Summary

“I’m not … I’m not some elf,” Lena argued, sneering as her thick eyebrows furrowed together, although her contempt was marred by the crack in her voice.

“Indeed. You are only half of one. No matter - your ears are pointed enough and you carry your father’s blood. They have already accepted the match.”

“Who? What match?” Lena demanded.

Arching an eyebrow in a cool, appraising manner, Lillian smiled sharply, her eyes clearly blue in the light of the room, yet frosty and hard. “The Seelie Court. You, my daughter, will keep the peace between our courts.”

    Chapter 1

                Lena swept up discarded stems, wilting petals and fallen leaves, the fragrant smell of the florists a comforting aroma as a warm breeze swept in through the propped open door. The summer evening was balmy and the dusty smell of the far off desert mingled with the car exhaust fumes and sun-warmed concrete sidewalks down the little side street. Glancing over at her employee, who was counting the cash in the register, Lena smiled faintly.

     

                “You can head off, Eve; I’ll lock up.”

     

                “Okay. Need me to take out the trash?”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively as she tugged the trash can closer, dying flowers, snapped stems and cut-offs piled up in the bag, she crouched to sweep the rest of the garbage from the cutting room floor into the dustpan with the little brush.

     

                “No, all good. I’ll see you tomorrow.”

     

                “Alright, have a good night.”

     

                Eve’s voice drifted further away, the sound of the cash register closing and the front door jerking open with the chiming of a bell. “You too!”

     

                Rising to her feet, Lena tipped the rest of the stray bits into the trash, banging the dustpan against the side of it. Wiping her hands on the apron tied around her waist, stained green from stems and leaves and streaked with powdery pastels from petals handled throughout the day, Lena dragged the trash can towards the propped open back door.

     

                Sunlight was lingering, the drawn-out dusk shrouding the city in lavender light, bright glints of orange light seeping through the cracks between skyscrapers to reflect off a hundred windows. The small enclosed garden behind her shop was filled with trash cans repurposed for composting, a small shed where Lena kept spare shears and glass vases gathering dust, coils of wire and an abundance of floral foam and a stagnant grey puddle from the overflowing drain. Hauling the trash can over to the nearest compost bin, Lena pulled on thick gardening gloves and transferred handfuls of wilting flowers and greenery onto the decomposing pile before checking the state of the others and slipping back inside.

     

                Tired from an early start, a wedding requiring the last, fresh finishing touches before she made the delivery across town, on top of the usual online orders of last-minute anniversary bouquets, birthdays and the walk-in customers buying flowers for themselves, Lena made her way back inside and locked the back door. She lived above the store, in an open-aired apartment that she’d spent a few years cultivating as her own space, relishing the simple act of being a self-made businesswoman, having something stable and enjoyable to accompany her through life.

     

                It had become a customary routine for her after packing up for the evening to make herself a small arrangement to take upstairs. There was something about flowers that had always been comforting to Lena, the way she was able to coax even the worst cases back to life, her touch making everything flower, everything thrive . It brought a sense of peace that she was yet to find in anything else, and she’d carved out a tiny corner of life for herself, doing what she loved.

     

                Selecting a few flowering daffodils and forget-me-nots and bluebells from the temperature-controlled cool room hosting dozens of flower species, Lena retreated to the spacious back room that acted as her workshop. Trimming the stems and rearranging the flowers in her hand, until it resembled a more aesthetically pleasing bouquet, she smiled to herself and breathed in the scent of the flowers. The bell above the front door chimed a moment later.

     

                “Eve?” she called out. “Did you forget something?”

     

                There was no sound and Lena frowned slightly, her hand holding her bouquet lowering as she cocked her head to the side and rounded the long trestle table scattered with wire and cutting boards, scissors and empty vases. Swathes of lingering light cut through the windows as she moved towards the open door leading to the shopfront.

     

                “Eve?”

     

                Stepping through the door, she stood in the middle of the empty shop and frowned. There was no response from the other woman and Lena clicked her tongue, feeling sheepish as she walked over to the front door and turned the key in the lock and slid the deadbolt across.

     

                Turning around, she let out a yelp, clapping a hand to her mouth as she pressed back against the door, finding a tall woman standing in the middle of the shop. 

     

                “Sorry,” Lena said, giving her a crooked smile as her cheeks warmed slightly. “You frightened me.”

     

                The woman cocked her head to the side, hazel eyes narrowing slightly as her mousy brown ponytail swished. She was wearing a leather jacket and all black, her lipstick dark and eyes unnervingly attentive. Lena’s smile faltered and she cleared her throat, reaching for the lock.

     

                “We’re actually closed for the day; I can take an order for you if you’re looking for a special arrangement. We do pickup and deliveries.”

     

                As she brusquely explained, she watched as another woman stepped out of the workshop where Lena had just been, fiddling with a pair of pruning shears. Her stomach lurched and she let out a nervous laugh.

     

                “Um …”

     

                “Is it her?” the other woman asked.

     

                “Fetch Pestilence.”

     

                Confusion flashed across Lena’s face and she opened her mouth, speechless for a moment. “I- sorry, you both have to leave.”

     

                She paled at the sight of a third woman emerging from the staircase leading up to her apartment, holding a framed photo of Lena and her mother.                 They all looked normal enough, somewhat ethereally beautiful, some luminescent quality to them that made them look radiant, but there was something ever so slightly off about them as well. Lena couldn’t place it but there was something that unnerved her, that made the hairs on her arms stand on end. Like called to like, some part of her finding them familiar in some sort of way as if she’d seen them before, or someone who looked similar. She couldn’t quite place the feeling though.

     

                “I’ll call the police,” she whispered, her voice quietly trembling as she reached behind her for the key in the door.

     

                The first woman let out a quiet laugh, her hazel eyes shining with delight as she took a slow step forward. “Oh, how amusing.”

     

                Her voice was warm but there was an undercurrent of a warning, making Lena’s heart pound in her chest. All pretences of politeness, of her cool customer service demeanour, vanished. She was frightened but that just made Lena calmer, her mind sharpening to serene focus as she reached for the key and twisted it in the lock, whipping around to fumble for the deadbolt. Three women who’d somehow managed to find their way into her store, the store she was sure she’d locked up tightly, was a cause for panic, that much she was sure of.

     

                “I wouldn’t.”

     

                Long fingers wrapped around her wrist, stopping her from pulling the bolt across and Lena jerked herself around. The other woman towered over her, standing far too close, and Lena inhaled - whether to speak or scream, she was unsure of. A hand shot out and wrapped around her neck, pulling her closer and digging in tightly. Lena’s lips twisted in a silent snarl as she reached up to pull her hand away.

     

                “Feisty. You might just survive us yet,” the woman murmured, amusement lacing her words as she leaned in close.

     

                Glancing back over her shoulder to the newcomer, the woman jerked her chin. “Purity.”

     

                Nodding, the other woman turned and made for the back door, opening it and stepping outside. Lena put up a struggle as the tall woman grabbed her by the shoulder of her shirt and dragged her to the door, her sneakers squeaking against the wooden floorboards, her fingers just falling short of a vase of flowers, the broom handle, the frame of the back door. She was outside in the lingering dusk, in the small garden enclosed with tall brick walls, wondering what they meant to do with her now.

     

                There was nowhere to go, the back gate securely chained - she definitely hadn’t unpadlocked that one today - but that didn’t deter them. First, the one called Pestilence stepped into the puddle, the shadowed corner of the garden seeming even darker as Lena watched her step into the murky water, a scum of oil and rotting leaves eddying by the disturbance. Only, she didn’t walk towards the gate, she just seemed to sink, as if walking downstairs, and was gone before Lena could comprehend what she’d witnessed.

     

                And then she was being dragged towards it, her breaths quick and frantic as she scratched and cursed the woman holding her, kicking frigid water everywhere, soaking the hems of her jeans as her skin rippled with goosebumps. The last thing she was aware of was the woman grabbing the back of her neck and thrusting her face down towards the deceptively deep puddle as her knees were kicked out from under her.

     

                She came to an unknown amount of time later, her head splitting with a headache and a crumpled expression on her face as she woke slowly, imagining herself waking from some strange dream. Only, when she opened her eyes, it wasn’t to the white ceiling of her apartment but to a canopy of trees, the air so much greener than the quality of her home with its abundance of potted plants. The light was strange, a violet twilight as it filtered through the faraway canopy overhead. Blinking slowly, she realised she was moving, being carried by the woman who had dragged her to wherever they were.

     

                Suddenly thrashing violently, she tumbled from the woman’s arms, catching her by surprise, and sprawled on the leaf-strewn floor of the forest. Scrambling to her feet, Lena shot off in a random direction, figuring that she couldn’t be too far from the nearest city block or the nearest road. She couldn’t have been out for very long if the sun was still setting, which meant she must be in one of National City’s parks. Although, the trees seemed impossibly tall and spread too far apart for it to have been anywhere but some remote, undisturbed place. Lena was too caught up in getting away from whatever strange thing she’d gotten wrapped up in to notice any of that.

     

                Her dark hair whipped around her grave face and she glanced back over her shoulder, breathing quickly, startled like a frightened rabbit as she shot off as fast as possible. But something tripped her before she’d gotten very far and she slammed into the ground, biting down on her tongue as the hot, coppery taste of blood flooded her mouth and she found herself dragged backwards. Something was wrapped tightly around her ankles, pulling her, and Lena scrabbled at the black earth, tearing up mud and leaves and weeds as she tried to grab purchase of something to anchor herself. Glancing back over her shoulder, her eyes widened and she let out a soundless cry of bewildered fear at the sight of snaking roots lashing themselves around her ankles, calves, thighs, snaking higher and higher as they pinned her.

     

                Then her attention was drawn to the approaching woman, stalking towards her with an amused look and a slight sneer on her face. Sinking to a crouch beside Lena’s head, she reached out to cup her chin in her hand, her nails, filed to sharp points, digging into Lena’s cheeks as she sighed heavily.

     

                “Do not try to run again; I don’t wish to hurt you, but I will do what I must.”

     

                “Reign, we must go. The sun sets - they’ll be awaiting her arrival.”

     

                Reign hummed a moment and then wiped a bead of blood from Lena’s lip before pushing herself back to her feet. She seemed transformed in the shadows of the forest, something otherworldly about her, and as the roots loosened their grasp on her and she was free to shakily climb to her feet, Lena realised the women had changed into new clothes. They were all barefoot now and dressed in fitted leathers, elegant patterns worked into the corsets, hair unbound and woven with silver and onyx. And there, parting Reign’s hair either side of her head, delicately pointed ears that made Lena feel lightheaded as she reached up to touch the tip of her own ear, not as prominently pointed but still a similar echo. 

     

                She felt faint, felt nauseous and shaken, her stomach fluttering as she quelled the hollowness in her chest. This was all so wrong, wrong, wrong . Here the trees were vast, a single one wouldn’t have fit in the width of her flower shop. Unfathomably large. There was a distracting humming in her blood and Lena felt as if she’d been transported to an entirely different world, everything seeming ever so slightly off. It wasn’t anything she could pinpoint exactly, but there was a general malaise that felt uncomfortably familiar. It was as if her soul knew another world existed beyond the human realm and she stared around, the suffocating silence of the forest almost peaceful, if it had been under different circumstances, the sight of leaves gently falling and the sweet smell of decay so fresh. It only kindled agitation in Lena though.

     

                “Come. We’ll not tarry any longer,” the one called Reign said, beckoning her with two fingers, the nails seeming dangerous.

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena hesitated and then turned, trying her hand at escaping again. The undergrowth was all shadows, ferns and moss and tangled weeds, and she didn’t make it more than a few steps before a quiet snarl sounded and the tight lashing of yet more weeds ensnared her. The one called Pestilence clenched her hand and Lena suddenly found herself being forcibly dragged towards her by the roots, her eyes widening as her arms were pinned to her sides, no amount of struggling able to free her from their vice-like grasp.

     

                “She’s persistent.”

     

                “That will serve her well,” hummed Purity.

     

                Snapping her fingers, Reign bared her teeth as she shot the other two women a dark look. “Now is not the time for this; it’ll be dark soon. Our heads will be on spikes if we lose her to the forest.”

     

                “Shall I bind her?”

     

                “Quickly, now.”

     

                There was an anxious edge to the woman’s words as she glanced around, her eyes restless. It was only then that Lena caught the hilt of a sword strapped to her back catching the last bit of light, glinting dully as her hair parted around the hilt and sheath. Suddenly gripped by the fear of being lost in the forest alone at night, unable to find her way back, unsure of where she even was, Lena didn’t protest as her wrists were bound with roots and Reign grabbed her bicep, painfully hard, and dragged her along.

     

                There was a profound silence to the forest, a stillness that she dared not break as she was silently hurried along, her breaths shallow and seeming too loud as they walked past vast trees, broad with age, their trunks whorled and knotted as white lichen crept up the bark. The ground was thick with moss and delicate flowers, blurred and grey in the waning light as the thick canopy overhead kept the fading sunlight at bay earlier than it should have. Their footsteps were silent, the moss and ferns muffling the sound, and it was the breeze rustling through branches above them that provided the only noise that Lena could make out.

     

                It must have been miles they walked, her wrists chafing at the bonds, the air growing colder and the darkness gathering until she couldn’t see more than a dozen feet before her, three feet, past her nose. It seemed endless and Lena stumbled and tripped as she found herself unable to see through the suffocating darkness, the rustling of ferns and the soft hooting of an owl the only things she could make sense of. She fell more than once, bracken and moss and fallen leaves softening the impact, but she was filthy and scraped and bruised, hauled back to her feet and told to keep moving.

     

                Eventually, she was led down an overgrown path of wax myrtle and prickly holly, unseen to her, and there was a faint glow visible ahead. Her stomach lurched and she staggered onwards, shoulders slumped and sore from hours of tense walking, the three women close around her, swords bared at their sides. None of it was comforting to Lena and she felt like things would only get worse from here, with no sign of her impending freedom approaching.

     

                Still, it looked like they were arriving somewhere and she blinked back black spots as the orange glow of lamps suddenly cast everything into vague form. The path beneath her feet became worn dirt and she could make out stone archways and yet more trees, twisting into whimsical shapes, melding with the sprawling assortment of buildings, as if they’d sprung straight from nature itself. She couldn’t make out much and was led onwards, barely daring to breathe as she caught sight of someone moving.

     

                Figures materialised from the shadows, orange light limning their lithe bodies, all of them inhumanly beautiful, their thin faces sharp and serious and wickedly clever. Their eyes seemed to almost glow in the dark, watching her like she was their prey. Bedraggled and wide-eyed, dragged along with little say in the matter, Lena felt cold fear spread through her, her throat painfully tight and her teeth clamped together in an effort to stop her bottom lip from trembling. She jutted her chin forward in a stubborn manner, refusing to let her fear show.

     

                It was a few minutes later that she heard the faint rippling of a pond, the smell of standing water on the edge of the breeze, and Lena looked around in quiet awe as she was led into a clearing. A wide pool of water filled the space, water lilies holding small lit candles as they spiralled across the surface of the water, cicadas singing and frogs quietly croaking while fireflies darted around. It was almost peaceful, the warm glow of the place illuminating the water and the trees ringing the pond, giving the illusion of privacy. And there, in the centre, an oak tree so huge that its thick roots jutted over the water, creating little grottoes for ducks, so vast and unreal in its size, with its leafy branches sighing with the wind, that Lena didn’t see the small throne nestled amongst the woven platform the tree’s roots formed.

     

                A woman rose, tall and imposing, bathed in silver as a full moon hung impossibly close and huge over the trees. It took everything in Lena not to shrink back as she took in the woman with dread, but Reign dragged her closer, against her wishes.                 “Your Majesty.”

     

                Holding a hand up and waving in a dismissive manner, the three women slinking back, Lena was left to face the towering woman alone, standing at the edge of the pond as she watched the woman walk the length of a worn, twisting root and stop before her. Swallowing thickly, she raised her chin and took in the hard lines of the woman’s face, smooth and ageless - she could have been forty or sixty - her caramel hair cascading past her shoulders and some bizarre crown of black thorns, emeralds and amethysts encircling her brow. She was dressed in deep green with a cloak of black feathers falling from her shoulders, so beautiful and intricately detailed, yet so foreign, like something out of a fantasy novel.

     

                Lena was silent beneath the woman’s scrutinising gaze, her pale skin luminescent in the moonlight, her eyes black and glimmering, and she didn’t think she would have been able to speak even if she’d wanted to. Walking around her in a slow circle, the woman stopped before her again and waved a hand, the roots binding Lena’s wrists falling away at her command. Rubbing at the raw pink skin encircling her wrists, Lena inhaled shakily.

     

                “She resisted,” Reign warily supplied.

     

                The woman made a small sound of amused acknowledgement, her stare so piercing that Lena found herself forced to look away. She could feel a dozen eyes on her, sure more of these strange people were watching her, and she fought the urge to restlessly shift, her shoulders tense and the moment weighted with expectation. Although, what they were expecting from her, she didn’t quite know.

     

                “Take her,” the woman eventually drawled, her voice deep and cool with amusement, a faint smile twitching her lips as she beckoned at a woman.

     

                She had tanned skin and dark hair, her eyes a piercing blue as she appeared at Lena’s side, bowing slightly to the woman before taking Lena by the arm, gently leading her away. It took Lena a moment to resist, yanking her arm from the woman’s grasp, only to find it return, albeit harder, a quiet hiss speaking volumes until Lena stopped struggling. Dragged away from the open space, down a path that went from dirt to worn cobblestones and moss, Lena blinked at the sound of some foreign language whispering through the trees from the assembled people watching from the shadows of trunks and the branches of trees. They were, all of them, slender and agile, more beautiful than any humans had a right to be, dressed in the colours of the forest and flowers and water, all of them barefoot. 

     

                Lena felt dizzy, felt panic set in as she drew in shallow breaths, squeezing her eyes shut as she was led along the path. Everything felt suddenly wrong , inescapably wrong, and Lena stumbled once more, her knees giving out beneath her as she sank down to the path, letting out a ragged breath.

     

                “Hush,” the woman said, not unkindly, although she was rather brusque in her manner, trying to drag Lena back to her feet. “It’ll be alright.”

     

                “Where am I?” Lena whispered, frightened to hear the answer. “What the fuck is this place?”

     

                She was hauled to her feet a little rougher then, the woman stunningly beautiful up close, and solemn as she stared at Lena, her blue eyes roaming over her face before she hesitated, a pucker forming between her eyebrows.

     

                “The Unseelie Court.”

     

                Mouth falling open, Lena was left speechless and rooted to the spot as the woman turned and continued walking. She paused after a few steps and let out a withering sigh before turning back and snatching up Lena’s hand, dragging her with her.

     

                “Unseelie Court. Is this … some sort of fantasy roleplaying? I mean … I’m just- I’m confused, so if you could just tell me what the hell is going on … that would be great.”

     

                The woman didn’t answer and Lena felt anger slowly burning in her chest as she was dragged through an open door and into the hallway of a stone building. They made a right turn at the end of the hallway and down a short staircase before going left and then through the tall, wooden double doors. The room was damp and muggy, steam curling from the wide natural spring in the floor.

     

                Giving her a once over and wrinkling her nose distastefully, the woman’s mouth thinned, “undress.”

     

                “I’m not doing anything ,” Lena fumed, balling her hands into fists. “What the fuck is going on here? I- are you kidnapping me? I mean … get off me.”

     

                Lena backed away as the woman reached out to grab the hem of her shirt. Pushing against her, cheeks heating with anger as she scowled, Lena tugged the hem of her shirt back down, her lips twisting derisively.

     

                “Don’t touch me.”

     

                “The Queen has asked me to prepare you. We can do this with no quarrel, or else I will resort to harsher methods, but either way you’ll obey. The choice is yours.”

                

                “I don’t give a shit who asked-”

     

                “If you insist on making it difficult, you’ll only make it worse. You look horrific; take a bath.”

     

                Cheeks reddening with indignation, Lena straightened, her pride and vanity rankled by the comments of this stranger, looking at her with a wrinkled nose as if her appearance offended her. Lena opened and closed her mouth, but looking down at herself, taking in the mud covering her, the damp jeans, leaves and grass stains and scrapes and bruises, she knew she looked far from elegant and beautiful.

     

                In contrast, the woman was dressed in a midnight blue dress, like gossamer, a night sky of tiny beads of quartz and threads of silver, shimmering in the orange glow of the bathing room. They stared at each other for a few long minutes, the silence full of tension, of expectation, both of them waiting to see who would win in a battle of wills. But Lena didn’t doubt the other woman’s intentions to follow through with her threats and so she bristled as she cleared her throat.

     

                “A little privacy would be nice,” Lena said in a brittle tone.

     

                The woman let out a loud bark of laughter, retreating to the other side of the room as she watched Lena kick off her muddy sneakers, sinking down onto a delicately carved bench. It seemed that was all the privacy she would be afforded and, for a second, Lena considered making another break for it, sizing up the woman and confident that she would be able to overpower her if she needed to.

     

                Examining her nails with feigned interest, the woman hummed softly and Lena blanched at the sight of narrow tongues of fire shooting from each fingertip. It was a silent warning, as if she’d read Lena’s mind, or seen her thoughts written on her face. Pale and sweating, confused by how the woman could do that and how the others had handled water and roots so easily, Lena fumbled with her clothes and undressed.

     

                She stepped into the steaming hot spring, finding it shallow, and plunged her head underwater before re-emerging, an apprehensive look in her green eyes. Her slightly pointed ears were more prominent with her wet hair slicked back, revealing the tips, and she watched as the other woman took note of them, watching her closely with open curiosity. It wasn’t leering but Lena still felt uneasy as she stayed submerged to her shoulders, her mind reeling with everything that happened, not entirely sure it wasn’t still a dream.

     

                Being kidnapped and taken to the middle of the woods and forced to walk to some strange building made her feel like she’d been abducted by a cult. If it wasn’t for that strange feeling of familiarity singing in her veins, a serenity in her chest, beneath her emotions, Lena would have been even more terrified than she was. As it was, she was willing to see it through and find out what they wanted with her, knowing her attempts at escaping were futile. 

     

                Fetching a small carved soap from the side of the bath, she scrubbed herself clean, the smell of pine perfuming the steaming air as she washed away the dirt. Her body ached , purplish bruises already forming and her wrists an angry pink from where the bonds had chafed. Resentment welled up inside Lena, cutting through her anxious fears, and she shot the stranger more than one dark look, before finishing up.

     

                Wrapping herself in a towel as she climbed from the hot spring, Lena stood dripping and uncertain on the stone floor. Wiping her face dry, she reached for her abandoned clothes but the woman was quicker. Snatching them up, she walked over to a brazier burning in the corner and tossed Lena’s clothes in.

     

                Letting out a startled sound of anger, Lena took a threatening step towards her, although they both knew she wouldn’t so much as lay a finger on her. Gesturing lazily towards the brazier, the woman smiled faintly as the flames grew, the orange glow brightening to white-hot as her clothes were burned to cinders.

     

                The door opened then and Lena clutched the towel to her chest as she watched a blonde woman walk in. A blonde woman who she knew. Mouth falling open, Lena’s eyes widened and she watched her employee duck her head.

     

                “Eve?”

     

                “Andrea,” Eve murmured, scurrying past Lena as she avoided her gaze, “she’s to be ready soon. Her Majesty will come.”

     

                Taking the bundle from her, Andrea nodded, while Lena watched on with a slack look of shock on her face. She wasn’t sure how this all tied together quite yet, but the guilt on Eve’s face all but assured Lena of her participation in it. She vanished back out of the door as Lena stood rooted to the spot, the water on her skin evaporating as she stared numbly at the door.

     

                “Dress.”

     

                Shaking herself out of her shock, Lena flinched away from Andrea and scowled at the emerald green bundle being held out to her. Depositing the bundle onto the bench, Lena plucked a pair of cotton undershorts and a brassiere that was laced at the front, all but confirming her fears that she was joining some sort of cult who only wore medieval clothes.

     

                Pulling them on as she cursed under her breath, Lena was left with the green dress next, embroidered with silver and other green hues as they detailed little flowers and plants. She struggled into it, to the amusement of Andrea, the dress well-fitting yet loose, the silken fabric of it like water as it pooled around Lena’s bare feet. There were no shoes she realised a moment later.

     

                “Come.”

     

                She has no choice but to follow Andrea, the stone cool beneath her soles as she scurried through the warren of hallways, feeling small and lost in wake of the confusing turn her evening had taken. Lena longed for her apartment, the fresh bouquet she’d made herself and a cup of tea as she made dinner for one. Her quiet life was something she prided herself on, caring for herself as no one ever had, even if the loneliness threatened to overwhelm her at times.

     

                They ended up in a spacious room, three of the walls made from stone and the other a strange web of roots, the bark smooth and worn as the roots reached into the room. There was another brazier lighting the space and woven rugs and tapestries, the patterns nagging at the back of her mind as she stared at the circles and knots. 

     

                “Sit.”

     

                Gestured onto a low stool, Lena gripped the sides of it and swallowed thickly, watching Andrea’s movements as her heart pounded in her chest. It seemed the worst she had to suffer from the woman was allowing her to brush her hair and plait it into intricate styles, Andrea seeming uneasy by the task as she deftly wove the strands together, the end result looking rather effortlessly simple. There were tiny emeralds and amethysts, beads of silver and diamonds woven into her dark hair before a silver circlet of thorns were plucked from a crushed velvet cushion. It circled her brow, the thorns passing above her ears and then down over the tops of her prominent cheekbones with an emerald the size of Lena’s thumbnail cradled in the middle of her forehead.

     

                Rings were slid onto almost every finger and a slender necklace of diamond florets and then Andrea stepped back. She eyed Lena and hummed to herself, reaching forward to part her hair more around the pointed ears, tugging at the flowing sleeves of the dress, letting the rippling fabric hang properly over her hands before she was satisfied. Once she was finished, Lena stared at her reflection in a polished sheet of silver, finding herself alien and just as otherworldly beautiful as the fae creatures she’d already encountered.

     

                Languidly stretching out on a divan, her work done, Andrea promptly ignored Lena, although she cast furtive glances her way from time to time as Lena sat rigidly on her stool, waiting. Neither of them spoke - no desire to on Lena’s behalf, and she doubted if her questions would be answered even if she voiced them - and the silence dragged on.

     

                The wood in the brazier cracked as the flames slowly consumed it and Lena felt exhausted. She didn’t know what the time was, couldn’t see a clock or even a plug socket that indicated there was electricity there. It felt like hours later when the door was thrown open and the Queen from earlier strode inside, irate and impatient, snapping her fingers at Andrea, whose effortlessly nonchalant demeanour quickly stiffened into willing obedience as she ducked her head in a small bow and vanished from the room.

     

                “Stand.”

     

                Lena obeyed the woman, her commanding aura enough for her to forgo her churlish, obstinate personality, although Lena was starting to get sick of these one-word orders. Still, she stood before her, hands clenched into fists and her shoulders tense and hunched, avoiding the sharp eyes of the Queen as she circled Lena, hands clasped behind her back. Her bearing was regal as if she’d never been denied a thing in her life and never expected to be.

     

                Even without shoes, she towered over Lena, and, this close, it was unnerving. Stomach tying itself into knots as she fought the urge to fiddle, Lena stared stoically ahead until she felt cool fingers touch the tips of her ears. Jerking her head aside, Lena’s mouth thinned as she shot the woman a wary look of unease.

     

                “You look like her,” she eventually said, coming to a stop in front of Lena, standing uncomfortably close and reaching up to grasp her chin in her hand. “Your mother.”

     

                The air rushed from Lena’s lungs as a flicker of panic flashed in her eyes, her lips moving soundlessly for a moment. “How do you know what she looked like?”

     

                With a scornful scoff of laughter, a muscle twitching in her jaw, the woman dropped her hand. “I knew her. Elizabeth. Those of Celtic blood have always been close to the fair folk; your father couldn’t help himself.”

     

                “I don’t have a father.”

     

                “Not anymore, no.”

     

                Brow creasing with confusion, Lena eyed the woman warily and spoke slowly. “Who- who are you?”

     

                “Ah, you do not remember me? A pity.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena’s frown deepened. “We’ve never met before.”

     

                “Oh, but we have. Although, you may not remember. Indeed, you were a child of six when your mother took you from our court and ran. I had thought more of the fae world would have remained with you, but perhaps your human blood is stronger than I imagined.“

     

                “I- what are you talking about?” Lena bitingly asked, her patience wearing thin.

     

                “I’m Lillian. Queen of the Unseelie Court. I’m your mother.”

     

                Choking on a breathless laugh, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Lady, you’re crazy. You just said you-“

     

                “Your father was Lionel - King of the Unseelie Court. He was my husband. Seeing as you’re of his blood … I claim you as my heir.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena couldn’t even form a single thought past the uneasy amusement, the urge to laugh building in her chest.

     

                “I knew keeping you alive would serve a purpose one day. And here you are to fulfil it. You may thank me for my mercy.”

     

                “I- sorry?”

     

                “I said you may thank me for sparing your life. When my hunters tracked down your mother, they lost you.”

     

                “Wha- my mom drowned.”

     

                “Ah. You remember it. Yes, Purity has a knack for it. I spared them the task of finding you - you were of no use to me then, a child of six.”

     

                Lena could feel the blood drain from her face, stiffening as an ice-cold feeling swept through her body. The words rang true to her, somehow, speaking to the blurred memories that still haunted her, twenty years later and still leaving her with that disturbing feeling that something had gone horribly wrong that day at the lake. The early years of her life were dim in her memory, only vague snatches of glades and her mother’s laughter, of red hair and flowers. Lena never quite knew where she grew up, only that one day her mother drowned and she found herself in the foster system, alone and abandoned.

     

                “You … you killed- no, I-”

     

                “It’s no matter now. You may call me mother and we’ll put this behind us. It was the done thing; I couldn’t have my husband’s mistress and her half-breed bastard threatening the monarchy, but now … well, now I have need of you, Lena.”

     

                Eyes flat with anger and fear, a prickling feeling running up her spine as she trembled, Lena let out a caustic laugh, the sound catching in the back of her throat. “I don’t know who you are or what the fuck you’re talking about, but you are not my mother.”

     

                She didn’t see the slap coming, the pain blossoming on her cheek as her head was whipped to the side by the force of it, vision dimming for a moment. Raising a hand, Lena touched the warm skin, already reddening, and gave Lillian a hateful glare. 

     

                “I am what I say I am. Who are you to defy me? You should be on your knees thanking me for bringing you home; it is an honour to do one's duty - especially a duty so important as this one.”

     

                “I’m not doing anything for you. Take me home right now or I’ll-”

     

                “You’ll what, child? What threats can you possibly make to me?”

     

                Mouth dry, Lena swallowed thickly, a burning pressure building behind her eyes as the urge to cry, so confused and frightened and angry, too much for her body to contain, built within her. “I’ll call the cops,” she whispered, “I’ll … sue. Whatever this place is-”

     

                Lillian let out a chilling laugh and grabbed her chin, pulling her close as she loomed over her, her grasp painful. “Haven’t you been paying attention, you foolish girl? You’re not in your world anymore. This is the Unseelie Court; the only way back is closed to you. Unless you want to follow your mother to the bottom of a lake, you’ll do as I say. Am I understood?”

     

                Breaths sharp and quick, Lena swallowed the urge to spit in the woman’s face, some feral side of her awoken by the quick temper of the fae Queen. A slow smile spread across Lillian’s face and she let out a quiet, smug laugh as she dropped her hand and pulled back.

     

                “You’re a quick learner. Good. It will serve you well here.”

     

                “I’m not … I’m not some elf ,” Lena argued, sneering as her thick eyebrows furrowed together, although her contempt was marred by the crack in her voice.

     

                “Indeed. You are only half of one. No matter - your ears are pointed enough and you carry your father’s blood. They have already accepted the match.”

     

                “Who? What match?” Lena demanded.

     

                Arching an eyebrow in a cool, appraising manner, Lillian smiled sharply, her eyes clearly blue in the light of the room, yet frosty and hard. “The Seelie Court. You, my daughter, will keep the peace between our courts.”

     

                She was left stammering speechlessly, perplexed and outraged in her finely embroidered dress and jewels that would have been worth millions if she’d hawked them back home, as Lillian walked towards the doors, opening one and slipping out into the hall without another word. 

     

                Andrea was back a moment later and no amount of questions, insults and curses hurled at her gave Lena any answers. Her fear swiftly gave way to anger, locked inside that room - she tried the door to no avail, pounding on the wood while Andrea lounged and sighed - and Lena’s growing frustration became destructive. She overturned the brazier, cherry-red logs burning holes in the rugs, the smouldering sparks quelled by the clenched fist of the other fae woman, who looked bored and unimpressed, the table of jewels and pins and the soft-bristle hairbrush used to make Lena presentable was overturned, an ewer of water smashed against the stone wall.

     

                It was only when Lena made to tear the clothes from her own body that Andrea moved, deceptively fast, appearing before her with a small dagger in hand. It was wickedly sharp, engraved with a swirling pattern, and the fae woman held it to her throat, hissing something in that foreign language that Lena had heard before. She stilled, throat bobbing at the thought of the keen edge pressed to her skin, and she felt that uneasiness of something she should have known nagging at the back of her mind.

     

                “That language. I know it,” she murmured, sure of herself.

     

                “Of course you do,” Andrea dismissively replied. “And you will know my promise if you keep that up.”

     

                Her words confused Lena, whose face crumpled, and she retreated back to her divan, tossing the knife up and catching it by its hilt as nonchalantly as if she was amusing herself with a baseball. Sinking down to a crouch, Lena wrapped her arms around herself and glowered at the fae woman, not quite believing what Lillian had told her. 

     

                Fingering the tips of her ears, Lena was sullen and pouting in deep thought as she contemplated the story. Her ears had always been a sore point for her, the thing at the endless parade of foster homes and orphanages that had made the other kids laugh at her. She’d always been strange, an oddity, with her made-up language and tales of elves and otherworldly creatures she’d eventually grown out of. It was only in plants that she’d ever felt like she belonged.

     

                Hours dragged by and Lena’s eyes prickled with exhaustion, bloodshot and dry with the urge to cry. She felt strung out and hungry, her stomach aching and her skin cold and clammy. She wanted to sleep but wouldn’t allow herself to, huddling on the floor as the light of the lonely brazier she hadn’t overturned kept the shadows at bay. 

     

                It was past midnight when the doors were thrown open by two beautiful men, dressed in soft tunics embroidered with flowers and thorns and birds, barefoot and swords sheathed at their sides. They had thin mail armour and overlapping scales, so delicately wrought that Lena couldn’t believe it was for anything more than show, and there, beyond them was Lillian, her cloak of feathers back in place and half a dozen more fae behind her, all of them richly clad and heartbreakingly beautiful.

     

                Lillian gestured for Lena to come and she uncurled her stiff body, rising unsteadily to her feet as she swallowed thickly. “Where are you taking me?”

     

                Her new mother didn’t reply, disappearing back down the hallway and leaving Andrea to drag Lena along behind them. The mixture of fae fell in around them, most armed and all of them looking like royalty, and Lena could feel their curious eyes watching her, taking in the sight of their new Princess. Her status hadn’t even dawned on Lena, and she was too absorbed in thoughts of what they were going to do with her now. Was she a sacrifice, to be executed to make peace? Was she to be a prisoner here, a bargaining tool? The possibilities seemed endless and Lena had no way of escaping or contacting someone.

     

                It was pitch black outside, the moon high above them, masked by the canopy of the trees. Lena couldn’t see well, stumbling along the path bordered by rose bushes, thorns reaching out to snag on her dress, roses blooming as she passed by. The other fae were all graceful and silent, not so much as a sound made by any of them, and Lena felt claustrophobic, trapped in the middle of the retinue as they shepherded her along, her heart hammering away and her palms sweating with fear. She wasn’t sure in what way, but the whole procession had a threatening aura and she knew to run would make things worse for herself. The pain on her cheek had gone but the ghost of the slap still lingered, and the faint shadows of bruises around her neck, the chafed skin of her wrists, spoke of casual cruelty at a whim.

     

                They walked a while, leaving the buildings nestled amidst the trees, as if they’d grown there rather than been built, the layout of the sprawling stone and wood indecipherable to Lena as she was led this way and that in the dark. They passed smaller buildings and hollowed out trees, the sound of laughter and music drifting through the trees, the occasional sight of a lantern bobbing past like a firefly against the darkness, and Lena was led to believe that it was some sort of city, perhaps. A city of fae - the thought was ludicrous and she had the urge to let out a hysterical laugh, kept at bay by clamping her lips together in a thin, bloodless line.

                

                Eventually, they came upon a clearing, a few more faes there, standing beside the shadowed forms of horses. Their soft whickering and snorting were familiar to Lena in the dark, although she couldn’t recall ever having seen a horse in person before. Lillian made for a pitch-black mare, practically invisible in the dark, and Lena watched her pull herself up onto its back, no saddle or bridle to keep her seated. Looking down on them, her face a pale blur in the night, Lillian’s piercing stare was still felt, making Lena’s skin crawl.

     

                “Reign, she rides with you. Do not let harm befall her.”

     

                The woman bowed her head and murmured something in that foreign language, a solemn vow from the tone of it, before she dragged Lena over to a chestnut mare, too tall for her to climb on herself. Leaping gracefully onto the horse’s back, Reign reached down and hauled Lena up by her biceps, fingers cutting in deep, before depositing her in front of her and caging her in with her arms on either side as she grabbed a fistful of the horse’s mane.

     

                Lena felt the horse shift beneath her and sat rigidly, uncomfortably waiting until everyone was mounted and they all fell into formation. They set off slowly, the horses lightly picking their way through the wide spaces between the trees, and Lena hunched over the horse’s neck, her teeth bared uneasily as she held on. She could feel Reign’s amusement behind her and felt a flicker of stubborn irritation, resolved to not complain or voice her discomfort.

     

                Once they were past the borders of the sprawling city, light and laughter and music fading behind them, they picked up the pace and Lena was jostled around, bumping along with the lurching gait, as she ground her teeth together, waiting for it to be over. Wherever they were heading, it was some distance though - far enough to warrant horses, which hadn’t been a requirement for the trip to the court. 

     

                The hours and miles passed by in a blur, hooves thundering through the ferns and then over mossy stone, packed earth and cobblestoned bridges spanning narrow rivers and streams. The forest seemed endless and wild, vines and roots and logs barring their way, thorny bushes running wild and snagging in the hair of the horse’s tails. There was also a general malaise of unease in the company, quiet orders rippling back and forth, Lillian and Lena nestled safely in the middle while swords and arrowheads glinted around them, ready to attack some unseen predator. More than once, Lena caught sight of glowing eyes, heard distant howls and heard the thundering sound of feet striking the forest floor, bushes rustling and panting breaths. Those sounds and glimpses of unknown things frightened her more than the fae holding her captive and she hoped they knew how to use the weapons they held.

     

                Eventually, in the grey hour preluding dawn, after hours of riding through the chill night, nothing to warm her save for the thin dress, Lena watched the shadowed figures come to a stop. They were shapes of faded blues and greens and copper, their horses monotone and still, pawing at the mud as their riders dismounted, coats lathered and rib cages expanding and contracting like bellows at a forge. Lena was stiff and numb on the horse, barely able to feel her toes, and she tipped her face to the pale light of the early sunrise, closing her eyes and exhaling a soft cloud of white. 

                

                Hands pulled her down from the horse, and Lena struggled a little, a dark look clouding her fine-boned face at being manhandled so frequently by these strangers. She bristled and drew herself up to her rather unimpressive height, made up for by the haughty bearing that seldom came out but was so imperiously similar to her unknown father and brother that the fae didn’t doubt their Queen for a second. While she looked like her mother, there was something fae about her that extended deeper than the slight points of her ears. 

     

                Swords were sheathed and arrows swiftly nestled back into quivers and Lena caught Lillian’s eye as she looked around, the shadows slowly lifting, revealing details as she took in the sight of wildflowers and oaks and willows, a squirrel scampering up a trunk while the muffled sound of ducks quacking and rippling water echoed in the fog that came to her knees. She shivered in the cold air and rubbed her arms, scowling around as she wondered where they were.

     

                The three hunters who had captured her fell into formation around her, dressed in the supple leathers, embroidered with water, leaves and swirling flames depending on which woman she studied, and Lena was led along a wide, worn path beneath the overhanging branches of the thick maple trees lining the way. Their leaves carpeted the path and Lena eyed the snowdrops and crocuses thrusting up amidst the weeds and ferns, which soon gave way to reeds as the sound of water grew louder.

     

                They came out in a half-moon clearing on one side of a wide river and Lena looked around in wonder. Columns sprouted from the ground like ancient trees in a petrified forest, forty feet tall, spindly but still miraculously upright, beautifully carved by hands that were most certainly not human. Across the river, through the haze of fog, she saw the columns mirrored, the decaying remains of an ancient waypoint that created a circle spanning the water. The river itself was a slow-moving ribbon of steel, reflecting the light of dawn, and Lena hung back as she watched the fae high-folk gather around, murmuring in their foreign language as they warily looked across the narrow bridge spanning the gap.

     

                It was a simple path, no handrail and patched with moss and russet leaves, the tall sentinels on either side reaching over with their long branches, creating a sparse web overhead. Lena craned her neck, looking up, the trees so impossibly tall that she couldn’t even comprehend how old they were - older than the redwoods she’d visited at national parks back home. The canopy overhead dwarfed the columns and she watched as a leaf drifted down towards her, falling more than a hundred feet as it swirled in the breeze. 

                

                Her attention was broken then by the sudden sound of an owl softly hooting, setting her heartbeat wild in her chest. And then she watched as her mother drifted across the bridge and on the other bank, a trio of fae made for the bridge too, meeting Lillian in the middle, a comfortable distance left between them. A quiet conversation, too soft for Lena to hear, took place before Lillian turned and beckoned.

     

                Reign gripped Lena’s arm and towed her along, the stone of the bridge slick with moisture from the fog, the furred moss soft beneath her feet as she warily looked over the side, to the few feet drop into crystal clear water, made reflective by the fractured pattern of sunlight seeping through the canopy. Swallowing thickly, Lena’s eyes landed on that of a fae woman, taller than her and golden. Her eyes were cerulean, her skin glowing and her hair so blonde that it seemed to shine, woven with threads of silver, with tiny sapphires and pearls and a silver circlet around her head, reminiscent of waves. She wore a velvet robe, the colour of stone blue, embroidered with silver and grey whorls of waves and fish, left open over a pristine white shirt and grey leather leggings. Her feet were also bare and a belt around her waist held a sheathed sword.

     

                She was, to put it simply, the most beautiful woman Lena had ever seen. There was an open curiosity to her piercing blue stare, a smattering of freckles on her nose, and her long blonde hair parted around the prominently pointed ears that were still a shocking sight to Lena. They stared at each other for a long moment as Lena was walked towards her until Reign let her go and she came to a stop.

     

                Lillian softly hissed impatiently and grabbed Lena’s forearm, dragging her forward and then to an abrupt halt, until she was a mere foot away from the golden fae woman. Lena watched as she pulled a dagger from her waist, silver and beautifully wrought, much like everything else she’d encountered in this realm, and she baulked, trying to shrink away as her fears of her throat being slit to appease some old feud resurfaced. Lillian’s threats about her ending up like her mother made Lena pale, standing on that narrow bridge.

     

                Twisting her arm and pulling her to a stop, Lillian pulled a dagger from her own person and jerked Lena’s left hand so her palm was facing up. Limp fingers curled inwards slightly and Lillian splayed them flat with the hilt of the dagger, shushing Lena before she turned the dagger and slashed it across her daughter’s palm in a swift cut. Pain blossomed and a small gasp of pain escaped Lena, vivid red blood welling up as she watched with wide eyes. Looking up, she saw the other fae doing the same before sheathing her dagger and reaching out with her left hand, fingers stained red - surprisingly ordinary - as her blood dripped onto the stones beneath them.

     

                Lillian thrust Lena’s hand forward and she was powerless to stop her, a stricken look of disgust and fear on her face as the fae woman’s fingers wrapped around her wrist, their palms together, blood mingling, slick and warm. The whole thing made Lena queasy but she couldn’t pull away and her fingers involuntarily wrapped around the other woman’s wrist to balance herself, much to her horror. 

     

                And then she watched as roots snaked up from the depths of the riverbanks, algae and mud and debris caught in them and wrapped around their clasped arms, tight and wet, before water rose up at the subtle gesture of the other woman, similarly entwining their hands, soaking into the thin fabric of Lena’s dress. She was taut and leaning as far back from it as possible, feeling faint and sick but unable to look away.

     

                The roots and water melted away a moment later and Lillian let go of her daughter, who wobbled unsteadily on her feet as she cradled her bleeding hand, a dazed look in her eyes. Stepping back, Lillian nodded her head.

     

                “It is done. Remember our agreement.”

     

                The other woman nodded, a wary flicker in her blue eyes, and Lena found herself being surrounded by the other two women - one with russet hair, shaved on the sides and long on top, and the other with dark skin and wide, dark eyes, clad in buttery yellow and gold. They blocked Lena from her mother and shepherded her across the bridge, gentler than the Unseelie had been, but just as brusque - perhaps even more so.

     

                Panic seized Lena and she looked back over her shoulder, wide-eyed and lost. Of course, she felt no more comfortable with the Unseelie but there had been something there, some hidden knowledge of her childhood that was at least familiar. Yet, she’d been handed over to these strangers with little fuss, Lillian already swinging back up onto her horse, black-feathered cloak draping over its flank as she grabbed a fistful of its mane and watched Lena for a long moment before wheeling around.

     

                The woman in blue swiftly crossed the bridge and stopped beside a dappled grey stallion, his mane and tail pure white and standing a whole head taller than Lena, who was guided over to it. The blonde was a few inches taller than her and was able to pick Lena up with ease, placing her on the horse before hesitating. Reaching into an inner pocket, she shook out a clean handkerchief and reached up for Lena’s left hand, carefully wrapping it around her palm. It was an almost tender gesture, and the kindest since Lena had wound up here, the thought making her want to cry.

     

                “Make haste,” the stony-faced one with the copper hair and brown eyes said, the finely wrought mail clinking softly as she mounted.

     

                Silently sharing a look with the woman, the blonde hauled herself up behind Lena, sitting close behind her, their thighs touching and her arms holding her steady in their circle. Gently touching her bare heels to the horse’s flank, she took off and the other dozen fae followed suit, splitting away from them and vanishing into the forest.

     

                Dark hair whipping around her face at the speed, the air was stolen from Lena’s lungs as she looked around at the steadily lightening forest. Inch by inch, the sunrise stole it back from the darkness, the air suffused with a purplish light, revealing the ever-changing landscape. Here it was flat and the trees set far apart for room to grow, ferns and flowers and brambles easily leapt over by the quick horses, offering a clear view of their surroundings. And then an incline, hooves tearing up dirt and loose stones, thick roots blocking the next turn in the twisting path before it sloped down to a valley, stone walls on either side of them, worn smooth where a river might have once passed through and carved it away before drying up.

     

                They passed through empty meadows of wildflowers, grassy knolls with cherry trees and splashed through shallow fords. The fae peeled off, one by one and in a pair one time, until it was just the trio that had stood on the bridge. Even then, the other two women departed together after a few more miles, a softly shouted conversation had before they were alone.

     

                Lena felt like she ought to be frightened, but she was thinking about the woman’s voice. It had been gentle and melodic, a weary sigh, higher than she’d anticipated. She still hadn’t spoken a word to Lena, and she hadn’t understood that fleeting snatch of words, only felt the rumbling of her chest against her back, sure that the women were exchanging warnings and reassurances.

     

                Still, after a few more miles, the prickle of fear in Lena grew. An ice-cold panic seeped through her numb body and she was suddenly terrified of what awaited her. She was alone on a horse with a stranger, sleep-deprived and starved after hours of subjected worry and assaults, passed from hand to hand. And speaking of hands, her palm hurt , the spotless white handkerchief stained with blooming patches of red. 

     

                Eyes stinging with tears as her throat closed up, Lena curled her fingers over the bloodstains and swallowed. She closed her eyes for a moment and steeled herself before inhaling deeply, knowing she was about to make an incredibly stupid decision but growing more desperate with each passing minute, while they showed no signs of stopping. 

     

                Tensing for a brief moment, she squeezed her eyes shut, clenched her teeth and threw herself from the saddle. Fortunately, she’d timed it well, as they galloped through ferns and weeds and a thick carpet of rotting foliage, the sweet smell of the forest heady and thick in the still air, but, on the other hand, there was no fortunate side to throwing oneself off a horse moving that swiftly.

     

                She struck the ground hard, her fall only slightly broken by a sprawling patch of wood anemone, the white perennials flattened beneath her, but she managed to land on a concealed log as well, hollowed out by mice and cracking under her stomach, the impact hard enough to bruise. Winded, Lena lay dazed for a moment, almost forgetting to run as she blinked back stars and coughed, biting back a groan.

     

                Barely managing to push herself to her knees, clutching at her stomach, Lena let out a sharp hiss and cursed her stupidity. Already, the sound of hooves retraced their steps and she found herself being gently guided to her feet, anxious blue eyes fixing her with an alarmed look.

     

                “Come. We cannot stop; it isn’t safe yet.”

     

                Lena blinked dumbfoundedly as the fae woman spoke to her for the first time. She couldn’t even form a reply, didn’t even have the chance to before the woman was carefully steering her back towards the horse and lifting her onto it as if she was a child. Tasting blood at the back of her throat, a headache throbbing at the base of her skull, Lena sat there, limp and resigned, as the woman pulled herself up behind Lena.

     

                The sun had fully risen and then climbed even higher by the time they started to slow. The horse snorted and tossed his mane as he plodded along and the fae woman didn’t seem quite so nervous, passing into a land that was relatively flat and quiet, birds singing back and forth and wildflowers growing everywhere in colourful patches. It wasn’t until they came upon a massive lake, so big that Lena couldn’t even see it in its entirety, that they stopped.

     

                It was flat and like glass, a clear blue as it reflected the expanse of sky. It was even bigger than Lena could make out, its misshapen form disappearing around jutting fingers of land, of thick trees reaching out to shade the water. The sight of so much water made Lena shiver - she’d never so much as been to the beach, a swimming pool or a river in the years since her mother’s death - and she wondered what sort of animals made it their home. A multitude of fish, surely, ducks and birds in the reeds, otters and frogs and other creatures who came to drink from it. 

     

                But there, a hundred feet from the bank of the lake, was a delicately built tower, eighty feet tall and made of a stone the palest shade of grey, rising from the water. The sight was absurd, like something out of a fantasy novel, but when the woman dismounted, she realised that this must have been their end destination. Throat constricting, her mouth dry and her skin clammy, she watched as a lone peregrine hovered midair for a moment before it dove for the surface of the lake.

     

                “Come.”

     

                Blinking, Lena looked down at the woman looking up at her. She was reaching for Lena expectedly, an earnest look of innocence in her blue eyes, and Lena shied away from her touch.

     

                “Where are you taking me?” she asked, although she already knew the answer.

     

                The woman pointed to the soaring tower, its domed roof of pale slate, the open archways that gave the tower a rather elegantly skeletal look as if it contained nothing and was nothing but a long-standing structure. What they were doing there, Lena didn’t want to know. Was she to be drowned in the lake? Was she to be chained at the top of the tower like the Princess she apparently was?

     

                “Argo. You’re safe here, I promise.”

    Chapter 2

                Argo.

     

                The fae woman said the name as if it held any meaning for Lena, who blinked as she stood there, trying to process everything. Her face felt numb and she didn’t so much as move, staring impassively as she waited for the joke to be over, the nightmare to end. But if it was a nightmare, it was a beautiful one. The fae said something else in that language, making Lena’s skin prickle beneath her dress as she narrowed her eyes, giving her a wary look. 

     

                Beckoning with her extended hands, the woman nodded and Lena swallowed before she reached out for her, hands gingerly resting on her shoulders as strong, tanned hands gripped her waist. Gently pulled from the horse, Lena was set down on the grassy banks of the lake and watched as the woman murmured something indecipherable to the horse, stroking its nose before she gave it's back a pat and the horse moved on.

     

                Shrinking away from the water, arms wrapping around herself, Lena’s stomach knotted itself with fear. Moving towards the lake, the woman glanced back over her shoulder and gave Lena a warm, yet reserved, smile. She beckoned her again.

     

                “Come.”

     

                A caustic laugh of disbelief clawed its way up Lena’s throat as she shook her head, shrinking back further, holding herself tightly. “I’m not going anywhere with you.”

     

                A look of confusion clouded her face, still beautiful and a little naive, Lena thought, and she took a step back towards her, her hand still extended. Her expression was pained and understanding and she stood there, waiting patiently, while Lena scowled at her, fear curling up her spine, although she had the quiet thought that this fae woman wouldn’t harm her.

     

                Cocking her head to the side, the woman smiled faintly, “it’s not safe out here. You must be tired; I’ll show you to your room.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena made a breathless choking sound. Anger flashed through her, hot and fast. “I already told you - I’m not going anywhere with you.”

     

                “I … don’t understand,” she slowly replied, her voice unhurried and gentle, softly crossing the gap between them as she tactfully kept her distance. “You agree to wed me, yet you refuse to share my home? That’s … complicated.”

     

                “Excuse me?”

     

                “Forgive me, I thought the treaty entailed-”

     

                “Wed? What the fuck are you talking about? I didn’t agree to marry you.”

     

                Looking increasingly confused with each passing moment, blue eyes wide and childlike and a pucker between her brows, the woman fiddled with her slender fingers, making a nervous habit look graceful. She let out a quiet laugh, the sound so delicate and bewildered, and her eyes creased at the corners in an endearing fashion.

     

                “Ah, they’ve given me a humorous wife, I see. I didn’t think an Unseelie capable of that .”

     

                “I’m not your fucking wife . Look, I don’t know what the hell is going on here but I’d like to go home. I didn’t ask to get dragged to this- this shitty forest and be forced into these shitty clothes and- and passed around like some doll .”

     

                The other woman visibly paled as Lena’s words sank in, her eyes widening with panic and horror, and no small amount of anger as her shoulders slumped and her hands hung limply at her sides.

     

                “You mean to say … you didn’t agree to this?”

     

                “No,” Lena snapped, bristling as she swallowed thickly, on the verge of tears. “No, I fucking didn’t.”

     

                Storming towards her, the blonde woman looked murderous and Lena’s lips parted as her eyes widened. But the woman swiftly drifted past her, the breeze of her passing making Lena’s dark hair ruffle slightly as she turned to look after her, even more confused. Hurrying away from the lake’s edge as they left the tower behind them and went deeper into the trees, Lena felt her chest constrict with panic.

                

                “Where are you going?”

     

                The woman let out a clear whistle, the sound drifting through the trees, echoing slightly, before she turned to look at Lena, her mouth a thin line of regret. “I’m taking you back.”

     

                “Back?”

     

                “I’ll have no part in your taking,” she brittly fumed, a haughty superiority to her words as she gripped the hilt of her sword, a muscle twitching in her jaw. “We were led to believe that you would be coming to this union of your own free will.”

     

                “Free will?”

     

                “It’s an honour to serve one’s court,” the other woman murmured as her brow creased. “Surely your mother-”

     

                “She’s not my mother. I don’t even know where I am.”

     

                “I … don’t understand.”

     

                “I’m not from this world,” Lena snapped, her patience wearing thin.

     

                That caught the fae by surprise, her mouth opening and closing for a moment as she stared at Lena with incredulity in her blue eyes. “We were aware you were only half-fae while brokering the treaty, had heard of the half-fae Princess, but … your- Queen Lillian made it seem like you- that you had been raised at court.”

     

                Cold and even haughtier than her companion, Lena jerked her chin up, “I promise you, I was not . All I know is that those people showed up in my home last night and dragged me through some … puddle. I- none of this makes any sense. I think- I … I need to sit down.”

     

                “I should have known better than to trust the Unseelie at their word,” she said as her mouth twisted derisively. “But I’ll play no part in their wicked treachery.”

     

                Lena turned at the sound of hooves striking the ground and watched as the dappled grey stallion returned, tossing his mane and snorting. He slowed as he neared them and Lena watched the woman fondly stroke his nose and whisper something, her tone full of regret and apology even if Lena didn’t know what it was she said. 

     

                “Come.”

     

                Wariness crept over Lena and she shied away from the offered hand. “I … I’m not sure I want to go back.”

     

                Mouth curling into an uneven smile, eyes softening with guilt and regret, the woman gave her a pained look. “Forgive me, but I- if you will not stay here, I must take you back. I thought you would understand, but … we are at war. This was supposed to be the union that brought peace between our Courts; I dare not antagonise them further.”

     

                Panic swept through Lena tenfold and she moved towards the woman, grabbing the shoulders of the open velvet robe she was wearing, her face pale and taut with fear as she ducked her head, unable to stop herself from her desperate plea as she hoarsely begged her.

     

                “Please don’t. Please don’t make me go back there. I don’t want to go back.”

     

                Rooted to the spot in her surprise, the woman was slow to react, reaching up to gently grasp Lena’s biceps and ease her back, putting some distance between them. Her gentle face was taut and she winced slightly before turning to the horse.  “Come.”

     

                “Please-”

     

                “I’ll not let them harm you.”

     

                She glanced back over her shoulder and took in Lena’s tense posture, rigid as a statue as she clutched fistfuls of the skirt of her dress, and her expression softened. Murmuring something in that strange language of their people, she smiled softly and Lena felt the tension in her body bleed away, filled with some unearned trust that made her walk over to her side and let the fae lift her into the saddle.

     

                Leaping up behind her, she cradled Lena in her embrace and urged the horse onwards, back the way they’d come. As exhausted as she was, uncomfortable and aching and so hungry that she imagined her stomach was eating itself, she couldn’t stop the tears that filled her eyes, the flush in her cheeks at the embarrassment of crying before a stranger, even if she was hiding it.

     

                She’d thought she was hiding it well but it turned out she wasn’t, and when the fae woman let go of the horse’s mane to touch the back of her hand, a quietly reassuring gesture and the most kindness Lena had been shown all day. Her tears came freely then, the pent-up sob breaking free as her chest heaved, vision blurring as they sped through the trees.

     

                And behind her the whole time, this aloof stranger who seemed uneasy by the whole thing, gingerly patting her hand whenever Lena let out a choked sob, although she did little else to comfort her as if she was unused to such human displays of emotion. Did they cry? They looked human enough but they were spiteful and cruel from what Lena had encountered and what she knew of half-forgotten fairytales and it chilled her to think of what they would do to her now, delivered back to the hands that had taken her by the only one who had been kind to her, which was, in itself, the cruelest thing of all.

     

                Neither of them spoke during the long ride back, hours passing by in a blur of thick forest, tangled brambles and grassy glens, rising hills and warrens of ravines. Lena imagined she slept, although the lurching gait of the horse bumped her around so much that she knew she hadn’t, and she fell into a sort of stupor, red-eyed and mindless as the forest passed by. At times they slowed to a walk and turned aside, the fae woman’s hand straying to the silver sword strapped to her side, sheathed in a scabbard wrought like overlapping fish scales, the hilt made of mother of pearl with a pale blue larimar stone the size of a quail egg set into the pommel. She never drew it, but she heard the distant sounds of creatures that she wished were further away and tried to put more distance between them.

     

                Lunch came and went with no rest and no food, and a day and a half without sleep and hours without food - the last thing Lena remembered eating was a kale salad picked up from her favourite salad bar down the street - left Lena in a quiet daze. She was helpless to stop it but she knew that when it came to it she’d struggle and fight.

     

                It was early in the afternoon, hours since they’d thundered across that narrow bridge, with such speed that it would’ve terrified and exhilarated her if she’d been paying attention, when the woman galloped straight past the borders of the city Lena had come from. Fae watched with surprise, a murmur of unease rippling through them as they watched their enemy charge in unchallenged. Thus was the nature of their new treaty, which no one wanted to break so early.

     

                Still, it didn’t stop the woman from urging her horse right through the city, pulling up sharp in that peaceful clearing with the thick, sprawling tree growing up from the pond. Lena blinked, dry-eyed and stiff as the fae woman leaped down from behind her, lithe and graceful, radiating power and fury as she fell into stride, making for the throne on that gnarled platform made from the ancient tree.

     

                “Your Majesty,” she stiffly called out.

     

                Lena watched from the back of the horse, clinging to it with the urge to flee, to make her escape before anyone could stop her, vanish into the woods and be spared this political feud she’d been thrust into the centre of. She didn’t though, just clung to the horse’s neck as she watched Lillian rise from the throne, in a dress of deep grey now, making her eyes icier as she walked forward.

     

                “What is the meaning of this?”

     

                “I will not take her,” the woman called out, “I have been deceived .”

     

                “How so?” Lillian challenged, raising her chin imperiously.

     

                Seething, the blonde woman squared her shoulders. “I was led to believe it was a marriage we had both agreed to, only to find as soon as I returned to my lands that my new wife was not what I had expected.”

     

                “She is an Unseelie Princess, is she not? Bastard of my late husband.”

     

                “You have taken her.”

     

                “She is mine to take, as the heir.”

     

                The sword at the woman’s waist was drawn swiftly in one sharp motion, the rasping sound of metal singing through the trees as she stood, bristling with the sword in her grasp, afternoon sunlight gilding her in a yellow light that made her seem crafted from gold. The answering chorus of swords drawn and bowstrings creaking filled the clearing and Lena looked around, sunlight catching on a dozen fae pointing weapons at them. And yet, the fae woman seemed unafraid, holding her ground just before the dappled horse - either brave or foolish and perhaps a bit of both.

     

                “I refuse -”

     

                Lillian cut her off with a slight smile, amused and mocking. “You’ve already made the oath - do you intend to break the treaty between our Courts?”

     

                “I- no . But I will not hold her captive-”

     

                “I tire of this conversation; she is no concern of mine and you cannot return her. She’s yours to do with what you will,” Lillian said as she waved her hand dismissively, already turning away. “Take her. And ensure you’re both here at the changing of the leaves to uphold your oath.”

     

                The woman stood there for a moment, the air brimming with the tension that centuries of war had brought, the hatred saturating the air as the fae waited for her to move, to strike so they could fill her lean body with arrows.
