Pale with worry, Lena looked around, her fingers knotted in the horse’s mane as she willed the woman to sheath her sword. 

     

                She did so a moment later, her delicate face flushed with her anger and embarrassment, the tips of her ears a gentle pink where they parted her hair. Lena met her eyes, her own wide and uncertain, and she straightened as the fae pulled herself up behind her and spurred the horse into motion.

     

                Lena could feel the bristling tension in her wiry muscles where they pressed together and felt the urge to apologise, although she was weak with relief at being evicted from the city. The thought of another night there was hellish and the tightness of her muscles loosened as they fled, almost as swiftly as they’d entered.

     

                It wasn’t until they crossed over a different bridge hours later that they slowed, and Lena had the distinct impression that they were on Seelie territory. Yet, they kept a leisurely pace, no longer hurrying as the dangers of the ancient forest bore down on them, and Lena was confused when they came to a stop. She was carefully lifted from the horse’s back once the fae woman dismounted and Lena was struck with the sudden fear that she was about to be turned loose to the trees, spurned by both Courts.

     

                “Where are we going?” Lena hoarsely asked.

     

                Gently patting the horse’s flank and sending it on its way, the woman turned and gave her a blank look, her ocean eyes piercing, yet unreadable. “I’m taking you home,” she replied after a long pause.

     

                Whatever answer she’d been expecting, that hadn’t been one of them and Lena stammered for a moment as she blinked. “I- home?”

     

                “Yes. Come.”

     

                Stumbling, her legs numb from so many hours on horseback, the inside of her thighs rubbed raw and her gait lurching and unsteady, Lena followed her through the trees until they came to the edge of a small pond. It was perhaps five feet across, an irregular circle that was much the same as the dozen other ponds reflecting the dim light seeping through the canopy around them. Some were bigger and a few mere puddles, gathering in the dips in the forest floor.

     

                Wading into the pool they stood before, the fae woman turned and held a hand out to Lena, who readily took it, her touch warm and soft as she guided her new wife into the water. It was no deeper than Lena’s knees at first but she waded in deeper and found herself slipping under and away.

     

                It was no more disorienting the second time, although she was spared the embarrassment of passing out, but not the embarrassment of vomiting against the wall she was suddenly facing as she doubled over, sour bile clawing up her throat. Ashen and wet, the thin fabric clinging to her skin and cold metal clinging, her hair damp around her face in straggling strands, Lena straightened up to find herself in her small enclosed garden behind her shop.

     

                The air rushed from her lungs and she hurried over to the back door, yanking it open and stepping inside. It was dark and a film of dust covered the shop, flowers wilting in buckets, mail clogging up the letterbox in the front door. The air felt stale and close and a sudden headache knifed through her head, the smell of the air nauseating after the clean air of the forest. 

     

                The fae woman stepped inside behind her and looked around in fascination. She seemed a pale imitation of her golden regalness in the forest, where she’d seemed like a mythical goddess come to life, yet there was still that ethereal quality to her that assured Lena that all of it had been real. If the clothes weren’t enough to convince her, this strange creature in her shop was irreconcilable proof.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena said after a long pause of silence.

     

                She felt uncertain in her own home, in her own shop, reaching out to fiddle with the limp petal of a wilted rose to avert her gaze from the intense stare of the fae woman.

                

                “Forgive me,” she murmured, her voice low and smooth in the darkness of the shopfront. “I assure you I had no intention-”

     

                “I know,” Lena whispered, believing her.

     

                She nodded and seemed to relax a little as if it mattered what Lena thought of her. It didn’t - they would never see each other again after that night. And yet, Lena knew she’d think of her often, and it would be with gratitude for bringing her home safely, for delivering her from that strange world that felt so familiar that it nagged at the back of her mind, begging her to be remembered. 

     

                “What will happen to you now?” Lena asked, suddenly gripped with concern for the fae.

     

                A small smile curled her mouth and she shrugged nonchalantly. “War. But we have been at war for centuries, so I’ve known nothing else in my life.”

     

                A flicker of guilt ran across Lena’s face and she nodded, ducking her head down. “I’m … sorry.”

     

                “Please, do not apologise; it pains me to hear you say it. Even if you are my enemy.”

     

                Lena didn’t know how to respond to that, her mouth opening and closing. After a second she let out a confused laugh, her face crumpling. “You’re not my enemy - I don’t even know you.”

     

                “And yet, by circumstances of birth, we’re enemies, nonetheless. I’ll leave you now.”

     

                She nodded her head, just a little deeper than a normal nod, as if she respected Lena, bowing ever so slightly. Then she turned to go, hand on the pommel of her sword, which should have looked cheap coupled with her costume, like a campy Lord of the Rings cosplay. But she was undeniably beautiful and it struck Lena at that last parting moment that she would never see her again.

     

                “Wait,” she called out, the fae pausing to glance back at her, features blurred by the shadows. “What’s your name?”

     

                “Kara.”

    Chapter 3

                The fae woman left Lena standing alone in the dimness of her shop, afternoon waning as night crept in, a crimson sunset ushered in over the city. The silence was deafening, her ears ringing faintly as her head pounded and her body sagged limply with two days’ worth of exhaustion.

     

                It was a long few minutes before Lena forced herself to move, stumbling up the steps, catching her toe on the wood, and not feeling a thing as she walked up to the apartment. Her rumpled bed was the same as yesterday morning and her things were where she’d left them but there was a foul smell in the air and dust motes spiraled through the shafts of sunlight slipping through a gap in the skyscrapers and through her window. Her plants were wilted and half-dead as well and Lena stood on the dusty floorboards and sneezed. 

     

                The sound was too loud in the cramped space, so stale after the open space, the wind whistling through the trees, and she looked around before slowly sinking down to the floor. Curling in on herself, she hugged her arms around her knees and frowned thoughtfully at the wall. Lena was left with the vaguely unsettling feeling that her entire world had shifted and would never be the same again.

     

                She wasn’t sure how long she sat there, almost as if time was moving at a different speed, hours passing by in the blink of an eye. When she came back to herself, dazed and confused, it was dark and the muffled sound of sirens and drunken shouts came in from outside. She was cold and stiff and it took her a long minute to uncurl herself and climb to her feet.

     

                Shedding rings with jewels worth more than the city block her shop and apartment were located in, Lena let the dress pool to the floor and staggered into the bathroom, turning on the hot water in the shower. Stepping beneath its scalding spray, she sank down to the bottom of the bath as her hair was plastered to her head. Unmoving, she stayed wrapped up in her thoughts as the hot water stung the cuts on her palms, the scrapes on her knees and the raw flesh around her wrists, mud swirling down the drain as the water washed her feet clean.

     

                Eventually, she reached for her soap and scrubbed herself clean, suds forming on her skin as she washed away the smell of fear, the small bathroom filled with the scent of freesia. It was comforting and slowly but surely her knotted muscles loosened and Lena washed her hair and climbed out. Wrapping herself in a towel, she wiped the condensation from the mirror and stared at her ashen reflection. The hot water had put some pink into her grey pallor but her pupils were still dilated with fear and Lena stood there, watching the water run down her arms and shoulders and drip onto the tiles, her mind elsewhere, until a shiver wracked her body.

     

                Changing into pyjamas, the pilled grey sweatshirt of her National City University crewneck from when she’d gotten her business degree feeling familiar and soothing. As exhausted as she was, Lena needed to eat something before she collapsed into bed and she crossed the open space to the kitchen. Yanking open the fridge, glass bottles of milk and juice clinking in the door, she made a heaving sound of disgust at the fetid smell of rotten food that assaulted her. 

     

                Clamping a hand over her nose, she stared with disgust and uneasiness, taking in the strawberries that were furred with mold, the wilted spinach, blackened and turned to mush in its container, the leftovers from the Chinese takeout on the corner that smelt sickly sweet, the oil seeping through the cardboard container. None of it should have been off, none of it should have rotted so fast since yesterday and Lena slammed the door shut on it, drawing in a gulp of air, still laced with the stomach-turning smell of it.

     

                Turning around, she looked at the apartment with fresh eyes and the prickling feeling that something was amiss. She ignored the sensation and went to bed, affording herself the time to sleep for as long as she desired, bone-deep weariness knocking her out cold for sixteen hours as she rose late and stretched, filled with the confusing sensation that she’d had the strangest dream. But no - the cut on her palm was there, stinging and scabbed over, and the jewels and dress too. It left Lena’s mouth dry and she stayed in bed a while longer, dwelling in her thoughts.

     

                It wasn’t something she’d ever be able to explain to someone without coming across as clinically insane but it bothered her. How could she have been dragged to some fairy realm and suffered a great ordeal in a matter of hours and come home and pretend that nothing was amiss? Digging the heels of her palms into her eyes, she exhaled roughly and ran a hand through her hair before climbing out of bed.

     

                No matter her feelings, she had the shop to look after and was already behind on her day. Taking a brisk shower and changing into her usual attire of a linen shirt and a pair of jeans, twisting her hair and clipping it up, Lena contemplated breakfast as her stomach ached and remembered the fridge from last night. She made quick work of tossing the entire contents of it, coughing at the rotting smell and opening all of the windows in the place to let the breeze chase it out. 

     

                After watering the house plants, watching them greedily drink as if it had been days, perking up beneath her care, Lena snagged her sunglasses, slipped on a pair of Birkenstocks, and grabbed her purse. Feet thundering downstairs, she came to a sudden halt inside the shop as she stared around at the array of plants, her lips parting in surprise. It was much worse than she’d thought the night before, the wilting bouquets not just wilted , but dead and rotting, the floor littered with petals and leaves, flowers shriveled up and dried out, buckets that had held water the night before bone dry and the stems yellowing or brown at their trimmed ends.

     

                “Fuck,” Lena swore, taking in the hundreds of dollars worth of products now dead and gone to waste - except for a single rose that she’d touched last night, flourishing and thriving despite the decay around it. 

     

                Pushing her sunglasses up onto her head, Lena quickly rushed through to the workshop and yanked open the door to the cool room housing thousands more flowers, the air rushing from her lungs as her skin pimpled at the frigid air in the cool room. She’d had a delivery made only two days before but the flowers were already dying, the low temperature not enough to preserve them for another week and Lena’s face crumpled. It would put a dent in her profits, that was for sure and she wanted to kick something.

     

                Squeezing her eyes shut, she stood there for a moment, breathing in the dank smell of stagnant water, the mingling aroma of flowers, and the earthy scent that still clung to them, cut through with the sweetness of rot, and pinched the bridge of her nose. Exhaling, she turned and stalked out, unlocking the front door to the shop and stepping out into the street.

     

                It was a mild day, mid-summer blue skies clear overhead as she briskly walked down the street, shoulders tense and a strained look on her face. So much had gone so wrong in the course of a single day and Lena didn’t even want to begin thinking about how she’d have to hire a replacement for Eve. Instead, she made the three-block walk to her favourite café, ordered herself the biggest matcha latte they offered and a bagel with cream cheese. Sitting near the window, a swathe of sunlight cutting across her table, she forced herself to breathe slowly and take stock of things. She was home and she was safe - that was good fortune given her bleak outlook on her circumstances only this time yesterday.

     

                Sipping her latte slowly and forcing herself not to wolf down the bagel, Lena lingered there a while longer before she climbed to her feet and left. Stopping by a small supermarket on her way home, she grabbed a basket and started filling it with things to replace the spoiled food in her fridge, grabbing a bottle of oat milk, fresh spinach, and a few caps of mushrooms, basking in the normalcy of it all as she tried to convince herself that it had been nothing but a nightmare. Or perhaps it was some psychotic breakdown, a delayed trauma response to everything that had gone wrong in her childhood.

     

                It was a lie, of course, and she would never have been able to convince herself otherwise, the cut on her palm stinging as a reminder of the truth. Swallowing, she shook her head and reached for a carton of eggs, depositing them in the basket before she grabbed two bottles of wine and made for the checkout. Standing there as a young girl scanned her items, Lena’s attention snagged on the day’s newspaper on a stand beside the checkout. Tearing a copy from the rack, Lena’s eyes honed in on the date as icy fear slid down her spine. 

     

                Breaking out in a cold sweat, she licked her lips and reached for another copy, aware of the girl’s apprehensive stare. The date was the same. A panicked laugh built up in Lena’s chest and she ran a shaky hand across her damp brow, looking up at the girl and giving her a wavering smile.

     

                “They printed the date wrong. On the newspaper. It’s wrong.”

     

                “Today’s the twenty-sixth,” the girl slowly said as confusion flashed across her face.

     

                Paling, Lena jammed both copies back into the rack, paper tearing, and rubbed at her brow as she inhaled sharply. She was jittery and panicked, her heart hammering in her chest, and she knew what she must have looked like, brimming with agitation, strung out on drugs or perhaps drunk at this time of day, but she felt like her mind was unraveling at the seams.

     

                “No, no, no,” Lena whispered to herself as she tried to piece it all together.

     

                She knew for a fact that she’d been taken in the evening and held overnight in that Unseelie Court place, ridden out in the late hours after midnight and handed over to that fae woman - Kara , Lena’s mind supplied - at dawn. It hadn’t even been a full day that she’d spent in that land, as long and agonising as it felt, yet now she was confronted with the fact that she’d been gone for nine days. 

     

                “Ma’am, are you alright?” the girl asked as she finished bagging up Lena’s groceries.

     

                Tossing a hundred-dollar bill onto the conveyor belt, Lena grabbed her bags with shaking hands, a lump in her throat as she swallowed thickly. “Thank you.”

     

                She hurried out in a daze, the world seeming to tilt as her perspective changed. The spoiled food, the dusty apartment, the dead flowers. Time had slipped by in that realm without her even noticing and she was left feeling hollow and uneasy. Stumbling home, her vision narrowed and her ears rang, the air too hot and polluted, a throbbing headache at the base of her skull that made her blood pound in her ears. She fell once, dropping her bags and scraping her palms on the grimy sidewalk, watching as the shallow cut from the dagger reopened, blood pooling in her palm.

     

                A hand touched her shoulder and she flinched away from the man trying to help her up. Sweat poured down her face and she blinked slowly, her lips parted and her throat dry. Picking up her bags, she ignored the man and carried on home, letting herself in through the shopfront and falling back against it as screwed her eyes shut and stayed there for ten minutes, trying to process everything. 

     

                Finally forcing herself to move, she made her way upstairs and put away her fresh groceries before looking around the apartment. In a flurry of motion, she stripped her sheets and put on the washing, vacuumed the floors and mopped, lit candles to chase away the lingering smell of dust as the breeze swept through, and watered her plants some more. The entire time there was a tremor to Lena’s movements, a fluttering in her stomach as if she was about to be sick.

     

                Afterward, she turned her attention to her business. In nine days, there had been orders, deliveries, the new stock that hadn’t been accepted, an influx of emails, and missed phone calls on her dead cell phone. It wasn’t just the loss of the flowers, but the refunds she had to issue, the negative reviews online, the voicemail left by a hysterical bride when her flowers hadn’t shown up on Friday. The only excuse Lena could make as she sent refunds through, wincing as her profit margin drastically dropped for the month, was that she’d been hospitalised. She offered no other details as to why , but it certainly felt like she’d just endured a psychotic episode worthy of it. 

     

                But no, the jewels, the dress, the bloodstained handkerchief. She went to fetch it from the bathroom where she’d discarded it and ran the thin cloth through her fingers before dropping it onto the pile of laundry to do next. She ended up keeping it for some strange reason, the bloodstains removed yet the strangeness of a simple piece of cloth a reminder that she hadn’t gone mad. 

     

                In the following days, as she cleaned up the shop below, reordered new flowers, and took new orders, she kept it in the pocket of her jeans, occasionally pulling it out to run it through her fingers. A week slipped by and yet she couldn’t let go of what had happened. It was like this was the dream world and Lena found her mind elsewhere on more than one occasion - in the middle of taking an order, at the store, while she cooked dinner - consumed by memories of hair like spun gold, roots winding around her ankles and dragging her along the ground, the dampness of clean forest air. 

     

                She was paler than usual, a feat in its own right, and distracted, barely eating a thing as headaches plagued her. Every night, dreams plagued her as well, the sound of water threading through her subconscious, the sound of hoofbeats and a soft voice, musical and gentle, saying a name. She dreamed of eyes like the ocean and pooling blood, the suffocating darkness and the feeling of being watched. 

     

                Once, when she’d been arranging bouquets in the shopfront, she’d seen a blonde woman walk past and dropped the vase onto the wooden floor, water soaking into her feet and petals and sharps of glass glittering in the light. She’d gone pale and wide-eyed as if seeing a ghost, and it took her a moment to realise that the blonde was too platinum, a product of bleach, the stature too short and not nearly as elegant. Lena had squeezed her eyes shut and frowned before cleaning up the mess and going about her business as usual.

     

                Five days after that, Lena caught the bus as far out of National City as she could, out to one of the tourist spots to tour the national park, sandstone foothills, and sparse shrubbery giving way to spruce and trickling rivers and then giant sequoias. She’d picked a hiking trail and walked as if in a dream, the peace of the trees paling in comparison to the cool tranquility of that forest she’d been led through. Her muscles ached as she climbed the trail, the air dusty and dry, the sun hot as it worked its way through the canopy overhead, the redwoods standing two-hundred feet tall and still not nearly as tall as the thick, dark woods. 

     

                The thoughts consumed her, called to her, sang to her and Lena kept walking as if searching for something. The desert started on the other side of the national park, sand and rock stretching out beyond, so different to that place she’d been, and Lena knew she could spend all day in the confines of the acres of soaring trees and wildlife and still feel that pull towards nature, that kernel of dissatisfaction. The truth was, she’d looked upon something otherworldly, and anything on earth would pale in comparison to it now.

     

                And there, beneath the ache in her chest, the disgruntling knowledge that this was far from the green paradise she’d walked through - under awful circumstances, of course, but familiar all the same, as if she’d been called home - was the shocking longing to go back. It had grown in the back of her mind like a seed planted. The past two weeks had left Lena with that nagging feeling of something wrong, something out of place, and she was starting to think that it was her . She with her slightly pointed ears, her affinity for plants, and her longing for something more . Even her flower shop and her contentment with her life had always left her longing for more, to know who she was. 

     

                It was almost out of frustration that she went hiking through the trees as if hoping it would quell that restlessness that had yawned open inside her. Instead, as she slung her backpack off her shoulders and set it on the leaf-strewn earth, pulling her water bottle from the side of it and drinking deeply, her skin pink and sweaty from the heat, Lena only felt anger at how wrong it all felt. She could feel it in her bones. 

     

                Screwing the lid back onto the bottle, she climbed to her feet, her face pale, bags beneath her eyes, and a pucker between her eyebrows. The bottle slipped from her fingers and she exhaled slowly as she moved towards the nearest tree, a rowan tree, the meaning lost on Lena at the moment even as she was drawn to it, laying her hands against its rough bark. 

     

                The tree was gnarled and twisted and its trunk was hollowed out, and Lena’s fingers brushed over the rough bark as she stared up at the branches, the small green leaves and the clusters of berries. Inhaling deeply, her skin tingled faintly, a whine in the air, and she let out an airy sigh, her eyelids fluttering closed. Here was the peace she’d craved, the touch of the tree beneath her palms warm and comforting, and then suddenly not there as she seemed to slowly tip forwards.

     

                She fell so slowly that time seemed suspended for a moment until she landed face-first on a mossy floor. Slow to move, Lena blinked as her eyes adjusted to the dimness, the thickness of the canopy cast the forest in a green shade of light as she let out a small groan and pushed herself to her knees. Tipping her head back, she looked up and knew exactly where she was, her stomach jolting with surprise. She shouldn’t have been able to do that, she knew she shouldn’t have been able to get back here alone, and yet she’d somehow fallen through.

     

                Scrambling to her feet, Lena whirled around, her eyes wide and stricken. Looking down at her palms, she frowned, yet her blood sang in her veins, and her skin prickled with that eerie feeling of being home again. The familiarity was overwhelming this time and it took Lena a few minutes of standing there to get her bearings, the dull throbbing at the back of her head that had lingered for weeks now, suddenly gone , that ache in her chest lightening. Inhaling deeply, she felt her chest expand with clean, cool air and marveled at the feeling. 

     

                Shaking her head, Lena turned and stared at the rowan tree, twice as tall as the one she’d been touching only a moment before, and yet still dwarfed by the tallest trees surrounding them, and she touched her palms to it again. Nothing happened. Frowning at her hands, Lena willed them to move through the trunk and let out a spluttered sound when she found herself still standing there.

     

                Confused, she turned again to survey the forest. It was midday, or so she surmised, and it didn’t seem quite so terrifying this time. In fact, there was a beauty to it that spoke to her and she found herself quickly forgetting about the rowan tree. Taking a stumbling step forward, she looked around, taking in the straight soaring trunks, the squat sprawling trees, the ferns and rocks and blackberry bushes, the distant sound of trickling water and the trilling of songbirds. Lena could have stayed forever, she thought at that moment, a laugh escaping her as she turned in a slow circle, a look of serenity crossing her face as something old and ancient wound through her body, some magic in her blood binding her closer with each moment spent in this fae world.

     

                What harm could it do to linger a moment? Lena was a lover of nature by heart, the beauty of the wildflowers she spotted springing up from the ground beckoning her. Without the haste of the three Unseelie fae and their fear of the forest at night, Lena forgot to be terrified of this land, of what hid amongst the trees, and perhaps that should have been her first mistake, but the human half of her succumbed to the fae magic of the place, leaving her mind susceptible to its tricks as she stumbled towards the flowers. Breathing in the air, she smiled softly to herself and caressed a petal, the botanist in her knowing better to enjoy the sight of it than pluck it daintily and keep it for herself.

     

                Moving onwards, she found herself enticed by the blackberries she found growing on a bush, plucking one and eating it, the flavour sweet and tart on her tongue, staining her lips purple as she reached for another one. She wandered almost without meaning to, straying further from that rowan tree, reaching out to touch the lichen-covered trunks of trees that had lived for thousands of years, watching as squirrels scurried past and a spider spun its web in a batch of brambles that was slowly spreading across the land.

     

                It was all fascinating to her and Lena lost track of time, until the fae part of her, tuned in to this world, subconsciously aware of the web of wildlife around her even if she didn’t know how to listen to it, brought her out of that trance-like wonder. Blinking, Lena found herself standing in a clearing, unfamiliar and darker, the trees so far spaced apart that she could see all around her, this part of the forest so ancient that it made her skin prickle. There was a palpable feeling of unease that made her stomach knot itself and she was filled with the sudden urge to go . 

     

                Looking around for that rowan tree, Lena picked a direction and set off, alarmed at how much the light had faded since she’d arrived in the forest, hours slipping by unannounced. She wondered how long that was in the human world and was filled with the strange reluctance to go back. Escape this part of the forest, yes, but go back to the filthy concrete jungle, troubled by constant headaches and that sense of loneliness that came from being an orphan, but also other. Coming to an abrupt halt, she frowned.

     

                She could stay. The thought came to her mind with such sudden surprise that she blinked. The breath escaped her as she ran a hand through her hair, dark strands having come loose from her clip as she’d wandered, her face pinched with confusion. Shaking her head, Lena set off again, leaves rustling beneath her feet as she pushed forward in her chosen direction.

     

                Yet, it was as if the forest was warning her against that way - or perhaps keeping her in. The feeling that came over her was oppressive, the very trees seeming to hinder her, the underbrush growing thick and difficult to navigate until it occurred to Lena that this wasn’t the way she’d come. The forest floor was thick with leaves chewed by worms and branches reached out to scratch her arms and cheeks like claws. Everything smelled of damp and decay, cut through by the bitter sharpness of cold and she let out a small cry of panic as she stepped on the bleached bones of a dead fox, the carcass picking clean and being reclaimed by the earth and moss.

     

                Lena found herself having to go around the massive trees blocking her path more than once as brambles snagged at her clothes and her skin grew clammy. She wanted a drink of water but couldn’t hear the sound of a river so pushed onwards, her palms brushing tree trunks as she hoped that one of them would drag her back through to her world. Although, the thought of that dry forest, with its small trees and searing heat, didn’t sound appealing and she had to wonder if her heart was really in it.

     

                But even as she thought it, dread grew like ivy inside her, creeping through her veins, wrapping around her bones and squeezing tight, and she found herself startled for some unknown reason, her head pounding in her chest. Drawing in a shallow, rapid breath, Lena turned, green eyes wide and nervous as her skin prickled with the feeling of being watched. And then she started to run.

     

                Crashing through the underbrush, lines of fire cutting her skin as her running shoes pounded over the dark earth, Lena heard the sound of something chasing after her, panting breaths and loud footfalls. Her first mistake was looking back and she stumbled at the sight of a huge beast streaking towards her, staggering forward as she tried to regain her balance before she sprawled into a fern. 

     

                Gasping, she struggled to her feet and carried on, but it was no use. She couldn’t run as fast as the thing that pursued her and it was only a moment later that a paw bigger than her back flattened her to the ground. Facedown in the earth, breathing in the rich, damp smell of it, Lena felt a growl reverberate through her chest as the hot, rotting breath of the creature made her gag as it lowered its muzzle to her.

     

                It sniffed at her and growled, the sound making Lena’s stomach lurch with terror, and when the pressure of its paw lifted a moment later she scrabbled at the mud, trying to drag herself forward. A snarl tore through the forest and she let out a gasp of shocked pain as large fangs clamped down on her arm, dragging her back like a ragdoll.

     

                The beast tossed her aside and Lena collapsed in a heap, this time on her back as she scurried back, the feeling of hot blood trickling down her arm, making her feel light-headed as she came face to face with a wolf. Except, it was no ordinary wolf, bigger than an elephant in size with moss coating it in patches, tiny purple and white wildflowers sprouting from it, along with trailing vines of ivy, giving it an ethereal beauty, despite its brutal danger. Its teeth were longer than daggers and saliva dripped from its jaw as it snarled and prowled towards her.

     

                It was then that Lena realised she’d fucked up enormously by coming back to this forest, for allowing it to get under her skin and entice her with its otherworldly beauty, and yet, even as the wolf walked towards her, its eyes such a pale shade of grey, shining as if they held stars within their depths, she couldn’t bring herself to regret it. Its sharp claws tore through her abdomen like she was made of paper and she couldn’t do much more than whimper and shrink back against the base of a sprawling oak tree as she waited for it to take her head in its jaw and break her skull like an eggshell.

     

                Only, it never came as she huddled in on herself, eyes shut and teeth bared. The next thing Lena was aware of was a loud shout distracting the massive wolf before it could snap at her and Lena looked up, pale and shaking, to watch as a fae man in silver armour barrelled into the side of the wolf. He was tall and broad, his skin dark and a shield held aloft, strapped to his left arm as he went down on one knee and blocked the swipe from the wolf.

     

                It snarled, muzzle peeling back over its gums, and sank lower to the ground. The man thrust a hand towards it and the wind whistled between the trees, a vortex slamming into the wolf’s side, throwing it off balance before the man yanked a sword from the sheath strapped to his back and drove it into the beast’s side.

     

                It let out a strangled yelp and recoiled before dashing off through the trees. Lips parted and a disbelieving look on her face, Lena looked up as the man approached, the sound of hooves pounding towards them as a few more fae arrived. Nestled into a dip between the roots of the oak, Lena pressed her hands to her wounds as her mouth went dry with fear.

     

                As horses were reined in, the one in silver armour stood over her, his shadow cast across her curled-up body, and she sluggishly blinked as her vision furred at the edges. Dropping to a knee in front of her, bloody sword sheathed at his back again as a deep grey cloak pooled around him, he reached out with a gloved hand and brushed her hair aside, careful not to touch her ears as he revealed the points.

     

                Lena promptly passed out then, blood soaking into her clothes and the adrenaline coursing through her too much for her to process. Glancing over his shoulder, the man looked at his companions as his mouth thinned.

     

                “This is the Unseelie halfling Kara wed.”

     

                “You mean the one she returned,” said a man with brown hair dressed in deep maroons, like an autumn maple leaf. 

     

                “Nevertheless, she’s still her wife. We can’t leave her here, Mon-El,” said Imra, her face furrowing beneath the hood of her burgundy cloak.

     

                “Do as you will, I care not; I tire of the hunt anyway. Night will fall soon.”

     

                James swiftly cradled Lena’s small form in his arms and carried her over to his horse, which had caught up to him, and he managed to get her over its back. He swung up behind her and urged his horse on, the pack of five galloping through the woods as they left behind the darker reaches of the forest.

     

                They moved swiftly and the trees became closer together, shorter and the canopy not quite as dense as late afternoon sunlight filtered through. There was a blue quality to the light and they splashed across a shallow ford in their haste, James urging his horse on as he glanced down at the woman before him. Her skin was so pale it seemed translucent, greenish veins stark against her pallor, the smudges beneath her eyes even more prominent.

     

                Eventually, he burst through a thicket of trees and pulled up short, his horse rearing and stamping. The sound of a lyre and laughter cut off and he swung down from his horse and pulled Lena down with him. The scene before him was one of leisure and Kara rose to her feet, her silken blue dress like deep water as it shifted with her movements, surprise crossing her delicate features.

     

                Alex sat up from where she lay with her head in Kelly’s lap and Querl glanced up from the book he’d been reading from. There were others there too, indulging in a picnic of a sort, on the banks of the river where they’d spent the day swimming, eating food, and drinking golden wine, basking in the midsummer warmth. 

     

                “I found her,” James said by way of explanation.

Stopping before James, she looked down at Lena’s face and her expression hardened at the greyish pallor her skin had taken on, the blood soaking the front of her human clothes.

     

                “Where?”

     

                “In one of the older parts of the forest. We found her being attacked by one of the wolves.”

     

                Kara glanced up at him, meeting his dark eyes in a fleeting look of worry before she reached out to relieve him of the burden of her wife. Mouth thinning as her expression darkened, she awkwardly shifted her in her arms to press her fingers to her pulse, feeling the weak flutter of her heart.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                James bowed slightly and Kara ducked her head before she turned from him, her eyes landing on her sister, who rose to her feet in a fluid motion, snatching up her discarded sword. Alex met her halfway and peered down at Lena with a hard look of anger.

     

                “Unseelie?”

     

                “A wolf.”

     

                “Kara, she cannot die.“

     

                “I know. I know. We’ll have to go by horse; she can’t make the trip herself.”

     

                “Take mine,” James offered, beckoning his dun stallion over.

They would though - Kara knew they’d follow to protect her along the way, the fate of their peace treaty depending on the two of them surviving. She was dimly aware of hoofbeats following after her and cursed at the miles separating her from her home.

     

                Still, the horse was fast and the journey swift as she held Lena securely in place, her hands coated with the woman’s blood. She’d been flippant when making a comment about how all the two Courts knew was war but this had been a valiant effort to broker peace, and despite her returning Lena, the treaty had remained in place. What she did when she was supposed to be on Seelie land was none of Kara’s concern, and if the Unseelie wanted to drag her back in their seasons, so be it. 

     

                That wouldn’t matter if she was dead though, and Kara knew who would be blamed for such a deed. If word got out that the Unseelie Princess was mauled to death on their side of the river, she knew it would be seen as a declaration of war, even if it hadn’t been intentional. That was just the volatile way their politics worked and she didn’t want to be the El that started a war when so many had died in the last one.

     

                Eventually, they neared her sprawling lake and Argo thrust up from the water, shimmering indigo in the twilight as dusk fell around them.                 The entire structure was open to the elements, a series of arches leading into the flooded atrium, ankle-deep as a barren white tree rose up from the stone floor. There were four slashes on her abdomen and a bite wound on her arm bled freely and deep and Kara winced slightly. Rising to her feet, she saw her sister materialise on the stairs.

     

                “Fetch bandages and medicine, please.”

     

                Alex nodded and carried on up while Kara found a shallow pewter bowl and grasped the water in the lake below and pulled it up to her. It sloshed as it settled into the bowl and Kara made her way back over to Lena. With her magic, she cleaned out the wound as best as she could, healing the edges back together, stemming the flow of blood.

     

                When Alex returned a minute later with rolls of linen cloth and an assortment of herbs, Kara rose to her feet and let her sister treat the wounds. She’d always been better at it than Kara was and she took to the wound with a fishbone needle Kara used for sewing, pulling the edges together. Making a paste out of herbs when she was done, Alex washed away the blood and smeared the salve over the wounds, and bound her with linen bandages.

     

                “She will be in much pain; she should rest.”

     

                “She’ll stay until she’s healed.”

     

                “How do you think she got here?”

     

                Kara’s eyebrows drew together in a troubled look as she fiddled with one of the sapphire rings on her fingers. “I couldn’t say, although … I must state the obvious answer, for how else would she have gotten here?”

     

                “They’re a treacherous sort. Do be careful around her as well.”

     

                “She’s half-fae and knows nothing of this world. I’d hardly deem her a threat. If anything, she’s a naïve burden I’ve been saddled with, and all to serve a purpose that could’ve been achieved without a union.”

     

                “And yet, you agreed. Lay the blame elsewhere, if you will, but don’t forget you took an oath as well.”

     

                With a scoff, Kara’s mouth twisted ruefully. “I haven’t forgotten.”

     

                Alex rolled her eyes and gave her sister‘s arm a quick squeeze. “I’ll leave you now. Give her willow bark for the pain and make sure she doesn’t overexert herself. She may be faint for a while; she lost quite a bit of blood.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Dipping her head in a nod and giving the unconscious woman a curious look, Alex turned and left, her footsteps disappearing down the curved staircase. With a sigh, Kara picked up Lena’s bloody clothes and wrinkled her nose at the coarse feeling of the fabric, depositing it in a pile and then tidying up the mess.

     

                Afterward, she scooped Lena up, the woman murmuring softly as her grey face perspired and crumpled with pain. Trying not to jostle her too much, Kara took her upstairs to the quarters that had been prepared for her some weeks ago and had lain empty ever since.

     

                The furniture was all made out of grey wood, and Kara set Lena down on top of the stone blue linen sheets. Gently easing the covers back, she tucked her in to keep her warm and moved over to the empty brazier in the middle of the room, where driftwood logs lay, starting a fire in case she felt chill when she woke.

     

                Lingering, Kara watched her with a clouded look on her face, fiddling with her rings as her blue dress stuck to her where Lena had bled through the thin fabric. She was still staring when Lena stirred and let out a faint sigh.

     

                Blinking slowly, her eyelids heavy, Lena let out a low hiss and involuntarily curled in on herself as pain tore through her abdomen. Squeezing her eyes shut, she bared her teeth and took a minute to collect herself as she tried to arrange her thoughts into sense.

     

                “You should lay still.”

     

                Jolting at the sound of that voice, the voice that had wound through her dreams for weeks, Lena’s eyes snapped open and she took in the sight of the fae woman. It was getting dark out and she was more shadow than radiant gold, but no less beautiful for it. Her hair was intricately braided and threaded with gold and crystal beads that made it look like droplets of water had gotten caught in the strands of spun gold, and she was wearing a dress that would’ve been beautiful, like the rippling surface of a clear blue river, if not for the unsightly bloodstains. Lena realised her hands were covered in blood as well and her stomach lurched.

     

                “It’s you,” she whispered, her voice shy and apprehensive. “I thought I’d dreamt you.”

     

                “What are you doing here?” 

     

                Laying back against the pillow, Lena blinked up at the stone ceiling, vaulted and carved to look like waves. She felt sluggish and exhausted as she lay limply in the bed, blinking slowly as she tried to latch onto her memories.

     

                “I … I don’t know. I was hiking. I fell through a tree.”

     

                “How?”

                

                “I touched it. It felt … right. I’ve felt so … ever since I left, all I’ve been able to think about is- is this place. I’ve been losing my mind.”

     

                She breathlessly babbled and Kara drifted over to her bedside, her gentle face marred by a severe look as she stared down at her. 

     

                “You were foolish to come back here. Do you know how close you came to plunging us back into war? If you’d died, you would have condemned us all to death for your … stupidity.”

     

                Kara’s sharp tone caught Lena by surprise and a slow flush of embarrassment put some colour back into her cheeks. Turning her head aside as her eyes smarted with tears, Lena swallowed thickly.

     

                “I- well, I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to; I got … lost.”

     

                Exhaling sharply, Kara stood there a moment longer, a muscle twitching in her jaw as her mouth thinned with regret.

     

                “Sleep. We’ll speak of this no more until you’ve rested.”

     

                Turning, she was gone with a quiet rustle of fabric, leaving Lena alone in that unfamiliar bed, listening to the rippling sound of water far below. It took her a disorienting moment to realise that she was in that tower, in the middle of that lake, and she felt sick as the breath caught in her throat.

     

                The night had grown too dark for her to make out much by way of details, aside from the shadows of furniture and a flickering blue light amidst the flames of the brazier as the salt burned off the driftwood. Gauzy curtains fluttered in each archway and if Lena had known each one opened up to empty air and a swift drop down to the lake below, she wouldn’t have slept so peacefully.

     

                As it was, lulled by the sound of water and the sigh of the wind, her whole body aching with a dull pain, she did manage to fall asleep. Some part of her felt like it was a dream again and was able to let her limp body relax into the soft down mattress, and the hours slipped by without her knowing. Kara appeared on the open floor every couple of hours, her face troubled and strained as she observed Lena and then left again, the woman sleeping undisturbed. 

     

                Oblivious to it all, Lena dreamed. The dreams were tidal, consumptive, chaotic. No one had faces, but one was recognisable by her gleaming golden hair, and she heard voices, layered on top of one another, a cacophony with one cutting through with bone-deep familiarity that seemed to run through Lena’s veins like electricity. All of them spoke that ancient language that she couldn’t comprehend, talking to her, and she broke out in a cold sweat as she restlessly shifted in the bed before she finally woke up talking. Lena couldn’t remember what she’d been saying, only that she was driven to keep saying it.

     

                When she opened her eyes, it was to the pale light of dawn. The air was frigid and there was fog curling past the thin curtains, giving the space a hazy look as she blinked back sleep and shifted up. Shivering as she pulled the blankets to herself, Lena was aware of the fact that her clothes were gone and she bristled at the thought of being undressed while unconscious, but the spotted bandages spoke of her wounds being tended to.

     

                Sitting up slightly against the pillows, she looked around at the place she was in. The bed was set near the centre of the room, the layered blue blankets warm and the mattress and pillows soft beneath her. Everything seemed pale and subdued, shades of grey and white and blues, tranquil and peaceful. Across from the bed were a low chaise lounge and a few stools made from the same pale grey wood as the bed. 

     

                Woven rugs of shades of blue were scattered around the room and Lena took in the sight of a writing desk, a vanity with a polished sheet of metal as a mirror, a carved chest, and a wardrobe. It was all so beautiful, the attention to detail so fine that nothing was simple, not even the tiny glass-blown bottles neatly laid out on the vanity or the legs of the armchairs.

     

                She was still marveling at it all from her bed, her head spinning at how strange it all was, how open and light and cold , when Kara materialised, summoned by the sound of her murmurings. Lena met her blue eyes from across the room and felt shy and uneasy beneath her stare. 

     

                Kara had traded her blood-stained blue dress for a linen shirt and pants in light shades of bluish-grey smoke, matching the curls of ink on her slender fingers. She looked like a freshly woken storm, brooding and restless, or a beautiful nightmare come to life to personally haunt Lena. She was something out of the very depths of her dreams, dangerous and ethereal, wound through her subconscious so tightly over the past few weeks that Lena felt nothing other than a strange sense of intimacy, of knowing her despite not knowing her at all.

     

                In her ink-stained hands, Kara gripped a wooden tray and her knuckles whitened slightly before she padded barefoot across to Lena. Setting the tray down on the edge of the bed as Lena warily shied away, Kara stepped back and clasped her hands behind her back, her shoulders squared and her bearing regal. Lena wondered who she was and what she’d done to be saddled with a half-fae stranger for a wife.

     

                “How do you feel?”

     

                Kara spoke softly, her earlier anger absent in her words as she looked at Lena with perhaps a little more kindness. Running a hand over her face, feeling stiff and uncomfortable as pain knifed through her arm and her abdomen, and a little more on her upper thigh too, Lena shrugged. Her eyes looked sunken as dark purple smudges gave her a haunted look and she hugged the blankets to her as she shivered.

     

                “It’s cold.”

     

                “The morning fog will vanish soon; it looks to be a clear day.”

     

                “Where are my clothes?”

     

                “They’re ruined; I’ll fetch you something clean to wear. I haven’t yet procured a wardrobe for my wife so my own clothes will have to suffice, although, I should think they’ll be too big, perhaps.”

     

                Giving her a wary look, Lena nodded and looked down at the tray. A steaming cup of pale green tea lay beside a small loaf of bread studded with seeds and a grilled mackerel, its silvery scales browned and the head and tail still attached as it stared blankly with a milky eye.

     

                “I caught and gutted the fish myself,” Kara stated as if it was an honour, and Lena looked up at her with a furrowed look of bewilderment. 

     

                Clearing her throat as she tugged at the embroidered cuff of her shirt, Kara seemed almost as uneasy as Lena by her presence. “I was harsh when we spoke before; forgive me. I didn’t mean to lay the blame at your feet, only that … there’s a lot at stake with our union.”

     

                “With the war, you mean?” Lena rasped.

     

                “Indeed. None of us are anxious to break the peace treaty so soon after the oaths have been taken. Your safety is paramount to us to guard it and … I hadn’t thought to expect you here. You least of all should wander alone in the forest.”

     

                Wariness flickered in Lena’s green eyes as she opened and closed her mouth for a moment before replying. “I felt this … pull. I’ve been dreaming of this place since I left and I … it wouldn’t go away.”

     

                “No, indeed. The forest is invasive. Once you breathe its air, touch its earth, bathe in its waters … it's inside you. Humans are occasionally pulled through the old ways and once they’re returned they experience bouts of madness. It’s the forest in them; it fades with time, and the memories too, but it tries to pull all those who have visited back once more.”

     

                “I ate some blackberries,” Lena murmured, touching her lips, “I wanted to stay. I thought … I-“

     

                A faint smile played on Kara’s lips as she nodded. “Yes. Those of fae blood feel that pull to a greater extent. None of us can bear to be parted from our realm for long, although there are those amongst us who revel in the mischief of visiting mortal lands for a brief while. The longer you stay, the harder it will be to leave.”

     

                Rubbing at her forehead as she breathed slowly, Lena swallowed thickly. “Last time I was here … it was only a few hours. Days had passed when I got home. I- how can that be possible?”

     

                “Like all things in the forest, time is strange and mischievous. A second here can be a month there, a year here can be a minute there. It’s a contrary mood and of its own design - you will find that things here are rather … sentient, and not always friendly. Be wary of even the most innocent of things. Trust nothing.”

     

                “Does that include you?” Lena asked as a wry smile curled her lips.

     

                Stiffening slightly, Kara looked away, a muscle working in her jaw as she seemed to rock on the balls of her feet. Exhaling softly, she looked back at Lena with a solemn look on her face. Lena thought she was perhaps a little older, but Kara’s slim face was I worked, no lines, no dark half-moons beneath her eyes. She seemed ethereal, unloved in, except for those blue eyes that spoke of warmth and mirth. She could imagine her laughing with ease.

     

                “We are enemies, you and I. Of course it should include me.”

     

                “Enemies?” Lena said as she choked on a laugh, taking a hand through her hair, tangled with leaves caught in it. “I already told you; I don’t even know you.”

     

                “And as I responded, by nature of our births, we are. And yet, by the oaths of our marriage, we are the peace between our Courts, and that is perhaps more complex. I bear you no ill will though, you may trust in that if nothing else.”

     

                “I- that day on the bridge. Was that- that’s when you and I-“

     

                “Your mother made the oath on your behalf; she informed us of your inability to connect with your element.”

     

                “She’s not my mother,” Lena snapped, suddenly taut with anger as her face darkened.

     

                Blinking in surprise, Kara cocked her head to the side, thumbing a ring on her index finger as she frowned. “She had claimed you; by the laws of our lands, she is your mother. As is my mother.”

     

                “I don’t give a shit about your laws,” Lena hissed.

     

                “No, indeed. You would selfishly condemn thousands to die as easily as you would breathe the air of the same place you hold with such contempt,” Kara snapped, striding closer to the bed.

     

                Lena spluttered as she tore back the blankets and climbed from the bed, her cheeks feverishly pink as she bristled with indignation.

     

                “Selfish? I’m selfish? I’ve been kidnapped, manhandled, married off like a bargaining chip, and mauled and you say I’m being selfish? I never asked to come here and I never said I’d be your wife. So don’t blame me for some war that I’d never even heard of until two weeks ago.”

     

                “I don’t blame you,” Kara haughtily replied. “But your disdain for that which you know nothing about is foolish and naïve.”

     

                “Who are you to tell me how I should feel? Who are you? I mean … why the fuck would you even agree to this?”

     

                Lena’s anger trailed off into mystified disbelief. She couldn’t comprehend what would bring someone to agree to this treaty of their own free will. Was it made for her as well? Kara seemed to think it an honourable sacrifice which made Lena think that she’d readily agreed to it.

     

                Mouth flattening, Kara gave her a derisive look. “I am Kara, daughter of Zor-El and Lady of the Waterfolk. I agree to this out of a love for my people and grief for what I’ve lost to the Unseelie. You know nothing of my pain and sacrifice that would bind me in an oath with those who took so much from me, and yet, I do not hold you accountable for it when you know so little. I only ask that you keep your opinions on the matter to yourself. There are those in both Courts who look on our union unfavourably.”

     

                Hands curled into fists as she stood beside the bed, skin rippling with goosebumps as a shiver wracked her and a flicker of pain ran across her face, Lena licked her dry lips. “Well …”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, her anger spent and an air of sadness shrouding her, Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners. “It’s of little consequence to you; rest. You will stay a few days until I’m satisfied you’ll not pass from your injuries. Drink your tea and eat. I will fetch you clothes.”

     

                Lena was left speechless as Kara quickly strode from the room, vanishing upstairs. Sinking down onto the edge of the bed, a hand pressed to the bandages on her side, dried blood spotting them, Lena stared at the stone floor and suppressed a shiver as a gust of cold air blew through the place. Already the morning was brighter and the fog had dissipated, the air slightly warmer and the sound of birds sounding beyond the arches. 

     

                Kara returned a minute later with a folded pile of clothes and Lena’s rumpled and stained ones dangling from her fingertip as she held it aloft. “These are yours; I’ll have them mended for you to wear upon your return.”

     

                Nodding, Lena stared at her with a guarded expression, watching as Kara deposited her armful onto the bed. There was a linen shirt similar to the one Kara wore but in a faded sea green and soft grey leggings. Lena could see the embroidered pattern of seafoam and shells on a cuff in an ivory thread.

     

                “Your bandages need changing,” Kara off-handedly continued as she gestured to Lena.

     

                She covered the bandages with a hand and frowned. “I’ll manage.”

     

                With a quiet huff of laughter, Kara closed her eyes and swallowed before sighing heavily and giving her a grim look of exasperation. “I’ll not force you, of course, but it will be at your own detriment. If the pain becomes unbearable, I’ll fetch you medicine at your request. The tea is made from nettles and willow bark - it should help some.”

     

                Making a vague sound of acknowledgment at the back of her throat, Lena ran her fingers over the woven fabric of the bedsheets and waited as Kara lingered a moment longer, uncertain and expectant before she finally turned and left. Alone, Lena let out a pent-up breath as her shoulders sagged and she ran a hand through her hair.

     

                Reaching out for the tea, which had cooled considerably while they argued, she drained it in two gulps, the taste green and earthen as it whet her throat, and then she climbed to her feet and looked through the clothes. Pulling on the pants took no small amount of effort as she had to bend over, the pain in her stomach so great that it left her panting and sweaty, her face returning to its ashen pallor, and she winced as she dragged the shirt on afterward. Kara was right - the cuffs were a little too long and the leggings ruched slightly around her ankles. Still, she felt warmer and they were perhaps the most comfortable clothes she’d ever worn, gentle against her skin as she ran a finger over the carefully stitched motifs. 

     

                Next, Lena smoothed out her own clothes, taking in the shirt drenched with blood and the tear in the thigh of her jeans, likewise bloody, and all of it grass-stained and muddy. Her pockets were empty save for the carefully folded handkerchief she’d found herself unable to part with and Lena hesitated, running it through her fingers as her lips twitched ruefully. She slipped it into the cuff of her shirt and roughly folded her clothes before depositing them on the floor and turning to the meal.

     

                The milky eye of the fish was off-putting, as was it's still attached head and tail, yet Lena picked at it and found it delicious, her appetite slamming into her with surprise as she wolfed down the white flesh and the soft bread, finding it more heavenly than anything she’d ever tasted before. It shocked her how such simple food could taste so good and she finished everything off without even meaning to.

     

                Afterward, Lena carried the tray over to the circular table set near the open staircase, which curved around the outside of the tower, no balustrade offering support, just smooth stone steps spiraling up and around each floor. It intrigued Lena but she wasn’t brave enough to leave the floor she was on. It must have been a hundred feet across, with carved pillars reaching up to meet the vaulted ceiling in strategic places. The pillars were carved trees that rose to bare branches which turned into swirling patterns of water and Lena ran her fingers over the smooth stone as she wandered around the place.

     

                There were tapestries of water, of grey skies and the depths of the lake, of grey herons and swimming fish. They were fascinating to her, as were the books - all of which were unintelligible to her eyes as she opened open and found herself staring down at scrawling runes loping across the page in indigo ink. She shut it and returned it to the standing shelves she’d taken it from and turned to the pitcher of water beside the wide stone basin, dipping her hands in and finding it cool. She washed the blood from her hands and the dirt from beneath her fingernails, dirtying the water, and carried on her careful inspection of the place, until she grew tired and her wounds ached too much for her to ignore.

     

                Climbing back into bed, Lena stared up at the ceiling and breathed slowly, listening to the sounds of nature and finding it peaceful. She’d never known a peace quite like it and there was the unsensible part of her mind that conjured up the thought that she might disappear into the forest and never be seen again, if only to wrap herself up in such serenity for all of eternity. That was the last thought on her mind as she slipped away to sleep.

    Chapter 4

                Exhausted, Lena slept all through that first day, sprawled across the wide, comfortable bed, oblivious to the breeze that stirred the curtains, the cry of waterbirds outside and the fae woman pacing up and down the tower, pausing on the stairs each time she passed Lena’s floor. She brought her lunch and dinner, carrying the trays up from the kitchen herself, and then removing them when the food turned stale and cold. 

     

                She never so much as stirred at Kara’s presence, sleeping peacefully as the forest wended its way through her body, binding her just that little bit tighter with each inhale of the clean air. Kara wore a troubled expression whenever she stopped and checked in on her, unused to having someone in her home, unused to having someone who seemed so obstinate and jaded, with no give.  

     

                Waking late-morning, the sun already up and peering over the top of the soaring trees, cutting through the gauzy curtain at an angle as it fell across Lena’s face, she felt marginally better. Still, the stitches pulled when she pushed herself up, stretching her aching limbs out, hunger gnawing at her stomach. She couldn’t remember the last time she’d ever felt so well-rested, no headache plaguing her, no aches - other than her injuries, of course - and it took her a moment to remember why as she ran a hand over her pale face.

     

                Climbing out of bed, Lena smoothed over the grey sheets and arranged the pillows, pressing a hand to her stomach as she grimaced and then walked over to one of the open arches. Pulling a gauzy curtain back, her stomach swooped at the dizzying height of the drop down to the lake, and Lena closed her eyes as she felt the blood drain from her face, her skin clammy from the sight of so much water. 

     

                Letting the sheer curtain fall back into place, the sun shining through it and the wind making it ripple, Lena backed up a few paces and pressed a trembling hand to her brow. Her pulse fluttered in her throat and Lena was still standing there, safe away from the edge, when the sound of someone gently clearing their throat interrupted.

     

                Whirling around, hand going to her chest, and then her side as she winced, Lena stumbled as the stitches on her thigh and stomach pulled. Kara’s eyes widened a fraction and her lips parted as she took a step forward, stopping when Lena stepped back. 

     

                “Good morning,” Kara greeted her.

     

                Lena raked a hand through her hair, mouth twitching as she gave the woman an appraising look. Mid-morning sunlight seeping through the sheer curtains outlined Kara in gold, her hair sleek as it fell past her waist, while the pale shades of grey of her tunic and leggings were stark against her suntanned skin and warm glow the sun seemed to infuse her with.

     

                Nodding, Lena felt uneasiness prickle up her spine and she curled her hands into fists, watching Kara closely. She held a tray laden with bread and fruit and a pot of tea, steam curling up from the spout, and walked further onto the open floor given over to her wife. When Lena wasn’t forthcoming with a reply, Kara pressed on, seeming uncomfortable with the silence.

     

                “How do you feel?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena curtly murmured.

     

                Kara nodded, setting the tray of food down on the table, gesturing to it as she met Lena’s gaze. “Breakfast. I took the liberty of adding herbs to the tea; I thought your injuries might be bothering you.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Would you like me to tend to them?”

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lena’s lips twitched with a faint smile. “I know how to keep stitches clean.”

     

                “Oh. Okay.”

     

                Lena slowly drifted towards the table, where Kara had backed up a few steps, and she raised the lid from the pot of tea, staring into the depths as a cloud of steam brushed her cheeks, the smell earthen and a little acrid. “Willow bark?”

     

                “You’re knowledgeable on plants,” Kara noted with mild surprise. 

     

                “A little.”

     

                Lena picked up a speckled pear, perfectly soft as she held it gently, and then the bread and crumbling chunks of cheese - goat’s she assumed - before her eyes landed on a spring of lily of the valley. Sincerity and humility. The symbolism came to Lena’s mind unbidden, years of creating bouquets with intent, with meaning, allowing her to take note of the flower’s symbolism, even if that hadn’t been Kara’s intention by including the tiny white flowers on her breakfast tray.

     

                Gently caressing a drooping bud, Lena’s face softened imperceptibly and she set the pear back down before looking up. Kara was watching her with open interest, and no small amount of nervousness, and when Lena cocked her head to the side, raising her eyebrows, Kara blinked.

     

                “Was there something else?”

     

                “Would you like to eat dinner with me tonight?” Kara hesitantly asked, a flicker of doubt in her eyes as she rubbed at the back of her neck. 

     

                “Do I have a choice?”

     

                “You’ll always have a choice.”

     

                “Oh, really?”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Kara ducked her head down, the tips of her ears reddening. “That was out of my control or knowledge. I regret my naive trust in the Unseelie, but I’ll not force you to dine with me if you’d prefer privacy.”

     

                Narrowing her eyes slightly, Lena jerked her chin towards Kara. “And you’d prefer my company?”

     

                “I would prefer … that we perhaps understand each other a bit more. I admit to my ignorance of human ways, and, while I know you’ll be returning to your home soon, I’d still like the opportunity to try and be amicable while you heal.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                Shrugging nonchalantly, Kara reached up to trace the whorled pattern of a wave engraved on a slender pillar. There was a cautiousness to her, a shyness that surprised Lena as she watched her closely, the warm breeze ballooning the gauzy curtains caressing her back as she stayed across the room.

     

                “Shouldn’t I know my wife?”

     

                “Is there any point?”

     

                “Curiosity?”

     

                “What’s there to be curious about?” Lena challenged.

     

                Kara let out a soft laugh, her eyes creasing faintly at the corners. “So much. You’re half-fae. That’s interesting.”

     

                When Lena didn’t respond, Kara gently cleared her throat and raised her pale eyebrows. “And aren’t you interested in the fae?”

     

                “No,” Lena lied, her voice low as she ducked her head. “Not particularly.”

     

                “Oh. Well … we don’t have to talk at dinner either. It’s entirely up to you. You should still eat though.”

     

                Brow furrowing with bewildered amusement, Lena shook her head, taking in the pattern of the woven rug beneath her feet, the silvery fish embroidered onto it, tiny minnows and koi. She wanted to run her fingers over it, study the intricate details, follow the thread picking out the subtle tides in white and grey and pale shades of blue, enthralled by the craftsmanship of everything she’d encountered so far in this strange forest. It felt familiar, unnerving . 

     

                “Will you answer my questions?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Truthfully?”

     

                Kara gave her a wry smile, “if you could understand the old tongue, I would answer them all in that language so you’d know I wasn’t lying.”

     

                “You can’t lie?” Lena blinked in surprise.

     

                “Not in the old tongue. We use it for our binding oaths, for promises, for anything important. Like marriage vows.”

     

                “So that’s why you can’t break it off?”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “Divorce rates must be low,” Lena quipped.

     

                Kara’s brow furrowed. “Vows aren’t taken lightly. One can only be freed upon death, and when one lives millennia, that can be a lengthy marriage if chosen poorly.”

     

                “How old are you?”

     

                “Forty-six.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Lena’s face. “Oh. I was expecting you to be … two hundred years old.”

     

                “Not quite,” Kara softly laughed.

     

                “So why would someone so young choose to make a vow they’ll have to live with for thousands of years? If it’s not something you make lightly.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara hummed softly and then smiled, eyes creasing at the corners. “Ask me again at dinner.”

     

                Lena let out a short bark of laughter, Kara’s smile growing at the sound before the latter waved a hand in a vague manner. “You’re free to wander the tower - I only ask that you don’t leave. It’s not safe to wander alone, as you know.”

     

                Kara’s eyes strayed to Lena’s hidden wounds and she cleared her throat, nodding to herself as she fiddled with a pearl ring on her finger, backing away. “If you require anything, ask.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “I’ll see you at dinner.”

     

                She was left alone after that, dragging out one of the pale wooden chairs at the small table and sinking down gratefully onto it. Pulling the tray towards her, she picked up the pot of tea and poured a green stream into the thin white clay cup. A small paring knife was on the plate and Lena cut the pair into wedges and then used it to spread the crumbling cheese on the soft bread. It was studded with nuts and dried fruits and she could’ve eaten a second helping after so many missed meals but was contentedly full as she sipped her tea.

     

                After a full investigation of her quarters, Lena pulled off her borrowed clothes as she stood before the basin of tepid water and dabbed at the scabbed stitches, wiping away dried blood as she winced and hissed through her teeth. She visibly paled at the realisation that her wounds had healed inhumanly fast thought - Lena had felt the claws raking through her stomach, felt how deep it had been as her skin had been rent by the sharp points, and yet the stitches looked to be holding shallow scabs together. 

     

                Dressing again, rebandaging her wounds, she finished her snooping and then hesitated at the stairs. Making her way up first, Lena wandered through floors with sitting rooms hosting divans and ottomans, low tables and carafes of pale gold and green wines, ones with shelves full of books - some in English and some in runes that made her skin prickle with familiarity - writing desks with clipped quills and pots of deep navy ink, almost black in the glass, she stumbled upon a rather austere floor near the top, the wind howling through the arches and pillars, thin padded mats covering the stone floor in the middle of the wide space, while racks of gleaming swords - some curved, others short and leaf-shaped, other nothing more than thin needles - stood off to the side between chainmail and scalloped breastplates, racks of other weapons, everything reminiscent of fish and the water. It was beautifully made and Lena ran a hand over a polished shield and lifted a long, unstrung bow carved with motifs of shells.

     

                She walked up through the levels, marvelling at the sights and finding that the tower was much taller than her initial judgement from the shores of the lake. The air grew colder and the wind rougher with every level she passed through, and she quickly backed out of quarters that bore signs of use - a bed with slightly rumpled sheets, books scattering the desk, a wine glass with golden dregs at the bottom - making her way the last few levels to the top. It was empty save for dozens of birds gathering in nests built on the edges of the open space, at the base of pillars - and some of the smaller ones in the place where the pillars forked to uphold a ceiling that wasn’t there. Lena had never been fond of birds but recognised some of them; snowy owls, sleeping through the day, storm kestrels, a rather large albatross, pale grey and white doves cooing and a few geese and pigeons. 

     

                It was bizarre but they paid her no attention as she stood there watching them for a long moment before she walked further into the open space and looked up at the expanse of blue overhead. The sight of a few telescopes and the like, rolled up star charts and other astronomy tools made her realise that Kara must have liked to watch the night sky from there, in the open space where the forest didn’t obscure it.

     

                As she stepped back onto the stairs, used to the open sky a step beyond the edge of the tower, with no balustrade to cling to, after the steady spiralling walk up to the top, Lena stared out at the lake. Its blue surface shimmered with sunlight and she was surprised by the size of it, rivers flowing in and out, hidden corners that she hadn’t been able to see from the entrance to it, and a small figure standing in a tiny boat, paddling along the still surface of the water.

     

                Lena hadn’t seen her in her hours spent exploring, and despite her apprehension about the open air and the fearful sight of so much water below, she sank down to the stone top of the steps and curled her knees to her chest, watching the woman. It was a curious predicament to be in, staying in the home of this stranger, nothing in common and seemingly at complete odds on things, yet Lena didn’t quite know how to feel. It was peaceful and she resolved to treat it like a vacation - aside from the injuries - but still didn’t know what to make of Kara and her resolve to honour this arranged marriage they’d been forced into.

     

                Watching her for a while, the breeze strong but still quite warm, Lena eventually grew sore from sitting on the stone floor for so long and climbed to her feet, her gait a little stiff as she started back downstairs, wondering what Kara was up to. It didn’t seem like she had a job - from what Lena had seen so far, she lounged around drinking wine, milled about the tower and spent her time on the water. 

     

                Passing back through the floors, she made her way past her quarters and down to more rooms, partitions separating studies from sitting areas, a game that looked rather like chess but with polished river stones on the checkerboard replacing the usual pieces, braziers with unlit driftwood and paintings. One floor seemed like a kitchen, with long trestle tables set with rising loaves of dough, fresh fruits and worn pots and pans, clay pots of herbs and strings of garlic and sacks of potatoes. There was another room with fishing gear that Lena poked around in, finding small boats on stands, freshly sanded planks fitted in amidst old, worn ones, heavy spears and an elegant trident leaning against pillars, rods and tangles of nets, and half-crafted paddles. She wondered if perhaps she’d married a fisherman.

     

                The last floor - the ground floor - was an empty foyer that was a foot underwater with a pale, leafless tree growing up from the ground.
