Lena halted on the stairs when she realised this, out cold when Kara had brought her into the tower, wary of stepping into the water, no matter how shallow. Once she stepped off the last step, she would be surrounded by water and the thought made her shiver, her skin turning clammy and cold as she sank down onto the steps.

     

                It was mid-afternoon, the late summer day showing signs of the rapidly approaching autumn as the sky deepened slightly, the sun already sinking behind the taller trees encircling the lake, and Lena was still sitting on the steps when Kara arrived a few minutes later, her small boat scraping against the stone of the mooring point. Climbing to her feet, her stomach jolting, Lena caught her eye and watched as Kara straightened slightly as she finished wrapping the rope through a rusted loop, pulling it tight. 

     

                She gracefully hopped out, two strung fish in hand and walked through the shin-deep water, heedless to the soaked leggings clinging to her calves. Lena almost believed the water was reaching for her as she watched Kara climb onto the bottom step, the water seeming to rise with her before sloshing back down, gently rolling as it settled. Fiddling with her hands, Lena cleared her throat and looked down.

     

                “I caught us dinner,” Kara said by way of greeting, holding the trout up for her to see.

     

                Lena’s mouth thinned in response, staring at the dead eyes and turning to walk up a step. “Delicious.”

     

                “Did you eat lunch?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Then I shall arrange for dinner to be cooked now.”

     

                “Arrange with who?” Lena snorted, her snooping revealing that they were entirely alone - save for the birds.

     

                She glanced over her shoulder and found Kara nearer than she’d thought, masking a wince as she rose up another step to put more space between them. Kara’s eyebrows rose a fraction at her question.

     

                “The water.”

     

                “The water?” Lena echoed with a snort. “Is the lake a chef?”

     

                “No, but the elementals are. They’re not really sentient in the way of fae - or humans, I suppose - but they’re corporeal forms and they help out with chores, under my control.”

     

                “So … you have … water servants?”

     

                Shrugging as her brow puckered slightly, Kara hummed. “More like water … friends.”

     

                “Friends, right. And what do they get out of it?”

     

                “Well, the water is part of my lake.”

     

                “Such a privilege.”

     

                Sensing that Lena was mocking her, Kara’s cheeks turned slightly pink as she muttered, “it is the biggest lake in the Seelie Court.”

     

                “So, what is it you do all day? Just … row your boat around, fishing?”

     

                “I’m a Lady of the Water Folk,” Kara said as a confused look crossed her face.

     

                “So you’ve said,” Lena exasperatedly replied. “That means nothing to me.”

     

                Kara laughed and reached out with a hand, water drawing from the air and coalescing in the palm of her hand. Stumbling in surprise, Lena almost pitched herself out through the archway as she lost her balance, and it was only Kara’s tight grip around her arm that stopped her. Pale as a cry tore from her lips, Lena stared up at Kara with wide eyes.

     

                “Watch your step,” Kara murmured, releasing her and leaving a wet handprint in her wake.

     

                Tugging down the cuff of her tunic, haughty as she drew herself up, Lena cleared her throat, her voice clipped as she spoke. “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding as she gestured for her to continue, Kara carried on. “The Fae fall into four elements, with varying types of control. I’m of the Water Folk and hold the seat on the Council that my family has held for millennia. The Seelie Court Council votes on all important matters and we govern our domains to keep the peace.”

     

                Kara stepped off the stairs and into the kitchen, leaving Lena a step above the archway and left with the choice to follow after her or make her way back up to her room. Hesitating, Lena hurried back down and into the open kitchen, late afternoon sunlight streaming in through the open arches, the curtains tied back as vaguely humanoid-shaped bodies of water whirled around the place. 

     

                Alarm and disbelief crossed Lena’s face as she watched one take a step, turning into a ribbon of water before it reformed before a table, picking up a knife and quartering a potato. Looking at Kara, Lena raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Um …”

     

                Setting the fish down, Kara smiled, “as I was saying, as a Lady of my own holdings, it’s my job to … well, govern over them. I may leave here by myself, but there are Fae who live on my land surrounding the lake, who use the lake for fishing, for water, the land for wood and food. It’s my duty to manage them, to ensure that there are conservation efforts for the wildlife, that water levels don’t rise or fall too drastically, that there are enough soldiers to protect the borders, that everyone’s needs are met and the law is followed.”

     

                “So … you’re a politician?”

     

                “Yes. I’m a Lady.”

     

                Kara stated it so matter-of-factly as if it was all the explanation she ought to have needed, and Lena hummed dubiously. It seemed archaic to her, although, perhaps it wasn’t quite so different to how the government worked anyway, and Kara seemed gravely serious and all her talk of honour and sacrifice made Lena wonder how such positions were held here. It seemed like a burden to have to give up the freedom to choose who to marry, to sacrifice so much for people, but it must have been an esteemed position for Kara to be worthy of marrying a Princess.

     

                Not that Lena really considered herself a Princess - growing up in the foster system and a cycle of group homes with no money, no family and second-hand donations didn’t exactly scream royalty - but that was the truce Kara had found herself agreeing to. It was still somewhat jarring to find her in that place, amidst so much elegance and understated wealth, and a part of Lena still wasn’t entirely convinced she wasn’t in the midst of some psychotic breakdown.

     

                Watching apprehensively as one of the humanoid water figures started gutting the fish that Kara had caught, Lena didn’t offer any reply and Kara grabbed a bottle of wine and two glasses before touching Lena’s elbow, causing her to jump, and leading her upstairs.

     

                They were in one of the dining rooms, a long table set in the middle of the open space, on top of a large carpet embroidered with mermaids, crabs and shells, and Lena sat as far from Kara as possible, until she realised that it put her directly opposite her at the other end. Kara gave her a knowing smile and pulled the stopper from the bottle of wine, filling both of them and then climbing to her feet before she walked the length of the table and set one before Lena.

     

                Returning to her seat, Kara sank back down onto it, her movements graceful and fluid, almost effortless as she raised her glass to her lips and took a sip. Watching her for a moment, Lena hesitantly tasted her wine, reassured that it wasn’t poisoned, and was pleasantly surprised at the cool sweetness of it. The smell of peaches and freshly mown grass enticed her and she drank some more, the wine going down easily as she shrewdly eyed her wife down the length of wood.

     

                They didn’t speak much and Lena stiffened as those eerie water figures started laying the table with dishes. Once dinner was set, she hesitated, watching as Kara pulled a bowl towards herself and started spooning a salad onto her plate. Lena didn’t move and Kara met her eyes a moment later.

     

                “The crab is especially good.”

     

                Lena nodded but still didn’t make a move to serve herself as she watched Kara for a long minute. Every move she made was graceful, measured, even as she wielded the strange two-pronged fork and the small sharp knife, cutting into the white flesh of the trout. She chewed slowly and sipped her wine, and when she looked up and met Lena’s eyes again, finding her staring, Lena quickly reached for a bowl of buttered peas and scooped them onto her plate.

     

                “So, what are you so interested in knowing?” Lena asked.

     

                “Well … everything.”

     

                “Everything?”

     

                “What did you do in your world? Do they really use lightning to power things over there? Where did you grow up?”

     

                Lena let out a quiet scoff of laughter as her mouth twisted and she helped herself to some crab. “I was a florist. I made bouquets of flowers for people.”

     

                Surprise crossed Kara’s face, “oh, intriguing. I didn’t know that was a profession. So those dead flowers in your home …?”

     

                “That was my shop.”

     

                “Ah, fascinating.”

     

                “And we don’t use lightning - we use electricity. Lightning is a form of that but … it’s different for TV and lights and phones.”

     

                “I’ve heard about TV,” Kara eagerly shared, “it’s where you watch plays, isn’t it?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose slightly, Lena shrugged. “Kind of. They’re like … moving photos from a camera.” At the blank look on Kara’s face, she tried again. “Like … a painting? With real people.”

     

                “I should like to see one.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “Now, where did you grow up?”

     

                “Does it matter?” Lena asked, arching an eyebrow. “You wouldn’t know it anyway.”

     

                Floundering for a moment, mouth opening and closing, Kara’s cheeks turned pink. “I may not know much of the human world, but I take an interest in my wife’s upbringing. Especially when I was misled in believing you’d been raised here.”

     

                Quiet for a moment, taking another sip of wine and then leaning back in her seat, Lena ran her fingers over the arm of the chair. “National City. It’s a warm place, on the coast and surrounded by desert and national parks.”

     

                “Your mother took you from your Court to raise you there?”

     

                A ripple of pain crossed Lena’s face and her voice was a flat murmur as she replied. “My mother is dead.”

     

                “I understand that. She fled with you and Lillian had her killed. That is the sum of my knowledge.”

     

                “So why ask?” Lena brittly asked.

     

                “I would like to know of your life after.”

     

                Snorting as a muscle jumped in her jaw, Lena didn’t reply for a long moment. “I was in and out of foster care until I went to college. And then I opened my shop. That’s it.”

     

                “What are foster care and college?”

     

                Sighing heavily, her mouth thinning as her eyes shone with annoyance, Lena stabbed at a potato and cut it in half with a quick slice of the knife. It was small and sharp and she turned it over in her grasp.

     

                “Foster care is where they put children with no family to raise them. Sometimes you move from house to house, different families looking after you for a while before you go to the next one. And college is … school. You go to lessons and you live there until you graduate. You’re … qualified for a trade or something.”

     

                Kara stared at her for a long minute, her lips slightly parted and her face tender with surprise. “You … weren’t raised with a family?"

     

                "No, I’m an orphan. You already know that.”

     

                “But … no one claimed you as theirs?”

     

                “That’s not how it works there,” Lena snapped.

     

                “I- well …”

     

                “I don’t want to talk about it anymore.”

     

                Nodding, Kara took a sip of wine, a confused look of discontent on her face as she tipped back her glass and set it back down. After helping herself to more food, she cleared her throat.

     

                “I shall tell you what you wish to know as well then. My family were all slaughtered by the Unseelie. I was taken in by my new mother - one of the Wind Folk - and raised alongside her daughter in the mountains. When I was younger, it was prophesied that I- I would kill the one that I loved so I deigned to never fall in love. Which is why I agreed to wed you. It will never be a marriage of anything but convenience.”

     

                “Wonderful.”

     

                “But … I do hope we can be amicable.”

     

                Lena pressed her lips together and narrowed her eyes before she looked at Kara, tapping a finger on the table in idle distraction.

     

                “What happens at the changing of the leaves? That’s what Lillian said when you tried to take me back.”

     

                Kara winced at the mention of it and cleared her throat, choosing her words carefully. “As … part of the truce that was struck … it was decided that we both would spend two seasons out of the year in each other’s courts. You would spend the summer and winter months in the Seelie Court, and come autumn and spring, I would spend my time in the Unseelie Court.”

     

                Surprise crossed Lena’s face as she cocked her head to the side. “I take it that doesn’t please you?”

     

                “To live amongst those that have killed all that I loved? No, it doesn’t. But my people come first and it’s a sacrifice I willingly made for this peace.”

     

                “And what happens when I don’t show up on the first day of autumn?”

     

                Kara’s lips twitched and she looked away - long enough for Lena to slip the knife from the table and tuck it beneath the waistband of her leggings. When she shifted, she felt the tip of it dig into the skin at the top of her thigh and she leaned back in her seat.

     

                “Perhaps I will lose my head if the Queen is feeling particularly vindictive. She’s … rather mercurial though, so perhaps I shall be imprisoned for the next two centuries instead. I suppose we shall see.”

     

                “Aren’t you going to plead your case to change my mind?”

     

                Kara blinked at her, a v forming between her brows. “No. Why should I plead for my life with someone who has already made up their mind? It would be demeaning and futile. It was always with the risk that I would pay with my life that I swore my oaths to you.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena snorted. “Okay, I get it.”

     

                “Pardon?”

     

                “You’re proud. You’d rather die than swallow your pride and ask someone to help you. It would wound your ego too much.”

     

                Scoffing as the tips of her ears reddened and a rather peevish expression crossed her face, Kara reached for the decanter of wine and refilled her glass before she rose to her feet. Walking the length of the table, she paused at Lena’s side, ignoring the way she stiffened slightly, and refilled her glass for her as well.

     

                “Is it pride, or is it the intelligence to know when it is a lost cause to beg for something from someone who will never give it?” she murmured.

     

                Her voice was a low murmur and it made Lena’s skin prickle with goosebumps, her stomach clenching and her heart lurching in her chest. Reaching for her glass, Lena took a sip of wine and then turned slightly in her seat, glancing up at Kara.

     

                “And how do you know that I wouldn’t give it?”

     

                There was an unreadable flicker that passed Kara’s face like a shadow before she smiled faintly. “You have made your opinions on being here very plain. It would take a great deal to convince me you’d chosen otherwise of your own volition. Have you?”

     

                Looking down at her lap as she tracked Kara’s movement back to her seat from the corner of her eye, Lena’s lips twisted with a hint or a smile.

     

                “No, I haven’t.”

     

                Nodding slightly, Kara cleared her throat and picked up her fork again. “So, we’re in agreement that to ask would be a waste of everyone’s time.”

     

                “Perhaps. Maybe I just like to hear people beg,” Lena quipped, watching as Kara stilled, giving her a wary look as she gripped her knife and fork tightly.

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter, Kara raised her eyebrows a fraction. “You’re humorous. Remind me again, who has the bigger ego?”

     

                “Ah, well you never asked about mine.”

     

                “Indeed, the question had slipped my mind. Although, perhaps I already knew that.”

     

                “How?”

     

                “By your confidence, Lena.” Kara sipped her wine, oblivious to the stricken look on Lena’s face at the sound of her name coming from the elf’s mouth, sounding so sweet and delicate. “It takes a great deal of arrogance or foolishness to go through an ordeal such as yours with such jaded wit. I admire it, and you don’t strike me as a fool.”

     

    Shrugging nonchalantly, Lena straightened in her seat, feeling the point of the knife gouging into her thigh as she reached for more trout. 

     

                “Maybe I’ve been through enough bad things to know that snark is a good cover for fear.”

     

                “I don’t believe you’re afraid - not anymore, at least.”

     

                “You’re not very frightening,” Lena haughtily replied.

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara studied her for a moment before finishing off her wine and pushing her chair back from the table. Climbing to her feet, she kept her eyes trained on Lena.

     

                “I think perhaps I’m finished eating. You may stay as long as you please.”

     

                “I’m good,” Lena said, jerking her chair back. “I’m not really hungry anyway.”

     

                Nodding, Kara walked around the table, her pace slow and elegant before she stopped at Lena’s shoulder and hesitated, giving her a clouded look before she cocked her head to the side. Lena’s pulse jumped at her throat, and she raised her chin slightly beneath Kara’s searching gaze, her wife’s eyes piercing with none of the chill of her supposed mother’s.

     

                “One more thing,” Kara murmured before she reached out and grabbed Lena’s right arm.

     

                Lifting it, Kara reached down and brushed up the shirt, revealing a small spot of blood on Lena’s thigh and the outline of something hidden in her leggings. Lena’s cheeks pinked slightly as she swallowed and allowed Kara to pull the knife she’d stolen from the dinner table from the waistband of her leggings.

     

                Holding it up, Kara stared at the bloodstained tip of the knife and gave Lena a bewildered look before she tossed it onto the table with the remnants of their dinner. Lena tensed as she gave her a haughty look and Kara let out a gentle laugh as her brow furrowed slightly and she reached for the buckle of the slender belt at her waist, a dagger sheathed on it, undoing it and then pressing the dagger into Lena’s hands.

     

                “If you wish to protect yourself then I will arm you with something better than a dinner knife,” Kara softly murmured, the brush of her fingers warm and featherlight as she pulled back from Lena’s hands. “Although, I hope you believe that I don’t intend to do you any harm. I would defend you with my life to honour the truce.”

     

                “That’s … alarming.”

     

                Kara afforded her a small smile, almost shy, and looked down, smoothing her fingers over the thin cotton of her tunic, wrinkled where the belt had cinched it around her waist. “It’s … loyalty.”

     

                Lena’s eyebrows shot up and she let out a cold laugh of surprise, “loyalty? I don’t want your loyalty; I don’t even know you.”

     

                “It’s not about knowing. I took an oath - a binding oath - and I intend to keep it, whether you return the sentiment or not.”

     

                Falling silent as she looked down at the dagger, Lena slowly drew it from its sheath, staring down at the slightly curved blade, gleaming and thin with a keen edge. Its hilt was inlaid with pearls and turquoise and Lena turned it over as she eyed it. She moved quickly, pressing the paper-thin edge of the blade to Kara’s throat, watching as the fae woman stilled, the mild expression on her face making Lena’s stomach lurch as she realised that she’d let Lena do that. 

     

                It suddenly struck her as pathetic and her mouth dried as she drew in a shallow breath, licking her lips and adjusting her grip on the hilt. “And what if I intend to do you harm?”

     

                Lena blanched as Kara pressed into the blade, looming over her with a solemn look on her face. “I wouldn’t lift a finger against you,” Kara murmured, her voice barely above a whisper. “But you and I both know you could no more hurt me than I could hurt you - binding oath or not.”

     

                Jerking the dagger back, Lena watched as a bead of vivid red blood rolled down Kara’s throat. Reaching up to touch it, Kara stared at the drop on her fingertip before shaking it off, the drop of red splashing on the stone floor as clear water. Looking up sharply, Lena’s mouth opened and closed and she looked back down at the dagger before roughly sheathing it.

     

                “You don’t know what I would and wouldn’t do.”

     

                Reaching out, Kara eased the dagger out of its sheath again and put it into Lena’s hand, guiding it up to her throat again, where the small nick had already healed over. “It’s a curved blade with a double-edge. You want to cut with the long edge; it’ll be easier and a longer wound.”

     

                Staring up at her, feeling the spots where Kara’s fingers touched her wrist like brands, Lena swallowed thickly, her eyes wide and lips parting. Kara jerked her arm down and pressed the point against a soft spot on her stomach, pulling Lena slightly closer as she emphasised stabbing herself.

     

                “A dagger is good for close quarters. You want to go for the abdomen, away from any bones. Ideally, you’d have a blade that isn’t curved so you can pierce the internal organs. Curved blades are better for slashing.”

     

                “Why are you telling me this?” Lena hoarsely asked.

     

                She pulled her hand back and Kara willingly let go, Lena sheathing the dagger again with a slight tremor in her hand. Clasping her hands behind her back as her lips twitched regretfully, Kara stared out at the blue surface of the calm lake.

     

                “Just because I intend not to harm you, it doesn’t mean others won’t.”

     

                “I’ll be leaving tomorrow.”

     

                “That,” Kara said with a grave look over her shoulder as she made for the stairs, “is another day.”

    Chapter 5

                The next day came and went with Lena still inside the tower, her neat stitches almost fully healed, much to her surprise as she prodded them the next morning before washing them and rebinding with fresh bandages, and she spent most of the day avoiding Kara once more. It wasn’t necessarily hard, watching as Kara paddled through the low mist of the early morning in her pale paddleboat, the water like a copper penny with the orange of the rising sun. She left ripples in her wake on the glassy surface of the lake and returned a few hours later, wet and serene as she walked up through the tower.

     

                Lena had lingered on her floor, pacing, sitting, laying down, the remnants of her breakfast tray set on the table as she lingered alone. She caught glimpses of Kara walking up and down the twisting tower steps, too often for her to be occupied with business on so many floors, and eventually, Lena rose to her feet as she spied Kara walking upstairs again. 

     

                At her movement, Kara paused on the steps and gave her a mild look of politeness, the blue of the dress she’d changed into making her eyes positively piercing. She stepped off the staircase and padded barefoot inside, silk rippling like water around her legs as she hovered a few feet inside.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “Morning.”

     

                “How do you feel?”

     

                Lena’s mouth twitched with a ghost of wry amusement. “Fine.”

     

                Twisting her hands before her, Kara nodded as she ducked her head, her blonde hair like a river of gold down her back as her pointed ears parted it around her face. She was hesitant to the point of nervousness and Lena cocked her head to the side, studying her as she waited. There was no doubt in her mind that Kara would say what was on her mind; she seemed unfailingly honest, and Lena had to wonder if that was a personal trait or something all Fae were predisposed to. If Kara was to be believed, if they spoke in the old tongue it was impossible to lie.

     

                “I should like to check your wounds today,” Kara finally said, peering up with uncertainty on her delicate features. 

     

                “I should like many things,” Lena mused, narrowing her eyes, “but it doesn’t mean I’ll get them.”

     

                A shallow furrow formed between Kara’s eyebrows and she faintly sighed before nodding. “That’s true enough.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena’s mouth thinned and she sank down on the edge of the bed, hitching up her shirt. “Quickly.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Kara hesitated a moment, until Lena quirked her eyebrow and she quickly crossed over to her, hands extending before she paused and gave Lena a cautious look. “I’m well versed in healing, but should you feel uncomfortable-”

     

                “Just look so I can go home and we can both move on with our lives.”

     

                Nodding, Kara reached out and started unwrapping the bandages around Lena’s torso, her touch cool and light as it skimmed over Lena’s skin, which rippled with goosebumps as she bared her teeth against the reaction. Closing her eyes as she held her shirt up to expose her stomach, Lena tried to relax beneath Kara’s touch but her shoulders were taut and she could feel the rapid beating of her heart.

     

                “You haven’t torn your stitches, which is good. I can remove them now but you should rest here another day before I take you home.”

     

                Muscle twitching in her jaw, Lena nodded as she looked across the room, avoiding Kara’s gaze. She briefly departed to fetch her things and knelt at Lena’s feet as she assembled her tools, a stone pestle and mortar used to grind herbs into a paste in her deft hands before she plucked a tiny blade from a soft grey roll.

     

                “Lay back for me,” Kara murmured, jostling the mattress as she sat beside Lena.

     

                Following her instructions, dark hair fanning out around her as she stared up at the delicate stone ribs of the ceiling, Lena breathed shallowly. Her whole body was stiff and she jerked at Kara’s fingers splaying on her stomach, her eyes dipping to stare at the blonde, who met her eyes with a firm blue stare.

     

                “You mustn’t move.”

     

                Making a faint sound at the back of her throat, Lena watched her with a severe expression on her pale face, taking in the way Kara hunched her shoulders, her head ducked low as she quickly ran the knife under each perfect stitch and snipped the thread with precision. The lines on Lena’s stomach were faint pink but were nothing like the puckered scars that should have resulted from the injury she’d sustained and she frowned as she considered it.

     

                “I’ll need to take them out of your leg as well.”

     

                Suppressing a sigh, Lena pushed herself up, a muted ache of protest in her abdomen, and yanked the leggings down to reveal the bandage. Rising from the bed, Kara resituated herself on her knees beside Lena’s leg, one tanned hand splayed over her pale thigh as the other snipped the stitches. Arms braced behind her to prop her up, Lena bared her teeth in an uncomfortable grimace, hating the feeling of someone’s hands on her.

     

                “Can you hurry up,” she said through her teeth.

     

                Glancing up, Kara’s pace slowed and she gave Lena a searching look of concern. “Does the pain bother you?”

     

                “No, I- just be quick.”

     

                Lips pressing together as if stifling the urge to say something, Kara bent back over her work and cut the rest of them out and used the tweezers to pull the thread free. It itched and Lena curled her hands into fists in the sheets. 

     

                When Kara motioned at the bowl next, her hands manoeuvring the water into a strand that pooled between her palms, Lena froze and watched with trepidation. The water was cold as Kara lowered it onto her skin, and Lena made a sound of surprise as she watched some of the lingering redness in the lines fade. The process was repeated on her stomach before Kara hesitated, holding the stone bowl of ground herbs in her hand.

     

                “Would you prefer to do this yourself?”

     

                Lips twitching ruefully, Lena took the bowl from Kara and started smearing it over her skin, the green sweetness of the herbs almost soothing - it was reminiscent of her flower shop, even if the herbs weren’t her usual fare - and she started to rebandage herself when Kara’s fingers wrapped around her wrist. Lena stilled and swallowed as Kara pried the bandage from her hands.

     

                “You’re not doing it correctly.”

     

                “You do it too tight.”

     

                “I don’t do it too tight; the purpose of bandages is to apply pressure to the wound to prevent blood loss or bones moving.”

     

                “My bones aren’t broken and you just pulled my stitches out so I doubt I’m going to bleed to death. Suffocate , maybe.”

     

                Kara’s movements slowed as she fixed Lena with an exasperated stare before she continued to wrap the bandages around her stomach. There was a barely perceptible loosening of the bandages though and Lena fought hard to hide a smug smile as she stood before Kara, unnervingly close, and breathed in the smell of water and salt that clung to her, even though Lena was sure the lake was freshwater. Once the one-sided awkwardness of being tended to subsided, Lena pulled her leggings up and arched an eyebrow at Kara, who rinsed her hands in the bowl of cool water and wiped them on a rag.

     

                “Satisfied?”

     

                “Moderately,” Kara murmured in agreement.

     

                Snorting, Lena sank back down onto the bed and Kara tilted her head to the side, watching her for a moment. “If you’ve grown tired of your quarters, I thought you might like to go out onto the lake so-”

     

                “No.”

     

                Lena’s blurted response was quick and sharp and Kara blinked, taken aback as her expression clouded. She bristled slightly as if the instant dismissal wounded her feelings. “Well …”

     

                “I don’t like water,” Lena tightly confessed.

     

                Mouth opening and closing, surprised anew, Kara’s mouth curled upwards at the corners as her eyebrows drew together. “You don’t like the water? And what about it offends you so much?”

     

                Lena’s pale cheeks flushed and she rose to her feet, turning her back on Kara as she walked across the room. She didn’t like the teasing edge in Kara’s voice and her knuckles whitened as she gripped the back of a chair, teeth grinding together. Feeling the warmth in her cheeks, Lena felt it radiate all the way up to the gentle points of her ears.

     

                “Ah,” Kara awkwardly murmured. “I see; you’re afraid of it.”

     

                “You don’t see anything,” Lena snapped, whirling around with a hard look on her face. “Leave me alone. Or better yet, take me home. I don’t want to stay here anymore.”

     

                Sobering up as she clasped her hands in front of her, a small pout on her lips as she bowed her head, masking her hurt feelings, Kara let out a soft sigh. “You really ought to-”

     

                “Take me home. Now.”

     

                “This evening,” Kara relented. “You should rest a while longer. I’ll fetch lunch for you.”

     

                Nodding, Lena was silent as she dragged a chair out and heavily sank down onto it, running a hand over her face. Kara walked over to her and removed the breakfast tray and replaced it with lunch. Staring at the small soup with open mussels resting in the creamy broth, Lena didn’t manage more than a few mouthfuls and abandoned the rest of it in favour of standing a few feet from the edge of the open archway.

     

                She wasn’t afraid of heights but the sight of so much blue was terrifying and she had to curl her hands into fists as she let the light breeze cool the clammy sweat on her face. Any closer and she would have been petrified by the thought of pitching out of the tower and falling into so much water.

     

                The rest of the day dragged by, water birds crying out as they swooped down, snagging little silver fish from the shoal darting around, Lena flipping through one of the books in her quarters, fascinated by the paragraphs of glyphs scrawled on some of the pages, the little watercolour paintings of sea creatures, of fae and birds and trees. She couldn’t read most of it but still read over every page, the hours passing by until Kara reappeared once more.

     

                “You should eat before we travel.”

     

                Uncurling from her huddled position on the chaise, Lena abandoned her book and climbed to her feet, following Kara down to the dining room they’d eaten in last night. Neither of them spoke and Lena forced herself to eat, knowing that she would never find anything equal to the simple freshness of it once she was back home. Perhaps that thought made her savour the taste of the fresh salmon, seared to perfection, the salad of alfalfa, arugula and other wild herbs better than any other salad she’d ever tasted, and the wine - Lena wanted to sneak a bottle home with her and stretch it out over years, the small drops of bottled sunshine a reminder of her time there.

     

                Eventually, they finished and there was no need to delay. Kara handed Lena the patched clothes she’d come here in and Lena went upstairs to change, leaving the borrowed shirt and leggings in a folded pile on the table. She was itching for a bath and a coffee but there was almost a note of sadness to the moment as she looked around the room, marvelling at how beautiful the place was. No matter how much she wished to go home, she couldn’t deny that it was a peaceful place to stay. She’d never felt so well-rested, so serene and content. If things had been different, Lena imagined she would have liked to grow up there. 

     

                Things quickly took a sharp turn as Lena trailed Kara downstairs and then faltered at the sight of the water-flooded ground floor. It wasn’t so deep that she wouldn’t be able to walk, so shallow that it wouldn’t have even hit her knees, but Lena’s breath caught in her throat and she struggled to clear it. Kara turned to look up at her, the bottom few inches of her dress floating around her in the water before water bled into the silk and it elegantly sank.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                “I- it’s the water,” Lena said, her voice breathless and wavering, staring out at the deep blue water stretching out all around them from the bottom of the tower. 

     

                There was no distinct point where the tower ended and the lake began, the water overtaking the bottom floor to make it seem as if the tower just sprouted right through the surface of the lake. Kara rose up a step, extending a hand.

     

                “I’ll not let you come to harm. I carried you across while you were injured; I can do the same again.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena’s face rippled with strained amusement and she shook her dark head, closing her eyes. She looked pale and clammy and Kara stared at her for a long moment, unsure.

     

                “What would you have me do? Shall I fetch my boat?”

     

                “No. Just … give me a second.”

     

                Obliging, Kara retreated back down into the water and Lena pressed her palm to her brow, breathing slowly. Her heart hammered in her chest and she could feel the unbalanced shakiness as she lingered a few feet above the water. Lena had never learned how to swim, could just about stomach being in a hot tub, but nothing bigger than that, and to be stranded in the middle of so much water was a personal nightmare. If she didn’t force herself to leave, she would stay in that tower forever. It was tempting to stay, but she couldn’t cower there forever as the wife of some stranger.

     

                She removed her shoes and forced herself down the last few steps and into the water, her teeth bared as she gingerly stepped in. The water was cold and the stone slippery in patches where algae covered the floor. Lena’s entire body tensed, hairs standing on end, and she shuddered at the feeling of water seeping into the cuffs of her pants. 

     

                Kara reached out a hand again, taking Lena’s with surprising tenderness, her rough palm encircling Lena’s fingers as she squeezed gently. Swallowing, her throat dry and tight, Lena didn’t even remind herself to snatch her hand away, and let Kara draw her forward.

     

                The water warmed as she adjusted to the cool temperature, and the smell of the water filled her nose as she breathed shakily, crossing through to the open archway pointing towards land. It seemed impossibly distant, like they would never be able to walk to shore, but Kara guided her out into the first stepping stone, submerged a few inches underwater.

     

                Lena’s jaw was tightly clenched and she had to stop herself from trembling, embarrassed by such a childish fear that she’d never overcome, not even after being forced to take swimming lessons, to no avail. She’d almost drowned herself with the panic that left her floundering in the deep end of a public pool after a foster parent had pushed her in, thinking a physical approach would make her learn faster. Still, she made it across the first stepping stone and told herself not to look down at the deep, murky water in the gap between her and the next one.

     

                Kara didn’t drop her hand once, slowly leading Lena across each stepping stone with quiet understanding. Lena expected mockery from someone who was so in love with the water, seemed to revel in it and its powers, but Kara was patient and gentle. And when Lena stumbled between one stepping stone and the next, her leg plunging down into the gap as she blanched, her face a ghastly grey as a cry escaped her and her eyes went wide with terror, Kara’s arm encircled Lena’s waist and lifted her with ease.

     

                One leg soaked to the knee, shaking all over, Lena clutched at the silk of Kara’s blue dress and breathed raggedly for a moment. Her eyes were squeezed shut and she could feel Kara’s warm breath on her cheek, the two of them standing almost nose-to-nose. She was oblivious to the way she clung to Kara, bunching the fabric over her stomach in a white-knuckled fist, the feel of her hard muscles lost on Lena. It took her a long minute to let go, and only then at Kara’s murmured urging in response to her breathless pleas.

     

                “Don’t- don’t let go. Please, don’t-”

     

                “I have you. I won’t let you fall.”

                

                Swallowing thickly, her eyes still shut, Lena slowly forced herself to let go. It was a long, tense moment but Kara didn’t remove her arm from Lena’s waist until she was sure she was steady on her own feet. She still didn’t drop her hand.

     

                It took a lot longer than it should have to cross the stepping stones back to shore, and Lena missed Kara’s anxious looks at the lengthening shadows and setting sun as she focused on each step. By the time they reached the shore, Lena was damp with sweat and shaking all over, and she waded through the shallows, foam the white of old fishbones creating a scum around the edge of the lake as her feet sank into soft mud. The sensation made her shudder, the silt and slime in the pewter water kicked up by her footsteps.

     

                Lena wanted to flop down on the grassy banks the moment she was safely on it, exhausted and sore from the tension in her muscles, which had quickly gone slack with relief, but Kara kept ahold of her hand and towed her onwards into the trees. The shade from the dense canopy darkened the path completely and the air was warm, perfumed with the scent of flowers while a constant droning of bluebottles accompanied them in the green gloom.

     

                Once they were just out of sight of the lake, Kara let out a trilling whistle, like birdsong, and they waited. It wasn’t long before that grey dappled horse they’d ridden on last time appeared, stepping over clover and wild perennials and tossing its head once it stopped beside Kara. She gave the bridge of his nose a tender stroke and then hesitated.

     

                “May I?”

     

                Lena held her arms up to allow Kara to grasp her waist and sit her on the high back of the stallion as he twitched his snowy tail, swatting gnats as they congregated in the shadowed dampness of the forest. Gracefully pulling herself up behind Lena, Kara grasped a fistful of its mane and nudged the horse onwards at a quick pace, hooves thundering across the forest floor as they shot off.

     

                Much to her surprise, Lena was growing used to the breakneck races through the forest, only a little uneasy at the speed at which the stallion expertly dodged tree trunks that seemed to appear before them before she could even comprehend they were there. The thought that the horse would trip on a snaking root and snap a leg, flinging the two women from its back, never quite left Lena but she no longer felt completely out of her depth. Still, she hadn’t ridden on a horse anywhere near enough to not be sore when they dismounted what felt like hours later.

     

                The forest was quiet now, a prelude to dusk as the shadows thickened and pooled in the hollows, a bluish tint to the grove they stopped in as the sun sank and the lingering light of it kept the dark at bay for a moment longer. Kara swung down off the horse first, patting its nose affectionately to steady it before she helped lower Lena to the ground. Stumbling slightly, she was steadied with a gentle touch and then Kara jerked her chin toward the tree that Lena had ventured through.

     

                “You will need to leave by your own power; it’s always better that way.”

     

                Nodding as she stared at the rowan, Lena swallowed and turned to Kara, a strange look on her face, wary yet soft with wry amusement. She rubbed her palms together and pursed her lips, green eyes bright as she looked up at Kara, ethereal and like a dream in the midst of the darkening forest. 

     

                “This is goodbye then,” Lena said with a small smile curling her lips. “Thank you for your help. And sorry for intruding.”

     

                Kara laughed softly, the sound making Lena’s arms ripple with goosebumps, intimately close in the small clearing where the trees pressed in all around. She felt like they were the only two in the entire forest and her stomach clenched. Eyes creasing faintly at the corners, Kara tilted her head to the side as her blonde eyebrows rose a fraction.

     

                “My wife is welcome any time she pleases.”

     

                “For both of our sakes, let’s hope we never see each other again,” she replied with wan amusement, giving Kara a thin smile.

     

                But a shiver ran down Lena’s spine, from the nape of her neck to her lower back. Suddenly she had an ominous premonition as to the feeling that things were far from settled and over. She couldn’t quite place why she felt that way, only that she felt certain that this wasn’t the last she’d see of Kara.

     

                Their goodbye was drawn out a moment longer, both of them unsure of how to behave around each other, as indifferent and awkward as they were. Kara’s impassive face betrayed nothing but there was a restlessness to her as she clenched and unclenched her hands, looking around before she cleared her throat.

     

                “You must go. It’s getting late and the forest …”

     

                Lena touched a hand to her stomach and nodded before turning to the rowan tree. She glanced back over her shoulder, “how do I- last time I couldn’t control it. What if I can’t-”

     

                “Try,” Kara softly ordered her, jerking her chin towards the tree. “It’s too dangerous for you to waste time.”

     

                Biting back a disgruntled comment, Lena pressed a hand to the bark and closed her eyes, trying to feel that strange sensation from last time, as if the tree was talking to her. She was silent, her palms pressed firmly against the trunk, her eyes screwed shut and a pucker of concentration between her eyebrows as she grit her teeth. After a moment, she let out a frustrated sigh.

     

                “I don’t think-”

     

                She trailed off as she opened her eyes, blinking at the sudden light filtering through the sparse, dry woods of National City’s foothills. It was pre-dawn and at the sharp exhale of surprise, Lena’s breath fogged before her. It was cold . She hugged her arms around herself, a troubled look on her face, and looked around. She was alone, of course, the fae forest gone and Kara with it, and it took Lena a moment to orient herself back in her own world.

     

                A headache blossomed at her temples and Lena blinked, running a shaking hand over her face. After a minute, she caught sight of something half-hidden beneath fallen leaves and dirt and dug out her backpack from when she’d hiked to the spot she was in now. Everything was still there, her phone flat and her purse untouched, and Lena picked it up and put it on her shoulder, wishing she wasn’t damp and wearing something warmer as a brisk wind rushed through the skeletal trees.

     

                Making her way back to the trail, she encountered no one as she walked back down. She was pink-cheeked from the cold and slightly breathless when she reached the main road, finding herself stranded. Lena didn’t know when the next bus would be and she walked along the edge of the road, suddenly sagging beneath the heaviness of being back in her world. Her senses seemed heightened and she could taste the exhaust fumes from cars that had passed by and smell the heavy pollution of the city on the wind. Gone was the smell of dew and flowers and Lena’s eyes smarted at the dusty breeze on her face.

     

                A few cars passed by before one of them stopped, taking pity on her as the grey sky opened and rain lashed at her face, morning fully breaking as she walked, and Lena didn’t even hesitate to climb into the passenger seat. A middle-aged woman cranked the heating and told her she could take her as far as the bay and Lena was breathlessly grateful as she shivered, evading questions about what she was doing walking through the foothills in the middle of winter. Lena was too afraid to ask what the date was, what year it was, feeling pale and hollow as it became clear that it was no longer the late summer she’d left behind.

     

                Dropped off just before the bridge, Lena huddled in a bus shelter and scraped together enough change to buy herself a ticket into Downtown, sitting at the back of the bus and trying to read the date on the front of the newspaper the old man across from her was reading. She got off three blocks from her home and walked through the drizzle with the weary anticipation of a hot shower and her bed, worrying about the state of her shop and the orders she’d missed. 

     

                When she finally arrived out front, it took her a moment to realise that it was her shop. Or rather, it had been. Gone was the sign above the awning and the door and the windows were boarded up with clapboard and covered with old newspapers, yellows and rumpled. The front door was locked and sealed with tape, an eviction notice stuck to the front and a larger Under Offer sign over the top. Lena’s chest constricted and she struggled to breathe for a moment, her breaths shallow and strangled as she rummaged in her bag for her keys, hands shaking too badly to even fit it in the lock.

     

                “Fuck, fuck, fuck.”

     

                The door got stuck as she jerked it open and the old bell chimed in the dusty stillness. A breathless sob escaped her as she took in the trashed interior. Cracked buckets strewn around the place, graffiti on the walls and litter and leaves covering the floor. The glass in one of the boarded-up windows had been broken and she stepped over cigarette butts, empty beer cans and chip packets and looked around with horror.

     

                Her shop was gone.

     

                Taking the steps two at a time as she ran upstairs, Lena was positively grey as she took in her smashed furniture, the ransacked cupboards and charred spots on the floor that spoke of fires set by rebellious teenagers hanging out there, a few half-smoked joints littering the place with empty pizza boxes and a bottle of vodka that still had a few inches left in it. 

     

                She wanted to cry. She might have as well, time seeming suspended indefinitely until it was almost noon and Lena hadn’t moved from where she’d sank to her knees. Climbing to her feet, she found the electricity shut off, of course, and the water and gas too, which left any hopes of a shower shattered. And Lena wouldn’t have slept on the bare mattress of her bed for anything, not wanting to think about who had been on it while she’d been gone.

     

                It took her a while to climb to her feet and try and take stock of things. Firstly, Lena needed to make a few calls, her flat phone meaning she had to charge it first, which required somewhere with power. She had enough cash in her purse to buy a charging cable at a convenience store and make it to the library, plugging it into the clunky computer and doing some research while she waited for it to charge. It was the middle of January - six months after Lena had left, gone in a matter of days in that other realm.

     

                Her phone was out of credit but she managed to use one of the free phones in a booth at the front of the library. Her first phone call was to the bank, where a wary woman explained that her accounts had been frozen. It took half a dozen more phone calls to get to the bottom of it all; her bank accounts were overdrawn, with each payment on her business loan sapping at her savings until there was nothing left, the bank had seized her shop once the payments had stopped, her loans had accrued interest and she’d been declared bankrupt. Not only that, but a quick search revealed a small line in the local newspaper about her being missing.

     

                Lena wanted to break the computer, wanted to cry and punch a wall and shout at someone. How had her quiet life she’d worked so hard to build, despite coming from nothing and having no one, gotten so completely fucked in what was a matter of days in her mind? A mere handful of days to her. She found it hard to breathe as she sat in the library, hands grasping fistfuls of her hair in an agonised manner as she hunched over the computer keyboard. Feeling half-delirious, as if she was slowly going insane by everything that was happening, unable to stop considering that perhaps she was losing her mind to vivid hallucinations as a result of her years of trauma. 

     

                It wasn’t an unreasonable assumption, and more reasonable than she’d been taken by Fae to some other world that had slowly been consuming her, but Lena knew that none of it was a hallucination. Although she failed to consider that even the most clinically insane person might have thought they were perfectly sound of mind from their perspective, she just knew that those missing months weren’t born out of a dissociative period. Nor did Lena consider herself creative or imaginative enough to have thought up another world in such detail. But the reality was harder to swallow than the thought of being mad because where did that leave her now?

     

                Homeless, broke and unemployed. Not to mention that Lena was technically missing, perhaps some cold case at a local precinct that had pushed her file to the bottom of the pile when no information was forthcoming. Would it help to reach out to the police? She had her social security number and her ID was in her purse, but what would she even tell them? She’d been kidnapped by creatures from myths and legends, whisked away to a forest as a Princess? If she didn’t consider herself clinically insane now, she knew they’d hospitalise her if she came out with that story.

     

                Eventually, she forced herself to her feet and out of the library, the hours slipping away to nothing and the sun already setting over the city. Hungry from a fruitless day of trying to piece together what she’d missed, Lena bought pizza and sat in a nearby park, the thick grease almost making her gag at hour awful it tasted after the fare she’d been on in the forest. She could almost imagine the forest whispering at the back of her mind, reminding her of how much better it had been there - cleaner, unpolluted, fresher and beautiful. The memory of the taste of the wine made Lena’s throat constrict and she felt the prickling urge to return. 

     

                It was like a faint ringing in her ears, calling her until she shook her head a moment later and came back to herself, sitting on a park bench in the noise of the city. Lena shivered at the uneasy feeling knotting her stomach as she choked down her pizza and shivered in the cold. The wind was bitter and she didn’t have a jacket, and she knew the park was no place to sleep - she’d run away more than once in her teenage years and knew the kinds of things that happened there in the middle of the night - so Lena reluctantly went to try her hand at a shelter she’d occasionally frequented as a stubborn seventeen-year-old who wouldn’t stay in foster homes. 

     

                It was a fifteen-minute walk and she queued with the other women and girls to claim a spot, her breath fogging before her as night fully crept over the city. Inside it was dismal but warm and she managed to get a bed for the night in a crowded room, hauling herself up onto the top bunk and staring at the ceiling as she lay on her back on the thin mattress, using her dirty backpack as a pillow. Sleep was hard to come by with the sound of people coughing, shifting, babies crying and the bunk beds creaking with each movement. It was something Lena thought she’d left behind, a part of her old life that she’d never return to with the help of her business degree and her little florist with the well-loved apartment above it. 

     

                The day she’d signed the lease to the place was the happiest of her life, and when the owner had put it up for sale and accepted her offer to buy it, she’d felt confident she’d be comfortable. Her business, while not particularly big, did well with constant clientele, the need for flowers for all manner of events leaving her busy with the endless orders. And Lena had loved what she did, but now her shop was gone, trashed and empty, and the dread that spread throughout her body left her cold and numb.

     

                Dawn came with the sinking feeling of helplessness and Lena skipped the breakfast that was offered in favour of the cold city air, her skin pimpling at the intense cold as she quickly walked away from the shelter. The thing was, Lena didn’t have friends. She’d had Eve, a good employee for the short duration she’d been there, and the delivery guys with her supply of flowers, but she was relatively isolated by her own design. The occasional fling had amounted to nothing but it had never bothered Lena - she was still young and she was in no rush to saddle herself with someone else’s problems when she had so much baggage she’d yet to fully deal with herself. 

     

                The longer she wandered, the more prominent the nagging feeling that had plagued her last time she’d returned, a sensation so strong that it made Lena restless and agitated. She must have looked strung out or drunk to the pedestrians passing by as she fiddled with her fingers, murmuring to herself, running a hand over her weary face and walking block after block. Lena flinched at times, catching snatches of trees at a corner park, seeing it for something else for a brief moment - something better - and almost walking into a blonde woman, seeing Kara’s face until she blinked rapidly and the features melted into someone rather ordinary and plain.

     

                Lacing her hands behind her neck, Lena blew the air out of her lungs as she lingered in the doorway of a Starbucks, eyes closed and her teeth clenched as she agonised over what to do. How could she reclaim her identity without answering a thousand questions, how was she supposed to get a job or an apartment with bankruptcy hanging over her head? How was she supposed to adjust back to a normal life that didn’t exist when every part of her was itching to go back there. That was it, the true fear inside her that twisted her stomach; Lena could feel the hooks of the forest deep in her skin, the feeling of something eldritch and enticing wending through her blood, calling to the parts of her that weren’t human. She could feel it right up to the tips of her ever so slightly pointed ears.

     

                But that was out of the question, a solution that she could only resign herself to if she was truly desperate. Lena wasn’t quite there yet, so early in the day that it seemed like she had enough time to figure things out before it grew really bad. But as she walked and grew hungry, her last five-dollar bill stretching to a meal at Big Belly Burger, where she lingered well past lunchtime, occupying a table until she was politely asked to leave by an employee who looked mildly disgusted, misjudging her for a homeless person, which was exactly what she was. It was something Lena hadn’t dealt with for years and she felt her cheeks burn as she shoved her trash in the bin and stalked out, eyes stinging with tears at how lost she felt. 

     

                Lena had to go back to that shelter again for the night, her sleep ruined by uneasy dreams of walking through glades she knew she’d never seen before but could only have existed in one place. In her dreams, she caught sight of golden hair and blue dresses disappearing behind trunks, always slightly out of reach as she tried to catch up, the smell of salt and water enticing her even amidst all the greenery. When she woke, it was to an ache in her chest.

     

                For four days Lena existed in some sort of purgatory, her days following the same helpless routine of waking in the shelter, accepting the meals given to her now that she was out of cash, and trying to formulate a plan. There wasn’t much she could think of, all of her phone calls for free legal advice were rather pointless, and she spent hours sitting in various parks, letting the trees and sparse winter plants inspire some love for her old home. 

     

                Each day, she felt that pull back to the forest just that little bit stronger. Her days spent there, drinking the water, eating the food, breathing in the air and the pollen and the touch and feel of the place, bound her tightly to the forest. It became so bad, that yearning that grew so overwhelming that it hurt to breathe, that Lena couldn’t even think straight. It was like her mind had been consumed by it, ravaged by some inexplicable thing that had gotten inside her. It felt invasive but it was so compelling that she sometimes found herself pressing a hand against the rough bark of an elm, a birch, a yew without even knowing she’d walked over to it. Yet, she remained firmly in her world, which was both a relief and a disappointment.

     

                It wasn’t until the fifth night that Lena finally broke. Wearing the same clothes she’d stumbled out of her world and back into it again in, she waited until it got dark and made her way back to the shelter, joining the end of the queue as she buried her hands in her pockets and shivered in the cool air. The last few days had taken their toll on her, her face thinner and exhausted, dark circles under her eyes and a defeated slump to her shoulders. Lena looked awful and she was keeping it together by a thread as she tried to figure out what to do.

     

                The last straw was when the middle-aged woman emerged from the shelter ten minutes after Lena had joined the queue, illuminated by the harsh white light spilling out of the place as she clutched a clipboard in hand and shouted down the line of women and children waiting.

     

                “We’re full. We don’t have any beds left for tonight.”

     

                A small sound of objection escaped Lena as her face fell and her stomach lurched. She hurriedly stepped out of line, almost tripping over herself in her haste. “I- but … I don’t have anywhere else to go.”

     

                The woman gave her a pitying look as her mouth thinned with regret. “I’m sorry. You should try the one over on Fifth Avenue.”

     

                Blinking back tears, Lena couldn’t even reply around the tightness in her throat as she turned away. She could feel the pressure in her chest, painful and constricting as she drew in a shallow, ragged breath, and she rubbed at her sternum as she stumbled away.

     

                “No, no, no,” she whispered to herself, her eyes filling with tears now, unable to keep them at bay as she grit her teeth.

     

                The shelter had been the only thing offering her any chance of sorting her shit out and Lena couldn’t stop herself from screaming a curse as she kicked at a trash can. The thud drew attention and she dug the heels of her palms into her eyes as she bowed over, aware of the wide berth people were giving her.

     

                Straightening up after a long minute, she wiped her face on her dirty T-shirt and sniffed, looking around. She was hungry and it was getting late, too late to be on the streets, and Lena had nowhere to go and nothing to eat. Rifling through her backpack for anything and coming up empty-handed, she patted down her pockets and stiffened.

     

                Pulling out a creased handkerchief, Lena swallowed thickly as she ran a hand over the fine quality of the fabric. She wanted to cry all over again as she clenched it tightly in her fist, knowing she was out of options. 

     

                Would it be so bad to go back there? Realistically, she knew that Kara was far from awful, but Lena didn’t know her and, more importantly, didn’t want to be her wife. Going back meant honouring an oath she’d never agreed to in the first place and the thought made her sick with worry, the idea of living with a stranger she’d been bound to, the two of them existing in some awkward state of forced politeness as they tried to avoid each other while honouring the agreement sounding like the last thing Lena wanted to do.

     

                But standing on the street with no other option, Lena knew it was only the second last thing she wanted to do. What was worse; living on the streets, begging for food and knowing from experience how difficult it would be to get back on her feet, or returning to a place she’d never wanted to go back to, living with a woman she barely knew - her wife - and being afforded some sort of wealth and comfort as a supposed Princess. It didn’t seem like a difficult choice to make but Lena cursed her bad luck as she stood on the sidewalk, at a loss for any other alternatives.

     

                In the end, it really was the only other option, and she could swear her body was calling out to the other place. Suddenly, it was as if her mind wasn’t her own, whispering to her to go, to go home, back to a pace she’d been foolish to ever leave. How could this dismal city, foul and cramped, ever compare to the wild beauty of the old forest? It seemed laughable to even consider coming back to her sad life. 

     

                The more she thought about bending her pride, the more enticing it sounded. It was the safest option, despite a somewhat tentative truce between an ancient civil war, and Lena shivered at the uneasy memory of that premonished feeling that she would see Kara again. It was as if the very forest had been laughing at her naïvety to ever think she could escape its clutches again; some part of her had known she would be back.

     

                It took almost an hour of asking for enough money to catch the bus back over the bridge and as far as it could take her out to the foothills. Desperate for any sort of answer to her problem, Lena was intent on making it back to the forest as soon as possible, and the national park she’d hiked through was the only way she knew how to do that. She was new to all of this and didn’t understand a single bit of it, but if it could get her back there, she’d be able to track down Kara again, she was sure of it.

     

                The thought of giant wolves and other deadly creatures claimed by the old forest was lost on her as she rode at the back of the bus. Her only real fear was that too much time had passed again - could it have been decades? Longer? What would happen then? What if she’d instigated war by not showing up at the Unseelie Court, or what if Kara’s vow had somehow been broken? Would she turn Lena away if she had no obligation to help? She didn’t seem so cold and unfeeling but Lena knew she was acting out of her perceived duty.

     

                Her mind was consumed with anxious thoughts of her future, and she was too distracted by them to fear the man that picked her up when she flagged him down, too preoccupied as she recklessly hiked through the pitch black of the winter night, the temperature drastically colder in the hills. All Lena could think about was that damn forest and the Lady of the Water Folk with her blue eyes and infuriating coolness. 

     

                But hours later her worry was for nothing, reaching that clearing with the hollowed rowan tree, drawn there by some inexplicable internal compass, and pressing her palm against the bark as a violet dawn rose over National City. 

     

                She pitched forward, a ringing in her ears and a tingling in her fingertips, eyes closed as she let herself fall through one world and the next. 

     

                Her eyes stayed shut for a moment. Nothing moved. The hour felt late, stretching out. It was palpably warm, it was summer, and when Lena opened her eyes it was like no time had passed at all.  Walking away from the tree in her blue dress, blonde hair rippling down her back, was Kara as Lena had left her. And at the sound of the disturbance coming from the rowan tree, she turned, unabashed shock on her face.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “Kara,” Lena breathlessly gasped, staggering forward and then promptly passing out on the forest floor.

    Chapter 6

                Blinking slowly, Lena stared up at the dusk-washed pale stone bones of the ribbed ceiling and felt shockingly empty, yet serene, as she got her bearings. Turning her head to the side on the soft pile of pillows, the warmth of summer leaving her slightly clammy beneath the blankets, soft linen smelling of salt and lavender as she gripped the edge and pushed them down. Kara was sitting in one of the pale wooden dining chairs dragged over from the table, still wearing her blue dress and looking like she hadn’t moved in hours as she stared at Lena, a shadow in the blue tint of twilight.

     

                “Is this some attempt at humour that’s lost on me?” she asked once Lena met her eyes.

     

                Rubbing at her forehead as she slowly pushed herself up, Lena closed her eyes and made a low sound of annoyance at the back of her throat. “And what part of this is funny?”

     

                “You’re like a released pigeon who keeps returning,” Kara replied, a brooding look of frustration clouding her face. “I had imagined that was the last I’d ever see of you, and get no more than a dozen feet from that infernal ash and you’re back. Yet again .”

     

                Lena scoffed as tears pricked her eyes and she flopped back down onto the pillows. “I thought I was always welcome back here. Or was that just you trying to be polite before you booted me out of the forest?”

     

                “Of course it was politeness, although I couldn’t in good conscience turn you away if you ever found your way back. I only imagined it might be years later, not seconds.”

     

                “It was days for me. And … it’s been months since I- everything was gone .”

     

                Kara’s face softened with pained understanding. “Ah. So, I was a desperate last resort.”

     

                “Obviously,” Lena snapped, pinching the bridge of her nose. “I didn’t have anywhere else to go. I-”

     

                “Is it money you’ve come to ask for?”

     

                “No, I-”

     

                “As my wife, you’re entitled to a regular stipend but-”

     

                “I don’t want your money!”

     

                Kara cut off and her brow creased with confusion as she leaned forward in her chair, gripping the underside of the seat as she cocked her head to the side. “Then I’m afraid I don’t understand what it is you expect from me.”

     

                Opening and closing her mouth, Lena closed her eyes and exhaled sharply, her cheeks colouring as she tried to swallow her pride. “My shop is gone. My home is gone. I … would be bankrupt and I’m missing . I don’t- I don’t know if I can go back .”

     

                “Oh,” Kara murmured, perplexed, before her face went slack and she gave Lena a piercing stare. “Oh. You wish to stay.”

     

                “I-” Lena started before faltering, “no, not particularly, but I don’t have anywhere else to go.”

     

                “No friend who might take you in?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “And no family, of course.”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Ah. Then I’m bound to my duty; I won’t turn you away, but you must be very sure of your decision. If you leave, you can’t return when you feel like it - we will most likely be in a civil war, and I won’t enjoy you complicating an already complicated situation. If you stay, you must prepare yourself to leave for the Unseelie Court in a few weeks. Autumn is near and we’ll both be obligated to spend the season there.”

     

                Digging the heels of her palms into her eyes, Lena let out a scathing exhale, a muscle twitching in her jaw at her frustration, at her confusion and disbelief that this was all happening to her. “Fine,” she bitingly replied through clenched teeth.

     

                “I won’t tolerate any affront.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena pushed the blankets fully back and scooted over to the edge of the bed, the stone cold beneath her bare feet as she rose to her full height, which still wasn’t quite as tall as Kara’s regal bearing as she stared her down. A faint smile twitched Lena’s lips and her eyes were sharp with annoyance.

     

                “Then don’t.”

     

                Disgruntlement clouded Kara’s face as she pursed her lips, looking a little sour. “I expect you to listen when I give you rules.”

     

                Lena laughed in her face, surprise making her eyebrows rise a fraction and her mouth wing up at the corners with amusement. “Are you fucking kidding me?”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena turned around and started making the bed, straightening out the linen sheets as she bristled with anger. A warm hand grabbed her arm and pulled her around as Lena tore herself free, face twisting with anger as she quietly snarled.

     

                “Get your hands off me.”

     

                Backing up, a flicker of panic crossing her face, Kara blinked. “I don’t mean that I expect you to obey me. Only … if I tell you to stay out of the forest at night, it’s for good reason.”

     

                “I’m not likely to leave this tower,” Lena snapped back, “or have you forgotten that we’re surrounded by water? Staying here means I’m going to be a prisoner .”

     

                Shifting uncomfortably, Kara opened her mouth but didn’t speak, her brow furrowing together as her mouth turned down at the corners. “Well … you’re not actually a prisoner,” she hedged.

     

                “Just in all but name. How lovely.”

     

                “I’m doing you a favour,” Kara bristled. “I could just as easily send you back and leave you there to sort through your mess yourself. It’s not my responsibility to care for you if you’re not here. This is my tower.”

     

                “As if I could forget. This is the last place I would want to be if I had any other choice.”

     

                “I’ve given you a choice; you rejected my offer of money.”

     

                “It’s not that easy,” Lena sharply replied, “there’s the law, there’s the government and police and banks. People I’d have to sort everything out with - to open a business, to get a new house, a new loan for a shop, register a new business. I don’t have anywhere else to go. It’s not as simple as building a house in a fucking forest and foraging for berries every day. Even if it was, I wouldn’t accept anything from you anyway. I’m not after a handout.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara rolled her eyes. “Ah, it’s your pride. I see. Well, I’ll be in my office, doing my duty to my people. In case you have any other insults you wish to exchange.”

     

                “Just stay out of my way,” Lena wearily warned her.

     

                Letting out a light laugh of surprise, eyebrows rising and falling quickly, Kara smiled tightly. “You have some nerve to command me in my own home. You should be careful with your attitude; I understand your frustration, and that your anger is misplaced in me, but once we’re at the Unseelie Court, your mother won’t be so understanding.”

     

                “She’s not my mother,” Lena hotly shouted at Kara’s retreating figure.

     

                Her anger felt sharp and too loud in the emptiness of the tower as Kara vanished upstairs, leaving Lena to stew in her misery and frustration. She spent the rest of the evening pacing, freezing at the sight of one of those strangely humanoid water figures appearing, shimmering in the waning light as it deposited a tray on the table and then somehow lit the brazier full of driftwood. Bluish flames licked at the bleached wood and Lena sat at the table, tearing apart the cut of salmon, the thick slices of bread and the selection of soft cheeses and fruit. She was starving and didn’t have the fortitude to starve herself on principle at that moment.

     

                Collapsing into bed afterwards, she struggled to quieten her mind and eventually fell asleep to the sound of lapping water and wind, the bone-deep rightness of it unnerving but preferable to the sound of hacking coughs, groaning mattresses and people talking at one of the shelters she’d spent the last few nights in. 

     

                Sleeping deeply and late into the morning, making the most of the safety the tower offered, Lena rose feeling leaden but content as she rubbed the sleep from her eyes. Straightening out the blankets, she found clothes waiting for her - a thin billowing shirt and soft leggings - and a breakfast of cold oats with nuts and fruit and a cooling pot of tea that she still gulped down, the smell of the herbs calming as she lounged in the chair, the picture of ease.

     

                At the sight of Kara appearing near the stairs, her serene demeanour vanished, and Lena scowled as she straightened up, rigid in her seat. Crossing the room, Kara gave her a blank look, her expression unreadable as she stood in a near-identical outfit to Lena, although it looked far more natural on her.

     

                “Good morning. I trust your mood has improved.”

     

                Giving her a stony look of silence, Lena gripped the arms of the dining chair hard enough to turn her knuckles white. She wasn’t sure why she was so annoyed by the fae woman - perhaps it was an underlying fear of her, while knowing she wouldn’t hurt her, no matter how rude or angry Lena was - but everything about her grated against Lena’s nerves.

     

                “Come.”

     

                Forgetting her sullen silence, Lena half-rose from her seat, a wary look creeping onto her face. “Where?”

     

                “To train.”

     

                Narrowing her eyes, Lena warily wound her way around the table and the other chairs, hands curling into fists as her shoulders went taut. “For what?”

     

                “I told you; you need to prepare yourself to leave for the Unseelie Court. You won’t be sitting idly until then. We have work to do.”

     

                Lena’s wariness only grew at her words but she found herself following after Kara, feeling like she didn’t have much of a choice. They made their way to the spacious floor full of weapons and armour and Lena froze on the stairs as she watched Kara shift some thin leather mats on the floor and then pick up her sword.

     

                “Sword fighting?” Lena sceptically asked.

     

                “Not for you. A sword takes decades to master and you wouldn’t be able to do much more than swing it. You’d have a better chance of impaling yourself than someone else.”
