                Rankling, Lena gave her a disgruntled look and moved further into the space, while Kara fished out the dagger she’d given Lena before and unsheathed it. Handing it to her, hilt-first, Kara unsheathed her sword and swung it through the air, eliciting a faint whistling sound as it cut through with such speed that it was nothing more than a silver blur.

     

                “Come,” she prompted Lena, beckoning with slender, tanned fingers. “Attack me.”

     

                Lena looked down at her dagger and then back up at Kara, her expression clouding momentarily before she lunged forward. The point of Kara’s sword was at her throat before she could even blink, making her shrink back, swallowing thickly.

     

                “Dead.”

     

                Flushing slightly as anger curled through her, Lena gripped her dagger tighter as her hand dropped to her side. Kara looked indifferent and beckoned her again, this time knocking the dagger from Lena’s hand with a well-aimed flick of her sword, before it was pressed against her chest.

     

                “Dead.”

     

                They repeated this over and over, Lena was blocked at every turn by the bright steel of the sword as she tried her hardest to get past Kara’s guard. She was getting so frustrated that she imagined she might actually plunge the dagger into the woman’s chest if the opportunity presented itself. Instead, she found herself growing sweaty and pink-cheeked from the exertion, teeth clenched, while Kara remained as composed as ever, which was even more infuriating.

     

                “Dead.”

     

                “If I’m not going to be able to defend myself then why are we bothering?” Lena eventually snapped.

     

                “Because I owe it to you to give you a fighting chance,” Kara stiffly murmured, blocking Lena’s path with her sword as she tried to stalk off, having had enough for the day. “You’re quicker than you think; your fae abilities have been softened by your life in the mortal world. Try, just a little , and you might surprise yourself.”

     

                Lena scoffed and rolled her eyes, pushing Kara’s sword arm down and stepping around it. And then it was there again, blocking her path and adding fuel to her anger as she gave Kara a sharp look.

     

                “Stop.”

     

                “Make me.”

     

                A scathing laugh worked up Lena’s throat as she stared at Kara for a long moment, tense and brimming with anger before she lashed out with the dagger. Kara’s wiry fingers grabbed her wrist and jerked her arm down and Lena twisted sharply in her grasp, breaking her hold. She was inside Kara’s guard, meaning she had the advantage, but when she raised the dagger in an over-handed stab, Kara grabbed her wrist again, dropped her sword and then wrenched the dagger from Lena’s hand, pressing the keen edge to her throat and leaning in close.

     

                “Dead,” she whispered.

     

                Lips twisting with anger, Lena wrenched herself away, too sudden as the edge of the dagger shallowly bit into her throat, beads of blood welling up as she turned around. And then her anger was muted by the shock of her blood as she touched a hand to her neck and came away with a bead of vivid red on the pad of her finger, flinging it off and watching with horrified disbelief as it turned into a small petal, the palest shade of lilac.

     

                Feeling grey with unease, Lena slowly turned around to look at Kara, her fingertips touching the bleeding nick. “Why is it doing that?” she rasped.

     

                “You’re much more than human,” Kara softly told her, “you shouldn’t forget it.”

     

                Mouth thinning as she swallowed, Lena looked down at the stone floor, feeling faint and aching all over from her multiple attempts at overpowering Kara. Pressing her palm to her forehead, she closed her eyes and drew in a long breath.

     

                “I’m done for today.”

     

                “Very well. We’ll resume tomorrow.”

     

                Kara sheathed the sword and dagger and then made for the stairs, leaving Lena to stumble into motion, her attention still snagged on the solitary petal skittering across the stone floor in the breeze. It bothered her, and she couldn’t say for what reason, except maybe she’d been expecting this whole thing to be a joke, but her blood had turned to petals , just like Kara’s had turned to water.

     

                Struggling to make her voice work as she followed Kara back downstairs, Lena regained some of her previous indignation and haughtiness as she avoided looking over the side of the steps, going slowly as she pretended like there wasn’t a long drop to deep water below.

                

                “I’d like to wash,” she proclaimed.

     

                Kara didn’t turn, just gestured through the open side of the tower. “By all means.”

     

                “I don’t like water,” Lena stiffly reminded her.

     

                Softly sighing, Kara clicked her tongue, as if she couldn’t imagine anything more absurd than being afraid of the thing that was like a second home to her, if not first.

     

                “Do you have a bath?” Lena pressed.

     

                “Yes, there’s a tub that you may use.”

                

                “Thank you.”

     

                Her cordiality gave Kara pause as she glanced back over her shoulder before continuing on her way. Pausing at one of the floors, Kara gestured dismissively as Lena looked past her, at the paper-thin screen decorated with water birds hiding the brass tub behind it, the low ottomans and chaise lounge and carved benches with handmade soaps in the shapes of shells and tiny bottles of perfumes and creams.

     

                “Your bath.”

     

                Wandering inside, Lena found that the tub didn’t have any plumbing attached to it and spluttered before stalking back out, bare feet slapping against stone steps in her haste to catch up with Kara, whose sigh greeted her before the sight of her did.

     

                “Yes?”

     

                “There are no taps.”

     

                “Taps?”

     

                “Plumbing.”

     

                “I don’t follow.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena gave her a withering look. “You turn the tap,” she mimed, “and hot water comes out. There’s nowhere for the water to come from.”

     

                Giving her a bewildered look, unsure if she was being mocked, Kara frowned slightly. “The water will need to be heated and brought up.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “It will take some time, if you care to eat while you wait.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena relented and followed Kara down to the kitchen, where she took a seat at one of the long benches and watched as Kara fetched food for them. Simple fare - fresh bread that had been baked that morning, crabs that had been steamed and gone cold, wild greens and a lemon cake that they ate with cups of tea tasting of lavender as they lingered in silence.

     

                Neither of them knew what to say or how to behave, Lena positively frosty and Kara unused to living with someone else, unused to a prickly half-fae who didn’t know the first thing about the forest, about the danger of politics and the history of their conflict. Lena was bitter at losing everything she’d ever had as a result of being dragged through to a different world, and it was hard for her to reconcile that with Kara’s intention to keep her safe. If she hadn’t agreed to marry her in the first place, it was possible Lena wouldn’t have been brought there at all. 

     

                But no, she knew that was a naive thought, knowing Lillian would have made them find her anyway, would have used her as a bargaining chip in some other way, if not in marriage. She might have kept her prisoner there just for the sake of it, taunting her for her own enjoyment, so Lena couldn’t really be that angry that she’d gotten the better bargain in the end. Although considering that she’d be back in the other court in a few weeks, perhaps she should be that angry.

     

                “The bath is ready for you.”

     

                Breaking herself out of her thoughts, Lena blinked at Kara and then nodded, forcing her stiff body to stand and walk toward the stairs. Climbing back up to the room with the tub, she found it waiting for her, steaming and fragranced with small white flower petals. Wondering how Kara had controlled the water from down in the kitchen, those humanoid figures boiling a portion of themselves and sprinkling flowers in for her. It was unnerving and she still didn’t quite understand it but as she stripped off her clothes and stepped into the tub, it didn’t seem to matter.

     

                Basking in the heat as it turned her skin an angry red and made the small cuts prickle with pain, Lena luxuriated in the feeling of being clean as she scoured her skin with the small soaps gathered from the tray set on a stool with a towel. And somewhere in the middle of her bath, she started to cry, her chest aching at everything she’d lost and how a simple bath could elicit such a strong response for her.

     

                And once she started, she couldn’t stop, the tears flowing faster, dripping into the water, washed from her cheeks as she slipped beneath the surface and tried to hold her sobs in her chest. It only made her gasp between choking sobs as she resurface, spluttering water, and wiping at her face, letting her misery well up and consume her as she rested her head against the rim of the brass tub. For all the richness of the forest, the cleanliness of the air and the water, the warmth of the summer and the wealth and care of everything crafted here, she misses her bed and her flowers and the comforting loneliness of someone who has sought out solitude and prefers it. Despite her decision to stay, there’s a part of Lena that abhors the thought of wasting away in the tower, her life slipping through her fingers with no purpose and nothing to show for, except as a piece used to broker a tenuous truce. 

     

                Lena would almost prefer war. She would at least feel some sense of urgency to help solve the conflict, and might have even offered herself up willingly to be bound to some irritable fae woman who seemed opposite to her in every way if it meant saving her own skin. Lena’s self-preservation triumphed over everything, but she didn’t feel like she was threatened with anything more than being imprisoned with a boring woman who loved the water.

     

                Eventually, the bath cooled and her sobs subsided and Lena wallowed in the tub, fingers trailing through the cloudy water as she lingered a while longer, nothing else to occupy her time, which seemed to stretch out infinitely ahead of her. It was relaxing to have nothing demanding of her time, but Lena didn’t handle idleness well and foresaw boredom consuming her as days stretched into weeks, stretched into months.

     

                She didn’t hear the quiet footsteps, didn’t have the telltale sound of scuffing shoes to alert her, and was startled in the bath at the sound of Kara’s voice, suddenly there on the other side of the screen. Water sloshed onto the stone floor, darkening it, and she scowled.

     

                “Are you alright?”

     

                “Don’t you know how to knock?” Lena bitingly asked, her calm mood disturbed by the arrival of the other woman.

     

                “But … there aren’t any doors here.”

     

                Lena had to choke back a surprised laugh, unwilling to give her that flicker of amusement, and scooted down further into the lukewarm water. “A bit of privacy would be nice.”

     

                “You’re behind the screen.”

     

                “Just … leave me alone,” Lena wearily sighed, feeling hollow and exhausted.

     

                Kara was silent for a moment but Lena knew she was still there, standing tall and regal as usual, insufferable and condescending. But there was a hesitation and sheepish guilt to her words when she finally spoke, sounding uncomfortable and a little peeved to be having this conversation.

     

                “I heard you crying.”

     

                “And?” Lena asked, her cheeks turning red beneath the lingering pink the fading hot water had painted her pallid skin.

     

                “I wanted to see if you were alright.”

     

                “It’s none of your business.”

     

                “You are my business, whether I will it or not. I’m sorry if my brusqueness has upset you; I only mean to give you a fighting chance in the Unseelie Court. Your anger is too quick, too careless, to your own detriment.”

     

                Struggling to swallow, Lena sank further beneath the water, until it was up to her chin and she stared broodingly over the rim of the tub as if she could see Kara through the screen. “Being here is to my own detriment. I think I’ll go mad if I have to put up with no one else but you for company.”

     

                “That can be rectified.”

     

                A faint sneer crossed Lena’s face and she sat up, water sloshing back and forth in waves, and pushed herself to her feet. Stepping out of the bath, she grabbed the towel and wrapped it around herself, her dark hair plastered to her pale skin, almost black as water dripped from the ends. Rounding the screen, Lena wiped a hand over her face.

     

                “I don’t need you inserting yourself into my business, okay? I’m happy by myself. If I’m staying here, then that’s that. It doesn’t mean we need to get along. We don’t need to be friends or- or care about each other-”

     

                “We could at least be cordial.”

     

                “What’s the point? I irritate you, clearly, and I don’t have the energy to pretend I like you, so-”

     

                “And what is it about me that you don’t like?” Kara asked, affronted and bristling as her soft expression crumpled with annoyance. 

     

                It was almost as if no one had ever disliked her before, as if she’d never had to deal with not getting along with people in her own court. Maybe she hadn’t, the shining lady of her house, rich and beautiful and gentle, but Lena wasn’t one of them and she had plenty of reasons to dislike her. It didn’t matter that she was the only person who had helped her, the only one who had protected her and kept her safe, it was the principle of it, and Lena was nothing without her principles. She was determined to stick to her distrustful opinion of Kara while she tried to settle into this strange new life as well as possible.

     

                “You shouldn’t take it personally,” Lena murmured, “I don’t really like anyone.”

     

                Trying to appear like she wasn’t sulking, Kara raised her chin and gave her a hard stare, although her blue eyes looked far too sad and unsure of herself to have the desired effect. “I just came to ask if you’d like me to do your hair.”

     

                Snorting, Lena arched an eyebrow, “what, are you going to braid shells into it?”

     

                Drawing herself up to her full height, Kara rolled her eyes and softly clicked her tongue. “It’s exactly comments like this that will find you in hot water. Only water folk braid shells into their hair. You’d likely have … thorns . Like your mother.”

     

                “Call her my mother once -”

     

                “It’s our laws.”

     

                “I don’t care!”

     

                “You might try being less prickly then,” Kara said with a cool, dismissive look. “At the moment, you’re doing a fine impression of her. One might even believe that you were her daughter.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena vanished back behind the painted screen and dried off, dressing in the shirt and leggings again and re-emerging to find Kara gone. Making her way back up to her room again, Lena sank down onto a chair and drew her knees up to her chest, propping her chin on top and wondering if her life had been reduced to this open room with nothing to entertain herself with.  Half of the books were indecipherable and there was nothing else for her to do to pass the time. Sitting and stewing in her annoyance, she listened as the first notes of a harp started drifting through the tower. 

     

                Curled up on the chair, it lulled Lena to sleep, as if the sound was a drug, the forest weaving its way through her mind, burrowing down to her bones and binding her tighter to this place. She was helpless to resist sleeping, enchanted by the warm air, the smell of the damp forest and sweet wildflowers as white-breasted cormorants sang out through the afternoon.  Lena slept all through the afternoon and long into the night, her dreams slipping in and out unobtrusively with snatches of a long-forgotten language, of glades in summer and blue eyes, like falling into a deep lake.

     

                Undisturbed, Lena slept on as a soft dusk-blue blanket was pulled over her just before the moon hit its peak, a spectral woman standing over her, all her golden beauty turned to soft orange from the light of the brazier she’d lit upon entering.  Kara stayed a while, watching Lena sleep and puzzling through this stranger in her home, trying to pick apart the knotted unease in her chest as her feelings for the woman, for her wife , clouded everything. It was just beginning to dawn on her, now that Lena would be staying and that she may have made a mistake by agreeing to marry her.

    Chapter 7

                Days passed by in a slow procession, each one stretching out like an infinite summer day of nothingness. Each day she was made to endure another sparring lesson, nothing coming of her ineptitude with a dagger, although it made for some colourful exchanges with Kara, who would be pink-cheeked with annoyance by the end of each lesson, and uptight as she tried to retain her polite composure. They’d gone from bruque strangers to bickering cohabitation and Lena found the wary fear of the fae woman dwindling down to nothing. 

     

                Kara was no more frightening than any of the numerous foster parents Lena had been sent to live with for short periods of time, with their rules and their flaws and vices. Except Kara was her wife and that was an entirely foreign concept to her - even moreso than this vaguely familiar forest that nagged at the back of her mind like an itch. The forest was perhaps the only thing that did make sense to her, like a balm soothing an old wound that had been bothering her for so long that she hadn’t noticed it. In its absence, the ghost of it was glaringly obvious.

     

                Still, even the forest couldn’t stifle the loneliness that latched itself around Lena’s heart as her empty days turned into a week, then two, with nothing to show for it. At times, she felt like she didn’t exist, like one day was repeating itself over and over in some loop, the only thing changing being her clothes and the prickly conversations with Kara. It was hard for Lena to see the end of it all and believe anything would get better.

     

                But it wasn’t all bad, and there were moments where Lena imagined doing that for the rest of her life, and it filled her with a strange serenity. There were the mornings she rose terribly early, before the sun had even slipped over the treetops, and she would sit on the edge of her room, where the stone floor met open air and the lake beyond, and watch the slim shadowed figure cut through the water in graceful motions. 

     

                Kara would return from her dawn swim and light a fire in the kitchen, making mint and dandelion tea for them and sweetening it with honey as sunlight began to flood gold into the aquamarine sky on the eastern horizon as the darkness lifted. They’d eat a breakfast of cold pears and cheese and Kara would take her downstairs to the bottom level, where Lena would sit on the last few steps, above the lapping level of the rippling water, while Kara stood calf-deep, educating her on the political history of the Courts and the socioeconomic impact of the long-standing war. She’d skip stones on the water while speaking, her voice smooth and rippling like water, and Lena could envision her doling out advice and calmly advocating for her people at the Council.

     

                On one such morning, indistinguishable from the others, Kara surprised Lena as she skimmed a flat stone across the still surface of the lake. It bounced six times and then vanished into the thin fog lingering in patches. Turning, she cleared her throat and her blue eyes landed on Lena for a moment as she picked up another stone, turning it in her slender fingers and then gazing out at the lake, a swan gliding past as ducks splashed in the shallows.

     

                “There’s a Council meeting today. I must attend, of course.”

     

                “Alright.”

     

                “You must promise me you won’t leave the tower,” Kara said, her eyes meeting Lena’s again, her stare piercing and solemn.

     

                A wry smile curled Lena’s lips and she leaned back, the step above cutting into her lower back. Narrowing her eyes a fraction, she gestured lazily with a hand. “As discussed, I’m not wading through a lake full of water to escape any time soon.”

     

                Nodding, Kara hesitated and then skimmed her stone before wiping her palms on the thighs of her leggings. Water darkened them past her knees and she waded towards Lena, bypassing the pale, skeletal tree in the middle of the foyer and climbing onto the bottom step. A few droplets of cold water splattered Lena’s sleeve, the thin fabric sticking to her skin, the chill of the water eliciting a small protest from her as she straightened up.

     

                “You would be surprised what someone might do in danger. But know that you’ll be better protected if you stay in the tower, no matter what happens. There are older things in the forest that have less rational thoughts than a fae looking to break the peace. Don’t forget.”

     

                “How could I?” Lena replied, her voice nettling as she touched her abdomen, where puckered scars should’ve marred the smooth skin.

     

                Climbing to her feet, she made her way upstairs to her room, which was slowly showing signs of being lived in - Kara’s clothes strewn around the place, trays from dinner, rumpled sheets and stacks of books she was trying her best to decipher. The water servants hadn’t made the rounds yet, straightening out the sheets and leaving the occasional splash of water on the table and the stone floor as they moved around the place in formless shapes that solidified into something humanoid to pick things up. 

     

                She was puzzling her way through a scroll in that foreign language, trying her best to make sense of the glyphs as if staring at them would make them arrange themselves into English, when Kara appeared in her room, standing on the threshold with her hands clasped behind her back. Lena glanced up and then did a double-take at the opulence of her outfit. She’d changed in a crushed velvet robe of a faded teal, cinched at the waist with a silver belt studded with pearls and diamonds and aquamarines, and her hair was elaborately braided with silver and drops of pearls and jewels like raindrops caught in her golden locks. It was a similar look to the first time they’d met, the sword sheathed at her waist, the detailed stitching hemming the exquisitely crafted robe with motifs of water, and Lena blinked.

     

                “I’ll be off soon. If you might accompany downstairs first.”

     

                It was a request disguising a command and Lena stared at her for a long moment before uncurling herself from the chair and tossing the scroll onto the table. Fluidly rising to her feet, Lena arched an eyebrow and gestured for Kara to leave, following after her as she studied her from behind, taking in the small braids, wondering if she’d done them herself with deft fingers, the broad width of her shoulders from years of rowing on the lake, the faint, puzzling smell of salt that seemed to cling to her, even though the lake was freshwater.

     

                They reached the foyer and Lena hesitated on the steps at the sight of a short woman with dark skin dressed in yellow. She had black hair to her waist, woven with gold, topaz and amber and she smiled softly as her eyes alighted on Lena. Wariness curled through Lena and she reached out to brace herself on the stone of the archway, watching as Kara stepped into the water, which quickly soaked it up and sank beneath the surface, fanning out around her as she walked forwards.

     

                “This is Lena,” she introduced her, half-turning to gesture back towards her with a hand laden with rings, the other one grasping the pommel of her sword.

     

                Lena’s brow creased with confusion, a flicker of recognition in her green eyes as she slowly descended another step, sure that she’d seen the woman before but couldn’t place when. She was pretty, with that inhuman fae quality that made her seem to glow from within, her movements graceful as she glided through the water and reached out for Lena, smiling softly.

     

                “Lena. It’s an honour to finally meet you properly.”

     

                “Um …”

     

                “I was present at the wedding. Normally, we would’ve enjoyed an evening of revelry, but out of concerns for your safety, we didn’t get the chance to formally be introduced.”

     

                “Kelly,” Kara informed Lena. “One of the Airfolk.”

     

                She was still reaching out for Lena, whose eyes darted between her and Kara before reaching out to shake her hand. Kelly looked down with bewilderment in her dark eyes and let out a quick laugh, the sound light and amused, before she turned to Kara.

     

                “How odd she is.”

     

                Lena furiously blushed as she folded her arms over her chest, bristling indignantly when she caught sight of Kara’s faint smile. The mirth in her blue eyes died as she met Lena’s gaze and she sobered up, clearing her throat.

     

                “Kelly will be accompanying you while I’m gone. She’ll keep you safe.”

     

                Spluttering in protest, Lena stormed down another step but pulled up short at the lapping water, her face pale and taut. “I don’t need a babysitter.”

     

                “I’ll return at dusk,” Kara said in parting, making towards the archway leading to the submerged stepping stones.

     

                “You-” Lena started but faltered, her brow pinching and the words dying in her mouth.

     

                Her mouth parted as a desolate look of disbelief crossed her face, as if she couldn’t believe Kara was leaving her there with a stranger . Lena had barely gotten used to having Kara around all the time, let alone this new woman who she most definitely didn’t know and was to trust to keep her safe.

     

                With an unperturbed look of serene gentleness on her face, Kelly mounted the first step, making Lena flinch back at how close they were, scurrying up the steps as her eyes darkened with a clouded look. She had a golden shield slung across her back and she adjusted the strap as she raised her eyebrows in a politely enquiring look.

     

                “Shall we retire to a sitting room?”

     

                Fixing her with an unreadable expression, Lena blinked and Kelly’s smile faltered as she found her way barred. 

     

                “Look, lady, I don’t need a babysitter,” Lena scowled, her distrust evident on her face.

     

                “I’m not familiar with that term. I’m also not a Lady.”

     

                Lena opened and closed her mouth and then exhaled sharply through her nose, her frustration spiking. Was everyone in the forest so irritating, or was it her poor misfortune that had brought her to the company of the two people who seemed to obliviously increase her blood pressure every time they opened their mouths?

     

                “I don’t give a shit what you are, I just- I don’t need … a carer? An attendee ?”

     

                Realisation dawned on the woman’s face and her face creased with a warm smile, “oh, well, I’m not here to serve you. Kara only thought you might find a need for a friend - another one, aside from her.”

     

                A laugh got stuck in Lena’s throat as disbelief flashed across her face. “I am not friends with her.”

     

                “That’s secondary to the cause. I’m not here to watch over you; I’m here to keep you … entertained?”

     

                “And how’re you planning to manage that?”

     

                Giving her a once over, Kelly smiled faintly and gestured at her. “Well, first of all, I think we should do something about the state of your clothes. Kara’s rather inexperienced at managing other people’s affairs; she’s good at many things, but can be quite oblivious at times. I imagine she’s been so consumed with her work that she’s forgotten to do anything about it.”

     

                “She’s been lending me some of her own clothes.”

     

                “Mm, yes, well … her style leaves something to be desired. Leggings and shirts might be appropriate for splashing around in a lake all day but they most definitely aren’t court fashion. If you showed up at your mother’s home in them, you’d be held with nothing but contempt, I’m sure.”

     

                Lena snorted, arching an eyebrow. “I don’t think it’s the clothes that would elicit such a reaction.”

     

                “No? Well, a few appropriate pieces wouldn’t go amiss, anyway,” Kelly distractedly murmured.

     

                She gave Lena a quick grin and then started moving forward, forcing Lena to step aside or engage in some sort of stand-off that would have been awkward for both of them. Stepping aside, Lena allowed the shorter woman to brush past and then hesitated before following after her, a thoughtful look on her face as she realised that Kelly was familiar with the tower.

     

                “And how do you know Kara?” she demanded as she quickly caught up.

     

                “I’m wed to her sister.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Alex. You’ll not have officially met her either, and she’s needed at the meeting. You may remember her from the day of your own wedding.”

     

                “I’ve tried my hardest to block it out,” Lena witheringly replied.

     

                Kelly let out a quick laugh, “you’re very amusing. It’s a pity Kara’s kept you away from us all; you’d make a welcome addition to our parties.”

     

                Lena stared at her back with a wary, brooding look as she followed her upstairs despite her reservations. In one of the sitting rooms, Kelly rifled through a desk drawer and found paper, a quill and an inkpot before settling down on a sofa. She wrote swiftly as Lena hovered awkwardly before her, rocking on the tips of her toes with her arms crossed over her chest, craning her neck to get a good look at the paper.

     

                “What’re you writing?” she asked, eyeing the glyphs that Kelly was jotting down.

     

                “Your measurements.”

     

                “You don’t know my measurements.”

     

                “I have an interest in clothes; I often make my own in my spare time, but you require finer things for court. I imagine my measurements will suffice, but should you need any alterations, I’ll be able to help.”

     

                “I don’t want … fine clothes,” Lena replied with evident frustration, her brown puckering and her tongue tripping over the unusual formality of the words.

     

                Kelly smiled patiently as she looked up, dark eyes warm and faintly amused. “We don’t all find ourselves in situations we desire to be in. Some of us must make do with our circumstances and be content with that.”

     

                “Did you marry … Alex for some truce as well?”

     

                “Oh. No. No, no, we love each other - very much - although I’m sympathetic to your plight. You should know … if you were to be forced into an arranged marriage with anyone, Kara is the best you could’ve hoped for.”

     

                “Then I’d hate to see the worst,” Lena darkly muttered.

     

                Humming, her mouth turning down at the corners, Kelly made another note as her eyes evaluated the width of Lena’s neck. “Mm, you most definitely would.”

     

                Standing there for a few more minutes, Lena eventually lowered herself onto a seat to Kelly’s right, tense and watchful as she waited for the woman to finish writing. When she was done, Kelly leaned forward and set the ink and quill down before neatly rolling the paper in her hands to create a scroll. She drifted from the room with graceful steps and vanished upstairs, leaving Lena watching the stairs as she waited for her to return. 

     

                “What’re you doing?”

     

                “Sending my measurements and instructions. There are birds upstairs; have you seen them?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “They send letters, when necessary,” she informed Lena, who snorted. Raising her eyebrows a fraction, Kelly cocked her head to the side. “And you can’t read.”

     

                Lena bristled, scowling as she jerked her chin forward. “Of course I can read.”

     

                “Ah, let me rephrase - you can’t read fae glyphs.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena exhaled softly. “Of course I can’t. But … they’re … familiar . I feel as if I should know how to read them.”

     

                “You were raised at court for a while; you would have learnt them and then forgotten once you left this realm.”

     

                “How can the forest just … make me forget?”

     

                “It’s more sentient than you give it credit for.”

     

                Scoffing dismissively, Lena gazed through one of the gauzy curtains as it balooned inwards and offered a glimpse of sparkling blue water and the thick forest stretching out for miles beyond. It was hard to think the forest had any sort of sentience, but she’d been in it, felt the uncomfortable feeling of being watched, of being herded in a direction, barred from a way by thick brambles, as if the forest objected to her presence. It could only be called sentience, but she hated the thought of the trees, the ferns, the flowers, the earth, water and mere air she breathed having some sort of power over her. And yet, here she was, still there, bound tightly to the place and willingly choosing to remain - although if it was binding her tighter with each passing second, how much of the choice was actually hers?

     

                “Here,” Kelly said, breaking Lena from her brooding as she walked over to her and picked up a blank piece of paper and dipped the quill into the ink.

     

                She sank down to her knees before the low table and slowly etched a glyph. “This one is shah.”

     

                “What?”

     

                Glancing up at Lena, she gave her a pointed look and gestured for her to join her on the floor. “Our glyphs. You should know them. Come.”

     

                Hesitantly sinking down to the floor, the stone cool through the leggings she was wearing, Lena shifted a little closer, peering over Kelly’s arm to stare down at the paper. She eyed the strange, flowing symbols, tracing the fluid lines with her eyes. 

     

                “This is khao,” Kelly said as she swirled the nib of the quill over the page, the soft scratching punctuating the silence.

     

                They spent the next few hours going through them over a plate of fish and steaming bread, Lena feeling clumsy and stupid as she tried her best to mimic the graceful arcs of each glyph with the quill. Kelly was patient and Lena found it hard to be angry at her calm deamanour which bordered on patronising as they worked through all thirty-three glyphs, Lena learning the names for them all before they moved on to the language. Kelly wrote a few glyphs and then the translation in the Latin alphabet used for English, the letters arranged in such confusing ways that Lena had no clue what words they translated to in actual English.

     

                “This word means flower,” Kelly said, dotting beside a word she’d just scrawled. “Your family are people of the Earth. I wonder how much power you’ll have over the element as a half-fae.”

     

                Lena didn’t give any indication of her aptitude for botany and slipping between realms through the trunks of ash trees. Shifting slightly, she copied out the glyphs and thought of her family with some resentment. They were as foreign to Lena as the rest of the forest, the dim memory of a father veiled in the back of her mind, much like her mother, and it angered her that Lillian was the person she saw with clarity when her family was mentioned. She was nothing to that woman, and yet, here it was as good as if she’d been born and raised by her for her entire life.

     

                “What’s the point of all this element stuff?” Lena asked as Kelly wrote down a few more glyphs for water, air, fire, earth, river, lake, tree. The list went on, each word written in a comprehensible alphabet with a foreign sounding word that somehow managed to roll off her tongue with that prickle at the back of her mind that she already knew it.

     

                “It’s our birthright,” Kelly said with surprise, “we’re, well, I suppose, just as much creatures of the forest as the animals that live here. We’re attached to nature; it’s in our blood, our bones, our lungs. With that comes a natural affinity. It’s hereditary.”

     

                “So is there like … a dominant gene?”

     

                “I don’t quite understand.”

     

                “You know, biologically?”

     

                “Biologically?”

     

                “Don’t you know science?” Lena asked, exasperatedly.

     

                Kelly arched an eyebrow, “science?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena sat back, leaning against the sofa and twirling the quill in her fingers. She’d always been rather adept at science, intelligent enough to excel at chemistry and human biology and physics - had even considered a career as a botanist before deciding on the stability of a business major after a childhood full of uncertainty - and she dipped the quill into ink and drew a Punnett Square. 

     

                “See, two parents with blonde hair carry recessive genes. This means their child will have blonde hair. While parents with black hair have dominant genes, but could be a carrier for the recessive blonde trait. If both parents have this recessie gene, that means there’s a twenty-five percent chance of having a child with blonde hair, while seventy-five with black hair. You know math right?”

     

                “Mathematics? Of course.”

     

                “So … does that make sense?” Lena haltingly asked, raising her eyebrows as she gestured to her squares.

     

                “Yes, it’s well known that offspring will inherit traits from either parent. If black hair is absent in the parent, it’ll be absent in the child.”

     

                “Yes, but … it’s science,” Lena stressed. “It’s about genetics.”

     

                Kelly let out a light laugh, “those are terms that don’t exist here.”

     

                Huffing impatiently, Lena stabbed the nib of the quill at the page before her. “How often do parents with dark hair have children with light hair?”

     

                “Not often. Although, Kara was one such child.”

     

                “See? It’s because of dominance with genes. It’s less likely to happen.”

     

                “And how does this relate to the elements?”

     

                Lena gave her a rare smile, almost smug in her curiosity. “I imagine there are rules against relationships within the same families? Lands? What actually makes up the court?”

     

                “Oh, well, it’s split into different affinities, I suppose. Each lake, river and piece of the sea has its own Lord or Lady. Same with the forest and the mountains. Then there are those who live within the boundaries of the land. As you say, relationships within families are forbidden, but there are many families that make up the retainers of each Lord or Lady. But everyone is free to marry between affinities, of course. I’m Air, Alex is Fire.”

     

                “Right, so if two people have a child … how does the child gain their element? Is it just based on what their parents are or can you be any of them?”

     

                “It’s chance. But, of course, Kara was born to two of the Waterfolk - one of the sea, one of this lake - so she would never have had an affinity for another element.”

     

                “So it is genetic.”

     

                “I … don’t follow,” Kelly slowly said.

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Lena set the quill down. “It doesn’t matter. It’s for my own curiosity.”

     

                “Do you have an interest in your family’s history?”

     

                “My mom’s dead; that’s all the family I’ve ever had.”

     

                “I’m sure once you’re at the Unseelie Court, your mother-”

     

                “Not my mother.”

     

                “Oh … um, well …”

     

                “Continue.”

     

                “Lillian will be able to inform you of the rest of your brethren. It might help you understand the diplomacy and relations between different families. The strengths and alliances that bond each one through generations of marriage and treaties.”

     

                Lena scoffed quietly, her lips twisting derisively. “I’m not really interested in alliances. Or history. None of this concerns me.”

     

                Raising her eyebrows in a quiet look of surprise, Kelly took a sip of pale golden wine from the glass in hand. “It should; you, yourself, are one such alliance. Arguably the most important one we’ve ever had.”

     

                With a thin grin, Lena cocked her head to the side and tossed the quill down, “and why do you think I don’t care? Maybe I would have more of a reason to if I’d been given even the slightest choice.”

     

                “Kara said you’d chosen to remain here.”

     

                “After I’d already been wed to her and told that nothing would be able to dissolve our marriage, short of dying .”

     

                Humming, Kelly glanced sidelong at her and shrugged nonchalantly. “You still made your choice. I would imagine it’s time to take accountability for that; you could have left.”

     

                Lena’s voice was brittle and her face hard as she replied. “I understand that, but I’ll never take any responsibility for getting married off. I chose to stay - I didn’t choose a wife .”

     

                “Choosing to stay was choosing Kara.”

     

                “That’s irrelevant,” Lena dismissively replied, “they can force us to marry, but it’ll be a union in appearance only. I understand that a marriage of convenience serves a purpose in diplomacy, as a truce between the Courts, but it’ll never be anything more than that and I’ll never be content with it.”

     

                Kelly’s expression was soft and she reached out to touch Lena’s arm, her fingers falling through empty air as Lena yanked her arm away, alarmed and offended at the idea that she’d touch her. Softly sighing, her mouth thinned as she looked at Lena, dark eyes somewhat sad and disappointed.

     

                “You sound just like Kara, but … it doesn’t have to be that way. Love can bloom even in the darkest of places if given the chance. It might surprise you both what could come of this union, if only you let yourself entertain the idea.”

     

                She opened her mouth to retort but Kelly fluidly rose to her feet and disappeared from the sitting room, leaving Lena stewing in her indignation as she snapped her mouth shut and ground her teeth together. 

     

                Everyone she’d encountered so far only seemed to serve her frustration and she reached out for the silver jug to refill her glass with wine, draining half of it in one gulp and savouring the sweetness of it as she frowned at the pages littering the table. The glyphs only served to frustrate her more, familiar but just out of reach as she stared at the swirling patterns, willing them to make sense.

     

                “And what has you scowling up a summer storm?” Kara asked by way of greeting, stepping into the sitting room looking weary and rumpled.

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena looked up and her face crumpled with a solemn expression, distracted and rather sombre as she raked a hand through her hair and then reached for the wine again. Kara’s blonde hair was a little windswept and the neat folds of her robe were creased and ballooning over the top of her belt as she sank down onto a chaise lounge, sighing loudly. She ran a thumb over her right eyelid and then looked at Lena expectedly.

     

                “I’m imagining my short lifespan before boredom kills me,” Lena wryly replied, gesturing with her cup of wine and rolling her eyes.

     

                Kara leaned forward and picked up Kelly’s empty cup, eyeing the dregs and then nonchalantly topping it up and taking a swig. The gap between the two of them closed and Lena could smell baked bread and the hint of something green, like crushed grass, clinging to her. It felt wrong, the salt tang of water, that damp odour of the lake that clung to her diminished from her time away from the tower.

     

                “Mm, yes, a life of leisure is so awful,” Kara replied, her eyes sliding to Lena with a piercing look.

     

                “Where’s Kelly?” Lena asked, changing the topic.

     

                “Gone.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Kara smiled faintly, tilting her head to the side and raising her eyebrows. “Does it bother you that she left without telling you? I hadn’t imagined you’d care about niceties like that.”

     

                “I don’t,” Lena defensively replied, shifting on the floor.

     

                “She likes you,” Kara admitted, leaning in. “Perhaps once we return to the Seelie Court in winter, you might get to know each other better.”

     

                Surprise flitted across Lena’s face as she turned her head to look up at Kara, sitting on the chaise lounge above her. “We won’t see them while we’re there?”

     

                Mouth thinning with dismay as her shoulders slumped slightly, Kara shook her head. “As a general rule, we tend not to cross the borders of each Court without good cause. Obviously, in a time of peace, such as now, there’s little risk, but tensions are still high. It would only need one insult to incite a skirmish.”

     

                “Oh. So you won’t be able to see your sister?”

     

                Stilling on the sofa, Kara looked down at her, the fading light of dusk making her look bluish and shadowed as her stare cut through Lena like a knife. “We all must make sacrifices for the sake of peace.”

     

                “Is there really so much danger even with the truce?” Lena snorted.

     

                Silent for a moment, Kara set her cup down and then climbed to her feet before stooping down to grab Lena’s arm and haul her up. Blinking in surprise, spilling some of her wine, Lena looked up at her, shrinking back slightly at how close they were. Kara’s face was impassive but there was a look like a brewing storm in her eyes.

     

                “Come. Else your ignorance causes you to offend someone at Court,” she murmured, her tone prickly as she let go of Lena’s arm and stalked off, leaving her wife with the ghost of her touch felt through the thin linen of her shirt.

     

                Lena hesitated, reaching up to touch the spots that felt as if they burned , like salt in a wound, and then followed Kara out of the room. Descending the few towers down to the ground floor, Lena hesitated and watched as Kara waded through the water in her already damp robe, turning and holding out a hand.

     

                “Come.”

     

                “No.”

     

                It was getting dark, the sky a brilliant amber streaked with honey and persimmon as the sun sank behind the trees, leaving twilight falling over the lake. A crescent moon hung low over the dark water, turning the still surface to ink, and the sight of it made Lena shiver with a prickle of unease.

     

                Kara fixed her with a long, searching stare before she walked towards her. “There are things you must see. Your fear of the water blinds you to the real fears beyond the shores.”

     

                Lena’s brow crumpled with confusion and she reached out, allowing Kara to lift her from the steps, silent and stiff as she was carried through the shallow foyer in her arms, Kara holding her almost at arm’s length, revealing the truth about her strength. She waded over to one of those bleached rowing boats knocking against the stone pillar it was tied to and Lena tried to object as she was lowered into it, the puddle of water at the bottom a shock of cold on her bare feet as she was set down on the bench at the stern.

     

                Leaping in beside her, Kara grabbed a paddle from the bottom and untied them, the little rowing boat immediately drifting free of its moorings as Lena huddled in the boat, staring out at the water with trepidation. She hugged her arms to herself and watched as Kara settled down, dipping the end of the paddle into the water and steering them away from the tower with a powerful stroke. Closing her eyes to the sight of so much water surrounding her, Lena startled with every drop that splattered her, no matter how careful Kara was, and she felt the adrenaline pound through her body as her bottom lip trembled.

     

                The hushed sound of the water lapping over sand and earth forced Lena’s eyes open moments before they ran aground. Kara climbed out first, grabbing the prow of the little boat and hauling them further up the bank. Lena remained seated and Kara sank to a crouch beside her, reaching out to touch her arm and then jerking it back as Lena flinched, her eyes sharp as they alighted on her.

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena brusquely replied, “it’s just … cold.”

     

                Kara’s face creased with confusion at Lena’s statement on such a mild evening, but she must have realised it for the lie it was as her expression went blank and she fluidly rose to her feet. Looking down at Lena, she hesitated before offering a hand anyway and Lena eyed it as she grit her teeth, before allowing Kara to help her out. 

     

                She staggered a little, damp mud and grass beneath her feet, and Lena tipped her head back, breathing in deeply. The mingled scents of the reeds and the stagnant water pooling in pockets and the warmth of the day, hot sand and warm apples in the trees, gave her something to focus on for a moment. Bees droned around them, enjoying the last days of summer, and the sound seemed to intensify the silence as they worked their way through the wildflowers near the shore.

     

                “Was that your first time in a boat?” Kara asked.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You should let me take you out more often,” was all the reply Kara offered before gesturing for her to follow.

     

                They moved deeper into the woods, betraying every warning Kara had previously given Lena about straying into the overgrown thickets and glens. She supposed it was alright to do it when she had the tall fae woman with the sword strapped at her waist to protect her, but Lena’s stomach twinged with the ghost of sharp claws rending her abdomen and she inched a little closer to Kara.

     

                They didn’t go far - not far at all. Lena might have ventured so deep herself without fearing what lay further in the ancient forest, the eldritch beasts making their homes in the old pockets where everything was rotting and tainted, and she thought she might be able to see the sun through the gaps in the canopy if it had been during the day. The forest was dim with the encroaching dusk, the deep blue of the sky offering very little light to see by as Lena stumbled and tripped over roots, stopped from sprawling half a dozen times by the quick grasp of her wife reaching out to right her.

     

                Eventually, Kara straightened and called out, a shadow in the dark but no less radiant as though power and strength emanated from her even when she wasn’t limned in gold by the sun. Lena was meeker beside her, shivering from the darkness of the shadows as her eyes adjusted remarkably well to the waning light, still able to distinguish the oak from the elm, from the pine. 

     

                “Nia?”

     

                A fleeting reply came from somewhere nearby and Kara honed in on it, trampling through the underbrush as Lena trailed after her, somewhat skittish as night truly invaded the forest. She had good reason to be wary though because a moment later the darkness lifted a fraction and she watched as Kara stepped over a prone body and drew up short as she realised the person was dead.

     

                Choking on a breath, Lena’s head snapped up to look at Kara, who had turned to watch her reaction, her eyes dark in the night but no less piercing as she took in the shockingly white shade of Lena’s face. There was an air of regret about her, to the flat line of her mouth and the resigned slump of her shoulders, but there was also a firmness to Kara, as if she was determined for Lena to be taught this lesson.

     

                Behind her, in between two thick trunks of yew trees, a younger woman with silken dark hair falling to her waist was coiling a whip near a small fire. She was wearing deep blue with silver armour, wave motifs identifying her as one of the Waterfolk, and Lena wondered if she was one of Kara’s relatives. Perhaps a cousin. Stepping in from the left, a whip thin short man with dark hair and tanned skin stepped forward, hands clasped behind his back and a few dark spots on his face that Lena didn’t recognise for blood, and nodded at Kara.

     

                “We’ve dealt with them,” he said.

     

                “Thank you, Querl,” Kara sighed, rubbing at her cheek as her eyes roamed around the few corpses visible by the sheen of their armour.

     

                “There’s still one left,” Nia said, gesturing off-handedly to a fae man bound and gagged to a slender aspen.

     

                Lena took in the sight of his cropped hair, not unusual from what she’d seen here, but not quite so common as long hair, and the lean hardness of him. He was bleeding at his hairline and his lips were twisted in a sneer, his armour dark with swirling designs of fire etched into the pieces and Lena stared at the golden mask in his lap.

     

                Walking over to him, Kara sank down to a crouch and picked up the mask, eyeing it before she lowered it and cocked her head to the side. Reaching up, she removed the gag. “General Lockwood,” she murmured. “You were supposed to be dead.”

     

                “Not dead, just working for a greater cause,” he said with a grin.

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Kara climbed to her feet and looked over at Nia and Querl. “Have you gotten everything you can?”

     

                Querl nodded, a shadow behind his dark eyes, and Kara nodded. Her shoulders were squared and her eyes mournful as she turned to Lena and walked over to her, guiding her closer to the bound man and then pulling her down to a crouch before him. His eyes drilled into Lena and she felt unsettled by his stare, the violence within him that simmered just below the surface. This was a man sent to kill her, to take her, that much was overwhelmingly clear to her. It made her stomach lurch, panic constricting her chest, and she subconsciously grabbed a fistful of Kara’s robe.

     

                “There’s no place for traitors in either Court,” Kara murmured, turning to look at Lena and then reaching out.

     

                The scraping sound of the dagger being unsheathed made Lena look down to her waist, watching as Kara removed the blade, the edge catching a flicker of light from the small fire that Querl was now stamping out. Lena stared at Kara with a blank look on her face, not comprehending the severity of the moment for a long second, before Kara’s eyes met hers.

     

                “There’s no honour in fighting a defenseless opponent, but there’s no honour in broken vows,” Kara quietly stated before turning to the bound General.

     

                A muscle twitched in Kara’s jaw as she raised the dagger and set the curved edge to the man’s throat and horror dawned on Lena as she watched him raise his chin, offering up an unobstructed path for the dagger. Lena reached out as a small cry fell from her lips, and Kara held an arm out to keep her at bay before she quickly jerked the knife across the man’s throat.

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena watched with wide eyes as blood poured from the man’s cut throat in a river of red, coating Kara’s hands as she held onto him, waiting for him to take his last breath. Once he drew in a final, rattling breath, blood pouring from his mouth and over his chin, turning to ash where it pooled on the ground, Kara let go of him, her movements jerky and stiff as she pushed herself to her feet. 

     

                Remaining on her knees before the corpse, Lena only had eyes for the dead man as her throat closed up. She’d seen her mother drown, dragged down beneath the surface to never come back up, but that had been a panicked moment of fleeing for Lena. She’d never actually watched someone die in such a brutal way, throat coat as he choked on his blood and the light dimmed in his eyes. It was a struggle to even process what she’d just seen as she kept blinking, feeling hollow and confused.

     

                “Come,” Kara said, her voice low and wavering.

     

                Head jerking up to look at her, Lena blinked in surprise, taking in the shaking hand held out to her. It was covered in blood, the other one still clutching the dagger in her fist. Lena hesitated but allowed Kara to pull her to her feet, feeling numb with shock but no more frightened of her than she’d ever been. It was strange but even after watching Kara kill a man, there was something so deeply sad and gentle about her; Lena didn’t believe she’d ever be capable of hurting someone in cold blood.

     

                Even as she faced her now, her eyes trained on Kara’s face, Lena could see the way the act unsettled her. Grim and regal, Kara set the dagger back into the sheath at Lena’s waist and met her eyes for a brief moment before she looked away. Wiping her hands on her robe, Kara nodded to Nia and Querl and then glided off, leaving Lena torn between eyeing the numerous corpses that she realised Kara’s friends must have killed and watching Kara’s retreating figure. She only hesitated for a second before following after her.

     

                As they walked back through the forest, the adrenaline started to wear off and Lena was shaking horribly as she stumbled after Kara, her mind trying to process what she’d seen. By the time reality had managed to sink in, the sound of the lapping water of the lake was audible over the sound of frogs burbling quietly in the reeds. Feeling numb, Lena abruptly stopped as the caustic taste of bile crept up the back of her throat and it was only as she turned and doubled over, vomiting on a moss covered rock near the shore that Kara doubled-back, her fingers suddenly brushed the back of Lena’s neck as she held her hair back for her.

     

                Lena imagined she would have cringed from her touch but she just coughed and spluttered, eyes streaming, and felt a stone of dismay settle in her stomach. Once she was done, she wiped the back of her mouth on the sleeve of her shirt, flecks of blood dotting the sleeve, and she let out a choked sound.

     

                Kara didn’t speak a word as she urged them onwards and helped Lena into the rowing boat before pushing out, bobbing in a stomach-lurching way that threatened to make Lena vomit again into the inky water. Feeling clammy and shaky, Lena huddled in the boat as Kara paddled them across the still surface, the ripples of her paddle disrupting the image of the crescent moon as they cut a path towards the tower, crossing the distance with the ease of someone who’d grown up on the water.

     

                As they knocked against the pillars of the tower, Kara grabbed a rope and leapt out, splashing into the shallow foyer and hauling the boat closer before looping the rope through a rusted ring embedded in the wall. Mooring it, she held a hand out for Lena, who was staring distantly as she trembled. When it became clear she wasn’t going to move, Kara swept in and lifted her from the boat, holding her closely to her chest. Lena tried not to think about the damp blood on her robe, even as it seeped into her linen shirt and made it cling to her skin.

     

                Carrying her across the foyer to the curved staircase, Kara didn’t glance at the pale tree in the middle, the roots webbing through the pale stone that bound it there, creeping across the foyer, and so, didn’t notice how the tree seemed to breathe at Lena’s passing. And Lena had her eyes closed, blind to it all as she endured the disorienting spiralling up through the tower, until she was set down.

     

                Standing on her own two feet, Lena blinked in the light of the brazier and candles, her mouth dry and the sour taste of bile making it hard to swallow. She blinked owlishly and watched as Kara’s eyes appraised her, her mouth a flat line before she disappeared again. Lena’s eyes stung as she blinked back tears, feeling disoriented and drained and she hadn’t moved an inch when Kara returned a few minutes later and reached out to take her hand.

     

                Leading her to the floor with the bathroom, where water was steaming in the tub, Kara left her to undress, the pale imprint of blood on her clothes as they pooled to the floor. Lena’s movements were jerky as she climbed into the tub, the water just a little too hot as it made her skin sting. Submerging herself as if welcoming the fear of drowning to fill the hollowness of witnessing death, Lena stayed submerged until her lungs ached.

     

                Resurfacing, she brushed her hair out of her face and then grabbed soap off the tray beside the tub, scrubbing her skin clean as if she could erase the memory of blood spilling from his neck. After a while, she heard light footsteps on the floor and closed her eyes, feeling raw and weary. Too weary to deal with her supposed wife.

     

                “I’ve brought you clean clothes,” Kara said, the sound of shifting around beyond the screen following as she set the bundle down.

     

                Lena didn’t respond as she rinsed the soap off her arms. She heard Kara sigh softly, followed by a moment of silence before she spoke again, her voice gravelly and strained.

     

                “You understand why I had to, don’t you?” she asked, sounding small and uncertain.

     

                “Yes,” Lena whispered.

     

                “I’m sorry if I frightened you, I-”

     

                Sniffing, Lena struggled to swallow, “you didn’t.”

     

                “There are factions within the Courts. They oppose the truce. You may resent me for leaving you with a stranger all day, but … it was for your own safety. My friends have guarded the tower all day, anticipating an attack from them. I’d hoped … we would be wrong. But this is a lesson for you - this is … it’s serious. Politics are deadly, your life's at stake here. These are the sacrifices I make for peace; committing murder, marrying my enemy. It’s- it’s not easy for me. I don’t enjoy it - there are pieces of myself that have been lost to this cause, in the hope that one day I’ll never pick up a sword again. It’s not this day.”

     

                “I know,” Lena bit back. “You didn’t have to take me out there-”

     

                Then Kara was around the partition, her hair damp and curling around her pale face, the golden light within her dimmed somewhat after their excursion. She’d washed the blood from her hands and wore leggings and a billowing shirt, looking as ordinary as she could without her finery from earlier on. There was a brooding look of sadness and defeat, her blue eyes mournful as she met Lena’s eyes.

     

                Staring back at her, Lena gripped the sides of the tub as if she was anticipating an attack. Instead, Kara fiddled with her fingers, a muscle in her jaw working as she grit her teeth.

     

                “I did . You’re like- you’re like me. Not so long ago … I refused to see the violence, the way the Court was coming apart. My parents died. My aunts and uncles. My cousin. I’m all that’s left of my family, and I had to learn that the hard way. So did you, or else you wouldn’t understand the severity of it.”

     

                Blinking back tears, Lena felt ashamed at how much she cared about someone she’d never met before, a man that had been sent to kill her, to use her as leverage, or as a piece to dispose of. Wiping at her eyes with damp fingers, Lena cleared her throat and Kara let out a long breath, sinking to a knee beside the tub.

     

                She draped one arm over the edge and studied Lena’s pale face before her other hand held a white water lily aloft, twirling the short stem between her fingers. Placing it in the bath, she watched it float and then met Lena’s somewhat apprehensive stare, disbelieving as the moment took an oddly intimate turn.

     

                “A water lily. I’m quite fond of them,” Kara murmured, a pucker forming between her eyebrows. “And what’s your favourite?”

     

                Choking on a laugh at how bizarre the innocuous question was, Lena frowned slightly. “I may have been a florist but I’ve always preferred trees.”

     

                “Oh. Why?”

     

                “A tree struggles to bloom for a year, but people only care about the flowers that bloom quickly. They don’t care about the trees when they finally blossom; they’re too distracted by beautiful things instead of hard work.”

     

                Kara cocked her head to the side and studied her for a moment, her fingers dipping into the bath as her eyes flitted over Lena’s face. Feeling self-conscious at her admission, Lena looked down at the water lily, breaking the tension of the moment. Clearing her throat, Kara swiftly rose to her feet and wiped her fingers on her clean shirt.

     

                “We’re leaving for the Unseelie Court in three days,” Kara informed her. “Autumn is upon us.”

    Chapter 8

                The sky was apricot with golden clouds on the morning of the first day of autumn.

     

                Lena sat cross-legged in her room, bent over the frustrating array of runes as she tried to memorise them, to puzzle through the sounds that Kelly had written down phonetically beside the neat letters. Dawn was only just breaking, the cry of a waterbird keening across the peacefully still lake beyond the open arches, and Lena was enjoying the solitude of the morning, soon to be broken.

     

                “You’re awake.”

     

                Glancing up, Lena set the quill down and rolled her knotted shoulders, her eyes giving Kara a dismissive once-over as she watched her step a short way into the room. “Obviously.”

     

                “What are you doing?” Kara softly enquired, mild curiosity lighting her delicate features as she swiftly crossed over to Lena’s side, glancing down at the pages her wife was quickly trying to hide. “You’re … writing?”

     

                “Kelly taught me some runes,” Lena dismissively replied, shuffling the pages into a pile as she hid the childishly clumsy letters she’d managed to scratch out in blue ink with the swan quill.

     

                “You have an interest in academia?”

     

                Frowning, Lena looked up. “I have an interest in not being bored out of my mind all day.”

     

                Straightening at the sharp annoyance in Lena’s voice, Kara smoothed a hand over the front of her rumpled shirt, beaded with water from her morning foray out onto the lake. She was holding a bundle wrapped in soft grey cotton in her arms and moved to set it down on the sofa behind Lena.

     

                “Then perhaps you should find something which brings you pleasure.”

     

                “What, like paddling around in a little boat?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Lena found it hard to mock Kara at times, her little barbs rolling off her back with little effect. She wasn’t sure if it was a conscientious effort to ignore her on Kara’s part, or whether the fae weren’t accustomed to sarcasm. But no, she knew Kara picked up on her sarcasm, and grew exasperated by it, so it was certainly an effort to ignore Lena’s petulance, which only served to further annoy her.

     

                “You have an interest in plants, no? Perhaps tending to nature would pass the time.”

     

                Gesturing around, Lena resisted the urge to roll her eyes. “As I’m well surrounded by nature, of course.”

     

                “Not here ,” Kara patiently replied. “At the Unseelie Court. As a queen with the same element as you, Lillian has cultivated extensive gardens. Or so Sam tells me.”

     

                “Sam? An Unseelie spy?”

     

                Kara let out a short laugh. “Of a sort. You shall meet her soon; she’s to be our escort through the lands. She’s something of an emissary, although her loyalty lies with the Unseelie, where she grew up.”

     

                “I hadn’t imagined you’d trust anyone from the Unseelie Court.”

     

                “Trust is a strong word. You’re right; I wouldn’t.”

     

                “Not even me?” Lena coyly asked.

     

                Hesitating, Kara fixed her with a piercing stare as a faint smile graced her lips. “Especially not you.”

     

                Spluttering with indignation, not expecting her to answer as such, Lena’s cheeks burned as she scowled. “I don’t trust you either,” she haughtily replied, although it wasn’t altogether true.

     

                Sighing as she paced at a leisurely speed, bare feet scuffing the age-worn stone floor of her home, Kara’s smile grew a fraction. “I hadn’t thought you cared much for my opinion of you.”

     

                “I don’t.”

     

                “Then it won’t offend you to know that my lack of trust in you is due to how unknowable you are.”

     

                She arched an eyebrow as she paused mid-step, glancing over at Lena to gauge her reaction. When she was met with nothing but an indifferent stare, Kara resumed her measured pacing. 

     

                “The Unseelie Court are predictable. They hate my Court, and I hate theirs. We are of the same mind, the same kind, all of us weary of war and mistrustful of peace, yet duty-bound to uphold any truces and treaties made. Now, you . You are unpredictable, you are a threat. I do not trust you, Lena, because I do not believe you will control that hatred for Lillian, your contempt for the half of you that binds you here, and that is dangerous to me. We are not of the same mind, and you’re a threat to both Courts if you decide to sabotage us in our peace. You very well nearly did by leaving.”

     

                Uncrossing her legs as she rose to her feet, Lena gave her a thin smile, eyes narrowing slightly in a contemptuous look. “I think you’ll find that I’m not so unpredictable or unknowable as you imagine. The only thing I want, more than anything in the world, is to be far away from here and even further away from you.”

     

                Kara flinched slightly, drawing herself up taller, her spine straight and shoulders back, before she cleared her throat, trying not to react, to give Lena what she clearly wanted to fuel her annoyance. Waving a hand dismissively at the bundle, Kara half-turned away from her, her profile limned in the golden morning sunlight.

     

                “Your new garments,” she murmured. “We leave as soon as our escort arrives.”

     

                Suppressing a sigh, Lena’s curiosity for the better of her the moment Kara was out of her room, her fingers quickly untying the bundle to reveal clothes in varying shades of greens. Linen, leather, velvet, cotton and silk slid through Lena’s fingers as she took stock of everything - the britches and shirts, the cloaks and soft dresses, the stark white nightshirts and jerkins, bodices and skirts. All of it was embroidered and more beautiful than anything she’d ever owned herself, delicate patterns of leaves and flowers and thorns, small bees and birds and other little creatures, beaded with diamonds, emeralds, amethysts and jade. She had half a mind to show up in Kara’s shirt and britches, in water motifs with no finery.

     

                Instead, she washed clean from the basin and selected one of the fluid dresses, the thin cotton of it soft against her skin, the sage green of it making her eyes pale and piercing. She fiddled with the layers of the skirts, of the undergarments, feeling restless as she paced, fishing out the jewellery tucked away in her room and slipping rings onto her fingers and toying with the circlet as she resorted to pacing. Her letters were abandoned in favour of the knots her stomach tied itself into, preoccupying Lena’s mind.

     

                A while later, while she was standing close to the edge of an open archway, her stomach swooping with sickening nerves as the wind snatched at her and she watched the lake ripple with the force of it, Kara stepped inside. Lena didn’t notice her arrival at first, but turned at the first sound of a scuffing foot, quickly jerking away from the edge as the thought of falling, plummeting down to the lake, made her shiver.

     

                “You’ll need to wear a cloak,” Kara said, noticing the shiver.

     

                Lena hummed, running her hands over the arms of her dress, the sleeves ballooning slightly before they cinched at the cuffs. She eyed Kara, taking in the rare display of wealth and luxury in her blue dress, a pattern of silver raindrops dropping down to the swirling waves at the hem. Pearls beaded the dull blue of the fabric, and Kara had a cloak already thrown over the top, her sword sheathed at her waist and as many rings and jewels as Lena. It was a show for both of them, and neither looked pleased, although Kara looked radiant, her long hair threaded with silver and quartz and the circlet she’d worn the day they’d met on that bridge.

     

                Fiddling with her own rings, Lena warily watched as Kara ducked her head down, gliding a step forward as she shrugged beneath the weight of her cloak, adjusting it at the clasp and then resting her hand on the hilt of her sword as she looked up. Her eyes were piercing and firm and her mouth a flat line as she hesitated, taking a step forward.

     

                “I know that we don’t trust each other,” she murmured, a grave look on her face. “You’re evidently not fond of me, and I admit that you get the better of me at times, which I don’t like. But we shall have no friends in the Unseelie Court, no one to aid us in the coming season, and so … we shall need each other, I think.”

     

                Lena looked at her with surprise and Kara gave her a strained smile, worry flickering in the depths of her eyes. When she reached out and cupped Lena’s shoulders in her hands, Lena didn’t shrink from her touch, a perplexed look clouding her face as she swallowed, her mouth dry.

     

                “We’re not friends, but we’re bound to each other,” Kara continued, “and so, perhaps we should agree to be allies. For a time.”

     

                “Allies?” Lena echoed, a hesitant note in the word.

     

                After a moment, she nodded, somewhat reserved and wary, her eyes darting up to meet Kara’s. It would be just the two of them, as it had been for Lena for weeks now, but she was realising that Kara was losing a whole network of friends and family, allies and retainers and soldiers. A sudden jolt of panic shot through her at the realisation that they were giving up the relative safety of Kara’s lands and her pretty tower and her lake for the wild danger of the Unseelie Court. They would have no one but each other - no guards or friends or hope of help if anyone came against them. Nothing but Lillian’s word that the truce would be upheld.

     

                Kara seemed to deflate a little and nodded, giving Lena’s shoulders a quick squeeze before she dropped her hands. Her eyes gave Lena an appraising once-over before she gestured to the vanity. “Come. I’ll braid your hair for you.”

     

                Sitting without complaint, although Lena hated having her hair done, she allowed Kara to gently brush her dark hair until it was silken. She was gentle, a little apprehensive even, and Lena tried not to shiver at the touch of her slender fingers smoothing over it, carefully plucking and twisting strands until Lena was left with an intricate web of braids woven with silver and tiny gemstones. Setting the circlet on her brow, Kara stepped back and viewed her work.

     

                “There. Now you look the part.”

     

                Lena had never wanted to look less like the part but murmured her thanks before she gathered up her cloak and pulled it around her shoulders. Fiddling with the clasp, she frowned and peered down at the heavy velvet, struggling against the weight of it until Kara clicked her tongue and walked over to her.

     

                “Here.”

     

                She fastened it with ease and then shifted the fabric forward, pulling it around Lena so it enveloped her in a deep green, warm and heavy. Lena nodded, looking a little pale, and she shifted the sheathed dagger at her waist as she cleared her throat.

     

                “My clothes …”

     

                “I shall fetch you a chest to pack after breakfast. We should be off then.”

     

                Following her down to the dining room, Lena sat at one end, in what was now her chair, while Kara sat at the other end.
