Eating warm oats and slivers of crisp green apples, drinking hot tea and buttering freshly baked bread, they avoided speaking, and it wasn’t until the sound of splashing footsteps sounded that Kara reacted to any of her surroundings. A shout called out and Kara called back in a flutter of incomprehensible words as Lena studiously ate.

     

                A moment later, Alex was standing there in her armour, her eyes skipping over Lena and landing on her sister before she took a seat near Kara and dragged a bowl of tiny waterfowl eggs, boiled and still in their shells, closer and began peeling one with deft fingers. 

     

                “You’re ready?”

     

                “As ever.”

     

                “You’re sure-”

     

                “I have given my word, Alex,” Kara softly interrupted, a firmness to her as she nodded slightly. “It was I who volunteered my services to the Council; I will not falter now. It is for peace.”

     

                Looking grim and anxious, a muscle twitched in Alex’s jaw as she looked over at Lena and found her watching closely. She said something in their fae language and Lena took a bite of her bread, tuning them out as she basked in the fading moments of peace. She wouldn’t return until winter had broken.

     

                “Trust is a thing forged,” Kara replied in English, her voice weary and gentle. “I have no cause to believe that I will be betrayed in this truce. By anyone.”

     

                Her eyes darted over to Lena, who was staring back at her with blank indifference before a slow smile twitched the corners of her mouth. There was a challenge to it, a sharpness that made Kara raise her eyebrows a fraction, seeing right through Lena’s goading smile.

     

                “We should pack,” Kara said after a few more minutes of disgruntled conversation with her sister.

     

                A chest was waiting in Lena’s room as she went on ahead, a teacup in hand and a weariness to her steps. Pale wood banded in bronze, it was open for her to deposit her belongings inside. All Lena had was her brand new clothes and she tucked them in with care before hesitating and adding the bundle of paper, quill and ink pot she’d been using that morning. What else would there be to do?

     

                “We must go.”

     

                Kara was standing on the stairs, ducking her head inside with a grim look on her face as she beckoned to Lena. Closing the chest and locking it, Lena reached down to pick it up and jumped slightly as Kara was suddenly beside her, relieving her of it with ease.

     

                “Go.”

     

                Nodding, Lena went on ahead, reaching the bottom and hesitating on the steps. Alex waited at the bottom and gestured for Lena to go to her, but she refused, remaining on the steps as Kara plodded down after her, laden with the box. Quietly cursing at the realisation that Lena wouldn’t step into the water of her own free will, Kara set the chest down and scooped her up, a small squawk escaping Lena as she scrambled to hold onto her wife.

     

                Splashing through the water, Kara set her down in one of the small rowing boats, where her own chest was stowed, and then went back for Lena’s. Climbing in, the sopping hem of her dress and cloak soaking the bottom of the boat, Kara untied them and pushed them free of the tower. Alex loped along the submerged stepping stones, quicker than Kara rowed them, and Lena looked back at the tower and the bare tree in the foyer with a pang of regret. She couldn’t believe it, but she would actually miss it there.

     

                Kara beached them on the banks of the lake, stepping into soft mud and grass before lifting Lena from the boat and setting her down on a patch of grass. Their horses were already waiting for them, and Lena wondered how they were managing to take their belongings with them as she looked for a cart. Hauling the boat up by the rope, Kara left their trunks there.

     

                “You’ll see to their delivery?”

     

                “I’d hand deliver them if they would let me through,” Alex grumbled, her worry evident in her brown eyes. 

     

                Lena observed the exchange and could sense Kara’s worry too, her uneasiness and reluctance to leave her home, her sister. They said their goodbyes, foreheads touching, tight hugs and murmured words before Kara relinquished her hold. She stepped into the shallows of the lake and cupped a handful of water, letting the droplets run through her fingers as morning sunshine spun her hair into threads of gold, and then walked over to Lena’s side. 

     

                “Alex and Kelly will be our guards to the river border. Nia and Querl will scout, and Sam will guide us. We should be fine, but news of the terms of the truce will have spread and people will know we’re to leave today. If anything happens …”

     

                Kara trailed off, a muscle jumping in her jaw as she clenched her teeth and then continued. “If anything happens, go with Alex or Kelly. Do not go to the Unseelie.”

     

                There was a frantic urgency to Kara’s words that made Lena frown, opening her mouth to question her further. Kara didn’t tell her, but if she was felled, she would have Lena be a bargaining chip for them to use than let back in Lillian’s clutches. Keeping that to herself though, she gave Lena a stern look, eyebrows raised in a silent question to whether she understood.

     

                “Plotting treason against my Queen?”

     

                Kara turned to look at the woman riding in on a dark horse, absent her leathers in favour of the robe she wore. A smile crossed Sam’s face as she came to a stop, shifting on horseback as she surveyed the party. Lena blanched, the blood draining from her face as stared at Reign, at the familiar hunter who terrified her, if she was being honest. She almost tripped over her feet in her haste to retreat.

     

                “It’s alright,” Kara murmured, her hands reaching out to balance Lena. “Sam is a friend.”

     

                “No, she’s not,” Lena hotly replied, her body tensed with panic as she shrank back, her hands grabbing fists of Kara’s velvet cloak as she slipped behind her, potentially prepared to use her body as a shield.

     

                She knew the hunter, the woman in leathers, a hardness to her face and her steel grip as she hauled Lena through the forest, stealing her from her home. It made her shiver with a prickle of fear, those memories of that twilight as she tried to run, only to be dragged back, the unease that threaded through the trees as something sinister lingered in the lengthening shadows. That moment had been the catalyst for all of this. If Lena had never been dragged into the forest, it never would have burrowed back beneath her skin, making itself at home in the places it had rested when she was a child, like a second skin that bound her to the place.

     

                Maybe she would have still had her shop and her home if it wasn’t for Reign. As it was, Lena knew the creature before her well enough to make up her own mind, regardless of how Kara viewed her. Still, there was something off about her, dressed in the deepest shade of purple, her hair tumbling around her shoulders and a softness to her face. Alex let out a short laugh and Lena wanted to push her into the lake, wondering why everyone was just standing around.

     

                “Forgive me,” Sam murmured, a sadness to her hazel eyes as she pressed a hand to her head and bowed slightly. “You’ll be familiar with one half of me, but … my sisters and I, we’re split. One might explain it as bouts of madness, slipping from one person to another as we slip between Courts. We have our loyalties to both, although the Queen keeps us close at hand for her own benefit.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena frowned as a flicker of surprise shot through her. “You have a personality disorder?”

     

                Sam’s eyes flickered to Kara with a question. Stepping from before her, Kara rounded on Lena and narrowed her eyes with confusion. “Then you’re familiar with this … affliction?”

     

                “Not really. I just know of it.”

     

                “I would have thought you wouldn’t know of it. I mean, to whom do humans split their loyalty between?”

     

                Mouth closing as she furrowed her brow, Lena hummed softly. “Okay, now you’ve lost me. Having multiple personalities is a- a mental health disorder. What do you mean by loyalty?”

     

                “Sam was born to Seelie and Unseelie fae. Her loyalty is split between the Courts, her oaths are to both. She cannot disobey either side, which makes her an effective emissary. That’s why she was sent to fetch you, along with her brethren born of similar circumstances.”

     

                “I don’t think we’re thinking of the same thing,” Lena slowly replied, feeling even more confused.

     

                “No? It’s of little consequence. Sam and Reign are two distinct people; you shall learn to love the friend that shines through and be wary around the hunter forged by your- Lillian. As it is, Sam is here to guide us through the lands of both Courts. She, who has the freedom to come and go as she pleases with little interference.”

     

                Still somewhat wary, Lena skirted around her to the horse that Kara gestured her towards. She was helped up onto its back and Kara hauled herself up behind Lena, shifting her forward and encircling her in her embrace, their thighs touching and the warmth of her palpable through their cloaks. It was becoming unnervingly familiar to be on a horse with her, and Lena knew that it was only out of a necessity for them to ride swiftly without Lena falling off every five minutes. She was no seasoned rider herself, and even though the extra weight would slow them down, it would be quicker in the long run and less risky than Lena riding alone.

     

                “Remember what I said,” Kara murmured in her ear, so close that it made Lena sit rigidly, her skin prickling with goosebumps. 

     

                She barely made a vague sound of acknowledgement before they were setting off, hooves digging into grass and lurching into the forest. Lena glanced back over her shoulder for one last glimpse of the tower, the white stone glimmering like a spike of pearl thrust against the pale sky. Turning back around, she tried to force herself to relax, limiting the soreness of the long ride ahead.

     

                Sam took the point, followed by Kelly and then Lena and Kara, with Alex bringing up the rear, and none of them spoke as they set a quick pace, alternating between galloping, trotting and walking to make sure they didn’t push the horses too hard. All of them were vigilant and Lena felt uneasiness wind through her as she watched the trees. 

     

                The deeper they travelled, the older and larger everything grew, the trees that had clustered near the banks of the lake now spaced further apart, looming huge and impenetrable around them as they picked their way over thick roots and sloping ground. Lena barely dared to breathe, the sunlight struggling to pierce the heavy canopy overhead, and what little that came through tinted green, and she felt her skin prickle with the feeling of being watched.

     

                “Kara-”

     

                “I know,” she replied, her voice low and tight, frustration colouring her words. “Don’t say a word.”

     

                Swallowing her fear as she kept her eyes trained straight ahead, she heard the growl of some distant creature, heard a muffled scream. An eerie howl wound through the trees, chilling, and Alex shouted something over her shoulder. Kara’s arm tightened around Lena’s waist and she hunched protectively over her, moments before a strange buzzing sound filled Lena’s ears, followed by the thwack of something driving home into a tree.

     

                A strangled sound came from further behind them, lurking in the dimness of the dark forest, and Lena squeezed her eyes shut. There was a tremble in the ground and the air felt foul to her, so close and humid as her skin prickled with sweat, the taste of the air so tangibly green . Opening her eyes again, Lena was met with the sight of a tangled snarl of bare branches and thick underbrush, thorns and roots blocking them in, the trees somewhat menacing in a way that led Lena to believe there was a sentience about them.

     

                But Sam was in front and her hands blossomed with fire a moment later, burning everything that lay before them as the temperature turned blisteringly hot. Lena sucked in a searing hot breath, gasping a little as it got caught in her chest, and watched as one of those terrifying wolves shot past, fur on fire and filling the trees with the smell of burning, rotten flesh. A spear struck home in its ribs a moment later and someone cut across on horseback before wheeling around and changing the trajectory of their charge.

     

                A snarl built in Kara’s throat and Lena ducked down over the horse’s neck, too concerned with making herself as small as possible, to process what Kara was doing behind her. But she heard the sound of grating metal unsheathed and felt Kara move behind her, her warmth fading.

     

                “Keep going,” Kara murmured, her hand grabbing a fistful of Lena’s cloak as she crouched on the back of the horse, her eyes tracking the rider as they made a beeline for them at an angle.

     

                “Kara. Don’t,” came Alex’s sharp shout, riding parallel to her sister with a bow in hand, an arrow knocked.

     

                She didn’t even look as she sent an arrow loose, taking a man in the chest, her eyes drilling into her sister as her face hardened. There was a tight look of disapproval in the sharp lines of Alex’s severe expression and Lena looked at her, eyes wide and questioning as she gripped the horse’s mane, wondering what was happening behind her that she couldn’t see.

     

                Lena didn’t have to wonder for long as the hand gripping her cloak suddenly vanished and a blur of blue dove past her, right as the oncoming rider came within range. Kara slammed into the woman in the saddle, tackling her out of it and dragging her down to the forest floor. A cry slipped past Lena’s lips as she watched with wide eyes, clueless and helpless as she blew past Kara, craning her neck over her shoulder to watch. 

     

                Gripping the mane, Lena made to pull the horse around, unsure of how to make it stop or listen to her, and as she watched Kara land a fist in the woman’s face, she felt a jerk on her sleeve, someone bumping into her. 

     

                “Don’t you dare stop,” Alex growled at her, releasing Lena’s arm so she could pull a small knife from the strap across her chest and fling it into the eye of another wolf, which let out a keening cry.

     

                Helpless to do anything but carry on, wondering if now was the moment she went with Alex to be spirited away to some secret home, away from Lillian, allowing war to inevitably break out. The wind whistled behind her, a fierce gale as Kelly sent a vortex of high-speed winds through the trees, a branch cracking somewhere, rebels buffeted backwards and a monstrous wolf sinking to a crouch as its muzzle pulled back in a snarl.

     

                Closing her eyes again, Lena grit her teeth and let her horse follow after Sam, Alex close behind with Kelly still in the rear. She didn’t know if Kara was still alive or not, didn’t know how to feel about it either way, but no one else seemed to be panicking beyond a normal amount, so Lena just clung to the horse and hoped the arrows whipping past would miss. She followed the others up to the bridge - not the one she’d been wed on, but an ancient one, with pitted stones and stains of lichen as a narrow stream gurgled under the single arch, bitter cold water meandering along.

     

                Behind her, she heard a shout. No, not entirely behind, but up as well. Glancing over her shoulder as the horse pounded over the bridge, Lena watched as a slim shadow dropped from a branch overhead, sword held point downward and streaming down to the wolf stepping into the water. Kara slammed down on the back of it, sword driving into the back of its neck, and then lost her grip and flipped into the stream.

     

                Relief flooded through Lena, much to her surprise, and she managed to bring herself to a stop, much to Alex’s angry shout as she blew past her. Watching as Kara resurfaced, spitting dank water as she wrenched her sword from the corpse of the wolf, Lena’s horse stomped a hoof, anxious to be off again. She watched as Kelly crossed the bridge, slowing as she brought her arm up and then sliced it down, compressed air slamming into the old stones and breaking them apart as they collapsed into the stream.

     

                One hit Kara’s shoulder, knocking her off-balance, and she staggered around, up to her waist and brimming with violence, before her eyes alighted on Lena. A scowl darkened her face and she threw up a hand, a wall of water rising from the stream as Lena watched on with increasing shock, everything so overwhelming, so unreal and inhuman that she thought she might pass out. With a dash of her hand, Kara sent the wave of water crashing over the fae pursuers, only one of them managing to part it with their own skill, before she was clambering up the riverbank and springing up behind Lena, digging her heels into the horse’s flank before Lena could react.

     

                Soaking wet and brimming with adrenaline and anger, Kara gripped her tightly with her left arm, sword held aloft in her right. “I told you to go.”

     

                Sharp retort dying on her tongue with the speed they were moving, swerving around wide trunks, jumping over roots and narrow gullies, reckless but frantic as they made for the main river bisecting the two Courts. Lena bounced on the horse’s back, jolting with pain as she stiffly held on, listening to the sounds fade behind them, their retinue falling back in, looking strained and stony with concentration.

     

                They crossed into the Unseelie Court with little fanfare and no further problems, except that Alex and Kelly suddenly peeled away, their parting shouts falling behind them as they stayed on one side of the bridge and the remaining trio crossed over. A moment later, two dark shadows emerged on horseback and Lena’s stomach lurched at the sight of Purity and Pestilence, as menacing as the first time they’d come for her.

     

                Only two more attacks waylaid them on the way through the rather more overgrown and wild lands of the Unseelie Court, dispatched with ease as Lena watched Pestilence wrap a man in thorny vines and tear him to pieces with the mere wave of her hand. It was horrifying but effective and the small attempts at rebellion, at war were squashed by the hunters as they made a protective trio around Lena and Kara.

     

                An hour after the last attack they started to slow, and Lena felt a stab of relief that the trip was nearly at an end. Noon had come and gone and she was hungry, stiff, tired and cold as they trampled through a grassy patch, the ground littered with mushy brown apples from the laden trees, shorter and squatter in this patch. A myriad of dosy bees meandered drunkenly over the fruit, their hum filling the space as the air filled with the sweet, rotting smell.

     

                Onwards they continued, until the trees and bushes became interspersed with flowers and groves of fruit trees and wild herbs. The air was perfumed with lemon, geranium leaves, hyacinths and narcissi, patches of colour propping up in the dimness as the trees started thinning out. Lena felt every muscle tense as individual trees resolved themselves out of the shadowy mass ahead, the dread growing with each heavy footfall of the four horses. 

     

                As they finally entered the boundary of the sprawling palace grounds, it was all pale shafts of sunlight peeking through the canopy, wisteria hanging in thick clusters from stone buildings built around thick trees, fae lounging on sun-warmed stone, their soft voices, light laughter and the trilling sound of flutes and lyres drifting through the trees. It was all so beautiful, but that was part of the lie, and Lena saw right through it.

     

                It felt as if the palace hid something foul under its lovely exterior; beneath the smell of blooming lilacs, something was in the last stages of decay, a rotten core to the place that started with their Queen. 

     

                They went along a large bed of violets, dismounting after a while and walking barefoot along the path, the two women hedged in by the hunters and trailed by curious fae. Feeling as if she was there for the first time all over again, escorted through the winding paths of the sprawling palace, eyes watching her from shadowed corners, exuding so much hostility that it brought a lump to Lena’s throat.

     

                Hearing the water first, much like last time, Lena soon found herself in that strange grotto, the pond of water half-claimed by the wide oak’s roots. It was bathed in sunlight instead of moonlight like the first time she had been there, dappled green light spilling onto the throne nestled amidst the roots as swans ruffled their feathers and ravens darkened the branches overhead. There was the sweet smell of decay laced with stagnant water from the pond and Lena’s stomach turned as she watched Lillian climb to her feet.

     

                In her absence, Lena had forgotten how tall she was. Six-foot and radiating power, her thorny crown on her head and a dress of deep purple, like the darkest shade of foxglove, poisonous but beautiful. A sharp smile crossed her face and Kara stood beside Lena as they came to a halt before her. Kara gave her a curt half-bow, while Lena stood rooted to the spot, aware of Lords and Ladies lazing about in patches of sunlight or deep shade, amusing themselves with wine and chatter in their Queen’s midst. It was silent now, the atmosphere tense.

     

                “My daughter,” Lillian proclaimed, spreading her arms in a welcoming manner, although there was a hint of mockery and mirth in her chilling voice. “Returned to me at last. Come, you may kiss your mother’s ring.”

     

                Bristling, Lena was equally as haughty and cold, scorn taking the place of mockery in her reply. “I would but I believe she’s at the bottom of a lake.”

     

                Kara’s hand snapped out and grabbed Lena’s arm, squeezing tightly, a warning. Lillian just let out a laugh, the sound airy and nonchalant, but her pale eyes told another story. Lena just jerked her chin up a fraction, stubborn as anything.

     

                “Ah, it seems your manners are in need of some refinery. How so like the Seelie to allow such vulgarity. But it has been a long trip; you must be tired.”



                Lillian snapped her fingers and gestured sharply and Lena watched as that young woman who’d cared for her last time peeled off from the sidelines. Her blue eyes were piercing and playful as she smiled, arching an eyebrow, and she gave Lillian a flourishing curtsy, while Kara gave another stiff bow. They were dismissed.

     

                Following their attendant, Lena felt stiff and somewhat terrified, this time knowing exactly what she was getting herself into. The whole place felt beautifully deceptive and the thought of three months trapped inside the pretty prison, sitting amongst the rotting flowers and ominous trees, was almost too much to bear.

     

                “You should not have done that,” Kara muttered as she stared ahead, walking beside Lena down the narrow path bordered by brambles.

     

                Giving her a sharp look, Lena sneered slightly. “No? Perhaps I’m less of a coward than you are, if you’re afraid of her.”

     

                Even as she said it, Lena knew her words were hollow and childish. Kara, who was damp and a shade less grand than she’d hoped to appear before her enemies, who’d brawled in the dirt and was splattered with bloodstains and had commanded a stream at a whim. She wasn’t a coward and they both knew it. Lena was just angry and had no one else to be spiteful towards.

     

                “Your quarters, Princess.”

     

                The woman - Andrea, Lena remembered her name being - gestured to the closed doors. Lena reached for the handle and opened it to the room beyond, expansive and opulent, and dim. She never thought she’d miss the airy tower with its lack of proper walls and the water beyond, but the stone room carved underground, with no windows, was suffocating. 

     

                “If you’ll follow me, my Lady,” Andrea was saying to Kara.

     

                “I’ll have quarters near my wife,” Kara objected, remaining rooted to the spot.

     

                “Your rooms have already been prepared for you elsewhere. These rooms are for the Queen and her family.”

     

                Giving her a placid smile, Kara’s posture seemed relaxed and harmless, but her hand still rested on the pommel of her sword and there was blood on her soft face.

     

                “I believe I now belong to the Queen’s family,” Kara said, casually gesturing to Lena. “And if I’ll not have quarters with my wife, I shall have them as near as possible.”

     

                Smile hitching higher as she cocked her head to the side, Andrea cleared her throat and then ducked her head. “As you wish. You may present your case to Her Majesty herself, as she designated the rooms herself.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara sensed a test and nodded. “Let’s not waste time then. I’m in much need of a bath; the forest is positively feral on this side of the river.”

     

                “Is it?” Andrea mildly asked. “I heard the sound of wolves could be heard miles away to the west, but perhaps the Queen’s intelligence was wrong.”

     

                “Must be,” Kara curtly replied. “After you.”

     

                As Andrea set off, Kara glanced over at Lena, who was standing just inside her room. Reaching out, Kara grabbed the door handle and pulled it shut, leaving Lena alone.

     

                Muscles suddenly going slack, Lena sat down heavily on a divan and buried her face in her hands. A fire lit the room, the smell of wood smoke somewhat pleasant, although it lacked the salty tang of Kara’s driftwood. She eyed the space, taking in the woven tapestries and rugs, the blankets and the rooms leading off the sitting room, one with a gigantic bed and another with an office and full shelves. 

     

                Eventually, Lena’s curiosity got the better of her and she rifled through her thighs, finding clothes in her size already filling trunks, unfurled maps of the Unseelie Court lands, the designated borders of pieces given to Lords and Ladies notes, picked up carved pieces of marble to observe them and sniffed the flower arrangements. It was homely in an unnerving way, just another enticing thing convincing her she’d be happy there.

     

                Making her way back out to the sitting room, Lena found a tray laden with delicacies on the round dining table. A small sugar loaf with cherry preserves, a steaming pot of dandelion tea and fresh peaches, so soft that she bruised the skin picking one up and took a bite. Pouring herself a glass of blackberry wine as she overlooked the tea, Lena took a sip and wished it was something stronger.

     

                Left to her own devices, Lena passed the remainder of the afternoon alone. It had already been creeping towards dusk by the time they’d arrived, and although she had no windows to see, she knew when night had settled over the palace. There was a hushed quality to the place, a hum in the ground and the walls that let her know that the day was winding down.

     

                A short while later, dinner was brought to her on a tray, and Lena was relieved to know that she wasn’t expected to dine with Lillian. She half expected Kara to show up as she dug into the pheasant and potatoes, the carrots and parsnips and leeks so filling as she ate her first proper meal since dawn. Her wife remained absent though, and Lena wondered whether she’d won the battle of her quarters or if she was currently tucked away in some forgotten corner of the palace. Strangely, Lena hoped she was nearby, enjoying her own meal and close enough for Lena to find her if necessary.

     

                As the evening wore on and Lena drank more of the blackberry wine, staining her lips a deep purple as it started affecting her in an odd manner, Lena decided she wanted a bath. Saddle-sore, aching from head to toe, and feeling dirty from the cold sweat that had made her feel clammy all day, she stepped out of her room and stopped the first fae she saw to ask for directions to the hot pool she’d been brought to last time.

     

                The young girl led her right to the baths, which turned out to be a collection of different rooms with pools of varying sizes. Asking for the smallest one, Lena slipped inside and was greeted by a humid wall of heat. Quickly shutting the door behind her, she exhaled softly.

     

                The bath steamed and the air was fragrant with flower petals as Lena shed her clothes, the soft cotton and heavy velvet sliding from her skin with relief as she rolled her shoulders, feeling light. The room was bathed in the warm glow of the braziers and Lena dipped her fingers into the water, the heat making her rush to climb in when she found it pleasantly warm. It was milky and whatever herbs and flowers they’d used to perfume it felt slightly oily against her skin as she sank down into the deep bath.

     

                One thing that was an improvement here was the baths, that much Lena could agree with. There was no waiting for the water to heat, no narrow tub, just a multitude of hot springs ready for her to slip into. Of course, she went for one of the smaller ones, one of the ones where she could touch the floor standing, where she could reach for the sides with ease, as opposed to the one she’d found herself in the first time she’d been trapped at the Unseelie Court.

     

                Lena didn’t want to think about that though. Didn’t want to linger on the idea of being trapped in this place for an entire season, three months of being surrounded by strangers. At least with Kara, they had been alone - Lena hadn’t even entertained the idea that there were perhaps small towns grown from the very foundations of the forest and mountains and lakes - but here, there were so many people that the idea was overwhelming. Even if it had just been Lillian, Lena imagined that would have been too much to bear as it was. 

     

                Gritting her teeth, she closed her eyes and held her breath, slipping beneath the water as she tried to empty her mind. She could smell lavender and sage, a hint of lemon from the bobbing slices and the musky sweetness of rose petals as they clung to her skin, yet none of it was enough to make Lena’s muscles unwind as she drifted. She couldn’t help herself; she was so on edge that she was irritable and sharp, a vicious edge to her waiting to lash out at the first unsuspecting person to cross her path. It was a leftover response to years spent alone, spent cycling through homes and families, her defences a necessary part of her survival, and she knew that she was in more danger at Court now than she’d ever been in her life.

     

                And yet, she enjoyed her bath with the ignorance of someone who evidently had not been raised at Court. She’d snubbed Lillian as her mother before everyone, as if it was a petulant argument between a parent and their child, easily forgotten about, brushed aside in light of Lena’s reluctance to be there. But she was there, basking in the heat of the bath as she made the grave error of thinking she would be safe there as part of the truce. No one would kill her when it would mean breaking the tenuous peace between the Courts, one that had only just been established.

     

                As she submerged herself again, skin turning a delicate shade of pink as steam curled around her, Lena was deafened to the quiet sounds of the door opening and bare feet crossing the stone floor of the space. When she resurfaced, drawing in a breath as she wiped the water out of her eyes and got her feet under her, Lena felt strong fingers wrap around her throat before she could even process that someone was there.

     

                It happened so quickly, her deep breath, the bite of fingers digging into her throat, and then the taste of the sweetened water filling her mouth as scrabbled at the hand holding her underwater. Panic shot through Lena - no, it was worse than panic, this was the stuff of nightmares, her biggest fear brought to life, old memories of watching her mother thrash in that small lake as three fae beings killed her at the orders of a spiteful Queen. And now it was her turn to thrash, struggling as she kicked water everywhere, her lungs burning with the desire for air, her teeth grit as her nails gouged into the back of the hands and wrists holding her beneath the surface.

     

                In the end, she inhaled, which was perhaps the biggest mistake she could have made, her body bucking beneath the water, kicking the legs of whoever was in the bath with her, holding her under. It was a feeble kick, the one of someone drowning, who was running out of oxygen as her vision dimmed, the orangeish glow above her furring around the edges.

     

                And then she was being hauled up, choking and retching as water streamed off her, her hair plastered around her face as she blinked back black spots. Throat on fire as she drew in short, rapid breaths, her chest rising and falling quickly as she gripped the wrist of her would-be murderer for support. Lena barely had a chance to collect her bearings before another hand grabbed a fistful of her dark hair and yanked her back.

     

                Breathing shallowly as the stone edge of the pool bit into the back of her neck, Lena balanced herself with her hands against the rough stone walls of the bath, her eyes darting around wildly, the whites of her eyes clearly visible as she tried to make sense of the dim room. She found herself staring at Sam - or rather Reign, as she was known to the Unseelie - dressed in her black leathers, up to her waist in the hot water, the lines of her body taut with violence. 

     

                The cold edge of a knife touched her throat then, yanking her head back further to expose the pale length of her neck, and Lena’s breaths turned more panicked as her chest rose and fell quickly. She knew it was a knife purely based on the violence of it all, and wondered whether this was a threat or an assassination as her whole body tensed with anticipation of either outcome. There was no point fighting, so Lena waited. Only for a moment.

     

                “It seems I haven’t made myself clear, daughter,” Lillian’s cold voice murmured in her ear, brittle but laced with amusement as the knife she wielded bit a little deeper. “If you were under any assumption that you have any free will here, that you could defy me in my own court, you thought very wrong. Now, I know things may be difficult for a half-breed to comprehend, and perhaps being raised away from Court has made you rather dense, but let me spell it out for you very clearly.”

     

                Despite the ice-cold anger in her mother’s voice, Lena felt a flicker of relief, the tension fading just a little. Lillian wouldn’t kill her unless she offered no purpose or was too much of a hassle to contain, which meant that Lena wasn’t going to die there, dragged beneath the water as she choked for air until her lungs filled and her heart stopped. Still, she didn’t move a muscle, didn’t speak as she breathed shallowly and tried to slow her pounding heart, her pulse fluttering at her jugular. 

     

                She swallowed thickly and felt her throat bob beneath the pressure of the knife. Cold fear coiled around her spine and Lena was helpless as she listened, her throat aching, inevitably going to bruise, and she didn’t dare speak. Before her, Reign was trailing a hand through the water, her hazel eyes trained on Lena’s shockingly pale face, thick steam swirling up to her elbow as the water became uncomfortably hot. Beneath the surface, Lena thought she could see guttering flames and bubbles obscuring the hunter’s hand.

     

                “You will do exactly as I tell you to. You may have been wed off to that backwater Seelie with her little pond, but you are mine to do with as I wish. Your use to me is contingent on how well you follow orders, and in the event that I find that you have no use to me anymore, I’ll dispose of you without hesitation. I have no qualms about getting my own hands dirty in that event, so listen closely; obey or else you’ll find yourself with a red smile across your throat. I’m not to be trifled with, I can assure you. Have I made myself understood?”

     

                The knife was curved and Lena could feel every inch of its length as Lillian dug it in a little further, her hand pulling hard on Lena’s hair. “I have asked you a question, daughter.”

     

                Lena floundered for a moment, breathless with her fear as her lips numbly moved. “Y- yes. Yes,” she rasped, her voice barely audible as it hitched.

     

                “Yes, what?”

     

                “Your Majesty.”

     

                Lillian clicked her tongue impatiently. “Again.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena shut her eyes and clamped her lips shut. Inhaling sharply, she swallowed her burning anger and exhaled softly. “Yes, mother.”

     

                “Better,” Lillian murmured, her fingers relinquishing their tight grasp on Lena’s hair as she tenderly stroked the soaking locks.

     

                She heard her shift to her feet behind her, the sharp edge of the blade vanishing, and Lena hunched forward, her shoulders taut as she curled in on herself, a shaky hand going to her throat. 

     

                “Get to bed,” Lillian instructed her, her voice sharp and commanding. “You will rise early for your lessons. It seems your wife has been negligent in your education.”

     

                Lena didn’t turn her head to look at her, just stared ahead at the hunter standing in the water a few feet from her, half anticipating her to start drowning her again. Reign just smiled at her, all signs of the softer woman from that morning gone, something predatory taking its place as she raised her hand, orange tongues of flame solidifying at her fingertips before she blew on them, the fire extinguishing and acrid wisps of smoke drifting towards Lena’s face. It stung her throat as she inhaled.

     

                “Come, Reign,” Lillian called out.

     

                Wading through the water, Reign hauled herself up, muscles shifting with her easy movements, and Lena shuddered at the thought of how much power lay in her lithe form, behind her graceful movements. Water streamed from the soaked leather britches and the woman’s bare feet slapped against wet stone as she passed by Lena’s head, the smell of wood smoke and ashes lingering in her wake.

     

                Lena let out a shuddering breath once the door shut behind them, a small cry escaping the back of her throat as she quickly clapped a hand over her mouth. Now that she was alone, she let her fear creep back in, a coldness seeping into her bones as she shook. It was painful to swallow and her fingers lightly glided over the tender skin of her throat as the ghost of Reign’s tight grip lingered along with the sting of the shallow graze left in her new mother’s wake.

     

                Not a fan of water at the best of times, just about stomaching a bath because of how relatively hard it was to drown herself, unless intentional, Lena was suddenly seized with the urge to get out of the steaming pool. Clambering awkwardly out of the water, the stone bit into her knees as she hunched over, wracked by a coughing fit as she spat out the lingering taste of her bath, her lungs aching with the effort. 

     

                The humid air dried the water running off her skin in rivulets as she stayed kneeling, gasping as she collected herself. Eventually, Lena ran a hand over her face and then raked her fingers through her hair, snatching up a towel and shakily running it over herself before she pulled on the heavy silk cloak, balling up the dress and the jewels and her little dagger, a pitifully small thing in a pathetic hand. 

     

                Gathering up her things, Lena made a swift exit, her wet hair straggling around her face, her skin so pale that she seemed luminous in the dark hallways of the palace. Weeds sprouted wildly in between bricks and through cracks, vines - some flowering and others thorny - crept over walls, and it was a beautiful nightmare of a place, claimed by nature as the fae dwelled amidst the roots and stone under the rule of a creature that Lena didn’t dare call human. She half expected to see eyes in the dark, watching her scurry back to her room, frightened, but it was quiet and still, something suffocatingly rotten about the whole place.

     

                Barging through her door, Lena slammed it shut behind her and fell back against it, her breaths quick and ragged as she hugged her bundle to her chest and ground her teeth together against the building urge to cry. A moment later, there was a knock on her door and Lena hesitated, stepping away and forcefully jerking the door open again.

     

                She was met with the point of a sword at her throat and her wife standing regally in the hallway, still dressed in her finery, which she wore with such ease that it only sparked Lena’s anger even more as she let out a lazy murmur.

     

                “Dead.”

     

                Heat flushing her ghostly face as she was confronted with that stupid game, chosen at quite the absolute worst moment on Kara’s behalf, Lena threw her armful of belongings at Kara as she snarled, tears stinging her eyes. “Oh, go and fuck yourself.”

     

                The tip of Kara’s sword dipped as her lips parted in surprise at Lena’s anger, the rumpled dress falling heavily to her feet with the tinkling of silver and diamonds and emeralds. Mouth opening and closing, Kara looked down and then back up, caught off guard by the reaction as she picked up Lena’s things and stepped inside. 

     

                Back to her as she seethed, shoulders taut beneath the velvet robe, Lena rubbed her fingers over her eyelids as she swallowed the painfully thick lump in her throat. She could feel the tightness in her chest and felt as if she was about to burst at any second. The forest had tempered most of her resentment over the weeks since she’d arrived there for good, the very being of the place settling into her bones like home, but at that moment, Lena didn’t think she’d ever hated it so much as she did then - not even the first day, dragged from her shop and married off to Kara.

     

                “Is something amiss?” Kara softly asked, her languid arrogance falling away. Following after Lena with a mild look of concern on her face, sheathing her sword at her waist and depositing Lena’s belongings on a divan, Kara's stomach twisted.

     

                A caustic laugh burned its way up Lena’s throat as she whirled around, eyes damp and stinging as she stamped down the urge to cry. Before she could even utter a word, Kara was before her, her eyes trained on Lena’s neck. She reached out and brushed her dark hair back, the pads of her fingers rough and warm against her cheek, before she cradled the side of her face and tipped her head back. Her storm blue eyes narrowed as she examined what Lena imagined to be a mottling collection of bruises and an angry red mark, a lingering threat. She hadn’t seen herself in a mirror, but Lena could read the stiff anger on Kara’s face.

     

                “Who did this to you?” Kara asked.

     

                “Why do you ask such stupid questions?” Lena snapped. 

     

                Bristling slightly, Kara dropped her hand from Lena’s neck and squared her shoulders. Holding Lena’s gaze, she waited for her to explain herself, but Lena moved away from her, fluttering her fingers in a dismissive manner.

     

                “You can go.”

     

                “I should think not,” Kara brittly replied, affronted. “Tell me what she said.”

     

                “Does it even matter? What, will you go and threaten her? Do the same to her?”

     

                Blanching as shame washed over her, knowing that she wouldn’t be the one to break the truce, Kara hung her head for a moment, fingers touching the hilt of her sword. “I would know what it is that made her behave badly.”

     

                “It’s because I snubbed her. This is about her pride, and now she-” Lena gestured angrily, her expression clouding with disdain. “She’ll have me at her every word, with her little lessons and whims. Otherwise, she’ll kill me.”

     

                “She can’t without breaking-”

     

                “Like she gives a shit about the truce,” Lena cut her off, her eyes blazing as she rounded on Kara, stepping in. “She’s playing nice because it suits her, and when it doesn’t she’ll cut my throat. She said so herself. And if you trust a word she says, you’re a bigger idiot than I anticipated.”

     

                Kara accepted her little barbed insults with serene composure, clasping her hands before her as her golden face softened into pitiful understanding. “You’re upset. I understand, so I’ll forgive your-”

     

                Balling her hands into fists, Lena bared her teeth as her face screwed up with anger, and she gripped the front of Kara’s cloak, pulling her closer. Kara glided like water, cocking her head to the side, the few inches of height she had on Lena making her seem more imposing, although her bearing was demure.

     

                “Don’t patronise me. Don’t pretend that you know a single thing about me. You’re nothing to me; they can call me your wife, they can say we’re legally married, but don’t think for a second that you will ever have any stake in my life. You know nothing about what I’m feeling, so you’ll forgive nothing .”

     

                Reaching up, Kara gently grasped Lena’s chin in her hand, her blue eyes solemn and resigned as she ducked her head slightly. Her voice was a whisper and the smell of saltwater and fresh rain and storms made Lena’s stomach tie itself into knots, her skin prickling from how close they were, from the thought of drowning. Everything about Kara was tied to the water, and to stand before her was to feel like Lena was drowning in her presence.

     

                “Don’t presume to tell me what I can and cannot do. You resent me? Fine. But I will have your respect,” Kara sternly murmured.

     

                “Then earn it,” Lena said through her teeth, her heart stumbling as her stomach lurched.

     

                Kara just let out a small laugh, cocking her head the other way before her fingers left Lena’s chin and moved to brush her dark, wet hair out of her face. As she did so, Kara’s fingertips brushed the short point of Lena’s ears, eliciting a sharp inhale as Lena’s eyelids shuttered with surprise. 

     

                Her ears had always been something of a sore point for Lena growing up. They were nowhere near as prominently pointed as Kara’s, the tips longer and sharper, but they were distinctly inhuman and something of a novelty to anyone who had ever noticed. Kids had laughed at her when she was younger, especially once The Lord of the Rings movies had been released and there had been elves, not quite so dissimilar to the kind she was amongst now, Lena wryly thought, and she’d been self-conscious whenever she’d gone to the hairdressers, hating the brush against the tips of her ears, so sensitive that it would make her whole body tense.

     

                She tensed then, her whole body prickling at the audacity of this woman before her, and Lena’s mouth went dry as any objection died on her tongue. Kara seemed to remember herself, snatching her hand back as two spots of colour flooded her cheeks.

     

                “Forgive me, that was … unbecoming of me.”

     

                Lena considered her mumbling reply and paused, understanding that the apology was for touching her, not for what she’d said. Still, Lena took it upon herself to accept it as an apology for her words, jerking her chin up in a haughty manner as she kept her cloak wrapped around herself, frighteningly aware that she had nothing on underneath and was feeling a little restless as the tips of her ears burned.

     

                “You should go,” she eventually rasped, nothing more to be said.

     

                Hesitating, Kara nodded, turning towards the door and then pausing again. She reached out and pressed a hand against the wood before looking back over her shoulder. “Come.”

     

                Considering ignoring her order, Lena relented after a moment and drifted over to her side, feeling the presence of her keenly as Kara took one of her hands and laid the palm against the wood.

     

                “From today onwards, you will lock yourself in every night. The door is wood - it will obey you if you will it.”

     

                “I don’t know how.”

     

                “Figure it out. You must also eat nothing that isn’t served to you by one of your mother’s servants. Do you understand me? And might I offer a suggestion? It would be unwise to offend Her Majesty in her own Court.”

     

                A sneer twisted Lena’s face as her soothed annoyance at Kara reared its head once more. Folding her arms over her chest, she ground her teeth together and frowned beneath her heavy eyebrows, her face like pale marble.

     

                Whether oblivious or just blithely pleased that she’d managed to nettle Lena just a little, although Lena was willing to give her the benefit of the doubt, Kara opened the door and paused in the doorway. Giving Lena a scrutinising look, Kara’s expression softened minutely, her mouth curving with the slightest smile that Lena later deemed mocking, although she couldn’t quite convince herself of that, and she gave her a small nod.

     

                “Goodnight. Wife.”

    Chapter 9

                Come sunrise, that infernal woman was back again, breaking through Lena’s flimsy attempt to lock her door by melding the wood together, and bringing the brasier to life until it filled the room with an orange glow. Lena had woken upon her intrusion, rubbing the sleep from her eyes as her heart pounded, and now she frowned at her.

     

                “Good morning,” Andrea cordially invited her. “Breakfast will be served shortly; you must dress.”

     

                She’d brought a bundle of clothes with her and gestured to them, but Lena was stiff and still as she watched her closely. Not one who was naturally inclined to trust, Lena stayed in bed, her hand gripping the hilt of her dagger beneath the down pillow as she tensed, waiting to see whether there were any ulterior motives.

     

                Glancing over at her, Andrea raised her eyebrows in a patronising look. “Quickly now.”

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                Letting out an airy laugh, Andrea smiled thinly. “You must be. Even if you’re not, you’re to eat breakfast with your mother shortly. She is not known for her patience.”

     

                Pulling the blankets back over herself, Lena turned on her side, closing her eyes with the determination to pretend that she wasn’t there. It was futile, of course, and moments later the blankets were torn off her, cool morning air violently replacing the warm cocoon of embroidered cotton.

     

                Offended, Lena sat up, her teeth grit in annoyance as she watched Andrea ball the blankets up in her arms. Moving across the mattress, Lena reached for the blankets and was jerked forward as Andrea stepped back. Sprawling on the earthen floor, the air rushed from Lena’s lungs and she rubbed at her chin before scrambling to her feet. Pale and haughty and bristling with anger, Lena took a step forward.

     

                Setting the blankets on the edge of the mattress, Andrea glanced sideways at her, violence in the lines of her lithe body as she waited for Lena to move. Scoffing, the Princess turned and reached for the blankets again, but wiry fingers closed around her wrist stopping her. Breaking Andrea’s weak grip, Lena shot her a dark look and the woman arched an eyebrow, reaching out to grasp her wrist again, this time tighter. Lena struggled to break it this time and tried to twist away from her before shoving her with her other hand.

     

                A laugh escaped Andrea, who used the backwards momentum to drag Lena with her and then spin them around. Forcing her up against the wall, she cocked her head to the side, blue eyes curiously appraising her, before Lena shoved back. Clicking her tongue, Andrea yanked her arm aside and propelled her forward, her other hand coming up to grab the back of Lena’s neck before forcing her down, doubled over.

     

                “Are we to do this again?” the woman asked, her voice laced with amusement as she jerked Lena’s arm up, eliciting a gasp of pain.

     

                “You can’t make me get dressed, or eat.”

     

                “You’ll find that you can be made to do a lot of things, under the right circumstances.”

     

                “If you don’t let me go, my wife will gut you.”

     

                “I see no wife,” Andrea murmured. “Only a farce of a marriage with a woman who detests you, and who you detest in turn.”

     

                Still, a moment later, she let Lena go, drifting away from her to hold up the deep green dress embroidered with silver leaves and white flowers. “Get dressed.”

     

                Standing there, fists clenched tight enough to turn her knuckles white, Lena gave her a hateful look. “I’ll wear my own clothes.”

     

                “You wore that yesterday and your luggage is yet to arrive. You’ll wear what I have brought or nothing.”

     

                “Then I’ll wear nothing.”

     

                A smile crossed Andrea’s face, “you’re quite amusing, you know. I think we’ll become fast friends-”

     

                “That’s not likely,” Lena scoffed.

     

                “But you ought to know Her Majesty has given explicit instructions to use any force necessary with you. She is of the opinion that you’re too uncooperative to see sense. I would prefer not to lay a hand on you, but …”

     

                Crossing over to her, Lena snatched the dress from her hands and shooed her out of the bedroom. Cursing under her breath, she stripped off her nightgown and into the dress, shifting with discomfort as she tried to make it sit right. She wasn’t used to wearing those sorts of dresses, the kind that made her feel like she was attending a renaissance fair, and Lena grumbled to herself as she smoothed her hands over the fabric.

     

                “Good,” Andrea said as she emerged, barefoot with her dagger belted around her waist. “You must fix your hair. Come, sit, I’ll assist you.”

     

                Raking a hand through the tangled mess from the aftermath of her bath the night before, Lena curled her lips derisively. “I’ll pass.”

     

                They stared at each other for a moment and it was Lena who caved first. She hunched her shoulders as she skulked over to the low ottoman and ignored the quiet laugh from the other woman as she drifted closer. Her fingers made quick work of Lena’s dark locks, intricately braiding it all into something beautiful yet understated. 

     

                As soon as she was finished, Andrea stepped back. “Come. Her Majesty does not like to be kept waiting.”

     

                Lena would have liked to keep her waiting a while longer but Andrea ushered her out of the room and she had no choice but to follow. A part of her was curious to see what would happen if she slipped down a side corridor and got herself lost, if she’d be dragged back for breakfast or if she’d be allowed to keep her own company, as long as it was within the walls of the royal residence. Tempted, she stayed the course instead and was brought to a web of roots growing over each other and tangling into the shape of two doors, flanked by guards who opened them at her arrival. Andrea shrank back and Lena proceeded alone.

     

                Her mother was already sitting at the head of the table, cold and harsh in a dress of rich emerald green adorned with patches of decorative armour - the girdle there, the gorget at her throat, the bracers, all of it finely filigreed with wildlife and flowers - sipping a cup of blackberry tea that stained her lips purple. Her eyes were sharp and watchful as Lena stepped inside, and she set down her thin clay teacup to appraise her daughter.

     

                Lena stood for a moment, reluctant and recalcitrant, before Lillian gestured impatiently. “That will suffice, I suppose. Sit.”

     

                Making for the chair that was furthest away from Lillian, and wasn’t directly across from her, Lena dragged it out and moved to sit before her mother made a sharp sound of objection. Clicking her fingers at the seat adjacent to her, Lillian arched an eyebrow.

     

                “Here.”

     

                She wanted to break her fingers for the rude arrogance of the gesture but settled for continuing to sink down onto her seat without a word. At a glance from their queen, one of the fae soldiers stepped forward and grabbed Lena’s upper arms to haul her to her feet but was interrupted by the quiet hiss of a blade being unsheathed and the keen edge set against their throat.

     

                Kara stood tall and regal in blue, like a sea during a storm as the lines of her body went taut, the long silver blade held still as she gave the man a flinty look, her eyes like blue granite. Without even saying a word, she made her intentions clear with the sharp edge of her curved sword and the soldier glanced at Lillian, who watched the exchange with interest, before holding a hand up to dissuade him from escalating things.

     

                He unhanded Lena, who sank back down onto her seat, scowling as she rubbed at the tender spots on her arms where he’d gripped her, and Kara sheathed her sword a moment later, once she was sure the threat had passed. The soldier retreated back outside, leaving the three of them alone. A dangerous mistake. Jerking a chair out beside Lena, strategically putting herself between mother and daughter, Kara cleared her throat.

     

                “That is twice in less than a day that you’ve laid hands on her,” Kara conversationally started, picking up the small knife on the long wooden table and turning it between her fingers.

     

                Setting it back down, she reached for the tea and filled cups for herself and Lena before her eyes cut to Lillian, who was lazily cutting a plum with her own knife, her slender fingers nimbly working through the soft flesh. 

     

                “My soldiers will enact my orders for me, if one tries to disobey me at my word.”

     

                “I suggest they enact them without touching ,” Kara replied, clicking her tongue and then taking a sip.

     

                Lena sat rigidly beside her, not touching a single thing, not even a mere sip of cool water from the glass carafe before her. She wasn’t used to this gentle, barbing politics, the exchange seeming polite on the surface but holding a threatening undercurrent. Who was she to think she’d be able to resist any of them if it came down to it? Lena couldn’t use a sword, couldn’t overpower any of these soldiers, couldn’t even begin to navigate her way through a ruthless Court. Her neck was tender and her throat sore and she resolved to sit there in quiet defiance. Perhaps that would serve her better.

     

                “They will enact them however I see fit.”

     

                “Then I will react accordingly.”

     

                “You forget yourself,” Lillian coldly replied, “you are not the ruler of your own holdings here; you are bound under the terms of the truce.”

     

                Kara hummed slowly, a picture of ease as she spread soft goat cheese over fresh bread and then picked up a few pears, testing the ripeness of them before picking up her small knife and narrowing her eyes at it. Slowly halving the pear, she gouged out the seeds and then cut it into slices.

     

                “Indeed, I am well-versed in the terms. Perhaps more so than you if you think drawing a knife on my wife is acceptable, Your Majesty. I’ve seen the marks on her neck and need to look no further than this room to deduce where they’ve come from.”

     

                “You accuse me of breaking the terms of our truce?” Lillian challenged her.

     

                Turning the knife in her hand, Kara thrust the blade down into the wood of the table, lodging it two inches deep as she shot Lillian a dark look. “The terms are vague, I admit, and perhaps it’s not an act of war to drown one's daughter while bathing, but I will not stand for it.”

     

                Lillian scoffed, her eyebrows rising and falling in a quick look of amusement, “do you mean to threaten me? Do try. I’m in much need of amusement.”

     

                “I’m not one to make threats - in fact, I despise them,” Kara murmured, “but let me make one thing clear, you will not touch her again.”

     

                Her voice was soft and serious and Lena stared at her side profile, taking in her tanned skin, her hair turned golden by long days in the sun, and her earnest blue eyes trained on her breakfast. Kara owed her no loyalty, no defence, and yet she took her vows to Lena with grave sincerity, kindling some small amount of gratitude in her wife, even if Lena still resented her for things out of their control. Who else could she blame but the one who’d willingly entered their marriage without a second thought, so gullible and noble with her sacrifice?

     

                A smile curled Lillian’s lips, enjoying herself very much as they muddled through one of the most uncomfortable scenarios Lena had ever found herself in. She’d never felt so much hostility cloud the air, so much bristling tension between two people. Even the hatred she felt paled in comparison, too many centuries of feuding muddying the waters between the two Courts for her own fury to hold a candle to theirs.

     

                “You’re not nearly convincing enough,” Lillian said, her voice like velvet as she draped herself in her high-back chair, a picture of boredom, using her knife to point to Lena and her mottled throat as she narrowed her eyes. “I would try more violence if I were you. It speaks louder.”

     

                The water in the carafe before Lena started to ripple on the surface and her brows pinched together with a disconcerting look as she cocked her head to the side. Reaching out, her fingers alighted on Kara’s tense forearm, feeling corded muscle hard beneath her touch. Flinching at the contact, Kara shot her a sharp look and abruptly shot from her chair.

     

                “Sit down,” Lillian ordered her.

     

                Standing for a moment, staring at the queen who wasn’t her queen, the woman who wielded all the power here, Kara defied her order for a second as she bristled with so much anger that Lena thought she might slip the water from the jug and drown Lillian with it. After a tense hesitation, Kara sank back down, a muscle working in her jaw.

     

                Reaching for her knife, she yanked it out of the wood and Lillian clucked her tongue. “You Seelie really are quite boorish. Especially you Waterfolk - so unrefined and unappreciative of anything that’s not miserably wet.”

     

                Hand lashing out, Kara let the knife go as it spiralled towards Lillian’s head. It was a warning, not an attempt, and with their fast reflexes, Lillian had plenty of time to shift her head to the side slightly. The knife slammed home in the wood of her chair, stuck fast beside the queen’s head. But Lillian just laughed, the sound cold and aloof as she wrapped her fingers around the hilt and jerked it back out.

     

                She threw it back at Kara, the blade spinning through the air. Kara caught it, blade-first, in her fist, red blood splattering on the table as clear water, with a tang of saltwater scenting the air. Lena startled backwards, her eyes squeezing shut with the shock as if she expected the knife to impale her. Kara uncurled her fingers and set the knife back down, her palm stained red but the droplets splashing clear as rain on the wood and food as the deep slice bled freely. 

     

                “I tire of this,” Lillian said, waving dismissively.

     

                “I find my appetite has vanished,” Kara stiffly replied, climbing to her feet once more. 

     

                Looking down at Lena, Kara crooked her fingers in a beckoning gesture, but once Lena pushed her chair back and tried to climb to her feet, Lillian softly cleared her throat and levelled her cool stare at them both. Her lips twitched with a smirk of satisfaction.

     

                “You may do as you please, but I have not dismissed the Princess.”

     

                Lena let out a bark of disbelieving laughter, gripping the arm of the chair. She rankled at Kara beckoning her but it wasn’t as fierce as Lillian acting as if she had any right to control Lena. It wasn’t specific to her - Lillian’s word was law to all fae, but Lena didn’t believe she should fall under her jurisdiction on account of her not being a part of the Court, no matter what she said.

     

                Glancing sideways at her, Kara shrugged dismissively and stepped around her chair. “Do as you will; I care not.”

     

                Stomach lurching with shock, a complaint started to form on Lena’s lips as she watched Kara take her leave. Twisting in her seat, she couldn’t believe she was actually going to leave her there, and she expected her to turn and take her with her at any moment. But she didn’t and the guards closed the doors behind her again, leaving Lena alone with her mother.

     

                “I take it she’s not fond of you,” Lillian murmured with glee.

     

                Shooting her a scowl as she gripped the arms of the chair with white knuckles, Lena made a scathing sound at the back of her neck. “And why would she be? We don’t even know each other.”

     

                “Marriage is usually a warmer affair.”

     

                “Well, yes, that usually happens when you get to choose to be married, and who you’re married to,” Lena ground out.

     

                “Royals are rarely afforded the luxury of a choice, daughter. You’d do well to learn that lesson fast. Shall we consider it your first lesson of the day? The others will be far more taxing, I’m afraid.”

     

                Giving her a dismissive look, Lena sniffed and sat back, folding her arms over her chest. They didn’t speak for a moment and Lena breathed in the damp sweetness of the room as she felt the grain of the wood beneath her fingers and brooded. 

     

                “Eat something,” Lillian off-handedly suggested.

     

                Ignoring her, Lena rigidly occupied her chair as her stomach rumbled and she intentionally avoided eating a single bite of food spread out before her. The half-starved orphan inside her hated the thought of so much waste, knowing what it was like to go hungry, to be denied meals and not have enough change to fill the gnawing feeling in her stomach, but her mouth was dry and she didn’t trust her hands not to shake if she took something. There was a nauseous knot in her stomach as well and she barely spoke to Lillian, who seemed content with silence as well.

     

                Wanting nothing more than to be gone from that room, she didn’t attempt to leave again. Not until Lillian finished the dregs of her blackberry tea and set the cup down, clearing her throat as she rose to her feet. Lena moved her head minutely, her eyes not quite landing on her, and waited expectedly.

     

                “You rise when I rise,” Lillian haughtily informed her.

     

                Wearily pushing herself up, Lena softly sighed. Rounding the table and walking down its length, Lillian paused before her, a threatening aura emanating from her as she reached out to put a finger under Lena’s chin and tilt her face until their eyes met.

     

                “And you bow your head in my presence until I tell you otherwise. Before the Court, you kneel and kiss my ring, and I always take precedence. You will take your meals with me, you will accompany me to Court and sit quietly. You will not speak unless spoken to, you will sit upright,” Lillian ranted, her tone swimming with disdain as she reached out to push Lena’s shoulders back, correctly her posture. “You will attend the lessons I set you, you will obey my orders and instructions, even if they are presented secondhand by my subjects, and you will keep the peace. Am I understood?”

     

                Lena arched an eyebrow and gave her a derisive look. “Perfectly.”

     

                A sharp smile crossed Lillian’s face, her pale blue eyes alight with amusement, and she nodded. “Your first lesson will be language with Andrea. She will be reporting your behaviour to me; don’t bring shame upon our line.”

     

                Lips twitching and her face hard, Lena didn’t reply and turned to leave. A vice-like grip stopped her and Lillian gave her a pointed look, one eyebrow raised as she cocked her head to the side.

     

                “Are you not listening to me, daughter? I always take precedence. You may not walk ahead of me.”

     

                Quietly scoffing, Lena gestured towards the door, the motion full of sarcasm. Giving her cheek a quick pat, a mockery of affection as she chuckled, making Lena scowl, Lillian swept out of the room and gestured dismissively to Andrea as she went on her way.

     

                “Bring her to me at dinner. I don’t want to catch sight or sound of her until then.”

     

                “Yes, Your Majesty.”

     

                Watching Lillian leave, Lena’s lip curled and then her eyes slid over to the woman left in charge of her. They stared at each other for a moment and Lena was struck by how beautiful she was - they all were, in a most annoying way - but that didn’t mean she felt anything other than an irritation to be left with her. A pretty face only took you so far - Lena knew that firsthand, and she had to admit that if looks were enough, she probably would’ve fallen for Kara the moment she’d first seen her on that bridge, beautiful and golden. Instead, Lena would’ve been begging for a divorce, if it was even a thing that existed there.

     

                “Come. We have work to do,” Andrea eventually broke the tense silence.

     

                She turned and walked down the hallway, leaving Lena to follow her once more, until they reached a large room with shelves of books and a few sturdy tables and lamps to read by. Andrea was no teacher by any means, but it was a simple task for her to teach Lena the strange elvish tongue that seemed so familiar in a way that made her brain itch. Andrea would point to a book or chair or body part and say the word for it, making Lena repeat it over and over until they turned to the glyphs she’d already been deciphering herself. She surprised Andrea there, although the woman snorted at her clumsy penmanship.

     

                It was mid-morning by the time they finally stopped, Lena flexing her cramping fingers as she leaned back in her chair. A flicker of movement caught her eye and she turned to stare at Kara, who was leaning against a shelf of scrolls with a handful of blueberries, testing the surface tension of each one between thumb and forefinger before popping it in her mouth. 

     

                They stared at each other for a long moment, the tension between them so unbearable as Lena’s ears started to ring, and then she leapt to her feet, the chair toppling to the floor. Crossing the space between them, Lena bristled as Kara quickly backed away, scattering blueberries as a mild look of surprise crossed her insufferable face.

     

                “You left me there,” Lena fumed, her pale cheeks flooding with two spots of colour as anger snaked through her.

     

                “You seemed content to sit there, indifferent to my attempts to help you,” Kara replied, wiping her stained hand on her clothes.

     

                Spluttering, Lena grabbed her arm, her grip like a vice as she bared her teeth. “Indifferent?”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara raised her eyebrows in a mild look. “You’re normally so vocal in your opposition, I assumed you must want to stay.”

     

                “You’re an asshole,” Lena snapped, shouldering past her.

     

                Kara cursed as Lena checked her, making her stumble up against the shelves, wood biting into muscle. She made to go after her but Lena didn’t get very far before Andrea cleared her throat.

     

                “We still have lessons,” she called out.

     

                Pausing, Lena glanced back over her shoulder, her expression positively haughty. “I’m tired of your lessons.”

     

                Continuing her exit, Lena got herself lost in the hallways, growing increasingly frustrated as she tried to find the exit, until she eventually stumbled upon Andrea, who was leaning against a wall as if she’d been expecting her. Perhaps she had; Lena wasn’t sure what these people could do with their odd ways and powers. Raising her eyebrows, she smiled faintly.

     

                “Ready to continue?”

     

     

                Her days became a cycle of lessons. Every morning she endured breakfast with Lillian and Kara - the latter who never left early again - before she met with Andrea for lessons in speaking and reading and writing. Then there were etiquette lessons, where she made Lena walk and sit correctly and tried to teach her to dance, to which her student firmly objected. 

     

                They’d break for lunch and afterwards, Lena was subjected to hours of sword training. Kara always came for that, watching Andrea beat Lena with ease every single time without fail. Lena wondered if perhaps it brought her enjoyment, but Kara watched in silence for the most part, or spoke to Andrea as if Lena wasn’t there, telling her to train her with her dagger, that perhaps she’d be more adept with a bow, that she needed to spend more time of formations and grip before they duelled. One thing was clear - if Lena ever had to use a sword to save her life, she’d be dead in a heartbeat. Yet, Lillian had insisted on it, calling it a noble art, despite Lena’s aching muscles and bruised skin from long hours. 

     

                After the afternoon whittled down to a few hours before sunset, Lena was taken to a few select scholars for lessons in history and politics and law. She hated to admit that she was interested, although she didn’t outwardly show it, and it was perhaps her favourite part of the day. Andrea would sit silently while Lena was lectured on topics, and once they were done she’d deliver her to Lillian for dinner, if she hadn’t been summoned to stiffly sit beside her on her throne and listen to politicians bicker back and forth about resources and money.

     

                Dinner was always a tenuous affair, Lena’s patience worn thin after a long day, Lillian’s amusement needling at her and Kara’s pride and duty downright insufferable. Once they’d finished, Lillian would take Lena to a room and try to coax her slumbering powers out of her. It had shown itself, that much they were sure of, and Lillian was determined to get it out of her, to make her control it, use her birthright as some sort of claim that she was Lionel’s daughter.

     

                Every night, she returned to her quarters after the baths, depleted and exhausted, and tumbled into bed with no time for anything else. Over two weeks passed by in that fashion, and Lena was oddly grateful for the distraction of it all, in some ways, but was utterly miserable in every other way. But even she couldn’t deny that she’d never felt better. Continuing the weapons training that Kara had started had given her a sliver of muscle that hadn’t been there before and the fresh fare served at every meal was better than anything she’d ever eaten before, despite the simplicity, not to mention the clean air of the forest that filled her lungs, clear and green. Her persistent headaches were gone, the aches that had bothered her, almost without her noticing, had faded, and Lena’s senses seemed sharpened.

     

                Still, she rankled at the thought of being kept there. The loneliness of it ate away at her, even more so than it had in the tower on the lake. Lena had never really had any friends but she’d served dozens of customers, day in and day out, and had familiar delivery people coming and going constantly. She’d never had to search for social interaction, but now she positively shunned any attempts at it, with people speaking at her rather than to her.

     

                After another failure of a lesson with the unwieldy training sword she’d been handed, Lena was surly and tired as she sank down to the base of a gnarled oak growing inside the cavernous sparring room. Sitting amidst the roots, she closed her eyes and tipped her head back against the bark, the feel of it like a balm to her.

     

                “You’re supposed to get better, you know,” Kara said with faint amusement as her shadow cut across Lena.

     

                Cracking an eye open, Lena glowered up at her. “Perhaps I don’t want to.”

                

                “Oh. No. I don’t think that’s it,” Kara laughed, “you’re just not very good at it.”

     

                “I’m glad you find it so funny.”

     

                “I do find it funny,” Kara agreed. “If only because it vexes your mother so much to know her bargaining chip to sue for peace is so overwhelmingly unsuited to this place. She’s not happy with your progress.”
