                Struggling to her feet, Lena’s lips twitched and she clenched her teeth. “I don’t need your opinion, thank you.”

     

                “Oh, well, it wasn’t an opinion,” Kara hummed, a pinched look of consideration on her face as she reached out to help Lena up, and found her hand battered aside. “It was more of a fact.”

     

                Stepping out into the hallway, Lena looked both ways and hesitated. Kara followed after her as if she didn’t have a care in the world, as if Lena wasn’t praying for her to go and bother someone else.

     

                “God,” Lena hissed, “will you go away?”

     

                “Why?”

                

                “You’re irritating.”

     

                “No, I’m not. I’m being honest; that irritates you. I’ve found self-reflection is a good way to analyse flaws-“

     

                “I’m going to smother you.”

     

                A quick grin cut across Kara’s face. “I’ve seen your sparring skills and I’m not confident in your ability to carry out that threat. I’d stick to …. what is it you’re good at again? Arranging flowers?”

     

                A scathing laugh rasped up Lena’s throat and her fingers touched her neck. “Yes, I’m well aware that I’m useless here.”

     

                “Then we are both in agreement on that opinion,” Kara softly agreed.

     

                Flinching back as if she’d been slapped, Lena pressed her lips in a flat, angry line, her eyes sharp with venom. She opened her mouth to speak then, inhaling sharply, and then closed it again. With a huff of sour disbelief, she turned and stalked off, the ground cold beneath her bare feet as she set off through the warren of roots and rock and dirt.

     

                “Don’t wander far,” Kara called after her.

     

                That only served to irritate Lena further and she found her way outside. The afternoon in the strange, sprawling dwelling in the forest was tinted green by the sunlight filtering through the impossibly tall canopy, making Lena feel dizzy as she glanced upwards. The dirt beneath her bare feet was freezing and damp and she shivered in the dress she’d been put in but couldn’t bear to go back inside.

     

                Gripping her biceps as she hugged her arms to herself, she hunched her shoulders and set off quickly, following the slightly sloping path upwards, a lingering fog wreathing around her ankles. Slipping further away from the underground hovel of stone and roots and too many plots and threats for her to make sense of, she strayed into the forest, the undergrowth crunching beneath her feet, leading her towards the heart of the forest.

     

                In the daylight it was hard to see the homes, so cleverly coaxed from the base of trees, gnarled roots creating lattice-like walls with knots where windows and doors were. It was all so expertly camouflaged that if Lena didn’t know what she was looking for, what she stood amidst, she might have thought she was amidst derelict ruins of some ancient civilisation, the occasional wall of grey stones looking out of place, but actually carefully melded with the nature surrounding her. 

     

                It was late yet she barely saw a soul, save for a young girl carrying a basket of freshly picked strawberries and a man smoothing the velvety nose of a horse as he softly sang to it. Lena wasn’t sure whether she ought to be sneaky or if she was allowed out; she thought the former was more accurate so she tried to stick to the deep shadows near the roots.

     

                She couldn’t be sure if she was beyond the homes of the Unseelie Court so she continued onwards, deeper into the forest until she was sure. The underbrush was thick and overgrown, brambles and ivy and rotting logs laying in her path. Larch and pines grew amidst the sycamores and hickories and thick elms and oaks, slivers of the dull sky visible through the gaps in the canopy as she walked onwards, as if in a dream.

     

                It didn’t rain, despite the grey sky, and she watched pollen through the shafts of light falling down to the leaf-strewn ground, blackberry bushes and strawberry and raspberry plants being pecked at by birds, while squirrels scampered around, storing nuts, and foxes slunk through the shadows for prey. It was verdant in the Unseelie Court, something that seemed unsettling, as if the place should have been decaying and rotten, just like it was beneath the veneer of courtesy they’d been greeted with. Instead, she found mushrooms, plucking them and watching as her nails bruised the soft bulbs of them, wondering at their variety and watching as spores drifted around her, amidst the plethora of wildlife.

     

                Lena had the sudden urge to seek out the darkest part of the forest and disappear. She could escape this tiresome game as a pawn and spend her days foraging for berries and acorns until she forgot her own name and let the forest claim her, let her body rot and get eaten by animals and reclaimed by moss and dirt until her bones were covered by the autumn leaves and winter arrived without her. It was a dangerous thought to have in a place where the very forest itself seemed sentient and watchful. It would be an easy thing to get taken.

     

                Perhaps it had been foolish of her to leave the town after all, but Lena still hadn’t burnt off her anger and she couldn’t stand to be around anyone else right now. Lillian would undoubtedly be furious at her impudence but she couldn’t bring herself to care about her missed lessons. Lena needed the peace of the forest, the serenity of the rustling leaves and the damp air, green from the abundance of plants and wildflowers. Breathing slowly as she walked, the air cool in her lungs as her fingers grazed the dew-dusted branches and fronds of plants, Lena felt some of the knotted of frustration unwind. 

     

                She headed deeper into the twisting wildwood warrens of the forest, so big and green and old in places that it was hard to believe that there had ever been a time when the trees were young. She gravitated to the untamed parts, where the trails were muddy and the air smelled sodden, bloated with dampness. The mud was thin from recent rain and it caked her feet as they sank in deep, and Lena had to admit there was something to be said for the lack of shoes worn by the fae. It was like she could feel the roots underfoot, knowing every part of the forest intimately. 

     

                As she walked, the shadows burned off as the cloud cover retreated and patches of eggshell blue seeped through, and she began to wonder if perhaps she’d made a mistake going so far. Only a few weeks ago, wolves had attacked them, people who would see her dead, and that was not to mention any unrest within the Court that she was unaware of. Still, she kept walking, her feet finding their own path.

     

                Perhaps it was the forest working against her, but Lena became hopelessly lost soon enough. She heard voices as she ducked beneath the roots of a tree spanning the narrow gully carved through the earth, and Lena’s heart lurched in her chest at the thought of being caught. Shrinking into the narrow space, she waited for the voices to drift further away and then emerged from her hiding spot, feeling rather exposed.

     

                Standing at the base of an ancient walnut tree, she looked for handholds and made quick work of hauling herself up to the first fork in the branches. Lena had loved to climb trees when she was younger and she was as adept at it now as she climbed through up the branches, wondering if perhaps it was some leftover skill from when she’d supposedly lived here. Had she climbed trees then? Had she run around barefoot in russet and green and violet and spoke in that strange tongue and made the plants grow wild? It felt impossible that she could forget all but the vaguest sensation that it was true, but if she was to believe what she’d been told, humans forgot their time at Court fairly quickly.

     

                She ignored how sweaty her hands got as she climbed higher and higher, the walnut taller than any she’d ever seen on earth. Her breath rattled in her throat as her mouth grew dry and Lena didn’t dare look down. A while ago she’d passed from safety to a good vantage point, but still, she continued, determined now to go high as she could.  Lena worked her way up until the branches grew slender and soon would support her weight. Settling into a crook that was almost comfortable, she glanced around her. 

     

                The ground stretched below, but the leaves fell around her and rustled in a sigh as the wind blew through. Her breathing calmed and she closed her eyes, listening to the leaves and their whispers, sure that they almost made sense if she just listened a little closer.

     

                She was high up in the canopy, thrusting above some of the small surrounding trees, and beyond the green ranges fading into the fiery colours of autumn, Lena could see the verdant green of the land, braided with muddy rivers and rolling hills, and hazy mountains in the near distance. Clouds still lingered on the horizon and it smelled like rain. Lena wanted to drown in the scent, her whole body slack at the comforting smell of petrichor.

     

                Staying up there for far longer than she intended, Lena realised with a jolt that the sunlight was waning and she still had to get back. Climbing back down the tree was a lot more nerve-wracking as she had to look down, the floor a dizzying distance beneath her and her footing made more clumsy for it. Half sliding and falling down some of the branches, she was scratched and rumpled by the time she made it to the leaf-strewn floor.

     

                Then, Lena got hopelessly lost.

     

                She came to the sound of running water nearby, following it to a brook babbling with movement, but the water was dark and smelled stagnant. She picked up a stone and dropped it into the stream. It disappeared with a small splash, swallowed by the murky water and giving no answers to its depth. Lena hadn’t crossed water on her way though, certain that she was heading in the wrong direction.

     

                Turning back the way she’d come from, she hugged her arms to herself with a prickling feeling of unease. All she could think of now was getting back to familiar territory, knowing that somewhere she must have made a wrong turn. She couldn't find the path that led home. Round and round, past oak trees and through myrtle thickets, she searched. A slow panic crept in as everything seemed to blur in shadowed sameness, the light fading quickly and leaving Lena stumbling on quicker as her breaths became sharper.

     

                Lena reached a dark clearing - the kind of place she would have liked to come on a warm summer’s day and linger awhile - spread beneath the branches of five oaks so dense only thin fingers of fading sunlight filtered through the canopy, highlighting patches of violets and bluebells. Lena didn’t remember coming that way but pressed on anyway, fear lodging in her throat as she started to regret her hasty actions and quick temper.

     

                The balmy nights of summer were vanishing behind them, the year was turning towards the darker months as a chill seeped into the ancient forest. As the sun began to fade beyond the horizon, ushering in true darkness, a cold wind made her shiver as she clenched her jaw against the effort. Summer was truly at an end and she could smell the sweet decay as she walked, rotting apples littering the ground as she passed through a grove, feeling a lurch of hope - where there was food, there had to be people nearby to tend to and harvest it. But nothing. Nothing but the cold and empty dusk. And then she felt it.

     

                She was being watched.

     

                The sensation sent a streak of cold racing through her chest. The hairs on the back of her neck prickled, rising in anticipation of some unseen horror lurking in the shadows, waiting to attack her, to drag her through the mud and brambles and slit her throat in a ditch. The breath caught in her throat and she swallowed painfully as she tried to be quiet, trying to mimic the silent, padfoot way Kara walked, cursing her feet for every crisp leaf and tiny twig they trampled. Each footfall felt like she was shining a spotlight on her location, beckoning them towards her. 

     

                There was a faint rustle then and her heart jumped into her throat, her stomach plummeting as she gave up all pretences of sneaking and started to run. The forest was tinted a dingy teal, the fading light casting everything in shadow as the thick foliage blocked her path, and Lena expected claws to rake down her back at any moment, rending her skin open to water the earth beneath her. 

     

                Instead, she collided with something solid and warm a moment later and let out a scream, which was quickly cut short by the hand clamped over her mouth, a hissing sound of worry silencing her. The scream was still stuck in her throat and Lena couldn’t move or catch her breath as she caught the faintest whiff of the sea on the hand pressed over her lips. 

     

                “Quiet,” Kara sharply whispered.

     

                Relief flooded Lena’s body and the air fled her lungs as she went slack against Kara’s body. Surprised, Kara’s arm wrapped around her, pressing them flush together as she held Lena’s weight, keeping her on her feet. Her blue eyes seemed silver and reflective in the dark as they flitted about, and after a tense moment she grabbed Lena’s hand and towed her away hastily.

     

                “How did you find me?” Lena asked.

     

                Her breaths hitched unevenly and her voice was hoarse with thirst. Kara shushed her, a panicked hiss, her hand tight on the hilt of her sword, ready to unsheath it at the first sound of trouble. Lena swallowed any other questions and tried to keep her feet beneath her, while Kara sighed and tutted impatiently at the racket her feet made as they snapped every twig between the grove and the Court.

     

                They didn’t see anything on their way back, and Lena knew she would've stayed lost in the forest if it had come down to finding it herself. Kara was annoyed, that much was clear by the set of her shoulders as her long strides left Lena scurrying after her, her hand clammy in Kara’s tight grip. She was disgruntled to be towed along like a child, her shoulder aching after a while, but she kept her mouth in a flat line until Kara suddenly relaxed, her grip on her sword going slack, her pace slowing. There was the faint orange glow of lanterns ahead, lifting the veil of darkness that had blanketed the forest on their return. Lena felt relief rush through her.

     

                Only once they were within the boundaries of safety did Kara finally speak, glancing sideways at her as they passed by armed guards staring into the darkness or perching in trees with their strung bows. The smell of woodsmoke and bread and flowers filled the night air, laced with the threat of rain, and Lena was more glad than she’d anticipated to be back within the relative safety of the Court.

     

                “The forest is dangerous at night; you endanger us both with your reckless stupidity,” Kara quietly fumed.

     

                Even her anger was a gentle thing, the tips of her ears pink and her brow furrowed in a look that was disapproving but still ethereally beautiful. Lena couldn’t imagine her shouting; not the loud, brash rage of her foster parents or the drunks she’d seen fighting outside bars, the customers who’d yelled down the phone over wilting flowers they’d left in the car all day. It seemed that they were all like that, their contempt a smooth thing that they kept reined in, using carefully chosen words as precise barbs that cut deeper than any shouting could.

     

                “I never asked you to come after me,” Lena snapped back, tearing her hand from her wife’s grasp. “Maybe I wanted to run away, did you consider that?”

     

                “You would die out there. I would give you a day, and that’s generous . You would think the memory of almost being disembowelled would have instilled some sense in you, but alas.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena bristled as she jerked her chin forward. “Well, maybe I mean to get myself killed so I don’t have to put up with you.”

     

                “Then take your dagger and put us both out of our misery.”

     

                Lena was silent a moment, only a little offended by the cool indifference of Kara’s tone, stinging slightly. After a pause, Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners and her face furrowed with consternation.

     

                “I did not mean-“

     

                “No, your meaning is perfectly clear, but if you want me to die then why did you come after me?”

     

                “I’ve told you before; I swore an oath to you, which means I’ll protect you with my life if it comes to it, if it means I must search through the forest to drag you back safely, whether you reciprocate the sentiment or not. I may not care for you or particularly like you, but I will do what I swore to do until you get one or both of us killed. I feel relieved to know that your childishness will hasten our deaths, so I shouldn’t have to do this for much longer.”

     

                “Childish?” Lena spluttered, “it’s not childish to want to escape the prison I’ve been confined to. You’d do the same if you were in my shoes.” 

     

                “I am in your position. Do you think I wish to be trapped in the den of my enemy? The people who killed my family? Any more than you wish to be here? No, but it’s my d-”

     

                “Duty,” Lena mocked, “yes, yes, you’ve prattled on about it enough. But I don’t give a shit about duty. What do I owe anyone here? Hm? You’re maybe the only one I do owe anything, and even then I wouldn’t owe you a thing if I hadn’t been kidnapped and brought here. Kidnapped , mind you - against my own will.”

     

                “Yes, that is a defining point of being kidnapped,” Kara said, rolling her eyes, “but you came back. You came back and asked to stay, so what is your problem? You can’t hold me accountable for your decision to come and live as my wife and honour the terms of the truce. If you didn’t want to do it, you shouldn’t have come back. Now, I’m saddled with the responsibility of your life as well as mine.”

     

                “Do us both a favour and get over trying to make me into a burden; I didn’t ask for you to save me. Any of the times.”

     

                “I suppose I have more of a conscience than you do then. I doubt you’d do the same for me.”

     

                “Mm, you’re probably right.”

     

                Lena wasn’t sure at what point they passed into the private gardens of the royal residence, only that one moment she was trying to keep up with Kara’s long strides, and then they were confronted by the sight of Lillian and her guards. The light of a few hanging lanterns illuminated the small clearing, the open mouth of a door and the creeping rose bushes signalling an entrance to the warren of the underground dwelling behind her mother. But Lena would have to pass her first to make it that far.

     

                “You were told of your lessons, and yet you abandoned them and disobeyed my orders,” Lillian frostily greeted her. “Now, perhaps your half-breed blood has made you dim-witted, but I thought I had made myself explicitly clear.”

     

                “Make yourself whatever you want; I’m my own person,” Lena scornfully replied.

     

                She’d been subjected to the Queen’s violence numerous times already, so it was no surprise to Lena as she watched Lillian’s hand strike back and swing towards her, too quick for her to do anything but flinch in anticipation of the stinging blow.

     

                Except the slap never landed. Kara stepped forward with lithe speed, grasping Lillian’s wrist in her hand as her face contorted with a silent snarl. She wasn’t as tall as the Queen, by a few inches, but her solid presence was intimidating enough to rival Lillian’s relaxed air.

     

                “I have warned you already what will happen if you lay hands on my wife again.”

     

                Four guards stepped forward, swords unsheathing, and Lena winced with pity for the first one to step forward, reaching to grasp Kara’s shoulder. Shoving Lillian away, Kara unsheathed her sword in one quick, practised motion, one hand gripping the hilt and the other flat against the pommel as she twisted and drove it straight into the stomach of the surprised fae man.

     

                Wrenching it free, blood spattering before it curled up in wisps of air, vanishing, Kara backed up against Lena and turned slowly. Red-slicked blade held aloft, she wrapped an arm around Lena, protectively but also in a manner that made Lena feel like she was held hostage, and moved her sword in a warning arc through the air.

     

                “I have no desire to hurt any of you,” Kara hoarsely said. “Let’s not break the truce over this misunderstanding.”

     

                Lillian had her hand held up to keep her soldiers at bay and took a slow step forward. Kara was stiff behind Lena and moved in front of her as the Queen approached, but it was Kara her focus was trained on. Stopping before her, her lip curled contemptuously, she let out a quiet huff of cool laughter and reached up.

     

                Grabbing Kara’s chin in a tight grip, her sharp nails digging into her tanned skin, Lillian’s cold eyes flitted over her face. Sword at her side, but her arms tensed to snap it up at the first sign of trouble, Kara was still before Lillian and her appraising stare. 

     

                “I should have you killed, or imprisoned, for attacking one of my personal guards defending me.”

     

                “Then do it,” Kara softly encouraged her. “I have warned you that I don’t own to threats; my actions succeed my words. I’m not a coward and I won’t betray my honour by speaking in vague ultimatums to no end.”

     

                Lillian let out a harsh laugh and pushed Kara away by her face. Gritting her teeth but enduring the indignity of the treatment, a Lady in her own right yet powerless here, she kept her piercing eyes on Lillian, each shift in her body a betrayal of how ready she was to fight.

     

                “Would that I’d had a daughter like you,” Lillian lamented with a sigh. “Instead, I’m saddled with … well, I don’t know what she is. Disobedient. Soft. Foolish. Everything a Princess shouldn’t be. And yet, she evades her lessons in favour of the forest; she is her father’s daughter, I suppose.”

     

                Heaving another sigh, Lillian waved a hand dismissively and turned, continuing to speak. “I tire of this. Take her to a cell; she can think on her actions overnight.”

     

                Two guards stepped forward, one of them knocking the pommel of her sword against Kara’s wrist to disarm her, her silver sword dropping to the ground. They took an arm each as Kara bared her teeth in disdain, her eyes cutting to Lena. Lillian snapped her fingers at the third guard, who was trying to help the fallen man.

     

                “Take her as well. May as well make it a lesson.”

     

                Lena’s squawk of protest died in her mouth as she gave Lillian a scathing look, the remaining guard grasping her with bloody hands. She struggled but even that was a half-hearted attempt, more to feel a small sliver of satisfaction that she didn’t go willingly - like her wife - than anything else. Propelled into the building and down a spiralling staircase that vanished underground, damp stone and black earth filling her nose as she stumbled after Kara’s back, Lena felt a prickle of anger towards the fae woman.

     

                They were locked into adjoining cells made in the bedrock of an underground cavern, dim lanterns offering some light and the iron bars separating them. Lena gripped the wooden bars of the cell door and tugged on them with no luck as she glared daggers at the retreating guards. She didn’t have much experience with cells, aside from episodes of CSI and Law & Order, but as far as they went, it wasn’t awful . There was a cot with blankets, a small stool and a stand with a pitcher of water and a measly candle. Honestly, she’d stayed at worse shelters.

     

                “Well …” Kara said after a lull.

     

                Turning to her, eyes blazing, Lena stalked over to the shared wall of bars and gripped them as she scowled at the other woman. Cocking her head to the side as she surveyed her wife’s face, Kara reached through to touch Lena’s scratched cheek, an anxious note in her voice when she spoke.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                Flinching away, Lena turned her head aside, not looking at her as she put a foot between them. Having to swallow several times to get the lump down, she cleared her throat and her voice was tight when she spoke.

     

                “Fine,” she curtly responded. “But you didn’t have to make things worse.”

     

                “Me?” Kara spluttered, “I’m lucky I have a head because of you.”

     

                “I didn’t ask you to stop her.”

                

                “Oh, so I should have let her lay hands on you? I should let her leave more marks?”

     

                She gestured flippantly to the vanished bruises Reign had left on Lena’s throat, courtesy of Lillian’s instructions. Reaching up to self-consciously touch the healed skin, Lena’s expression soured.

     

                “I’m not some damsel in distress. You think I haven’t been slapped before? Many times? I’ve had worse, believe me, and no one had to die to stop them. That’s all you lot seem to do; feign politeness and run each other through with swords when you run out of things to say.”

     

                “Because you’re so well-versed in the art of politics,” Kara laughed.

     

                Lena turned and retreated over to her cot, but even that wasn’t far enough away for her liking. She could still see Kara and hear her as she continued, heedless of Lena’s desire for silence between them. 

     

                “Never do that again.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena curled her lip as she looked over at her. “I’ll do as I please, thank you.”

     

                “You must listen to me.”

     

                “And why is that?” Lena asked, snarky and annoyed.

     

                “Why must a child listen to their mother? You’re worse than a child; blundering and loud and brash.”

     

                “You know nothing about me.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara scoffed, her eyebrows rising as she smiled faintly. “I know that you like to read and you’re afraid of water. You prefer white wines and soft cheeses. You’re intelligent yet your emotions get the better of you. You’re happiest around nature and that makes you more tolerable to be around as well. You’re stubborn, which is admirable, at least - I don’t think I would respect you so much if you weren’t willing to fight. You’re a restless sleeper; I admit to checking up on you at home. I wonder if you’ve always done it, or if it’s being back here, in the forest. You talk with your hands a lot - and your eyebrows. I find it … endearing , perhaps, in some way.”

     

                As if remembering herself, Kara cleared her throat and turned away from the bars. She crossed her cell to sit on the edge of the bed as Lena was left feeling unsettled by the fae’s perceptiveness. Putting her back to the bars of the cell as she resolved to ignore Kara did little to block out the murmured words that reached her slightly pointed ears, soft and insistent.

     

                “I’m more attentive than you give me credit for. Perhaps it’s you who knows nothing about me. ”

    Chapter 10

                The evening in the cell dragged on, a meal of soft bread, cheese and duck brought to their respective cells. It was cool in the deep confines of the earth and Lena huddled on her cot with her platter of food, sipping the water and picking at the food. 

     

                After a while, she abandoned it and climbed to her feet, aware of Kara watching her as she ate her own dinner. Pacing back and forth, somewhat restlessly, Lena closed her eyes and breathed in the damp smell, finding some comfort in the earthy dampness, the prickle of awareness of burrowing tree roots, which was odd in itself and made Lena feel unbalanced. There was something inside her that answered the call of the forest, that she struggled to put a name to, that had always been with her, even at home. Here, it manifested as some cognisant prickling that made the hairs on her arms stand on end when it came on too strong.

     

                Walking back over to her cot, Lena dropped down onto it and brought her knees to her chin, hugging her legs close. The fear of not knowing what was happening to her, or being subjected to things out of her control and people who wished her ill had taken its toll on her. She didn’t want to think about the forest, the intoxicating poison of it drawing her in, suffusing her body like an enticing drug. Squeezing her eyes shut, she shifted onto her side and pulled the blanket over herself, blotting out the candlelight and resolving to sleep. Lena wasn’t afraid of the dark, but she couldn’t bring herself to endure the suffocating blackness of the cell.

     

                Lena didn’t find any solace in sleep though, restlessly tossing and turning as her mind conjured nightmares of the forest ensnaring her, roots binding her tightly, dragging her down into a bog, her lungs burning for air until she was left with the sensation of being consumed, moss growing over her bleached bones as flowers sprouted from between her ribs. She woke in a cold sweat, jolting upright as her chest rose and fell quickly, eyes wild as they looked around the cell. 

     

                “You’re safe.”

     

                Squeezing her eyes shut and then blinking rapidly, Lena raised her head and pushed her dark hair out of her pallid face to scowl at Kara. Her wife was turned towards her, as serene and beautiful as ever, and Lena felt embarrassment curl through her, flushing her cheeks as she ran her dirty sleeve over her face.

     

                Hunching over, Lena cradled her forehead in her hand and tried to shake off the unsettled shakiness in her stomach. It was just a dream; she’d been plagued by bad ones since she was a child. Only, she’d slept quite soundly since she’d arrived at Kara’s tower, and had forgotten what it was like to be dragged into the dark recesses of her mind. Her dreams had always related back to a forest, to the ominous feeling of being watched, of some eldritch horror eating away at her, nettles scratching at her skin and bogs slowly consuming her. A part of her now thought the forest was trying to call her home, but now that she was back, it hadn’t stopped entirely.

     

                “Are you alright?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena tersely replied.

     

                Kara nodded and continued her pacing, each step slow and measured, her hands clasped behind her back. She looked pensive and as restless as Lena felt inside, still awake despite the lateness of the house. They didn’t speak for a long stretch, didn’t acknowledge that the other was still awake, although Lena clearly hadn’t gone back to bed.

     

                “You don’t sleep?” Lena eventually broke the silence.

     

                Kara stopped her silent pacing and looked at her, mostly in shadow and limned in orange candlelight. There was a pause before she answered, her voice a low murmur so as not to disturb the peaceful night.

     

                “Very little. I find my mind too preoccupied with the burden of my duties to find much rest in sleep. Especially so far from home and from the water.”

     

                “Do you miss it?”

     

                Drifting over to the bars, Kara let out a quiet huff of laughter and cocked her head to the side, putting her arms through the bars and resting her forearms on the horizontal slat. Her posture relaxed and she smiled wryly, head cocked to the side.

     

                “If you told me I must cut my heart out of my chest or never step foot in a body of water again, I would hand you my still-beating heart and die happy in a mere puddle.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, Lena wandered over to the bars, standing in front of her and gripping the cool iron in her grasp. She let out a quiet hiss and jerked her hands back, shock flashing across her face. Kara chuckled, turning her arms and holding her hands open for Lena’s. 

     

                Hesitating before setting her hands in Kara’s, Lena frowned and looked down at the shadows of her palms, visibly marked even in the dimness of the cells. It would’ve been an angry red if she’d looked at them in the light.

     

                “The bars are iron,” Kara murmured. “Surely you know enough of human fae mythology to know that iron is not agreeable with us.”

     

                “How would I know that?” Lena replied, disgruntled. “I’ve been around iron loads of times back home.”

     

                “It has a more subdued effect there. The times I’ve visited the mortal realm, I was merely subjected to an awful aching in my head.”

     

                Lena blinked at the memory of the persistent headaches that had plagued her for days at a time, to the point where she’d needed a prescription from a doctor for migraine medication. It hadn’t been a constant pain, but there were times when she’d be using shears to cut the stems off her flowers when she’d feel like her head was splitting open, when she’d need to lay down and let the nauseous feeling abate. Not once had she considered it might be because of iron , and rarely did she even deal with it that it wouldn’t have occurred to her even knowing what she knew about herself now. Still, reluctant to give away anything about herself - especially anything that could make her look stupid - Lena turned her head.

     

                “Why aren’t those bars iron too?”

     

                She pulled her hand from Kara’s and gestured dismissively towards the door to the cell before depositing her hand back in Kara’s. Smiling faintly, Kara hummed low at the back of her throat, the touch of her thumb gently stroking along her fingers oddly intimate, making Lena want to pull her hands free again. 

     

                “The guards have to open and close those doors to admit us. We should not be so familiar with each other to need to touch these bars.”

     

                “How come it’s not burning you?”

     

                “My arms are covered by my sleeves. Once again, your hastiness has landed you in hot water; you must not be so rash.”

     

                Trying to pull her hands free, Lena scoffed and frowned, a flicker of annoyance in her eyes. Kara’s fingers encircled her wrist though and held her fast. Lip curling slightly, Lena narrowed her eyes a fraction.

     

                “You’re very quickly becoming my least favourite person in this place,” Lena lied.

     

                “I would say the same, if not for your mother,” Kara murmured, amused.

     

                Grinding her teeth, Lena snorted. “You know how I feel about the m word.”

     

                “Forgive me - if not for your Queen.”

     

                Smiling wryly, Lena rolled her eyes and her smile grew a fraction more. Closing her eyes, she let out a weary sigh.

     

                “You look tired,” Kara whispered, her voice so close that Lena’s stomach jolted.

     

                Opening her eyes, Lena’s mouth thinned and she slipped her hands from Kara’s, her fingers grazing along her palms. Still, she stood there for a moment longer, locking eyes in the darkness of midnight. Giving her a smile that was almost tender, Kara reached up and pressed the cool pads of her fingers to Lena’s face, burning points splayed across her jaw, before pulling her hand back.

     

                “Sleep. Your dreams cannot harm you here. Peace flows like a river; do not fight the current.”

                “Goodnight, Kara,” Lena wearily said before turning back around and walking over to her bed.

     

                She sank back down onto the cot and wrapped herself in the blanket, making sure her feet were covered as the chill burrowed into her toes. As she finished getting comfortable, she heard a murmured reply.

     

                “Goodnight, Lena.”

     

                She slept a while after that and woke to find Kara sitting on her cot, indifferent to the cold, indifferent to her surroundings as she didn’t even stir at Lena’s movements. She was awake though, occasionally shifting, and they both waited until they were let out of their cells and led back upstairs. It was still dark and Kara went straight out into the open forest, standing still beneath the canopy of the trees as dawn crept in beneath the cover of grey clouds, lightening their surroundings a fraction.

     

                The ground was damp beneath their feet and the forest was foggy, Lena breathed in the wet air as she tasted the decay surrounding them, autumn slowly overtaking the forest as it all rotted away in anticipation of the coming winter. Neither of them spoke and when Kara vanished back inside, Lena lingered a while longer before following.

     

                In her room, she changed into one of the green tunics that had arrived in the trunk of her belongings, leggings snugly fitting to her legs and a soft robe of a deep green that was almost black thrown over the top to stave off the chill. Belting her dagger at her waist, she made her way to breakfast and endured the stiff exchanges with Lillian, until Kara arrived and took a seat beside Lena.

     

                She poured blackberry tea for them both and Lena inhaled the sweet aroma, wrapping her hands around the cup and taking a sip. It warmed her through and she eyed the food but didn’t eat much, feeling particularly resentful that morning as she cast Lillian scathing looks every so often. Her back was aching from the cot, although Lena had certainly slept on worse beds in shelters, and she was stiff and disgruntled as she barely paid attention to the forced niceties exchanged by her wife and her mother.

     

                “I think training with the sword is a waste of her time,” Kara said, which caught Lena’s attention.

     

                Blinking, she turned to look at her, mild interest on her face as she set her tea back down. Lillian’s lip curled slightly and she coolly arched an eyebrow. “You would prefer her to go undefended? Swordsmanship is an art, even then. It would do her some good to bear some knowledge of Court activities - even if it’s that of the skill of a child.”

     

                “I have already instructed her in using the dagger I gifted her,” Kara cordially responded, “albeit, we didn’t have much time to hone her skills. But Lena doesn’t have the swift fluidity of the water in her; much like all Earthfolk, she’s rather rooted . And stubborn. To have her practice with a sword is to watch a bear blundering about - all force and no finesse. I think perhaps a bow would present a better opportunity for one without the foundational footing of a swordmaster. It would take decades for her to show any real skill in that, while I’ve always found the bow a rather … rudimentary tool, and it is the preferred weapon of your Court, is it not?”

     

                It was a snide remark that Kara said somewhat arrogantly, and Lena fought back a sleeting smile as she picked her tea back up. Taking another sip and clearing her throat, Lena deliberated for a moment and arched an eyebrow.

     

                “Do I not get a say in my own lessons?”

     

                “No,” Lillian flatly said, her eyes cutting to Lena and then back to Kara. “A bow will do her a disservice if she ever finds herself in close-quarter combat.”

     

                Kara let out a quick laugh, the sound warm and bemused. “With all due respect, Your Majesty, I think any weapons in your daughter’s hands would do her a disservice if she ever found herself in close-quarter combat. She’d be as likely to stab herself as her opponent and would undoubtedly perish, regardless of sword or bow at hand.”

     

                Unable to argue against Kara’s words, Lena still bristled slightly in her seat, rankled by the laughter lacing her wife’s words as she criticised Lena’s lack of skill. She would die if it was left up to herself to defend her own life, but she scowled at anyone else pointing out her lack of skill. 

     

                “I don’t believe she has the strength to wield a bow; that’s why I picked the sword instead of our preferred weapon.”

     

                “Anyone who can wield a sword can draw back a bowstring. A few months ago I may have agreed with you, but she’s had weeks of training to condition her arms. I’m proficient with a bow and willing to undertake her training myself.”

     

                “Why, when I have so many who are undoubtedly more skilled than you?” Lillian haughty asked.

     

                Gesturing off-handedly, Kara smiled thinly. “Undoubtedly so, Your Majesty, but considering the peace between our people is precariously balanced on my marriage to your daughter, it would be prudent to allow us the opportunity to get to know one another, don’t you agree? How can we be expected to foster a relationship between our Courts when we haven’t fostered one within our marriage?”

     

                Lillian’s response was a sneer of contempt, her pale eyes flashing with mirth as she waved her hand dismissively. “As you wish. She’ll continue her practice with the sword but you shall have sole responsibility for her once a week so my advisors can make better use of their time than lecturing the Princess.”

     

                Her eyes then slid over to Lena and her lips twitched derisively. “And you … I have appointed one of my own personal guards to accompany you and ensure you attend your lessons. Reign has strict orders to not let you out of her sight.”

     

                The fae woman stepped forward, her face too gentle for the malice Lena had seen beneath the surface. She was dressed in her customary black leathers and her lips were stained dark, hazel eyes appraising Lena like a predator assessing its prey. Lena was struck again by the kind woman she’d been greeted with in the Seelie Court, a stark contrast to this version of her, twisted by the Unseelie Court.

     

                Climbing to her feet, Lillian tossed down the knife she’d been using to cut slivers of a green apple away from the core and pulled her cloak of black feathers over her shoulders. Purity stepped out of the corner, reading to escort her from the room, and Lena eyed the other woman with curiosity, wondering what she would be like in the other court, and wondering if this place would poison her in a similar manner.

     

                “You may have her today,” Lillian dismissively told Kara, carelessly gesturing, “I will be busy this evening; I won’t be at dinner.”

     

                Pushing her chair back and standing, Kara politely ducked her head and then glanced sideways at Lena. Hesitating, she followed a moment later at a slower pace, her insolence rankling Lillian, who said nothing even as a muscle twitched in her jaw. 

     

                Standing as she swept from the room, they reclaimed their seats once she was gone and Lena sighed as she slumped. Filling a plate, Kara set it before Lena and then refilled their cups of tea. 

     

                “Eat. You will need your strength.”

     

                “I’m not hungry.”

     

                “It’s not a matter of appetite,” Kara softly started to lecture her, “dinner last night will not be sufficient enough to keep your energy up. If you don’t take care of your body, your body won’t take care of you. How can you deny it food and expect to be able to fight for your life?”

     

                “I don’t think a poor diet is going to be the reason I get killed if I’m ever attacked.”

     

                Kara let out a quick chuckle, “no, I don’t believe so either, but it will be a long time until lunch if you don’t eat now.”

     

                With great reluctance, Lena picked at a bowl of cherries and delicate speckled eggs soft-boiled, sipping her tea in between and finding that she was slightly relieved to be spending the day with Kara instead of enduring more lectures about the history between the Courts and the socioeconomic impacts of their endless wars. Only slightly though, and she wouldn’t have told Kara that.

     

                Finishing off what she was willing to eat, she pushed her chair back and stared at her new guard, disgruntled at the thought of Reign skulking around after her. Not least of all because Lena was a little bit frightened of the other woman. Kara followed after her and Lena groaned as they were joined by Andrea in the hallway beyond, the four of them making up an unlikely quartet that was largely comprised of people Lena didn’t like.

     

                “You can go,” she told Andrea. “My wife is in charge of me today.”

     

                “Your wife is in charge of your education today,” Andrea corrected her with an easy smile, “I am still in charge of your schedule and composure and keeping you out of places you shouldn’t be in.”

     

                “That’s what she’s for,” Lena said, gesturing to Reign.

     

                “No, I’m to make sure you don’t do anything foolish, like try to escape.”

     

                “I wasn’t trying to escape,” Lena scoffed, put out as she grit her teeth. “I was enjoying the solitude, which I clearly don’t get enough of with you lot hanging around.”

     

                Kara smiled in that infuriatingly serene manner and cocked her head to the side, eyes creasing slightly at the corners. “Come. I shall fetch my bow and we’ll see if you have the making of a marksman.”

     

                “You mean we’ll see what other ways you can laugh at me,” Lena scoffed. 

     

                Laughing quietly to herself, Kara set off and Lena was helpless to follow, Reign hemming her in from behind and Andrea at her side. Even if she’d wanted to escape, the three fae women wouldn’t have let her get more than a step before stopping her, their easy grace masking their speed, their agility, the wiry strength that didn’t match their lithe bodies. They were beautiful and dangerous, like poisonous flowers, and Lena wasn’t entirely immune to the charm of their appearances. Perhaps if she’d been human, she would’ve succumbed easily, but there was a prickle of unease around them that came from the deep-rooted knowledge of what they were really capable of, and even then she’d barely scratched the surface.

     

                Kara fetched a finely carved bow made from a pale wood, and a quiver of grey-fletched arrows, slinging it over one shoulder and then exiting her suite before Lena could do more than glance around inside. It was nearly identical to her own quarters and not really that interesting, but she hadn’t stepped foot inside it since arriving at Court and didn’t really know all that much about her wife - other than she was maddening . 

     

                Leading their group above ground and beyond the grounds of the royal residences, Kara picked her way through to an open space just beyond the circle of safety the Court provided. With the four of them so near the invisible boundary of patrolling soldiers and carefully concealed buildings, no harm would befall them as Kara strung the bow and beckoned Lena closer.

     

                “You must hold it like this,” Kara instructed her, fitting the bow in her left hand and then pressing two fingers against the taut string. “And pull back like so. Hand to mouth, exhale slowly and then loose. Then with an arrow, like so.”

     

                She demonstrated knocking the arrow, pulling it back with the bowstring in one fluid motion before letting the arrow fly across the wide space between the cavernous trees, striking the tiny eye of the whorl in the trunk of an ancient oak. Turning to Lena, she held the bow out.

     

                “Now you.”

     

                Lena accepted an arrow from Kara and attempted to knock it, feeling clumsy with the length of the arrow and the lack of something to brace it against as she tried to fit it on the string. Then drawing the arrow back itself was its own problem, her muscles straining against the taut string, her left arm shaking slightly as it fully extended.

     

                “You’ll hurt yourself doing it like that,” Kara softly clucked.

     

                “Then how do you suppose I do it?” Lena muttered, her body tense as she tried to retain her grip on the bow and pulled the string without letting the arrow fly widely.

     

                “If you’ll allow me to assist you-”

     

                “Isn’t that what you’re doing?”

     

                “Your form is wrong.”

     

                “You haven’t shown me how my form’s supposed to be.”

     

                “That’s why I offered to assist you.”

     

                “You’re a terrible teacher.”

     

                “You’re an abysmal student.”

     

                Glancing at Andrea, Reign’s lips twitched slightly, hazel eyes appraising the bickering married couple. “Are they always like this?”

     

                “Much to my entertainment,” Andrea said. “Although, it gets weary after a while.”

     

                It went on for hours, with Lena struggling to knock an arrow and fire it in a somewhat straight arc, while Kara’s demonstrations became increasingly smug as she struck the knot in the tree every time without fail. Eventually, she did it with her eyes closed, behind her back and tossed one of her gold rings in the air and shot the arrow straight through it. By that point, Lena had had enough and knocked the bow out of Kara’s hand when she offered it to her for her next go.

     

                “If you’re not going to teach me properly then find something better to do with your time.”

     

                “If you were more willing to allow me to help-“

     

                “I am willing,” Lena heatedly replied. “Telling me to aim higher or don’t let my arm shake isn’t helpful.”

     

                “Here,” Kara impatiently replied, her pointed ears turning pink as she snatched up her bow and put it in Lena’s hands.

     

                Before Lena could even say anything else, Kara pulled an arrow from her quiver and stepped up behind Lena. Bracketing her between her arms, Kara reached around to close over Lena’s hand in the bow, her fingers working hers apart, adjusting her grip, before she knocked the arrow and grabbed Lena’s right hand, putting her fingers on the fletchings. Using Lena’s hands as her own, Kara drew the arrow back in one swift motion, raising Lena’s hand to her cheek and adjusting her sight down the shaft of the arrow.

     

                She was crouched slightly behind Lena to see from her height and let go of the bow to nudge her elbow to a slight bend before nudging the other elbow higher. Straightening up, she was smug as she stepped back.

     

                “How difficult was that?”

     

                “You say that as if I haven’t made it this far yet.”

     

                “You haven’t. Not with a good form … which is slipping, by the way.”

     

                “Stand in front of it,” Lena snapped. “If my form’s so bad I’m sure I’ll miss you.”

     

                Stepping in close behind her wife, Kara let out a small laugh, lilting and shot through with warmth, making Lena’s skin prickle as her stomach clenched with surprise. She didn’t like that her close presence, her laughter even, could affect her so much. Mouth dry as her lips tightened at the corners, Lena swallowed and Kara closed her hands back over Lena’s, steadying her shaking grasp and nudging her elbow higher again.

     

                At the touch of Kara’s fingers slipping back over her fingers, Lena let the arrow fly, hitting the tree for the first time all morning. It wasn’t anywhere near the centre of the thick oak, but it had struck wood, which was an achievement in itself. But it was soured by the pleased note in Kara’s voice, her lips so close to Lena’s ears that it made her tense.

     

                “Now, how difficult was that?”

     

                “I’m done for today,” Lena managed to hoarsely tell her after a moment.

     

                She turned and stepped back, too close to Kara for her liking and feeling oddly hot despite the autumn chill. Thrusting the bow against her, Lena didn’t look her in the eye but glanced over at Reign and Andrea, who’d both long since grown complacent enough to drape themselves over gnarled tree roots, waiting for them to be done.

     

                As she strode past Kara, disturbing Reign and Andrea as they climbed to their feet to retake their positions as her shadows, Lena was irritated to find Kara keeping pace with her.

     

                “You know, considering your mother has entrusted your education to me for the day, I could disagree with you. But as I’m not in the business of deciding for others, I think it’s quite time for lunch, don’t you agree?”

     

                Lena scoffed and stopped, scuffing damp leaves as she turned to look at Kara. Her expression was cool and dismissive as her eyes raked over her wife’s tanned face, her eyes so blue that Lena was beginning to feel grateful for the grey skies so she could escape the reminder of how perfectly it matched the colour at dusk.

     

                “Get over your holier-than-thou attitude,” she softly told her, although there was steel behind the words. “You continue to tell me how you would never force me to do anything as if I should fall at your feet and praise you for it. You’re not better than anyone else here for not taking advantage of me; it’s the least I would expect from our sham of a marriage.”

     

                Setting off again, Lena was restless and annoyed as she walked back the way they’d come - or in a semblance of the direction, steered by Andrea when her lack of direction started to deter them from the path - while Kara stayed behind to pluck her arrows from the tree. Seated in a small antechamber where she took her meals when they weren’t with Lillian, Lena lounged in a chair and drank far too much wine with little food to soak it up, and as lunch dragged into the afternoon with no sign of her wife, Lena felt a prickle of guilt and then unease and then outright worry at her absence. 

     

                Spilling a bit of wine on the table, Lena cleared her throat, the tips of her slightly pointed ears pink as a blush crept into her cheeks. She looked at Andrea and bit her lip before speaking.

     

                “Do you think … I mean … she made it back okay, didn’t she?”

     

                “Who? Your wife?” Andrea asked with indifference. “I would assume so.”

     

                “She enjoys food too much to miss lunch,” Lena brooded aloud, a clouded expression on her face.

     

                Running her finger over the finely wrought silver wine glass, Lena pursed her lips. Draining the rest of it and climbing to her feet, a little unsteady and a little pouty, she swept out of the room and down the hallway until she eventually came out above ground. Wandering the grounds of the royal residence with her two shadows, Lena eventually stopped in a small meadow dotted with the last wildflowers of the year and keeled over into the soft grass.

     

                Weak sunlight streamed through the canopy overhead and she listened to birdsong and the sound of droning bees as she closed her eyes and brooded. The gentle caress of the wind grew colder as the afternoon wore on, overcast skies blanketing the forest, making it dimmer as she pulled her cloak tighter around herself and lingered. She was surprised that Andrea or Reign didn’t drag her back inside against her will, and enjoyed the peace as she breathed in the fresh air, laced with impending rain, and let her head swim sluggishly from heady wine.

     

                A shadow cut across her face, blotting out the weak sunlight, and Lena cracked her eyes open as she frowned. It took her eyes a moment to adjust, to make out the figure standing over her, and then she sat up quickly, the sweetness of the wine turning sour on her tongue.

     

                “What are you doing?” Lillian asked, her voice chilly.

     

                “Meditating.”

     

                “Get up.”

     

                Staggering to her feet, Lena swayed a little and squared her shoulders, blinking rapidly as she tried to stop the sense of vertigo trying to tip her off-balance. Lillian gave her a disapproving stare as Lena raked a hand through her hair and cleared her throat, wilting beneath the stare of the imposing woman. 

     

                “You’ve been drinking.”

     

                “You have nice wine.”

     

                “You should be at your lessons? Where’s your wife?”

     

                Lena gestured vaguely, “Oh. She’s … around.”

     

                “Around?”

     

                “I misplaced her.”

     

                “And how does one misplace a person?”

     

                “My mother did it quite effectively.”

     

                Lillian let out a sharp huff of laughter, catching them both by surprise as her cold eyes narrowed slightly and her mouth twisted with a reluctant smile. “Get inside. I’ll not have you wasting your time lying about; if your wife has abandoned her duties, we shall continue our lessons.”

     

                Letting out a weary sigh, Lena waited for Lillian to walk off before trailing after her at the correct distance, keeping her chin up and her back stiff as she followed her back inside and through to the empty chamber with a latticework of tree roots overhead and a mosaic floor of stones depicting wildflowers underfoot. It was Lillian’s preferred room to teach her in, making Lena stand in the middle, beneath the creeping roots as she tried to make them move with every fibre of her being.

     

                It was to no avail, leaving her clammy and frustrated by the end of their session together, Lillian’s cold amusement at her lack of ability only made Lena more stubbornly determined to make them move. She’d done it before, had exhibited little fragments of power as flowers decayed at a slower rate and trees let her fall between realms, but she could no more master the easy way Lillian manipulated trees and plants and earth than she could any of the other elements. The Queen enjoyed it though, clearly pleased by her failings as she made snide comments about the human half of her polluting her blood and her abilities. 

     

                When she was finally summoned to dinner, the two of them and their guards dining alone, no conversation to ease the tension between stepmother and stepdaughter, Lena sullenly picked at the salad on her plate until Lillian was finished. With a terse goodnight, Lena swept down the increasingly familiar hallways and bypassed the door to her room for the one next door.

     

                Banging on it, she waited impatiently for Kara to answer and then crouched, slipping free one of the jewelled pins Andrea had slipped in her hair that morning and jammed it into the lock. It was a simple mechanism, for all their artistry with their designs, and she flipped the tumbler quickly and pushed the door open, turning to face Reign and raising her eyebrows pointedly.

     

                “Goodnight.”

     

                “Enjoy.”

     

                Making a scathing sound of disgust at the insinuation, she slammed the door shut and prowled through the suite, finding the rooms bare. Resolving to wait as her stomach twisted with unease, having not seen Kara since noon, Lena settled on one of the chaise lounges after stoking the smouldering brazier to warm the chill room.

     

                An hour must have passed by and Lena lightly dozed, before the door opened and she startled awake, heart pounding and a moment of relief cutting through her as she sat up, face soft, and then slammed her defences back into place. Kara paused at the sight of her, a v forming between her brows as her hair hung around her face, damp and the colour of burnished brass.

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Where were you?” Lena asked, feeling stupid a moment later when Kara pointedly replied, pink-cheeked and soft from the hot springs. 

     

                “Taking a bath.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lena smiled thinly. “All afternoon?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “You didn’t meet me for lunch.”

     

                “No,” Kara replied again, although her tone was different, her answer hesitant and agreeing.

     

                Mouth twitching at the corners, Lena climbed to her feet, smoothing a hand over the rumpled clothes she’d worn all day. She struggled to speak for a moment, shifting with uncertainty. “I should go.”

     

                “Why are you in my rooms? And how did you get in?”

     

                “I picked the lock.”

     

                “You didn’t answer my first question.”

     

                “I was waiting for you.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Because you didn’t meet me for lunch.”

     

                “I ate elsewhere.”

     

                “I waited for you.”

                

                “I never said I was eating lunch with you.”

     

                Feeling foolish and still somewhat under the effects of alcohol, Lena was tongue-tied and embarrassed, which made her haughtier as she tried to stave off the warm feeling of a blush creeping into her pallid cheeks. Clearing her throat, her voice held a faint rasp as she brushed past Kara, careful not to touch her, and then stepped out into the corridor before returning to her own rooms. 

     

                Sleep was a fitful thing that night, dreams of salt and water and burning lungs and the cool caress of a lake as it dragged her down keeping her company through the long hours of the morning, and Lena was cranky when she woke. Dark circles ringed her eyes and her mouth was like cotton as she let Andrea do her hair. 

     

                Her days resumed their usual monotonous drag of lessons and curt conversations with people she didn’t care about, and who didn’t care about her. She endured hours spent at Lillian’s side, listening to a circle of Lords and Ladies converse in that language that she felt like she knew but was only just learning, catching the occasional word but not much else. Lena often felt like a well-groomed pet at the Queen’s side, set on an elaborately carved tree stump in her finely wrought dresses and increasingly thicker cloaks as the weeks went by and the weather forged onwards into autumn. 

     

                Kara taught her archery once a week, both of them cool and aloof with each other as they held a bow each and spent hours firing arrows at their claimed oak tree. Lena had steadily improved, although it was still a rare thing when she managed to get an arrow to lodge itself firmly in the tree bark. Kara was more patient with her as well, although they didn’t speak all that much to voice their frustration with each other.

     

                Lonely and miserable, Lena ended up snapping one morning, finally having enough of her sword-fighting lessons. She tossed the sword down and made a frayed sound of annoyance at the back of her throat, her back smarting from the rap of Andrea’s blade a moment before.

     

                “I’m tired of this.”

     

                “Pick up your sword,” the other woman said, gesturing with her own.

     

                “No. I’m done. It’s a waste of time.”

     

                “You’re done when I say we are. Pick it up.”

     

                “You-“

     

                The tip of Andrea’s sword pricked Lena’s throat, her blue eyes bright with amusement. “You’re dead.”

     

                Reaching up, Lena pressed her palm against the flat edge of the sword and angrily pushed it down. Andrea swung at her and Lena blinked in surprise, stumbling backwards, dodging another swing a second later as Lena let out a spluttered squawk.

     

                “If you choose to fight without a weapon, so be it. Defend yourself against me with your hands and let us see if you’re any better at that.”

     

                Drawing away, green eyes wild and body tense, a part of her not entirely convinced Andrea wouldn’t cut her - just a little - as part of her lessons, Lena licked her lips and tried to find an escape. Stumbling back from another slash, she tried to sidestep Andrea and grab her arm, but the fae woman was too quick, lightly laughing as she danced away and beat her back, which only enraged Lena further. She could feel her composure slipping and knew she’d slip up in a moment, Andrea cutting her deeply.

     

                She didn’t though because a moment later, Kara twisted her arm and then struck the sword from her grasp. Her other hand shot out to encircle Andrea’s throat as her pretty face flushed with anger. She’d waited to see it unfold, but at the first sign of it going too far , she’d risen fluidly and swiftly crossed the room to her wife’s defence.

     

                “Have you lost your mind? You’ll kill her-“

     

                “I wouldn’t hurt her - much,” Andrea pouted, “she’s in good need of a proper lesson.”

     

                Pushing her away, Kara’s mouth thinned but she didn’t object. Reign watched with interest, pausing the idle cleaning of her nails with a small knife to watch the exchange. 

     

                Moving over to Lena, Kara reached up and pressed the pad of her thumb to Lena’s throat, blotting the bead of blood before glancing back over her shoulder. Lena stared daggers past her as Andrea arched an eyebrow and shrugged indifferently.

     

                “Lessons are finished for the day,” Kara frostily declared.

     

                “You don’t have the authority-“

     

                “Take it up with your Queen.”

     

                Grabbing Lena’s arm, Kara towed her from the room, bristling as a storm brewed inside her. Reign followed but Andrea stayed behind, and Kara led the trio out to the grounds and then beyond. As they passed the boundary of the Court’s security, Reign drawled something from behind them and Kara curtly responded, towing Lena further into the wildness of the forest before they eventually slowed.

     

                It looked like it was on fire, a blanket of orange and yellow and red everywhere Lena stepped, while the rest was claimed by moss and brown pine needles and butter-yellow mushrooms growing out of rotting logs and half-buried rocks. Breathing in the sweetness of the air, Lena felt some of the tension bleed out of her body and glanced at Kara, who was still gripping her arm, a little too tightly for comfort.

     

                “What are we doing?”

     

                “Getting you away before you make me do something I’ll regret.”

     

                “Me?” Lena spluttered.

     

                Kara’s eyes cut across to her and she gave her an exasperated look, unwinding her fingers from around Lena’s bicep. “It would appear that being in your presence brings out some of my more … undesirable qualities.”

     

                “Oh, that’s why you’re avoiding me,” Lena said with a sharp laugh that cut through the stillness of the forest. 

     

                “I’m not avoiding you,” Kara quickly replied, her cheeks and ears turning pink. “Only … I don’t like to lose my composure, but I feel … protective of you, and that makes me lose control of emotions better reined in.”

     

                “Lose control?” Lena snorted. “I wish you would . You’re the picture of serenity; why don’t you ever just yell? Just shout out me, tell me to fuck off, that you wish I would die. It would be a lot easier to hate you if you were just honest about how you felt.”

     

                Kara’s mouth thinned with displeasure. “None of those things would be honest . But you’re welcome to hate me all the same if that’s what you’d like.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena turned away from her and took a step forward, cold without the warmth of her cloak, which she’d taken off for practice. She’d gotten used to not wearing shoes, the constant movement of her schedule keeping her toes warm, but her leggings and tunic were too thin for the wind howling through the trees.

     

                The warm weight of Kara’s embellished pale blue robe settled on her shoulders and Lena looked up, surprised as she reached for the collar to stop it from slipping off. She could feel Kara’s hands where they rested on her shoulders and took in the resigned tenderness in her wife’s blue eyes as she smiled faintly, her tan fading now that summer was over, leaving the freckles smattering her nose stark against her paling skin.

     

                “Aren’t you cold?”

     

                “I don’t feel it so much. Waterfolk swim in freezing waters at midwinter, largely unaffected, so a bit of wind isn’t much of a problem. You have more of an effect on me.”

     

                She froze at the admission and then cleared her throat as Lena shrugged the voluminous robe on. The sleeves were a fraction too long and too wide to be practical, and Kara wore it with more ease than Lena ever imagined she’d have, but it was warm from her body heat and Lena secretly enjoyed it. The smell of salt and smoke clung to the thick fabric and she surreptitiously breathed it in as she turned, Kara’s hands sliding from her shoulders.

     

                “How do I affect you?”

     

                “You make me … impatient. Argumentative. And I find that I enjoy it more than I should, which isn’t admirable.”

     

                Lena let out a shuddering laugh, her face creasing with bewildered amusement. “Oh, you like it when we argue, do you?”

     

                “A little,” Kara confessed, an innocent note of open curiosity in her response.

     

                The coy amusement of the moment vanished then as Lena hugged the robe tighter to herself, looking around. It was still morning, bright, pale sunlight passing through leaves and needles to dimly light the forest. 

     

                “Isn’t it dangerous for us to be out here?”

     

                “Yes,” Reign interjected, reminding them both that she was there.

     

                She was inspecting her nails, one arm crossed over her chest while she toyed with little flames above each finger, bored by their marital affairs as they bickered and teased and were vaguely vulnerable in such quick succession that it felt like whiplash at times. Lena’s eyes flickered over to her and then back to Kara, who looked faintly sheepish as she smiled slightly.

     

                “You’re less irritable outside, and further from the Court. I thought it might mellow you to have a moment of peace out here.”

     

                Tipping her head back as she closed her eyes and inhaled deeply, Lena let out a shaky laugh that filled her chest, hands hanging limply at her sides. “Nature brings me peace,” she confessed. “It’s … grounding. Trees and leaves and dirt and flowers … I feel calmer because of it.”

     

                “I know. That’s how the water feels for me.”

     

                “I would stay out here forever if I could.”

     

                “We can stay awhile.”

     

                She lowered her head and stared at Kara, a searching look in her eyes as she tried to find some ulterior motive, some game. But Kara wasn’t spiteful, she didn’t enjoy tormenting Lena for the sake of it, and she was actually quite kind at times when Lena wasn’t purposely rankling her. It was nothing more than a small gift of a moment’s peace.

                

                Seizing the opportunity, Lena walked onwards, her pace slow as she basked in the tranquillity of the forest. It seemed odd that something that offered her so much peace could hold so much malice within it, so much danger that it seemed thick in the air at times, a palpable feeling. The sentience of the forest still made her uneasy, the vague notion that the trees were talking and eyes were watching, never fully leaving her, even during the day as she walked beneath the high canopy and watched yellow leaves drift down around her, cradled by the gentle wind. Every so often there would be a screaming wind that blew the leaves around in a flurry, snatching at their clothes and hair, gritty dirt and dried pine needles stinging their cheeks.

     

                A patchwork of grey clouds blanketed the sky, casting a gloomy pall over the day, although the rain held off. Lena’s lungs burned a little from the cold as she walked up gentle inclines and sloping dips, winding past convoluted roots and over logs. The smell of freshly disturbed earth was rich and damp, the sweetness of berries in the air as they passed overgrown blackberry bushes and strawberry plants half desiccated by birds and mice, mould and moss and rain mingling into a heady aroma.

     

                At one point, they heard the sound of running water and followed it to a milky green river, bordered on both sides by choking weeds and the trailing fingers of weeping willows, algae and moss adding a putrid edge to the dank smell of slow-moving water. There was a lichen-spattered stone bridge crossing the narrow stream and Lena moved onwards, the other two women following after her, despite knowing they should all turn back now.

     

                The wind picked up as they walked through a patch of sycamores, thousands of yellow leaves streaming around them as they stood on a rise, staring down at the overgrown brambles and bogs and weeds. They fluttered on the wind drafts and Lena drew in a deep breath, taking in the dark clouds behind the treetops as they stood a little closer to the canopy, the trees not quite so big there.

     

                Though it was midday, they were deep in the forest and once they’d passed through the thicket of sycamores, everything turned bleak and dim, the trees crowding back in and rain starting to fall. It hissed as it pattered on the canopy, falling through and running down trunks and over the mud-slick paths. Kara murmured that they should go back but Lena ignored her for a while, her feet digging into the soft earth as she shivered onwards until coming to a grove of trees. They were blackened husks, their bare branches fanning outwards, a lonely sight between the drenching sheets of rain, and Lena felt a pang of sorrow.

     

                “What happened here?”

     

                “What always happens in war,” Kara murmured. “They should not have touched the trees though.”

     

                Lena’s brow creased with a stern look of deep thought, taking in the blackened trunks, and the scorched ground. The grove was half submerged by deep pools of stagnant water as well, the air thick with midges and flies, and Lena felt something off about the place. Kara reached out and touched her arm, her mouth turned down at the corners with discontent.

     

                “We shouldn’t linger here. There’s too much death.”

     

                And then Lena’s mind made sense of the shapes breaching the shallow pools, the curves of ribs, broken bones and a patch of white that might have been a skull, covered by moss and reclaimed by nature as the body lay where it had fallen. Her chest constricted, the breath catching in her throat, and Lena took a slow step back and slipped, falling down into the mud.

     

                Kara reached down, looming over her and putting her hands on Lena, who looked at her with wide eyes. Her soaked linen shirt clung to her narrow body, the little dip of her navel, the prominent lines of her collarbones, her shifting arm muscles. She pulled her to her feet with ease and Lena grabbed fistfuls of linen as she wobbled and then steadied herself, her eyes glued to the sliver of Kara’s sternum visible at the neck of her shirt. Looking up, she blanched at the sight of Kara’s rain-wet mouth and swallowed thickly, allowing the touch for a moment longer before stepping back.

     

                She stepped onto the moss, the dampness of it soaking the soles of her bare feet, and Lena cleared her throat as she looked down, her hair hanging around her face in lank strands. The rain started to let up then and she listened to the caw of a raven somewhere in the trees, the patter of droplets intermittently falling breaking the stillness of the moment as Lena took in the barren wasteland of this corner of the forest. 

     

                “We should go back,” Reign said, a firmness to her voice as she looked around.

     

                If she was nervous, Lena knew it was time for them to go. Turning, she found herself sandwiched in between Reign and Kara, stumbling forward as the chill got into her bones, making her joints still. They’d walked a while, the three of them silent as they enjoyed the peace of the forest, even the two more in tune with other elements, and Lena was surprised how much time had passed by. The light was already waning, even though it was early afternoon, but dusk was a while off yet, giving them plenty of time to get back.

     

                Before long, she was cut and bruised from stumbling, grateful for Reign’s lithe form winding through the trees. The rain had softened the ground and Lena was ungainly on her feet as the ground sloped down to shallow ravines snaking beneath thick roots, and Kara helped her down each time, gripping Lena’s wrists and slowly lowering her over the edge until her feet met the ground. 

     

                Lena wasn’t sure what it was that suddenly made the other two women freeze, alarm shooting through their bodies as their eyes met past her, but their voices were low as they sank to crouches, Kara dragging Lena down with her by the hem of her robe.

     

                “How many?” Kara asked.

                

                “I can’t be certain. It would help if our Princess could read the ground and tell us.”
