                Glancing up at the sky, which was darkening towards dusk, Kara considered for a moment. “We’re losing the light, and I wouldn’t like to leave them behind us in the dark. Seeing as we’re here, we’d better deal with them.”

     

                “Give me a moment to scout.”

     

                Kara tersely nodded, the quiet hiss of metal unsheathing breaking the suffocating silence of the moment. Reign leapt up out of the narrow ravine, her swords still sheathed at her back, and she scuttled up the trunk of the beech tree shading them, skulking along the thick branches as she tried to get a vantage point on their surroundings. It was a tense five minutes before she dropped back down beside them, startling Lena, which was quickly silenced as Kara slapped a hand over her mouth, giving her a withering look.

     

                “A bear,” Reign murmured, somewhat relieved but still unsettled.

                

                Kara sucked her teeth for a moment and then nodded, a hum catching low in the back of her throat. “We can probably sneak past.”

     

                “Probably.”

     

                Reign’s eyes landed on Lena and then moved back to Kara. Rolling her eyes, Kara climbed to her feet and sheathed her sword roughly, helping Lena up and then moving over to the rock and crumbling earth of the ravine they were in. She laced her fingers together and jerked her head to Lena as Reign leapt upwards past them. 

     

                “You run and you don’t stop,” Kara whispered, “do you hear me?”

     

                “I hear you,” Lena wearily replied.

     

                “You run fast.”

     

                A lump formed in her throat and she blinked a few times, fear coiling in her stomach. “I’m not very fast. I won’t be able to keep up.”

     

                “I’ll not leave you, Lena. Just run and don’t look back.”

     

                She boosted her wife up and then landed next to her, grabbing her hand and setting off at a sprint that almost dragged Lena off her feet. Slowing, although frustrated by it, Kara eventually glanced sideways at her and then tugged her a little more insistently. Lena ran as her lungs burned for air, twigs and rocks gouging the soles of her feet as she ran as if death was chasing her, which a bear apparently was.

     

                Lena tried not to let the weakness in her legs slow her but she stumbled a moment later when she felt a large roar rattle around in her head, jarring her teeth. Eyes flying wide open, she looked to her right and saw the biggest creature she’d ever seen lumbering through the trees. It wasn’t as tall as the soaring trees, but it was easily thirty feet on all fours, the black coat of the bear covered with the forest, a whole ecosystem growing over it as it rubbed up against a trunk, flower petals cascading from the wildflowers and weeds growing rampant on its mossy back, the groaning of wood filling the forest as the roots tried to cling to the ground.

     

                It raked its claws down another tree, stripping bark and scoring deep lines in the trunk. Lena was fascinated as much as she was horrified, and they raced past like mice, unnoticed and inconsequential to the giant bear. Once they were a safe distance away, they slowed and Kara let go of Lena’s clammy hand.

     

                “I haven’t seen a bear this close in a while,” Reign said, a note of unease creeping into her voice.

     

                “I haven’t seen one in the Seelie Court in years,” Kara murmured, equally as worried. 

     

                “What the fuck?” Lena rasped.

     

                They both looked at her and smiled wryly. Reign’s hazel eyes glimmered with mirth and she moved a strand of hair out of her face, “welcome to the old forest.”

     

                A second later an arrow struck her in the chest.

     

                Lena was left staring at it as the sound of ringing steel cut the stillness of the moment, Reign drawing twin blades as Kara unsheathed her long sword. The former snapped the shaft off the arrow and Lena stammered helplessly, her eyes trained on the wound punched through the leather as a figure dropped from the sky, silent and stealthy, sliding down a long rope. The sound of clashing metal drew Lena’s attention as Kara sparred with one figure before the other dropped down beside her and she found herself fending off two . Another arrow whistled past and pierced the muscle of Reign’s calf as her leg buckled, her tanned skin taking on a grey pallor now as two arrows bled her. 

     

                Helpless and confused, Lena turned in their midst, her hands shaking as she looked around and watched it unfold. Reign was on one knee and whipped one blade through the air, whistling as it turned tip over handle to impale a man, before she staggered up and cut another’s head off.

     

                “Get down,” she snarled at Lena, jerking her head aside to dodge the next arrow as another slammed down into the ground at Kara’s feet.

     

                Not needing to be told twice, Lena dropped to a crouch and let out a hoarse shout as the next arrow cut her cheek, whistling past almost close enough to bury itself in her face. Covering the shallow cut, she fell back and scuttled away, a man bearing down on her as he raised a sword high. Lena kicked his knee out and he staggered forward, about to fall on top of her until Reign ran her sword across his throat and Lena squeezed her eyes shut to the spray of hot blood on her face.

     

                The body crumpled to the ground and Lena’s eyes landed on Kara, who was still fighting one of them, while a woman had taken the place of the fallen man. She watched as the man kicked Kara’s leg out, dropping her to one knee as her sword slipped from her hand, and the man swung his sword down to behead her. A cry escaped Lena and she threw herself forward, scrabbling at the mud, and watched with shock as roots erupted from the ground, ensnaring the man until he was fully enveloped, before he was dragged beneath the black dirt without another sound. 

     

                Floundering, Lena blinked as she watched a knife jam into the woman’s eye socket, courtesy of a knife throw from Reign. There was one man left and his sword fell from his hand as Reign slammed the pommel of her sword against his temple, knocking him out cold.

     

                “Why did you do that?” Kara sighed. “We could have interrogated him here.”

                

                “I will do it back at Court.”

     

                “You’re injured, it’s getting late, and we have miles to go while protecting the Princess . We don’t have time to waste dragging a would-be murderer through the forest, just to kill him anyway.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Reign went rigid as her jaw muscles clenched, trying to mask her pain as she let out a shallow, shaky breath. Making a grunt of annoyance, she reached down and snapped the fletching off the arrow through her leg. 

     

                “You take care of that,” Kara said, jerking her chin towards Reign. “I’ll wake him up.”

     

                “As you like.”

     

                Lena was still on the ground and watched as Kara went over to the unconscious man and started slapping his face to rouse him, moving on to cut a length of rope. As Kara dragged him over to the narrowest tree she could find, stringing him up with the rope, Lena watched as Reign crouched, her leg out at an awkward angle, and yanked the arrow from the muscle, teeth clenched against a low growl of pain.

     

                Blood flooded from the hole, turning to ash and cinders as it spilt on the forest floor and she lit her thumb on fire and then pressed it into the wound. The smell of charring flesh made Lena’s stomach turn as Reign cauterised her own wound, and she looked away, slightly terrified of the hunter and the brutal way she tended to her own injuries. Stomaching turning, Lena climbed to her feet and stepped past the dead bodies, staring at the faces and the blood.

     

                She walked away and breathed in the damp air, trying to clear the hot iron stench of spilt blood from her nose as she closed her eyes and swallowed her gorge. Kara managed to get the man awake and asked him a series of questions in their native tongue, her voice sharp and unforgiving as he gave halting, rasping responses at the edge of her sword.

     

                When she was finished with him, she dashed his head against the trunk and his head lolled as he slumped back into unconsciousness. Reign had finished treating her wounds, managing to free the arrowhead from her chest and seal the edges closed before joining Kara. They conversed for a moment in low voices before Reign yanked her sword from the fallen woman’s chest, but Kara stilled her with a hand, her eyes sliding over to Lena.

     

                “You will do it,” Kara told her, and Lena didn’t have to ask what she was talking about.

     

                Lena blanched, shrinking back as her eyes widened and her mouth went dry. “Wha- I- I- no. I’m not- I’m not a murderer. I can’t- I can’t kill someone.”

     

                No one mentioned the man her power had so clearly dragged underground at her desperate command to save her wife. He was undoubtedly dead or would be soon enough via suffocation if the tightly wound roots hadn’t snapped his ribcage in a vice-like grip as they’d buried him alive.

     

                “None of us is until we do it, and we all have the capacity for it. You will not truly understand the severity of our circumstances until you confront the ugly side of this war. Come, wife,” Kara said with faint bitterness, “do your duty. His fate will not be any different should another hand wield the blade.”

     

                “Then you do it.”

     

                Swallowing regretfully as her eyes darkened, Kara shook her head. “I have already experienced the difficulty of a first kill. It’s an invaluable lesson, which would serve you well. As Andrea said, you’re in need of a proper lesson.”

     

                “Fuck your lessons,” Lena ground out through her teeth, white with fear as she stood rigidly, hands curled into fists.

     

                “Oh, just get on with it,” Reign complained, wincing as she tried to put weight on her leg.

     

                Kara ignored her and reached out to snag Lena’s wrist, her eyes assessing the trees as the shadows deepened around them. “There are worse things in the forest than a killer. It’s dangerous for us to linger and we can’t set him free. He must die for his actions. Harden your heart; you will thank me for it once you understand.”

     

                “I won’t thank you for anything,” Lena bristled.

     

                Reaching out for the dagger sheathed at her wife’s belt, Kara pulled it free and worked the hilt into Lena’s stiff fingers. Taking it, albeit reluctantly, Lena stared down at the keen edge of the blade and then her eyes darted up to the man. Her heart raced in her chest and she couldn’t swallow, her throat closing up so painfully tight that she could barely breathe.

     

                “How do I-“ Lena started and then faltered, her voice a hoarse croak.

     

                “I will help you,” Kara whispered, her voice like the sigh of the wind, regretful and soft.

     

                She stepped up behind Lena, setting a hand on her waist and holding her right wrist in the other. Guiding her forward, Lena’s bare feet stumbling over the carpet of damp leaves, Kara raised her arm to situate the edge of the blade against his neck. Lena was grateful that she’d knocked him unconscious again, that his head lolled a little and his eyelids were shut.

     

                “I’ll do it myself,” she stiffly managed to grind out. “If I have to do it, I’ll take the full burden of it. I don’t need you to carry it for me.”

     

                Kara’s touch faded and she softly cleared her throat, “very well, then.”

     

                Moving to the man’s side, she grabbed a fistful of his hair and jerked his head up to expose more of his throat for Lena. Eyes flitting to her wife’s, Lena licked her chapped lips and adjusted the grip of the dagger in her hand as Kara nodded a grim encouragement.

     

                A cold sweat crept over Lena’s body and she shifted restlessly, time slipping by and the shadows growing longer. Kara grew agitated but didn’t rush her, although her attention was no longer solely focused on Lena’s as she listened to the wind, to the leaves and the sounds of the forest, assessing them for any threats as Reign made her impatience evident. The birds were still chirping though, which was always a good sign.

     

                Eventually, Lena inhaled sharply through her gritted teeth and squeezed her eyes shut. Jerking the edge of the blade across the man’s throat, not quite as easily as she would’ve liked, she felt the warm spray of blood on her already bloody face from the close proximity. She didn’t flinch, just let her arm fall limply to her side as her eyelids fluttered and she watched blood trickle from his throat. 

     

                She’d seen it before when Kara had taken her to watch the other traitor die but that had been different. That had been swift, blood spilling from his throat in a torrent of red. This was a slow trickle, her slice too shallow to kill him quickly - if at all. There was a moment of tense silence and then Reign laughed at her failure. Panic set in and Lena’s mouth opened and closed as he started to stir, Kara letting go of his hair so his head lolled, chin against his chest, and he made a gurgling sound at the back of his throat.

     

                “Wha- I-“ Lena stammered until the scraping sound of unsheathed metal greeted her ears.

     

                Kara was tense, ready to deal the killing blow herself, but Lena was quicker, her fingers curling around the hilt and her hand rising from her side to stab it into the soft part of his belly. She stabbed instead of slicing, the horror of how easily the dagger plunged through his skin and muscle with the force she put behind it shocking her. 

     

                Pulling the dagger free again, Lena let it fall limply from her bloody fingers, the breath sharply expelled from her throat. 

     

                “Oh. Oh … no,” she murmured, blinking as if she couldn’t quite believe what she’d done. 

     

                Reaching out, she pressed her fingers over the wound, blood welling up quickly and spilling over her hands. She fell to her knees before him, her eyes level with the stab wound until his body went slack against the rope binding him to the tree, the blood from his cut throat dripping onto her upturned face as her lips parted in shock. 

     

                A ragged sound escaped her when she realised the man was dead, and she pulled her hands back, bathed in red, the cuffs of the sleeves saturated as they slipped back over her forearms. Lips moving wordlessly, she couldn’t bring herself to speak. 

     

                Kara came to her then, crouching next to her, smelling of pine and rain and blood, her fingers gentle on Lena’s cheeks as she made their eyes meet. “Come away. We must leave.”

     

                “He’s dead.”

     

                “You did well.”

                

                Turning, Lena vomited at the man’s feet, one last insult to injury, and Kara swiftly pulled her to her feet, picking her dagger up for her and sheathing it at Lena’s waist. Guiding her away, they rejoined Reign and set off through the forest at a quick pace - or as quick as they could with a trembling princess, a limping hunter, and a weary noble. 

     

                There was something primal about the forest as they passed through it, the dimness of it lengthening the shadows, the needles and leaves muffling their hurried footsteps as they rushed past trees and bushes and brambles. They ended up looping an arm around their shoulders to bear Reign’s weight as her leg troubled her, and Lena felt her skin prickle as a change stole over the forest.

     

                Something lurked at the edges of her awareness, some terrifying presence that wasn’t any less terrifying for the lingering hours of daylight still ahead of them. They were in a part of the realm that was ancient, that was wild and malicious and rarely disturbed. It unnerved the three of them and Lena was starting to resent Kara’s peace offering as she was filled with anything but peace. 

     

                A howl started up a way away, distant and muffled but chilling, and autumn burnished the woods into something beautiful and deadly, a forest fire of crimson and gold. The afternoon was turning towards dusk, and it had fallen a few degrees colder, Lena’s bottom lip trembling as she felt grey all over.

     

                And then they were back, suddenly past the perimeter as autumn wildflowers dotted a grassy clearing beneath the shaded canopy. Bees lazily hummed between the buds, butterflies drifting past, white and delicate like flower petals in the breeze, and birdsong floated across the space. There was some sort of revelry going on, silver goblets clinking, wine flowing and laughter growing louder as they stumbled upon the party, softened somewhat by the sharpness of the wind. Flowers in shades of purple sprouted in abundance, fuelled by the drunken powers of the fae gathered, and trails of white, flowering ivy draped from branches.

     

                Fae women in crushed velvet dresses and wolf masks reeled about in some graceful dance, men in fox and rabbit masks drinking deep purple wine and playing flutes and lyres, laying about in the long grass and stuffed pillows. Platters of food were positioned on low tables and lower-ranking fae carried them around, squirrel and bird masks hiding their faces as they offered up sweet cakes and rosy apples, slivers of pear and bread smothered with honey.

     

                And then the trio stumbled upon them, disrupting the moment with the blood soaking into them, their bedraggled appearances and the injured hunter slung between the other two women. A flute died off as a lyre continued to fill the air with sweet music, eyes landing on them as conversations trailed off. There were dozens more who continued their glassy-eyed dancing and laughing, and Lena thought she spotted a dazed human or two partaking as they fed a woman grapes from a vine, heedless to the violence that had just wandered into their midst. 

     

                “Quickly,” Kara murmured, carrying onwards, forging a path through the throng of fae.

     

                Reign’s face was sweaty and grey, each step causing a grimace, and Lena ran through a list of herbs that could stave off the pain. They didn’t have proper medicine here, didn’t have proper antibiotics and sterile equipment, and, despite her dislike of the woman, Lena was concerned.

     

                Nearing the royal residence, they were greeted by alarmed guards and the other two hunters, Purity running forward to take Reign from them. Pestilence eyed the overwhelming amount of blood staining Lena’s front and arched an eyebrow.

     

                “Good hunting?”

     

                “She’s cauterised her wounds. See her to a healer,” Kara curtly told them before taking Lena’s hand and pulling her forward.

     

                In a daze, her eyes unfocused as her mind wandered free of her body, Lena passed through hallways and corridors, fae servants backing away and watching her pass with startled expressions. Most of them inclined their heads respectfully and murmured vague pleasantries, but they fell on deaf ears as Kara escorted Lena through the hallways, unkempt and with a face like a summer storm.

     

                Lena didn’t really process anything until she found herself standing in one of the chambers with the hot springs, the air humid against her cold cheeks as wisps of steam curled from the shallow pool. Kara was in front of her, carefully pulling off the robe.

     

                “Here. Undress. You need to bathe.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena gave up on words and tore herself away from Kara. Turning her back on her, she fumbled with her clothes and tore them free before walking over to the edge of the pool and staring down into the dark water. It was crystal clear, but the dim lighting of the cavern as the brazier burned away made it impossible to see the bottom.

     

                “It’s quite shallow,” Kara murmured.

     

                Slipping into the warm water, the tiny cuts and scratches marking Lena’s skin stung fiercely and she dunked her head underwater before resurfacing. Water made the mud and blood streaky at the dried edges, but it had dried completely and was caked onto her skin. Leaning back against the edge of the pool, Lena closed her eyes and swallowed the sour taste of bile at the back of her throat.

     

                A splash of water made her open her eyes again and Kara was in the pool too, making Lena tense as she straightened. The pool was still deep enough to come up to her collarbones but Lena was wary of being so vulnerable around other people, her eyes dark as she watched Kara settle on the other side.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Kara murmured.

     

                Closing her eyes again, Lena tipped her head back, feeling weak with exhaustion as the adrenaline started to wane in wake of safety. She didn’t think her legs would be able to bear her weight if it wasn’t for the water’s buoyancy, and her whole body ached. 

     

                The door opened a few minutes later and Lena quickly turned around, wading away from the edge as her heart thundered in her chest. Lillian swept inside and paused as her eyes landed on her bloody daughter. Cocking her head to the side, she arched an eyebrow and gave her an amused look.

     

                “Are you hurt?”

     

                “No harm came to her,” Kara answered for her.

     

                Lillian’s pale eyes swept to her and she sneered, “fortunately for you. You should not have taken her beyond the Court; I forbade it yet you disobeyed me.”

     

                “Forgive me, Your Majesty-“ Kara started, appropriately abashed. 

     

                “It was my idea,” Lena rasped, coming to and dragging her gaze up to meet Lillian’s as she felt the sudden need to protect Kara from the Queen's wrath. “I wanted a break from court, from training.”

     

                “Need I remind you of what happened last time you abandoned your lessons to wander the woods? Do you prefer a cell? I can arrange permanent accommodation for you there if it’s to your liking.”

     

                Lena let out a strained laugh, her eyelids shuttering, and Kara waded forward, jerking her chin forward. She chose her words carefully, pausing as she searched for ones that fit.

     

                “The Princess has had a long day, Your Majesty. She … she saved my life and took the lives of two others. One of which was with the use of her powers. It’s been quite a shock, I’m sure.”

     

                Surprise made Lillian falter for a second, losing her cool composure as she sharply looked at Lena. “Is this true?”

     

                Not trusting herself to speak, Lena managed a shallow nod, her bottom lip trembling as she ducked her head down. Hesitating a moment, Lillian drew herself up and hummed dubiously.

     

                “Well, it seems there is something of your father in you after all. Very good.”

     

                “Goodnight, Your Majesty,” Kara murmured, a polite dismissal that she risked to try and rid them of her as soon as possible.

     

                Without another word, the Queen swept from the room and the doors were closed behind her, shutting them back into their bubble of privacy. The breath hitched in Lena’s throat and she let out a broken sound as tears blurred her eyes. Reaching up, she angrily swiped a bloodstained arm across her face, water smearing it and making the droplets run pink down her arm.

     

                “Hush, it’s alright,” Kara gently comforted her, moving over to Lena.

     

                A proper sob escaped Lena this time as she kept her head ducked down, teeth grit against the horrible feelings weighing heavily in her chest. Kara reached out and picked up her hand, plucking a washcloth from the stack at the edge and soaping it up before she gently dragged it over Lena’s hand and arm.

     

                She worked slowly, carefully, wiping away the blood and dirt as Lena cried. At first, she’d been embarrassed but unable to stop herself, but once she’d fully caved to her emotions, Lena felt a release inside her. For weeks - no, months - she’d bottled so much of it away that to fall apart in a hot bath after a horrifying day granted her the opportunity to vent every pent-up feeling she’d locked away inside. 

     

                Tears cut down her cheeks and dripped into the water and Kara crooned softly to her, a tenderness to her voice that cut cleanly through Lena’s heart. It was more kindness than she deserved, but then she remembered how Kara had told her to do it and couldn’t find any kindness in that act. 

     

                “I hate you,” she whispered, her voice ragged. “I hate you for making me do that.”

     

                Kara audibly swallowed, dipping the cloth in the water and wringing it before she reached up and smoothed it against Lena’s cheek. Eyes opening, Lena stared right at her even though Kara didn’t meet her eyes. Cleaning the blood away, her touch featherlight and frighteningly comforting as Lena allowed her to touch her, shocked by the intimacy of it, standing so close together, naked and each nerve frayed by the touch of Kara’s hand on her arm, her neck, her cheek.

     

                It would’ve been so easy to kiss her, to allow that hatred to boil over into something else, the unbearable tension broken by the angry desire that welled up. But she was tired and heartbroken, guilt threatening to swallow her as she tried to stamp down the breathless sobs. So Lena numbly let Kara wash her until her skin was clean and the chill that had seeped into her bones had vanished.

     

                Once she’d finished rinsing off Lena’s back and working fragments of leaves and pine needles from her dark hair, a painstakingly long process as she tenderly washed each lock, Kara briskly washed herself. Pink-cheeked and soft from their lengthy baths, they emerged and dressed in their dirty clothes, Kara bundling up her bloody robe and gripping her sword in hand.

     

                They skipped dinner and walked straight back to their suites, and when Lena opened her door, Kara stopped her. Her hand was gentle as she reached up and stroked Lena’s flushed cheek, her blue eyes filled with sorrow and a plea.

     

                “Forgive me,” she murmured.

     

                Lena closed her eyes and swallowed. A moment later, Kara leaned in and pressed a delicate kiss to the arch of Lena’s cheekbone, her lips soft and warm and the smell of rain on her skin. Lena’s eyelashes fluttered and her lips parted as a quiet breath escaped her and Kara murmured a parting apology.

     

                “I wish you a kinder sea.”

    Chapter 11

                Lena was quiet and brooding over the following few days, effectively ignoring her wife as she attended her lessons and performed miserably, or made no effort at all, so deeply tangled up in the recesses of her mind as she thought endlessly about the man she’d killed. It was different to how she’d expected it would feel, with no glory but no horror, just an odd sort of emptiness that made her feel nauseous and left her hands shaking at times. 

     

                Her sleep was plagued with nightmares too, but then hadn’t they always been? Roots cutting into her skin, dragging her beneath the ground, filling her mouth with the damp mud and rotten foliage of the forest floor, the flesh withering from her bones as she suffocated and let the forest reclaim her. She was powerless in her dreams, her apparent skill with earth and plants failing her as she was buried alive. It was better than the dreams about water though, but Lena still woke up in a cold sweat in the early hours of the morning, shivering and panting in the dim light of the banked fire.

     

                If Kara noticed the dark circles beneath her eyes, she didn’t question Lena about them. In fact, she was relatively quiet as well, her usual attempts at awkward conversation dwindling to tense silence between them as they sent arrow after arrow at their targets, side by side with a safe distance separating them. She found herself frequenting that clearing they’d claimed for themselves more often now, seeking some comfort in the blank rote of knocking an arrow, drawing it back and letting it loose. Lena was by no means good, but she’d been improving with the hours spent out in the woods as a cold rain poured between cracks in the canopy and her fingers grew stiff and numb around the curved wood.

     

                The days started to become indecipherable, one blending into the other without much difference. It grew colder, so cold that the frigid earth burrowed through the soles of Lena’s bare feet as she trampled over damp ground and dew-covered leaves in fiery shades of autumn as the season wore on. It was at its halfway point now, sweet decay and impending winter leaving Lena’s breath hanging in the air before her whenever she stepped foot beyond the confines of her warm quarters for her lessons. 

     

                Still, she basked in the fresh air that burned her lungs and the cold that made her joints and muscles ache, bewitched by the dangerous beauty of the forest. Even when fae went missing at night, the unfortunate guards on watch winding up with their throats cut or mauled to death by the bolder creatures prowling the wild. There had been an instance as she’d gone on a walk with Kara and Reign, leaving the safety of the nearby Court to venture into pockets of ominously oppressive vegetation, where they’d found a fae man pierced through by thorns as long as Lena’s forearm, blood spilling from his mouth and eyes as the forest claimed him. They’d left him there, not wanting to interrupt this delicate ecosystem of hunter and prey in case the vengeful forest claimed them next.

     

                If she wouldn’t describe it as feeling settled in her new home, Lena didn’t feel quite so out of place. The routine of it gave her a welcome distraction, in comparison to the empty days at Kara’s home in the Seelie Court, and Lena supposed she should feel grateful for the scholars who chastised her and lectured her and made her spend far too many hours hunched over dusty books and scrolls, which wasn’t altogether unpleasant, but Lena missed being surrounded by things that were alive. She only ever felt really peaceful out in the forest proper, amidst the bracken and beneath the trees as her lungs gratefully drank in the sweet poison of the forest. Even if she could leave now, Lena was starting to suspect that she wouldn’t be able to.

     

                Rising for breakfast when Andrea roused her, Lena was quiet as she fought back a yawn and blearily blinked through the ordeal of having her hair brushed to a silky sheet and simply braided. A dress was laid out for her with a woollen cloak in shades of deep greens and Andrea threaded gold through her hair and slipped a couple of rings onto Lena’s fingers before she was satisfied with her charge’s appearance.

     

                Lena arrived last, as usual, always taking a few extra minutes to drag her feet before she was all but shoved into the room with her mother and wife. She’d gotten over her stubborn determination to half-starve herself out of spite and helped herself to breakfast after a stiff curtsy sent Lillian’s way in greeting. She’d gotten quite good at them but never allowed herself to make it look anywhere near as graceful as Kara’s respectful bows.

     

                “It’s the mid-autumn festival today,” Lillian informed Lena towards the end of breakfast. “You’ll attend the celebrations.”

     

                Lowering her spoon from the speckled boiled egg before her, Lena glanced over at her mother as her expression clouded. “What sort of celebrations?”

     

                “Revelry.”

     

                “Revelry,” Kara gently scoffed, coring a pear and then quartering it, adding a section to Lena’s plate. “Of course the Unseelie Court would celebrate mid-autumn with inebriation.”

     

                Giving her daughter-in-law a chilly look, Lillian sipped the hot cider that had started frequenting their tables over the last week to ward off the penetrating cold. “Ah, yes, I’ve heard much about the ascetic reflections of your Court. One would think a solstice would bring more cheer than that, but then you’ve always been a solemn folk. It’s any wonder you know how to laugh at all.”

     

                “Perhaps our humour misaligns. At any rate, I’ll keep to my people’s ways, Your Majesty.”

     

                “You’ll join the Court’s festivities,” Lillian replied, an unrelenting hardness to her words that left no room for Kara to object.

     

                Still, she opened her mouth as if she was about to, inhaling and then letting the breath loose in a resigned sigh. Nodding, she spread honey over bread and carefully layered the pear that she’d cut into slivers.

     

                “As you command. I only ask that the Princess and I observe tradition beforehand, out of respect for the union of both Courts.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, irritated by the prolonged conversation, Lillian fed the soft yolk of an egg to the raven perched as she made a low sound of annoyance at the back of her throat. Lena had gotten used to Lillian’s brusque orders, snide comments and easy dismissals the moment she tired of their presence or the sound of their voices. It had rankled her at first, but there were worse things than being ignored, even if it meant she lived at someone else’s whim. But her mother was a Queen and she fell under her command, even if she was a Princess in her own right - which most days it felt like she wasn’t.

     

                Finishing off her breakfast, taking slices of bread with honey from Kara’s plate and giving her wife a sweet smile. Long since tired of Lena’s antics, Kara just spread honey over more slices and diligently cored another pear, setting more food in front of Lena as they waited for Lillian to leave. It wasn’t long, both of them accustomed to the Queen eating little and drinking moderately more before leaving to deal with tenuous politics and finances for things that exhausted Lena just to think about. Only the day before she’d been subjected to a lecture on grain storage and seasonal trade, although it never seemed like money exchanged hands or anyone starved, as far as she could tell. 

     

                Lillian left shortly after and the two of them remained seated beside each other at the table, a palpable tension dissipating as Lena refilled their cups with a mint tea. Sipping her tea, Kara sat upright in her seat, while Lena immediately deflated into a slouch, drawing her legs up onto the chair and tipping her head back, eyes closed.

     

                “Thanks for the heads up that it’s the autumn solstice.”

     

                “I didn’t think it would interest you to know,” Kara cordially responded.

     

                “And why is that?”

     

                Lena cracked an eye open to watch her. Glancing down, Kara raised her eyebrows as she wryly replied, “because you’ve shown so much enthusiasm towards fae culture until now.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena straightened up and reached for a green apple, turning it in her slender fingers as she brooded. “If I thought I could’ve gotten out of a party by … doing whatever it is you do, I would’ve pretended to be, wouldn’t have I?”

     

                “Would you? That would mean spending more time with me.”

     

                Deliberating, Lena smiled thinly, “preferable to my mother’s company.”

     

                “I thought she wasn’t your mother.”

     

                Freezing for a moment, Lena stammered as she tried to make excuses for the oversight in her wording. “I- well, it’s- that’s what she calls herself. Not that I- ”

     

                “Don’t worry, I won’t tell her,” Kara said with a spark of amusement in her eyes. “Bring your apple, quickly. I’ll show you the proper way to celebrate the autumn solstice then.”

     

                Taking a bite of it, Lena pushed herself to her feet and gestured for Kara to lead the way. The way turned out to be out into the forest, Reign following close behind like an unwelcome shadow, although Lena had grown used to her presence and even managed to elicit some frightening conversations out of the woman. It was still dark, the dawns arriving later with each day as the season crept towards winter, and Lena cursed and stumbled after Kara, who eventually sighed and took her arm to escort her with a little more ease. A low fog blanketed the ground and the two fae women were stiffly on guard, hands on hilts, as the trio moved through the forest like wraiths.

     

                “This is far enough,” Reign eventually said, stopping on a slight knoll thrusting up amidst a patch of hawthorn.

     

                Nodding, Kara turned in a slow circle, looking up at the high canopy overhead. Early morning dew had dampened her hair and it curled slightly at her temples, a sheet of pale gold in the dimness of pre-dawn grey. Drifting down the side of the knoll, she fetched rotting branches and created a neat structure on top of the knoll before looking at Reign and politely raising her eyebrows. From her words, Lena caught the gist of her asking for a fire. 

     

                Reign obliged, unusually cooperative, and stepped back to observe with surreptitious curiosity, which Lena assumed was the reason behind her willingness. With a crackling fire blazing on the knoll, Kara sank down and produced a few stalks of barley, hesitating and handing one off to Lena before glancing up at Reign, who lingered back.

     

                “Would you like to join?”

     

                Holding her hand up as she snorted, Reign shook her head. “You keep your ways, Seelie, and I’ll keep mine.”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Kara handed another one to Lena, who gave her a pointedly clueless look. Patting the damp grass beside her and waiting for her wife to kneel beside her, Kara kept her voice low, all three of them hyper-aware of the fact that they were beyond the safety of Court and it was still somewhat dark out. Dark head ducked in close, Lena ran her thumb over the dried-out stalk and the heads of grain and listened to Kara talk.

     

                “The old ways dictate we light a fire, so even in the coming darkness there will be light, and with autumn being the season of the earth - your season - we give thanks to the earth and all things that come from it.”

     

                Tossing her barley into the fire, she watched as Lena copied the motion and then picked up her wife’s hand. Lena had taken a couple of bites of her apple on the walk and held the half-eaten remains in her left hand now. Taking it from her, Kara gave her a quick smile and then tossed that into the fire as well.

     

                “My people keep with tradition,” Kara continued as the sun started to rise, lightening the forest to the colours of autumn, “so all solstices are celebrated at dawn and dusk beneath hawthorns or rowans. Sacred trees that mean-”

     

                “I know what they mean,” Lena murmured.

     

                Nodding, Kara continued, “of course, your lessons have progressed greatly. It’s an element that old Celts took from us, although they adopted their own meanings for their practices, and we look fondly upon those humans for their love of our traditions. Perhaps you’re familiar with some of theirs, through your mother.”

     

                Stiff and awkward, Lena cleared her throat. “No, the forest- I don’t recall much of my mother, except her death after we left. I’ve never set foot in Ireland.”

     

                “A shame. It’s a beautiful place.”

     

                “You’ve been to Ireland?” 

     

                “Of course. I’ve spent many days there. In many of the old countries, in fact. The Scottish Highlands. Welsh valleys. English moors. Scandinavian forests. Even the Appalachians. I must admit, I find myself very unsuited to your cities though. Too much pollution, one can barely breathe. But the pockets of wilderness … they’re familiar, in a sense. I think you would thrive there, in your homeland.”

     

                Lena let out a small huff of laughter, producing a puff of white in the air before her. The intense heat of the fire warmed one side of her and the other half was slowly freezing as she breathed in the acrid smoke.

     

                “I think I would thrive anywhere but here.”

     

                Giving her a long, searching stare, Kara hummed dubiously, “I think … you would thrive well enough here if given half the chance. It’s a feral, dangerous place, no mistake, but … well, you are half of it. And you can feel it, which is why you so stubbornly resist, isn’t it?”

     

                She didn’t reply, but Lena’s face said it all as she rolled her eyes and then jerked her chin towards the fire. “Go on, what’s next?”

     

                “Blood.”

     

                “Blood?”

     

                “Just a little bit.”

     

                Kara had a small knife in her hand a moment later, slicing through her palm without so much as a spasm of pain on her face, before holding her fist out daringly close to the orange flames, red blood hissing where it hit the fire as beads of water. She held the knife out to Lena, who deliberated over the sanitation of sharing a bloody knife and quickly ran it through the folds of her cloak. Faltering for a moment with the sharp edge of the knife hovering above her skin, Lena bit her lip as she anticipated the sting of pain, the quick jerk cutting through her skin with ease as blood welled up in her palm.

     

                Flinging the blood over the fire, a shower of pale violet petals drifted into the flames and filled the air with the sweet smell of them burning. Wincing faintly at the sting, Lena curled her fingers over the cut and felt the warmth of blood seep through her fingers, held in her palm. She jerked slightly as Kara’s warm fingers grazed her knuckles and she opened her hand, almost involuntarily.

     

                With a thin ribbon of cold water, Kara washed Lena’s palm free of the blood, her fingers waving slowly over the pale skin and clean cut before she produced a spotless white handkerchief and carefully wrapped the cut and tied it off. The tenderness of the gesture made it hard for Lena to breathe, her throat constricting as she watched Kara closely, golden head bowed and serene attention to her wife’s injury with no concern for her own palm, which was steadily dripping water to the forest floor.

     

                “Is that it?”

     

                “Yes, that’s it,” Kara murmured. 

     

                She turned shy then, pushing herself to her feet and reaching a hand down to help Lena up. Tucking a long lock of hair behind her ear, Kara’s cheek shallowly dimpled. 

     

                “It’s a grander affair at my home. All of the fair folk come together, regardless of affinity - the meeting point changes with the seasons and who it belongs to - and we all pay our respects to the forest. There’s drinking and dancing too, yes, but … not with the debauchery of this Court.”

     

                Reign snorted and gave Kara a withering look. “Let’s go,” she ordered, “we don’t want to miss the debauchery .”

     

                The flames dimmed and Kara let out a small cry in protest, taking a hasty step forward. “Leave the fire, Sam. It should burn until nightfall.”

     

                “As you wish. I hope it warms the wolves when they arrive with the smell. We’ve probably lingered too long as it is.”

     

                Murmuring a low agreement, Kara took Lena’s uninjured hand and gave it a distracted squeeze. Walking with her, holding hands with a surprising familiarity that felt natural by this point, Lena took in the early morning sunlight dappling the trees and leaf-strewn floor, catching beads of dew caught on webs spanning the distance between branches or trunks. 

     

                “You did well,” Kara murmured approvingly.

     

                Lena hated the glow of satisfaction that praise brought her, craving any sort of validation after a childhood without anyone to supply it, and turned her head, dark hair curtaining her face as she awkwardly cleared her throat. 

     

                “Careful, Kara,” she coyly replied, “that almost sounds like a compliment.”

     

                “It’s the truth. I hadn’t thought you’d be able to manage an entire ritual, especially not for something you view as primitive - mostly due to scepticism and stubborn rejection as opposed to cowardice-”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                “But I’ve either underestimated your natural curiosity for your heritage or your determination to oppose the Queen at every turn. I initially thought it was the latter, but you wouldn’t willingly spill blood over a trivial matter when bearing witness would have sufficed. Which leads me to the conclusion … the forest has changed you. Imperceptibly, but a small change all the same. You seem more … pliable. I don’t know if that’s the correct word, but your anger has simmered enough for you to see with a clear mind.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Lena’s eyebrows rose in a sceptical manner. “An interesting theory.”

     

                Kara laughed and gave her hand a quick squeeze as if it was the most natural thing in the world for them to be so comfortable around each other. It bothered Lena a little that she did feel comfortable around Kara now - comfortable enough to not hold her tongue, to not rein in her emotions, to let out every thought and ounce of bitterness without fear of repercussions - but in a way, she was the only friend she had in this place, if she could call her a friend, and Lena was alone without her. For all their resentment and bickering and irritable, petty knack for getting under each other’s skin, they only had each other to rely on because no one else cared about them beyond a symbolism of peace.

     

                “Don’t change too much, Lena,” Kara murmured as they carried on, an odd note of fondness in her voice. “I wouldn’t like it.”

     

                Making a disconcerting sound at the back of her throat, Lena’s lips twitched and she kept her eyes on the forest, absentmindedly holding her wife’s hand as they walked back towards the Court. Rabbits scampered past and they saw more than a few squirrels trying to bury nuts for the winter, and when they passed by a chestnut tree, Kara dropped Lena’s hand to run at the trunk, propelling herself up to grab a low-hanging limb on the fifty-foot tree and shook free a raining torrent of nuts as Lena scurried backwards, scowling as Kara’s light laughter drifted down.

     

                Dropping from her branch, Kara made a basket out of her billowing shirt and plucked as many as possible from the ground. Her cheeks were flushed, largely from the cold but also with the bright-eyed delight that was almost childish, and unusually unserious for Kara.

     

                We can roast them in the fire later,” Kara said as she ferreted another one out from amidst the carpet of leaves and loamy earth. “It wouldn’t feel like the autumn solstice without roasted chestnuts.”

     

                “Of course not,” Lena dryly replied, hesitating before sinking into a crouch and pooling her dress to gather them in. 

     

                Reign watched with her usual aloof remoteness, arms crossed and eyes darting around in a hawk-like watchfulness. Once the two women had gathered as much as they could, they left the rest to the wildlife and trekked the rest of the way back in silence. Stopping at Kara’s room, next door to Lena’s, they set the chestnuts in a basket that Kara emptied of scrolls and letters and essays she’d been working on and Lena brushed the black dirt off her hands, the heady smell clinging to her palms after the fact.

     

                “You should get ready before your mother’s patience is tested,” Kara said. “Come. A bath would do nicely; you look half frozen.”

     

                “It’s a wonder I haven’t lost any toes to frostbite,” Lena grumbled.

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara frowned, “don’t be ridiculous; it’s far too warm for that.”

     

                Still, the cold seemed to burrow into Lena, the constant dampness of the earth and pockets of mould and spores in the air leaving her feeling like she was on the verge of sickness with increasing frequency over the last few weeks. The hot springs were a welcome reprieve from it all, steaming water stinging her extremities as she managed to withstand the uneasy ordeal of having a bath. It no longer bothered her quite so much, with showers out of the question and a need to be clean, and she stayed huddled against the rough-hewn wall as steam flushed her cheeks and plastered her dark hair to her temples and she watched her wife bask in the joys of a pool of water.

     

                Kara was far from self-conscious and Lena often had to focus her attention on something else, not for any shyness or sense of modesty but because there was a part of her that wanted to stare, taking in the toned golden muscles of Kara’s lithe form. They were wives by name only and Lena could never have felt anything other than tolerance for Kara, but she was undeniably beautiful to look at. And sometimes Lena wanted to look.

     

                After she’d dried and dressed, Lena went back to her room to find Andrea laying out a dress caught somewhere between a deep purple and maroon, embroidered with a myriad of flowers and thorns in delicate gold thread. It was the nicest dress Lena had, even nicer than the one she’d been married off in, tailored to her size and appropriate for the autumn solstice. Sitting still, Lena endured the elaborate braids - even more elaborate than usual, on par with how Andrea had made her up like a doll to wed Kara - her head feeling heavy with the unfamiliar presence of a gold circlet and topaz and amber threaded through her dark hair with small hairpins wrought into tiny flowers and bees. More ornate rings in similar autumn tones filled her fingers and Lena could see herself losing more than a few of them with ease throughout the day.

     

                Left alone in her quarters, Lena grew antsy and ended up barging into Kara’s rooms, finding her fixing her own hair into something simpler but elegant. She eschewed the richly gilded tastes of the Unseelie and stuck to her water tones in blues and greys and tinges of greenish or silvery hues woven through, the fabric of her clothes always reminiscent of running water. Today was no different, although the shades had steadily grown darker as the warmth of summer had vanished, and she wore a dress of indigo blue shot through with silver, like capped waves on a moonlit night.

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured as she watched Kara twist a section of her hair and wind the silver wire around it, weaving a complex pattern that looked like waves once the effect was finished.

     

                “What is it?” Kara murmured, eyebrows rising with patient expectancy.

     

                Brow creasing, Lena lingered inside the door a second before shutting it behind her and stepping further inside, making herself comfortable. “Oh, um, nothing, I just- I thought you’d already be ready. And … your dress is nice.”

     

                Mouth curling into a smile, Kara gestured to a divan for Lena to take a seat, “thank you. You look like a maple tree come to life.”

     

                Narrowing her eyes, Lena hummed, “I’m not sure how to take that.”

     

                “Well.”

     

                “Alright then. You should hurry; Andrea’s gone to check with the Queen if she’s ready and we apparently have to accompany her procession.”

     

                Grunting, Kara twisted another part of her hair with painstaking care and finished it off before letting out a quiet huff, her shoulders dropping slightly. “You know, I rather prefer the simplicity of my people’s traditions over this extravagance.”

     

                “I think I’d prefer it too,” Lena sighed, draping herself over the furniture as she brooded.

     

                “The winter solstice is aligned with water, so it’s of particular importance to me and my kin,” Kara said, sliding on a few silver rings. “We shall celebrate it together once we return home.”

     

                It was a bold statement to assume Lena’s home was at Kara’s, but she did feel a pang of longing for the serene isolation of that tower. Living in a royal residence crowded with guards and servants and nobles was too overbearing for Lena, who was innately suspicious and didn’t take well to letting her guard down around other people. She’d stayed in packed shelters and crowded group homes and learnt quickly that too many people were a hazard, whether it be her things stolen, caught in the midst of violence or simply not having enough resources to feel fed, safe and rested.

     

                “That’s a long way away.”

     

                “Too long a time,” Kara agreed, longing colouring her words and anguish creasing her elfish features.

     

                Lena didn’t touch on Kara’s evident homesickness and there was a knock on the door a moment later, Andrea’s impatient form waiting in the hallway as Kara poked her head out with a mild look of irritation.

     

                “Oh. You.”

     

                “You’re late. She’ll have your head if you don’t meet her in the outer courtyard immediately. And where’s that infernal wife or yours? She’s less of a Princess and more an escape artist.”

     

                Giving her a wry look as she squeezed past Kara, Lena laughed. “If only I was so lucky to escape this place.”

     

                “Well you can’t and you’re late. Come along,” Andrea briskly ordered with a snap of her fingers.

     

                “You do recall the part where I’m a Princess - your Princess, I might add. You order me around like a dog.”

     

                “A dog is better trained.”

     

                “To that I can agree,” Kara murmured behind Lena as she followed.

     

                Coming to an abrupt stop in the passage, Lena purposely angled her arm so that when Kara ran straight into her, her elbow winded her. Making a breathless sound of displeasure, Kara nudged Lena to keep walking.

     

                They were outside a mere minute later, the Queen’s cold demeanour sharpened by her wintery gaze, piercing Lena as she stepped outside into the late morning pale sunshine. Lillian was wearing an identical shade to Lena’s dress, although was more richly adorned and had her usual cloak of sleek black feathers falling away from her shoulders, while Lena had been allowed a crushed velvet half cloak that didn’t mask the extravagance of her dress.

     

                “You’re late,” Lillian snapped as Lena dipped into a weary curtsy.

     

                Stepping past Lena and politely bowing, Kara then turned slightly, her body curving around Lena’s as she hesitated. There was a flicker of wariness in her blue eyes as her lips parted and then she touched her fingertips to Lena’s cheeks, the featherlight warmth of her touch making Lena’s chest tighten.

     

                “Forgive us, Your Majesty,” Kara demurely replied before Lena could offer some brash response. “We were spending some much-needed time alone and lost track of time.”

     

                Reaching out, Lillian smacked Kara’s hand aside and scoffed contemptuously. “Don’t seek to fool me, girl. I have more wits than my daughter; I can see through you with perfect clarity.”

     

                “Then I must apologise, Your Majesty, for clouding your vision just this once - we were together, were we not?”

     

                Kara’s eyes landed on Lena and then slid to Andrea, who looked hesitantly suspicious as Kara spoke truthfully in the fae tongue, understood by Lena, much to her surprise. Lillian arched an eyebrow at Andrea and the noblewoman lowered her head deferentially, or perhaps trying to seem more unnoticeable.

     

                “I fetched them together from Lady Kara’s quarters.”

     

                “Inconsequential,” Lillian dismissively replied, “it’s almost noon and you’re late.”

     

                Lillian walked off, tall and graceful as her cloak rustled the leaves of the overgrown courtyard, and Lena hurried to take her place at her right hand, a step behind with Kara to her left. Green eyes cutting over to her wife with irritation, Lena could feel the touch of her fingers on her cheek and her face clouded with suspicion.

     

                “What did you do that for?”

     

                Kara glanced at her at the muttered words and raised her eyebrows. “Do what?”

     

                “You know what you were insinuating. And what’s the point? Everyone here knows we can’t stand to be around each other.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara softly sighed, reaching out to take Lena’s hand, raising it to kiss her knuckles before she safely tucked it in the crook of her arm and led her onwards. “But we have the upper hand here; say we keep people guessing at our true feelings for each other … well, then they’ll be unsure about how to manipulate us, how to use us against each other to fracture the peace or hurt one another. People divulge things depending on how you present yourself - as someone who despises me, one might tell you of a way to get rid of me and gain an advantage in the next war, yet as someone who loves me, others may come forward with ways to strengthen the peace between Courts, to promote trade and land treaties. We shouldn’t let our moods dictate our greatest asset, but our minds. Rational thought and logic are weapons in their own right, and while you’re no master of the blade or bow, you have a sharp tongue and more wit than the rest of the Court. Use your advantages to their fullest and we’ll come out on top.”

     

                “You make it sound like it’s life or death,” Lena rolled her eyes.

     

                “It very well could end up being so.”

     

                Lena made a noncommittal sound of doubt and let her attention drift as she followed her mother to that shallow pond with the large tree growing out of it, assembled Lords and Ladies in finery already waiting for them. There was an air of arrogance and languid aloofness amidst the crowd as if they were already tired of waiting and would prefer to be deep in their cups and dancing to music. Whether they knew Lena was the cause of the delay or not, they still cast sharp glances her way, full of judgement and shrewd malice.

     

                Flowers had sprouted in abundance, and Lena mentally named them all as she walked amongst foxglove and bluebells and hanging wisteria mingling with tree branches and ivy. There were more than usual, coaxed forth by her mother and her ilk - Lena hadn’t managed anything earth-related since Kara’s life had been at risk - and the pond was almost choked with water lilies. The dank shadows of the clearing made the air sweet with stagnant water and moss and Lena drew in shallow breaths as she followed Lillian along a wide root and stood stiffly at her right-hand side, with Kara on her right in turn.

     

                Lillian’s voice was coy and drawling as she gave a short speech, owls and doves and ravens in the branches of the tree while swans glided through the crowded surface of the pond, the oddly serene beauty of the place lost on everyone but Lena as she ignored the incomprehensible language to focus on it. Motes of pollen swirled past as she could taste the sweetness of rotting apples in a nearby orchard and the honey from the hives. Closing her eyes, she fell into a sort of stupor, her fingertips tingling at the headiness of the forest as she let it lull her into a peace, which she was violently dragged from at the sudden sound of musical instruments and voices.

     

                Blinking back the dazed feeling, Lena stumbled alongside Kara for a moment as she tried to shake her head and followed in Lillian’s shadow. The Queen led them through to a grove of hawthorns and rowans, tables laden with food and casks stacked nearby, wine and mead and ale ready to serve. Ribbons and vines of flowers fluttered in the breeze and Lena took it all in as her feet trampled tiny buttercups and daisies, brought forth again with the odd fae power, even though it was long past their time to flower.

     

                “A drink?” Kara offered up in suggestion.

     

                “A dance,” Lillian cut in.

     

                Glancing up at her mother, peeved by the mere act of having to look up such a way, Lena’s mouth thinned. “I don’t dance.”

     

                “That’s why I’ve made you take lessons.”

     

                “And I still don’t dance.”

     

                “You will dance because I tell you to.”

     

                Trying to dispel the tension, Kara smiled with ease, taking Lena’s hand in her own and bowing slightly, her eyes flashing a warning to behave. “So we shall dance, Your Majesty. Come along, wife.”

     

                “I’m going to step on your toes,” Lena threatened under her breath.

     

                Chuckling as she escorted her over to a grassy patch of earth, Kara twirled her in a circle, which Lena stiffly endured, before taking her into her arms. Jaw clenched and radiating discontent, Lena forgot every dancing lesson she’d been forced to take and allowed Kara to try her best at coaxing her through the steps. And she did step on her toes - numerous times.

     

                “It’s not so bad,” Kara murmured, her lips just above Lena’s ear.

     

                “That’s your opinion,” Lena shot back, “you’d find a better partner with someone else.”

     

                “I could find a worse one too.”

     

                Snorting, Lenap pulled back a fraction to give her a droll look. “That’s a lie.”

     

                Grinning, Kara shrugged and didn’t reply. She smelled like impending snow and Lena suppressed a shiver, drawing closer to Kara’s contrasting warmth. Allowing herself to be lulled by the music and the dancing, Lena lost track of time, the afternoon passing by quickly without her knowledge. Kara was attentive, procuring food and drink without Lena even being aware that she’d gone, and she could easily believe humans would dance themselves to death, their feet worn down to bloody flesh and bone after days and nights spent swept up in it all. She was only half immune to it and felt a little off as the day wore on.

     

                She was dancing with Kara again, somehow, against her will - or rather she thought it was against her will - and felt flushed from sweet wines and warm despite the chill of the afternoon. Kara’s hand was rough in hers and Lena’s stiffness had thawed a little, the soles of her feet dirty and damp, and she’d forgotten about her earlier annoyances until Kara had the misfortune of opening her mouth again.

     

                “Your fingernails are like fish scales,” Kara said, holding Lena’s fingers tightly as she kept her in motion, the music surrounding them as everything took on a disoriented feeling.

     

                Lena scowled, her green eyes bright with annoyance as her mouth turned down at the corners. She brought their dancing to an abrupt halt and made a contemptuous sound at the back of her throat, tearing her hands free.

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                Floundering with a stricken look on her face, Kara couldn’t formulate a response as her wife stalked off through the dancers. Pushing her way to the edges of the sprawling gathering, Lena snatched up a glass of cherry wine, a rich red, almost like blood. Hesitating as she surfaced through the fog in her mind, she closed her eyes and banished memories of the coppery tang in the air and hot spray on her skin, forcing the cup back and swallowing painfully.

     

                “Oh, that won't do,” a tall fae woman tutted, her fingers trailing over Lena’s hand as she worked the chalice free and tossed it into the grass. 

     

                Hand moving so she could trail a long finger along the underside of Lena’s jaw and prop her chin up on the tip, the woman gave her a sharp smile. It was wolfish and dangerous, reminding Lena of the chilling first encounter with Reign, Purity and Pestilence in the shadowed shopfront of her florist. There was no kindness on the woman’s ethereal face and it rankled Lena slightly, being toyed with.

     

                She slapped the woman’s hand away, her lips twisting derisively. Andrea was beside her then, saying something about being careful as Lena struggled to catch half of the words thrown at the other woman. 

     

                “We’re just having fun , aren’t we?”

     

                Her eyes cut to Lena, coy and gleeful, and Lena scoffed and opened her mouth to reply before a cup was procured. “Perhaps something stronger? You must be having a dismal time with that Seelie wife of yours.”

     

                There was venom behind the words and she felt as if she should defend Kara but didn’t have time to as a cup was pressed to her lips, tipped to let a strong blackcurrant brandy sear a path down her throat as she quickly swallowed. Streaks of deep purple cut down the sides of her mouth as she made a sound of protest at the back of her throat and Lena coughed at the burning feeling as she wiped at her mouth.

     

                “Sit,” Andrea murmured to her, gripping her arm and leading her over to a low divan in the shade of a rowan tree. “Careful how you compose yourself, Your Highness. The Queen shall have both of our heads if you cause a scene.”

     

                “Oh, it’s mid-autumn,” the fae woman proclaimed as she followed after them, “we’re supposed to be celebrating, and what’s a celebration without a drink, no? Eve, why don’t you fetch us something stronger?”

     

                The woman raised her voice to call out to Lena’s ex-employee, and Lena scowled at her as she slumped and then straightened at Andrea’s hand pressing against her spine, forcing her upright. Giving her a snarky look as Andrea arched an eyebrow, unbothered by Lena’s annoyance, Lena rolled her shoulders and jerked her chin forward. Behind them, Reign leaned against a tree, her ever-present shadow lurking around ominously for any sign of a threat against the Princess, and Lena ignored her as she sat rigidly, sandwiched between her attendant and this stranger.

     

                “Here. Drink.”

     

                Looking at the cup held out to her, Lena blinked and found Eve standing there with a laden tray in front of the fae woman. Taking a cup, Lena took a sip of the contents and found it bitter but strong. That was good enough for her if she was forced to be at the celebrations, ash smeared on her cheeks and a brooding look of annoyance on her face. The least she could do was drink enough for her discomfort to soften into a haze of drunkenness.

     

                “Oh? Perhaps you’re interesting after all. You and I shall have some fun; I don’t imagine you encounter that often in the presence of your brooding wife. I could never suffer those Seelie and their infernal arrogance. One must feel horribly trapped in a marriage with one. All for the pretence of peace, when I say war should be preferable.”

     

                “Veronica, you overstep,” Andrea warned her quietly.

     

                Letting out a sharp laugh, the woman - Veronica - sprawled on the carved bench, so close to Lena that it was rather uncomfortable, the smell of ashes on her skin and smoke on her clothes. 

     

                “You shared the same sentiments until it was your father’s life at risk for treason. What do I care for peace? There’s more profit in war.”

     

                “Only for the winning side. Of which we were not.”

     

                Humming, Veronica’s dark eyes landed on Kara’s form, tall and slender and easily discernible from the Unseelie fae gathered in the forest. Lena had never noticed it, but there was something about her wife that marked her as different, for all the similarities between the Courts. Yes, they were all inhumanly beautiful and graceful and dangerous, but there was a radiant softness to Kara, in her cornflower blues and stone greys and all the shades of seas and rivers, that marked her as an outsider. 

     

                “Unfortunately for us, we’ll never find out which side would have prevailed in the end, although, now we’re graced with the presence of our new Princess. Oh , would you look at how small her ears are,” Veronica laughed, “it’s a wonder she can even hear us with the size of those tips.”

     

                Frowning, Lena self-consciously touched her fingers to her ears, the small, prominent point hidden by the gesture. Veronica just laughed again and Lena found herself quickly disliking the woman more and more with each passing moment as she sipped her wine, the woody taste of nuts and tart fruits not entirely palatable as she drained another chalice. There was a pleasant warmth in her stomach though, smothering the clenched knot of discontent, and Lena did like that as it blurred her annoyance a little and softened her anger. 

     

                Still, she stiffened when Veronica reached up and brushed her hair away from her face, fully exposing her ear instead of the slight tip that had parted her dark locks. A crease formed between her brows and she shifted uncomfortably, Andrea murmured a low warning which Veronica ignored as she touched a fingertip to Lena’s ear. Going rigid, Lena jerked her head to the side, her green eyes clouded with annoyance.

     

                “Sensitive,” Veronica coyly said, a few laughs rippling through the nearby audience.

     

                Lena opened her mouth to excuse herself but didn’t have the chance to formulate a response before Kara was there, her fingers tightly encircling Veronica’s wrist in a white-knuckled grasp. Stiff and pink-cheeked, Kara ground out a few words and Veronica shrugged, her fingertip brushing the slight point of Lena’s ear as she removed her touch. Kara let go of her and said something else, her eyes cutting to Andrea and Eve and the others standing around them, tension clouding the air for some inexplicable reason Lena couldn’t decipher. Draining the cup of wine she was holding, refilled at some point without her even noticing, Lena set it down on the bench beside her and then found herself hauled to her feet, letting out a sound of protest as Kara drew her to her side.

     

                Her wife’s anger was evident in the taut lines of her body as she stood over the other woman, her voice low and trembling slightly with the effort to retain her composure. Veronica stared up at her, indifferent and now draped over Andrea’s lap with a half-eaten plum held between slender fingers. Her nonchalance only incensed Kara’s anger, the exchange too quick and complex for Lena’s basic language skills to cobble together into sentences. A cutting remark from Kara made Veronica let out a purring laugh at the back of her throat before she made a dismissive response that had everyone within earshot tittering and muffling laughs.

     

                Flushing red, Kara clenched her hands into fists and her eyes slid to Andrea. Jerking her chin, she made a sharp string of words and then grabbed Lena’s arm, towing her away as gently as possible. Feet slipping over damp, trampled grass, Lena scowled, trying to wrench her arm free.

     

                “Why are you so angry?” she snapped.

     

                Kara pushed through a patch of brambles as she stalked away from the group, cutting a path through the wilder patches of the sprawling party and coming out near a reeling group of dancers in the midst of weeping willows. The trailing branches caressed Lena’s shoulders as she was led into their shade and through to the other side, and then onwards, away from the revelry. 

     

                They approached the dim mouth of a tunnel boring down through the earth and into the damp bowels of the royal residences and stepped inside, blotting out the blue dusk as sconces lit the way. Tearing her arm free, Lena came to a stubborn stop as Kara rounded on her. Eyes dark with a wounded look of betrayal, cut through with black anger, cheeks pink in the torchlight and voice low with contempt, Kara stepped in close as she softly exploded.

     

                “You- you are intent on making as much trouble for me as possible. You are selfish and arrogant and possibly the most ignorant human to step foot in this forest.”

     

                Lena let out a choked laugh, shock crossing her face. “Excuse me?”

     

                “I tirelessly devote myself to keeping the peace and all the while you flaunt its fragility in plain sight of the whole Court, without even an ounce of care for appearances, for how much you weaken us-”

     

                “Are you really so incapable of going a single day without blaming me for some ridiculous rule I’ve broken? What have I done this time? Please, by all means, tell me what’s so offensive . What did I flaunt? ”

     

                “You let her touch your ears,” Kara quietly fumed. 

     

                Caught off guard, Lena couldn’t do anything other than laugh. It was a choked, halting thing at first as it worked its way up her throat, but then she laughed outright in Kara’s face at the absurdity of her statement. Stiff and evidently embarrassed, a muscle twitched in Kara’s jaw. She was close enough that the clean scent of rain cut through the dampness of the earth, and she saw a few nicks of blood on Kara’s cheek and neck from the overgrown brambles she’s torn her way through.

     

                “My ears? You’re mad because someone touched me? Are you really that possessive? Or is it jealousy?” 

     

                Her tone lightened with amusement and then turned mocking, which only served to deepen Kara’s scowl as she ground her jaw. Lena was surprised she didn’t crack a tooth from the effort.

     

                “I am not jealous,” Kara frostily replied, “what cause do I have to be jealous? Although, perhaps I’m envious of the fact that they are not married to you.”

     

                “By all means, have your fun with other people, if that’s what this is about. Do you think I care about who’s in your bed at night? You think too highly of yourself if you think it bothers me.”

     

                “It should bother you. Not for any fondness for me, but for how it affects our marriage. How it impacts the truce. You’re a Princess, and one might expect you to present yourself with more decorum than that.”

     

                “The Queen, perhaps, but then I was never in agreement with her anyway,” Lena lazily drawled, committed to getting deeper beneath Kara’s skin now.

     

                Kara loomed over her, anger making her beauty somewhat wilder, a tempest held at bay in her storm-blue eyes as she filled the narrow hallway. “You may not be in agreement with her, but you are your mother’s daughter.”

     

                “You’re ridiculous,” Lena scathingly replied. “She touched my ears - big deal. Should I get mad when Andrea brushes my hair? When Reign drags me back to training when I try to leave?”

     

                “It’s different,” Kara ground out, flushed and agitated,

     

                “You know, every time I start to think that maybe you’re not the biggest pain in my ass, you go and open your mouth and ruin it. I’m starting to think the only good thing about you is how you look.”

     

                Opening her mouth, Kara was struck speechless and looked peeved at that. Clamping her mouth closed, she scowled and her face reddened and after a moment she brushed past Lena hard enough to knock her into the wall.

     

                Letting her go, Lena hesitated and then turned, seized by a sudden urge to defend herself further. “They’re ears . Do you understand how fucking crazy you sound?”

     

                Kara shot something back over her shoulder as she stepped out of the hallway, the words meaningless to Lena, who made a ragged sound of frustration and slammed the side of her fist into the earthen wall, which responded by parting. That was even less satisfying than the bruising pain of impact she’d been anticipating and only made her madder.

     

                Stalking back to her room as she muttered under her breath, Lena slammed the door and shed her half cloak. It was warm in her quarters with the lit brazier and she wiped her brow on her sleeve as she started to pace. Her chest felt tight and she was flushed with anger, finally settling down in the room with her writing desk and modest collection of accumulated books.

     

                Fingers itching to do something, get around something, Lena set a blank piece of parchment before her and dipped a quill in ink. Breathing slowly, she practised her glyphs by writing various sentences she’d learnt over the weeks.

     

                An hour slipped by and then two, her head clearing somewhat from the strong wine and brandy, the taste of it clinging to the back of her throat. She cleared her throat and then glanced at one of the lit candles, trying to measure the time; it had been not far off dusk when Kara had stalked off and she hadn’t returned yet. Lena wondered if she would at all, or if she was already squirrelled away in her own quarters, sulking.

     

                Her eyes were heavy and her head was aching when her door opened. Dropping the quill to the desk, Lena paused before climbing to her feet and stepping out from behind her desk as she waited. Cupping her elbows, she gave Kara a severe look. Her wife was pink-cheeked from the cold, bringing the smell of rain and pine sweeping in with her as she brandished a bloody sword. A jolt ran through Lena as she momentarily panicked before watching Kara move through the space with ease, uninjured.
