                “I thought you would’ve rejoined the party,” Kara murmured. “Andrea said she hadn’t seen you since.”

     

                “I didn’t want to go in the first place,” Lena snarkily replied.

     

                Grunting, Kara brushed damp hair out of her face. “It surely would have improved your mood; as it is, I’m sorry for my part in souring it. My anger was misdirected but they were … they were making a mockery of you.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena’s forehead furrowed as she faltered, embarrassment washing over her as it made her haughty. 

     

                “Oh. How so?”

     

                Softly huffing, her eyes flinty with annoyance, Kara shook her head. “Don’t trouble yourself about it.”

     

                Glancing down at the bloody sword, Lena shifted restlessly and nodded at it. “Did you- did you do something stupid?”

     

                Snorting, Kara shook her head as the corner of her mouth twitched. She didn’t offer a reply and Lena made her own conclusions, taking in the flecks of blood and the smell of pine and wet earth.

     

                “You’ve been into the forest,” Lena noted, an accusation to her words. “Alone. ”

     

                Kara gave her a quick glance, wiping her sword on an oilcloth and then sheathing it. “There are many of us who enjoy the privacy of the old forest by ourselves. All of us have grown up in the midst of it, spent decades, centuries, millennia walking through groves and valleys and dells, and know all there is about the dangers that lurk in the wild corners at night. You are not one of them.”

     

                Spluttering with indignation, Lena jerked her chin forward, “I seem to recall only getting into trouble in the forest when I’m with you.”

     

                Setting her sword down, Kara moved quickly, her fluid movements too graceful for the speed she turned on Lena, tall and intimidating yet so very very gentle as she reached out and traced her fingertips in reminiscence of a monstrously large wolf’s claws. Lena’s throat closed up at the feeling of Kara’s fingers moving over the cotton weave of the dress she was wearing. 

     

                “I seem to recall a time I was not with you,” Kara murmured.

     

                Scoffing as her cheeks reddened with annoyance, Lena shoved Kara’s arm away. “Well, you didn’t tell me there were wolves here, did you?”

     

                “Are there no wolves in human forests? Where else would you have imagined them to live? As well as the bears, the deer, the birds-”

     

                “I haven’t seen any plane-sized birds around here.”

     

                “I have never seen a plane; I’m not sure how they would compare in size.”

     

                “And there aren’t any elephant-sized wolves growing their own ecosystem in their fur back home either. That’s- that’s … not normal.”

     

                “What is normal?”

     

                Clenching her teeth, Lena let out a soft hiss, “yes, please, wax philosophically to me right now. It’s just what I would like.”

     

                Kara’s brow gently creased as she clasped her hands behind her back. “I’m not much of a philosopher-”

     

                “Thank God for that.”

     

                “Your Gods don’t exist here-”

     

                “No, I- I’m not religious, it’s an expression.”

     

                “Odd. Religion. Such a baseless human notion to believe in something you can’t even see. We don’t believe in anything but the trees, the water, the air and fire. Tangible things that provide for all life, and that which we return to upon death. Simplistic, perhaps, but you can feel it, can you not? The forest is alive , it behaves by its own will, its malice and poison. That’s why you shouldn’t walk alone beyond the borders of the Court. Not unless you can feel that.”

     

                “Oh, believe me,” Lena said with disdain, her lip curling slightly, “I’ve felt that since the moment I stepped foot in this cursed place. It’s- it’s suffocating. As bad as you are.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, an alienness to her ethereal beauty that reminded Lena that she wasn’t speaking to anything even remotely human, and was only half of one herself, Kara blinked. A slow smile spread across her face then, heartbreakingly sweet as she seemed lit from within by a golden glow, her eyes as blue as the sea, her hair silken wheat and her slender height sylphlike and delicate. Lena’s stomach knotted itself with unease. 

     

                She now knew how easy it would have been for a dazed human to allow a creature like this to coax them through to this realm, to drink wine and eat the fruit and stay forever, a blissful prisoner. Beneath the otherworldly beauty, there was a danger that made the hairs on the back of her neck stand on end, and Lena supposed she should have been grateful for the immunity her fae blood offered her. If Kara had stepped out of a puddle in the small courtyard behind her shop and beckoned Lena to follow her through, she wouldn’t have stood a chance.

     

                “I am not suffocating you,” Kara gently replied, “I’m keeping you safe.”

     

                Trying not to sound too bitter, as grateful as she was resentful, Lena’s mouth twisted derisively. “Both can be true.”

     

                “Then let me give you the space you so desperately crave,” Kara roughly replied, frustration making a soft pink blush creep up her neck and tint the tips of her pointed ears.

     

                She snatched up her sword and turned away, the fluid velvet folds of her navy cloak rippling like midnight as she strode off a few steps.

     

                “You’re too sensitive,” Lena called after her. “It’s never been personal; I just don’t think we need to pretend to get along.”

     

                Stopping in the doorway, Kara stared straight ahead for a moment, square-shouldered and bristling, before she deflated, seeming to shrink before Lena’s eyes. “There is every need.”

     

                Roughly sighing as her mouth turned down at the corners, Lena crossed her arms over her chest. “You know, you really piss me off.”

     

                “We share that sentiment.”

     

                “Why are you always so … uptight? You have everything you could ever want and you act as if I’ve ruined your life.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara considered that. “You have, in a way.”

     

                A disbelieving laugh scraped Lena’s throat as she blinked, taken aback by Kara’s candour for something she didn’t believe she was guilty of. The deal had been made before Lena had even been dragged from her home one inconsequential evening, forced to wed Kara without so much as a moment’s notice for the nuptials, yet she had ruined Kara’s life? Perhaps they were both the cause of each other’s happiness, but Lena hadn’t been a willing participant in it.

     

                She was still scrambling for a cutting response when Kara grimaced. “Forgive me, that was rude of me to say. I admit to feeling resentful that I’m here, in part due to you, instead of in my own Court, but the blame shouldn’t fall to you.”

     

                Aloof, Lena remained silent. Maybe it was childish, her surly expression making Kara’s own face slip deeper into apologetic pleading, woefully guilty and tender, but Lena was tired and drunk and feeling too warm in all of her layers. She tugged at the neck of her dress and cleared her throat but couldn’t find any words to respond as Kara waited for her to speak.

     

                Pausing a moment longer, Kara eventually let out a long sigh. “I shall see you tomorrow. Hopefully my company will not be too unbearable for you.”

     

                Rolling her eyes at her wife’s melodrama, Lena fiddled with the rings on her ink-stained hands and then crumpled up a piece of paper she’d been using to write out the names of flowers and trees in her increasingly improving fae script. Dropping it onto the littered desktop, Lena let out a hissing breath through her teeth and braced her hands on the edge of the desk, mouth a flat line and green eyes brooding.

     

                Her throat was dry and she tried to clear it as the glyphs on the pages before her blurred, her pallid cheeks strangely flushed as a damp sweat made the thick cotton cling to her skin. She tried clearing her throat again and coughed, the coppery taste of blood filling her mouth. Frowning as she swallowed, it got caught in the back of her throat and Lena let out a spluttering cough.

     

                Red speckled the creamy pages before her before and she was wracked by a coughing fit, more and more red flecking the paper as she tried to speak, her head spinning, her ears ringing. Drawing in a ragged breath, she managed a pitiful word.

     

                “Kara.”

     

                Her wife had already turned near the front door of the quarters at Lena’s coughing, and as Lena’s fingertips came away stained vividly red, petals falling from them, her eyes landed on the pale face of her wife filling the doorway. Fixing her dizzying gaze on Kara for a moment, Lena swayed unsteadily on her feet as it started to dawn on her that she’s been poisoned. And then she collapsed to the ground like a sack of stones.

    Chapter 12

                Within moments, Kara had Lena in her arms and was striding out of her quarters, her heart pounding in her chest and the clammy feeling of fear creeping up on her. She made a few turns as her body acted on its own, leading her away from Lena’s rooms, away from further danger as she tried to get her somewhere safe. 

     

                A young boy dressed in the livery of a kitchen hand appeared at the end of the hallway, carrying a basket of apples, on his way to the party. He paused at the sight of her, his mouth slack with shock, and dropped his basket, apples rolling in every direction as he stared at the bloodstains coating Lena’s chin and neck.

     

                “Fetch the Queen,” Kara hoarsely barked.

     

                The young boy floundered for a moment, his face ashen and eyes wide as he took in the limp form of Lena in Kara’s arms, his eyes darting between Lena and Kara as he shrank backwards as if Kara was the threat.

     

                “Now.”

     

                Turning, he fled, his movements graceful even in his haste as he vanished down the hallway. Kara heard his footsteps on the worn stones set into the packed earth as he climbed the few steps of a side exit leaving the Royal Residence. Resuming her hurried pace through the hallways, Kara didn’t even break stride as she turned her torso and held Lena’s limp form out of the way, shouldering open the doors to Lillian’s quarters. To stay in Lena’s suite would have been to risk someone showing up to ensure the deed was done, perhaps with a red smile across the Princess’s throat, and the Queen’s quarters was the safest alternative Kara could think of.

     

                Making for a chaise lounge, Kara carefully set Lena down and ran a shaking hand through her hair as she thought. While relatively skilled as a healer, as most Waterfolk were, she wasn’t an expert at poisons and it took her a moment of panicked thinking to try and find a solution. Sewing flesh wounds was something she was capable of, but purging the body of a slow killer wasn’t quite as tangible for Kara. 

     

                Her eyes landed on the cold fireplace and the charred lumps of wood amongst the ashes, and Kara remembered watching a healer make a child who’d eaten holly berries drink a slurry of charcoal and water to help him vomit. A pitcher of water stood on a sideboard and Kara grabbed it and quickly snatched the burnt wood, almost to the point of charcoal, and pulverised it in her hand before dumping it in the water. Swilling the jug around, she walked back over to Lena and cradled the back of her head before setting the lip of the jug to her mouth and pouring.

     

                Grey liquid streamed over her face and one might have been mistaken in thinking Kara was trying to drown her wife as Lena roused slightly, coughing and spluttering and blinking the gritty water out of her eyes. She made her drink until Lena convulsed, twisting in her arms and vomiting onto the earthen floor, a torrent of poisoned wine and lumps of charcoal heaved up. Coughing as her eyelids fluttered, Lena made a mewling sound of confusion at the back of her throat as her head turned, trying to seek out someone to ask what was going on. 

     

                “Lena? Lena?” Kara roughly said as she set the half-empty jug down and cupped her wife’s cheek in a calloused hand. 

     

                Head lolling to the side, Lena let out an incoherent mumble and seemed to deflate again, her body going limp on the lounge. Quietly cursing, Kara pinched the bridge of her nose and scrambled for any other snippets of information. Her skill with water could usually help aid in healing, flushing out wounds and encouraging the edges to seal again, but she couldn’t do much but place her hand against Lena’s chest and feel the remaining water in her stomach and pull it from her throat in a long ribbon, hoping that was all of the poison. The portion already absorbed into her bloodstream was a different matter.

     

                Using the cuff of her sleeve, Kara wiped Lena’s face dry, although she couldn’t clean away the blood which had started to dry on her chin and neck. She checked her pulse, still slow but present, which was all that mattered, and Kara poured some more of the liquid down her throat, until Lena brought it all back up again, until she was sure her stomach had been emptied. Kara’s limited knowledge of poisons meant she couldn’t be sure how long ago Lena had ingested it, or how much, her symptoms only providing evidence that she had been poisoned.

     

                The open doors meant she heard the approaching footsteps before she caught sight of Lillian, although Kara didn’t so much as turn as she heard the Queen cross the threshold of her own quarters. Under different circumstances, Kara knew she would be accused of spying for being in Lilian’s rooms uninvited, and might have been dragged down to the dungeons and interrogated, but as it was, she couldn’t bring herself to care about the consequences of invading Lillian’s personal space, so long as it meant Lena would be fine.

     

                “You summon me on the evening of mid-autumn?”

     

                Kara glanced up, pale-faced and tense, as Lillian strode into the room, her mouth turned down disapprovingly at the corners. Her harsh voice faltered at the sight of Lena’s listless form draped across the chaise and Kara watched her eyes narrow as she drew herself up to her full height. It was impressively intimidating yet Kara didn’t quail before her as she straightened, shoulders stiff and an edge to her stare.

     

                “On account of your daughter’s health, Your Majesty,” Kara haughtily replied, “yes, I do.”

     

                “What has happened to her now?”

     

                “We were talking and she collapsed. She’s been coughing up blood; I would assume poison, but I don’t pretend to be overtly knowledgeable on the subject. That’s your forte, is it not?”

     

                Shrugging in a lazy, dismissive manner, Lillian held back a moment before drifting towards her daughter. She loomed over her, cocking her head to the side as she studied the chalky pallor of her face, the blood staining Lena’s skin and the shallow rising and falling of her chest. Pressing two fingers to Lena’s throat, Lillian felt her weakening pulse and hummed dubiously.

     

                “Yes, poison,” she agreed after a moment.

     

                Kara was growing impatient, fighting the urge to bite back a sharp retort for the Queen to do something. Each minute that the poison spread through Lena’s veins, was absorbed into her bloodstream and wound towards her heart, was a step closer to death, and Kara didn’t intend to fail Lena on that count.

     

                “Your court is rife with it, it’s no small wonder, Your Majesty, that someone has been able to so easily assassinate my wife.”

     

                “She’s not dead yet,” Lillian sniffed derisively. “Perhaps this shall test the strength of her mettle - if her weak human constitution can survive it.”

     

                Kara’s voice was an unrecognisable snarl that rose from some visceral part of her as she clenched her fists, water shooting up in a tall jet from the jug she’d been using to make Lena drink down the charcoal slurry. Glancing up at her, Lillian arched an eyebrow and straightened, inches taller than Kara and faintly amused.

     

                “Help her. Save her.”

     

                “Careful. You do not want to make demands of me.”

     

                “I do demand it. We were assured of our safety with the alliance of our marriage. I will not stand for her to suffer as a result of the Unseelie Court’s negligence.”

     

                “Negligence? You speak of negligence - where were you? Your wife is your responsibility, and yet I find her on death’s doorstep. I find it most interesting.”

     

                Lips thinning to a bloodless line, a dangerous air about her, Kara gestured to Lena with barely controlled anger in her voice as she ran a hand over her face. “Please. She cannot die; you and I alone know the importance of that. You may not care for her but you must help her. If not you, one of your healers who knows better than I how to help her.”

     

                “Dar-Essa,” Lillian noted. “It’s swift in large doses, but suffering can take hours or days in smaller doses. Death is usually inevitable. It’s a favourite of mine; one can get so many answers out of a person when they believe their life is at risk and a cure dangling before them. Although, I usually find a knife more efficient for coaxing out information. Immediate pain always provides swift results.”

     

                “Have you poisoned her?” Kara demanded, her chest rising and falling quickly as panic kept her in its clutches. “Answer me quickly; have you poisoned your daughter?”

     

                Lillian’s demeanour was frosty as her eyes flashed dangerously. “Be careful who you accuse, Seelie. I might cast suspicion on you just as easily. It is interesting to me that the two of you were alone after she left the revelry in good health and now-”

     

                “Alone but not for long. I went for a walk, to clear my head.”

     

                “Clear your head?”

     

                “Your daughter has … a natural ability to get beneath my skin.”

     

                “And you would be better off without the yoke of marriage to her, wouldn’t you?”

     

                Kara’s mouth flattened and her cheeks coloured as she cast her eyes down. “I would never behave so dishonourably- I would never hurt her-”

     

                “Wouldn’t you? I find it rather convenient-”

     

                “As you said, I would also prefer a knife. There’s no honour in poison, only cowardice. I’m not a coward and … I must admit to not wanting to rid myself of the Princess quite so much as you might imagine.”

     

                “Your fondness for her grows,” Lillian murmured, cocking her head to the side, something predatory about her piercing stare as she tucked the information away for further use.

     

                All of them were aware of the risk of any sort of feelings developing between the married couple, whether they were ones of fondness or contempt. To sway either side of ambivalence meant to throw each other into danger, risking the ease of manipulation as factions on both sides would try to tip the scales in their favour. To love someone from a different Court, to develop any sort of romantic feelings would be to paint a target on each other, run the risk of either of them being used against the other to further hidden agendas or outright dispose of them to resume open war. 

     

                For Kara to hate Lena would have been slightly more negligent, leaving her vulnerable to attacks, such as poison so easily slipped into a cup of wine and drained to ease the discomforting feeling of being the hen amongst the wolves. But Kara didn’t hate Lena, had defended her on numerous occasions, bloodied her sword for her, killed for her, and yet someone had bypassed her overbearing protection to try and dissolve the marriage, one way or another. It wasn’t uncommon for such things to happen in the Unseelie Court, and she had to admit there were assassinations in the Seelie Court too, both sides playing a long and dangerous game spanning centuries or longer. 

     

                But Kara didn’t hate Lena, which raised the concerning question of what was the goal of the attack. A simple solution to push the war forwards, battling over the no man’s land on either side of the river, stealth attacks in the dead of night in little villages and holdings nestled in pockets of the unruly forest? Or perhaps a misconstrued personal attack, thinking Kara cared for her wife more than she did, would be willing to seek revenge and start the war herself, absolving any other guilty parties from the blame of instigating it, and leaving others free to retaliate. War was expensive, but Kara knew it could be profitable for the right people.

     

                Lillian didn’t say anything else as Kara detailed her efforts in a clipped tone, Lillian stepping around the pool of charcoal, water and wine to lean over her daughter while she dispatched Purity and Pestilence to fetch a few healers and track down Reign. The healers arrived quickly, a glassy sheen to the eyes of two of them from too much to drink, and they all crowded around the unconscious form of the Princess as they worked. Kara hung back, pacing restlessly as she waited to find out if Lena would die or not. Silently making plans for how she would slip out of Court and escape back home. It would no doubt entail a bloody chase through the forest, hounded by wolves and a potential bear, foxes seeking corpses to scavenge, and multiple dead - possibly herself as well. 

     

                “It’s easily curable with a tea brewed from the leaves if that eases your concerns.”

     

                It did and Kara felt the knot of tension in her chest loosen slightly. She kept her hands clenched into fists to hide the fact that they were shaking terribly and she tipped her head back, eyes closed as she breathed in the cool air of the room, earth and sweet flowers on the verge of decay seeming overwhelming for someone used to the open-aired tower on the water. Her skin was damp from her fear and she tucked herself away in the corner as the healers tended to Lena, a fire coaxed to life in the remaining ashes of the hearth, the pale pink blossoms stripped of their leaves so tea could be brewed. 

     

                The room became stiflingly hot with too many people crowded inside it, the quiet bur of voices overlapping as the fae discussed dosages and treatment methods, one of them affiliated with water repeating Kara’s process of emptying Lena’s stomach while another brewed a different kind of tea and another wiped Lena’s brow. The Princess stirred on the sofa, restless and agitated as her bloodless lips moved wordlessly and a few sighing mumbles escaped her. Kara watched on with a brooding look on her face as Lillian likewise held back, no maternal instinct leading her to her daughter’s bedside. There was no room for feelings in the Queen’s suite, from anyone, and they all played out their parts with an air of nonchalance to Lena’s fate.

     

                There were concerned murmurs and the air was oppressively hot. Enough so that Kara slipped out a minute later, a white-knuckled grip on her sword hilt, still bloody from her earlier foray out into the forest, and returned to her rooms. Thoughts spiralling down into despairing hypotheticals about the worst-case scenario, Kara paced the sitting room for a few minutes, hand anxiously running through her blonde hair, until it was no longer tame and silken, but lank and dishevelled. She looked haunted, agonised, afraid.

     

                Whirling around, Kara made the sudden decision to leave. If Lena was going to die, she couldn’t stay and meet her own death. Not like this. Entering the bedroom, her mind latched onto the act of packing her things, travelling with whatever essentials she would need and abandoning the rest if need be, Kara came to an abrupt halt just inside the doorway. Her face visibly drained of its blood as she stared slack-jawed at the scattered pink flowers covering her bedsheets.

     

                A strangled sound of panic escaped Kara as she lurched forward, picking up a flower and turning it between thumb and forefinger. She didn’t have to question what the flower was, even if she hadn’t been familiar with the sight of it, having grown up around freshwater and watched it bloom every spring since her birth. Dropping it, Kara’s eyes darted around the bed and then she hurriedly started to gather them up. 

     

                Using her skirts as a basket, she swept flowers into the depression, scrabbling at fallen petals as her throat went dry with fear. Out in the sitting room, she tossed them into the empty brazier and fumbled with the logs and kindling to start a fire, spending a rare moment cursing her affinity with water instead of fire as the wood struggled to light and the petals smoked. 

     

                Eventually, she managed to get the fire burning properly, sweet smoke billowing out of the grate, filling the room with the cloying smell of it. Coughing as she turned away from the brazier, Kara reached for the small shutters at the top of the high ceiling, letting in a gust of cold air as she glimpsed grass and gnarled roots through the foot-sized window. Letting the fresh air sweep away the evidence of poisonous flowers, Kara returned to her room and quickly started to pack, bundling shirts and leggings, grabbing anything edible scattered around her room and an empty canteen she’d travelled to Court with and hadn’t touched in the weeks since.

     

                Shoving it all into her canvas bag, Kara buckled everything safely inside and changed into travel clothes, pulling a cloak over the top in the hopes that no one would notice she was dressed ready to flee. Adjusting her sword belt and loosening her sword in its scabbard, Kara swallowed thickly, leaving her bags in the middle of the bed as she went to make sure the flowers had all been reduced to cinders in the brazier. She was just stirring up the ashes when there was a knock on the door.

     

                Stiffening, Kara gripped her sword hilt tightly and managed to walk over to the door as if nothing was amiss. Instead of the armed guards she’d been expecting, Andrea stood there alone. Her eyes gave Kara a quick appraising look, taking in her white knuckles, the pinched look of worry on her face and the change of clothes. She arched an eyebrow coolly.


                “I would have thought you’d at least have the uptight honour to stay at her bedside until she woke.”

     

                Some of the tension bled out of Kara’s shoulders as she blinked. “She’s awake?”

     

                “She was. Briefly . Brief enough to assure the healers that the antidote had worked before they set her to dreaming with some other brew.”

     

                Nodding, Kara’s mouth thinned and she considered it for a moment. To leave Lena behind now would be antithetical to everything she’d been striving for, their peace crumbling to nothing and guilt and shame consuming her as she left her wife - albeit, not one who cared for her much - behind to suffer at the hands of strangers. As much as Kara and Lena were strangers, Lillian and the rest of the Unseelie were more so, and they weren’t shy about their hostility. 

     

                “I should see her.”

     

                “Ever the dutiful wife,” Andrea murmured as Kara stepped out of her room.

     

                Giving her a cutting look, Kara stormed down the hallway with a look on her face that was reminiscent of a thunderstorm, and she was rankled by the following footsteps of her wife’s attendant following after her. Lena had to be shadowed and guarded but Kara disliked the feeling of being watched, although she felt the constant skin-crawling feeling of Lillian’s creatures watching her from their hiding spots. No doubt her every move was reported back to the Queen, who trusted Kara as much as Kara trusted her.

     

                Despite the terms of the truce worked out between Lillian and the Seelie Council, of which Kara had dutifully offered her own hand in marriage for the sake of peace, Kara knew that Lillian had only conceded to it to allow for more time. Whether in a year or a decade or perhaps a century more, the Unseelie would renege on the truce and blood would flow freely once more. They weren’t so much as living peacefully but on borrowed time and Kara would try and buy as much of it as she could, even if it meant miserable months spent amidst her enemies, harbouring her resentment for the people who had killed her family.

     

                Lena was still draped over that chaise lounge in her blood-stained dress, her cheeks pallid and her dark hair curling in damp strands at her temples. Her mouth was still stained pink from the blood and her eyes rolled beneath closed eyelids as her lips moved soundlessly, a restlessness to her sleep even with the steeped tea the healers had given her. Lillian was gone, no longer needed with the assurance that the fragile peace would hold another day, and Kara sank to a knee at Lena’s side.

     

                Sighing heavily, she touched bloody fingertips to Lena’s neck, feeling her rapid pulse and the faint warmth of her skin, very much alive as her chest rose and fell in deep, even breaths. Leaning her forehead against the velvety feel of Lena’s sleeve, Kara lingered a moment before climbing to her feet, her throat faintly rasping from the smoke that had filled her room.

     

                “Move her to my quarters,” Kara commanded the two fae guards left behind with a healer. “She needs proper rest, in a real bed.”

     

                They nodded and murmured their obedience and Kara stalked back out of the room, craving fresh air as her feet took the familiar path through a side entrance to the forest beyond. It was still relatively early, the muffled sounds of laughter and music drifting through the trees as dusk descended over the forest. She tipped her head back and moved through the trees, past the delicate flowers of deadly foxglove, past creeping roses in full bloom despite the lateness of the year, through a tunnel of woven wisteria, the purple flowers gracefully hanging over her as she moved through the rich plantlife until she hit the water.

     

                Kara had subconsciously sought it out, reeling herself towards the gentle undercurrent of the trickling stream a league away from the Royal Residence, which still wasn’t far enough to escape the foreboding weight of it. The dank smell of algae, moss-slick rocks and running water washed over her with a loosening in her chest and a pang for her big lake and her freshly caught fish and her little boats bobbing in the gentle swaying of the current. 

     

                Sinking down onto the muddy bank of the stream, Kara watched as the faltering light turned the bark of the pines a bloody crimson, too alike to Lena’s blood splattering her face for comfort. As she watched, a swan flapped its wings as it swooped down to the water, landing gracefully as a few crows cawed and ruffled their feathers, the entrails of a frog forgotten about as they hopped about, irate at the disruption. 

     

                Dipping her fingers into the water, Kara closed her eyes and let it invigorate her. It was frigid and numbed her fingertips, but it felt like life. She loved the forest, loved to touch the trees, loved the mountains where Alex dwelled, the feeling of the air on her skin, loved fire and the comforting woodsmoke and warmth, marvelling at everything as she felt the natural order of existence and her place amidst it all. She was an infinitesimal part of the forest’s ecosystem, a part of her down to her very bones, born and raised amidst the spores of pollen and molecules of water, bound to the place as tightly as any that had lived their whole lives there. But it was water that called to Kara’s soul in a way that the other elements couldn’t, even as she appreciated them accordingly. 

     

                She would have drowned herself in water rather than be parted from it and the keen sense of being out of place lingered in the subterranean quarters of the Unseelie Court, surrounded by too much greenery and not enough damp things. Slipping down the gentle slope of the bank, she found her feet firmly planted in the shallow bottom of the stream, the water barely brushing her knees as she wriggled her toes in the silken silt that had built up over centuries as the water carved its path through earth and stone, wearing it down. The water turned cloudy where Kara stood, the disturbed sediment stirring up grit and sand and detritus and she turned until her body was parallel to the flow of the water, tipping backwards and letting the water consume her.

     

                Drifting, letting the world fade away in a reckless disregard for self-preservation, Kara cleared her mind and thought of nothing as she felt more herself than she had in days, weeks . The water scoured her of her worry as the chill of it burrowed into her, rinsing away blood and dirt and memories and emotions. Limp as she let her buoyancy keep her afloat, Kara breathed slowly as her body unwound. It was like a sliver of home and Kara mourned the small slip of fresh, cold water, a paltry replacement for the deep, sprawling lake she’d left behind. Winter couldn’t come soon enough.

     

                Eventually, she pulled herself from the water, rivulets running off her as she climbed up the bank, her skin pallid and her hair brassy as it hung around her in wet ropes. Covering her face with her hands, she inhaled sharply, the taste of dank water on her tongue, the comforting feeling of her clothes hanging heavily off her tall frame, weighted by the water. Despite the cold evening air, Kara walked back through the forest, her footsteps slow with reluctance, and let the river water drip from her clothes, leaving a splattered trail in her wake, the forest quickly drinking it up like it was consuming little pieces of her. 

     

                She was only slightly damp by the time she reached the perimeter of the Unseelie Court, her reckless endangerment creeping up on her as the shadows grew a fraction too long for her to be wandering alone. But she was already back safe now, reeking of the forest and river water, and she wearily listened to the sounds of the celebrations, even louder now, lights from bonfires and torches and lanterns visible in snatches of warm yellow amidst the wide tree trunks and thickets. Kara’s enthusiasm for mid-autumn couldn’t have been lower and she wasn’t inclined to join them, slipping back into the dim tunnel and following the route back to her quarters.

     

                A guard was outside, nodding sternly to her as she passed through, and the other was in her sitting room with the healer. Kara nodded to them and continued through to her bedroom, where Lena was tucked in beneath the sheets. Lingering in the doorway for a minute, Kara exhaled softly and walked over to her, pressing the back of her cold hand against Lena’s feverish brow, letting her fingertips graze down her temples to her flushed cheeks, rosy despite the sallow look of her narrow face from the ordeal of being poisoned.

     

                Kara felt guilt rear its head as if she should have been able to protect Lena from an invisible enemy and she pulled up a stool beside the bed, perching on it as she watched her wife sleep and brooded a while. The hour grew late, the quietness of night descending over the buried residence, and Kara’s eyes were heavy from the exhaustion of the day, yet still, a while later she rose and dismissed the healer and the guard and lit another fire in the cold brazier. In the silence of her quarters, Kara roasted the chestnuts they’d picked only that morning and breathed in the wood smoke, the smell clinging to her clothes, mingling with the dank smell of water and moss and pine, all the scents of the forest shrouding her.

     

                She ate a few of the chestnuts and filled a bowl, fixated on the bizarre notion that Lena would be hungry when she woke up, and Kara had promised her roasted chestnuts, even if it had been an indulgence for herself more than for her wife. Sitting at her bedside, Kara resolved to remain there until Lena woke, which was not long before midnight, the blankets stirring as her head rolled back and forth on the pillows and her brow furrowed with a familiar look of annoyance. A ghost of a smile touched Kara’s lips as she blinked away the stupor she’d slipped into.

     

                “Ah. She awakens,” Kara murmured, wry humour in her exhausted words as she straightened on her stool.

     

                Lena looked around at the unfamiliar quarters, the shades of blue of clear pools of water, of the ocean on a sunny day, on a stormy night, of the silvery sheen of water in the moonlight. Without asking, she knew she was in Kara’s bedroom, a place that had been out of bounds to her before, and now she was in her bed. 

     

                “I- what-”

     

                “Be cautious. Your body will be weak for a number of days, or so I’m assured. Your throat likewise will be sore; let me fetch you some water.”

     

                She shot to her feet, eager to be useful, to mask the relief that left her jittery as she turned her back on Lena. Lifting the jug of water, Kara’s hands shook fiercely as she let a stream shoddily fall into the cup, a few drops spilling onto the earthen floor. Drawing in a deep breath, she fixed her face into a serene look and turned back around, passing the cup to Lena as she reached her bedside. 

     

                Lena’s expression was wary but she knew Kara would never feed her poison and slowly sipped, letting the cool water whet her rough throat. She finished it off and cradled the cup between her palms until Kara plucked it from her and set it safely aside and Lena scrubbed a hand over her face, feeling stiff and clumsy, her eyelids heavy and a pressure in her head and her chest that made her want to sleep for longer.

     

                “What happened?”

     

                “Poison.”

     

                “I know that,” Lena replied with chagrin, a muscle jumping in her jaw.

     

                Pursing her lips, Kara collected her thoughts for a moment. “I sent a serving boy to fetch your mother. She fetched her healers. They brewed the antidote and gave you some tea, and then I told them to bring you to my room. You’ve slept through the entire thing, or rather, you weren’t very conscious when you were awake.”

     

                Humming dubiously, discontent etched into the lines of her face, Lena sank back against the pillows and stared up at the ceiling with a stormy look of worry in her green eyes. Kara studied her profile, drinking in the sight of her, brooding and prickly and jaded, as ever, and felt something in her chest soften. It was deeper than relief but that was the overwhelming feeling filling her. She didn’t even want to begin considering what that deeper feeling was and turned to the bowl of chestnuts instead.

     

                “Roasted chestnuts,” Kara murmured, cupping the bowl between her palms as she gave Lena a wan smile.

     

                “Well, it wouldn’t be mid-autumn without roasted chestnuts,” Lena managed to choke out past the tightening in her throat.

     

                Sitting up slightly, she took one of them from the bowl and turned it over in her fingers. She couldn’t remember ever eating chestnuts before and was surprised by how comforting the taste was as she chewed, sweet but savoury, the slightly charred edge giving it the taste of the forest, of woodsmoke and greenery, and Lena’s weak mockery died in her mouth. They filled her with the vague notion that it wouldn’t be mid-autumn without them, that perhaps she’d celebrated mid-autumn this way before, her memories wiped clear of the act as the forest had been purged from her in the human world. She reached for another one.

     

                Her throat was scratched and stinging but she swallowed anyway, unsure of what else to do. Latching on to the activity of eating, she was able to buy a few moments as she tried to pull herself together. Finishing her chestnut, she rubbed the faint oily sheen on her fingertips in the light weave of the sheets and exhaled deeply, exhaustion leaving her spent.

     

                “Sorry. You were almost free of me for good.”

     

                Kara’s face furrowed with a severe frown, her blue eyes bright with irritation as she quietly scoffed. “Do you think I’m so callously cruel as to wish for that?”

     

                “No,” Lena admitted, “no, I don’t think that. It would be preferable though, wouldn’t it?”

     

                “War would be preferable to marriage to you? No, I don’t believe so.”

     

                “Ah, well, others might agree.”

     

                They shared a wry smile and Lena rubbed her forehead before picking up another nut. “These are good.”

     

                Kara nodded, elbows on her thighs, her shoulders tense. She was lost in her own thoughts for a minute as Lena chewed her chestnut and watched her closely, studying the tiny flecks of blood on her cheeks, almost mistaken for freckles from her long days spent on the water, the discontented downturn of her mouth, the slender fingers with silver rings that she steepled, her chin perched on top. 

     

                With a weary sigh, Kara straightened up, a grave look of worry on her face. “We need to tread carefully now. Now we know others are willing to make bold moves, it’s no longer just the threat of harm, but a reality. It was a very close call tonight, and I- … I regret that I was not as observant as I should have been to notice a poisoned drink passed on to you. From now on, I would see us by each other’s sides at all times.”

     

                “Now that’s a challenge,” Lena said with a hoarse laugh, “I thought we’d discussed earlier how suffocating it was already. We’ll be down each other’s throats about everything if we never catch a break.”

     

                “Rather down each other’s throats than a knife across it because of negligence. Although, in regards to earlier, I’m sure it’ll take some considerable effort to not let my temper get the better of me so I don’t abandon you to the wolves.”

     

                “At least the wolves are honest about their intentions.”

     

                “Indeed, it’s those hidden behind flattering masks that are most dangerous.”

     

                Lena hummed, the sound frayed and on the edge of hysteria. Her hands trembled as she fiddled with another chestnut and she had to blink rapidly. Her throat hurt and her chest hurt and her stomach too, her whole body aching and bone-deep exhaustion leaving her spent against the pillows. It was worse than having her stomach torn open by claws, a tingling sensation in her extremities leaving Lena feeling oddly out of touch with herself as she listlessly sighed and slowly blinked, fighting the urge to sleep for a week.

     

                “Are you alright?” Kara murmured, the attempt at levity vanishing as Lena’s thoughts crept back in.

     

                Tears floated into the crescents of Lena’s eyes, and she wasn’t quite sure why. It was all just a little bit overwhelming, that palpable unease that kept her on edge for weeks too much for her to handle right now. She just wanted to feel safe, but every day in the forest felt precarious like she lived and died at the whim of some malevolent thing she couldn’t even see but felt so deeply that it made the hairs rise on her arms to think about it. 

     

                Digging the heels of her palms into her eyes, Lena let out a choked laugh. It might have been a sob, but she hid it well, trying to feign nonchalance at how close she’d brushed with death - again. Her sanity and patience were a thin veneer these days and Lena wasn’t sure how much more she could take. Even Kara’s tower would be preferable to the Unseelie Court, the remote place surrounded by Lena’s biggest fear seemed safer than sitting amidst bloodthirsty people vying for the chance to kill her. 

     

                “I’m okay,” she whispered, pressing her fingers against her eyelids as she inhaled deeply.

     

                Her lungs ached as they expanded and she started to cough, Kara producing a pristine handkerchief for her as Lena coughed flecks of vivid red blood into her palms. Wiping it off, Lena’s lips twisted contemptuously and she swallowed, the taste of old pennies coating the back of her throat. 

     

                “I guess I’m lucky you came back at that time.”

     

                “Lucky, ” Kara scoffed with laughter, “I suppose you’re plagued by a type of luck. Even if it’s not good .”

     

                “It’s luckier than I’ve been in a while. I thought- I thought the forest … it’s got its hands inside me now, I’ve swallowed all the bad bits of it and I can feel it in my blood and lungs and I just- I thought maybe it was … killing me. It seems inevitable, doesn’t it? I’m not made for this place.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara’s face creased with a bewildered smile. “But of course you are; you were born here. It’s in your bones. You’re not as weak as you believe yourself to be, in fact, you’ve proven more resilient than even I imagined. You might say I was almost free of you for good but at this rate, I think you’ll outlive me.”

     

                “Well, I’ve had my fair share of near-death experiences. I think it’s only fair if the next one is yours,” Lena said with a wry smile.

     

                A quick laugh escaped Kara and Lena’s smile grew a fraction, both of them tied together by the sham of a marriage, by the danger it posed to them both, by the sheer act of living in such close proximity, guard and Princess. There was an odd dichotomy between them but there was a kernel of trust growing larger as the days went by. They might annoy each other, might be sharp with their honesty, resentful of the burden they posed to each other, but at the end of it all, they both knew they were alone there, save for each other. Lena was sick of being alone. 

     

                The feeling choked her up, fear a cold weight in her tender stomach as she blinked back tears and balled her hands up into fists on the bed sheets. The urge to cry clawed at her throat and she let out a strangled laugh, an ache between her ribs as her heart lurched in her chest.

     

                “How does it ever get better than this?” she asked, sobering up as sadness slammed into her.

     

                “I can’t promise it will,” Kara admitted, “but I can promise I’ll keep you safe. I’ll do better next time-”

     

                “It wasn’t your fault.”

     

                “But I’ll do better,” she insisted, her voice firm, a coal of anger in her blue eyes as she squared her shoulders. “You’re staying with me; I’ll ask your mother for a shared suite. I’ll sleep at the foot of your bed if I must. No harm shall befall you again, I swear it to you on our wedding vows.”

     

                Lips twisting ruefully, Lena made a small sound of disgruntled amusement at the back of her throat and sniffed. “Please never ask me to do the same; it would be a worthless promise coming from me. Not all of us are as … noble as you are.”

     

                “I wouldn’t ask a thing of you,” Kara said, earnestly as her eyes shone with sincerity. “Only to trust me. In that, I know the price may already be too high. I regret that my failure-”

     

                Lena covered Kara’s hand with her own and let out a withering sigh, closing her eyes as she fought back a smile. “You really won’t let that go, will you? You didn’t fail and I’m alive, so …”

     

                “Merely alive is not enough for me.”

     

                “No? What is?”

     

                She cracked open an eye and let her head loll to the side to take in Kara’s rigid posture, the clouded look of confusion, wariness, and caution. “Your happiness. Your safety. Your comfort.”

     

                “You know, for all her faults, at least Lillian picked a considerate wife for me. I think I could do a lot worse.”

     

                “I think perhaps you could do better. We’re … not well suited, I think.”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena whispered, her lips twitching with dry amusement. “I think we might be the only people willing to put up with one another. In that, we’re the perfect match.”

     

                Reaching for Lena’s hand, Kara held it in her calloused palms like she was cradling something precious. She hesitated momentarily and then ducked her head over it, placing a gentle kiss on the back of it and then straightening as she patted it comfortingly. Lena stared at her, bewilderment forming a crease between her eyebrows as she warred with herself. How could she feel so grateful for the kindness shown to her by someone she wanted to hate so badly? It would’ve been easier if she did hate Kara, but at best she was just mildly affronted at times by Kara’s uptightness. Even that, Lena couldn’t really hold against her.

     

                “Kara, I-“

     

                The sound of clinking armour suddenly filled the suite and Kara fluidly rose to her feet, sword halfway unsheathed by the time Purity and Pestilence stepped into the room. They wore dark chainmail as usual, lithe and dressed in dark leathers, danger radiating from them in a threatening aura. Lena and Kara were both tense as a familiar dislike for Lillian’s personal guards shot through them.

     

                And then came Lillian, a little smug, a little arrogant as she stood regally in the doorway, illuminated by dim candlelight. There was a triumphant tilt to her chin and she raised her eyebrows as she beckoned to Kara, who had slammed her sword back into its sheath, the cagey violence draining out of her as soon as she’d realised there was no threat. Not an immediate one at any rate, although there was an undercurrent of violence in the postures of Lillian’s guards and Lena felt the uneasiness of the moment.

     

                “Come away,” Lillian commanded, cool amusement lacing the steel in her voice as her lips twitched slightly. “There are questions for you to answer. I would see you cause my dear daughter no further harm.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Lena’s face as she pushed herself up slightly, blinking back the sluggish feeling in her mind as she honed in on the meaning of Lillian’s words. Eyes darting to Kara, Lena’s mouth opened and closed and she fought to find her voice, even as it scratched the sides of her throat.

     

                “Wha-” Lena objected, confusion etched on her face. “It wasn’t her , don’t be so ridiculous.”

     

                “Hush,” Kara quietened her, reaching out to briefly caress the side of Lena’s face.

     

                It was a quick gesture, and intimately affectionate, stilling Lena as she shrank back down on the mattress. Her cheeks were flushed pink with the feverish effects of the poison lingering in her system, and her body was leaden as her heart lurched in her chest. Visibly paling, Lena gathered her strength and kicked the blankets off as Kara clapped her hands together and chuckled quietly, weary and already resigned to her fate as she endured it with bitter humour.

     

                “You hurt her-” Lena started to threaten, a tremor in her voice as she knelt on the rumpled bed sheets.

     

                Lillian gave her a cutting look as Purity grabbed Kara’s arm, jerking her harshly, and the rest of Lena’s threat died in her mouth. Eyes drifting over to Kara, who jerked back, bristling with indignation, Lillian’s lip curled as her eyes appraised her with cool indifference.

     

                “Oh, don’t worry. I’ll make sure your wife is returned to you in good health - unless, of course, interrogation proves she was involved in the attack on your life. Then I’ll make sure she’s returned without a head.”

     

                “You-”

     

                Lillian stepped towards the bed and cupped Lena’s chin in her hand, her grip tight as her lips curled in a contemptuous smile and her nails dug in deep. Raising her other hand, she uncurled her fingers to reveal the pale pink petals of a flower nestled in her palm.

     

                “You will be ignorant of the fact that the Dar-Essa flower is native to the Seelie Court and grows in abundance near water. Imagine my surprise when Pestilence ferreted out a few heads of the flower in your wife’s rooms earlier, as well as her packed bags. She intended to flee and leave you behind, dead.”

     

                Lips parting as the bristling tension bled out of her, Lena sank down, her eyes landing on Kara, whose cheeks were rosy as she scoffed at Lillian’s words. But there was guilt as well and Lena’s eyes landed on the packed bags dropped onto the end of her bed a moment later.

     

                A wounded look of betrayal bloomed in Lena’s eyes as she tried to make sense of it all, unable to speak as her forehead pinched with confusion. Lillian tipped the petals into Lena’s lap and she picked one up with a shaky hand, running her thumb over the velvety feel of it as her mouth went dry.

     

                “A word of advice, Lena,” Lillian haughtily spoke, “never trust a Seelie.”

    Chapter 13

                It was two days of constant surveillance from her wife’s bed before Lena was finally deemed fit enough to leave the quarters. Her weakness surprised her, barely walking to the front door leaving her chest heaving and a cold sweat prickling her skin, her chemise sticking to her and the heavily embroidered robe over the top almost making her knees buckle beneath the weight.

     

                Andrea attended her, looking as ethereally polished as usual, and Reign was at her door, returned to her post and preternaturally still. They both looked at her, taking in the greyish tint to her skin and the hollows beneath her eyes, and Lena’s mouth thinned with annoyance.

     

                “Don’t say a word.”

     

                “Come on,” Andrea sighed, “let me help you, Your Highness.”

     

                Hating to be touched by other people, by people she didn’t trust and held only irritation for at best, Lena endured it as Andrea looped her arm around Lena’s waist and Lena’s arm over her shoulder. Sniping at each other as they made slow progress towards the bathing rooms, Lena was pink-cheeked and exhausted by the time they reached the hot springs, the damp and chill making her cough rattle while the poison did the rest.

     

                “Leave me,” she dismissively murmured, leaning against the rough stone wall as her vision dimmed and swayed. “Fetch my wife.”

     

                “Your wife is still imprisoned,” Andrea murmured, her eyes darting to Lena’s face, watchful and curious.

     

                Fighting to keep her expression impassive, although there was a slackness in her muscles, Lena cleared her throat. “Oh. And will my mother be releasing her anytime soon?”

     

                “Potentially,” Andrea coyly replied.

     

                “What do you know?” Lena impatiently asked.

     

                “Only that Reign has discovered an accomplice. Whether to Lady Kara or some other assassin remains unknown. The Queen will do her due diligence and ensure that your wife is innocent before releasing her.”

     

                Pressing her mouth into a flat line, Lena turned abruptly and walked towards the edge of the pool. Shedding her robe, she let it pool to the stone floor, watching steam eddying from the surface, making her face prickle from the heat.

     

                “Tell my mother I’d like to speak with her once I’m presentable.”

     

                “I’ll relay your message.”

     

                “Good. You can leave,” Lena curtly replied, waving a hand dismissively.

     

                She knew she wasn’t being very likeable, and hadn’t given the Fae folk she’d been around much incentive to like or protect her, but she was tired and frustrated. Without Kara at her side, things felt unbalanced and she didn’t know how to navigate it properly. It was perhaps for the best that she’d been bedbound, limiting the damage she could do in the meantime.

     

                The doors squeaked closed behind her and she shed her shift, tossing it aside and gingerly slipping into the hot water, teeth bared and shoulders tense as the water closed around her. Closing her eyes, Lena breathed in the smell of damp rock and water and waded a little further out, but close enough to touch the edge if need be.

     

                She washed thoroughly, days of sweat and sickness and the lingering odour of stale wine washed away with pine soap, fresh and comforting like the forest. Lena was itching to get outside, to feel fresh air on her cheeks and the life that was tangible around her but just out of her reach.

     

                Climbing out and drying off, she donned her robe and picked up her chemise before walking back out. Dark hair hung in wet ropes down her back and she left a trail of water droplets behind her as she walked back to her quarters, hesitating on the threshold and then entering for the first time since she’d collapsed.

     

                Andrea returned halfway through Lena trying to dress herself, clicking her tongue and muttering in the Fae language that Lena was slowly grasping the basics of. Bundled into heavy velvets and linen and cotton layers, kept warm against the damp chill, Lena suffered the process of her hair being intricately braided and adorned with only a small amount of silver and gemstones before she grew impatient and climbed to her feet.

     

                “Where is she?”

     

                “Meeting with her advisors. Your request has been passed on.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes. “It wasn’t a request.”

     

                “She’s the Queen; at most, you can request. You don’t make demands of her, Lena.”

     

                Anxiously chewing her lip, Lena hesitated and then sighed. “Fine. Then I’ll make my own decisions.”

     

                “For what?” Andrea demanded.

     

                Fixing her with a sharp look, Lena didn’t trust the woman much at all and just let out a small laugh. “I’m not going to tell you but you can come if you insist on keeping me out of trouble.”

     

                “She’ll have my head if she knows you’ve been walking around after being poisoned.”

     

                “I’m fine. She’d be happy if she could keep me locked up permanently, I think. It seems that’s what she’s trying to do to Kara, anyway.”

     

                They were walking down the hallway now, an odd trio, and Lena was tired but determined. Andrea let out a withering sigh beside her and Lena glanced sideways.

     

                “You may as well let her stay there. It would offer you more peace of mind and it’s not as if you hold the fondness of a real marriage.”

     

                Mouth thinning as she considered her attendant’s words, Lena hummed dubiously. “No, I don’t but it’s still a real marriage. And I’m not a bad person; I won’t leave her to rot there for the Queen’s amusement when we all know she didn’t try to kill me.”

     

                “Do we know that?” Reign drawled behind her.

     

                “You tell me,” Lena asked, coming to a stop and turning to face her. “Who was the accomplice?”

     

                Giving her a wry smile, hazel eyes shining with amusement, Reign shrugged. “It’s of little consequence to you.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena scowled and turned back around. “You both drive me insane. Literally so unhelpful and suffocating. The least you could do is help me out a little bit; someone did try to kill me and I’d like to find out who it was.”

     

                “Perhaps you have to look no further than your wife,” Reign mused. “Maybe it was her accomplice after all.”

     

                “I don’t buy it,” Lena firmly replied. “You’ll see soon enough.”

     

                She led them down to the dungeons and the other women had little choice but to follow after her, if they couldn’t stop her to begin with. Other guards kept watch over the few occupied cells and they straightened at the arrival of Lena, gracefully ducking into shallow bows as she swept past, her voice growing loud and sharp with anger.

     

                “Where is she? Kara?”

     

                “At the end,” came the slightly echoing response.

     

                Straightening, an odd pang of relief and longing shooting through her, Lena forged ahead with renewed strength. Her relief was short-lived as she flagged at the sight of Kara sitting in her cell, exhaustion washing back over her and anger flaring to life. Her worry had muffled the disgruntlement Lena had felt at Kara’s plans to leave but now it filled her again, once she was sure that Kara wasn’t hurt - beyond a few scrapes and bruises.

     

                “Hello, wife,” Lena acerbically greeted Kara, wounded and resentful as she gripped the bars of the cell.

     

                “Good evening, wife,” Kara replied, her voice a weary murmur as she climbed to her feet, shoulders bowed with exhaustion. “Or has the moon passed its zenith into the morning?”

     

                “You were leaving?” Lena hissed, ignoring her question.

     

                That sheepish look of guilt crept into Kara’s features again and she sighed as she came to a stop on the other side of the bars, her face half in shadows and half in the flickering firelight of the torches. Mouth thinning, she looked at the floor, brooding, Kara cleared her throat.

     

                “I planned for the possibility of it, yes.”

     

                “You were going to leave me here.”

     

                “If you succumbed to the poison, yes. Yes , I was going to leave your body here. I don’t believe that’s an offence on your behalf.”

     

                Lena spluttered with indignation. “I hate it here. I hate it here more than you do and you’d happily just … leave me?”

     

                Sighing, Kara reached up to lay her hand over Lena’s fingers wrapped around the bar, quietening some of her anger. “The next time that you’re staring death in the face, I promise I shall take your body with me when I flee for my life.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena scowled as she tore her hand free from beneath Kara’s touch. “Don’t mock me.”

     

                “I’m not mocking you. If it means that much to you then I promise it, on the purity of my lake’s waters. And if I break my promise, let it be polluted with all sorts of rotten things as punishment.”

     

                Kara’s expression softened and her voice with a gentle murmur, sincere and almost tender. Lena’s hardness wavered and some of the tension bled out of her shoulders, a haunted look of wariness lingering in her eyes though, ringed with purple shadows and the exhaustion of her ordeal. It would be days before she felt strong again after the poison, and she shouldn’t have been up and walking. 

     

                “You should rest,” Kara reminded her.

     

                “I couldn’t sleep.”

     

                “What concerns you?”

     

                “You. Always you.”

     

                A faint smile curled Kara’s mouth, “do you fear I’ll come for you in the dark if you let your mind rest?”

     

                Clicking her tongue, a look of annoyance tightening her face, Lena turned her head to glance at a nearby guard, keeping her voice down. “I don’t believe you would ever hurt me.”

     

                “No? The flowers were in my room.”

     

                “Conveniently. I think if you’d been trying to assassinate me, you’ve had plenty of opportunities to see it through, and half of them would've been accidents that would’ve kept your hands clean.”

     

                Brow pinching with grave confusion, Kara cocked her head to the side. “Do you trust me?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena cautiously confessed. “And do you trust me?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Good,” Lena said, letting out a shaky breath and then unsheathing Kara’s dagger at her waist. 

     

                Kara blinked, looking down at the blade winking in the dim light of the dungeons. Wariness wended through her and she looked up at Lena, blue eyes clouded with concern. Looking a little pale, her hand trembling as she tightened her grasp around the hilt, Lena reached through the bars and wrapped her free hand around Kara’s throat, squeezing just tight enough for it to look convincing. Raising the dagger, she pressed the tip of it to Kara’s cheek, digging it in slightly, a bead of blood welling up and rolling down her cheek.

     

                “Did you think I’d be so easy to leave behind,” Lena snapped, raising her voice, drawing attention from the guards. “You were stupid to even try it, to underestimate me. If you want to turn your back on our marriage and plunge us back into war, I could slit your throat right here and damn the truce. It’s what you’d deserve and no one could stop me.”

     

                “Your Highness,” Reign murmured, warily stepping forward.

     

                “Forgive me,” Kara gasped, playing her part well, eyes filling with tears. “I was foolish to even consider leaving you behind. I had thought all else was lost, otherwise, I would never have conceived such an idea. Never . I will cut my heart out here and now to prove it to you. I’m loyal to you - only you.”

     

                Lena wanted to laugh at her theatrics, and when one slipped out she forced another sharp laugh, colder and contemptuous, channelling Lillian’s cruelty. This was her chance to not appear weak, to not make her attachment to Kara look weak, armouring herself against the things that could be exploited. She’d taken what Kara had said to heart and now she was ready to play the game or find herself dead in a ditch out of her own stupidity. 

     

                Digging the knife in deeper, watching Kara’s blue eyes sharpen with annoyance and feeling a flicker of guilt as more blood welled up, Lena leaned in closer. “You would do well to remember whose Court you’re in, wife. My mother will have your head at my word and we’ll- we’ll bleed your Court into your … pretty lakes and rivers and take it for ourselves.”

     

                Collapsing heavily to her knees, Kara slipped out of Lena’s grasp, looking up at her with achingly sad eyes, tears freely falling now, the tracks shining in the dim lighting of the torches as one of the guards drew nearer. Lena could feel the heat of her torch on the left side of her face and made sure to harden her features, masking her nervous doubt and panic at hurting Kara.

     

                “I would deserve no less. I’m yours to command; loyal to you and the peace between our Courts. If there is a way for me to make amends, speak it and I will see it done the moment I have my freedom from this prison. If I have betrayed your trust irrevocably by bringing danger upon you, then tell me now and I will give my blood to you at your feet.”

     

                Sinking down to her level, Lena reached through the bars and touched a finger to Kara’s cheek, smudging the blood, and heaved a resigned sigh. “Let no one say the Princess is unreasonably cruel and unforgiving. I will entertain no apologies from you but, um, I will- I will expect you to do better to strengthen our marriage. Or I won’t give you another chance.”

     

                “I’ll do better, I swear it, on my honour and life.”

     

                Startled by the Fae language that rolled off Kara’s tongue, binding her words as true and meaningful, Lena’s expression clouded with wariness. Her bloody fingers fell away from Kara’s cheek and she swallowed, her mouth dry, kneeling before her for a moment longer as the pretences fell away. 

     

                “I’ll get you out as soon as I can,” Lena whispered.

     

                “I’m okay. Just look after yourself. Please, for me. You should be resting.”

     

                “I’ve spent days in bed,” Lena sighed, her expression turning wry. “Your bed. And it smells like the sea.”

     

                Kara let out a soft chuckle, shifting closer to the bars, holding them tightly as she smiled slightly. “You smell like pine; it’s odd that I should have missed it so much. Missed you so much.”

     

                Frowning, Lena drew back a fraction. “Why would you miss me?”

     

                “One becomes terribly bored in imprisonment. Even your irritable scowl is a balm against the loneliness of the dark.”

     

                A surprised laugh escaped Lena and she paused before sighing. “I’ll get you out. I promise.”

     

                “Rest.”

     

                She left after that, unsettled by the discontent she felt for her wife tucked away in the dark dungeons. Andrea forced her back to bed once they returned to the main level of the royal residence and Lena didn’t protest, her face flushed and a slight fever to her brow.

     

                Stripping off the layers of her clothes in favour of a new nightgown, Lena crawled back into Kara’s bed and idled away the remainder of the day by brushing up on her glyph literacy. Eating sparsely and drinking plenty of tea, she eventually gave up on doing anything, her body aching and weak, and let her mind drift.

     

                Alone in Kara’s room that night, Lena lay in her bed, breathing in the smell of rainwater and moss and something briny like the sea, oddly comforting and familiar against the damp earthy smell of the room. Still, Lena was restless, tossing and turning, dark hair splayed across the pillows like spilt ink, her pale face creased with brooding unease as her dreams were plagued by nightmares of stinging saltwater stuck in her throat, of bogs dragging her down into the muddy puddles, her lungs aching for air, the coppery taste of blood filling her mouth as she scrabbled at roots and rough rock, scraping her fingertips raw as wave after wave lapped over her. 

     

                Waking in a cold sweat, dark hair clinging to her brow and cheeks, Lena was slow to realise she wasn’t alone. She wasn’t sure what tipped her off, the room pitch black save for a sliver of grey light filtering in through the narrow window up near the eaves of the room, showing a patch of grass and roots beyond the underground residence. All Lena knew was that there was a prickling awareness at the back of her neck, her heart pounding in her chest, and she bolted upright, her hand reaching beneath her pillows for Kara’s dagger.

     

                Her grip tightened on the hilt as she saw a shadow move, of middling height and rather stocky for a Fae. Lena was seized by a second bout of panic when she realised her paranoia had been correct and someone was in her bed chamber. Quickly shifting onto her knees, Lena held the dagger out in a shaky hand.

     

                “Don’t come any closer.”

     

                The person moved quickly, wiry fingers encircling her wrist, twisting it hard enough to make her hiss with pain. The dagger was taken from her with ease, fingers stinging as her tight grip was roughly broken, and Lena cradled them in her good hand as she scowled, breaths coming in shallow and quick through her nose as she shrank in on herself.

     

                “A dagger is no way to show courtesy to kin,” a low voice hummed with amusement. “I shall forgive the transgression. After all, we are as strangers at the moment.”

     

                “Who are you?” Lena asked, fear lodged in her throat.

     

                The man chuckled, the sound cold enough to make the hairs on Lena’s arm and nape stand on end. Her visceral reaction to him was the same as it was to the forest when confronted with the darker things lurking in the pockets of unruly wilderness and she was struck by the urge to flee. Lena was smart enough to know that she wouldn’t get far though, something entirely predatory about this man as he stood beside her bed.

     

                “You would have forgotten me in your time away from Court. I may have forgotten you too, for you have grown much, if not for your looks. You are remarkably like your mother.”

     

                “How do you know my mother?”

     

                “Ah, it was hard not to know the King’s mistress for one at Court so often. A gentle woman with a lovely voice. Foolish though, to try and leave. No matter now - the dead are of little consequence to me.”

     

                He laughed as if it was some inside joke and Lena stared expressionlessly at him. Blinking, she waited to see what would happen next, tense and still as she hardly dared to breathe. The smell of the forest clung to him, thick pine and dirt and a sweet cloying decay mingling on his skin. The weak moonlight highlighted a shaved head and harsh features, angular and sharp and unsettlingly familiar as he twirled the dagger between his fingers.

     

                “The work of the Waterfolk. She has her mark all over you; you smell like a rainstorm.”

     

                Snorting, he tossed it aside, the metal ringing as it struck the edge of the trunk pushed up against the foot of Kara’s bed. Pacing back and forth at her bedside, he ran a hand over his shaved head, his movements fluid and dangerous, like a panther, and Lena sank onto the mattress, her thighs aching from the effort of kneeling still.

     

                “This peace is unforgivable. To marry you off to one of them , a Seelie - kin to the people who killed father, no less - is a sign of weakness I hadn’t anticipated. I should have slit her throat in the forest and let the chaos unfold but you were always the weaker target. It matters not now; the deed is done.”

     

                Lena noticed his hands were dark with blood then and faltered as the breath got caught in her throat. Her eyes darted towards the black mouth of the door and she licked her lips, calculating her chances. They were slim but she’d grown up slipping out of dangerous situations, and her months in this realm had improved her reflexes and strength, hours of sword fighting and archery adding a small amount of muscles to her arms and back.

     

                As the man muttered to himself, she wriggled to the opposite edge of the bed inch by inch and then made a run for it. She landed hard on the bare floor, almost tripping herself up, and staggered forward. Making it out into the open living space of Kara’s quarters, she was brought up short by a sharp pain in her scalp as the man caught her by a fistful of her hair. Lena let out a shout of panic but was quickly cut off by the velvety sweetness of flower buds shoved into her mouth, choking her silent as she spluttered around it.

     

                The man kept his hand clamped over her mouth and Lena inhaled sharply through her nose, the coppery smell of blood overwhelming. She could feel the stickiness of the not quite dried blood on her chin and cheeks where his fingers splayed and he softly hushed her.

     

                “We’re in the middle of a conversation, Your Highness,” he murmured. “I didn’t give you leave.” 

     

                He wrestled her to the ground, turning her over as he pinned her, and Lena spluttered out a few petals, the powdery taste of them cloying on her tongue amidst the mingling blood. She still had most of the bud and thorns trapped in her mouth as the man grabbed her chin, fingertips digging into her cheeks.

     

                “Shush, now,” he whispered, “we don’t want to alert anyone to my presence. That wouldn’t end well for anyone.”

     

                Her muffled question was incomprehensible but he caught the gist of it, letting out a quiet huff of laughter as he let go of her.

     

                “We’re watching,” he warned her, his voice low and menacing. “You are easily reachable, Lena. By me or anyone I send your way. You’re fortunate the Queen saved you but you won’t always be so lucky and your weak wife is easily done away with.”

     

                “Don’t,” Lena rasped around a mouthful of petals and thorns, pricking her tongue and the insides of her cheeks. “Don’t hurt her. Please.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                “Please.”

     

                Cocking his head to the side, he looked bemused and she tried to reach up and remove the mouthful of flowers. He stopped her and the smell of blood clinging to him made her stomach turn with fear. Eyes pricking with tears as her throat closed up, Lena sniffed.

     

                “Did you kill her?”

     

                “No,” he eventually replied. “You should be wishing I had. It will be you or her eventually. It just depends on who gets there first. Unfortunately, my little spy made the error of opposing my orders and feeding the poison to you . Old resentment, perhaps? Who knows. Next time, the arrow might strike the correct target.”

     

                Feeling weak with relief at his words, trusting his honesty, Lena went slack and barely listened to anything he said. 

     

                “I’ll be back for you. Don’t let the burden of being heir weigh too heavily on you; the mantle won’t be yours for much longer.”

     

                Then he kissed her cheek in a gentle manner and was gone before Lena could scramble upright, coughing and spluttering and gouging out the flowers and thorns. The inside of her mouth was cut to shreds and she found herself sitting with the mess of Dar Essa flowers in her bloody palms, her eyes widening as she tried to see through the darkness where the man had gone. The whole encounter felt off and unsettling and Lena rinsed her mouth out with elderflower wine, spitting it into the lit brazier along with the flowers.

     

                Sleep evaded her for the remainder of the night and dawn arrived a few hours later, grey and pale through the slit of a window.
