Fingers rubbing at the dark bruises beneath her eyes and the lip split by thorns, the taste of blood still lingering and the cuts inside her cheeks stinging, Lena anxiously paced Kara’s quarters. Andrea arrived earlier than usual, bearing a deep scarlet dress embroidered with maple leaves in fiery shades. She dressed Lena and made her presentable, eyeing her face as she fixed a cloak around her shoulders with a thorned broach. 

     

                “What happened to your lip?”

     

                “I- my knees gave out last night,” Lena mumbled, feeling the urge to lie. “Caught myself on the edge of the end table.”

     

                Snorting with laughter, Andrea shook her head. “And we’re supposed to make a leader of you. Well, we’ve established you have more brains than coordination so perhaps you’ll be a ruler of words one day, instead of brawn. Your wife will balance you well; those Seelie half-wits are good with swords if nothing else.”

     

                “She’s smart enough to rule her own holdings,” Lena defensively replied.

     

                “A few backwater villages of Waterfolk are easily ruled. Give them a pond or a little stream and they’re all too happy to spend their days fishing and swimming.”

     

                “That doesn’t seem stupid to me. It’s probably the smartest decision anyone I’ve met here has made. Give me a little garden with flowers and I’d be just as happy.”

     

                “Well, you’re made for better things than that,” Andrea curtly replied, slipping a ring onto Lena’s finger.

     

                Raising her chin in a haughty manner, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners. “Better isn’t the same as happier.”

     

                “No,” Andrea conceded, “but then not everyone is fortunate to be happy.”

     

                “Are you happy? Doing this?”

     

                A strained smile twitched the woman’s lips as her pale blue eyes shone with bitterness. “I used to be happy until my betrothed died and my father conceded to this truce. Now, I’m … content.”

     

                “To be a babysitter?” Lena asked, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “It does feel somewhat like minding a child at times,” Andrea snorted, “but one day my loyalty and my position at Court will pay off. I’ll be rewarded for my efforts in making you a presentable Princess.”

     

                “Don’t get too ahead of yourself; I have no interest in being presentable or a Princess.”

     

                “Be that as it may, you are - the latter, anyway. And appearance-wise, you’re presentable enough for your mother, who has requested your presence.”

     

                “Oh, so she can make requests while denying mine?”

     

                “That is generally how ruling works. Now, hurry. And keep that mouth closed. She’s not in a good mood.”

     

                Led to Lillian’s council chambers, where the Queen was feeding the tiny hearts of rabbits to a couple of ravens perching on the back of her tall seat. The room was situated inside the hollow cavern at the base of a wide tree, as most of the upper floors of the royal residences were, and gaps in the gnarled roots allowed in the chill fresh air as birds came and went, cawing as the wind quietly howled and dead leaves skittered across the floor.

     

                Curtsying with some difficulty, finding it hard to regain her balance as she came back up, her limbs still somewhat weak, Lena stood before the Queen and fixed her with a hard stare. Lillian fed another heart to a raven and stroked its dark feathers before glancing sideways at her daughter.

     

                “You are proving quite hard to kill,” she approvingly greeted her.

     

                “Maybe they’re just not trying hard enough.”

     

                Lillian laughed at her bravado and turned her full attention to her. “Your attitude hasn’t been dimmed by the effects, I see. Perhaps there’s more of your father in you than I had initially assumed.”

     

                “No, I’m my mother’s daughter,” Lena firmly replied before faltering slightly, a sour expression crossing her face. “Which one, I’m not quite sure.”

     

                A slow smile spread across Lillian’s face. “Are you here to flatter me for sympathy?”

     

                “No,” Lena indignantly scoffed, “I’m here to ask you why my wife is still imprisoned. Surely several days are long enough to question her. Just ask her in your language and she won’t be able to lie to you.”

     

                “Ah, and there your naïvety shows we are not alike,” Lillian sighed with irritation, rising from her chair and stalking towards Lena, tall and imposing. “There are many ways to lie. Many ways to hide a secret, many ways to twist the truth or circumvent it.”

     

                She cupped Lena’s chin and frowned slightly, her thumb smoothing over the cut on Lena’s lip. 

     

                “You’re reckless. You should have more care.”

                

                “Let her out. I know you found the person who did it.”

     

                “You don’t know who?” Lillian asked with mild surprise, clicking her tongue. “I’d thought you’d be more curious to ask. It was Eve; the one I sent to spy on you and confirm my suspicions before my hunters dragged you home.”

     

                “Eve?” Lena echoed, shock making her blanch. “Oh, um … okay. Why?”

     

                “That is what I’ve been trying to figure out,” Lillian snapped. “Amidst all your excuses for your wife, she may very well have been involved.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes, “oh, come on. Ask Eve, I’m sure she’ll tell you the truth if you threaten her enough.”

     

                “That will be difficult considering her throat was cut last night.”

     

                The off-handed way Lillian said it made Lena’s face go slack with surprise, her spine stiffening as she recalled bloody hands covering her mouth, the smell of copper in the air. The man had spoken about his spy and perhaps that had been his intention the whole time; to make sure they remained blind about who the real enemy was. Lena’s breaths turned shallow and she wiped her clammy palms on her dress, wondering whether to tell Lillian what she’d seen. That would sound like she was making something up to defend Kara though, and Lena didn’t know if that would be helpful in the end.

     

                “Oh. Well … it couldn’t have been Kara. She’s been in a cell the-“

     

                “I know that,” Lillian sharply cut her off. “That doesn’t absolve her of any guilt.”

     

                “Then ask your questions and let her out. You can’t keep her locked away on a suspicion; that could be grounds for war if word reached Seelie ears.”

     

                “And who will tell them? You?”

     

                Jerking her chin up, Lena clenched her jaw and her hands into fists. “Yes.”

     

                She thought Lillian was about to slap her and flinched slightly when a pat on the cheek came instead. Blinking, she swallowed as her mother laughed.

     

                “You cannot be loyal to both Courts and I will not let you be loyal to them.”

     

                “I’m loyal to her,” Lena admitted through numb lips, perhaps even to herself for the first time. “She’s the only one who has shown me any kindness or respect.”

     

                “She would not be so kind if you didn’t serve a purpose. She would gut you like a fish if given the opportunity for more bloodshed.” 

     

                “If that’s your opinion, that’s fine. I think I know her a little better than you do and I’d like her returned to me in one piece. Please.”

     

                Sighing heavily, Lillian swept back to her chair and got settled, her gaze piercing and heavy. “Amuse me; why do you fight so strongly on her behalf when you have fought this marriage every step of the way.”

     

                “I didn’t want to be forced into it, I didn’t say I wanted her dead. Or to suffer or be locked away like a criminal.”

     

                “You aren’t foolish enough to soften your heart for her, are you?” her mother said, her voice low with a warning.

     

                Scoffing, Lena looked offended at the mere idea of it. “Of course I’m not. What sort of Stockholm syndrome do you think this is?”

     

                “Let’s pretend I know what that means; it would be unwise for you to forget your purpose and let yourself believe something that isn’t real. You’re a tool for peace and that is all. You’re not even fit to be heir but you’re all that is available so we all must do our best with that, but you are not to fall in love with a Seelie. Do you understand?”

                

                “Don’t worry,” Lena snorted, her lips twitching wryly. “There’s no chance of that happening. I can promise you.”

     

                “Good. See that you keep it. I’ll return your plaything to you shortly.”

     

                Surprise flashed across Lena’s face and she swallowed her haughtiness to curtsy, perhaps more differentially than usual as she bowed her head as well. “Thank you, mother,” she murmured.

     

                Lillian extended a hand adorned with rings and Lena crossed the gap to kiss the signet one. The gemstone was cool beneath her lips and she rankled at the display before straightening. Fluttering her fingers dismissively, Lillian reached for a rabbit carcass on the table beside her seat and tore out a liver, clicking her tongue to coax a raven close.

     

                Stomach turning, Lena swept out of the room and let out a pent-up breath. Stopping a short way down the hall, she leaned against a wall and closed her eyes.

     

                “You should rest,” Andrea warned her.

     

                “I’ll be outside. Bring Kara to me.”

     

                She stalked outside, a headache pounding at her temples, and breathed in the fresh air. It was bracing and sweet and Lena ran her fingers over the rough bark of a nearby trunk, over brown leaves and little nuts and furred patches of moss. Birds called and she could hear someone playing a harp amidst the trees and it filled her with so much peace that she wanted to cry as she absorbed it all.

     

                Waiting outside for half an hour, she turned when she heard footsteps and felt an unbidden smile cross her face as Kara emerged from between two roots. Dishevelled and dirty, she still looked ethereal and noble and Lena had to stop herself from throwing her arms around her. She settled for meeting her halfway and arching an eyebrow.

     

                “Did you enjoy yourself yesterday,” Kara asked, disapproving and flushed as she hugged her cloak to herself. 

     

                She drew Lena further from earshot of Reign and Andrea, keeping her voice low, but they couldn’t truly escape the surveillance of her attendants. 

     

                Giving her a smug smile, Lena laughed. “I did, thank you for indulging me.”

     

                Rubbing her cheek, Kara rolled her eyes. “I didn’t have much say in the matter.”

     

                “I’m sorry for nicking you. I had to make it look realistic,” Lena sheepishly replied.

     

                “It’s but a scratch. You might’ve choked me harder if you wanted it to look convincing though. Bruises would have been good evidence to have.”

     

                “Well, I didn’t want to hurt you.”

     

                “You can’t expect it to be believable and not put in the effort. Here; squeeze tightly at the sides but not my windpipe or else you’ll crush it.”

     

                “You- excuse me? I’m not going to choke you.”

     

                Lena’s voice was loud in the stillness of the gardens and Kara hissed to quieten her, drawing her into the cover of a weeping willow and pressing her up against the trunk. “Quiet, Lena, or else you’ll be fooling no one. Now, if you’d like to make it convincing, you’ll have to commit to the act. Are we to be turbulent and unbalanced or doting and secure?” 

     

                Apprehensive now that she was faced with a more difficult situation, Lena anxiously chewed her lip, considering it for a moment. “I can’t hurt you.”

     

                “Then love it will have to be,” Kara said with a sigh. 

     

                “And what about what happened in the dungeons?”

     

                With a wry grin, Kara waved airily. “What’s love without a little anger at times? A slap wouldn’t be amiss in an argument from one who seems so temperamental as yourself.”

     

                “I’m not going to slap you.”

     

                “And therein lies the issue; you want to play pretend but as a child pretends, without any conviction or substance to it. If you can’t bring yourself to be unkind to me you’ll have to be tender, and I fear you don’t have that in you either.”

     

                Spluttering, Lena scowled, the tips of her ears reddening. “I can be tender.”

     

                “Indeed? Could you kiss me? Love me? Feel fondly for me? No, I don’t believe so.”

     

                “I could.”

     

                Kara laughed, her cheeks dimpling and her eyes creasing with amusement. “Not convincingly. You already look like you’re in agony to be in the near vicinity of me, so I won’t torture you further by making you kiss me unnecessarily. In fact, it would look like a farce to think our feelings for one another have changed so suddenly and intensely after I’ve been accused of attempting to murder you.”

     

                “What should we do then?”

     

                Running a hand through her long golden hair, the gesture unusually stressed for Kara as her silken hair fluttered in the breeze, Kara stared thoughtfully at the long fronds of the willow branches. Mouth pressed into a flat line, eyes the blue of the sky before a storm, she hummed thoughtfully for a moment before returning her eyes to Lena.

     

                “For now, we’ll walk through the gardens arm-in-arm and you can teach me the names of all the plants as the Court watches. I will look appropriately chastened and reined in and you will do your best impersonation of your mother’s haughtiness and they will all think that the Unseelie have come out on top in this battle of wills.”

     

                “I hate this.”

     

                “I dislike it too but my hands are tied and I must bow before my pride for the greater good,” Kara grumbled.

     

                She offered her arm to Lena and gave her a crooked smile. “Come. I suspect there may be red helleborine growing nearby but you will know better than I.”

     

                Swallowing past the lump in her throat, Lena looped her arm through the crook of Kara’s elbow and ducked her head as they stepped through the willow branches, their bare feet leaving faint impressions in the carpet of moss as they returned to the dirt path. Kara led them to the patch of wildflowers which she had correctly identified as red helleborine, as confirmed by Lena, and they bypassed white oleander and yellow daffodils, foxglove and late blooming roses and clover growing in between everything else while lichen-marked branches and trunks in patches of white and green and yellow, vivid in the gloominess of the forest. 

     

                Kara pointed out hanging wisteria and maroon carnations, little snowbells and wild daisies, the dandelions and buttercups that sprouted everywhere they could fit, weeds tenderly grew alongside all manner of plantlife as the Fae treasured both individually. There seemed no rhyme or reason to the sprawling, unruliness of the gardens and the forest beyond, but nothing was wilted or dead, choked by ivy or mint or roots drying up the soil. It was a carefully constructed chaos, a riot of life that Lena could feel in her tingling fingertips as Kara prompted her to name every flower or shrub they came upon.

     

                Indulging her, Lena had a morose look on her face as they walked around, somewhat sulky and brooding as her lips barely moved, her skin crawling with the sensation of eyes watching. Kara had been right; Lena didn’t think she could play along with an act well enough to convince anyone else. The best they could hope for was a tense peace that portrayed their feelings well enough, and she hoped her private stunt in the dungeons would spread enough for people to think she wasn’t as weak as she appeared to them.

     

                And it was peaceful to walk with Kara, who smelt of river water and moss and whose voice was the drone of constant running water. As far as companions went, she was one who had grown slightly on Lena, as water wore on a stone, smoothing it over time. Not that Lena felt anything more than mild irritation for her but her earlier anger and resentment at their predicament had softened into a mutual understanding. They would do things together now which was the source of her feelings of betrayal at the thought of Kara leaving her body to decay in this Court, left behind. Lena hated the thought of being alone there, even if it was her bones that would be left there. She would rather be buried on the banks of the lake she feared than spend an eternity giving life to a place that was poisonous. 

     

                "Our time together feels like a storm,” Kara said with a weary sigh. “Something too big to handle but too powerful for us to escape. I hadn’t expected marriage to pose such a risk to either of us but it is like a dreary rain that never ends, one tempest after another."

     

                “Kara?” Lena murmured, surprisingly vulnerable. “Please be careful. I’d hate to lose my only friend at court and … I don’t think the poison was meant for me.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara stared at her for a long moment. She averted her gaze then, mouth thinning as she rubbed her brow.

     

                “The first time I saw you, I formed a very poor opinion of you,” Kara admitted. “I thought you had no common sense and no character, and wouldn’t last a day wed to me in this place. I’m glad to be mistaken.”

     

                “Barely,” Lena gravelly replied, her worry scratching her throat. “There’s something I have to tell you.”

     

                Making a small sound of acknowledgement at the back of her throat, Kara turned to look at Lena, eyebrows rising slightly, blue eyes curious and a faint smile at the corners of her mouth. She was gentle and kindled some warmth in Lena, her kindness so easily given when they weren’t purposely antagonising one another.

     

                “The Prince,” Lena started before she faltered.

     

                Expression clouding over immediately, Kara’s mouth thinned. “You mean your brother?”

     

                Rankling slightly at the idea, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners and she exhaled through her nose, a weary sigh. “I guess. What was he like?”

     

                “Arrogant, conceited, proud, vain, selfish, witty, sharp, aggressive. There are many words that could be used to describe the Prince. I think I would sum him up in one with cruel.”

     

                “But … what did he look like?”

     

                “Oh, well, he took after your father in almost every way. Their likeness was uncanny, merely the younger and older versions. Dark hair, dark eyes. He had your mother’s bearing though. One might say he had the worst qualities of both parents.”

     

                “What bad qualities did my dad have?”

     

                Kara contemplated her question for a moment, raising her chin a fraction as a breeze raced through the trees, rustling her hair and swirling leaves and petals across the forest floor. “I saw him but once, at a distance. He struck your brother to the ground and cut the head off one of his hunting dogs for some perceived insolence. I don’t believe he was a good man. I- but you don’t … remember anything?”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena strained her memory for things that lay hidden from her, things that had faded or made out to be distant dreams as the years away from the forest leached her of her childhood. But there was a lingering unease that had wound through Lena’s mind over the years, that feeling of wariness, skittishness and anxiety at loud noises, raised voices, and quick movements. There had always been the distinct impression that they hadn’t been the product of foster care but Lena had never been able to pinpoint where exactly they’d come from.

     

                Her mouth felt dry and she cleared her throat, staring down at the carpet of lush grass underfoot, dew damp on the soles of her feet and a chill creeping into her joints, pleasantly numbing her against the ache in her bones. Her lungs still felt raw and bruised and the searing cold of the air was a nice balm against the lingering effects of the poison.

     

                “I remember … bits of it.”

     

                “Oh. I won’t press you on things you’d prefer to leave buried.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena whispered, a tight smile briefly twisting her lips. “I hope you don’t mind me pressing you on things better left buried. What happened between our families?”

     

                “Ah,” Kara murmured, tipping her head back and blowing the air out of her lungs. It hung in the air for a brief moment, a haze of faint white. “It wasn’t between our families so much. Not at the beginning. Our Courts have been at war for centuries, millennia, and there have been prominent families on both sides involved in the thick of it, the pivotal moments that defined the war. Three centuries ago, my grandfather killed your grandfather. In retaliation, your father killed him a century ago. My father and my uncle - twins, a rarity - killed your father twenty-two years ago. My uncle perished in the fighting and your brother hunted down my father and killed him and my mother and my aunt fifteen years ago. My aunt and uncle on my mother’s side defected to the Unseelie Court and were killed as traitors by the Waterfolk of the Seelie Court. My cousin was our greatest fighter left and led the latest war five years ago.” 

     

                Kara paused for a moment, her eyes sliding sideways to Lena’s pale face, brimming with troubled thoughts and not-so-distant memories. She drew Lena in a little closer and cleared her throat, a muscle twitching in her jaw.

     

                “It was bloody. Everybody lost someone. I was one of the few who had no one left to lose, but even then the family who took me in, Alex’s father, died. It lasted four years, merely the blink of an eye to us, but it was terrible. Your brother was vicious and bloodthirsty and some of the smaller ponds are still red with the blood he helped spill. You saw the dead that time we were out in the forest; there are many sites like that from the battles, surprise invasions we traded on either side of the great river. It ended with my cousin and your brother fighting in the shallows. It was a mistake on your brother’s part, to fight near so much water. But your brother was very skilled with earth and he pierced my cousin's body with thorns as long as my arm. No amount of water could heal him. He was like a shrike, knowing he would die but pushing himself further onto the thorns, and I watched as he did it, tired and bleeding and helpless. He grabbed your brother and let the water take them both. Neither of them came back up. When the fighting stopped, we pulled my cousin from the thorns, the life already gone from his eyes, but your brother was lost to the river.”

     

                The forest was quiet around them, save for the hum of nature; leaves rustling, birds calling, the scrabbling of squirrels and a blundering badger in the undergrowth, trickling water nearby and the rhythmic dripping of last night’s rain off pine needles. Letting out another sigh, a pinched look of old worry on her face, Kara rubbed her brow.

     

                “I had already assumed my family’s titles as Lady of the Lake and the Sea. As a seat on the Council as part of the Water Delegation, we entered negotiations with the Queen of the Unseelie for a peace treaty. The proposed idea was to call a truce to the blood spilt, to let it end with my cousin and your brother, with ties of equal importance. As the sole survivor and heir of my family, I took it upon myself to offer my own hand when a marriage proposition was put forward. There were a few suitors that the Council deemed too insignificant to withstand the truce until your mother mentioned the bastard Princess, hidden away. You were our last hope for peace, for us to regrow what was burnt and ruined and slaughtered. It’s unfortunate how you came to be here but it’s been a blessing for many. You will be well-liked when you assume the throne.”

     

                Speechless for a moment, Lena opened and closed her mouth and her voice was raspy when she found it. “Assume the throne?”

     

                “You are the heir. It may not be for a thousand years but yes, you will inherit it one day and unite our Courts through our marriage. That was the intended purpose.”

     

                Coming to an abrupt halt, Lena was even paler than usual as she looked at Kara with wide, uncertain eyes, a grave furrow between her eyebrows and a stiffness to her face. She was afraid suddenly, her arms prickling with goosebumps beneath the sleeves of her dress, and she pulled her arm from Kara’s and hugged them to herself.

     

                “I think I saw him.”

     

                “Who?”

     

                “My brother,” Lena gravelly replied, fear making the word come out rough and shaky. “I think I saw him in my room.”

     

                Kara let out a small laugh of confusion. “What do you mean? I just told you he drowned.”

     

                Fumbling for an explanation, Lena raked a hand through her elaborately braided hair, her pulse fluttering at her throat. “I know but … I’m sure of it. He was quite short, dark eyes, a shaved head-”

     

                Sucking in a sharp breath, Kara’s expression turned severe. “A shaved head?”

     

                “Yes, he has a buzzcut and the things he said-”

     

                “It goes against our nature to shave our heads, to cut our hair,” Kara interrupted, looking perturbed by the idea. “Only those who have forsaken the natural order of our Courts in favour of the wilds would do such a thing.”

     

                “Doesn’t that sound like something he would do?” Lena warily asked.

     

                Mouth pressed into a hard, flat line, Kara gravely stared out at the forest, a tense set to her shoulders as she took Lena’s hand in her own and then started to tow her forward. Hand in hand, looking like they were merely a couple taking a walk through nature, a natural pastime for all Fae, they hurried further down the path until they reached a small brook.

     

                Water ran past, the tinkling sound of it masking the sound of their voices and Kara rounded on Lena, cupping her shoulders and ducking her head in close. “What did he say?”

     

                “I asked him how he got in and he said he’d grown up there and knew every inch of the place. He made some insinuations that made me think … well, that he’s- he’s my brother. I think it was him, behind the poison, I mean. He asked how I was feeling. I was- … I felt scared.”

     

                Brushing Lena’s hair back, Kara cupped her cheek, her voice low and firm. “You have nothing to fear. I’ll let no harm come to you.”

     

                It wasn’t lost on Lena how many times Kara had promised that, but she didn’t think it would be fair to hold it against her how many times Lena had somehow wound up hurt. Closing her eyes, she felt the reassuring warmth of Kara’s hand on her cheek and let out a shallow breath, a knot of worry in her chest.

     

                “Speak of this to no one-”

     

    “You don’t believe me,” Lena huffed in disbelief as her eyelids snapped open.

     

                Digging her fingers in slightly, Kara gave her a stricken look. “I believe that someone was in your room, and I believe them to be a threat. I’ll not be hasty in assuming it was your brother; I was there that day, I saw how long he was under and that he didn’t come up for air. I’ll not discount your suspicions either. But you must keep silent about this. Please, Lena, for me. Things are fragile enough as it is and there will be panic by those who fear what violence he could bring back or worse, that his supporters will become more ruthless and gather in support of him if whispers start to spread.”

     

                Pale and rigid, Lena took in the fear on Kara’s face and managed a stiff nod as the corners of her mouth tightened. It wasn’t as if she had anyone to gossip with anyway and she knew Lillian couldn’t care less for anything that came out of her mouth. 

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “Thank you,” Kara said with relief, wrapping Lena in a tight embrace.

     

                It loosened something inside Lena, the act of being securely held by strong arms, and after a moment she hesitantly returned the hug. Her face pressed into Kara’s shoulder and her face crumpled with grave concern as she clutched fistfuls of the navy cloak falling from Kara’s shoulders.

     

                “What can we do?”

     

                “Autumn is over halfway through. All we can hope now is that winter arrives quickly so we can leave for my mother’s ancestral home.”

     

                “We won’t be going back to the tower?” Lena asked with surprise.

     

                Pulling back, Kara gave her a small smile, laced with yearning and sadness. “No, not until summer. We’ll be making for the coast instead, to my lands near the sea.”

     

                The thought of so much water made Lena visibly blanch, her stomach already tying itself into knots. “Near the sea?”

     

                Kara gathered her hands into her own and gave her a wan smile of understanding. “You needn’t worry. You managed well in the middle of the lake, so I would think you’d fare better on the shores. You wouldn’t need to set foot in any water the entire time we’re there. I think you’ll find it a welcome reprieve from so much overcrowding here; the trees press in rather oppressively, do they not?”

     

                “The trees are the only things keeping me sane,” Lena murmured.

     

                “Ah, well, we have differing opinions on which is better. Still, the salt air and sea grass will be to your liking, I think. You’ll grow to love it. I find it creeps up on those that have misgivings initially. Quite like myself.”

     

                Her smile elicited a shuddering laugh from Lena, who closed her eyes and pressed her lips together to stop any other betrayals of amusement kindled by the Fae woman she felt conflicted about. Cupping the side of her head, Lena let her head loll to the side and let out a weary sigh.

     

                “What if I don’t want to grow to love it?”

     

                “That’s the thing,” Kara said with a quick smile, “you don’t realise it’s creeping up on you until it’s already got you in its grip.”

     

                She raised Lena’s hands to her lips and pressed a quick kiss to her knuckles, her smile growing a fraction. “Don’t worry, I shall announce my presence if ever I should start to sneak up on you. That way you’ll never have to fear growing to love me. And it should be a consolation to you that I, myself, am destined to never love anyone out of fear of killing them, so you have nothing to fear from me.”

    Chapter 14

                In the following days, Kara made a request for a suite with two bedrooms for them to move into, for the sake of safety by close proximity - although, Lena had only been next door and had still been slipped poison so she wasn’t quite convinced that being kept closer to Kara would do much - and when no accommodations were immediately made, Kara bid Lena sleep in her bed and moved the chaise lounge into the room so she could sleep near the foot of her bed. Lena wasn’t sure if she felt safer in her presence, but she definitely felt disquieted. 

     

                A week passed by quickly, the two of them practically glued to each other’s side as they took their meals together and Kara accompanied Lena to her lessons, making a conscientious effort to ensure she was with her at all times. To Lena, it felt like she had two guards with her, Kara jostling for position at Lena’s side as Reign stalked behind and Andrea escorted her through her regimented schedule. 

     

                At night, Lena found herself restless. She didn’t know if it was the sound of someone else in the room with her, or the fact that Kara’s pillow still smelled of the sea, of running rivers, of deep lakes. She rolled over, she caught a whiff of salt, she pressed her face into the pillow and inhaled the stagnant scent of algae and wet stone. It was maddening.

     

                One night, she woke in a panic, the gritty taste of dank water and silt in her mouth - or rather, the faded memory of it as she relived her mother’s drowning, trying to swim to the shore of the small lake, hunted and frightened - and it was the fresh smell of rain filling the room that oddly calmed her. Lena blinked up at the dark ceiling, her heart pounding in her chest, and she wondered how the water could be soothing yet so terrifying at the same time. Or rather, perhaps it wasn’t the water that was soothing but the familiarity of Kara. She hated to admit it but there was a sense of peace in that familiarity.

     

                Perhaps even more maddening than the brine and freshwater scents that mingled in their shared bedroom was the fact that Kara snored. Lena hadn’t slept close to her before, didn’t know that insignificant detail about her until she was roused the first night by the quiet rumbling sounds as Kara lay stretched out on the chaise lounge without a blanket and one of the pillows after an argument about the sleeping arrangement that had left them both pink-cheeked and irate. It seemed that Lena’s insistence that Kara wouldn’t be comfortable on the chaise had been for nothing; she seemed to be fast asleep, deep and peaceful and content.

     

                By the end of the week, Lena had enough of her snoring though. It wasn’t particularly loud but the persistent droning kept her from sleeping, while Kara was free to slip away almost as soon as her head touched the pillow. It was a marvel that she could slip away so easily while Lena’s mind was weighed down with her thoughts of the day but it was adding insult to injury that she snored, further disrupting her wife’s sleep.

     

                In a fit of frustrated annoyance, Lena launched her pillow across the room, the soft thump of it striking Kara’s chest following. The snores broke off as Kara jerked awake, the glint of a dagger in her hand as she bolted upright, one foot going to the packed earthen floor, and through the dark grey of the room, her eyes met Lena’s.

     

                “Wha-”

     

                “Stop. Snoring,” Lena hissed.

     

                Bristling, Kara scowled and threw the pillow back onto the bed. “I don’t snore.”

     

                A laugh of disbelief caught in Lena’s throat at Kara’s stubborn objection. “Yes, you do.”

     

                “Well, you talk in your sleep.”

     

                “I do not ,” Lena indignantly replied.

     

                “Yes, you do!”

     

                Jutting her chin forward in a stubborn manner, Lena raised her eyebrows. “What do I say then?”

     

                “Nothing,” Kara grumbled, rubbing her bleary eyes. “You speak in childishly clumsy Fae. It’s nonsense.”

     

                “Well, at least it’s not snoring that is loud enough to wake the whole Court.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara pummelled her pillow into a more comfortable lump. “That’s a ridiculous notion; you were right next door and never complained once. I know that means you couldn’t hear me because you’re not prone to holding back your complaints.”

     

                “You make me sound so miserable.”

     

                “Have you tried being less miserable?”

     

                “I’m not miserable. Or … it’s this place that makes me miserable.”

     

                Softly sighing, Kara gave her a searching look. “So are you miserable or not?”

     

                “What does it matter?” Lena murmured as she tugged the blankets up and burrowed into the bed. 

     

                “It matters a lot - to me.”

     

                Lena closed her eyes as her mouth thinned. “I’m tired. Go to sleep.”

     

                Kara didn’t reply and the silence seemed suffocating. They were both aware that the other was still awake, not least of all because Kara’s snores were absent, and Lena tossed and turned, irritable and restless until she sat up.

     

                Pushing the blankets off, she let out a rough sigh, raking a hand through her dark hair. Climbing out of bed, she reached for a robe to pull on over her thin nightgown and felt the chill earth burrow into the soles of her feet. Kara shifted up on the chaise, her blonde hair shifting around her shoulders as Lena’s acute eyesight pierced the gloom of night.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “I can’t sleep.”

     

                “So what are you doing?”

     

                “I don’t know … going for a walk?”

     

                “It’s the middle of the night.”

     

                “And?”

     

                “Do you want me to list your near-death experiences over the last few months?”

     

                “No need, I remember them vividly.”

     

                Kara climbed to her feet, pulling on her own robe, fastening the clasp and gently pulling her hair from beneath the back of the neck, the long strands running down her back in a river of what looked like liquid silver in the dark. Lena blinked, casting her a wary look as if expecting Kara to wrestle her back into bed.

     

                “What’re you doing?”

     

                “I’m not going to let you go alone,” Kara choked out, horrified by the idea. “You’ll end up as a pin cushion for every unsheathed dagger in this place.”

     

                Snorting, Lena’s lips twitched with a smile. “Am I that bad with my sword?”

     

                “You don’t have a sword. And yes. You’re not bad with a bow, though,” Kara reluctantly conceded. “If you had the patience.”

     

                “Not as good as you,” Lena said, her eyes cutting sideways to Kara as she stopped near the doorway.

     

                “No, but I was raised as a fighter. You were raised as … a gardener?”

     

                “Florist,” Lena peevishly replied. “And I wasn’t raised as one; I started a business.”

     

                “Of course, your natural affinity for the earth would have made it your calling. I’m sure being outdoors when you were young was something you craved though.”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched with annoyance at Kara’s correct assumptions. She hated that someone she didn’t consider a friend, wasn’t close to in any way except proximity, could know her well enough to simply state the truth. She didn’t want Kara to know what made her feel trapped, what made her happy or sad, what she thought of certain philosophies and her most secret memories. They were becoming too entwined in each other in a way that was unsettlingly intimate, without any semblance of something fond growing between them.

     

                Continuing out of their shared quarters, Lena hugged her robe to herself and frowned as she walked the halls illuminated by the orange glow of candles periodically placed. There were a few Fae still awake within the Royal Residence and Lena curtly nodded at each curtsy she received from the nobles and the guards, kitchen staff and scholars, lawmakers and Lillian’s council. If they wondered at her presence, walking the halls at midnight in her bedclothes, they didn’t question it, only eyed the wives with renewed interest, drawing their own conclusions.

     

                “Wait,” Kara murmured, snagging Lena’s arm when she made for an exit to the bitter night beyond. “You should stay inside.”

     

                “Well as you’ve guessed, I crave being outside, so …”

     

                Sighing, Kara dropped her arm and followed Lena out, her hand itching towards the sword she’d buckled on, never trusting any Unseelie enough to walk without it. They stepped outside to the sharp sting of late October, the darkness pitch black and only their acute eyesight allowing them to see where they were going.

     

                The ground was rock hard and damp beneath Lena’s feet and she shivered as her breath plumed before her, mist swirling around her ankles as she disturbed it. They were like ghosts, the sound of nearby revelry almost eerie in the middle of the night, sharp laughs and the keen sound of instruments. Lena didn’t want to know what they were doing.

     

                Moss carpeted the ground as she led them further from her home, the ferns growing as high as her shoulders, the rough trunks and smooth boughs of trees beneath her fingertips as she inhaled the sharp scent of wet pine needles, invigorating and heady. Running her fingers through soft foliage and prickle needles, Lena’s feet sank a little into the ground as it became sodden, the faint scent of decay filling her nose now. The long summer days had quickly yielded to darkness and she could almost taste winter in the air, a metallic edge to the damp freshness of the forest.

     

                “We shouldn’t go any further,” Kara softly cautioned her.

     

                Nodding, hearing the distant howls of wolves that let Lena know they were closer than they sounded, she didn’t protest. Instead, Lena glanced at the lichen-splattered trunk of a towering white oak and craned her neck back before she planted a foot against it and reached for the lowest branch. Warm hands stayed her as they settled on her waist, branding her through the thin cotton of her nightdress.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “Climbing,” Lena managed to get out as her throat closed up.

     

                Wearily sighing, perhaps even regretting her decision to escort her, Kara just lifted Lena higher so she could grasp the branch easily and then scuttled up after her. They wound through the branches, climbing higher and higher as the wind cut through the trees, making the leaves rustle and the low-lying autumn fog eddy across the forest floor.

     

                Once the branches grew thinner with the new growth of the ancient forest, Lena became more careful but was still insistent on breaching the canopy. When she finally poked her head through at the top of the white oak, a bitter wind scoured her pink cheeks and her fingers were almost purple where she clung to the branches like a little squirrel. It was dark but silver moonlight washed the forest in its weak light, the stars so impossibly bright and near and numerous, the haze of nebulas visible against the velvety black sky awe-inspiring.

     

                Staring out at the rolling expanse of trees in every direction, right up to the slopes of the distant mountains to the north, Lena breathed in the cold air as it burnt her throat until some of the tension bled out of her. When the wind became too rough, she shrank back into the cover of the canopy to find Kara lounging along a branch, slowly whittling a piece of wood with a dagger. 

     

                Their eyes met in the gloom and Lena shrank down into the fork of the tree with Kara, curling in on herself as she shivered and wrapped her cloak tighter around herself. Neither of them spoke as they listened to the forest; the whistling wind, the rustling leaves, creaking branches, the occasional hoot of an owl and scratchings of nocturnal animals, which Lena hoped were all normal-sized and cuddly forest creatures instead of the eldritch horrors that had stalked and chased her through the woods, an ecosystem in itself. 

     

                “Feel any better?” Kara eventually asked.

     

                Lena’s voice was scratchy from disuse, dried out by the cold air, and she had to clear it twice before she could reply. “Yes.”

     

                Nodding, Kara carved off another sliver of wood and blew on the small creation she was shaping. Lena couldn’t tell what it was but the faint rasp of the blade’s edge against wood was soothing and she sank down into the pocket where they lay, the initial chill fading as the close proximity to Kara warmed her through.

     

                Lena’s eyes grew heavy and she thought she could have slept there, a hundred feet in the air, nestled in the boughs of the tree. It was oddly comforting but her mind kept her awake, even when her body grew heavy.

     

                “You become different in the forest,” Kara noted, not for the first time.

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “I wonder if I seem the same around water.”

     

                Considering her musings for a moment, Lena hesitated, her eyes half-lidded and watchful. “You seem freer.”

     

                “Do I?”

     

                “Yes. You’re not happy here. I think … maybe if my mother was near more water, if you could fish and swim every day … maybe you’d like it more.”

     

                “I think so too,” Kara agreed, her voice a low murmur. “I’m fond of trees, and all living things, as all our kind are but … you’re right. I find the trees suffocating - just a little - and they box me in like water doesn’t.”

     

                “What a pair we make. I hate the water, you hate the forest. A match made in hell.”

     

                “It’s not hell to be with you. I’ve actually become quite fond of you.”

     

                The open earnestness of her statement shot through Lena like she’d been electrified, as if Kara had been reading her earlier thoughts. Her face was pale in the gloom and she was stiff as she stared straight back at Kara, the tension thickening.

     

                Breaking off first, Kara ducked her head as she continued to carve, clearing her throat as deft fingers cradled the wood. “I don’t expect you to think otherwise. We’ve both been torn from our homes as a result of this, subjected to loneliness and the whims of others, but … at least I’m not out of my depth. I can still swim in the comfort of familiar culture, expectations, rules and laws. You’ve forgotten so much that you’re learning from scratch. It’s a pity.”

     

                “Can I be honest?” Lena haltingly asked, her stomach plummeting at her own words as she cursed herself for even considering opening up an inch. But she felt compelled to speak.

     

                Kara’s expression was solemn but open and she nodded quickly, her blue eyes piercing as she stopped her carving and listened intently as if Lena was about to impart the secrets of the universe on her. 

     

                “The only thing I really had back home was my shop. I didn’t have … family or friends. No one to miss. I’ve always been good at being alone because … after my mom died, I couldn’t get attached to anyone. I’d go to a home and then be back at an orphanage or at a different home within a month. It’s not the familiarity of life that I miss. If I’m being honest … maybe I would’ve leapt at the opportunity to be here - if it had been my choice. I think I could’ve been happy if I had more freedom, more choice to do as I please. The only way for that to happen would be if I was out from under Lillian’s control.”

     

                “I suppose that’s another way it’s easier for me; I chose to put myself in this situation and I’m my own master.”

     

                “Doesn’t sound like much of a choice,” Lena snorted.

     

                “It was a choice out of necessity,” Kara conceded. “And I no longer need to concern myself with lover’s spats and quarrels outside of our marriage. A relief as well.”

     

                Snorting, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Common before, were they?”

     

                Giving her a reproving look, Kara’s mouth twitched at the corners as she fought back a smile. “Yes.”

     

                “Oh. Interesting. I thought with that prophecy you always go on about, you wouldn’t have risked a relationship.”

     

                “I never said relationship, I said lovers. There’s a difference.”

     

                Spluttering with laughter, Lena’s eyes creased at the corners. “I’m well aware of the difference. You just don’t seem like the type.”

     

                “Why not? Do you still think I'm so uptight?”

     

                “Well … yeah. Only a bit though. I think I’ve tested your patience enough to warrant it.”

     

                “Hm, maybe. I still think you don’t know me well enough to be making that assumption.”

     

                “Changed now that you’re a married woman, huh?”

     

                Kara gave her a withering look and Lena grinned as she got beneath her skin a little. “I’ve told you numerous times; I take my marriage vows seriously. It also wouldn’t hold any weight with the truce if people didn’t think we were committed to each other. How would it look if I was draped over someone else at a party, letting them touch my ears?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena toyed with a knot in the wood, following the whorls with her fingertip as she pursed her lips slightly. “Well, apparently not good based on your reaction to me. And here I was, flattering myself that maybe you were jealous.”

     

                Giving her a level stare, Kara raised her chin a fraction. “I don’t get jealous. I don’t let myself develop those sorts of feelings for other people. If I did then it would be too close to caring enough to possibly love someone, and that’s not something I can bring myself to do.”

     

                “You’d find me hard to care about, anyway. That’s not a new feeling though.”

     

                Kara’s response was so quick that it seemed like she spoke without pausing to think first, scoffing with laughter as she shook her head. “It wouldn’t be hard at all.”

     

                Her laughter trailed off into deafening silence as Lena stared at her, blinking and still. It took her a minute to respond, surprise winding through her as the new feeling of not being entirely unwanted crept over her.

     

                “Why not?” she murmured, doubt clouding her expression.

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Kara’s face creased with confusion, her nose crinkling, a furrow between her eyebrows. She held her dagger and chunk of wood in one hand and idly toyed with the tip of her ear as she considered the question - considered answering it as well. After a moment, she sighed and averted her gaze, and if it had been lighter Lena might have seen the faint flush of pink in her cheeks.

     

                “You’re … enigmatic.”

     

                “Enigmatic?” Lena laughed, “and that would make it easy to care about me?”

     

                “Yes. The enigma you present is … confident but vulnerable. Hard but soft. Suspicious but trusting. Smart but ignorant. You’re a contradiction and … I quite like it. There are few things that surprise me in the Courts; I’m pleased that you can, or I should’ve grown bored already. I’m not good at being bored.”

     

                “And here I thought you hated my bad qualities.”

     

                “Hate? No. I find myself irritable when concerned though, and your bad qualities are usually a cause to be concerned for. I think … under different circumstances, you would be seen as quite desirable at Court.”

     

                “Desirable? I’m a bastard who is a failure at every Fae cornerstone of skill and knowledge. No one would be lining up to marry me if I hadn’t been sold off like a cow.”

     

                A smile curled Kara’s lips and she cocked her head to the side. “You forget the most important thing. The one shallow thing that would allow anyone to overlook your shortcomings. The thing that has entreated our kind to entice mortals to visit us for millennia. You happen to be very beautiful, Lena.”

     

                Coy, Lena’s smile wavered slightly as she let out a breathless laugh. “Am I?”

     

                “Don’t be self-deprecating; you know that you are and you don’t need me to tell you.”

     

                “It’s nice to hear it all the same.”

     

                “Well, now you have.”

     

                They lapsed into silence for a moment and Lena watched Kara shrewdly from the corner of her eye as she watched her return to her woodcarving. Words on the tip of her tongue as the urge to speak grew in her throat, until she felt as if they would spill out of their own accord if she didn’t speak them, Lena cleared her throat.

     

                “You are too, by the way. I’m sure you know it as well. I thought … when I came here, as terrified as I was with all these strangers dragging me through the forest and putting me in their strange clothes and telling all these stories … I saw you and I thought it was a dream. You were the most beautiful person I can remember ever seeing.”

     

                “And then you were wed to me and any good opinion my looks may have bought me is at the bottom of the sea.”

     

                Lena laughed, her eyelids shuttering as her cheeks dimpled. “You’re not so bad. I’ve had worse.”

     

                “Have you? You said you didn’t have anyone to miss. Curious - I never did think to ask if you had been torn away from a lover to be brought here.”

     

                “No, I didn’t have a lover,” Lena said with amusement. “I have had them but I’m in a similar boat as you. I’m not going to kill anyone if I fall in love, but … I still can’t bring myself to be in a relationship. I think … I’ve been abandoned too many times.”

     

                “You can rest assured I won’t leave. Not only because of the truce. You’re … something of a friend to me now, I think.”

     

                “A friend? I’m touched.”

     

                Softly sighing, Kara gave her an exasperated look, her expression increasingly visible as the sky lightened to bruise blue. “You don’t need to make a joke out of everything. I know you feel uncomfortable by anything that would make it seem as if there’s a bond between us. But there is. We’ve endured a lot in our short time together; I think we’ll become good companions after we get used to each other.”

     

                “Companions? God, I hope that excludes anything sexual.”

     

                Snorting, Kara rolled her eyes. “Very funny. I wouldn’t go near you in that manner.”

     

                “And yet you just said I’m attractive.”

     

                “Beautiful,” Kara corrected. “I said beautiful.”

     

                “They’re synonymous.”

     

                “Not necessarily.”

     

                “I don’t know whether I should be offended or not.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Doesn’t everyone want to feel like they’re attractive to people?”

     

                Blinking, Kara arched an eyebrow. “No.”

     

                “Maybe I’m just vain.”

                

                “You’re not vain.”

     

                “Maybe not. It’s hard to be vain when you have someone reminding you that they’re repulsed by you.”

     

                “You put a lot of words into my mouth. I did call you beautiful, as discussed.”

     

                “Just not attractive.”

     

                Kara sighed, getting peevish now. “I didn’t say that either. I said they’re not mutually exclusive.”

     

                “So which is it? Am I attractive or not?”

     

                “Why is it important to you?”

     

                “Because I’m used to being attractive and if I’m not then maybe I need to reevaluate my opinion of myself. I wouldn’t want to be too arrogant if it’s a turn-off.”

     

                “And who are you trying to lure?”

                

                A quick smile crossed Lena’s face as she shifted. “No one. It’s always good to be seen as desirable though, isn’t it? Especially in a position of power. Charming people would be more effective than cutting their throats, a method my mother seems to have not learnt yet.”

     

                Kara hummed in agreement and returned to her carving. Lena was in a particularly tense mood though, restless for some inexplicable reason, and she didn’t want to let the silence stretch between them. Instead, she fought back a smile as she toyed with Kara, the satisfaction of her weary responses entertaining at least.

     

                “Or maybe I’m trying to lure you,” she flippantly replied, tossing her hair before leaning against the branch beneath her.

     

                Stilling, Kara kept her head ducked down but she looked at Lena through her lashes and let out a quiet scoff of laughter after a moment. Sighing, she shook her head and her nimble fingers continued their artistry.

     

                “Ah, you’re enjoying this, aren’t you? You do strike me as a tease.”

     

                “Am I?” Lena nonchalantly asked, pretending to inspect her nails.

     

                “And what if I were to call your bluff?” Kara asked, gently blowing on the wood and smoothing her thumb over a patch.

     

                “What bluff?”

     

                “If you’re trying to lure me and I allow myself to be lured, your bluff would be called.”

     

                She raised her head and looked at Lena then, her blue eyes serious and unwavering as they stared at each other. Raising her eyebrows a fraction, it was almost a challenge. Pursing her lips slightly as she tried not to seem too petulant, Lena shrugged indifferently.

     

                Laughing, Kara suddenly sat forward and Lena looked almost horrified as the distance between them shrank, Kara reaching out a hand to prop herself against a branch above them. Slinking down, Lena stared up at Kara with wide eyes, surprised as she found herself penned in by her wife.

     

                Leaning down, Kara’s breath was warm on Lena’s lips and she let out a small laugh. “You’re not so brave,” Kara murmured, reaching with her other hand to gently thumb Lena’s bottom lip. “You would never allow me to kiss you. You’re all bark and no bite, wife.”

     

                Bristling with indignation, a dark flush staining her cheeks as she scowled, Lena knew that Kara was right as her bluff was called. But that instilled a sense of stubborn determination to prove her wrong by doing the opposite of what Kara expected. And even though Lena didn’t want to kiss her - or did she? Her feelings were always kept safely under wraps as she maintained her general aloof air - she did so purely out of spite.

     

                Quickly pushing herself up, catching Kara by surprise this time, Lena’s lips pressed against hers in a fleeting kiss. Jerking back, Kara’s blue eyes widened and her mouth opened and closed as she lost some of her composure, that somewhat flustered person she was shining through for a moment as her cheeks reddened.

     

                “What are you doing?” she hoarsely demanded.

     

                Lena let out a small laugh, a grin of satisfaction crossing her face even as her stomach knotted itself. “Calling your bluff. You’re not as clever as you think and I’m not a coward. Two can play these games, wife.”

     

                Chastened, Kara sat back in the crook of the bough she’d been occupying and didn’t say anything. Lena couldn’t tell if she was surprised or annoyed and when she broodingly returned to her carving a moment later, Lena snorted.

     

                “Are you going to ignore me now?”

     

                “No, I just don’t have anything to say,” Kara curtly replied.

     

                “That’s surprising; you never seem to be able to shut up normally.”

     

                “I’ll spare us both and stay quiet then.”

     

                “That’s not what I meant,” Lena wearily replied, rolling her eyes as she sighed. “I didn’t say it bothered me-“

     

                “Oh, really? At this rate, I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anything about me that doesn’t bother you.”

     

                “Your laugh,” Lena blurted out.

     

                Kara’s peevishness slackened into surprise as she quickly turned her eyes to Lena’s face, blinking. Mouth parting as her eyes widened a fraction, caught off guard by the answer that had slipped from her without thought, Lena struggled to force down the lump that got caught in her throat. Running a hand through her hair, she cleared her throat and realised she couldn’t take it back now so she may as well explain herself.

     

                “I mean … you have a lovely laugh. It reminds me of running water.”

     

                Still staring at her, Kara’s annoyance thawed a little and she gently cleared her throat, nodding in reply. The sky was lightening around them, dark navy lifting to deep blue and then greying as the yellow sliver of the sun crept over the hazy edge of the forest on the horizon. 

     

                “We should get back,” Kara announced shortly after that, when they could see each other clearly.

     

                Pushing her stiff limbs up off the branch, the cold settled in her bones and making her extremities numb and raw pink, Lena let Kara go first and followed her down. Landing lithely on the leaf carpet forest floor, Kara half drew her sword as she glanced around attentively, her blue eyes darting around, as close to the boundary of the Court as they were. Something crashed through the undergrowth and the hairs on Lena’s arms raised as she landed beside Kara, the soles of her feet stinging from the impact.

     

                Gesturing for her to back up, Kara slowly eased away from the gloomy forest, darker over a hundred feet down from the canopy. Feeling dwarfed by the overwhelming size of the forest, the thickening ominous air that smelled of sweet decay and pollen and rain and warned of darker things beyond. Lena almost imagined she could taste the metallic bite of blood, coppery and thick, on the edge of the breeze as she silently crept away.

     

                They made it back to the grounds and slipped through a guarded tunnel leading underground. Hesitating, Kara turned and reached for Lena’s hand, the cold of her fingers making her smile slightly before she suggested a bath. 

     

                Retreating to their own sides of the steaming, shallow pool, they let the hot water thaw them slightly and scrub dirt from their skin and pine needles from their hair with the soap. Feeling marginally better, Lena dried off and dressed in her nightgown and robe and let her hair dry in the humid air as she let Kara linger a while longer, moving through the water like an eel, basking in the feel of it. From her seat, Lena only felt unease at the thought of being submerged like that, surrounded by so much water, her lungs aching.

     

                When they returned to Kara’s room, Andrea was already waiting inside, Lena’s clothes laid out for her. She eyed them both dubiously, taking in the damp hair and the flush of pink from the hot water, and then instructed Lena to get changed for breakfast, helping her into the woollen layers, getting thicker as the weather turned colder.

     

     

                Life followed its usual routine for the next week, Kara insisting on accompanying Lena to her Council meetings with Lillian, even though the Queen insisted it wasn’t Seelie business. They were inseparable and Lena found a sort of comfort in Kara’s presence, duelling with her even though it was a lost cause, her amateurish skills with a sword making her lose each time, sitting beside her as she was lectured and quizzed on her lessons, Kara speaking slowly with her in the Fae language that Lena was gaining a clumsy understanding of. 

     

                She no longer felt quite so out of her depth as the weeks passed, some of her lessons imparting knowledge to her and helping her adapt. Lena had always been smart, information getting stuck in her mind without little effort on her part, and while she was stubborn and aloof and cold out of fear, still uncertain of her position at Court and the dynamics, she had a better understanding of the laws, of the way her mother governed the Unseelie. Lena had been taught how to sit with the correct posture and which dishes were eaten when and the correct greetings and titles for the nobility, the rituals of certain events or phases of the moon, how to make bluebells grow from seeds despite the frost that made the ground hard and would wither them by dawn. It was with great resentment, but she learnt.

     

                The weather cooled to a raw grey, leaving changing and falling, the forest turning somewhat sparse and skeletal, save for the pines and conifers. Finding herself in a foul mood of late, forced to stay inside by Lillian’s insistence as the weather worsened and a few light flurries of snow dusted the forest, Lena felt suffocated and cooped up. Her lessons continued, endless hours spent reciting Fae poetry that tripped her tongue up, or hesitantly making the tree roots of gnarled structures forming the Royal Residence shift slightly into something that looked like a knitted chair or a woven door, and Lena resented it all. 

     

                In the evenings, which were cold and damp, she huddled near the hearth in the new suite given to her and Kara - separate rooms now, which left her feeling oddly alone with a stone wall between them - and drank jugs of hot apple cider. In the last few remaining weeks of her time at Court, Lena couldn’t bring herself to feel excitement over the prospect of leaving soon, and instead, she spent her time plotting.

     

                One evening, Kara wandered out of her own room and was drawn to the scratching sound of a quill on paper. Hovering in the doorway for a moment, she observed the figure of her wife bent over the desk, dark hair running down her back like ink. Lena was wrapped up in a thick green dressing gown and her face was limned in orange light from the fire. Kara drifted inside uninvited, knowing Lena heard her approach.

     

                “Working hard at your studies? And here I thought you didn’t care for the arduous task of assigning grain allotments to each holding.”

     

                “It’s not homework; I’ve figured out a solution to our problem,” Lena distractedly told her, setting down her quill.

     

                “Which problem?” Kara asked, leaning against the desk as she looked down at her wife, cradling her cup of wine as she smiled slightly with amusement.

     

                “Our marriage. The truce. Two birds, one stone.”

     

                “And what is our stone?”

     

                Leaning back on her chair, Lena pressed her lips into a flat line for a moment before her eyes cut up to Kara. She anxiously chewed her bottom lip before speaking.

     

                “We stage a coup.”

     

                “A coup?” Kara exclaimed, straightening as shock made her expression go slack. “Are you insane? What would possess you to even think, let alone speak that word in this Court.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes and shifted her page closer as her eyes scanned over her words. “Just think about it; we stage a coup, depose my mother and instate me as Queen - reluctantly, albeit - we agree to keep the peace between the two of us as representatives of both Courts. No need for a marriage then, obviously, and I have no interest in war and I’m not a liar, so the truce would stand.”

     

                Setting her wine down, Kara snatched up the paper, turning whiter with every word she read. Finishing, she gingerly held the page in hand and gave Lena a frantic look.

     

                “Have you written anything else down?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena said, reaching for a few more sheaths of paper. “But I’m not an idiot; it’s written in code. Flowers for meaning.”

     

                A broken sound of disbelieving laughter escaped Kara as she snatched the pages from Lena and crumpled them in her fists. Lurching towards the brazier, she cast the evidence into the low-burning flames and watched them catch alight. The tension bled out of her slightly then and she whirled around on Lena, pink-cheeked with anger.

     

                Turned in her chair to watch, Lena spluttered indignantly. “I worked hard at that, thank you.”

     

                “Is it not enough to have a death wish for yourself, now you conspire to have me implicated in treason so I can lose my head along with you,” Kara snapped.

     

                Scowling as she snatched up Kara’s wine, Lena drained it. “It’s a good idea,” she protested. “Cut the head off the snake-“

     

                “And what happens then? Hm? You think they will accept you as ruler because you are the bastard of the late king? You’ve spent two months in this Court; they will slit your throat the second you sit on the throne.”

     

                “Well I wouldn’t stay here,” Lena snorted. “I can’t wait to get away from here.”

     

                “So your plan is to kill the Queen-“

     

                “I didn’t say kill.”

     

                “It would be only slightly less stupid if that’s what you intended; they wouldn’t be able to reinstate her that way. But say she’s dead and you leave, you’ll plunge a whole Court into a civil war for a power struggle, probably spark the war with the Seelie Court again as a result, and any noble will seize power for themselves. They will stage a coup against you in your absence; the only difference being you will have no friends to back your claim and fight in your defence. You’ve not made a good impression so far, Lena. In fact, you’d be lucky to have a single person back such an idiotic plan as this.”

     

                Cheeks flaming, Lena drained the wine and slammed the goblet down on the desk. Climbing to her feet, she gave Kara a scathing look. “At least it’s a better plan than twiddling our thumbs and waiting to be killed instead of eliminating the threats ourselves.”

     

                Stepping into her path, Kara gave her a pleading look, shoulders going slack as she exhaled softly. “To twiddle our thumbs is the safest option. I cannot protect you from everything, much as I would like to. And if you were right about your brother … that poses another threat we can’t account for in reckless plans like a coup.”

     

                “Then what do you think we should do?” Lena demanded, her cheeks flushed red.

     

                Kara gestured sweepingly to the brazier with the ashes of Lena’s evidence, her face tight with panic and anger. “Not that. I’ll hear no more of it.”

     

                Pushing to her feet, the chair scraping backwards, Lena gave her a look full of anger and betrayal, her hands balled into fists. “You’re not in control of me and I’m not going to waste my life doing the bidding of others.”

     

                A rueful smile curled one side of Kara’s mouth as she nodded. “Rest assured it’ll be a short life if you continue down this path. I won’t walk it with you, Lena. I told you I’ll be loyal to you, but my people come first. Jeopardise that and I’ll do what I have to.”

     

                “So will I,” Lena said with a challenge.

     

                Nodding, Kara swallowed thickly, her expression clouded with worry. “Then on your own head be it.”

    Chapter 15

                Lena didn’t let it go.

     

                It wasn’t that she didn’t agree with Kara that it was a reckless idea that would get herself - possibly both of them - killed but that Lena would rather try than sit around and do nothing. It was a last-ditch effort, knowing that Kara was right in that she would have absolutely no support, but then it occurred to Lena that it didn’t have to be her. She just needed someone who would be in a better position to take over the throne, who would have no reason to want her married to a Seelie or the truce to last.

     

                In a final act of desperation, Lena scrawled a note on a scrap of parchment and climbed onto the trunk of clothes set against the wall beneath the foot-wide gap between the roots that allowed fresh air to stream inside. Setting a rock down on the note, she was confident that she was being watched and the note would be seen. She waited four days before a response took its place.

     

                Archery at dawn.

     

                The three words were written in a jagged script that took Lena a few moments to decipher as she consulted her dictionary by candlelight at her desk. A jolt of anticipation ran through her as she pieced together the glyphs and her heart raced in her chest before she tossed the scrap into the brazier. She was right about being watched and apprehensive about venturing beyond the wards alone but Lena didn’t feel as if she had much say in the matter. She was either committed to her cause or not.

     

                After a sleepless night, she rose early and dressed warmly, opening her bedroom door and creeping towards the front door. She hadn’t even made it to the door before Kara’s door was opening, her wiry form a dark shadow in the banked embers of the fire from the night before.

     

                “Where are you going?” she asked, her voice gravelly and thick with sleep.

     

                “To bathe.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Is that alright?” Lena asked, her tone slightly nettling as her pulse stuttered at the thought of being caught.

     

                Kara mumbled something too low for her to hear before slipping back into her room and Lena quickly stepped outside, pulling her cloak tight to herself and glancing at the night guard she wasn’t overly familiar with. The only time she was without Reign shadowing her was at night when her guard slept and this night guard wasn’t nearly as immovable as her mother’s pet. It was a simple thing for Lena to tell him she was bathing, watching him shift with uncertainty before nodding. 

     

                Relief flooded through Lena and she walked down the hallways as if making for the bathing pools before ducking down a side corridor and taking a back exit, emerging from between two roots and slipping through a hedge row and through the gardens. She was no spy, no hunter, no light-footed fae archer used to stalking creatures through the woods but no one paid attention to Lena’s quiet blundering through the underbrush as she circled back around to the path leading to her clearing. She hadn’t brought her bow and it seemed like a risk in hindsight, going beyond the confines of the Court with nothing but the dagger Kara had given her. If someone was close enough for her to use her dagger, Lena had to admit she was likely already dead. 

     

                Still, nothing disturbed her, in fact, it seemed almost unnaturally quiet. No soft hooting of owls, no early morning twittering from the other birds or the slow crash of badgers and foxes and other nocturnal animals crossing over with the stirrings of daytime forest dwellers. Drawing her cloak tighter, Lena made it to the clearing and felt the hairs on the back of her neck rise as she found herself alone, her breaths gusting out in pale clouds as she turned slowly, the air feeling wrong somehow. She rarely felt uncomfortable in the forest and to feel so on edge now should have been all the warning she needed to leave, but she stayed.

     

                A minute later, with nothing but the creaking trees and the dripping of melting sleet that coated the branches as the wind howled through, a ghastly screech that only served to set Lena even further on edge, a shadow materialised through the mist. Lena’s fingers itched to grasp her dagger at the apparition but it solidified into the sight of the man who’d appeared in her room a few weeks ago.

     

                He wasn’t covered in blood this time, his head freshly shaved and his clothes showing the wear and tear of the forest, leaves and dirt clinging to him, a slightly feral edge to his harsh features. Lena could see him better than in the dark confines of Kara’s old rooms but she still couldn’t see anything of herself in his features - or Lillian for that matter, except for in his mannerisms.

     

                “Your Highness,” he mockingly greeted her with a shallow bow.

     

                “You’ve been watching me?” Lena asked, her voice uneven.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Did you kill Eve?”

     

                He gestured helplessly, no remorse on his face - not that she expected to see any. It was a cruel and ruthless Court, lacking the idyllic peace of Kara’s home, and Lena knew that the stakes were higher for the Unseelie. No one would outright kill each other but midnight assassinations weren’t uncommon. Lena was surprised she hadn’t fallen victim to more attempts if anything.

     

                “A necessary sacrifice.”

     

                “Why? Because she would’ve talked?”

     

                “She only knew a little. You haven’t talked though, have you?” he murmured, expression clouding with bewildered surprise.

     

                That wasn’t entirely true - Lena had told Kara her suspicions. They hadn’t been readily accepted but she’d told her nonetheless. Still, Lena shook her head, rooted to the spot as he slowly prowled in a circle around her, making her stomach pitch like a roiling sea.

     

                “Good.”

     

                “You’re my brother, aren’t you?” Lena warily asked.

     

                He smiled thinly, his dark eyes glittering in the gloom. “Ah, so you did piece it together.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Good. I was beginning to think you were as dull as the other human pets they keep around Court. I am surprised you sought me out; I don’t believe I made a good impression on you last time.”

     

                Her stomach knotted with unease and Lena couldn’t say she felt comfortable around him, her muscles so tight that her body ached where she stood. Throat dry, she cleared it quietly, trying to summon some courage as she faced the man she didn’t know, yet shared blood with. Lena had always viewed herself as an only child and it was an odd thing to suddenly think about a family she’d never had before. Lillian was already too much to bear. Enough to want to rid herself of her.
