                “No, I don’t think you did,” Lena murmured in agreement, her curiosity still piqued enough to endure the risk. “But I thought you might- maybe you could help me.”

     

                “Help you?” he asked, arching an eyebrow in a manner that was so much like his mother.

     

                Cold fear slid down Lena’s spine, her back dampened with sweat despite the chill of the pre-dawn forest, and she toyed with her fingers, anxiety squeezing her chest tight. Clearing her throat again, she gestured off-handedly, trying not to betray the panic she was trying to hide.

     

                “You said last time that you would be coming back for me. That I shouldn’t worry about being heir for long. I … did you want to be heir?”

     

                “It is my birthright,” Lex drawled.

     

                “Everyone thinks you're dead.”

     

                “But I am not.”

     

                “Do you think you’ll be a good ruler? I mean … if you were on the throne, would the people back you?”

     

                “They will have no choice. I’m strong . Not like my mother, who’s weak enough to form a truce.”

     

                “Would you start the war again?”

     

                “It wouldn’t be a war; the disorganised rabble of the Seelie Court wouldn’t stand a chance without their best warriors.”

     

                Mouth thinning as she second-guessed her plot, wondering if she was asking for aid from the wrong guy. But then she’d only heard what he was like from Kara, and while her wife wasn’t known for lying, she would be biased, of course. Kara didn’t like anyone from the Unseelie Court, while Lena thought some of them were tolerable at least. 

     

                “I’ve heard you’re cruel,” Lena hesitantly replied.

     

                “From whom? Your wife? She would believe that of me,” Lex said, his expression darkening into brooding contempt. “Our family has slaughtered almost all of hers; I might believe the same of her for efforts against our own people. Perhaps she’s right though but a ruler must do cruel things at times for the sake of their people. I would keep us safe if I were in power - and not by cowardly means.”

     

                “Would you let me go?”

     

                “Go where?”

     

                “Wherever I wanted,” Lena wistfully sighed. “Out of this marriage, this truce.”

     

                He gave her an easy smile then, toying with his dagger. “But of course. I would have no need for your wife or a truce.”

     

                “If you help me, I won’t stand in your way. You won’t ever have to see me again.”

     

                She kept her expectant stare level, fingers knotted in a white-knuckled grip in her skirts as she waited for him to reply. Lex was silent, twirling his knife as he pretended to consider it before a slow smile spread across his face.

     

                “I’ll help you but you shall have to help me to do it.”

     

                Licking her lips, Lena hesitated, her throat dry. “What do you need me to do?”

     

                “I can have Dar-Essa flowers slipped to you. You will need to find a way to slip them to our mother.”

     

                “I- I don’t know if-”

     

                He moved in close, his expression stern and intimidating. “You will.”

     

                “Okay. I’ll do it.”

     

                “Alright then. Once she’s out of our way, you shall be free from your marriage and truce and I shall be free to claim the throne. That is the bargain you would like to strike, is it not?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena rasped.

     

                Guilt needled at her at the thought of civil unrest and political upheaval the assassination or imprisonment of the Queen and instating her brother, returned from the supposed dead, would wreak on the Unseelie Court, and Seelie too she supposed if he got the war up and running again. But this was a thing that had been ongoing for centuries, millennia, and a paltry four months was a mere blink in time for the fae who had endured this for as long as they’d been alive. 

     

                Lena wasn’t responsible for the lives of these strangers, for the bad blood between the Courts. Lena just wanted a quiet life with her flowers and without being foisted upon someone else as their bride. It felt selfish - it probably was selfish - but why was it her responsibility to sacrifice her hard-earned contentment with the life she’d struggled to achieve so strangers could peacefully hold their parties in the forest and dance through the trees?

     

                “Then we have a deal.”

     

                Lex slashed his palm and held the knife out to Lena, who wavered before making a small, stinging cut on her own. Her brother gripped her hand in his, a tight hold as they stood close together, his relatively short stature still intimidating as she took in the cold hardness of his face, wondering again if she was making a mistake. Was he as callous and calculating as he seemed? Perhaps he was just patriotic and understood the history better than Lena to know why the truce could not endure. Was he really so bad as Kara had said, or was her wife obligated to lie to make the death of her family seem unjust instead of the cost of war?

     

                “It’s winter in three days so I’ll be leaving Court then. It needs to be before then.”

     

                Lex reached out and cupped her chin, urging her head up, and Lena met his flat stare with uncertainty. Her chest tightened with unease as the back of her neck prickled and she swallowed thickly as her brother smiled thinly.

     

                “Don’t fret. All will be as you wish. Leave the planning up to me, just be ready to do your part.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena said with more conviction than she felt.

     

                She nodded to reassure herself, restless with agitation as a lump got caught in her throat. Wiping his palm clean on a handkerchief, Lex held it out to Lena to staunch the bleeding of her own shallow cut and then took it back.

     

                They were left staring at each other for a moment and Lex’s dark eyes were assessing, taking in the measure of her before his lips twitched with amusement. Straightening, he gave her a piercing look and nodded in parting.

     

                He was gone a moment later, a lithe shadow that was quickly swallowed up by the dimness, which was slowly lightening. Lena was left shivering in the mist that writhed around the trees, shrouding her lower legs as her hair was left damp against her cheeks and shoulders as she lingered. After a minute, she forced herself to move, the cold having crept into her muscles and joints, making her stiff as she stumbled back towards the Royal Residence, knowing her window to bathe without rousing Kara’s suspicion of what was taking so long was shrinking rapidly.

     

                Hurrying through the hallways, she burrowed down through the warren of earth and found an empty bath, shedding her clothes quickly and stepping into the steam. It was hot enough to make her frozen feet sting as the cold was chased away and Lena quickly submerged herself, surfacing quickly as the sensation of water closing over her head made her chest constrict with panic. 

     

                Settling against the wall, she basked in the warmth for a few minutes and then hastily scrubbed herself clean with a bar of soap before climbing out of the bath. Drying herself off, she dressed in her damp clothes and tried to wring as much water from her hair before winding her way back towards her quarters. 

     

                Reign was still hovering outside the door and gave Lena a once-over, taking in the flush of pink in her cheeks from the bath before Lena slipped into her room. The door to Kara’s quarters was open as Lena crossed over to her own, directly across from it, pausing as the sound of her wife’s voice drifted from her suite. 

     

                “You were gone for a while. I almost came looking for you.”

     

                Quietly snorting, Lena changed her trajectory and poked her head inside Kara’s bedroom and then crossed the threshold. She was behind the desk, dressed in one of her thin shirts with the sleeves rolled up, leather leggings undoubtedly fitted to her lithe form beneath the desk, and she was making hasty notes, the swirling figures of runes materialising with such fluid ease that Lena was envious.

     

                “Do you think I’m so dimwitted that I’d get lost on my way to bathe?”

     

                Glancing up, Kara’s blue eyes flickered with amusement. “No, but I wouldn’t put it past you to somehow suffer an attempt on your life on the way.”

     

                Lena couldn’t argue with that and rolled her eyes, annoyance twisting her lips before she flexed the fingers of her cut hand. The gesture caught Kara’s attention, eyes immediately landing on the red line crossing her palm. 

     

                “What happened to your hand?” Kara asked, setting down her quill and rising to her feet.

     

                Screwing her eyes shut for a moment, Lena opened and closed her mouth before shaking her head and running her other hand through her dishevelled, damp hair. “Oh, um, cut it on the edge of the pool.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Kara was in front of her, cradling Lena’s hand in her own as she reached out with her other hand, summoning a ribbon of water. Directing it into a crystal sphere, Kara lowered the cool water to Lena’s palm, soothing as it flushed the shallow cut clean. Flinging the water into the brazier, Kara produced a clean handkerchief and wrapped it around Lena’s hand.

     

                “No attempt on your life but an injury nonetheless,” Kara sighed. “What am I to do with you?”

     

                It was said almost fondly and Lena’s stomach swooped as she met her eyes, her own stare unreadable. She had no sarcastic retort for her wife, although Kara stared at her almost expectedly. Mouth thinning, Lena cast her eyes aside, taking in the orderly state of the room; scrolls and books, a tray with the remnants of tea from last night, her deep blue robe folded over the back of an armchair and her sword leaning against the wall. It was lived in and homely, in contrast to Lena’s rather bare room, holding nothing but the chest with the clothes and jewels she’d accumulated over the months. Even in the court of her enemies, Kara was more at home than Lena would ever feel there.

     

                “You should get changed for breakfast,” Kara murmured after a moment. “Your attendant is already readying your clothes and you’re sure to rankle her if you’re late.”

     

                Sighing, Lena pulled her hand free and turned, leaving the bedroom and making for her own, where Andrea was setting out a warm dress and pairing the jewellery and cloak to go with it. She glanced up with disinterest as Lena entered and rolled her eyes at the damp mess of her hair, gesturing her to take a seat before fetching a comb.

     

                Lena allowed her to work out the tangles and braid it plainly before she was helped into the clean shift and dress. Her feet were cold but she knew better than to grumble about shoes or even a pair of socks, and she hovered near the brazier as Andrea handed her rings to slip on. Belting on her dagger, she smoothed her hands over her dress and then sighed wearily before slipping out of the room.

     

                Kara met her at the door and they stepped out into the hallway, their usual quartet making their way to breakfast. As they swept into the dining room together, Lena faltered for a moment, sure her mother would be able to see the guilt on her face, but she lowered her gaze as she dipped into a shallow curtsy and took her usual seat with her wife beside her.

     

                They didn’t speak all through breakfast as Lena sipped her tea and ate slivers of figs and warm bread. As soon as they had finished, they withdrew and Lena dismissively rejected the scheduled lessons as she took the lead down the hallway, making her way through to one of the rooms stocked with weapons. Filching a worn, ornately engraved bow and a quiver of arrows, Lena slung the latter over her shoulder and stalked back out into the hallway and then out into the cool morning.

     

                The sky was grey through the canopy overhead and a brisk wind whistled through the trees as she made her way to their usual clearing, just beyond the safety of the boundary guarded by soldiers. No one stopped them but Lena was aware of the presence of the soldiers at the fringes of her consciousness, a hair-raising feeling of being watched stealing over her. Kara had long since stopped trying to convince her to stay within the confines of the safety the Unseelie Court’s royal seat offered but she loosened her sword in its scabbard and was vigilant as they took up their usual positions.

     

                Stringing the bow, Lena let herself fall into the relatively peaceful monotony of archery, loosing her pent-up frustration, her fear, her unease as she sent arrow after arrow towards the nicked bark of the wide trunk. Her aim had marginally improved, as had the ease with which she could draw back the bowstring, some of her softness diminished by the muscle she’d gained from hours spent in that clearing. 

     

                She stayed there until her muscles burned from the effort and returned to her quarters, loose-limbed and tired, her mood soured by that as lunch was brought to their rooms for them. It was warm in their quarters with the fire going and Lena curled up in a brooding ball on the chaise as she watched steam drift from the fresh tea and ignored the bowl of stew. Kara ate hers with trepidation as she cast sideward glances at Lena in between mouthfuls before plucking up the courage to question her.

     

                “Is something weighing on your mind?”

     

                Sharply looking at her, Lena frowned. “No.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Why would you think that?”

     

                “You’re uncharacteristically quiet. Ordinarily, you would have said at least three unkind things about my presence or our marriage by lunchtime. You’ve yet to say one at all so far today.”

     

                Looking bewildered for a moment, Lena just hummed distractedly. “Oh. Yes, well … I’m just thinking about leaving.”

     

                “I would have thought you’d seem more pleased with the prospect. If not for excitement at visiting my second holdings but to be free from this place.”

     

                “One prison is much the same as the other.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara sighed as her shoulders sagged. “You aren’t a prisoner with me. You have your freedom. Always.”

     

                Lena’s smile was thin and crooked, an eyebrow arched as she let out a quick laugh and reached to pour herself some tea. Hesitating, she poured a cup for Kara as well and nudged it along the low table towards her. Meeting her gaze, Lena’s eyes narrowed a fraction.

     

                “So I could choose to go and stay somewhere else once we’re back in the Seelie Court? I could take my diamonds and sell them in the human realm and live there for the season and you’d be okay with that?”

     

                Opening her mouth, Kara hesitated before her expression turned sheepish. “I couldn’t let you go back; there would be no guarantee you would only be gone for the season. You might hold to your vow and try to return in three months but you could just as easily come back through a decade in the future. And as for staying somewhere else, I wouldn’t be able to keep you safe.”

     

                “Right,” Lena flatly laughed, unsurprised. Taking a sip of her tea, she glanced sideways at Kara again and let out a small sigh. “I wouldn’t leave again. I would have stayed gone if I had thought I had the means to rebuild my life.”

     

                She couldn’t quite keep the bitterness out of her voice, taking another sip of tea as her expression soured. Kara was sympathetic to the loss of her florist, to the loss of her home and ordinary life but she could never feel guilty about Lena’s presence with her. In fact, Kara would be terribly selfish and never let her stray from her side if she could help it. She would never admit it to Lena but she enjoyed her prickly company, the departure from the stiff formality of ruling, of laws and politics. She enjoyed it more than she would admit to herself.

     

                “You could take the diamonds, as you said,” Kara pointedly replied.

     

                “And I still couldn’t get back the life I lost. Yes, it would probably be better but what’s the point if it’s different? I may as well build a new one here. At least I don’t have to deal with debt and homelessness here. At least I … understand myself better here. Regardless of how I feel, I don’t think I could leave anyway; it has its teeth in me, the forest. You and I both know that.”

     

                “Then you’ve decided?”

     

                Kara’s question was tentatively posed, a note of hope in her voice, and Lena let out a huff of laughter. Running a hand over her face, she shook her head and drained her tea before refilling her cup again. It was warm, even if it did little to soothe her. Sighing, she shrugged helplessly.

     

                “It’s not much of a choice though, is it? I suppose I have though. Now I just need to wait for the pieces to fall into place.”

     

                “What pieces?”

     

                Giving Kara a tired smile, Lena closed her eyes. “This is far from over, Kara. You can feel it too, can’t you? This peace. It’s so … fragile . I’m not even from here and I can see the cracks. There’s not much for us to do except wait to see what happens next and take it in stride.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara reached out across the gap between them and touched the back of Lena’s hand. Freezing, Lena looked down at her fingers and then up at her wife. She grudgingly had to respect the sincerity in Kara’s eyes, the determination to take whatever came at face value, with none of the sly manipulations Lena had seen by others and was slipping into herself.

     

                “It’ll be okay. Whatever may come, at least we can say we tried to put a stop to it with our marriage and the truce.”

     

                Lena felt as if she visibly paled, thinking about how willing she was to weasel her way out of the promise she’d never made, ignorant of the plot to wed her away until it was upon her, and yet she’d never pretended to have more morals than Kara. Only that Kara had the freedom to choose and she had not, and Lena had never said she would have chosen the same if she’d been given the option. Clearly, her choice would have been different. If it wasn’t, she wouldn’t be planning on helping the brother onto the throne in exchange for her own freedom. 

     

                Once that was bought for herself, Lena planned on getting as far away as possible, as quickly as possible, and forgetting any of this had ever happened. The obvious choice would be going back to her home, perhaps to another city, where she could disappear into the masses of a metropolitan area, gone without a trace. But then there was the forest. The forest with its clean air and the hum of life in every facet of it, from the dank ponds infested with mosquitoes and frogs and little minnows to the lichen and moss-covered rocks and trees, the nests of birds and rabbit warrens, the palpable hum of root systems and brambles heavy with blackberries and stalks of wild garlic, branches laden with apples and pears. It was intoxicating, right down to the rotting foliage carpeting the floor, the rough bark beneath her calloused palms from hours spent holding a bow that she was semi-confident could feed her if she had to hunt, to the lazy bees spreading the pollen that was in her lungs as surely as the water was in her veins. Lena was so enmeshed in this world that it seemed an awful waste to pry herself free from its vice-like grip for a smoggy city of exhaust fumes and oil and garbage. 

     

                She didn’t want to confess to not trying very hard so Lena just settled for a weak smile and moved her hand away from Kara’s touch before drinking her tea. They milled about the place for the remainder of the afternoon, reading in their respective rooms, Lena always far too aware of Kara’s presence for her liking. 

     

                After dinner, she was left to read by candlelight in bed, although she was far too distracted and couldn’t make it through a single page, the puzzle of deciphering the glyphs not enticing enough to hold her attention. Instead, she turned over the possibilities of what her brother would do and fretted long into the night as sleep evaded her once the hour grew late enough for it. She didn’t end up falling asleep until a few hours before dawn, and at one point she thought she heard footsteps outside her door but was left undisturbed. 

     

                The next two days passed in a blur and she was too preoccupied with her heavy thoughts to engage in the verbal sparring with Lillian as her mother stared at her, cold and calculating in her assessing gaze. Lena went through the motions by rote, her lessons in decorum and history going over her head as she idly made notes and blundered her way through questions with the wrong answers and mumbled confusion, her expression clouded. Kara watched her closely through all of it, not saying a word until it was the night before they were set to leave and Lena was coiled tight, her whole body stiff and jerky as she watched Andrea pack her things for her in a trunk to be sent after them.

     

                “You should come with us,” Lena blurted out as she watched Andrea lay out her clothes for the morning, felt leggings and a woollen dress split at the back and front for riding.

     

                Andrea glanced over her shoulder at her. “And why would I do that? Is it not enough for me to attend to you here, now you expect me to do it for you in her Court?”

     

                “I-” Lena started before the words died in her mouth.

     

                She didn’t particularly like Andrea, or Reign for that matter, but she’d grown accustomed to their presence the way she’d grown accustomed to Kara. Lena didn’t know what would happen once Lex wormed his way back into the Court but she felt the least she could do was try and help the people who had helped her, albeit grudgingly and with difficulty as she made their jobs as hard as possible for them, but they were the only ones who’d had any sort of interaction with Lena beyond the sly manipulations of the court or the stiff manner of those ordered to teach her by Lillian. 

     

                “I just thought it would give you a break from this place,” Lena shrugged dismissively. “What else will you do, sit around and wait for me to come back in the spring?”

     

                Andrea laughed quickly. “I have a life outside of pandering to your every whim.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena’s mouth twitched. “You’ve pandered to no one but the Queen.”

     

                “Your belongings are packed. Will that be all?”

     

                Nodding, Lena gestured towards the door and then ran a hand over her face, all but collapsing onto the armchair set near the brazier in the corner of her room. Brooding over the following day, she didn’t hear her wife approach but the faint tang of salt water and rainstorms flooded into the room ahead of her arrival and Lena looked up, her expression unreadable as her hand fell from her face.

     

                “You are worried.”

     

                Shrugging nonchalantly, Lena rubbed her fingertips over her lips, her green eyes darting about restlessly as she avoided looking at Kara. Stepping into the bedroom, Kara crossed over to her and dropped to a knee, her expression tender and earnest as she looked up at Lena, trying to catch her eye.

     

                “What troubles you?”

     

                “It’s not your concern,” Lena mumbled with less ire than intended.

                

                “Of course it is. Your concerns are mine, as is everything shared in a marriage.”

     

                “Well, I don’t want you to concern yourself with it. It’s- it’s nothing. I just- I can’t wait to be away from here. I hope I never have to come back.”

     

                With a soft, resigned sigh, Kara’s shoulders slumped and she grimaced, setting a hand on Lena’s knee. “We shall return in the spring. The season away from here will do you good; it won’t feel so bad upon our return, you’ll see.”

     

                “Your unfailing optimism that this will all work out is starting to get on my nerves,” Lena sighed, letting her head loll to the side as she gave her wife an exasperated look.

     

                Expression softening with amusement, blue eyes bright, Kara raised her eyebrows. “Starting to? Am I losing my touch or are you growing accustomed to me?”

     

                Straightening, Lena inhaled deeply and then exhaled heavily, her lips twitching with a smile as she reached up to press her fingertips to Kara’s cheek for a moment, an intimate gesture that she quickly put a stop to, hands dropping as if she’d been burnt. Still, the ghost of a smile lingered a moment longer as Lena replied.

     

                “You’re losing your touch. Obviously.”

     

                “I’ll endeavour to try harder then. I wouldn’t want to go all soft on you.”

     

                “No, we wouldn’t want that. You would be poor company if you let me get my own way all the time.”

     

                “Rest assured, I will remain as stubborn as a stone battling the constant wear of the river. I won’t yield to your commands just yet.”

     

                Eyelids shuttering, the corners of Lena’s mouth twitched. “Good.”

     

                They fell silent for a moment, Kara still kneeling, her hand still on Lena’s lap, a comfortable ease between them. Lena broke it with a sigh, her shoulders caving as her eyebrows drew together in a stern look.

     

                “I’m glad to be leaving.”

     

                “Me too,” Kara whispered, reaching for her hand and squeezing it gently. “You’ll be safe enough once we’re home. I promise.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                She faltered before squeezing Kara’s hand in return, perhaps tighter than necessary, as if clinging to the one person she could trust. And in return, she was willing to wash her hands of any further involvement in this sham to rid herself of her wife. Her kind and trusting wife, who had too much loyalty and honour than was good for her. Lena just hoped Kara stayed clear of the fallout of it all, remained at her tower and her lake as Lex ransacked the Unseelie Court and got his revenge however he planned. Kara didn’t need to be courageous and pick up her sword; she deserved a quiet life too, spent fishing and swimming and boating. A quieter life without a wife to bicker with.

     

                The brief resurgence of guilt was enough to make Lena’s eyes sting with tears, her throat closing up around her swallow. Drawing in a shaky breath, Lena stared at their entwined hands and knew she should tell her the truth.

     

                “Kara, I-”

     

                “It’s okay. I know you have mixed feelings about all of this. You don’t need to explain yourself.”

     

                “But-”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Kara looked up at her with a sweet, seraphic look on her face, golden hair like an unbound river, blue eyes like deep wells, so deep Lena could drown in them and for once she didn’t think she’d be afraid of it. The fight drained out of her and she rubbed her forehead, unable to even put into words the conflicted feeling in her chest. She just wanted it to be over, meant no malice or hatred towards anyone else - perhaps a little towards Lillian but Lena wouldn’t have minded if she lived, so long as she was free of her - and was tired of going through the motions of the useless farce that she was a Princess doing her duty to keep the peace.

     

                “Sleep well, Lena. We have a long and dangerous journey in the morning,” Kara murmured, squeezing her hand and kissing her knuckles.

     

                Kara left then and Lena heard the soft hooting of an owl through the gap in the roots a moment later and watched as a flutter of movement caught her eyes. The pale buds of a Dar-Essa lay on the packed earthen floor, delivered to her to assist her brother in their joint plot to get what they both wanted and Lena held them delicately in her cupped palms, the memory of coughing up blood, of the tingling at the back of her throat and leaden exhausted that persisted for days making her second-guess herself. Hiding them beneath her pillows, she went to bed.

     

                She slept fitfully, tossing and turning all night, mumbling in her sleep as she dreamed of a shallow lake, murky with moss and weeds and gnarled roots, the latter ensnaring her, pulling her down, down, down. Water was in her mouth, in her nose and eyes, her heavy clothes making it hard for her to fight as they grew sodden. Despite it being only to her knees, Lena dreamt she was drowning, coughing up the dank taste of stagnant water, her hair plastered to her cheeks and forehead, lips tinged blue from the cold as roots wound around her throat as she clawed at them, pale petals spilling from her lips as she found her throat full of flower buds. 

     

                It was dark when she went under again and Lena let out a hoarse cry as she startled awake, eyes darting around wildly as she found herself sitting upright, chest heaving and her nightdress clinging to her sweat-slick skin. Kara was standing at her bedside and Lena flinched at the sight of her before raking her hand through her sweat-dampened hair. Sniffing, she swallowed thickly and drew in a shallow, shaking breath.

     

                “You were dreaming.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Was it a nightmare?”

     

                Kara’s inquisitiveness made a flash of irritation run through Lena. Closing her eyes, a muscle twitched in her jaw and she nodded slightly. The mattress jostled as Kara sank onto the bed uninvited. Eyelids flashing open, Lena gave her a flat look but Kara was unperturbed by her apparent annoyance.

     

                “Yes,” Lena softly admitted.

     

                Digging the heels of her palms into her eyes, she inhaled sharply and exhaled roughly. The silence of the early hours of the morning was deafening and she tried to will Kara to leave without her having to tell her, the embarrassment of her bad dreams of something so trivial as water , murky memories of drowning dredged up with it, making her cheeks warm.

     

                “Would you like to talk-”

     

                “No.”

     

                “I’ll fetch you some tea then.”

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                “Tea tastes just as good when one is fine as it does when one is not.”

     

                She had no argument for her wife’s logic and decided it was easier to let her complete her task, and at the very least give Lena a minute or two to compose herself. The nightdress was so thin that her sweat had turned it sheer in places and she had to pluck it loose from her clammy skin as she kicked back the blankets and climbed out of bed. It was cooler out from beneath the warm quilts and she paced for a moment before Kara returned, having relayed her order to the guard and come back with a laden tray.

     

                Hovering just inside the door, she watched Lena closely and then set down the tray and crossed over to her quickly, pressing the back of her hand against Lena’s brow. Jerking away, affronted, Lena scoffed and rolled her eyes.

     

                “I’m not sick.”

     

                “Just a precaution. You look … off.”

     

                Bedraggled and flushed, a strained look on her face, Lena let out a shuddering laugh and plucked at the front of her nightgown. “It’s this place. It’s getting to me. I’m just- I’d like to be away from here as quickly as possible. Something isn’t right.”

     

                “Yes,” Kara slowly agreed, wariness flashing across her face as she poured from the teapot with a pensive furrow between her brows as she held a cup out. “I have had the same feeling of late.”

     

                Pausing in her idle pacing, Lena fixed her with a piercing stare and then took the cup of tea. “Have you?”

     

                “Yes. Well, more so than usual, I should say.”

     

                Kara paused, hesitating as suspicion crept into her features, and she clasped her hands behind her back, clearing her throat before she shook her head and spoke. “Come, since we are awake we should bathe and ready ourselves for the journey. It will be longer and colder than the one here and I do not like the taste of the air this morning.”

     

                Lena gave her a sceptical look as she said it and Kara looked faintly sheepish as she shrugged helplessly. “It tastes of steel.”

     

                Making a quiet scoffing sound at the back of her throat, Lena pulled on the heavily embroidered robe and belted it at her waist, raking her damp hair out of her face. It had grown unnaturally fast since she’d been in the forest, hanging almost to her waist and unruly when it wasn’t braided out of the way, a sheet of inky satin that made her look like a mediaeval painting or mythological creature come to life when she was trussed up in her finery. Kara reached out and touched one of her cheeks, gone cold as the sweat had dried, and Lena’s eyelids shuttered at the gentle touch of her, feeling her fingertips slip up towards her temple, brushing a loose lock of her hair back behind her ear, mindful of the short, pointed tips.

     

                “The baths,” Lena murmured, her voice gently rasping, and Kara nodded, dropping her hand and walking out of the room.

     

                They made their way through the corridors to the steaming pools, choosing Lena’s preferred shallow one as they let the heat warm them through and scrubbed themselves clean, the smell of pine sharp in the air. Kara seemed on edge the whole time, as noticed by Lena’s furtive glances as she took in the corded muscles of her arms and back, shoulders tense and her head turning towards the door whenever she heard a sound.

     

                Returning to their quarters, they went to their respective rooms and dressed, Lena pulling on warmer clothes than she’d worn so far, the felt leggings thick and the split dress heavy over the thinner linen shift beneath it. Tucking the flower petals in the sleeve of her dress, she picked up her cloak and steeled herself for the courage to poison the Queen.

     

                With her cloak over the top, she was bundled up a little too warmly for the confines of her room with the small ventilation hole between the roots and found herself eager to be off, if only for the fresh air of the forest. The only thing she could smell on the breeze was the telltale hint of impending rain, which wasn’t enough to dampen her mood at being away from the Court.

     

                Making their way to breakfast together, they sat beside each other and Lena deliberated over the tea before choosing the blackberry her mother preferred, shifting the pot towards herself and allowing the petals to fall into the top before filling her cup and then hesitating before filling Lillian’s, the Queen’s shrewd stare snagged by the act. Filling Kara’s cup for her with a peppermint tea, Lena found herself with less appetite than usual, cracking the top of a soft-boiled duck egg and dipping warm bread into the yolk as she forced herself to swallow and avoided her tea. Lillian ate slivers of raw rabbit hearts and fed them to her ravens in turn as they flocked to her high-backed chair, her sharp stare never straying far from Lena’s face.

     

                “So, you have survived the season against my expectations,” Lillian eventually drawled, taking a sip of her tea and setting the cup down. “I should commend you on your stubborn determination to survive, daughter, but I won’t. It seems it was a matter of sheer luck instead of quality of character. Nevertheless, you’re alive for now and the peace holds in my Court.”

     

                “As it shall in mine,” Kara smoothly interjected, her stare unwavering as she rolled a ripe raspberry between thumb and forefinger, awaiting a response for a moment before popping it in her mouth and chewing slowly.

     

                Lillian fluttered her fingers in an irritated gesture of dismissal and Kara’s lips twitched with amusement. Sitting rigidly in her seat, heart pounding in her chest at the excitement of this being the last meal she had to endure with her mother, the last day for months - hopefully ever - that she’d have to be in her company against her will. 

     

                As eager as both women were to be away from the Court, now that it was the first day of winter and they held no obligation to remain - Lena was almost surprised that Kara hadn’t woken her at midnight to leave immediately, and thought she might have if it was safe to travel by night - they were forced to wait as Lillian lingered over her breakfast. Eventually, she finished off her second cup of tea, hesitating momentarily and pressing her lips together before she cast Lena and Kara piercing looks.

     

                Clearing her throat, she set down her cup and arched an eyebrow. “You are both restless this morning. Is something amiss?”

     

                “We are eager to begin our travels, Your Majesty,” Kara politely replied. “We have a long distance to cover before we reach my home. Winter is never a good time to be in the forest for long; I would see us off soon.”

     

                Giving her a shrewd look, Lillian licked her lips, stained a faint purple from the tea. She leaned back, appraising them both as her eyes narrowed a fraction and Lena’s stomach swooped as she wondered if her mother would keep them there against their agreement. After a tense minute, Lillian swept to her feet, birds scattering as their harsh caws filled the room. 

     

                Feathers drifted around her and a flutter of wings filled the silence. A moment later, the chairs of the two wives scraped back in unison as they rose to their feet. Waiting for Lillian to sweep out first, they trailed after her and were led down the main hallway and up above ground, the trio flanked by guards as they emerged in formation to the early dawn.

     

                “A red sun rises,” Kara murmured through thin lips as she looked around. 

     

                Lena saw the faint wisps of pink through the canopy, the bloody sunrise visible through patches in the cloud cover. A shallow furrow appeared between her eyebrows and she shivered involuntarily as she took in the branches overhead, which had steadily lost their leaves since she’d arrived, carpeting the ground underfoot. She drew in a shaky breath, so cold she felt as if it scoured inside her throat, her exhale hanging before her for a moment as her eyes darted around. She felt the skin-crawling feeling of being watched and glanced around, trying to spot what was wrong and finding nothing.

     

                “What ails you?” Kara whispered, her blue eyes full of concern as she glanced sideways at Lena, taking in her pallid cheeks, hollowed eyes and pinched expression.

     

                “Nothing,” Lena tightly muttered, hugging her cloak tighter to herself.

     

                Two horses were waiting for them, the same ones they’d arrived on, and Kara let hers nuzzle her palm as she watched an attendant buckle her bag to a saddle. Lena stood beside her own, eyeing it with dismay as she thought of the sore journey on horseback, thinking that perhaps she should have spent more time riding while at Court so she wouldn’t find it so uncomfortable this time around. Lamenting how sore her thighs would be by the time they stopped later that evening, Lena’s eyes flickered sideways at the approach of her familiar guard, dressed in her usual dark leathers and looking wary and uncertain as she raised her arm.

     

                Turning to her, Lena’s eyes dropped to the bow and quiver Reign dangled from two fingers. Her lips twitched with a thin smile, hazel eyes intense as she cocked her head to the side. “Hopefully you’ll be a better shot when you return.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes and took them, the bow unstrung but a good weight, slightly different to the one she’d been practising with. The feathers were fletched with the feathers collected from ravens and Lena ran a thumb along the trimmed edge of one before slinging the quiver over her shoulder.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Then she couldn’t resist herself, arching an eyebrow. “Is this your way of saying you’ll miss me?”

     

                Andrea brushed past then, scoffing as she cast Lena an exasperated look. “A chance for some peace and quiet? Not likely, Your Highness.”

     

                “Don’t get too bored without me,” Lena crooned.

     

                They drew back without another word and Lena’s eyes landed on Lillian, who was watching the proceedings with a cool air of disinterest. Her mother’s eyes sharply found her then, narrowing a fraction as her lips thinned. Freezing like a startled deer, Lena hesitated before meekly approaching, ducking her head slightly as she tried to make herself as unimportant and small as possible, to escape her notice with any further problems.

     

                Clearing her throat, Lillian narrowed her eyes again as Lena glanced up, her own face clouding with confusion. She didn’t think she’d done anything to warrant her mother’s contempt recently - only her mere existence, which she would have assumed Lillian had grown accustomed to of late.

     

                “Goodbye, Your Majesty,” Lena murmured, dipping into a curtsy.

     

                Her demure tone made Lillian pause again, that suspicious look sharpening her hard features. Then she coughed again, hard enough to bring a little colour to her cheeks, her pale eyes brightening with delighted venom. 

     

                “You foolish girl.”

     

                “I-” Lena managed to stammer out, brow creasing as she stumbled back a step, fear twisting in her stomach at the sudden violence that crept into the Queen’s bearing.

     

                Coughing again, Lillian dissolved into laughter, the flash of her teeth showing them stained pink with blood. “Did you think you could get rid of me so easily with a little bit of poison?”

     

                Confusion crumpled Lena’s face as she opened her mouth to protest. “Wha- no, I didn’t-”

     

                Face twisting derisively, murder written in the harsh planes of it, she reached out for Lena, her mouth a snarl. “Did you think I wouldn’t notice? I knew something was amiss at breakfast with how nervous you seemed. You and your infernal wife. I would know the taste of Dar-Essa anywhere . I’ve been poisoning myself with it for years, you arrogant bastard, against this very eventuality.”

     

                As she snarled her torrent of accusations and explanations, her hand found Lena’s neck, sharpened nails digging in painfully deep, choking off any explanation or defence Lena could have formulated. All that escaped through her trembling lips with a small gasp of pain, dissolving into a choked whimper.

     

                “Unhand her. Now,” Kara demanded as she shouldered her way through the small group of attendants, guards and officials. “She has done no such thing.”

     

                “I can forgive the transgression of your insolence, your disobedience, your utter contempt for the laws of the Courts but I will not forgive this insult against my life. You have chafed against this truce since you arrived, caused more inconvenience than purpose served, and I believe I have no further use for you now. You will leave this Court today, but not with your life. Neither of you.”

     

                Her eyes cut to Kara’s face, which whitened with each word, and then back to Lena as her lips twitched, smug amusement on her face as her pale blue eyes brightened with mirth. “Did you really think you could kill me?”

     

                “No,” Lena breathlessly replied, the word slightly strangled as she tried to breathe deeply around Lillian’s gouging fingers. “Please.”

     

                “You will violate the truce if you harm her. Do not force my hand, Your Majesty. Neither of us will like the outcome, I can assure you that.”

     

                “More threats in my own Court,” Lillian clicked her tongue, her eyes flitting to Kara’s momentarily. “You will find it hard for vengeance with your throat slit, Lady Kara. Shall I let you both rot in a cell first so you can contemplate your transgressions? Or shall I do away with you now? Which is fonder of the other, I wonder. Perhaps I shall torture it out of both of you and then make her watch as I cut off the other’s head.” 

     

                A bout of coughing stole over Lillian, who reddened with anger as the poison she so diligently dosed herself against still mildly irritated her, even if it paled in comparison to the effects Lena had endured. “Guards!”

     

                At her call to action, Lena heard the scrape of metal unsheathing and blinked at the arc of silver that flashed before her. Lena was still rooted to the spot as the pressure around her throat vanished and she found herself sprayed with warm blood, trying to process the bleeding stump of her mother’s hand, where before her hand had been, wrapped around Lena’s neck. Her shock got caught in her throat, her face bone white, pale enough to rival Lillian’s rapidly paling face as pain and utter rage blossomed there.

     

                Meanwhile, Kara continued with the motion of her sword, stained red from her decisive act to incite violence to gain the upper hand. She moved like water, twisting fluidly, her sword arcing around her in a graceful dance that seemed too gentle for the blood and death it left in its wake. Lena turned in a daze and felt the hot splatter of blood on her cheeks as Kara opened the throat of a guard that had been advancing upon her. Mouth opening and closing, her hand gripping her bow tightly as the quiver of arrows hung loosely on her shoulder, Lena was utterly useless as she watched with building horror and cluelessness.

     

                And then an arrow with brown fletching caught a guard straight through the throat, taking the man down with a strangled gurgle as blood spilt from his open mouth, and Lena looked around wildly for signs of the archer. It was quickly becoming chaos and Lena whipped her head back and forth, panic welling in her chest.

     

                Then Kara was on her, bloody sword held out, face severe as her blue eyes darted around, her lips a hard line as she bodily shepherded Kara out of the fray. Pausing to slash at a guard bearing down on her, Kara drove the woman back and had to relinquish her hold on Lena to grip her sword two-handed and hack at her again, steel skating over the breastplate. Then a woman with dark hair appeared, a red handprint of dried blood pressed to an ornate golden mask covering her face, and Kara faltered, unsure whether she was friend or foe for a brief moment before she scored a line across the woman’s arm, between the edge of her engraved breastplate and vambraces, drawing a shallow cut which had the woman cursing her.

     

                Lena found herself pitching forward then, a mouthful of dirt and the coppery taste of blood as her teeth bit the inside of her lower lip, scrabbling at roots as she tried to drag herself forward. Rolling, she swept her hands up and used the unstrung bow to fend off the man on top of her. He bore a similar beautifully wrought golden mask as well and Lena remembered seeing one for the first time that night Kara had cut the throat of the man in the forest. 

     

                A moment later, blood splashed over her chest as twin blades cut through tendons and muscles and Lena let out a ragged sound of horror, scrabbling backwards on her elbows as she kicked herself free. Reign loomed over her, her teeth bared, blood coating her hands, hazel eyes darting around as she relished the mania and fear flashed through Lena as she wondered whether her mother’s hunter was going to slash her throat next. 

     

                Eyes locked, they stared at each other for a moment before Reign whirled away, taking down one of the other invaders that Lena knew were there at her brother’s behest. Staggering to her feet, she found Kara again, her breaths coming sharp and quick as she grabbed her hand and ran towards the horses unbothered by the violence, bred for war and skirmishes like this. 

     

                Kara all but tossed Lena up into the saddle before mounting her own, slapping the flanks of Lena’s mare with the flat of her blade before she leapt into motion on the back of her own. Reaching across, Kara tore the unstrung bow from Lena’s grasp, grit her teeth as she bent the wood to string it and then grabbed an arrow from Lena’s quiver, loosing it behind them. Lena didn’t turn, trying her best to stay in the saddle, but from the sound of the thud the arrow had struck home.

     

                Balancing her sword across her knees as she managed to keep riding while stealing arrows and sending shaft after shaft toward their pursuers, Kara seemed only slightly perturbed by the sheer number of them, seemingly appearing from nowhere. It wasn’t just the Unseelie either, after them for the attempt on their Queen, but the rogues as well, fighting each other even as they pursued the fleeing women. 

     

                As they streaked through the forest, the wound around wide trunks, rain-battered golden leaves clinging valiantly to branches as the sunrise cast their surroundings in a dismal grey, sunlight struggling to pierce the thick canopy of overarching branches tangled up in each other. Lena couldn’t keep up with Kara’s gruelling pace, struggling to cling to the reins and saddle as her breaths came sharp, the frigid air burning her lungs and scouring her bloody cheeks, knees trembling as she tried not to jostle too much with the motion. It was unbearable though, fog masking mossy trunks and hiding bracken and underbrush, boulders and fox dens, snaking roots that could trip up her mare and snap her leg in an instant. 

     

                They rode for what felt like hours, outpacing their pursuers quickly and then slowing their pace once Kara was confident they were safe, not wanting to tire the horses too soon. Lena was stiff and frozen as she bumped along uncomfortably, miserable and confused, the sharp turn of the morning more than she’d anticipated. And why did the man in the golden mask try to hurt her?  

     

                Eventually, the gentle sloping of the forest floor marked the land’s slow melt into the river dividing the Courts in a line of quicksilver catching the dawn’s light. It was still too far away for Lena to make out but she heard the quiet music of the running water and felt a rush of relief run through her at the idea of crossing over it. She knew realistically they weren’t much safer in the Seelie Court but there was a chance anyone who found their trail would honour the truce between their Courts and remain on the Unseelie side.

     

                Leaves were falling from the larch and alders as the horses picked their way down the sloping ground, flat, yellow leaves on the sandy ground, the oaks and the greasewood bushes rustling in the breeze. As they approached the banks, soft mud giving way to the river of quick, frigid water, teeming with little minnows and grasses and tiny white flowers, Lena had the feeling of something being wrong. The forest was too peaceful, the forest was too quiet for the violence that had led them there swiftly, and her eyes scanned the long green and black bulrushes growing along the banks before she hesitated and then followed Kara into the brackish shallows of the river’s edge.

     

                The horses went slow, the current making them cut across at a slight angle, the autumn rains had swollen the banks, the frothy churning of the disadvantageous crossing point making Lena’s stomach pitch at the thought of being swept away. She was too focused on trying not to think of drowning, of the lead-coloured river slicing through the heart of the forest, the dank smell of water surrounding her, grazing the soles of her feet, making her feel faintly nauseous. Then an arrow, the tip sharp as a razor’s edge, sheared through the air with a quiet hiss and the twang of a bowstring, missing her by an inch.

     

                Lena pitched out of the saddle out of fright and struck the surface of the river hard. Her heavy dress and cloak dragged her down and she was rolling and tumbling beneath the water, kicking up reeds and mud and stones as her feet found the bottom. Panic settled in as the dim light of the first dawn of winter struggled to pierce the surface of the water, letting her know which way was up, her lungs aching for air, the taste of silt and algae filling her mouth as she thrashed around, feeling like a child again, still incapable of swimming and finding herself bogged down in the water. It was so cold it felt like fire, her struggling sluggish as her limbs burned, clawing at the dark water. She wouldn’t die, she wouldn’t drown, she refused.

     

                And then she was aware of a lithe figure cutting through the water with all the elegance Lena presumed the Waterfolk were famous for. Strong arms wrapped around her and bore her to the surface, where she sucked in a lungful of freezing air, spluttering and gasping as she thrashed around, heedless to Kara’s hissing warnings as she towed Lena across the rest of the river. Dragging her wife up the bank, Kara let Lena collapse to her knees in the mud, soaking wet and bone white as she gasped at the fresh air, the horses behind them, shifting restlessly as they waited to be off. The sun was still rising yet, the shadows shifting around them, and Lena wiped the water from her eyes, numbed from the shock of the water.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena gasped at Kara’s feet, watching as a dozen fae materialised out of the trees on the opposite bank, all of them wearing golden masks, all of them moving with the unnerving grace and confidence of those who knew they held the numbers.

     

                “It’s not your fault,” Kara murmured, quietening her as she drew her sword.

     

                But Lena knew that it was, that she’d gambled with their lives for the assistance of the brother she didn’t even know and had been wilfully ignorant of the warnings Kara had given her, cautioning her against this reckless plot. Of course, it would never be so easy as letting him have the throne once Lillian was deposed; Lena was still a threat. She was his successor and if she could help him do away with one ruler, why not another?

     

                As the gathering on the other side of the river parted, Lena’s shoulders sagged with defeat as she heard Kara suck in a surprised breath, Lex decked out in resplendent silver armour made to look like he was ensnared by silver thorns. He held a bloodied sword in one hand and a thorned helmet tucked beneath his other arm, his eyes landing on her kneeling form and a slow smile of malice spreading across his face.

     

                “Ah, how fortuitous,” he called out as his eyes went to Kara. “I am to rid myself of two threats at once; my father’s half-breed bastard and the last of the pitiful House of El.”

     

                “You ,” Kara snarled, squaring her shoulders as the water turned into a still ribbon of ink, the surface tensed ready at the fae’s command.

     

                He gave her a shallow, mocking bow and then straightened, the tip of his sword burying in the ground as he leaned on the hilt, a casual air of disinterest. “Surprised to see me? I hear your cousin wasn’t so lucky but then, only the best may win. As you will soon find out. I should thank you, sister, for aiding me in bringing this moment to fruition.”

     

                Kara sharply looked down at Lena and behind the look of blistering animosity reserved for Lex, confusion quickly spun into doubt and then grim understanding, reading the guilt so plainly written on her wife’s face. Lena couldn’t even bring herself to speak, her shoulders curling in as she ducked her head down, cheeks flaming with embarrassment at her obvious blundering mistake.

     

                Hesitating with uncertainty, Kara’s mouth thinned and she reached down to drag Lena closer, her hand going to her dark hair to grab a fistful and yank her head back. Lena drew in a shallow, frantic breath at the chill, sharp edge of Kara’s sword laid against her throat, her grip so tight that Lena was left wondering whether she would actually do it or not. There was only so much grace her wife should be expected to give her and she’d watched Kara open throats before. Lena didn’t want to believe she’d be able to do it to the woman she’d been wed to for months now, even in light of what Lena had done.

     

                “If she’s so important to you, do not come a step closer or I shall spill her blood on the banks,” Kara firmly called back across the river, her face a tense scowl, her hand steady even if her heart pounded.

     

                A small gasp escaped Lena as the sharp edge dug into her skin, scoring a shallow line that threatened to go deeper. Pushing herself back against Kara’s thighs, she tried to put a scant distance between her and the blade but Kara’s pursuit was unforgiving, holding Lena firmly in place as she kept the blade’s edge levelled, ready to slash across if it came to it. White with fear, Lena curled her hands into fists to stop herself from shaking, closing her eyes to the sight of the flat water and gilded soldiers.

     

                Lex’s answering laugh to Kara’s threat made the hairs on Lena’s body stand on end, cold and haughty. “You think she’s important to me? I will gut her the moment I am done with you. She is nothing to me but a thorn that will undoubtedly plague me if I don’t cut her down, as my mother should have done.”

     

                “If you do that … you violate the peace-”

     

                “It has already been violated,” Lex cut her off. “Thanks to you. Thanks to the Princess. My mother will be dealt with quickly once I am done here and then the rest of your Court will know no peace until I am done with them too.”

     

                Hesitating, licking her lips, Kara’s eyes darted back and forth as she weighed her options. Lena was silent, knowing she was way out of her depths here, helpless and at the mercy of her wife. Even if Kara didn’t kill her where she knelt, there was a very high chance they would be run down by the fae milling on the opposite banks though, and for a brief moment, Lena thought she would prefer it if Kara did it herself. At least it wouldn’t be done in cold blood.

     

                “I’ll do it,” Kara warned him, her voice cracking as her conviction wavered.

     

                A dozen arrows were concentrated on them and Lena knew if Lex willed it, they’d be cut down by a volley quicker than Kara could finish cutting her throat. She wondered if Kara would see it as a fitting sacrifice or a waste and wanted to tell her to go, that she’d stand herself and let her wife go free. It was the least Lena could do for her.

     

                “Kara,” she whispered.

     

                “Shut up.”

     

                “Kara, go. Let him have me.”

     

                “Shut up.”

     

                Lex laughed again, cocking his head to the side. “You cannot even say it in our language because you know it to be a lie,” he mused. “You cannot bring yourself to kill her, even knowing you may die for her mistaken trust in me. Don’t worry, Seelie.”

     

                He grabbed a bow from the nearest fae and fit an arrow to it, drawing the string back in one smooth motion. “I’ll do it for you.”

     

                The arrow didn’t miss her this time and Lena hadn’t even had time to think or react. Kneeling in front of Kara as she had a second to comprehend his act as he grabbed the bow. Lena knew she wouldn’t be quick enough to move out of the way, still kneeling in the mud with a sword pressed to her neck, and even if she was it would leave Kara exposed behind her. 

     

                The best she could manage as Kara’s sword dropped away and her wife thrust out a hand to raise a wall of water to cut off the loosed arrow, too slow to stop it, was to shift to the side. Instead of taking her in the throat, the arrow thudded into her shoulder with enough force to send her into Kara’s knees, taking her down with her. A numbness radiated through Lena’s left shoulder, the breath forced from her lungs as she sprawled on top of her wife. 

     

                Her wife who was quickly shuffling out from beneath her, dragging Lena to her feet by her sodden cloak as she scrambled further up the banks. Splashes followed after them and Kara was seized by her anger as she shoved Lena towards the horses and then turned, one hand commanding the water into a churning, seething force of rage as the other twirled her sword as she moved towards the river.

     

                Knees going weak as Lena braced herself against her horse, unable to drag herself into the saddle as her left arm hung limply at her side and the dull throb of pain started to voice itself through the numbness, she watched her wife. Moving like a blur of grey as silver steel and the slate blue of her cloak moved too fast for Lena to distinguish, she cut down the first two to make it across the river. Three more had gone under in the roaring mass of waves Kara conjured up and they hadn’t resurfaced yet, four more hanging back uncertainly with Lex. 

     

                Another six were still struggling across the river, one of them struggling to keep their flame alight as Kara doused them in river water again and again. One buffeted her with gusts of wind, spraying water, mud and algae every which way as they tried to carve a path through the river. Kara was fending them off alone and Lena’s eyes darted between her and Lex, watching as her brother raised his hand, the roots of trees lining the river bank twitching at his command.

     

                A scream tore through the forest, wrenching and panicked, and it took Lena a moment to realise it had come from her. A sharp crack like a tree branch being snapped in two nearby as she thrust a hand out, forgetting to breathe as fear constricted her chest. The forest was still dim, no more than a few minutes passed by since Lex had arrived, and the leaves were thick, heavy overhead, the weak sunlight failing to do more than lighten the deep shadows that lingered. There was a groaning in the earth and a cold wind blew, howling as the bite of it chilled Lena in her soaking wet clothes as she clung to the saddle, swaying unsteadily on her feet.

     

                The ground split open in front of Kara, cleaving the edge of the river bank away from the ground, turning it to churning mud that made it hard for the approaching fae to clamber up the bank. Still, one of them loosed an arrow that scored a line across Kara’s bicep and another set a tree on fire to her right, the smell of pine resin mingling with the acrid smoke as Kara coughed and ran one of the men through. She hacked the head halfway off a woman as her golden mask slipped from her face and earned herself a deep cut to her thigh, making her right leg buckle but Kara was fending them off well, even as Lena tried to assist her.

     

                But Lena didn’t know what she was doing, hadn’t meant to tear up the riverbed, but her inexperience made her instruction blind and wild as she felled a large larch, branches crushing as it toppled into the river, damming the current as the water level quickly raised, buffeting the straggling fae against the sharp points of broken branches. Lena winced as she saw one speared on the tree, still screaming as the water was forced down his throat as he tried and failed to battle against the current and free himself from the branch.

     

                The ground had shaken from the force of the tree and it bought Kara enough time to hack off an arm and throw a small knife into the soft spot between neck and shoulder and forge a clear path up towards the horses. She was bloody and wet, bleeding freely from several cuts, and her expression was livid, made even more so when she saw Lena standing there.

     

                Without a word, Kara picked her up and set her down on the saddle before mounting her own and circling around as she bought Lena a moment to get her leg astride and grab the reins. She managed to coax her horse into motion and set off straight ahead, plunging into the forest with Kara following close behind, sword held aloft, shouting to urge the horses faster. Lena still had the arrow lodged into her shoulder, the fletching visible in her line of sight even without looking down at the two feet of wood sticking out of her, and she fought to stay conscious as the awareness of their dire circumstances made her vision dim.

     

                They fled as quickly as possible, taking the easiest path presented to them as Kara ended up in the lead, winding down sloping declines that led to passages burrowing beneath overarching root systems of towers oaks and spruces overhead, coming out the other side to skirt around rocking outcroppings that the horses would’ve spent their much-needed energy scrabbling over. In Kara’s mind, it didn’t matter which way they went, as long as it was as far away as possible from the Unseelie Court and their pursuers. 

     

                Shivering in her soaked clothes, Lena followed after her, exhaustion making her sway unsteadily in the saddle as she bumped along, each jolt making the arrow in her chest twinge, making her vision fur at the edges. Each breath was a ragged knife and Lena was sweating profusely as they went on and on, bleed seeping into the damp fabric as the hours dragged by. Kara didn’t exhaust the horses but she pushed them as hard as she was willing, sweat lathering their sides as their chests heaved from the relentless pace that was set.

     

                They should have stopped to staunch their wounds, stopped to stretch their legs and eat, stopped to give the horses a rest but they didn’t. Lena lost track of time, grey-faced and verging on unconsciousness as her eyes stared vacantly at the forest. The terrain slowly changed as they rode, descending into a valley where moss-covered boulders hemmed them in and the forest floor was thick with fallen branches and rotted pine needles. The place seemed to deaden all sound. The forest felt old and deep, and the sound of their horses’ hooves was an intrusion.

     

                The boulders grew larger, the tree canopy overhead thicker as moss and vines hung in thick ropes, brambles and thorns choking the underbrush as the horses stepped warily. The valley seemed bottomless, deciduous larch, aspen, and black cottonwood trees surrounded them, all in shades of fiery orange, lemon yellow and hyacinth red as the retreating autumn set the trees alight. There were paper birches with bright red leaves dotted throughout the evergreen spruces and they followed the run-off of a trickling stream, shimmering lilac under the dense canopy as the sunlight faltered and a lilac-hued twilight stole through the forest. 

     

                It had gotten so cold that Lena’s lips were tinged a faint lavender, along with her nails, and she was so stiff that each shiver that wracked her, which was endless, made her whole body ache in protest. Eventually, she couldn’t stay in the saddle any longer, her stiff fingers going slack on the reins as she pitched sideways at the next jostle of her horse, falling left ways to the ground and catching the side of her face on a rock as she fell heavily. The force of her impact with the mossy ground drove the arrow the rest of the way through the muscle of her shoulder, just below her collarbone, and out through the other side, the bloody tip glistening wetly in the dusk.

     

                The ragged sound of pain that escaped her filled the tense silence and Lena’s eyes were squeezed shut as she lay helplessly in a heap, the wet heat of blood slick on the left side of her face as the coppery taste filled her mouth. Unable to move, so exhausted that it was all she could do to stay conscious, the slow loss of blood and the dull throb of pain so draining, Lena couldn’t even raise her head as she vomited, convulsing with the effort as her mind dimmed, threatening to drag her under. 

     

                Cold hands were dragging her up then, cursing softly as she was propped up against the side of a large boulder, sagging against the stone as Kara positioned her carefully. It was getting dark, lingering sunlight fading quickly, and Kara looked around anxiously before her eyes strayed back to Lena’s face, pinched with agony and grey from the arrow piercing her.

     

                Muttering beneath her breath, Kara pulled her dagger free and started lifting patches of moss from the carpeted ground beneath them, making a quick pile of it and then scrambling for enough twigs, leaves and bark in the near vicinity to make a fire. The sparks took an age to catch on the damp pile she made but eventually, she had a smoking tongue of flame near them, her hands shaking from the adrenaline that had persisted all day. She had two broken fingers herself, along with a few ribs she suspected, the gash in her thigh mercifully missing her femoral artery but soaking her leggings in blood, the other cuts and scrapes leaving her aching and a little faint herself. 

     

                Of course, it was not so bad as the arrow gone right through her wife, the arrow Kara had thought would be fine stuck in her chest to stem the flow of blood until they were somewhere safer. She hadn’t imagined Lena would fall off her horse and ram it straight through the other side of her chest, but then she’d always underestimated what her wife would do. 

     

                Angry at her for a multitude of reasons, Kara set about cleaning off the edge of her dagger and then heated it in the pitiful fire before cutting the fletching off the arrow, practically all that was sticking out of Lena’s chest. Pouring water from her canteen belted at her waist into the wound, Kara shushed Lena as she groaned, writhing at the pain of it. She eased her up then, shedding her sodden cloak and tearing open the dress, splitting the seams at the shoulder and sleeve until she bared the site of the wound. Reaching behind and gripping the back of the arrow shaft, Kara carefully pulled it out an inch as Lena grit her teeth, the tendons in her neck taut as she stifled a scream. Packing moss over the front of the wound, Kara pressed a hand against her wife’s pallid skin, as clammy as a freshly gutted fish and almost as pale, and dragged the arrow out of her back.

     

                This time Lena couldn’t swallow the hoarse shout as blood sluiced from the gaping wound in her back. It was briefly numbed by the sheer coldness of the water Kara poured over it, flushing it out before padding it with moss. Tearing the hem of her shirt, she bound the linen around Lena’s shoulder as best as she could, her breaths coming quick as she listened to the forest, the baying of wolves making her skin ripple with goosebumps at the thought of them being hunted, the scent of blood heady in the air. Kara knew she couldn’t keep them both alive in another fight now. 

     

                Their best bet would be riding as far as they could and hoping they made it to a safe holding before night fully set. Kara knew where they were now, in that deep valley surrounded by sheer cliffs and soaring trees, and as far as her memory served her, the nearest spot she trusted was half a day’s ride by horse. They wouldn’t make it that far in Lena’s current state before they were hunted down, whether by beast or fae. Lena started mumbling incoherently, her tone pleading and apologetic, and Kara’s anger dimmed momentarily before she dragged her cloak back over her and drew as much moisture from her clothes as she could, expending some of her dwindling energy reserves to keep her wife warm.

     

                She was still deliberating what to do next as Lena babbled apologetically, her cheeks wet with tears, the left side of her face covered in blood and vomit. Gently shushing her, Kara tore another piece from her shirt and soaked it from her canteen, dabbing at the mess as she scrambled for a way out, cradling Lena in her lap as her eyes flitted around anxiously for any signs of danger.

     

                That’s when a howl split the hush of twilight, so close that it made Kara’s blood freeze, spooking the horses, which ran off with their supplies, and leaving her helplessly alone as she huddled against a boulder with her wife’s unconscious body draped across her. Her eyes scanned the trees until she saw a monstrously large wolf pad through the shadows, hackles raised, eyes glinting in the gloom, flanked by two more as their muzzles pulled back over their teeth. 

     

                Sniffing as she shifted Lena to the ground, Kara ran her grimy sleeve over her clammy face and hobbled to her feet, unwilling to greet her death without a fight at least as she sent a prayer to the old forest and raised her sword.

    Chapter 16

                As Kara steadied herself, chest rising and falling quickly, bleeding from a few cuts and scrapes as her damp clothes clung to her, her knuckles whitened on the hilt of her graceful sword and the skin raised on her arms. The near-distant snap of branches and logs, of heavy footsteps thundering through the trees approached with a faint tremor in the ground underfoot. They were near water but Kara doubted her ability to fend off multiple wolves with Lena muttering nonsensically behind her, in the shade of the large boulders. If it was just herself, she would have been able to squirrel herself up the trunk of a towering tree and wait out the wolves but she stood her ground before her wife.

     

                The first one padded out of the treeline with a snarl pulling its muzzle back over long canines. Kara had been in this position before, though not nearly as sorely outnumbered as she was now, and she licked her lips, eyes flitting around as she saw the luminous yellow eyes of a few more shifting in the shadows. The hulking mass of the first one was blanketed by lichen and moss, white caps of mushrooms sprouting between the coarse grey fur of its pelt, the musty smell of decay and the deep belly of the forest drifting on the wind. The blight of the forest that made them seem so terrifying, burrowing into the bones of creatures, overtaking them until their muscled bodies were reclaimed by the earth, plagued the five that skulked out of the shadows and Kara could smell rotten blood and meat from their previous meal fouling the air. 

     

                They paused, a blood-chilling howl running between them as Kara’s bravery wavered momentarily before she stepped forward, away from Lena without leaving her exposed, and yanked her long hunting knife free. Clashing the side of the knife against her sword in a clear ringing sound of steel on steel, she ground her teeth together.

     

                “Come on, you bastards. Have at it,” she snapped, her eyes bright with anger, with determination and frustration at the whole ordeal. 

     

                If they’d left on good terms with the Unseelie, neither of them would have been hurt and even Lena’s shoddy archery skills would have been an asset under the circumstances. If they’d left without being hunted to the river, the peace treaty in tatters, they wouldn’t have run the horses ragged to the point where Kara had been forced to bring them to a stop and then lost them in the process. And perhaps most wistfully, if they’d followed the path they should have taken, Kara knew in her bones her sister would have been waiting for them at the crossing point, a safe escort to take them home to their mother’s on the way to her winter residence. Instead, Lena had derailed their plan in three, increasingly angering ways.

     

                The four flanking the leader of the pack spread out, the furthest on each side creeping forward as they tried to arc around so they could draw the net tighter around Kara when it came to a fight. She held her blades aloft, eyes flitting back and forth as she tried to gauge the coiled movements of the wolves to see which one would move first. They were still two dozen feet away, inching closer with a low, rumbling growl sweeping through them as they approached their prey. Stepping forward to meet them, trying to cover Lena while putting enough distance between herself and the boulders that backed her, Kara twirled her sword and then bounded forward, crossing ten feet in the blink of an eye.

     

                Slashing across the flank of one of the wolves, she ducked and avoided the snapping jaws of the one to its left, rolling beneath the stomach of the first and shoving her hunting knife into its belly. Hot blood splattered her face, thick and coppery in her mouth, and Kara felt a sliver of pity at the high-pitched whimper of agony. Rolling out the other side, she saw a pair of wide-open jaws ready to snap her up and thrust her sword up, the momentum of the wolf driving the blade up through the roof of its mouth. One of its canines punched through the muscle of Kara’s arm but she didn’t falter as she dragged her sword back out in time to be side-swiped by a claw.

     

                Skittering across the mossy ground, Kara rolled onto her back and reached out for the water, dragging up a spray to drive back the wolf sniffing towards Lena. Getting her feet back under her, Kara hacked at a muzzle, at a foot, drawing blood along a foreleg and using a net of ivy taken root in one of them to haul herself onto its back. The wolf shook itself and Kara went flying off the side of it, slamming into the side of another with enough force to give her a nosebleed, teeth biting down on her tongue.
