                “You have both been tossed to the wolves. I envy neither of you but … I would see you happy.”

     

                “My duty comes before my happiness,” Kara dismissively replied, a muscle twitching in her jaw out of frustration. “I am not you. It is different for us.”

     

                Exhaling roughly, Alex sank to a crouch at her side and stared up at her with a grim look on her face. Kara glanced down at the feeling of her sister’s calloused hand covering her own. “It is different for us but it doesn’t mean you have to sacrifice one for the other. Do your duty, as you will, but … find the light in this too, if you can.”

     

                “I have searched for it,” Kara mumbled, “yet I remain in the dark still.”

     

                “I will not pretend to know her well, and if I knew it was not from ignorance I wouldn’t think too kindly of her, but … I pity her. She is drowning, she is lost. It is plain to all that she is adrift in this world. She is your wife and if you are so committed to your duty, then is a part of it not to help her in this?”

     

                “I am trying . She is opposed to it, as I said. In the event that she wasn’t, I don’t believe she would be the light in this dark, or offer me any of the happiness you would have me find. You know that I cannot-” Cutting off, Kara cleared her throat and tried again. “You know I cannot bring myself to have any feelings of affection for someone.”

     

                With an exasperated sigh and roll of her eyes, Alex’s mouth twisted wryly. “The thing about a prophecy is it usually happens regardless of what you wish to happen. Perhaps the fact that you are so stubbornly against seeking happiness with her is a sign that you think you would feel fond of her if given half the chance.”

     

                “I don’t need your illogical reasoning right now,” Kara sighed, giving her sister a withering look. “She’s ill; I will have time to think about what comes next. Whether she is better off here with mother-”

     

                Alex scoffed and pushed herself to her feet again before gently smacking the back of Kara’s head. “You are not leaving your wife in our mother’s care.”

     

                “Ow.”

     

                “Don’t give me that, Kara Zor-El, or I shall dry out your skin with fire and make sure there’s not a drop of water in these halls for you to dip your toes in.”

     

                Giving her a dour look, Kara rubbed the back of her head, although in truth it hadn’t hurt in the slightest, and she flicked her fingers towards the bowl of water, directing the contents onto the front of her sister’s flowing tunic. Squawking indignantly, Alex patted the wet patch and kicked a leg of the stool Kara sat on, almost tipping her over.

     

                Hissing through her teeth, Kara slapped Alex’s thigh. “Sh, you’ll wake her.”

                

                “Well, do you care for her or not? If you care for her, you’ll not abandon her, and if you don’t care for her, it won’t matter if we wake her or not.”

     

                “All this time away has reminded me of how aggravating you are,” Kara grumbled.

     

                Chuckling, Alex gave her cheek a quick pat and retreated a step. “I’ve missed you too. You never broke your fast and it’s midday already; you must eat.”

     

                “I shouldn’t leave her alone.”

     

                “Then you have your answer. I’ll bring you some food.”

     

                Pensive and more troubled than she cared to admit, Kara cupped her chin in her hand as she turned her attention to Lena once more. Nodding absentmindedly as Alex moved to the door, Kara softly sighed.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Her mind weighed twice as heavily now with her sister’s words ringing in her ears, Kara was almost oblivious to the food that was brought in. Kelly was with Alex and didn’t intrude further than poking her head past the curtain and murmuring a sympathetic encouragement before both women left. Alone with her wife again, Kara was left to dwell on things as she considered this new development. Ordinarily, she wouldn’t have been parted from her sister for long at all, with Alex a frequent guest at her winter residence near the sea, and now that she was reunited after a season apart, Kara was still parted from her sister in favour of her wife.

     

                Confused, she ate the thick stew that her sister brought up, fresh bread and honey cakes and crisp apples accompanying the hot tea and the watered dandelion wine making for a better meal than Kara had eaten in days. There was some for Lena too but Kara was reluctant to wake her yet, not while the fever still kept her brow damp with sweat and her frayed voice whispering mostly nonsense. Instead, she spooned the broth down her throat for her to have some sustenance, trickling water and tea after it to keep her hydrated.

     

                Andrea made a surprising visit in the middle of the afternoon, inquiring about Lena’s health in a coy manner that made it seem as if she held no fondness for her Princess. Kara knew some fraction of loyalty had been forged in the autumn though but she was in no mood to entertain the Unseelie noblewoman and quickly shooed her away. 

     

                Dinner was brought to her in that room as well, steaming hand pies of vegetables that warmed her through as Kelly lingered to converse, so much transpiring between the two women since they’d parted ways at the start of autumn. It felt good to be surrounded by her family again and Kara was able to shake off the grey moods of longing and despair that had plagued her for months, bearing her burdens alone. Eventually, Kelly left as well and Kara eyed Lena’s pie until her hunger won out against the expectation that her wife would wake soon enough to eat it.

     

                Eating slowly as the evening passed her by, Kara was grateful for the lull, so long spent tense and suspicious leaving her emotionally drained at the comfort of being safe at home. The most she had to worry about was betrayal from Andrea or Reign, but the latter was already entrenched in her Seelie mind, a brief visit from Sam earlier showing the gentle side that Kara was familiar with. Not having to concern herself with who might be plotting against her, where the daggers and poison might come from, was a weight off her shoulders and if it wasn’t for Lena’s troubling fever, Kara would have felt perfectly content.

     

                Instead, she was a silent presence at her wife’s bedside, for no other reason than she didn’t want Lena to be left alone. She had a mind to stay there all night, although she was still exhausted from the journey and her own injuries, the tumultuous few days and the hard ride through the forest, something that would take more than one night’s rest to recover from. In the end, Eliza had to convince her to leave, showing up with another strongly steeped healing brew.

     

                Kara gave her little more than a glance as her mother stepped inside, setting down her laden tray and handing a cup of tea to her daughter. Draining it quickly, the faintly bitter tang of it lingering on her tongue, Kara turned the empty cup in hand as she watched Eliza feel Lena’s brow and trickle tea down her throat.

     

                “Her fever has broken. That is good.”

     

                “Mm,” Kara distractedly hummed, a clouded look in her eyes.

     

                “Come. Leave her to sleep now,” Eliza coaxed her away. “She will be fine and you need your own rest.”

     

                It was with great reluctance that Kara left, settling down on her own bed next door and thinking anxiously over her conversation with Alex, her complicated opinion of Lena and a way out of it. Despite her opinion a few days prior that the truce was broken, Kara hoped some shred of it still held, and if it didn’t, she wasn’t entirely sure her marriage to Lena would be null and void. At any rate, she would have to consider herself wed for the time being and hope for a good turning point in their relationship, or else she would be in for a bad winter secluded with her wife at the seaside.

     

                She slept deeply once sleep came to her and woke to the chill of her room, absent the smouldering embers of the usual fire she kept in the fireplace. Thoughts of Lena’s own room cold with the chill of the stone encasing the halls, a mountain bearing down on them, Kara roused herself and went to light a fire for her wife, dusting her hands off once she was done and turning to find Lena looking at her, eyes half-lidded, face pale and a shallow pucker between her eyebrows as she lay on her side, waking slowly.

     

                “Ah, you are awake,” Kara murmured, pleased.

     

                “You say that as if it’s been a while,” Lena mumbled, blinking slowly.

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Kara crossed over to the slab and sat at Lena’s feet, resting a hand on her covered calf. “You went to bed two nights ago and spent all of yesterday feverish.”

     

                Making a low sound at the back of her throat, Lena rolled onto her back and ran a hand over her face. Sighing softly, she didn’t say anything for a moment as she stared up at the ceiling and Kara watched her closely, the silence between them thick. Tongue-tied, Kara swallowed thickly and drew in a shuddering breath.

     

                “How do you feel?”

     

                “Awful,” Lena snorted. “How’s your leg?”

     

                Kara gingerly patted the bandaged lump of her thigh. “I have had worse.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                They lapsed into silence for a minute, which seemed far longer as the weight of it shrouded the gloomy room, flickering firelight making shadows on their faces as Lena avoided looking at Kara and Kara couldn’t take her eyes off her. As she watched, she saw the tiny changes in Lena’s expression, the taut look of worry and pain faltering as her carefully constructed mask fell away piece by piece. First, it was the way her eyebrows drew together in a mournful, aching look, then the flattening of her mouth before it turned down at the corners, the dimpling of her chin as she clenched her teeth to stop it from wobbling. Lastly, her eyelids fluttered shut over bright eyes.

     

                “I won’t apologise,” Lena hoarsely whispered, her voice anguished and uneven.

     

                Wearily sighing as her face softened with grim amusement, Kara gave her leg a quick pat. “No, I don’t suppose you would.”

     

                It felt awkward between them, their angry and defensive words from two nights before and the forced reconciliation that was reluctant and insincere leaving them both tongue-tied as they didn’t know what to say next. Kara committed herself to letting it go, like silt settling to the bottom of a lake, and cleared her throat.

     

                “You should eat something filling. You have had nothing substantial since we arrived here.”

     

                Without another word, she climbed to her feet and made a quick escape. Making her way to the kitchens, she murmured greetings to her sister and Kelly and helped herself to breakfast, setting a tray with porridge, fresh bread and ripe raspberries and blackberries. Making tea and serving the other two women cups full, Kara slipped out of the room and carried the tray back to Lena’s room, finding her still in bed, and silently served her wife breakfast. Shifting her stool across the room, Kara took a seat and ate her own portion, not looking directly at Lena as she spooned her porridge into her mouth in between mouthfuls of tea and berries. 

     

                “Would you like to bathe?” she asked once they’d both finished eating.

     

                “I’m tired.”

     

                Nodding, Kara climbed to her feet, adding another log to the fire before she gathered up their dirty bowls and then left without a parting word. Muttering curses to herself in the kitchen as she washed the dishes and avoided the burning feeling of her sister’s eyes on her back, Kara made herself scarce afterwards, marching straight through the hallways to the entrance and out into the cold day.

     

                Walking to the edge of the mountainside, Kara’s breath misted before her and the tips of her pointed ears started to turn pink as she stared distantly across the horizon, taking in the grey clouds, promising rain or worse. They were not so high up that the early winter weather would force them indoors just yet but it still made the world chill and grey as Kara took in the steep, broken cliffs and jagged ravines of the mountain range spreading out to the north-east. 

     

                Drinking in the freezing air as it scoured her lungs, Kara felt a rush of peace flood through her but she knew the serenity would be fleeting. Shaking her head, she turned aside and followed a path to the pool of water that had become a small haven for her in the mountains, the run-off from the snow that had not yet settled in, the ice riming the edges of the pool not quite hard enough to stick yet as she crunched through the thin layer, Kara let the sting of the water burrow into her. She could feel every drop, a heaving mass ready to obey her direction as she closed her eyes and let it invigorate her.

     

                Shedding her clothes, she waded in, her skin rippling with goosebumps as it blanched white and then red from the intensity of the cold. Up to her shoulders, she inhaled deeply and plunged beneath the inky surface of the dark water caught in the depression of the surrounding rocky landscape. Staying submerged until her lungs ached, Kara burst up to the surface and shifted onto her back, arms and legs spread as she breathed quickly, shallowly, basking in the buoyancy of the water. It was not her lake, it was not her sea but it was a third home to her, that view of the open sky overhead, the surrounding mountains and the familiar howl of the wind. 

     

                Staying until snow started to drift down, white specks swirling in the empty air beyond the mountainside, turning the green pines, the black rocks, the brown river below into grey ghosts, Kara emerged from the water feeling as if her mind had been scrubbed clean of her troubles. Flinging the water from her skin and hair with a flick of her wrists, she dressed in her clothes and dusted off the fine flecks of snow before making her way back to the mouth of Eliza’s halls and going in search of tea.

     

     

                With the snow, a wind came down from the northern shore, blowing for a few days without ceasing as Lena holed herself up in her room, silent and morose as she spent her time in bed, either sleeping or pretending to sleep to avoid speaking to anyone. It was hard to sleep at times, the wind howling haunting songs that sometimes sounded like screams instead of the soothing flute-like melodies that otherwise swept through the halls. She found no comfort there, even though it was safer than she’d been in months. Still, Lena refused to leave her room.

     

                It was easy at first, waking from her fever and lying about her exhaustion, her pain, drinking the teas that were given to her by Kara or Eliza and sleeping again as the herbal remedies left her drowsy. But her wound was healing quite well and the teas became more infrequent and the insistence that she eat dinner in the hall with them, that she bathe and change into something else more frequent. Lena was nothing if not stubborn though, usually to her own detriment, and she was committed to her own unhappiness, no matter how hard Kara tried to coax her out.

     

                She was trying again, a few days later, sitting on the small stool that remained in Lena’s room for her visits, although Lena didn’t know why she still bothered to show up. They both knew that they would have preferred to go about their own business, neither of them interfering with the other. It would make for a peaceful marriage that way and Kara could have better spent her time with Eliza and her family. Still, she was there again, trying.

                

                “Nia, Querl and James have arrived. Winn, Mon-El and Imra yesterday. Will you come to greet them?”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Will you not eat dinner with us all tonight? I know your injury plagues you but … surely you have recovered enough strength to eat outside of your bed tonight.”

     

                “I don’t want to. I don’t want to eat with you, I don’t want to talk to you, I just- I want to be left alone and then I- I want you to take me … as far away as you can think, as far away from all of … this as I can get, and then just- just leave me there. And then you’ll never have to see me again and we’ll both be happy. Just leave me alone. Please.”

     

                A regretful look crossed Kara’s face and she sighed softly. “It would make me very sad to never see you again. I’m not sure why you think otherwise.”

     

                The air was forcefully expelled from Lena’s lungs and she choked on the inhale, lips parting over gritted teeth as she dug the heels of her hands into her eyes. The next breath hitched and the sob was more blatant this time, the Princess kicking the sheets off as she rolled over, covering her face with her hands, shoulders curled in as she tried to make herself smaller. Shoulders slumping, Kara scooted along the bed, raising her injured leg up on the slab as she angled herself to reach out for Lena, cupping her arm.

     

                “Hush, it’s alright.”

     

                A whimper caught at the back of Lena’s throat and her breath hitched on another sob before she choked out another. Clicking her tongue, Kara sighed and squeezed her arm gently, uncertainty leaving her swimming in deep waters as she committed to muddling her way through her wife’s contrary moods. Alex’s words rang in her ears and Kara’s jaw was stubbornly set as a grave look crossed her face.

     

                “Hey, ” she murmured, shifting closer, her thigh pressed against Lena’s back. Hunching over, she rested her chin on Lena’s upper arm and furiously rubbed her shoulder in an effort to soothe her. “It’s alright, Lena. All will be well.”

     

                “No,” Lena ground out through her teeth as she struggled for her composure. “No, it won’t. For you maybe but I- … I’m so lonely. I am so alone.”

     

                Her strangled words were said through her clenched jaw as she tried hard to fight against the sobs building in her chest. Angrily dashing tears off her pallid cheeks, she screwed her eyes shut, lashes wet and ink-dark from her tears, Lena drew in a shuddering breath. Pulling her closer, Lena’s head almost on her leg, Kara’s blonde hair spilling across them both as she turned her head, cheek pressed against the side of Lena’s shoulder.

     

                “You are not alone. Not if you don’t wish to be.”

     

                “I don’t. Of course I don’t. But I am. ”

     

                “You have me.”

     

                Lena shrugged her off and sat up, her face crumpling with anger as she wiped her tears on her sleeves and gave Kara a scornful look. “What good are you to me?”

     

                Bristling, Kara brushed her long hair back, disgruntled as she was rebuffed again. “I am all you have.”

     

                “And I’m not all you have. You get to come home to your family-”

     

                “They are yours too.”

     

                “I don’t know these people!”

     

                “You have been here not yet a week-”

     

                “That isn’t the point. I- you get to spend the next three months happy with your sister and her wife and your mother. Your friends . And what about me? When do I get to be happy? You’ll be forced to be miserable half of the year and I’ll be forced to be miserable the whole of it. And you bring me here, knowing that it’s not my home, even if it’s one of yours, and expect me to be fine. I don’t begrudge you the chance to spend time with your family, I just- I have no purpose. I’m an outsider. No one cares for me, you and I tolerate each other at best-”

     

                Shifting with agitation, Kara toyed with her fingers. “I regret that we cannot be on friendlier terms. As your wife-”

     

                “You said it was over,” Lena snapped. “Don’t call me that.”

     

                “It won’t be over until the rivers start running red, believe me. Until that eventuality, which you have almost ascertained, you are mine, as I am yours. Until that eventuality, we should get to know each other better, you and I, now that we are somewhere safe. Rest and heal; you will find your loneliness will not stay long in these halls.”

     

                Snorting as she tossed her dark hair back, Lena closed her eyes, mouth thinning regretfully as she tipped her head back, and drew in a rattling breath. After a moment she let out a spent breath and sagged on the thin mattress covering the slab, a bitterness to the twist of her mouth as she replied.

     

                “It’s stayed with me for twenty years; it’s not going anywhere.”

     

                “You have not had me for twenty years,” Kara softly replied, climbing to her feet, shifting her weight off her injured leg and holding out a hand. “Come. It will not all seem so bleak with fresh air and sunlight on your face, although I cannot account for much of the latter. It is a dreary day but even that is preferable to so much rock, don’t you agree?”

     

                Lena gave her a sullen look for a prolonged moment before she folded her arms over her chest and drew her knees up. She remained firmly seated. With a sigh, Kara sank back down onto the edge of the bed slab and set her hand between them, upturned in invitation.

     

                “Please, Lena. You have shut yourself in here for three days already; you must leave at some point.”

     

                “Oh, must I?”

     

                “You are being stubborn. You won’t be helping yourself to hide away in here, hoping it’ll get better.”

     

                “I’m not hoping for that. I’m just hoping it won’t get worse.”

     

                “Well, it will . If you do nothing but feed into your own misery, you will make yourself heartsick with your own grief.”

     

                “Can’t you just leave me alone?” Lena ground out.

     

                “No.”

     

                Alex barged inside a heartbeat later and stormed over to her sister, dragging her up off the bed by the collar of her shirt as Kara let out an exclamation of surprise. As soon as her lanky legs found their balance beneath her weight, Kara straightened indignantly and looked down at her sister, inches taller than her as they stood so close. Alex arched an eyebrow, unimpressed.

     

                “Alex, what-”

     

                “You may be bigger, stronger and faster than me, sister, but you are not as feral and I am not as tolerant. Get out.”

     

                “I am Lady of the House of El. Last I checked you were not Lady of these halls yet to command me,” Kara petulantly replied.

     

                Still gripping her collar, Alex grinned wolfishly. “I am not but I’m older than you and will still stick you full of holes if you don’t make yourself scarce.”

     

                “This is a private matter.”

     

                “Your marriage concerns everyone, thus, it’s a public matter. Off with you. Now.”

     

                She dragged Kara away slightly and then let go of her collar, letting her sister shrug her shirt into place, scowling as she left pink-cheeked. Lena was still sitting with her back against the wall and gave Alex a stricken look, her face pale in the firelight.

     

                “Sister,” Alex drawled. “Come. Let us talk.”

     

                “You’re not my sister,” Lena scornfully rasped.

     

                “Kara is my sister and you are her wife, so you are my sister. You may have us or your own family; I believe us to be better company than your mother and brother. Now, come.”

     

                Lena didn’t reply, just turned her head aside, haughtily raising her chin as she averted her gaze. Sighing impatiently, Alex reached out to grab the shoulders of Lena’s nightgown, repeating the act of dragging her sister-in-law off the bed. Jerked forward, Lena spluttered and a moment later she had the dagger Kara had gifted her in a trembling hand, pointed at Alex. Her chest rose and fell quickly as she licked her lips, a panicked look on her face.

     

                Snorting, Alex rolled her eyes as she let go of Lena and then moved too quickly for her to follow. Striking the inside of Lena’s wrist and then yanking the dagger free, Alex pressed the point against her forefinger as she twirled the hilt, clicking her tongue as amusement flickered in her brown eyes.

     

                “Don’t play with toys if you don’t know how to use them. Now, put it away before you hurt yourself and come with me.”

     

                “I don’t have to do what you say just because you asked.”

     

                “I didn’t ask.”

                

                A laugh escaped Lena despite her annoyance, and she found that Alex’s particular brand of tough love was more palatable than Kara’s uptight attempts at dutiful companionship. Still, Lena wasn’t in the habit of doing what she was told and she scrabbled beneath the pillow for the dagger’s sheath and slid it home.

     

                “I’m tired. I want to rest.”

     

                “You have rested for days. I lack my sister’s diplomacy and patience to allow you to spend another day holed up in here quarrelling-“

     

                “Actually, she’s ignored me, for the most part.”

     

                “Put on some real clothes, go outside and take a bath. You smell rank; your shoulder will fester if you don’t keep it clean.”

     

                Spluttering as her cheeks heated, Lena was well aware of the fact that there was still the coppery tang of old blood and sweat clinging to her from her journey. It was that more than anything that eventually made her climb out of bed, and Alex squared her shoulders before gesturing towards the door.

     

                Hugging her arms to her chest, Lena scowled the entire way to the spacious room Alex led her to, a circular raised tub with ink-dark water. Lena drifted over to it and dipped in her fingers before snatching it back at the icy temperature, Alex muffling a laugh behind her before she stepped up to the edge of the shallow tub and thrust both hands in, the surface beginning to furiously boil a few moments later. Withdrawing her hands, Alex gave her a quick wink.

                

                “It pays to make friends, you know,” the fae woman said.

     

                Face stiffening slightly, Lena crossed her arms over her chest and waited for Alex to leave before she stripped off her clothes and unwrapped her bandaged shoulder before hesitantly stepping into the tub. It was as shallow as it seemed, halfway up Lena’s chest once she had sat down, legs stretched out before her, and she slipped down further to submerge herself fully, gritting her teeth and spitting water at the stinging heat in her shoulder.

     

                But it was hot and Lena felt marginally better as the warmth of the bath burrowed into her stiff joints and cold bones, the fire of her austere room not enough to combat her reluctance to move from the bed for days. There was a soft soap that melted on her skin like cream, the warmth of honey washing away the filth of the last week as she gently soaped herself up, working it through her lank hair as well.

     

                “Lena!” Kelly warmly greeted her as she swept inside in the midst of Lena washing her hair, startling her so badly that the bar of soap slipped from Lena’s hands and she splashed water everywhere trying to anchor herself before she went under. “It’s good to see you healthy. You have been hiding from us, it seems.”

     

                “What are you doing?” Lena hoarsely asked, dragging wet hair out of her face.

     

                “You and Alex are of a height and you are in need of clothes until your new ones are finished. Here.”

     

                She raised a bundle and then set them down at a safe distance. 

     

                “How is your shoulder faring? It looked a nasty wound.”

     

                “Fine,” Lena warily replied.

     

                “I’m glad to hear it. And your glyphs? Did you practice while you were gone?”

     

                “I- yes.”

     

                Smiling, Kelly nodded. “Good. You will have to show me.”

     

                “I- maybe- maybe some other time?”

     

                “Oh,” Kelly blinked. “Forgive me, would you like some privacy?”

     

                Dipping her chin in a shallow nod, Lena shifted her wet hair off her shoulder and tracked the woman’s movements to the door before she sighed and slipped deeper into the water to wet her shoulders and continued washing. Once she was clean and feeling more refreshed, she climbed out of the tub and wrapped herself in a towel.

     

                Drying off quickly, she stayed wrapped in the towel as she sifted through the pile of clothes. Brown leather leggings worn soft from use were thick and warm, creases and the nicks of blades marking it, with a russet cotton shirt, followed by a burgundy tunic that fell to Lena’s knees, split for riding with flames worked into the cuffs and collar. A leather vest went over the top of it, sturdy as it kept the layers secured, the belt with Kara’s dagger going around her waist, and then a long robe the colour of mahogany over the top, even more ornate, the twisting tongues of golden flame giving way to smoke wrought in silver. 

     

                Feeling warmer than she had in days, the stickiness of her fever washed away, leaving her comfortably cosy, Lena wrapped her hair in the towel and walked over to the open doorway, sticking her head outside. The two women chattering quietly together drew apart at the sight of her and Alex fixed her with a long look before speaking.

     

                “Well, you cannot go outside with your hair in that. You will catch a chill and Kara may drown me in the river. Or then again, maybe she won’t.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena folded her arms over her chest and was helpless to stop them from herding her through the hallways to their shared room, the mess of their belongings strewn about the place. Bidding her to sit on the floor before the fire, which burned big and bright, almost stiflingly hot, Alex lit her hands on fire and held them near Lena’s head, sighing when her sister-in-law jerked away.

     

                “Don’t fret, I shall not burn you.”

     

                Wary, Lena sat still as the warmth of the flames drew the moisture out of her hair, leaving it a tangled, frazzled mess. Clapping her on her good shoulder, Alex climbed off her stool and gave her a quick grin.

     

                “I will let more capable hands braid it for you, or else you will look like a bird’s nest.”

     

                Relenting against the inevitability of it, and used to Andrea doing it for her by now, Lena let Kelly take a seat on the stool and work a comb through her dry hair, along with some sweet-smelling oil that made it shiny and smooth. Deft fingers braided sections into neat, elaborate patterns and when she was satisfied, Kelly rose to her feet.

     

                “Much better. You look more the part now.”

     

                Staring down at her fire-emblazoned clothes, Lena felt that she most definitely did not look the part of an Unseelie Princess with an affinity for the earth, and a small smile curled her mouth at the idea of Lillian seeing her dressed as such. That was enough for her to think better of the clothes than she had before, rising to her feet and twisting her hands in the heavy wool of her robe.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Come along now,” Alex said, gesturing to the door. “We shall have a chat, you and I.”

     

                “I think I’d prefer to lay down.”

     

                “You may do so after. Quickly; Kelly read the clouds and says it will snow soon. I have never known her to be wrong.”

     

                She said it with a smug edge of pride, kissing her wife quickly before striding towards the door. Lena felt only a flicker of envy at the thought of a marriage so easy, so loving. Not that she wanted that with Kara, she reminded herself. Only that it would have made things a lot better if it was even slightly warmer. Of course, she knew she was complicit in making that impossible, putting up walls, biting and fighting tooth and nail against any progress. Except, they had made progress, some truce between them until she had ruined it all with her reckless plot. They were something of friends, or had been, spending countless hours together walking through the forest, Kara teaching Lena archery, helping her practice her speaking skills, climbing trees, bathing together, sharing their quarters and meals. They had even kissed. Now, they would barely meet each other’s eyes.

     

                Reluctantly following Alex out of the room, Lena trailed after her at a distance, as if they both just so happened to be walking in the same direction without walking together. Alex paused a few times, turning to give her an impatient look, but Lena was aloof and chafed at being ordered about so committed herself to taking her time. She did start to slow with genuine reluctance when she saw the cavernous white mouth of the exit, the air colder as the wind gusted in, but she forged onwards, the stone growing colder beneath her feet.

     

                At the mouth of the plateau, Lena shifted from foot to foot at the icy stone against her soles, watching with disbelief as Alex walked outside without so much as flinching, glancing back over her shoulder and raising her eyebrows impatiently. Mouth thinning, Lena frowned as she drew the robe tighter around herself.

     

                “I don’t have anything on my feet.”

     

                “There is little snow; you won’t need shoes until it settles for good. A week or more yet.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena exasperatedly stepped outside, the damp rock almost treacherous in some places as the weak sunlight hadn’t managed to thaw the thin veneer of ice coating it yet. Struggling onwards, Alex slowing her pace for her now, Lena stared out at the view, the freezing breath catching in her throat. The forest was a fog-wreathed thing stretching as far as she could see, which was some distance with her fae-enhanced eyesight, and she felt a deep ache for the cover of the trees, the smell of sap and pine and rich mud. Lena had always loved nature but being in the forest for so long and then being taken away from it left her feeling oddly vacant and desperate for it. She wondered if that was how Kara felt about being away from her lake.

     

                Alex led them to a small patch of leafless trees, gnarled and twisted where they’d managed to grow between the rock, none of them taller than ten feet. Coming to a stop in the middle, Alex turned on her and gave her an appraising look.

     

                “You have a lot of frustration inside you,” Alex mused. “It makes you angry. We shall work on that, so you stop taking it out on my sister.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena swallowed her annoyance and hung her head. “I don’t mean to. She’s just always … there.”

     

                “And she always will be. My sister is loyal to a fault. Now, she has many faults, I’m sure you know, and she is too gentle with your stubbornness. You are too soft, Lena. There are some in the Unseelie Court who still hold to the old ways of leaving a child out in the forest alone to test their mettle. You are already older than they are when it’s done but you would fare poorer than them, I think. It is time for you to toughen up.”

     

                A flash of anger swept through Lena and she rankled at Alex’s words. “You have no idea what I’ve been through.”

     

                Making a scathing sound at the back of her throat, Alex moved quickly, grabbing Lena’s arm and moving behind her to twist it up at a painful angle, forcing Lena to fold in half as she grunted with annoyance. Alex jerked her back up and laughed softly, letting her go.

     

                “You have been through much but that doesn’t mean you’re equipped to handle it. But we shall try, at the very least. How is your skill with a blade?”

     

                “Shit,” Lena sulked, crossing her arms.

     

                “And the bow?”

     

                “Better but … well, you wouldn’t want me guarding your back.”

     

                Alex laughed as amusement flashed across her face, giving Lena a quick smile, and she withdrew a small throwing knife from her belt, holding it up. “Until your shoulder heals, let’s see how you fare with knives.”

     

                She turned and let loose her knife, striking the heart of a knot on one of the trunks. At a closer look, Lena could see that it bore the marks of thousands of strikes and she glanced back at Alex as a knife was held out to her. Taking it with apprehension, Lena turned it over in her fingers and gripped the hilt tightly.

     

                “Not like that,” Alex snorted, producing another knife and standing beside Lena as she showed her how to grip it before she sent the knife hilt over tip towards the trunk again.

     

                Lena tried to emulate the motion but ended up tossing the dagger a few metres away before her shoulders slumped and Alex laughed, not unkindly. Going to fetch all three of them, Alex handed one to her again and prompted her to have another go. Trying to heed the instructions given to her, to use more force, to loosen her grip, and to angle the knife at a particular degree, Lena only managed to strike the trunk once and the knife didn’t stick at all.

     

                Still, she kept at it, letting the knives free, fetching them again, and spending her energy as some of her frustration was vented. The toll of the cold also helped wear her out as she fought against the stiffness that settled into her bones, her shoulder pleasantly numb after a while, and eventually, she could barely stand to raise her arms again to set the knife free. Hands hanging limply at her sides, she exhaled forcefully, cheeks bitten from the cold and wind, and handed the knives to Alex.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Better?”

     

                “Much.”

     

                Nodding, Alex’s expression was solemn as she tucked her knives away. “It is healthy to find a way to expend your energy in a physical manner. Archery is not nearly as satisfying, in my opinion, but there is a certain ruthlessness in knives, don’t you agree? When your shoulder is better I will- I said scarce , Kara, not spy.”

     

                Lena turned as Alex’s voice rose, cutting off mid-sentence to draw attention to her sister, skirting past the edges of the rocky clearing. Their eyes met briefly and Kara paused before she shot her sister a withering look.

     

                “I was going for a swim,” Kara curtly shot back, although the pink in her cheeks wasn’t from the cold.

     

                Still, she went on her way and Lena drew in another sharp breath of cold air, her green eyes tracking her wife’s progress along the snow-dusted rock. Alex stepped up beside Lena and folded her arms, watching her sister as well for a moment before she turned to her sister-in-law.

     

                “Tell me you do not like her.”

     

                “I don’t like her.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Alex huffed, “again, in our tongue. You are proficient enough now, or so she tells me.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena’s mouth twitched but she was obstinate at heart and knew enough of her own feelings. Fumbling around the clumsy words, she found herself faltering, hitting a wall. “I don’t- I don’t-”

     

                A flicker of satisfaction warmed Alex’s eyes as her lips twitched with a smile. “Good. That is a start.”

     

                “A start for what?”

     

                “For a good marriage.”

     

                Lena rolled her eyes and kept her opinion to herself as she turned her back on Kara’s retreating figure. Moving over to the gnarled tree, she jerked the knife out of the knot and tapped it against her palm.

     

                “You could have gotten worse, Lena. She is prideful and too serious most of the time, at the cost of losing her family young. I don’t know what you know of her-”

     

                “I know enough. I know exactly who I’m married to.”

     

                Eyebrows rising, Alex gave her a dismissive once over. “Do you? You know her whole family was slaughtered, yes. Do you know that five generations back, thousands of years ago now, her family were royalty? You may be a Princess by blood but so should she have been, until the House of El abdicated in favour of a more democratic ruling body. That is why she was deemed the most suitable match for you, after long deliberation over eligible suitors. Should I tell you of the others who almost had your hand? James - Kelly’s brother, you remember? - a placid man, slow to anger but harbours long grudges. Mon-El, a terrible man who would drink and whore his way around the Courts without an ounce of sympathy for your circumstances. It could have been Lucy, the sister to Kara’s dead cousin’s wife, a kind woman but hard, a general who would have you fall in line like her soldiers or leave you at home to your own devices. Or-”

     

                “You’ve made your point,” Lena bitterly interrupted. “I didn’t say I could have done better. I know she is kind, more tolerant than I deserve, a pain in the ass most of the time but still forgiving, even if her patronising makes me want to pitch myself off the side of this mountain. She is not the problem! Do none of you understand that? The problem is- is … this.”

     

                She gestured around with frustration, her cheeks starting to warm now as she worked herself up. “I am not used to this life. I’ve gotten used to it, to sitting about twiddling my thumbs, to being dragged around and made to do what I’m told but that doesn’t mean I have to like it. Your sister is … beautiful and I’m sure many people would want to marry her if she wasn’t cursed - hell, maybe even though she is - I’m not arguing that-”

     

                “What is your argument then?” Alex curiously asked.

     

                “I should have the freedom to choose for myself, right? I never got to choose if I wanted a wife. I chose to be here. I admit that I willingly came back and asked to stay after I- it was all taken away from me but … what’s my incentive to make this marriage work, huh? What do I get out of it?”

     

                “The incentive is you have someone willing to die for you - and she cannot say the same. While you want to cry about your loneliness and then turn your back on the chance to have a family who would care for you? I’m not telling you to let go of your anger and frustration, only that if you were less stubborn you might find some genuine happiness amidst it all. Is that not better than the two of you making each other so miserable that you-”

     

                “She doesn’t make me miserable. You haven’t been there for three months , you don’t know anything ,” Lena hotly replied. “I tried to make her leave me on the riverbank, to save herself but she wouldn’t. You think I don’t know it was my fault? You think I don’t feel guilty about it? Stupid? But I was trying to get us both out of this shit situation because she seems happy to just … have a wife and-”

     

                Alex was cool in the face of Lena’s confused frustration as she spoke with her hands, cheeks red and eyes bright with helpless anger. After a minute, Alex roughly sighed and reached out to shove Lena, mindful of her shoulder, straight into a snowdrift piling along the edges of the small cliffside clearing. A sound of protest escaped Lena as she struggled to sit up, frowning.

     

                “What the fuck was that for?”

     

                “You talk too much. You used to never speak at all but if this is how conversations are between the two of you … I might stage my own coup for a bit of peace and quiet, or else we’ll all have a miserable winter.”

     

                Pushing herself up and then slapping Alex’s offered hand away before staggering to her feet, her cheeks rosy, shallow breaths hanging before her in puffs of white as she hugged her cloak tighter around herself, Lena scowled.

     

                “Funny.”

     

                “Come on, you have had enough, I think,” Alex murmured, putting an arm around Lena’s shoulders and shepherding her back towards the gaping mouth of the tunnel. After a moment, she sighed heavily and dropped her arm. “You know, she is not opposed to having a wife because … she lost all of her family and she has been slowly finding a new one. She will never bring herself to love someone because of that cursed prophecy but … she wants to be alone no more than you do.”

     

                “She’s not alone; she has you.”

     

                “And you have her. Funny how that works, isn’t it? If you let people in, the loneliness grows smaller. Let in enough people and it may leave altogether.”

     

                Lena hummed dubiously at the logic and hugged her arms to her chest. They walked the rest of the way back to the entrance in silence, slipping through the wide doorway as the tug of the wind lessened, although it howled and created its strange music, haunting melodies produced by the holes bored through the stone. 

     

                She was glad for the escort as Alex led her back to her rooms, knowing she would have gotten horribly lost in the near identical-looking hallways that wound through the mountain. They passed by staircases going up and down but never took them and Lena wasn’t sure she’d like the idea of venturing deeper than the sprawling warren she’d been quartered to so far. She was almost surprised when Alex stopped outside her room and brushed aside the curtain for her, and hovered uncertainly as she fiddled with her fingers.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena found herself saying, feeling oddly relieved and some of her frustration vented without bruising feelings and egos of the only person she gave the slightest shred of fondness for.

     

                Nodding, Alex stepped back and then paused, anxiously biting her lip as she cocked her head, listening closely, and then determined Kara was not holed up next door in her own room. Looking at Lena, she gave her a wry smile.

     

                “Look, no one is asking you to love her. It would just be nice if you both found a sliver of happiness in your companionship.”

     

                Lips twitching, Lena shrugged, staring down at the floor. “Perhaps.”

     

                “I shall see you at dinner.”

     

                Alex said it as if it was an order instead of an assumption and Lena watched her leave before she retreated further into her room and sank down onto the stone bed, the thin mattress giving slightly beneath her weight. The fire was warm and she considered sitting before it to thaw out her pink feet, not nearly as immune to the cold as the other fae seemed to be but having some greater tolerance or else her toes would have been black from frostbite after so long standing outside. 

     

                Idling away the rest of her morning and afternoon, Lena skipped her midday meal as she took the initiative to wander, listening closely for the sound of anyone before she ducked inside a room or slipped down a side hallway. Her mind was too busy for conversation and she had a lot to think about as she walked, finding a large hall filled with books, another with sacks of grain and flour and dried lentils and beans and nuts adjoining a larger kitchen, where she could hear voices inside and quickly backtracked the opposite way. Finding a dozen sitting rooms of different designs, some with narrow windows overlooking the mountainside, others with fireplaces on every wall, and more yet with shallow wading pools with odd pale-bellied fish. 

     

                The place was wondrous, a marvel of creation and skill as much as the other places Lena had encountered. She was still completely enamoured by the detail and craftsmanship of everything the fae seemed to create, from the delicate embroideries on almost every article of clothing, to each pillar, each chair and table leg, the soaring ceilings, the wrought sconces and braziers and fireplaces. There were paintings too, of course, and tapestries, all of them showcasing scenery and historical battles and fae, and perhaps family too, and Lena admired their evident appreciation for beauty in all things. Even a plain, simple spoon was lovingly carved with someone’s labour and she had to admit she enjoyed the act of slow, simple living for the sake of enjoyment. She just didn’t have anything that brought her enjoyment, save for flowers. There were no flowers in the halls.

     

                She spent the entire afternoon exploring, finally bringing herself to venture down a level, up a level, trying not to get lost. It was impossible to keep track of where she was and many of the hallways were pitch black and ominously dark - she didn’t stay there long - and it wasn’t until her stomach started rumbling that she figured she should eat. Trying to navigate her way through the halls, Lena eventually heard the sound of voices and warily approached.

     

                Stepping into the massive doorway of a dining hall, she hesitated and the conversation dropped off as everyone turned their attention to her. Rising from her seat, Kara stared at her, waiting for Lena to speak first but Lena couldn’t speak, her mouth opening and closing, her throat painfully tight. Eliza rose to her feet as well, from the head of the long table, smiling as she beckoned.

     

                “Come and eat, daughter. Sit with me.”

     

                Pausing, her mouth flattened and she nodded, ducking her head down as she strode purposefully across the carved stone floor, stopping at Eliza’s side and sinking down onto the stone chair that was pulled out for her. It was a table big enough to seat fifty people, running down the middle of the room, and everyone was spaced out near one end, a few chairs separating some as they grouped together.

     

                Eliza sat alone, two chairs on each side of the table perpendicular to her own vacant, while Kara sat with Alex, Winn and Nia, Kelly sat with James, Querl sat with Mon-El and Imra, and then further down, Andrea and Sam. Trays and dishes littered the table and Lena kept her eyes cast down as there was a smattering of murmured greetings sent her way, making her wince as a few muttered Your Highness before the conversation picked up again.

     

                “Eat. You must keep your strength to heal your shoulder,” Eliza softly ordered her, gesturing to the plates.

     

                There was an empty seat between Lena and Kara but her wife leaned across the gap with a pitcher of steaming apple cider to fill Lena’s goblet. Murmuring her thanks, Lena kept her eyes down as she scooped roasted potatoes from a bowl, buttered peas, some carved chicken and warm bread before she ate quietly. Eliza spoke to her a few times over the course of dinner, kind in a way that didn’t belie the firmness beneath, and was otherwise content to watch Lena, gaining the measure of her daughter-in-law. Kara didn’t say a word to her, although she occasionally set a dish down in the space between them; a vegetable pie, soft cheese with herbs, a sweetened rhubarb pie with thick cream to pour on top.

     

                Once she was finished, Lena drank more cider as it warmed her through, feeling full and content, although out of her depth with discomfort at the company. She was grateful no one paid her much attention but it did sting a little to watch Kara engage in conversation down the length of the table, her laughter coming easily, stories told back and forth of old jokes and events that Lena was clueless about. She had no one to laugh about old stories with.

     

                As soon as Andrea and Sam made their excuses and left the group of friends to their drinking and reminiscing as the odd wind figures whisked away dinner at Eliza’s direction, Lena used their departure to make her own. Quietly thanking her mother-in-law, she pushed her heavy chair back and rose to her feet, slipping out practically unnoticed.

     

                She made it almost halfway down the long hallway before she heard Kara’s soft voice calling after her. “Lena!”

     

                Slowing, she turned to look at her before coming to a stop as Kara’s long strides worked to close the gap between them. Clearing her throat, her wife fumbled in the pockets of her navy robe as she reached her.

     

                “I have something for you.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Here,” Kara murmured, holding out a shapeless woollen lump. “I have been making them for you.”

     

                Lena took the item and realised it was two pieces, holding them up as she blinked in surprise, a smile curling her lips. “Socks.”

     

                “I know how you are always complaining of cold feet,” Kara explained as she shifted from foot to foot, her own bare against the cold stone. “I’ll make you shoes for riding through the snow before we leave.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena’s eyes creased at the corners as her cheeks dimpled shallowly. “It would be nice to keep all of my toes.”

     

                Giving her a wavering smile, Kara nodded, fiddling nervously with her hands as she looked at the socks in Lena’s hands instead of meeting her eyes. Lingering in the awkwardness of the moment, Lena sighed after a moment and pulled on one sock and then the other, wriggling her toes inside the soft wool as the burrowing cold was lessened. Her smile grew a fraction.

     

                “Perfect.”

     

                And they were, delicate wool intricately knitted in deep forest green with little white roses. She hadn’t known Kara was such a proficient knitter and it made her soften slightly, touched by the gesture. 

     

                “I picked roses,” Kara blurted out, brushing her hair off her shoulders and clearing her throat before she continued. “I wasn’t sure what your favourite flower was - strange that I shouldn’t know such a thing about my own wife after so many months - so I picked roses. I think- I think it’s very fitting; much like a rose in full bloom … you’re also beautiful. Very beautiful. Um …”

     

                Taken aback by the compliment, Lena’s lips parted in surprise and she didn’t know what to say for a moment, eventually stammering out a response. “Lily of the valley. It’s lily of the valley. My favourite.”

     

                “Oh. Well, for the next pair then.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara finally met her eyes and her shoulders sagged slightly, an aching look in her blue eyes. “Can I walk you back to your room?”

     

                Relief flooded Lena and she let out a breathless laugh as her shoulders dropped, her expression softening with a wry smile. “Please. I have no clue where I’m going.”

     

                “Don’t worry, I will guide you true.”

    Chapter 18

                It was easier after that day, if not quite peaceful. Lena was able to tolerate it better, dragged out into the bitter wind and light snows every morning by Alex as her sister-in-law committed to sapping as much of Lena’s frustration as possible from her, the physical exhaustion numbing her emotions somewhat, leaving her less irate, more amenable. Likewise, Kara seemed far more untroubled around her family and friends, that tense, uptight demeanour born from her wary worry diminished by the safety of her mother’s halls. It helped that Lena was afforded more free time than she knew what to do with, almost bored without the stiflingly overbearing lessons Lillian had filled her days with but it also provided an opportunity for the two women to spend more time together.

     

                It wasn’t that they did everything together, only that they were always near each other. If she was puzzling her way through a complex essay plucked from the cavernous library room, Kara would be nearby knitting with a sudden passion for it that had eluded Lena’s notice before. If Lena was answering questions in quiet conversation with Eliza and Kelly, Kara was playing stones with Alex or Winn, if Lena was throwing knives with Alex and taking advice from James and Mon-El, Kara was swimming in her little lake a short while away. 

     

                And there was that awareness of each other too. If Lena rose to go and ask Kelly a question, her new teacher as she helped Lena practise with the glyphs, Kara would look over. If Kara got up to refill her cup of tea, Lena glanced up. They didn’t speak that much but Lena was, if not shy, reserved around almost everyone else and remained close to Kara whenever possible. They sat beside each other at all of their meals and Kara would wait to escort her through the halls, which were still disorienting to Lena, who hadn’t made much headway in mapping out the place, wary of getting lost in the dark hallways.

     

                After a couple of days, Lena didn’t resent being there so much. It helped that her shoulder was healing well, daily poultices and fresh bandages staving off infection, the pain fading to a stiff ache but nothing like it had been initially. That alone improved her mood and her sheepish guilt dimmed as well, the halting peace between her and Kara offering something of a fresh start. Lena couldn’t admit that she cared about her wife, that she felt anything but tolerant towards her, on account of her defiance against the arrangement but it was there. It didn’t fill that pit of loneliness but she recognised the truth to Alex’s words that she couldn’t do it alone and there were people willing to help. Lena started to let them - just a little.

     

                Coming from the baths after her morning spent throwing knives at the trees in the small clearing outside, Lena was dressed warmly in some of Alex’s borrowed clothes, nothing of her own to her name yet, and bumped into Kara on the way back to her room. Coming to a stop, blinking in surprise, some of that old awkwardness still lingering somewhat, even if they were nothing less than cordial and polite with each other now, Lena opened and closed her mouth for a moment.

     

                “Morning.”

     

                “Good morning,” Kara slowly said, a faint crease between her eyebrows.

     

                They’d already seen each other, Lena escorted to the kitchen by Kara for breakfast, which they’d eaten across from each other with copious amounts of tea and fresh bread, still warm from the oven. Their conversation came to a halt and Kara waited expectedly for a moment, giving Lena a bemused look before forging onwards.

     

                “I was coming to find you.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Here,” Kara murmured, holding out a pair of folded socks.

     

                Lena cocked her head to the side, taking them and unfolding to see the pattern of little lily of the valley flowers against the dark green pattern. A smile curved her mouth and she looked up at Kara, curious and grateful.

     

                “Thank you. They’re perfect.”

     

                Ducking her head, Kara glowed with delight, her cheeks turning faintly rosy and a smile on her lips as she clasped her hands before her. “I made these ones thicker, for warmth once we depart.”

     

                “Thank you. I never would have imagined you as much of a knitter,” Lena said with bewildered amusement, running the fine woollen socks through her fingers.

     

                “There is much you do not yet know about me, but it is an egregious error on your part to believe someone who was raised on the water, weaving nets and tying knots, would be a stranger to the simple task of knitting socks,” Kara lightly teased, her face softening with a smile. 

     

                Mouth twisting ruefully as she narrowed her eyes a fraction, Lena hummed in agreement. “I suppose that’s true enough.”

     

                “Still … plenty of time. We shall have all winter.”

     

                “Am I going to be spared the rigorous education my mother attempted to impart to me this autumn?”

     

                “Ah, well, we shall have to find something for you to do to pass the time. I don’t believe you will like sailing or fishing, nor swimming-”

     

                “Swimming? We’re heading north; I imagine it would be freezing in the sea this time of year.”

     

                “Not quite freezing, although it takes a strong constitution to withstand the bite of it. My friends aren’t fond of partaking in that act either, they believe the water is too glacial.”

     

                Snorting, Lena raised her eyebrows. “So, you’re the only one without any sense then.”

     

                Grinning, Kara shrugged nonchalantly, “some might say I am the only one courageous enough to brave it.”

     

                “And does Alex join you on these swims?”

     

                “No, she has a natural aversion to too much water, given her affinity with fire.”

     

                “Ah, I see. Your theory doesn’t hold up then.”

     

                “How so?”

     

                Taking a slow step closer, almost conspiratorial as she lowered her voice, a spark of laughter in her green eyes, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Your sister is far from a coward, and frightening enough to convince me to listen to her, so I’m not so sure it’s your bravery that has you going for a dip in sub-zero waters. Maybe a lack of wisdom.”

     

                Kara let out a quiet scoff of laughter, hands clasped behind her back as she teetered forward slightly on her toes. “Is that so? And you are one so wise in your years.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes. “I might not be wise but I’m clever enough to stay where it’s nice and dry - and warm. How you haven’t gotten frostbite is beyond me.”

     

                “Strong constitution,” Kara reminded her. 

     

                “Maybe more like a genetic predisposition to withstand colder temperatures.”

     

                “And what is a genetic predisposition?”

     

                Kara’s amusement turned into curiosity as she questioned Lena, an open look of naïvety on her face as she patiently waited for a response to this foreign concept. Smiling slightly, Lena hummed dubiously for a moment as she tried to find the words to explain it.

     

                “Well, I guess it just means that you were born with a superior resilience to the cold. Maybe that’s because your family grew up around water, so the environment over the last few generations shaped you in the best way to handle being near so much cold. I would hedge a guess and say that your sister can withstand heat a lot better than you can.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “And your mother or Kelly don’t get lightheaded at high altitudes.”

     

                “That’s correct.”

     

                “Those would be genetically superior traits that suit their lifestyles and environments. How long can you hold your breath underwater?”

     

                “Quite some time, but the same goes for all Waterfolk. It is a product of our magic.”

     

                “Yes, but- well, it’s the same way you were born with blonde hair and blue eyes. Your genes are passed down from your parents and grandparents. You’re … quite tall, actually, so that would typically make you a better swimmer. Your height comes from your genes so, say, you had a great-aunt that was very small, arms and legs too short, not enough surface area to, you know, stay buoyant, well, maybe she’d drown in the lake because she couldn’t keep herself afloat, couldn’t fight against the current. If she drowned, that would eliminate those genes from the gene pool; she wouldn’t pass them on. If she had a sister who was taller and stronger in the same situation and she survived, those would be advantageous genes to pass on. That’s a … very basic overview of it, and I’m no scientist, but basically, it’s survival of the fittest, you know?”

     

                “Oh,” Kara softly exclaimed, realisation dawning on her face. “You’re speaking of the runt of the litter. Drown the weakest to conserve resources for those with better traits.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena’s face furrowed, “well … no, that’s not- not exactly what I mean. That’s called eugenics-”

     

                “Eugenics,” Kara slowly tested the word. “And what does that mean?”

     

                “I- that’s off-topic. Anyway, just imagine … someone might die of shock in cold water because they’re not used to the cold but you are so you’re fine. I would fall into the former category so no, no, I don’t believe I’ll be taking any swimming lessons from you this winter.”

     

                Hesitating slightly, Kara’s face furrowed with concern. “Can you swim? I have not seen you do so yet but it would be troubling to me to surround you with so much water and not have you know how to safely navigate it.”

     

                “No,” Lena quietly crowed. “What makes you think I would be able to swim? I avoid it at all costs. A bath is almost too much. You had to drag me out of the river not even two weeks ago!”

     

                “Ah,” Kara murmured, her mouth thinning with dismay, “I thought as much. Is that … something you would be interested in learning?”

     

                Spluttering as she blanched slightly at the suggestion, Lena firmly shook her head, mouth flattening to a tight line. “No. No, thank you. I- you love the water and I respect that so long as I’m in your company I’ll be subjected to that but … my mother-“

     

                “Of course,” Kara murmured, apologetic as she reached out to touch Lena’s hand, cutting off any further need for explanation. “Forgive me, I should know better than to suggest you face your fear, given where it has come from.”

     

                Fiddling with the socks as she ducked her head, a nervous shakiness in her stomach, Lena swallowed thickly. “It’s alright. I know it must seem stupid to you.”

     

                “Nothing that is important to you will ever seem stupid to me.”

     

                Peering up through her lashes, Lena faltered for a moment, eyebrows furrowing together. She drew in a shuddering breath but was cut off as Kara quickly filled the silence, looking a little flustered as she rocked on her heels.

     

                “I was going to go for a walk if you would care to join me. Of course, if you would prefer to be smart enough to stay where it’s warm and dry, I wouldn’t hold it against you.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, um, sure. I could do with some fresh air,” Lena haltingly agreed, wary of Kara’s light teasing.

     

                Nodding, Kara gestured ahead and they fell into step together, walking through the halls until they reached the open mouth of the entrance, a steel-grey sky visible beyond. The air tasted like metal, the tinge of approaching snow, and Lena immediately felt the bite of the cold as they stepped outside, frozen rock beneath her feet, the thin veneer of slick ice felt through the socks covering them. She loathed to ruin the socks Kara had made for her but going about barefoot in the early winter chill was more than Lena could bear, even if everyone else seemed nothing more than mildly uncomfortable.

     

                They took the familiar path Lena had taken with Alex every day since that first day she’d been forced outside, skirting the sparse trees bearing the nicks of many knives thrown at their trunks and downwards, beyond where Lena had been before. The air was bracing, making her lungs ache, although they were not nearly as high up as they could be, and she basked in the silence as she followed Kara’s lead. She could feel the restlessness in her wife before Kara plucked up the courage to speak, breaking the peace of the morning as Lena dragged her attention from the snow-capped peaks to listen.

     

                “I would like to ask you some questions if that’s alright?” Kara asked, uncertainty on her face as she looked sideways at Lena. 

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena’s eyebrows rose a fraction and she gave her a dubious look. “About what?”

     

                “You,” Kara said with a quiet laugh, reaching out for her wife’s hand and looping it through the crook of her arm. “So that I may understand you better. It has become apparent to me that I have done a poor job of knowing you. I know your temperament and your qualities and flaws, the measure of you as a person and a wife but I don’t believe I know very well what you like or dislike.”

     

                “Oh. I guess not. And I probably don’t know that about you either,” she grudgingly confessed. 

     

                Giving her a crooked smile, Kara raised her eyebrows. “So? If I ask you a question, shall I answer it as well? It is only fair.”

     

                “Am I allowed to ask any of my own?”

     

                “Of course but you must also repay the fairness of answering the question too.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes. “Fine, Kara, I’ll play fair.”

     

                Looking pleased with herself, Kara hummed for a moment, eyes narrowing a fraction with deep thought. “I now know your favourite flower is lily of the valley; it might interest you to know my favourite flowers are also lilies - water lilies.”

     

                “That wasn’t a question,” Lena wryly replied.

     

                A flicker of surprise crossed Kara’s face and she let out a quick laugh. “You are funny sometimes. I know that much. No, indeed, it wasn’t a question; I’m trying to think of an appropriate one. Ah, what is your favourite gemstone?”

     

                “My favourite gemstone?” Lena dubiously echoed with a quiet scoff. “And how is that important?”

     

                “It is the act of knowing that is important, not the significance of the information.”

     

                “I quite like nephrite.”

     

                “Nephrite? Oh.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “I thought perhaps you’d like something more precious. Diamonds, emeralds, rubies.”

     

                “Let me guess, yours is sapphire?”

     

                Snorting, Kara gave her a withering look. “Aquamarine, actually.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “And your favourite book?”

     

                Glancing sideways at her, the look coy and vaguely sarcastic, Lena’s lips twitched with a smile. “Familiar with human authors, are you?”

     

                “Ah, I suppose not. Nevertheless, I would like to know.”

     

                “The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett.”

     

                “And what is it about this book you like so much?”

     

                “I- … I don’t know,” Lena faltered. “I guess I just- it’s a story about an orphaned girl who gets sent to live with relatives and meets some other children. They’re a bit entitled and one of them is sick but they become friends and they help each other out and there’s a secret garden … it’s just a nice story.”

     

                “And I’m sure the garden was fascinating to you.”

     

                Kara said it in a gently teasing manner, her blue eyes bright with amusement as she ducked her head in conspiratorially to softly say it, and Lena let out a huff of laughter, her cheeks pink from the biting wind and her breath hanging before her. She attempted to fold her arms over her chest while still clinging to Kara, her lips twisting with feigned annoyance.

     

                “Too many years being shifted from home to home, away from any gardens or parks, does make one wish for a secret, overgrown garden all to themselves.”

     

                “Is that what you would have liked for yourself? A garden? I have seen your store; you did not have one then.”

     

                Humming as her mouth turned down slightly at the corners. “I think I would have liked that, yes. Maybe once I was older, once the store was successful enough for me to move out of the city a bit. Buy a nice, big property, plant my own flowers and then make bouquets and arrangements in a workshop.” 

     

                “Does it not make you sad to cut short the life of a flower to make these bouquets?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose slightly, Lena shrugged. “Does it not make you sad to take water from your lake to drink or wash in?”

     

                “An interesting approach to ethics,” Kara murmured. “I will have to consider my answer.”

     

                “And what about your other answer?”

     

                “Which?”

     

                “Your favourite book?”

     

                “Oh. I suppose you wouldn’t know mine either. A tale of Firebird and Nightwing.”

     

                “No, I don’t know it. What’s it about?”

     

                Looking a little sheepish as she bit her lip, looking down, Kara let out a short laugh. Looking at Lena, she wrinkled her nose endearingly, the faint freckles crossing the bridge scrunching with the motion as a v furrowed her brows as well. Lena’s stomach plummeted at the expression, an odd sensation as she blinked mildly, her lips parting, pulse quickening slightly. She’d had the bizarre urge to reach out and smooth away the crinkle, an almost tender impulse that made her suddenly nervous.

     

                “Ah, well, it’s a romance,” Kara admitted. “They’re both legendary warriors from Fae history, tens of thousands of years ago. One Seelie, one Unseelie. Wed together against all likelihood.”

     

                “Oh. That seems almost concerningly ominous.”

     

                “In what way?”

     

                Gesturing to herself and then Kara, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Unseelie. Seelie. Married.”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh as her eyebrows rose a fraction, Kara shook her head in a bemused manner, as if surprised Lena would ever assume a connection like that to the story she knew nothing about. Shallow dimples appearing on her face, Kara gave her a coy look of enjoyment to break the news to her.

     

                “They were in love , Lena, Star Crossed lovers if you will. Not a political marriage to sue for peace. A love for the ages, until they met on the battlefield and fell at each other’s side, together in death as was denied them in life. A romance but also a tragedy.”

     

                “Oh. Will you- will you read it to me sometime?”

     

                Surprised by the question, Kara gave her a genuine smile in response, ducking her head as her face softened with delight. “Of course. I have a copy of it in my winter residence library.”

     

                Her answering smile a little uncertain, Lena nodded in return. “Good.”

     

                Kara resumed her series of questions, from Lena’s favourite colour to her favourite meal, favourite time of day, favourite tree, favourite instrument, favourite type of tea and favourite season. They seemed endless and nonsensical, offering nothing of importance but each answer seriously considered and then tucked away safely. In return, she offered up her own responses to the questions, unprompted, and any others that Lena thought of, which followed in the same vein of unimportant, yet significant enough to want an answer to.

     

                They’d wound up on the shore of the little lake of water Kara came to swim in each day, and Lena had watched with mild horror as Kara waded up to her knees in the stinging cold of the stagnant water, unbothered by the numbing sensation of it as she proceeded to her waist. And Lena knew it was cold because she’d stayed a safe distance from the rocky shore but crouched to dip her fingers in it, letting out a quiet gasp of shock at the bite of it. 

     

                Smiling placidly, eyes closed and serene pleasure on her face, Kara almost tenderly stroked the surface of the water, palm ghosting over the surface rippling in the strong wind, smoothing out the wrinkles and taking pleasure in the feeling of the water as she asked the questions that came to mind. On her thigh, Lena spotted the faint limp of an almost fully healed wound, that tug of guilt making her mouth twist derisively until there was a lull in the conversation for her to politely clear her throat. 

     

                “Your leg is healing well.”

     

                Glancing over her shoulder, Kara nodded. “It is the water, it helps. You might try it too, for your shoulder.”

     

                Shivering, and not entirely from the cold, Lena shook her head and let out a husky laugh. “No, thank you. I’ll stick to baths and those foul poultices your mother keeps making for me.”

     

                “As you wish.”

     

                Once Lena was too cold to withstand it any longer, Kara emerged from the lake and spread her arms, the water drawn from her clothes and skin by the command, the flecks of it hovering around her in a shimmering nimbus before she flicked her fingers towards the lake. Dressing in her folded clothes, Kara gave her a bright smile, rolling her shoulders and picking her way carefully across the rock. Turning her face skywards, she paused for a moment.

     

                “It’s about to snow.”

     

                Lena glanced up, brow creasing. “Probably soon.”

     

                “No, now,” Kara corrected her.

     

                “How can you tell?”

     

                “I can feel the moisture in the air freezing. Come, it’s almost noon and there will be hot cider and a fire indoors. A game of stones too, if you’re interested. You should rest while you can; we’ll be leaving in a few days.”

     

                Sharply looking at her with surprise, Lena gave her a questioning look. “In a few days? And when was this decided?”
