                “This morning. Kelly read the clouds; the weather is worsening and the paths we must take will drive us higher into the mountains before we come back down to the forest on the other side of the range. It’s best we leave before the passes become too treacherous.”

     

                Lena’s eyes strayed to the looming mountains spreading out away from them. It wasn’t lost on her that they were quite low down, in the foothills more than anything, and she gazed up at the cloud-obscured peaks with trepidation. Kara reached for her hand and gave it a quick squeeze.

     

                “You needn’t worry. We won’t go nearly high enough for you to fear the heights. And we shall have bows to fend off the birds.”

     

                “Birds?”

     

                “Well … you’ve seen the size of the wolves,” Kara weakly explained, her smile wavering.

     

                Lips parting, aghast, Lena looked at her with wide eyes. “You’re joking. I’m not … walking through the mountains so a gigantic … I don’t know, eagle can swoop in and haul me off.”

     

                Sheepishly apologetic, Kara shrugged slightly. “If it helps, you’ll be riding.”

     

                “No, Kara, that actually doesn’t help,” she replied, her tone brittle. 

     

                A smile twitched Kara’s lips, spreading into a grin before she let out a huff of laughter. “Sometimes I forget how new this all is to you. Strange to think I’d anticipated a halfling wife who had been appropriately educated at Court.”

     

                “Sorry to disappoint.”

     

                “Oh, no, you’re not a disappointment at all. Quite a handful, I will admit but I think that is more to do with your nature than not being raised at Court. I think perhaps you would have been even more defiant if you’d been raised by Lillian.”

     

                Snorting as she glowered resentfully, Lena’s eyelids shuttered and there was a ghost of a smile on her lips. “If I had been raised by Lillian, I would undoubtedly currently be residing at the bottom of a ditch.”

     

                Considering the response for a second as she cocked her head to the side, Kara nodded in agreement. “I think perhaps you’re right. How fortunate you were to be completely ignorant of half of yourself for nearly three decades so that you might end up in my company instead.”

     

                It was said in a slightly self-deprecating manner and Lena’s mouth twitched at the corners as she narrowed her eyes against the glare of the snow and pale sky. Holding Kara’s hand, she relied on her wife to help her navigate some slippery patches of rock and they found themselves on the shelf outside the entrance again. Kara didn’t relinquish her hold on Lena’s hand though, escorting her into the dark hallway before the light of a few sconces lit the way.

     

                “So, what shall it be? Hot cider with a fire and a game of stones or back to your room?”

     

                “Will there be food involved with the cider and fire?”

     

                “Undoubtedly. Although, I would bring your midday meal to your room if you sought solitude instead. I wouldn’t see you starve if you objected to my company.”

     

                “I don’t object to it,” Lena mumbled indignantly, a brooding look on her face as she pouted slightly.

     

                Humming quietly, Kara glanced sideways at her and her eyes creased at the corners with amusement. “No, you’ve been rather agreeable these last few days. What is it my sister said to you? You may ignore it if she was inappropriate but tell me first so I know whether she needs a cuff around the ear as well.”

     

                “Hm, I’m not sure I like your odds; she had you up and out of my room with ease.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Kara smiled slightly, “Alex is more bark than bite. I, on the other hand, am more bite than bark. Sometimes it’s easier to pick battles.”

     

                “Yes, I’m beginning to learn that myself,” Lena wryly replied, “which is partly why I’ve been more agreeable, as you say. Your sister didn’t give me much choice in the matter - she loves you.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “She wasn’t particularly pleased with the way we’ve handled things. Our poor effort to get along. Anyway, apparently I need to vent my frustration with physical exertion instead of taking it out on you.”

     

                “Oh. Well, yes, Alex has always been one who prides herself on her physical prowess. She would resort to physicality rather than any sort of mental understanding for anger or frustration. You needn’t worry though, you may take it out on me whenever you would like. Even physically,” Kara earnestly replied before she faltered a moment, face furrowing as she hastened to correct herself. “That is- I only meant- if you needed a sparring partner, we could- we could do that, if that’s the sort of physical exertion that you were after.”

     

                Surprised by Kara’s flustered explanation, uncharacteristic and amusing, Lena couldn’t resist the feigned ignorance of her teasing as she narrowed her eyes a fraction, pursing her lips. “What other physical exertion did you think I would have in mind?”

     

                The tips of her ears turning faintly pink, Kara opened and closed her mouth, staring at the floor as she towed Lena along, her pace increasing ever so slightly. “Archery,” Kara waveringly replied, swallowing thickly as her eyebrows drew together before continuing. “Um … you seem to enjoy individual physical exertion. I mean that you- you seem to take more pleasure in doing it alone- ah, that’s not- daggers! Yes, close-quarter combat is a great way to vent frustration- oh.”

     

                Wincing, Kara ran a hand over her face and let out a barely audible groan as Lena shook with quiet laughter. 

     

                “I- do you remember when I tried to help you with that dagger I gave you?” Kara said with a baleful look at her wife.

     

                “Oh, that’s what you’re insinuating,” Lena said with feigned surprise, pressing a hand to her heart as she gave Kara a wide-eyed look of panic. “I thought you were suggesting consummating our marriage.”

     

                Kara brought them to a stop and gave her a stern look, her lips twitching with a thin smile as she tried to hide it. “Lena, you’re bothering me.”

     

                Narrowing her eyes, Lena pursed her lips. “You wound me. Would you prefer it if I held a grudge against you for holding a sword to my throat not yet two weeks ago?”

     

                “That would depend on whether you’d prefer it if I held a grudge against you for instigating a coup.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena hummed dubiously. “Probably not. I was just starting to believe you liked me. Well, I thought you liked our kiss too but apparently not that much.”

     

                Giving her a reproving look, Kara’s mouth thinned with exasperation but her blue eyes were bright with hidden laughter. “I never said I didn’t like it but I wouldn’t insult you by expecting anything more than you’ve already given.”

     

                “How gallant,” Lena teased her, rolling her eyes. “I’d forgotten I was dealing with the most noble Fae in both Courts.”

     

                “You’re testing my patience now,” Kara warned her with no real conviction, the corners of her mouth curving up the tiniest bit.

     

                Sobering up, Lena cocked her head to the side and gave her a searching look. “You never told me your family were royalty.”

     

                “Because they are not,” Kara replied, the words lightly clipped.

     

                “But they were.”

     

                “Yes, they were but the throne was abdicated in favour of a democratic Court. And now my hands have been washed of any obligation to lead the Seelie and I am free in my duties as Lady of the Waterfolk.”

     

                Mouth twisting derisively, Lena was only a little resentful as she gave Kara a shrewd look. “And it’s just me who has to worry about the inevitable duty of leading the Unseelie.”

     

                Patting her hand in a placating manner, Kara continued onwards, guiding Lena to the dining room. “You shouldn’t fret too much about that. That would require your mother and brother dying now.”

     

                “And that’s not likely at all , what with the new war we’ve instigated.”

     

                “It’s the same war, just renewed. However, your brother is an unwelcome surprise and addition to it. He was … well, quite manic before. A very good strategist, which helped the Unseelie Court’s edge, admittedly not enough, but … things may escalate quickly now that he has returned. The war became almost stagnant after what transpired between your brother and my cousin. It merely continued out of obligation until the truce was struck but your brother has a vengeful streak and I would imagine he will bring back the ferocity and horror of brutalistic warfare. There’s no art to that sort of butchery.”

     

                “Ah, there’s that noble streak again. Is one form of killing not the same as any other?”

     

                “No. There is respect in fighting one with honest intentions. Trickery and deception are not honourable.”

     

                Kara’s voice was firm and Lena didn’t protest. She supposed it had to be different, growing up amidst a war, in a place that didn’t have the same social views and expectations. It all seemed very mediaeval, from what she’d seen so far, albeit a rather sanitised and idyllic version for the most part. Even the death and blood and threats had a veneer of dismissive normalcy to them, as if it was common, expected even. Lena hadn’t quite gotten used to that yet but she imagined if Kara thought something was horrifyingly brutal, it must be even more sickening than Lena could imagine.

     

                Giving Lena’s hand another placating pat, Kara gave her a warm smile. “Let us not discuss such matters further when we’re about to eat. Instead, tell me more about this internet.”

     

                Letting out a small laugh at Kara’s bewildered delight in the human technology Lena described to her, she launched into a deeper explanation of their previous conversation on the top as they walked the rest of the way to the dining room. They entered in easy conversation, heads close, arm in arm as they angled their bodies towards each other, and Kara looked up with surprise at the quietness of the room, the scattered figures of her friends and family staring at them intently.

     

                Nodding to them all with warm smiles, Kara led Lena to the chair she’d occupied at every meal since that first time and claimed the one beside her. Continuing her line of questioning in a quiet voice, Kara poured them both fresh water and cups of hot peppermint tea, which Lena quickly wrapped her hands around, still feeling the chill of the outdoors. 

     

                Watching as Kara started to fill their plates, selecting things she’d seen Lena serve herself before, Lena was filled with the odd sensation that they did know each other. Of course, they’d already agreed they knew those sorts of things about each other but it was meaningful . She knew Kara would serve herself the buttered potatoes and would choose the green apple over the red. She would have two cups of tea and then the honey wine, would steer clear of the kale and beets but happily dish up turnips and leek. There would inevitably be a serving of dessert as well, with the remains of Lena’s, her wife’s surprising sweet tooth apparent.

     

                Eating her own lunch in relative silence, Lena answered the occasional question Kara gave her and felt the eyes of Andrea and Sam on her face as they tried to make sense of this new development. They’d never been privy to the meals with the wives and Lillian but there was a palpable shift in things between them that hadn’t been apparent during the hours the two Unseelie had spent escorting them around. It had been obvious before, of course, both of them too wrapped up in each other, even in their bickering and anger, for it to not raise eyebrows by anyone witnessing it but this was a different sort of development that had only been teased before. They’d spent too much time around each other for there to not have been some fondness for each other as the months had gone by, with no real reason to hate each other beyond the confines of their circumstances. Now, they’d come to a more peaceful truce without the overbearing expectations of Lillian’s sly plots.

     

                As promised, after lunch Lena joined Kara for a game of stones, which she’d been introduced to over the last week and found similar to checkers, an easy game for her to pick up, and was warm by the fire as she sipped her cider and thrashed Kara twice before the favour was returned. Warm and content, the ease of being away from the Unseelie Court was a welcome balm against the prickly parts of Lena as she enjoyed her freedom and the languid chance to do nothing but read, sleep, eat and socialise at her whim. 

     

                Their remaining few days passed in much the same manner, although there was a general hum of preparation to depart. Lena spent odd hours alone as the flitting language of the gathered Fae ran back and forth with orders and plans that were made without her input, rations bundled up, clothes packed, horses shod and readied in the stables, weapons sharpened and Fae from nearby dwellings in the mountain passes delivering requested supplies to their liege as Eliza ensured they had everything they would need.

     

                The morning of, Lena had a hot bath after sheepishly pleading with Alex for the assistance of her fire, lingering in the steam as she basked in her last chance for who knew how long. Lena wasn’t looking forward to the trip through the mountains, frozen to her saddle with birds of prey hunting them for sport, or so she imagined, and she was somewhat glum about leaving the mountain hall. It had been a brief reprieve, a welcome refuge as she recovered from her injuries, delaying their onward journey some but with little complaint from her wife and family as they dwelled longer than anticipated.

     

                Emerging from the bath pink and warmed through, Lena dressed in her borrowed clothes and slipped on her thick socks made for the journey. The little lily of the valley flowers made her smile as she wriggled her toes inside before setting off in search of everyone. She had nothing by way of belongings, the caravan of chests that should have followed them from the Unseelie Court no doubt lost or still sitting in their room at the Royal Residence, so Lena had nothing to take from her room. Hovering in the main hallway running from the exit, Lena stood off to one side as she watched everyone ready themselves, uncertain by the number of them.

                

                “Is everyone coming?” she asked Kara in a low voice when her wife passed her by, snagging her arm to stop her. 

     

                “Yes. I gave Sam and Andrea the option to find refuge elsewhere but they are both committed to accompanying you. The rest of my friends will be escorting us there.”

     

                “I- why? We never needed that many people before.”

     

                “We were assured of peace before. It was better to travel in small groups when the forest was the only threat to our safety but now numbers will serve us better in case we have been tracked here. It is not quite so deep into winter yet for most creatures to have bedded down for the season. The bears, yes, but other predators will be seeking out weak prey and easy targets, even in the mountain passes. You needn’t worry; I trust all with my whole heart. I wouldn’t entrust your livelihood to anyone I doubted.”

     

                It wasn’t just mistrust that had Lena brooding as she folded her arms and leaned against the wall, she also didn’t like it with too many of them around. Her differences were more apparent as she watched the Fae socialise, cobbling together broken sentences as they spoke too quickly, all of them oddly serious or bewildering to her, their lithe grace and unruffled demeanour in any circumstances lending them an unnatural beauty that she was a little envious of. There was a natural ease and confidence to them, talking of matters she had no knowledge of, some of them speaking to her politely but with condescension and placid smiles of pity at her upbringing away from Court. 

     

                And perhaps there was a secret part of herself that was envious of sharing her wife with these people, after months of having Kara all to herself, to tease and complain to, bicker and argue with, encourage to bend her steel will and give Lena her own way. Things were better between the two of them but it wasn’t lost on Lena that a large chunk of their time together now revolved around numerous other people within the nearby vicinity, vying for their friend’s attention too.

     

                Somewhat surly and impatient, Lena was left undisturbed, useless with the horses, reluctant to stand outside in the cold, too clueless to attach saddlebags and navigate the hallways to ferret out forgotten things for last-minute packing. It wasn’t until Eliza sought her out that she had anything to do.

     

                “Here,” Eliza said, presenting Lena with the thick, folded fabric, which was shaken out to reveal a warm cloak, embroidered with birds and clouds in silver against the steel grey of the wool. “There wasn’t much time to have more than this made for you, given the shortness of your stay, but it will keep you warm on your travels through the mountain passes.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena earnestly replied, surprised by the gift.

     

                Nodding, Eliza reached out to cup her shoulders, giving her a kind smile. “You will do well.”

     

                It was said with utter conviction, no doubt in her mother-in-law’s words as she squeezed reassuringly. “Be safe. Look after yourself, Lena, as much as she looks after you.”

     

                Her eyes flickered over to Kara and then back to Eliza, confusion slowly blooming on her face. “Are you- you’re not coming with us?”

     

                Concern shot through her, surprising as Lena realised she liked Kara’s mother and had enjoyed their gentle conversations amidst so much overwhelming confusion and frustration. It had been a balm, some maternal tenderness heaped onto her by the Fae woman, stoking an ache in Lena for the mother that had been torn away from her and the absence of a replacement. It didn’t help that they were all concerned with the ramifications of Lena’s coup, Kara’s amputation and Lex’s resurrection. Who knew what would happen next?

     

                “No, I have my own halls to tend to,” Eliza said with a soft smile, cupping Lena’s face in her hands. “But we shall see each other at Midwinter.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, okay, um … thank you. It’s, uh, it’s been nice meeting you and thank you for letting me stay.”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Eliza tilted Lena’s head down and kissed her brow before wrapping her in a hug that made Lena stiffen with the surprise of how badly she’d wanted to be held by someone else. The loneliness was slowly eating away at her and no amount of cordiality from Kara could make up for the cavernous desire for someone to like her, to be tender with her, affectionate with her, in the purest sense of it. 

     

                Swallowing thickly as she extracted herself from the hug, worried that she’d never let go if she didn’t pull away herself, put up her walls, Lena held the cloak to her chest. “Thank you.”

     

                “I shall see you soon.”

     

                Nodding, Lena shifted aside, holding the cloak up with a furrowed look of concentration on her face. Slender hands gripped the edges of it and her arms lowered to reveal her wife standing on the other side, taking the cloak from her.

     

                “I shall have your measurements taken for a new wardrobe once we arrive,” Kara said as she draped the cloak around Lena’s shoulders and then fastened it with deft fingers before she reached out to touch the deep maroon of Lena’s robe beneath. “This colour becomes you but I find it … disconcerting to see you in fire and wind instead of flowers. That is to say … you are not Lena of the Earthfolk if you are not in green.”

     

                She felt her face heat, although her expression was inscrutable, and watched as Kara’s cheeks coloured, blinking rapidly as her lips parted in surprise at her own words. Looking down, face furrowing slightly with confusion, Kara fiddled with her rings and then turned. 

     

                “That almost sounded like a compliment,” Lena softly called after her. 

     

                Pausing, glancing back over her shoulder, Kara smiled slightly. “Yes, it did.”

     

                Her face twitched with an answering smile and then she looked away, hugging her new cloak around herself and waiting until the last few adjustments were made. Kara brought her a pair of simply made leather shoes before they left, merely a few pieces stitched together to enclose Lena’s feet and provide a sturdier sole than the woollen socks against the cold and wet. Assuring her that proper ones would be made for her once they arrived at their destination, Kara knelt and helped slip them over Lena’s feet before she straightened and moved towards her mother.

     

                Kneeling, Kara let Eliza place a hand on her head, saying something to her too softly for Lena to hear before she rose to her feet, embraced her mother and was kissed on the forehead in a similar fashion to Lena. Alex and Kelly said goodbye as well and Kara crossed over to her wife, pressing a hand against her back and urging her towards the exit. 

     

                It was still dark, night retreating, the muffled sound of birds flitting through sparse trees seeming loud in the overwhelming quiet of the mountain. Lena wouldn’t have even known it was morning if it wasn’t for the faintest lightening on the horizon but it was still too early and painfully cold as she huddled in her cloak, wishing for something heavier, something lined with fur as her feet crunched through the layer of snow that had fallen during the night. Hands jammed into her armpits, Lena let Kara guide her over to the horse saddled for her, boost her up and grab the reins tightly as she gingerly sat astride.

     

                “Whatever happens, stay close to my side,” Kara told her, voice low and tense. “If I tell you to flee, you flee, do you understand?”

     

                Letting out a soft sigh, her breath hanging in the air before her, Lena gave her a weary look. “Yes, Kara, I’m not an idiot, I won’t let a bird carry me off due to stubbornness.”

     

                “It’s not birds I’m worried about,” Kara said, her lips reluctantly twitching with a smile, “but that is good to hear. It will be slow going through the mountains; the altitude and snow will make it harder and it is quite steep at some points but do try to stay in your saddle.”

     

                “Don’t worry, my hands will be all but frozen to the reins very soon, I think.”

     

                Eyes glancing down to Lena’s pale fingers clutching the reins tightly, Kara’s mouth thinned. “Gloves. Why did I not think of gloves for you?” she muttered to herself before moving to Lena’s saddlebags, rummaging around until she found socks. “Here, these will have to do for now. It will be better than nothing until I can find better. Unfortunately, most of us don’t need such garments often, if ever, so it may take some time.”

     

                “It’s fine,” Lena murmured as Kara unrolled the socks and slipped them over Lena’s hands for her, squeezing and then nodding with satisfaction, reassured they’d help somewhat.

     

                Everyone else was already mounted and the horses were shifting restlessly when Kara let go of Lena’s hands, the two of them brought out of their little bubble. Gripping the reins tightly, Lena glanced over at Eliza, standing in the mouth of the entrance, and gave her a small wave, the farewell returned as Kara swung up onto the back of her horse and Alex set off at the front of their retinue.

     

                “How far is it?” Lena asked, Kara at her side, the horses taking up the width of the path clinging to the edge of the mountain pass. 

     

                Lena was pressed against the sheer face of the mountain, away from the dizzying drop down to the rock and forest below, which she was grateful for as she bumped along with the shifting motions of her horse. Kara seemed unbothered by the height and glanced over at her, eyebrows rising slightly as she processed the question.

     

                “Only three days if the weather holds. During bad spouts of weather, it has taken more than a week to clear the passes. It will be quicker once we’re through the mountains though.”

     

                Nodding, Lena’s mouth thinned grimly and she prayed for good weather as she fell silent, quickly becoming stiff from the burrowing cold as the wind buffeted them, despite the attempts of the Wind Fae to mitigate it. Snow was falling by the time they rode to the switchback path leading higher into the mountain, towards the pass cutting through the closest peaks. White specks blew on the wind, melting as soon as they touched the cloaks and horses but soon heavy enough to make the travellers damp.

     

                Quickly spiralling down to misery, Lena was silent and stoic, not wanting to complain with so many Fae surrounding her, their opinions and quick judgement of the halfling Princess making Lena rankle at the prospect of being seen as weak or pampered. Still, her cheeks were bitten red where they were exposed and her fingers were stiffly locked around the leather reins as her thighs chafed against the saddle with the ongoing pace that was set.

     

                They didn’t stop for hours, trekking upwards on rocky paths that were already covered by deep snow drifts that had settled in during the autumn, miles above the milder weather of Eliza’s home. The air was like a raw knife down Lena’s throat with each breath, fire in her chest as she shivered and was locked tensely on the saddle, barely feeling her fingers or toes, staring at the horizon, obliterated by the snow, which was coming down steadily now. The higher they climbed, the more she had the dizzying sensation of not knowing where the sky ended and the world began, skeletal trees and patchy rock visible through thick snow doing little to offer perspective. 

     

                The sky was the same shocking white by the time they stopped, offering no suggestion of whether it was noon or not, the sun obscured behind the heavy clouds, but the others must have had a better grasp of time as they came to a halt in a wide corridor between the two looming peaks of the mountain range. Lena couldn’t make herself move, teeth chattering as she hunched over the neck of her horse, and Kara had to lift her down, holding her steady as Lena’s knees buckled beneath her.

     

                “Are you alright?”

     

                Making a frayed sound of amusement at the back of her throat, Lena met Kara’s eyes, snow caught in both of their lashes. Her lips were badly chapped but she gave Kara a wavering smile, nodding as she wrapped her sodden cloak around herself. 

     

                “Come,” Kara urged her, an arm around her back. “I will ask Alex to light a fire. Boil some water for tea.”

     

                Everyone else seemed largely unaffected by the weather, stretching out sore limbs, parcelling out food and muttering about the snow with nothing but vague annoyance at the inconvenience. Still, Alex had a fire going and Sam was quickly at her side, both of them cursing the cold as they reached for the flames. Lena was inclined to agree with them, her jaw aching from trying to stop her chattering as she all but sagged at the side of the fire, pulling off her damp socks to hold her pink hands over the flickering tongues of heat.

     

                Alex melted a patch of ice and Kara directed the stream of water into a kettle she’d procured, setting it over the fire, which her sister heated to an intense purple until the water sputtered and steamed. Making a quick tea, nothing more than a few sprigs of mint and dried hibiscus thrown in to stave off a cold, they parcelled out cups of it and Lena clutched hers tightly, leaching the warmth from it until it started to cool and she was forced to drink it before it lost the capacity to warm her through. She felt slightly refreshed and wolfed down the chunk of bread and cheese given to her, Kara cutting an apple in half and feeding her slices as she squatted at Lena’s side.

     

                Drawing as much moisture out of her wife’s clothes as she could, Kara ushered Lena back onto her horse as they all mounted and set off again. Despite everyone’s best efforts, they couldn’t keep the weather at bay and Lena suffered the worst of it, more susceptible to the cold despite her bundled layers as the snow continued to fall. It muffled everything , offering a strangely quiet landscape as they forged a path through the snow drifts, Kara leading them ahead to help carve a path without altering the natural order of things too much.

     

                The wind whistled and the few trees they encountered, buried to their lowest branches, creaked and groaned, laden with snow. When Winn started to sing, his voice was flattened by the thick coating of snow, making each word sharply stand out. She couldn’t understand the words but they washed over Lena in a calming torrent as a few of the others joined in. When Kara’s voice joined, Lena sharply glanced at her, surprised at the smooth velvet of her voice, blinking when Kara met her gaze and gave her a quick smile. Lena frowned, disconcerted, turning her attention back ahead.

     

                Riding until it was almost too dark to see, which was saying something, considering their eyesight was so sharp, the dark air seemed to glitter with frost as Alex held a hand aloft, orange flames flickering over the austere land. They were so high up that Lena felt dizzy and nauseous and she huddled in her cloak as they all came to a stop, waiting until Alex let out a triumphant shout and urged her horse towards a crack in the side of the mountain pass they were nestled in. One by one, they all slipped through it, the sides so close that it made Lena’s chest tight with claustrophobia, blindly letting her horse guide the way as the breaths sawed in and out of her aching lungs.

     

                They came to an even darker mouth then, leading into the heavy rock of the actual mountain, and Lena had no arguments as she followed Kara’s flank inside, the wind dropping away almost immediately, although the air was still frigid. Following the naturally formed tunnel deeper inside, the air dank and musky, Lena came out into a cavernous space, Alex’s fire illuminating stalactites overhead, ten feet long and poised to impale them, and the rough floor of the cave. She spied bones on the floor and wrinkled her nose, recognising the place for the abandoned den of an animal - a wolf, a bear, she didn’t care so long as it didn’t come back.

     

                They’d brought wood with them, bundled up and lashed behind the saddles, and a fire was quickly built up, Kara shifting water with a wave of her hand to fill the three pots that hung over the flames. Tea was made and a stew was started, while the other was heated until it was warm enough to steam so they could all wash their hands and faces. Lena was limp beside the fire, the haze of smoke smarting her eyes, her body wrung out, hands and feet numb. Kara dipped a clean cloth into the hot water and murmured indiscernible nonsense to Lena as she wiped her cheeks, the heat making it sting, and then removed the wet socks to wash Lena’s raw palms as well, wrapping them in the cloth for a minute as the heat burrowed in, making the pink tips even redder.

     

                “Tomorrow will be easier,” Kara murmured as she pressed a cup of tea into Lena’s hands.

     

                Nodding as she swallowed thickly, Lena took a sip of her tea and closed her eyes. She would have been happy to sleep right there, regardless of her hunger, regardless of her wet clothes but Kara coaxed her up. Dry clothes were procured to replace the top few layers and her cloak was draped over the ground near the fire to dry after Kara had drawn out more moisture. Wrapped in blankets, Lena was then allowed to sit and eat the stew, hastily made with vegetables that didn’t take long to cook, chunks of carrot and cauliflower drifting amidst the white flecks of chicken. 

     

                Full and warmer than she’d been since that morning, Lena was heavy-lidded as she huddled into a ball, pressed up against Kara’s side, the quiet chatter falling on deaf ears until Kara softly asked if she’d like to sleep. They made do on the stone floor, the blankets piled on top of her as she curled up on her damp cloak, her back to the fire and her feet in Kara’s lap to keep them warm. Alex took enough pity on her to remove a smooth, polished stone the size of a saucer from her saddle bags, heating it with her hands and wrapping it in a spare shirt before tucking it in with Lena, who held it tightly to her chest. The others all stayed up to drink tea and talk a while longer, used to the arduous task of travelling and feeling nothing more than the usual weariness of a long day.

     

                The next morning, she had to be woken, Kara sheepishly shaking her with an apologetic look on her face as she knelt by Lena’s side. Groggy and sore, Lena pushed herself up slightly, muscles stiff as her body protested at the movement. There was enough space beside her with the angle of her body to realise that Kara had slept beside her.

     

                “Breakfast is ready,” Kara was saying as Lena rubbed her tired eyes, dry and gritty from the smoke.

     

                Sitting up, she was given more tea, desperately wishing for the buzz of a strong cup of coffee, and a bowl of porridge with a side of dried pork and a soft-boiled egg. Eating her food with little relish, Lena was silent as everyone else chatted and packed up, breaking down the camp and readying themselves for the next leg. It would be another long day of riding and Lena was already irritable.

     

                “Here, let me sort out your hair,” Andrea said as Lena finished and sat beneath her blankets, waiting as she kept warm.

     

                Sitting still as she suffered through the familiar routine of Andrea brushing her hair out and then braiding it back, a more suitable style for riding than her usual ones, Lena felt faintly uncomfortable as she shifted beneath the glances of the others. Murmuring a quiet thank you once her old attendant was finished, Lena rose to her feet and walked over to her horse, rubbing the velvety nose of the mare as she waited for everyone else to get their affairs in order.

     

                They were back out in the snow all too soon, the sky not even lightened by the dawn yet, and Lena was sullen and glum as she hunched her shoulders, the hood of her cloak pulled over her dark hair, socks over her hands. There was little conversation and Mon-El and James roamed ahead to scout the way while Alex went back to check for fresh tracks. She returned with the grim news of wolf prints fresh in the snow, which put them all on edge, bows strung, swords loosened in their sheaths. Lena’s skin prickled with unease, her heart in her throat as she understood enough of the exchanges to cobble together an explanation.

     

                Plodding onwards in tense silence, there was no singing or conversation this time and Lena felt her stomach turn at the faint screech of a bird of prey, casting her eyes skywards as she made out the small dot of something circling far overhead. It wasn’t comforting to know how far away it was but Lena was just grateful she couldn’t verify the true size of the bird, her horse shifting restlessly beneath her, sensing her agitation. 

     

                The snow turned to sleet before long, soaking them all through, and Lena felt like crying as she squared her shoulders and suffered through the deluge as they wound up higher, until the sleet turned to snow again and their clothes froze on their bodies. Anxious and overbearing, Kara rode at Lena’s side and kept trying to talk to her, offering gentle encouragements, trying in vain to help Lena, sapping away as much water as she could from Lena’s clothes, asking Kelly to blunt the wind and Alex to heat up the stone again, which only grew cold quickly and slowed them as Alex had to shift her horse up and down the line. Lashes frozen together and face red and windburnt, Lena was silent with a glazed look of detachment on her face, her breaths pluming before her, lungs burning from the cold as she stopped focusing on how her body felt and just let herself be jostled along on the horse. 

     

                When the white wolf leapt at them, she did nothing but watch as four fletched arrows struck the beast, along with two knives, a wall of wind, tongues of fire and a wave of water as all Fae leapt into action. It was dead before it could do much more than carve a large furrow through the deep snow, a hair-raising howl escaping it before it growled and was slaughtered a moment later. Where there was one, there would undoubtedly be more sniffing out their trail though and they were off at a rigorous pace through the treacherously slick path until well after lunch, beyond when they should have stopped, hunger gnawing at Lena’s stomach as she stiffly sat astride her horse and wished she was anywhere else, even back in the Unseelie Court.

     

                By the time they did stop, she fell off her horse, knees striking the icy ground as she didn’t wait for Kara, bruising herself from the impact and skinning her palms through her sodden gloves as she fell face-first into it. There was a quiet bark of laughter off to her left from one of the men but Lena didn’t know who, beyond caring as she weakly pushed herself up, Kara’s strong hands on her then as she tried to help her up to her feet. Lena refused though, leaden as she knelt on the stone, cheeks burning, frustration welling up in her chest, stronger than she’d felt in almost a fortnight.

     

                “W-why did we h-have to come h-here?” Lena asked through clenched teeth, scowling and resentful.

     

                “It’s the only way through the mountains. Don’t worry, we’ll be clear of it tomorrow morning. It will be an almost easy day’s ride through the forest after that. It will be another eighty miles to the sea but we’ll make up for lost time.”

     

                Shaking her head before she was wracked by another violent shiver, Lena’s jaw tightened and she swallowed thickly. “W-we could’ve gone b-back to your lake. T-to Argo.”

     

                “I have people to care for,” Kara gently told her. “I have been gone too long already, it was necessary.”

     

                “For you.”

     

                “And you as well. Don’t forget that your brother will be hunting you. The mountains will offer protection through the winter - protection you might not have needed if you hadn’t-”

     

                “I-I know what I-I did,” Lena shakily snapped.

     

                “Then do not blame the wrong people,” Kara softly rebuked her. “Let me help you. Alex is making a fire; I’ll make you some tea-”

     

                “I-I don’t want a-a cup of fucking tea. I w-want to go inside.”

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter as she climbed to her feet, dusting off snow, Kara shrugged helplessly, spreading her hands. “What do you want me to do? The quicker we’re on our way, the quicker we will get there. It is not ideal-”

     

                “I-ideal?” Lena scornfully echoed.

     

                “But it is what it is and we will endure it for a while longer yet. Come. On your feet.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Sighing, Kara’s voice turned wheedling as she quietly pleaded, “Lena, please. The hard part is almost over. We will begin descending soon. It will be much quicker and not so cold once we are lower down, and then tomorrow will be easy .”

     

                “Of course it’s easy f-for you. E-everything is. You could’ve left m-me with your m-mom. Why did you b-bring me here?”

     

                “You are not wed to my mother,” Kara curtly replied. “You are not her responsibility. You are mine, however, and I will not let you slow us all down any further.”

     

                Scowling as she petulantly crossed her arms over her chest, Lena closed her eyes. “W-what do you want me to do? I can’t ride a-a horse , you know that.”

     

                “No, indeed, there is not much you can do, is there? It is fine for you to complain while you sit and have everything done for you,” Kara hotly chastised her, voice low but not quietly enough for everyone else to not hear them, although they were polite enough to pretend that they weren’t eavesdropping. “While we cook for you and clean up after you, scout ahead and brush your hair and make your fire. Everyone here is here to escort you safely; they would die for you if it came to it, out of their loyalty to me. Is that not enough for you, Your Highness?”

     

                “I can look after my-myself,” Lena fumed. “I-I looked after myself a long time before I had y-you so … just leave me. If I’m slowing you d-down th-that much, leave me for the birds. I-I don’t care.” 

     

                Looking down at her for a moment, Kara’s mouth was a thin line and she paused before reaching down to haul Lena to her feet, holding her upright for a moment, an inch off the ground, until Lena had no choice but to set her feet firmly down at the disorienting sensation of not being on solid ground. 

     

                “I’ll have no more complaints,” Kara murmured, cupping Lena’s cold face in her hands as she gave her a firm look, broaching no protesting.

     

                Lena’s scowl just deepened as she jerked her face out of her wife’s grasp, her mouth twisting with annoyance, her frustration making her prickly. “You’re an asshole.”

     

                Mon-El mumbled something, a sneer on his face as he raised his eyebrows sarcastically, earning a snort of laughter from James, both of them falling silent as Kara’s head whipped towards them, her ears turning pink.

     

                “You insult her, you insult me,” Kara scathingly snapped back, her blue eyes bright with anger.

     

                Remaining rooted to the spot as a fire was made off the side of the path, Lena stubbornly jutted her chin forward and avoided looking at the group assembling around the source of heat, warming themselves through with tea and a sparse lunch of increasingly stale bread and some fruit and cheese. Kara tried to bring her something but Lena ignored her, and then Kelly tried as well, to no avail, and lastly Andrea.

     

                “You should eat and drink. Quickly, now. We’ll be off in a moment.”

     

                “I-I don’t want anything.”

     

                “Don’t be childish.”

     

                “I’m not.”

     

                “You are, Your Highness-”

     

                Sharp eyes snapping to Andrea’s face, Lena’s cheeks turned rosier in the biting air. “D-don’t call me that.”

     

                “Come,” Alex called out, clenching her fist to quash the fire, a stern look on her face as she gave Lena a piercing look that felt so dismissive that she rankled at the appraisal. “We don’t have time to waste. Anyone who does not wish to eat now can wait for supper.”

     

                Turning away, her lips twitching contemptuously, Lena waited beside her horse with a stiff set of anger to her shoulders. Arms folded over her chest, she watched everyone else haul themselves up into the saddle and Kara cast her a brooding look as she walked towards her before her sister intercepted her, clapping a hand on her shoulder and directing her to her own horse with a low murmur.

     

                Once everyone was astride their horses except for Lena and Alex, the latter rounded on the Princess and raised her eyebrows in polite inquiry. “Were you coming with us, Princess?”

     

                “Obviously,” Lena bit out, all eyes on her. “Where else am I g-going to g-go?”

     

                “Well, you had better climb on your horse then.”

     

                Clasping her hands behind her back, Alex gave her an expectant look and Lena let out a breathless scoff, clenching her teeth and reaching for the pommel of her saddle with her socked hands. Balancing herself as she tried to get a foot in the stirrup, Lena’s grip on the pommel slid and she staggered back, her cheeks flaming as she avoided looking at the patiently waiting Fae, who were undoubtedly amused by her clumsiness. Trying again, Lena landed on her ass on the hard ground, the air fleeing her lungs, blinking back black spots as Alex’s shadow cut across her.

     

                “Now that was a poor effort. Up. Again.”

     

                Hurriedly climbing to her feet, brushing off the worst of the clumps of snow as she tried to stifle her anger and embarrassment, Lena reached for the saddle but didn’t have the strength to pull herself up. Pausing, she set her jaw and gave Alex a reluctant, sideways glance.

     

                “I can’t get up.”

     

                “Then that is a bit of a problem, is it not?”

     

                “Alex-” Kara curtly interjected.

     

                Holding up a hand, Alex kept her brown eyes fixed on Lena, unwavering and determined. “You should go on ahead while we have the light - we may be here a while.”

     

                Everyone started to file out, Kara and Kelly both lingering back as their horses shifted restlessly beneath them, Kara’s shoulders caving as she eventually shook her head and pulled on the reins to guide her horse after Kelly’s. Lena refused to look at Alex as she stood at her horse’s side, aware of the other woman’s eyes fixed on the side of her hood.

     

                “You have been here for months and yet you can’t even mount a horse without assistance,” Alex said after a tense minute. “That is pathetic.”

     

                “Well e-excuse me f-for not finding time to prance around th-the forest on a horse in between all of m-my other lessons,” Lena snarkily replied, the effect dimmed somewhat by her chattering.

     

                “I don’t care what you were doing, we will not be leaving here until you are on that horse by your own hands. Now, mount up or there will be nothing left for supper by the time we catch up and you will rue the decision to turn your nose up at your lunch.”

     

                “This is fucking ridiculous,” Lena muttered to herself, shaking her head.

     

                Alex moved quickly, her strides covering the ground between them to grasp a fistful of Lena’s cloak and jerk her around roughly enough for the hood to slip back. She looked less than impressed and Lena thought that if she’d been taller she might have feared her more, but they were of a height and so she met her gaze steadily.

     

                “You will listen to me loud and clearly; you are not here to take advantage of your ignorance, you are not here to be pampered like in the Unseelie Court, and you certainly are not here to cause trouble for my sister. For the rest of this trip, you will not eat, drink or sleep until you have earned your fair share of it, do you understand me? We are not your servants and you need to toughen up.”

     

                Batting Alex’s hand aside, Lena’s lip twitched with a faint sneer, incensing Alex, who grabbed her again and gave her a rough shake. “Do you hear me?”

     

                Pulling herself free and then giving the other woman a quick shove, Lena glowered as she shrugged her shoulders, righting her cloak. “You don’t get to order me around.”

     

                Stumbling back a step, looking mildly surprised, Alex let out a quick laugh and smiled. “I do because if you decide not to listen to me, you will be in for a very cold and lonely night, and I don’t believe you will offer much of a fight for the next wolf. Now, have I made myself clear?”

     

                “You know,” Lena mused, narrowing her eyes as she turned back to her horse, “I was s-starting t-to like you but I m-might have to change my opinion.”

     

                “If you are as helpless as you seem right now, I shall have to change my opinion of you too, which will matter a lot more to you than yours does to me. You don’t have many friends here, Lena, and you will burn through them quickly and wear out your welcome if you do not make more of an effort to assimilate.”

     

                “Who s-said I wanted to assimilate a-at all?”

     

                “You would not have come back here if you did not want to stay and adjust to this new life. It was an egregious exploitation that was done to you, we will all agree to that, but you came back and have spent months learning under your mother’s instruction; now it is time to use that knowledge and make the truce worth it. Otherwise, it is not just your time that has been wasted. Now, enough of this; get on your horse.”

     

                “I-I’m trying.”

     

                It took her almost ten minutes to climb into the saddle, bruising what felt like every inch of her until she was angry, embarrassed and finally warm from the exertion. When she finally managed to do it, it was a less-than-graceful mounting, clambering over the oiled leather and pivoting her body around until she was awkwardly sprawled across the horse’s back. Righting herself, Lena got her feet into the stirrups and gripped the reins in her sore hands, giving Alex a rather smug look, to which the other woman rolled her eyes and then smoothly mounted her own horse, clicking it onwards and telling Lena to keep up.

                

                They kept a brisk pace until they caught up to the others, Lena avoiding Kara’s surprised glance, and she was silent and aloof as Kara rode on her left side, close by and attentive as usual, although there was an awkward tension in the air after their argument. A prickle of shame washed over Lena at her own helplessness, her own frustration that was so hard to keep a lid on, but she kept her mouth firmly shut as they rode onwards.

     

                It was getting dark when the next wolf found them, a disturbance up ahead as it launched itself from the white snow-capped rocky ledge and bowled Winn out of his saddle. Within mere moments, it was taken care of, Alex galloping ahead with her fire, Kara’s hand on her sword as she reached out to stay Lena’s horse at her side, away from the fray. A forceful gust of wind from James ensured that it was truly dead, slamming the bloody body against the stone side of the cliffside path they were on, the sickening crunch of bone making Lena’s stomach turn slightly as it struck just ahead of her, effectively separating Kara and Lena from everyone else.

     

                Then her stomach lurched for a different reason, feeling a faint twinge in her awareness that lifted her eyes upwards, to the sloping side of the mountain above them, tons of snow and rock that had been disturbed by the tremor of the wolf’s impact. She realised what was happening a split-second before everyone else, a cry tearing from her lips as she looked at Kara, who was directly beneath where the avalanche would strike before swiping them off the side of the mountain, and then threw herself at her.

     

                Lena’s feet were still in her stirrups and her horse careened into Kara’s, pitching them towards the rocky wall to their left, and Kara’s mouth was open with shock as she fell sideways, torso twisted so her back was to the stone. Feeling something give in her ankle, a flash of white-hot pain, Lena freed herself in time to make solid contact with her wife’s warm body and send them both crashing into the wall, falling to a heap with Lena on top of Kara, her hands up, palms towards the sky as if to hold the weight of the world in them.

     

                Stone shifted, jutting out from the mountain and sloping down over them and the horses, Lena’s eyes owlishly round as she felt the rumbling of earth, stone and snow barrelling over them, over the slanted sheet of rock she’d thrust over them. The panicked whinny of the horses was barely audible over the thunderous roar of the mountain crumbling above them but Lena was shockingly aware of the sound of Kara’s shallow breaths in the closeness of their faces, feeling the warmth of it fan over her mouth, strands of her dark hair brushing her wife’s cheeks. Stunned by her own actions, Lena couldn’t process anything as she stared at Kara and Kara stared back at her, waiting for it to pass.

     

                It felt like an eternity before the rumbling faded and they were left panting in a clumsy tangle on the icy ground, Kara’s horse standing over them as Lena glanced up to the underside of the saddle straps. Her own horse was on its knees beside Kara’s, forced down by the sheet of rock that had saved them all from being pitched thousands of feet off the side of the mountain, and Lena started to violently shake as the adrenaline of what had happened set it, heart pounding, mouth dry.

     

                After a minute longer, Kara shifted out from beneath her and probed at the blocked end of their shelter, where ice and rubble buried them. Lena was helpless to move the stone over them, staring at her socked hands with surprise, as if she hadn’t imagined she had the capacity to do that, the power she held still new and unnerving to her. It took Querl shifting the ice as he returned it back to its liquid form and Mon-El shifting the earth and rock to free them, a task that took the better part of an hour before the two women and two horses were bared to the bitter air of dusk.

     

                Leaning against the stone wall, sweating in her layers, even though the chill had settled back in, Lena couldn’t put any weight on her right ankle and was too dazed to even speak as her horse was righted and she was safely deposited back in her saddle. Everyone looked a little startled by what she’d done, including her, but there was renewed interest and some grudging respect as well, as if they’d underestimated her too much. Lena didn’t think they had; she hadn’t known what she was doing, only that Kara was in the way and she’d instinctively hunched over her, as if that alone would have stopped an avalanche from coming down on them.

     

                “Now that is how you earn your supper,” Alex said with wry amusement, clapping Lena on the shoulder as she passed by, slowing to bring up the rear.

     

                Throat tight, Lena didn’t speak at all, not even when they came to a stop for the night, a spacious overhang offering a ceiling for the night, enough space for the horses and them to shelter beneath. A roaring fire was quickly built up with the remainder of their firewood and Lena remained seated on her saddle after everyone had dismounted, her face bone white and pinched as they all set about making tea and dinner and drawing lots for sentry duty with familiar ease.

     

                “Are you alright?” Kara asked, holding her arms out to help Lena down, more sympathetic than her sister.

     

                Jerkily looking down at her with that glazed look of disbelief in her eyes, Lena opened and closed her mouth for a moment before she managed to speak. “I think … m-my leg is broken.”

     

                Anxious concern crossed Kara’s face as she quickly hauled Lena down, shifting her weight so she could get an arm under her knees, the other around her back, and carry her over to the fire. The heat was an immediate relief, stinging and overbearing but welcome all the same. Ashen-faced and numb, Lena could do little more than blink as Kara removed her boots and socks for her as she inspected her legs, the right shoe full of blood where the bottom of Lena’s fibula had snapped and pierced the skin. 

     

                The conversation slowly petered out as the others realised what had happened and Lena was deaf to the gentle probing questions posed to her by Kelly and Sam. Vision swimming, Lena’s eyelids fluttered and she blinked rapidly at the warm touch of Kara’s rough fingers on her cheek.

     

                “You’re okay. You’re alright.”

     

                Tears filled Lena’s eyes and she drew in a hitching breath before letting out a breathless sob, the sound getting caught in her chest as everything caught up to her. Hot tears spilt down her cheeks, freezing almost instantly, and there was a palpable hum of hurried worry as the water was boiled, clean linen bandages procured and willow bark tea steeped strong and bitter. Kelly was the best at healing, having trained with Eliza, and Lena was barely aware of her own body until a strip of leather was put between her teeth after a cup full of boiling tea she choked down. 

     

                Holding her head in her lap, Kara wiped her face clean with hot water and a moment later Lena felt the blinding agony of bone being wrenched back inside, so sudden and unexpected that she heaved, vomiting all over herself as she spat out the leather and strained to sit up. Murmuring softly to her, Kara cleaned her up as best as she could, her own face taut with worry and guilt, and Lena let out pitiful sobs, tightly gripping her wife’s sleeve as Kelly stitched the bleeding wound together and then thickly bandaged her leg. 

     

                By the time Kelly was done, Lena was sobbing freely, turned on her side, her face buried in Kara’s lap as she clung to her damp robes, the ordeal of the last two days catching up with her. No one said a word, a little uncomfortable by her open display of agony, exhaustion and frustration, and Kara just rubbed her back as Kelly tucked her in with as many blankets as was offered up by everyone else, murmuring soft reassurances to her wife until Lena let out a ragged sigh and let unconsciousness drag her away with relief.

    Chapter 19

                Heavy eyelids cracking open a fraction to a swathe of blinding white, Lena screwed them shut again as her face furrowed with annoyance. She felt stiff and cold, as if she hadn’t moved in a long time, and she burrowed into the heavy blankets piled over her, cheeks ruddy where they’d been exposed to the biting wind all night. There was a pain in her ankle and she let out a rough sigh of discontent as she tried to go back to sleep, blotting out the muttering voices around her as she made herself comfortable - or as comfortable as one could be on the rocky ground of a mountainside.

     

                “You’re awake,” Kara’s relieved voice cut through the muffled background noise, forcing Lena to crack open an eyelid. “Good.”

     

                Scowling, Lena closed her eyes again, making a low, disconcerting sound at the back of her throat as she clung to the fog of sleep, feeling pleasantly woollen-headed as she stubbornly refused to wake. Kara shifted closer, the touch of her fingers gentle against Lena’s face as strands of dark hair were brushed aside.

     

                “You should eat something. You didn’t eat a thing last night.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “Come on, Lena,” she gently coaxed her, wan amusement in her voice, although her face was solemn and there were faint signs of stress in the tight corners of her eyes and mouth.

     

                Everyone else was agitated and restless as they lingered about, the horses saddled - sans the stallion James had been riding, which had been carried off in the night by an eagle. Down a horse, the sun already halfway to its peak and the early winter hunger of the other predators lurking about, the mood was tense and dismal. They all wanted to be on their way but Kara was reluctant to move Lena until she had rested and awoken herself.

     

                “There is breakfast. And tea.”

     

                “Do you have any Tylenol?” Lena grumbled.

     

                Kara’s response was a beat too late and confused. “Um … no, but the tea is really good. And we’ll be off the mountain soon so … it’ll be warmer at least.”

     

                Reluctantly, very reluctantly, Lena sat up, the blankets going with her as the wind Kelly was shielding managed to block the worst of it, while the fire Alex kept fueling cut through the rest. Pale and tired, her ankle hurting and her body too stiff to obey without protest, Lena felt worse than she had since she’d been shot with an arrow and jolted through the forest on horseback for hours afterwards. At least it hadn’t been anywhere near as cold then, snow coming down beyond the overhang sheltering them, the day shrouded in white. Her breath plumed before her when she turned her head away from the fire and she could feel the intensity of the cold in her lungs.

     

                Hot porridge was handed to her in a bowl, as well as some tea, steeped strongly with willow bark for her pain, and she tried to force herself to eat but just felt queasy. Kara hovered at her side, anxious and attentive, trying to encourage Lena to eat more as the others idled about with varying levels of sympathy and patience.

     

                “One more bite,” Kara quietly pleaded.

     

                “I’m not hungry,” Lena rasped, looking quite grey-faced.

     

                “We’re losing valuable daylight,” Querl noted, wringing his hands nervously. 

     

                Kara gave him a firm look, “we will delay as long as need be.”

     

                “I can ride,” Lena listlessly replied, not convincing in the slightest but too stubborn to admit the thought of being in the saddle all day was unbearable.

     

                “If it’s any consolation, we lost a horse during the night so we will be riding double,” Kara told her, her mouth a grim line at the thought of slowing their process. Querl was right, they were losing valuable daylight, and that was without the burden of two to a horse.

     

                Lena blinked at her, expression vacantly bewildered. “Lost a horse? How do you lose a horse? There’s nowhere for it to go.”

     

                Opening and closing her mouth, Kara looked sheepish as she shrugged. “An eagle.”

     

                “An eagle? An eagle stole a horse?”

     

                “Fortunately, just the one.” Kara’s smile was weak and she picked up the cooling cup of tea sitting beside Lena and held it out to her. “Drink up, at least.”

     

                Draining the cup, Lena grimaced and shivered at the bitter taste of the tea before she eased the lump of her leg around to climb to her feet. Her right ankle was bandaged with a bit of spotting seeping through the linen and her rough boot wouldn’t fit back over it - nor would her sock. On the matter of that, Kara gave her a grim look.

     

                “I shall have to make you new socks, on account of the other one being soiled with your blood.”

     

                “That’s a pity. They were the best socks I’ve ever owned,” Lena sighed.

     

                Smiling, Kara climbed to her feet and then helped Lena up, her right leg bent as she kept her foot off the ground, hands tightly gripping her wife’s arms for balance. Everyone was quickly in action, the fire quenched, the wind howling as Kelly abandoned her shield, Nia rolling blankets and Andrea holding the reins of Kara’s horse as she carried Lena over to it. Settling her in the saddle first, mindful of her ankle, Kara climbed up behind her, arms bracketing Lena’s waist as she grabbed the reins in hand and then adjusted her grip, her left arm encircling Lena fully.

     

                “We shall stop when you need to stop,” Kara murmured, her lips so close to Lena’s ear that it was hard for her to determine whether the goosebumps were from the cold or the proximity. “But rest for now - I will not let you fall.”

     

                They set off then, Sam already ranging ahead to scout the mountain pass down to the rolling forest below, Alex scouting the rear for trouble pursuing them. The mountains were eerily quiet as they plodded through the fresh snow, hooves leaving deep furrows as new snow fell around them. With Kara at her back and her arm around her middle, Lena was warmer than she’d been in days, despite the lack of one shoe, and she found herself relaxing against Kara’s chest, despite her best efforts.

     

                Still, the jostling of the horse’s movements made her ankle ache in a near-constant dull throbbing that made it hard for her to rest. And the cold did still harry her, fingers in socks, clinging to the pommel of the saddle, her cheeks exposed to the air even as she turned her head aside, hood covering the worst of it. With her face leaning against Kara’s chest, she could hear the steady pounding of her heart and closed her eyes, sagging against her wife as she let the hours pass by. 

     

                It was noon before she knew it, the cohort coming to a stop somewhere in the sloping foothills of the mountain, the wind milder, the snow turning to sleet and damp patches of grass and foliage springing up amidst the soil and rock. It was only mildly better, the wind less aggressive in exchange for the smell of damp wool and horse from the sleet. Lena didn’t eat as she curled up on the rock Kara set her down on, the bare branches of a tree shielding her from the worst of the sleet as everyone else wolfed down rations and then got back in the saddle. The cup of tea she sipped helped warm her from the inside and that was enough for Lena, who had a banging headache and was feeling the pain of her broken ankle more now that the previous tea had worn off. 

     

                The descent through the foothills was treacherously slippery, the slow plod of the horses dislodging shale and cascades of pebbles, thawing snow and ice leaving a wet path for them to follow down a rather steep incline. Lena was bumped around by the motion and found her eyes wide open, face pinched with worry at the steep drop of the switchback path they were taking, as she watched them near the forest canopy below. Perhaps almost as disconcerting as the height of their descent down the mountainside was the run-off of melting snow and ice that couldn’t stick this low down, creating cascading gullies of water where the waterfalls ran in the spring and summer. It was nowhere near as rough, Kara assured her, but Lena found it off-putting to watch so much water tumble down the mountain alongside them, churning the patches of soil to mud and sprouting moss and lichen in slick patches along the rocky path where water had splashed and melted in the weak sunlight. 

     

                The air tasted green the lower they descended, the smell of decay and damp soil unknotting something inside Lena’s chest as if she hadn’t realised how coiled she’d been, so far away from the trees, the loamy earth, the bracken and brambles and plants and flowers. Her skin seemed to tingle with the viridity of the forest, even in the early days of winter, in contrast to the white and grey landscape she’d endured for a fortnight now. Inhaling deeply, she closed her eyes and a small smile played on the corners of her lips. She could smell wild garlic as they brushed past nettles, dark and tangled in the gloom of the forest, the crush of leaves under the hooves of the horses, moss and lichen covering every available surface, even as the leaves abandoned the branches to carpet the floor, allowing for pale, unfiltered sunlight to wash over them as they walked past the first few trees.

     

                “You are happy,” Kara murmured.

     

                Hesitating, Lena turned slightly, not quite able to see her face but responding anyway. “Yes. Yes, I think I am. I’ve … missed it.”

     

                “It … it will be within distance,” Kara haltingly explained. “But … well, I do not live on the doorstep of the forest as I did at Argo, you understand.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                She was tired and already grieving the loss of the forest again, in favour of the coast this time, which was worse than the mountains, and Lena didn’t have the energy to talk. Her ankle hurt, her body was sore and chafed from more riding than she’d done in months, and they weren’t making quick enough progress to satisfy anyone, although she never asked to stop. 

     

                Forging onwards, they plunged deeper into the forest northwest of the mountains, crossing streams several times, where the run-off from the mountain carved through deep gullies with steep banks the horses had to scramble up and down. The water ran clear, save where the horses’ hooves muddied the tranquil current, absent minnows and tadpoles at this time of year. 

     

                They crossed a river as dusk settled in, the banks’ sandstone and soft, worn away easily into soft curves, the water thick and gritty as the horses trod the riverbed into the wide, shallow waters. Cresting the pitted edges on the other side, there were the signs of a badger’s den hollowed out and deep enough to make Lena’s stomach lurch. Skirting around the animal’s den, they followed a broken path that had half fallen into the river and followed its winding path westwards for a while before the light started to falter. 

     

                They were hours away yet, half a day even, and there was a quiet, hissing conversation in Fae that Lena only half followed along with before it was determined they would continue onwards a while longer before stopping for the night. From what she could gather, they would continue until they made it somewhere safe, although she couldn’t have said where that was or how long it would take. In the end, it turned out to be several hours, torches lit, those with fire holding hands aloft as others strung bows and loosened swords in scabbards, ears strained to listen to the creaking and groaning of the ancient forest, wary of any danger creeping up on them.

     

                They made it to the ruins of an ancient structure with no distractions though, a cracked and moss-coated domed watchtower rising a hundred feet from the forest floor, built into the side of a cliff near the top of a valley, giving a sweeping view of the sloping grounds to the south. It was carved out of the sandstone of the cliff, showing signs of relative disuse and abandonment, cracked and missing sections of the domed roof where it had caved in on itself. Kara was confident it was safe though when Lena questioned her on the structural integrity of the ruins, and Lena soon found herself trying to sleep at the side of the fire built in the tall ground floor, smoke escaping through a portion of the collapsed wall, refusing supper as her body all but sagged from exhaustion as soon as she was lowered to the ground. It was a lot warmer there though, the mountains looming further behind them with every mile they travelled, which was consolation at least.

     

                She slept soundly until she was roused, pitch black outside with the flickering firelight to see by. Rubbing the sleep from her eyes and blinking owlishly, Lena was limp and defeated, aching for more sleep but coaxed awake and onto the back of the horse again. If she’d been able to walk on her ankle, it would have been with the lurching gait of someone whose thighs were saddlesore, her tailbone feeling bruised as Kara set her down on the horse and climbed up behind her. 

     

                All of them moved through the forest like wraiths, keeping up a quick speed as they pushed the horses as much as they were willing, crashing through the underbrush and through stagnant puddles and short clearings of brambles and weeds. After a couple of hours, the forest gave way to gently rolling flatland, crossed by shallow streams with high-banked channels, the waxing moon shining through a gap in the clouds as the bitter night assaulted them and snowflakes hissed as they melted in the heat of the torches, pale moths drawn to them in a fluttering cloud. 

     

                The arable flatland soon gave way to marshy wetlands and with her keen eyesight, Lena could see the shadowy rippling of water as they forged deeper into it, the terrain levelling out and the air turning dank with the smell of standing water. She could hear things splashing about and the quiet sounds of water birds nesting in the reeds and grasses as they slowed their pace somewhat, mindful of the sudden change in the landscape that could plunge them into the deep, stagnant puddles or muddy bogs. Soon, the horses were splattered by black mud and gnats bothered them all, the tinny buzzing of them annoying Lena as she lingered somewhere between sleep and consciousness.

     

                It wasn’t much further once they reached the marshland and as the sky lightened somewhat on the horizon, Lena was able to see the slipstreams, lagoons, creeks and estuaries weaving through the green grass to the sea. Soon enough, there was the tang of salt on the breeze, and then the distant crash of the waves, before their path skirted westwards and they approached their destination at the edge of the cliffs, dropping off to the sea below. Before the cliff gave way though, there was the long limestone building of Kara’s home perched on the edge of it, blocks hewn out of the cliffside to build on top, leaving a three-storey residence that was beautifully ornate and belied what was hidden from view below.

     

                Reining in their horses as they came to a stop, there was a palpable air of relief and delight to have finally arrived, the gruelling pace and unforeseen delays making the welcome all the sweeter. The early morning was quiet and peaceful and Kara coaxed her horse to the front of their party, bringing it about as her face softened with a smile that Lena couldn’t see. A man was waiting for them, dressed in navy winter robes etched with tiny snowflakes and studded sea glass, his hands clasped behind his back and a warm smile on his face. 

                

                “My Lady.”

     

                “J’onn,” Kara said with weary relief, dismounting fluidly as the older man pressed a hand to his heart and bowed politely.

     

                She strode towards him and hugged him briefly, her fondness evident but Lena’s state more pressing as she gripped his shoulder and glanced back over at her wife. Concern crumpled her face and she swiftly moved back over to the horses, stopping beside Lena and holding the bridle to keep it steady.

     

                “Forgive me, we shall have to talk later, it has been an arduous trip,” Kara brusquely told him, reaching up to lift Lena out of the saddle, holding her in her arms as she faced her Steward. “I must see to my wife’s needs first.”

     

                His eyes slid to Lena and he nodded politely, smiling slightly. “Princess.”

     

                Lena offered up no response, save for a slow blink of confusion, so exhausted and in pain that her thoughts were muddled by the teas she’d been given. The only thing she made out in the grey of early dawn was a pale stretch of stone and wide steps leading into the open mouth of the ornately carved dwelling. Inside was cool and held the smell of the sea and Lena knew they must have been close, hearing the roar of the waves even if she hadn’t caught sight of it yet.

     

                Kara carried her down two flights of stairs, through the fortress carved into the limestone cliffs overlooking the sea, and brought them down to the lowest floor, level with the quay and the waves that lapped into the open rooms facing northwards. Striding into a room that held a half-moon tiered pool, open to the frigid sea, where residents could bathe in the saltwater that swept in with the current, Kara set Lena down a safe distance from the open mouth of the room on a stone bench and slipped into a small storeroom, emerging with a wooden tub. It was deep but not very long and she set it down on the smooth limestone floor and thrust her arms at the half-moon pool, guiding a ribbon of water into the tub and then glancing towards the door.

     

                “Alex!” she softly called out.

     

                It took a minute for her sister to appear, calmly stepping foot into the room and glancing at the silvery sea before looking at her sister. “Would you mind?” Kara asked, gesturing to the tub.

     

                Crossing over to the tub, Alex thrust her hands in, wetting the sleeves up to her elbows, and had the water steaming within moments, withdrawing her hands and splattering salt water over the damp floor. Kara nodded her thanks and fetched a clean towel and soap, her eyes trained on Lena’s grey face as her wife sagged on the bench.

     

                “I’ll ask Kelly to brew something stronger for her and ready a room,” Alex murmured, lingering a moment longer with uncertainty.

     

                “The one across from mine, away from the sea,” Kara said, meeting her eyes. “Can you bring something warm of mine for her too? Thank you.”

     

                “Are you sure you don’t need assistance? It will not be pleasant.”

     

                “She doesn’t need an audience to her pain.”

     

                Nodding, Alex left and Kara looked at Lena and let out a heavy sigh, her mouth thinning. Her blue eyes were regretful and somewhat sheepish as she crossed to Lena and knelt at her side, taking a limp, pale hand in her own.

     

                “It will be painful,” Kara admitted, her mouth turning down at the corners. “The salt will be agony against the wound but it will help stave off infection and help you heal quicker. The water will warm you through though; it will help some.”

     

                Shivering in a damp heap on the bench, Lena thought she would have withstood any amount of pain to be warm again. Nodding as she swallowed thickly, her face pinched with reluctant trepidation, she allowed Kara to lift her to her feet and carry her to the bath, her wife quietly instructing her to grip the side of the tub for balance as Lena kept the weight off her right foot.
