                Unclasping her cloak for her, Kara was gentle as she undressed her wife, removing the outer robe with the sodden hem, the thick tunic beneath, the wet boots and thick bandage and the wool leggings, hesitating with the billowing cotton shirt and watching Lena’s face intently as her wife averted her gaze, a muscle jumping in her jaw. Kara could see her fluttering pulse at her throat and had the bizarre urge to brush her lips over it, forgetting herself momentarily as she pulled off Lena’s shirt and held her tightly by the waist, her hands like hot brands as her wife’s stomach jolted.

     

                Shifting slightly, a wince rippling across her face as she twinged her ankle, Lena looked almost nauseously green and let go of the tub to wrap an arm around herself. “This is becoming far too common for my liking,” Lena muttered as her face puckered with annoyance.

     

                “Don’t worry, I’m not looking,” Kara murmured, expression earnest as Lena gazed out at the sea and the lightening day outside. 

     

                Letting out a gravelly laugh, Lena’s eyelids shuttered and she smiled thinly. “Thanks but I’m not sure how you’ll get me in the bath without an eyeful.”

     

                “You underestimate me.”

     

                Lena let out another laugh, her face furrowing slightly, wanting to be upset but Kara’s tenderness and gentle jokes distracted her from her feelings. Sobering up, Kara’s hand slid up her back and Lena felt a lump lodge itself in her throat as she blinked at her wife, too close for comfort, given Lena’s current state of undress and the shocking revelation that she would have liked Kara’s warm hands to hold her a little while longer. The thought startled her, blinking as she flinched slightly, Kara’s grip tightening as her lips parted, immediately thinking it was Lena’s ankle, that she had put too much weight on it.

     

                “Brace yourself,” Kara instructed her, tipping Lena slightly and hooking a hand beneath her right knee, lifting her with ease and lowering her into the hot water.

     

                It was an immediate balm to the brisk wind blowing in from the sea, and Lena’s skin smarted at the intensity of it, little nicks she hadn’t been aware of stinging slightly as she settled in the tub until it was just her lower right leg remaining aloft. Fixing her eyes on Lena’s face, Kara was tense as she lowered her leg into the hot salt water. It was like fire, the sting of it immediate as Lena let out a ragged sound of pain, sitting up as she sent water sloshing over the sides. A strong hand pushed her back down, pinning her firmly in place with a sheepish glance, as Lena choked on a breath, her eyes smarting with tears as she scowled.

     

                “It will pass,” Kara soothingly told her, face torn with guilt and pity. “Breathe deeply through it; it will pass.”

     

                Mouth clamping shut, Lena inhaled sharply through her nose and made a small, plaintive sound at the back of her throat. Kara held her in place for a long minute as the blinding pain in her ankle finally dimmed, or rather she became used to it and was able to stamp down the agony, making it small enough for her to forget about it. Letting out a ragged breath, she panted as her chest heaved, cheeks pallid and green eyes wide and stricken. 

     

                “Good, that’s it, that’s good,” Kara murmured, letting go of her.

     

                As her breathing slowed, Lena tipped her head back against the rim of the tub and swallowed the acidic taste of bile, eyelids fluttering as she caught glimpses of the stone ceiling, carved with marine life and the whorls of the current in the soft limestone. Laying spent against the rim of the tub, Lena let the hot water burrow into her bones, her energy failing her as her stiffness thawed and every scrape, bump and bruise made itself known. 

     

                She jumped slightly, splashing water, when Kara dipped a clean cloth into the bath, meeting her gaze with mild surprise, and began to lather up the soap. Gripping the edge of the tub, ever on edge around water, Lena was stiff and hawkishly watchful as Kara started to wipe away the accumulated dirt and sweat of travel from the arm closest to her. Lena didn’t say a word, her eyes fixed on her wife’s face as Kara dutifully committed herself to the task of bathing her wife, being gentle but thorough. 

     

                Finding it within herself to relax, Lena was limp as she stayed warm in the bath, even after the dawn came and the grey sky beyond the bathing room turned to a steady patter of rain, the waves rolling in frothy white and rough as they dashed against the tiered steps of the pool. A few lapped over, white foam rippling towards the tub, soaking Kara’s feet and the cuffs of her leggings and hem of her cloak as she knelt beside the tub, careless to it, or perhaps grateful for the invigorating rush of the cold sea. 

     

                She washed Lena’s hair for her too, an act that was so tender that Lena was shocked by the overwhelming craving for the contact, Kara’s fingers working through her dark locks, untangling knots, washing it clean and scooping handfuls of water along Lena’s hairline, carefully keeping it from running onto her face. It loosened something in Lena’s chest, that horrible pit of loneliness that she couldn’t fill, no matter how hard she tried - and Lena had tried very hard over the years. It felt bottomless, always starving, no matter what she fed into it, and now she could barely speak as she lay in the bath as the wife she had never wanted washed her hair and made her think about how nice it would be to be looked after in such a manner all the time, not just when she was injured.

     

                Once Kara made it to Lena’s injured ankle, the stitched edges of the wound where the bone had pierced the skin, she looked at Lena through her lashes, her movements slower, gentler as she dabbed at the crust of blood. Mouth thinning imperceptibly, Kara swallowed and looked back down at Lena’s ankle, an unreadable expression on her ducked face.

     

                “You saved my life,” she haltingly murmured after a moment.

     

                Opening her eyes as she sat up slightly, Lena let out a strained laugh, disbelieving as she covered her face with her hands and softly groaned. “That’s how fucked up everything is.”

     

                Letting out a small laugh of surprise, Kara shook her head, a wry smile on her lips. “Thank you,” she firmly replied. “Thank you, Lena, for saving my life.”

     

                “The favour was long overdue being returned. I think I still owe you half a dozen more times though.”

     

                “You owe me nothing.” 

     

                Shrugging noncommittally, Lena watched Kara wipe away the dried blood with a brooding look on her face, her elbow propped up on the edge of the tub, her cheek on her fist. Once Kara had finished, she wrung the cloth out and climbed to her feet to fetch a towel and the clothes Alex had brought in unobtrusively mid-bath. Returning with the bundle, Kara set it down away from the outgoing tide and helped Lena to her feet before wrapping her in the soft length of fabric and lifting her out of the tub. Wrapping the towel tightly around herself with one hand as she gripped the tub for balance with the other, Lena watched as Kara raised the bathwater and pushed it towards the writhing sea, joining the rippling tide with a splash and a fine spray.

     

                “Do you have something against doors?” Lena shakily asked as a tremor wracked her with the gust of wind drying the water on her skin.

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter, Kara shrugged. “It is easier to be by the water when there are fewer obstacles inhibiting the access to it.”

     

                “Certainly an interesting decision to come here during the winter,” Lena snidely commented.

     

                “It may be somewhat warmer south, away from the coast, but you would not thank me for living in a wallless tower, even in the mild storms.”

     

                “Mm, perhaps.”

     

                “If it appeases you, your room will have four walls and a brazier for a fire, which I shall endeavour to have burning nonstop. Come, let us get you dry and clothed; you will feel much better then.”

     

                Briskly towelling herself off, Lena had to accept Kara’s help to get the clean clothes on, obediently putting her arms through the holes on the chemise and then the thicker nightgown, the cotton softly pilled and smelling of lavender and sea salt, beautifully embroidered with shells in the same off-white. A heavy wool robe was pulled on afterwards, the washed-out blue of the sea on a rainy day, verging on grey, and Kara belted it firmly at Lena’s waist, holding the folds closed, blocking out the worst of the wind and falling almost to her feet.

     

                “I bet you didn’t expect to be doing all of this when you took me as a wife.”

     

                “I took you as my wife expecting to care for you; I admit I have not done as well of a job as I intended but yes, I did expect to be caring for you. Albeit, I expected you to be more … suited to our lifestyle. I didn’t anticipate your lack of skill with any weapon or self-defence, or living in the forest, or speaking our language, or-”

     

                “You’ve made your point,” Lena said with somewhat bitter amusement.

     

                Kara smoothed out her robe and then cupped her shoulders, giving Lena a tired smile, eyes grave and bluer than the sea. “That is to say, I am sorry for my harsh words on the road. You are not to blame for your inability to build a fire or saddle a horse.”

     

                Shrugging as she glanced aside, mouth twisting wryly, Lena swallowed thickly. “I mean, I could have made more of an effort to learn those things.”

     

                “There is still time. More time than you have had thus far to fill with what you please.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena nodded and looked out at the sea as it rushed back in, lapping up over the top tier but not flooding close enough to touch her feet. Still, she shifted restlessly and Kara squeezed her shoulder gently.

     

                “Come, you should rest. I will take you to your room.” She hesitated, uncertainty flashing across her face. “Would you like to walk or should I carry you?”

     

                Lena softly snorted and rolled her eyes, “I can walk, if you lend me your arm.”

     

                Holding her left arm out, Kara gave her a gracious smile and let Lena hobble out of the room, leaning heavily on her every other step. It was slow going but Kara was patient, affording her the choice to make her way upstairs by her own means, and she led them down a wide stone hallway and came to a stop at a seemingly random door, curtains hanging in the open mouth of it. Holding it aside, Kara helped her across the threshold and Lena found herself looking at a rather bare room, a large bed made of limestone and driftwood monopolising the middle, a lit brazier set off to the side of it for warmth, and her two sister-in-laws standing near a wooden table on the other side, steeping tea and making a poultice, side by side.

     

                They glanced up slowly at the arrival of the other two women, which made Lena think they’d already heard them coming, and Kara helped her over to the bed, an arm around her back as she eased Lena down onto the mattress. Swinging her leg up and adjusting herself against the soft pillows, Lena felt she could have fallen asleep right then, the room pleasantly warm, although it could’ve been hotter after the snow she’d endured, and she let out a heavy sigh.

     

                “Your ankle will need to be bound again,” Kelly said as she set the pestle down and moved over to the bed, perching on the edge of it near Lena’s foot. “But first I will apply a poultice to help with infection and rebind it later. You should not walk on it any further.”

     

                Her dark eyes slid to Kara, who had pulled up a small stool beside the bed, nodding as she agreed with the advice. Lena watched as she reclined on the pillows, getting a good look at the curved row of stitches, the wound faintly red from the abrasive salt water and heat of her bath, and felt her stomach swoop slightly at the thought of the bone piercing the skin. Watching as Kelly carefully applied the muddled herbs and honey in a thick paste, Lena felt the residual tension bleed out of her, feeling safe despite the latest set of unfamiliar surroundings. 

     

                “Here, drink this,” Alex instructed her, carrying a steaming tin cup over to her and pressing it into Lena’s hand.

     

                The smell was bitter and it didn’t taste much better as Lena took a sip, her mouth turning down with distaste as she swallowed. “That’s foul.”

     

                “It’s good for you,” Alex retorted. “Drink it. All of it. You will thank me later.”

     

                Doubting that very much, Lena murmured something intelligible beneath her breath and tipped the cup back, draining it in two swallows and coughing as her face screwed up. She caught sight of Kara smiling slightly and gave her a withering look, which made her wife smile more, nose crinkling, eyes creasing.

     

                “We should leave you to rest,” Kara murmured once Kelly had placed a sheer piece of linen around the poultice. 

     

                Climbing to her feet, Kara helped Lena beneath the blankets and tucked her in, her wife’s pale face furrowing with confusion, her eyelids already heavy. The tea Alex had given her was strongly steeped and filled with several herbs to make her drowsy, and Lena made a low sound at the back of her throat, acknowledgement of Kara’s departure, ready to sleep in a bed for the first time in days.

     

                Kara slipped out of the room after her sister and sister-in-law, hovering a moment to glance backwards at her wife, pale and small amidst the sea of pillows and thick quilts, face peaceful and dark hair fanning out across the pillows like spilt ink. She sighed softly and let the curtain fall, obscuring the room behind it, running a hand over her face and hurrying a step to catch up to the other women.

     

                “I should meet with J’onn,” Kara murmured. 

     

                “There will be time enough for politicking,” Alex rolled her eyes, wrapping an arm around her sister’s shoulders. “Go and swim in the sea for a while; it has been months since you have had the pleasure.”

     

                Humming distractedly to herself, Kara rubbed her forehead, glancing back over her shoulder. “I shouldn’t go too far - she might need something.”

     

                “She will be asleep for hours, if not most of the day,” Alex snorted. “I brewed it strong enough to put a bear to sleep. I don’t believe her constitution is that strong, although she is not as soft as I initially thought.”

     

                “She’s proud. That’s what it is. She will hate that she cried in front of everyone, that she couldn’t keep up. You saw her; she was miserable the entire ride but she wouldn’t take more rest than the rest of us, and the snow wasn’t nearly as bothersome to you or I. And she’s barely eaten a thing in days. I should have fetched her something to eat before she slept.”

     

                Kelly let out a soft laugh, looping her arm through Kara’s, sandwiching her between the two women. “You sound almost as if you care for her.”

     

                “I do care. Of course I care. She is my responsibility.”

     

                “Do not twist the truth on me,” Kelly murmured as she bumped Kara with her hip. “If you mean to lie, speak English instead of talking circles around the truth to get away with it.”

     

                “I’m not-” Kara went to retort, the words cutting off as her throat closed up.

     

                Scowling, her cheeks reddened and she shook off the touch of both women, picking up her pace. “I think I will go for a swim. The salt air will clear my mind more than your meddling words.”

     

                Taking the nearest staircase at a brisk pace, Kara left a stream of clothes in her wake as she followed the familiar path to the sea, the ghosts of her childhood brushing faintly against her mind from the years she had been raised there. She was in her shift by the time she reached the stone quay that extended into the sea, making a left and walking until the quay gave way to sand. Shedding her chemise, she waded out into the shallows, heedless of the cold, picking her way over the pockmarked rocks and the slippery seaweed clumps floating haplessly in the surf, until she was up to her thighs as her skin prickled with goosebumps, stinging as the salt got into minor cuts and abrasions, scouring her skin. The sea was greyer than she had remembered as she plunged into the water, letting it close over her head and feeling the current tug at her.

     

                For a moment, she was surrounded by the strange silence that came with the sea blotting out its own sound, the absence of the crash of waves like a sort of deafness as the salt stung her eyes and she cut through the water, catching sight of little minnows in the shallows. Kara went with the motion of the waves, letting it lull her in and out as she drifted aimlessly, the water invigoratingly cold, making her teeth ache as her extremities tingled. Once she was far enough out, she resurfaced, inhaling cold air as waves lapped at her face.

     

                Submerging herself again, Kara swam around until she was tired, which was too soon for her liking, tired from their travels, and cut through the waves to sit on the beach a mile down the coast. She had always loved that section of the beach, the unending stretch of green marsh and forest, the ever-changing colour of the water, the little pebbles and shells nestled in the golden sand before the rolling dunes gave way to damp soil and the shallow ribbons of the estuaries that eventually met the sea.

     

                Emerging from the sea, she flopped down on the sand and stared up at the cloudy sky, her chest rising and falling, grains of sand sticking to her skin and the brisk wind drying the water. Closing her eyes, Kara lost herself in her thoughts for a while before sitting up, watching the waves lap at the shore as gulls careened overhead, whitecaps marking the grey sea as the waves rolled in, the swell big and rough. It was cold by the sea but she hardly felt the chill in the air, a brooding look on her face as she hugged her knees and listened to the creatures around her, drinking in the familiarity of it that she had sorely missed. Frogs croaking in the wetlands behind the dunes, birds nesting in the tall sea grass, crabs scuttling along the beach and the splash of fish in puddles of water gathered in the dips and valleys of the terrain.

     

                She stayed out there for an hour, the bracing air helping to straighten out some things before she climbed to her feet, brushing off the sand and walking back towards the carved cliffs further down the coast. Picking her way over pitted rocks, driftwood and dried seaweed, Kara felt the knotted tension that had persisted for months, even lingering somewhat at her mother’s hall, bleed away, as if the sea was a balm for all of her problems. It felt criminal to have been away from it for so long, like she was recovering a piece of herself that had been stolen, and she tried not to think about how quickly the season would pass, unsure of what it would bring afterwards.

     

                Along the way, she picked sea violets in shades of cream, powdery blue and lavender as she wandered the dunes, verging on where the sand gave way to soil, and gathered a fistful as she walked purposely towards home. As the dunes gave way to the soil, the landscape climbed up as the sand gave way to rock, the limestone residence that had belonged to her family for thousands of years rising from the top of the cliff and burrowing into it over the lower two floors. She came at it from the lower floor, level with the sea, rounding the rocky outcropping of the cliff as she skirted through the shallows, shells and stones underfoot, sand shifting with the tide, and caught sight of Alex sitting on the smooth worn steps of the side entrance.

     

                Her sister rose to her feet and picked up a heavy robe with her, holding it out as Kara approached. Mindful of the flowers, Kara took the robe and slipped her arms through, belting it at the front and giving her sister a rueful smile. Alex cupped her shoulders and sighed heavily, her brown eyes aching with concern.

     

                “You should not feel angry for your feelings.”

     

                “I’m not angry,” Kara replied, the words ringing true. 

     

                “Frustrated then. It is alright for you to care for her, you know. No ill can come of that if you insist it is not love.”

     

                “It isn’t in the way that you mean.”

     

                Hesitating, trying to see the trickery in Kara’s response, the way she might have been able to skirt around the meaning, Alex seemed to accept her words without argument and nodded. “Alright then. Just in case you do care for her, I have checked in while you were off swimming and she has not stirred. She is fast asleep.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                “Now, come and eat. You will have missed the fresh catches, I’m sure.”

     

                She had, wistfully thinking of the taste of brine in the freshly caught variety of fish, crabs, oysters and mussels, octopus and squid, lobsters and little cockles and the soft seaweed baked into bread or eaten raw, silky and overwhelmingly salty. Walking to the vast kitchens with her sister, Kara found a clay cup and filled it with fresh water before depositing the handful of flowers into it and taking a seat at one end of the kitchen. Bread had already been baked and there was a basket of oysters for shucking. Tearing the end off a fresh loaf, Kara picked up a discarded knife and started to prise open an oyster, eating without preamble as her sister clicked her tongue and moved about.

     

                While Alex prepared vinegar with shallots and garlic, nudged fresh butter across the table with a plate of little sardines, silvery in the light of the kitchen fires, and started filleting a hunk of salmon, Kara wolfed down a dozen oysters and the bread, incorporating the other foods as her sister passed them to her. The sharp vinegar cut through the brine with a pleasant sting and Kara felt she could have eaten the entire contents of the kitchen, so homesick that she wanted to fill herself up with the place. She couldn’t count the days her father had taken her out with nets, wading through the shallows, or on a little boat, tying knots and reeling in fish, sometimes staying along the reef as she learned how to hunt with a trident, as proficient with it as any weapon she’d been tutored in. What Kara wouldn’t give to go shrimping with him once more.

     

                Eating her fill, joined by Alex, Kelly, Nia and Querl as they trickled in, the others off resting in guest quarters or busying themselves with other interests around the place, Kara felt content and idled away the rest of the morning until she went in search of J’onn, stopping by Lena’s room first to deposit the cup of flowers on the table and then seeking out her Steward. He was in a small office dedicated to his use while she was away, making notes in a thick ledger. Glancing up at her arrival, he rose to his feet and smiled warmly at her.

     

                “You’re looking well.”

     

                “This is the best I’ve felt in months,” Kara admitted. “The sea air agrees with me better than the constant confines of the forest and nary a lake to swim in.”

     

                “And is married life agreeable to you?”

     

                Giving him a weary look, Kara pulled out the chair on the other side of his desk and curled up on it, legs crossed and robe arranged over her thighs and knees. “It is … an adjustment.”

     

                “Even the ones that are chosen for love are never smooth sailing. I know that better than most.”

     

                “And how is M’gann? I did not see her when we arrived.”

     

                “She’s well. She’s gone fishing for the day; if we had known you would be arriving I’m sure she would have stayed but you are days later than expected.”

                

                “Trouble on the road. Twice over, in fact. I assume word has not passed the mountains yet?”

     

                “It’s been peaceful waters all since you were here last winter. The catch has been good, trade has been stable, and the water levels have been managed well. The stores are nearly full to bursting to get us through this winter and we had a few new additions to our stables. The worst that happened was we lost one of the bigger boats to a nasty shark during the summer; fortunately, no one was injured.”

     

                “Thank you, J’onn. You are a rock amidst this brewing storm. I fear it will get worse yet; I … well, I have cut off the hand of the Unseelie Queen-”

     

                “Pardon?”

     

                Giving him a droll look, Kara smiled thinly and ran a hand over her salt-crusted curls. “It was in retaliation to a threat on mine and my wife’s life the day we were to leave their Court. Due to unfortunate circumstances, the Prince is also alive. A shocking revelation that caused quite a skirmish as we fled. We were both injured and had to spend a few days recovering at my mother’s hall, and then Lena was injured again on the way here. A broken leg on account of her saving my life.”

     

                “A brave woman indeed. One could not expect less from a Princess raised by the Unseelie.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara said with a crooked smile. “That was a lie, in fact. News does indeed trickle here slowly. She was raised by humans , unbeknownst to the Seelie when we made the truce. More Unseelie trickery, which should have been expected in hindsight, but she is learning the ways of our people - albeit slowly. We will make a Fae of her yet.”

     

                “Then you are committed to your vows for the sake of peace?” J’onn delicately inquired.

     

                Grimacing, Kara shrugged half-heartedly and watched as a humanoid water element set down a tray of tea, summoned by J’onn. “Yes. Even now, I cling to the shreds of the truce and hope it has not all been in vain.”

     

                He poured tea for them both and Kara stirred honey into hers, murmuring her thanks and then leaning forward to tap the open ledger. “We should begin. I have been gone far too long.”

     

                They sat in his office for most of the afternoon, Kara asking questions as they went over figures, letters and documents, J’onn pulling out sheaths of paper and rattling off their stock of certain goods and how much was traded. They had more tea and shared a late lunch together, picking at the tray of food as Kara was brought up to speed on her lands, prospects and people. 

     

                After they were finished, she thanked J’onn wholeheartedly and felt a little more in control of things now, her life feeling less like a mess of indescribable proportions and more of a compartmentalised mess. It was a relief to not have to worry about the state of her holdings, although Winn would be returning to Argo for her to manage it in her stead, as he had been through the autumn, and she was eager to speak to him as well and feel reassured in her decision to make him a Steward in her stead. 

     

                Satisfied for the time being, Kara went for another swim, leaving her robe on the quay and sticking to the shallows as she twisted beneath the hulls of little bobbing rowing boats, basking in the sting of the salt and the prickling cold of the water. She didn’t emerge until the day was inching towards dusk, the grey clouds dimming as the sun struck westwards to the distant horizon, the surface of the water shimmering silver.

     

     

                Lena woke to the smells of the sea, brine and seaweed drifting in on the early winter wind. The distant sound of gulls crying brought her from the grasp of sleep and she sat up in bed, feeling as if she’d been given a horse tranquiliser. Running a hand through her salt-tangled hair, she felt gritty from the seawater and her face furrowed with displeasure at the tang of it clinging to her skin beneath the cut of fresh soap. She was alone in her room, that much was apparent, but her eyes snagged on a little clay cup of violets in pastel shades, sitting on the table against the wall. Someone had checked up on her; Lena didn’t have to ask to know it was Kara.

     

                Pushing back the heavy blankets, Lena climbed out of bed, balancing unsteadily on her good foot, drawn forward by the sound of the crashing sea. Hopping forward as gracefully as she could, Lena ducked her head through the curtain as she leaned on the carved door frame and looked up and down the hallway. The sprawling house she’d only caught a glimpse of felt like a water-worn pebble, the driftwood furniture and porous walls of the limestone like parts of the cliffs that had been battered by the sea for however long the place had stood. It felt as if it had always been there, weather-worn and lived in and loved. Lena shivered at the sea wind that blew in through the rooms connected to the hallway running the length of the floor and remembered that Kara had requested a room across from her own.

     

                Continuing her shuffling hop towards the billowing curtains of the room directly across from hers, Lena gripped the door frame and brushed the curtains aside as she ducked her head in. The room was more spacious than hers, a bed similar to her own situated with the headboard backed to the stretch of sea that Lena could see through the open wall of ornate pillars and arches that dropped off to nothing but the sea and rocks below. There was a paper screen painted with herons standing in marshy waters, a driftwood vanity with a mirror of polished silver and a few chairs and tables scattered about with woven rugs, baskets of bound scrolls and shelves of books. It was lived in and comfortable, a towel discarded on the back of a chair, wet footprints on the pitted limestone floors.

     

                Kara was standing in the open archway, her hair damp and curling from the salt, a long robe pulled on over skin that had dried with the tidemarks of salt from her second swim. She turned at the sound of Lena’s arrival, her expression softening with amusement.

     

                “Why am I not surprised you would ignore Kelly’s advice and walk on your broken leg?”

     

                Shrugging slightly, Lena gave her a wan smile. “I woke up alone.”

     

                “I was listening,” Kara lightly informed her, Lena’s face furrowing slightly, uncertain and wary. 

     

                The wind was strong as it blew in off the coast, salt spray crashing up from the powerful waves and dotting the edge of the room. Lena blinked in surprise, shivering in the bitter cold at the proximity to the water as the northern wind whipped against her cheeks. She wasn’t sure how Kara could stand to sleep in a room like that.

     

                “Here,” Kara murmured, crossing the room to her and taking her arm.

     

                She led Lena over to a chair facing the sea, nestling her down on the wide seat and then fetching a few thick blankets, tucking her in and briefly meeting her gaze. Lena shivered and she wasn’t sure it was entirely from the cold, although the sight of the sea bucking and heaving in great swells below and as far as she could see did little for her comfort. It wasn’t quite dark yet, the grey sky still light enough to hold the sun, but it was getting late and Lena could feel it in the slow stillness of the early evening, listening to the gulls cry out. One banked and perched on the edge of the room, cocking its head to the side and clicking its beak before it took off again.

     

                Lena stared at the grey-green water rolling in, unable to see the way the waves dashed against the walls below, crashing through any openings and lapping up to the far walls of the rooms set on the sea. It was a long drop down, the ceilings of each floor twenty feet high. She had no desire to look, to see the cold sea below in the waning light of the deep grey sky as the waves were dragged out with the tide and lapped back against the cliffside, backed by the strong winds.

     

                “What is this place?” Lena asked after a long minute of silence as they listened to the sea and the wind.

     

                Looking down at her, mildly surprised by the answer, Kara smiled sadly. “This is the last home of the rulers of old. The home of my ancestors for millennia. It’s where I was raised - mostly.”

     

                The way she said it was indifferent, brusquely, as if wanting to get the explanation out of the way quickly. Lena knew it was a front, knowing it was a piece of Kara’s grief that she didn’t like to talk about in the same way that Lena didn’t like to talk about losing her own mother. She left it alone, grasping at the other flippant comments with interest.

     

                “This is where your family lived when you were still royalty?”

     

                “Well I never was,” Kara mused. “There were four royal families. This was long before the Courts, so long ago that only a few of us are old enough to remember that time. One for each element. There are different cultural groups within that, of course, and it was the Seafolk side of my family that were the rulers of all the Waterfolk, holding dominion over every river, lake, sea, stream, puddle. The same went for the other elements but … we are not a perfect race. There were fights that became territorial battles and then full-blown warfare and bloodshed. It was endless, for thousands of years, until there was an attempt at peace. The four rulers met and three decided to abdicate in favour of democracy. One did not. There were those who didn’t agree with the idea of a Council, of a democratic approach to leading after so many millennia of Kings and Queens, and there were those who were tired of being ruled by one person. It split the land, right down the river, creating the divide of the Courts into Seelie and Unseelie once there was no clear divide between elemental loyalty. Families were torn apart and alliances were formed. The bloodshed never stopped. The Seelie have always been more numerous, had more land, yet the Unseelie have never relinquished their throne or given up on their desire to claim more territory.”

     

                “So … my family are the original Earthfolk that have ruled for thousands of years?”

     

                “Yes, after a fashion. Lillian is not of royal blood but is Queen out of marriage to the King and no apparent suitable heir - you were believed to be unsuitable given your mother - but … well, I suppose Lillian changed her mind out of desperation and had no choice but to instate you as her heir to make the deal more valuable to the Seelie Court. Of course, she would not have abdicated in your favour, despite your blood claim.”

     

                “Thank God for that,” Lena snorted. “Although, I do think I would make a less murderous Queen, regardless of how long I actually kept the throne. Which wouldn’t be long, according to you.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Kara’s cheek dimpled and her eyes were bright with amusement. “If it pleases you, I would slaughter everyone that attacked you, for however long you were on the throne, until I fell before you.”

     

                “That’s … almost sweet,” Lena slowly replied, wrinkling her nose. “You know, you don’t always have to be so self-sacrificing though. If you save me too many times … well, I might just start relying on you too much.”

     

                “Would that be so awful? To rely on your wife?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena was quiet for a moment, staring out at the sea with a pensive look on her face. Eventually turning her attention back to Kara, she let out a soft sigh, her expression turning almost tender. “No, it would not be so awful for me at all. But … perhaps unfair to you.”

     

                “Why is that?”

     

                Biting her lip, Lena cast her eyes downwards, staring at the length of Kara’s shins visible beneath the hem of her long robe. The robe was decorated with little seed pearls and silver and cream thread against the deep grey of it and Lena picked out little seahorses and starfish as she swallowed past the tightness in her throat.

     

                “I would hate to be a burden to you.”

     

                Fluidly sinking to her knees, moving like water itself as she folded, her robe pooling with her, Kara straightened as she leaned forward, cradling Lena’s face in her hands. Her palms were pleasantly calloused against Lena’s cheeks and her eyelids shuttered at the contact as Kara smoothed the pad of a thumb over her cheeks. She smelled of salt and Lena had the thought that she would taste like it too, the tang of the sea cutting through the clean scent of rain that usually clung to Kara. 

     

                Eyelashes fluttering, it took a concentrated effort to meet Kara’s intense stare, unable to move as she remained still, seated with the pile of blankets over her lap. Giving her a wavering smile, hesitant but earnest, Kara swallowed thickly.

     

                “You’re not a burden to me.”

     

                “I’ve been a burden to everyone who has been given me,” Lena murmured, surly and vulnerably childish as she looked at Kara through her lashes, wary and trying to act unaffected. “They always want to get rid of me in the end.”

     

                “Then I shall be the first to keep you, so speak no more of burdens of abandonment. I will not give you back, even if your mother comes with all the strength of the Unseelie Court,” Kara insisted. “You are mine and I am yours, and that is not a burden, it is a marriage.”

     

                “Until we can break it.”

     

                “Break it?” Kara asked, confusion flitting across her face.

     

                Wariness crept into Lena’s features at the bewildered look she received and she licked her lips, a fleeting smile crossing her mouth. “Well, yes, once there’s no need for a truce, we can end it. We’ll both be free from the vows. That was the plan, right? My plan, anyway. It’s what- it’s what Lex promised me. To be free of my marriage vows.”

     

                Sinking, sitting on her heels, Kara opened and closed her mouth for a moment before delicately clearing her throat. “Lena … there is no breaking an oath sworn in the Fae tongue. Nothing short of death. We may one day live apart, live our separate lives, but we would still be wed, even if in name only. Your brother … well, it is evident he intended to have at least one of us dead, so to that event, I suppose he would have upheld his end of the bargain. But … it is not so simple as to renege on words that were said with binding truth. I’m sorry if I misled you-”

     

                “It’s fine,” Lena quickly cut her off, the ghost of a smile that crossed her dazed face slightly bitter, her green eyes unfocused beneath creased brows. “It’s … my mistake.”

     

                “I hope one day it is peaceful enough for us to live separately - if that is what you wish.”

     

                “Is that what you wish?”

     

                “I- you know what fate is in store for me. Regardless of our marriage vows, I am to love someone and bring about their death. If you should choose to stay at my side … I hope you will not think me too monstrous in that eventuality.”

     

                A thin smile crossed Lena’s face and she slumped in the chair, her scepticism written plainly in the corners of her mouth and the faint creasing of her eyes.

     

                “I wouldn’t think that. Mostly because I don’t believe you would ever kill someone you love.”

     

                “The prophecy-“

     

                Shrugging, Lena lazily fluttered her fingers, “is a bunch of words. How can they predict your future? Unless you let it.”

     

                Face furrowing with a severe look of stubborn insistence, almost surprised by Lena’s audacity to contradict her beliefs, Kara spluttered. “You don’t understand-“

     

                “I do. We have fortune tellers and psychics and other hacks in my world too, you know. They tell everyone they’re going to meet the love of their lives and they’re communing with a dead relative. It’s a cheap trick. You can believe it, that’s fine, but I’m not too worried about it. I mean, regardless, you won’t be the thing to kill me so it doesn’t concern me in the slightest.”

     

                Kara flinched slightly as her brow creased and she bowed her head, fiddling with her fingers in her lap as she was silent for a moment. “Well, you see, it is a rite of passage amongst our kind, not … a cheap trick, no charlatans or fanciful tales involved. Everyone is taken to a seer to determine their fate. A record is made of each prophecy; I have not known them to be wrong yet. Not a single one. They may not arise the way anticipated but, nevertheless, it always transpires.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena’s scepticism faded to doubt as she blinked in surprise. “Oh.”

     

                Looking up, Kara gave her a placid smile and straightened, pushing herself to her feet and ducking to press a kiss to the middle of Lena’s brow as she tipped her head to look up at Kara, a pinch between her eyebrows. “But that is not for you to concern yourself with, as you say.”

    Chapter 20

                The rise and fall of crashing waves, muted by walls but distinct, was the first thing that pricked Lena’s awareness as she woke. The heavy blankets and furs covering her fell back slightly as she shifted into a more comfortable position, rubbing her eyes and feeling the dull ache in her right leg as she moved it. 

     

                A few days had passed since their arrival at Kara’s ancestral home, and her ankle was healing well, inhumanly quick, under the care of those who came to bathe the stitched wound with saltwater and slip herbal teas down her throat. It was an isolating experience to be bed-bound in a strange place, spending hours staring at the carved cornices, door frame and ceiling as she made out the little creatures and plantlife in the whirling designs, picking up the occasional snatch of conversation as someone walked past, waiting for one of Kara’s periodic visits.

     

                It was early, the grey light of dawn streaming in through the covered windows behind her, the cold breeze of the night chill sweeping in, making the flames of the small brazier waver as the fire kept the chill of early winter at bay in her room. The room was airy and the natural light filtered in high above, high enough to stop anyone from easily accessing her quarters, and Lena hated how draughty the place was, how the roar of the sea seemed unending, almost maddening as she breathed in the tang of salt and brooded over the variety of seafish soups she’d been brought to aid in her healing and keep her warm. 

     

                Alone in her room, she was left abed by the strict orders not to walk on her ankle, which she obeyed only because it did hurt whenever she tried to hobble about, and she found her loneliness frustrating, a pressing ache in her chest. Determined to not squander another day with only a handful of minutes of conversation to occupy her otherwise empty time, Lena tried to think of something else to do.

     

                It wasn’t long before the sounds of voices reached her ears, and she recognised the soft tones from one of them, muted by the walls, but definitely Kara. Waiting until the voices neared and the others faded, her sensitive ears could pick out her wife’s footsteps across the hallway. Hesitating, biting her lip, Lena pushed herself up on the mattress and shifted to the edge of the bed, sliding off it and keeping her weight on her good leg.

     

                Steadying herself, Lena dragged on the heavy robes folded over a stool and began a painful hobble towards the doorway, taking her first steps beyond it since she’d been confined there days before, parting the curtains as the frigid stone floor burrowed through the sole of her left foot. She wasn’t quiet by any means but Kara must have been distracted by her thoughts because when Lena stopped in the wide doorway to her room, Kara didn’t turn. 

     

                Lena lingered a moment and watched as Kara undid the robe she was wearing, the heavy velvet sliding over her skin, still holding onto a summer tan earned from years outdoors on the water. Knowing she should leave, or at least have the courtesy to look away, Lena took in the expanse of tanned back, nicked with old scars, silvery again Kara’s skin, the way her spine arched, a swan-like grace to her wife’s posture and elegant movements as she set the robe over the back of a chair set before her vanity. 

     

                She moved slowly, deliberately and eternally patient, her willowy figure cast against the dark grey sea visible through the open north archways like a painting. Of course, Lena had seen her undressed before - somewhat - but she’d never had the chance to openly observe her wife, to take in the muscles of her back, the length of her legs, the way her blonde hair fell in a shiny sheet to her waist, unbraided at that time of the morning, without Kara observing her in turn. 

     

                After a moment, she blinked and shook her head slightly, feeling a stab of annoyance for intruding. Making to leave, her left foot scuffed the floor as she turned slightly, intent on heading back to her own room. The quiet sound broke through Kara’s reverie though, the fae’s body stiffening momentarily, and Lena froze. Kara turned slightly, her eyebrows rising in mild surprise, although her quick judgement on whether the sound was a threat had already alerted her to the fact that it was Lena. 

     

                Opening and closing her mouth as she leaned heavily on her good leg, Lena smiled with uncertainty. “Sorry, I didn’t mean to disturb you.”

     

                Reaching for her freshly shed robe, Kara shrugged it on, belting it at the front and then turning to face Lena. “It is no disturbance; I was just about to swim.”

     

                “Oh, well, I won’t impose.”

     

                “You are not,” Kara lightly replied, cocking her head to the side, a faint smile in the corners of her mouth and crease of her eyes. “A swim is not so important in comparison to being sought out by one’s wife.”

     

                “Maybe in a real marriage.”

     

                “Is ours not real? We said the vows.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena quietly scoffed, folding her arms over her chest as her lips twisted with wry humour. “You know what I mean.”

     

                Smile widening a fraction, Kara acquiesced with a nod. “So … what troubles you?”

     

                “Hm?”

     

                “What troubles you? It’s not often you seek me out for the pleasure of my company. In fact, it would seem that most often you find no pleasure in my company.”

     

                She said it lightly, a teasing edge to her words, but there was a wounded flicker in the depths of her blue eyes that Lena could read from across the room. It was even more unbalancing to hear the words, given her reason for being there.

     

                “Oh … um, actually … well, I haven’t really spoken to anyone in a few days. It was getting a little … lonely. So I guess you’re wrong; I am seeking the pleasure of your company.”

     

                Kara had visited daily, several times in fact, usually around mealtimes, before she’d taken her own with whoever of their party remained, but they were fleeting, pleasantries and inquiries as to how Lena’s ankle was healing before she was swept off with business. Lena didn’t begrudge her the busy schedule of her position, or the indulgence of her swims and boating excursions as Kara made up for lost time away from the sea and any big body of water. Still, it didn’t lessen her loneliness to be content with the way of things.

     

                Surprise flitted across Kara’s face and she stepped forward, her expression softening. “Forgive me, I had thought you needed rest.”

     

                Ducking her head in a nod, Lena smiled thinly. “I did. I’m just not good at being bored.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing for a moment, Kara drew closer, her long velvet robe swaying around her shins as she drew nearer, the smell of salt on her skin, ink staining her fingertips from hours spent working on ledgers at her desk. Extending a hand, Kara flipped it, her calloused palm held out to Lena, who slid her own hand into the rough grasp without consciously deciding to.

     

                “Forgive me for my lack of attention. How fares your leg today?”

     

                “It’s healing quickly. It doesn’t hurt so much.”

     

                “It’s the saltwater; it aids in healing. I have a gift for you until it has fully healed though. Come.”

     

                She led Lena further into her airy room, settling her onto a low driftwood stool before moving over to the table covered in a variety of belongings; pieces of driftwood, oyster shells, quills, curls of wood shavings and stacks of books, rolls of parchment and a few daggers and half-fletched arrows. Lena was surprised by the mess of Kara’s rooms, so used to her orderliness, but she supposed Kara had never had all of her things with her in the Unseelie Court, that perhaps her wife usually left clutter and half-finished projects in her wake.

     

                Hefting a length of wood leaning against one end of the long table, Kara smiled as she ran a hand down the length of it. It was ornately carved with flowers and vines, little thorns and leaves, and she turned it in her grasp with a pleased look on her face as she crossed over to Lena. Kara smiled softly at her, holding it out as Lena took the stick with some confusion.

     

                “It is to assist your walking until your ankle can bear your weight again. I carved it myself.”

     

                Lena’s eyes studied the intricate carvings before they flitted back up to Kara’s face. Her eyebrows furrowed together in confused fondness, thinking of the hours Kara must have spent each evening, each spare moment, carving the motifs into the length of wood, turning something ordinary into a work of beauty. 

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding nonchalantly, as if the act was nothing, Kara cleared her throat gently. “Do you think you’re fit for a walk?”

     

                “Now?”

     

                “Yes, now. It would seem I have been a negligent wife.”

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter, Lena gripped the walking stick tightly and pushed herself to her feet. “Not negligent. Busy.”

     

                She used the walking stick to hobble forward, keeping the weight off her right ankle, and Kara stepped in to loop her arm through Lena’s, steadying her and offering her something to lean against as they made for the wide door. The entire palace seemed a fraction too large, the door big enough for them to walk through side by side, the ceilings soaring above them, and Lena felt dwarfed by the sheer size of the place as Kara led her down the hallway. So far, she’d only had a brief glimpse of the sprawling place, and she looked around with interest as Kara led her downstairs and through adjoining hallways, until she took Lena through a side entrance and their bare feet hit sand. 

     

                “The fresh air will do you some good,” Kara informed her as the first gust of the brisk sea air buffeted them.

     

                Lena’s dark hair whipped around her and she shivered in the heavy layers of her clothes, already dreading the worsening weather, which seemed inevitable. They were already a few weeks into the early days of winter and the sky was an overcast grey, turning the choppy water to steel as Lena breathed in the cold wind, chilling her through as it got into her lungs. 

     

                “The seaside agrees with you,” she commented as Kara led them along the beach, leaving an odd trail in their wake of three feet, the walking stick and the occasional light impression of Lena’s right toes. 

     

                Glancing sideways at her, Kara smiled slightly. “It does. But not with you, I think. You are already missing the forest.”

     

                Lena’s eyes strayed to the south, the haze of trees in the distance striking a pang of longing in her chest. She frowned slightly, taking in the would-be enormous pines, birches, oaks, maples and firs, the speckled golds and reds of autumn leaves on the cusp of yielding to winter, turning over Kara’s assumption as they slowly walked, wearing the idea smooth.

     

                “I didn’t realise that I could miss it so much,” Lena said, trying to articulate the confused feeling in her chest, that ache that hadn’t been there until she’d reached the mountains. “When we went to your mom’s home, when we were so far above it, it was like I’d physically lost something. How is it possible to miss it so much? The trees. I used to like getting out of the city, to go for hikes, but I never missed it like that.”

     

                Stopping, Kara stooped and picked up a broken shell, turning it between calloused fingertips before she took Lena’s hand. “It will sting a moment.”

     

                A faint gasp escaped Lena’s parted lips as Kara gouged the jagged edge of the shell across her fingertip, ruby-red blood welling up fast. Turning her finger over, Kara gave Lena’s hand a gentle shake, dislodging the blood, both of them watching as the beads turned into petals, drifting down to the sand with the breeze. Slashing her own palm with more carelessness, Kara tipped it and let the pool of blood splatter against the sand in a shower of water. 

     

                “You miss it so much because it is a part of you as you are a part of it. The same for myself and all of our kin. The elements are what give us life - water, food, air, warmth - and we feed off it, as it feeds off us, binding us to it. You ache for water when you are thirsty, you ache for air if you hold your breath, ache for fire when you are cold; is it strange to ache to bury your hands in the earth and feel the life around you? You had been gone from that magic a long time, starved of the forest and its sweet poison binding you to it. Now … you are home, and you are more in tune with yourself than you’ve ever been.”

     

                Lena let out a frayed hum, rubbing her eyes as she tried not to think about it. She didn’t like the reminder that the longer she stayed, the less inclined she would be to leave, that breathing in the air of this other plane, drinking the water and eating the food, was tying her to it, that the blood in her veins was not as ordinary as she’d thought. It was an unsettling thought and she chafed at it, rolling her shoulders as her mouth turned down at the corners. 

     

                “I’ve always known myself quite well, actually,” she murmured, hobbling on a step as Kara retook her arm to escort her.

     

                “We can only know as much as is tangible to us at the time. Your memories, faded and gone as they were, left a hole in yourself that you are only now starting to fill. The longer you remain here, the more yourself you become.”

     

                “And how are you so confident to tell me what I know and don’t know about myself?” Lena brusquely replied, somewhat nettled by Kara’s patronising words. “You don’t know me as well as I know myself; you just know more about this place.”

     

                “I don’t mean to presume I know you better than you know yourself, only that you do not know yourself in its entirety.”

     

                “Even that is presumptuous.”

     

                “How so? I speak truthfully. Your life before you were here-”

     

                “You don’t know a thing about my life before here,” Lena frustratedly cut her off, pulling them to a stop. “I know you’d like to think that my life was shit and I was miserable, and how it’s so much better here and I’m so grateful that I’ve been brought home so you can feel less guilty about the circumstances I was brought here by, but it’s not true. My life was great! I loved it. I wasn’t rich, I didn’t have jewels and palaces, but I was safe, I was proud of what I did for myself. I loved my shop, I had a coffee shop I went to every day, I had regular customers and a favourite bar, a favourite restaurant, a favourite book and- and movie and album. Do you know what it’s like to have interests, likes, and dislikes, and then they’re no longer possible? I didn’t have any family or friends to miss me but I had a whole life there. And now I’m here, and I don’t feel like I know myself any better because I am failing miserably at adjusting to this place, and I just- I wish I could read a book I like and listen to some music and make bouquets and go on shitty dates with people.”

     

                She was getting worked up now, her frustration turning into a breathless tirade as her face turned blotchy, her eyes glassy as her lip wobbled, her arm freed from Kara’s grasp as her knuckles whitened around her staff. Lena swallowed thickly, staring at Kara’s mild look of surprise and hating that she couldn’t keep her emotions under wraps like that, stamp them down until she was cool and unaffected.

     

                “I wish I was adjusting better than I am because at least then it wouldn’t be so hard, but every time I think that it’s okay it just- it’s one step forward, three steps back.”

     

                “Then let me help you,” Kara softly pleaded, reaching for her hand.

     

                Lena snatched it away, scoffing as she averted her gaze. “Help? This is the longest conversation we’ve had in days. And you say you’ve been a negligent wife but how can I hold that against you when you have what you wanted? You get to be in your home with friends and family and that’s great that you can be so happy and keep yourself busy running your holdings but it doesn’t stop the fact that I am lonely.” 

     

                “Then tell me what you want. If it is within my power to provide it, I will. Do you wish for duties? Are there any pastimes you would enjoy? I will procure whatever you need; books, quills, seeds.”

     

                “Things will not make me feel less alone, I know that. I’ve always been a lonely person, even before, but at least before I could- I could … do something about it. Do you know how easy it was for me? I had my pick of anyone that I wanted to take home.”

     

                “That is your desire then, is it? You want to have lovers?” Kara replied with annoyance, gesturing dismissively. “I will not stop you if that’s your wish. I will even make a list of suitable candidates if that eases your loneliness.”

     

                “Would you stop it,” Lena snapped, raking a hand through her hair as she scowled. “Firstly, I don’t need your permission, I also don’t need your help -”

     

                “Then what do you need? As it stands, all I can see is that you need to pick a fight. I will not lose my temper but you are spoiling a perfectly good walk.”

     

                Shoulders sagging as she leaned heavily on her walking stick, Lena gave her an aching look. “I just want to belong. I want … friends, I don’t want to struggle, I just- I would like to be wanted. Completely. I’m not used to this sort of isolation. I … I hate the beach. I don’t like the sea; I hate to look at it. I wish we were still in the forest. Even the Unseelie Court would be preferable to here.”

     

                Kara’s expression turned painfully aching, a sheepish look of embarrassment, of helplessness as the thing she loved the most was the thing that Lena hated the most. They could never be happy in the same place because it would require either one of them to be separated from the thing their very beings ached for. Lena knew she wasn’t being fair and she said as much. 

     

                “I know it’s not fair to you,” she said, her voice lowering, tired. “I know it makes you happy to be here, but this is not my happiness. I don’t need you to fix it, I don’t need you to fret over me, I just- I need to complain about it to someone . And I need you to listen . I don’t need you to tell me what I know or don’t know, or feel or don’t feel, or that it will all be okay, just … listen. Please. I know you mean well, I know that- this isn’t easy for either of us and I- I care about you and I’m sorry for ruining your life but-”

     

                Lena was promptly cut off as Kara seized her face in her rough palms, cradling her face gently, and kissed her softly but insistently. It surprised Lena, catching her off guard as her grasp went slack around the walking stick, her other hand hanging limply at her side as her eyelashes fluttered, and she could taste the salt on Kara’s lips, her own parting instinctively beneath warmth. 

     

                After a brief moment, clarity shot through her and she jerked her head back, eyes widening with panic. Her mouth opened and closed and she clamped her mouth tightly shut for a moment, making a disconcerting sound at the back of her throat as her eyebrows furrowed together, before she managed to speak.

     

                “Why would you do that?”

     

                “Forgive me,” Kara murmured, somewhat breathlessly, her eyes on Lena’s mouth. “I did not know how to make it clear that you have not ruined my life, that I care for you too, and that I don’t wish for you to feel lonely.”

     

                Silent for a moment, wary as she licked her lips, adjusted her grip and balance on the stick, she arched an eyebrow slightly. “Words usually help.”

     

                Opening her mouth, Kara faltered, snapping her jaw shut as she flushed. After a second, she conceded, “yes, they usually do.”

     

                Things felt awkward, a tension in the air as the wind blew and the clouds thickened overhead, warning of future rain. Shifting unsteadily on her good foot, Lena cleared her throat and gestured off-handedly. “The walk won’t finish itself.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Kara didn’t offer her arm again, clasping her hands tightly behind her back as she started to walk off, her pace quicker than Lena’s, even as she attempted to move faster. It was difficult, the end of her walking stick sinking into the sand, but she was content to follow in her wife’s wake as she let the fresh air clear her muddled mind. 

     

                They didn’t speak, naturally, and they walked some distance, Lena surprised to find that the clean air and the salt filling her lungs was a good balm to her restlessness of being kept indoors, even if there wasn’t a tree in near sight. The stretch of beach sloped upwards on their left, into dunes and seagrass, and Kara led them overland, as the limestone cliffs that had been quarried formed beneath their feet. The damp grass smelled fresh so early in the morning and Lena walked the cliffside path along the commanding bluffs, vibrant forest and marshland teeming with life stretching away from the coast, while the grey sea glittered in the weak sunlight seeping through pale grey clouds. 

     

                Following the edge of the cliffs, Lena didn’t look down at the dizzying drop into the churning waters below, but was content to listen to the cry of gulls and other waterbirds, the marshland with its estuaries and streams running towards the sea filled with the sound of frogs and dragonflies, gnats and ducks and swans, starlings, even a few pelicans gliding along as swallows fitted through the sky. It was pretty, Lena had to admit that, teeming with life, and even more in the water below and on the beach they’d crossed. How many crabs, fish, octopi, eels and the like had they unknowingly passed by? Perhaps Kara was aware of it, but that attention evaded Lena.

     

                After a mile or two, Kara slowed and turned, her usual composure back in place, and she smiled slightly at Lena. “Come, let me show you something.”

     

                She waited for Lena to close the gap between them and then walked at her side, leading her to a path worn down to the pitted limestone beneath the layer of grass, soil and sand. Taking her elbow, Kara kept Lena from slipping as they followed the path down to sea level, giving way to golden dunes as the cliffs ended and the shoreline started once more. 

     

                They rounded a few towering rocks before they arrived at the base of the cliff they’d just walked along and Lena slowed, her eyebrows rising a fraction at the glimpse of a statue, a hundred feet high, waves lapping over the carved toes of the aged structure. Craning her head back, she took in the face of the being, the tiny details that had been softly worn by wind and water for however many centuries it had stood there, the folds of the robes and fish-scale armour pitted and cracked with time. A sword was held in clasped hands before the fae’s stomach, point nestled between the statue’s feet, and Lena startled at a particularly rough wave that exploded over the base of the statue in a spray of white. 

     

                Staying safely away from the sea, which rushed up the beach towards them, tracking seaweed in its wake, Lena tried to crane her neck out to see past it. She caught a glimpse of three more statues lined up along the cliffside, evenly spaced apart, all of them similar in garb and style from what she could tell. Kara gave her arm a gentle tug and Lena turned to look at her, and then past her, to where her wife’s attention was; where the statue had been carved out of the cliffside, the rest of it had been excavated beyond, darkness beckoning them as Kara led her towards it. 

     

                The darkness was unnerving and Lena’s bare foot faltered at the damp touch of limestone underfoot, worn smooth from decades of footsteps over them, but she let Kara lead her further inside. Once she was past the initial threshold of the cavern beyond, her eyes adjusted quickly, sunlight filtering in through the wide gaps between the statues. The place was mostly rough-hewn, the walls and ceiling uneven and natural rock, save for the floor, which was smooth and flat. The place smelled strongly of brine, salt crusting the base of the statues and riming the floor in tide marks near where the cavern was open to the sea. 

     

                As she looked at the backs of the statues, she wondered at the place. It must have been a hundred and fifty feet across, the statues carved as solid pieces, with the ceiling seeming to rest on their heads. It wasn’t as deep as it was wide, less than a hundred by her judgement, and the first twenty or so feet gave way to the sea before even steps climbed to the limestone floor they stood on. Hugging the right-hand wall, Lena was hesitant as she followed Kara along the limestone, although she was eager to be further away from the churning water beyond.

     

                It was a brooding day and the sunlight cast the place in deep shadow still, so Kara dropped Lena’s arm and moved over to a sconce on the wall and lit the dried driftwood with two rocks taken from the pocket of her robe. Lifting the torch from the sconce, she lit another further along the wall, a small circle of light and warmth cast over them. Drawing closer to it, Lena turned her back to the rough wall behind her and stared out at the sea, inky at its closest point before it turned to metal grey further out.

     

                “What is this place?”

     

                “My kind quarried here for centuries,” Kara explained as she lit another sconce, lightening the wall to buttery yellow as the shadows lifted. “The cliffs of my home were quarried for the limestone that was used to build the rest above ground. This place was quarried for similar needs; watchtowers along the coast and the borders and strategic points in what was once exclusively Waterfolk land. It was jealously protected, you see; we almost had a monopoly on salt, on freshwater, seafood. Many wars were fought over resources, so the watchtowers gave us an advantage. The limestone itself was also coveted, of course. Once all that was necessary had been quarried from this place, it was made into what it is now, to this day; a place for thought, for reflection and peace. A place to honour the old rituals as well. Come midwinter, there will be many who visit these halls, as well as their respects to me.”

     

                Lena looked around at the place, the smell of wet stone, of fresh air not unwelcome but chilling all the same as she tugged her robe around herself. It was by no means dank but there was something to be said for wet stone in early winter that wasn’t hospitable to Lena’s taste and she wasn’t keen on staying long. Still, Kara finished lighting the back sconces and paced the open hall, a serene look on her face as her robe billowed around her with the brisk sea breeze sweeping in past the statues.

     

                “Do you come here often?”

     

                Facing her wife, Kara smiled softly, her blonde hair burnished amber in the orange glow of the sconces, making her look younger, more doe-eyed without her braids. “Quite often when I am home. When I tire of my duties and have swam to exhaustion, I come here instead. It is quiet; I am disturbed less here.”

     

                “Who disturbs you? There’s hardly anyone that lives there.”

     

                “My memories. I am disturbed by the memory of my parents, my lost family. These days I am also disturbed by thoughts of being caught here unawares, my back to the sea, which you will not willingly step foot into. I wonder at times if you would hate me terribly if the Unseelie sought us out here, or your brother, and I took you out there on a boat, threw you to your deepest fears to save your life.”

     

                She said it off-handedly but Lena could read the tension in her voice, the way her eyes flitted over Lena’s face with uncertainty. Throat feeling tight, Lena toyed with the walking stick, looking at the carved motifs as she chewed on the inside of her lip.

     

                “I wouldn’t hate you at all. I would feel sorry to have made you abandon your home; I don’t think my mother or brother would let it go unscathed.”

     

                “No, I don’t suppose they would. Until such eventuality, life must go on and I am to be busy with affairs that have been long overlooked. J’onn is excellent at managing them for me but it’s unbecoming for me to be so ignorant of my affairs. Perhaps you might have an interest in it.”

     

                “What would that be?”

     

                She had questions, she realised, and voiced them as she leaned against the wall, until her leg started to ache from all of her weight put upon it, and she sank to the floor, injured ankle stretched out before her. Kara paced as they talked, her voice soft but drifting across the gap between them as she explained her responsibilities, areas of governance, both of their ancestries and alliances - old and new - that had shaped the fate of the Court, grudges that had been held onto for centuries or longer, blood feuds that had existed for longer than anyone could remember why . Lena was curious and Kara was forthcoming with as much information as she could supply.

     

                After Lena’s questions had almost run out, Kara spent some time in the sea, walking down the steps and cutting through the water with ease as she swam out to the statues, where clusters of oysters had latched onto the base of them, growing in abundance. Kara pried handfuls free, swimming back and forth until she had enough to satiate their growing hunger, Lena forgetting she hadn’t eaten yet as the morning tracked towards noon. 

     

                Kneeling on the limestone floor, Kara used the edge of an oyster shell to pry open another, handing it off to Lena with a smile. They sat and ate their oysters, a pile of shells amassing in their laps and on the floor between them, and when Kara opened one to find a pearl nestled amidst the flesh, she grinned as she plucked it free and held it up between thumb and forefingers before extending it to Lena.

     

                “A pearl,” Lena murmured, taking it and rolling it between her fingers, the creamy sheen of it so perfect. “Maybe they can stitch it onto a new dress for you.”

     

                She reached out to hand it back and Kara’s warm fingers curled over her own, closing Lena’s hand over the pearl. “For you. Perhaps it can be stitched into a new dress for you.”

     

                Quietly snorting, Lena withdrew her hand and uncurled her fingers to stare down at the pearl. “That must be sacrilegious to sew Waterfolk items onto an Earthfolk garment. Surely.”

     

                “Sacrilegious?”

     

                “Disrespectful.”

     

                “Oh. No, it wouldn’t be. We have love for all elements - look, I have flowers embroidered here,” Kara said, holding her arm up so Lena could take in the wide cuff, embellished with silver thread. “We just have a particular fondness for our own. Don’t worry, I will find you enough pearls so that they may be stitched into flowers. That way you may stay true to your roots, as deep and stubborn as they are.”

     

                “I take it as a compliment.”

     

                “As you should. It is maddening at times but a good quality - you know this, I need not tell you that.”

     

                “Oh, but it does charm me to this place to be flattered,” Lena said with a teasing smile, tucking the pearl safely in a pocket. 

     

                “Ah, is that what it will take for you to feel more welcome? Perhaps I shall have to flatter you more,” Kara replied, a little coy, a little shy as she leaned in, playing to Lena’s teasing.

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes and picked up another oyster, turning it in her palm, taking in the tiny scruff of seaweed as she thumbed the ridges of the shell. “That would only work until you ran out of compliments, and then we’d be back to square one.”

     

                Kara laughed, shoving handfuls of opened oyster shells into her pockets and then pushing herself to her feet. She reached down to help pull Lena up, who grabbed her walking stick and gripped the unopened oyster tightly, making sure her wife had her balance as she gripped her arms, cupping her triceps for a moment longer than necessary.

     

                “It could be an endless list - if you wished it to be,” she said, her laughter softening to kindness.

     

                “Is that right? Maybe with insults. You’re not going to tell me my hair is like seaweed again, are you?”

     

                Kara gently scoffed, her cheeks flooding with colour for a quick moment as she turned her head aside. Staring at her profile, taking in the bridge of her nose, the bow of her lips, the freckles splattered across her cheeks, and the warmth in them, rosy and warm to the touch if Lena hedged a guess. She might have reached out to check if her hands weren’t full, and felt fortunate that they were. Tucking a strand of wavy, salt-crusted hair behind the pointed tip of her ear, Kara’s cheek dimpled with regret and Lena felt a spark of curiosity for her evident embarrassment.

     

                “It’s fine, I didn’t take it personally,” Lena reassured her. “I’ve said much worse to you so that would be a little hypocritical. If that was an attempt at an insult though, I think it needs more work.”

     

                Opening her mouth to respond, Kara looked down at the floor, rubbing her thumb over a knuckle as she faltered for a moment. Lena spared her the discomfort by laughing, easy and light, reaching out to tap Kara’s arm with the walking stick.

     

                “Let’s go.”

     

                Nodding, closing her mouth as her smooth brow furrowed briefly, Kara took a step forward and then absentmindedly reached out to hook her arm through Lena’s. They talked a little on the way back and despite her great reluctance and dislike of the sea, she found that the walk and the bracing salt air had helped alleviate some of her frustration, that the open space and the company of her wife had made her rankle less at being there, had lifted some of the weight off her, made her loneliness smaller. It seemed that getting out of her room after days spent bedbound had been good for her, even if her ankle twinged when she accidentally put weight on it at times while walking back to the distant hall of Kara’s home. 

     

                It started to rain on the walk back, the stinging beginnings of raindrops splattering Lena’s exposed skin, whipped into a frenzy by the wind, and she shivered as she held her robe closed, hunching her shoulders. Kara waved a hand above her and Lena looked up to see the rain diverting around her, commanded so by her wife, and she looked at Kara, who was being battered by the quickening raindrops, hair turning brassy as it plastered to her cheeks, robe hanging a little more heavily on her frame. She seemed to enjoy it though, her eyes darting sideways to Lena, cheek dimpling shallowly before they continued onwards.

     

                The sand was dimpled and grew firmer as they went, due to the rain that soaked it, blades of wet grass clinging to their feet and ankles once they made it to the cliffs. Occupied by her thoughts, walking slowly as she stared up at the dark clouds overhead, the grumble of thunder approaching off the coast, Lena breathed in the cold air and found that she didn’t mind the cold so much, that it wasn’t so unbearable now that they were at a lower altitude - even if the wind blowing southerly was strong enough to steal the breath from her lungs. She had no doubt it would get stronger as the weather worsened, strong enough to bowl her over if she went for a walk without Kara’s anchoring presence at her side.

     

                Returning to the hall, Kara helped her up the steps and paused as she gave Lena a quick once-over. “Would you like a bath?”
