                Thinking of the hot bath on her first day there and the absence of a proper bath since then, of how damp and cold she was, shivering where she stood, Lena’s shoulders slumped slightly as her expression perked. “I’d love one.”

     

                Kara smiled slightly, nodding as she changed their trajectory and led Lena through the lower level, the sound of water crashing over rock growing louder as they made it to the northerly facing side of the cliffs, carved open to the elements. This low down, it was frightening to Lena, the water rushing in, the whole place damp and cold and lined with old tide marks of salt. She had the paralysing thought that the waves would flood the entire ground floor and Kara paused momentarily at the sudden stop before Lena shook herself out of it and continued onwards.

     

                Stepping into that open chamber that she’d been brought to on the day she arrived, Lena was no less struck but the strange, austere beauty of the place. Aside from the carvings, it was bare, water lapping up the steps of the tiered circular pool and Lena hesitated, baulking at the thought that she’d have to bathe in there , the freezing water churning about her, the open sea sweeping through the open wall and the current tugging at her. A cold sweat crept over her and she glanced quickly at Kara, green eyes flickering with panic.

     

                Her wife bustled about, fetching that tub Lena had bathed in last time, and Lena felt weak with relief and her eagerness for a bath was renewed. Filling the tub with water straight from the sea, Kara murmured for Lena to wait and returned a few minutes later with Alex in tow, brusque and all business as she walked in, rolling her sleeves up, and plunged her hands into the frigid water, steam curling off the surface a moment later. Nodding to Lena, she gave her sister an unreadable expression and then left without a word.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena murmured in her wake, directed to Alex and Kara.

     

                Hovering with uncertainty, Kara wrung her hands and cleared her throat. “Do you need help?”

     

                She’d already fetched the soap, a clean towel and a pitcher of fresh water to wash off the lingering salt, making sure Lena had everything she wanted, and Lena’s ankle had healed enough for her to manage getting in and out of the tub. Kara probably had better things to be doing than babysitting her wife, and while Lena appreciated the help last time, as exhausted and injured as she had been, she didn’t want to take up more of Kara’s time. She’d already taken up her morning and vented her frustration on her - Lena could occupy herself for the rest of the day.

     

                “No, thank you. I’ll manage. You should have your swim.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara gave her a crooked smile and nodded. Nodding in return, Lena set her walking stick down a safe distance from the tub and shed her robe. Turning away, Kara walked towards the sea and started to undress, Lena’s eyes darting over to her and then back to the tub, an odd knot in her stomach as she finished undressing, removing the bandage from her right ankle and easing herself into the bath. The salt made her ankle sting and she leaned her head back, tendons in her neck going taut, but revelling in the heat as it worked wonders on her stiff muscles and the chill in her joints. 

     

                Dunking her head and then surfacing, brushing dark hair out of her face as she breathed heavily, eyes shut and the taste of salt on her lips, Lena waited until she relaxed into the heat before she opened her eyes again. The wind howled through the massive chamber, waves crashing and seagulls crying creating a peaceful melody to her clouded thoughts, and she caught sight of Kara submerged up to her chest as she sat on one of the limestone tiers and let the waves break over her shoulders. Her eyes flickered over to Lena across the gap between them.

     

                “That’s not a swim,” Lena softly spoke, knowing her wife could hear her.

     

                “You do not like the water; I’ll not leave you here alone for my own enjoyment of the sea. I will swim later.”

     

                “Even I would be hard-pressed to drown in a bathtub,” Lena snorted, even though she knew it was easily done and a bath was just about all she could stand. “Go on. Leave me to relax; I’d like to take my time.”

     

                “Is that an order?” Kara asked with mild surprise. “You would like to be left alone?”

     

                Eyes closing, a fleeting smile tugging at her lips, Lena hummed at the back of her throat. “If I ordered you, would you listen?”

     

                “I always listen to you.”

     

                “That’s news to me.”

     

                “No it isn’t,” Kara scoffed. “You just don’t listen to me.”

     

                Lena let out a contented sigh, sinking an inch deeper into the water. “I’ll be fine, Kara.”

     

                Still, she couldn’t help but smile faintly to herself, ducked down enough that her wife couldn’t see as she gave her a final look to make sure she was certain before setting off in an easy stroke towards the open archway leading out to the open sea. Lingering in the water until it started to cool, Lena sat up and leaned over the side of the tub for the soap, working it into her hair and scrubbing her skin clean before she rinsed herself off and then used the jug of fresh water to rinse off the salt. 

     

                Wrapping herself in the clean towel, she dried off quickly from the brisk wind and was shivering as she donned her layers. She could have done with some clean clothes but as long as she was warm, that was all she cared about in the immediate future, even though her damp hair made her unpleasantly cold as the wind dragged at her locks. 

     

                Kara resurfaced right as Lena was towelling off the dripping ends of her hair, emerging from the sea like one of the Nereids from Greek mythology, tanned and golden as water streamed from her and the sea churned in her wake. She cast off the water from her skin and hair and pulled on her discarded robe before moving over to Lena, flicking her fingers in a lazy gesture that pulled the moisture from Lena’s hair, leaving it dry, if a little frizzy.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara clasped her hands behind her back for a moment, swaying slightly on her heels. “Are you finished here?”

     

                Lena folded the towel and nodded, letting Kara take it from her and set it beside the tub, picking up her walking stick for her. Taking it from her, Lena leaned on it and turned to go, Kara falling into step beside her as they left the bathing room and walked down the hallway. Lena remembered the way from last time, having seen so few places in these halls yet, and she slowly climbed each step as Kara patiently waited, affording her the independence of doing it herself.

     

                When she reached her room, Lena paused on the threshold and gave Kara an uneven smile. “Thank you.”

     

                “If you require anything else, you need only ask.”

     

                Nodding, Lena slipped through the archway and set her walking stick against the wall before she shed the outer layers of her clothes and eased herself down onto the edge of her bed. Reaching into the pocket of her shed robe, she fished out the pearl and turned it between her fingers as she brooded over the events of her morning. Despite her reluctance to spend so much time alone in her room, she found herself tired, and as she sat and thought and fiddled with her pearl, she made herself comfortable on top of the heavy blankets and pillows, and somewhere in the middle of it, fell asleep, pearl clutched tightly in a fist.

     

                Kara found her there a few hours later, still peacefully asleep, in her worn dress with dark hair spilling across the pillows. The room was dim, only narrow beams of light sifting through the high arrow-slit windows, the sunset not far off, and there was no fire lit in her brazier. Stepping inside, padding as she set her laden tray down on the table, Kara moved over to the brazier and picked up pieces of driftwood to coax a fire to life for warmth and light. She worried about Lena’s propensity for the cold and didn’t want her to wake up to the dark cold.

     

                She needn’t have worried, the quiet rasping of the flint rousing her wife from her nap as Kara tried to get the sparks to catch. They did a moment later and she blew on the glowing embers amidst the kindling, the air fanning them into little tongues of flame, which caught quickly, spreading and growing until Kara was confident the driftwood would catch. Straightening up, fanning the air before her to dispel the smoke, she glanced at Lena and found her watching her.

     

                “Forgive me, I didn’t mean to disturb you,” Kara whispered, sheepish as she crossed the room and set the flint down on the table.

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena mumbled, her voice thick with sleep as she rubbed her eyes with a fist and then uncurled her fingers to find the pearl in her palm.

     

                Kara watched her study it for a moment, the way her dark eyebrows drew together, lips pursed ever so slightly. Pocketing it in her dress, Lena raked her hair back and then met Kara’s eyes again.

     

                “What time is it?”

     

                “Dusk is not far off. You have slept the afternoon away.”

     

                “Oh.”

                

                “I brought you your evening meal; I did not realise you were still sleeping.”

     

                Lena’s eyes strayed to the tray. It was set for two, she realised, sitting up straighter against her pillows. “I’m awake now.”

     

                “Are you hungry?”

     

                “Sure.”

     

                Nodding, Kara picked up the tray and turned to the bed, setting it down on the blankets and removing Lena’s cloak, folding it carefully and setting it on the low stool. Satisfied, she gave Lena a small smile and nodded, hovering a moment before she turned to go. Lena’s eyebrows rose slightly in surprise and her eyes took on a yearning look.

     

                “Wait!”

     

                Pausing, Kara glanced over her shoulder, not quite turning around. A politely inquiring look gave her a more serious expression as she cocked her head to the side slightly.

     

                “I- aren’t you staying?” Lena asked, confusion crumpling her face as she gestured to the tray. “It’s set for two.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara murmured, restlessly shifting as she wrung her hands. “It was my intention but I know you prefer your own company when you have just awoken so I shall leave you be.”

     

                “Stay.”

     

                “If you like.”

     

                “I would.”

     

                Lena’s voice softened with uncertainty and she looked down at the tray, bewilderment and a rush of annoyance at her blatant desire for Kara to stay flitting across her face. Kara had changed since they had parted ways, one of her billowing shirts tucked into leather leggings, and she sank onto the edge of the bed and started to roll up her sleeves as Lena took stock of things. There was a steaming jug, two cups, two bowls and a beige clay pot with a lid clamped down on top. A loaf of dark rye bread was wedged in alongside butter, a bowl of blackberries for sweetness, and a bowl of some unidentifiable-looking sludge. She watched as Kara lifted the steaming jug, noticing the fresh ink stains on her fingertips and felt a smile twitch the corners of her mouth at her wife’s devotion to her ledgers and letters.

     

                “It is mulled cider. I thought it would chase away the cold nicely - I’m assuming you are cold?” Kara glanced up, eyebrows rising slightly, a curl to her mouth as she teased her. 

     

                “Ah, well, you know me.”

     

                “Here. It is quite delicious. This one is from my apple trees at Argo; it’s warmer there so the growing conditions make for a sweeter wine. Better for winter, I think, although the cider we make from my orchards here is quite pleasant in the summer. You will need to try some for yourself.”

     

                Lena accepted a cup with murmured thanks, thinking of still being there next summer. She wasn’t sure whether the thought of the rest of her life spent in the forest was what bothered her, or whether it was the quiet doubt that she would get to spend much more time breathing at all. There was the unshakable feeling of unease at things that were left unfinished; her brother, her mother, whatever else lurked in the forest which wished them ill. Even she knew her enemies weren’t just limited to the Unseelie Court, and that as secluded as they were so far north, there would still be those plotting. Perhaps they’d wait for warmer weather but that only gave them more time to iron the kinks out of their plots.

     

                “You are preoccupied,” Kara noted.

     

                Taking a sip of her cider, the pleasant warmth of it tracing a path down her throat, Lena shrugged indifferently. “Just thinking.”

     

                “Do you wish to share?”

     

                Lips twisting ruefully, Lena’s eyes were bright with bitterness as she met Kara’s open stare. “I was wondering if we would still be here next summer.”

     

                “We will be in Argo again, as we have already-”

     

                “Not here … alive.”

     

                “Oh. I should think so.”

     

                “How can you be so confident?”

     

                Blinking, Kara looked puzzled for a moment before she took a swig of her cider and then set her cup down on the floor. She removed the lid from the clay pot to a cloud of steam and the fragrant smell of garlic, fennel and something briny. Mussels, Lena realised, taking in the dark shells opened to reveal the flesh inside.

     

                “I am confident because I will not let anyone hurt you. You know I would intend to keep you safe, no matter the cost.”

     

                “Surely there’s a limit.”

     

                “How so?”

     

                “Well … is it ethical to kill however many people to keep one person alive?”

     

                “No, perhaps it’s not ethical, but your life is worth a thousand people’s lives to me. Others would disagree but that is how I feel. Your life is as precious to me as my own sister’s, my family’s. Even more than my own.”

     

                Letting out a scoff of laughter, Lena paused midway to taking a sip of her mulled cider. “Is that meant to be romantic?”

     

                “It is not meant to be anything,” Kara shrugged. “It is true. If you doubt that, I will repeat it for you in fae.”

     

                “I don’t doubt you. It just worries me that one day you will be forced to act on your words.”

     

                “Why would that worry you?”

     

                “Because I don’t believe one life should be worth a thousand. Sorry, but I don’t know if I could kill a thousand people to save you.”

     

                “I would not expect you to.”

     

                “And why do you think I expect you to?”

     

                “Because I am a trained warrior and you are not. If I do not save you, who will?”

     

                “And if you can’t save yourself?”

     

                “My sister would die for me. She would do anything I asked of her, as I would do for her.”

     

                “Hm. That’s a lot of trust to have in someone.”

     

                “Do you trust me?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Good. Now, eat before it gets cold.”

     

                “Did you make this yourself?” Lena asked, setting her cup down on the floor too and then picking up a bowl.

     

                Kara nodded, plucking a mussel from the pile and prying both halves apart. She used one half to scoop out the flesh and then dunked it in the broth and spooned it into her mouth. Lena followed likewise and then tore off the heel from the loaf, buttering and dipping it into the broth as well.

     

                “Here,” Kara said, picking up the little bowl with the congealed mass inside. “Try this with the bread and butter.”

     

                “What is it?” Lena sceptically asked.

     

                “Seaweed.”

     

                “Seaweed? Are you trying to be funny?”

     

                “How could this be construed as a joke? It is food.”

     

                “When you insulted my hair by saying-”

     

                “It was not meant as an insult at all,” Kara softly interrupted. “In fact, it was meant as a compliment.”

     

                “A compliment? In what world would that be seen as a compliment?”

     

                “Mine.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow sceptically, Lena paused momentarily. “Right.”

     

                Letting out a resigned sigh, Kara gestured to the archway of Lena’s door, the thick walls hiding the glimmering sea beyond. “The water … that’s where seaweed comes from, and this kind of seaweed is very soft, almost like silk when it’s wet.”

     

                “Oh … right.”

     

                “I’m quite fond of seaweed.”

     

                Realisation crept over Lena and she blinked, unsure how to process this new information, that her wife was a little strange and a little awkward, but well-intentioned even if Lena didn’t realise it at the time. She hadn’t realised it for the compliment it was intended to be and she didn’t know how to take it now, except to take the bowl from her wife and scoop some onto a chunk of buttered bread, shoving it into her mouth before she could say something stupid.

     

                Chewing quickly, she slowed as her tastebuds assessed it and found it foul. She had to force herself to swallow, her face crumpling with disgust, even as she tried to mask it, and Kara laughed at her as she managed to get it down, coughing as she reached for her cider. Rinsing the taste away, Lena hummed dubiously.

     

                “I don’t think that’s for me,” Lena said with a wry smile.

     

                “No, it’s not for everyone but I’m quite partial to it myself,” Kara murmured, her eyes flitting over Lena’s face.

     

                “More for you, I guess.”

     

                She handed the bowl back and gave Kara a reserved smile, her stomach jolting slightly as their fingers brushed, and she quickly picked up another mussel and opened it. Kara slathered her piece of bread with butter and seaweed and seemed pleased as she ate it and there was a brief lull in conversation before it picked back up.

     

                They finished their dinner together as the sun set outside, darkness stealing over the room as the bluish tint of the driftwood fire kept it at bay, and as they were on the last dregs of the cider and finishing off the blackberries, Lena felt satiated. Not by the food, but by the day. It had been refreshing, outside of the confines of her room, for the most part, the outdoors doing her some good and a relatively easy day with her wife’s company a balm to her loneliness. She thought she could handle the winter there, on the coast, if her days were like that - perhaps a little busier and more fulfilling, but content with it all the same.

     

                “Today was not such a bad day,” Lena haltingly admitted.

     

                Kara’s face softened minutely with delight and some relief and she nodded in agreement. “Not such a bad day.”

    Chapter 21

                The next morning, a lead blue dress was dropped off by a humanoid water figure, the thick wool adorned with blue water hyacinths stitched up the skirt and sleeves. As Lena laid it over her rumpled bed, she wondered if Kara knew the symbolism of blue hyacinths - sincere care - and if she’d picked the dress out herself from her own wardrobe. It wasn’t made for Lena, dragging on the floor slightly when she changed into it, but it was warm and clean with the underlayers that had come with it, and when she belted on her dagger, she felt more refined than she’d felt since leaving Eliza’s halls.

     

                Kara came to escort her to breakfast, where Lena found a few of their party still remaining - with Sam and Andrea too - and there was polite conversation and plans made. After finishing her breakfast, Lena didn’t know what to do with herself until Kara stood, rounding the table to stop at her side and softly clearing her throat before she asked if Lena wanted to accompany her outdoors.

     

                Two horses were saddled when they exited through the main doors on the above-ground floor, a dappled grey and a snow-white mare. Kara helped Lena onto the back of her own first and then mounted the white, keeping them both together as they set off at a walk. Kara thought it would be good for Lena to grow more accustomed to riding and Lena was just happy to fill her time, even if she wished she’d brought her cloak and the tips of her ears grew cold as the wind blew over them.

     

                That night, they ate dinner together in the dining hall, Lena at Kara’s right hand, and her wife escorted her back to her rooms before lingering. She pulled a book from the pocket of her surcoat, small but thick, the pages thin onion paper and the leatherbound cover covered in glyphs.

     

                “It’s the tale of Flamebird and Nightwing,” Kara had explained. “I told you that it was my favourite story, that I would read it to you. I know you do not have your favourite story here but perhaps this could become a new one.”

     

                She stayed for an hour, sitting on the stool beside Lena’s bed, her wife tucked beneath the blankets, and read aloud from the book. Lena thought she had a nice voice for reading aloud, gentle and warm but precise, rising and falling with the inflexion of her words and occasionally gesturing with her hand as she became absorbed in the story. Listening intently, Lena was likewise consumed by the story, but mostly due to Kara’s voice, the pitch of it lulling her into a peaceful stupor as she couldn’t tear her eyes away from her wife.

     

                When Lena’s eyes grew heavy, Kara left her to rest with the promise of more in the future, and Lena was left to her quiet room, the lit brazier flickering and throwing off shadows as she listened to the muffled roar of the sea and breathed in the salt. It so keenly smelled like Kara that she could keenly feel her wife’s presence long after she’d left, a sort of freshness lingering like a rainstorm had scoured her salt-rimed room clean.

     

                The next few days followed much the same pattern, riding or walking along the shore or coast, although they never went very far, while Kara pointed out birds and inlets, places she’d fished, or they collected shells and driftwood, oysters and mussels and even an octopus once, when Kara had an elegant trident with her, piercing the creature on its tines and showing Lena how to prepare it. There were hours in between when Lena emerged from her room more, playing Stones with Alex, with Kelly eagerly asking if she could help Lena with her glyphs, the two of them writing together in a parlour with honey-sweetened tea. Kara showed her how to weave nets and quietly knitted Lena new socks in between, beaming with pride each time she presented a new pair to her pleased wife.

     

                New clothes in shades of the forest trickled in, along with belongings for Lena’s room. She acquired a mirror of beaten copper, clear enough for her reflection and spotted green with age at the edges, combs of whalebone and little pots of creams and perfumes that Kara gifted her like a grey shrike trying to woo a mate. She had a local fisherman come and play the harp one evening for them, a cobbler made Lena a pair of sturdy boots, uncommon for their kind but well-made, brought her a palmful of more pearls and large, polished pieces of larimar and turquoise to assist with the energy of Lena’s room. 

     

                Andrea arrived one morning, bustling in and waking Lena as she set down a basin of hot water and roused her from sleep. They bickered back and forth as her attendant insisted on resuming her duties, now that Lena was on the mend, and Lena hastily washed and was subjected to the quick braiding and adornment of what little jewels she still owned. It became a routine after that, and Lena endured it out of the realisation that it gave Andrea a sense of purpose away from the Unseelie Court, as much as it gave Lena company. After that day, she was never far from Lena, and Sam lurked about as well, sweeter than her counterpart but still armed to the teeth and that uneasy feeling Lena couldn’t shake that her guard might turn at any second.

     

                The sudden inundation of gifts and attention was almost too much for Lena, who had spent the few days before that relatively alone, but she couldn’t say she hated it. In fact, she craved more, asking if she could sit with Kara as her wife conversed with J’onn and went through her ledges and papers and penned letters. Kara explained her work to her and let Lena practise her penmanship by making notes or writing letters for her. It gave Lena more of a purpose, even if she thought it was boring, but she did have a head for business and numbers and Kara was pleased by her wife’s affinity for it, roping her in to help more often.

     

                Perhaps the best gift her wife gave her over that week was the carefully poised request for help when Kara asked if she would be so kind as to consider making a few floral arrangements to decorate the halls. Lena saw straight through the request, knowing it wasn’t for Kara’s benefit at all but pleased to be asked all the same. She scrounged up a wicker basket from the kitchens and walked through the nearby coastline and marshy beginnings with Sam in tow, cutting what flowers and greenery she could find, ensuring to leave the roots so they could regrow. 

     

                She spent an entire morning foraging, filling her basket with bluebells and foxgloves, sea campion and pink thrift, wild onion and salt grass and reeds. Once her basket was full, she returned to the halls and found an empty room with a long table inside, spreading out her findings and spending the afternoon on the laborious task of arranging the bouquets. She ended up with five of them, finding appropriate jugs to put them in with fresh water and distributing them to the main areas. The offcuts were used to make two smaller arrangements, one brightening up Lena’s room and the other nervously held in hand as she hovered outside her wife’s door that evening.

     

                “You may come in,” Kara’s voice drifted to Lena.

     

                She was alone, without her accompanying shadows, who had both tired of her quiet work arranging her cuttings and figured she was safe enough alone in Kara’s home, so she swept inside. The hem of her jade green dress brushed the smooth worn limestone and her right ankle held beneath her, fully healed in a matter of a week, thanks to their quick healing. The row of neat stitches were still in place though and they itched as she found her wife sitting cross-legged on the floor with silver chainmail rippling like water in her hands as she oiled it with careful attention.

     

                “Don’t get up,” Lena said as Kara made to move.

     

                Settling back down, Kara gave her an expectant look as she carefully worked at the mail, making sure it didn’t rust so close to the salt and sea. Lena saw the scattered parts of the rest of her armour, wrought like fish scales and so beautiful that she couldn’t comprehend that it could be made in such a place, without the aid of machinery and power tools. The filigree we so fine and detailed that she had the urge to run her fingers over the cool metal as her eyes drank it all in.

     

                “I just wanted to bring you this.”

     

                Setting her oilcloth aside, Kara beckoned her forward, reaching out as Lena approached and handed her the flowers. Kara’s fingers brushed the backs of Lena’s as she took the little bouquet, raising it to her nose and then tipping her head back to smile up at Lena, eyes creasing at the corners as she took Lena’s hand and pressed her lips to the knuckles.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Lena left her hand in Kara’s grasp until her wife let go, setting her chainmail aside to climb to her feet, and then covered it with her other hand, running a thumb over the ghost of Kara’s lips there. She turned, tracking Kara’s movements across the room as she fetched an empty silver cup, filled it with water from the wash basin and nestled the flowers in it. Turning back to Lena, Kara gave her another smile, letting a fingertip trail over the petals of a foxglove.

     

                “Did you enjoy your day?”

     

                Inhaling deeply, Lena slowly breathed out, feeling the faint ache in her shoulders of hours spent hunched over, gathering flowers and arranging them, and her lips twitched with a smile as she nodded. “Yes.”

     

                “And your foot? How is it healing?”

     

                “Oh, um, yeah, I think it’s pretty much healed now. The stitches are a little itchy.”

     

                “I could remove them for you if you like.”

     

                “Now?”

     

                Kara shrugged and gestured off-handedly, “I am not busy and if you are certain your foot has healed enough for them to come out …”

     

                “I mean, I’m not a doctor - healer, whatever - but it seems fine to me.”

     

                “Come, sit. I’m no healer but I know enough from my mother to judge whether it is healed enough to remove them.”

     

                She moved aside a breastplate on her bed and patted the rumpled sheets. Hesitating, feeling like it was too comfortable, too rote for her liking, Lena sank onto the mattress as Kara dragged a small stool over to her bedside and sank onto it. She had a small box in hand and rifled through the contents until she came up with a pair of scissors wrought into the shape of a crane. Lifting Lena’s foot into her lap, she eyed the red edge of the stitched wound and hummed a moment before nodding.

     

                “It has healed well. You should still be gentle a while yet.”

     

                Her fingers were gentle as she snipped the thread of the stitches and carefully tugged them free, and Lena was left staring at the small line of where her bone had rent her skin and the tiny dots on either side. It was strange that she healed so well, and always had, bruises vanishing within the day, falls as a child that should have resulted in broken bones only leading to aches, but she was grateful for it. Within a couple of days, she thought the scar would fade to white like the ones on her thigh and abdomen from the wolf.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena murmured, rubbing her foot and rolling her ankle to test the motion.

     

                “I hope that will be the last of your injuries,” Kara said with a wry smile, which Lena matched with a droll look.

     

                “Wouldn’t that be nice? I’m on my way to amassing an unseemly amount of scars; I should be grateful I’ve already been married off before someone could find me hideous.”

     

                “You are lovely.”

     

                “You’re too kind.”

     

                “You think me kind now? And here, you thought I was insulting you at every turn, until recently.”

     

                “Okay, well, you have unusual compliments so how was I supposed to know?”

     

                “I’m aware, as Alex-”

     

                Kara trailed off, putting her scissors away in the little box and climbing to her feet. Cocking her head to the side, catching the thread of Kara’s abandoned sentence before she could let it go, Lena raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Alex what?” she lightly pressed.

     

                There was a sense of enjoyment as Kara ducked her head, turning as a flush crept up her neck. She put away her things and moved the stool, her movements slow and measured, as graceful as ever, and then cleared her throat, gesturing vaguely as she stooped down to pick up her discarded chainmail and oilcloth.

     

                “Alex pointed out that perhaps you would not understand the compliments of Waterfolk, that I should … speak to your own ideas of flattery.”

     

                “You asked your sister how to, what, flirt with me?”

     

                The idea was baffling as much as amusing, and she watched as Kara quickly opened her mouth, rushing to defend herself. “No, I’m not flirting with you - nor would I presume to court you, if you are getting the wrong idea about my gifts - only that … I would hope that it might make you consider me as a friend.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena’s expression furrowed slightly. “I do consider you as a friend. You don’t need to flatter me to get me to like you.”

     

                “It is true, nevertheless, so why should I not speak truthfully?”

     

                “I don’t know, it might give the wrong impression.”

     

                “What impression are you under?”

     

                “I never said it would give me the wrong impression.”

     

                “Yours is the only impression I care about.”

     

                “Is it?”

     

                “Of course. You are half of this marriage; it only concerns the two of us.”

     

                “Interesting. How many times have I been accused of selfishness for not considering the many other people our marriage affects? Too many to count if you ask me.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara smiled with wry fondness, “very well, Lena, it is as you say; our marriage concerns many others. It is still only your impression I care about, so tell me, what is your impression?”

     

                “My impression? My impression is that you care for me, that you also see us as friends, that you will say or do anything to make things easy between us, that you are not interested in anything but keeping the peace for the sake of ease.”

     

                “That is not entirely true. I am interested in many things about you, not just for the sake of peace. And I think I have made it clear that I will not say or do anything to make things easy; I have said and done things that have caused the opposite at times, much to my regret. But I do care for you, that is true. Perhaps more than I had wished to.”

     

                “Don’t worry,” Lena said with a teasing smile, leaning back slightly with her legs stretched out in front of her. “I’ll make sure it’s not more than it currently is.”

     

                Snorting, Kara toyed with her chainmail, smiling as she shook her head. “Oh? And how are you going to manage that?”

     

                “I can be horrible when I want to be.”

     

                “Unfortunately, I have never found you to be horrible, so I’m not confident that will work.”

     

                “I haven’t tried very hard.”

     

                “Now, I believe that is a lie - you don’t strike me as someone who does not try at things. Say it to me truthfully in fae or I shall not believe you.”

     

                “Is that right?” Lena laughed before clumsily trying to force the words out and coming up speechless as her throat tightened around the lie. “Alright, I’ve done my worst.”

     

                “And I did not find you horrible at all,” Kara confessed in fae, no lies tripping her up.

     

                Lena’s mouth curved with a reserved smile and she ducked her head down, sitting up straight as she toyed with her fingers in her lap. They both sobered up after that and she pushed herself to her feet, absentmindedly reaching out to touch the back of Kara’s hand.

     

                “I should leave you to more important things than flattery. I just wanted to bring you the flowers.”

     

                “It’s nothing important,” Kara murmured. “Just oiling my armour.”

     

                “Some might say that’s very important. I can’t imagine rusty armour would do you any good in a fight. Although, I think that many pieces weighing me down would make me a sitting duck, regardless of rust or not.”

     

                “It is quite light. Come, see for yourself.”

     

                “Hm? You mean put it on?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Wary surprise stole over Lena and she eyed the chainmail in Kara’s grasp with scepticism. “I don’t know, I mean, I wouldn’t have any use for it.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara set down the oilcloth and let the chainmail slither into the shape of a long shirt. “I can’t think of anyone who would have more use for it. Consider it a lesson in warfare; you should know the parts and where the weak spots are. It may very well be a matter of life and death for you one day, and I would see you appropriately educated.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes. “I do know the parts; that’s chainmail.”

     

                “A chainmail hauberk. And what is this?” Kara asked, reaching past her to pick up a shaped piece of ornate metal.

     

                Pursing her lips and narrowing her eyes, Lena shrewdly eyed the piece for a moment before sighing. “It’s the shoulder piece.”

     

                “What is it called?”

     

                “Do I need to know the names if I know what it’s for?”

     

                “Well, it’s not a proper lesson if you don’t know all of the information, is it? It’s a pauldron. Take off your dress.”

     

                “Has your flirting progressed to seduction so quickly?”

     

                “Very humorous. I will let you keep your underclothes on.”

     

                “How generous of you. And what’s the point of this, exactly?”

     

                Still, Lena climbed to her feet, unbuckling the belt at her waist, setting her beloved dagger aside and then toying with the clasps on the outer layer of her dress before she slowly undid them. Shedding the outer layer, she still had the heavy skirts and loosely tied bodice on over the shift beneath and she unfastened the ribbons and let the skirts pool onto the floor before stepping out of them.

     

                “The point is for you to get the feel for it, to see its usefulness, to know how to move it and put it on.”

     

                “You can just do it for me,” Lena said with a goading smile.

     

                Sighing, Kara rolled her eyes as she stepped forward and crumpled the hauberk to the neck before slipping it over Lena’s head. “Arms.”

     

                Obediently slipping one arm through a sleeve and then the other, Lena felt the chill of the little steel rings through the thin cotton of her shift, and then the weight of it as Kara let it unfurl, falling to Lena’s knees. It was lighter than she’d anticipated though, and she held her arms slightly aloft, as Kara adjusted it over her shoulders and arms.

     

                “Well, think about how fierce you will look in armour.”

     

                “How do you know I aspire to look fierce?”

     

                “Beautiful then.”

     

                “You must think me awfully vain. Do you think I care if people think I look hot?”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Kara turned and picked up the breastplate. It had leather buckles on the sides and she had Lena put one arm through and quickly fastened the sides and shoulder, checking the ones that were still fastened for good measure.

     

                “You are always so cold, but I would think so much metal would make you look very hot once you started fighting.”

     

                “Not that hot. Attractive hot.”

     

                Brow creasing, Kara reached for the forget as her nose wrinkled with confusion. “How does your body temperature make you attractive?”

     

                “No, it means attractive. It’s slang, you know? Informal language.”

     

                “That doesn’t make any sense.”

     

                “It’s like saying women in armour get you off.”

     

                “Off what?”

     

                “Christ,” Lena muttered, pinching the bridge of her nose as she tipped her head back. “Like arousing. Physically attractive.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara suddenly exclaimed, looking mildly alarmed at her ignorance. “Well … that’s odd.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes. “Go on then, what’s that bit for? A neck collar?”

     

                “It’s a gorget. But yes, for the neck.”

     

                “See? I’m good at this.”

     

                “Just keep still or your hair will get caught.”

     

                Kara fastened each piece to her, the additional weight settling into place as the vambraces were strapped to her forearms, pauldrons were buckled to the sides of the gorget and under her arms, sinking to her knees to fasten greaves to her shins. Lastly, Kara grabbed her scabbard, attached to her sword belt, and buckled it around Lena’s waist before stepping back.

     

                “How do I look?” Lena asked, spreading her arms as she grinned.

     

                Considering the question as she rubbed her chin, Kara met Lena’s gaze, her blue eyes shining with amusement. “Hot.”

     

                Snorting, Lena reached out to give Kara a playful shove and her wife grabbed her arm, jerking it up quickly and suddenly twirling a knife in her fingers. She pressed the tip into Lena’s armpit with a raised eyebrow.

     

                “Mail will protect the worst of it, but a well-aimed thrust at a weak spot will still injure your opponent,” Kara explained as Lena patted the empty dagger sheath on the belt.

     

                “You would ordinarily be wearing a gambeson underneath as well for extra padding,” Kara explained, twirling the knife again before she balanced the point on her finger and then caught it by the hilt as it fell, jerking it up under Lena’s chin. “And a helmet, of course, so always go up through the jaw when possible. And here.”

     

                Kara dropped her hand to Lena’s thigh, the edge of the knife slipping through the split front of the chainmail as she laid the edge against the thin cotton of Lena’s shift. The cold metal made Lena’s skin prickled with goosebumps, although it very well could have been from the touch of Kara’s knuckles so high on her legs

     

                “A cut here will have your life’s blood on the ground within moments.”

     

                “I’m aware of the femoral artery.”

     

                Then Kara grabbed a fistful of Lena’s dark hair, jerked her head back, and stepped behind her before Lena could respond. Propelling her towards the table, Kara pressed the edge of the knife against Lena’s throat as her wife slammed her palms on the table for balance, caught off guard by the turn of things.

     

                “This is why it is dangerous to fight with your hair down,” Kara murmured, her lips close to Lena’s ear as she lectured her. “We all hope we may fight nobly, but there is always the risk that someone will dishonour the art of war to spill more blood. Be careful Lena - I would hate for someone to catch you unawares.”

     

                “Would you?” Lena rasped, her heart pounding in her chest, throat dry as her head was tipped back, Kara standing so close behind her. “You sound as if you’re enjoying yourself. How many times have you dreamt of slitting my throat? Should I be concerned?”

     

                Letting out a withering sigh, Kara loosened her grip on Lena’s hair and her fingers brushed the back of Lena’s neck. She kept the dagger in place though and Lena was rooted to the spot, the cold edge pressed to her throat. “I-”

     

                “Am I interrupting?”

     

                Startling so violently, Lena almost cut her own throat as she jerked her head around, Kara yanking the knife away with shocking speed, sparing Lena a line scored from ear to ear. They both sprang apart so quickly that it almost felt as if they’d been caught doing something forbidden, something untoward, like sneaking teenagers. Alex held a crammed tray in hand and arched an eyebrow at the sheepish, evasive looks on their faces.

     

                “No. No, not at all,” Kara quickly replied, moving away as she picked up a flint stone and started lighting lamps. 

     

                Dusk had crept over them as they’d talked and the shape of the world had blurred at the edges, a chill creeping into the wind as the tide swept in and crashed over the lower levels of the hall. The stars were veiled behind a haze of clouds as blue twilight stole over the sea.

     

                “I was just giving a lesson.”

     

                “Well, you have both missed dinner; I anticipated you would be together so I brought enough for two. I hope I haven’t intruded.”

     

                “Kara was just showing me how to put on armour.”

     

                “So I see. It becomes you, Your Highness. Don’t you agree, sister?”

     

                Back to the two of them as she lit another lamp, Kara waved a hand distractedly. “Yes, yes, Lena is aware of how beautiful she looks in armour. She is not fond of flattery; it will not make her like you more.”

     

                “It’s not flattery,” Alex laughed, setting the tray down on Kara’s cluttered table. She rounded on her sister-in-law and her eyes darted down to her foot. “I am just curious to see how long the Princess intends to delay her other lessons. We had a deal that I would instruct her in a few skills.”

     

                Groaning, Lena gave Alex a grim look. “If you’re talking about kicking my ass, I can wait a bit longer for the humiliation. I’m not in a rush to repeat last time.”

     

                “Then perhaps that will be more incentive for you to perform better this time. I should think the absence of any wounds would help. Do you need a few more days for your leg to heal?”

     

                Wriggling her toes as she balanced on her left foot, Lena shrugged. “It feels fine.”

     

                “Tomorrow then,” Alex declared with a savage grin.

     

                “Fine, but I’m not wearing armour. I’ll be rattling around like the Tin Man if you expect me to fight in this.”

     

                “Armour is typically expected to be worn for a fight,” Kara chimed in. “That is its purpose.”

     

                “It’s also the purpose of fire to be hot but that doesn’t mean it can’t burn you.”

     

                “Ah, now that is logic from the mouth of Firefolk,” Alex said with approval.

     

                Kara gave her sister a droll look before shifting her eyes to Lena, maintaining her expression. She picked up the jug of fresh water Alex had brought and poured a measure into each cup. “You are both maddening. I should think you’d be fast friends.”

     

                “That will depend on the feelings your dear wife harbours for me tomorrow. I will leave you two to … whatever it is you have planned for your evening,” Alex said with a vague wave between the two of them, looking mildly suspicious - or perhaps hopeful. “I hope it is enjoyable.”

     

                “Sleep peacefully,” Kara called after her sister’s retreating figure.

     

                Silence fell over the room after Alex left, the two women hovering uncertainly from their respective spots, with enough distance between them that it felt awkward. Clearing her throat, Lena gestured to the breastplate.

     

                “I should probably take this off.”

     

                “Keep it on. You should grow accustomed to moving with the weight of it.”

     

                “Oh. Okay.”

     

                “Are you hungry?”

     

                “I could eat.”

     

                Kara moved the tray onto the floor, fluidly sinking to her knees with it. She handed the cup of water up to Lena, who took a sip and then sat somewhat heavily, metal clattering at her ungainly movements. It wasn’t uncomfortable though, nor heavy, as Kara had assured her, and she accepted a bowl of soup. Chunks of crab and root vegetables floated in the creamy broth and Lena spooned it into her mouth and dipped bread into it. There was an assortment of fruits and cheeses as well and Kara carved a green apple into slices for her with her dagger, sharing it with soft brie on buttered bread. The bread had seaweed in it, Lena noticed, but it wasn’t unpalatable when baked into it and she finished her portion quickly and helped herself to some of the wine that had been sent up in a clay jug. 

     

                She filled Kara’s empty water cup with some too and they sat in companionable silence as her wife ate her fill and slowly mopped the dregs of her bowl with the heel of her bread. Content, Kara leaned back on her elbows, legs crossed at the ankle as she stretched out, and she gave Lena a tender smile.

     

                “It really does become you, you know,” she off-handedly commented, gesturing to the armour. “You look every inch the warrior princess.”

     

                “I look like I’m about to attend a renfaire.”

     

                “I’m not sure what that is, but I shall take your word for it.”

     

                “A renaissance fair. People dress up in fantasy mediaeval clothes and pretend they’re a knight or a peasant or even an elf. Maybe a witch or a princess too. Whatever takes their fancy.”

     

                “Is that how you view being here? Dress up and make believe?”

     

                “If it was dress up and make-believe, I’d like to think I’d have fewer scars and near-death experiences.”

     

                “I cannot promise you will not be subjected to more, but if my word means anything to you, I will try my best to ensure any ill directed to you will befall me first before it strikes you.”

     

                “Do you not care about getting hurt? About your scars?”

     

                “If I am scarred in the act of defending my wife’s life, I will wear them with pride for all to see. And if I fall to my wounds, I will die with relief, knowing that I never loved one enough to kill them.”

     

                “How do you know that’s true, though? I mean, don’t you love your sister? Your mom? What if it’s them?”

     

                “Of course I love them, but it is not them.”

     

                “How do you know that?”

     

                “I am quite certain. The prophecy was quite specific.”

     

                “In what way? Sorry, am I prying? I’m just curious.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Kara took a sip of wine. “Curiosity is always welcome. The prophecy ascertained that it would be the one who holds my heart; at present, that’s no one. Familial love is not the same as the feeling of cutting one's heart out of your chest to give it to another for safekeeping.”

     

                “How would you know?”

     

                “Do you? You speak as if you know the truth of love and that I am ignorant of it.”

     

                “No, I’ve never loved anyone. No, that’s not true - I loved my mom. I was so young but that felt like ripping my heart out of my chest, to lose her.”

     

                “That is a different matter; it was ripped out of you unwillingly, not freely cut out and gifted.”

     

                “Doesn’t matter,” Lena said with faint bitterness, “it’s the same. Love and grief are two sides of the same coin. It’s a knife’s edge between the pain of the two.”

     

                “It is different. I know it,” Kara insisted, her voice lowering to a brooding murmur. “In my bones, I know that when it happens, it will be different and it will make me wish it had been me instead so that I may selfishly be spared the agony of my guilt.”

     

                “Then I pray you never fall in love; I would hate to lose you to the grief of losing someone you love.”

     

                “I have lasted so long alone, I will undoubtedly endure alone for a while yet longer.”

     

                Kara’s crooked smile was filled with wavering doubt, her dark blue eyes like deep wells of worry, and Lena’s expression softened with pity. Hesitating, she bit her lip and reached out to rest a hand on Kara’s knee.

     

                “You aren’t alone. We’re tied together, whether we like it or not, and I might not be the person you’d cut your own heart out for but I’ll be the person who is at your side through it all. I have no other choice, as you’ve said, so … I don’t know if that’s comforting or not but … well, through all of my foster families and group homes, I’ve learnt that it’s better to have someone than no one. ”

     

                “Then how come you have never had someone?”

     

                “Me? Well … no one has ever wanted me. It’s made it pretty difficult to get someone to stick around and … I don’t trust easily. Not after everything. I just know that I was a little girl who so desperately wanted a family, that even the worst people they put me with were better than nothing, and it just- it never stuck. I was never a good fit. Kind of messes with you, going through something like that. It made me stop hoping I’d find a good family, good people who wanted me. I guess- I guess all I really needed was to be handed off to someone who couldn’t get rid of me.”

     

                “Lena-” Kara started, then cut off with a sigh.

     

                Her expression softened and she reached out to take Lena’s hand in her own, squeezing her fingers reassuringly. Lena could feel the hard callouses, see the tiny scars from fish hooks and knife nicks, the searing heat of Kara’s tanned skin as her fingers tightened around Lena’s soft hands.

     

                “I would not get rid of you even if I could,” she continued in fae.

     

                Lena’s stomach jolted at the truth. It felt wrong to hear it, to know that it was honest, that Kara truly meant it. It went against everything that Lena felt inside, that inner turmoil of a child so unwanted, that endless loneliness that still dogged her even now, even with Kara sitting across from her. Some wounds would never heal, partially because Lena would never allow herself to be in a position where there was the chance that the person would only add to her pain one day, that they wouldn’t stick around.

     

                Knocking back the rest of her wine, she clumsily climbed to her feet, clearing her throat. “I should get going.”

     

                “You can stay, you have nowhere else to be.”

     

                “No, I- I really should go. Um, let me just- how do I-”

     

                She fumbled with the buckles, growing agitated as she scrabbled at the leather straps, growing hot inside the metal encasing her. It was even worse that she could feel the heat creeping into her pale cheeks and she couldn’t meet Kara’s eyes when her wife climbed to her feet and started to help her, quickly relieving her of the pieces of armour. 

     

                Once the chainmail was dragged off her, Lena turned and left, still in her shift, the layers of her dress abandoned on Kara’s bed. Although she didn’t call out, Lena could hear Kara’s footsteps shadowing her to the door, a silent question left unspoken as she let Lena go. Crossing the hallway and slipping through the archway of her own bedroom, Lena sank heavily onto the bed and curled up on her side.

     

                Her room was dark, the brazier down to coals, and it was colder than she expected. The sun from earlier on that day had vanished and she could hear the wind screaming through gaps in the halls, the hiss of rain as the threatening clouds started to roll in off the coast. She dug the heels of her hands into her screwed-up eyelids and tried to stamp down her frustration. Lena couldn’t pinpoint why it bothered her so much for Kara to speak it in fae, so sincere that she truly believed that she wanted Lena around, only that it did. 

     

                No one could honestly say they’d ever wanted to fight to keep her around, that if they were given the chance they’d still choose her - only her mom. Her mom who was still at the bottom of that lake, as far as Lena knew, had drowned to save her daughter and made it so that Lena would never have anyone love her so selflessly ever again. There was a lot to be said for a mother’s love, but it could ruin you for the lacklustre love that others offered, and Lena had been knotted up inside ever since she was a child because of it.

     

                She slept fitfully, the sound of the rain growing stronger, the rumbles of thunder gradually growing louder, interspersed with flicker lightning that startled Lena from her sleep. Twice she woke from nightmares of her usual sort, dank water and the musty taste of weeds and silt in her mouth, the burning in her lungs, roots and rotting branches snagging on her skirt as she struggled. Covered in a cold sweat both times, she rolled back over and listened to the storm until she fell back asleep, waking with that leaden, wrung-out feeling of exhaustion.

     

                Despite her exhaustion, she was awake early, sitting against her pile of pillows with her knees drawn to her chest when Andrea came to help dress her. Her attendant swept in with a bundle of clothes in her arms and paused, surprise crossing her face.

     

                “Oh, you’re awake. Good. Here - your wife gave me these.”

     

                She set down the bundle of clothes and Lena poked through the items, finding a pair of soft leather leggings, a thick cream cotton shirt and a woollen jerkin embroidered with leaping fish around the neck. Lena briefly washed over the basin with the hot water Andrea had carried in with her and then changed into the clothes before allowing her dark hair to be simply braided out of her face. Pinning her grey cloak on before putting on a new pair of socks Kara had knitted her, Lena laced on her tooled boots and swept out of her room with Andrea in tow.

     

                “You know you don’t have to stay here, right?” Lena said as the Unseelie fell into step beside her. “There’s a good chance you’ll have your head chopped off alongside mine once whoever’s after us manages to reach us here.”

     

                “Where else would I go?”

     

                “Wherever you want. I’d kill for that kind of freedom.”

     

                Andrea laughed, “many would kill to be in your position.”

     

                “Shall we trade?”

     

                “I could never be married to a Seelie . She is so serious that one would wonder if she has ever laughed once in her life. Not to mention the backwater notions of the Waterfolk, I-”

     

                “Hey,” Lena snapped, coming to a stop as she interrupted the other woman. “Don’t talk about her like that. You don’t even know her but you’re here by her good grace so don’t piss me off because she might be nice but I’m not .”

     

                “Do you know how to laugh too? Heavens, you’re a pair well matched, I should think. Find your own way to breakfast if you are in such a foul mood.”

     

                Scowling at Andrea’s retreating back, Lena scoffed and then continued on her way. She did know the way but it still nettled her for one of her few … friends wasn’t the right word but Andrea was one of the only people Lena regularly interacted with and she rankled at being snubbed. It didn’t help that she’d slept so poorly either, shadows beneath her eyes as she stepped into the long hall they had breakfast inside every day.

     

                Tapestries were hung on the walls, pillars soaring to the vaulted ceiling, the stone carved and sweet rushes of lavender and herbs sprinkled over the floors to scent the space. It had the clean tang of salt water as well where the floors were regularly scrubbed by the waves when the tide rose high enough to flood the lowest levels of the halls, and Lena took a seat on a stone chair rimed with salt. Kara was at the head of the table and she sat at her right, nodding solemnly as she reached for a jug of something steaming. Tea.

     

                “Good morning,” Kara greeted her, scooping mackerels onto some bread.

     

                “Morning,” Lena replied, somewhat curt as she filled the cup set at her place, pausing before filling Kara’s for her. Her eyes flitted to her wife’s and then to her sisters-in-law. “Morning.”

     

                J’onn, Sam, Nia and James were also in attendance and they shared friendly nods as Lena eyed the smoked salmon, mackerels and grilled cod and helped herself to porridge instead. It warmed her, a chill to the air of the breakfast hall from the wet night, but she had little appetite, toying with her food as her thoughts preoccupied her.

     

                James left first and then J’onn in his wake, and even though Alex had already finished her breakfast, she lingered, talking rapidly in fae with Kelly and Kara. Lena picked up one out of every three words when her sister-in-law slowed every so often but she wasn’t listening closely, nothing of interest catching her ear, and it wasn’t until her spoon clattered to the rim of her half-empty bowl that Alex cut off mid-sentence and scraped her chair back.

     

                “Excellent. Let’s go.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Alex, let her breakfast settle first,” Kara sighed as she rolled her eyes.

     

                “No, no, we’re doing it now.”

     

                “Oh, our lesson?” Lena assumed, her brow furrowing. She was distracted and just waved a hand dismissively. “Sure. Fine. You’ll kick my ass anyway - may as well get it over and done with.”

     

                Sighing again, Kara climbed to her feet as Kelly did the same, and she shot her sister a stern look. “You will be gentle.”

     

                Pressing a hand to her heart, Alex bowed slightly as she grinned, backing out of the door and then turning as she set off towards the exit leading to the beach. Kelly followed after her and Lena made for the door but was cut off by Kara’s arm barring the way. Eyed flitting up to her wife’s face, Lena blinked blankly at her.

     

                “You do not seem yourself.”

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                Reaching up to cup her face in a hand, Kara thumbed the lavender bags beneath Lena’s eyes. Eyelids shuttering at the gentleness of her touch, Lena swallowed thickly, resisting the urge to lean into her warm touch.

     

                “You look tired.”

     

                “Bad dreams.”

     

                “Oh. I did not know they persisted.”

     

                “Always.”

     

                “You can tell me of them … if you ever want to.”

     

                Giving her a wan smile, Lena moved her head, shaking off Kara’s touch. “I don’t. But thank you.”

     

                Nodding, uncertain with worry as she fiddled with a ring on her thumb, Kara didn’t know what else to say and exhaled as she stepped aside, gesturing for Lena to go ahead. She followed after her and the two of them made their way out into the grey day.

     

                The sand was wet and Lena’s boots gouged furrows into it as she walked towards the two women waiting for them. Alex had unbuckled her knives and set them on the rock that Kelly had settled down on.

     

                “No weapons,” Alex assured Lena, looking eager at the prospect of sparring with her.

     

                It made no difference to Lena either way; she was guaranteed to lose.

     

                Almost as if she sensed Lena’s accepted defeat, Kara laid a hand on her shoulder and stepped forward, removing her sword belt and leaning it against the same rock as Alex’s knives. She untied her robe then, the wind ruffling her unbound hair as she raised her eyebrows suggestively.

     

                “I’ll go first. Kelly?”

     

                “As you wish,” the other woman humoured her, removing her cloak and rolling up the sleeves of her shirt.

     

                Kara moved back over to her sword and yanked it free, giving Lena a quick wink before she took the dagger as well. Hefting the hilt in her hand, she flipped the dagger and caught it by the blade before offering the dagger to Kelly.

     

                “Unless you’d prefer to fetch your spear and shield?”

     

                Waving aside the offer, Kelly took the dagger from her. “We all know you will best me with any weapon. It shall be a welcome session all the same and a dagger will do nicely.”

     

                Testing the weight of the dagger, Kelly put some distance between her and Kara and beckoned her for her to start. Swinging her sword through the air, the blade whistling through its trajectory, Kara closed the distance slightly, angling towards the sea as Kelly circled with her. 

     

                Kara moved first, lunging forward with a slashing cut to Kelly’s arm, scoring a shallow line that welled up red through the cut cotton. Stomach jolting, Lena straightened, her whole body attentive as she leaned forward, serious concern on her face. Alex lounged beside her, arms folded over her chest as Kelly spun away from the sword and thrust her dagger towards Kara’s abdomen as she remained inside her guard. Lena’s grip tightened on the rock as her shoulders went taut, but Kara was quick. So quick that she could hardly keep track of her movements.

     

                When Kelly thrust a hand towards Kara a moment later, a gust of wind drove her towards the sea, and Kara summoned a wave with her left hand, funnelling the water into a malleable ribbon that she used to lash at Kelly like a whip. It became even more interesting then, a game of weapons and power, stinging sand lashing Kara’s exposed skin, while the sea churned behind her, waves rushing up the beach to pull at Kelly’s ankles. They each bore a few cuts and Lena watched vivid red droplets turn to rain or vanish into an eddying swirl of wind as they bled freely from superficial wounds.

     

                Even though there was no ill intent in the fight, Lena watched with an anxious edge to her face as her eyes darted back and forth. For her part, Alex heckled the two women in fae from the sidelines, laughing when Kara launched a wave at Kelly that swept her to her knees, and again when Kelly’s hand vised shut a moment later, trapping the air inside Kara’s chest, leaving her gasping, her mouth opening and closing like a fish on dry land.

     

                It took Lena a moment to realise what was happening as Kara stumbled backwards, even as Kelly surged forward, dagger cutting towards her sister-in-law’s chest. Ocean blue eyes widened as she staggered away, knocking the dagger away with her sword, Kara’s expression turned serious and she struck back, again and again as Kelly fended her off with a grin on her face as Kara’s face started to redden, very quickly verging towards purple. 

     

                When Kara stumbled, falling to a knee, her sword raised to deflect a downward strike, Lena couldn’t stop the stab of panic that had her off the rock before she even realised she was moving. It wasn’t until she felt the resistance of Alex’s hand snagging on her cloak that she was brought to a stop, face bone-white as she whirled around, stricken.

     

                “She’s fine,” Alex insisted.

     

                “Are you fucking crazy? She’s turning blue,” Lena shouted, trying to tear her cloak free and then scrabbling at the fastening when Alex held on tightly.

     

                “Look.”

     

                Fingers slowing on the clasp, Lena watched as Kara dragged in the sea behind her, churning around Kelly’s feet as the sand underfoot shifted with the current, unbalancing the fae and allowing Kara to tackle her around the knees. As she fell, Kelly’s grasp on her power slipped and she fell back onto wet sand as Kara gasped, chest heaving, and climbed on top of her before she could move, sword held poised over her heart, ready to thrust down.

     

                “Yield?”

     

                “A good fight,” Kelly relented with a grin. “I thought I had you there.”

     

                Kara breathlessly laughed, giving her a quick smile as she pushed herself to her feet and then reached down to help Kelly up. “Almost.”

     

                Still standing there with her hand at the clasp at her throat, Lena could feel her heart hammering, a hollow shakiness inside her as she considered that she’d actually thought Kara was in danger. Of course, it was ridiculous to think that her family would hurt her, but then Lena didn’t exactly have a good opinion of family in the fae world, considering her own had threatened her numerous times. 

     

                Kara and Kelly were laughing, bleeding and wet as they traipsed the short distance back to their respective partners and Lena felt some of the tension bleed out of her. Her throat was still painfully tight and she knew her hands would be shaking if she uncurled her fingers from their white-knuckled fists, adrenaline coursing through her.

     

                “After you, Princess,” Alex gestured to the stretch of golden sand as if nothing was amiss.

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena undid her cloak and folded it up, setting it on the rock. She kept her boots on and considered rolling up her sleeves, but it was cold and she didn’t think the length of her sleeves would delay the swift defeat that was heading her way. Alex looked entirely too gleeful at the prospect of pinning her to the ground, now that Lena wasn’t injured in any way, and she wondered if perhaps it had been a mistake to let the woman convince her that she needed a physical outlet for all of her frustration. She should have stuck to archery, perhaps horseback riding at most. It was too late for that now though and Lena was grim as she kept as far from the water as she could.

     

                “No powers, Alex!” Kara called out. “You know it’s not a fair fight if you use fire.”

     

                “It’s not a fair fight regardless,” Lena muttered, scowling as she tried to shake off her lingering worry.

     

                It bothered her that she’d thought for a moment that Kara’s life was at risk, that she could lose her. She shouldn’t have cared that much, shouldn’t have felt the vice-like pressure in her chest as she’d watched Kara struggle to breathe. Shaking her head to clear her mind of the thoughts, Lena told herself it was just a projection of what her mom’s last moments must have been like, the old loss still haunting her, even though Elizabeth would’ve been choking on water, not suffocating. They were two different things entirely but Lena had to rationalise her worry somehow.

     

                “Are you alright?” Alex quietly asked, her face crumpling. “You look frightened. You shouldn’t; I will not harm you.”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena tightly replied, squaring her shoulders.

     

                Nodding, Alex beckoned for Lena to advance and Lena was cagey as she shuffled forward, her whole body taut as she curled her hands into fists. Was she supposed to punch Alex? It felt wrong to do it but there were no weapons and Lena didn’t think she’d have the strength to wrestle the other woman to surrender if it came to it. 

     

                She inched closer and almost slipped on the sand as it shifted beneath her feet, a snort of laughter escaping Alex as she patiently waited. Righting her balance, Lena flushed and took another step forward. Quickly tiring of the timid approach of her opponent, Alex moved quickly and slapped Lena’s arm. It was gentle but the impact was still felt and Lena’s scowl turned affronted as she rubbed her arm. Alex gestured for her to continue.

     

                Going slowly again, she found herself pitching backwards as Alex hooked her leg with a foot, sending her crashing to the sand. Scrambling to her feet, Lena was starting to get annoyed now, her meek approach hardening to irritation as she dusted off her palms and then forged onwards, arm swinging. Alex grabbed it and punched her in the stomach, just hard enough to wind her, leaving Lena gasping for a moment as her eyes widened with outrage.

     

                Swinging again, Lena only felt air, Alex moving quickly, so easy for her that Lena failed to see how she got any enjoyment out of it at all, except at Lena’s embarrassment. Alex didn’t strike her as cruel enough to want to embarrass her for her own enjoyment. To teach Lena a lesson in humility, sure, but at least that had a purpose. Trying again, her wrist was grasped and Alex hesitated before gently slapping her face. That was even worse than being punched, Lena sourly thought as she jerked her arm free.

     

                “Keep going,” Kara called from the rock, where she was reading an old book with a worn wooden cover in between glances at the sparring, handling the tattered pages carefully. “Try and actually hit her this time!”

     

                Swallowing a scathing sound, Lena continued her attempts. She slipped more than once, covered in sand, and once Alex had gotten the measure of her, she started giving her advice. Move her feet faster, bend her knees more, and read the tension in Alex’s body. It wasn’t very helpful - Lena knew she was slow, wasn’t as athletic as these faes who had trained in warfare their entire lives - but she stopped being so timid.

     

                Their bout went longer than Kara and Kelly’s on account of Alex holding back. She started to hold back a lot more as Lena got into it, allowing her to see how it would play out if they were the same speed. Still, she got in a good many hits as she coached Lena on how to block them, making her learn the hard way, and when Lena attempted to emulate her movements, she even let her get in a punch or two. Lena wasn’t good at pulling hers but they were softer than Alex was used to and she smiled approvingly each time. 

     

                The next time Lena found herself flat on her ass, Alex held out a hand to help her up, but Lena grabbed a fistful of sand in hand and flung it into Alex’s face. Jerking her head back as she raised an arm to protect her face from the stinging eyeful, Alex let out a loud laugh of surprise.

     

                “Very good.”

     

                Climbing back to her feet while she had the chance, Lena felt a prickle of pride at catching the fae by surprise. It didn’t matter though, Alex darting past her guard to remind her that she was by no means skilled. Circling behind Lena, she grabbed her arm, jerking it back and forcing her to double over before Alex shoved her to the ground before she could recover.

     

                Face pressed into damp sand, Lena bucked and struggled as Alex pressed a knee to her back and then rolled her over. “Yield?”

     

                Lena licked her lips, grimacing at the tiny grains of sand in her mouth, and she briefly considered it. But then she knew that she would gain more respect by fighting to the last, that perhaps she had too much pride and would have preferred Alex punching her to unconsciousness before she gave in. Her mind made up, jutting her chin forward, Lena’s green eyes hardened with determination and she mustered her strength as the fae leaned over her, pinning her arms beside her face. 

     

                Urging her head up with as much force as she could manage, Lena’s forehead smacked Alex in the nose, hard enough for an audible crack and the hot splatter of blood on Lena’s brow and cheeks as she broke it. The pain was felt first, Lena’s vision blackening as nausea swept through her, and she struggled to sit up as Alex sat back on her haunches, pinching her nose.

     

                Rubbing her forehead and then pulling her hand away to stare at the blood, she blinked back stars as she stared at the fae. Blood streamed from Alex’s broken nose, turning to ash as it hit the sand, and she laughed at the wide-eyed look of panic on Lena’s face, seemingly unbothered by her newly broken nose.

     

                “An admirable attempt. I would suggest that next time you avoid that unless you’d like to knock yourself out in the process.”

     

                Feeling woozy, her head hurting, Lena squeezed her eyes shut, aware of Alex climbing to her feet. She felt hands on her arms then, lifting her to her feet and she drew in the cold sea air as she shook her head.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                “Do you yield?”

     

                Snorting, Lena closed her eyes and then shook her head. Alex laughed and clicked her tongue as she backed up a few steps.

     

                “You are stubborn; I admire that. Foolish, though.”

     

                “That’s the general consensus,” Lena snarkily replied, wiping her face on the sleeves, streaks of ghastly red left in its wake. 

     

                It made her stomach turn but she didn’t have time to react as Alex advanced on her, her movements lazy, her face stained red, but predatory and lethal all the same. Swallowing, Lena wondered if she could yield now, knowing that she was in for a brutal payback, even if Alex didn’t repay the favour of any broken bones, as Lena had inflicted upon her. 

     

                They kept at it, Alex’s punches sure to leave bruises as she put Lena through the wringer, tiring her out and calling out instructions and pointing out her mistakes at the same time she landed a strike for good measure. The distance between them had closed and it was a close-quarter fight for the most part, Alex getting Lena in a chokehold and coaching her through getting out of it, then jerking her arm behind her back and yanking it upwards so it strained Lena’s shoulder, then striking her in the kidney, gently so that it didn’t hurt too much but emphasising how it could hurt a lot, especially with a knife - Kara had already taught her that lesson before - and Lena was breathing heavily by the end of it.

     

                When she was certain that Lena had tired herself out, Alex drove her point home, exposing all of Lena’s flaws - her slowness, her poor footing, her weak defence - as she drove her backwards with a lazy assault that took almost no effort. Struggling to stay on her feet, Lena grimly hoped that Alex was enjoying her payback, right up until the moment that her sister-in-law raised a leg and planted her foot against Lena’s chest before pushing with all of her might.
