                Reeling backwards, Lena didn’t realise how close she was to the water until a wave washed over her as she landed on her back ten feet away from Alex, dousing her as she got a mouthful of saltwater before it retreated, churning white froth surrounding her as the sea dragged itself back out. Her mind was immediately seized by terror and she couldn’t move as the tide shifted the sand beneath her, hands sinking to her wrists, her chest rising rapidly as she breathed frantically, anticipating the next wave getting ready to crash over her. 

     

                But then Kara was there, one hand raised towards the sea while the other grabbed a fistful of her sister’s shirt. Lena didn’t look behind her as she shivered, soaked through on the wet sand, not wanting to see the wall of water held at bay behind her, but she knew it would be there, that Kara was holding it back. Staring at her wife, eyes fearful, lips parted as she breathed quickly, Lena couldn’t move. Not until Kara jerked her head and Lena scrambled to her feet, staggering off and rushing towards the entrance without pausing to fetch her cloak.

     

                As soon as she was away from the shoreline, Kara let the sea have its control back, the wave booming as it crashed onto the sand, water spraying over the sisters as Kara jerked Alex close, her expression hard. Her sister seemed puzzled, trying to parse the meaning of Kara’s sudden anger as she squared her shoulders.

     

                “Why did you do that?”

     

                “It was just a bit of fun.”

     

                “She is frightened of the water,” Kara snapped. “Her mother drowned . ”

     

                “Oh. Forgive me, I did not think-”

     

                “No, you did not.”

     

                Blinking in surprise at her sister’s clipped tone, uncharacteristic, Alex’s brows drew together over brown eyes. “It was not my intention to scare her. If I had known she feared it, I would not have done it.”

     

                “You will not do it again,” Kara warned her.

     

                Alex nodded and Kara seemed to remember herself, blinking as she shook her head, unknotting her fingers from her sister’s shirt as she let her go. A pucker formed between her eyebrows as she tried to come up with some explanation for her actions, to alleviate the odd tension in the air but she closed her mouth and turned, stalking after her wife without another word.

     

                It didn’t take her long to find Lena; she could hear her heartbeat almost as soon as she stepped foot inside the dwelling, following the sound of it until she reached the dead end of a short corridor. Pausing at the mouth of it, she quietly approached her wife, Lena’s back to her as she faced the limestone wall. Kara could hear her ragged breaths, see the tense set of her shoulders as she hunched over, dark hair damp and straggling down her back and in her face as she buried her head in her hands.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                Her voice was a low rasp, gentler than she’d been with Alex, but no less anxious. Lena didn’t respond and Kara inched closer, reaching out a hand and crooking a finger, drawing all of the water out of her wife’s clothes and hair. She flung it carelessly aside, splattering it on the stone floor, and crossed the remaining few feet separating the two of them.

     

                Outstretched hand pressing flat against Lena’s back, Kara stepped in closer and slowly turned her. She gripped Lena’s wrists and tried to pry her hands from her face, a pitiful sound escaping Lena’s lips as she tried to resist but was too limp with exhaustion to put much effort into it. Still, she kept her head down and Kara relinquished her hold on one wrist to brush her dark hair out of her face, fingertips tracing her cheek, down to her jawline and then tilting her head up.

     

                Lena’s sorrowful eyes met Kara’s, bloodshot from the few tears she’d let slip free and the many more she’d fought back, and she ducked her head again. The pallid look of fear, of embarrassment and grief wrenched Kara’s heart and she softened slightly, giving Lena’s hand a gentle squeeze.

     

                “It’s alright. You are safe.”

     

                Lena didn’t say anything and Kara could hear the loud pound of her chest, rising and falling quickly as she hadn’t quite regained control of her breathing. She’d correctly presumed that quiet sobs had been gasped out in the dim recess of the corridor and she could hear the way the breaths caught in Lena’s chest. Her wife closed her eyes, an errant tear slipping down her cheek, and Kara reached up to wipe it away before she pressed Lena’s hand against her chest and then slowly pressed her hand over Lena’s heart. 

     

                Stepping in closer, so that scant inches separated the two, Kara breathed slowly to keep her heartbeat regular for Lena to feel beneath her palm and listened to the sound of her wife’s heart as it slowly but surely started to level out. She watched her closely, Lena’s slightly ducked head slowly smoothing out the taut lines to one of weary resignation, the hunched stiffness of her shoulders slackening as Kara’s heartbeat lulled her away from the terror of her memories.

     

                “Forgive me, I should have been paying closer attention,” Kara whispered. 

     

                “It’s not your job to protect me from everything,” Lena hoarsely muttered.

     

                “If it is not mine, then whose?”

     

                Raising her chin, Lena’s eyes met Kara’s and her lips parted as if she was going to respond. She didn’t say anything though, just lowered her gaze, and Kara leaned in to touch her forehead to Lena’s. They stood that way for a few moments, the breath shared in the small space between their mouths, and Lena’s fingers twitched against Kara’s chest, clawing in the fabric of her shirt as she leaned in slightly, without meaning to, drawn to the other woman and her warmth, her safety. 

     

                She could feel Kara’s warm breath fanning over her lips and gently bumped her nose as her stomach tightened, that old, familiar pull of desire that occasionally reared its head to trouble her flickering to life. Suddenly aware of what she was doing, at risk of pursuing, Lena suddenly jerked back, her expression turning sulky with derision as her eyes flitted over Kara’s face.

     

                “You smell like the sea.”

     

                Her voice was quiet but contemptuous, making it sound like the insult she clearly thought it was, and she shouldered past Kara without another word, stalking off down the hallway until she’d walked the breadth of the halls and wound up in a small storage room, amidst crates of wine, sacks of flour and barrels of dried fish. 

     

                Sinking to the floor, guilt needling at her beneath the hollow shakiness of the sea closing over her, Lena let out a gasping sob as hot tears prickled her eyes. Reaching for a clay bottle of wine, she unstoppered it and took a swig. It was spiced and strong, the sweetness of blackberries on her tongue as she chugged half of the bottle in one go before she started to cough and splutter. Sitting in the dark, she finished off the bottle in between her quiet crying, tears cutting through the blood speckling her cheeks as she wiped her nose on her sleeve and tried to swallow her sobs in between mouthfuls of wine.

     

                She was on the second one by the time footsteps started down the hallway and a shadow filled the grey dimness of the open archway. Lena didn’t look up, just toyed with her bottle of wine, and a moment later Alex stepped across the threshold and sank to her haunches before Lena, reaching out to snag the bottle of wine from her hand.

     

                “Forgive me.” 

     

                Wiping her face on her sleeve, Lena didn’t say anything but she glanced surreptitiously at the other woman. Her face was free from blood and her nose looked straight, so Lena assumed she’d been tended to, but Alex looked regretful as she took a sip of wine to fill the heavy silence. 

     

                Clearing her throat, she forged onwards. “I was aware of your mother and your aversion to water; I did not think amidst things. I would not have sought to frighten you intentionally.”

     

                Reaching forward, Lena tugged the bottle of wine back and took a long drag from it. Watching her for a moment, Alex reached out and took the bottle back, noticing the second one already empty beside Lena.

     

                “You will make yourself sick if you drink more.”

     

                “I will have to feel if I don’t.”

     

                “The fear will pass.”

     

                “That’s not the only thing I don’t want to feel,” Lena confessed.

     

                “What else are you feeling? You may not trust me but I will listen if you wish to talk. If you do not wish to talk to me, that’s fine, I will fetch my sister for you.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Lena blurted it out in a panic before she could stop herself, the prospect of seeing Kara, of being in close proximity to her unbearable. She hadn’t even allowed her mind to stray towards the unwelcome feeling that had stolen over her as Kara tried to soothe her and after too much to drink, Lena knew she might do something irrevocably stupid. 

     

                “If you think her complicit in hurting you, I will absolve her of the blame for you. It was by my hand alone that you ended up in the sea and she will have my head if I repeat the mistake,” Alex brusquely told her before she softened. “She’s not the worst of us, you know. Not by a long way.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena let out a weary sigh. “I know. All I have known of her myself is kindness.”

     

                “Yes. My sister is like sunshine; she will bring light and warmth wherever she goes. It has been … difficult at times to be born as I was, like dull rain clouds in contrast to her radiance but I am blessed in her shadow. I think you will understand that.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “She will not let any harm befall you. She will only bring you light and warmth if you let her in; she has suffered much but her heart is still good, even if she will pretend that she does not feel so keenly as she does. Do you understand me? She will always care more deeply than she will admit. About everything. Even about you.”

     

                “Don’t worry, I’ve promised her that I won’t let her care for me more than she already does. And don’t I do a bang-up job of pushing people away?” Lena said with a hollow laugh, giving Alex a crooked smile. 

     

                “As she already does may be too much for her to bear to lose one day,” Alex muttered to herself, so softly that Lena didn’t quite catch it all, looking troubled as she touched the tender bridge of her nose. Speaking louder, she continued, “you will not push her away. And by extension, you will not push me away either, or any of your kin.”

     

                “You’re not my kin, and I’m not your responsibility.”

     

                “There may come a day when you’re grateful for being wrong on that matter. It will not be today but perhaps today you will be grateful for being left alone. I will see that you are not bothered but do not drink yourself to despair; it is a bleak hole, Lena. One that I have ventured into myself on occasion. Light and warmth are better company.”

     

                She moved to leave and then hesitated before nodding to her, genuinely respectful. Slipping out of the door, Alex left her alone and Lena pushed herself to her feet a while later, wishing she was more drunk than she was. As it was, she felt a little unsteady on her feet, her mind pleasantly foggy as it leached away some of her frustration and unease.

     

                Exiting her hiding spot, she wandered through the halls and made her way outside, slipping through the exit on the eastern side of the hall, opposite to the beach she’d been on this morning. Walking up a path cut into the steep cliffside, she was grateful for the grass underfoot and set off alone, no cloak or dagger to keep her company against the frigid wind as the clouds darkened overhead. The rain held off though and Lena walked until she reached where a few tributaries winding through the marsh met the mouth of the sea, slipstreams of water mingling as birds cried out and wildlife rustled amidst the weeds.

     

                She had to admit there was a particular beauty to the wetlands and marsh, and she spent a while watching a cormorant dive for fish in the shoal sparkling amidst the shallows. Idling away the remainder of her morning a safe distance from the water, Lena tried her best to suffer the closeness of it, trying to stamp down her fear as she confronted it as best she could from the damp patch of grass she curled up on.

     

                In the end, it did start to rain, but she lingered outdoors, noon passing by and leading to afternoon. Saturated in her clothes, Lena lay splayed on the grass, feeling the earth beneath her and wishing for trees to shade her, for the mossy, dank depths of the forest. It would not have been so bad if she had the forest. Instead, she had dirt, and she clutched fistfuls of clumped earth and grass and felt the roots beneath her, feeling them as extensions of herself as she focused on her breathing and let the rain patter down onto her.

     

                She didn’t move until the rain gave way to hail, peppering her with pea-sized pellets that stung her face. It was starting to get dark now, the afternoon a deep grey, sunset already on the horizon as winter made the days shorter, and she caught sight of movement in the distance, someone watching her from afar. For a moment, she thought it was Kara, but the darkly dressed figure melted away and she knew it was Sam, her shadow keeping an eye on her, possibly at her wife’s request as she resolved to give Lena her distance. 

     

                Walking back quickly, arms over her head as the hail lashed at her and then turned back into rain, thunder cracking as a storm rolled in, turning the sea to monstrously large, grey waves, Lena was eager to be out of her wet clothes and into her bed. It had been a draining day on a few accounts and her body was stiff, bruised and shivering. It was a relief to see the wet limestone building in the distance as Krypton came into view, and she entered through the front door this time, taking the quickest route to her bedroom.

     

                Tiptoeing to the door as if avoiding being spotted, even though she couldn’t hear Kara in her room, Lena stepped inside and stripped off her wet clothes, leaving them in a pile before she sank onto her bed. Shifting beneath the blankets, she rolled onto her side and closed her eyes, damp and cold and exhausted. Still, she didn’t sleep and hunger gnawed at her stomach, but she had no appetite, faintly nauseous from the copious amounts of wine she’d consumed that morning. 

     

                While she didn’t sleep, her mind did drift, her hair slowly drying into frizzy waves as she huddled beneath the heavy blankets and tried not to think at all. As committed as she was to not feeling a thing, it took her a moment to realise that someone was standing at the door, some unknown length of time later. 

     

                Jerking up, bringing the blankets with her, Lena stared through the gloom at her wife. Holding a cup in hand and a grey cloak under her arm, Kara hovered on the threshold with uncertainty, her eyes filled with hope and concern.

     

                “Hello.”

     

                “Hi.”

     

                “I don’t mean to disturb you, I just- I made you some tea. I, uh, I thought … it might help you sleep. I brewed it with herbs to help with that so …”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena awkwardly replied, unable to make herself look at Kara, feeling somewhat tongue-tied.

     

                Kara stepped inside, taking her gratitude as an invitation, and set Lena’s cloak down without a word. Hesitating, she walked over to the bed and gingerly extended the cup, trying not to get too close as Lena tried to understand the reason for her odd behaviour. Then it hit her with the smell of lavender and honey and a glistening, telltale sign of perfume at her throat and wrists that showed how Kara had tried to hide away the hint of saltwater and sand that had clung to her since their arrival. It made her stomach plummet as she took the cup and shamefully thanked her wife.

     

                Nodding, Kara rounded the bed and stoked the brazier to chase off the chill and Lena took a sip of her tea, bare arms prickling with goosebumps as she clutched the blankets to her chest and watched her wife closely. The fire built up quickly and the room warmed marginally, Lena furtively glancing at her wife as she cradled her cup in her palms.

     

                Dusting off her hands, Kara rounded the foot of the bed and surveyed Lena before gesturing to the cup. “Drink. It will keep your bad dreams at bay.”

     

                Lena didn’t bother contradicting her but she quietly scoffed her scepticism before taking a sip. It tasted earthy and sweet and she rolled the taste on her tongue as she stared at her lap, trying not to dwell on the awkwardness that descended between the two of them.

     

                “You were upset today. It saddened me to see you hurt alone; I would have liked to help,” Kara haltingly admitted, toying with a ring on her finger as she studied Lena.

     

                Feeling a hot flush sweep through her, knowing that her confusion for the sudden and unwanted rush of longing was not Kara’s fault, Lena sank on her pillows, pulling the blankets up higher as the tips of her ears burned. She didn’t know what to say, that she wasn’t averted to Kara’s help, that it was more than ending up in the sea that had her so knotted up and affronted, that it wasn’t all hurt but something that troubled her deeper than the known root of her fear of the water. In the end, Lena didn’t say anything.

     

                Kara’s mouth thinned with disappointment as her face fell, slightly crestfallen. Stepping closer to the bed, she hesitated before she smoothed a hand over Lena’s dark hair and then pressed a soft kiss on top.

     

                “I will leave you to your sweet dreams,” she murmured.

     

                Toying with her cup as Kara made for the door, Lena’s stomach twinged and she drew in a quick breath before the moment vanished. The smell of lavender and honey was strong in her nose and it was all so wrong. She couldn’t stop herself from speaking.

     

                “Kara? Don’t wear the perfume; you don’t smell like yourself.”

     

                Pausing, half-turned, her face delicately furrowed with confusion, Kara cocked her head to the side. “But you don’t like the sea.”

     

                “No, but I like you.”

    Chapter 22

                It was morning, judging from the angle of pale sunlight slanting through the high window, and Lena groaned as she pushed herself up off her pillows. She didn’t remember dreaming, didn’t remember waking, and she slowly sat up as she rubbed her eyes, the lingering taste of the tea Kara had brewed her at the back of her throat. Pondering that, surprised by its effectiveness, Lena had time to take stock of her body, every inch of her tender, every muscle feeling stretched to breaking. All of her injuries were superficial though; bruises, strained muscles, sore joints. 

     

                Groaning as she climbed to her feet, Lena felt a stiffness in her movements as she dressed slowly, but as she stretched, she could feel her muscles loosening. As tired as she was, she didn’t feel plagued by the exhaustion of a bad night’s sleep that had dogged her for months, perhaps even years, predating her arrival in the fae realm. 

     

                She would have liked a hot bath then, but Lena finished dressing instead, digging through her piles of clothes to find appropriate attire for movement. Fitted leggings were laced up at the front, a billowing shirt tucked in and a thick jacket that wouldn’t restrict her movements but was padded enough to stave off the cold fastened over the top. Her dagger was belted at her waist, as usual, and she pulled on socks and her boots before stepping out of her room.

     

                Making her way down to breakfast, she found a few of the others already there and murmured hellos as she took her usual seat. Kara was there and Lena gave her a slight nod as she settled in, perusing the spread before her before Kara reached for the pot of tea and poured Lena a cup - she always picked the same one. Lips twitching slightly at the service, Lena glanced briefly at her wife, as Kara looked at her, blue eyes meeting green.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “How did you sleep?” Kara murmured, setting the pot back down.

     

                Clearing her throat, Lena took a sip of her tea as her face furrowed with contemplation. “Better. Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara sipped her own tea and returned her attention to her plate. Serving herself from the array of food, Lena ate her toast, fruit and oats as she periodically glanced at Alex, who paid her no attention. 

     

                Finishing quickly, Lena remained seated until Alex was finished, rising to her feet. Quickly standing as well, Lena was staring determinedly at her and Alex slowed, raising her eyebrows slightly at Lena’s unusual behaviour.

     

                “Again,” Lena said, her tone almost a demand.

     

                “Again what?”

     

                “I want to go again.”

     

                A slow smile spread across Alex’s face and she jerked her head to the door. Hurriedly following after her, Lena was subjected to a brutal hour of Alex’s uncompromising lessons. Her willingness to persist made her lesson that morning harsher, more demanding, and embarrassing too, although that wasn’t Alex’s intention. Punches were still pulled and Alex withheld any fire, but Lena felt like it wasn’t so much a lesson but a bout of humiliation as she was knocked on her ass time after time. 

     

                Still, it kindled something in her, sparking the drive to forge onwards. Lena was tired of being helpless, tired of letting the others do things for her, and even if she would never hold a candle to the skill of the fae who had been learning the arts of war for decades, it was better than being defenceless if it came down to it. If she was attacked, at least Lena would have the means to try and protect herself, even if it wouldn’t make a difference in the end.

     

                And it didn’t, fighting Alex and getting nothing but air, finding her pinched blocked, the wind knocked out of her as Alex retaliated. After the hour was up, Alex determined that they were done and Lena was left to pick herself up, breathing heavily, damp and covered in dirt and grass as they’d practised on the high ground outside the entrance to the halls.

     

                Not quite ready to give up yet, she asked after a bow and some arrows and spent the remainder of her morning recovering the calluses she’d lost over the last few weeks. Archery was by far her better pursuit so far, although she was only passable at that, but Lena enjoyed the meditative aspect of it more than she’d anticipated when she’d picked it up in the Unseelie Court. It felt good to come back to it then, setting herself a target on the rotting log of a tree set fifty yards from where she was standing.

     

                She missed more often than she struck the target, and it made her back and arms ache, grateful for the thickness of her jacket as it dulled the scrape of the bowstring when she messed up. Still, Lena got a sense of pleasure out of it and decided to dedicate more of her time to it, as well as hand-to-hand combat with Alex.

     

                “You should not give up on the sword,” Sam called out as she skulked nearby, that half of her that had sworn to Lillian that she would guard the Princess holding fast, even in the Seelie Court. 

     

                She had spent that morning much like the last few weeks, watching over Lena if she was outside alone - which wasn’t often - and while there was a warmth to her and she was generally kinder and more talkative, there was still that slightly unnerved feeling inside Lena whenever Sam was around her. It wasn’t that she didn’t trust the fae, only that Lena didn’t really trust anyone - except Kara - and she wasn’t sure what to make of the woman who belonged to both Courts and the loyalty she’d sworn to the Queen. Still, Sam seemed earnest then as she rose from the grass and took a few steps forward.

     

                “You will never be adept at it - or not for many years to come, at least - but you should not give up on it either. I remember, vaguely, of our lessons. If you have an interest in resuming them, it would make good use of my time here.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena bit her bottom lip as she considered it. She had no love for the sword, as heavy and unwieldy as she found it, her arms too weak to effectively swing it without trembling from the effort, her movements laughably clumsy. She almost flushed at the thought of the others watching her try her hardest in vain; Kara had been there in the Unseelie Court, but Kara had always been more sympathetic to her shortcomings. Hesitating, Lena winced slightly as she clutched her borrowed bow tightly in her hands.

     

                “Could we- could we do it in secret?”

     

                “Secret? I hardly think there are any secrets here, Your Highness.”

     

                “I know,” Lena murmured, frustrated as she scuffed her boot across the grass. “I just don’t want them to see how bad I am. After a while, it sort of becomes … embarrassing, you know?”

     

                Sam’s hazel eyes softened slightly and her mouth curved with a kind smile. “Do not be embarrassed. I will help you; we shall have to find a secret place.”

     

                “Now?”

     

                Pausing, Sam’s expression furrowed and she glanced at the limestone hall behind them and deliberated momentarily. “Very well. I will find a suitable sword for you. Wait for me here.”

     

                Deciding to make use of her time by loosing a few more arrows, even as her blistering fingers protested at the motions, but her attention wasn’t really in it, all of her shots missing the target as she waited for Sam to come back. Lena didn’t know why she was so jittery about it, knowing she had the freedom to do what she pleased there, as everyone else did, but she had mostly milled about in her room unless coaxed outside by Kara, and it somehow felt wrong to sneak about without telling someone. But Sam would be with her, so what was the worst that could happen?

     

                When Sam returned, she had her own sword sheathed at her side and another under her arm. Hurrying past Lena, she jerked her head for her to follow. Quickly recovering her arrows, Lena shoved them all into the quiver, slinging it over her shoulder and followed after Sam, glancing back over her shoulder to look back at the limestone hall with reservations. It looked like it might rain and she hoped it would hold off as long as they were outside, but Sam took her along a familiar path as Lena caught up to her, wringing her bow in her hands.

     

                “The temple?”

     

                “I’ve been here before and know it isn’t frequented that often. I should think we’d have the place to ourselves, away from prying eyes for now, and an excuse as to our presence if we are discovered. You may have to assume piety,” Sam said with a sideways glance at Lena as her cheek dimpled with a smile. “If you can find it within you to feel any sort of deference to the elements.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes and continued in step with her guard, casting her curious glances as they walked along the cliffside. “Why do you follow me around? I mean, you don’t have to guard me just because Lillian made you.”

     

                “Ah, but I do. There is something of my vow that lingers even in the Seelie Court,” Sam murmured, touching her brow. “I am split in half and it … confuses things, but my vows hold true no matter who I am. So, I shall protect you until I am released from my vows. I try to keep my distance as much as possible but you must understand that a vow is unbreakable, and so I must honour it when it becomes too overbearing to ignore my duty.”

     

                “Right. Well, thanks, anyway. I hope it’s not completely boring.”

     

                “I find myself with more time than I have had in decades since you have come along. Before that, I was a constant guard for your mother, and she demanded more of me than occasionally trailing after you does. I cannot complain.”

     

                “You can vent your frustrations on me now, I guess,” Lena snorted as they started down the path down the cliffside.

     

                Making sure she stayed close to the limestone as she kept a watchful eye on the grey waves crashing in, Lena slipped into the ancient temple and eyed the statues as Sam moved further inside. It smelled of brine and damp stone and Lena felt her arms prickle with goosebumps. Setting her bow and quiver aside, she stepped into the middle of the open space and stared expectantly at Sam.

     

                “Aren’t you going to light the braziers?”

     

                “No. Your eyesight is good enough. It will be good training for you.”

     

                “But I-”

     

                “Here.”

     

                She tossed a scabbard to Lena, who clumsily caught it. Gripping the ornate hilt, she drew the sword and studied the polished length of engraved metal, beautifully crafted of course, and just a little too heavy for her. It was shorter than the ones she’d practised with before but still almost as long as her arm, a cumbersome extension of her body as she set the scabbard aside, removed her jacket and swallowed thickly.

     

                “Did they not have any practice ones?” she asked with a shaky laugh, uncertain about her decision now.

     

                “As before, the best way to learn is the hard way. Injure or be injured.”

     

                “Fucking hell, can’t any of you do things the easy way for a change? In case you’ve forgotten why we’re here, I’m shit at swordplay and I don’t feel like being cut to bits for sport.”

     

                “I will not hurt you beyond anything superficial. You may try your hardest though. Come.” 

     

                Rolling her eyes as she let out an exasperated sigh, Lena rolled her shoulders and then gripped her sword in two hands, lunging forward. Sam had her sword in her hand before Lena could cross the space between them, the clang of metal striking metal ringing out in the hollow space. Shoving her away, Sam clicked her tongue.

     

                “Do not anchor your feet. You do not want to set roots or you will be easy to unbalance.”

     

                Nodding, bouncing slightly on the balls of her feet, Lena tried again. The sounds of their collisions filled the silence and Lena soon worked up a sweat as she stubbornly pressed on again and again, earning a few shallow scrapes across her ribs and arms as her cotton shirt was cut into tatters by the other fae’s sword. Sam was gentler in her tutelage than Reign had been, more helpful and kinder as she coached Lena through corrections.

     

                Sweating profusely as her chest heaved, Lena found her back, arms and shoulders aching so badly that she didn’t think she could hold the sword any longer. When she found the sword knocked from her grasp for the twelfth time, she staggered off-balance and closed her eyes.

     

                “Pick it back up.”

     

                Eyelashes fluttering, she opened her eyes and wiped her bloody sleeve over her face before stooping to fetch her sword. Ready to go for another round, despite wanting to give in so badly, Lena adjusted her grip and then found Sam beside her instead of across from her.  “Follow me.”

     

                Watching as Sam started to slowly work her way through a series of motions, the blade flowing quickly, elegantly through the air as she cut and slashed in a graceful dance, Lena tried to emulate it. They crossed the stone floor from one end of the hall to the other, and then back again. Repeating it a dozen times, Lena’s muscles were practically seizing by the end of it, and she didn’t feel as if she was moving any better or had gained any information from it. Still, when Sam sheathed her sword, she gave Lena an approving nod.

     

                “You have not forgotten all of your lessons. Practice the forms we just went through, and they will offer you some balance and flexibility; it is invaluable in a fight. It will also help empty your mind of your troubling thoughts.”

     

                Face furrowing with annoyance, Lena went to fetch her belongings, sheathing her sword and slinging bow and quiver over her shoulder. “My thoughts aren’t troubled.”

     

                “Everyone has troubling thoughts.”

     

                “Even you? Aren’t yours mostly locked away in your other half’s head?”

     

                “Even me. They may be locked away but there is … an overlap. I am aware of my atrocities, I am aware of dragging you through the forest, I am aware of the people I have killed. My orders have not always led me down honourable paths. Your mother-”

     

                Shifting restlessly, Lena studied the other woman’s face, weary with regret, and had to swallow thickly. “My mother … drowned. Lillian said it was Purity.”

     

                “Yes, she is my sister out of our shared affliction as children of both Courts. And Pestilence too. Her affinity for water was what killed your mother, but we three were all sent to hunt her on the Queen’s orders. I do not remember to regret it as Reign but … I do regret it. All of them.”

     

                “My life was ruined that day,” Lena murmured, closing her eyes to the stinging feeling building behind them. “And then you ruined it again when you brought me back here. It’s a cold comfort to know that you do regret it, at least.”

     

                “I do. And I will help you get your revenge.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena smiled humourlessly as she opened her eyes. “I don’t want revenge. Not against you.”

     

                “Perhaps not, but I will train you to be an accomplished swordfighter so that one day you may kill me if that is the retribution you claim.”

     

                To Lena’s surprise, Sam said it in Fae, binding it as a promise, and she didn’t quite know how to feel about that. A huff of laughter escaped her and she arched an eyebrow before nodding. “I’ll meet you here tomorrow.”

     

                “Tomorrow.”

     

                “Don’t tell anyone.”

     

                “On my life, Your Highness.”

     

                She stowed the sword at the back of the hall and then left first, head bowed against the harsh wind as she fumbled with the buttons on her jacket, wishing she’d had the good sense to bring her cloak. The rain held off until she was back at the hall, entering from the top level and going straight to her room as she set the bow and quiver down at the foot of her bed, keeping them for now.

     

                The sound of footsteps neared her door and she turned to watch as Kara appeared. Her blue eyes seemed to pierce Lena through, a question in them, and Lena didn’t know what to say or do, at a loss as she stood helplessly on the spot. Kara didn’t seem to know what to say either, toying with the rings on her fingers as she gazed at her, mystified.

     

                “You missed mealtime. I looked for you.”

     

                “Oh … um, yeah, I was- I was practising archery,” Lena said, spreading her fingers as she showed Kara her red palms, blistered and raw.

     

                Frowning as she stepped into the room, Kara took Lena’s hands in hers and clicked her tongue, her callused fingers gentle as they ghosted over the back of Lena’s fingers. “You should not work yourself so hard.”

     

                “Hard,” Lena snorted, her mouth twisting wryly. “If I worked hard, my hands wouldn’t be this soft.”

     

                “I will fetch saltwater. It will sting fiercely but help the healing.”

     

                “I’m fine, but thank you. I think I might take a bath.”

     

                Hesitating, already headed towards the door, Kara faltered and then nodded. Giving her a thin smile, eyes evasive, Lena fetched a clean dress with a chemise and followed her wife to the door. Walking down the hallway, Kara followed her and they walked together in silence, down to the lowest level, where Kara filled the tub with water for her and went to find her sister to heat it for Lena.

     

                Once the water was steaming, Lena thanked them both and kicked off her boots a safe distance from the bath. As she made to start undressing, she felt Kara touch her sleeve, glancing over at her as she raised her eyebrows. Face clouded with confusion, Kara cocked her head to the side.

     

                “I know you were not outside practising your archery the whole time.”

     

                Staring blankly at her, offering no confirmation or contradiction to Kara’s words, Lena swallowed and waited for her to say something else, to demand where she’d been, to press her for information. Instead, Kara’s mouth twitched slightly at the corners and she dropped her hand.

     

                “You should not wander far alone.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena murmured, ducking her head in a slight nod before she turned her back on her and fumbled with her buttons.

     

                Kara left her to it and Lena undressed quickly, the air so cold as she got a good glimpse of the treacherous waves through the open wall of the room. It had started to rain, droplets lashing the sea’s surface, the sky a gloomy grey as water rushed in. It was not as peaceful as she had hoped, a storm brewing and the beginning mutters of thunder rolling in, but she relaxed in the hot water after the initial stinging pain in her palms and fingers reduced to a dim ache. 

     

                Her muscles ached profusely as she let the hot water work at them, hands gripping the side of the tub as she rested her head against the rim. Eyes closed, Lena breathed slowly, trying to focus on emptying her mind. Sam was right; her thoughts did trouble her, and Lena knew she had to learn to sort through the tangled feelings, the conflicting emotions trapped inside her, content with her lot one minute and then angry at the same circumstances the next. There was no easy way to sort through it, most of it boiling down to the untapped potential of futures that were forever out of reach to her now. That went as far back as her mother’s death, her life unravelling in such a confusing way that Lena had never been able to feel things normally since.

     

                Sitting in the tub of hot water until it started to cool, she contemplated her situation and her feelings, a large portion of her thoughts taken up by Kara and strictly off limits to pursuing any wary inclinations of something more to be concerned about there. Lena had enough on her plate without trying to deduce her relationship with Kara. They were married and would be until either of them died, and that was an easy enough way to encapsulate their situation without needing to make it unnecessarily personal. 

     

                Hoisting herself out of the tub after she’d scrubbed herself clean and rinsed off the milky residue of soap, Lena dried off quickly, the howling wind of the storm quickly reducing her to shivers as she struggled with her clothes. The waves that swept in and dwindled to nothing started to lap over the top of the tiered depression, rushing further and further inside as the sky darkened to positively black, and Lena dressed as quickly as she could, the hairs on the back of her neck standing on end at the thought of being in that room as it slowly flooded. 

     

                With an armful of her clothes, she made her way upstairs, leaving wet footprints behind as she carried her boots in hand, and holed herself up in the warmth of her bedroom. Someone had lit a fire in the brazier and a tray laden with tea and biscuits was waiting on the side table. There was a pot on there too with a handwritten note, familiar to Lena as she picked up the piece of paper and tried to decipher the whirling glyphs.

     

    For your hands.

     

                Setting the note down, Lena smiled faintly as she removed the lid of the pot and found a thick cream inside. Spreading it over her palms and fingers, she smelled the sweet milk and honey of it and let it seep into her raw hands as she served herself some tea and sank onto the edge of her bed, the little note on her lap as she studied the three words and listened for Kara’s heartbeat across the hall. She wasn’t there so Lena sipped her tea alone and enjoyed the biscuits before she fell asleep without even meaning to.

     

                Sleeping through dinner, oblivious to the presence of no less than three residents passing by to fetch her as they made their way to a smaller dining room, the one on the ground floor prematurely flooding with the bad weather, Lena didn’t wake until late. Stiff and groggy as she blearily looked about, she climbed to her feet and stepped out of her room. It was dark and silent and she glanced about, unsure of what time it is as she shivered in her dress.

     

                Without a word, Kara appeared in the doorway of her own room, as if summoned, her face pale and solemn in the gloom. Raking a hand through her unbrushed hair, Lena blinked owlishly at her, silent for a moment as an odd tension descended between them.

     

                “I fell asleep.”

     

                “Go back to bed,” Kara softly coaxed her, jerking her chin.

     

                Hesitating, Lena frowned, rubbing her forehead before she shook her head and then turned. Stepping back into her room, she walked over to the brazier and added another log, rubbing her arms as the chill worked into her bones, before she tried to undo her dress. Stripping down to her chemise, she was pulling back the blankets when Kara stepped into the room.

     

                A steaming cup was held in her hand and she crossed over to Lena, who was climbing into bed, and handed it off to her. “Tea. For your nightmares.”

     

                Gratitude flooded Lena, who had worried she wouldn’t be able to sleep again, and she took a scalding sip, then another, until she’d drained the cup. Kara watched her do it and then fetched the salve she’d left for Lena earlier, sinking onto the edge of the bed and taking the empty cup from her hands. Taking her wife’s hands in her own, one after the other, Kara scooped the cream out and slathered it over the blisters and reddened skin of Lena’s abused hands, her touch pleasant and gentle as Lena’s eyelids shuttered, basking in the simple touch of her wife caring for her.

     

                “These are not from a bow,” Kara murmured as she finished up. 

     

                Opening her eyes, Lena stared at her and Kara let out a quiet laugh, a quick smile crossing her face. “Or you are worse at archery than I recall.”

     

                “I fell,” Lena confessed in Fae, which wasn’t a lie, as she had fallen numerous times on the limestone floor of the ancient quarry.

     

                “What am I going to do with you?” Kara sighed as she gave Lena a tender look of amusement. “I fear to let you out of my sight or let go of your hand, you are so prone to injuries.”

     

                Her hands cradled Lena’s for a moment and then Kara quietly laughed, raising their hands to her lips and pressing a kiss to Lena’s fingers. “Be more careful. If you make a habit of hurting yourself, I will run out of salves to heal you.”

     

                “That would teach me a lesson, wouldn’t it?”

     

                “No, it wouldn’t; I would scour the forest to harvest the herbs with my bare hands and make a salve for you myself if there was none to be had. And if there were no herbs to be found, I would trade my land and fortune, every ounce of salt and every drop of water, in even the smallest stream under my ownership, to acquire some.”

     

                “You shouldn’t say such things,” Lena softly chided her. “You make me feel too self-important when you talk like that, you make me feel like I’m …”

     

                “Like what?”

     

                “It doesn’t matter. I wouldn’t be able to make a beggar of myself for you though; don’t you think that’s unfair?”

     

                “Not all is equal. In any such case, I am not so clumsy as you to need you to give up your things and pick herbs by the moonlight to heal me,” Kara teased before she sobered slightly. “I mean it though, I will keep you safe. Always. Even if that means from yourself.”

     

                With a crooked smile, Lena’s cheek dimpled as her eyelids shuttered. “I’ll try my best to reciprocate.”

     

                “You have already given so much of yourself, just by being here. But you should sleep now - the hour grows late.”

     

                “You’re still awake - and you didn’t sleep away your afternoon.”

     

                “I was not knocked about all morning.”

     

                “You must think me foolish,” Lena murmured, wrinkling her nose as she flushed, eyes on the quilt as she let the salve soften into her skin.

     

                Reaching out, Kara tucked Lena’s dark hair behind her ear. “I have never thought that. I find you anything but that. But I shall if you do not rest. Goodnight, Lena.”

     

                “Goodnight, Kara.”

     

                Giving her a quick smile, gently squeezing her wrist, Kara left her to sleep and Lena lay back on the pillows, her hands pressed over her heart as she closed her eyes and felt the slightly elevated thump of her heart. She didn’t remember falling asleep but she slept soundly, waking to another morning of stiff limbs and more bruises mottling her pale skin.

     

                Her mind made up, and sheer stubborn determination keeping her on course, Lena’s life followed much the same pattern for the next two weeks. Midwinter was fast approaching and she filled so much of her day with learning how to fight, in any capacity. Mornings, straight after breakfast, she sparred with whoever was willing to fight her - usually Alex, sometimes Kelly, occasionally Kara, Sam or Andrea and even J’onn at one point - slightly improving as she grew quicker on her feet and was not so easily caught off guard anymore. After that, she would practice her archery for a couple of hours, her back and arms permanently aching, although it became easier as she recovered what she’d spent countless hours on in the Unseelie Court after weeks of abandonment, her aim marginally improving by the end of the second week, even if she was no marksman. 

     

                Then there were her secret sword-fighting sessions with Sam, which yielded to a few ruined shirts to the point that she’d had to start reserving them just for their lessons together so she didn’t run out of them. She started timing it so that she attended lunch and then slipped away, spending a couple of hours going through forms and being drilled by the fae, earning scrapes and cuts and bruised muscles as the flat side of the blade sometimes whacked her with intent. Lena wouldn’t say she was passable by any means, but she did find it easier to absorb instruction with Sam than with Reign, the forms making her movements somewhat graceful, even if she had to go through them slowly to complete them properly. 

     

                She was always exhausted after that, Sam usually pitying her enough to heat a bath before they parted ways for the evening. More than once, Lena noticed Kara watching her, or caught the slightly curt edge of an exchange between her wife and Sam, although Kara never spoke to her about anything directly. If anything, Kara seemed to be around more, talking of anything but the others residing there with them, and she never pried but she was always seeking Lena’s company, seeing if she would be interested in going through the ledgers, if she would like a game of stones, presenting her with new socks and fine dresses and shirts, pearls fetched from the sea and silver and gold rings taken from the wealth of Kara’s inheritance. 

     

                Lena wouldn’t say she didn’t enjoy the company, but she was usually too tired and quiet for Kara’s earnestness and desire for conversation, worn out from a hard day of training and looking forward to bed. If Kara was ever disappointed by Lena’s brief answers or excuses to pardon herself, she didn’t show it, and each night, no matter what, Lena went to bed with a steeped cup of tea ready for her to make sure her dreams - if she had any - were only pleasant.

     

                Those two weeks were the best that Lena could remember so far, and the only thing that could have improved it would have been if she was surrounded by forest instead of sea. The weather took a turn but she enjoyed the briskness of it, the frost on the grass and in the reeds and puddles, rain and storms growing more prevalent with each passing day. But she had purpose and drive and that made all the difference to Lena as she decided to get herself out of the rut she’d been existing in. It was by no means easy or perfect but if she wore herself out, she forgot to focus on her mixed emotions and brood over her dogged loneliness.

     

                Waking early that morning, a freezing fog from the sea had swept in and she could smell the heaviness of salt in the air as she made her way downstairs. Winter in full swing, ice had started to rim the shoreline and the limestone wharf as the waves grew steep and dangerous beyond. Lena preferred to stay above the cliffs as much as possible, even the booming crash of the waves breaking over golden sand or limestone sending a chill down her spine at their power. She didn’t like the sea, and no matter how much time she spent on the coast, or even on the banks of a lake, she would never warm to the water, that much was very clear.

     

                That morning, Kelly was her sparring partner, shorter than Lena by a couple of inches but by no means the weaker opponent for it. She was quick and light on her feet, and even without using her spear or control of the air, Kelly was an imposing fighter, her strikes hitting vulnerable points on Lena’s body. Staggering around, Lena grew frustrated with each punch, pulled to cause minimal pain and injury, trying to keep her mind empty, trying to stay quick on her feet, unrooted but still immovable. For her part, she usually only managed to land one or two direct hits, and even then Lena thought it was out of pity rather than any skill.

     

                After a few rounds, Lena was breathing hard and nursing a few sore spots as she rose to her feet again, a stubborn set to her jaw. “Again.”

     

                “I think we are done for today,” Kelly replied, unrolling the sleeves of her shirt as she gave Lena a warm smile. “You fought well.”

     

                “I’m not finished.”

     

                “You should not push yourself.”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena insisted.

     

                Sighing, Kelly nodded and beckoned for her to attack. Wasting no opportunity, Lena darted forward, hands balling into fists, and aimed a punch at Kelly, which was blocked by the other woman’s forearm. Kelly’s own punch landed in Lena’s stomach, just hard enough to wind her as she staggered backwards, struggling to breathe for a moment before she swung again. Still unbalanced by the hit to her solar plexus, Lena was no good as Kelly got an arm around her neck and nudged the back of her knee, legs buckling as she was lowered to the damp ground once again.

     

                Twisting out of her grasp, Lena shot to her feet and then tried to tackle Kelly, who was quick to rise as well. Getting her arms around the other woman’s waist, Lena drove her back a few steps before Kelly anchored herself and broke Lena’s hold on her. Straightening, chest rising and falling quickly, Lena moved forward but found a foot firmly planted against her chest as she was kicked back. Tripping over her own feet, she fell onto her back and bit her tongue hard, the coppery taste of blood in her mouth as she blinked back black spots. Scrambling up again, Lena spat blood and ran her sleeve across her mouth before she squared her shoulders. Kelly held up a hand, brown eyes soft with amusement, not unkind but still evoking a sense of embarrassment or pity for Lena that she didn’t take too kindly to.

     

                “We are done for today.”

     

                “I haven’t yielded,” Lena objected.

     

                “Then yield now.”

     

                Lena refused, throwing herself at Kelly once more, only to find herself facedown on the ground, shaking her head as she blinked, trying to make sense of what had happened. Pushing herself to her feet again, she turned and looked at Kelly with surprise, the fae giving her a stern look as she folded her arms over her chest.

     

                “Do you yield?”

     

                “No.”

     

                Moving forward again, Lena suddenly found her lungs not working, face furrowing in confusion as the oxygen fled her and she scrabbled at her chest. Staring at Kelly, who had a hand crooked in her direction, Lena tried to make sense of things. None of the others ever used their powers against her, knowing it was already an unfair fight even without them, but now Kelly was stealing the air from her and Lena found herself suddenly helpless. Lurching forward as her pale face slowly started to redden, Lena floundered, mouth opening and closing as she grew angry and then panicked. Was this how her mother had felt in her last moments? Gasping for air, even if it was dank water that had flooded her lungs instead of this odd sensation of nothing.

     

                Face a bright red then, Lena still moved towards Kelly, even as her vision dimmed and she stumbled. Feeling as if she was about to pass out, Lena suddenly came to on her knees, gasping and retching as she blinked at the sudden clarity, the ease of breathing as she panted, gripping fistfuls of grass and sandy soil. A second wave of anger and embarrassment washed over her at being so easily overpowered with nothing more than a flick of a wrist, and she shot to her feet again.

     

                Only this time, she pulled up short at the rasp of metal and the unexpected appearance of a familiar sword at her throat. If she hadn’t stopped, Lena would have scored a line across her neck, and she felt her heart stutter in her chest before her eyes glanced to Kara, who held the hilt of the sword, betrayal in her green glare. 

     

                “There is wisdom in knowing when to yield, and there is honour in acknowledging a better opponent,” Kara softly informed her, a firmness to her words that belied her tone. “You have been bested; you will yield.”

     

                With a quiet scoff, Lena batted the sword aside and swallowed her pride as she met Kelly’s sheepish expression before she turned and stalked off. She didn’t make it more than a few steps before Kara was at her side, sword sheathed and a hand in the damp cotton of Lena’s muddy shirt. 

     

                “Your behaviour does not become you. It demeans Kelly to have a less worthy opponent challenge her so. It is a difficult lesson to learn, to swallow one’s pride and admit defeat to a finer opponent, but there is no shame in it. There is shame in not knowing when to stop, a foolish pursuit that will only serve to embarrass you.”

                

                “And how do you suppose I get better if I can’t challenge you all to push me to be better.”

     

                “You yield, and yield, and yield. As we all did when we were training. It is a lesson in humility and respect. Refusing to yield when you have been bested so, when a fight is over, is not respectful.”

     

                “Was it respectful to kill all the people we have to make it to where we are safe?”

     

                “That is life or death. The only honourable thing in that situation is affording your enemy a swift death if you can. A duel, on the other hand, has more honour than that. You will learn that hard if you do not heed the lessons our friends impart upon you here.”

     

                “If it comes to a duel, I will be a dead woman walking regardless of the lessons I’ve learned.”

     

                “If it comes to a duel, I will be your champion,” Kara said with a quick laugh. “Fortunately for you, I am an excellent fighter and have learned many lessons over the years.”

     

                “Lucky me,” Lena snarkily replied. 

     

                They had walked most of the distance back to the main entrance by then but something inside Kara caved, a sudden change of mind, of disposition as she reached out once more to grab Lena’s sleeve and pull her to a stop. Reaching up to cup her wife’s face in her palm, Kara gave her a searching look and Lena tried avoiding her gaze. Despite her dreamless sleep, Lena had lilac shadows beneath her eyes from how exhausted she was, running herself ragged to be better , and even though she’d never spoken a word to Kara about her secret lessons, Kara sensed there to be something more, something troubling her.

     

                “Get changed,” Kara said as she dropped her hand.

     

                “Changed for what?”

     

                “We are going for a ride.”

     

                She swept onwards and Lena stared after her, expression slack with surprise before her brow furrowed with confusion. “Where are we going?”

     

                Kara ignored her question and Lena hurried to catch up with her, but was met with nothing but silence. Sighing, Lena returned to her room and changed into clean clothes suitable for riding. While she’d ridden a few more times on horseback at Kara’s suggestion, Lena was by no means an adept rider, but she’d gotten better at least and didn’t detest the idea of going for a ride. Perhaps the bracing sea air as they plodded along a cliffside path would help shake off some of her frustration.

     

                Tucking a clean shirt into a pair of leather pants, Lena donned a padded jacket and swung a cloak around her shoulders, fastening it at the neck. She was pacing on her boots when Kara appeared in her doorway, dressed similarly, in soft grey leggings and a navy doublet, a cloak fastened at her left shoulder as her scabbard poked through the gap. There was also a leather bag under her arm and she stooped to pick up Lena’s borrowed bow and quiver, extending them.

     

                “Bring this.”

     

                Rising to her feet, Lena took them from her, slung the quiver across her chest and took a moment to string the bow. If Kara wanted her to bring it, Lena anticipated having to use it at some point, wondering if she was going to receive a lesson in horseback archery. If so, that was beyond her capacity, but she kept her mouth shut.

     

                Outside, they walked to the far east of the top level, where a large archway led into an open stable. The horses were free to come and go as they pleased, with no stalls and no rope tying them up, and there were usually at least half a dozen there at any given time, seeking shelter and food as winter drove to warmth and safety. The smell of hay and manure struck Lena as she stepped inside, finding Alex there with two horses waiting for them, already saddled. It was Kara’s dappled grey and the one Lena had ridden from Eliza’s hall to Krypton, a gentle thing who was patient with her nervousness.

     

                “Let Kelly and I come with you,” Alex burst out in Fae as soon as they were inside the stable.

     

                Shaking her head, Kara gave her sister a confident smile, taking the reins of her horse and stroking the mare’s velvety snout. “We shall be fine, sister. I do not intend to go far, but distance is the purpose. It will defeat it to bring all of you with us.”

     

                “Not all, just-“

     

                “Trust me,” Kara interrupted, gripping Alex’s shoulder. “Just the two of us is necessary. I shall see you tomorrow evening.”

     

                Lena had caught most of the conversation as she feigned ignorance, but her attention sharply turned to Kara at the last part. Watching her wife kiss her sister’s cheek in parting before hauling herself up into the saddle, Lena’s lips parted as she stared up at Kara with a wide-eyed look of wariness.

     

                “Mount up, wife,” Kara said with a faint smile. “It is still early enough to make good use of our time.”

     

                “Where are we going?”

     

                “You shall see.”

     

                Reluctantly mounting her horse, the motion getting easier each time, Lena made herself comfortable and balanced her bow across her knees as she stared at Kara. She trusted her, of course, but Lena didn’t like to be left clueless and she didn’t trust this wild land, even if she trusted her wife. It made her restlessly uneasy to not know what they were doing.

     

                Alex similarly looked unconvinced, her mouth turning down at the corners as her brown eyes flickered with annoyance. Squeezing her sister’s knee, she nodded and stepped back, arms folded over her chest. “I will come looking if you are not back before nightfall tomorrow.”

     

                “I would expect nothing less. Enjoy your evening, sister. Try not to drink all of my wine.”

     

                Seeming in high spirits, Kara gave Lena a quick wink before urging her horse onwards. With little choice but to stay behind or blindly follow after her, Lena sighed and shook her head before she set off after Kara with Alex’s quiet laugh trailing after her.

     

                Setting off at a trot, they were quickly far enough away from Kara’s home to pick up the pace, galloping along the path that they usually took, heading westwards. Lena jostled uncomfortably, not entirely comfortable with galloping yet, feeling as if she was going to come flying off her horse at any moment, but she caught up to Kara as her wife started to slow at the end of their first mile.

     

                “Where are we going?” Lena asked again, this time more demanding.

     

                Slowing to a walk, Kara fell in beside Lena and looked over at her, a tender expression in her blue eyes as she gave her a crooked smile. “We are going away for the night.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                Kara didn’t respond, just urged her horse to a slightly quicker pace, something they could, and did, keep up for miles. Swallowing her frustration, and the temptation to obstinately come to a stop and refuse to continue without any answers, Lena spent the next hour riding in silence with Kara. Unfortunately, the bracing sea air did little for her temperament.

     

                The further they went, the more varied the landscape became, the sea to her right as the horses plodded through long grass, waves slamming onto the beach or cliffs below with loud booms, audible over the sound of the wind, as they came apart and washed back out. Still following the coastline, they continued for hours and the land slowly sloped downwards, giving them a spectacular view of the marshland, the estuaries rimed with ice in the shallow beds, enormous sweeps of grass and channels of rushing water as oaks grew wide and tall, shading the creeks and stagnant ponds, green with the grass and plants that grew in abundance. Even in winter, it was beautifully austere, a thin fog lingering in patches, everything grey and damp and decaying, the air sweet as the wind blew it towards them.

     

                Brilliant white herons and storks stood amongst the reeds as they approached the wetlands, stretching as far as the fae could see, inland and westwards. As the horses carefully picked their way through the narrow paths of solid earth, Lena breathed in the rotting perfume as she took in the transparent sheets of ice filming puddles, quiet tributaries of the estuary crusted white at the edges, even as the day warmed, the warble of birds and frogs and insects that couldn’t be curbed by the cold filling the space with noise. It felt like the perfect joining of earth and water, a serene wilderness that made Lena feel at peace as the horses plodded over bleached and withered grass, weaving between birch trees and shrubs, their hooves gouging tracks in the softer patches of mud.

     

                They reached a racing river a few miles in, Kara silently guiding them south without Lena even realising it, until they came to the glinting bank of rushing water as it rushed over rocks and carved a wide path through the marsh. Keeping a safe distance from the banks, Lena watched the sunlight dapple the surface as she followed Kara’s tail, wondering what was so important that she had brought them miles away from safety.

     

                They followed the course of the river for several miles, the marsh slowly giving over the wide green moors choked with gorse and bracken. Small conifers crowded in amongst the mosses and sedges, a blanket of green everywhere Lena looked as she caught a glimpse over the tops of the short trees, feeling terribly lost as she tried to feel her surroundings to make sense of herself. She could feel the life there, just beyond her fingertips, malleable and almost eerily sentient, as if knowing she was there and patiently waiting to do her bidding. Lena had so rarely used that strange power though, and usually only when in peril, and she did nothing as they rode onwards.

     

                At the end of the moors, they reached rolling grassy plains, grass brushing her knees even as she was seated on horseback, and Lena could see the ground sloping downwards as the river narrowed slightly, coursing downwards over rapids. A broad valley descended a few hundred feet, large crags of mossy rock jutting out of the side of the valley as lichen covered the trunks towering trees dotting the wide space, the air smelling earthy and green as the forest encroached on the foot of the valley, just within reach.

     

                Fog lingered in the bowl of the valley and Kara brought them to a stop just above it, dismounting on the riverside in the shade of a willow, branches trailing in the water, and helping Lena down from her horse. Rummaging through her packed bag, Kara removed a wrapped bundle and a skin of water, offering the latter to Lena first before setting the bundle down on a nearby rock and tending to the horses, which she set to grazing.

     

                “Why?” Lena asked again, once Kara turned to face her.

     

                Taking the skin from her, Kara drank some water before stoppering it and letting out a quiet sigh, her shoulders slumping. “Because … you have been pushing yourself hard lately, and you seem … distant. I see how troubled your mind is, even if I cannot read the thoughts within it. I thought … perhaps it was best to take a break from it all, take you someplace you can pause and … mull it all over, I suppose. Just you and I.”

     

                Wariness flickered across Lena’s face as her expression clouded. “Oh. So … we’re not- we’re not going to meet anyone or …”

     

                “No, we are just spending some time outdoors.”

     

                Eyes straying to the looming shapes of trees in the nearby distance, Lena felt an ache in her chest to slip beneath the canopy and lose herself to the forest. Her fingers itched to bury themselves in the loamy earth, to let roots grow over her, and her eyelids shuttered as she swallowed thickly.

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                “Come and eat,” Kara murmured, her fingers brushing Lena’s damp sleeve.

     

                Unwrapping the parcel, they sprawled on the grass and shared a small loaf of bread and a few little mackerel. Kara unsheathed her dagger and picked up a green apple after they’d finished the rest, cutting wedges away from the core and handing them off to Lena, slice by slice, eating her own in between, her slender fingers, nicked with scars, so deft as she worked meticulously and ate her pieces from the edge of the blade as Lena furtively watched her.

     

                “If you care to share what is troubling you, there is nought by the trees and my ears to hear,” Kara said after a long stretch of silence.

     

                “I’m not so troubled as I was,” Lena hedged, drawing her knees to her chest and hugging them to herself.

     

                “Perhaps not, but troubled you still are.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena stared at the turbulent river as she felt a sudden pressure in her chest, the feeling unable to be named but oddly affecting her as she huddled beneath her grey cloak and tried to scramble for an excuse. That was all she had, excuses for the things she said and did, not wanting to dig any deeper than that to understand why she felt the way she did. 

     

                “It doesn’t matter.”

     

                “It matters to me.”

     

                “Well it shouldn’t,” Lena sharply replied, a muscle twitching in her jaw.

     

                “But it does.”

     

                Fixing her wife with an exasperated look, Lena sighed. “Okay, I’m not going to sit here and bicker with you like a married couple.”

     

                “Dear wife, that is what we are,” Kara said with a wry grin.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena’s mouth thinned and she took another slice of apple offered up to her. She chewed slowly, staring at the long grass, the winter wildflowers dotting it, cold and stiff after so long swaying in the saddle. Lena could feel Kara staring at her but didn’t meet her gaze until her wife lay back on the grass and sighed.

     

                “You’ve been spending a lot of time with Sam.”

     

                Sharply looking down at her, Lena frowned. “What makes you say that?”

     

                With a slight smile, her eyes still shut, Kara gestured off-handedly. “I can smell her all over you. Like smoke and ashes.”

     

                “And you’re so sure it’s Sam and not your sister, who has been tackling me to the ground for sport every day for two weeks?”

     

                 “It is a different kind of smoke and ashes.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “It is your prerogative to spend your time with whoever you choose, of course,” Kara hurriedly continued, a faint flush to her cheeks as her eyelashes fluttered slightly before she screwed her eyes shut. 

     

                “It is.”

     

                “And I have told you before, I would not begrudge you seeking comfort in someone else.”

     

                “Right.” There was a tense beat of silence and Lena smiled slightly, eyes glimmering with amusement as she cocked her head to the side. “Are you jealous?”

     

                Considering it, Kara let out a huff of laughter, opening her eyes. “Perhaps I am. That it could be so easy for you to enjoy the company of someone else but so difficult for you to confide in me.”

     

                Snorting, Lena plucked a few blades of grass and let the wind sweep them away, wrinkling her nose as she squinted at the glare of the pale sky. “Well, for the record, it’s hard for me to confide in anyone. And I’m not enjoying little trysts with Sam - do you think I would so easily be able to sleep with one of the women sent to hunt down my mother and me when I was a child?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Kara pushed herself up onto her elbows. “Oh. No, I suppose not. I had forgotten- it can be easy to forget that Sam is someone else at times. She is so kind around the Seelie, and then she is back in that Court and her vows and the Queen’s orders bring out the worst in her. It is a pity.”

     

                “Regardless of that, she isn’t my type.”

     

                “No?”

     

                Lips twitching with a smile, Lena shrugged indifferently. “I’ve never been too fond of brunettes.”

     

                “Oh,” Kara murmured, staring up at the sky as she hesitated. “I have.”

     

                Humming, Lena lay down beside her, watching a kite circle overhead, hunting for food. She folded her hands on her stomach and breathed slowly, the freshness of grass and greenery invigorating despite the cold. She wished they were closer to the forest so that she could hear the rustle of the leaves in the trees but she couldn’t hear the sea, and that was a gift in itself. It almost felt too quiet without the incessant crashing of waves and Lena didn’t like how quickly she’d gotten used to it.

     

                “So … what were you doing with her then?” Kara asked after a few minutes.

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, eyes creasing at the corners as red crept up her neck and into her cheeks, Lena rubbed the bridge of her nose, wincing slightly. “Ah, she’s, um, she’s been secretly giving me sword fighting lessons.”

     

                Sitting up, Kara looked down at her with surprise, bewildered amusement in the lines of her face as she arched an eyebrow. “Truly?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena sheepishly said in fae. 

     

                “Why in secret?”

     

                “I, uh, I didn’t want anyone to hang around watching. It’s bad enough I can barely shoot an arrow or throw a punch, I didn’t need the mockery of how bad I am at swinging a sword. And everyone else is so good at it, so when Sam suggested I keep training … well, I asked if she’d help me in secret.”

     

                “So that is where you have been vanishing to each day?”

     

                “Mm, to that old quarry temple place. I’m shit, obviously, but at least I can say I’m trying.”

     

                “Trying is all that we can do,” Kara nodded approvingly before climbing to her feet. 

     

                Brushing grass from her cloak, she walked off to search the low-hanging fog for wood, returning five minutes later with appropriately shaped willow switches, perhaps a little too thin but long enough to serve their purpose. Smiling triumphantly, Kara twirled one in her fingers and then extended it to Lena, who frowned.

     

                “Come then. Show me what your lessons have taught you.”

     

                “Did you miss the part where I said I’m shit?”

     

                “You do not have to be good, I am merely curious.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena relented after a moment, wearily sighing and then unclasping her cloak, leaving it in a puddle on the grass. Turning the willow switch in her fingers, Lena cast her wife a weary look as Kara lazily swished hers to get a feel for it, a faint whistle as it cut through the air. Giving Lena an encouraging smile, she bowed slightly, a little cocky but clearly enjoying herself.

     

                “After you.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena gripped the switch in both hands and lunged forward. Kara was quick, batting it aside and following up with an overhead swing, which Lena just managed to block with her switch. The clack of the slender sticks filled the valley and Kara seemed as if she wasn’t trying at all as Lena kept herself on her toes, ducking and weaving as she kept moving no matter what. The sting of the switch fell on her arms and once with a playful hit on the ass that earned Kara a withering look as her wife grinned.

     

                As they came apart, Lena trying not to grumble too much at the sore spots that would leave little more than red marks, she shrugged off her jacket and tossed it beside her cloak as Kara raised her eyebrows and unclasped her cloak. Going at it again, Lena hammered at Kara with the switch, striking overhead in rapid succession until her switch snapped in half, the top portion of it careening into the grass. Pausing to glance at her switch, Lena looked surprised and then looked at Kara, hesitating a brief moment before she hurled the stick at her wife.

     

                Kara cut it out of the air with a quick cut of her willow switch but wasn’t quick enough to stop the tackle that wrapped around her waist. Bringing her to the ground, Lena knocked the wind out of herself as she lay sprawled on top of Kara, both of them breaking out into laughter as it rang along the riverside. 

     

                It wasn’t over then though, Lena too breathless to stop Kara as she rolled them over, the solid warmth of her pinning Lena to the damp grass as her strong hands encircled Lena’s wrists and pinned her arms either side of her head. Cheeks flushed pink, strands of blonde hair spilling around her face, tickling Lena’s cheeks, Kara suspended herself above her, eyes glimmering with delight as they faced each other, scant inches apart. Unnerved by how close she was, and pinned by her capable hands too, Lena tried to buck and squirm beneath Kara’s weight but stilled at the mortifying tug of desire in her gut that made her go suddenly limp.

     

                Oblivious to the inner turmoil, Kara’s mouth curved into a smile as she raised her eyebrows a fraction. “Do you yield?”

     

                Hesitating, feeling hot all over, dizzy with the smell of salt and water clinging to her wife’s skin, Lena licked her lips, torn between pride and composure. “I yield,” she rasped a moment later.

     

                Sitting up, Kara straddled Lena’s lap and pulled her up with her, then all the way to their feet. Looking proud, Kara cupped Lena’s chin affectionately in a warm hand. “You fought well. Sam has made good on her lessons so far.”

     

                Tucking in the tail of her shirt that had come free from her pants, Lena hummed dubiously before rubbing her left arm. “I would disagree; if we were using real swords, I would have been cut to pieces.”

     

                “Progress is progress. One cannot hope to be a master in a day, nor even a year. I’m confident that with years of training, you will be proficient enough to rival a good opponent in skill.”
