                “But not you,” Lena said with a distracted smile as she tucked her hair behind her ears and fetched her jacket, feeling too flushed to put it back on just then.

     

                “No, not me,” Kara agreed. “But war is not for everyone and there are nobler pursuits than being good at shedding blood. It is not my skill with a sword that I hope to be remembered for one day.”

     

                “I should hope to be remembered at all.”

     

                Moving in close, Kara picked up her hand and smiled softly. “You will be remembered. Not as a fighter but as one who sacrificed much for the greater good of unifying the Courts under a banner of peace.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena pulled her hand free and wrung them as she looked down at the grass underfoot. “Not that it lasted very long. Although, I still think it would have been better to go through with the coup. I wouldn’t have to look very far to find a better alternative for a ruler.”

     

                She gestured to Kara, who looked surprised. “I would not want a throne. It goes against the democracy of the Seelie Court, which was established with the abdication of my own family’s crown generations ago. I would not pick that mantle back up again.”

     

                “Good. I wouldn’t want to spend more time in that place than I have to.”

     

                “You are worried about spring,” Kara murmured with understanding. At the grim twitch of Lena’s lips, she reached for her hand and squeezed reassuringly. “Don’t be. I have told you before, if it means war to keep you here, with me instead of with them, I will gladly welcome it.”

     

                “Even if it means hundreds, if not thousands of Seelie will die?”

     

                A ripple of pain ran across Kara’s face and she swallowed thickly. “It is why I would make a terrible ruler; I cannot help but be selfish, as much as I wish I could be the hero. I would save you first.”

     

                Eyelids shuttering, Lena smiled sadly, haltingly shaking her head. “I don’t like it when you talk like that.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                “It makes me think- it makes me think of all the times my foster families would promise me things, would make me think that it was permanent, that I would stay forever. And then I’d be back in an orphanage, waiting for the next family, hoping for adoption. Until I got old enough to realise that no one would ever put me first, that I would have to do that for myself. When you- when you talk like that … I can’t help but feel like … you’re lying to me. That you’re going to make me promises you won’t keep.”

     

                “I promise you,” Kara firmly whispered in Fae, her hand so warm as she held onto Lena, standing so close. “I will save you first, I will put you first, above all else. When the day comes to give my heart to the one I will kill, this promise will still hold true and I will put you above them and let them die to keep my word to you. I will hate myself for it but I am no oathbreaker, Lena, so I promise you now. I am not a fickle human and I do not make promises lightly. They mean something to us, and you mean something to me. We are already promised to each other, now I bind myself to you twice over. Does that satisfy you?”

     

                Opening her eyes, Lena stared at Kara, mystified as her gaze flitted over her face, solemn in her haughty beauty. “What are you saying?” she murmured mostly to herself, confused and curious, catching only half of what Kara had said and missing a chunk of the intent.

     

                A tired smile crossed Kara’s face, resigned and tender, and she reached up with her free hand to cup Lena’s face in her palm, brushing a featherlight kiss to her high cheekbone before pulling away. “I am saying you are wrong.”

     

                A hoarse laugh of surprise escaped Lena and she shook her head, smiling crookedly as she looked at Kara through her lashes. “That’s not the way to a woman’s heart.”

     

                “What is?”

     

                “Depends on the woman,” Lena coyly replied.

     

                “To yours?”

     

                “God, I hope you’re not trying to make me fall in love with you. You’ve made it very clear you’re never going to fall in love so that’s very unfair to trick me into unrequited feelings for you.”

     

                Rolling her eyes good-naturedly, Kara’s cheeks shallowly dimpled with a faint smile. “That is not my intention, but can I not be considerate of my dear wife’s proclivities?”

     

                “Flowers. It is always flowers.”

     

                “Above jewels and finery?”

     

                “Above anything. Flowers are the most romantic thing in the world, especially when you know the language of them.”

     

                “I did not think they talked,” Kara teased her before striding away and stooping to pluck a flower from the grass. “What does this one mean?”

     

                Lena took it from her, twirling the stem between thumb and forefinger. “Pink hellebore. Affection and gentleness.”

     

                Nodding, Kara wandered a few steps away, plucking a few more and then a lenton rose, holding it aloft. “This one?”

     

                “Serenity and peace.”

     

                She found a few cyclamen and Lena told her they symbolised lasting affection, love, and camellias for inner strength. Plucking them sparingly, ensuring not to take too many and to leave the roots behind, Kara handed them off to Lena one by one as they walked through the valley. The fog had burned off as the day warmed, only a few thin fingers of it lurking in cool, damp corners near the craggy rock face, and Lena enjoyed the lush green of the grass, her gaze straying to the trees in the distance. It was enough to stand beneath the boughs of one of the willows for a few minutes though, as she gripped her handful of flowers.

     

                “Come, let us go,” Kara declared after a few minutes.

     

                A pleading look softened Lena’s face as her shoulders sagged. “So soon?”

     

                “I did not say we were going home.”

     

                Perking up slightly, Lena tried not to show her surprise or pleasure. “Oh. Where are we going then?”

     

                “We are spending the night in the forest.”

     

                Staring blankly at her, Lena blinked as she paused. “Sorry, we’re … spending the night? Like … camping?”

     

                “Yes, at the ruins of a watchtower. Similar to the one we made camp at on our way to Krypton” 

     

                “Will we be safe?”

     

                “You are always safe with me.”

     

                Lena didn’t protest, the thought of even a night in the forest something to look forward to, despite the memories of wolves and bears and fae trying to kill her. They walked to the horses and Kara suggested they walk a while, not wanting to exhaust the mares, and Lena fondly patted the velvety muzzle of hers as she walked beside her, Kara to her left as she walked alongside hers. 

     

                It was a pleasant day, bitterly cold of course but no rain on the air and no snow either, only the howling wind to contend with as they walked the broad grassy field of the deep valley, their view of the forest extending inland for miles ahead. Lena briefly worried that if she slipped into the first, she would never come back out again, whether willingly or not.

     

                As they walked, they asked each other questions as they came to mind, and Kara rambled on about topics that caught her interest, explaining goose seasons, fish habits, how to read the weather in the clouds and the different types of waves and currents. She explained how to walk quietly, how to follow animal tracks, the best way to snare a rabbit and listen to the forest. If it went quiet, she impressed on Lena that she shouldn’t make a sound but should find a high hiding spot immediately. In return, Lena talked of flowers and herbs, the seasonal varieties of fruits and vegetables and which poisons she’d encountered. Kara listened with rapt attention, even though she was somewhat knowledgeable on most of what Lena told her about, but it was the act of sharing, of talking, that she really enjoyed.

     

                Approaching the fringe of the forest, Kara brought them to a stop at the side of the trilling river, submerging their skins, one after another, as the water ran cold over her wrists. Then she took them deeper, through a hollowed-out copse of trees, where grass and bracken had been flattened into a narrow track through the thick undergrowth of the ancient trees. As she padded, twisting out of the way of snagging brambles and creeping roots, she murmured the history of the place to Lena.

     

                “The watchtower we will be staying at is not far - some would say it is still within the fringes of the forest - perhaps a mile or two. Millennia ago, it was the tallest structure from where it stands to the sea, used to watch for any Waterfolk marching on the lands of Earthfolk, but then there was peace and the Courts divided and the forest claimed it for itself. This valley was nothing more than grass, with herds of horses and deer too - not blighted by the forest yet, so ordinary enough to hunt and eat - but trees have since taken root and grown taller, to where we are now. The watchtower is still there, the rock worn smooth and parts tumbling down, but it serves its purpose as a safe refuge for travellers. My father would bring me at times, teach me the things I now teach you.”

     

                “What was your childhood like?” Lena asked. “You know about mine but you never really talk about yours.”

     

                “You do not talk much of yours either. But mine was … idyllic. I spent my days at the beach, crabbing, fishing and swimming. My mother taught me how to weave nets and read the currents, how to set pots for lobsters and use a spear. My father taught me how to read and write, how to cook shellfish and how to whistle bird calls. I was an only child so all of their time when not at war was devoted to me. Unfortunately, that was not much of their time, and they did have duties to the land as well. Once I had been taken in by Eliza, she taught me what I know of healing and Alex taught me how to ride horses and hunt, to read the trails left behind by animals. We would spend nights in the mountains in summer, once we were trusted to keep each other safe. I even rode an eagle once, the big ones in the mountain pass. I grew older and learned the arts of war, I campaigned with my sister, sustained injuries and killed my share of Unseelie. We had revelries, too much wine and too many lovers to count, so much laughter and many good times. I suffered so much loss but I experienced so much of life too.”

     

                “I’m glad you got to live first. I’m sorry that it was cut short.”

     

                Glancing over her shoulder at her, Kara smiled crookedly, her face dappled by the occasional fingers of sunlight breaking through the shaded canopy overhead. “I am still living. It is not unenjoyable for me to be wed, you have not curbed my wilder inclinations or rebellious nature. I was tired of them before you arrived, saddled with my duties at such a young age. I have always been of a serious disposition; it is why I did what I could to honour my family by putting myself forward for your hand.”

     

                “Would they be disappointed you chose peace over revenge?”

     

                “No. My family dreamed of peace above all else. They only fought out of duty to protect our people, but they would have chosen peace if it had been an option. It is perhaps I who would choose to seek revenge if given the chance, but it would have dishonoured their legacy to snub what they would have wanted to sate my desires first.”

     

                “Will you kill Lex?” Lena haltingly asked.

     

                “If the opportunity arises, yes. Though I will not seek him out willingly; my priority is to keep you safe.”

     

                Something loosened in Lena’s chest, her shoulders slumping a little and Kara paused at that, turning fully around so they stood a few feet apart. “You are relieved at that.”

     

                Colouring slightly, Lena opened and closed her mouth, shifting uncomfortably. “No, I- well, yes. It’s just- I wouldn’t want to say.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                Cringing slightly, Lena looked down. “It’s selfish. And it- it would contradict your feelings.”

     

                “I would like to hear it anyway.”

     

                Closing her eyes and tipping her head back, Lena heaved a sigh. “I’m relieved because … if you went after him and killed him … I would be heir again. And as awful as my brother is, and as much as he deserves to die, I selfishly hope he doesn’t because … if anything happened to Lillian, that would mean the crown would be mine. And if you don’t want it-”

     

                “I would stay at your side while you ruled though,” Kara interrupted. “You are naïve to our ways, clueless about our history and laws, but if I had the option to kill your mother and brother, I would kill them in a heartbeat. Perhaps that is selfish of me, now that I know your feelings on the matter. Even then, I would still do it. Forgive me.”

     

                Looking at her, Lena smiled thinly. “There would be nothing to forgive. How could I hold that against you?”

     

                “Would you truly not want to rule?”

     

                “You said it yourself, I would very quickly lose my head.”

     

                “They would have to take off mine first, I can assure you of that.”

     

                They’d started walking again and Lena let out an exasperated laugh, narrowing her eyes with amusement as she followed on her heels with her horse at her side. “Always so quick to try and sacrifice yourself first. What have I done to earn such loyalty?”

     

                “You married me.”

     

                “I don’t believe I had much say in the matter.”

     

                “You did it all the same. And since that moment, I have endeavoured to be a worthy wife.”

     

                “It’s not you who should be trying. You were worthy from the start.”

     

                “How so? I married a woman against her will.”

     

                Kara said that with some bitterness and Lena’s expression furrowed as she stared at her wife’s back. “The moment you found out that I had no idea about it, you tried to give me back. Is that not showing your worth?”

     

                Back stiffening, Kara quietly scoffed but didn’t turn. “I tried to give you back to my enemy, who I knew had stolen you away from your life. I don’t believe that was very honourable of me. If the Queen had accepted the return of you … I would have left you there.”

     

                “You could have left me there, whether she’d accepted it or not. Instead, you took me with you and returned me to my home. It was unfortunate it was gone, I will admit, but you did the honourable thing, knowing it would mean war by autumn if I hadn’t come back.”

     

                “Sometimes … I wish you had not,” Kara confessed.

     

                Lena’s stomach dropped slightly and she swallowed past the lump in her throat. “Why?”

     

                “Because I live with a fear inside of me that grows stronger each day.”

     

                “What fear?”

     

                Silent for a few minutes, nothing but the sounds of the horses, birdsong and Lena’s footsteps filling the forest, Kara eventually responded. “I do not wish to burden you with my thoughts.”

     

                “It’s not a burden.”

     

                “Then I do not wish to frighten you away.”

     

                “You couldn’t. Where else would I go?”

     

                There was a wry smile in Kara’s voice by that point. “Then I do not wish to give voice to that which may be nothing but the foolish thoughts of a foolish woman.”

     

                “You’re not foolish. I actually think you’re very wise at times.”

     

                “I do not consider myself wise. I just manage to not repeat the same mistakes.”

     

                “One could argue that is the definition of wisdom.”

     

                “One could, yes.”

     

                “Always so diplomatic.”

     

                “Always so argumentative,” Kara sighed, her voice laced with amusement before she sobered up. “Leave it be, Lena. Do not press me on it any further. It is for my sake as well as yours.”

     

                Frowning slightly at the discomfort that twisted her stomach, the uncertainty of what Kara was eluding to exactly, Lena fell silent. They walked on for a while, Kara eventually leading them off the narrow animal trail as it disappeared into a thicket of underbrush too dense for the horses to follow. There were mushrooms along the way and Kara eventually started to pick some, informing her of the edible ones, cutting open the white flesh to point out greyish patches of the ones that would make them ill. It caught Lena’s curiosity and she listened intently. The tension seemed to dissipate somewhat over the next hour, the trees starting to grow further apart, leaving a wide enough gap for them to ride on horseback for the remainder of the trip.

     

                Eventually, they came upon the side of the valley, where it widened near the bottom, the forest continuing beyond it in every direction. Lena almost didn’t see it at first, carved into the side of the valley’s rock face, but there was the elegantly wrought protrusion of a tower, worn with age and crumbling with disuse. Lichen and moss covered the old stones where they still stood, and Lena could make out the old carvings of vines and leaves beneath the patches of green, white and yellow. 

     

                Dismounting, Kara cocked her head to the side and listened as Lena tried to tune in to her surroundings too, hearing nothing but small animals and birds in the trees. Climbing off her horse, Lena joined her, rotting foliage muffling her footsteps as she gripped her bow in hand and padded forward on Kara’s heels. Stepping through the mouth of a half-collapsed arched doorway, Lena was hit with the musty smell of damp stone and undisturbed air, no people stopping by for a long time. 

     

                They weren’t the only ones there though, and she let out a hoarse shout when she crunched a few old bones underfoot and startled some sleeping bats from their roosting in the eaves of the ceiling. The leathery flapping of their wings as they swooped over her head and out into the late afternoon made Lena jump and she felt her cheeks warm as Kara reached out to steady her, quietly chuckling.

     

                “Fret not - we’re alone. The animals will not hurt you.”

     

                “Not unless a bear tries to force its way inside,” Lena unevenly replied, still a little shaken.

     

                “Come, let us set camp and get a fire going. You will feel calmer with some light.”

     

                It was a dingy place without a fire, the narrow arrow slits for windows not offering much light as the greenish tint of pale sunshine filtering through the canopy trickled inside. Gathering as much wood as she could find on the forest floor, Lena made a pile of it inside as Kara unsaddled the horses and sent them off to graze with parting gifts of apples and a quick rub down. 

     

                Inside the watchtower, Kara made her way up an old winding staircase, some of the steps sunken and cracked, and set down their saddles and the bag she had brought on the top floor of the watchtower, rummaging through until she found flint and some tinder. She had a fire going within minutes, the damp wood smoking as it struggled to light until she drew out some of the moisture from the wood and had a dry crackle going in no time. Lena watched from the mouth of the staircase as Kara worked, and was surprised when her wife climbed to her feet and held a pole up.

     

                “Have you ever fished?”

     

                “No. You have to get too close to water for my liking.”

     

                “Ah, well, you will be safe with me if you would like to try. We shall have to catch our supper.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes and turned, carefully picking her way downstairs. On the ground floor, she stepped aside so Kara could take the lead and followed after her, ducking under low branches of saplings, her cloak snagging on thorns as she tried to will them away with her hands. Lena was no good at that though, hadn’t quite the knack for manipulating roots and dirt without a threat to induce it. Instead, she had to struggle her way through the forest, which always felt somewhat sinister beneath the serenity it offered, as if it loved her so much, wanted her to stay so badly that it would smother her, trap her so she could stay forever. 

     

                She heard the trickling stream before they came upon it, following the sound through the alders and river birches until she caught a glimmer of silver rushing through the wet ground. It was so narrow Lena felt she could jump across it if she tried her best, and it ran slowly, despite the noise of it, too much ice obstructing the free-flowing water as frost clung to the banks and patches of the surface looked like glass. 

     

                “Right, we’ll probably have the best luck with grayling here. They do prefer warmer water but it’s downstream from the river so they’ll wash through. Floating is the best method to catch them,” Kara informed her as her fingers moved quickly, tying sinew to the end of the stick she’d brought with her and then finding a little piece of wood and testing its buoyancy before tying it to the string. 

     

                She had little fishhooks in a folded piece of felt she opened to reveal the spread of little pointed pieces of bone and steel. Selecting one, she showed Lena how to thread it on the line and a knot to tie it off, a little weight attached to make sure it sank as well. Explaining the method for fishing, of which bait different species preferred, she hooked a maggot from the supplies she’d brought and then climbed to her feet. Lena remained crouched a safe distance from the edge of the stream and watched Kara cast the line into the water.

     

                Lowering herself down beside her wife, Kara stretched her legs out before her and held the rod in hand, giving Lena a quick grin. “And now we wait.”

     

                “For how long?”

     

                “Until a fish bites.”

     

                “What if a fish doesn’t bite?”

     

                “Then I hope you aren’t too hungry,” Kara teased.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena clicked her tongue and managed to unwind some, sprawling on the withered grass along the banks of the stream as she toyed with the blades of grass. It was quiet, the wind screaming through the trees, the melodic trickling of water and the occasional splash of a frog or something else in the water. Eyes closed, Lena breathed in the clean, cold air, savouring the lack of salt on the wind as she let it soothe her. The air smelled green and sweet, laced with the chill that spoke of bad weather sweeping in off the coast.

     

                “You have been practising.”

     

                Kara’s voice broke the silence, pulling Lena from her reverie, and she blinked as she opened her eyes, giving her wife a curious look as she made a sound at the back of her throat. Gesturing to the patch of earth in front of Lena, Kara smiled faintly and Lena looked down to find a patch of lush grass and the withered weeds she’d been toying with back in full bloom.

     

                “Oh. Um … no, I don’t know-”

     

                “Yes, you do. You are good with plants,” Kara softly interrupted, adjusting the fishing rod and trying to catch a glimpse of the float to make sure it was still bobbing along with the current. “You may lack the finer control of your powers, the ability to ensnare us in roots or break the earth unless you are startled into it, but you have always had an affinity for plants, haven’t you?”

     

                “I- yes, my flowers always lasted longer, never wilted in the store. My, uh, my customers used to say I had the best bouquets in the city.”

     

                “I do not doubt it. You are good at giving life to that which is decaying, even if you do not see it.”

     

                “I don’t.”

     

                “You give life to me. You say I have lived before and I say I am still living, but it has been … a despairing existence for many years. There is much I have feared to do with the worry of falling in love. You have taken some of that worry away, have eased the fear in my heart.”

     

                Lena swallowed thickly, her expression clouded as she stared at her wife. “Kara … you know that … you can still fall in love even if we’re married. I can’t stop that from happening.”

     

                Giving her a wan smile, Kara shifted her position and turned her gaze back to the stream. “I know that. But you are a welcome distraction because if I devote my time and energy to you, I will not have time to fall in love with another. So while I can fall in love, by living my life as a faithful wife, I will not fall in love. And it is because of you that I am not afraid to enjoy my life without that overwhelming bleakness of my fate. So thank you, Lena. I do not thank you often enough.”

     

                Laughing awkwardly, Lena smiled shyly, staring at the side of Kara’s face. “Yes, you do. You thank me more than you have to. More than you should. I don’t think I thank you enough.”

     

                “There is no reason for you to thank me.”

     

                “There is every reason. I’m only here because of you, only alive because of you. If I didn’t have you to look after me … I’d be lost.”

     

                “I will always look after you, Lena. You are special to me.”

     

                Cheek dimpling with a crooked smile, Lena just watched her without saying a word, a glow of warmth in her chest. The leaves rustled and the stream continued to flow and she had the odd sensation of thinking she could stay there forever, fishing in the golden hour of winter, sitting along the water with her wife, the whole world quiet and peaceful. 

     

                “Ah!” Kara suddenly exclaimed, her soft triumph breaking Lena from her daydreaming. “I think we have our supper.”

     

                She brought in the first grayling and then coaxed Lena into having a go, helping her hook the bait, covering her pale hands on the rod with her warm, callused palms, showing her how to cast the line into the water and sitting beside her as their knees touched while they waited for another fish. They were quiet, the silence amicable, and when Lena felt a tug on the rod, she almost let go of it, only Kara’s quick reflexes reaching to grab it before it was yanked into the steam. She put it back in Lena’s hands and had her arms wrapped around her by the time they’d reeled the fish in as Kara tried to show her but did most of the work.

     

                Content with their two, Kara showed Lena how to gut them, how to clean and fillet them, and then left the entrails in an offering to the forest and the wild creatures half-starved by winter. Returning to their watchtower, they cooked the fish over the crackling fire and ate the white flesh on the bread Kara produced. She had a bottle of winter wine as well, bold and dark, spiced strongly enough to stave off the cold as she informed Lena it was going to snow that night.

     

                Lena didn’t know how she knew, but Kara always seemed to be correct in her prediction of the weather. It was no surprise when the temperature plummeted with the encroaching darkness and Lena caught a glimpse of billowing white through the narrow window as the snow blew in, a gentle flurry of flakes dusting the trees. The sky was a deep blue through the arrow slits and Lena stood there a while after they’d finished eating, watching the flakes thicken until the wind was a gale and she thought a blizzard was coming.

     

                It was freezing inside the watchtower, even with the little fire that Kara kept adding branches to, and Lena rubbed her palms together when she finally returned to her spot. Tired in a pleasant way, her muscles stiff from her wrestling and sparring, thighs aching from hours on horseback, Lena couldn’t stop yawning and Kara eventually laughed and pulled a blanket from the bundle she’d packed.

     

                Making a bed for her beside the fire, she assured Lena she would not be awake much longer herself. She stayed up hours after though, her words in English so easily deceptive as she watched her wife sleep, tugging the blanket securely over her, stoking the fire to keep her warm as her mind weighed heavily with her worries. Kara still wouldn’t give voice to them but they nagged at her all the same, and she could not stop her eyes from straying to Lena’s face often.

     

                She did sleep though, in the dark hours of night, stretching out beside her wife. They only had the one blanket, and their cloaks, but Kara did not feel the cold as Lena did and was content to lay at her back with only her cloak for warmth. It didn’t stop Lena from rolling over at one point, grasping a fistful of Kara’s cloak as she mumbled in her sleep, pressing her face into her back. Kara was fast asleep, oblivious to her wife and her nightmares.

     

                And she did have nightmares, Lena's dreams haunted by the odd feeling of her mind deteriorating as she stumbled through the forest, ensnared by roots, dragged down into hidden bogs that she hadn’t noticed underfoot, drowning in muddy water as flowers grew over her bones. She woke with a gasp to the pale brightness of the rising sun, covered in a cold sweat with the cool dampness of fresh water in her nose. 

     

                Hurriedly sitting up, the blanket slipping off her, Lena blearily blinked at the sight of Kara, her face soft as she slept soundly. Rubbing her eyes as she frowned, highly aware of their close proximity, Lena staggered to her feet and paused, adding some wood to the glowing embers of the fire and blowing the coals to life before she made for the stairs. Quietly descending with care, she slipped out of the watchtower.

     

                Daylight was beginning to illuminate the western edge, but it was too low to peek over the top of the watchtower, early morning hoarfrost coating the ground in patches of white as her head was wreathed in steam as the breath gusted out of her. The air was so cold that each breath felt like fire, her nose and cheeks reddening quickly as she stood in the damp chill of the early morning. 

     

                Snow lingered in a shallow coat, with the leaves of the trees glazed with ice as the flakes had settled there and hardened overnight. It was beautifully stark and she looked around at the forest before her, the broad trunks and gnarled roots, weeds and brambles and the nearby sounds of the horses slowly plodding about as they grazed. Even as she watched, she could hear the sound of dripping water as the forest warmed slightly, the blanketing fog lifting somewhat as mist ribboned towards the canopy. It was wet and alive and Lena closed her eyes, standing outside the doorway as the cold burrowed into her.

     

                Eventually, she started to shiver, her fingers so cold that they were numb, her lips cracked and lashes sticking together as the moisture froze. Kara was so quiet that Lena didn’t even hear her approach, but she felt the blanket being wrapped around her shoulders and startled before glancing over her shoulder at Kara. Giving her a tired smile, Lena clutched the blanket closed in front of her as her breath plumed before her in the stillness of the morning.

     

                “It’s cold out here,” Kara murmured, touching her arm a few minutes later. “Come back inside and warm up.”

     

                Drinking it in for a moment longer, Lena turned and followed her inside. Upstairs, they drank tea and broke their fast on the remainder of their rations before stamping out the fire and packing up their things. They hadn’t come with much and had even less to take back with them, the food and wine gone, and it was a quick departure, gone before the sun had even fully risen. The horses were nearby and easily summoned by a quick whistle from Kara, who saddled them swiftly and boosted Lena into her saddle.

     

                The ride back through the forest was slow and quiet, the whole world dripping as they rode through the creeping fog, Lena feeling freezing mud splatter her legs and the mare’s flanks as they plodded onwards. The sound of birds calling to each other kept them company through the morning, and Kara passed the time by emulating them, much to Lena’s amusement as she laughed and listened to the same species respond in like. 

     

                When they reached the valley, they were greeted by a fog so thick that Kara made Lena ride at her side so she did not lose track of her, and the fog didn’t let up for miles and miles. Even once they’d crested the valley, the marsh clung to the fog and had not warmed enough to completely melt the frost and snow that had swept over the coast like a white blanket. They were splattered with frigid water and mud, the cold in their lungs as the horses doggedly carried onwards at Kara’s instruction, hardy creatures, and Lena felt her hands grow stiff and numb around the reins as Kara kept their course.

                

                It was a slower return, partially due to Kara setting a leisurely pace, drawing out their time alone together. She was vigilant as well though, her sword loose in its sheath as she kept an ear out, the noises in the marsh sounding different in the fog, but nothing troubled them. The marsh gave way to the estuaries she had grown up in, sailing little skiffs through the myriad of waterways, the thin rivulets and broad avenues, some shallow with sandbars and marshlands, others deep with grass and algae masking the bottom. She was knowledgeable of the ever-changing area though and led them safely through it.

     

                It was afternoon by the time they reached the cliffs, ice still clinging to the grass and the sea a churning mass beyond the shore, treacherous waves rolling in as deep grey skies spoke of more bad weather on the horizon. Kara informed Lena that the best of the winter weather was behind them now, storms, blizzards and cold spells ahead of them, which made Lena wonder what was in stock for her, as cold as it had been so far. National City was never that cold and Lena rubbed her arms as she frowned at the sea and the clouds, wondering how much worse it would get and whether she should anticipate losing any toes.

     

                Twilight was approaching by the time they made it back to Krypton, the yellow limestone a beacon of warmth and rest as they spotted it in the distance. They picked up the pace a little, and even Lena had to admit she was eager for a hot bath, dry clothes and a warm meal, even if it meant leaving the forest behind in favour of salt and sea. The homely glow of light was visible as well and Lena felt in higher spirits as they neared Kara’s home, finding welcoming as well, despite her usual surliness at being holed up there.

     

                When they came to a stop in the stables, they dismounted and Kara’s family and friends were quick to appear, seemingly out of thin air. Kara murmured a brief summary of their evening and antics as the horses were unsaddled, and Lena dutifully brushed down her mare and let Kelly help her with a grateful smile, while Kara likewise cared for her own. Alex had vanished inside to heat a bath for Lena, an act that was almost enough to earn a kiss from her sister-in-law, if Lena had ever felt such fondness for her. Instead, it was her wife who earned that fondness, everyone else disappearing back to their hobbies as Lena and Kara walked across the frosted grass to the main doors of Krypton.

     

                Before they walked inside, Lena stopped Kara with a touch on the arm and quickly leaned in to press a gentle kiss to her cheek, giving her a tender smile. “Thank you.”

    Chapter 23

                The snowstorm that had blown in lingered, blanketing the surrounding wetlands in white as the snow hardened. Frost rimed the shoreline and the stretch of grass along the cliffside was slick with ice, sleet assailing the sprawling building sitting on the edge of the cliffs. It was damp and cold, relentless bitter winds blowing from the north as winter arrived seemingly overnight. It was a surprise to Lena, who had gotten used to the damp chill and suddenly found herself cold to the bone, never quite warm and always shivery slightly.

     

                That wasn’t to say efforts weren’t made to keep her warm, a fire burning in every room as Kara asked her sister to light them every morning and stoked them herself every evening, piling on driftwood that was collected from the shoreline. Furs were piled onto Lena’s bed and her clothes became thicker and more layered but the wind still found its way inside through the numerous open archways and uncovered window slits. 

     

                Still, it wasn’t all bad and Lena found herself sweating and rosy-cheeked as the wind bit her cheeks and dried her lips, slipping on the icy grass as she attempted to land a punch on Alex. As reluctant as she was to even get out of bed, she had committed to her lessons this time, creating a routine of hand-to-hand combat lessons - usually with Alex - in the mornings as she was knocked to the ground over and over again, and then sometimes Alex would linger afterwards and help Lena learn how to throw the little knives strapped to her sister-in-law’s belt. Afterwards, Lena would somehow manage to get her freezing fingers to draw back her bowstring as Kelly took up a position beside her, her affinity for air allowing her to guide the arrows to the target with ease, offering advice on Lena’s stand and aim. Once she’d tired of that, Sam would materialise and they would slip off to the temple for their sword fighting lessons. And through it all, Kara would sit and watch in silence.

     

                They would go for walks sometimes, or take the horses out on clear days, feet or hooves breaking through the thin crust of ice. The rides would take them out further, to open grassland and little thickets of trees with occasional lakes and rivers in the east, or deeper into the wetlands and marsh to the west. Sometimes, if the sea was relatively calm, Kara would lead them along the beach to explore sea caves and rock pools, bringing home octopus and winkles, crabs and driftwood or seaweed gathered from the shore at low tide, the briny smell clinging to their hands and clothes afterwards.  

     

                Two weeks before mid-winter, Lena woke early to a frosty morning and it took her a good hour to warm up enough to face the day, her body equal parts stiff from the cold and the bruises that mottled her pale skin. Buried beneath the pile of blankets and furs, she curled up and wished for sleep again, the sharpness of the air against her cheeks when she’d woken alluding to a frigid day. It was Kara who roused her, amused by the lump on the bed as she stepped inside, a steaming cup of tea in hand.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “I can’t feel my toes,” Lena grumbled, pushing back the blanket covering her face so she could give her wife a disgruntled look. 

     

                “Well, if you can feel your hands, wrap them around this cup and the tea shall warm you.”

     

                Peering over the mound of blankets, she glanced at Kara’s hands and then made an effort to sit up slightly against her pillows, reaching for the tea. Kara handed it to her, the scalding feel of the clay between Lena’s palms chasing the cold away as she breathed in the fragrant blend of herbs, and Lena let the steam caress her cheeks as she smiled slightly.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “It snowed again last night. That is the dryness to the chill this morning,” her wife informed her, sinking onto the mattress, close to Lena’s side.

     

                “Oh. Will it stick?”

     

                “It is no more than a foot so some will melt. The sea will wash it away on the beach. Although, it is two weeks until mid-winter, so I would anticipate more snow on the horizon. Kelly can smell it on the wind, and I can feel it in the clouds.”

     

                Taking a sip of tea, heat mercifully tracing down her throat to nestle in her stomach, Lena grimaced. “Remind me again why we came here instead of to the middle of the forest?”

     

                “My tower has no walls.”

     

                “Right. And your mother’s home?”

     

                “I must see to my people, Lena.”

     

                “Right. Well, did your family have to build a fortress on the edge of a cliff?”

     

                Laughing, Kara reached out to gently stroke Lena’s knuckles before dropping her hand to the blankets. “You may stay in bed all day if you wish. I will bring you food and tea and whatever else you wish if you deem it too cold to get up.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena fixed her with a dour look. “I’m afraid Alex might come and drag me out by my ankles so she can pummel me to the ground again.”

     

                “Alex is currently in bed as well, cursing my ancestors the same as you. Fire is not too fond of ice and she is lamenting her absence from the south. Although, as she has yet to inherit her birthright, she is often here with me in the winter. She just enjoys complaining about the cold as much as I enjoy complaining about the heat.”

     

                “Do you?”

     

                “Very much so. It wrings all of the water from me,” Kara said with a crooked smile. “It makes me feel rather dry, like a riverbed in summer when the water levels are low. There are some mountains here where lava oozes from the rock and if my sister had it her way, she would find herself a nice cave and bask in the heat of it year-round. I, myself, do not share that preference.”

     

                “Well, I’d gathered that much. How are you still swimming in the sea at this time of year? It’s beyond me.”

     

                “It’s invigorating.”

     

                “Or terrifying. I’m just glad I can stay warm and dry inside here while you enjoy your death wish.”

     

                “I would advise you to do the same today. Perhaps we can spend the day together for a change.”

     

                “You spend every day with me. I thought you’d be too busy to sit around watching me have my ass handed to me, but you sure do make an effort to be present for my humiliation.”

     

                Kara frowned at Lena’s dry amusement. “I am never too busy for you, and a few hours each morning does not qualify as spending the day with you. And that is not why I come to watch. You have Alex teaching you hand-to-hand combat and knife throwing, Kelly is teaching you archery and Sam is teaching you sword fighting. You have not come to me for anything; if I did not seek you out myself, I don’t believe you would have any use for me.”

     

                Swallowing her mouthful of tea, Lena’s brow furrowed together and she was quick to respond. “That’s not true. Well, it is - I don’t have any use for you, you’re not someone I keep around because of what you can offer me. Not that I had much of a choice in the matter, but that’s irrelevant right now. I just- don’t you have better things to do than babysit me?”

     

                “Do you think so little of yourself that you think I would prefer to work than spend time with you?”

     

                “No, but a lot of our time spent together is you teaching me about things. About harvest yields and water levels, how much stone was quarried and how much wood we have, how much wool we traded for and how you balance your books. Even teaching me about your history … all of that has to be tiring after a certain point.”

     

                “Then what shall we do today?”

     

                Pausing, lips pressed together as she thought for a moment, Lena gave her a wary look. “What do you enjoy doing that isn’t related to the water?”

     

                Considering the question as she cocked her head to the side, Kara smiled. “I like to play the harp. I enjoy reading, as you know. Sometimes I play stones with my sister. Knitting - although, it is a skill I learned through making nets, which is related to the water. I enjoy practising my swordcraft, cooking, and riding. There are many things I enjoy doing, so you have your pick of what you would like to do from those - or none if you would prefer. I do not believe our interests would overlap much.”

     

                “Well, you’re lacking any sort of garden patch or flower bed, so I’ll rule out gardening,” Lena mused, “I do like reading, and music if you’d like to play your harp for me. I’m a decent cook myself, so we could make lunch together if you’d like. You could show me how to knit a pair of socks, I’m sure that would free up more of your time. And you could be my sparring partner today if your sister isn’t available.”

     

                She finished with a quick smile and Kara returned it shyly. “Get dressed and I will bring you some breakfast first.”

     

                “What are we going to do?”

     

                “All of those things. The day is long.”

     

                Sweeping out of the room without another word, Kara vanished and Lena was left to sip her tea in the comfort of her bed, the brazier burning low as it ate away at the wood that had been thrown on it last night by Kara as she made the rounds to warm the halls of Krypton for her wife. Lena had just reached the dregs of her cup when Kara returned with a laden tray, setting it on the mattress and immediately reaching for the pot of tea. She refilled Lena’s cup first and then filled a clean one for herself, nursing it while Lena ate.

     

                The porridge was drizzled with honey and studded with walnuts, hot and filling, and there was fresh bread and a pot of currant jam. Lena ate bits of everything while Kara cut slivers from a pear. 

     

                “Where would you like to begin?” she asked, handing over a piece.

     

                Lena shrugged as she spread jam over a piece of bread, exchanging it for the slice of pear. “I don’t mind. You can pick.”

     

                Taking a bite of the bread, Kara thoughtfully chewed, her eyes narrowing a fraction. “Well, seeing as you are still in bed, why don’t we read first and you can remain in bed a while longer? We have tea and I shall build the fire up for you. Is there anything you wish to read in particular?”

     

                “Sounds good to me. But unless you have children’s books in your library, I don’t think I’ll be much use at reading them. Kelly’s a good teacher but I’m not that capable of understanding glyphs.”

     

                “You have gotten better with fae though,” Kara said approvingly before hesitating, “that is when you deign to speak it.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena lightly responded, accepting another piece of pear and fitting it in between a mouthful of porridge. “But seriously, do you have any kids’ books?”

     

                “Children are taught to read from our history books. They do not simplify them for their benefit; it is important they learn the hard way.”

     

                “Must everything in this damned place be learned the hard way?”

     

                “If it was easy, there would be no sense of worth in life. Although I have not lived so long myself, I can only imagine eternity gets quite tiresome if there is nothing to strive for.”

     

                “Eternity,” Lena murmured, her expression clouding for a moment. “I know you said before that our lifespans are … very long. Um … how old is the oldest-“

     

                “Three millennia. Unfortunately, most of our people are struck down in battle. There have not been many Fae to reach a millennia in the last few centuries, with endless war claiming so many lives. There have not been many children born either, not enough to replace the countless that have been lost. Our light is dimming but … perhaps we shall be the last generation to endure such sadness.”

     

                “Would that mean … you and I- if we lived that long, we’d be married the whole time. Thousands of years.”

     

                “Potentially. Although, we do not yet know what the seers have said of your fate.”

     

                “What makes you think they’ve said anything?”

     

                “If your father did not have them read your fate when you were a child, they could read it as an adult, if it was your desire to know.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, as sceptical as always, Lena smiled slightly. “I think I’d prefer not to know. You know, the whole thing about sitting around waiting for your fate to happen to you thing. There would be no sense of worth in that, now, would there?”

     

                Rolling her eyes at Lena’s mocking words, Kara cut her another piece of pear and then finished off the rest before climbing to her feet. Crossing over to the brazier and the stack of driftwood piled in a willow basket, she added more to the low-burning fire and built it back up before facing Lena.

     

                “Reading it is then. I shall be back soon.”

     

                Lena remained in bed, sipping her tea and picking at the remains of breakfast and it wasn’t long before Kara was back, a few books tucked beneath her arm and another pot of tea in hand. She shifted some things around on the table off to the side, filled their cups from the remainder of the old pot and then set that aside so the new one could take its place. Spreading the selection of books across the blankets, Kara gestured to them.

     

                “I brought a few options. This one is one I loved as a child; it’s the tale of a man named Rao, an ancestor of mine who lived ten thousand years ago. He was one of the Firefolk and a valiant warrior. I also brought-”

     

                “I’ll just read that one,” Lena said before she could continue, wanting to know what about it Kara had loved so much. 

     

                Handing the book over, Kara picked up her own selection and then stacked the others on the table. She spied the small stool and snagged a leg with her foot, drawing it closer before settling on it, opening it to the first page as Lena thumbed the corners of her own. Looking up through her eyelashes, Lena cleared her throat as she opened her book.

     

                “You can sit in bed if you’d like.”

     

                Kara looked up, mild surprise crossing her face. Slipping a finger between the pages, she shut her book and slowly climbed to her feet. Stepping forward and turning around, Kara perched on the edge of the bed and let her book fall back open. Rolling her eyes, Lena shifted to the left side of the bed, careful not to jostle the tea tray, and then dragged that with her so it was in the middle of the bed before she patted the right side.

     

                “At least make yourself comfortable. Aren’t you cold?”

     

                “I’m content,” Kara assured her, dressed warmly for the day with fur-lined clothes and thick wool layers.

     

                Still, she climbed to her feet again and sat where Lena had indicated, over the top of the blankets but feeling the warmth of where her wife had lain. Clearing her throat, Kara settled against the pillows and picked up her cup of tea as a comfortable silence filled the room. It was comfortable, but that didn’t mean Lena didn’t feel a faint tension, her stomach knotted as she drew her knees up beneath the blankets, resting her book against her thighs as she looked at the first page again and tried to puzzle through the handwritten glyphs.

     

                After a few minutes, she set the book down and climbed out of bed, the shock of cold air a slap after the warmth of so many layers. Kara glanced up at her, tracking Lena’s movements to the table across the room, where she’d amassed belongings since her arrival. Fetching paper and a stick of charcoal, Lena climbed back into bed, hurriedly covering herself with the pile of blankets again and picking up her cup of tea to take a sip.

     

                Settling back in with her book, she broke down the sounds of the glyphs that she had learnt through hours of lessons with Kelly, trying to piece together the sound of the word and then translate it to English. It took her an hour to get through the first page, stringing the sentences together on her empty pages, reworking the order so they made sense and then reading them together. 

     

                It was painstaking work and wasn’t the pleasurable morning of reading that she’d anticipated, already tiring of it after translating merely the first page. With a sigh she snapped the book shut and set it aside with her notes on top, rubbing her eyes with the heels of her palms as she kept her charcoal-stained fingers away from her face.

     

                “This is stupid,” she sighed, “it’s all gibberish to me.”

     

                “Gibberish?”

     

                “Nonsense.”

     

                “Oh. Well, I can read it to you if you tire of translating it.”

     

                Kara closed her book and set it down, exchanging it for Lena’s as she opened it to the first page, took a sip of tea and then started to recite the glyphs. She read it in fae, insisting that it sounded better, and Lena did concede that there was a musical quality to the lilting of her voice as she read through the first tale far quicker than Lena would ever have been able to translate it. They were halfway through the second tale, both of them subconsciously shifting closer to each other on the bed, their heads ducked in, just the tea tray separating them, when Alex appeared in the doorway.

     

                She had on almost as many layers as Lena, sans the blankets, and cast a wary look around the room. “What are you doing?”

     

                “We are reading, sister. Surely you know what that is, no matter how many hours you spend with your knives,” Kara replied, turning the page.

     

                “You did not break your fast with us.”

     

                “Lena was of a mind to stay where it is warm for a while longer.”

     

                “A wise choice. I have half a mind to do the same if there is nothing entertaining to do. Fetch me if you decide you’ve had enough of reading.”

     

                Departing almost as quickly as she’d arrived, Alex vanished back to her room at the other end of the hall and Kara finished off the second tale. Once she’d finished, she paused and glanced at Lena.

     

                “Do you wish to read another or shall we move on to something else? Perhaps practising your swordsmanship will warm you. And then I shall drag my sister out of bed to heat a bath for you to wash and warm yourself through even further. By that point, you should be warm enough to endure tea by the fire and a lesson in knitting.”

     

                “Sounds like a plan.”

     

                “Alright, well, I shall fetch my sword.”

     

                Leaving Lena to pluck up the courage to leave the bed, Kara walked across the hallway and into her own room. With a reluctant sigh, Lena threw back the covers and climbed to her feet. She’d slept in her robe, a thick winter nightgown with a chemise, leggings and socks on, and hastily changed into something easier to fight in, keeping the robe as she buckled it closed with her belt and dagger. The sword she practised with had become hers without anyone objecting so she’d taken to keeping it propped up against the table instead of hidden beneath the bed, and Lena buckled that to her belt as well before stepping out of the room, finding Kara waiting patiently for her.

     

                They made their way downstairs to a rather bare room, big enough to make the sound echo faintly as they both unsheathed their swords. Lena was nervous about sparring with Kara, even though she’d done so before and had been watched for the last few weeks by her wife, some part of her not wanting to embarrass herself and the other part of her seeking her approval. Kara gave her a playful bow and Lena rolled her eyes before mirroring her. 

     

                Kara prowled silently and Lena moved to follow her movements, keeping distance between them as she adjusted her grip on her sword. After a tense minute, Kara darted forward, found her way past Lena’s guard and had the edge of her sword pressed to her wife’s throat. Hand pressed to the small of her back to keep her from falling over, Kara gave her a small smile, her blue eyes shining with amusement.

     

                “Do not drag out your attack. You will only serve to give your opponent more time to find a weakness. Take advantage of the element of surprise.”

     

                She pulled away and they went again, this time with Lena charging straight into attack, the sound of clashing metal filling the room. Kara blocked her at each turn but her counterattacks were measured, testing Lena’s skill rather than speed, to see if she guarded herself well, if she could anticipate where Kara would strike next. In the weeks since Sam had resumed teaching her, Lena had surpassed where she had previously been, her dedication to it this time proving to make her a quick learner, and what she lacked in skill and fitness, she made up for in sheer stubborn determination.

     

                Long past the point of exhaustion, she pushed herself to keep going, a few of the others slipping in and out as the noise drew their attention. It was only when Kara parried her blow and Lena gritted her teeth, pushing back against her immovable strength, that they stopped, when Lena grabbed the edge of her sword and pushed back, the bite of steel across her palm as blood welled up and Kara quickly jerked back. With a quiet bark of triumph, as she got past Kara’s guard and pressed the tip of her blade against her sternum, Lena grinned.

     

                Less than pleased, Kara scowled as she batted Lena’s sword aside, wrenched from her wife’s grasp as it clattered to the floor, and snagged her wrist, jerking her close as she turned her hand to look at her palm. It wasn’t a deep cut but it was bleeding enough to run down Lena’s wrist, disappearing beneath the sleeve of her robe and jacket. Clicking her tongue with annoyance, Kara sheathed her sword in one smooth motion and then produced a handkerchief with a flourish as petals drifted from Lena’s dripping blood, falling to their feet.

     

                “Reckless,” Kara brittly told her. “And foolish. You could lose your fingers if you tried that in a real fight.”

     

                “I still won.”

     

                “You won because I did not want you to injure yourself further. Your enemy will not share that sentiment.”

     

                Smile growing a fraction as she let Kara tie her handkerchief around the cut, stemming the bleeding as it soaked the spotless white cotton, Lena raised her eyebrows. “But you admit that I won.”

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners with disapproval, Kara gave her a withering look. “Come. I will have Alex heat a bath for you. Your hand will sting but perhaps it will serve as a lesson for you to not be so rash.”

     

                Picking up Lena’s sword and sheathing it for her, the smell of salt clinging to her flushed skin, Kara turned and swept out of the room. Following after her, palm smarting from the slash across it, Lena bristled and was silent as she followed Kara downstairs and into the open-aired bathing room. 

     

                The view beyond the semicircular tiers was bleak, dark waves crashing on the limestone steps and white forth churning over the stone as it swept in. The sky was a deep grey and the air bit at Lena’s exposed cheeks and hands as she stared out at the black stretch of sea. It was frightening to her and she didn’t want to get any closer, rubbing her arms as she hung back, staring at the low clouds as she breathed in the strong smell of brine.

     

                Without a word, sensing her unease, Kara fetched the tub and lifted it with some difficulty due to its unwieldy size, walking out of the room and finding a small antechamber on the other side of the hallway. It was bare of anything not made of stone, due to the nights when the sea flooded the lower level, and she set the tub down in front of an empty fireplace before summoning a torrent of water from the sea and filling the tub.

     

                She left Lena sitting on a low stone stool and returned ten minutes later with a towel, soap, a jug of steaming water, and a stack of firewood under her other arm. Alex followed her in, thrusting a flaming hand into the tub as Kara arranged some wood in the swept fireplace, and then lit that too before grumbling about going back to her own fire.

     

                “Take your time,” Kara murmured, “I will swim a while.”

     

                Reluctantly stripping off her clothes, Lena quickly scrambled into the hot water and sat down, submerging as much of herself as she could. Even her hand, which did sting as she hissed and curled her fingers around it as the salt got in. The heat of the water was pleasant though, burrowing into her, even if she could have done without the briny tang of it and the way the salt dried on her skin. Lingering as long as she could, until the heat started to wane somewhat, she grabbed the soap and washed herself clean before rinsing her hair with the hot freshwater in the jug.

     

                Then came the difficult part of getting out of the bath, too cowardly to brave the frigid air as she mourned gas heating and the balmy winters of National City. She did force herself out though, almost tripping on the lip of the tub in her haste before she staggered towards the fire and righted her balance. Dropping to snatch up the towel, she wrapped it tightly around herself and shivered before the wall of heat radiating from the fire as it saturated her with the smell of wood smoke. After a while, it started to sting her eyes and throat but Lena didn’t move away from the heat, even as it reddened her skin, not even to get dressed.

     

                Kara found her there ten minutes later, pausing in the doorway to study her wife, towel wrapped around her like a cloak and dark hair tangled against her back and shoulders as she gazed distantly into the fire. When her wife stepped into the room, Lena broke herself out of her reverie and looked at her, expression softening at the familiar sight of her. 

     

                “Warmer?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You should dress before the storm blows in.”

     

                “Another one?”

     

                “It will not be so bad.”

     

                Moving towards her neatly folded pile of clothes, Lena started to dress in her undergarments, pulling on layers that she’d gotten used to fastening after months in the Courts, and she stayed near to the fire as she dressed, her bare skin prickling with goosebumps as she had to abandon her towel. Lingering just inside the doorway, Kara waited patiently and after a tense minute, Lena broke the silence.

     

                “Can I ask you something?”

     

                “You know that you are always free to do so.”

     

                “If you can control water, and ice and snow are just another form of water, why don’t you stop it? I mean … if it snows, can’t you just turn it into water?”

     

                Smiling slightly with amusement, Kara’s cheeks dimpled and she raked a hand through her damp hair. “Ah, you have stumbled upon the question we have all asked as children. The answer is quite simple; if I were to never let snow touch my land, it would disrupt the natural cycle of the seasons, ruin the harmony of living in nature. It is not for me to decide when it should snow.”

     

                Nodding as she absorbed the explanation, Lena pulled her robe over her layers and started buckling on her belt, the sword and dagger sheathed at her waist. “I suppose so.”

     

                “You agree?”

     

                “It’s like planting invasive species of flowers or trees and changing the biodiversity of the region. Native species can’t thrive when these invasive ones are taking over and it can change the habitat and food sources of native animals. Same thing as introducing pests to a region, taking away resources from native animals. I guess I just never considered that there was a conscientious decision to not intervene with nature here. As you said, you all live in harmony with it, but I guess I figured you would have shaped the land to your will, in a way.”

     

                “You have forgotten the wildness of the forest and the seas. It would be foolish of us to try and shape that which is so feral and dangerous that we cannot take more than what is necessary. There is a beautiful balance in the order of things here. It is to kill or be killed for all creatures, hunt or be hunted. To try and tame the forest would be to think oneself more powerful than nature.”

     

                With a quiet laugh, Lena crouched as she laced on her boots. “And I bet it helps that the forest has everyone wrapped around its finger with the spores of it in the water and air, poisoning you to never leave.”

     

                “Yes, there is that too. We are a part of it as it is a part of us. It is the cycle of life.”

     

                “You are happy to just be part of the cycle?”

     

                “I eat my fill of fish and one day the fish will eat their fill of me, and I will be bones at the bottom of some river, lake or sea. There is something comforting in that knowledge that life will continue, that it will be sustained and nourished by my body. Think of yourself and your love of flowers and trees; you eat the apples from a tree and one day you may be buried with the seed of an apple tree, and that tree will grow from the bones of your body as it feeds off your flesh and grows apples for someone else to eat. Is that not a comforting thought to you?”

     

                Expression clouding, Lena straightened and walked towards Kara, retying the bloody handkerchief around her palm. “Yeah, I don’t know if that’s comforting or weird. I try not to think about my own burial, especially with how very possible it is that it’ll be soon. Is that normal for Fae though? To give your body back to nature?”

     

                “Yes. Earth or water. It is impossible to give one's body to the wind, of course, and to give oneself to the flames would deprive nature of the life that can be born from flesh and bones. To have your body burned is something that is reserved for traitors or enemies who do not deserve the respect of a proper burial. Even between Courts, death rites are honoured, except for the rarest of blood feuds.”

     

                “Well, for my peace of mind, can you promise to make sure I’m given to the earth when I die? I’d hate to become a pile of bones at the bottom of a lake. No offence.”

     

                “Of course I would ensure that. I know how much you hate the water; I would not let your rest be unpeaceful.”

     

                “And I know how much you love it so I can only imagine we wouldn’t be buried together.”

     

                Looking surprised at the mere idea of it, Kara slowed her steps as she blinked at Lena. “Well … I haven’t given much thought to us dying but I would imagine you’re correct. Perhaps we will plant a tree on the banks of the river so that we can remain near each other. Would that do?”

     

                It was Lena’s turn to look surprised, although hers was more so due to the nonchalant way they were discussing where they would be buried together instead of the notion of them being buried together or not. Clearing her throat as her expression furrowed for a moment, she shrugged indifferently.

     

                “I guess so.”

     

                “Good. Now that matter has been resolved, shall we have some tea?”

     

                Continuing the way to the large hall where everyone congregated in their spare time, Lena allowed Kara to drag a chair closer to the roaring fire, sitting as her wife fetched a thick blanket and tucked it across her lap. A writhing mass of water bore a tray, leaving droplets in its wake as Kara controlled its movements, and she poured tea for them both, waiting until Lena was comfortable before she pulled out a willow basket of wool and started to show her how to knit. 

     

                Lena didn’t have the dexterity of someone who had grown up weaving nets, used to tracking stitches and tying knots, mindful of the tension and keeping the wool or rope untangled. She made a mess of her piece, while Kara’s needles swiftly clacked as she worked on her latest piece. It was peaceful though, listening to the snap and crackle of the flames, the taste of mint on their tongues and the sweetness of warm buns with currants and nuts baked into them as they passed the time together.

     

                After an hour of knitting a shapeless form, Lena sighed and dropped the wool and needles to her lap. “I’ve had enough of this. It’s beyond salvageable at this point.”

     

                Looking up from her own, Kara softly chuckled and set her neat rows of stitches down. “Shall we do something else now? I can play for you if you’d like.”

     

                She gestured to the beautifully wrought harp safely stowed in the corner of the room, far larger than the little one Lena had spied in her bedroom, bigger even than the one she’d heard Kara play from time to time in Argo. Nodding, Lena drained the dregs of her tea and drew her knees up to her chest, chin propped on top as she wrapped her arms around her legs and watched Kara move across the room. 

     

                The first strum of the strings was a gentle trill, which Kara quickly spun into a melody that made Lena’s skin ripple with goosebumps. Watching her wife play, slender fingers moving across the strings in an elegant rhythm, Lena was quietly awed as she listened to the music, relaxing in her seat as some residual tension bled out of her. Closing her eyes, she listened to the endless stream of music, realising how much she had missed it, the simple act of turning on the radio in her workshop, whatever pop music was trending drifting through the speakers as she worked. There were no words to this but it was enjoyable all the same, evoking a peace that Lena wished would never end.

     

                Eventually, it did though, the notes dwindling to silence, and Lena opened her eyes, lashes fluttering as she moved, a certain stiffness and heaviness to her body, as if waking from a nap. She smiled sweetly as she roused herself, watching Kara rise from the stool set beside the harp and drift towards her.

     

                “That was beautiful. You’re very good.” 

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “Do you sing as well?” Lena asked after a moment.

     

                “I do. You would not know our ballads though.”

     

                “Must one understand music to enjoy it?”

     

                Kara conceded to that point and promised to sing for her next time. The idea of a next time, of more music, filled Lena with inexplicable delight and she gave her wife a small smile as Kara hovered nearby. Toying with her fingers, Kara raised her eyebrows as she smiled slightly.

     

                “What next?”

     

                “Well … seeing as I have no skills other than arranging flowers, or talking about flowers, or growing flowers,” she mused with a wry smile, “I suppose I can … cook us dinner? I can manage okay in the kitchen if you’re hungry.”

     

                “If you have a mind to cook.”

     

                “As long as it’s warm in there.”

     

                It had been a long time since she’d had to cook and Lena was surprised by how much she’d missed the simple act of fending for herself. Her meals were brought to her or spread out before her, her clothes were laundered and mended for her, sheets changed and bed made, her every whim catered to. It gave her more free time than she knew what to do with, and only now that she’d managed to fill it with practising for the off-chance of killing someone did she have any semblance of a busy day.

     

                In the heat of the kitchen, the air humid from the steam as it caressed her pink cheeks, tendrils of her dark hair sticking to her hairline, Lena chopped vegetables taken from the larder and worked lumps of cold butter into flour. She intended to make a pie, hoping for chicken and ending up with some plucked quail, which was better than the endless diet of seafood she’d been exposed to recently. As much as she’d loved seared salmon or chilli mussels back home, she didn’t enjoy them enough to warrant fish and molluscs for every meal.

     

                As she cooked, Kara watched her closely, the way Lena thumbed through the hanging bundles of dried herbs, identifying what she needed with ease, the way she quickly ran her knife over them, chopping them finely, the way she roughly kneaded the pastry with the heels of her palms and how her dark hair spilt down her back in an inky river as she tried to keep it out of her face. Kara fought the itch to round the kitchen bench and braid it back for her. 

     

                There was a loaf of fresh bread as well, left to rise as Kara made them raspberry tea and Lena paused a moment to sip it as they chatted. There were no windows in the kitchen, carved into the cliffside as it was, but on the north-facing side of the hall the light was already fading, although the clouds to the east had started to bruise. The smell of rain was heavy on the salt air as Kara glanced through the open doorway, as if she would be able to see through the hallway wall and beyond to the expanse of sea and sky.

     

                Tea break over, Lena was back to work, flour dusting the front of her quilted jacket as she egg-washed the pie and then set it and the scored loaf into the stone oven. Rinsing off her hands, she stepped back and gave Kara a quick smile.

     

                “Sorry, we might have to wait awhile.”

     

                “It looks like the wait will be worth it. Would you like some more tea?”

     

                Gesturing vaguely, Lena smiled wryly. “I swear all I do here is drink tea, but sure, tea sounds great.”

     

                “Tea is one of the simple pleasures of life. I don’t believe you can ever have too much.”

     

                Lena didn’t disagree as Kara rummaged around in the jarred assortment of blends and withdrew her choice, filling the iron kettle with a wave of her hand and setting it to boil. Once it did, she steeped the leaves in the hot water and then filled their cups, nursing her own as she sat on a stool and studied Lena as she gently blew on the steaming surface of her tea.

                

                “What is next after we eat?”

     

                “That’s everything on our list.”

                

                “It is not yet suppertime. We must find something else to do to fill the evening.”

     

                “What is it you’d like to do?”

     

                “Me? I’m content with just the pleasure of your company.”

     

                “Just content?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara sipped her tea. “Perhaps more than content.”

     

                “How about stones?” Lena asked, raising an eyebrow as she tried to hide a smile.

     

                She was good at the game, or as good as one could be with no knowledge of its existence until a few weeks ago, relying on slim knowledge of chess to fill in the blanks. It was one of the things she’d come to enjoy of late, that chance that she would beat her opponent - usually Alex - at something for a change. Winning with the absence of bruises was a small triumph in Lena’s eyes, her body seeming to always be covered with a smattering of purple, green and yellowish brown lately as she earned too many bruises for her body to heal them quickly enough before the next batch was delivered with swift precision by a jab or a restrained sword edge. 

     

                “I’m sick of being bad at everything we’ve done today so maybe I’ll have a chance to beat you,” Lena explained with a glimmer of competitiveness in her eyes.

     

                “Well, we haven’t eaten yet, and it smells very promising, but if you wish to play stones afterwards, we shall play stones. Although, do not think you will win so easily; I have been playing this game far longer than you have.”

     

                “But I know how to play chess, and it’s not that dissimilar. So maybe we’re on equal footing for a change.”

     

                “Does it bother you to not be equal to me at all things?”

     

                Hesitating, Lena turned to the oven and she pressed her lips together, buying herself a second as she checked on the pie. “No, it’s not about you. I’d just … like to be good at something here. Hell, even a board game is better than nothing, isn’t it? I’m not good at anything else so …”

     

                “You have many talents.”

     

                “Do I? If I do, they’re lost on me.”

     

                “As mentioned before, flowers-”

     

                “That’s not necessarily a talent. It’s some inherited power that wasn’t fully realised until I came here.”

     

                “It is a talent to know them all, to identify their meaning and what they are used for. You would make an apt healer, if you desired to be. My mother would gladly teach you some of her knowledge during her visit.”

     

                “Your mother is visiting?”

     

                “For midwinter. She should be arriving from her mountain halls any day now.”

     

                Humming dubiously, Lena wrung a tea towel in her hands. “Maybe. It would give me something to do at least. Instead of wasting my time doing nothing.”

     

                “You aren’t wasting your time. It is important to stand still for a while, a little rest amidst the journey of life.
