Your boat is just dropping anchor at this harbour for a time, and after you have rested, you can set sail again for the next adventure.” Kara paused and then let out a short laugh, her face crumpling with bewildered amusement. “We should be glad for the peace we have after so many ordeals and disruptions.”

     

                Lena could hardly argue with that and removed the pie and bread a short while after that, serving up wedges of the pie and slicing thick pieces of hot bread as Kara fetched butter and forks. They sat together at one end of the long trestle work bench and Kara kept up a stream of compliments for Lena’s cooking, almost verging on too enthusiastic to be genuine, if she hadn’t said many of them in Fae to dissuade Lena’s scepticism. 

     

                “It really is delicious. I could eat this every day,” Kara earnestly assured her again as she scooped up another forkful of pie.

     

                “You know, I don’t think I’ve ever received such vocal praise for my cooking before,” Lena snorted as she gave Kara a droll look, “perhaps I’ve missed my calling as a chef, or maybe you’re a little too full of shit.”

     

                Giving her a stern look, a smile tugging at the corners of her mouth, Kara swallowed her bite and cleared her throat as she reached out to cover Lena’s hand with her own. “Can I not praise my wife?” 

     

                Opening her mouth to respond, Lena was interrupted by Alex entering the kitchen, a rigid set to her shoulders as she quickly made a beeline for her sister, a piece of paper in her hand and her brown eyes alight with adrenaline. Kara set down her fork and raised her eyebrows as she watched her sister approach.

     

                “Sister, come and taste the pie Lena baked, it-”

     

                “A red sunset,” Alex cut her off as she stopped on the other side of the workbench and braced her hands on the wood. “And a raven from the south-eastern outpost.”

     

                “What message do they bring?”

     

                “Unseelie have crossed the river further south. They can’t be certain of the numbers; the original message was from a scout who retreated to send a warning, but a score perhaps. Not so many for us to easily deal with.”

     

                She held out the message and Kara quickly read the glyphs as Lena frowned slightly, trying to decipher them herself. Whoever had written the message had a messy hand though and she was not so well-versed in reading Fae to make much sense of the swirling symbols. With a sigh, Kara crumpled it in her hand and set it down with a regretful look of sorrow on her face.

     

                On her feet a moment later, she was moving quickly as Lena floundered for a moment and followed after her. Alex was following as well, the two of them making rapid plans as Lena was left trying to piece things together, so unused to talk of strategy and the different landmarks and distances they spoke of. This was not for her ears but she felt so helpless and adrift that she trailed after her wife, rather than sit in the kitchen alone. After all, they were spending the day together.

     

                Crossing the threshold of Kara’s room without pause, Lena came to a stop and then hovered with uncertainty as she watched Kara head straight for her armour. She’d never seen her wear it, had never seen the radiance of her wife in a suit of gleaming armour, beautifully wrought like the sea and scales of a fish, but she could vividly imagine the sight. Lingering, she watched with interest as her wife started to strip off some of her clothes and dress for battle.

     

                Catching sight of Lena as she turned away from her sister, heading off to don her armour, Alex paused and then turned back towards Kara. “You should bring her,” Alex said in Fae, her eyes sliding sideways to Lena.

     

                Stiffening, Kara continued to change. “Absolutely not. I will not unnecessarily put her in harm’s way when it can be avoided.”

     

                “She is not a fragile flower, sister. She is an Unseelie Princess; she should know what it is to battle and spill blood. Perhaps it will encourage her to honour peace one day.”

     

                “One day? We are in peacetime now. I will not sully the promise I made by waging war.”

     

                “When you speak of peace, I am unable to see it. It is a sweet sentiment, I admit, but it is not possible when they commit acts such as this. The things we have done to keep the Seelie Court safe make it as such and any attempt at peace was forfeit the moment you chopped the hand off their Queen. Will you let the Unseelie raid your land, kill your people, pollute your waters and sit in your home as you leave them defenceless?”

     

                Kara’s cheeks coloured and her voice was terse when she replied. “You know that I will not. That does not mean I will bring my wife with me. I forbid it.”

     

                “She should see that firsthand, to witness the ongoing feud and someday - perhaps someday - bring about the peace you wish to see in the world.”

     

                Finishing tying the front of her quilted gambeson closed, Kara turned on her sister, her expression hard. “This is my land. I am leading the party, I decide who goes.”

     

                “I speak for myself,” Lena cut in with an arched eyebrow, surprising both women, who had overlooked her passable understanding of Fae as they’d talked freely.

     

                “Then what say you, Princess?” Alex asked.

     

                Crossing her arms over her chest, Lena anxiously chewed her lip as she considered it. She wasn’t much use with a sword, and was only slightly better with a bow, but was that enough for her to consider a skirmish with Unseelie who had been fighting for longer than she’d been alive? Not to mention the ride through snow and sleet on horseback, which she admittedly had gotten better at but wasn’t sure she wanted to suffer through the cold for. But the alternative to that would be to stay behind, to stay with guards no doubt, while Kara went off to fight and left Lena wondering about what was happening, who had been hurt, if someone wasn’t coming back.

     

                Swallowing her fear, she licked her chapped lips, looking a little pale at the prospect of being thrown back into the middle of fighting, which she had witnessed enough of already, dragged between Courts, Lena forced herself to nod. A wounded look of betrayal crossed Kara’s face and she abruptly turned her back to her, reaching for her mail as she tried to stamp down her anger at her sister and her fear for her wife. Gesturing dismissively, Kara’s chin dimpled as she clenched her teeth, mouth a grim line.

     

                “Go and prepare yourself then.”

     

                Rankling at the brusque dismissal, a stab of guilt cutting through her at Kara’s clearly hurt tone, Lena turned and left quickly, haughty and indignant in her own right. Once she was in her room, she didn’t know what to do, what she needed to prepare, having no armour to don and only a borrowed sword, bow and quiver of arrows. As she lingered with uncertainty, Lena heard furious whispers across the hallway, although she couldn’t make out any words - by design, she surmised - and a moment later footsteps grew louder and approached her room.

     

                “Come,” Alex curtly instructed her.

     

                With nothing else to do, Lena followed her to the other end of the long hallway and into her rooms. Kelly was there, donning her own armour amidst the furniture and their belongings, hers finely wrought steel with swirling clouds and birds gilded in gold on the gorget, breastplate and her greaves and vambraces. The latter she was tying on as she sat on the edge of the bed, looking up at the arrival of the two women.

     

                “Take off your clothes. We will have to make do with spares for you.”

     

                Hurried unbuckling her belt, sword and dagger carefully set aside, Lena shed her robe and then her flour-dusted jacket. She had a thick wool shirt and then a thinner cotton one beneath, shedding the first and hugging her arms to herself as she shivered in her shirt and leggings. She was of a height with Alex, who handed her a spare gambeson in a deep rust colour, shoving her arms through the sleeves and then fumbling with the ties. Alex brushed her fingers aside and fastened it quickly for her, turning back to her trunk and rummaging through the contents.

     

                “Kelly, do you have spare gloves? Mailed ones? I only have the one pair with me.”

     

                “I have armour for her.”

     

                They paused, three of them looking to the door, where Kara was mostly dressed, her polished armour catching the orange glow of the lit fire in the room, limning her in warm light. Her expression was still hard and she stared at Lena with his ocean-dark eyes, blonde hair spilling around her shoulders like a river of gold. Lena thought she looked like a pre-Raphaelite painting of a soldier, standing in the doorway as the burnished glow of her armour displayed the water motifs carefully hammered and wrought into the metal, like a river goddess come to life. 

     

                “Come with me.”

     

                Turning to glance at the other two women, Lena hesitated and let out a soft sigh, snatching up her sword belt and bundling the sheathes in her arms as she walked out. Lena didn’t walk beside her, somewhat annoyed by Kara’s cold shoulder, and chose to walk behind her instead, to one of the rooms she’d merely poked her head into before and moved on without much thought for the contents. It was an armoury of sorts she supposed, two sets of armour on stands and a variety of weapons sheathed or safely stowed.

     

                Without a word, Kara unbuckled the smaller breastplate in the waning light coming through the narrow window, setting it aside and then removing other pieces until she held a finely made coat of chainmail in her hands. She turned to Lena and raised it, Lena ducking her head as she donned it, following the motions of Kara piecing the armour together on her that they’d gone through a few weeks ago, casting furtive glances at her wife’s slightly reddened eyes.

     

                Still as Kara dressed her, raising her arms when necessary as buckles were cinched tight and more pieces were added, Lena felt her fear rise. She was no fighter, she wasn’t someone worth dressing up in armour to be slaughtered immediately, but she had agreed to go and knew she wouldn’t stand to be left behind. Not unless they all stayed with her, and then who would protect the borders of Kara’s lands?

     

                The smell of oil and metal clung to the armour and Lena felt the increasing weight of it settle on her as each piece was attached. Once Kara was finished, she picked up a helmet and a small shield, shaped like a scalloped shell, and handed them out for Lena to take. Giving her an appraising look, she tugged on a few pieces and then walked out of the room. Pausing a moment as she determined whether or not she was supposed to follow, Lena went after her, the armour surprisingly easy to move in.

     

                Kara walked back to her room, gesturing to the floor at the foot of her bed. “Sit. I will braid your hair for you.”

     

                Sinking down with some awkwardness, Lena felt the mattress jostle behind her a few moments later as Kara sat cross-legged behind her, the touch of her fingers on her hair making Lena’s scalp prickle as Kara started combing it into segments, moving quickly. It felt more intimate than when Andrea did Lena’s hair, perhaps because Kara had never been an attendant, had never had the daily duty of making Lena presentable, yet was taking the time to do her hair now. She did it silently, and Lena could feel her hurt and anger coldly radiating from her. Swallowing thickly, she closed her eyes and breathed in slowly.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Don’t be. As you said, you speak for yourself.”

     

                “You don’t want me to go though.”

     

                Kara’s hands stilled near the end of Lena’s braid and she was silent for a moment longer as she finished it off, tying the end to secure it, and then rested her hands on the cold metal of Lena’s shoulderplates. “Of course I do not want you to come with me. Why would I desire to see you in harm’s way? To be distracted in the middle of battle by thoughts of your safety?”

     

                Mouth thinning, Lena felt her throat constrict. “I’m not yours to be minded.”

                

                “If not mine then whose?”

     

                As she murmured the words, her fingertips tenderly brushed Lena’s neck. Closing her eyes, trying to stifle the shiver that ran through her, Lena bowed her head. “The armour will protect me,” Lena replied, diverting the conversation without answering.

     

                “It did not help the last person who wore it.”

     

                Withdrawing her touch, Kara climbed off the bed and crossed over to a trunk, rummaging through and pulling out a cloak of deep navy, adorned with leaping fishes and water lilies along the hem. She beckoned to Lena, who climbed to her feet with some difficulty, meeting her halfway.

     

                “Who did it belong to before?” Lena asked, running her fingers over the filigreed Waterfolk motifs on the chest plate, trimming the pauldrons and vambraces. 

     

                Fanning out the cloak as she approached, a pin clamped between her lips, Kara draped it over Lena’s shoulders and adjusted it until it sat properly, fastening at her right shoulder. Pinning it securely in place, Kara smoothed her fingers over the thick wool and met Lena’s gaze with shadowed eyes.

     

                “My mother.”

     

                Lena’s stomach dropped and she didn’t know whether she should have anticipated that answer or not. There were many relics scattered through the various rooms of the holding, breastplates, shields and swords mounted on the limestone walls alongside tapestries, the scratched and aged wood of old oars and canoes leaning against walls beside rusting tridents and spears. There had been no reason to think that the suit of armour Kara was dressing her in had belonged to her dead mother. 

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena didn’t know what to say, an ache in her chest. “Kara-”

     

                Reaching out, Kara touched her fingers to the filigree, tracing the curve of a fish scale on the overlapping pattern. “Fish and water will have to do; I do not have any armour fit for an Earthfolk Princess.”

     

                Closing her mouth, Lena closed her eyes too, for a brief moment, her stomach knotting. Opening her eyes again, she shook her head slightly, trying to shake off the nerves, the unease, and looked at Kara and her loose hair.

     

                “Would you like me to braid your hair for you?”

     

                Kara smiled thinly and grazed her fingertips over Lena’s cheek in a featherlight brush. “I do not need mine brushed out of my face. It will not hinder my ability to fight.”

     

                She didn’t take insult to Kara’s assumption that she would be cut down easily if momentarily inconvenienced by her hair blinding her or getting blown in her face, just nodded as she wrung her hands, the mail-backed gloves softly clinking. Turning from her, Kara started to gather the remainder of her belongings, donning her cloak and hefting a trident that was taller than she was, slinging the strap of her shield across her chest so it covered her back.

     

                “You must listen to my instruction once we leave these walls,” Kara softly ordered her. “It is dangerous, for all of us, and any poor decisions on your part could very well mean the life of someone else. If you insist on coming, then very well, I will not stop you, but you must stay atop your horse. You are passable with a bow, so fire from horseback and try not to hit any Seelie. If you are unhorsed, flee and find cover. I will find you afterwards but you must get away or they will cut you down. Do you hear me, Lena?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Turning back to her, face shockingly pale and pinched with fear, Kara’s blue eyes were pleading in the dwindling light of dusk. “Will you do as I ask?.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Thank you. It will ease my mind to know that you are not in the thick of it. As much as I wish you were here, safe behind these walls.”

     

                “If I was to stay, would you stay with me?”

     

                Hesitating, Kara grimaced. “No, I would have to see my duty through.”

     

                Stepping forward, Lena rested an arm on the cold steel of Kara’s vambrace. “Then I will do mine. Is it not my duty as much as it is yours? Even if- even if I don’t kill someone, Alex is right and I should know what we are fighting to stop.”

     

                “It should not be happening at all. It was an egregious mistake on my part to cut your mother’s hand off and ruin any chances of the truce lasting.”

     

                Reaching up, Lena cupped her cheek in hand, marvelling at the warmth of her. For someone who loved the water enough to swim in mid-winter seas, Kara was so warm, not the clammy cold-bloodedness of sea creatures. “It was ruined the moment I let my brother’s words get to me.”

     

                “No, before then even,” Kara murmured, her eyelids shuttering as a muscle twitched in her jaw. “I do not believe there was ever anything to ruin. We have never known peace; it was merely a farce, a moment to recuperate amidst centuries of war.”

     

                “One day it will be real. If it’s up to us to decide, we can make it happen.”

     

                The hard edge to Kara’s expression softened as she smiled slightly. “One day, yes. But for now, I must pick up my sword and bloody it once more. Gather your things; it will be a long night and perhaps even longer than that.”

     

                Feeling like she was playing dress-up in her armour, the gravity of her reality not quite fully settling in yet while she was still in the safety of Krypton, Lena fetched her bow and quiver, slinging the latter over her shoulder and keeping the bow unstrung. She checked her borrowed sword and gifted dagger in their sheaths and wondered at what else to take. Fortunately for her, she didn’t have to deliberate too long, Alex sweeping past and pausing before thrusting out saddlebags to Lena.

     

                “Here. Bring a blanket and fill the rest with food. Kelly is in the kitchen; find her.”

     

                It was all so organised and militaristic that Lena knew they’d done this a thousand times together, all of them working together like a well-oiled machine, knowing what part they had to play. Except for Lena and the Unseelie who had found themselves on the opposing side - away from the fighting on Andrea’s part. Lena found her helping wrap food in squares of linen, her fresh bread tied into a bundle with hard cheeses, the remainder of her pie - now cold - cut into wedges and similarly wrapped. 

     

                “Surely you’re not going,” Andrea blurted out at the sight of Lena, laughing as Lena bristled.

     

                “You’re not?”

     

                “I came with you to get away from the bloodshed your family inflicts. I’m no warrior and there is no shame in that. You should heed my words.”

     

                Raising her chin as she crossed over to the larder, fetching a sack of oats and the teas she’d come to know Kara preferred, hurriedly packing them away as her cheeks warmed. “Just because you don’t want to go, it doesn’t mean I don’t want to go.”

     

                “On your own head be it. I, on the other hand, will enjoy the peace and quiet by a warm fire, I think.”

     

                “It is a noble choice to defend one’s land and people,” Kelly declared, dunking canteens into barrels of fresh water. 

     

                “It is also noble to know when not to strike. A lesson that we have yet to learn as a collective.”

     

                “On whose end is that lesson not heeded?”

     

                “Do not cast blame on one Court. Both are to blame. Even now, the truce we were all to put our faith in was broken by your beloved Lady of the Waterfolk; I was there to witness it myself.”

     

                “You’re wrong,” Lena harshly snapped, setting down the saddlebags and quickly cramming in whatever she could. “It was I who broke it, not Kara. Don’t speak ill of her when she has been more committed to peace than any of us. Even now, she doesn’t want to go but she has to out of duty.”

     

                “And why do you go?”

     

                Faltering, Lena swallowed thickly as she buckled the saddlebags, a stab of fear cutting through her. “Because … I don’t want to be left behind. Let’s go.”

     

                She hefted her belongings and rounded the workbench, Andrea’s words drifting after her. “Good luck to you, Princess.”

     

                Walking alongside Kelly with their burdens slowing them, they went straight to the stables, where Kara and J’onn had saddled the horses and Alex was attaching her saddlebags filled with herbs, bandages, tinder and wood. They shared the burdens across their mounts, M’gann and Sam showing up in full gear shortly afterwards with a sulking Andrea in tow, still reluctant to come and lingering back as she watched them ready to leave. 

     

                As better as she had become at riding, Lena struggled to get in the saddle with the bulk of her armour making it more difficult, and J’onn boosted her up before he snagged the bridle of his horse and mounted up. Kara was fetching a saddle for Sam’s smoky horse, now that she was tagging along too, and the others restlessly waited as the women hurriedly tightened straps and fastened saddlebags and a bedroll. Five minutes later, they were all in the saddle, too many horses shifting in the confines of the stable as they were finally ready to leave.

     

                “If a message comes, send the raven on to the eastern outpost,” Kara instructed Andrea, who nodded and then seemed to melt into the shadows as she returned to the warmth of the hearth inside the halls.

     

                They filed out with Kara at the lead, setting a quick pace as night was ushered in. Lena wasn’t too keen on riding in the dark but she’d grown to trust the mare she frequently rode, knowing the horse would keep up with the others and place her hooves carefully, so she clung to the reins and moved with the motion of the trot as the cold stole over her. The wind was brutal and she snagged the hood of her cloak, pulling it up to try and block the worst of it from her face, but Lena could feel the burn in her throat with each breath of frigid sea air, her lungs aching and the ghostly shapes of the freshly falling snow Kara had foretold silently falling around them.

     

                No one spoke for well over an hour and Lena couldn’t feel her fingers or toes, although they’d been riding through spare woodland for the last couple of miles, which had lessened the wind somewhat as bare trunks and branches interrupted it. The moon was nearly full, offering some silvery light to guide them by, their keen eyesight making up for any other shortcomings, and Lena wondered how far they were going, how long it would be before she had to face the terror of battle. It was starting to dawn on her now that it was an awful decision to come along. Kara’s anger now seemed warranted, the stupidity of thinking she would be able to keep up with these Fae, who had been fighting their whole lives, now very apparent to Lena as she rode in the middle of their group, trying not to slow everyone down but knowing they kept her carefully contained in the middle so nothing ill befell her.

     

                It wasn’t lost on her that every minute of delay could mean a life lost for a Seelie somewhere, wherever the Unseelie were currently prowling, and she remained steadfast in her determination to not slow them down. Not even when Kara fell back somewhat, letting Alex guide them for a short turn as she queried her wife’s wellbeing and asked if she needed to rest. It had been more than two hours of riding by then and Lena obstinately refused, her lips a pale lavender and her jaw stubbornly set as she rode on. The miles seemed endless as they rode through the changing landscape, leaving behind the coastline and the wetlands as they cut a southerly path through the east of the Seelie lands.

     

                Riding for hours, the land eventually stretched out, low and rolling grassland interspersed with occasional thickets of forest as they rode through shallow streams, shallow glens, rising fells in the shadow of the mountain foothills and moorlands. Once they turned to the south, fingers of the forest reached towards the north and started to thicken, Lena feeling something give inside her at the smell of wet and rotting foliage, the earthy smell of bark and mud and moss so sweet that she was glad to have come along just for a ride through the trees. 

     

                Of course, that was not the reason for their trip and they led the horses onwards at a brisk walk, already tired from hours of riding, despite their stamina, coming across old crumbling stones amidst tall patches of grass, wildflowers and weeds and towering trees with deep roots as the trees still grew relatively far apart. Lena could still see the stars through the wide gaps in the canopy, aided by the bare branches of the deciduous trees, while a carpet of needles muffled the sounds of so many hooves as the coniferous trees filled the air with the smell of pine. 

     

                It wasn’t long before the weather took a turn, the snow they had left behind turning to heavy clouds that blotted out the stars and the moon and unleashed a torrent of bitingly cold rain. It was relentless as they all plotted onwards, drenched and stumbling over uneven ground in the gloom as the horses struggled to keep their footing as the rain turned the hard ground to mud. As the storm swelled, rain stinging their faces and beating harder upon them, Kara led them onwards along the path she had been setting, none of them stopping, not even as midnight came and went, until they finally reached the watchtower that had sent the raven. 

     

                It was a beautiful stone tower half built into a towering beech tree, ivy, moss and lichen obscuring some of the carved birds spiralling around the curved walls, and they were greeted by half a dozen arrows pointed at them from narrow windows and watch platforms built into the spreading branches of the beech. Kara was already talking, dismounting as she conversed in Fae, some of her words lost on Lena with the pattering of rain as it continued to fall, pinging off their armour and soaking them to the bone. 

     

                A familiar man appeared from the mouth of the arched doorway leading inside, tall and broad, wearing armour that matched his sister’s and a cloak that would have been the golden of an ash tree in summer. James was grave but he looked pleased to see them, hefting his giant axe as rain sluiced down his face. Kelly was off her horse within seconds, wrapping him in a hug, their foreheads touching in greeting before Kara hugged him as well, immediately turning to business.

     

                From what Lena could gather as she slithered off her horse, James had been manning the watchtower with a few of his warriors since leaving Krypton, and it was he who had sent the letter at the behest of a scout who had ridden north from an outpost to the south. Since the previous morning, when the raven had been sent off to Kara’s holdings, he had been keeping watch for a sight of any of the Unseelie heading north. Lucy was there as well, stepping outside and greeting her friends before ushering them inside, giving Lena a surprised look but gesturing her inside all the same.

     

                Inside, it was dry and instantly warmer, a fire built up on one side of the room, and Lena looked around with interest at the design of the place. Stone merged with wood in such a way that she wasn’t sure if it had been built into the tree or if the tree had been grown around the stone, a perfect blend of both, and Lena studied it as she shivered, water dripping off her as she strayed closer to the fire, tucked in the corner out of the way as urgent voices overlapped and the whispers of the Fae in the levels above them as they held their positions. Overlooked, Lena was grateful to have a moment to not be doing anything, quietly stamping her feet and breathing into her gloved hands as she tried to warm herself up.

     

                After some conversation, Alex, Sam and M’gann slipped out into the night again and Lena met Kara’s gaze from across the room. Her wife was tense as she crossed over to her, blue eyes dark in the firelight as she came to a stop before Lena, giving her an appraising look and then gesturing with a crook of her fingers for the moisture soaked into Lena’s hair, clothes and armour to withdraw. Suddenly dry, right down to her toes, Lena blinked in surprise at the oddity of the sensation, a laugh catching in her throat.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding distractedly, still wet herself, although it didn’t bother her, Kara rubbed her eyes and grimaced. “You rode well.”

     

                Surprised again, a small glow of pride flooded through Lena’s chest and she smiled unevenly, nodding in acknowledgement. Reaching out, Kara traced the filigree of Lena’s pauldron, her expression clouding momentarily - Lena didn’t have to ask to know it was at memories of her mother - and sighed as her hand slipped free.

     

                “Rest now. Scouts have been sent out to scour the forest; we will wait idly until word reaches us or they brazenly attack.”

     

                “Is it not dangerous for them to be out in the forest at night?” Lena asked, her voice hoarse.

     

                “Winter is the most dangerous time to be in the forest. We can only hope the starving animals find them before we do but I would not count on it. They must be desperate indeed for them to attack so deep into winter but Alex, Sam and M’gann are excellent hunters and trackers. I have faith they will return to us unharmed. Come, have a hot meal and then sleep.”

     

                The cold stole any appetite from her but Lena followed after Kara anyway, their saddlebags piled inside the doorway as Lucy helped Kelly tend to the horses, and Kara rummaged through them to find the tightly rolled blankets and food stores before making her way upstairs. She made her way up to the top level of the tower, the stone steps giving way to wooden ones as they continued up through the hollowed tree trunk to the platforms above, exposed to the elements as those on sentry duty kept careful watch in the rain.

     

                On the top level, there was a small fire with a pot bubbling away. Kara murmured polite conversation to the Airfolk warriors that lived in the nearby mountain halls that James had inherited from his father, replenishing their supplies with what they had brought and fetching stew and a cup of tea for Lena. Huddled in the far corner, a blanket draped over her shoulders as Kara stood restlessly at her side, Lena ate her food and sipped her tea, noticing that Kara didn’t get any for herself.

     

                Once she had finished, a little warmer for it, Lena’s empty bowl and cup were plucked from her hands and set aside before Kara made her way down a level. Unfurling the bedroll she’d had tucked under one arm, Kara gestured to it and Lena hesitated.

     

                “Do I keep the armour-”

     

                “Yes, keep it on. Keep your weapons within reach and your dagger at hand. I do not believe they will attack us here but for my own peace of mind.”

     

                Shedding her shield, helmet, bow, quiver and sword belt, Lena felt the ache in her back and shoulders now that the extra weight was gone. Sinking to the bedroll, she unsheathed her dagger and drew her cloak around her, tossing the blanket over her legs as well. Dropping to a knee at her side, Kara lifted the edge of the blanket and tucked her in, reaching out to brush away a few flecks of mud that had splattered Lena’s cheek.

     

                “Sleep well.”

     

                “You’re not sleeping?”

     

                “I will keep watch through the night so others may rest. Including you; you must be tired.”

     

                Lena was, feeling it in her bones. She would have been more comfortable without the bulk of her armour but she knew she would sleep regardless. “You’ll wake me if-”

     

                “I will,” Kara cut her off, her thumb continuing to tenderly stroke her cheek. “But sleep peacefully. No harm will come to you while I stand guard. You have my word.”

     

                She said the latter part in Fae and Lena felt at ease as the truth to Kara’s words washed over her, a strange sensation to wholeheartedly believe someone because they said so. It didn’t come naturally to her to trust but she trusted Kara and settled down, feeling her wife’s hand against her cheek for a moment longer before Kara stood and moved to one of the arrow-slit windows looking into the dark forest beyond. 

     

                Eyes heavy, Lena fell asleep quickly, despite the cold and the noisy patter of rain, her hand curled around the hilt of her dagger as the hours passed by. She didn’t stir at the low murmurs of voices, at the sound of footsteps moving up and down the winding staircases, the whicker of horses grazing as they dispersed through the trees, and her sleep became more peaceful when the rain stopped and snow silently started to fall, the flakes thickening to a flurry as the forest was blanketed in a ghostly white. 

     

                Waking to grey light streaming through the window, Lena was stiff and exhausted as she lifted her cheek from her arm, the pattern of her vambrace embossed on her cheek as she tried to blink the heaviness from her eyes. Moving slowly, a yawn crumpled her face as she sat up, she rubbed her eyes and then blinked owlishly, catching sight of Sam sitting on the floor nearby, her back to the stone wall as she watched Lena intensely.

     

                “Oh. You’re back.”

     

                “For some time now.”

     

                Looking around, Lena smoothed a hand over her braided hair, noting the obvious absence of her wife. “Where’s Kara?”

     

                “She is scouting.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “They are breaking their fast downstairs. If you are finished sleeping, I will take my turn now.”

     

                Realising that Sam had taken over Kara’s guard upon her return, instead of seeking her own rest, Lena quickly scrambled to her feet, almost overbalancing as she stooped to pick up her assortment of armour and weapons, strapping them all back on as quickly as she could. Stepping aside, she gestured to her rumpled blanket and smiled apologetically.

     

                “You can sleep here.”

     

                “That is most generous of you,” Sam said with a warm smile, climbing to her feet.

     

                Despite their long hours spent sparring together, Lena was still unable to shake that feeling of unease at times, knowing there was another personality lurking inside her guard’s head. One that would gladly threaten her life at the command of her mother. Still, since she had been in the Seelie Court, whatever vows split her loyalty between both Courts seemed to have held to her loyalty to Kara and her friends, and Lena was somewhat glad to have someone watch her back, even if she half expected the knife to come from her guard at times. She should have known that Sam was above reproach when in the Seelie Court though, because Kara wouldn’t have left Lena alone in her protection if she ever thought she was a threat.

     

                Plodding downstairs, Lena felt the wind as soon as she reached the ground floor, the open archway allowing it to sweep inside with a flurry of fresh snow. She paused at the sight of so much white beyond and then found Alex and M’gann near the fire, hastening her pace as she crossed over to them. Extending her hands over the fire, she looked to her sister-in-law.

     

                “Morning.”

     

                “Ah, you are awake. Here, I imagine you are as cold as I in this miserable weather,” Alex grumbled, picking up her empty bowl and filling it with hot porridge for Lena, who took it gratefully.

     

                “You complain too much,” M’gann said with a quick smile, standing a little further from the fire than the other two women. “The air is merely brisk. You should spend more time up north.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex bickered good-naturedly with M’gann as Lena wolfed down her breakfast and was then handed a cup of tea once she had finished eating. Antsy as her eyes kept glancing to the open doorway, Lena sipped her tea as she stared out into the barren stretch of forest, the snow falling and no sign of her wife returning.

     

                “You needn’t worry,” Alex said as she finished off her latest cup of tea, catching Lena’s attention as she cast her a quick look. “She hasn’t been gone long. She will likely not be back for hours yet.”

     

                “How is that a cause for me not to worry?” Lena grumbled as her expression clouded.

     

                Letting out a quiet laugh, Alex grinned, a teasing edge to her smile as her brown eyes shone with amusement. “Do you care for her, Princess?”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes, the tips of her already pink ears warming as she ground her teeth. “Why would that be funny to you?”

     

                “Well, I was there on your wedding day, and for your subsequent insistence that you be returned to your home, that you did not wish to be married off to my dear sister. It would be most amusing to me now if you had come to care for her after your time of tribulation, your stubborn determination to despise it here, no matter the effort spent trying to enarmour you to our life, our culture.”

     

                “I’m glad it amuses you.”

     

                “Oh, don’t be sour about it. I, for one, am glad that the two of you seem to be getting along. I could not understand your dislike of her before; my sister is a spot of sunshine even in the bleakest winter. Once you get to know her that is. I would be surprised if you had not come to care for her after the long months you have spent together.”

     

                Fixing Alex with a blank look, Lena felt irritation nettle her but didn’t show it. “I didn’t say I care for her. Keep your assumptions to yourself.” 

     

                Turning, she walked to the doorway and stepped outside, resolved to enjoy the rest of her tea in the snow as she felt a twinge of anxiety. Staring at the bare branches and ancient trunks, Lena’s breath came out in plumes of white as she waited, slowly pacing as it grew too cold for her to remain rooted to the spot, snow sticking to her armour and the moisture in the air frosting over the pieces as her cheeks reddened and her lips further chapped. It was midmorning and Lena didn’t stop her pacing until noon.

     

                At the sound of hoofbeats thundering through the forest, somewhat muffled thanks to the foliage and fresh snow blanketing the earth, Lena’s stomach jolted and her heartbeat picked up. Suddenly, she wasn’t alone, James and Alex standing outside with her, the latter grabbing a fistful of Lena’s cloak and dragging her backwards, a long hunting knife in her other hand as she tried to listen. Softly whistling the trill of a robin, Alex cocked her head and relaxed somewhat at the faint whistle drifting towards them.

     

                A minute later, a dappled grey mare burst appeared, Kara, ducking below a long branch as she wove between the trees on horseback, coming to a quick stop in front of them. Her cheeks were red and she had her helmet under her arm, a severe expression on her face as her blue eyes shone with anger.

     

                “I have found their tracks along the riverbed. They crossed back into Unseelie territory hours before; there was snow starting to settle in their footsteps. They do not have horses.”

     

                “Then we must look to the river to track them,” Alex declared.

     

                “What if- what if they’re not coming back?” Lena asked. “I mean … could it just be a raid? Did they take food at the outpost?”

     

                “They burned it down. They did not come to raid but to destroy.”

     

                Kara looked at Lena as Alex responded, her stare unwaveringly intense as she swallowed. “You will stay.”

     

                “What? But I-”

     

                “Do you wish to track them along the riverbed? Do you remember how wide it is? How deep? Last time you fell in. We cannot have cause to delay this time - more is at risk than just our lives. Hostiles on my land will not be suffered and I cannot manage your fear of the water while I track Unseelie through the waterways of the north. I am not asking you to stay out of spite but out of care for you. I do not wish you to be frightened.”

     

                Voice softening the more she went on, Lena stumbling towards her horse, reined in as she looked up at her wife with a pleading look on her face, Kara looked tired and resigned, faint shadows beneath her eyes as she sat atop her horse. As her voice grew softer, wearier, the others hurried about, making arrangements, and Lena clung to a fistful of Kara’s cloak as she stubbornly set her jaw.

     

                “Take me with you. I won’t slow you down, I won’t be a burden, I-”

     

                “You are not a burden. You are just … unseasoned.”

     

                “If you leave me behind, I will saddle my horse and follow you, and I will wake the entire forest while I call for you to wait for me, and when I catch up to you, I will not be turned away, no matter how much you beg me to. Not even if you tie me to my horse and send her away, not even if you tie me to a tree to wait for you to come back for me.”

     

                Kara let out a huff of surprised laughter, her eyes creasing at the corners as she smiled crookedly. “You are as stubborn as a rock.”

     

                “I mean it,” Lena said in Fae, her voice wavering slightly with unbridled frustration. “You say I’m unseasoned, that I haven’t learned your ways enough, that I haven’t pulled my weight. How can I if I’m not given the chance?”

     

                Silent for a moment, Kara pursed her lips and sat a little straighter in her saddle before reaching down to pry Lena’s fingers from her cloak. “Off with you then. Saddle your horse and be ready when the rest of us are, or we shall leave without you. And if you fall into the river, you had better swim or grow gills.”

     

                Already turning away, a flicker of triumph lending her more determination than she really wanted, knowing the dangers and the possible outcome, knowing the relentless journey and the toll it would take on her body - and that was without accounting for having to fight as well - Lena wound through the trees to find her horse. She found the mare and led her back to the tower with gentle coaxing and found her saddle amidst the neat piles stacked inside. Trying to be quick, she struggled to throw the saddle across the horse’s back and fumbled with the straps and buckles as everyone else mounted up and started to ride off, James heading east with J’onn, M’gann and Sam in tow, while the rest of his warriors went south and two stayed behind as guards. Kara shifted restlessly in the saddle and Alex hurried around, talking aloud.

     

                “Sorry, sister, I know I have packed it somewhere. It’s my best knife, as you know. I couldn’t abide going into battle without it.”

     

                “You may stop your feigned searching; she has fastened the front cinch,” Kara sighed.

     

                Alex glanced over at Lena and smiled impishly, “ah, good. Just in time; I have found my knife.”

     

                “Help her mount; we must go.”

     

                Giving Lena a quick boost, winking at the murmured thanks for stalling, Alex mounted up and set off with her sister, while Lena quickly followed. Anxious about being left behind, she rode on Kara’s flank, unwilling to fall back, even as she already felt the saddle soreness of a long ride ahead of her. They quickly caught up with the others and there was a subtle reshuffling of their order, Kara at the rear with Alex, penning Lena in with the middle of their party as James led them onwards. 

     

                An hour into their ride they reached the river, the banks iced over, snow heaped on either side as the river moved slowly, thin sheets of ice breaking free of the shallows and floating downstream. It was almost peaceful but they didn’t have time to stop and enjoy the scenery, pummeling the hard earth into mud as snow and dirt were churned together by so many hooves pounding along the winding path of the river. 

     

                They saw no other tracks as they rode, not for hours, the light already starting to fail, until James spotted the signs of footsteps in that morning’s snow, pointing westwards, a sure sign someone - or multiple someones - had crossed from the Unseelie Court. Their path turned away from the northern route they had been taking and they had to pick their way carefully over the uneven ground, the trees giving way to the open, undulating grassland as the stretch of deep blue sky spread out around them, ushering in dusk.

     

                The wind was brisk and they only stopped once, momentarily to drink some water and wolf down bread and cheese with it, before donning their helmets, stringing bows and loosening swords in their sheaths. The atmosphere was tense and Lena strung her bow with a lump in her throat, unsure of herself as she wondered whether it would even be any use to try and shoot it, but she strung it anyway and held it across her lap as she gripped the reins and looked ahead, her peripheral vision somewhat blocked by the helmet, making her a little uneasy as they set off again.

     

                Her unease only grew as they carried on, the tracks long behind them with no new signs as they cut a north-westerly path, crunching frosted grass under their horses’ hooves as the miles slipped by. It was the dark of full night now, although it couldn’t have been that late at all, not yet a full day passing since they’d left Kara’s home in pursuit of Unseelie, and Lena felt numb as she followed on the heels of Sam in front of her, keeping her eyes on the unchanging landscape of rolling hills interspersed with shrubbery and thickets. It felt almost peaceful, the night silent, save for the wind, and she wondered at what point they would give in and rest or turn back.

     

                The sky was veiled with clouds, blotting out the stars and the moon, and Lena could feel the night growing colder as what little warmth the sun had instilled upon the day vanished quickly. She just hoped the rain would hold off a little while longer, but her wish was unfortunately not heeded, a drizzle quickly turning to a downpour as they found themselves slowly plodding down the gently sloping sides of a glen. It was vaguely familiar to Lena, or the land all looked the same to her, but she was sure they’d ridden through this one the night before, which made her worry about how far they were from Krypton.

     

                Their quarry wasn’t as close to Kara’s lands as she’d briefly considered though, because they hadn’t quite made it through the sparsely forested glen when the sight of a horse came streaking towards them from the northern mouth of the glen. Lena’s stomach jolted as she reined her mare in, their party of eight coming to a stop as weapons were readied, eyes scanning their surroundings for more attackers, and Lena reached behind her, stroking the fletching of an arrow as her horse shifted beneath her, wondering whether now was the time to knock and draw.

     

                She decided against it, on account of only one horse appearing before them, knowing one of the others would have the rider unseated before she could fit the arrow to her bowstring. It didn’t matter anyway, Alex urging her horse forward a moment later as she stood in the stirrups, her keen eyes picking up the familiar glint of her wife’s armour.

     

                “Hold! Hold, it’s Kelly!” she called out, a panicked edge to her shout as she kicked her horse into motion, galloping towards her, fearing her wife was injured.

     

                The rest of them spurred their mounts onwards as well, relief cutting through the tension as they’d feared the worst, but their relief was short-lived. As the distance between their party and Kelly shrank, the other woman’s shouts became audible as she urged the wind to carry her words to them.

     

                “They’re coming!”

     

                Lena’s blood ran cold and she went rigid on her saddle, jostled uncomfortably as her mare carried on. Fingers tightly curled around her bow, Lena shallowly breathed as her eyes nervously darted around, and then made out the shadows of figures on foot running through the long grass as they descended through the shallow valley, weapons glinting. They weren’t so far away, swift on foot, even if their opponents were faster on their tired horses, but Lena quickly counted the shadows and concluded with a nauseous stab of fear that they were greatly outnumbered. Whoever had determined a score had been wrong, almost double that number creeping towards them, in comparison to the nine of them that their party now made.

     

                Kara fell back a moment, hefting her trident in hand as she cast Lena a quick glance. “Remember what I told you. Stay safe.”

     

                Before Lena could formulate a response, her wife dug her heels into her horse’s flank and surged forward, leaving Lena behind as she surpassed the rest of the group and raised her trident. Lena was still charging forward as well, purely by her mare’s instinct to follow the others, and she watched as Kara drew her arm back and launched her trident thirty feet, the power behind her throw sending it swiftly into the armoured chest of the nearest Fae. They buckled beneath the force of the impact and Lena watched their body topple as Kara quickly crossed the remainder of the ground separating her from the corpse and jerked her trident free.

     

                Then the other eight of their party were on the invaders, and Lena realised that she was on the fringe of the fray as well, the sound of clashing metal and shouts overwhelming as her horse, used to warfare, forged onwards. Trying to rein in the mare as she reached for an arrow, Lena shifted in the saddle, her breaths shallow and quick as tried to make herself useful. Drawing back the bowstring, Lena’s left arm moved aimlessly as she tried to hold it, trying to sight a target, but everyone was moving too fast and it was so dark. 

     

                In the end, she shot at a dark figure in the distance that she thought was an enemy, unsure whether her arrow met its target or not, and reached for another arrow. As the fight unfolded, the dark was illuminated with sudden flames, smoke choking the air, which was then pushed around by whoever seized the currents at that time, and Lena was somewhat desperate as she loosed her arrows, wishing she had better control over the earth, knowing there was no body of water, save for the rain falling around them, for Kara to use her gifts. She might have been more useful if she’d been better trained, as opposed to keeping flowers alive for longer than they should have been.

     

                As the fray dissolved into chaos, figures in gold masks with bloody handprints pressed across them and their mismatching armour surrounding them, the realisation that these were Lex’s band of rogues and not an organised Unseelie attack dawning on the Seelie, Lena suddenly found herself within the battle instead of lingering back. At the sight of a spear thrusting towards her, she lurched sideways, avoiding the point, and grabbed it in her right hand. Trying to jerk it out of the hands of her attacker, Lena found herself dragged from her saddle instead, landing in a heavy heap on the floor as she was unhorsed.

     

                There was a heavy blow to the side of her helmet then, as she knelt in the grass and dirt, the taste of blood in her mouth as her ears rang and head ached, and she dropped her bow to the ground, pulling her helmet off. Sweat-dampened hair sticking to her cheeks and hairline, Lena breathed raggedly as she looked around, wild-eyed, and then felt a blow to her left shoulder. Fortunately, her armour muted the force of it and she turned sideways, yanking her dagger free as she turned around and rammed it into the stomach of the man with the spear. 

     

                Freezing as surprise slammed into her, Lena’s mouth parted as her eyes widened, blood spilling over her mailed gloves as she removed the dagger in a daze. The man’s pale eyes widened as well behind the gold mask, his hands moving to the gap between his cuirass and tassets, trying to stifle the blood. Mouth soundlessly opening and closing, Lena was still on her knees as she looked at him with panic, and then hot blood flecked her face as a hunting knife lashed out over her head, drawing a gash across the man’s throat. 

     

                Finding herself hauled to her feet, trying to make her legs bear her weight, Lena blinked in surprise as she stared at Alex. Her sister-in-law was splattered with blood as well, her brown eyes alight in the flames wreathing her shoulders, and Alex reached out to briefly cup Lena’s face in a gloved hand before she turned and twirled her long knife in hand. Unsure whether she was supposed to follow after Alex, relying on her kin to protect her, or heed Kara’s advice she’d promised to follow and flee to cover, Lena held her dagger in a tight fist as she helplessly looked around, blood on her lips as she felt the pain of her fall. 

     

                Shifting her dagger to her left hand, Lena jerked her sword free, moving in a circle as she looked about before she caught the glint of a blade coming towards her. Jerking back, narrowly avoiding having her throat cut, Lena batted it aside and quickly backed up, a tall woman bearing down on her, mask slipped free to reveal a snarling face as she hacked at Lena again, who managed to block that one as well, wishing she’d had time to strap her shield to her arm so she could at least cower behind it. Instead, she was forced to keep backing up, until she slipped on a patch of icy grass and went down heavily, winded as she lay on her back, gasping for air and trying to gain enough momentum to roll onto her stomach. 

     

                Instead, Lena watched the woman spin her sword in hand and then drive it down into the chainmail in the gap below Lena’s chest plate and tassets, issuing her the same injury she’d just inflicted on the Fae man. Except, Lena had a coat of mail on beneath her armour and that softened the blow a bit, but the rings weren’t able to fully fend off the downwards thrust of the woman’s sword as it pierced through the mail, through the padded gambeson beneath and into Lena’s hip. Hissing with pain, Lena dropped her sword and grabbed the woman’s blade in a gloved hand, holding it fast as she struck fast with her left hand, plunging the dagger into the soft flesh of the woman’s thigh, parting leather, skin and muscle as she slit the femoral artery and wrenched the blade in the wound to seal the kill.

     

                The woman’s leg buckled beneath her weight and she fell to a knee, her hand slipping from the pommel of her sword as it fell aside, and she half fell on top of Lena, reaching out to grab her face in her hand. Feeling the woman’s grasp, strong enough to bruise, on her chin, Lena struggled beneath her, managing to push the woman’s head aside, near enough to the gleaming edge of the blade beside them so that when Lena grabbed a fistful of the woman’s shorn hair, barely a few inches long and hard to keep ahold of, she was able to pick up the sword and smash her head against it, the metal cutting into her cheek and jaw, and then at a different angle, her throat. 

     

                Despite the noise of the fighting, Lena could still hear the choked surprise of the woman as she died, not as quickly as Lena hoped, blood spilling over Lena’s breastplate, working itself into the grooves of the engraves and filigree motifs. Managing to push the woman off her, Lena tossed the sword aside and grabbed her weapons, the pain in her left side sharp and hot and terrifying, black eating the edges of her vision as she managed to get onto all fours, staggering back to her feet again.

     

                This was different to any death and violence she’d been exposed to before, mostly because she was in armour, fighting alongside the others, instead of hiding or relying on their protection. That wasn’t to say that the others weren’t fighting their hardest to kill the Rogues as quickly as possible, handling the brunt of them as they expected Lena to still be on horseback - save for Alex, who had already saved her once - but caught in the thick of it, the smell of blood, sweating in all of her layers, despite the cold, Lena felt sick. It wasn’t what she’d expected, and she couldn’t quite compute that she’d already killed two people - definitely one, and a hand in the other at the very least - stumbling onwards, her sword and dagger in hand, the edge of one stained black in the darkness, luck seemingly on her side as she evaded death.

     

                She caught sight of James fighting from horseback with his heavy axe, hewing two in rapid succession, Kelly on horseback at Alex’s side as she blasted a masked figure backwards with a gust of air and then sent two arrows into the man’s chest and neck, Sam surrounded by an inferno of fire as she fought with two swords, hacking off an arm and then decapitating the woman, M’gann’s horse rearing and kicking a man in the chest as the woman dealt with another. They all moved so quickly that Lena felt out of her depth, picking her way over corpses, trying to stay out of the way, afraid she might be mistaken for one of their enemies as she found herself on foot.

     

                And she was doing well as well, the pain in her side white hot, hot blood on her skin at odds with the biting wind, but nevertheless still on her feet and still alive, until she lurched, an arrow sprouting from the side of her leg. She half-turned, looking down at it, puzzled, before she looked up and saw the archer removing an arrow from their quiver and fitting it to the bowstring. 

     

                Panic shot through Lena as she sank to a crouch, dropping her sword as her body processed it all quicker than she consciously could. The leather strap of the shield crossing her chest was in her hand and she slashed her dagger across it to sever it, the shield falling off her back as she reached behind her and dragged it in front of her body, catching sight of the arrowhead glinting in the firelight right as the arched finished drawing the bowstring back.

     

                The arrow thudded into the shield with so much force that it punctured the steel. Eyes screwed shut, Lena felt the force of the impact, jarring her locked elbows as she gripped the edges of the shield tightly. Opening her eyes, she found the tip of the arrow an inch from her left cheek, letting out a ragged breath as she scrambled backwards, pulling up damp grass as she tried to back away, seeking shelter in the shrubbery as the thorns scraped against her armour.

     

                It was dark and she was on the fringes of the fight, overlooked and surrounded by bodies, and she didn’t have to try and defend herself as she saw someone - she thought it might have been Kara’s trident, or perhaps J’onn’s spear - impale the archer and move on to the dwindling numbers of the remaining Rogues. Exhausted, the arrow shaft sticking out of her leg as her thigh went numb, Lena didn’t think she’d be able to stand, holding the shield over herself as she hid behind it.

     

                She didn’t know how long the fight lasted, everything happening so quickly, her multitude of injuries sustained in a mere handful of minutes, but the night suddenly felt quiet as the shouting died and a few last sounds of clashing metal filled the air. They died off quickly and Lena listened to the moans of the injured, dying slowly, and the snuffling of the horses as they lingered about, some still retaining their riders. 

     

                Reluctant to lower her shield, afraid that there might be someone nearby and not wanting to give up what little protection she had, only her dagger left to defend herself with, Lena stayed where she was. The lifeless corpse of a woman with her head caved in, golden mask crumpled from the blow, lay to her right, roots wrapping around the woman’s wrists as if she’d been calling for the earth to shroud her, and Lena was hit by the hot, cloying smell of blood and brain matter. The smell caught at the back of her throat and she had to close her eyes to stop herself from looking, unsure if it was safe to drop the shield until the unmistakable sound of her wife’s voice cut through the quiet of the wind ruffling the grass

     

                “Lena? Lena!” Kara’s hoarse shout grew nearer as she removed her helmet, frantically looking around. “Where is she? Lena?”

     

                There was a desperate edge to Kara’s voice and Lena had to force her stiff limbs to move, shield dropping from her hands as she lurched unsteadily to her feet. Taking a staggering step forward, her right leg dragging, Lena felt a dizzying wave of tiredness slam into her all of a sudden, her hands hanging limply at her sides, dagger still clutched tightly in one fist, as she stepped forward.

     

                “I’m here,” she wearily replied, utterly spent, her dark braid coming undone, blood, mud and grass on her face as she moved unsteadily on her feet.

     

                The ragged sound of relief that escaped Kara wasn’t lost on anyone else, trident carelessly tossed aside as she crossed the gap to her wife in four long strides. Catching her wife in a crushing hug, cupping the back of her head in one hand, bloodied sword still in her grasp as she encircled her waist with the other, Kara closed her eyes and felt a knot loosen in her chest. 

     

                For Lena’s part, she sank into Kara’s arms with the shocking realisation of how badly she was trembling, how cold she was, oblivious to it all until she had felt the warmth and strength of her wife’s embrace. Fearing her leg was about to give out beneath her, Lena sagged into Kara, hugging her tightly as she buried her face in her wife’s neck, smelling the sand and seawater of the coast beneath the blood, sweat and steel, a comfort as the rain pelted them.

     

                Kara’s fingertips pressed against Lena’s scalp as if she was trying her hardest to hold her closer, and her voice was wavering and low as she spoke. “Are you hurt?”

     

                “A little,” Lena sniffed, the adrenaline waning as she felt the bright spots of pain.

     

                Not only her leg and her side, but a pounding headache, the ache of her jaw, the pain in her left shoulder from the spear that had found the gap between chest plate and pauldrons but failed to penetrate the chainmail. There would be a multitude of other bruises as well, falling from her horse, scrabbling about on the ground, but Lena couldn’t feel those as the fiercer pains took priority of her awareness.

     

                “Show me where.”

     

                Pulling back quickly, Kara’s eyes roamed Lena’s face, tracing her jaw with the shadow of its bruises, her touch gentle as she wiped away the rain that shone like tears on Lena’s cheeks. Swallowing past the thickness in her throat, Lena stared down at her shaking hands, blood dripping from them as the rain washed the red away, her chin wobbling as she put all of her weight on her left leg.

     

                “My leg,” she whispered, angling it to show Kara the arrow sticking out of the back of her thigh, just below the knee. 

     

                Sinking to her knees in the churned-up ground, Kara carefully cradled Lena’s leg in her hands, taking in the angle of the arrow, where it had pierced the skin between the tassets and mail covering Lena’s thigh and the greaves covering her shin. Looking up at Lena, rain running through the blood coating her face, her blue eyes were full of guilt and her skin pale beneath the grime as she moved one hand to the shaft of the arrow.

     

                “It’s not so bad,” she murmured in reassurance. “Straight through the muscle, no bones or arteries. Hold steady.”

     

                Opening her mouth to object as she anticipated Kara yanking the arrow free, Lena couldn’t even formulate a sound as she braced herself against her wife’s shoulder and felt the arrow twinge slightly in the wound as Kara snapped the fletched end of the shaft off. Her vision dimmed momentarily but at least she wasn’t in danger of knocking the arrow against anything, only a couple of inches of wood sticking out of her leg now.

     

                Tossing aside the shaft, Kara’s eyes found the blood at Lena’s hip, her hands following a path up to the patch of rent mail, bleeding slowly, not an immediate risk to Lena’s life but packed with the torn hem of Kara’s tunic all the same, and she climbed to her feet, asking after anything else, her hands running over her armour, eyes roaming over her body, anxious to confirm that Lena was okay. She wasn’t, of course, injured and overwhelmed by it all, but Lena was alive and her injuries weren’t severe, which was better than Kara could have hoped for as everyone else nursed their own injuries. 

     

                James had two arrows sticking out of him, Lucy was bleeding from a head wound, Alex had a deep gash across her arm, Kelly and Sam were picking long thorns out of their limbs, J’onn’s armour had been melted, burning through to his skin and M’gann had suffered a fall from her horse. Kara seemed fine to Lena, but even she was nursing injuries and masking them well as she focused on her wife. It was a relief to Lena’s ego that none of them had come out of it unscathed, as outnumbered as they’d been, and she didn’t dwell on the fact that they’d all been in the thick of the fighting, while she’d been on the edges of it and had still wound up injured the most. 

     

                As Kelly started to check on everyone’s injuries, Alex prowled amidst the dead or dying with Sam, doling out mercy whenever they came across someone clinging to life. They were swift to end the suffering but Lena still had to look away from it, so many lifeless forms dotting the slopes of the glen, and she let Kara break her from her stunned stupor, her gentle coaxing making Lena blink herself back to what she was saying.

     

                She was trying to guide Lena to her grey mare, lifting her onto the saddle and turning to face her friends. “I must ride for Krypton.”

     

                “Go,” Alex ushered her. “Tend to her; we will see to the dead.”

     

                “These traitors do not belong to either Court - burn them.”

     

                Nodding, Alex sank to a crouch and straightened out a body before dragging another one next to them, the others all doing their part as they arranged the dead and recovered their lost weapons, leading the horses away to graze while they managed the rest. Kara climbed into the saddle behind Lena and bracketed her with her thighs and arms as she gripped her reins and clicked the horse into motion.

     

                “The sword, my bow, I- your mom’s shield-”

     

                “They will bring everything back,” Kara softly interrupted, letting go of the reins with one hand to give Lena’s fingers a quick squeeze. “Rest now. We are closer to home than I thought we would track them but it will be a long ride yet.”

     

                Lena felt the warmth of Kara’s breath against her hair, thought she felt the brush of her lips, although she was so exhausted that she might have been imagining it. Either way, she felt safe, sinking back against her wife as she tried to burrow into her warmth, unattainable with their armour between them, and leaned her head against Kara’s shoulder, her body limp as she moved with the motions of the horse. 

     

                It continued to rain but Lena was too tired to care, her cheek pressed against Kara’s pauldron, the shape of scales marking her cheek as she fell asleep, her wife managing to raise her hood without waking her, trying to cover her with their cloaks as well. Through the darkness of night, Kara led them through familiar land, retracing the path they’d taken only the night before, and despite the earlier chaos, it was quiet and peaceful, the rain pattering off leaves and iced-over puddles, owls hooting and smaller animals rustling about in the dark of the cold winter night. Tired and in pain, Kara rode onwards with a fiercely protective grip on her wife, heedless of anything else.

     

                Midnight had long since passed by the time the land became familiarly homely, the sound of the waves audible over the wind and rain as the horse wearily plodded along the limestone cliffside. Kara had spent many days thundering across this stretch of land and felt relief flood through her to be so close to home, an hour or two at best, depending on how fast her flagging horse could manage the trip. The sense of urgency diminished and as much as Lena leaned back against Kara, Kara leaned into her as she breathed in the fresh grass smell of her, intoxicating beneath the blood, sweat and steel, tired as she rested her cheek against Lena’s back and kept them both in the saddle.

     

                When the low limestone building became visible in the distance, a mere shadow against the darkness, Kara urged the horse into a brisk trot for the last few miles. Trotting right into the stables, her mare came to a stop and Kara was out of the saddle in an instant, murmuring to the horse as she carefully lifted Lena down, waking her wife. Blinking slowly, looking pale in the dark, Lena put all of her weight on her left leg as she looked around, the smell of hay, manure and damp stone a dead giveaway that they were back in the stables.

     

                “Can you walk?” Kara rasped.

     

                Trying to put her weight on her injured leg, Lena let out a whimper as it buckled slightly. Sparing her the pain of trying to limp down two flights of stairs, Kara scooped her up, leaving Lena lightheaded for a moment, and swept through the dark archway. She was on the middle floor when the sound of footsteps approached, Andrea materialising in the dark with a dagger in hand, dark hair unbound and flames blooming in her palm.

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Kara’s eyes fell on the flame and she jerked her head. “Follow me.”

     

                Hesitating a moment, Andrea quashed the fire and padded after her. Carrying her wife down to the room where she’d left the tub before the fireplace, now empty of water, Kara carefully set her down on the floor and gestured to the chopped logs stacked neatly in a basket on a raised plinth.

     

                “A fire, please.”

     

                Andrea silently reached for a log and Kara crossed to the bathing room, dragging a stream of water out of the sea and directing it into the small room and the tub. Lena shivered on the floor, soaked to the bone as her teeth chattered, and Kara asked Andrea to heat the water before she knelt at her wife’s side, removing her gloves and brushing dark hair out of her face.

     

                “Let’s get you cleaned up.”

     

                Legs stretched before her, bracing herself on her hands as she lay sprawled on the floor, Lena let Kara start undoing the buckles and clasps of her armour. Her cloak was undone, the soaked wool heavily pooling on the floor, then the vambraces were set aside, the breastplate undone, the pauldrons, tassets, greaves, boots, then the chainmail, gambeson, shirt and leggings. Andrea left once the bath was steaming and Kara lifted Lena to her feet at the side of the tub, finishing off undressing her and helping her step into the scalding tub.

     

                Kara’s hands were warm on Lena’s clammy skin, a searing heat that was impossible to ignore as Lena’s heartbeat stumbled, and Lena felt cold when her touch was gone, missing it, even though she wasn’t in the frame of mind to process that. She was too focused on gripping the high sides of the tub and lowering herself in, her chest rising and falling quickly as she breathed rapidly, anticipating the agony of salt in her wounds. Her leg was submerged first, hissing at the pain as she gritted her teeth, then her hip, an even worse pain as Lena had to clamp her mouth shut to swallow the whimper, her vision going black for a moment.

     

                A warm hand pressed against her spine, trying to comfort her as her whole body went tense, the tendons in her neck and shoulders taut as she tried to adjust to the pain. Kara undid Lena’s braid and ran her fingers through her dark tresses, murmuring to her as she took in the multitude of bruises scattered across Lena’s back, a particularly nasty one just below her armpit, in the muscle of her shoulder, where the spear had failed to pierce the mail but had been thrust with enough force for the skin to mottle black and purple.

     

                Slowly but surely, Lena’s tense muscles unwound, the heat of the steaming water working into her bones, easing some of her aches and pains as the saltwater sting ebbed to a smouldering throb. The fire helped as well, warming the room and casting a rosy glow over the chamber, and she closed her eyes, basking in the feeling of being warm, if not yet dry. She knew she would have to move soon, wash and dry off, but she couldn’t bring herself to move as the water slowly clouded, pink and grey as blood, sweat and dirt mingled.

     

                After ten minutes of letting her silently soak, Kara picked up the cloth that Andrea had brought in - a stack of towels, dry clothes, soap and hot water silently set down on the floor before she vanished, presumably back to bed - and dunked it in the water. Carefully, she wiped the back of Lena’s neck and across her good shoulder, slowly going through the motions of washing her wife’s back, working soap into the cloth as she took her time, being gentle around the bruises, then working along her arm, then the other. 

     

                Kneeling at her side, facing her now, Kara reached out, metal softling clinking, and cupped Lena’s chin in her hand. Lips stained with dried blood, eyes ringed with dark circles and a shadowed look in her gaze as their eyes locked, Lena swallowed thickly.

     

                “I killed someone. Maybe two,” she whispered.

     

                Pausing, Kara dunked the cloth into the water and then started to wipe the blood from Lena’s cheek, taking a moment to respond. “You must have fought well.”

     

                A strangled laugh didn’t quite make it past Lena’s lips and her face furrowed as she started to cry. Softly shushing her, Kara wiped the tears away with the blood and dirt and Lena closed her eyes, bottom lip wobbling as she tried to compose herself.

     

                “I tried to stay on the horse like you told me to. They dragged me off, I-”

     

                “It’s okay. You did well, Lena. You should be proud of your courage - I am.”

     

                Those weren’t words Lena had ever heard and that only made the urge to cry even harder to stifle, letting out a pent-up breath as she hunched over. The only person she’d ever had to be proud of her had been herself, and it was a tender thing to hear it come from the mouth of someone who had spent months caring for her more than anyone else had since her mother had died. Putting her head in her hand, Lena felt the brush of the cloth against her other cheek as Kara continued to bathe her, and leaned into the touch as she craved the contact. She was injured and vulnerable and she might have been out of her depth but she had her wife.

     

                They didn’t speak again as Kara continued to wash her, then her hair, working grass and dirt free as her fingers massaged Lena’s scalp, pleasant and calming as Lena felt her eyelids grow heavy. As afraid as she was of the water, she thought she could easily slip down into the bath and drown a content woman, so long as Kara continued to wash her hair, the warmth of the water making her sleepy. 

     

                Eventually, she had to get out though, the soap and salt rinsed out of her hair with the warm jug of water, a towel around her shivering form as she stood unsteadily and was enveloped by her wife’s embrace as she wrapped it around her. Setting her down in front of the fire, Kara told her to stay right there as she vanished, returning minutes later with all manner of healing paraphernalia and more saltwater in a basin. Spreading everything out on the stone floor, wet as the water dripped off Lena as she dried in front of the fire, Kara made a quick judgement and helped adjust the towel to bare her wife’s hip so she could assess the stab wound.

     

                It was deep, a little more than an inch, forced through the mail and layers to impale her on the sword’s point, and perhaps two inches wide, bleeding slowly but steadily for hours now, even though Kara had packed the wound as best as she could. It needed stitches and she gave Lena a pained look, pressing a small bladder of brandy into her wife’s hand and bidding her to drink it as she readied a little bone hook to sew the wound closed. Firstly, Kara had to clean the wound out though, using saltwater for that as Lena bit down on her tongue to keep herself from crying out, the pain blinding as she went rigid on the floor, held in place by her wife.
