                Once it had been cleaned and Lena was sufficiently numbed by the brandy, or as much as she could hope, Kara checked with her to see if she was ready before she worked the point of the hook through one side of Lena’s wound. It was nauseatingly painful and Lena lay back flat against the stone floor, teeth gritted as she covered her face with a hand, covering her tears as she tried not to move. It didn’t matter how much she’d had to drink, she could still feel it, the pain of it not something she’d get used to no matter how many times she’d been stitched up.

     

                Fortunately for her, Kara worked quickly, so many years of working with hooks and fishing line, of her mother’s healing lessons, making her nimble fingers swiftly manage the task. Then came her leg though, Kara pressing down Lena’s right shoulder to pin her as she reached down to the few inches of the arrow shaft left sticking out of Lena’s right leg and yanked it free in one quick motion. Lena couldn’t stop the shout of pain that escaped her then, sweat prickling her brow as she panted, blood rushing out of the freshly opened wound. 

     

                That one took longer for Kara to manage, despite being smaller. It was deeper and bleeding freely, no clotting or tamping over long hours affording an easier time of it. Still, Kara tended to it with the same care and precision as the hip wound, cleaning it with saltwater and stitching it up before she smeared both injuries with a mixture of honey and herbs and bandaged them tightly. She dressed Lena then, undergarments and a thick nightgown that Andrea had brought for her, a robe loosely belted over the top before she urged her to her feet.

     

                The sun was just about to rise by that point, the morning bitterly cold but the darkness lightening to grey after so long spent riding home and tending to Lena, and she didn’t think she had the energy to even make it upstairs. Leaving the armour where it was, Kara didn’t ask before sweeping Lena off her feet and cradling her against her chest, trying to be mindful of her injuries and the fact that she was filthy herself, still in her armour. Carrying her upstairs, Kara set Lena down on her bed and pulled the blankets over her, tucking her in.

     

                “I’ll make you some tea to help with the pain.”

     

                Slipping out, Kara vanished downstairs to set water on to boil and used that time to strip off her armour, abandoning the filthy lot as she went against her principles of taking care of her armour after each battle, hastily washing herself in the sea. She watched the sunrise as she bathed, salt and soap on her skin as she rinsed away the blood and sweat, her left arm broken, the right side of her ribs a nasty purple from the heavy-handed blow of a warhammer, which had dented her breastplate. While she’d been focused on Lena, her pain had been secondary but now it was catching up to her, along with the exhaustion. 

     

                Climbing out of the water, Kara padded naked to the kitchen, steeping herbs in the boiling water and then pouring two cups, carrying them upstairs and pausing to don a shirt and leggings before heading into Lena’s room. Her wife lightly dozed as she waited for her, and Kara padded over to the bed and gently roused her, handing her cup to her and then taking a sip of her own before she moved to the brazier and started a fire.

     

                Once the flames caught, Kara turned back to the bed and sank onto the edge, giving Lena a searching look of concern. “Are you all right?” 

     

                Lena managed a tired smile, but it was thin. “I’ll live - thanks to you.”

     

                “I’m sorry it hurt so much. The tea will help.”

     

                “You’re drinking it too. Are you- are you hurt?”

     

                Her question was halting and Kara gave her a thin smile in return, taking another sip of her tea as she held her left arm in her lap at an awkward angle. She would ask Kelly to set it for her properly when she returned, before it healed wrong, but for now, she would endure the dull ache of it. There was nothing to be done for her bruised ribs though, and Kara had suffered far worse than some bruising, even if it pained her to move too much.

     

                “I’m well.”

     

                “But … are you hurt?”

     

                At the wide-eyed look of distress on her wife’s face, Kara considered lying to her, or at the very least giving her another evasive answer, but she knew that Lena was too perceptive for her lies to be very effective. Even if she’d answered in Fae, Lena would have picked apart the answer to see how Kara could have twisted the truth.

     

                “Minor injuries. Nothing for you to concern yourself with.”

     

                “Where? Show me.”

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter at the demand, Kara gingerly raised her left arm. “I took a blow to the arm; I believe it to be broken. And my ribs were dealt a blow as well but suffered only some bruising.”

     

                “Show me,” Lena repeated.

     

                Draining her tea and motioning for Lena to do the same, Kara pulled up the hem of her shirt to expose the bottom of her ribcage and the beginnings of the bruise. Lena wasn’t stupid though and leaned forward to yank the shirt the rest of the way up, a soft gasp escaping her as she took in the swathe of bruising down Kara’s entire right side, unable to stop herself from reaching out to lightly graze her fingertips over the injury. Shifting away from her touch, Kara’s movement could have been mistaken for jerking away in pain and Lena was quick to apologise, not realising that it was the intimacy of Lena touching her bare skin that bothered her more than it being over a fresh bruise.

     

                “What happened?”

     

                “A blow, as I said. It will be gone in a matter of days, it is nothing to be concerned with.”

     

                “You’re sure nothing’s broken? It hasn’t … I don’t know, punctured a lung?”

     

                “No, nothing of the sort. My arm pains me more, in truth, but even that is nothing worse than what I suffered as a child, falling off a horse or out of a tree. Come, sleep now. All will be well with a little rest.”

     

                Mouth opening, Lena inhaled to speak and then thought better of it, closing her mouth and casting her gaze down on the pile of blankets. The same blankets they’d shared the day before, albeit, Lena beneath several layers and Kara stretched out on top. So much had happened since then and Lena felt saw raw and vulnerable that she couldn’t abide the thought of being all alone.

     

                “What is it?” Kara gently asked, reaching out with her good hand to cover Lena’s in her warm, calloused grasp.

     

                Smiling wanly, Lena closed her eyes, feeling a little embarrassed to admit it. “Nothing, I just- I was going to ask …”

     

                “You may ask anything of me, you know that I will give it to you if it’s within my power.”

     

                “I know, it’s just- it’s stupid.”

     

                “Not to me.”

     

                Opening her eyes, Lena gave her a pleading look as her shoulders sagged, the tea and brandy pleasantly numbing her as her eyes prickled with tiredness. She didn’t have the energy to be coy or as prideful as usual, so Lena decided to be honest.

     

                “Will you stay? I just- I don’t want to be alone and … I don’t want you to go.”

     

                Softening, Kara took Lena’s empty cup from her and climbed to her feet. Setting them down on the side table, she turned back to the bed and pulled back the blankets as her wife’s anxious expression turned to one of relief as it became evident that Kara was staying. Slipping beneath the obscene amount of blankets, Kara shifted the pillows into a more comfortable position and leaned against them, head lolling to the side as she breathed in deeply, the smell of grass, pine and earth clinging to them so strongly that she briefly considered stealing one for her room, to sleep with every night.

     

                Staring at her wife, Kara gave her a small smile and reached across with her good hand to tenderly thumb the hair out of Lena’s face. “Sleep now. I’m here.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena whispered, meek and grateful.

     

                She hesitated a moment before shifting closer, and then closer still, crossing a boundary that they hadn’t consciously crossed, despite the times they’d fallen asleep beside each other. Pressing herself up against Kara’s uninjured side, Lena slowly settled down with her head on her wife’s chest, listening to the steady thump of her heartbeat as she relaxed against the warmth of her. In turn, Kara felt her body relax as well, the press of her wife against her side a surprising turn but comforting as she finally gave in to the exhaustion of two sleepless nights and the weight of the worry she’d carried for Lena. 

     

                Finding peace in each other’s presence, they fell asleep together, unaware that that morning was the catalyst for so many things yet to come.

    Chapter 24

                Kara was nowhere to be found the next day as Lena woke alone in bed, well past noon and looking around with bewilderment as she rubbed her eyes, wondering if it had been a dream. Her side pained her as she pushed herself upright and then paused, leaning over to the other side of the bed and pressing her face to the pillows.

     

                The smell of salt and rain was refreshingly strong, and Lena’s eyelids fluttered shut as she let out a quiet breath. Her shoulders slumped and she frowned slightly before pulling back, confused by her actions and even more so by the truth of her memory. 

     

                She couldn’t hear Kara across the hallway and there was a stillness to the place that gave Lena the vague sensation that she was home all alone. Climbing out of bed, the pain making her wince, face crumpling with the effort, Lena shrugged on a few layers and had to settle for her socks, her boots elsewhere after shedding them for her bath. Her leg could barely hold her weight and she retrieved the carved walking stick Kara had made her when she’d broken her leg, leaning on it as she hobbled out of the room.

     

                Making her way downstairs, she picked up on voices and pinpointed Kara’s coming from the kitchen. Slowly, Lena walked towards the room and stepped into the doorway, conversation pausing as a few faces turned to her. Kara had her arm in a sling and was spreading seaweed on fresh bread at one end of the long benchtop, while James poured tea for everyone, sitting beside his sister, and Alex and Lucy sat across from him. At the sight of her, Kara climbed to her feet, bread set down on a plate as she crossed the room to Lena, her eyes so blue and full of concern.

     

                “You are awake,” she stated the obvious. “I had considered waking you but thought you must have direly needed the rest.”

     

                “Yeah, I think so,” Lena said with a droll smile. “How’s your arm?”

     

                Raising it slightly in its sling, Kara shrugged nonchalantly. “It is no bother. Kelly is just overly cautious of her patients; she will no doubt want to check my handiwork once you are amenable.”

     

                She gave Lena a quick smile and then extended a hand. “Come, sit. You should rest your leg, and you are in need of a good meal, I should think. And tea, of course. One can never have too much of it.”

     

                “No, of course not,” Lena teasingly murmured.

     

                There was a slight shuffling of seats, Alex’s eyebrows rising and falling quickly as she shifted her plate along without a word, freeing up room for Lena to sit at Kara’s left hand. A clean plate was procured by her wife and Lena realised she was quite hungry, and judging by the fact that everyone else had made it back, it must have been quite late in the afternoon.

     

                Tea was poured for her and Kara softly inquired about her injuries, if she felt okay, her warm fingers briefly pressing against her forehead to check for a fever when the others were occupied. Lena rolled her eyes but suffered it without complaint and let Alex ladle stew into a bowl for her before reaching for a piece of bread, her face whitening as the stitches in her side pulled.

     

                Fingers encircled her wrist as Kara stopped her. “Do not strain yourself; you will make your injuries worse.”

     

                “I’m fine. Don’t fuss,” Lena wearily chided her. 

     

                “Oh, yes, she may ride into battle but fetching her own bread is too much of a risk,” Alex laughed.

     

                “She would not have ridden into battle if not for you,” Kara softly replied with some iciness to her tone, clearly harbouring some resentment for her sister and the hand she’d had in it all.

     

                “She acquitted herself well though, no? Did you not say she slaughtered two? Very well done, Your Highness.”

     

                Rolling her eyes at Alex’s wry praise, Lena spooned stew into her mouth. Truthfully, she felt no pride in what had happened, her feelings muddled by her terror and pain, the tightness in her chest from the panic, the disorientation of staggering about in the dark, trying to make sense of everything as it happened so quickly. She hardly even considered one of the kills her own, considering Alex had slit the man’s throat, regardless of whether or not her stab wound had been fatal in its own right. Mouth thinning at the corners, Lena broke off a piece of the bread her wife got for her and didn’t respond.

     

                She ate slowly, her bowl refilled once she neared the bottom of it, and much of that eaten as well, her hunger ravenous, much to her surprise, and then Lena was fed slices of pear as Kara cut them for her, handing them off one by one. Eating each slice in between mouthfuls of tea, Lena felt full and warm and would have been perfectly content if not for the aching of her wounds. As if sensing her discomfort, Kara touched the back of her hand to get Lena’s attention, their eyes meeting as her wife gave her an expectant look.

     

                “Would you like me to make you a drink for the pain?”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, eyelids shuttering, Lena nodded. “If you wouldn’t mind.”

     

                Already on her feet, Kara’s expression softened with sympathy. “Of course not. If you would prefer to stay up a while before returning to bed, I can escort you to the fire in the great hall.”

     

                Nodding, Lena eased herself off her seat, the others still chatting and enjoying the remainder of their dinner, pitchers of cider and wine scattered amidst the plates and bowls as they unwound after the battle. They all looked clean and somewhat rested, their respective injuries treated and bound, and Lena was envious that they could come out of it looking so unaffected while she was treated like a delicate flower, feeling all of her injuries to their fullest extent.

     

                Kara took her arm to provide more support and Lena relied on her and her staff to walk to the hall, a fire roaring in the hearth, Sam and M’gann both already there, playing stones in the corner. Dragging a chair closer to the fire, Kara eased Lena onto it and made her comfortable before she vanished, leaving her by the warmth of the flames, the air tasting of smoke, listening to the other two women move the little polished stones on the board. They didn’t speak to her and she was glad she wouldn’t have to make small talk or discuss the battle, how poorly it had gone for her, although she’d managed to survive, which was a miracle in itself.

     

                Returning ten minutes later with a pot of tea and a clean cup, with a blanket under her arm, Kara sank to her knees at Lena’s side. Pouring the steeped herbal tea into the cup, she offered it up and then draped the blanket over Lena’s legs, tucking her in and pressing the backs of her fingers to her brow again to reassure herself there was no fever.

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena insisted.

     

                “No doubt you are,” Kara agreed, mollifying her in a way that seemed almost patronising.

     

                It chafed Lena a little but she knew her wife was worried, which was amusing in and of itself, so she couldn’t bring herself to feel too irritated that Kara wouldn’t take her word for it. She knew Lena would hate to admit any weakness so would make the extra effort to watch over her herself, taking her health and well-being very seriously. 

     

                “Is there anything I can get you? Anything you need?” Kara asked, curling and uncurling the fingers of her good hand anxiously.

     

                Considering it for a moment, Lena shrugged lazily and looked up at her wife through her lashes, a faint smile at the corners of her mouth. “If your arm wasn’t broken, I would ask you to play for me, sing me a song.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara murmured, looking down briefly before she raised her head. “I am skilled enough to play with one hand. A simple tune, I admit, but perhaps sufficient enough?”

     

                Smile growing a fraction, Lena jerked her chin in an arrogant manner, which was amusing to them both. “Off you go then.”

     

                Nodding, Kara made her way over to the harp and managed to lift it with one arm around the narrower part near the base, resting it against her shoulder as she lugged it over to Lena. She set it down awkwardly and gave her wife a quick grin before going to fetch the stool as well.

     

                “There. Now I shall not have to shout or disturb anyone,” Kara declared as she sat at Lena’s side, back angled away from the fire.

     

                “How dare you disturb anyone in your own home,” Lena teased her.

     

                “Quite right.”

     

                Her wife’s response was serious though and she bowed her head as she put the fingers of her good hand to the strings. With the speed of her playing, she may as well have been using two hands, moving too quickly for Lena to keep up as the soft melody filled the silence. The firelight limned Kara in orange, making her blonde hair seem like burnished brass, her face shadowed as she closed her eyes, playing intently. Her voice joined in after a few measures and Lena drained her cup of tea and propped her chin in her hand as she watched her with rapt wonder. Kara’s voice was sweet and although her wife had been right, that she couldn’t understand the quick lyrics of the ballad in its entirety, it was beautiful to listen to.

     

                At the end of the song, Kara refilled Lena’s cup again and made her drink more before she resumed her playing with a different tune and new lyrics. She played three in all, refilling her wife’s cup again in between songs, and by the end of it, Lena was drowsy and relaxed. The music had calmed her and her eyelids were heavy as she opened them, pulling herself from her reverie to realise that the others had trickled in at some point; Alex darning tears in her clothes, Kelly reading a book, James carving something out of driftwood. 

     

                On her feet, Kara laid a hand on Lena’s shoulder. “Come to bed.”

     

                Humming in agreement, Lena stood as she let the blanket fall from her lap, stooping to pick it up as Kara reached for it as well, their hands overlapping in the wool. Giving her hand a gentle squeeze, Kara set the blanket down on the seat and waited for Lena to get her bearings with the staff before offering an arm for her to lean on. They didn’t speak as they walked out and made their way upstairs, the hallways cold as the bitter wind swept inside, stirring tapestries and howling as it whistled through gaps in the limestone.

     

                Inside Lena’s room, she sank onto the edge of her bed and removed a few layers, bundling them up and setting them on the floor. Kara leaned her staff against the edge of the table and moved to the fire, which was burning low but had been carefully maintained throughout the morning to ensure Lena hadn’t been cold while she slept. Watching her wife build it up higher made Lena’s throat tighten slightly, the simple act of being cared for reminding her once more of what her life had been like before.

     

                “Did you leave before they came back?” she found herself asking, her thoughts of people leaving, of never having anyone, surfacing and bringing the question to the tip of her tongue before she could stop herself from speaking.

     

                Glancing over her shoulder, Kara looked momentarily puzzled. “Leave where?”

     

                “My bed.”

     

                “Oh.” Setting in the last log and straightening, Kara dusted off her hands and cleared her throat. “No, I heard them arrive. It was then that I left.”

     

                Nodding, trying to make sense of the relief and slight prickle of betrayal, Lena fussed with the blankets. “Good.”

                

                “Good?”

     

                “Yes, good. It would get them talking if they found you asleep in my bed. I don’t want them starting stupid rumours about us, especially when they’re not true at all. I wouldn’t want people to get the wrong impression of us, that’s all. I know we’re married but we’ve made it perfectly clear that it’s in name only, and that you and I would never have picked each other if we’d had a say.”

     

                She talked too much, watching Kara’s neutral expression as she gazed at her, and wanted to bite her tongue off to shut herself up but found herself overexplaining it instead. Finally trailing off, Lena cleared her throat and settled back against the pillows. Pausing, as if waiting for her to continue her tirade, Kara then nodded rounding the foot of the bed.

     

                “As you say, we are married in name only. Although, the reason for my departure from your bed this morning was not out of concern for what others may have thought to find me there. It may be in name only, but you are still my wife. It would not be so unseemly to think I would keep watch over your injured form as you sleep.”

     

                A shallow furrow appeared between Lena’s eyebrows as Kara spoke. They both knew that Kara hadn’t stayed for that purpose, that it had been Lena asking her that made her agree, that they had both been sleeping, but for the sake of ease, Lena let the white lie slide. Nodding, she pulled the blankets up over her shoulder as she turned onto her right side.

     

                “Goodnight.”

     

                “Sleep well, Lena.”

     

                Kara slipped away without a sound and Lena felt mildly annoyed as she tried to get comfortable, and then remembered the unfortunate presence of the pillows her wife had slept on in the early hours of that morning. Breathing in the smell of salt and rain, Lena felt restless as she sighed heavily, pummeling them into shape and pressing her cheek to the place where Kara had rested hers. She slept fitfully, dreaming of the sea, of being under the water, but woke with her arms wrapped tightly around the pillow and her face pressed into it.

     

                Rising slowly, rubbing her eyes and breathing in the cold air, making her wonder if it had snowed again overnight, Lena climbed out of bed. In contrast to the stillness of when she woke yesterday afternoon, there was a flurry of activity that morning, the halls filled with voices and footsteps as everyone efficiently went about their tasks. Curious, Lena pulled on a robe and belted on her dagger, finding another pair of socks to combat the iciness of the stone floors, and fetched her staff to lean on as she wandered out of her room.

     

                Making her way downstairs, she saw Kara’s friends dressed warmly for travel, carrying coils of rope, nets, oars and planks of wood, folded piles of cloth that Lena didn’t recognise for sails, and bundles of salted mackerel and barrels of fresh water. Confused by the activity, Lena sought out her wife and found her at the western point of the lower levels, staring out at the sea as she listened to the sandpipers.

     

                The sky outside was a dull pewter grey, clouds pushed around by the force of the wind as a storm brewed in the distance. Slowly walking inside, Lena stepped up beside Kara, watching the stretch of dark waves churning through the archways, shivering at how exposed she felt to the sea.

     

                Continuing to stare straight ahead, Kara’s side profile was sternly handsome as she raised her chin a fraction, looking troubled. “How do you feel?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena replied, hesitating before she stated the obvious. “Everyone’s busy today.”

     

                Turning her back to the sea, Kara bowed her head, rubbing her brow as she was silent for a moment. Then she clasped her hands behind her back as she paced away a few steps.

     

                “I am to leave this morning.”

     

                Mild surprise crossed Lena’s face as she raised her eyebrows, green eyes wide with anxious curiosity. “Where are we going?”

     

                As she strayed a few steps further away, silent for a moment, staring at the giant tapestry hanging on the wall, Kara let out the softest sigh. “You will not be going anywhere.”

     

                Caught by surprise again, Lena’s mouth opened and closed as her expression fell. “What do you mean I’m not going?”

     

                Turning, Kara gave her a resigned look, guilt flickering in her eyes. “You are recovering from your injuries.”

     

                “We all are. We all got injured,” she sharply retorted.

     

                “And it is a risk I am unwilling to take again. I head east, towards the boundaries of the Courts, to warn my people and our allies against enemies. I would not see you in harm’s way once more, not so soon.”

     

                Anger flushed Lena’s pale cheeks as she clenched her jaw, eyebrows furrowed together. “It’s not your decision to make. You agreed with that last time; nothing has changed since then.”

     

                “I make this decision for you, out of kindness,” Kara gently replied, a pleading look on her face. “We are to sail.”

     

                Some of her anger guttered at that but Lena wouldn’t give up that easily, spluttering before she gestured sharply. “Well, take the horses instead. We don’t have to sail.”

     

                “It is quicker. Urgency is of utmost importance.”

     

                “It’s not safe.”

     

                Kara let out a huff of laughter, “I know this land, even with its capricious nature. No harm shall befall me unexpectedly, least of all on the seas.”

     

                With a derisive scoff, Lena folded her arms over her chest and turned away. Panic flitted across Kara’s face and she reached out to snag Lena’s arm, stopping her from leaving as she stepped in, their faces close as Lena gave her a sullen look through her lashes, mouth turned down at the corners.

     

                “Do not be angry with me. Please. I shall not be gone for long and you will be well cared for in my absence.”

     

                “They’re all going with you. It’s not fair.”

     

                “There is no fairness in life.”

     

                Giving her an aching look, Lena clutched Kara’s sleeves, her shoulders sagging with dismay. “Send birds to deliver your messages. Let everyone else go without you. Stay here with me instead.”

     

                Running a hand over Lena’s silken hair, Kara’s mouth was a grim line as she gazed at her apologetically, her voice quiet with her guilt as she replied. “I must go and you must stay. I’m sorry.”

     

                Her anger flared back up and she scowled as her eyes prickled, although they remained dry. Lena had the unfortunate tendency to cry when she was mad but she wouldn’t give in to that now, wouldn’t allow herself to come off as pitiful or pathetic. 

     

                “Go then,” she flatly ordered Kara, letting go of her.

     

                Sighing, Kara’s eyes were pleading as she reached out to cup Lena’s face in a hand, grimacing when her wife sharply turned her head aside. “I do not wish to part on such terms.”

     

                “These are the only ones you’ll get, so stay or go, it’s up to you.”

     

                Exasperation made Kara’s expression strained but she just nodded at her wife’s surly words, meant to vex her and landing as intended. “Very well.”

     

                Making a brusque exit, her mood soured by Lena’s poor reception of the news she’d be staying behind, Kara went to help with the boat. The most adept at sailing, she helped ready the little ship, ropes and sails while her wife was left to seethe alone. Not for long, unfortunately for Lena, as she paced back and forth, her anger warming her as the brisk wind swept in, ruffling her clothes.

     

                “You’re not sulking, are you?” Alex laughed as she stepped inside. 

     

                She was dressed warmly in layers of burgundy and brown, her knives strapped to her and a peek of her mail beneath the leather and layers of wool. Lena scoffed as she folded her arms over her chest, her staff clamped to her side as she tried not to look too petulant. 

     

                “What is the matter?”

     

                “You clearly already know,” Lena bit out.

     

                “Yes, I imagine everyone within these walls heard your argument. And you deem it unfair , no doubt, that you are not permitted to come.”

     

                “Of course it’s unfair! How would you feel if Kelly left you behind?”

     

                Considering it for a moment, Alex walked over to her and then to the very edge, where the limestone lip of the room dropped away to sea. The waves lapped against the salt-rimed stone below and a few little rowing boats bobbed with the tide, rope tying them to the rusted rings set in the stone and Alex nimbly leapt into one of them, keeping her balance as the boat rocked at the disturbance. Glancing over her shoulder as the wind snatched at her hair, Alex raised her eyebrows suggestively.

     

                “You fear the water, no? Come, climb in with me and row us out beyond the surf. If you do, I will personally vouch for you, as I did last time.”

     

                Wariness flashed across Lena’s face, but even once she had ascertained Alex was being serious, she didn’t move an inch. Arms crossed over her chest and face pale and stiff with reluctance, Lena’s mouth tightened at the corners. Turning to face her fully, Alex spread her arms and shrugged.

     

                “No? There we have it then.”

     

                Leaping back up onto the lip of the room, Alex crouched a second as she caught her balance and then straightened. Crossing over to Lena, Alex cupped her face in her hands, making Lena scowl as she met her sister-in-law’s eyes with annoyance.

     

                “Your fear of the water is a weakness, and there can be no room for weaknesses in already perilous circumstances. We all must be aware of our weaknesses so we can overcome them and be stronger for them, but until you overcome yours, you will not be strong enough to sail with us.”

     

                Jerking her head out of Alex’s grasp, Lena scoffed, her cheeks and the tips of her ears reddening slightly as averted her gaze. With a quick laugh, Alex reached forward to gently prod Lena’s hip wound, eliciting a small sound of protest as the ache flared up, Lena’s eyes cutting back to her with indignation. Alex wrapped her in a tight hug before she could speak.

     

                “And you are injured, sister. Rest and be well; it is all she wants from you now. It may upset you to be left behind, but know it upsets her too, to leave you here. She does not deny you to be spiteful.”

     

                “I never said she did,” Lena muttered, frowning.

     

                She was stiff in Alex’s friendly embrace and was somewhat relieved when the other woman gave her back a quick slack and let her go. “Now, no more sulking.”

     

                “I’m not sulking,” Lena protested.

     

                “You have the freedom to do as you please here; make good use of your time. Keep practising your archery.”

     

                Glumly ignoring her, Lena stared broodingly at the sea and only felt resentment, no matter the valid reason for her to be left behind. Withdrawing from the room, Alex went to help finish with the final arrangements, and through the archways on the right side of the open wall, Lena could see the bobbing ship, and make out the shapes of the travellers as they readied the vessel. Kara had climbed the mast, checking the rigging on the sail, and Lena thought their eyes momentarily met before she decided it was probably too far for Kara to notice her lurking in the shadows of the westernmost room of the hall.

     

                As much as she denied her sulking, she was definitely brooding, time passing by slowly as she lingered in that room away from everyone else. No one disturbed her and she could hear them getting ready to leave, torn between her stubborn insistence that Kara wouldn’t get anything but her anger in parting and wanting to see her off properly, tell her to be safe. As she got over her sulking, it was her embarrassment at her behaviour that made her lean towards remaining tucked away in the far room, committed to them parting without another word passing between them, but of course, Kara wouldn’t have it that way.

     

                Lena heard her footsteps approach, slow and cautious, somewhat meek in the wake of upsetting her wife, and she didn’t turn as Kara stepped inside the room. They were both aware that Lena had heard her and Kara let out a soft sigh when she didn’t turn around or acknowledge her. Stopping behind her, Kara reached out to press her palm to Lena’s back, between her shoulder blades, her touch palpably warm even through the layers of Lena’s clothes.

     

                “I shall return to you in a few days. Take care of yourself; I will not be gone for long.”

     

                Mouth twisting with annoyance, Lena gripped her staff in both hands as she leaned on it, narrowing her eyes at the storm blowing in. She wanted to come off as stoic but her hurt was evident.

     

                “I know you do not wish to see us off but I could not part with you after angry words. I do not begrudge you your feelings but I would appreciate it if we could bid farewell to each other without any animosity.”

     

                Her hand trailed to Lena’s shoulder and she gently pressed against it, trying to coax her into turning. Slowly allowing herself to be moved, Lena’s eyelids shuttered with exasperation as her shoulders dropped. She wouldn’t meet Kara’s gaze but felt her wife’s fingers trace the line of her jaw.

     

                “I shall see you when I return. Be well.”

     

                Giving her a stiff nod, all she could bring herself to offer Kara, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners with anger and annoyance. Grimacing, Kara hesitated and then thought better of saying anything else, choosing to lean in and press a lingering kiss to Lena’s cheek instead, before she withdrew and left without another word.

     

                Left behind, Lena reached up to press her fingers to the lingering warmth of the kiss. She wasn’t left alone, finding Andrea embroidering something near the fire and J’onn going over ledgers, the sound of Sam off in her room on the floor above. Exhaling, Lena paused outside the open doorway to her room, reluctant to relegate herself to bed to further her sulking but not wanting to see anyone. Not that there were many left to see, the others on the ship below as she heard the sound of voices and creaking wood, the snapping of the sail as it was hoisted.

     

                Hesitating, wondering whether it was too invasive, she couldn’t help herself from stepping over the threshold of Kara’s room. She’d been in there numerous times before and wasn’t there to pry, but rather to cross over to the open wall, staying a safe distance from the edge as she leaned against one of the carved pillars and stared out at the little ship as they rowed it out through the surf. The wind was rough and the storm looked like it would hit soon and Lena’s stomach knotted with worry.

     

                “Should you be in here?”

     

                Startling slightly, Lena sharply glanced over her shoulder, frowning at the sight of Sam in the doorway. She’d acquired a bigger wardrobe since arriving and was dressed in a maroon doublet with a coat that fell to her knees, wrapped at the front and held in place by her belt. She wasn’t wearing her sword, only a long dagger. Her unbound brown hair and curious hazel eyes softened her face, making her look vastly different to the woman Lena had first encountered in her flower shop.

     

                “I’m always welcome in my wife’s room,” Lena grumbled.

     

                “Just not on her ship? Surely you do not intend to stand there all morning until they are out of sight.”

     

                “What else is there to do?”

     

                “We could throw knives? I would not want you to strain your injuries with swordplay just yet but a well-aimed dagger can take down a foe just as well as the thrust of a sword.”

     

                Taking in the salt-stained sail, ballooning with the breeze, the sight of six oars heaving against the current and the tiny deck crammed with supplies, the weak sunlight glinting off her wife’s golden hair, Lena pursed her lips. She hovered a minute longer until the boat was too far out for her to distinguish Kara from the others, the wind strong as it towed them out to sea and the spindly legs of the oars retracted, and then turned to Sam.

     

                “I’ll get my dagger.”

     

                The next few days followed a rather pathetic routine of stopping by various rooms facing north, on the off-chance that she would catch a glimpse of a white sail against the horizon to the east, and all time spent between then anxiously baking various pies, which she never ate, and checking in on everyone else to see what they were doing. J’onn let her assist him with the ledges and inventory, her business experience making her good enough with numbers to impress him as he shared the workload and answered her questions about laws and the economy. 

     

                Andrea helped her dress and lit her fires for her, the two of them annoying each other to ensure constant bickering as she tried to make Lena come down for meals and let her check her wounds, and Sam often wound up nearby as she kept tabs on her charge, watching Lena practise her archery and knife throwing, drinking tea with her and playing stones. It wasn’t half bad, but it had never been the prospect of the company that had made Lena so opposed to staying behind. Each day, she stared out at the empty sea and felt her stomach churn with unease as the waves angrily tossed about, rain and sleet and snow blowing in on the wind, depending on the day. Each day, her wife didn’t return.

     

                On the fourth day, she was watching the sea again, this time from one of the small sitting rooms on the lowest level, on the eastern edge of the halls, her hands red from the cold as a fire was absent in the small hearth, and her lips chapped from the wind. Her injuries had been recovering well, pink scars already replacing the scabs as the bruises faded, and she no longer needed the support of the walking stick to lean on as she watched and waited. Footsteps approached mid-morning and she bit back a sigh, wondering who was disturbing her peace now - her shadow, attendant or Kara’s Steward.

     

                “You seem more at peace here than I had anticipated.”

     

                Whirling around as she was caught by surprise, Lena’s eyes widened a fraction as her lips parted at the sight of her mother-in-law dressed in grey and silver travelling clothes. Despite the dampness and dirt, mud soaking the hem of her flowing riding dress and cloak, Eliza still looked elegantly serene, her hands hidden in the voluminous sleeves as she smiled softly at Lena, blue eyes calming.

     

                “I- Eliza,” Lena stammered, confused as she quickly ducked her head in a polite greeting.

     

                Gliding towards her, Eliza stretched out her arms as her smile widened. She kissed both of Lena’s cheeks and took her hands, affectionately squeezing them.

     

                “It is good to see you, Lena.”

     

                “It’s good to see you too,” she replied, a little uncertain in the company of Kara’s mother without her wife’s presence. “Um … Kara’s actually not here.”

     

                “Yes, J’onn has explained it all to me. I must have left before the pigeon was sent, but it is no matter. I’m sure my daughters will return soon.”

     

                Nodding, Lena pressed her lips together, toying with the buckle of her belt. “Was the journey okay?”

     

                Eliza gave her a thin smile, weariness etched into the lines of her face. “It was slow. There has been trouble south-east of the mountains as well; those who dwell in my land have spent most of winter fending them off through the mountain passes, in the foothills. I, myself, only had to contend with an eagle or two, much to my chagrin.”

     

                She shook out her sleeve in a vexed manner, glancing at her upper arm, and Lena’s eyes widened a fraction with panic. There was old blood staining the material where Eliza’s bicep was, hidden from view unless she angled her arm as she was then.

     

                “You’re hurt,” Lena stated the obvious.

     

                “A mere scratch.”

     

                “Should I- do you need someone to look at it? Um … Kelly’s not here-“

     

                Reaching out to ease her concern with a gentle hand on Lena’s shoulder, Eliza smiled warmly. “Fret not, I can tend to myself well enough. Although, I would welcome the company if you are finished here?”

     

                She ended up following her mother-in-law through the halls to the small room well-stocked with herbs and healing supplies. Sitting on a small stool, Eliza shed her cloak and the outer layer of her riding dress and worked her arm free, gently questioning Lena seemingly at random. How she found the weather, what she did to pass the time, how her injuries were faring, if she spent much time on the beach, what she thought of the brisk wind and the species of birds found in the area. It all felt rather unimportant but Lena obligingly answered as she watched Eliza clean the long scratches from the claws of the giant eagles and bind them with clean bandages. She offered her help with that and then Eliza repaid the favour by forcing her to sit and let her check on Lena’s almost healed wounds too.

     

                Afterwards, they had tea together in the kitchen and Eliza showed her how to make bread. It was another two days before Kara returned, a full week without her wife unnerving Lena, having spent very little time apart since she’d decided to stay in her world. Lena spent those two days either keeping watch for sight of the ship, although she did it in a manner that she thought could be played off as coincidence, spending all of her time in north-facing rooms and sitting or standing uncharacteristically close to the edge. At times, she was coaxed away by her mother-in-law, or otherwise joined by her, and Lena patiently answered all of Eliza’s questions as the older woman tried to familiarise herself with her daughter’s wife. Not that Lena minded, always polite and accommodating, but she had never been that great with people and found herself overthinking much of what was said, searching for some deeper meaning to Eliza’s questions.

     

                On the seventh day, past noon, she caught a glimpse of something in the distance as she idly paced along the lip of the room with the harbour, water lapping against wet stone, the smell of brine strong as algae and limpets dotted the jetties jutting out into the sea. There were a few little sailboats and rowing boats made for enjoyment tied up along the narrow limestone paths, and another bigger one like the one they’d sailed away in, and Lena had been eyeing the coils of rope and piles of nets, battered collection of oars leaning against the walls and a couple of kayaks and rowing boats in the midst of being carved or repaired as they rested on stands in the spacious room. Despite her hatred for the water, she was curious about it, or rather curious about her wife, and she knew that Kara often spent time in this room, fiddling with her boats, bending damp planks of wood and nailing them in place, sanding down driftwood and sewing holes in sails with the dedication of the truly devoted.

     

                Lena had never been in the room alone until Kara had left and had rarely ventured in before that - except to know of its purpose and occasionally track down her wife - and as her pacing slowed at the sight of the dot, she felt momentarily flustered at the telltale sign of a white sail pulling around the curved coastline to the east. Lingering a moment as equal parts anxiety and relief cut through her, she caught sight of golden hair and then turned and hurried out of the room, her week-old annoyance stoked at the impending return of her wife. Walking back upstairs, Lena deliberated for a few moments before deciding to hide in the library, amidst the stacks of shelves and books.

     

                Tucking herself away in the corner of the room, as far from the door as she could get, the light dim from the arrow-slit windows, Lena sat on the driftwood chair and pulled a book free at random. At first glance to decipher the glyphs, it looked to be a historical account of the tides, an utterly boring topic but a decent cover all the same as Lena cradled the book in her palms and pretended to study the pages. The whole time, she listened intently, minutes passing by as her body went taut, until an age later she heard the sound of oars, of shouting voices, the snap of the sail and knocking of wood as the ship docked at the harbour, voices audible now, laughter and indecipherable words of presumed relief or grumbling, and her heart thudded in her chest as a lump lodged itself in her throat and her skin turned clammy. 

     

                Her back to the opening between two rows of bookshelves, Lena propped her elbow on the table as she listened intently. It didn’t take long for her wife’s attention to turn to her, as soon as she had finished greeting her mother, and Lena listened as Kara’s footsteps came into her range of hearing. It would’ve been an easy thing for Kara to locate her, her sharp hearing picking out Lena’s heartbeat from within the depths of the library, and Lena was tense as she heard her come closer and closer, until the hairs on the back of her neck rose at the feeling of her wife’s eyes on her back. They both knew Lena was aware of her presence but Lena didn’t react until Kara spoke.

     

                “My eyes must have deceived me, for I thought I saw you waiting at the harbour for my return,” Kara greeted her as her footsteps stopped behind her, her voice weary but fond.

     

                Back straight, Lena was silent and still for a moment before she rose to her feet and turned, closing the book over a finger, as if she intended to resume where she’d left off. “They must have.”

     

                “How unfortunate; it would’ve been a heartwarming welcome to come home to.”

     

                Rubbing her thumb along the edges of the book, Lena looked everywhere but at Kara as she shifted restlessly before her. Clearing her throat, Kara gestured to her wife, her blue eyes flitting over her body, noticing the lack of a walking stick.

     

                “You have recovered well?”

     

                “Obviously.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara awkwardly deduced with a sheepish look of surprise. “You are still angry.”

     

                Piercing stare landing on her wife’s face, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Are you surprised?”

     

                Opening and closing her mouth, Kara was uncertain as she toyed with her calloused fingers and ran a hand through salt-crusted curls. Licking her wind-chapped lips, she shrugged slightly and nodded.

     

                “Yes. I thought you might have … come to understand.”

     

                With a scoff of laughter, Lena smiled thinly. “Oh, no, I understand, but that doesn’t mean I can’t be angry about it.”

     

                “Oh. May I ask why?”

     

                “You ask me to assimilate,” Lena softly snapped, gesturing widely. “You ask me to make an effort to fit in, to- to learn your ways, and when I try, I’m dismissed. As if it’s nothing.”

     

                “You were not made to stay behind because of your lack of assimilation, only out of your injuries and the danger it would put you in.”

     

                “That is bullshit.”

     

                “We were on a boat, Lena!” Kara exasperatedly reasoned, spreading her hands helplessly. “What would you have me do? Knock you senseless until we arrived so you were not sick with fear the entire time, just so you may not have felt left behind?”

     

                “There were other ways.”

     

                Kara stepped in closer, her mouth a grim line of annoyance. “Those other ways would have exposed you to more danger and would have unnecessarily delayed us. Not to mention you would not have even managed to stay on your horse for long. You are letting your feelings get in the way of reason; other lives were at stake - do you think your pride is worth more?”

     

                “It’s not about pride-”

     

                “No? Then why does it matter if you cannot use what you have learned here unless it’s to prove yourself?”

     

                “Because you don’t think I’m good enough. Oh, by all means, show me how to use a bow or a sword, teach me how to read , teach me your language but God forbid I use any of it. Tell me you wouldn’t be mad to be treated the same. It’s a waste of my time, trying so hard to earn your approval, only to be dismissed.”

     

                “You don’t-”

     

                “I see you two have not learned to exist in your marriage in your time here,” Eliza sighed as she interrupted. “I do not presume to lecture you on how you may conduct yourself in your ancestral home, daughter, but peace is more harmonious, do you not agree?”

     

                “Speak not of Airfolk platitudes of peace,” Kara said with exasperation, tired from her travels as she ran a hand over her face. “I have sacrificed more than most for peace.”

     

                “You speak derisively of Airfolk peace, yet I’m certain you have not forgotten a few instances of discipline that would remind you of the contrarian nature of the wind. It is not always a gentle summer breeze.”

     

                The wind picked up then, an almost eerie high-pitched whine as it caught in the cracks and corners of the room, ruffling pages and shifting books. Kara seemed unruffled by the showcase of her mother’s powers making her point, and she grimaced faintly.

     

                “Indeed, I have not forgotten. But much like the wind, Lena and I may bite but there can be a gentleness between us as well. As I’m sure my wife can attest to.”

     

                “Then make it gentle,” Eliza softly ordered her, her eyes sliding to Lena’s surly brooding, her arms folded over her chest as she stared at the floor. “Put it to rest and come and have some hot cider. I would like to hear of your trip.”

     

                Nodding curtly to her mother, Kara bowed her head as she clasped her hands behind her back, shoulders hunched forward. She waited for Eliza to leave, giving them enough privacy to talk quietly without being overhead, before raising her head and bringing her hands before her to fiddle with them some more.

     

                Mouth opening and closing as she sheepishly wrung her hands, Kara softly cleared her throat. “You are correct, of course - I would be mad. I assure you it was not my intention to hurt you, and if haste had not been paramount, and you weren’t injured, I would never have left you behind,” she murmured in Fae. “And I’m sorry for my poor behaviour. But I hope you know you do not have to earn my approval; you have it irrevocably. Always.”

     

                The corner of Lena’s mouth twitched at the corner, a flicker of annoyance passing her face as she didn’t quite catch every word on her wife’s lips. Then she softened slightly, her eyebrows pinched together as she grimaced, eyelids shuttering as she softly sighed.

     

                “I missed you.”

     

                Caught off guard by the words Lena hadn’t meant to say, Kara let out a small laugh and stepped forward to gather Lena up in a gentle embrace. “I missed you too.”

     

                From that moment on, Kara made a conscientious decision to only speak to Lena in Fae, unless it was to translate something for her understanding, and they resumed their daily sparring and Lena’s other accumulated hobbies. The weather was atrocious, storms so fierce the booms of thunder seemed to shake the cliffside and the rain soaked into the sand and the stretch of land along the cliffside, making it soft with mud and soaking them to the bone whenever they were outside. Lena still braved it on occasion, huddled in her cloak as she walked alongside Kara, collecting driftwood and shells, watching her fish from the shore as she perched on a rock a safe distance away, or gingerly climbed over slippery rock pools, helping to collect crabs and seaweed as the salt spray of the sea made the hairs on the back of her neck stand on end.

     

                There were many hot baths and days by the fire as well, Kara overly attentive as she tried to make up for leaving Lena behind. She knitted her more socks and gifted her with more pearls she’d pried from oysters on her trip, recounting the tedious meetings with minor Lords and Ladies who paid homage to her, insisting they remain in their dwellings for Midwinter so they could keep watch for any Rogues raiding along the borderlands. Lena’s annoyance thawed and she was more pleased than she cared to admit that she was reunited with her wife, although there was a strange undercurrent of tension between them.

                

                That tension only seemed to grow as the following week dragged on until, eventually, the day of Midwinter arrived, the sun rising late and the sky so dark it seemed a deep navy with the heavy cloud cover. It rained all morning, the tide crashing in and the main hall of Krypton filled with milling Waterfolk as they arrived in clothes of blues and greys, locals drawn away from the inlets, streams and little lakes they holed themselves up near in the long winter months. There were others there as well, her friends and a few fae from other elements, all of them honouring the day no matter their power, and Lena stayed out of the way for the most part. Hidden away in her room, she drank tea and ate porridge and let Andrea braid her hair as the Unseelie made herself scarce.

     

                A new dress had been made for Lena, little seed pearls combined with gold to embroider lilies of the valley on the deep green wool. The flowers covered the bodice and trailed down over the top of the outer skirt, which buttoned down to her waist before it parted similarly to the wide sleeves slashed to the elbows to reveal the ivory and gold brocade of the underlayer. Lena had anticipated a relatively quiet and respectful day, given the apparent solemnity and austerity of the Seelie Court, in comparison to the Unseelie, but apparently, there was still the expectation to feast.

     

                With that came the necessity for her to fit the part of Unseelie Princess and wife of a Seelie Lady of the Waterfolk, and Lena endured the long process of Andrea ensuring she wouldn’t be found lacking in any way. There was the chemise and then the heavily brocaded underlayer, before she was helped into the thick wool of the top layer, sleeves widely draping and skirts splaying to reveal the brocade beneath as the pearl buttons down the front were quickly fastened. Then there was a heavy velvet cloak on top in a deeper shade of green, elegantly draped and fastened with a golden broach, and a circlet of gold with emeralds and even more pearls, these ones larger and, unknown to her, gathered by Kara’s hands to make a gift of the circlet to her. Her hair was braided with gold and rings were slid onto her fingers before Lena was deemed presentable enough, her cheeks and lips faintly stained with berry juice, although she was sure the cold would’ve bitten them pink for her in no time.

     

                Once deemed ready, she swept across the hallway to Kara’s room to roll her eyes and grumble but stifled any grumbling as she watched Kelly braid Kara’s hair for her. There were pieces of sea glass and shells amidst the silver and Kara was wearing the same circlet Lena had first seen her in when they wed. Her dress was a far cry from the silken dress she’d wed her in though, not clinging to her like running water this time but pooling about her in sturdy wool, the brocade beneath white and sky blue, while the outer layer of it was a royal blue, silver thread, diamonds and quartz beaded around the hem and cuffs like tide marks.

     

                Kara glanced sideways at Lena as she tried to remain still, Kelly’s fingers deftly weaving in the last of the shells, and Lena saw her cheek dimple. Waiting patiently for them to finish, Lena ran her fingers over her heavy skirts in a soothing manner as she paced a few steps. When her sister-in-law finished, she slipped past, murmuring she needed to finish getting herself ready, Lena cleared her throat as she watched Kara don a velvet robe buckle on her sword belt, sword attached.

     

                “Well … this is a lot more finery than I imagined for the occasion.”

     

                “Water is the element of winter.”

     

                “I know, I just remember you giving the Unseelie a lot of shit for their debauchery during Mid-autumn, and that was my element’s time of year,” Lena reminded her with a quick grin. 

     

                Humming, Kara slipped silver rings adorned with diamonds, sapphires and turquoise onto her fingers and then plucked another from the collection, turning to Lena. “There is some revelry, of course, but not nearly as much debauchery. Here, for you.”

     

                As she neared Lena, she reached for her hand and slid a ring onto the forefinger of her left hand. The ring was gold, with delicately woven vines and leaves on the band and a polished piece of green stone set in the centre. It wasn’t an emerald but Lena smiled faintly as she met Kara’s eyes.

     

                “Nephrite. You remembered.”

     

                “I remember everything you tell me. Do you like it?”

     

                “Yes, it’s beautiful. Thank you.”

     

                Cheeks dimpling as her eyes creased at the corners, Kara smoothed her warm thumb over the ring and Lena’s finger, almost absentmindedly. Mouth opening and closing, Lena felt a little awkward as she cringed.

     

                “I don’t have a gift for you though. Sorry.”

     

                “Your presence is enough of a gift.”

     

                Lena let out a quick laugh and then gave Kara a quick once over. “I haven’t seen you in a dress in a while.” 

     

                “Mm, they’re not so practical during wartimes - or for fishing.”

     

                “You look … nice.”

     

                Kara’s smile grew a fraction and she gave Lena an appraising look before her smile widened even further. “You look like the first flower of spring.”

     

                Bowing her head to kiss Lena’s knuckles, Kara straightened and tucked Lena’s arm into the crook of her elbow. Walking arm-in-arm, Lena felt that tension again, perhaps to a greater degree now, the compliments, the gifts, the casual affection and contact that become increasingly commonplace. Their relationship was so odd, being wed under duress, thrown together and forced to get along in their unusual circumstances, and yet there was a genuine fondness there that verged on something else, and a frustration that made them bicker and find each other’s weak spots as well. Lena had increasingly felt the wary inevitability that they were bound to either fuck or fall out, walking the delicate line between the two possibilities.

     

                Leading her wife downstairs, Kara ducked her head in close to whisper to her, a hasty preparation for what was to come next. Lena had already been somewhat briefed on the number of people attending, all of them there to pay homage to Kara, welcomed with a sip of water and a pinch of salt, but she felt uncomfortable by the number of eyes on her as they entered the great hall on the lower levels of Krypton. Not all of the stares were friendly and Lena read more than one disapproving look as her Earthfolk dress was taken in, a few murmurs exchanged and glances at the short tips of her ears. 

     

                The large driftwood chair at the north end of the room, back to the sea, was for Kara to take and she let go of her wife’s arm to lower herself onto the smooth worn wood. Lena sat on a small chair beside Kara, hands folded in her lap and quiet as she watched. Fae trickled forward, one by one, kneeling before their liege and exchanging niceties as Lena listened, watching as a sack of barley and a bag of salt was gifted to each person by Kara, vital necessities for the curing of food and enough sustenance for the winter.

     

                It seemed endless, and Lena barely spoke more than a few words, and then only to those she knew, sitting rigidly beside her wife as she reevaluated her previous surprise that there was more finery than she’d anticipated. It was thoroughly dull to sit and listen to the same platitudes exchanged, water and salt shared and greetings extended as Kara warmly listened to her subjects, most of whom she’d known since her childhood. As bored as Lena was, she held up her end of things without complaint, cold and wary of the sea at her back, the wind snagging her hair as she tried not to shiver in the cold. That was all she needed, for them to think she was some frail, spoiled Princess of the Unseelie. 

     

                Eventually, it was over and Kara rose to her feet, extending a hand towards Lena. They didn’t look at each other as Lena took it and rose to her feet, feeling Kara’s warm fingers tighten around her cold ones. Pausing to raise her wife’s fingers to her lips, Kara glanced at her through her lashes as she gently placed a kiss, for the benefit of everyone else in the room, and then escorted Lena upstairs and out onto the expanse of grass outside the main entrance to Krypton.

     

                Long tables had been set with an abundance of seafood and other dishes, drinks already being passed about and more fae than Lena had been around in a long time milling about in groups or sitting on the damp grass as they conversed with neighbours and old friends. Alex handed Lena a cup of hot cider and she murmured her thanks as she took a sip, eyeing the platters of salmon, fresh oysters, scallops, and smoked mussels. There were fresh loaves of bread baked that morning and an assortment of cheeses alongside venison with rowan jelly and slow-roasted lamb with preserved lemons, roasted chickens and potatoes in butter and little honey cakes and fruit pies. 

     

                As the others dispersed to converse with familiar faces, Lena was joined by Sam, who sipped blackcurrant wine at her elbow, dressed in fire tones and a little more reserved, given her half status in both Courts. No one was discourteous to her but there was a notable lack of warmth in any greetings afforded to her, which was similarly doled out to Lena as well, so obviously out of place and aloof, even to the most amenable of Kara’s people.

     

                Thankfully it was the shortest day of the year, so the afternoon had limited daylight and allowed Lena to slink into the shadows of the long limestone building and nurse her second drink alone. She’d picked at some of the food and watched her wife dance with her friends, reeling to the sounds of flutes and harps, insisting she wasn’t jealous as she brooded in the shadows, the stretch of grass illuminated by lit braziers dotted about. 

     

                When it started to rain, Sam excused herself inside, leaving Lena to her own devices, considering slipping away as well until she noticed the absence of her wife. Kara had not bypassed her to walk through the open doorway of her halls, that much Lena was sure of, and she looked through the darkness of late evening as she tried to spot Kara, wondering if she had missed her amidst the others dressed in their finery. The last time she remembered seeing her was when her wife had tried to coax her to dance with her and accepted Lena’s reluctance and fetched her another drink before vanishing again. That must have been an hour ago perhaps.

     

                Drifting away from the revelry, skirting the length of the building as the conversation, laughter and music quietened somewhat, Lena hugged her cloak around herself as she listened to the crash of the sea. And then she knew where Kara would be; somewhere peaceful and alone, where she would be able to listen to the sea and escape the crowd of people she’d spent all day talking to. Deliberating over whether she should disturb her or not, Lena still found her feet carrying her forward, and she shivered in the drizzle as her breath hung in the air before her.

     

                Salt carried on the wind and the grass cushioned her footsteps as she followed the familiar curve of the cliffside to the shadowed temple in the distance. It was far enough away that she very quickly couldn’t hear anything but the howl of the wind and the crash of the waves as she walked onwards, descending through wet dunes and long seagrass until she reached the soft-worn limestone and stepped inside. 

     

                She heard Kara’s heartbeat before she even made it inside, the sound warming her slightly as she tried to be quiet. The sight of her wife’s kneeling form near the edge of the water, waves lapping against the limestone edge, made Lena pause momentarily, and she could tell by the way Kara’s head was angled slightly that she’d heard her arrival. She had shed her dress and jewellery and her chemise was a ghostly white in the dark.

     

                “I thought I’d find you here,” Lena said with faint amusement, her voice carrying in the cavernous temple as she slowly padded closer to her wife.

     

                Without looking up, Kara arranged a couple of small bowls in front of her. “For me, this is a sacred place. It’s where I feel most at ease.”

     

                “I know, that’s why I thought I’d find you here.”

     

                “Am I so predictable?”

     

                “No, I just know you.”

     

                The truth of her response made them both fall silent for a moment, absorbing that piece of information, that Lena knew her wife well enough to know where she would be when she couldn’t find her. She could have checked Kara’s bedroom first, or the coves to the east of Krypton, or the curve of shoreline between Kara’s ancestral home and the beginnings of the cliff face where the temple was. But she had gone straight there, knowing her wife would be inside the quiet peace of the old quarry.

     

                Clearing her throat, Lena continued to move in an arc, watching her in the gloom of the temple, the roaring of the sea keeping her away from the edge as her skin prickled with wariness. Her curiosity was too strong though and she slowed to a stop, head cocked to the side as she eyed the bowls, unable to make out the contents of them in the faint moonlight filtering in past the statues.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “I’m keeping the old ways,” Kara murmured, her golden hair spilling around her back and shoulders as she bowed her head. “It is midwinter. This is the season associated with water, so it is particularly special to the Waterfolk. I honour all seasons, but there are more meaningful offerings for me at this time of year. It is a time of reflection, of turning inwards to deepen our understanding of ourselves and reveal that which is hidden from us in this time of cold and darkness, to then be reborn in the spring, rested and restored with the tranquillity of a flowing river as time passes through to the next season.”

     

                “Oh. Is it a secret, or will you teach me?”

     

                Raising her head, her circlet gone, resting on top of the folded robe and outer layers of her dress beside her, Kara looked mildly surprised. Lena could see something dotting her skin and drifted closer, toying with the rings on her fingers as she took in Kara’s pensive expression, deliberating for a moment.

     

                “It’s no secret so I will teach you,” her wife conceded with a shallow nod, “but you would not like to participate fully in this ritual, I think. It involves submerging oneself in water to purify the body but we will make adjustments for you.”

     

                Smiling slightly, Lena nodded, “thank you.”

     

                “Kneel,” Kara said, gesturing across from her.

     

                Sinking onto the cold, damp stone, Lena’s glance shifted to her right, where the water lapped at the stone steps descending into the sea. She shivered involuntarily and Kara reached out to pick up her right hand, her touch warm and calloused.

     

                “Do not fear, I will keep the waves at bay for you,” she quietly reassured her, turning Lena’s hand in her own, cradling it in her palm as she smoothed a thumb over Lena’s fingers to flatten them. Her blue eyes were dark in the dim light, but no less piercing as their gazes met. “Much like mid-autumn, there is a blood offering. If I may?”

     

                Nodding, Lena watched her pick up a tiny paring knife, similar to one she’d watched Kara deftly shuck oysters with but looking a little more ornamental. In her wife’s hand, it was a small thing, the handle inlaid with fragments of shells and sea glass, and she made a small cut in the fleshy part at the base of Lena’s thumb, her blood seeming black in the dark as it welled up. As Kara set the knife down, Lena spotted a small cut on her hand from her offering.

     

                “You must give it to the water; the salt will make it hurt.”

     

                Moving Lena’s hand, making her lean over to reach, Kara dipped it into the water and Lena pressed her lips together, stifling a grunt of pain at the sudden sting of the cut as her blood mingled with the sea over the lip of the steps. The water was freezing, numbing Lena’s hand quickly after the initial sting, soaking into the flared cuff of her dress until Kara pulled her hand out, cradling her hand gently as she raised it and pressed a kiss to the cut before letting go. 

     

                Leaning over, Kara cupped her hands and filled them with water from the churning sea, murmuring for Lena to close her eyes as she pushed herself up on her knees, spilling water over her wife’s upturned face. It ran down Lena’s brow and cheeks, saltwater settling into the corner of her mouth and eyes and dripping into her lap. The cold sensation on her already damp skin made her shiver and she curled her hands into tight fists in the wool of her dress skirts.

     

                Clearing her throat, Kara shifted a little restlessly as Lena opened her eyes to look at her, noticing the way her wife avoided meeting her stare as she busied herself with a bowl of what looked like little periwinkle flower petals.                 “Periwinkles symbolise purity so they’re used in this ritual. It is customary to press them to your cheeks and ears.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “It is only that your ears … they will be sensitive to touch.”

     

                “I’m aware,” Lena lightly replied, giving her a crooked smile. “It’s fine.”

Meticulous with her work, Kara was silent and Lena leaned in, keeping still as she braced herself against her wife’s thighs, hardly daring to breathe as Kara worked carefully.

When their eyes met, Kara held her gaze, and she could see a trace of apprehension in Kara’s eyes. It almost felt intimidating to be so close to her wife, hands splayed on her thighs, feeling the warmth of her through the cotton of her chemise, but Lena kept her gaze steady.

     

                “Salt is also used to purify,” Kara explained, reaching out. “Open.”

Placing the salt crystals on Lena’s tongue, Kara met her gaze as Lena’s mouth instinctively closed around her fingers, the salt dissolving as the bitterness of it filled her mouth. She should have pulled back but she didn’t, the two of them kneeling so close to each other, Lena’s hands on Kara’s thighs, Kara’s fingers pressed between Lena’s lips, and Lena knew at that moment that she wanted her. And if she wanted Kara, she knew she would have her.

     

                A moment later, Kara withdrew her hand and Lena swallowed the mouthful of salt as her wife shifted away from her. Perhaps it was because she’d already had a few drinks to make her more susceptible to act on her thoughts, or perhaps it was because Kara had been touching her ears, an altogether maddening sensation, or better yet, maybe it was the urge that had been there for some time, but Lena pursued her as Kara moved back.                 Still with surprise, Kara didn’t respond to the kiss for a moment but then she seemed to sink into it, her shoulders slumping as her lips parted. Emboldened as Kara returned the kiss, Lena ran her tongue over Kara’s lower lip, tasting rain and salt, and felt Kara’s hand cup her cheek, warm and strong as the kiss lingered. 

     

                Pressing herself closer, Lena climbed onto Kara’s lap, straddling her as she cupped her face in her hands, fingers brushing the tips of Kara’s ears. The sound of her wife gasping into her mouth made Lena’s stomach clench and she traced her fingertips down the side of Kara’s throat, feeling her arms wrap around her. Lifting her with ease, Kara shifted them so that she laid Lena down, hovering over her as she gave her a searching look.

     

                Resting on her elbows, her chest rising and falling quickly, Lena didn’t move for a moment before she reached for the short row of seed pearl buttons on the front of the outer layer of her gown. Freeing her arms from it, Lena reached for the ties at the front of her brocade underlayer and pulled them loose, Kara working the embroidered skirts up and pulling the whole thing over Lena’s head, leaving her shivering in her chemise at the sudden cold. 

     

                Kneeling between her legs, Kara gave her a piercing look and Lena breathed shallowly as she waited with bated breath, before her wife removed her boots and socks for her, setting them safely aside, and then cupped the back of Lena’s calf and ran her palm up her leg as she loomed over her, fingers skating over her recent scar, courtesy of the arrow. Relief that her advances weren’t about to be rebuffed washed through Lena, and she met Kara’s kiss with an almost desperate need for her, her hands on Kara’s thighs again, ghosting upwards beneath her chemise, over her ass, to the small of her back, before Kara paused to remove it. 

     

                Lena wished she had a moment to drink in the sight of her but they were otherwise too preoccupied, her own chemise slipping off a moment later and Kara’s mouth kissing the curve of her throat, the ridges of her collarbones, as her fingers dug into her thighs. Grasping a fistful of blonde hair, Lena closed her eyes and basked in the feeling of Kara’s touch, the anticipation of it leaving her slightly breathless. It had admittedly been a long time, and perhaps she was desperate, but she felt as if she might explode if her wife didn’t fuck her quickly. Her patience was too thin to draw it out, for them to savour it, and she almost found herself pleading but had more dignity than that. 

     

                If her impatience was evident, Kara didn’t give in to her whims, taking her time as she lightly touched all of Lena’s scars from the injuries she’d sustained since arriving in the Courts, her mouth warm and soft as she kissed the one on her shoulder, working her way down. Of course, Lena knew Kara was good with her hands but it added another layer to the meaning as her wife touched her, first tentatively, gauging her response, and then bolder as she gained more confidence in Lena’s assent.
