Neither of them said a word, and Lena didn’t think she could feel her feet as she shivered, her clothes damp from the fog and the chill of night, her stomach tying itself into knots as she cringed over the inevitable.  

     

                Pausing outside their respective doorways, the awkward tension of unfinished business hanging between them, their eyes met before Lena quickly looked away. 

     

                “Goodnight,” she whispered.

     

                “Goodnight. We shall … talk again soon.”

    Chapter 26

                A rough shake abruptly tore Lena from her sleep, an affronted look on her face as she blearily peered through the dark. Andrea was looming over her and Lena frowned, tugging the blankets up to her chin as she closed her eyes. 

     

                “Go away.”

     

                “Your mother is here, which means you need to get up so I can make you presentable. It won’t do to have you running around in your usual state of undress in her presence.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena burrowed deeper into her pillows and blankets, ignoring her attendant. Unfortunately, Andrea still maintained her relative indifference to Lena’s status, heightened by their removal from the Unseelie Court and Lillian’s rigid rules, and Lena found the blankets snatched back, revealing her to the biting cold of her room. Curling into a ball, Lena made a low sound of annoyance at the back of her throat.

     

                “You’re very annoying.”

     

                “The feeling is mutual, Your Highness. Get up.”

     

                “Light a fire first - then I’ll get up.”

     

                Sighing and muttering in Fae, Andrea built up the fire in the brazier and fished out Lena’s dress from Midwinter. It was the finest garment she owned but Lena’s stomach lurched at the sight of it, bolting upright and kneeling in the middle of the mattress as she felt her face flush.

     

                “Not that one!”

     

                “Why not? It is your finest dress; it will make a good impression.”

     

                “I don’t care about a good impression. She can’t stand me; I hate her. Why does it matter?”

     

                “Appearances always matter. Very well, I shall fetch something else.”

     

                Annoyed, Andrea folded the gown and rummaged around in one of the chests Lena had accumulated. She came up with a dress that was moss green, embroidered in silver and little pieces of sea glass and shells beaded into the shapes of water lilies and dragonflies, and Lena was satisfied with that, the heavy wool plainer and sturdy enough to go about her day. More importantly, there were no memories of Kara undressing her attached to it.

     

                Washing her hands and face in the basin with a pitcher of hot water Andrea had brought up for her, Lena endured being dressed warmly in her layers and then had her hair neatly braided and adorned with more sea glass beads, shells and dried flowers found along the sand dunes and fringes of the estuaries and marshlands in the area. Adorned with rings and scented with what Lena was sure was merely saltwater, marking her as if she was one of the Waterfolk, she was deemed presentable enough for breakfast. 

     

                Moving through the halls, she wished she’d donned a cloak to keep the cold at bay as her breath faintly misted before her. Through the open doorways of the north-facing rooms, she could see it was dawn, the light seeping in a milky blue as a fog crept in. As soon as she reached the doorway of the dining room, she became reluctant to go any further thanks to the sight of Lillian sitting at the end of the table, directly across from Kara but with twenty feet between them. 

     

                Breakfast, which was usually a chatty affair, all of Kara’s house guests sitting in pairs or groups at varying spots along the long table, was suddenly tense as Lillian sat alone and Kara’s family and friends all clustered at her end. A chair had been saved for Lena at Kara’s left hand though, and at the prod in her back from Andrea, Lena crossed the threshold and made for her wife. 

     

                “Good morning,” Lena murmured to the room as she tried to ignore the tension.

     

                “Good morning,” Kara greeted her, leaning her head back and looking up as Lena passed behind her chair. “Did you sleep well?”

     

                “Decently.”

     

                “I had thought you would sit with your mother, considering the long time we have been apart,” Lillian called from the opposite end of the room.

     

                Tearing her eyes away from her wife, who was also dressed impeccably, in comparison to her usual practical leggings and billowing shirts, fit for fishing and sailing and swimming, Lena gave Lillian a blank look of indifference. Reaching a hand for Kara, Lena raised her chin a fraction.

     

                “We are in my wife’s halls, my place is at her side. As ever.”

     

                Taking her hand, Kara pressed a kiss to her knuckles and then covered it with her other hand. She raised her eyes to Lena’s, piercing blue and bright with amusement, and Lena felt her stare like a jolt of electricity. Trying not to appear flustered as the memory of their interrupted conversation last night came to the forefront of her mind, Lena took her seat and cleared her throat as she arranged her skirts.

     

                “You look beautiful this morning,” Kara said just loudly enough to be heard by all, pouring tea for Lena and giving her a small smile.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena warily replied as she leaned forward to help herself to some porridge.

     

                Kara reached for it as well, lifting the pot and setting it down closer. “I shall do it,” Kara murmured, spooning some into a bowl for Lena, who gave her a bewildered look.

     

                Her wife had always been attentive, pouring her tea, making sure she had what she liked, but she didn’t serve Lena directly and it was disconcerting. It was surely for the benefit of Lillian’s presence but Lena couldn’t see how it made a difference to have Kara dish up food for her instead of doing it herself. 

     

                Murmuring a quiet thanks, Lena silently spooned porridge into her mouth as the tense silence blanketed them again. She kept glancing sideways, down the long table, eyeing her mother and the hunters who stood behind her shoulders, forbidden from breaking their fast with the rest of them. Lena wondered how Sam felt about the whole ordeal - Andrea too, for that matter, considering they’d both abandoned the Unseelie Court at the first sign of trouble.

     

                “I thought we might go for a walk later on,” Kara suggested as she refilled Lena’s tea.

     

                “Sure. I’ll need to fetch my cloak.”

     

                “There is no need - mine will keep you warm enough.”

     

                Nodding, keeping her eyes on the table, Lena spread honey onto a slice of toasted bread and Kara deftly started to slice a pear, setting the slivers down on a little plate that she nudged closer to Lena. Setting the pear slices over her toast, Lena nodded her thanks and took a bite, eyes glancing up to Kara’s face and away again. The last thing she wanted after their unfinished talk last night was to go for a walk with her and rehash it all again.

     

                Once she was finished, rushing instead of enjoying the languid sort of breakfasts they all preferred, she scooted her chair back and excused herself. Climbing to her feet as she set the scrunched-up napkin on her plate, Lena gave Kara a quick glance as her wife rose from her seat as well, smiling at her as she waited for her to depart. Slowly slightly, Lena frowned and then went on her way, seeking solitude from practically everyone as she tried to mull things over.

     

                Unfortunately, her solitude was short-lived as she idly paced in one of the rooms facing the sea, hearing footsteps behind her. Turning, her mild expression quickly soured as her eyebrows furrowed into a scowl, her mouth flattening with contempt. Lillian swept into the room like it was her home to command, the thin smile on her lips faintly mocking as her cold gaze appraised Lena. She’d washed the dirt away and wore a deep purple dress split for riding, rather plain in comparison to the finery Lena usually saw her in, but no less imposing with her towering height and powerful demeanour. 

     

                Straightening her posture, Lena raised her chin a fraction as she stared down her mother. Neither of them spoke for a moment, staring at each other as the sound of waves breaking against the limestone filled the silence. After a tense minute, Lillian arched an eyebrow as her smile grew a fraction, wandering further inside.

     

                “You look well.”

     

                Lena let out a huff of laughter, rolling her eyes as she averted her gaze. “Is that all you have to say?”

     

                “What is it you would like me to say to you?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena spread her hands slightly. “Maybe a reason why you came here? When we parted, you were about to kill me. Kara chopped your hand off.”

     

                “I have not forgotten,” Lillian replied with steel in her voice. “As I am sure you have not, so it does not bear repeating. As for the reason why I came here … it is as was mentioned last night; we have been run out of Court and seek refuge with kin.”

     

                “Surely anyone else would be preferable.”

     

                “Believe me, I would have sought out another but, alas, I have no other kin. In wake of my son’s betrayal, I am forced to turn to you. If there had been another choice, it would surely have been preferable to this dismal cavern of a home and the wasteful presence of a daughter who would not draw breath if it were up to me.”

     

                Lena was stiff and angry as she curled her hands into fists. “I-”

     

                Footsteps approached the doorway and Kara stepped inside, hands clasped before her as she gave Lillian a flinty look. Standing just inside, Kara didn’t drop her gaze, her anger a slow-burning thing but present nonetheless as she slowly started to move towards Lena, while speaking to Lillian.

     

                “You will speak to her with the respect she is deserving of.”

     

                “What respect is a bastard deserving of?”

     

                “She is a Princess of the Unseelie Court and wife to a Lady of the Seelie Court, and more importantly than either of those, she is a good person, so you will speak to her with the respect that is deserving of or you will seek refuge elsewhere. I don’t believe my Seelie kin will be as welcoming of your kind as I.”

     

                Reaching Lena’s side, pink-cheeked and tense, Kara reached up to cup her wife’s face in her palm while giving her mother-in-law a sideways scowl. Lena’s eyelashes fluttered at the gentle caress of Kara’s thumb over her cheekbone, and she found herself drawn into her touch, leaning into it as she raised a hand to cover Kara’s. Pressing a kiss to her temple, Kara withdrew then, but kept her body facing towards Lena and her hand against her wife’s back, staking her claim.

     

                “You are in my halls now, Your Majesty, and you are most welcome here, but only at my leisure. A surefire way to find yourself adrift once more will be to insult my wife. I suggest you do not attempt it again.”

     

                “Fond of her, are you? A pair well-matched, I think.”

     

                “It seems we are in agreement,” Kara tightly replied. “Our bond has prevailed through turmoil and only grows stronger for it. How fortunate I am to have had a wife such as your daughter picked for me; I do not think I could have picked better myself.”

     

                Lillian’s smirk turned into a sneer and Kara brushed Lena’s hair off her shoulder as she gave her a small smile. “Shall we take some air?”

     

                Nodding, Lena kept her eyes on Lillian, even as Kara unclasped her cloak and draped it around her wife’s shoulders, pinning it securely in place and then fussing with the folds. Kara took her hand then and led her out of the room, leaving Lillian behind as they made for the exit, stepping onto wet sand. They walked a while, Lena withdrawing her hand from Kara’s and watching as her wife walked the tideline, heedless of the salt water that washed over her feet and erased her tracks. Lena watched her from the corner of her eyes, stepping over the straggling line of seaweed, shells and driftwood that marked the highest reach of the water at high tide. It was a clear day, the wind brisk as it blew the clouds clear of the sky.

     

                They didn’t wander too far, a mere ten minutes along the coastline, pausing midway between Krypton and the old quarry, out of earshot of anyone who might be eavesdropping. The roar of the tall waves would have drowned out their voices to all but one standing next to them anyway but Lena was grateful for the relative privacy, tense as she leaned back against the damp cliffside. Kara paced a few steps away from her, facing the sea.

     

                “You don’t need to constantly defend me from her, you know,” Lena murmured, frowning at the grey sea as she folded her arms over her chest. “Her opinion doesn’t actually matter to me, and honestly I can’t stand the woman - I fucking hate her - so why do I care what she thinks?”

     

                Turning, Kara walked over to stand at her side, likewise leaning against the cliffside as she worried her fingertips over slightly chapped lips. After a moment she spoke, her voice low and faintly hoarse.

     

                “I do not defend you because I think that you care what she thinks, only that her spiteful words are untrue and I despise cruelty. It is unnecessary and unwarranted. Also, I believe only good can come from her believing that we have grown closer in our time here.”

     

                With a quick laugh, Lena gave Kara a sideways glance. “It would surprise her to know just how close.”

     

                “Mm, I think it would be best not to reveal the specifics of that to her. It might give her cause to think she could use us as leverage against each other.”

     

                “As if I want anyone to find out anyway.”

     

                “Just because you don’t wish for anyone to know doesn’t mean someone may not find out.”

     

                Rubbing her hands over her gritty eyes, Lena’s expression turned even more brooding as she looked out at the sea, before turning towards Kara, damp sand shifting beneath the movement. Kara’s head was slightly cocked to the side as she studied her wife, expression rather blank, save for a faint tightening at the corners of her mouth.

     

                “Well, the only way they’d find out is if it happened again - and that’s not going to happen.”

     

                Nodding in easy acceptance of Lena’s decision, Kara stared at the sand for a moment before she softly sighed. “As you wish, but … we should finish our conversation from last night.”

     

                “I have nothing more to say.”

     

                “No? You are clearly … frustrated by something, and all I wish is to make sure you’re okay. I made my intentions clear last time, and I accept that you feel differently but you said that you wanted me and then you avoided me and I don’t like to be treated so contrary. It aches somewhat to be subjected to this hot and cold treatment, to not know if I have upset you in some way, or what is amiss between us. I do not wish to talk about sleeping with you again, only your feelings.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes and raked a hand through her hair. “I don’t need to talk about my feelings. Thanks for the concern but it’s not really helping to talk about it more.”

     

                “Then your frustration will only build.”

     

                “I can manage it just fine.”

     

                “At night?”

     

                “That’s no concern of yours,” Lena haughtily murmured.

     

                “Isn’t it? I would think I might be allowed to have some thoughts on my wife thinking about me at night while denying there is anything left wanting between us.”

     

                “I didn’t say I was thinking about you.”

     

                The quick blink of surprise was the only sign of Kara’s wounded feelings and she slowly backed away. Her expression retained its usual softness but her blue eyes were bright with annoyance as the corners of her mouth tugged downwards slightly. Hand propped on the hilt of her sword, she ducked her head in a shallow nod and looked everywhere but at Lena as she swallowed thickly and gestured vaguely in her direction.

     

                “Very well, I will … leave you to your thoughts of others. If you, uh, if you should change your mind regarding your need for conversation … well, you know where to find me.”

     

                Turning, she walked towards the sea, shedding her jacket as her shirt billowed around her, and let the water run over her feet and soak the hems of her pants. She went no further than that though, keeping Lena within easy sight and reach as a precaution. Her care only served to annoy Lena as she ground her teeth, angry at herself, angry at the heat of desire that had crept up on her as they’d stood so close, angry for pushing Kara away when she didn’t want to do that but didn’t know how to let her close without fucking things up. Her fear was deeply rooted in the concern that she might so easily develop feelings for Kara, feelings that she knew wouldn’t be reciprocated, whether Kara wanted to or not.

     

                “You know, this isn’t very easy for me!” Lena shouted, the wind whipping her words away. 

     

                Kara’s sensitive hearing easily picked them up though and she glanced over her shoulder, her cheeks flushed and a furrow between her eyebrows. “No, but you insist on making it harder than it needs to be!”

     

                Storming forwards, Lena crossed the stretch of dull golden sand and stopped a safe distance from the surf as it rushed up the shore. “I’m not doing anything.”

     

                “No, indeed, and that is precisely the problem. Everything is about what you want and when you want it. My own feelings be damned.”

     

                “I- well … that’s not true,” Lena spluttered.

     

                “Is it not? We talk when you wish to talk, we have sex when you wish to have sex, and we spend time together only when you wish to. I am the fool who must suffer for your indecisiveness, waiting for you to seek me out at your convenience. I am the one who must chase after you to see to your hurt feelings or wounded pride.”

     

                “I’ve never asked you to do that.”

     

                “No, you wouldn’t. You’d rather push everyone away instead of letting someone care about you, wouldn’t you?”

     

                A strangled laugh escaped Lena, her breath hanging before her as she breathed quickly, her chest rising and falling and the cold air like a knife to her lungs. “And you’re up to the task are you? You, who will never care about anyone-”

     

                “No, I will never love anyone,” Kara sharply corrected her. “I care for many people, including you, but I cannot love anyone romantically , and that is a great distinction.                 Wading deeper into the sea, up to her knees, Kara angrily set her shoulders and left Lena on the shoreline, knowing her wife couldn’t follow her any further this time. With so much left to say, Lena was brimming with frustration, guilt already nettling her beneath it, and she chafed at the barrier the sea presented, wanting to splash after Kara and continue their silly argument but too afraid to face the water. She wasn’t even sure what the real issue was, only that they were talking around a few different things that made a bigger mess than if they’d just talked directly. The worst part of all was that every word had been true, in some capacity, and she was left dejected on the beach as Kara vanished into the water.

     

                Left wallowing in her building frustration, Lena stood on the beach for a few minutes, arms folded over her chest as she hunched her shoulders before she let out a scathing sound at the back of her throat. Hugging Kara’s cloak tight to her body, she stormed back towards the halls and slipped inside unnoticed. It was still early and she would ordinarily have been at her lessons with the others, passing the time usefully, but she wanted to be alone. Instead, she went up to the stables, seeking the companionship of the horses.

     

                Upstairs, tucked away in the damp stable as the frigid wind, that much stronger so high up, froze her through, she brushed down the horses, one by one, removing dirt and dust, and combed out their tails and manes. It was calming, methodical work and even the smell of manure didn’t bother her after a while, the soft whickering of the horses as they bumped her shoulder with a velvety muzzle sweet as she fed them handfuls of oats and murmured to them. Content with her peace, she spent the rest of the morning there, stewing in her annoyance and guilt and embarrassment. In the end, her words had hurt Kara more than they had satisfied her, and Lena would only hurt herself by driving away the closest person she had to family.

     

                Once she’d had enough, smelling of horse and covered in straw, Lena made her way back inside and washed her face and hands before creeping through the halls, straining her ears to pick up on any sign of Kara. She made it to the kitchen without bumping into her but found Alex instead, using a small knife to deftly gut a sea bream that could only have come from her sister. Lena moved inside and picked up a green apple from the bowl on the long trestle table, rolling it between her palms as she hovered.

     

                “Is something amiss?” Alex asked, her eyes on the fish as she pulled out the murky grey entrails.

     

                Looking up, Lena raised her eyebrows in a mild look of surprise, her voice light but too quick as she responded. “Hm? No. No, I was just … where’s your sister?”

     

                “She has taken a sailboat out. Apparently, the catch will be good today.”

     

                “Oh. Okay. Good.”

     

                “Lena, your mood is one spark away from starting a forest fire,” Alex curtly noted, her knife moving quickly. “If something is amiss, tell me and I shall help you.”

     

                “Nothing is amiss,” Lena softly snapped. “Why does everyone have to get so involved in my feelings? Can’t I just be left alone?”

     

                Setting the knife down, Alex raised her head and gave her a level stare. Cheeks faintly flushed, Lena ground her teeth together as she met her gaze. After a moment, Alex picked her knife back up and slowly started to remove the fins.

     

                “If you wish to be left alone then, by all means, you may go.”

     

                Mouth flattening, Lena lingered a moment longer before she reached out and set the apple back onto the pile. Lifting her skirts a little, she turned and left, hearing the soft click of Alex’s tongue as her sister-in-law carried on filleting the sea bream. 

     

                Wandering about a bit, less cagey now that she knew Kara wasn’t there, she did make a stop by the room with the stone docks and a few little boats bobbing in the current as she double-checked for any sign of her wife on the horizon before continuing on her way to occupy herself. Spending an hour in the library, she managed to translate a chapter of text and filled a few pages with neatly copied glyphs, her penmanship greatly improved over the months since Kelly had first shown her how. It was peaceful and she was undisturbed but still restless.

     

                Her early afternoon wanderings led her to the wine cellar, picking up a jug and unstoppering it as she took a swig. It was sweet blackberry and she lurked in the dim room by herself, sitting on a cask as she ran over her talk with Kara that morning, trying not to wince at her callousness, torn between pushing her away or letting her in. This strange in-between they fell in wasn’t good for either of them, Lena’s contrary moods dictating their relationship for the moment. She hated to admit it but there had been some truth to Kara’s words about her selfishness. 

     

                She was brooding over that when she was discovered. For a moment, she panicked at the thought that it was Kara’s footsteps approaching, but Lena knew her wife’s gait and heartbeat well enough to know the person about to stumble upon her wasn’t Kara. Instead, it was Sam who found her there, dressed warmly with an exasperated look on her face as her hazel eyes gave Lena a quick once over.

     

                “Your absence was noticed at mealtime.”

     

                “I don’t want to see anyone.”

     

                Sam was silent for a moment, taking in the jug in Lena’s hand and grimacing. “You’re not going to get drunk again, are you? It was not enjoyable guarding you in the rain; I abhor the wet.”

     

                Lena snorted, taking another swig of wine and then heavily sighing. “I suppose I shouldn’t. The only thing that could make my mood worse is a nasty hangover in the morning.”

                Sam blinked, wary surprise crossing her face. “You are married.”

     

                “Oh, well, that doesn’t matter. Kara said I’m free to pursue anyone I’d like.”

     

                “You belittle the sanctity of marriage. The vows are not idly said - it is why marriage is rare amongst our kind, meant to be the greatest display of love, an even bigger commitment than having a child.”

                Opening and closing her mouth, Sam smiled gingerly, hazel eyes apologetic. “Forgive my boldness but … have you sought out your wife?”

     

                “I would rather anyone but her,” Lena bit out in English. 

     

                “Oh. That is rather unfortunate then, and dire indeed if you would seek out your mother’s killer first. May I ask what about her offends you so?”

     

                “Everything. Her voice, her face, her laugh, her smile, her touch, her attitude, her eyes, her-”

     

                “A rather extensive list. She is also very beautiful, and kind - she has been a friend to me for many years in my travels between Courts, always so understanding of my plight - I wonder if perhaps your ire with her may be solved with words between you two.”

                “You are talking to me.”

     

                “Well … you’re less annoying than she is.”

     

                “Ah, so she has done something to anger you.”

     

                “No, she is just so- so insufferably attentive. I would prefer it if she was not so kind. Maybe I’d like her less then - that would solve some of my problems.”

     

                Realising she’d said too much, Lena stiffened slightly and cleared her throat, trying to feign indifference as she ran a hand through her hair. “Regardless, I’ll just have to endure it I suppose.”

     

                “A word of advice, Your Highness, it is better to have someone be attentive than negligent. I was adopted as a child and my mother was less than kind to me.                 Quietly scoffing, Lena’s mouth twisted derisively. “Well, now you’re annoying me too. Just as well; I don’t actually want to sleep with you.”

     

                “Yes, I sensed that you did not.”

     

                Humming disconcertingly, Lena was quiet for a moment before she narrowed her eyes suspiciously and jerked her chin at Sam. “And who are you courting?”

     

                Freezing, her eyebrows rose a fraction and Sam gave her a faint smile. “Is it not so obvious?”

     

                “What, Andrea? Oh. I thought maybe you’d just banded together as the only Unseelie here.”

     

                “Surely we would have cleaved to you in that instance.”

     

                “Haven’t you? She wakes me up whenever she feels like dressing me like a doll, and then you … well, you’re a second shadow most of the time.”

     

                Wariness flickering across Lena’s face, she felt her stomach lurch with sudden panic. “You, uh, you haven’t been spying on me, have you?”

     

                “I only keep you within sight when you are not accompanied outside of these walls. Your wife is usually at your side, so no, I have not spied on you. You may rest assured your arguments remain private between you two alone if that is your concern.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                “You should eat,” Sam suggested.

     

                Nodding distractedly, Lena was left with much to think about as her shadow slipped out of the room and left her to her thoughts. Her stomach rumbled, a reminder of her missed lunch, and she reluctantly found herself taking the hunter’s advice, slipping into the kitchen to take an apple again, this time taking a bite out of it. Sitting at the trestle table, as near to the fire as she could get, she ate her apple and ferreted out nuts and then a bowl of soup from the pot hanging over the low-burning flames. No one disturbed her, off to pass the time how they pleased, but she still didn’t linger long, paranoid that Lillian would seek her out if she heard her. Their encounter that morning was just about all that Lena could stomach.

     

                Returning to her room, she ended up falling asleep beneath a pile of blankets, the blackberry wine making her more relaxed. She slept soundly, perhaps more so than she had in a while, and probably would've slept right through the evening if she hadn’t been disturbed. As it was, she was roughly awoken for the second time that day by her irate attendant, jolting awake so suddenly that her hand went beneath the pillow for the dagger that was still belted at her waist.

     

                Breathing heavily as she became aware of her surroundings, Lena raked her hair out of her face and gave Andrea a livid look. “Jesus Christ, do you have to do that?”

     

                “Do you have to undo all my hard work? Mucking out stables in your finest clothes,” Andrea shot back, stepping away from the bed and giving Lena a disapproving look. “You smell of horse and wine and your mother is awaiting your presence at dinner.”

     

                Rubbing her tired eyes, Lena fought back a yawn, disgruntlement creasing her face. “Well, I’m not going to dinner.”

     

                “It has been decided that you are , so I ask you to make it easier for us both and bathe yourself quickly.”

     

                Huffing, Lena tore back the rest of the blankets and stumbled out of bed. Andrea had brought hot water and a clean towel for her and tugged at Lena’s clothes as the Princess snapped at her in return, both of them bickering and getting nowhere. She had managed to do little more than undress and wet her hair, both women cursing each other in as many languages as they knew when Kara appeared in the doorway. She’d changed from her earlier clothes into an elegant blue dress, beaded and embroidered and making Kara appear younger and softer, her hair braided and a circlet of her Ladyship on her brow.

     

                “Is something amiss here?”

     

                “Your obstinate wife has made a mess of things, and I find myself trying to salvage it as best as possible.”

     

                “That does sound like her,” Kara agreed with faint amusement, her eyes flitting to Lena and then away again. “You needn’t offer her your help; she is grown enough to know her own mind. I dare say it will make life easier for us all if Lena may do as she pleases.”

     

                Giving Kara an equally withering look, Andrea clicked her tongue and shook her head, before tossing the chosen dress onto the bed. Kara stepped aside to let her stalk out of the room and there was a beat of silence, wives staring at each other as Lena held her towel to herself, dripping water onto the floor. Opening her mouth to speak, Kara decided against it and turned, walking off without another word.

     

                Muttering darkly to herself, Lena hastily finished washing as she shivered, pulled on her underclothes and struggled into the layers of the dress alone. Her hair hadn’t held onto the finery of the morning well but she managed to braid it, adorning glass and shells and all, into something she hoped was adequately presentable, before lacing on her shoes. Sighing as she resigned herself to another awkward meal, she slowly made her way downstairs.

     

                Upon entering the dining hall, she saw that someone had picked fresh flowers interspersed between lit candles, the floor strewn with sweet herbs that were crushed underfoot, and Lena warily looked around. Kara was settled in her customary chair, Lillian once again at the far end directly across from her, and Lena quickly took her seat at Kara’s side.

     

                She smelled roasted meat and took in the bowls of mashed turnips in butter, peas cooked with mint and potatoes roasted with the skin on. There was not as much fish as usual, she assumed for her mother’s taste, and Lena was glad for the quail and duck she saw, helping herself to pieces as a tense silence blanketed the meal. It was worse than it had been at breakfast, and she almost wished she’d taken Kara’s subtle dig as a free pass to miss dinner, but she’d come anyway, meek as she kept her head down, waiting for the chance to ask her wife for a moment alone. 

     

                It never came, Kara finishing her meal quickly and then murmuring her apologies as she took her leave. Lena couldn’t remember Kara ever leaving the table with everyone still eating and was left looking after her with surprise and a flicker of panic as she felt her opportunity slipping from her grasp. It was awkward but it would remain awkward between them until she swallowed her pride and apologised for her words.

     

                Firmly deciding to wait outside her room for her instead, Lena lingered over her dinner and then excused herself as soon as Alex and Kelly left, following in their footsteps. They made for different parts of the halls though and Lena ducked into the kitchens to make a cup of tea, carefully carrying it upstairs and slowing outside the doorway to Kara’s room. There was no sound of her inside but Lena was determined to wait, hovering a while, then pacing back and forth, then slipping downstairs to brew a fresh cup of tea when the original one cooled.

     

                Back and forth she went, eventually taking up a seated position as she leaned against the cold wall outside the open doorway. She didn’t think Kara would mind if she’d gone inside and made herself comfortable on a chair, but Lena didn’t want to be too presumptuous. She wasn’t planning on ambushing her, merely showing that she could wait for Kara to seek her out, had the patience to be uncomfortable for a while and not give in to comfort at the expense of patching things up. Her leaning against the wall led to idle pacing, and then sitting on the cold stone floor, and eventually, slumped against the base of the wall as she fell asleep waiting with the latest cup of tea in hand.

     

                It was almost midnight when Kara retired to her rooms, quietly padding down the hallway in plain work clothes and slowing at the curled-up figure waiting outside her doorway. She suppressed a sigh and walked over to Lena, watching her for a moment before she stooped down to gently shake her awake. Lena jolted awake with surprise, blinking slowly for a moment as she stared up at Kara before she remembered her purpose.

     

                “Go to bed,” Kara quietly instructed her.

     

                “I was waiting for you,” Lena hoarsely confessed, rubbing her tired eyes with a fist before she staggered to her feet, tea sloshing over the rim of the cup. 

     

                “Yes, I heard you.”

     

                Lena winced at the implication that Kara had heard her outside her room and had delayed returning to it to avoid her. Wiping tea off her fingers in the skirts of her dress, Lena cleared her throat and raised the cup.

     

                “I … brought you tea. Your favourite. I- well, it was hot when I brought it, um … that was a while ago though.”

     

                She made no mention of the frequent trips back and forth to brew a fresh cup to ensure it would be hot when Kara deigned to grace her with her presence. Lena hadn’t anticipated dozing off for however long it had been, letting the tea grow cold.

     

                “Thank you,” Kara murmured, somewhat curt.

     

                Still, she took the cup and had a sip anyway, lingering in the hallway for a moment. Casting Lena a quick glance, she walked into her room and Lena was unsure whether she was invited inside or if it was a silent dismissal. Either way, she had some things to say and followed Kara in. 

     

                Her wife set the cup down on a side table and rinsed her hands and face in a basin of cold water before pausing and then stripping off her dirty clothes. A few feet behind her, Lena watched the way the muscles of her bare back shifted as she shed her shirt, a warm flush moving through her as she looked down. 

     

                “I wanted to apologise … if you have the time to listen.”

     

                She watched Kara’s back stiffen. No response was forthcoming and Lena’s mouth thinned as she wrung her hands before she took a step forward. Pressing her palm to Kara’s shoulder, Lena felt the heat of her and had to stop herself from pressing her whole body against her warmth.

     

                “Hey,” she whispered, “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Alright.”

     

                Bending to pull off her pants, full of sand and soaked through, Kara managed to shrug off Lena’s touch without it seeming intentional. Fingers running down her back as she followed her wife’s movement, Lena sighed softly and stepped back, watching Kara change. She could smell the sawdust of wood shavings, and the tang of pine sap on her skin, almost eclipsing the salt and rain that always clung to Kara.

     

                “You were right, I’ve been … selfish. I know it’s not a good enough excuse but … with the way I grew up, no one was ever nice to me and I don’t- I don’t like feeling vulnerable and that’s how I feel when you’re there, making sure I’m okay, trying to get me to be honest about things. I just- it’s not how I’m built. It scares the shit out of me - so do you. I care about you, and it will never end well between us, just like it’s never ended well for me with anyone. I’ve only ever had myself, do you understand that? Only myself to rely on. And now I have you and I don’t know how I’m supposed to let you in without risking being hurt so I shut you out, and I don’t mean to but I don’t know any other way to be. I’m frightened.”

     

                Kara turned slowly, tugging down the hem of her chemise as she grimaced. There was a spark of frustration in her eyes though and she stepped in closer, raising her hand and letting her knuckles ghost over Lena’s cheek. 

     

                “You needn’t be frightened of me. I’m not going to hurt you or leave you; I’m trying to make sure you’re well, that you are … happy. I sometimes feel I don’t know what you’re thinking at all. It frightens me to think I am not looking after you well enough.”

     

                “No,” Lena murmured, closing her eyes. “No, you are … you are too kind. You do too good of a job, it makes me feel … overwhelmed. I’m not used to people like you and the closer we get, the more I- it makes me panic to think about how much I stand to lose now. I like you, Kara, but I don’t want to get closer to you. I’m afraid of what might come of it.”

     

                “Nothing can come of it, you know that it wouldn’t. I don’t say that out of any selfish desire to have you in my bed again - that is not important to me - only to assure you that you have nothing to fear by opening up to me. There is so much frustration in you, it is plain to see. It will not benefit you to let it fester. I only wish to help.”

     

                “I asked Sam to have sex with me,” Lena blurted out, looking at Kara as she watched surprise cross her face. She winced slightly and wrinkled her nose before elaborating in the wake of Kara’s silence. “She said no, which is good because I didn’t actually want to have sex with her. I just- yes, I’m frustrated - you are the root of my frustration.” 

     

                Lena laughed, pressing the heels of her palms to her eyes, the laughter trailing off to a groan. “I want you , of course I do. You and I both know it, no matter what I say, and of course it’s you that I think of but … that’s preferable to having you because that’s just one more thing that could hurt. Only it frustrates me more and I wish I hadn’t followed after you on Midwinter because maybe I wouldn’t be feeling this way, except … I don’t think it started on Midwinter.”

     

                Kara finally spoke, her voice low and cautious. “No, I don’t think it started then either.”

     

                Ducking her head as a smile twitched her lips, Lena swallowed thickly, a shakiness in her chest. Her whole body felt flushed, brimming with restlessness, and she was tired but her mind was too alert for her to go to bed. She knew that much. Rubbing her forehead, she was quiet as the silence thickened. With a soft sigh, Kara stepped forward and wrapped her in a gentle hug.

     

                “You think too much - that is the root of your frustration.”

     

                “Maybe. I’m sorry for being an ass though.”

     

                “You are not an ass, you are just … you isolate yourself too much. I find it hard to reach you.”

     

                “It’s by design.”

     

                “Well, you needn’t do that anymore. I will keep my distance.”

     

                “I don’t want that either. I feel lonely otherwise.”

     

                “Then tell me a good middle ground and I will meet you there.”

     

                “What about what you want?”

     

                Kara hesitated and Lena shifted slightly in her embrace, almost cheek to cheek with her, feeling Kara’s nose skim her face as she turned her head. “I have made my stance clear on all fronts. And it is not important to me, as mentioned. Although-”

     

                She trailed off and Lena withdrew from her hug, holding her waist at arms’ length. “What?”

     

                Kara’s eyes were dark in the dimness of her room, a storm at dusk, and Lena’s throat was dry as she held her gaze. Licking her lips, Kara hesitated and then let out a small laugh, reaching up to gently squeeze Lena’s chin.

     

                “Although, I am glad you did not have sex with Sam. I would hate to think it was just me you were opposed to and … I would be horribly jealous.”

     

                “I think I knew that,” Lena admitted, her brow creasing with displeasure. “I think … I was trying to find a way to hurt you. I’m glad I came to my senses before I could.”

     

                “Yes, I’m glad too.”

     

                Lena nodded, toying with her fingers as she hovered with uncertainty, her pulse quick, her mouth dry and stomach knotted, and her wife giving her a piercing look the entire time. Feeling a little flushed, she faltered as silence descended and softly cleared her throat as she forced her eyes to the floor.

     

                “Right, well … I should let you sleep.”

     

                As she turned to leave, Kara snagged her arm to stop her, mouth opening and closing for a moment before she softly spoke. “Thank you for the tea.”

     

                A crooked smile quirked Lena’s lips as her eyebrows furrowed together in amusement, and she nodded, pausing before leaning in to kiss her wife on the cheek. “Goodnight, Kara.”

    Chapter 27

                Four days later, Lena was feeling marginally less awkward around her wife, although they had yet to speak further about what she’d divulged to Kara, but was still brooding about the place, stewing in her discontentment as she sought her own company in the library, or on the grassy stretch of land with a bow and a quiver of arrows when the weather allowed. She could sense Kara tiptoeing around her, her quiet relief that things had been laid bare, but still wary of crossing a line that Lena wasn’t quite sure was there anymore. 

     

                She would have said as much, but that would have required admitting that she wanted it erased altogether, complicating her life a little more in the process. It was frustrating and she knew her morose silence wasn’t pleasant to be around as she pitied herself, suffering for her own cowardice. 

     

                Breakfast had been a quiet affair, refraining from any conversation as she ate quickly and had anticipated a day by the fire, the few days of rain, sleet and storms leaving it dismal and cold beyond the confines of Krypton if outside for too long. She’d taken to games of stones with J’onn once he’d finished poring over his ledgers with Kara, seeking something to occupy her time so her mother couldn’t swoop in to offer snide remarks and unwanted conversation. So far, Lillian’s ambushes had been few but Lena felt uneasy being cooped up inside with the possibility of another encounter in the cards. Escaping from the dining hall as quickly as possible, she hadn’t even made it to the stairs before she was caught.

     

                “Lena,” Kelly quietly called her name, catching her attention and cocking her head to the side as she smiled, beckoning her. “Come for a ride with us.”

     

                Us was Alex, of course, standing behind her wife with an expectant look on her face. Considering rejecting the offer, Lena hesitated and then nodded. At the very least, it would get her away from there, away from the uneasy feeling of her mother lurking about, ready to pounce at any second, watching her every movement. She was already dressed warmly for her brooding by the fire so followed them straight up to the stables, Alex helping to saddle her horse for her before the three of them set off at a walk.

     

                The sky was a stormy grey and she questioned whether it had been a good idea to join them as a light pattering of rain started to fall not fifteen minutes later. None of them turned back though, and she wouldn’t be the one to suggest it, just followed on Alex’s tail as the occasional flash of lightning lit up the sky to the north. They were heading westwards, hooves gouging into soft grass and mud, bloated from too much rain over the past few weeks, and Lena breathed in the salt-laced air as they skirted the marshes, bringing a tinge of moss and trees and rotting plant life to the breeze. She drank it in, eyes closing as the wind bit her cheeks and she felt a little bit of the tension leave her.

     

                Riding for over an hour, picking up the pace a few miles from Krypton, Lena had anticipated nothing but the freeing sensation of racing across the open land on horseback, much the same as the countless rides with Kara, but she was surprised when Kelly made for the overflowing banks a few miles south of where the estuary met the sea. The wetlands that sprawled from the shallow, brackish water teeming with life, the croaks of frogs, warbles of birds and rustling of little mice and shrews scurrying through the reeds and bushes creating an idyllic peacefulness. Sitting astride her horse, Lena looked confused as the other two women dismounted.

     

                “Are we … staying?”

     

                “For a short while,” Kelly said with a reassuring smile. “Come, dismount.”

     

                She steadied Lena’s horse by reaching for the bridle, and Lena’s boots squished into the soft earth. A veil of fog still clung to the damp grass and little hollows and dips in the landscape, everything so green and wet as she looked around, save for the dark expanse of water, an unnerving presence she could have done without, and Lena breathed in the frigid air, her lungs burning and fingers stiff where she’d held the reins tightly.

     

                “What’re we doing here?” she haltingly asked, uncertain now.

     

                Alex unclasped her cloak and spread it out, sprawling on it with a contented sigh, resting on her elbows. “We are enjoying the scenery, sister.”

     

                Frowning, Lena wedged her fingers into her armpits as she crossed her arms. “Oh. Okay.”

     

                “Take a seat. I have mulled wine if you care for some.”

     

                Mouth thinning, Lena rolled her eyes and then sank to a crouch, dismayed as the hem of her cloak pooled in the muddy grass. Alex passed her a wineskin and Lena took a sip, the wine still warm enough compared to the cold of the day. She passed it back and the three of them were quiet for a few minutes, watching the egrets, loons and cormorants on the water, before Lena cleared her throat.

     

                “Did Kara ask you to bring me?”

     

                “No, Kara is not aware you are here,” Kelly informed her.

     

                Wariness flickered through Lena, a cautious doubt she didn’t care to feel stealing over her as she eyed the two women. As far as her trust went in these parts, she didn’t think she had any reason to think Kara’s family would harm her, but Lena could be wrong. As if sensing her sudden panic, Kelly laughed softly, taking the skin from Alex and taking a swig.

     

                “You needn’t worry for your safety. You have nothing to fear from us; we are kin, and you will always have our protection for that.”

     

                “Right,” Lena murmured, unconvincingly.

     

                “You’re here so you can … unwind,” Alex exasperatedly told her. “You have been particularly tense. I would imagine most of it comes from your mother’s presence, but not all. You are entitled to your secrets, of course, if you do not wish to share them, but it is very apparent to all that you have not been in good spirits of late.”

     

                “And, what, you thought a picnic would help?”

     

                “It is not a picnic , but we did think a few hours away from that place might help. Away from the sea, your mother and my sister. You spend entirely too much time with her; I love her greatly but you are bound to bite each other’s head off in your current mood. So, why not enjoy some fresh air? We would have taken you to the forest if we would not be gone too long in the process.”

     

                “Is this an ambush?”

     

                “No! Why do you suspect the worst of us?”

     

                “Don’t take it personally,” Lena unevenly grinned, “I suspect the worst of everyone.”

     

                Kelly handed her the wineskin again, her hand lingering on Lena’s shoulder a moment longer. “Well, we are just trying to be your friend. You have made a poor effort to befriend us, so we will do it for you, even if that means coercing you into a ride with us so we may speak freely.”

     

                “Freely about what?”

     

                Alex was tamping tobacco leaf into the bowl of a pipe and gave Lena a weary look as she held the stem between her lips. Summoning a small flame, she lit it and puffed a few times before blowing a perfect smoke ring. With a flutter of her fingers, Kelly reshaped the smoke into a little bird, making it flap its wings as the wind current carried it higher before she let it go to smoke. Lena watched with a faint softening of amusement in the corners of her eyes and mouth before she met Alex’s brown eyes at the heavy sigh she let out.

     

                “Do you love my sister?”

     

                “What?” Lena exclaimed, loudly enough to startle a thrush from the branches of a gnarled tree nearby. “No. No, of course I don’t.”

     

                Her vehemence, coupled with her English, seemed too defensive, and she found herself spluttering for a moment, annoyance flashing through her. There was an undeniable prickle of panic as well that she didn’t want to acknowledge; paying any notice to it would lead to a line of thought she wanted to avoid. She had to smother the feeling, before it grew, knowing what the cause of her panic was, and why she had resorted to her native language to get her objection out. It would have caught in her throat if she hadn’t.

     

                “Right,” Alex dubiously replied, lounging on her elbows, legs stretched out with her ankles crossed as she smoked. “Will you at least concede that she is beautiful?”

     

                With a scoff, Lena rolled her eyes, resentful as she smiled wryly, her jaw set. “Of course she is. She’s beautiful, she’s smart, funny, likeable even. Far too serious and overbearingly protective but that’s not to her detriment. She’s good at everything and mean to no one, loyal to a fault, and a pain in my ass. She’s … she’s a remarkable woman.” 

     

                “Then what is it about her that deters you from love?”

     

                Spluttering, Lena laughed at the question. “What, am I supposed to force myself to love her because she’s nice?”

     

                “Not at all, only … you two have such a … strange relationship. Of course, your marriage was quite unconventional, but it is not only that. One might be- one might be led to think that you two have … come to love each other. But you deny it.”

     

                “Yeah, misled maybe. Maybe you should speak to your sister and she can set you straight too; we all know she’s not in a rush to fall in love.”

     

                “Yes, but she will fall in love. You see that, do you not? Whether she wills it or not, it will occur and … yes, a tragedy will come of it, but maybe not for decades, centuries even. If you did love my sister, and if she loved you, it would be a shame for the two of you to deny your feelings for each other when there could be many years of happiness to come first.”

     

                “I get what you’re saying but … you’re talking to the wrong person. I’m not in love with Kara. We- look, it’s complicated, and I care for her, I’ll admit that, but she and I … I’m not even going to go there. That’s a whole lot of mess I don’t want in my life. Now, please, leave it alone.”

     

                Her irritable response softened as her voice turned raw, green eyes bright as her heart pounded in her chest. It was meant to be a haughty request but it came out as a desperate plea, Lena’s hands fisting in the split skirts of her dress. Throat tightening against the building pressure in her chest, she couldn’t say anything else.

     

                “Okay,” Kelly whispered, reaching out to take her hand. “How about we shoot instead?”

     

                Kelly shot her wife a cautious look and Alex’s mouth thinned around the stem of her pipe before she put an arm behind her head and laid down, blowing smoke to the sky as she put it to rest. Lena allowed herself to be dragged to her feet, Kelly’s bow and quiver plucked from the ground. Pacing a few steps away, Kelly held her unstrung bow out to Lena, who went through the motions of bending the wood and stringing it, the waxed sinew taut as she ran thumb and forefinger down the length of it. 

     

                Slinging the quiver over her shoulder, Lena kept walking, damp grass underfoot as she scanned their surroundings and chose a suitable target. The weathered trunk of a short ash tree caught her eye and she removed an arrow, knocking it in a smooth, swift motion as she sighted down the shaft. The feathered fletching tickled her cheek as she breathed and then loosed it at the trunk, striking her mark as the arrowhead burrowed into the wood. 

     

                Shooting until she’d emptied the quiver and created a circle of tightly packed arrow shafts and grey fletchings, Lena was comforted by the familiar ache in her muscles, the movements she’d spent hours practising - not perfected yet, but that would come with time - and felt some of the tension dissipate as her mind was solely focused on hitting her mark. 

     

                “You are getting better,” Kelly approvingly told her as she stepped up to her side. “Shall we put your skill to the test? Let us see if you can bag something for dinner.”

     

                “Dinner?” Lena warily replied.

     

                “Yes. What do you think, my love?” Kelly called over her shoulder. “Swan or duck?”

     

                Alex had finished smoking and had her eyes closed as she lay stretched out on her cloak, enjoying the brisk, fresh air. “Duck.”

     

                “I- you want me to shoot a duck?” Lena apprehensively asked. 

     

                “If you are able to hit a moving target.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “What is it?”

     

                Wincing slightly, Lena rubbed the bridge of her nose, feeling a flush creep up her neck. “I don’t know, I just- I’ve never hunted anything before. Never … killed anything.”

     

                “You killed a person,” Alex interrupted.

     

                Cringing, Lena wrinkled her nose as she adjusted her grip on the bow. Looking down at the beautifully carved wood, she felt a pang of unease. Kelly gave her back a pat and then started towards the estuary, where birds congregated to gracefully glide across the surface of the water, nesting amongst the reeds and in the trees, dipping in and out as they hunted small fish, or just wheeled about overhead. There were plenty of ducks but Lena still felt uncertain about it.

     

                “That one there. Go for one that is moving; it’ll be good practice.”

     

                The one pointed out to her was an ordinary brown, quacking softly as it paddled along and occasionally dipped its beak in to eat weeds and roots that had ended up in the water. Swallowing thickly, she looked up as Kelly set the arrows back into the quiver, the weight startling her out of her brooding thoughts, and Lena took one out, taking her time to knock and draw it back. The duck wasn’t moving particularly fast and she tracked the movement of it for a moment as she breathed and then loosed it.

     

                The feather struck the duck in the breast and Lena jumped with shock at the splash as the duck was bowled over by the force of it punching through feather and muscle. Going white, she stood on the banks with her mouth open, guilt clawing at her as Alex and Kelly laughed with delight at her hitting her mark, the latter leaping to her feet to wade out into the shallow estuary and fetch the dead bird. Yanking the arrow out, Alex held the duck aloft by its slender neck, and Lena felt her stomach roil as she opened and closed her mouth. 

     

                “Oh no.”

     

                “An excellent shot,” Kelly complimented her.

     

                “Is it- is it dead?”

     

                “Of course it’s dead. You took it right through the lung. At least the heart will be in fine condition for eating; it’s always a shame to waste it.”

     

                “A few more and we shall return home with a nice brace,” Alex beamed, holding the arrow out for Lena to take.

     

                Ignoring the arrow, Lena held the bow out to Kell and let the quiver slide off her shoulder, catching in the crook of her elbow. Kelly waved it away with a smile. “No, no, you keep going. It’s good practice.”

     

                “It seems like such a waste.”

     

                “A waste? How so? We’ll eat it for dinner. I will show you how to pluck it.”

     

                Kelly was studying her face and took a slow step forward, cautious as if dealing with a wild animal. “Lena, are you well? You’ve gone all pale.”

     

                “I, uh, yeah, I’m fine, I just- I don’t want to do this. I don’t think … I’m made for hunting. That’s not … what I’m built for.”

     

                “Oh. Well, if you’re sure.”

     

                “Here, have a drink,” Alex urged her, stooping to pick up the wineskin and tossing it to Lena, who dropped the bow and quiver to catch it.

     

                She drank almost all that was left in it as Kelly recovered her bow and quiver and turned to the water, methodically picking off a few more ducks to add to Lena’s. Sinking to the grass, heedless of her cloak this time, Lena frowned as she hugged her knees, watching as Alex slit the duck’s throat and left it hanging upside down to drain the blood. Once she’d finished, Alex squatted near her, head cocked to the side.

     

                “Does it really bother you to kill the meat you eat with your own hands?”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes. “It’s not that , I just- this isn’t what I want to be doing. This isn’t me. I’m a florist! I like flowers, I like trees and pretty things that are alive. Not killing things.”

     

                “Death is a part of life, as much as life is a part of death. You kill the duck to eat it, and you live because of that, and then you die and you feed the weeds, which will feed other ducks. It is the way of things.”

     

                “I know that, I just … don’t think this is what I’m meant to be doing. I don’t know what I’m doing!”

     

                “And that is the root of your problem,” Alex told her, gently prodding her in the chest. “You are too confused. It has made you angry.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena murmured with weary relief. “Yes, I am angry.”

     

                “And you will continue to be angry if you do not vent the fire inside you. You are angry because you will not choose what it is you want, and that is making you frustrated. Almost half a year you have been here, and you pass the day with your interests, but there is no joy in you, Lena. Oh, yes, you have picked up our language and learned to ride a horse and shoot a bow, but you do not enjoy it enough to make it your life. It is as you said, you have no purpose.”

     

                Lips parting as a look of shock flitted across her face, Lena looked almost indignant as she closed her mouth and swallowed thickly. “I don’t know what I want.”

     

                “Yes, you do, you are just afraid. You will not know peace until you confront your fears, until you stop hiding , until you find the thing that brings you joy. It is not hunting, that much we are sure of,” Alex gently said, finishing with a smile as she gestured to the duck she had attached to her saddle.

     

                “I have decided,” Lena protested. “I’m here, aren’t I? I chose to stay. That’s not the problem-”

     

                “Then it is not what is frustrating you. Dig deep and feel it. You will feel better once you help yourself. You are afraid of the water and you hate it in Krypton, but you have not tried to dip your toes in the sea and make your fear smaller. You let everything grow too big until it consumes you. That is not good for the soul. You are disconnected from yourself and your surroundings; you will never be at peace if you do not reconcile yourself with your place here, in the Courts, in the forest, in your marriage. If you would only reach out, feel it all, feed into it, you would find yourself more aligned, you would find yourself less frustrated and angry and then it might become easier to know what it is you desire.”

     

                “I do feel it! I feel it too much. But what am I supposed to do with it all, huh?”

     

                Scowling as she grabbed fistfuls of wet grass in her hands, kneeling on it, Lena’s face was furrowed with frustration and she felt it spilling out of her. She was no good at making roots snake to her at her command or shaping rock to her will, not when she consciously tried to do it, but Lena had the unfortunate knack of letting intense emotions fuel her, and that seemed to be the catalyst for her powers to make themselves known. There was a faint tremor in the ground and she could feel it in her bones, the awareness of the deep fissures and layers of rock and dirt, feel it shift ever so slightly.

     

                The adrenaline of the earthquake sent a thrill through her, her chest rising and falling quickly as the surface of the estuary rippled at the disturbance, birds taking flight for a mile around. Raising her face skywards, she breathed deeply, feeling the ground shake as she funnelled her frustration into it, deaf to the alarmed words of her family nearby as they tried to calm the horses before they could bolt. Sweat beaded her skin, even with the brisk wind buffeting her, and she didn’t think she could unclench her fists in the grass as her stomach jolted with the feeling that she was going to split the ground in half, the panic that seized her as she found her mouth opening and closing, speechless as she fed her anger into the ground until she was spent.

     

                Sagging where she knelt, Lena breathed raggedly for a moment, blinking owlishly as her hands trampled in her lap, blades of grass clinging to wet skin. A shadow cut across her and she looked up, a troubled look clouding her face. Alex had her hands planted on her hips, mouth an exasperated line as her brown eyes shone with amusement.

     

                “Better?”

     

                “I- yes,” Lena rasped, wiping her face on her sleeve.

     

                “I should hope so. Were you trying to break us free from the mainland?” Alex laughed. “Come, on your feet.”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena swallowed the lump in her throat. “No, I’d like to sit for a bit. I feel …”

     

                “Drained? Yes, that’s a lesson we all learn. Use too much and you’ll wear yourself out quickly. In a fight, that can be life or death. It’s a lesson in control.”

     

                “Right, well, I think that lesson is a bit pointless for me. I’m shit at getting it to work on command so … nothing to control, I guess.”

     

                “Control is many things, not just keeping oneself in check. Your explosive emotions are something to control. If you do what you just did at Krypton, you could plunge us all into the sea.”

     

                A shiver wracked Lena and her mouth thinned as annoyance reared up. “You told me to reach out and feed into it! I was just doing what you told me to. Normally I can’t feel anything, so what are the chances of that happening again anyway?”

     

                “Well, if you allow yourself to regularly feel it all and regulate your emotions, I would imagine the chances of you grasping it would be higher, for one. Then you might have better control over this thing that had been dormant inside you for your whole life. Kara has spoken of your lessons to me - we are of the opinion that your mother may not have been the best person to teach you, as she surely fans the flames of your frustrations to the point of these outbursts. The trouble is, there is no one of the Earthfolk that we trust at Krypton to teach you, so we will do our best in their stead.”

     

                “Or I can just keep on ignoring it,” Lena said with a weak smile.

     

                “No, you have ignored so much for far too long. I have brought you here so you may be mad at me, or Kelly if you should choose, for speaking the truth that my sister does not want to. You must start making choices, and finding more purpose in life than putting your head in the sand and hoping for the best. This nonsensical notion of peace that Kara wished for is breaking; you cannot be dead weight when it comes to war.”

     

                “I don’t have the skill, I don’t have years of training. I- last time, I think it was pure luck that I killed her first - and him, even if you got there to finish it first - and I don’t know if I’ll be lucky again. But I’m not afraid to die, so … I’ll do it again, even if I die, I just- I don’t want her to try to die for me.”

     

                Alex cupped Lena’s chin and gave her a weary smile, “that is who she is. But you do not have to give her the opportunity to do it.”

     

                Nodding, Lena drew in a shaky breath and pushed herself to her feet. Pausing, she looked from Alex to Kelly and hesitated. “I have a stupid question …”

     

                “Ask it,” Kelly urged her.

     

                “When Kara dies, where does she want her body laid to rest?”

     

                “Oh, yes, that is odd. Alex?”

     

                “She has always desired the same burial rites as her parents.”

                

                “Which was?”

     

                “A boat sent out to sea.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Why do you ask?”

     

                “I- no reason. We just talked about it once. She said she’d plant a tree over my body so I could help it grow.”

     

                Nodding, Alex smiled slightly, “that would suit you well.”

     

                “It’s as good a funeral as any, I guess.”

     

                They were silent for a moment, the estuary rippling from the wind across its surface, birds settling back down now that Lena’s display was over, and Alex raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Are you ready to go?”

     

                Biting her lip, Lena gave her an apologetic look. “Could we stay a while longer?”

     

                “If you’d like. But we are not sitting idly the whole time, so how do you wish to pass the time?”

     

                Considering it for a moment, Lena raised her eyebrows suggestively. “We could spar?”

     

                “You aren’t dressed suitably.”

     

                “What if I need to know how to fight in a dress one day?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex conceded. “As you wish.”

     

                “And no pulling punches,” Lena insisted. “Your sister insists on being gentle.”

     

                “Your wife will have words with me if I bring you home beaten to a pulp.”

     

                Unclasping her cloak, knowing she’d warm up quickly enough, Lena laughed as she rolled her eyes in response. “I’ll be disappointed if you go easy on me.”

     

                “I never said I’d go easy.”

     

                Alex had unbuckled her assortment of weapons and set them safely aside as Lena had folded up her cloak, and then tried to take her by surprise by sweeping her legs out. Seeing it coming, subjected to a similar act a few times before, Lena backed up with a smile on her face, setting her shoulders, her hands in fists, elbows and knees bent slightly. Dodging the punch Alex threw at her, she missed the left-handed jab to her stomach and felt slightly winded as she reached out and grabbed the edge of Alex’s leather vest, yanking her in closer as she hooked a foot around her sister-in-law’s ankle. Lena went down with her, Alex rolling so Lena was underneath her.

     

                Grappling on the floor, Lena managed to trap her legs and dig her thumb into Alex’s throat, while she wound up with a knee to the stomach and a fistful of her hair caught in Alex’s hand. They separated and Lena managed to land two punches before receiving one of her own, striking the underside of her jaw, pain blossoming white-hot as she reeled backwards before recovering. Catching Alex’s arm on her next swing, Lena turned so her back was to Alex’s chest and used the momentum to elbow her in the sternum, turning back around and trying for a headlock that Alex easily broke. Taking a kick to the thigh, Lena’s knee buckled and she took another hit, this time to the stomach, doubling over as she wheezed. 

     

                Alex didn’t go easy, as promised, and Lena could taste blood as the fight went on, still on her feet, moving quickly but remaining grounded, her balance set as she dodged and ducked, on the defensive more than offensive, but still landing a few more hits. Hot and breathless, Lena enjoyed the distraction, the chance to be outdoors, away from it all, even if her body would hate her for it later, aching and bruised. 

     

                “You are better with your fists than a sword, I will grant you that,” Alex said, giving her a quick grin, teeth reddened with blood. “But you have forgotten something.”

     

                “What?” Lena panted, hands on her knees as she took a moment to catch her breath.

     

                She’d barely finished speaking before an arm wrapped around her neck and jerked her up straight. Kelly’s grip was tight, and even though Lena had a few inches on her, she was held fast as Alex smiled wider.

     

                “There will be more than one enemy to contend with. How do you fare against two?”

     

                Swallowing a groan, Lena rolled her eyes and stamped heavily on Kelly’s foot, kicking her shin and then ducking out of her grasp as her friend swore. Breathlessly laughing, Lena danced away, triangulating the two women, and Alex nodded approvingly.

     

                “Do not put your back to us.”

     

                That was easier said than done as they both started to circle around, feinting and testing her with quick jabs, lunging forward and prancing away. Kelly struck her collarbone and Lena ended up on one knee as she found Alex behind her, but tackled Kelly’s legs, tripping her into her wife.

     

                “Good. Use us against each other.”

     

                On her feet, Lena dodged a punch Kelly sent towards her nose, watching as Alex almost copped it, ducking aside before it could land, and then split a knuckle as she caught the buckle of Alex’s belt with a low thrown punch. She had her ears boxed and her lip split, swaying on her feet, but didn’t go down as they tested her skill, pushing her limits.

     

                “Faster.” 

     

                “You can throw better than that.”

     

                “Watch your balance!”

     

                Eventually, she had a stitch in her side and had jarred two fingers of her right hand, her body pleasantly exhausted and aching in many places, tender from the beating she’d taken. Holding a hand up, Lena smiled as she rolled her eyes, taking victory in the laboured breaths of the other two women, who’d have more than a couple of bruises each in the morning.

     

                “I yield.”

     

                “A good bout,” Kelly said as she clapped Lena on the shoulder before gently touching a tender cheek, laughing. “But Kara will be having words with us.”

     

                “You should’ve let me get in a few more shots; maybe she’d let you off the hook then.”

     

                “Oh, she’ll not care how many times we were struck,” Alex snorted, shaking her head. “We are not her beloved wife, wrapped in lambswool.”

     

                “Don’t start with that again,” Lena darkly warned her. “Not if you want us to be friends.”

     

                “Come. Rinse the blood away.”

     

                Lena lingered on the banks, wary of the water, and Kelly silently filled the empty wineskin with frigid water out of understanding, which Lena gratefully took as she poured some into her dirty palms and did her best to wash off the mud and blood, her knuckles fiercely red and split in places. Her face wasn’t any better and she could taste the blood as she licked her lips, water running down her neck as she cleaned herself up. Yet, there was a pleasant exhaustion to her body, her frustration spent for the time being, and she had to admit she felt lighter. They so rarely sparred with her in a way that injured her beyond a couple of bruises from pointed jabs, but this time Lena had worn herself out by venting the lingering tension the earth had not sapped from her. She would sleep well tonight.

     

                They spent a little while resting afterwards, and Lena wandered about nearby, picking ramsons that grew in the marshlands to flavour their dinner. Winter was sparse with its offerings but a few of the oak trees had acorns and Kelly used a gust of wind to rattle them loose from the branches after Lena pointed them out. She had to use her skirts to gather them into a pile, and Alex produced a clean handkerchief to form a bundle for the ride home. 

     

                After a short walk around the area, satisfying her curiosity and the invigorating feeling of being outdoors in nature, Lena started to feel the cold more keenly, damp and dirty, and asked if they could go home. Mounting up, the three of them set off at a leisurely pace for the first couple of miles, before they let the horses pick up the pace, trampling waterlogged earth as they headed north-east. The air burning her lungs, Lena grew stiff and felt each fresh bruise and ache with the jostling, but she was glad for the quick respite in the marshlands, even if it didn’t hold a candle to the forest to the south. What she would have given for another outing that far, but she knew the risks with her brother lurking out there somewhere, biding his time with his growing band of followers. How long would it be before even a few miles from Krypton was considered too much of a risk?

     

                The ride home was relatively quick, rain clouds breaking as they neared the last few miles. The sky was a deep grey over the edge of the cliffs as they skirted the coast, heads ducked down as they were soaked through to the bone, and Lena was thinking fondly of a hot bath and something warm to eat. They had been gone longer than anticipated, the other women caving to her plea to stay out there longer, which meant they’d all missed lunch. That eagerness drove them the rest of the way home in a hurry, and they dismounted in the stables with relief, chatting amongst themselves as they unsaddled their horses and gave them a brushing down before seeing to their own needs.

     

                Shivering as her sodden cloak dripped water on the stone floors, Lena followed Alex and Kelly straight to the kitchens. Andrea was in there and gave them all a cursory look as they filed in, setting down their ducks, ransoms and acorns on the long worktop and getting to work. Alex insisted on her knowing how to butcher meat herself so Lena was subjected to helping draw water from a barrel to boil it, the ducks set into the large pot until Alex deemed them fit for plucking, explaining to Lena how chickens were easier but the boiling water helped soften the ducks’ skin enough to make the job easier than dry plucking. Working at a slower pace, Lena plucked the one assigned to her and then got started on a second, until they had a brace of birds and a pile of feathers.
