                “We will leave them to hang for a few days,” Alex declared, gathering them all up by their slender necks and fetching some string to tie them up in the cool pantry, where they would be exposed to the airflow but kept away from the steam of the ovens. “We’ll butcher them once they’ve aged.”

     

                Nodding, Lena looked down at her hands, soft down sticking to them, and went to wash her hands before a hot bowl of stew was set in front of her and Alex heated a kettle for tea. Andrea was wordlessly cutting a loaf of bread into slices for them and Lena found herself seated next to where she stood, thanking her as a slice was set down in front of her, still slightly warm in the middle.

     

                “You hunted them yourself?”

     

                “Only one,” Lena shrugged, tearing her slice in half and dunking a corner. 

     

                “It was a fine shot,” Kelly said as she took a seat across from Lena with her own bowl, smiling.

     

                “And was there trouble?”

     

                Lena scoffed quietly, touching a particularly tender spot beneath her left eye. “No, no trouble. Just a little training session.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Andrea finished cutting the loaf and spread butter and honey on a piece for herself, leaning on the worktop. “You could have spared your face. At least your mother would not have been able to criticise your beauty, but alas, now we shall all have to hear about your appearance at dinner.”

     

                “At least I provide a constant topic of conversation.”

     

                “I, for one, am sick of it,” Andrea said with a quick smile, pouring herself some tea and then vanishing out the door.

     

                “You know, I believe she’s starting to like you,” Alex laughed.

     

                Lena scoffed and spooned stew into her mouth. In between bites of food, she sipped her tea and felt a great weariness wash over her, cold and wet and aching down to her bones as the heat of the fire did little to warm her up. Taking pity on her, Alex offered up a bath once she’d finished and Lena relished the sting of the bath in the multitude of little cuts she’d accumulated, settling into the steaming tub and hastily washing before changing into dry clothes. She opted for something nicer, knowing that Andrea would argue with her if she chose something plain, and spent some time transcribing a chapter of a book she was reading as she practised her handwriting, staining her fingertips with charcoal. 

     

                Kara found her there a while later, on her way back from fishing or swimming - Lena could never be sure what her wife had been up to when she came back sopping wet - pausing in the doorway to watch her. Glancing up, Lena’s lips pulled into a smile, making the cut sting as it reopened slightly. Kara raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Where have you been?”

     

                “Out for a ride.”

     

                “How many times did you fall off your horse?” she chuckled.

     

                Laughing, Lena raked a hand through her hair, still damp as it dried in waves down her back, and set the book aside. “Your sisters indulged me in a sparring session with no punches pulled. So … naturally.”

     

                “Naturally.”

     

                Quiet for a moment, Lena pressed her lips together as Kara hovered. “I shot a duck today.”

     

                “You shot a duck.”

     

                “Mhm. I hated it.”

     

                Nodding, Kara’s mouth twitched at the corners. “Yes, I don’t think you would much enjoy hunting. Nor even fishing.”

     

                “Yeah. I’m more of a … forager. Found some wild garlic, so … you know … plants.”

     

                Kara nodded again, “did you enjoy yourself at least?”

     

                “Yes. It was nice to get away - from her . It makes my skin crawl to know she’s … lurking about.”

     

                “You know I would take you out more, if you would like me to.”

     

                “You know that I would always like to.”

     

                “Would you? I confess, you are no longer avoiding me and we are friends as we were before, which is a great relief, but I don’t imagine you would want to be alone with me, away from here.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Lena was quiet for a moment, her mouth a flat line as she stared at the wall, considering her wife’s words. She responded slowly, “I think I would. I think I’d like to be anywhere with you. I enjoy your company too much.”

     

                “Oh. Well … that is good to hear. Perhaps we can go for another ride again soon.”

     

                “Sure.”

     

                “I should dress for dinner.”

     

                Nodding distractedly, surprised by how much of herself she had revealed, a nervous flutter in her stomach, Lena kept her eyes on the wall. She thought perhaps there was something to be said for exhausting herself to the point where she no longer felt the knot of frustration in her chest, making her more amenable, more honest and forthright with her thoughts. 

     

                Afraid to go any further down that train of thought, Lena picked up her book again but spent the entire time listening to the sounds of her wife changing across the hallway. The splash of water, the sound of fabric sliding over skin, the cinching of a belt and the clink of the buckle and rings. Feeling hot in her layers, Lena left her room to make her way downstairs, finding herself in one of the sea-facing rooms, the brisk air cooling her flushed skin as she stared out at the dark sea in the failing sunlight.

     

                Kara had been right that Lena didn’t want to be alone with her, in the sense that Lena did want to be alone with her and knew exactly what would happen if they were, unable to stop herself from caving to her desires. But Alex’s voice was at the back of her mind, nagging and persistent. Lena had lied to her earlier and she knew that her sister-in-law was on the right track with Lena’s feelings and her confusion about it. She was beating herself up inside for wanting Kara, purposely denying herself what she very well could have, over childhood fears of losing people and having no one. Lena didn’t want to be alone, but that came at the cost of keeping everyone at arm's length, and it wasn’t viable long-term if she was going to build a life there. And in that sense, she had avoided setting down any permanent roots beyond the decision to stay, which hadn’t been much of a decision when she’d had nowhere to go and no one to fall back on, save for the wife she’d never asked for. 

     

                But she was staying, and she couldn’t live the rest of her life wrapped up in her anger and resentment at herself for not being able to take what she wanted because she was frightened. What sort of life would that be? One that would be worse off than her life was now. At least for now, she had company, she had idle pastimes, even if she hadn’t set her eyes on anything substantial to fill her days. What happened when she burned through her options? Kara had promised she would never leave Lena, but there were many ways to stay and keep one's distance - Lena was in the midst of doing that herself. 

     

                Pacing back and forth, she was too consumed by her thoughts to notice the dark figure appear in the doorway, watching her with a cold gaze. It wasn’t until Lillian moved further into the room that Lena raised her head, dread snaking through her as her throat tightened. Cocking her head to the side, Lillian eyed her battered appearance and a slow smile spread across her mouth.

     

                “It appears you are still as weak as ever.”

     

                “Not quite,” Lena quietly replied. “I may not be strong by any means, but I’m resilient. I know how to survive here now.”

     

                “Is that so?”

     

                “Yes. I’ve even killed a couple of people.”

     

                “Oh? Well, perhaps there is something of your father in you after all - aside from your ears.”

     

                Slowly shaking her head, Lena’s face furrowed with a considerate look as she took Lillian’s judgement seriously. “No, I don’t think so. I didn’t like it much. Sorry to disappoint.”

     

                Lillian let out a quick laugh, eyebrows rising and falling quickly as she scoffed contemptuously. “ Something of him, but not much. It’s no surprise, given what a soft-hearted woman Elizabeth was. But then I guess that’s what drew him to her.”

     

                A desperate yearning filled Lena’s chest and she toyed with the rings on her fingers as she took a reserved step forward. Lena remembered so little of her mother and had known so little to begin with, so many holes in her memories, muddled and dimmed from her time spent away from the forest, and it felt so unfair that this woman in front of her, the woman who had ordered her death, knew her better than Lena ever would. She didn’t want Lillian to know just how desperate she was, but she couldn’t keep it off her face. 

     

                “Could you … tell me about her?”

     

                “Tell you about her?” Lillian quietly exclaimed, wandering further into the room, her eyes widening with disbelief. “Why would I want to waste breath speaking of her?”

     

                “I would like to know more about her, and you’re the only person left who knew her.”

     

                “Is it comfort you seek? You will not find it in what I have to say. You wish to know her? Very well. She enjoyed the outdoors and your father saw her one day when he was in your realm. He was injured by a piece of iron so she helped heal him - she was what you humans call a doctor - and they fell in love, or so he would have me believe. He brought her back here, to keep her at his side. She was delighted, for a time - the dances, the feasts, the dresses and jewels and the beauty of the forest - but she grew to hate it here. It is not a place for humans to dwell long but she was besotted and he would not let her leave, even when she came to resent him. His attention was fleeting but you were born and he gave you two everything that was desired, even what little love he was capable of. That was not enough for her; I suppose she saw the foul parts of him as well, finally saw reason enough to know she did not belong amongst our kind, and left as soon as she could. Foolish woman. Of course, I could not let her take you but you slipped through my fingers and she died. I suppose some might consider that a sad end for her but it was quick. Merciful, some might say.”

     

                Tears stung Lena’s eyes and she swallowed thickly, anger burning hot in her chest as her hatred solidified. “Thank you.”

     

                Her mother was standing close to her now, face pale and hard in the waning light, and her lip curled derisively. “You will be lucky if your brother is so merciful when he kills you.”

     

                An uneven smile crossed Lena’s face as she choked on a laugh. “I guess I will just have to kill him first.”

     

                A surprised laugh escaped Lillian and she arched an eyebrow. “Even if you were entirely your father’s daughter, you would not have the ability to kill him. You are not smart enough, you are not strong enough to be a kinslayer. The best you can hope for is to tuck tail and run.”

     

                “Yet, I’m still here.”

     

                Reaching up, Lillian cupped Lena’s chin and stroked her cheek with her thumb before pressing down on a new tender bruise. Letting out a quiet hiss, Lena tore her face from her mother’s grip, and Lillian’s mouth thinned.

     

                “You are a fool, just like your mother. He has not come for you yet. For your sake, hope he does not come for a long while yet.”

     

                Nodding, Lena turned her back to her mother, which meant looking at the sea. It was dark but the crests of the waves caught the faint moonlight from the crescent moon that was rising between heavy clouds, a shimmer of silver against the inky backdrop of endless water. Moving towards it, Lena stopped a safe distance away and let the wind ruffle her hair as she thought long and hard about what Lillian had said. She expected her mother to interrupt her but was relieved to hear footsteps pad away, leaving her alone. Lena suspected that Lillian would think it was torment enough to leave her with a glimpse of the mother she barely remembered. 

     

                She was still staring out at the sea when Kara found her. Lena knew it was her by the sound of her footsteps and it reminded her of why she had come downstairs in the first place. Kara was silent as she lingered in the middle of the room and Lena turned after a prolonged moment of nothing but the sound of the sea. There was gentle concern in Kara’s slightly widened eyes and Lena’s gaze flitted away from her searching stare. 

     

                “Dinner is ready?” Lena surmised.

     

                “Yes, if you wish to dine in the hall, but … it has been a long day. I would gladly make your excuses and bring something up to your room if you would prefer.”

     

                Giving her a weak smile, Lena shook her head. “It’s alright.”

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                “Just a lot on my mind. A lot to think about. It has been a long day.”

     

                “Will you tell me about it?”

     

                Throat tight, Lena managed a thin, wavering smile as she crossed over to Kara and took her arm. “No. Not right now.”

     

                Nodding, Kara escorted her out of the room and they walked to the dining hall in silence. Only Sam was there, sitting further down the table than their seats, and they exchanged polite nods. Taking her usual seat, Lena reached for the wine and offered it to Kara, filling her cup first and then her own before taking a sip. She asked about her wife’s day as they waited for a few of the others to turn up before serving themselves, and was correct in her assumption that Kara had been fishing, listening to the excitable way she gestured to the size of a lobster she had caught in a pot, eyes bright with delight. Lena couldn’t stop the faint smile on her face as she propped her chin up in her palm and watched her.

     

                When Kara asked about hers, Lena gave her a brief overview of their ride out west, the hunting, the little earthquake and sparring, barely scraping the surface on the depth of her emotions about it all. It had been a draining day and she tried to brush it all away to be present in the moment but she wasn’t up for much conversation, offering no further explanations or details, and Kara politely kept her questions to herself. As they talked, Kara’s family trailed in and they took that as a cue to dig in.

     

                Lena served herself a piece of salmon with kale and asparagus and a few potatoes, still hungry after her late lunch and tiring day, and she felt warm with the lit braziers and the wine she was drinking. There had been few days where she’d felt so content, but she would’ve been happy to sit in that room, warm as she slowly got drunk, for the rest of the night. Instead, she ate a dessert of stewed apples and then excused herself to her room, not up to a night of talking by the hearth. She wanted to lay down for a bit, mull it all over and straighten out a few things.

     

                As soon as she’d kicked off her boots and changed into a thick nightgown and robe, she was beneath the covers, her aching body relaxing into the down mattress, and she let out a weary sigh. Shutting her eyes, a divot between her eyebrows as she brooded, Lena tried to parse through the events of the day. It was true that she felt more relaxed, her body too tired to hold onto any frustration after she’d depleted all of her energy, and she was left feeling oddly vacant, thinking that perhaps an earthquake every now and again would be the solution to her problems.

     

                As Alex had mentioned, that wasn’t something she should aspire to create without proper control though, and as much as she disliked being situated on the coast, the last thing she’d want to do was plunge Kara’s ancestral home into the sea. Instead, she would have to slog through the age-old method of working through her problems herself. The most apparent one was the one she least wanted to confront, and the one that was likely easily solved. 

     

                Sweet Kara, who she kept at bay as much as possible, fending off her wife’s attempts to get closer, lapsing and letting her in only to shut her out again. It was tiring even for Lena, that losing battle of her feelings. It wasn’t that she loved her - or rather, Lena didn’t think it was a romantic love, perhaps something more platonic - so it wasn’t out of concern for her life that she pushed Kara away. It was the fear of being alone, and she had already deduced that she would be left, even though Kara had told her otherwise. How was Lena supposed to let her in if she didn’t confront that particular fear? And how would she give Kara the chance to prove that Lena’s trust wasn’t misplaced, unless she did give her the opportunity to stay? They were married, they were friends and now lovers, so what difference would it make to stop shutting Kara out? Except all the difference in the world to have someone she could confide in, be honest with and trust. 

     

                Lena didn’t get beyond agonising over her wife before she fell asleep. She hadn’t made it to what purpose she might serve in the Courts or how she might confront her fear of the sea. She hadn’t even given a thought to deepening her relationship with Kara’s family, of growing her circle of friends, and giving as much as she received. Instead, she slept soundly for a few hours, until her sleep was light and she dreamed. Dreamed of her wife, in her bed, of her hands and her mouth and her soft words. 

     

                Jolting awake, heart racing, Lena listened to the quieting rumble of thunder mutter into silence. Running a hand over her bruised face, she stared up at the dark ceiling and listened to the pounding in her chest slow as the dream burned at the front of her mind. And across the hallway, she could hear quiet movements as Kara evidently readied herself for bed. The sound of fabric, bare feet on stone, the quiet thud of a wooden chest closing and the trickling of water as she washed her face and hands. Lena listened, her body coiled tight with tension, with desire, her mouth dry and nails gouging half-moons in her palms as she curled her hands into fists, unable to shake off the dream.

     

                She could go to her, she knew that. Kara would almost certainly welcome her, and if she didn’t, then Lena would have what she’d always wanted. Except, she hadn’t wanted that at all, hadn’t wanted Kara to rebuff her, but hadn’t known how to let her in. Lena had spent her entire childhood futilely wanting , until she’d been too afraid to want and learnt to never want anything. That same fear that maybe she would want Kara so badly that she would inevitably be let down, just like the rotation of foster parents and guardians had let her down, dogged Lena even now. But she could go to her if she chose to confront this fear. Here and now, just nip it in the bud. This wasn’t the same as being eight years old and wishing for adoption, or twelve, just wishing for a permanent foster family, or fifteen, just wishing wherever she wound up for a few weeks would be nice, or seventeen, just wishing to be eighteen so she could get out of the shelters and go to college. This was Kara, her wife who never let her want for anything, and surely wouldn’t let her want for her.

     

                Throat aching with how badly she wanted to, Lena stared up at the ceiling, lips moving soundlessly as she tried to pluck up the courage. Kara’s room was silent now and she knew she’d be asleep soon, a small window of opportunity for Lena to act. Her heart was still thudding in her chest and she felt an edge of panic creep in, the urgency to get out of bed and go to her. Before she knew what she was doing, the layers of blankets had been thrown back and Lena was climbing to her feet, unable to stop herself now that she was moving, momentum driving her forwards.

     

                Her determination momentarily faltered as she found herself facing Kara’s doorway, but she didn’t talk herself out of it, drawing in a deep breath and squaring her shoulders as she stepped closer. The room was dark and still and she deliberated for a moment longer over whether or not to disturb Kara, who was surely on the precipice of sleep if she hadn’t been roused by Lena’s presence, before she spoke.

     

                “Kara?” she hesitantly murmured, hovering just inside the doorway.

     

                She could see her wife’s shadowed form beneath the blankets, the air freezing as the wind blew in through the open archways looking out onto the sea. Lena couldn’t make out the waves in the dark, the moon covered by thick clouds, but she heard the roar of it and shivered in her nightgown.

     

                At the sound of her name, Kara shifted, rolling over and pushing herself up onto her elbow as she peered through the dark. Pushing her hair out of her face, her voice was slightly hoarse as she spoke, but it didn’t sound as if she’d made it past drifting off.

     

                “Lena? Is something amiss?”

     

                Drifting inside, ghostly in her nightgown, Lena wrung her hands as she padded quietly across the cold stone. “Sorry, I know it’s late. I- I was dreaming …”

     

                “Did you have a nightmare?” Kara asked, her voice soft with concern as she sat up, bringing the blankets with her to cover bare skin.

     

                “No, not a nightmare. A good dream.”

     

                “Oh. Then-”

     

                “I couldn’t go back to sleep,” Lena confessed, her voice barely a whisper as she stood at Kara’s bedside. “I couldn’t stop thinking about it. It was about you …” Reaching out, she brushed Kara’s hair back in a tender caress and let her fingertips trace over the point of her ear, hearing the sharp intake of breath through her wife’s parted lips. “And me.”

     

                Reaching up, Kara stopped her with a gentle grasp of her wrist, her blue eyes dark in the night as her face furrowed with a serious look. “Don’t.”

     

                Stilling, Lena felt her face flush as her fear came true. “No?”

     

                “If you are here to share my bed and then snub me come dawn, then no. I will not allow my feelings to be trifled with to satisfy your fleeting fancies.”

     

                Drawing in closer, until her knees hit the side of the bed, her hand cupping the underside of Kara’s jaw, Lena swallowed, her throat dry and tight. “And if I didn’t snub you? If I wanted you again and again?”

     

                Freezing for a moment, Kara licked her lips and drew in a shallow breath, her expression unreadable as Lena gave her a wary look, shy in her vulnerability as she admitted what she wanted. Swallowing thickly, the corners of Kara’s mouth curled with a faint smile as she looked up at Lena through her lashes.

     

                “Then I would say it is far too cold for you to be standing there and you should come to bed.”

     

                A surprised laugh escaped Lena as the tense look on her face smoothed to amusement, smiling wryly as she felt Kara’s hands smooth over the hem of her nightgown, pushing it up until her warm palms ghosted over her thighs. Lena felt her heart stumble in her chest, a lightness there as she allowed herself to feel the relief of caving to what she wanted. She’d been tying herself into knots over something that felt so easy, in a way it never had with other people, always that distance Lena kept herself at, but futile when it came to her wife. Of course she’d known that, and it had been the primary reason why she had cautiously slammed on the brakes, to ensure she didn’t make herself too vulnerable, or give too much to someone who wouldn’t be hers.

     

                But she was hers for now. Looming over Kara, Lena cupped her wife’s cheeks as she ducked her head to kiss her slowly. Kara’s hands glided up to Lena’s waist as she pulled her closer and Lena all but fell on top of her, the mattress jostling as they both quietly laughed and she pushed herself up, straddling Kara’s lap. Kissing her again, with more fervour this time, her palms glided up Kara’s spine and she felt her wife’s arms tighten around her waist. Lena lost all sense of reason, any doubts banished to the corners of her mind as she sank into Kara’s touch with relief.

     

                She didn’t know how late it was, or how long they were in each other’s arms, trying to be quiet, swallowing groans, muffling sighs into pillows, only that her body ached anew, slick with sweat that the wind briskly dried on her skin, making her shiver. Eyelids heavy and her body slumped on the mattress, Lena didn’t think she’d be able to move again, and would gladly have fallen asleep right there, the taste of Kara on her tongue and the pleasant warmth of her wife beside her, pulling the quilt up over her bare skin. Lena hummed appreciatively and let out a content sigh, completely worn out and all too aware of her bruises where Kara had held her too tightly where she was already tender from sparring.

     

                They didn’t speak for a few minutes and Lena thought she was in danger of falling asleep if she didn’t shake herself out of it, finding her voice, even if she couldn’t find the willpower to move just yet. She had pressing words to get off her chest though, drawing in a shuddering breath to murmur into the pillows.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Why do you apologise?”

     

                It took her a minute longer to speak again, guilt and embarrassment coupling with the old pain of her youth as her throat tightened around the words.

     

                “I haven’t been fair to you. You’re right, that I’ve toyed with your feelings. It wasn’t on purpose but I- it’s difficult for me to say it. I mean, I said it the other night - I’ve wanted you the whole time, and it’s been confusing and frustrating - but … I don’t know, I just think that … if I weren’t so afraid of being left alone again, it wouldn’t have been so difficult to give in.”

     

                Kara stroked Lena’s arm as she whispered a reply. “You will not be left alone, I have vowed it. Above all, you will always be my wife, and that means that I shall never leave you alone, even should you wish for it.”

     

                Smiling, her eyes closed and the warmth of her wife at her back, Lena softly hummed. “It would be nice to not be left for a change.”

     

                “Go to sleep, Lena,” Kara softly told her. “You will not feel so afraid in the morning.”

     

                A prickle of dismay stole over Lena and she swallowed thickly, pushing the blankets back as she made herself move. “You’re right, and I should leave you to sleep as well.”

     

                Reaching out, Kara gently snagged her arm before she could do more than half-push herself up. Glancing over her shoulder, Lena’s eyebrows furrowed together, confused as her exposed skin started to prickle from the cold. Kara struggled for a moment before she tugged at Lena’s arm and let out a timid huff of laughter.

     

                “I did not say you should sleep in your bed. I can sleep just as well with you beside me, I should think. I have watched you sleep before - you do not take up so much space.”

     

                Uncertain for a moment, Lena hesitated, propped up on one elbow with her wife’s hot fingers encircling her arm as her heart pattered quickly in her chest. Licking her lips, Lena drew in a hitching breath and then nodded, easing herself back down and eagerly pulling the blankets back over herself. 

     

                “Just as long as you don’t snore.”

     

                “You know that I do at times. I only hope I do not have a pillow thrown at me this time.”

     

                “Well, if you do , know it was deserved.”

     

                Kara snorted and then made herself comfortable, and Lena pummelled the goose-down pillow into shape before setting her back to Kara and closing her eyes. The wind brushed her cheeks and she drew the quilt up higher, covering her mouth and cheeks, her stomach swooping at the proximity of her wife at her back. They were silent for a moment, listening to the sound of waves crashing and thunder muttering before Lena cleared her throat.

     

                “Goodnight, then.”

     

                “Goodnight, Lena. Sleep well.”

     

                Sleep was hard to come by though, as loose-limbed and tired as she was. Hyper-aware of Kara’s breaths, which soon evened out into peaceful sleep, Lena couldn’t stop thinking about how close they were, that she could merely roll over and throw an arm across her wife’s waist, she was that close, and perhaps she’d made the biggest mistake of her life by crossing that line in the sand again. But it wasn’t a mistake and there was no turning back now, not that she wanted to. Sleep was hard to come by, but it did come eventually, her mind racing as she tried to rationalise it to herself as she breathed in the smell of rain and salt on the pillows, the intoxicating smell of her wife, and found sleep in the comforting presence of it, and the safety of her wife asleep at her side.

     

                Hours later, she woke to the boom of thunder that seemed to shake and rattle the hall and its contents. Lena’s eyes shot open as her heart raced as she pushed herself up slightly, dark hair spilling around her and a singular quilt draped over her body as she lay in a bed that was not her own. The view of the raging sea and the dark sky through the arches was familiar, albeit from a different angle than Lena was used to, and despite the lack of heavy furs piled atop the blankets, she was quite warm with the sleeping form of her wife beside her radiating heat.

     

                Staring down at Kara’s peaceful expression in the pre-dawn grey, Lena felt her stomach swoop with momentary panic before she relaxed against her pillows. The smell of rain and sea enveloped her and she burrowed into the quilt and pressed her face into the pillows, eyelids fluttering shut as she lingered in bed, content to stay there all morning. Carefully turning so she didn’t wake her wife, Lena studied Kara’s face in sleep, the way her lashes fluttered, the freckles faded from a winter of weak sunlight, her summer tan faded, her golden hair spilling across the pillows as she breathed slowly, fast asleep. Another boom of thunder echoed through the halls and Lena burrowed deeper into the blankets as the wind swept inside with rain, splattering the limestone floor near the open arches.

     

                It was unnerving being in Kara’s room and she was glad to have her back to the sea, skin rippling with goosebumps as her heart thumped loudly in her chest, unease making her stomach clench at the thought of so much open water. Laying and thinking as the sky slowly but surely lightened at her back, Lena waited for her wife to awaken as the storm raged on.

     

                The day was dismal and wet, what sunrise there had been not doing much to lighten the sky, and Kara slowly roused to the dreary, grey morning, blinking as she came to. Her eyes settled on Lena and there was a creasing at the corners as a small smile curled her lips, the pattern of rumpled sheets impressed on her cheek as she lifted her head slightly.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “Morning,” Lena whispered.

     

                “How did you sleep?”

     

                “Not bad. I don’t know how you managed to sleep through the storm though.”

     

                Smiling, Kara rubbed her eyes. “When you spend winters on the coast, you grow accustomed to it. Not to mention learning to sleep in any condition on battle campaigns.”

     

                “Hm, guess I haven’t learnt that lesson yet.”

     

                “I pray you do not have to learn it. The sounds of people dying are not pleasant, no matter how tired you are.”

     

                “Mm, I’m not so eager to end up in a battle again. I think I’m running out of luck.”

     

                “You do not need luck when you have me to guard your back. Although, I pray you never end up in a battle again as well. It was … not pleasant for me last time, to worry for your safety while I fought. I-”

     

                “What?”

     

                “I have never allowed for such distractions before. My eyes … they searched for you each time they were not trained on the enemy.”

     

                Lena let out an awkward laugh. “Ah, well, I was hiding in a bush, so … nothing to worry about there.”

     

                Smiling, Kara closed her eyes, but there was a thickness as she swallowed, throat bobbing. “There is always cause for me to worry. I would hate to lose you.”

     

                Surprised by the shy vulnerability of Kara’s voice, Lena turned to study her face, taking in the oddly tense set of her face, the way she squeezed her eyes shut, mouth a flat grimace. “I wouldn’t willingly leave, you know. I know I tried - a few times - but I’m not planning on running away again.”

     

                The longer she had stayed in that realm, each night spent beneath the stars, around a campfire, each day spent walking along the beach or riding through the woods, it had muddled her feelings, until she couldn’t remember why she had protested so much against staying. Breathing in the air, tainted by the wildness of the forest as it dug its nails in deeper, built roots in her bones, binding her to the realm, eating the food and drinking the water, which was likewise saturated with the strange magic of the wilds, so intoxicating that she could never imagine anything sweeter. Her heart no longer yearned for the concrete and pollution of Metropolis.

     

                “Do you not miss your home? One day, I should see you returned, with jewels enough to rebuild your flower shop and a garden you may fill with a thousand blooming flowers to make your bouquets. It may not come for a long, long time, but I would see it happen one day.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Because my life is one of death, Lena. It comes from my hands, and it shall one day come from my love. But you … you are life. I would not be surprised if flowers grew from your footsteps. You deserve better than the danger this world brings.”

     

                She laughed quietly, opening her eyes as she turned her head to look at Lena. There was a pained look in her blue eyes, an aching remnant of guilt and sadness, and Lena frowned.

     

                “I missed it when I was first brought here, but … this place is home to me now. I- we’ve already spoken about this; I won’t be returning. I thought- well, I had my home, but it was … merely four walls and a bed and a shop, but I guess- I guess I was wrong because I thought that was all I’d ever wanted, a permanent home, but … I guess what I really wanted was a family . You know, people you love to be around, maybe even a few you hate to be around, but just … people who would never leave. I- well, I haven’t thought about home in a long time and thought of anywhere but here, with you.”

     

                Lena wanted to tell her all the ways she’d been withering away in Metropolis, bit by bit but surely withering nonetheless, but she didn’t know how to explain it, thank it wasn’t until she’d been dragged to the Unseelie Court that she had finally felt rooted to a place, entwined in the forest as she had never been anywhere before. It didn’t matter that she’d hated it, for a long time, because it had felt familiar in a way she couldn’t deny, that feeling of belonging that had avoided her for so long. And while she may have missed out on so much of the social culture by being raised amongst humans, she was born in the forest and would surely die there too, not to be parted from it again. 

     

                Silent for a moment, Lena chewed on her lip and then drew in a deep, shuddering breath before she made her firm declaration, nailing home her decision. “I will stay.”

     

                “To what end?”

     

                “To no end.”

     

                Kara looked at her, expression unreadable but rather serious, and didn’t speak for a long moment as she processed what her wife had said. Lena held her gaze, feeling oddly bare as she felt that self-consciousness creep over her with the admission of her true feelings. It made her feel defenceless to reveal that she thought of Kara as home, that she had found what she’d sought for so long in this place she’d sworn to never like. But feelings changed, and the wife she’d once been so committed to disliking, given the circumstances of their marriage, had burrowed her way through the thorny cage around Lena’s heart, whether she wanted to admit it or not. And if Kara had felt like reflecting on her true feelings, she would have confessed to the same. As it was, Kara silently tried to process Lena’s acceptance of her place there, at Kara’s side, and was silent for a few minutes before she abruptly changed the topic.

     

                “We should get ready for breakfast.”

     

                Nodding, Lena sat up, raking her hair back and looked to the floor for her nightgown. She couldn’t see it anywhere and sat further up, Kara letting out a small laugh as she slipped out of bed and stooped to pick it up, tossing it to Lena.

     

                “Is this what you’re looking for?”

     

                “Thanks,” Lena rolled her eyes, feeling the strange tension break, shrugged it on and then got out of bed.

     

                She wrapped her arms tightly around herself as the biting cold made her shiver, and watched as Kara fetched a robe from the back of a chair and lazily tied it shut, rather unaffected by the deep winter chill. Looking up, she slowed as she caught Lena watching her, tucking her hair behind her pointed ears before she smiled.

     

                “You look half-frozen; it almost seems a cruelty to oust you from my bed, but I do not think you would prefer the alternative of being found in it.”

     

                With a huff of laughter, Lena wryly smiled. “You’re right. It’s nothing a few walls between me and the open elements can’t fix. Maybe a cup of tea too.”

     

                “I shall have one poured for you before you have taken your seat.”

     

                “What if I get there before you?” Lena countered, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “Well, I don’t take nearly as long to get ready as you, so I find it very unlikely that will happen.”

     

                “It’s Andrea, thank you very much. She’s hell-bent on treating me like a doll half of the time. It’s impossible to get rid of her when she shows up to dress me. I should be glad it’s not every day, although I’m not sure why.” Kara laughed and Lena gave her a bewildered look. “What?”

     

                “She does not come to dress you on the mornings she is in Sam’s bed.”

     

                “Oh. So everyone knows about the two of them?”

     

                “Yes.” Lena cringed slightly at a stab of panic. Sensing the source of it, Kara gave her an exasperated look. “They are not as careful.”

     

                “I know it’s probably ridiculous to you, I just- I never had a lot of privacy growing up. I never really had anything that was … mine.”

                

                “Well, now you do,” Kara murmured, a tender look in her eyes before they brightened with amusement, a grin spreading across her face. “I shall see you at breakfast - when you deign to join us.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes and rounded the bed, making for the door. Before she reached it, Kara softly called out to her and she turned slightly, raising her eyebrows inquisitively. Opening and closing her mouth as she toyed with the belt of her robe, Kara took a moment to speak.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Brow furrowing together with bewildered amusement, Lena laughed. “For what?”

     

                “For staying until I woke.”

     

                Nodding, Lena felt a gentle twinge in her chest, a soft smile at the corners of her mouth as she turned and walked out. Gingerly crossing the hallway, the stone like ice beneath her feet as she padded back to her room, Lena pulled on a robe and some socks and added more wood to the low-burning brazier before huddling over it as the flames grew. She could feel her cold cheeks sting from the prickling heat as she warmed up, her breath no longer visible in the air as the four walls and minimal exposure to the elements made her room far warmer than Kara’s.

     

                She was pondering over her wife’s penchant for the open sea, knowing she would never be able to understand a devotion for it like that, although it must have been similar to the way she ached for trees and plants instead of this endless grass, sand and sea, when Andrea showed up. Bustling in with a steaming jug of hot water, she set it down next to the washstand with a clean towel and moved to Lena’s trunk.

     

                “You’re up early. I thought I’d have to drag you out of bed; it’s cold this morning.”

     

                “The storm woke me,” Lena murmured.

     

                Going still as Andrea came up with a dress and showed it off to her, she felt a momentary flicker of panic, worried that her attendant would get close enough to catch a whiff of salt on her skin. Mouth opening and closing, Lena cleared her throat as she scrambled for words.

     

                “You, uh, I- I can dress myself today. You can … go to breakfast.”

     

                “Oh, well … if you’re sure.”

     

                “I think it’ll be more of a … casual clothes day. Nothing with laces, maybe some pants, so … I’ll be able to manage that alone, I think. But thank you, and thanks for the water and the towel.”

     

                “Are you well?” Andrea said with some concern and a little bit of apprehension. “You’re behaving … very strangely.”

     

                “Me? I’m quite well. I just had trouble sleeping. The storm-”

     

                “Yes, you’ve mentioned.”

     

                “I think I’ll need another nap after breakfast,” Lena said with a quick grin. “But anyway … all good here.”

     

                Giving her an appraising look of scepticism, Andrea hummed at the back of her throat, unconvinced, and left her to it. Shoulders slumping slightly, Lena went to her trunk and fished out soft leggings, brown pants, a clean shirt and jacket, and then a fur-trimmed robe, washing thoroughly with the hot water and soap, smelling her skin as she tried to pick up on any trace of her wife. Smelling nothing but the milky trace of honey, Lena dried herself off and dressed quickly, picking up the sound of Kara dressing across the hall. 

     

                She was out of her room before her wife and felt a flicker of triumph as she hurried downstairs, a faint smile on her face as she neared the dining hall. Slowing near the doorway, Lena spotted wet footprints, and when she stepped into the open arch, the smile fell from her face at the sight of her wife sitting at the head of the table, the floor around her seat wet, and a damp sheen to her blonde hair.

     

                Kara was pouring tea into two cups and Lena had to fight to keep a scowl off her face as she crossed the threshold and plodded over to her spot. No one paid her much attention besides murmurings of good morning or polite nods as they enjoyed their breakfast and conversation.

     

                “Good morning,” Kara said with a smile as she nudged a steaming cup towards Lena, who was taking her seat. “How did you sleep?”

     

                “Not well,” Lena said, her mouth twitching with annoyance as she looked at the cup. “I was kept up half the night. The storm was rather loud.”

     

                “Yes, I was up quite late myself.”

     

                “And up early by the look of things; have you just come back from a swim?”

     

                “A quick plunge from my room,” Kara said with open delight. “A most bracing drop into the sea. Quite disorienting for a moment, but refreshing nonetheless. And a quicker way to breakfast.”

     

                “Well, I should be glad I don’t have to rush when I have you to make sure there’s a cup of tea waiting for me,” Lena said with a droll look.

     

                “Quite right.”

     

                Unable to be too disgruntled, Lena fought back a smile as she sipped her tea. She peeled softly boiled eggs for the two of them as Kara filled her bowl with porridge and Lena kept glancing over at Eliza, a few seats down on the opposite side of the table, as she made a small pile of eggshell. Setting a peeled egg on Kara’s side plate, Lena murmured her thanks and pulled her bowl closer, drizzling some honey on top and pensively digging in. She had been preoccupied with her thoughts on the matter at dinner last night, her conversation with Lillian - as sparingly as it had been - replaying in her mind. Last night had sidetracked her but with one problem solved for the time being, Lena turned her attention back to it.

     

                After breakfast, she thought about it some more, sparring with swords to let her bruises heal, then a bout of archery on the grass outside, the wind making it more difficult for her to hit the target as she made adjustments to her aim. Her heart wasn’t in it though and she was distracted, earning a shallow cut on her forearm as Sam berated her, and cutting her archery session short as she made her way back inside for lunch and then sought out Eliza once they had finished eating in the kitchens, tailing her out the door as the others lingered over the pie Sam had made. 

     

                “Eliza, may I speak with you for a moment?”

     

                Lena pulled up short as she reached her mother-in-law, who stopped and turned, giving her a warm smile as she raised her eyebrows. Reaching out, Eliza looped her arm through Lena’s and gave her hand a quick pat.

     

                “Of course, I was just on my way for a walk. You can accompany me.”

     

                Allowing herself to be swept along, Lena waited until they were outside and a decent distance from the halls before she spoke, her voice low and uncertain as the wind snatched the words from her mouth as soon as she spoke them. All the better, as she was nervous she would be laughed at.

     

                “I would like to be a healer,” Lena declared, keeping her eyes on the horizon as she squinted slightly. “And I would like you to teach me.”

     

                “Why?”

                

                Blinking, she opened and closed her mouth. “Why?”

     

                “Yes, why? Why would you like to be a healer and why should I teach you?”

     

                “Oh,” Lena faltered for a moment before she drew in a deep breath and launched into a rapid explanation with conviction. “I, well, I know a lot about plants. I can name most of them, what they’re used for, where to find them, what they symbolise. I used to be a florist, so I used to deal with plants a lot; I know how to store them correctly, which I think would be really important. I know which ones are poisonous, and which parts are useful - not just pretty in a bouquet - and I think I’d rather use that knowledge to help people than to pretend I’m any good at waving a sword around. I wasn’t raised a warrior, I was raised to survive, and I think that this is the way for me to do it, to find purpose in healing people. Life, not death. I think I’d be better at that. And you were so good at it when you healed us up in the mountains, and I know you taught Kara and Kelly some as well, and I think … maybe if you taught me, I would finally be good at something here. That could be my purpose.”

     

                She fell silent and nodded, her mouth a flat line of determination as she stared at the stretch of grass with a serious look on her face. Eliza was silent for a moment as well before she nodded, glancing sideways at Lena before the corner of her mouth curled into a smile.

     

                “Very well, if this is your purpose, I will teach you until I depart.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                “Yes. We will begin immediately.”

     

                “Oh. Okay. What are we doing?”

     

                “You say you’re knowledgeable about plants? Let us put it to the test.”

     

                A stab of panic shot through Lena, worrying that maybe she’d just thrown herself into the deep end, but she nodded and followed along as Eliza set off again. They were on foot so it was a good hour of walking before they had even made it a few miles away for other vegetation to begin creeping in. What little they saw, Eliza pointed out and had Lena name them and rattle off any uses she knew of. Relief shot through her and her confidence grew, the simple act of listing the properties of willow bark, identifying yarrow leaves and nettles amidst the wintry landscape something she was good at, didn’t have to try at.

     

                Eliza had her gather them as well, producing a little knife and handing it to Lena, who only took as much as advised, leaving the roots intact so they could grow back. It started raining but she worked without complaint, rain in her eyes, cloak growing heavy as her hands became covered in dirt, handing up cuttings of different herbs, flowers and weeds to Eliza, who cradled an armful in the crook of her elbow, her cloak draped over it to carry them. They talked the whole time too, not just about the properties of different plants and what ails they could be used for, but about Eliza’s life and how Lena was faring, how she had been filling her days and stories about Kara from her childhood. The latter greatly interested Lena and she found herself smiling as she snipped leaves and flowers, listening carefully.

     

                The entire afternoon passed in such a fashion and Lena had stepped into more than one puddle of mud, her boots and leggings caked in it, her face scratched from branches and a few bites from horseflies. Filthy and shivering, the walk home was a slog, not realising how far they had ventured through thickets of trees, along riverbanks and pockets of marshland, but there was a sense of satisfaction in the hard work, eyeing the pile of plants that Eliza carried bundled up in her cloak. She had promised Lena she would teach her more tomorrow, eyeing her daughter-in-law with amusement at Lena’s grateful eagerness. 

     

                Returning to Krypton under the full dark of night, Lena was in dire need of a bath and dinner. They had missed mealtime, the failing sunlight and heavy rain making the trip back trickier as they relied on keen eyesight to lead the way, and she made straight for her room upon arrival to strip off her sodden clothes and put on something clean, and more importantly, dry. She’d wiped her hands off on wet grass but they were still dirty, and beneath that, pruned from the rainstorm, the beds of her fingernails a shade of purple to match her chapped lips. 

     

                With a heavy exhale as she stepped into the warmth of her room, her shoulders sagged with relief at the sight of the built-up brazier with a pot of water resting in the flames, kept hot for her return. Lena hadn’t even managed to unclasp her cloak before Kara was at her doorway, curious and a little anxious as she gave Lena a once-over. After a moment, she smiled crookedly.

     

                “You look as if you have been swimming. I know that cannot be true.”

     

                Lena rolled her eyes, fumbling with the broach, her fingers numb and clumsy. Crossing over to her, Kara helped, standing so close that Lena could have kissed her if she’d wanted to, a bizarre thought to cross her mind - what they were left no room for affection like that. Clearing her throat as Kara undid her cloak and folded the sopping wool into a neat pile, Lena thanked her and stared down at her hands.

     

                “Are you well? You didn’t catch a chill, did you? You seem … feverish?” Kara cautiously spoke, taking in the flush to Lena’s cheeks, the brightness to her eyes.

     

                “What? No, I’m fine,” Lena breezily dismissed her with a smile. “I was out walking with your mom.”

     

                “Two days without your company - must I share you with everyone?” Kara said with a glance and a small smile as she lifted the pot from the fire and poured the hot water into a basin for Lena to wash with.

     

                “Did you miss me?”

     

                “I thought of you, yes. You vanished without a word; if you hadn’t been with my mother, I might have worried.”

     

                “You worry too much,” Lena scoffed, sniffing as she looked up through wet lashes, undoing the fastenings of her jacket and pulling it off, setting it on the stool near the brazier. “She was just teaching me some healing stuff.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Kara’s eyebrows rose and she felt a warm relief spread through her chest. “Oh! That’s what it is - you’re excited.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow as she submerged her muddy hands in the hot water and started to scrub the dirt free, Lena laughed. “I guess I am.”

     

                “I’ve never seen you excited before.”

     

                Humming, Lena lathered soap and cleaned her nails, dark hair hanging in damp tendrils around her face as she considered that for a moment. Her cheek shallowly dimpled with a flicker of old pain and she raised her head slightly, turning to the side to speak over her shoulder. 

     

                “I suppose you wouldn’t have. It’s a rare occurrence.”

     

                “Well, I’m glad that there is something good to come of you being here.”

     

                “Mm, I guess I should also be glad I decided to take some advice.”

     

                “Ah, is that the cause of your sudden changes of heart? And whose advice have you deigned to take, if I may be so bold to ask.”

     

                “Your sister’s,” Lena started in a clipped tone before she softly snorted and shook her head. “Your sister is very good at tough love. She said you have me wrapped in lambswool and … well, I think she was calling me a coward, just in a roundabout way, so … well, I’m deciding not to be a coward. And … I found out my mom was a doctor - a human healer - so … I guess I’m also taking your advice from when you told me I should ask your mom to teach me.”

     

                “I- firstly, you are not a coward,” Kara said, trying to process everything at once. “I do not believe that would have been what Alex meant to convey, whatever she might have said, but … that is wonderful news that you have decided to learn the art of healing. I am sure you will do well at it.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lena sheepishly smiled. “Do you remember when we arrived at your mother’s halls and she made us tend to each other’s wounds? I was sick the moment she had me stitching you up.”

     

                “Ah, well, you were injured, so we shan’t hold that against you,” Kara laughed, “and you were doing so well until then. I have faith you will own to it. After all, you have said it yourself, it’s in your blood. A healer for a mother and a king for a father; what will we make of you yet?”

     

                Kara’s voice was playfully coy and Lena’s stomach swooped as she looked back down at her hands, scrubbing slowly as her pulse jumped at her throat. “I guess time will tell. I just have to prove myself first, so … no more lambswool.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Kara took one of Lena’s hands in her own and plucked the scrubbing brush from the other, taking over for her as she worked the crescents of dirt out from beneath Lena’s fingernails. 

     

                “It pains me to see you hurt. Even now, covered in bruises that you welcomed, I would will it otherwise if I had it my way. I do not think that is unwarranted for me to wish for your safety.”

     

                “No, it’s not, but I’m not as fragile as you think. I’m not made of glass, you know.”

     

                “No, not glass, but you are mine to protect. Even if there comes a day when you best me in arms, or you cannot bear the sight of me any longer, you will always be mine to protect.”

     

                Raising her head to meet her gaze, conscious of how close they were standing, Lena swallowed thickly. “Have you considered that you might be mine to protect too?”

     

                “And who might I need protecting from?”

     

                “Me,” Lena said with a rueful smile.

     

                Kara cocked her head to the side, confused. “You?”

     

                “I have been a coward, more than once, and … I think I would have still been cowardly if I hadn’t had a fire lit under me yesterday. It was hurting you to be treated the way I’ve been treating you, so in that regard, it is for me to protect you from myself by doing better.”

     

                Letting go of Lena’s hand and the scrubbing brush, Kara cupped her face in wet palms, water gliding down Lena’s neck as she stared at her with slightly widened eyes. “It only hurts to see you hurt yourself by agonising over things you keep hidden.”

     

                “I know, but it still hurts you beyond that,” Lena unevenly replied, a pained smile crossing her face. “Don’t worry, your sister knocked some sense into me though.”

     

                Face furrowing with a frown, Kara’s thumb ghosted over Lena’s black eye. Letting out a hoarse laugh, Lena rolled her eyes. “Not literally. We just … had a nice chat and she was very reasonable. I think everything yesterday just … let me think about it more without being too frustrated to think clearly. I think I’ve been spiting myself for a while, um, just living inside of my fears a bit too much … and I decided not to do that anymore. So, last night …”

     

                Kara dropped her hands and resumed washing Lena’s for her, palms scratched and fingertips raw from her foraging as she willingly let her wife care for her. Cheeks faintly pink, Kara cleared her throat. 

     

                “Last night … did you mean what you said?”

     

                “Which part?”

     

                “That you would not snub me again?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena murmured, staring down at their joined hands in the basin. “Yes, I meant it. I meant all of it. To no end.”

     

                There was a tender look on Kara’s face as Lena raised her eyes to hers, a smile starting at the corners of her mouth. “I will not hold you to that, although it gladdens me to hear it.”

     

                “I’ve said it now, truthfully, so you know that I mean it.”

     

                Hesitating, her hands clean, although mud still flecked her face and dirtied the cuffs of her shirt sleeves, Lena looked down at herself and then back up at Kara. She was apprehensive at first but the earnest look on her wife’s face made her soften.

     

                “Maybe not tonight - I’m filthy and tired and cold - but … maybe tomorrow night I could come to your room again.”

     

                Voice hitching up at the end, making her suggestion sound like a question, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction. Face creasing with a smile, Kara leaned in and kissed her cheek, mindful of the bruises, and strayed towards the door.

     

                “Rest well. I will see you in the morning - and tomorrow night.”

    Chapter 28

                Worn out, Lena woke late to the bright whiteness of the sky slanting through arrow slits and hastily dressed for breakfast, catching the tail end of it, only Kara, J’onn and Sam left at the table when she arrived. She gave her wife a hesitant smile and sank onto her seat, slightly breathless from rushing, gritty-eyed from sleep and not nearly awake enough yet.

     

                “Good morning,” she mumbled, covering a yawn, her eyes flitting to Kara and then to the others. “Sam, J’onn.”

     

                Kara set a cup of tea down before her and Lena gave her a grateful smile, even though she wished it was coffee, and she’d barely set about spreading jam over a piece of bread when Eliza appeared in the doorway. Brightening at the sight of her, Eliza smiled and beckoned her.

     

                “You are up. Good. Come, we will get started.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena faltered for a moment before swallowing a complaint. Giving Kara a dour look at the amused look of innocence on her face, Lena climbed to her feet and took her cup of tea and piece of bread with her. Eliza didn’t wait for her to wake up gently, already rattling off a list of lessons to run through, skills and knowledge she would need to learn. Keeping up with her quick pace, Lena wolfed down her bread and tried not to spill her tea, following her mother-in-law all the way to the room well-stocked with healing supplies. 

     

                “Right, let us begin. You can identify plants in the wilderness, a useful tool when you are without resources, but how do you fare with them once they have been prepared and dried?”

     

                It was a rigorous morning, mentally at least, going through an inordinate number of boxes, jars and pouches, filled with different herbs, plants, barks and seeds as she was drilled on their names. She did quite well, all things considered, and Eliza praised her regularly for her correct answers, but it was plain there was a lot Lena didn’t know as well. 

     

                They took a break to fetch tea and food, sitting on little stools as Eliza started to speak of illnesses and symptoms in relation to different herbs. Willow bark for pain, chamomile for inflammation and relaxation, garlic for fevers and preventing infection, honey for coughs and burns, for stopping wounds from becoming infected. She handled them as she briefed on them all, the clean smell of mint and lavender lingering on her hands.

     

                Breaking again for lunch, they came back to the room and Eliza started a fire in the empty brazier, a twitch of her fingers sending a small gust of wind to fan the flames higher. Setting a pot of water on top to boil, she emptied out their teapot and had Lena carefully measure out doses of different herbs and set a pot of tea to steep. They repeated this a few times with what Eliza deemed the most important teas for her to know, Lena tasting them and finding a couple familiar from the times Kara had brewed her tea for her pain or to sleep. It was a nice thought to think that Eliza was teaching her the things she’d gone to lengths to teach her own daughters for their safety.

     

                Eventually, she was set the task of learning how to sew. Nothing fancy, just a quick running stitch, so she could at least close up a wound. Given a few cuts of white cloth and some thread and needles, she was left alone by the brazier, perched on a stool, and dedicated the early hours of her afternoon to embroidery. At first, Lena worked the point of the needle through the fabric and pulled the length of blue thread through, continuing the stitch as she envisioned it as if closing up a deep gash, lining them up as neatly as she could, which was still quite crooked, the stitches too long, then too short, creating an irregular row. 

     

                Filling three pieces of cloth with rows of stitches, somewhat neater as she went along, taking her time, knowing she wouldn’t be afforded the luxury on a bleeding body, she picked up another clean piece and then had the idea to embroider something nice. And then she had the idea to embroider something nice for Kara, who had given her so many gifts, the blue thread already suitable for the simple arcing wave pattern she tried out. It took a long time for her to stitch around each edge, her neck aching as she hunched over her work, and then she chose a darker shade of blue and repeated the pattern a few millimetres above the original one, a double wave in two shades, feeling pleased with herself as she tied off the end and snipped the thread. It was clumsy and nowhere near the elegance of the clothes that came, crafted by artisans, but Lena felt a prickle of pride as she smiled, running her fingers over it.

     

                Her back aching from hunching over for so long, she decided to call it a day and tidied everything away. Seeking out her wife, Lena checked along the ground floor first, checking in J’onn’s office and finding him working at the ledgers alone, then the room with a few little sailboats being repaired, and then continued further along, poking her head into rooms and listening for the sound of anyone around. Near the end of the floor, the opposite end to where she’d been holed up, Lena heard voices and lightened her tread as she crept closer.

     

                “-obey me, do you understand me? Your oaths are to me, to the Unseelie Court, and I will always be your priority,” Lillian hissed, looming over Sam, who was on her knees, each arm taken by one of her sisters, their hands pressed on her shoulders to keep her kneeling there.

     

                Hovering just outside the doorway, stumbling upon the scene, Lena’s mouth went dry. She didn’t know whether to make herself known or continue walking, no one else in the vicinity to fetch and an undercurrent of unease to the display of power. She didn’t like it one bit as she lurked in the shadows of the hallways.

     

                “You may have found the means to twist my orders by following her here in some pretence of guarding her, but from now on, you will be brought to heel. Have I made myself clear?”

     

                Sam didn’t speak and Lena was startled by the quick slap that followed her silence. As Sam’s head whipped to the side, her hazel eyes got a quick glimpse of Lena before Pestilence grabbed a fistful of her brown hair and dragged her attention back to her Queen. Lena noticed blood on her face, her stomach jolting at the deep red of it against her skin.

     

                “Have I made myself clear, Reign?” Lillian harshly repeated.

     

                Before she could stop herself, Lena was crossing the threshold, drawing in a quick breath as she squared her shoulders, heart pounding loudly in her chest, betraying her unease. “What’s the meaning of this?”

     

                “It is a matter that does not concern you, daughter. Leave us.”

     

                “I am not to be commanded in my wife’s halls, mother,” Lena curtly responded, her gaze hostile. 

     

                Pausing, Lillian glanced sideways at her, a rather chilling expression on her face, and she slowly turned to face her daughter. Giving her a piercing look as Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction, hands balled into fists at her sides, Lillian slowly cocked her head to the side. A faint smile graced her lips and she shrugged nonchalantly, gliding towards her daughter and pausing to trace a sharp nail over her cheek.

     

                “No matter. I believe I have made my point. Purity, Pestilence, come. Your sister may join us when she remembers her priorities.”

     

                Letting go of Sam, who sagged where she kelt, shoulders hunched forward as her hair fell around her face, the two hunters obediently followed after her mother as the three of them swept from the room. Rooted to the spot for a moment, Lena frowned and then turned to Sam, quickly crossing over to her and dropping to a crouch. Hesitantly reaching out, she set a hand on her shoulder and flinched slightly as the woman’s head snapped up, hazel eyes flat, face hard as she looked at Lena.

     

                “Hey, you alright?” Lena apprehensively asked.

     

                A furrow formed between Sam’s eyebrows and she blinked, her face crumpling with confusion for a moment as some clarity came back to her gaze. Lena gave her shoulder a gentle shake, concerned for her, much to her surprise.

     

                “Sam?”

     

                “I’m fine,” Sam replied after a delayed pause, raising a hand to her nose, which was the source of the bleeding, clearly having been struck before Lena had entered the room. 

     

                Producing a handkerchief with clumsily embroidered stitches vaguely resembling waves, as drawn by a child, Lena held it out to her and then pressed it to Sam’s nose when her guard didn’t take it. There was the faintest smell of smoke in the air from where her blood had dripped off her chin, ashes in her lap, and Lena watched as Sam blinked again and then took the handkerchief from her.

     

                “Wait here,” Lena instructed her before climbing to her feet and stalking out of the room.

     

                Purposefully striding through the hallways, she listened for the sound of Andrea and found her in the great hall at the fireside, reading and drinking some red currant tea away from the cold. There were others in the room and Lena quickly crossed over to her, keeping her voice down as she loomed over her attendant, casting a shadow over the page. Glancing up, Andrea gave her an expectant look.

     

                “Can I help you, Your Highness?”

     

                “Come with me.”

     

                “May I ask why? I am quite content, you see-”

     

                “No,” Lena curtly responded, reaching down to grab her arm and dragging her up.

     

                Spluttering with indignation, Andrea made a low sound of frustration at the back of her throat, almost a growl really, and knocked back the remainder of her tea before setting the cup on her seat with the closed book. Shooting daggers at Lena as she yanked her arm free of her grasp, Andrea reluctantly kept up with the brisk pace she set out of the hall, taking the stairs two at a time as they headed down.

     

                “What, may I ask, is so important that you need my help?”

     

                “Sam.”

     

                Pausing, lagging behind a step as she was caught off guard, Andrea licked her lips and hurried to catch up. “What of her?”

     

                “I know of the two of you. I caught my mother- well, I’m not sure what the full extent of it was, but she was angry at her and had her hunters knock her about a fair bit. I thought- well, I don’t know if Sam wanted anyone to know but I know if it was- well, I would want to know if someone I cared about was hurt.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, well … thank you,” Andrea murmured, her indignation quickly giving way to bewildered gratitude.

     

                Frowning, Lena forged onwards and then gestured to the doorway of the room she’d left Sam in. She didn’t want to intrude on a private moment, only wanted someone with more of a connection to her guard to care for her, so after a brief glimpse to watch as Andrea fell to her knees in front of her, reaching for the bloodied handkerchief, Lena left them to it, rubbing her brow as she walked the length of the hallway to head outside onto the beach for some fresh air.

     

                As she was exiting, head hanging as she smoothed away the lines of worry on her brow, looking down at the smoothly worn limestone underfoot, she was so absorbed in her own thoughts that she almost walked straight into someone. Strong hands caught her before they collided and she blinked in surprise as she jumped back, looking up at her wife, who was smiling slightly, head tilted to the side as she appraised her.

     

                “Careful.”

     

                “Oh. Sorry.”

     

                “Are you well? Is something amiss?” Kara quickly asked, her smile dying and her expression pinching with worry as she held Lena’s arms in her hands, taking note of her distracted tone and rather solemn expression.

     

                Mouth thinning, Lena sighed. “It’s- I don’t know, my mother and her hunters just had Sam … I don’t know, attacked? Beaten?”

     

                Surprise flashed across Kara’s face and she let go of Lena as she tried to brush past her. Blocking the way, Lena grimaced and gave her an exasperated look. “It’s alright. Andrea’s with her now, let’s just … leave them to it.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara nodded and Lena kept her hands planted against her shoulders for a moment longer as their eyes met, conscious of the small space between them, feeling Kara’s warm breath ghost over her mouth. Struck with the maddening urge to lean in and kiss her, Lena propelled her backwards instead, down the sandy steps and onto the beach with her. Kara let out a light laugh as she kept backing up, even when Lena’s hands dropped away, leaving footprints in her wake as she studied her wife. 

     

                “Sam will be alright.”

     

                “I know,” Lena said, wrinkling her nose as she looked out at the rough sea with a stormy look on her face. “It just- I don’t know. It didn’t feel right; something felt off about it.”

     

                Changing her trajectory, Kara walked towards her and reached out to cup her chin, blue eyes comforting and kind. “All will be well, Lena.”

     

                Nodding, Lena wrapped her arms around herself and rubbed her hands over the sleeves of her dress. Her expression was brooding as she paced a few steps away, eyeing the sky and the dark clouds that spoke of incoming bad weather. The air was frigid, a thin mist blurring the horizon offshore. In a month or so, it would be spring, but to Lena, it still felt like deep winter, although it hadn’t snowed in days now.

     

                Standing at her side, Kara stared out to sea and they lingered in companionable silence for a few minutes before Lena’s mouth twitched slightly at the corners. Keeping her gaze straight ahead, she swallowed and drew in a shallow breath.

     

                “I made you something.”

     

                Glancing sideways at her, Kara smiled slightly, cheek shallowly dimpling. “You made me something?”

     

                “Mhm. A handkerchief. Um … it wasn’t very good, and I’d give it to you, but I had to use it to wipe up the blood on Sam’s face. So … well, I don’t have anything for you now. Sorry.”

     

                Reaching down to give her hand a gentle squeeze, Kara’s smile grew a fraction. “Thank you. That was very thoughtful.”

     

                “I mean … it definitely wasn’t good,” Lena repeated with a huff of laughter. “I’ll make you a new one. Without bloodstains.”

     

                Laughing along with her, Kara gave her hand another squeeze and then looked at her from the corner of her eyes. “Are you alright?”

     

                “Mhm. Are you?”

     

                Running a hand through her hair, Kara blew the air out of her cheeks and shook her head. “I’m not sure. There is far more shadow than light in me these days. I do not care for it.”

     

                “What can I do to help?”

     

                Turning to her, dropping her hand, Kara smiled sweetly as she gave Lena’s chin a gentle squeeze. “You already help; you are much of the light. Come inside; you will freeze if you stay out here much longer without your cloak.”

     

                Lena nodded, despite the worry that nagged her, concerned for her wife and the things she kept close to herself. They were honest with each other and kept very few secrets - or she liked to think that they did - but she knew that Kara didn’t include her in most of what was going on, sparing her any responsibility or burdens of trying to solve their current predicament. Still, as excluded as she was from it, Lena was well aware of the rising tension and the unease that left everyone’s shoulders taut and expressions serious most of the time. 

     

                Making their way back inside, they wound up in the great hall together, Kara making her way over to her harp to quietly play in the corner, while Lena asked if anyone would be interested in a game of stones with her, M’gann joining her at the board. Warm and distracted, she played a few games, losing them all, and then followed the others out as someone decided it was time to eat and everyone followed suit. Dinner was a rather quiet affair, Sam and Andrea absent, Lillian tense and hard-faced at the opposite end of the table, and Alex and Kelly out scouting in the dark, leaving only a handful of them there to dine together. 

     

                Eating slowly as the awkwardness over the room left them mostly silent, cutlery and cups scraping, the wind howling, Lena finished and lingered for a few minutes before excusing herself. Making her way upstairs, she changed into warmer bedclothes and tied a robe on top before climbing into bed with a book she was slowly getting through, her mind distracted instead of focused on the glyphs. There was a feeling of apprehension, of nervousness as she thought about later on, the suggestion that she go to Kara making her stomach clench with anticipation. She had surprised even herself when she’d asked, never so forward with what she wanted, but Lena was glad she’d been able to ask for what she wanted, feeling a little more at ease. 

     

                Of course, she’d known that talking to her wife instead of avoiding her and letting her confusion and frustration bottle up until she lashed out was the better path to take, it had felt so difficult to do it at the time. Until two nights ago when she’d made a conscious effort to let her walls down and be honest for a change - with herself and with Kara - and it had felt so much better. She’d spent the last two days feeling like a weight had been lifted off her shoulders, and it wasn’t entirely attributed to good sex with her wife, but it was definitely a contributing factor. 

     

                The more she thought about it, the more she wanted to head across the hallway and seek her wife out now, undress her slowly and put her mouth in all the places she’d thought about on so many lonely nights, the places she’d put her mouth on several occasions already but found the prospect just as thrilling. Desire settling low in her belly, Lena was restless as the evening wore on, giving up on her book after an hour and then turning to her notebook, writing down the information she’d learnt that day with a stick of charcoal and then trying to spell it phonetically in and then in the swirling glyphs of the fae language.
