                She was well aware of the time when Kara came up to her room, slowing as she angled towards her bedroom, as if torn between going to her wife or waiting for her. The anticipation of it made Lena’s pulse quicken and her stomach swoop, but she still waited a long while before she climbed to her feet, putting her things away and washing charcoal from her hands before she tried to smooth out her wrinkled bedrobe and brush her hair back, and then finally slipped out of her room and into Kara’s, hovering in the doorway a moment.

     

                “Good evening,” Kara murmured as she looked up to meet Lena’s eyes.

     

                “Good evening.”

     

                Setting her quill down and climbing to her feet, Kara stayed behind her desk as Lena stepped inside, closing the distance between them. She was a little apprehensive, plainly written on her face, but she was drawn to Kara as surely as if she was being reeled in on a hook. Kara was likewise a little uncertain, a little shy, giving Lena a small smile as she neared her.

     

                “I wasn’t sure you would come.”

     

                “It was my idea.”

     

                “Yes, but there was nothing to hold you to it.”

     

                “I would be insulted by your lack of faith in me if I hadn’t given you good cause to be wary,” Lena quietly laughed.

     

                “It is not a lack of faith. I thought perhaps you might be tired; the hour is late.”

     

                “I wanted to make sure everyone else was asleep first. Sorry if I’ve kept you up-”

     

                “No, no, not at all. I have been making good use of the time.”

     

                Leaning against the desk, Lena tried to make sense of what she was looking at upside down. “Doing what?”

     

                “Taking stock of things and … making arrangements.”

     

                “What arrangements?”

     

                Turning one of the heavy ledgers so Lena could get a better look, reading the glyphs she’d memorised and fitting them together, pointing out one or two to Kara to double-check the meaning, Kara cleared her throat and ran her fingers lightly over the dried ink. 

     

                “This is how many barrels of freshwater we have here. This is the figure of sacks of grains - wheat, barley, oats, milled flour - and sacks of salt for curing meats. The number of my people willing to fight, in comparison to weapons and horses, in comparison to sea-worthy boats. J’onn has managed the trading well in my absence, and we have been well-stocked for this winter, but the arrangements … well, the arrangements are for war.”

     

                “War?” Lena softly echoed, raising her eyes to meet Kara’s.

     

                Hesitating, Kara nodded after a moment. “The reports … are not good. My mother intends to leave within the week; I’m sorry for that, I know you were looking forward to learning from her, but she is the Lady of her halls and must see to the mountain passes to defend against the east.”

     

                “No, that’s- of course she does. My lessons aren’t a priority,” Lena quickly replied, her throat a little tight from the panic of war. “Will we- I mean … do we have enough supplies? Are we … going to be okay?”

     

                Kara gave her a faint smile, not entirely convincing, and laid a hand over Lena’s, on top of the page. “We shall be fine, Lena. You shall be fine.”

     

                “I- what’s that supposed to mean? You’re not sending me away, are you?”

     

                Her panic grew and she felt a lick of anger, bristling as she straightened, mouth opening to plead her case or reason with her wife. Reaching out to gently cup her face, Kara tenderly stroked her cheek.

     

                “No, I will not send you away. As much as I desire to keep you safe, in truth I would not entrust your safety to anyone else, save my family, who are here with me. And I would not be able to part with you even if I were to send them with you; I would miss you too much.”

     

                “Good,” Lena breathlessly replied, hackles lowering as her shoulders slumped with relief. 

     

                “Is it good, that I should be so selfish as to endanger your life?”

     

                Blinking, her brow furrowing with consternation, Lena licked her lips as she took a moment to reply. “I- well, yes, obviously it’s good. I don’t want you to send me away, so how is it selfish of you not to? You couldn’t make me go anyway, so really, we’re both getting what we want. And isn’t that what you’ve been trying to convince me to do?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara conceded with a slightly aching look. “But that does not make it easier for me when I consider the danger we are all in.”

     

                “I thought we were safe here.”

     

                “We are removed from it all. The mountains and the wetlands make it harder for large parties to reach us, and small parties we can defend ourselves from. However, if a larger force were to reach us, we are penned in with our backs to the sea.”

     

                “You have ships.”

     

                “Yes, I have a few small sailboats for fishing or ferrying supplies. That does not mean we would not have to leave so much behind, but it would offer us a quick escape if we were overrun. It is not the issue.”

     

                “What is?”

     

                Shoulders slumping slightly as she grimaced, Kara gestured limply towards Lena. “I have told you before that I fear the day I must make you board a ship against your will. It is why I admit to having thought of sending you away now, while there is still time to send you west on horseback.”

     

                “Kara,” Lena softly sighed, a grim look on her face as she raked her dark hair back. “You and I both know that if it comes to it, I will be on a boat by my own choice, and I will not hate you even an ounce for it. I will just be glad to live another day.”

     

                “But you would be frightened, and I think I would hate myself for that even if you did not hate me.”

     

                “I could never hate you.”

     

                “We are all capable of hatred.”

     

                “Yes, but I could never hate you . You’ve done so much for me, all I can feel is gratitude. Granted, I haven’t always been grateful, and I haven’t always been nice to you, but that’s only because it’s taken me a while to accept it all. Now I- well …”

     

                “Now you what?”

     

                Lips pressed together, Lena rolled her eyes and let out a quiet huff of laughter, “now, I guess I have a better understanding of a lot of things, and I know you better now, so I find it hard to blame you for anything at all. Even marrying me in the first place. If I were in your position, I probably would’ve done the same, except I don’t think you would have made it so difficult for me.”

     

                “Ah, well, if you were in my position, I would be in your position, so I believe I would have made it similarly as difficult for you as you did for me. We are both stubborn, I think.”

     

                “Yes, we are,” Lena said with a faint smile, her cheek shallowly dimpling as her green eyes flickered with amusement.

     

                There was a brief moment of silence and Kara stared down at her ledger and eased it closed, done for the night as she moved over to the basin of cold water and washed dried ink from her hands. Clearing her throat, back to Lena, she spoke quietly, hesitantly.

     

                “I have rambled on for too long; you must wish to sleep.”

     

                “I didn’t come here to sleep.”

     

                “You didn’t come here to hear me talk either. It is late.”

     

                Easing off the edge of the table she’d been perching on, Lena cocked her head to the side and took in the bowed, golden head of her wife, the way she’d messily rolled her billowing shirtsleeves up, the glimpse of her tanned forearms, muscular and elegant. Licking her lips, Lena drew in a shallow breath.

     

                “I came here for your company - I didn’t specify which kind. But … I’m not tired yet, if you aren’t.”

     

                Drying her hands, Kara slowed as she glanced back over her shoulder, blue eyes shining with amusement in the dim lighting of her room. Straightening, she set down the cloth and walked towards Lena, pausing in front of her as they stared at each other. Lena could feel her heart stumble in her chest, quickening, as her stomach clenched, yet she kept her hands at her sides, some part of her still reluctant to reach out first, to claim what she wanted.

     

                Kara likewise stared at her, eyes searching as she appraised Lena, as if making sure she really wasn’t too tired to be there, and there was a prolonged pause. Then Lena let out a small laugh, a smile crossing her face as she raised her eyebrows.

     

                “What is it?” Kara murmured.

     

                “I don’t know, it just feels … different this time. I guess this is the first time it’s been intentional.”

     

                “Was it not intentional the other night?”

     

                “No, it was all very spur of the moment,” she blithely replied.

     

                “Do you prefer the spontaneity?”

     

                “I don’t know. Maybe. I think I have less time to think it through and talk myself out of it.”

     

                Giving her a small smile as she reached out to take her hand, Kara gently squeezed her fingers. “If you need to talk yourself into it, I think you should return to your room.”

     

                “No,” Lena murmured, frowning as she lowered her gaze. “I’m not talking myself into it, I’m just- it feels like it has more meaning if it’s intentional, and that’s difficult for me to come to terms with.”

     

                “In what way?”

     

                “Meaningful as in … I might delude myself into thinking there are feelings involved that neither of us want to feel.”

     

                Stepping in closer, the small distance shrinking down to nothing, Kara’s hand slid up Lena’s arm. “And what feelings would they be?”

     

                “Oh, you know, the ones that make me think that we care for each other more than we should.”

     

                “Then I do not think you would be deluding yourself into thinking that there are feelings involved.”

     

                Eyelids closing, Lena smiled wryly. “You misunderstand-”

     

                “I misunderstand nothing. You are concerned that there is love between us, but is there not? You are my family so my love encompasses you also.”

     

                “I’m less concerned with that than about getting the wrong impression.”

     

                “What impression would you like me to make?”

     

                With a quiet laugh, Lena tipped her head forward, brow settling on Kara’s shoulder. She let out a resigned sigh, shifting closer, pressing herself against her wife’s lithe body as her hands ran up Kara’s sleeves, feeling lean muscle beneath the billowing shirt, her body radiating a delicious heat.

     

                “I don’t know, just make it a good one.”

     

                Calloused fingertips carefully brushed dark hair back over Lena’s shoulders and then stroked the side of her neck, and she felt her pulse quicken at the touch, feeling Kara’s fingers move back up, over her jaw and to her temple, before circling around her ear to brush a loose strand back. Brushing the short tips of Lena’s ears, Kara stroked the side of her neck again and then softly kissed the pointed tips, making Lena’s stomach clench at the sudden arousal. 

     

                Feeling the soft brush of her wife’s lips kiss the path her fingers had just taken, Lena gripped her arms a little tighter, thumbs pressing against her biceps. She still had her brow resting on Kara’s shoulder and felt her wife’s hand cup her chin to gently urge her head to the side so she could kiss her. It was slow and cautious, Kara’s mouth warm against hers, and Lena’s lips parted as she grabbed fistfuls of her shirt, the enormity of her desire surprising her as any thoughts about wrong impressions were banished for the time being. 

     

                Kara lifted her onto the large desk and Lena let out a sound of surprise as she sent things scattering, spilling an ink well over a few loose pages, a pot with quills tumbling over and a little set of scales clattering loudly as the weights fell off the brass plate. Reacting quickly, Kara caught the pot before it could roll off the edge of the desk, breathing a little heavier as she gripped Lena’s waist in her other hand, her throat bobbing as she swallowed thickly.

     

                “Sorry,” Kara murmured, setting the pot down as her nose brushed Lena’s cheek.

     

                Letting out a quiet laugh, Lena recaptured her lips, kissing her once, twice. “Are you trying to summon an audience?”

     

                “I hope not. I would hate to have to stop.”

     

                Smiling against her lips, Lena felt Kara’s hands at the belt of her robe, deftly undoing it and then parting the front before she paused. Pulling back slightly, she gave her wife a searching look, expression momentarily clouding.

     

                “What’s wrong?” she whispered.

Each boat also had a store of Kara’s valuables; uncut jewels and stones, lumps of raw gold and silver, rings, necklaces and circlets. Anything that could be used by her enemy to trade for supplies or bolster meagre stores was depleted. She’d even gone so far as to bury several chests of family heirlooms along the coastline of her lands, places only she’d be able to recover them from afterwards. 

     

                The work wasn’t finished yet, and Kara motioned water from the sea, creating her humanoid figures as they bore crates, chests and barrels for her, rearranging things for ease of access, shifting damp coils of rope and freshly carved oars on board. It was strenuous to keep them moving and keep the water condensed enough to carry physical objects, but less taxing on her body than hauling the cargo about herself as she busied herself with maps and charts, rolling them into cylindrical leather cases and stowing a set on each boat in case they were separated. They would hopefully be able to stay within land at all times, and within sight of each other, but if it came to it, she wouldn’t have any of them stranded or without the means to survive at sea for at least a week.

     

                She worked sporadically as her mind drifted from task to task, and the morning passed her by until her hunger became apparent. Kara finished packing away her armour and loading it on board before she made her way back to the kitchen, where Lena still occupied the long counter. She had given up on sewing the fishes back together and was baking instead, a row of golden hand pies still steaming from baking over the fire. Now, she was working on some bread, kneading the dough with a clouded look on her face.

     

                Kara rounded the table and cradled her waist as she stood behind her, leaning in to brush her lips over the back of Lena’s neck. She felt Lena jolt in her grasp, shying away from her as she murmured. “Don’t do that.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                “Because we don’t do that. And anyone could walk in, so ...”

     

                “No one will sneak up on us without me hearing.”

     

                With a heavy sigh, Lena brushed her hair back and then cleared her throat. “I know,” she murmured. “Sorry, I just- I don’t want to leave.”

     

                Kara turned her in her hands and smiled slightly as she reached up to wipe away the streak of flour left behind by Lena’s hand. Blue eyes creasing at the corners, a smile still didn’t quite reach them as her shoulders slumped.

     

                “I know. I’m sorry for that.”

     

                “I don’t want you to be sorry.”

     

                “And yet, I am.”

     

                Turning back around, Lena continued to knead the dough as Kara watched her, before she cut it into even pieces and worked them into small loaves. Covering them with a clean square of linen, she left them to rise and washed off her hands before giving Kara a sulky look.

     

                “I just- I’ve moved around so much, my whole life, and no one has ever stayed, and now your mother is leaving and we’re leaving and I feel so … unrooted. I like your mom; she’s been good to me, and I’d like to know her better, but now she’s going home, and we won’t even have a home.”

     

                Moving in closer, Kara cupped her cheek and smoothed her thumb over the high bone, giving her a strained smile. “You told me your home was me, and I shall be with you always. It will be a mere few days by boat, I promise you, and then we will have horses the rest of the way. Our journey will take us to Alex’s home, and my sister’s hearth is mine, which is yours. We will be safe there.”

     

                “For how long?” Lena quietly demanded. 

     

                Dropping her hand, Kara’s mouth thinned with regret. “I cannot say.”            

     

                Nodding, Lena looked uneasy - not frightened, but just uncertain about it all, which surprised Kara even more - and reached for one of the hand pies. She held it up and smiled grimly. “They’re for your mother to take with her, but here. You can be my tester.”

     

                Softening, Kara smiled as she took it from her. “Thank you,” she murmured before hesitating and leaning in to kiss her wife’s cheek, a glint in her eyes when she drew back. “And we do do that.”

     

                With a quiet scoff, Lena softly whacked her with another square of linen as Kara laughed, before covering the pies with it. Taking a bite of her pie, Kara hummed appreciatively and gave Lena another eye-crinkling smile, this one genuine, before making herself scarce with a parting order for her wife to eat as well. She didn’t see her for the rest of the day, conferring with her friends and her sister, ensuring everyone was on the same page, ready to leave within a few days. There would still be a few things to arrange and Kara spent the remainder of her afternoon brooding over her list as her hands grew stained with ink and she itched for the refreshingly cold sting of the sea at her back. Duty came first though and she remained seated at her desk, writing letters and pressing her seal to the hot wax before sending birds to the wind with her letters tied to their legs. 

     

                Dinner was a sombre affair, even more so than it had been since Lillian’s arrival, and no one spoke much as Kara grimly awaited her mother’s departure as she picked at her food. It was dark and raining, the hour growing late, and no sooner had she finished eating did Eliza declare it was time for her to leave. Both daughters and their wives abandoned their own meals as they all rose to their feet as Eliza bid the other occupants farewell. She’d already changed into her travelling clothes, a heavy robe and cloak in the deep grey of storm clouds, the underlayers split for riding, and she retrieved her pack and weapons from her room before making for the stables with the four women in tow.

     

                Alex saddled her mother’s horse for her as she tried to reason with Eliza, cinching buckles. “Let us accompany you. Just through the marshes.”

     

                “Save your energy for your own safety. All will be well with me,” Eliza soothed her with a hand on her arm before she turned away.

     

                Kelly went to her first, saying her quiet goodbye, murmuring promises and looking rather grave as she nodded at Eliza’s advice, before bowing her head for her mother-in-law’s kiss and a quick embrace. She retreated and Lena found Eliza’s attention turned to her. Kara watched as her mother cupped Lena’s cheeks in her hands, smiling warmly at her. She couldn’t help but overhear the quiet conversation between the two of them as she hung back, waiting to part with her last. 

     

                “Thank you for all of your help,” Lena murmured.

     

                “My daughters will continue to teach you,” Eliza said. “Work hard and you will do well, I should think.”

     

                She paused, a shallow furrow between her brows as her mouth thinned. “Be wary of her as well, Lena. I am unsure of how, but I do not believe she should be trusted, even at her word. Whatever danger there is in the forest has twisted her too, a darkness within, that much is plain; she is smart enough to bide her time, but there will come a time.”

     

                Lena didn’t have to question who she was talking about, nodding gravely with her face still between her mother-in-law’s hands. Gently tilting her face down in her grasp, Eliza kissed Lena’s brow and then turned her attention to her daughters. Lena met Kara’s eyes briefly before she slipped through the door leading back inside, giving them some privacy to say their farewells. Moving forward, Kara smiled as Eliza pressed one hand to her cheek, and the other to Alex, looking between her daughters.

     

                “I do not need to tell you to be safe in these perilous times, but I will say it all the same. Look after one another and be wise. I will do what I can for you in the mountains; my people will hold the pass to the last of us if it comes to it, but you must flee.”

     

                Kara nodded, her throat tight. “I will do all that I can for peace.”

     

                Eliza stroked her cheek with her thumb as she smiled faintly. “Look after her. She has finally found the path but it is a long journey and she will fail without you. And, I think, you will be lost without her.”

     

                “I will ensure her safety. We are committed to the purpose of our marriage.”

     

                “Ensure that she keeps you safe as well.”

     

                A funny smile crossed Kara’s face and she let out a small laugh. “There is nothing she can protect me from that I cannot protect myself from.”

     

                “There are many ways to keep someone safe. Do not dismiss her yet.” 

     

                “I will not,” Kara murmured in agreement. “Travel safely, mother. We will see each other again soon.”

     

                She bowed her head and let Eliza kiss her forehead before hugging her, the embrace tight as they both secretly feared the tragedy of no future reunion. They wouldn’t speak it though, wouldn’t give voice to their doubts, but they held on a moment longer before parting. Stepping back, Kara let her sister say farewell, murmuring promises and letting Eliza impart her wisdom before she kissed and hugged her goodbye.

     

                They both stood back as they watched her mount her horse in one fluid motion, reins in hand as the horse shifted beneath her, and she smiled down at them, blue eyes tender with sadness to be leaving them once more. She’d stayed far longer than usual, due to the danger and the desire to help her children where she could, but Eliza had always needed to leave eventually, her own people needing her.

     

                “Send word once you are home safely,” Alex said with a shadowed look in her eyes.

     

                With a laugh, Eliza raised her eyebrows. “I have traversed these lands for many years longer than you have been alive; do not seek to caution me. I love you both.”

     

                She urged her horse into motion and they trailed it to the wide archway of the stables, watching as their mother set off at a trot through the sheeting rain. Shoulders slumping, Kara grimaced and clapped her sister on the back before they turned away and slipped back inside. They set off down the hallway as they quietly conversed, until they reached Kara’s room and lowered their voices as they turned to more serious matters.

     

                “J’onn and I have come to the same result again. We cannot leave any resources behind but it will slow us considerably to take it all with us. It will take us three days of quick sailing to reach the Guardian, and we shall be able to make a gift of the bulkier resources to Kelly’s mother there, hopefully in exchange for horses, but that is dependent on how many of us make up our party.”

     

                “Kara,” Alex started to protest, her mouth thinning with understanding. “They are not your people, nor your responsibility.”

     

                “Ah, well, she is my kin now, for good or ill, and I have extended hospitality to them all, so I am obligated to hold to it.”

     

                “Your hospitality ends the moment we flee.”

     

                “It would weigh on my conscience to abandon them here to die.”

     

                “It shall not weigh on mine so let it be my decision. We cannot all sail west, nor will they be welcome anywhere else. Yes, we need resources aplenty for our journey, and we cannot leave any behind to aid the Prince, but leave some for Lillian’s cohort and leave them to their own survival. The rest will be sorely needed by your vassals to the east.”

     

                “Yes, I have M’gann sailing with a ship full in the morning. Salt, meat, grain and cider. All that I can spare, all that will be left for him to plunder if it comes to it. I will serve my people first, of course I will.”

     

                “I do not doubt that, but you will serve our unwelcome allies too, and that is more perilous. They will outnumber us when we leave; we will all be endangered then.”

     

                Drifting to her desk, staring down at the plans they’d rehashed a dozen times already, Kara grimaced. “If we leave them behind, we provide him with the opportunity to ally himself with his mother, take her numbers for himself.”

     

                “She has little love for him now after he took her crown. It is more likely he will slash her throat to legitimise his claim. I doubt he will see the title of kinslayer as an obstacle to committing regicide.”

     

                “I fear you are right, and yet …”

     

                “You must do as you see fit as Lady of the Waterfolk, and I am beholden to your promise of hospitality, but the moment we flee, I will gut as many of the Unseelie rats as I can and toss them into the sea if it means we will not have our throats slit in our sleep.”

     

                “Do not make more trouble for me, I beg.”

     

                “You are making trouble for yourself, only further down the line. If you will not listen to me, then listen to our mother and the warning she gave your wife. Do not trust Lillian.”

     

                “I do not trust her,” Kara sighed, raking a hand through her hair. “I am just unsure of the wisest course to sail.”

     

                Alex sank onto the bed with a weary sigh, head bowed as she rubbed the bridge of her nose and then stilled. Kara was behind her desk, hands braced against the worn wood as she hunched over the arrangements. There was a moment of silence and Kara watched as Alex ducked down even lower to smell the pillows. Stomach swooping, Kara knew what she would smell; green apples and pine, and something earthy like the forest. Her sister straightened and her stare from across the room was cutting, no skirting around the truth between them.

     

                “Ah,” Alex murmured, grimacing, “so, you have had her in your bed then.”

     

                “A number of times now,” Kara softly admitted, hesitating a moment as she pressed her lips together before she sighed, her shoulders caving. “I will not ask you to keep secrets from your wife, but I ask that you do not tell anyone else. She does not wish for it to be known.”

     

                “As if it would matter,” Alex scoffed. “Wed half a year - I should be surprised it has taken so long, as beautiful as you both are. I suppose we can attribute her improved mood to your intimacy?”

     

                Kara let out a surprised laugh, cheeks dimpling as she eased herself onto her seat and slumped in it, rumpled robe draping around her as she tipped her head back. “Wrong, sister, but you may attribute her dismal moods to it.”

     

                Clicking her tongue and then laughing, Alex leaned back on her elbows. “Truly that bad? No wonder she resented being wed to you.”            

     

                Scoffing, Kara reached for the nearest object to lob at her sister - a particularly nice shell she’d once found - and fought back a smile as her sister lazily snatched it from the air. “It has been difficult for her to acknowledge what she wants. I will not betray her trust by speaking of her feelings with you, but … I suppose you are somewhat correct that her improved mood of late has been partially attributed to reconciling herself with those particular wants. She was not in high spirits at first, afraid it would not bode well for our friendship if we were intimate, but now ...”

     

                “Now?”

     

                Lips twitching with a small smile, Kara leaned forward for her cup of wine and knocked back the remainder of it before reaching for her jug. “Now, she trusts that I will not abandon her as everyone else in her life has.”

     

                Seeming pleased, Alex pushed herself to her feet. “Well, I will not deny that I am pleased for this change of heart between the two of you. It has been maddening to see you both so committed to your yearning dance, circling each other like sun and moon.”

     

                “Mm, she is quite like the moon, is she not?”

     

                “Please, do not wax poetically to me,” Alex groaned, “I have heard enough of your poor attempts at flattery. Any attempts to draw a comparison with the moon will surely only enrage her; cold, distant, remote.”

     

                “I thought perhaps beautiful, luminous.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex shook her head. “I will be leaving now.”

     

                Kara laughed as she took another sip of her wine, chin propped up in her hand as a tenderly pensive look softened her face. For all the worries she had, she looked less troubled when thinking of her wife. That was not lost on her sister, who trailed towards the door as she studied her, shoulders slumping slightly with relief as a small smile graced her lips.

     

                “I am truly pleased for you.”

     

                Waving her fingers in a dismissive gesture, Kara sighed as a wry smile quirked her lips. “You needn’t be pleased I have taken a lover. She is not the first, and I am sure there will be many others to come.”

     

                “I’m not pleased you’ve taken another lover,” Alex scoffed, “only that you seem happier now than I believe I have ever seen you. I do not know if she is solely responsible, but nevertheless, it warms the heart.”

     

                “We are on the brink of war and you think me the happiest I’ve ever been?” Kara softly exclaimed.

     

                Shrugging slightly, looking just as bewildered, Alex’s lips twitched at the corners with amusement. “Yes, I do. And I know it must be true, for we are on the brink of war, as you said, and such happiness should not be stoked in times like these. And yet …”

     

                “And yet.”

     

                “I should like to see how happy she makes you in times of peace.”

    Chapter 30

                Their week to finish their preparations was ultimately too optimistic. Word came from James of his soldiers retreating further from the river splitting the Courts, of more land yielded to the Prince and his growing band of Rogues. They worked quickly and slyly, small groups prowling through the forest and riverbank on the Seelie side of it, slitting throats in the dark and melting back into the shadows as they slowly but surely advanced. They just didn’t know how far back he’d been pushed with his thinning band of soldiers until they were practically on Krypton’s doorstep three nights later.

     

                She’d been in Kara’s bed earlier than night, worn out from a day of helping pack up resources and practising her stitching, embroidery and usual archery, sparring and wrestling. Bruised and aching but feeling stronger and more certain and grounded in herself, Lena had felt a certain bittersweet quality to the day, now that she knew her time in Krypton was ending. She hated the sea and was nervous - she told herself it was nerves instead of terror - about sailing on the open water, but she’d gotten used to her routine there, had actually found herself adapting quite well after so many months, finding some peace within herself there, despite the salt air and her small life on the coast. Looking back, so much had changed and so much had been learnt, some of it painfully so, and even the small steps she’d made seemed large in hindsight. Winter was almost at an end, half a year gone since she’d been dragged through to the Courts, and Lena couldn’t help but wonder if an autumn and a winter would ever mean so much again.

     

                It had been in the late hours of the night that she’d returned to her own bed, expecting to sleep the night away until dawn, but it could only have been a couple of hours when Lena jerked awake to the sound of someone shouting. It wasn’t close, slightly muffled as if snatched away by the wind, but the disturbance was obvious as her heartbeat quickened. The closer sound of bare feet on stone and a rasp of metal caught her attention and her eyes strayed to the door as she sat up in bed, blankets clutched to her chest, watching as her wife appeared. Naked with her sword in hand, long golden hair spilling down her back and a panicked look on her face as she beckoned to her wife.

     

                “Quickly. Leave everything - get to the boat. I’ll join you there.”

     

                Scrambling out of bed, Lena didn’t even pause to put on shoes, wearing only her nightgown and a heavy woollen robe over the top, just grabbed the sword and dagger attached to a belt and the unstrung bow and quiver of arrows as she tripped over her own feet in her haste. There were things she would have liked the time to gather up as well, but she didn’t hesitate at Kara’s fraught command. Anything that had been important was already stored on the boats downstairs.

     

                Out of bed, out of the room, she was ushered to the narrow staircase to the west of the building instead of the wide main staircase near the entrance, Kara’s warm touch on her shoulder for a brief moment before it was gone. Lena hesitated only once, at the top of the staircase, locking eyes with her wife, who was making sure she was safely on her way to their planned escape route before they parted ways.

     

                Feet slapping against the cold stone in her haste, Lena came out on the lowest level as she listened to the chaotic sounds of movement above, everyone roused from their beds by the sound of alarm, voices overlapping as questions were asked. She was the first one to reach the little harbour, the darkness of the sea through the open north-facing wall greeting her as she watched the ink-dark sea roil. The smell of salt was heavy in the air, the lap of water over the stones making her pause, a lump in her throat.

     

                She’d known this would happen eventually, that within the next few days, she’d be ushered onto a boat and they’d be cast out to sea, leaving Krypton behind. Ever since she’d arrived in Krypton, she’d wanted to leave, but not like this. And she couldn’t get onto a boat herself. Instead, she inched towards the harbour, stopping shy of where the biggest waves rushed over the stone floor, and took a moment to buckle on the sword belt, adjusting the weight of it on her hips, and then slinging the quiver across her chest. As an added precaution, Lena strung her bow, crouching on the floor, bending the supple wood and hooking the string until the bow stood taut. Rising to her feet, Lena plucked an arrow from her quiver for good measure, knocking but not drawing as she kept her eyes on the dark archway, the blood pounding in her head as she chewed her lip.

     

                Heart pounding in her chest as a cold sweat covered her body, Lena listened to the sounds of steel on steel, strangled screams and loud shouts, willing someone, anyone , to come so she wouldn’t be there alone. She heard footsteps then, the loud heartbeat of someone unfamiliar, and Lena had the sense to raise her bow and draw back the arrow, her shallow breaths and shaky hand making the arrow tip waver as she held it. When the person appeared in the doorway, she didn’t hesitate at the glimmer of a gold mask identifying them as the enemy, letting the arrow fly without a second thought. 

     

                Her unsteady hand set the arrow off-target, but the tip still caught the side of the man’s neck, ripping open his jugular vein with a spurt of blood. He staggered forward, a sound of surprise dying in his throat as he tried to clap a hand over the wound, and Lena let out a panicked sound as she watched him die, wide-eyed as she scrabbled for another arrow, feeling cold dread in her chest.

     

                Drawing the arrow back with the bowstring, Lena drew in sharp, shallow breaths as she slowly moved off-centre to the doorway, creeping towards the left side of the room, hoping it would give her an advantage, even just a few seconds to release. The next person to enter the room approached quickly, none of the tentative creeping, and Lena held the bowstring taut as she gritted her teeth, knowing she had to react quickly. She felt weak with relief when Andrea barrelled in a moment later, two long knives wreathed in flames in her hands, the smell of smoke clinging to her as she cast Lena a sharp look. 

     

                Relief punched through Lena, her shoulders caving as she slowly released the tension of the bowstring, and she watched as Andrea pivoted, her back to the sea now as she slowly retreated towards the boats, pale blue eyes on the door. Once she’d reached the short stone jetty extending into the sea, she glanced at Lena.

     

                “What are you waiting for? Get on the boat.”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena shifted uneasily. Making a low sound at the back of her throat, Andrea rolled her eyes and leapt onto the nearest boat, moving towards the anchor off the stern of the boat. She started to haul up the heavy chain, slick with algae and slightly rusted with age. Lena watched her, wondering whether she should do the same for the other boats, whether it would help speed up their escape. But she didn’t want to get on the boats, and she could buy whoever came in next more time by covering the door. She wasn’t quick with a bow, but at least she could provide some cover. That was better than nothing and at least she was being useful, one dead Rogue already cooling on the floor.

     

                The wind was brisk and she shivered, her bare feet feeling frozen as she held her position on the left side of the room. She could hear the fighting getting worse and fear pierced her heart as she trembled, ears strained for the sound of anyone approaching. It was consolidated upstairs, from what she could hear, but she willed them to hurry up, to retreat instead of fight. Why did everyone have to fight all the time?

     

                Chest tight, she felt her fear grow and felt an answering tremor through the stone. Mouth dry, Lena backed away from the door at the sound of people fast approaching, right arm pulling back as she drew the arrow. J’onn swept in first, a bloodied knife in his hand, M’gann at his back with a sword in hand and a pack over her shoulder as she fended off an attack. An unmasked Fae with golden hair followed but Lena didn’t recognise the woman, hesitating only briefly enough to watch her lunge for M’gann before loosing her arrow. It struck the woman’s shoulder and gave M’gann a much-needed second to hack into the side of the woman’s neck. 

     

                They glanced at Lena as they backed away from the door, J’onn reaching for his wife’s hand, tugging her towards the boats. He hesitated, reaching out a hand to Lena as he beckoned her, but she stood her ground. She might have been afraid, and she’d been cowardly many times and was maybe being cowardly again by not getting on the boat, but she wouldn’t leave without Kara. It was just unfortunate that Lena had married the most insufferably noble person in both Courts, who would undoubtedly be the last person onboard.

     

                “Next one! Next one!” Andrea shouted, gesturing to the boat at the next jetty as J’onn and M’gann changed their trajectory. 

     

                They split up, taking a boat each, weapons abandoned as they raised the anchors and hoisted the sails with the practised ease of those who’d spent their lives on the sea. Sounds of fighter grew louder as it came closer, Lillian sweeping in with Purity and Pestilence defending her, lethal as they fought off the five that approached, her mother trying to wield a sword in her off-hand, somewhat clumsy without her right hand attached. Lena was surprised she hadn’t been there first and as she sent two arrows into the fray in quick succession, the first grazing a cheek and the second pinging off armour, she watched as her mother boarded the boat with Andrea onboard. 

     

                “Get this thing moving,” Lillian ordered, glancing over her shoulder. “Purity!”

     

                Her guards hacked through the remaining two before falling back to her, heeding her call as they stepped over bodies, more shadows moving into the doorway, more than Lena thought they could stop. She had no idea how many were in Krypton but she felt terror constrict her chest, knowing Kara and the others were still out there. She shot arrow after arrow until her quiver was running low, killing or wounding more people than she’d ever imagined, unable to feel guilty right now as panic, self-preservation and adrenaline kept her body moving as her mind reeled.

     

                The next person through was familiar but shouldn’t have been there, James in his silver and gold armour, slamming a giant axe into the chest of a man, yelling down the hallway as he jerked his axe free. He ducked back out and Lena caught sight of a gold mask and sent another arrow streaking towards the person, catching them in the thigh and watching as they stumbled to one knee. A knife took them in the face and she watched someone jerk it free, hoping it was Alex for a brief moment when she caught sight of the shoulder-length hair, before the woman leapt into the room and ran to a boat. Lucy.

                

                There were others - soldiers that James shoved towards the boats as he shouted orders, Lillian’s Unseelie cohort, who had dashed across the beach to defend their Queen - piling onto boats until they were perilously close to being full. Lillian was still trying to get those on her boat to hoist the sails and cast off, a few ropes sawn through to remove the boat from its moorings, but none of them, including Purity, were adept at sailing or knew what they were doing.

     

                Lena had retreated back towards the boat as more people spilt in and more bodies scattered near the doorway. A few of James and Lillian’s people lay dead amongst them and Lena found it hard to swallow as she worried about Kara. She wanted to kick herself for listening to her and going straight to the boat, wanted to go and search for her too, but knew that would make it harder for them to find each other when Kara was expecting her to be at the harbour. It had barely been fifteen minutes by Lena’s reckoning, and she knew that wasn’t a lot of time in the grand scheme of things, and that Kara had fought longer battles and come through the other side, but fifteen minutes was long enough to have been slaughtered and her body grown cold while Lena lingered, unaware.

     

                And then she was there, dressed now, a blue robe belted around the waist with her sword belt, barefoot and angry, her face like a stormcloud, blue eyes black in the dark. Her sword dripped with blood and her skin was splattered with it, same as Alex, Kelly and Sam as the three of them followed her in, creating a small knot as they fended off the Rogues, more of them than anticipated, in a blur of wind and fire. There were more of James and Lillian’s soldiers as well, knives, daggers and swords flashing amidst a jumble of elements, no room for bows there, except for Lena, who kept firing, her focus solely on her wife, who kept looking around, distracted.

     

                Sam saw Lena off to the side and changed her trajectory to the boat, grabbing her arm and dragging her along with her. Lena twisted in her grasp, a hard set to her face as she tore herself free. “No.”

     

                Crossing the rest of the distance to the boat with her sisters, Sam lithely landed on the deck and Lena tried to stifle her panic as water lapped over her feet, so close to the churning sea. She wanted to call out to her wife but didn’t want to endanger her by making Kara lose focus, watching as she quickly removed an arm and cut a throat, moving with such elegance that it seemed wrong that she left death in her wake. And still, her head kept turning, glancing over her shoulder as she looked towards the boats.

     

                Lena couldn’t make out what Kara was shouting, but she watched as Alex sent two little throwing knives into the chest and belly of a man without a mask and yelled something back as she sent a jet of flame towards another, melting their gold mask on their face as they screamed in agony. Out of arrows, Lena slung her bow over her head and shoulder so it cut across her chest, jerking her dagger free as she lurked in the corner, where the jetty started, the hem of her nightgown and robe soaked from the water that she’d barely acknowledged, so focused on everything else, so focused on her wife . 

     

                Kara was merely a few feet from her now, sword still cutting through their enemies as those on the boats thinned the ranks with arrows, but her distraction wasn’t apparent until she sheared through a woman’s stomach and turned with the force of the slice, her gaze landing on Lena. Watching her wife’s eyes widen at the sight of her, relief mingling with panic, Lena watched Kara straighten, shoulders squaring as she blocked and parried an attack from someone else, pushing back against them as she tried to put as much distance between Lena and anyone else with a wall of water pulled straight from the sea. 

     

                It was her eyes, searching for Lena after every dispatched enemy, that did it, her attention on her wife instead of the fight. Lena was already moving towards her, not wanting to be penned in near the water or the wall, skirting behind Kara, who skewered someone and roughly shouldered them off her blade before her eyes strayed to where Lena had been. When she didn’t see Lena there, she started to look around in a panic, and Lena watched her shoulders slump with relief at the sight of her wife a few feet behind her, not seeing the figure approaching. 

     

                At the stricken look on Lena’s face, Kara whirled around, her sword rising as she blocked the downstroke of the woman, and Lena felt her heart stumble in her chest. Relief washed over her but not quite strong enough to eclipse the anger and urgency as she lurched forward, already reaching for Kara, dagger in hand as panic blossomed in her chest. She moved instinctively, jamming the dagger into the side of the woman’s neck, blood splattering on her face as she jerked it free and pushed her away before she turned to Kara.

     

                As she turned to her wife, Lena was caught by surprise as Kara sagged against her, the heavy weight of her bearing down on her making Lena stumble backwards a step as she steadied them. Pushing her back up, Lena’s face was pale, aghast and bewildered as she took in the sudden ashen pallor of Kara’s face before her wife’s gaze hardened and she straightened. Lena barely caught sight of the blood wetting the left side of Kara’s abdomen before she was being pushed towards the boat.

     

                “Go. I’ll be right behind you.”

     

                One of the boats was already moving away from the jetty, Waterfolk fighting against the current as they guided it out of the harbour, and Lena watched as Alex slit a throat and then sprinted towards one of the other boats. Kelly was quick to follow, strung bow slung over one shoulder and long hunting knives in her hands as she sheathed them and slipped her bow off. She was on the deck of the boat with one leap, sinking to a crouch and knocking an arrow, sinking it into the eye of a woman.

     

                It was just Lena, Kara and a few soldiers against the Rogues now, the second boat moving out to sea, and Lena was torn, agonising over it for a few seconds. She knew that Kara wouldn’t get on the boat until she was on there, and it was that thought that kept her moving, towards the last boat, her mother’s cohort finally sawing the last rope free, the sails ballooning with the wind. It was already moving away from the jetty, and it took all of Lena’s courage to run down the stone, slick beneath her feet as the spray of the waves soaked her, and throw herself across the steadily widening gap. 

     

                Strong hands caught her and hauled her the rest of the way over before she could fall into the churning sea, and Lena lost her grip on her bloody dagger as she was set down, the boat bobbing violently beneath her. She looked back towards Krypton, the limestone harbour a mass of shadowed movement, and there, her wife standing on the edge of it as she fought with a few stragglers still standing. She was injured, she’d been bleeding, and now she was slipping further away from Lena as the boat carried them out to sea, the Waterfolk on board towing them away as quickly as they could fight the current. The ocean looked malevolent, large waves glimmering beneath weak moonlight piercing the clouds, the depths a black darker than the sky.

     

                Scrambling to the front of the boat, the wind whipping her dark hair about her, Lena clung to the edge of the boat, her heart in her throat. Even her shout was a hoarse croak, barely audible over the rain, wind, waves and creaking boat, the rain lashing her, barely felt.

     

                “Kara!” she yelled and yelled until her throat hurt and they were almost too far away. The end of the jetty was ten feet away, then twenty, thirty. “We have to go back. Turn around.”

     

                She spoke to no one, her commands falling on deaf ears, and Sam clapped a hand on her shoulder to drag her away. “We must keep going. Come away.”

     

                Tears stung her eyes, so much fear in her chest that Lena could feel it like a physical weight, barely able to breathe as her throat tightened. She held out a hand, reaching for Kara, as if she could grab ahold of her and drag her onto the boat, to safety, so much pent-up emotions filling her that she was shaking. Sam had her arms around Lena, trying to drag her away from the edge of the boat, but Lena fought against her, struggling to reach for the boat again, her hands outstretched as Kara was reduced to a shadowed figure at the edge of Krypton's lowest halls.

     

                She didn’t even mean to do it, wasn’t intentionally trying to do anything except possibly fling herself off the back of the boat and swim to her wife, but it took Lena a moment to realise that the shaking wasn’t just her body, that she felt it on a gut level, the entire cliffside trembling. It happened slowly, her desperation creating fissures in the limestone as the floor of the hall started to split, until the portion of flooring Kara had been standing on was no longer attached to the rest of Krypton, dragging her away from the halls as Lena’s power boiled over. That wasn’t the end of it, Kara pitching backwards at the sudden feeling of being adrift at sea, while the entirety of her ancestral home came apart at the hands of her wife as, as predicted by Alex, Lena sent Krypton plunging into the sea. 

     

                The heavy blocks of limestone crashed into the sea with an explosion of water, an endless torrent of broken stone as three levels of beautifully carved motifs, furniture and heirlooms of a thousand years, were pitched into the sea by Lena’s unpredictable power. The breath caught in her throat, her chest aching as she stared at the collapsing halls with horror in her eyes, her wife nowhere to be seen.

     

                The other two boats were ahead of them, to the left, heading west, and there were shouts and exclamations of surprise drifting across the water as they watched it happen. Going limp in Sam’s arms, Lena’s mouth was open, slack-jawed, as she stared hollowly at what had been a beautifully wrought hall in the side of the cliffs until mere moments ago. It had all happened so fast that she was struggling to process it.

     

                They were all helpless to watch, those with the oars straining against the rough sea as they tried to put distance between them and the shore. Everyone else was silent, most of them uncaring or relieved to have made it away safely, and Lena felt a sharp pain in her chest as Sam dragged her away from the stern so Lucy could try and steer the rudder, dodging the boom as James adjusted the triangular sail, heaving corded rope and funnelling wind into the heavy fabric. 

     

                “No, no, no,” Lena murmured to herself, eyes darting around at the people crammed onto the small boat, almost a dozen of them amidst the packed deck, none of them concerned with the fact that her wife was not onboard.

     

                She tried to lunge for the back of the boat again but felt Sam’s arms tighten around her, forcing her to the floor, and Lena tried to elbow her in the gut. “Let me go.”

     

                “What will you do?” Sam tightly murmured in her ear. “Will you swim back to shore? You’ll both be lost to us then.”

     

                “I’ll-”

     

                Lena cut off as an armoured body suddenly flopped over the stern of the boat, coughing and spluttering. The man had lost his helm and he weakly scrabbled for purchase, James abandoning his rope, the boom swinging wildly as the wind returned to its normal course. He lunged for the man and dragged him overboard with one hand and then reached down as a second soldier appeared. One more was thrown up onto the boat before Lena saw the familiar sight of strong hands and the soaked cuffs of a sky blue robe, embroidered with little silver fish, grip the stern. 

     

                She threw herself forward as James hauled Kara overboard, not helping much but grabbing fistfuls of heavy velvet just for the relieved reassurance of laying hands on her wife. Sopping wet, blonde hair plastered to her pallid cheeks, water pouring off her barely clothed body, Kara breathed heavily as she sheathed her sword. Blood had already started drying on her skin, clothes and hair, some of it already washed away by the water, but she was unsteady on her feet and Lena didn’t know how much of the blood was hers. Definitely some of it; she’d been stabbed.

     

                Lena looked at her with a mixture of panic and concern, green eyes wide, expression taut as she tightly gripped Kara’s arm. Looking around, her wife took stock of things and gently prised Lena’s hand off her arm as she immediately took charge.

     

                “Take us back in. Now! We have allies on the beach. Your Majesty, your-”

     

                “Leave them,” Lillian dismissively instructed her, standing tall at the prow with a cluster of her Unseelie around her. 

     

                Kara floundered for a moment, surprised. “But they need our-”

     

                “They are as good as dead, girl. Leave them. Get us away, before my son sends others to follow in whatever craft is still afloat.”

     

                After a moment, Kara conceded with a nod. She was not happy about it, swaying on her feet as she cradled her side, eyes hard and dark in the night as she looked around herself and then out at the writhing mass of water surrounding them.

     

                “Oars in! Someone grab that rope and secure the boom! I need Windfolk filling the sails and Waterfolk working the current. We need to get out to sea; Lucy, starboard on the rudder! We’re drifting , we can’t sway, we’ll capsize.” 

     

                She moved about as she spoke, a hand pressed to the left of her naval, and even in the dark, Lena could see the blackness of blood seeping between her fingers. A fresh wave of concern and panic washed over her and she grabbed a fistful of Kara’s robe as the desperation of her oppressive feelings poured out of her.

     

                “Sit down.”

     

                “Do not fuss; I will manage until we are safely away.”

     

                “It was not a request. Sit down,” Lena softly urged her.

     

                Giving her a small smile, Kara reached up to stroke her cheek, thumb smearing the blood on Lena’s face in the process, and she let out a strained laugh. “I have endured worse, wife. I must get you-”

     

                “You will sit or I will take my dagger and stab myself and then you can decide whether sailing is more important than a bleeding wound.”

     

                They stared at each other, Lena’s expression hard as she clenched her jaw, looking angry, even though it was really fear. Her chest rose and fell quickly and neither of them moved for a moment, until she reached for her empty dagger sheath, forgetting she’d dropped it. Kara’s wiry fingers still encircled her wrist and then Lena grabbed her wrist, both of them locked together as her face spasmed with pain.

     

                “I mean it, Kara,” she firmly murmured. 

     

                Lena thought her eyes might’ve been swimming with tears, or maybe it was just because of the rain sheeting down her pale face in the darkness, but Kara wavered unsteadily for a moment. Reaching up to brush wet hair out her face, Lena gave her a pleading look, feeling her wife sag against her, barely able to stay on her feet. She had to bite the inside of her lip to stop it from wobbling as she silently willed Kara to listen to her.

     

                With a weak smile, Kara slumped, her eyelids fluttering closed as she let out a rasping sigh. “So be it.”

     

                Lowering her to the deck, the fight bleeding out of her wife as her strength waned, and Lena felt cold all over as she urged Kara back, until she was stretched out on the wooden planks, rain pelting her and her sodden robe heavily splayed about her. Reaching for the buckle of her sword belt, Lena fumbled with it and jerked it free, tossing it aside and then unbelting the robe. She kept Kara’s bare skin as covered as possible as she parted the robe, taking in the messy wound to the very left of her abdomen, bleeding steadily as Lena watched, swallowing a small cry of surprise. Glancing over her shoulder, she peered through the dark as she stemmed the blood flow with the hem of her nightgown.

     

                “I need a first aid kit,” Lena shouted, closing her eyes as her face crumpled. “A- a medicine chest. Please.”

     

                Lucy was still firmly holding the rudder to their course, and James had tied off the rope for the boom, quickly eyeing the number of crates, barrels, sacks and chests. They were marked with glyphs painted onto the wood or hemp material and he quickly rooted through the supplies and hauled a chest out from amidst it, the others on the boat all pressing in at the prow as they moved away. Wiping her face on her sleeve, not much use, given how wet she was, Lena brushed her sodden hair out of her face and opened the chest. It was too dark to see much and she quickly looked behind her, her eyes landing on Sam.

     

                “Sam!” she called out, “Sam, I need light. Please. Sam.”

     

                Her voice sharpened as she frowned, taking in the silhouette of her guard. Sam’s head was cocked to the side and her eyes were closed, a stiffness to her face. She didn’t have time for whatever was going on with her and her eyes searched for someone else until Andrea brushed past her lover and sank to her knees at Kara’s side. Flames blossomed over her palm, casting an orange glow over the dark wound and the contents of the chest.

     

                “I need alcohol,” Lena rasped, looking around. 

     

                Her gaze landed on a collection of clay jugs inside a net, hooked on the side of the boat. She lunged for it, pulling out one of the corked jugs and yanking the stopper out. Pressing it to Kara’s lips, she made her drink until she was spluttering, before swallowing a few gulps herself. It was mead, she thought, the taste of honey on her tongue, and she didn’t think it would affect her fast enough to steady her shaking hands as she pawed through the neat contents of the chest. Finding a hooked needle and some sinew, Lena swallowed the lump in her throat.

     

                Mind turning to thoughts of infection, of bacteria and blood contamination, of possible sepsis and any number of bad things, Lena hesitated. There was nothing to sterilise her hands with and they trembled as she looked down at her fingers. They looked clean but that wasn’t enough reassurance for her as she baulked at the thought of putting her hands on Kara. 

     

                “I need water. Freshwater.”

     

                James broke open a barrel of it and took the small cauldron nestled into the chest to fill it for her. Asking Andrea to heat it for her, Lena stopped her before it could boil and then washed her hands, until they were pink from the heat of it, before she hesitated and pulled her bloody nightgown away and poured the remainder of the water over Kara’s wound. Her wife went rigid against the deck, her body taut, tendons prominent in her neck, as she tried not to move at the pain. Lena watched as blood sluiced over wet skin and joined the puddle on the deck, wondering how much of that was from the rain and how much had seeped out of Kara and turned to water once it struck the wood.

     

                She’d done all that she could to make it as clean as possible and couldn’t delay any further. Still, Lena hesitated a beat longer, looking around at the others crowding the stern of the boat. “Can anyone- is there a healer here? Does anyone-”

     

                Cutting off, her throat tightening around the building urge to cry, Lena swallowed painfully. She wished she was on the boat with Kelly, that someone else could help. No one else spoke and Kara limply touched her hand, her face strained with the pain.

     

                “It’s okay. You can-”

     

                Lena wasn’t sure that she could. She’d practised on fish, with a completely different needle, with no blood or concerns for what injuries were within. Kara swallowed thickly and touched the tender skin around the wound. 

     

                “It’s a … clean cut,” she breathlessly assured her. “No organs, you- it’s … just like the fish.”

     

                Ghostly pale, Lena squared her shoulders as she bowed her head over the wound. Fingers shaking as she gripped the needle, she swallowed an apology as she gently placed her hand on one side of the wound, slightly easing the gaping hole together, and slowly pushed the needle through Kara’s skin. Her wife let out a hiss between gritted teeth, her face screwing up with the agony of it before she started to arch off the deck.

     

                Holding the flames aloft in one hand, Andrea roughly flattened Kara’s shoulder to the deck, holding her fast. James did the same on the other side, and Lena couldn’t help but apologise, breathlessly repeating it over and over again as guilt needled at her. It wasn’t the same as the fish, it was horrible , forcing the hook through Kara’s skin, over and over again, bringing the sides together as her wife suffered in silence for the most part. Rain continued to fall but Kara was sweating as well, her face a shocking shade of white in the gloom, and Lena tried to work quickly to make the suffering end as soon as possible.

     

                Once she was done stitching it, a dismal attempt but decent enough considering the circumstances and being relatively inexperienced, Lena rifled through an assortment of herbs, finding the ones Eliza had taught her. Hawthorn to help her heart, willow bark for pain, goldenseal and dandelion for infection and chamomile for tea. She passed the pot to James with a plea for more water and had Andrea heat it again before she added the herbs, letting them steep as she lifted a pestle and mortar from the chest, mincing garlic and cloves with burdock root and more dandelion roots and chamomile, wetting the dried herbs with a splash of the tea before pouring honey from a clay pot and mixing it into a thick paste. This, she smeared over the row of stitches so the poultice could draw out any impurities and the skin could absorb the properties of the herbs, and she finished it off with a torn square of linen pressed to the sticky honey. It was no use wrapping Kara’s abdomen in bandages yet when she looked like she was barely conscious, let alone able to sit and endure that, never mind the rain that would have soaked them through in minutes.

     

                Once she’d finished, Lena pressed the rim of the pot to Kara’s mouth and made her drink the steeped tea before she concluded she’d done all she could. Rest was the only thing left to offer her, and after tossing everything into the chest and shutting the lid, Lena lurched to her feet and crossed to the side of the boat before vomiting into dark waters. The honeyed taste of mead scraped her throat, turned sour from the bile, and she flinched at the cold spray of the sea on her face, her fear slamming back into her now that the more immediate fear of Kara’s wellbeing had diminished.

     

                Staggering away from the side of the boat, Lena sagged to the deck and closed her eyes. That only made the boat’s rocking motion more apparent, disorienting as she felt them pitch back and forth with the monstrous waves of the sea, the prow rising up them and then slamming down on the other side. They were too big for a vessel of their size, and the night was too dark for them to see much beyond the endless black of the sea, and Lena felt cold all over at the thought that they were going to die out there, capsized and drowned. The creatures in the forest were abnormally large and twisted by the forest; she didn’t want to imagine what the sea had done to the things held within its depths.

     

                Crawling towards Kara, trying to focus her attention on her wife so she didn’t have to think of their peril and her impending death, Lena wiped her wife’s wet face with the soaked hem of her robe. Kara’s wet lashes fluttered and she looked at Lena through slitted eyes, some of the tautness of her pale face softening minutely. Face strained, Lena attempted a smile and shifted her position so her back was against the side of the boat before she gently eased Kara’s head into her lap. Stroking wet hair, Lena let out a rough exhale as her whole body sagged, too tired to continue.

     

                Limply resting, Lena idly continued to stroke her wife’s hair as rain pelted them and the sea tossed them about, a few of the soldiers under James heeding his instructions as they set a course to follow the other two boats, funnelling wind into the sails and trying to manipulate the water to keep them afloat. Kara fell asleep at some point, her breaths still quite shallow and her entire being soaked through - Lena didn’t know if that was a bad thing for the Waterfolk, if Kara needed to be kept dry to keep chills and fevers, or pneumonia even, at bay, or if it wouldn’t bother her, her natural inclination to be submerged in water leaving her rather immune to those sorts of things - and Lena was glad she was resting, at least, the tea working as she’d hoped. 

     

                Andrea approached her an unknown length of time later, interrupting the stupor Lena had fallen into. She had a blanket in her hands and hesitated before extending it towards Lena, who murmured her thanks and started to shake it out, draping it over Kara and partially covering the side of her face. It would undoubtedly be soaked through in no time, but at least it would keep the rain off her for a little while. Looking around, Lena took in the huddled figures of the others on their boat, some sleeping, some quietly talking, while others shared wineskins back and forth, waiting out the rain and the cold night.

     

                She thought dawn would never come, lost to the nauseating rocking of the boat as she lightly dozed, waking in cold sweats from the nightmare of being out at sea, surrounded by water as far as she could see, only to realise it wasn’t a nightmare - except, she couldn’t see a thing. Not until the sky slowly but surely lightened a touch, black turning to deep grey as the cloud-covered sky continued to rain down on them. But it was lighter at least, growing steadily so as Lena watched, the sky vast overhead and the grey sea showed as their boat crested and plummeted the rough waves, the air smelling of pitch and wood and rope and salt and rain. The other two boats were visible in the near distance and as the sky lightened, they turned south-westerly, the waves pushing them along faster now.

     

                It was mid-morning by the time they neared the shore. A rocky coastline of little inlets and bays greeted them as soon as it was within sight, and Lena’s heart leapt at the sight, taking in the tall pines crowding the wet strips of golden sand, or pebbled beaches. They skirted along the coast for miles, following the other boats, Lucy declaring it too dangerous to bring them into the shallows where they were, the reef likely to beach them or tear a hole in the hull. Instead, they sailed westwards until the boat in the lead turned in towards a small cove. 

     

                Pine-covered cliffs of limestone, chalk, sandstone and clay in striated layers encircled the cove, save for the narrow entrance between the two reaching arms of the cliffs. The beach was grey from the sand and lime of the rock formations, and the water was a clear greenish colour, shallow enough to see the bottom, minnows darting about. They dropped anchor as close to shore as they could get without bringing them aground and before they’d even furled their sails, Alex was splashing through the shallows and hauling herself over the prow of the boat, elbowing through the soldiers and Unseelie to reach her sister.

     

                Her face was pale and severe, chestnut hair plastered to her cheeks, and she stared down at her sister with concern in her dark eyes. Kara had slowly been roused by the activity of making land, and she let out a listless sigh, shoving aside the sodden woollen blanket and laboriously sitting up.

     

                “Do not fuss,” Kara clicked her tongue. “It was merely a cut and I have already been tended to.”

     

                Blue eyes, bright with pain, met Lena’s, and Kara gave her a piercing look. The flat line of her mouth spoke of regret but there was a tenderness to her face as well, gratitude welling up in her eyes as she silently looked at her wife, as if she didn’t know what to say. Lena wasn’t looking for any thanks, but she did feel like yelling at Kara for her lack of self-preservation. Instead, Lena unsteadily pushed herself to her feet, joints stiff and the sour taste of vomit still at the back of her throat. She thought she might be sick again, belatedly, out of fear for all that she’d endured that night. Instead, she sucked down a few lungfuls of salt air and watched as an egret sailed by with a silver minnow in its beak, the tang of pine in the air. Closing her eyes, Lena breathed that smell in again, feeling the tension bleed out of her. It was almost like the forest, and at the very least, there were trees there. It felt like a mercy.

     

                Alex and James lifted Kara over the side of the boat as Lena watched from the deck, unsure whether she wanted to get off. It was one thing to be forced onto a boat, but another matter entirely for her to go wading through the shallows to make it to the shore. Up to her waist in the sea, the feeling of the current swirling around her calves, the sensation of sand beneath her toes, and water lapping against the back of her knees, was more than Lena could bear. Kara stood unsteadily at the side of the boat, extending a hand to Lena, who shook her head, arms folding over her chest as her skin prickled with goosebumps. 

     

                “It’ll be alright, it’s shallow here,” Kara tried to encourage her. “I’ll make sure you don’t fall.”

     

                Alex waded over to her sister and grabbed an arm, looping it over her shoulder. “You need to rest. James?”

     

                Towing her sister away, Alex jerked her head towards the boat, and James looked up at Lena. He gave her a warm smile and waded towards her, tall enough that even up to his thighs in the water, he was still shoulders above the top of the boat. Unfortunately for Lena, that meant she was almost helpless to oppose him as he reached for her. Trying to back away, she met the solid form of Andrea behind her, her hands gripping Lena’s shoulders and driving her forward, right into James’ arms. He scooped Lena up and draped her over his shoulder as if unloading a sack of flour from their cargo.

     

                “Sorry, Princess.”

     

                Spluttering, Lena couldn’t do much but remain indignant, her mess of salt-crusted dark hair dangling towards the sea as he waded through the water, the spray of it splashing up towards Lena in rhythm with his strides as she screwed her eyes shut, jaw clenched painfully tight.

     

                “Put me down right now,” she quietly demanded, her face flushing red with embarrassment.

     

                “I would gladly but we are still in the sea,” he apologetically replied.

     

                Helpless to dangle over his shoulder as James carried her the remaining distance to the grey shore, Lena silently fumed. Once they hit land, James bent his knees until Lena’s feet touched the damp sand, and she roughly jerked away from him, fixing her rumpled nightgown and robe with as much dignity as she could manage. Clearing her throat, she gave him a disgruntled look, a haughty tilt to her chin.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                James bowed his head slightly, the corners of his mouth twitching, and Lena heard a smattering of muffled laughter behind her. Whirling around, her sharp green eyes landed on the sprawled figure of her wife, robe parted over the site of her wound as Kelly peeled away the square of linen and inspected the wound beneath Lena’s poultice.

     

                “There is no shame in accepting help,” Kara assured her before Lena could speak.

     

                “You’ve changed your tune since last night.”

     

                “It was not out of shame that I snubbed your offer; there was nary a sailor onboard, save for myself. My skill was needed to get us away safely.”

     

                Sniffing, Lena crossed her arms over her chest. “Clearly you overestimated yourself; we got here in one piece without your help. And despite your stubbornness, you didn’t bleed out.”

     

                “You did well,” Kelly said, glancing up at Lena. “The stitches will suffice. Once supplies are unloaded, I shall bathe it and apply a new poultice.”

     

                “I shall do it,” Lena firmly replied, a stormy look on her face, as irate as she already was. “She is my wife.”

     

                Nodding, Kelly pressed the square of linen back over the wound and fixed Kara’s robe for her. Standing over her wife with her arms folded, Lena’s expression was sullen as Kara looked up at her, skin still shockingly pale and her exhaustion evident beneath her eyes. 

     

                “You almost left me.”

     

                “I think so.”

     

                Eyes prickling, Lena rapidly blinked to dispel the feeling. Her throat felt tight and she felt a fresh wave of anger wash over her, clenching her teeth to stop her jaw from trembling. “You said you wouldn’t do that.”

     

                “I did.”

     

                “Why didn’t you get on the boat?”

     

                “They would have followed, overwhelmed us, perhaps stopped our chances of sailing away. I had to ensure your safety.”

     

                “And what of your own? I am not the one wounded. Surprisingly, I’ll admit, but I’m fine. You’re not.”

     

                “It is nothing to be worried about. It is merely … the result of a lapse in attention.”

     

                “A lapse in attention?” Lena echoed. “You could have died.”

     

                “I was brought to distraction.”

     

                “Distraction . What could be so distracting that it was more important than the people trying to kill you?”

     

                Beckoning her, Kara’s eyes shuttered as she reclined on the sand. Sinking to her knees at her side, Lena’s mouth was a hard line of disapproval, her cheekbones sharp, giving her a severe look when coupled with the shadows beneath her eyes and her pallid skin, damp and dishevelled and feeling altogether rather pathetic as she slumped next to Kara. Reaching up, Kara smiled thinly, a tremulous thing as she reached up to press her fingertips to Lena’s cheek.

     

                “You.”

     

                Her voice was a whisper, soft enough that the words were for Lena alone. Mouth opening and closing, Lena let out a scathing sound of contempt, although her anger dimmed. “I was doing just fine.”

     

                “You were doing wonderfully . It is only what I have told you before - my eyes search for you. I cannot help but ensure that you are well, before my own safety. That is what is more important than my foes.”

     

                “I thought you were dead,” Lena said again, her voice a low murmur, vulnerable and petulant as she balled the damp cotton of her nightgown in her fists. It was bloody, torn and dirty from the events of the night and she wrung it tightly in her hands as she kept her eyes lowered beneath Kara’s gaze.

     

                “I’m sorry to have frightened you.”

     

                Pausing, Lena winced slightly and looked at Kara through her lashes, contrite. “I’m sorry I ruined your home.”
