                With a breathless laugh, Kara’s face spasmed with the sting of pain and longing, but she just nodded, rubbing her bruised cheek as she hummed. “I will confess, it took me by surprise to find myself hauled away on a chunk of stone. Even more so to find myself swimming amidst the ruins of my ancestral home. But I am more surprised I still draw breath, so that is something to be fortunate for.”

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “As am I,” Kara murmured, her fingers still touching Lena’s face, her calloused palm tender as she cupped her cheek in her hand a moment longer before lowering her arm. 

     

                They lapsed into silence and Lena turned, sitting with her knees drawn to her chest as the deluge continued, the rain almost unnoticed after so many hours exposed to its patter, and they watched the others unload supplies, hauling casks and sacks off the boats and pile them on the sand, out of reach of the surf rushing up the narrow beach. A few soldiers ventured up the cliffside, Earthfolk creating little crevices in the stone as handholds while Airfolk solidified air currents to bear them skywards, returning minutes later with armfuls of damp wood and withered pine needles, their Firefolk brethren creating several fires that gave off billowing clouds of smoke as the wet wood was forced to light under their scorching flames.

     

                In short order, a makeshift camp was created along the beach, everyone gravitating towards their own. Alex had started a fire near Kara, and they were joined by Kelly, James and Lucy, J’onn and M’gann, and Sam and Andrea. Lillian and her Unseelie gathered around their fire and James’ soldiers around another. Water scooped from a barrel was set to boil over the fire, little wooden cups soon filled with steaming tea and passed about as they all warmed themselves. With a faint furrow between her brows, Kara drew the water out of their hair and clothes and flicked the droplets to the sand, all of them drier for a moment as they shivered near the fire, even if it continued to rain.

     

                Lena wished they were up at the top of the cliffs, beneath the canopy of the pine trees, curled at the base of their salt-weathered trunks, the heady smell of pine soothing them to sleep. She felt so exhausted and miserable from the relentless rain, wishing for solid walls around her and a hot bath and dry clothes. Instead, she huddled in her bedclothes and let her tea warm her as much as possible, hands tightly clutching the cup. 

     

                Sam helped Alex sort through supplies and make breakfast for them, loaves of damp bread passed around and oats set in a pot of water with a mix of nuts, softening and congealing until it was ready to be scooped into bowls. They all wolfed down their portions and the hot food radiated warmth from their bellies. Andrea washed the pot with sand and seawater while Kelly pulled the medicine chest closer and opened it to reveal the contents. 

     

                With another pot of water boiling, Kelly told Lena to make some tea, coaching her on what to add, and then watched over her as Lena dipped a piece of linen into the steeping pot and used the herbal water to wipe the poultice off Kara’s skin and bathe the wound. After that, she made a new poultice, Kelly instructing her to add a few more herbs that Lena had overlooked the first time, and smeared the honey and herb paste over the stitches, before pressing a clean square of linen to it. Then, Kelly helped Kara sit up, slipping her robe off her arms and shoulder so it pooled at her waist, and Lena tightly bandaged her abdomen. Alex had clean clothes for them then, and Lena helped Kara into the loose shirt and pants before a thick hooded robe went over the top. Kara’s face was waxy and grey by the end of it, even though she insisted she was fine, quietly bickering with her sister and her wife as they made her rest and drink some more tea. Lena still hadn’t gotten past her worry, a pinched look on her face as she crouched near Kara, dirty and wet as she huddled, keeping her eyes trained on her wife to reassure herself she was fine.

     

                Spare sails were brought in from the boats and stretched out to make triangular shelters, rope and oars securing the flimsy structures in place as they created lean-tos against the cliff face. It kept the worst of the rain off them but the shelters weren’t very big, and it went by unspoken decree that the injured would be set beneath them. Kelly had gone on to treat the soldiers and her friends, and even the Unseelie who had made it on board, stitching up bleeding wounds, creating salves and smearing them over cuts and bruises, setting broken bones and doling out strong teas to fight infection and pain. Many were in bad shape, soldiers who’d ridden hard across the open land with Lex and his Rogues at their backs, and Unseelie who’d rushed from the temple and fought in the disorienting fighting in the hallways, unsure of friend or foe as they’d found their way to the boats and clambered aboard, unwilling to be left behind like some of their brethren. Lena tried not to think about the ones her mother had left behind to their deaths.

     

                Sitting beneath the edge of the taut sail, listening to the drumming of the rain, Lena was left with her wife, blankets procured as they rested, and her eyes itched with the desire for sleep. Her body was exhausted and she slumped against the cold hardness of the cliff as it neared midday. Kara was already asleep, the tea making her drowsy, the stiff pain on her face smoothed out as the pain was lessened by it, but Lena was still awake, sitting and thinking as she stared blankly ahead at the sail. She’d found herself under it when they’d erected it straight over Kara, and no one had said a word about her not being injured, which she supposed was because she was seen as so vulnerable by everyone. She would take the unintended insult if it meant she stayed semi-dry and out of the rain. Her train of thought was interrupted a moment later as sandy feet appeared to her left, quickly followed by the rest of her sister-in-law as she ducked down to peer under the sail.

     

                “She’s sleeping,” Lena murmured.

     

                “As should you be. You look as if you have not slept a wink in days.”

     

                Rubbing the dark shadows beneath her eyes, Lena hummed. Watching her for a moment, Alex gave her shoulder a quick squeeze. “Spare them no thought.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “It troubles you, to end a life. There is nothing weak about that; some people are not made for killing. But it took courage to remain on land while others boarded the boats, covered by your arrows. They would have killed you and the rest of us, if given the chance, so spare them no thought.”

     

                Lena let out an awkward laugh, her brows pinching together as she grimaced. “It wasn’t courage - I was scared . I don’t like the water, I didn’t want to get on it.”

     

                “Yet, you did. That is courageous as well.”

     

                Shrugging slightly, Lena broodingly stared ahead at the sailcloth. Giving her shoulder another quick squeeze, Alex gave her a faint smile. “Sleep, Lena. We will need to be gone by nightfall and you will need your rest.”

     

                Nodding distractedly, she watched her sister-in-law walk away to converse with the others near the fire. Exhaustion settled into her bones and she realised that she probably could sleep dreamlessly, as tired as she was. After a moment, she shifted down the sand to stretch out beside her wife and draped the blanket over herself before she huddled for warmth and pressed up against Kara’s side. She was out within minutes, her mind giving in as she nestled her face into the crook of Kara’s shoulder, breathing in the smell of salt and rain clinging to her skin, listening to the sound of her even breaths and steady beat of her heart. They were both alive, for now, and that was no small comfort.

    Chapter 31

                That evening, they were back on the boats. They’d distributed themselves a little better this time, friends grouping together and ensuring that there were capable sailors on each little sailboat. The rain continued to fall so the extra sailcloth was rigged to provide some shelter for those who weren’t funnelling wind into the sails or trying to manoeuvre them through enormous waves, and Lena huddled against Kara for warmth as water still found its way through to them. 

     

                It was a miserable night, Lena feeling nauseous and exhausted, despite her earlier nap, and the smell of pitch, pine, saltwater and blood mingled as the injured fae stretched out where they could. Everyone tried to sleep as much as they could, but that was almost impossible for Lena as she listened to the crash of the waves as their sailboat swayed to and fro, glad that she couldn’t see the sea as she sank down and closed her eyes, breathing in the smell of her wife as she tried to focus on her heartbeat instead. 

     

                A great storm blew in just before dawn the next day, cold and dark, the violent lash of rain and howl of the wind keeping her awake as Lena’s nails gouged crescents into her palms. Her heart thudded in her chest and she thought she might be sick as the boat rocked precariously and M’gann manoeuvred their craft through the perilous weather, turning the rudder hard as she steered them sideways up the wall of an oncoming wave, until they reached the lip and sailed down the other side. Lena felt her stomach lurch as they plummeted down the wave, the breath expelled from her lungs as cold dread suffused her, but M’gann was already steering them up the next wave, the boat pitching so far backwards that anything that wasn’t lashed down to the deck started to shift towards the stern - including sleeping fae, who were jerked from sleep as they scrambled for purchase, hands grabbing them - before they reached the top, right before they would have been capsized and swallowed by the sea.

     

                It was Lena’s worst nightmare, fear radiating from her as she gripped handfuls of Kara’s clothes, unable to make out much of anything, the sky black despite the morning hour. She couldn’t even sit upright, the motion of the boat jostling her about, the wind snapping the rigged sailcloth so fiercely she thought it was about to tear it off and leave them exposed to the harsh weather, the sudden savagery of the world. The storm pushed them up and down over the swell of the waves, up the wall of one and then down the other side, a relentless rhythm that did nothing to soothe Lena as she anticipated the worst every time. Despite the flimsy shelter, her hair was drenched and her clothes felt heavy and rough, sodden fabric chafing against her skin as she pressed her face into the crook of Kara’s neck, breathing in the smell of her salty hair and feeling the warmth of her through their clothes.

     

                “It’s alright,” Kara murmured, her voice a thin sigh as her hand ghosted down the back of Lena’s robe. “I’m with you.”

     

                Her words only marginally soothed Lena’s terror, and it was a long morning, the sky remaining a deep grey throughout, no breakfast for them as they sailed on through the poor weather, waiting for a reprieve. Lena wondered why they couldn’t just put in at shore, finding shelter literally anywhere , but when the storm died, thunder turning to a quiet mutter, rain a slow patter as grey clouds lightened to thick white, the sailcloth was pulled back to allow them all a bit of freedom to stand and stretch, she could see over the side of the boat that the coastline was mostly rocky. Even with her little knowledge of sailing or the sea, it seemed obvious that their little sailboats would have been dashed onto the rocks and turned to kindle, and she grimly admitted to herself that perhaps the terrifying pitching up and down the waves had been the best course, even if the endless stretch of sea made Lena sick with fear. If she’d had the ability to make her legs bear her weight, she thought she might be bent over the side of the boat, heaving her guts up.

     

                Instead, she drew her knees to her chest and closed her eyes, her face a waxy shade of grey as the wind whipped her dark hair around her face. She had never tasted air so clean though, drinking in deep lungfuls as she tried to quell her nausea, salt and seaweed and bracing as it scoured her lungs clean. She remained there for hours, legs stiff and cramping, a headache behind her eyes from the tension in her body, Kara’s head resting in the crook between her thighs and stomach as she slept on. Kelly checked on them both, offering Lena mint to chew on to alleviate her seasickness, a futile endeavour given the source of her fear, and touching Kara’s brow to see if she was feverish before leaving her to sleep. Lena knew she needed her rest more than anything, but she longed for her wife’s company to distract her.

     

                Eventually, the boats turned towards shore, wood scraping against rock as the sea roiled beneath them, oars moving in tandem as they tried to navigate through sharp rock without putting a hole in their hulls. They had to leave the boats twenty feet from shore, Lena forced to bend her pride to her fear and allow James to carry her to the wet stone that made up their camp for the remainder of the daylight hours. Cold and wet, shivering and exhausted, her eyes dry and gritty, Lena was miserable and quiet, her eyes darting to Kara every few seconds as she watched her wife’s face spasm with pain. Kelly tended to the wound as best as she could, making the rounds of all the injured fae, and the best Lena could do was force her limbs to move so she could start scooping fresh water into a pot and brew tea. 

     

                The rough stone bit into the soles of her feet and she felt slow and clumsy as she moved, nothing close enough to use for firewood but desperately needing something to burn to make her wife tea. Tearing lengths off the bottom of her filthy robe, Lena wadded it up and looked around, her eyes snagging on Andrea, and beckoned her over. She got her to light the fire, the damp fabric smoking but inevitably catching as Andrea’s intense flames didn’t let up, and Lena heaved the pot on top with arms that felt like jelly. It was still raining a little and she wiped her palm over her wet face, crouching awkwardly next to the flames as they quickly consumed the fabric. Lena kept ripping pieces of fabric free to feed it, until Alex touched her shoulder, dropping to a knee with an armful of wet wood foraged from the cliffs high above the rocky shore.

     

                “You need to rest, Lena,” she murmured, nudging her aside.

     

                “I’m making tea,” Lena rasped, “she needs tea. What if it’s infected? I don’t know if I- nothing was clean. God, it was so unsanitary. My hands-”

     

                “She is well, and you must rest. How you are still able to stand after expending that much energy, I don’t know. Although, I suppose it is the thrill of it all, keeping your blood running hot, keeping you awake. That is not good for your head or heart; you must rest.”

     

                Lena’s hands shook a little and she knew that Alex was right, that it was adrenaline keeping her going at the moment, her body in a low-grade state of panic and shock and fear. She’d dragged half of Krypton into the sea and could feel the hollowness in her stomach, the leaden weight of her limbs, the ache behind her eyes and in her head, at the base of her skull as if it was sinking into her spine. Her legs wobbled where she crouched and she gracelessly fell back, scraping her palms on stone, watching as Alex took over tending to the tea. As soon as it was steaming and had steeped long enough, she insisted on carrying a cup over to Kara, who was stretched out on her back, rain pattering against her cheeks, her skin pale and lips bloodless. Cupping the back of her wife’s head, she pressed the cup to her lips and made her drink.

     

                Alex took the empty cup from her and brought it back over for Lena, both of them quietly bickering until Lena drained it, the warmth of it radiating from her belly as she sat beside Kara. She felt drained, wanted to curl up on the cold stone and close her eyes, press her face into her wife’s neck and pretend she was in her bed. She would smell of the sea; Kara always smelled of the sea lately. That smell of water, whether it was the sea or fresh rain, had always made Lena’s stomach twist, vague memories too dark to dwell on surfacing in response to it, but now, she wanted to drown herself in it, face pressed to Kara’s throat, listening to the strong beat of her heart. There were others about though, and she was too wary to give in to that impulse, too scared to show that she cared that much.

     

                “What can I do?” Lena hoarsely asked, green eyes rising to Alex’s strained face as she loomed over her sister. “Alex, what can I do?”

     

                “Go to sleep,” Alex firmly ordered her, stooping to push Lena down. “You’ll make yourself sick, and that’s the last thing we need.”

     

                Lena leaned on her elbows as she mournfully stared up at her, itching to help, for something to do to distract her. Instead, she lay stretched out beside Kara as she watched the others move about, the spare sails rigged for shelter, someone building a better fire, another poking along the rockpools. They were all wet and tired but uncomplaining as the seasoned soldiers went about their usual making of camp, and Lillian’s cohort of gentry and assistants pitched in as well, some tension between the parties as they shared supplies.

     

                Beneath the canopy of the sail, with damp blankets thrown over her, Lena felt the tea slowly start to creep over her, making her drowsy as her eyelids drooped. Cuddling up to her wife, sharing their body warmth, Lena let out a weary sigh as her whole body went limp, an arm across Kara’s chest as she pressed her cheek to the hard stone. She slept soundly, despite the howling wind and crashing waves, out of reach of the spray, and was roused hours later by Alex. Blearily peering through the gloom of dusk, rain dripping off the edge of the sailcloth, Lena felt just as tired, just as limp and hollow.

     

                Alex was shaking Kara awake next, murmuring tenderly to her sister as she helped her sit up. Fetching two bowls for them, Alex handed them off and Lena stared down at the contents before taking a sip, the salty brine of winkle soup filling her mouth. It was hot and filling and she wolfed it down with the slightly stale bread and then washed it down with more tea. Kara ate very little of hers, listless and exasperated as she waved them away. She drank the tea though and Lena wrapped the blankets around her shoulders, her face etched with concern.

     

                Legs still a little unsteady, Lena forced herself to her feet to help, packing away belongings to be stored on the boats, palms scraped raw on the thick hemp ropes holding up the sailcloth as she clumsily coiled them, her back and shoulders aching where she’d drawn her bowstring over and over again. Anything to be of use, anything to get them quickly moving again, to Kelly’s family home, where Kara might receive proper care and be out of the elements long enough to dry off. Filling her with as many herbs as possible, Kelly packed away the remainder of her things and had J’onn carry Kara to the boat, setting her down in the middle of the deck where she could stretch out near the mast. James carried Lena and she was quick to sink to her knees, crawling to her wife and covering her with a blanket.

     

                Brushing damp hair out of Kara’s face, Lena gave her a wavering smile. “We’ll be there soon.”

     

                Giving her a weak smile, Kara’s eyelashes fluttered and she let out a soft sigh. “I’m alright.”

     

                Lena didn’t believe her in the slightest, tears stinging her eyes as she blinked furiously, aware of the others clambering over the side of the boat, water sloshing onto the wet planks, oars picked up and dipped into the sea, everyone quickly falling back into the rhythm of things. They wound their way back out to sea and the rain held off for the moment, J’onn insisting the reprieve would hold for now as he smelled the air for rain. Sitting with Kara’s head in her lap, her fingers tenderly combing through her wife’s hair as she tried to quell her anxious worry, Lena felt her stomach churn with the pitching and dipping of the swell as she fought to keep the winkle soup down. 

     

                They sailed back out to sea and as sunlight faded, Lena stared out at the endless stretch of black water as they sailed along at a cracking pace, still heading westwards. Before all light was gone, she saw that the clouds had started to bruise again, flickers of lightning veining the sky as the wind howled. The rest of the light faded quickly and the rain started back up with a rumbling shudder. It rained all through the night and they couldn’t see clearly enough to get the spare sail up for cover, so they all sat through the downpour, Lena staring down at Kara’s face through the wash of rain, doing her best to shelter her from it. Lena was drenched, her clothes clinging to her body like a second skin, her dark hair tangled down her back as she clung to her wife, the rain falling thick and cold until midnight came and went.

     

                A fog stole in just before the sunrise, thick and grey, leaving them barely able to see a stone’s throw ahead and the sound of the sea seemed muffled and distorted, the creaking of the boat and slap of water against the hull magnified, the waves a distant roar. The air was cold and lovely as Lena drew in deep lungfuls, tasting the salt, waving away oatcakes and dried herring for herself, trying to pass morsels through Kara’s lips as she coaxed her wife to eat. She held on to the next time they stopped, sandbars skimming perilously close beneath the grey surface, flagging from the events of the last couple of days.

     

                As they rested on the third day, a wind blew down from the north, melting the eddies of mist away and the weather felt calmer now - mostly - as they sat on a pebbly beach, the clouds breaking overhead. Nothing more than a veneer of mist remained by the time they set off again, stars visible through patchy clouds, a host of constellations drawing Lena’s face skywards as she focused on them instead of the inky velvet water below. The dark stole in again and it made it feel as if there was no end to the sky, as if they were sailing through it, the rough seas mellowing enough to reflect the sky above. She felt a little more at ease, her body going slack as she leaned against the thick mast and let the gentle rocking lull her to sleep.

     

                It took them four days of sailing before they arrived at their destination, sailing past slate cliffs that loomed over them, evergreens so dark they were nearly black leaning precariously, where they’d grown beneath the prevailing wind. Just past midday, they were greeted with hundreds of nesting birds, swooping and wheeling about, calling to each other, a sea of feathers and beaks and shimmering silver fish scooped from the shadows of the cliffs, and Kelly announced they were almost there, relief evident in her hoarse voice. It was still a few miles of cliffs and birds before they reached the cove that served as a wide harbour, at the base of cliffs carved into the home of James and Kelly’s family.

     

                Navigating through the narrow entrance to the cove, kicking up spray in rhythm with the tide, the wind dimmed and the air smelled of salt and pine, refreshing and gentle as they sailed to the wharf of little boats rocking in the current. Staring up at the grey slate as dusk started to arrive, the day taking on a purplish tint, Lena felt weak with relief, making out moving figures walking along corridors facing the harbour. Behind them, the way they’d come, Lena could see archers watching the entrance to the harbour, crenellations on the tall slate cliffs enclosing the cove. They docked alongside bigger vessels used for trading along the Seelie coast and the Waterfolk leapt to secure ropes to the marina, furling sails to steady the crafts, stowing oars and dropping anchor. 

     

                It was a buzz of activity before they all started to disembark, James and Kelly first, son and daughter of the Guardian, the westernmost point of the Seelie Court. Alex helped haul her sister to her feet and guide her off the boat before joining her wife, who was greeting her mother. Lena wrapped her arm around Kara’s waist, briefly touching her brow to Kara’s temple, and then led them further along the dock, her legs feeling like jelly to have solid ground that wasn’t a beach beneath her feet. Her clothes were still damp from the days of rain, and she could feel the gritty sand that had worked beneath the layers and still clung to her feet, chafing her skin and palpable as she padded along barefoot.

     

                Kelly’s mother was only slightly taller than her daughter, flowing robes of smoke grey embroidered with silver and gold birds with rings and gemstones adorning her as she cupped her daughter’s face in her hands,

     

                “Mother,” Kelly said with weary relief, letting the other woman kiss both of her cheeks before stepping aside to let her brother greet her.

     

                Alex greeted her next, murmuring quietly as she gestured to her sister and Lena, and then beyond, where Lillian and the Unseelie had disembarked further down the marina. Dark eyes cast appraising eyes over the few dozen guests arriving on her doorstep and Lena swallowed the urge to interrupt the niceties and demand medical attention for her wife. Clammy and stubborn, Kara shrugged out of Lena’s help and stepped forward, managing a bow without her usual elegance as she greeted Kelly’s mother and made apologies for their arrival. They’d sent word ahead days before departing, but she hadn’t meant for them to show up in such a state.

     

                “A number of us were injured,” Kelly explained, “I must see to her wound, mother. I will rejoin you shortly.”

     

                “I will see the rites performed before you depart,” her mother insisted.

     

                There were a few others who had accompanied her to the marina to welcome them, and they stepped forward with goblets of honeyed wine and platters of barley cake at their Lady’s beckoning. Despite being family in some regard or another, they all still took a sip and ate a bite before passing them along to the others. Murmuring her thanks to Kelly’s mother as she passed her by, her hands moving back to her wife’s waist, Lena felt a flicker of unease, wondering if the blame of their arrival would be cast upon her, bringing her mother, their enemy , in tow. She wondered if an Unseelie had ever breached the guarded arms of the cove before, or if she’d brought the first in with her. It was the least of her concerns now though, following after Kelly as she set off towards her childhood home with purpose and led them through the open brass doors of the main entrance. 

     

                Lena kept her arm around Kara’s waist as she anxiously helped her along, her wife softly murmuring that she was fine, that she shouldn’t fuss, yet barely seeming to bear her own weight as her face occasionally went taut with the pain. Alex had Kara’s arm slung around her shoulder on the other side, bearing the brunt of her sister’s weight as she followed after her wife, winding through the airy hallways as they were led to a quiet wing in search of a guest room. A chill wind blew in and Lena shivered in her damp clothes as she kept pace with Alex, eager to get her wife to bed, to a sterile place where Kelly could properly treat her wound. She’d tried her hardest not to think about infection, of dirt and sand getting into the wound, of butchered stitches and red, weeping edges of the stab wound, but the panic was starting to eat away at her now, a funny feeling in her chest as her throat tightened.

     

                Kelly swept through the white muslin curtains in an open doorway and as Lena stepped through, she found herself in an elegant room carved out of the same grey slate of the cove’s cliffs. They were through to the other side of it though, carved folding doors at the back wall open to let in the sweetness of winter flowers and water from a small brook that trickled past. Lena could hear the soft coos of doves as they rustled around in the trees beyond, the wind sighing through the leaves and stirring the muslin curtains. On the carved wooden platform in the middle of the room was a thick mattress of soft down collected from the seabirds nesting along the coast, and Kelly gestured for them to set Kara down on top of the thick woven blankets.

     

                Though she insisted she was perfectly capable of getting undressed by herself, Kara didn’t resist as Lena helped her out of the salt-crusted clothes while Kelly went to fetch healing supplies, asking her wife to help her. Left alone - truly alone - for the first time in days, Lena’s eyes flitted over Kara’s lithe body, taking in the spotted linen bandages and then up to her face. There were bruise-like circles beneath Kara’s eyes, her cheekbones sharper and her brow drawn tight as she tried to mask her pain. She looked worse than Lena had ever seen her, her wife always relatively unscathed, no matter the circumstances, and as she perched on the edge of the bed beside Kara, she covered her face with her hands and burst into tears. 

     

                “Why do you cry?” Kara asked, pushing herself up.

     

                Reaching a hand on to stop her from sitting up any further, Lena let out a breathless huff. “Don’t ask such stupid questions. You almost died.”

     

                “Oh. That was days ago now; there is no need for this belated concern.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena wiped her face with her fingers and sniffed. She felt ragged, bone-deep weariness in her and so much worry snarled in her chest that she could feel another sob building. She wanted to cry until she found relief in sleep, but instead, she looked at her wife, eyes a little bloodshot and expression so pitifully mournful that Kara couldn’t help but smile faintly.

     

                “You look awful,” Lena told her, face spasming with pain.

     

                “You look beautiful.”

     

                Shooting her a dark look, Lena grimaced. “Don’t make fun of me.”

     

                “I do not jest. I speak truthfully, for I always find you so. If it were not for my injury, I would ask you to come closer so that I may touch you, but I know that you will treat me as if I am wrapped in lambswool.”

     

                “Now you know how I feel.”

     

                “Would it change your mind to know it would make me feel better to have you closer? I would not ask for much, even a kiss will do, but it would greatly improve my spirits.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena scoffed and used the end of her robe’s belt to swat her wife’s bare thigh. She could see the strain in the corners of Kara’s eyes though, the way her chest shallowly rose and fell with quick breaths, the effort it took for her to force levity to comfort her wife, even while she was the one with a stab wound in her side. Even knowing that Kara was trying to assuage her worry, Lena felt the keen ache in her chest and couldn’t resist leaning down to kiss her anyway.

     

                Their lips were chapped and the taste of salt clung to them both, but Kara’s mouth was warm and Lena’s shoulders sagged with relief as some of the tension bled out of her, a sort of desperation to it. She gripped her wife’s face in her hands and kissed her softly, blotting out everything else as she felt Kara’s lips curve with an answering smile as she pushed up against her mouth. 

     

                By the time she heard footsteps approaching, Lena was too slow to react beyond shooting to her feet before Alex was brushing through the curtains. She couldn’t help but look guilty as she ducked her head and turned away from her wife, raking a hand through her knotted hair. Snorting, Alex set down a basin of steaming water, lilies and irises floating on the surface of it, while Kelly followed her in with an assortment of salves, herbs and bandages in her arms. 

     

                “We may move past this false modesty,” Alex wearily sighed, rolling her eyes. “We are aware of your frequent nights spent in my sister’s bed.”

     

                Eyes sliding to Kara, Lena gave her a pointed look. “You told them?”

     

                “My sister has more integrity than that,” Alex brusquely replied. “Her bed pillows, however, do not hide secrets nearly as well; the smell of you was all over them. I, for one, am glad. Now, may we move on to checking my sister’s wound?”

     

                Clicking her tongue with exasperation, Lena gestured to Kara and then sank beside her on the bed. She watched as Kelly untied the bandages and used them to wipe away the latest poultice, before dipping a clean cloth into the floral water and gently dabbing at the stitches. Lena itched to do it herself, but now that they were somewhere clean and safe, where something more could be done, she knew that Kara needed the best care, not her wife’s care. Still, she didn’t take her eyes off Kelly’s hands as they worked, watching her bathe the wound clean and mix herbs and honey into a salve, not unlike the ones they’d been applying on their brief stints ashore, before she placed a square of muslin cloth over the site and had Lena hold Kara upright as she bandaged her midriff. 

     

                While Kelly set about steeping a tea, Lena took another clean cloth and dipped it into the murky bowl of water and started to clean the rest of Kara. She started with her hands, working the cloth over her fingers as she held her hand tightly, then over the palm and knuckles, wrist, and forearm. She made her way up to Kara’s collarbone and wiped blood off her face, chest and neck, before climbing to her feet and sitting on Kara’s other side to repeat her ministrations. Then she rinsed her thighs and knees, calves and shins and sandy feet before setting the cloth in the bowl and drying her hands in her salty clothes. Looking a little cleaner, although her brassy hair was a snarled mess, holding patches of red where the blood hadn’t been washed out by the rain, Kara lay on her elbows with her eyes closed. 

     

                She must have felt Lena studying her because her eyes opened a moment later and her chapped lips curled into a smile, Lena’s stomach swooping with an edge of concern as she stared at her wife and reassured herself that she was okay. A minute later, Kelly carried the cup of tea over to Kara and handed it off, a stern look on her face.

     

                “Drink it all. You are recovering well, thanks to your wife-”

     

                “I suppose the stubbornness of Earthfolk has its virtues,” Kara mused around the rim of the cup, her eyebrows rising and falling in a quick goading look.

     

                “But you must rest,” Kelly continued, hands on the hips of her dirty clothes, dark braids crusted with salt and tired lines on her face. They all looked like they needed some rest.

     

                “Rest, yes, I hear you. Thank you, sister. I shall be well.”

     

                Kara flashed her a quick smile and drained the rest of her tea without complaint under Kelly’s patient but unforgiving stare. Taking it from her, Kelly softened slightly and Alex gave her sister a long look.

     

                “We shall have words now that we are somewhere safe,” she told her sister in a brittle tone. “Not today, but I will box your ears for your idiocy. Just wait until mother hears-”

     

                Spluttering, Kara bristled indignantly. “Well, you needn’t tell her.”

     

                “Oh, I will, Kara Zor-El, I will do far worse than tell her. Have you lost all sense? Has too much salt air addled your brain?”

     

                “I have lost neither sense nor the ability to wash your mouth out if you continue to berate me,” Kara grumbled, her fingers twitching towards the bowl of water as a column of it raised in threat.

     

                “We should all hope Lena does not berate you, or we might all end up in the sea this time,” Alex snapped back, all of the candles in the room suddenly flaring significantly higher as the flames wavered. 

     

                “Well, I think we should all stop talking and get some rest,” Lena tried to reason, raising her eyebrows as she folded her arms over her chest. “If someone could show me to my room?”

     

                Kelly looked from Lena to Kara and cocked her head to the side. “You do not wish to share quarters?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Lena looked at Kara, who looked back at her, almost affronted at her response. Mouth opening and closing, Lena looked from Kara to Kelly, and then to Alex for good measure, before back at her wife. Gesturing off-handedly, she shrugged.

     

                “She should rest.”

     

                “I will rest just fine if you are here. I would prefer to not let you out of my sight for the time being.”

     

                “No one will know you are here together,” Kelly sighed as she rolled her eyes. “We are in my wing; this is one of my guest rooms. Everyone else will be housed elsewhere. If that is your concern.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena mumbled, nodding before sinking onto the bed.

     

                “I will have someone bring food and clothes. And more water to wash with, Lena,” Kelly said.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kelly tugged on Alex’s arm and then dragged her wife from the room, closing the carved doors behind her. Letting out a weary sigh, Kara shifted up the bed and eased herself beneath the covers with a small groan. Eyes flitting down to her, Lena watched her settle against the pillows and let out a gentle sigh, before she paced away from the bed, towards the carved doors overlooking what lay beyond their room. The small brook trickled past and Lena realised it was a small garden, trees shading the space, winter flowers - snowdrops, hellebores and jasmine - flowering amidst the moss and shrubs. She breathed in the smell of life, of green things living, and felt her headache lessen somewhat, the flowers seeming to perk up a little, the canopy of the trees seeming to lift, as if they were responding to her presence. Lena would have stayed out there all afternoon, basking in the merest hint of rich earth and plant life, but Kara’s soft words pulled her away.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                Turning, Lena closed the doors and fixed the curtains over them before she padded to the bed and sank onto the edge of the mattress. Her expression was solemn and she let out a soft sigh. “Better now.”

     

                “Forgive me, I did not have time to tell you that she knew,” Kara whispered.

     

                Giving her hand a gentle squeeze, Lena kissed the back of her knuckles. “Don’t even worry about it. It’s not important.”

     

                “It was important to you.”

     

                “There are bigger things to worry about now.”

     

                Kara let out a soft huff of laughter, her eyelids shuttering. “They will not tell anyone else.”

     

                Shrugging half-heartedly, Lena smiled thinly. “It doesn’t matter.”

     

                “You needn’t share a room with me if you do not wish to. It is selfish of me to ask for you to stay here with me so I may be reassured of your safety, but if you do not-”

     

                “No,” Lena quietly cut her off, staring down at their joined hands. “No, it is as Kelly says; I do not wish for my mother to know of it. But I, too, will be more at ease here with you, knowing that you are safe.”

     

                “I do not wish for you to worry.”

     

                “I’ll still worry.”

     

                Giving her a tired smile, Kara’s eyelids closed for a beat too long before she opened them again, fighting against the heaviness. “You should rest too. You must be so very tired.”

     

                “I am,” Lena admitted, her whole body sagging with the confession. 

     

                She didn’t rest then though, waiting for the knock that came a short while later, a man bearing a laden tray and two women with a bowl of water and soap and a stack of cloths and clean clothes. Lena climbed to her feet as they entered, tense as she watched them set everything down; the tray of food on the table at the back of the room, where shuttered windows overlooked the garden, the basin of water to a small stand set in the corner, the clothes and cloths set on a low stool. Thanking them, Lena waited until they were gone before she moved to the table and fixed a plate of food for Kara. There was chicken, dates, pears, and some hard cheese and soft flatbread. Filling a cup with more of the honeyed wine they’d had on arrival, Lena carried it to the bed and set the tray on the sheets. 

     

                Moving over to the bowl of water, perfumed with the lilies and irises floating on top, she shed her filthy clothes and dipped a clean cloth into the hot water, the warmth of it blissful as she smoothed the cloth over her skin. Rubbing her face clean, Lena lathered up soap on the cloth and washed the rest of her, salt, sweat, blood and dirt wiped away with relief. Feeling refreshed, she slipped on a cotton nightgown, thinner than the ones she’d been wearing in Krypton, the enclosed walls of the Guardian and the protected cove making for a milder late winter than they’d experienced up north, exposed to the sea. 

     

                Clean and dry, although she was desperate to wash her hair and get a brush through it, Lena moved to the table and fixed herself a plate as well, knocking back a cup of wine where she stood and refilling from the pitcher before joining her wife on the bed. Sinking back against the pillows, Lena let out a weary sigh as she took a sip of wine and set the cup on the edge of the wooden platform.

     

                “I don’t think I’ve ever appreciated being dry as much as I do right now,” Lena said as she looked at Kara. “Or being clean. Or warm, or a soft bed, or something other than seafood to eat.”

     

                “You know, most of those things are directly opposed to my entire being, my very claim to the Waterfolk. If I didn’t know any better, I’d think you weren’t very fond of me.”

     

                “Ah, well, opposites attract, and all of that.”

     

                “How so?”

     

                “Oh, you know, like magnets? Right, you don’t have magnets, um … well, it’s science. Uh, some metals can be magnetised - it’s when the atoms- you know what, never mind - so you have two sides, a north and a south, and if you use two magnets, the north and south will pull together, but if you put two north ends together, it will repel. So in relationships, it’s like saying two people who are the complete opposite of each other are more likely to attract each other. You like the water and I like to be firmly on land. You’re warm and kind and I’m … well, sort of a bitch, but … you know.”

     

                Kara let out a surprised laugh, “I do not think you a bitch.”

     

                “No? You should. I’m not very personable. And I did plunge your home into the sea. Kind of a horrible thing to do.”

     

                “I don’t believe you intended to do that.”

     

                “No,” Lena whispered, her face crumpling in memory of her anguish. “No, we both know I couldn’t intentionally do it, even if I’d tried my hardest, I just- I wanted you to come to me.”

     

                “Seafolk are always drawn back to the sea, whether they want to be or not, so my halls have just returned home, in a way,” Kara shrugged. “And it was a feat of power that is not often displayed; you should rest now.”

     

                “Mhm,” Lena hummed around a mouthful of chicken. “I think I shall sleep for a week.”

     

                “If it pleases you.”

     

                “It will please me if you get better.”

     

                “I’m fine. Don’t fret, wife, I will be well enough in a few days. It would not have bothered me so much if it had not been so deep.”

     

                “That’s typically how stab wounds work.”

     

                “Eat your food, Lena. You get very brusque when you’re tired; I feel as if I’m being chastened by my mother.”

     

                “Your mom? You think I act like your mom? Please never say that to me again.”

     

                Raising her eyebrows, Kara took a sip of wine. “I thought you liked my mother.”

     

                “I do. She’s great, the best mother I know of. But no one wants to be compared to someone’s mother, especially not when one has frequently had their head between your legs.”

     

                Scoffing as her pale cheeks flushed, Kara threw the pit of a date at her. “Now I wish for you to never say that to me again. Hurry up and sleep; you are toying with me and I do not care for it.”

     

                “Oh, no, if I was toying with you, you’d know,” Lena said with a quick grin.

     

                Throwing another date pit at her, Kara rolled her eyes. “I could only be so lucky.”

     

                “You’re injured.”

     

                “That has never stopped me before.”

     

                “Oh, is that how you used to woo your lovers? Get all injured and on bedrest and then feel sorry for yourself until they come and kiss your wounds better for you?”

     

                “Very amusing. I am rarely injured this severely; some of us have been graced with more talent in the art of war than others.”

     

                Humming as she chewed a mouthful, Lena glanced sideways at her. “Well, in this instance - probably the only instance ever - I came out of it without a new injury, so now you have to do what I say.”

     

                “You killed many,” Kara whispered, reaching out to gently rest her fingers on Lena’s arm.

     

                Lena opened and closed her mouth but nothing came out. She’d tried not to think about that, or the tenderness that still lingered in her upper body as a result, about how many arrows had struck flesh, felling fae without little fanfare or fuss. It felt easy to cast off the blame for it when it hadn’t been up close, their blood soaking her hands and clothes. It was different to how it had been the other times; she’d been relatively calm, unwavering as she waited for her wife to come to her. With a shrug, Lena’s mouth twisted ruefully as she picked up her cup of wine and toyed with it instead of drinking.

     

                “I can’t always be a liability,” Lena murmured, “I just didn’t expect to ever become a … murderer to stay alive. I’ve been in some shit situations in my life - shelters aren’t always the safest places - but I never had to kill anyone to get out of them. But … it’s okay. I don’t like it, but it’s okay because you’re alive and … I can live with doing it again and again as long as it means you’re still alive.”

     

                “I do not wish for you to do things you do not-”

     

                “No one made me do it. I chose to do it. Each time, it’s been a choice, so that’s … fine. I just- I’m coming to terms with what it means for me to choose to do that. I’d prefer to help people instead, and that’s why I’d like to learn how to heal people, but until I’m any good at that, I’ll make myself useful however I can. Not that I’m that great at killing either, but …”

     

                “You are quite good with a bow,” Kara murmured. “Thank you for choosing to help us.”

     

                Lena let out a quiet laugh. “Some of it was self-preservation too. I’m too much of a coward to be brave like the rest of you.”

     

                “Yet, you could’ve gotten on the boat a long while before I arrived. You were still there.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena stared down at her wine. “Cowardice, again. I couldn’t get on the boat; I was too frightened of the water. I didn’t want to do it without you. I thought you- I thought you were going to …”

                

                Shifting closer to her, Kara put her arm around Lena’s shoulders and her lips brushed her hair. “I was buying us time. I was not staying. My folly has earned me a new scar, but I was never dying then; I have not killed my love yet.”

     

                Eyes stinging with tears, Lena scowled as she pouted slightly. “Okay, well, don’t fall in love. Not for a really long time, because I can’t- as long as you’re not in love, I’ll know you can’t die yet, not until you’ve killed them.”

     

                Letting out a huff of amusement, Kara nodded. “I also hope to not fall in love for a really long time. Not for my sake, though.”

     

                Leaning her head on Kara’s shoulder, Lena sighed, her weariness catching up to her. “Don’t let anyone put new holes in you either. For my sake.”

     

                “It will be nothing more than a scar in a few days. In time, it will fade, as the others have. See?”

     

                She pushed the blankets down a little, still naked as she’d foregone the clean nightgown brought in for her, and lightly touched the silvery scar on her collarbone, faded with age. Her hand moved to another on her ribs and then she twisted her left arm to show the little silver circle.

     

                “This is where an arrow went through, cleanly. This one,” Kara said as she showed Lena her right hand, two little scars, barely noticeable, at the fleshy base of her thumb. “I was barely a child when I got this one. My mother was teaching me to fish; I clumsily got a hook stuck.”

     

                Letting out a laugh, Lena touched the scar and then all of the other ones Kara had pointed out, her mouth warm against her collarbone as dark hair spilt around her head, sinking lower as she kissed the one on her ribs. Kara let out a breathless laugh as she tipped her head back against the pillows, her hand gently pressing against Lena’s spine.

     

                “I will not show you the one on my thigh. It will be unbearable to be teased so.”

     

                “Finish your food,” Lena murmured as she raised her head, amusement softening her face, and kissed Kara on the cheek. “Then you should sleep as well.”

     

                “I have little appetite.”

     

                Lena gave her a long, searching look. “Is something else wrong? I have never known you to not want to eat.”

     

                “I just … feel too weary for it.”

     

                “Should I feed you? The doting wife fulfilling her duties,” she gently teased her, climbing to her feet with her near-empty plate and cup of wine and moving over to the table. 

     

                A covered pot held soup and Lena knocked back the rest of her wine, letting it soften her mind, before she carried a bowl over to Kara. Sitting at her side, she crookedly smiled as she raised a spoonful with an arched eyebrow.

     

                “Open.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara’s lips parted and she let Lena spoon-feed her a few mouthfuls. “Satisfied?”

     

                “A little.”

     

                “You are so difficult to please.”

     

                “On the contrary, it’s quite easy ; just do as I say.”

     

                “It is a good thing you were born a Princess; you have the right qualities for it.”

     

                “Ouch. It hurts that I know you were being honest.”

     

                “I never said they were bad qualities.”

     

                “You were calling me bossy.”

     

                “In a way. Being a leader is not a bad quality though. And it’s a necessary one for the heir to the Unseelie throne.”

     

                Swallowing a few spoonfuls of soup, Lena scowled. “While I’d prefer not to be reminded of that - although, my brother is likely the heir, or King now, even - I thought we’d agreed I’d end up with my throat slit if I’d tried to take over.”

     

                “That was in the autumn. Now, it is almost spring. You have changed much.”

     

                “Well, let’s hope my mother lives a long and healthy life,” Lena said with a strained smile. “And let’s not talk about my family, the reason we’re in this mess, anymore. Go to sleep.”

     

                “You go to sleep.”

     

                “I am. I will be very annoyed if you snore tonight.”

     

                “Perhaps I should not have insisted you stay here with me.”

     

                On her feet, moving about the room as she set down the tray she’d brought to the bed for Kara, then circling the space as she blew out candles, made sure doors were closed and fetched her dagger, Lena finally returned to the bed. The room was dim and the sheets were soft as she climbed beneath them, eyes gritty, body heavy, and let her head sink onto the pillows as she stretched out on her side, looking at her wife.

     

                “I’m glad you did.”

     

                Reaching out, Kara gently stroked her cheek and Lena closed her eyes, relief and some semblance of peace sweeping over her. “Goodnight, Lena.”

     

                “Goodnight,” she whispered.

     

                She managed to open her eyes a few times to catch glimpses of her wife before she succumbed to her exhaustion, born of four days of little sleep and too much energy expended on ruining an ancient dwelling, and Lena didn’t stir again until late the following day. It had been just before dusk when they’d arrived and the room was just as dim when she woke again, groggy and uncertain of how much time had passed. Her limbs felt heavy and she could barely open her eyes past slits, realising she was entwined with her wife. Kara’s arm was draped over her and her breaths were slow and deep, one of her legs caught between Lena’s, and for a moment, Lena simply rested in the comfort of her presence, letting herself slowly wake.

     

                Remaining exactly where she was as she listened to the doves coo outside, Lena kept track of the quality of the light and came to the conclusion they’d slept the entire day away. Her throat felt dry and she was surprised to feel so hungry so soon, but she didn’t move an inch, her body sinking into the mattress as she slipped in and out of consciousness, dozing until she felt Kara stir at her side. Opening her eyes, Lena watched Kara go through the same groggy realisation as she took stock of her surroundings and her entangled position with her wife before she looked at Lena and the hawkish look softened into a smile.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “I think it’s technically dusk again,” Lena whispered, reaching out to tuck Kara’s hair behind her ear as she smiled. “Did you sleep well?”

     

                “Yes, although I wish to still be asleep. I’m terribly tired.”

     

                Humming in agreement, Lena idly stroked Kara’s hair as they lay together, neither of them speaking for a long while, the moment oddly intimate. The sound of footsteps nearing the door eventually disturbed them, a knock announcing the arrival of an unfamiliar heartbeat, and Lena climbed to her feet and went to answer it as Kara sat up, hair tousled and eyes still heavy with sleep. Opening the door, Lena thanked the woman who carried a tray, taking it from her and giving her a small smile.

     

                Jostling the mattress as she knelt on the edge of the bed, she set the tray in between them and climbed back beneath the covers. Kara reached for the pot of tea but Lena gently batted her hand away. “Let me. You rest.”

     

                Taking up the steaming pot, Lena poured two cups of tea and stirred in some honey before she handed one over. Side by side, they enjoyed their tea in companionable silence before turning their attention to their meal. There were slices of barley cake, a bowl of dates, little speckled boiled eggs, more of the cheese and a selection of fresh fruits and nuts. A little piece of parchment was nestled amidst two wooden bowls and Kara plucked it from the tray and read over the looping glyphs before setting it back on the tray.

     

                Meeting Lena’s gaze, she gave her a reassuring smile. “My sister. She and Kelly checked on us earlier but did not wish to disturb our sleep. They will leave us to rest until tomorrow morning.”

     

                Nodding, Lena started to cut a pear into slices for them and set half near Kara before she started to pick at the food. Tired and hungry, they didn’t speak much as they dwelled on their own thoughts, sipping their tea and refilling the cups, but it was a moment of peace amidst the chaos of the last week. In bed with her wife, Lena wanted to linger there with her for a hundred years.

    Chapter 32

                Lena woke again to the keening of the wind and a cold bed. She wasn’t sure if it was morning or night again, by the grey light seeping into the room, and she shivered as she sat up, pulling the blankets with her. Her momentary concern and confusion at the absence of her wife was dispelled as she heard the sound of her voice outside, in the private garden. Slipping out of bed, she winced as her feet touched the cold floor and wrapped her arms around herself as she moved over to the shutters, brushing aside the muslin curtains to open them.

     

                The rain had stopped for a brief moment but the wind was cutting, whisking away all of the moisture and leaving the air painfully cold and dry. A few thin clouds hung low overhead as Lena stepped outside, but it was rather clear, the sky dark as the sunrise broke. Trees growing alongside the narrow brook shaded much of the garden, needles of early morning light stabbing through the dense foliage, suffusing everything in a deep green-tinged light that made Lena feel warm. As the wind howled through the leaves, furiously rustling them, she heard a flutter of wings and watched the doves she’d heard yesterday flitter about with little grey sparrows and black-headed starlings. 

     

                Her wife was sitting on a mossy boulder situated in the weak sunlight between the walls of Kelly’s wing of her home and the nearest tree, her sister and sister-in-law with her. They were sipping tea and the other two looked refreshed and rested. Kara wore the nightgown brought for her the night before last, her skin still pale with circles beneath her eyes, but seeming to sit straighter, less bothered by her healing wound. She looked over at Lena at her arrival outdoors and smiled.

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “It is morning?” 

     

                “Yes. Come, join us for some tea and food.”

     

                Raking a hand through her tangled hair, Lena stifled a yawn, shifting from foot to foot on the hard-packed earth, like ice against her soles, wishing she had shoes, and picked her way towards them. The feeling of earth, of real dirt, and the smell of trees and moss was like a balm to Lena and she felt better out in the garden, even as she shivered in the wind. Sitting on the ground, the damp seeping into her nightgown, Lena was handed a cup of tea, something hot with a little sweetness to it. 

     

                A covered pot held oats and there were fruits, fresh bread and more barley cake. Kara piled a plate and filled a bowl and handed them off to Lena as she chatted animatedly, looking more lively than she had in a week. Eating slowly as she curled in on herself, Lena watched her closely, looking for any signs that she might be putting on a brave face. It didn’t seem that she was so Lena didn’t usher her back to bed, just sat and ate as the dawn passed into day, the sky turning a pale shade of blue between patchy cloud cover. Weak sunlight streamed through the canopy of the trees, trying in vain to warm the day, and Lena stared at the babbling brook. The water seemed dark green in the shade, and a murky brown in patches, leaves and dirt caught in small eddies. It was peaceful and she listened to frogs singing on the bank.

     

                Finishing off the dregs of her latest cup of tea, Kara climbed to her feet and stretched, wincing slightly at the pull in her abdomen. “Well, I am in dire need of a swim in a clear cold stream and then finding a nice big rock in the sun to dry off.”

     

                “You should-” Lena started to reason.

     

                Smiling down at her, Kara cupped her chin and wrinkled her nose slightly, eyes creasing at the corners. “I’m afraid this is non-negotiable.”

     

                “You should bathe properly as well,” Kelly said with a once-over at the salt-crusted and bloodied hair of both women. “I will have ewers of hot water brought for you both. And clean clothes too.”

     

                Kelly went off to find someone to assist while Lena refilled hers and Alex’s teacups and chatted quietly with her, the brisk wind slapping their cheeks. Kara had already stripped off her nightgown and unravelled the muslin bandages, standing knee-deep in the water. It was shallow enough for Lena to consider dipping into it without the nauseating panic that she would drown, knowing if she remained close to the banks, to the low branches of the ash tree nearby, she’d be able to wash properly. Despite the bowl of fragrant water and less grime coating her skin, she still didn’t feel clean.

     

                Finishing her tea, she watched as a woman carried in a bundle of clothes and towels and a man deposited steaming pitchers of hot water. Kelly resumed her spot on a low rock and Alex lit a pipe, puffing on it in between swigs of tea. Climbing to her feet, sorting through the piles and separating them into two, unsure of sizes until Kelly directed her to a buttery yellow tunic threaded with gold and dove grey leggings and a robe that were hers, a closer size to Lena than she was to Kara, who’d had to make do with the clothes borrowed from another. 

     

                Shedding her nightgown, skin rippling with goosebumps at the frigid air against her skin, she sank to a crouch at the bank of the flowing water, easing a foot in. The water was so cold that it hurt, skin tightening painfully as her foot went numb as she hissed softly. Removing her foot, the skin was bright pink and Lena’s chest rose and fell quickly, expelling gusts of white as her breath hung visibly. Grateful for her strong constitution, knowing that submerging herself in freezing cold water flowing from some distant mountain should have left her with pneumonia, or at the very least a nasty flu, yet she’d never been prone to illnesses, Lena put her foot back in as she gritted her teeth. 

     

                Setting her other foot in, she stood knee-deep, feeling the hard pebbles and stone and the soft silt and mud. Standing with her arms outstretched slightly for balance, Lena gingerly waited for the intense sting of cold to pass. Behind her, off to her right, she heard Alex laugh and shot her a withering look as she scowled.

     

                “Just get in . You will feel better if you get it over with.”

     

                Kara was drifting on her back, eyes closed and a look of bliss on her face as the water towed her along, towards the end of the garden, where it continued to trickle down a narrow ravine of rapids before dropping down to the sea. Lena watched as the current slowed and her wife seemed to drift back towards her, against the natural current, until Kara was almost parallel with her. Sitting up, crouching so the water submerged her up to her chest, Kara gave her a quick grin. She reached out a hand to Lena, her fingers pruned, and as Lena felt the earth between her toes, gratefully grounding, she felt the cold of the water as it flowed up Kara’s arm and over their joined fingers, cold as it crept up over her wrist.

     

                “She is right. Better to be done with it than inch in when it is this cold,” Kara murmured. “I have your hand in mine; I will not let go.”

     

                Tense and shivering, her teeth clenched so hard she thought they might crack, Lena gripped Kara’s hand so tightly she felt the bones move in her grasp, before gingerly lowering herself down into the water and stretching out on her back. Exhaling, she sank beneath the surface and felt her back brush the bed of the brook, before surfacing quickly, eyes wide and her body shuddering at the intensity of the cold.

     

                There was a bar of beeswax, scented with jasmine and lilies, and Lena sat shivering in the water as Kara rubbed it over her dark hair, lathering it and rinsing it away with a flick of her fingers, water sluicing down Lena’s hair and back. Her wife kept a hand on her at all times, on her shoulder, against her ribs or waist, and Lena was helpless as she sat there, unable to move as she folded her arms over her chest and let Kara wash her clean.

     

                Once the blood and dirt had been washed free, she abruptly staggered to numb feet and waded a step to the bank, stepping out of it and snatching up her ewer of hot water and dumping it over herself before wrapping herself in a towel. Sinking to the bank, she drew her knees to her chest and tried to ease the tremors as the wind scoured her pointed ears and cheeks as it rushed through. She dried herself off quickly and changed into the leggings and tunic Kelly had lent her, the cuffs of the tunic a little too short, and then she beckoned Kara closer, making her sit and lean back against the bank as Lena washed the dried blood and days of sweat, sand and salt from her hair. 

     

                Her wife stayed in the water a long while after she’d finished, and Alex and Kelly went inside to pass the time in other ways, while Lena pulled on the robe, which closed at the front with a wide sash tied around her waist. Sitting a safe distance from the water, in the shade of an ash tree, she looked up at the ribbons of light shining through its leaves and breathed in the fresh air, relishing only the faint tang of salt on the wind within the confines of the garden. Kara splashed about in the water for a while yet before emerging and rinsing off with her considerably cooler ewer of water and then doing as promised and finding a big rock in the sunlight to stretch out on and dry.

     

                Lena basked in the weak sunlight as well, with her back to the rock, breathing in the green taste of the air and not even minding the cold for once. At least there were trees and moss, and the sea was a little more removed from her immediate surroundings, even if the halls were on the doorstep of the cove. Beyond the cliffs, more trees and green grass were visible, as far as Lena could see over the top of the stone cliff-face that made the east-facing garden wall, and she was eager to run barefoot through the grass, feeling the dew and the tickling blades on her soles. They would be away soon, through a tree-lined gully and into rolling hills and grazing fields, or so Kara explained to her as they lingered outside a while longer. 

     

                Eventually rising to dress, Kara took Lena’s arm in the crook of her elbow and led her back inside, pausing long enough to buckle on her sword belt, and then winding through the hallways with some familiarity. They cut through to a walkway that spanned the length of the Guardian and Lena looked out through the carved archways. It was sunny and the view over the sea was serene, shining swells undulating beyond the cove, a stormy blue.

     

                Pushing open carved wooden doors to a sitting room, they found Alex and Kelly taking some tea near a square firepit set in the middle of the room. Smoke vanished up through a hole in the ceiling and there were low sedan sofas on each side of it, the two women taking up one each, small platters of olives, dates and cheese on a side table. Lena sank onto one and Kara lowered herself down beside her, stretching out with her head in Lena’s lap. A little surprised, and a little uncomfortable with the open glances from the other two women, Lena fiddled with her fingers and looked about as she warmed by the heat of the flames. 

     

                “This is where you grew up?” she asked Kelly.

     

                Lifting her attention from the book in her hands, Kelly smiled slightly, warm nostalgia in her dark brown eyes. “It is. My family has held the guardianship of the westernmost point of the Seelie Court for a thousand years.”

     

                “Do the Unseelie attack often?”

     

                “They have in centuries past. They are not so focused on maritime warfare though; they have few ships, although your brother has raided the western coast numerous times to disrupt trading. We are a crucial port and a stronghold; my father fell in defence of this place.”

     

                “It seems my family has a lot to answer for,” Lena replied with a short, flat laugh.

     

                Eyelashes fluttering, Kara looked up at her and gently touched her fingertips to Lena’s cheek. Looking down, dark hair cascading around her face, Lena raised her eyebrows slightly. “It is not your burden to bear.”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena murmured with a shrug. “I did decide to trust him, against my better judgment. Some of that is my burden, my thing to answer for.”

     

                “It is not a crime to wish for freedom, or to be deceived by one promising it.”

     

                “I guess I should be grateful he lied. Imagine what would be if I’d actually gotten rid of you.”

     

                Kara laughed as she withdrew her touch. “I am not that easily rid of.”

     

                “You are telling me,” Alex scoffed, drawing both of their attention. “When we were but children, after your family’s deaths, you were like a second shadow. I was not fond of my new sister following me everywhere, and yet I could not be rid of you.”

     

                “And aren’t you so grateful for that now?”

     

                “Yes, yes, you are the shield at my back, the sword at my side. There is no one I trust more, you are equal to my wife. As all marriages and families should be.”

     

                Her eyes slid to Lena, who rolled her own. “You would like to know if I trust you all? Sure. We might’ve gotten off on the wrong foot, but … yes, I do trust you. I can’t say the same for anyone else, and I don’t think all marriages and families should be trusting - my Unseelie ones for example - but I can at least say that my family within this room, and your mother, have earned my trust.”

     

                “And it was very hard-won at that,” Alex laughed.

     

                “Don’t tease her too much,” Kara smiled, looking up at her wife. “She is still learning.”

     

                Kelly rose to her feet, brushing off her robes, and gave Lena an expectant look. “Speaking of learning, we should resume your education in healing while we have some time to rest. Come, I will show you some excellent books to read.”

     

                Giving Kara’s shoulder a gentle pat so she’d sit up, Lena rose to her feet and told her wife to rest, nodding to her sister-in-law as she trailed Kelly to the door, and then glancing back to look at her wife once more before she left the room. It wasn’t that she thought any harm would befall Kara in Kelly’s home, only that Lena loathed to part from her. She hadn’t had time to think about it much, to think beyond the simple feelings of safety and danger, but she knew there was an anxious sort of attachment, that it was true that she trusted so few, but she didn’t have any friends besides Kara, and maybe that wasn’t a good thing, but she failed to see how it was that bad for now. She might be starting to trust the others a bit more, making more of an effort to spend time with them, but she would always cleave to Kara. 

     

                The morning passed by quickly as she sat in a large room, a wall of shelving holding an array of dried herbs and healing paraphernalia, a pot of tea on the table and a thick tome beside it as Lena deciphered glyphs with Kelly’s help, each paragraph leading to questions and answers and new information. It was warmer as far south as they were, much of the Guardian protected from the fierce winds sweeping in off the coast, and Lena would have gladly waited out the remainder of winter, and most of the spring, there if allowed. She knew they wouldn’t be though, too much at stake for any involved to just hide away as far west as they could possibly get. 

     

                Past lunch, they came to a stop, and Lena smoothed her hands over the whorls of glyphs, a thoughtful look on her face as Kelly started to return things back to their shelves. Meeting her gaze, Lena’s mouth thinned slightly. “Do you know what the plan is?”

     

                “To Alex’s home. It is in the Mid Vale.”

     

                “Yes, but when? How long will it take? Will we be safe there?”

     

                “We shall be gone again within a matter of days. My mother’s people are unloading our ships; supplies will be sent south, to travel upriver, and we will leave on horseback. It will take a fortnight, perhaps, with how many we number. It will be difficult to travel quickly with so many of us. Although, my brother and his soldiers will part ways with us as they take the path back to the war front. As for safety … we shall be as safe there as anywhere, with mostly the forest to contend with. Undoubtedly, the war will call us to it before it reaches us.”

     

                A wary look crossed Lena’s face. “And my mother?”

     

                “What of her?”

     

                “What are we doing with her?”

     

                “She will come with us. My mother will not suffer Unseelie in her home for long. And aside from rites of hospitality, which all will obey or face shameful consequences, she has no obligation to them. Not as you and Kara are beholden, as kin of hers.”

     

                “I wish that we weren’t either,” Lena muttered, resentment clouding her face.

     

                Giving her an understanding smile, Kelly slowly eased the heavy tome closed and tapped the cover of the book. “We will resume tomorrow after breaking our fast.”

     

                Nodding, Lena poured the rest of the tea out into her cup and then drained it in one go. Staring into the dregs, the grit of tea leaves clinging to the bottom, Lena was quiet for a moment. “What are you doing for the rest of the day?”

     

                “My mother is expecting me for a midday meal. Other than that, I imagine I will look in on those injured, if you care to accompany me.”

     

                “Sure. Just come and find me when you’re ready.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, Lena trailed her to the door and Kelly walked alongside her, weak sunlight shining in through the arches of the walkway. “You are free to roam wherever it pleases you while you are here; I only ask that you do not enter rooms with closed doors. This place is both harbour and small garrison, and there are more here in residence than at Argo or Krypton.”

     

                Nodding in agreement, she asked Kelly to guide her back to the bedroom she was sharing with Kara, and they parted ways as Lena opened the door and stepped through the curtains as they ballooned towards her at the sudden disturbance. She could hear Kara outside in the garden and crossed the room to step through the other set of curtains, drifting in the breeze of the open doors. Her wife had shed her robe and was knee-deep in the water again, her pale grey leggings soaked darker to her thighs, the deep grey tunic splattered with droplets. She turned at Lena’s arrival, hair a pale gold in the weak sunlight, and smiled.

     

                “You should rest.”

     

                “The water does me some good. I shall seek out the sea later; the salt will ease the heat in my wound.”

     

                “It’s not infected is it?” Lena anxiously asked, feet carrying her forward.

     

                Kara laughed, water writhing around her fingers as she spread her arms and tipped her head back, breathing in the fresh air. “No, there is no infection. Salt is merely good for healing wounds.”

     

                “So the folk stories say.”

     

                “You and I are folk stories, wife. Do not be so hasty to dismiss them.”

     

                Gesturing dismissively, Lena rolled her eyes. “Well, you’re very real to me.”

     

                “I should hope so, that I’m not a mere dream to you.”

     

                Looking at her wife, her handsome face bathed silver in the pale light, flaxen hair spilling down her back, pale clothes making her look ethereal as she stood amidst the gently flowing water, Lena wouldn’t have been surprised if she had dreamt the whole thing. Arms wrapped around herself, a small smile tugged at Lena’s lips, her gaze tender as she wondered if she should pinch herself. 

                

                “I wouldn’t be surprised if you were,” she whispered. “But I-”

     

                Falling silent, Lena lowered her gaze to the mossy ground underfoot. She heard splashing as her wife waded towards the bank, curious as she cocked her head to the side, waiting for more. Lena was tight-lipped though, vaguely embarrassed as she frowned at the dirt.

     

                “But what?”

     

                Drawing in a shuddering breath, Lena heavily exhaled. “But I hope that you’re not.”

     

                She could feel how close Kara was, a few feet between them as Lena stood a safe distance from the bank and Kara likewise did, remaining in the swirling current of the water. Water dripped in front of Lena’s, splattering the dirt, and she looked up, her wife’s hand extended to her. Taking it as she met Kara’s piercing stare, Lena let herself be tugged a step forward, as close to the water as she’d like to get, as Kara stepped in as well. Wet fingers cupping her chin, Kara urged her wife’s face down and leaned in to give her the briefest of kisses before pulling back and giving her a radiant smile.

     

                “I am not a dream.”
