                Shrinking away, Kara slid back into the shallow water with laughter, stretching on her back, arms and legs spread wide so that she almost touched either bank, drifting. Watching her, Lena was struck with the strange sense of insanity, that she must have suffered some psychotic break for this to be her life, that it still felt too unreal for it to be happening to her. She’d never felt crazy before but watching her wife splay on top of the water as her clothes darkened, sinking to just beneath the surface with a serene look on her face, she felt a certain madness to herself, the urge to wade into the water and join her, even if it meant drowning. She wondered if that was the forest at play, the hooks inside her, roots binding her to this place, to her wife. Only her prickling fear stopped her. 

     

                Sinking to a crouch right along the bank, Lena watched her wife. She didn’t know how long she sat there as Kara drifted peacefully, the wind rustling the trees, the cold stiffening Lena’s joints as she listened to the birds and breathed in the green air. It was the best she’d felt in weeks, since that trip to a little copse of trees near the estuary, perhaps even since before then. It felt more secure there, situated back and above the sea, only a relatively gentle harbour below, trees and plants surrounding them and fields of green sprawling behind them. Lena knew that Kara loved her home by the sea, and she felt guilt needle her to have ruined it, but she was quietly grateful to be away, even if she wished to have never left such destruction in her wake.

     

                They milled about the garden and their room for the remainder of the day, Lena eventually climbing to her feet and borrowing Kara’s sword as she went through stances and flowing movements with less grace than her wife. Kara eventually got out of the water, drawing it from her clothes and hair, dry within moments, and she joined Lena without a weapon. Despite being unarmed, despite being injured, Kara was quick and surefooted, ducking and weaving as she avoided her wife’s attacks, reaching out to strike Lena’s weak spots with a quick jab of her finger. It was frustrating to still be so inadequate against someone without a sword, but Kara merely chuckled as Lena finally let the sword tip lower to the ground, sweating as she drew in rapid breaths.

     

                Cupping her chin, Kara smiled crookedly. “You are getting better.”

     

                With a scoff, Lena gave her a withering look. “You keep saying that, but put me in a fight against you and you’d gut me like a fish.”

     

                “I did not say you were a sword master , only getting better . But if you need pick a weapon in a fight, I ask you choose a bow. You are more than better with a bow, plainly seen by all at Krypton.”

     

                “Yeah, well, I don’t think I’d be able to shoot a squirrel through the eye at fifty feet like your sister and Kelly.”

     

                “Not yet. But no matter what weapon you are armed with, you have a fighting chance now. Armour will help with the rest.”

     

                “Planning on throwing me into the thick of it again?”

     

                “Not anytime soon if I can help it, but we both know you will not sit by without complaint. You will insist on being at my side, so at least I may reassure myself that you are somewhat adequately acquitted for battle.”

     

                Lena bristled slightly and gave Kara a haughty look. “Maybe I won’t insist on being there if it means you’re going to be so distracted that people put holes in you.”

     

                “It was one hole.”

     

                “That makes it so much better then.”

     

                “It does, does it not?” Kara beamed, ignoring the sarcasm, as she took her sword from Lena’s grasp and replaced it with her hand.

     

                Gently squeezing, she tugged her wife towards the open door. Inside, Kara sheathed her sword and buckled it back on before leading Lena to a humid kitchen on one of the lower levels of the garrison, soldiers and sailors alike coming in and out, filling bowls from a massive pot and sharing honeyed wine. James was there with a few of his soldiers and Kara gave him a quick smile as she breezed past, fetching soup for herself and Lena and taking two cups of the wine as well before leading them to a secluded courtyard overgrown with flowers and bushes. 

     

                Stone had been quarried so that a square of pale sky was visible overhead, four stone benches situated in a square with a maple tree growing from the middle of them. Setting their food down on a bench, Kara sat cross-legged and handed some of the flatbread to Lena with a smile.

     

                “I thought you might like it here. My visits to Guardian have always led me here when seeking privacy; I am not often disturbed.”

     

                Sinking to the stone bench, lichen and moss furring it, Lena crossed her legs and cupped her bowl in one hand, dipping her bread into the broth. “It’s quiet.”

     

                “And there is no water.”

     

                Eyes sliding to her, Lena smiled thinly. “I’m not opposed to the stream in our garden. It’s peaceful to listen to, at least.”

     

                “That is glowing praise from you.”

     

                “It is nice to be near a big tree though,” she conceded, watching her wife smile widely with delight, pleased that her idea had been well received.

     

                They ate in relative silence as they enjoyed the peace and quiet, the wind lessened with the high walls enclosing them, the cold not so biting although they lingered in the shade, the midday sun already past its zenith. Her empty bowl beside her, glad for the lack of seafood, Lena sipped her honeyed wine as she stared up at the wide canopy overhead, thick branches spreading from the gnarled trunk, and she felt small and comforted in the shade of it. Finishing off her wine, she climbed to her feet, mossy ground underfoot, and stepped towards the trunk, laying a palm against the bark as she closed her eyes. She felt the tension bleed out of her and the tree creaked slightly, her eyes snapping open to watch it almost preen, little branches rustling and branches flexing as if the whole thing was stretching.

     

                “The trees are happy to have you back,” Kara said with a quiet laugh.

     

                “I’m happy to have them back. I can’t wait to be in the forest again.”

     

                “Do you not fear the creatures within it, the twisted depths of the wilds?”

     

                “I’d rather be in danger amongst the trees than on the coast. And it’s been far too long; I’d even take another season in the Unseelie Court if it meant I could be in the thick of the forest again.”

     

                A small smile playing on her lips, Kara climbed to her feet. “Now I know how dire your need is if you wish to be back in the wolf’s den again. Come.”

     

                Before Lena could question what they were doing, Kara was already scrambling up the trunk as she reached for the lowest branch. A small sound of complaint escaped Lena’s lips as she looked up at her wife. “Your stitches.”

     

                “Will manage just fine. Come; sit in your tree for a while and think of the forest. We shall be there soon enough.”

     

                Sighing, Lena gave in without complaint and followed her up, muscles aching as she pulled herself up, hand over hand, less nimble than her wife but sure-footed all the same. Through the branches, which grew slender the higher they went, she followed on Kara’s heels until her wife settled in the fork of a branch that would bear her weight. Picking her own branch to sit on, legs dangling on either side, Lena let out a slightly breathless laugh, the ground a dizzying drop below.

     

                A slight flush to her pale cheeks, Lena smiled as she met Kara’s eyes, both of them sitting comfortably high in the tree’s branches as they swayed slightly. Lena thought of a whole host of trees, of the thick forest, brambles and undergrowth taller than she was, roots thicker than a horse at the base of monstrously wide trunks, the canopy a hundred feet above her head at least. The thought of loam and leaves and sweet sap and soft mud was encouraging and although Lena was glad for the short reprieve they were offered there, she was eager to be on their way again, if only to be back east in the trees. Everything would be alright once they were at Alex’s home, someone safe and permanent to wait out the lengthy war amidst the forest and valleys and lakes. 

     

                Her time spent poring over maps told her little of the terrain they’d be traversing, how many fields and glades and sprawling halls they’d encounter, how far the forest stretched and how thick it would be, mountains cutting a path through them, but she knew enough to make her own assumptions. Verdant valleys and gullies, sheer passes through tree-filled mountain passes, the damp green sweet and heavy in the air. No trace of salt on the wind at all. It was all she wanted in her mind, thinking of being safe enough to sit outside and take it all in without the threat of death looming immediately over her.

     

                Eventually, climbed back down, Kara moving with ease despite her wound, and lifting Lena the rest of the way down as she neared the lowest branch. They carried their dishes inside and spent a little while in the kitchens, pitching in as they scrubbed them clean in large barrels of hot water, Lena watching the whirling tornadoes of air flit around, whisking dishes away and fetching ingredients as the Airfolk starting on dinner commanded them about. Staying to help make some bread, a simple task that she had gotten the knack of and enjoyed the mindlessness of kneading and of others eating that which her hands had made, Lena watched her wife leave as Kara mentioned a swim.

     

                By the time Lena had finished, there were a dozen loaves scored and rising, almost ready for the oven, and she washed flour and dough from her hands before leaving. Walking along the walkway, she looked out at the day, the shadows growing longer and the light fading somewhat. The surface of the harbour was relatively calm and she paused to lean against the waist-high stone wall, running her fingers over the motifs of sparrows, cranes and doves carved into them. Below, she caught sight of a sodden figure climbing out of the water, robe stripped off and golden hair a dull brass, watching as her wife set down a handful of something caught before turning and executing a perfect dive back into the harbour, powerful arms cutting through the water as she revelled in the open water of the harbour.

     

                Kelly found her then, and Lena accompanied her through the hallways, visiting sickbeds as Lena brewed tea while Kelly pounded herbs into poultices and changed bandages. It was fulfilling work that Lena enjoyed, making herself useful, helping others with her knowledge of plants, which was only growing. It passed by the remainder of the afternoon and by the time they were done, her wife had finished swimming. Kara entered the covered walkway the two healers were walking along and smiled at the sight of Lena. Barefoot and clutching her damp tunic and leggings, her robe belted over bare skin, Kara raked a hand through a mess of salty curls as she waited for them to catch up to her.

     

                “Am I late to supper?”

     

                “Not yet, but you should hurry before the best cuts of meat are gone,” Kelly goaded her as she ushered Lena along. 

     

                She led her to a large chamber at the very southern end, quiet and tinged with blue evening light from the windows carved along the western wall, bringing in the soft hissing of the sea below. A very stood around the large hearth, warming their hands and talking in low voices, while others huddled in groups with cups of wine, and others yet took their seats at the long tables. Kelly led Lena to the head table, directing her to an empty seat before she moved a few seats along to sit in between her mother and Alex. There was an empty seat between Lena and Alex that was obviously for Kara, both of them afforded places of respect with the Lady of the Airfolk. James sat to his mother’s other side, Lucy and a few others of importance taking the remainder to his right. 

     

                Others slowly trickled in and Lena looked for Kara, her attention overlooking the food until her wife arrived and took a seat at her side. Looking a little more refreshed, Kara gave her a small smile as she filled their cups with wine. Turning her attention to the fare spread out before them, Lena was pleasantly surprised to see roasted pheasant amidst the herbed potatoes, spiced pears and carrots. Bread still warm from the oven, possibly even the ones she’d made herself, were spread amongst the dishes and she took a little of everything onto her plate. The food was good and the wine sweet, and she ate her fill and watched the others at the tables, taking note of familiar faces scattered amongst the unfamiliar.

     

                The meal dragged on as everyone lingered over their food, especially those who had been travelling or camping along the river separating the Courts for who knew how long, quiet conversation not disturbing the peace as someone started to play a harp, another a flute, adding to the comfortable ambience of the firelit room. As some started to trickle away, the room emptied a bit, and Lena felt heavy and content in her seat, and probably could’ve fallen asleep where she was. Still tired down to her bones, wondering how long the exhaustion born of her erratic power would linger, she quietly excused herself from the table and bid Kara stay when her wife tried to accompany her.

     

                Exiting the grand hall, the sharp evening wind blew in her face as she stood on the walkway, taking in the damp mist that had descended, the clouds that gathered overhead, blotting out the starlight. Dew gathered on her hair and clothes as she exhaled puffs of white, feet cold against the stone floor, the night getting colder and the sea a glimmer of black and silver through the haze of mist as she walked along. 

     

                Losing her way as she tried to remember the path back to her room, she stumbled across a lone figure standing rigidly near an archway, staring out at the sea. Taking in the shadowed profile of the tall woman, Lena approached with curiosity. 

     

                “Sam?”

     

                There was no response, no indication that the other woman heard her, and Lena walked closer, a flicker of concern washing over her as she wondered if she should find Andrea. Shoulders square, a regal tilt to her chin, Sam stared out at the water and Lena drew near her side.

     

                “Sam, are you well?”

     

                Stiffening, the woman’s hand fell to the hilt of her sword as her head swivelled, eyes seeming black in the dark, hard and flat and entirely unfamiliar. It made Lena’s stomach plummet as a cold chill stole over her, something sinister in the lines of her protector’s face, something not altogether unfamiliar. She looked like Reign, which sounded like a silly comparison, considering they were the same woman, but Lena was left with a feeling of unease, even as she watched Sam blink, shaking her head slightly as her shoulders sagged and her hand dropped from the sword hilt.

     

                “Princess. You should not sneak up on one who is armed. Not in times like these.”

     

                “Oh, sorry, I tried to get your attention.”

     

                “Forgive me, I did not hear you,” Sam said, her eyebrows drawing together as she squeezed her eyes shut, wrestling with something for a moment before she quietly drew in a sharp breath. “My mind was … elsewhere.”

     

                “Right,” Lena said, confusion flashing across her face as she hugged her arms to herself. “Well … I’m heading off to bed. You should get some sleep too; I hear we’ll be leaving soon.”

    Chapter 33

                The few days of rest passed by quickly, much needed and restorative, especially for Kara, whose wound healed quickly with enough sleep and idle time. The day her stitches came out, they made plans to leave, Lena sitting in on meetings with her family and Kelly’s family, agreements being made for horses and provisions, Kara making a gift of some of the supplies they’d brought, and plans to send the rest to bolster the soldiers along the treaty line drawn up and left to be dealt with after they’d gone. 

     

                Two days later, they were up before dawn broke over the Guardian. Clean clothes, thick and well-made for travelling, had been brought to them the night before and a woman brought a basin of hot water for them to wash with before dressing. The leather leggings were snug, a wool tunic covered by a leather jerkin, and a grey cloak wrapped around their shoulders for added warmth. There were thin leather boots as well, tight around Lena’s calves as she relished the thought of shoes. Belting on her dagger, she felt fit for the road and smiled at her wife, who had a healthy glow to her face once more, and looked regal in the gifted clothes.

     

                They all ate breakfast together in the main hall, everyone dressed warmly for travel, looking more prepared than they had when they’d left Krypton in a rush, and Lena savoured the food, well aware of what they’d be eating on the road. The soldiers departed first, readying horses and supplies at the stables, and Lena lingered with her wife, sticking to Kara’s side until the remainder of them left. Lena had tried to argue for her mother to stay at the Guardian with the Unseelie, as far from battle and the Prince as possible, but Kelly’s mother trusted Lillian even less than Lena did and wouldn’t stand to have her remain. Lena glared daggers at her mother’s back as she watched her walk ahead, dressed in a similar fashion as the others, sans a hand.

     

                Reaching the stables, Lena looked at the mass of horses, a little over three dozen of them, the extras being used as saddle horses for the sheer amount of provisions they would need to keep a party of twenty-nine fed and watered for a fortnight. They could hunt along the way, providing the availability proved sufficient enough, but they couldn’t count on that to sustain them. Thanking Kelly’s mother, Kara and Lena went to find their mounts, directed to two horses set aside for them, of better stock than some of the others. Lena’s mare was a hand shorter than Kara’s and a sooty black with white fetlocks, and Kara’s was a buckskin with a dark mane, whickering softly as Kara smoothed a hand over her velvety nose and murmured a few friendly words. 

     

                “Lena,” Kelly called out as Lena made to hoist herself into the saddle, turning to look at her sister-in-law with an expectant look on her face.

     

                Giving her a small smile, Kelly extended a bow made from dark wood, unslinging a quiver from her shoulder in the process. Brown-fletched arrows filled the quiver. Confusion crossed Lena’s face as she took in the offered bow and then met Kelly’s dark eyes, bright with delight.

     

                “What’s that for?”

     

                “It’s for you.”

     

                “Me?”

     

                “Bows are the preferred weapons of the Airfolk. You will not find a bow equal in all of the Courts to one made here by my mother’s craftsmen. It is a gift to you, Princess; may you slay many enemies with it.”

     

                Lena smiled as she took the bow, turning it in her hands, running her fingers over the engravings. She tested the tension of the bowstring and then drew it back, her smile growing. “It’s beautiful, thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kelly handed over the quiver. “I hope it serves you well.”

     

                Slinging the quiver across her back and adjusting her cloak, Lena smiled brightly as her eyes met Kara’s, her wife already mounted. Hauling herself up into her saddle, Lena got her feet in the stirrups and admired the bow some more before leaning across to show it to Kara. 

     

                “Very appropriate,” Kara smiled, nodding as she eyed the bow before straightening in her saddle.

     

                James finished his farewells with his mother and the remainder of their party mounted up, everyone jostling for order as the towering gates carved out of heavy stone from the rock bed they were set into were dragged open. A tunnel perhaps fifty feet long was carved through the rock and angled upwards, an archway of light beckoning them through to the other side as their party started to leave, two by two. Beside her wife, Lena felt a thrill of excitement, aching for woods, for glens and thick forests, mossy valleys and narrow gullies winding beneath the roots of trees that were a thousand years old.

     

                They came out of the tunnel to open fields stretching far into the distance, the unending green turning into gently rolling hills in the distance. The mountains in the far distance were a mere smudge on the horizon, the forest a thick wall of deep green closer still. Lena would have happily gotten lost in the depths of the trees, feeling it tug her forward, a craving that needed to be satiated. A gentle pace was set, a little faster than a walk as everyone got their bearings, the horses well-trained and falling into line in short order, but they started to pick up speed a few miles away from the coast.

     

                “It is good grassland out here,” Kara explained to Lena as they trotted along. “Cows and sheep. A lot of farming too, plenty of wheat and barley grown in these parts. Further inland, near my sister’s home, is better for root vegetables and mushrooms, and you would not hunt any big game save for deer. You can smell how fertile the soil is here though; it is a region of sweet wine, honey and cheeses. If only we had time to savour a little more of it before we had to leave.”

     

                “Maybe we can come back one day,” Lena suggested.

     

                Meeting her gaze, Kara smiled warmly. “If you wish to.”

     

                “It would be nice, when it’s peaceful, to go and visit other places. To see your favourite spots. We could go. Just the two of us.”

     

                “Alright. We will. Just the two of us.”

     

                Giving her a droll look, Lena raised her eyebrows. “We just need to make it through these trying times first. Hopefully unscathed.”

     

                “Your words are very pointed, but I should remind you that it is not I who is most at risk of injury. Let us hope your new bow serves you well enough that you may remain out of immediate danger in any future battles.”

     

                Lifting her new bow, Lena laughed as she mimed drawing back the bowstring, letting go of the reins as she moved with her mare, knees and thighs keeping her steady. “Find me a target and I will do quite well, I think. That’s always the coward’s way, isn’t it? To kill from afar so I don’t have to see the blood on my hands. I’m pretty good at that, it seems.”

     

                Kara scoffed and clicked her tongue. “You are no coward, Lena.”

     

                “I don’t know. I’d rather other people did the killing for me, but if I have to do it, I don’t want to see them die. I’d rather take the easy way out of anything.”

     

                “You’ve fought hard in your life for the luxury of the easy way. No one would begrudge you that choice. Me least of all, if it meant you were safe. There are a thousand ways to be of use; your healing alone could save more lives than you might take in battle. Is that not of more use, to tip the numbers in our favour by your own hands?”

     

                “I don’t think I’m good enough at anything to tip things in our favour yet. Unless peace will be won by which Court has the prettiest arrangement of flowers.” She scoffed, shaking her head as she smiled wryly. “All we can do is try our best, right?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara softly agreed. “Although … I wish you would not try so hard . You do not have to be useful to be of worth. You are worth so much to me by merely existing; I would not think less of you if you offered nothing to the war. You may sit and bake bread and practise your archery and pick flowers if that is what you wish to do. A life is to be enjoyed if lived well.”

     

                “I know, but I can’t. I need something to do, I need to be useful or- or wanted, needed, desired. It would be easier if I didn’t feel that way, but if no one is beholden to me for anything, if I’m not pleasing people, making them happy, then I can be set aside and forgotten about far too easily.”

     

                “I would not easily forget you, and I would not set you aside, under any circumstance. You could be taken from me and I would fight my way back to you, even if I had to do it alone. That’s what it means to make a vow.”

     

                “I know you mean that, because you can say it, so I’m trying to accept it. I trust you, of course, but there’s a lot for me to undo before I can believe it.”

     

                “It’s okay if you never believe me; it would not make it less true.”

     

                “At the very least, I can promise you the same. I would fight my way back to you as well if we were ever parted.”

     

                “I will try my hardest to make sure that eventuality does not come to pass, but it is comforting to know you will fight. You are ever the survivor, my wife.”

     

                Kara gave Lena a quick grin and their conversation turned to lighter topics after that. Kara talked more about the landscape, the plants that grew there, which animals were in abundance, the river in the distance and the tributaries of it. She spoke at length about healing as well, the medicinal herbs in the area, how they could be used, and which ones to steer clear of. 

     

                Miles passed by in that fashion, the morning giving way to afternoon with barely a break to stretch their legs. They ate in the saddle, a cloudy sky overhead threatening rain, but Lena was glad to be away, the tang of salt on the wind receding the further inland they travelled. She breathed in the blessedly fresh air and dragged her windblown hair out of her face as she stared out at the lands, taking in the open moorland, green valleys and fern-filled gorges hiding waterfalls and lakes as the west of the Seelie Court spread out before her, foreign and exciting.

     

                They didn’t follow a road, nor had Lena seen a single one in all her time there, no disruption to the endless fields, white chickweed and violets dotting the grass, until they reached undulating hills, lush with bracken, red sorrel and gorse. The soil was black and everything was so green as they moved through the rolling hills towards the trees, winding up a knoll, horses knee deep in the heather, patches of rocky ground veining the green, wildflowers and weeds making for a picturesque view as the horses trotted along at a steady pace. It was a bewitching place, the western hills with its occasional tree shading a patch of grass, trickling streams cutting through the ground before them, the valley, mountains and vales ahead shrouded in mist.

     

                Now and then they heard birds, Kara identifying the call as a thrush, and Lena looked to the sparse trees dotting the hills, wishing they could rest beneath one for a while, perhaps enjoying a proper lunch beneath its canopy. Instead, they continued onwards, until the sky darkened and the clouds grew heavier, the rain starting up as daylight failed. They were in the open, the nearest thicket of trees a few miles away, so they pushed onwards until they reached what little shelter was offered amongst the seemingly endless stretch of hills.

     

                As they approached the thicket of trees, they all started to dismount, everyone moving with purpose as horses were unsaddled, wood was collected for fires, folded canvases were carried into the trees and waterskins were collected for filling at the nearest source of water. Lena made herself useful with the horses, brushing them down, checking their hooves, and setting them out to graze freely before turning her attention to the next one. By the time she finished with her last one, Lucy and another two soldiers finishing off theirs, a group had come back with filled waterskins, the canvases had been lashed to trunks, creating multiple shelters for them all to huddle beneath that night, and several fires had been started amongst the trunks, pots clustered over them, boiling water for tea or stew.

     

                Picking her way over roots, ducking beneath taut ropes, skirting around helmets and shields and packs, Lena sought out her wife. Kara had gone off to help with the water and was now crouched beside a fire, tearing foraged herbs into pieces and sprinkling them into a pot. She glanced up at Lena’s approach, wiping her hands on her cloak as she smiled.

     

                “Come, sit. Tea will be ready soon.”

     

                Sinking to the leafy ground, Lena let out a weary sigh. Her body ached, unused to such hard riding after a few months of relatively short forays away from Krypton for pleasure, and it was cold, her cloak damp and fingers pink. Holding her hands nearer to the flames, Lena was glad for the rest, looking about as she breathed in the air, feeling the roots beneath her, the rich earth and the awareness of the branches overhead. Looking up to the somewhat bare canopy, Lena cocked her head to the side, a thoughtful look crossing her face.

     

                Kara glanced at her as she pulled wooden cups from her saddlebags, setting them down ready for the tea before she glanced at Lena again. “Something amiss?”

     

                “No. I can just … feel the trees. More than before, it feels- I don’t know.”

     

                “We are not born with an affinity for an element, you know,” Kara explained. “It is not something a newborn babe can do - I imagine chaos if a tiny thing could set the forest afire with a mere tantrum - it is something that we are aware of as we grow. A few years from birth, we may feel it more keenly. I imagine your perception has been somewhat dulled in your years removed from the forest, and you have been away from trees these last few months, so perhaps you have not felt that awareness so keenly until now because there have not been many trees to contend with.”

     

                “But I’ve done things without meaning to. I know it’s there , that I can feel it if it’s forced.”

     

                “Yes, but being in tune with oneself and with the elements is not meant to be forced. It should be as if reaching a hand out to touch the falling rain, not as if you are wringing it from the clouds with your own hands.” She laughed, giving Lena a kind smile as she reached out to lay a hand on her knee, tenderly stroking her thumb over the soft leather. “It will grow stronger with time until it is as natural as breathing.”

     

                A small furrow formed between Lena’s eyebrows and her mouth turned down slightly at the corners, a pensive look on her face. Her dark hair was damp and her brooding gave her a clouded demeanour as she stared up at the leaves.

     

                “You know, sometimes I feel like I can’t even recognise myself anymore,” she confessed. “I’m not the same person I was when I first got here. I don’t think I’ll ever be that person again. But I don’t- I don’t think I’m who I’m supposed to be yet. It’s … confusing.”

     

                “You have changed a great deal, but that is what it means to be alive. We are all of us constantly changing, like a river slowly eroding rock over many years to carve a new path for itself. But we are still the same river, no matter what changes befall us, and it is inevitable that as we flow with the current, we will never go back. We can never go back to who we were, so one must continue onwards with the flow of time, ever-changing, always new. How exciting .”

     

                Kara gave Lena a tender smile as their eyes met. Her warmth was infectious, her blue eyes so earnest that Lena couldn’t help but believe she did find it exciting to always be changing, to never stay the same. She supposed when you had the opportunity to live for thousands of years, you couldn’t remain the same throughout it, too many variables, too much life lived to not change at all. Lena supposed that was true of a regular human life too, albeit on a smaller scale. 

     

                “Don’t change too much,” Lena whispered, her expression softening. “I like you as you are.”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Kara cocked her head to the side, eyes creasing at the corners and a faintly perplexed look crossing her face. It was gone quickly and Lena didn’t have to wonder what she’d been thinking; Kara was usually quick to speak her mind.

     

                “It is interesting you tell me not to change too much - Alex is of the opinion I have changed greatly of late. She attributes it to you.”

     

                “Really?” Lena blinked, surprised. “What change would that be?”

     

                Gesturing vaguely, Kara turned her attention to the boiling pot of tea. Leaning forward, she picked up the wooden cups and filled one each for them, handing Lena hers first before she replied, thoughtful as she considered whether her sister’s observation had any merit to it.

     

                “She said I’m happier now.”

     

                Cup almost to her lips, Lena paused, lowering it as she raised her head. Staring at her wife, she gave her a searching look. “Are you?”

     

                A funny look crossed Kara’s face, as if she found it amusing that Lena would ask such a question. “You’re my friend, my family. Of course I am happy in your company.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                At Lena’s mumbled response, Kara looked at her, eyebrows rising slowly in an expression of hope. “I hope it is reciprocated.”

     

                With a huff of laughter, Lena finally took a sip of her tea, swallowing the scalding mouthful as her chest spasmed with a strange feeling. “Of course it is.”

     

                “But … you are happy, aren’t you?”

     

                At the anxious edge Kara’s expression took on, Lena laid a hand over hers on the leaf-strewn floor. A placating smile softened her expression, her green eyes tender as she studied the slightly pinched look on her wife’s face. 

     

                “I think I’m … starting to be. I was content, but I think I’m starting to be genuinely happy. I’m happy with you - that’s enough.”

     

                “Is it?”

     

                “Yes. It’s more than I’ve ever had before.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena exhaled softly, a faint smile on her lips. “Kara, I- my life has never been particularly great. I’m not a cheerful person, I’m not … excitable or- or warm and loving. I don’t have to feel things greatly to feel it, you know? Just because I’m not jumping for joy, it doesn’t mean I’m not happy, and just because I’m not screaming and crying every day, it doesn’t mean I’m not upset. I’m an … even middle-ground, and I’m satisfied with that. It’s dependable, it’s consistent.”

     

                “That is a very Earthfolk quality,” Kara whispered as she smiled, one cheek dimpling as it hitched unevenly. She held Lena’s hand in her own, staring down at their entwined fingers. “But you are warm and loving, even if you do not see it yourself. To be loved by you, to be seen as worthy of it in your eyes, would make one the most fortunate of Fae.”

     

                “It’s not worth that much, I can assure you,” Lena said with an amused scoff.

     

                “Then I must disagree. Those who love you would crave the sentiment returned.”

     

                “Ah, now that’s a short list.”

     

                “You may put me at the top of it.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose as she leaned in slightly, lowering her voice as she smiled crookedly, Lena opened her mouth and then hesitated. “That’s because you’re married to me, and there wasn’t much choice in the matter.”

     

                “Ah, but I did freely decide to marry you, and I did not love you at the time. There was nothing in our oaths that demanded that of me, but you have become family to me regardless of our Courts and all our differences. You shall always be loved by me.”

     

                “Then I guess that makes me one of the most fortunate of Fae.”

     

                With a huff of laughter, Kara let go of Lena’s hand and took a sip of her tea. “I don’t think anyone loved by me is fortunate. It is a waiting game of loving people while living with the torment of not knowing who it is my love will kill. I try my hardest to resist, and yet … I am always weak in the face of it. Who does not wish to love and be loved? It would be a cold and empty life without it. I am not built for such loneliness, and so I am selfish.”

     

                “You aren’t selfish. A selfish person wouldn’t offer themselves up for an arranged marriage to make peace. A selfish person wouldn’t risk their life over and over again for others. You wouldn’t care for me as you do, you wouldn’t try so hard to make me happy, to be a good wife.”

     

                “It is because I’m so selfish that I do those things,” Kara admitted, opening her mouth to say something else before they were interrupted.

     

                Both of them jerked apart, surprised by the interruption and by how close they’d naturally gravitated to each other, an intimacy between them to anyone observing, and Lena sloshed some of her tea over her hands as she quickly put some space between them. It was just Alex, dropping an armful of firewood to the ground, the wood clattering loudly, and Kara gave her sister a pointedly exasperated look.

     

                “Should I pitch the two of you a private shelter for the evening?” Alex murmured too quietly for anyone else to hear.

     

                Kara’s legs were stretched before her and she knocked her foot against her sister’s ankle, her eyes flashing a disgruntled warning. With a quiet chuckle, Alex sank to a squat and helped herself to some tea, settling down beside her sister and glancing around the camp. Lena likewise turned her attention to the camp, any further conversation of sensitive or personal topics put to rest, and she sipped her tea as she eyed the groups that formed. Her mother and the handful of Unseelie who’d made it unscathed grouped together at their own fire and Lena watched as Sam and Andrea tended to their cookpot. 

     

                A flash of outrage ran through her, and she knocked back her tea and climbed to her feet, brushing leaves off her cloak. Picking her way through the trees, aware that she was being a little petty, Lena approached her mother’s group and stopped at the edge of the clear divide.

     

                “Sam, Andrea, come.”

     

                They paused mid-task, glancing over at her, taking in the clenched jaw, the haughty bearing. In the gloom of the trees, Lena looked hard and regal and there was a momentary pause before they glanced at Lillian and then at her daughter, before stepping towards Lena.

     

                “I have not given you leave yet,” Lillian called out, making them pause again.

     

                “It is fortunate they are my attendants then,” Lena retorted.

     

                “Yours at my behest. Now, I require them back. How un fortunate for you.”

     

                “You are in the Seelie Court; your command does not stand here.”

     

                “Yet, I am still Queen of my own people.”

     

                Lena’s voice was brittle and tight as she stepped forward, glaring daggers at her mother. “Well, you can’t have them. They’re mine. ”

     

                 “They are traitors to do with as I see fit. They should be grateful I am merciful enough to let them serve my meals and stoke the fire instead of removing their heads.”

     

                Ignoring them, Lena turned her heads to her attendants, who had been loyal to her since their departure from the Unseelie Court, keeping her safe and tending to her even before then. It wouldn’t have bothered her so much if they had been helping anyone else, it only bothered her because it was Lillian. Staring at her mother for a long moment, gaze flinty and unwavering, Lena turned to look at the two women caught in between it all, her voice softening as she jerked her chin up slightly.

     

                “Go to my fire - I will join you shortly.”

     

                Hesitating briefly, Andrea took Sam’s hand and pulled her into motion, the latter still and tense before she stumbled and seemed to wake. Expression clouding slightly, Lena turned her attention back to Lillian, cocking her head to the side before she jerked her chin towards the thinner outskirts of the thicket.

     

                “If I may have a word?”

     

                Her mother had somehow commandeered a small stool to sit on and rose to her feet with a look of amusement on her face. Intimidatingly tall and a little unnerving, something cold and dangerous about her that always put Lena on edge, she elegantly drifted away from the warmth of the fire, putting some distance between herself and her people for some semblance of privacy. Skirting around the group of Unseelie, ignoring the deferential murmurs of acknowledgement, Lena stalked after her mother.

     

                “What are you doing?” she hissed, rounding a tree trunk and scowling.

     

                Rain pattered down through the sparse canopy, dotting her cheeks as she gave her mother a surly look from beneath heavily furrowed brows. Lips twitching with a smile, Lillian arched an eyebrow.

     

                “You wanted to speak with me?”

     

                “You know what I mean.”

     

                “I am unsure what it is I have done to upset you. We have barely spoken in all our time together.”

     

                “You’re up to something,” Lena firmly insisted. “I can’t figure it out but you’re up to something and you’re not dragging them into it.”

     

                “They are mine to-”

     

                “They are mine,” Lena snarled. 

     

                “Are you so assured of their loyalty? You, who does not belong, who inspires devotion in no one , whose purpose is nothing more than a bartering piece, who has failed miserably at that. Do you think they see any strength in you worth following?”

     

                “I’m not strong, I know that, but I’m kind. That goes a long way.”

     

                “You cannot rule with kindness,” Lillian scathingly replied.

     

                “Why do you assume I want to rule at all?”

     

                “You’re my heir-”

     

                “Not anymore.”

     

                “You are . Your brother is a traitor, he has gone rogue, abandoning all morality in favour of his power-hungry scheming. He is not worthy.”

     

                “And you think I am?” Lena scoffed with laughter.

     

                “No, but you are of use to me, and that is worth more than my son’s sword at my neck. If you wish to know what I am up to, it is as simple as that. You are of value to me because I am offered safe refuge through you, and now, we find ourselves behind the fighting. He will need to fight his way through the forces of the Seelie Court before he can depose me.”

     

                “So I’m supposed to believe your only motive is … what, self-preservation? I don’t buy it.”

     

                With a sharp smile, her mother lazily shrugged. “Self-preservation can get you far in life.”

     

                “Well, hopefully far away from me,” Lena snapped. “I don’t need your meddling. I don’t need you making a mess for me, for the people I care about.”

     

                “Your first mistake was caring for anyone. It is a weakness.”

     

                “It may be a weakness to you, but it is a strength to me. It’s how I’ve survived this long.”

     

                Suddenly looming over her, face pale and hard, eyes flat and her mouth a contemptuous sneer, Lillian grabbed Lena’s jaw, nails biting into her skin, and rammed her back into the trunk of a gnarled yew tree. “You have survived this long because of sheer dumb luck. The only reason your body is not at the bottom of a bog is because of your brother’s unfortunate timing with that little coup you staged.”

     

                “Get your hand off me,” Lena whispered, her voice deathly quiet as she looked at Lillian, unafraid. “Or you’ll find yourself without your remaining one.”

     

                Glancing down, Lillian caught the glimmer of unsheathed steel in the waning light of the trees. Lena swallowed as she stared at her mother, Lillian letting out a soft huff of laughter as she raised her eyes back to Lena’s. After a moment, she let go, cocking her head to the side as she studied her.

     

                “You’ve grown teeth. Perhaps a spine.”

     

                She said it approvingly, appraising her daughter with a smirk on her lips. Scoffing, Lena angrily sheathed her dagger and fixed Lillian with a harsh stare. “Stay away from me.”

     

                Brushing past her, Lena took large strides as she swiftly put some distance between them. She could feel Lillian’s piercing gaze drilling into her back and chafing beneath it, although she refused to turn around, making a beeline for the fire, where her wife was sitting up straight, sword next to her hand, waiting for any sign of trouble. Sam and Andrea were there too, sitting with Kelly, J’onn and M’gann. Reclaiming her spot, pulling her cloak tightly around herself, Lena glanced at the two women, a sullen look on her face.

     

                “Stay away from her.”

     

                Nodding, Andrea stroked a hand over her lover’s hair, a brooding look on her face as her eyes briefly met Lena’s. Unable to shake the uneasy feeling her guard instilled in her, Lena stared at Sam a moment longer before she picked up her cup and moved to fetch herself more tea. She was quiet and contemplative for the remainder of the night, eating the thin stew they cooked over the fire, sharing the bread that was still thankfully fresh from that morning, and eager for bed as they all settled down, drawing lots for sentry duty. Stretched out beside her wife beneath the canvas shelter, listening to the gentle thud of rain, Lena breathed in the faint tang of salt clinging to Kara’s hair and skin as she pressed up as close to her, sharing in her warmth as she drifted off to sleep.

     

                Waking the next morning to the sharp pinch of the cold, bundled beneath a blanket and a cloak as she breathed in the smell of damp earth and fresh rain, Lena pushed herself up and rubbed the sleep from her eyes. There was a hum of activity in the camp, everyone rousing one by one, building fires back up, starting on breakfast, pouring oats into pots of water and brewing tea. Lena had been spared sentry duty and only Kara and J’onn were awake from their group, so Lena joined them at the fire and took over tending to the porridge, stirring it slowly as she stifled a yawn, adding in dried fruits and nuts, accepting a cup of tea from J’onn and returning her wife’s sleepy smile.

     

                They were off soon enough, resaddling the horses, breaking down camp as they put out the fires and repacked their shelters and bedrolls, waterskins full for the day ahead. Sore but relishing the activity, Lena rode alongside her wife, both of them resuming their conversation of the day before, pointing out herbs, listing uses, dangers, and defining features. Kara spoke of her childhood as well, recounting hunts in these parts with her parents, trips along this route with Alex, Kelly and James often accompanying them, drawing a picture of the surrounding land they didn’t pass through. 

     

                It was a wet day, the rain heavier than the day before, and they all rode with the hoods of their cloaks up, staving off the wet as much as possible. The horses plodded on at the steady pace they set, the ground becoming swollen with mud as the day passed by and the rain grew heavier. Birds swooped low and settled in the branches of oak and rowan trees that sprouted from the hills, wildflowers growing in clusters in shades of white and yellow, and the thin border of the forest approached with each mile. 

     

                It took them the remainder of that day to even reach the outskirts, the hazy patch of green finally within reach as distinguishable trees, ash and black elder, willow and oak growing tall across the horizon. Lena’s heart soared at the sight as they approached, dusk ushered in, the gloomy, wet day offering little light as they continued onwards through the last few miles, determined to make it to the forest before resting. Once they reached the fringes, they pushed onwards a little way longer, any lingering light non-existent as soon as they were beneath the canopy of the trees. 

     

                The crushed-moss fragrance mingling with the rain was heavenly as their horses picked their way through the trees, past thick trunks and snaking roots making the ground uneven. Lena wanted to drown in that smell, let it burrow into her pores, seeming to come alive as she straightened in her saddle, her green eyes bright with eagerness as soon as they passed the first sparse row of trees. Kara watched her closely, taking in the way her expression softened, how the tension bled out of her, the way she inhaled deeply, eyelashes fluttering, a faint smile curling her lips.

     

                Onwards they went, a mile further, darkness falling and the chill of night with it. Their breaths plumed before them and the Firefolk amongst them illuminated the way with palmfuls of flames, casting an orange glow over the forest. It was quiet, everything hushed beneath the prickling watchfulness of the trees, small creatures scurrying about through the soft carpet of leaves, pine needles and moss. The trees seemed to grow closer together the deeper they went, their trunks getting wider, the canopy higher as they reached forty, fifty feet. Lena knew they would get even taller once they were deep into the wilds, a hundred feet or more, dwarfing the Fae and everything within the forest. Almost bewitched by the peace that suffused her, Lena would gladly have wandered into the wildest, most untamed depths of the forest and gotten lost, never to be seen again. Mind muddled, intoxicated by the smell, the feeling of the forest, it almost felt like a drug.

     

                At a small stream trickling before them, they carefully picked their way across the lichen-covered ruins of a bridge, the horses choosing their steps carefully, jumping across the broken masonry, and the woods got thicker from then on, shadows so deep as to be impenetrable, even by the keen eyesight of the Fae. There seemed to be a specific destination in mind, and Lena was content to continue through the darkness, hunger gnawing at her stomach and her muscles tight and sore, so long as it was within the forest. Their destination didn’t become apparent to her until she found herself following right behind Kara, past large blocks of stone grown over with moss, like a velvet blanket carpeting the ground. Shortly, they were all dismounting, horses unsaddled and tended to, Lena taking to her tasks without a word as she wondered where they were, staring at the hollow wreck of what she assumed had once been a watch tower, now reclaimed by the forest as young trees sprung up inside the hollow walls, moss and ivy growing over everything, roots climbing through walls.

     

                Lena was glad to see the ruin, the idea of walls - albeit, crumbling ones - a promise of some protection, given their exposure to the elements and any danger nearby, encouraging. As she finished helping with the horses, left to roam freely through the trees, nibbling on what vegetation they could find, she picked her way across the springy ground, her boots leaving faint indentations in the moss, and made her way through the old entrance. Fires had already been started, cookpots already bubbling with that evening’s stew. Wet and shivering, Lena made her way to the closest fire with familiar faces. 

     

                Kelly was sitting on a block of stone, and Lena sank down beside her, rubbing her hands together near the flames as she closed her eyes, breathing in the smell of damp stone and earth, trees and rain. It was heavenly. Gently bumping her with her shoulder, Kelly smiled as she glanced sideways at her. “You are glad.”

     

                “Beyond words,” Lena agreed, a smile creeping onto her face. 

     

                “She waits for you.”

     

                Confused for a moment, Lena looked at her sister-in-law and then followed her line of sight. Kara was near a hole in the back wall, half in shadow, staring at Lena with a patient expression on her face, which perked slightly as their eyes met across the distance. Jerking her head towards the hole, Kara vanished through it and Lena climbed to her feet, abandoning the warmth of the fire with only a tiny flicker of regret. Giving Kelly a crooked smile, she sighed softly.

     

                “Enjoy the warmth.”

     

                With a quiet laugh, Kelly raised her eyebrows and reached her hands out to bask in the heat of the fire as Lena pouted slightly, moving away from the warmth. Crossing the ruins, the smell of smoke, wet wool and horse was left behind, a biting wind caressing her as she stepped through the hole and glanced around, finding a soldier on sentry duty, a bow knocked but not drawn, Lena nodded to the woman, whose eyes slid off to Lena’s right. It seemed a pointed look, so she turned and followed that direction, almost blind in the complete darkness of the forest, her breathing and heartbeat loud to her ears as she strained her hearing. 

     

                Rounding the trunk of a large aspen, Lena found Kara leaning against a spruce, waiting for her. Straightening, Kara smiled and took a step towards her, feet silent on the damp leaves. Hugging her arms to herself, Lena had to clench her jaw to stop her teeth from chattering. They met each other halfway, Kara reaching out to pluck a few pine needles from Lena’s hair, her expression unreadable as their eyes met. 

     

                “I hope you have a good reason for stealing me away from the fire,” Lena lightly warned her.

     

                “And what is your definition of a good reason?”

     

                “Well, if you were planning to … I don’t know, ravish me against a tree, I’d say that was pretty good.”

     

                “Ravish you against a tree?” Kara snorted, a quick smile crossing her face. “You deserve more decorum than that. Or is that what you fantasised about when you thought of me while you-”

     

                “Shut up,” Lena scoffed, rolling her eyes.

     

                Stepping in closer, a few inches taller than her, making it seem a greater difference than that with her domineering presence, Kara had Lena backing up slowly but surely without even realising it, until her back hit a trunk. Reaching behind to steady herself, bark rough beneath her fingertips, Lena swallowed as Kara braced a hand beside her head, leaning in as she ducked her head. Her lips barely grazed the side of Lena’s neck, and Lena’s eyes screwed shut, lips parting as her breath hitched.

     

                “Oh, you did,” Kara gleefully murmured.

     

                “You’re getting a bit too big for your britches.”

     

                “Admit it.”

     

                Fixing her with a droll look, Lena arched an eyebrow. “No.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Arms encircling her, Kara let out a quiet laugh, almost nose to nose with her wife as she held her close. “Then tell me what it is that you think about.”

     

                “What, are you going to reenact them for me live?” Lena laughed.

     

                “Maybe I shall.”

     

                “Is that why you brought me out here?”

     

                “Who knows? I do consider myself a very giving lover.”

     

                Lena let out a quick laugh, reaching up to give Kara’s ribs a quick squeeze, right where she knew she was ticklish. “Oh, you’re funny.”

     

                Letting her go as she flashed her a quick grin, Kara took up her hand instead and towed her away from the tree, further through the trees. “As much as I would very much enjoy a quick tryst with you, I don’t care for a nearby audience; it is bothersome to try to remain quiet to evade discovery.”

     

                “Mm, the downside of sensitive hearing, I suppose.”

     

                “We may have all been cooped up together in Krypton, but my sister’s home has many dark corners we can enjoy together.” Her eyes glittered in the dark as she glanced sideways at Lena, her hand tightening a fraction around hers. “But my purpose for this evening was for you to enjoy the forest.”

     

                “Enjoy the forest?”

     

                “You have been away from it for so long. The ache of missing the trees has never been more evident than upon your return to the confines of the forest, so I thought you might enjoy the opportunity to walk amongst the trees alone - save for me, of course - and bask in the feeling, the smell, the sound, whatever it is you love most about the forest. A moment of privacy to feel all that you do, away from the others.”

     

                Looking at her, face pale in the dark, Lena’s expression tenderly softened as her heart twinged in her chest. “Thank you. That’s very thoughtful.”

     

                Nodding, Kara pulled her ahead of her and set Lena to take the lead, following silently a few steps behind her. Lena heard only the faintest rasp of her wife unsheathing her sword, always careful, always prepared for danger. She knew it was a precaution so Lena didn’t let it worry her, drifting through the old trunks of trees that pre-dated her by centuries, her hand brushing against rough bark, moss and lichen, itching to take her shoes off and nestle her feet into the earth. She closed her eyes, feeling it all, basking in the smell - that was what she loved the most - and occasionally stumbling over a root or slipping in a patch of wet leaves, pushing through bracken and thorns, her wife’s hands gentle as she reached out to steady her.

     

                Eventually, it was too cold and Lena was hungry and tired, turning to Kara and staring at her for a moment. Moving suddenly, she gripped her wife’s face in her hands and kissed her roughly, her gratitude and delight unspoken in the act, before she pulled back and gave her a small smile, taking her hand and starting back the way they’d come. Kara guided them back to the ruins of the old tower with not a single word between them, but Lena held her hand and felt the warm glow of contentment in her chest as they walked in peaceful silence.

     

                Back at the fire, they ate their portions and drank tea, everyone talking quietly amongst themselves as they unwound from a day of riding before they bedded down for the night. It was a little warmer within the confines of the crumbling walls, but the forest was colder in general, making for a bitter start the next morning, waking to frost and dew coating everything as they all stiffly roused themselves and went through the motions of the previous days.

     

                Within the hour, the morning still gloomy as the sun struggled to rise, made that much harder to reach the forest floor through the canopy, they were winding through the trees, huddling on horseback as the wind blew through the forest. Without sunlight to warm the ground, it was a bitterly cold morning, Lena alternating which hand was jammed into her armpit for warmth, a veil of mist lingering on the ground even as the day brightened, everything tinted green as the trees grew thicker. The deeper they went, the wilder the forest grew, mushrooms in great variety sprouting in patches, a few red deer startling as they passed by, owls swooping overhead as they made for their nests, low-hanging branches blocking the way, brambles and bracken making it a slog to get through the damp walls of it. 

     

                The ground slowly rose, and occasionally they came to rocky cliff faces or deep ravines as the ever-changing forest made for an interesting ride, skirting along the base of the cliffs until they reached a sloped incline the horses could scramble up, finding a slope down into a ravine so narrow they had to go in single file, stone and earth pressing up on either side, until they cut up the other side of it, miles to the south but apparently taking them along the best route. At the top of a particularly high knoll piercing the canopy of the trees, Lena got her first good glimpse of the area as she looked at the Court spread out around her, verdant patches of green and brown to the west, dark pools of lakes and silver threads of rivers cutting through the south-west. To the northeast, much of it was mountainous, low clouds obscuring what she assumed must be Eliza’s home, at least a fortnight away by the vague smudge they appeared to be. Deep ravines formed in between, rivers winding through, or so Kara explained to her, and as she glanced west, Lena could just make out a hint of the sea they’d left behind, secretly grateful for it even though she felt guilty for that at the longing on her wife’s face as she stared west a moment longer.

     

                It was slower going in the forest, the uneven ground making it more treacherous, and with the lowered visibility of anything lurking ahead - even with scouts ranging a mile before them - they were all relatively quiet. Enjoying the peaceful sounds of the forest, Lena didn’t mind it so much, occasionally meeting her wife’s eye, so much said between them without a word as Kara was as attentive as ever. They stopped only once near midday, sharing dried meat and the bread, which was now slightly stale, before they rode onwards again. As eager as she’d been to leave the coast behind, Lena quickly tired of the monotony of riding miles each day, becoming saddle sore, never seeming fully dry. She consoled herself with the fact that at least she wasn’t cold and wet on a boat this time.

     

                It was nearing twilight, day and night blurring together, when trouble found them. The forest was full of shadows, everything a deep green or brown in the waning, wintry light, when Alex, at the front of their party, held a hand up. There were too many of them for it to be sudden but they came to a halt, the horses whickering, a whisper running down the length of their party, the trees creaking and groaning and wind howling, wondering what it was that had caught the attention of Alex’s keen ears. 

     

                After a tense minute, Lena picked up on a snuffling sound, close enough to be audible but far enough for them to not know the source. With a few silent gestures, Alex nodded sharply and dismounted, Kara likewise dismounting. She looked up at Lena, whose expression sharpened with confused panic, and gave her knee a quick squeeze of reassurance before she padded after her sister. Kelly and Lucy followed after them, the four slipping through the trees without a sound. 

     

                Lena felt her stomach twist with unease, her mare sensing that as she shifted beneath her, and it was a tense few minutes as they all waited with bated breaths. A loud squeal cut the tense silence and everything erupted into chaos then, Lena sitting astride her horse as a flurry of activity filled the forest, soldiers urging their mounts forward, a few dismounting to go on foot, and others fanning out so it wasn’t so crowded and confusing. Lena had her strung bow slung across her chest with her arrows and briefly considered pulling it over her head and knocking an arrow but knew the close confines would make it hard to know what she was aiming at, and if it was something the best fighters in the Seelie Court couldn’t handle, she had little hope of managing it herself with a couple of arrows.

     

                But Kara had gone that way and it only took a moment for her to calculate the risk and grasp her reins in hand, about to urge her mare onwards when a hand grasped her reins and jerked them the opposite way. Sharply looking up, Lena scowled at Andrea, who tugged insistently, her blue eyes wide with worry.

     

                “Come away.”

     

                “But-”

     

                Lena blinked, a flicker of unease crossing her face as she turned her head back towards the sounds of shouting and squealing, splintering wood and the panicked whinny of frightened horses. She winced as she caught sight of someone in armour going flying through the air a dozen feet in front of them, knocked through the air by the unseen danger. The thick trunks obscured her line of sight and she had no clue what happened to the soldier, Andrea slapping Lena’s mare on the rump to get her moving.

     

                “It’s a boar.”

     

                Her attendants shout followed after Lena, who glanced sharply over her shoulder, panic on her face. They were dangerous enough at a normal size and she feared for her wife, unsure of how big this one was. Within the forest, one could never be sure whether they were encountering a normal-sized creature or something that had been twisted into a monstrously huge beast, half-reclaimed by the forest already. The sound of splintering wood and a loud shout of pain made Lena jerk her reins, heart thundering in her chest as she couldn’t help but hear Kara in the sound. It could’ve been anyone, but she couldn’t shake the thought that it was her wife, mauled by a huge tusk, trampled beneath large cloven hooves. 

     

                Andrea cursed her as she drew up short, grabbing her reins again to keep them moving. Lena was out of the saddle, landing awkwardly, twisting her ankle as she sucked in a hiss of pain, hobbling onwards as she got her feet beneath her and moved on foot, running hard through the brush as she backtracked. She was so intent on the roars of anger and clamouring voices that she didn’t hear anyone else approaching until she barrelled straight into someone. Biting her tongue as they fell down in a tangle, Lena groaned as she cupped her bruised elbow, rolling onto her back as she blinked back black spots. 

     

                “You imbecile,” her mother hissed, hurriedly on her feet again, her hunters grasping an arm each as they assisted.

     

                Casting her a dismissive look, Lena shouldered through them, dimly aware that Sam was with them as well, and barely got a few feet away from them before her eyes widened. Ahead of her, the colossal moss-covered hide of the boar was visible as she stared at the side of it, hooves gouging deep furrows in the earth as it trampled everything, soldiers visible through the brush as they lobbed spears and arrows into its side. Mushrooms and lichen speckled its bristled hide and she breathed in the dank smell of rot, black blood splattering the trees and the earth. As Lena paused, tense and transfixed by the unnatural sight of it, the thing surely weighing two hundred tons, thirty feet tall and solid, she watched it swipe with its tusks, flinging aside two of their party, gouging a deep gash in the trunk of a spruce tree before she found herself staring at its face. Little black eyes shone above its wet snout and Lena felt her stomach drop.

     

                Turning, she bolted as quickly as she could, her ankle paining her a little but forgotten about as adrenaline shot through her, heart pounding in her ears. Her mother was there and Lena caught a glimpse of Sam but lost track of the others, unsure of where Andrea was too as she weaved through the trees, hearing branches snap as the ground trembled underfoot. She would have gone right over the edge of the wide gorge if she hadn’t noticed the lack of trees ahead, skidding to a halt as rock plunged away to nothing, the roar of water a hundred feet below. Arms windmilling for a moment, she stepped back, turning as she heard the boar barrel towards them.

     

                Purity and Pestilence were there then, fighting as the smell of burning flesh filled Lena’s nose, the ground violently trembling as Lena felt her heart in her throat. She looked for Kara, knowing she must be nearby, knowing that she would come, wishing for the comfort of her presence, Lena watched the others fight, knowing her arrows were useless here, and that her dagger was less than useless, unless she planned on scaling its bristly back and plunging it through an eye, and even then, she doubted the best of them could manage that feat. Penned in with her back to the water, her mother and Sam alongside her, biding their time to escape and circle back around, Lena watched as an alder tree was felled, as someone’s leg was trampled as they let out a scream of pain. 

     

                The weight of the boar too close to the edge was an unaccounted-for danger that no one even considered, and perhaps if the boar hadn’t been their main concern, at the very least Lillian should have felt the fractures in the ground beneath their feet. Lena could be afforded some grace with that, considering her fledgling abilities, and as she watched the Fae corral the boar away from the edge, they might have assumed they were safe then, but as the boar charged back the opposite way, the edge of the cliff finally gave way.

     

                With everyone herding the boar away, it was only the three of them who knew what happened next. As the ground gave way beneath her feet, Lena barely had time to let out a surprised cry before she was dropping, rock sheeting away from the face of the gorge. Her mother fell beside her, her one hand scrabbling for purchase on the rock as she managed to find a handhold on a piece of rock she moulded at her will. Lena was not so fortunate, but then a tight grasp encircled her wrist, and Lena found herself staring up at Sam, who had her other hand around her mother’s wrist, holding a woman in each as her hazel eyes widened with panic. She was not so strong that she could haul them both up singlehandedly, and Lena watched her slip a little, half-dangling over the edge herself, tendons taut in her neck as she clenched her teeth, trying to bear their weight.

     

                “Sam,” Lena gasped, her free hand scrabbling for purchase as her feet kicked helplessly at air.

     

                “Reign,” Lillian firmly commanded her attention.

     

                “Sam,” Lena whispered, her face pale in the fading light as she drew in shallow breaths, her skin prickling with dread as she dangled a hundred feet above the surface of the writhing river below. 

     

                “Reign,” Lillian snapped, her pitch rising as panic filled her now, standing on a little ledge she’d made for herself whilst leaving her daughter to dangle over empty air. She only had the one hand though and Sam’s grasp slipped slightly on the stump of Lillian’s right hand. “Remember your oaths. You are sworn to me. Let her go.”

     

                Panic knifed through Lena as her head whipped around to look at her mother, aghast with disbelief. But then she really shouldn’t have been; her mother had warned as recently as two nights before that she would do whatever she had to out of self-preservation. Still, it shocked Lena then to hear her so callously instruct her hunter to drop Lena straight into the river below, and Lena’s expression took on a desperate edge, her throat tightening around her pleas as they came out a rasping gasp.

     

                “Sam, please. Please don’t.”

     

                “Let her go.”

     

                “Please,” Lena whispered a final time, watching Sam’s expression harden into that blank void that had unnerved Lena for weeks now. 

     

                And with that final plea, her guard’s grip went slack and Lena plummeted into the gorge, down to the ribbon of violent water rushing along below.

     

     

                Black blood sheeted down Kara’s forearms as she thrust her trident up through the boar’s heart, teeth bared in a snarl as she fought against the strength of the beast, her feet gouging furrows in the earth as momentum pushed her backwards. With dying squeals, it collapsed heavily, two hundred tonnes shaking the earth as Kara swiftly jerked her trident out of the wound and staggered back, the boar’s snout almost grazing the front of her leather jerkin, its final breath warm against her skin. Standing between its monstrous tusks, curving on either side of her, Kara drew in deep breaths, flicking blood off her fingers as relief flooded through their party.

     

                They were scattered throughout the trees, soldiers trying to tend to their fellow warrior who had been gouged through the stomach, steel rent with ease by the massive tusks, while Alex struggled to catch her breath where she’d been knocked into a tree, looking a little pale as she bled from a head wound, but otherwise fine as her wife crouched at her side. Many of them were bruised and bleeding from superficial wounds as Kara turned in a slow circle, a stern look on her face as she took stock of everyone, eyes sliding past faces as she searched for one in particular. 

     

                As the chaos settled, splintered trees heaved out of the way, an Unseelie with a broken leg hefted to her feet by friends, soldiers retrieving arrows from the hide of the boar and from the dirt surrounding it, James soothing horses as Lucy whistled for some that had strayed away, Kara struggled to find Lena. Only two of their party had perished as far as Kara could tell - the warrior who had been gouged through the stomach, a soldier sliding the man’s eyes closed with bloody fingertips, and an Unseelie who had been stomped into the dirt - but as she looked for her wife, Kara felt the keen cut of worry when she couldn’t find her.

     

                “Lena?” she called out, her voice loud as she moved away from the boar, stepping over splintered bark and snaking roots. 

     

                There was no response and panic flared up as Kara moved further away from the dead boar, her trident limply held in her grasp as her blue eyes darted around, wild with fear as she felt her stomach swoop with unease. Turning, trampling earth as she moved the other way, towards the rear of the fallen beast, she tried to remember the last time she’d seen her wife. She looked for her, always, her eyes never seeming to stray too far from her wife, and she was sure she’d seen her backing away from the boar near the edge of the gorge. 

     

                “Lena!” she shouted, her voice cutting through the hum of voices, sharp in the air, fear filling her chest now, a heaviness there as she drew in shallow, ragged breaths, her frantic searching taking on a desperate edge. 

     

                “She’s not here.”

     

                Pausing momentarily, Kara’s head whipped around to face the Queen and she stormed towards her, face white, blue eyes stormy as her brows furrowed together, bewildered and uneasy. Lillian was inches taller than her but Kara struck an intimidating figure as she cut across the distance separating them, her face taut and jaw clenched.

     

                “What do you mean?”

     

                “It is as I say, she is not here. This beast was set upon us. We were backed to the gorge; the weight of the boar must have weakened the edge. The ground gave way. She fell.”

     

                “She … fell?” Kara hollowly echoed.

     

                “Yes, she fell.”

     

                Anger flashed across her face, eyes bright and cheeks reddening as she tightened her grip on her trident. “I don’t believe you. No, she- that is a lie.”

     

                “I speak truthfully. My hunter was with us, were you not, Reign? Tell the Lady Kara what happened to my daughter.”

     

                Shoulders tense and a length of steel in her grasp, hazel eyes hard, Sam stood rigidly to Lillian’s right and Kara gave her a pleading look, a heaviness in her chest as she silently begged her to reveal it all for a lie. “Sam?”

     

                Blinking slowly, her eyes meeting Kara’s, Sam seemed confused for a moment, reaching up to touch her brow as she frowned. “I- forgive me.”

     

                “Is it true?” Kara demanded, her voice wavering.

     

                “Yes, she fell.”

     

                A sharp breath was expelled from Kara’s lungs, her eyes stinging as cold dread suffused her. Tossing her trident aside into the bracken, she ran towards the edge of the gorge, evidence of the spoken truth visible in the crumbled edge of the cliff, rock and dirt broken free. Below, a hundred feet down, the swift-moving river ran west out to sea, and Kara’s vision blurred as she stared into the water, knowing her wife couldn’t swim. 

     

                Reaching for the buckle of her sword belt, Kara fumbled to undo it and felt her anger flare white-hot as someone grabbed her arm. Turning, brimming with too many emotions to control herself, she grabbed them by their leather jerkin and dragged them in close. She was not a particularly threatening person, too gentle and kind to inspire fear, but she was not herself then, seeing surprise blossom in her sister’s eyes as she held her by the front of her jerkin. 

     

                “You cannot,” Alex softly told her, gripping her arm tightly.

     

                Tossing her sword aside, Kara swallowed past the painful tightness in her throat. “You will not stop me.”

     

                “I will.” 

     

                “She cannot swim,” Kara said, her voice breaking.

     

                “I know, which is why you cannot go after her now. She has been gone too long; you should not find her in such a state, to be alone in the river with her-”

     

                Alex cut off, ducking her head. Feeling tears on her cheeks, Kara let go of her sister and reached up to touch them, surprised by their presence. She knew what her sister wouldn’t say, that Kara would be alone in the river with her body once she found her, a hundred feet down from land, unable to do anything but let the river take them to the sea.

     

                “I can’t leave her-”
