                “No, I would not ask you to do that. We are three days from Guardian; we will go back-”

     

                Tearing her arm free from her sister’s grasp, Kara let out a huff of anguished disbelief, her voice sharp with outrage as she cut Alex off. “I will not go back to find her body without looking for her.”

     

                “Sister-”

     

                Casting Alex a wounded look, Kara stepped towards the edge. “She is mine to protect; I will not abandon her.”

     

                Without another word, Kara stepped over the edge and dropped like a stone, air rushing about her and the water glimmering below. Feet first, arms at her sides, Kara clenched her teeth and beckoned to the water, the river rising to meet her before she slammed into it. She couldn’t think of what it must have felt like for Lena to slam into it, filled with the fear of drowning. As she sank deeper into the river, Kara wondered if she had been knocked unconscious, trying to see through the murky water as silt was stirred up by the disturbance of her arrival, trying to spot a pale body with dark hair. She tried not to think about her being dead as she swam deeper, letting the current take her.

     

                In the end, she searched for more than an hour, slowing the current, feeling the water around her for anything large disrupting the flow, anything out of place or abnormal in the natural order of the river. She would have stayed down there longer, swimming further away, but the sun had been setting when the attack had happened, and what little light hit the bottom of the gorge had quickly waned, darkness making it hard to see her own hands as she swam through the water, let alone anything else. Fear that she’d already passed her by made Kara turn back, fighting her way upstream as she pushed her senses to the limit, ears strained for the faintest echo of a heartbeat in the water, even though she knew it would have been impossible for anyone to be alive underwater without air for so long. 

     

                Reaching the point where she’d entered the water, the sky pitch black overhead but the sound of voices audible above the trickling water, Kara made her way over to the cliff face and used the water to push herself up to where she could find a handhold. Dragging herself up, using crevices and bumps as finger and toe holds, she reached the lip and scrabbled for purchase, dirt and loose stones beneath her fingertips before a hand grabbed her wrist and she was hoisted the rest of the way up. Soaking wet and empty-handed, Kara sagged as she knelt in the dirt, her blonde hair hanging in wet strands around her bowed head as she let out a breathless sob.

     

                “She may yet live,” Alex reassured her as she knelt before her sister, a hand on her shoulder for comfort. “She is intelligent and resourceful and has survived this long in a wild place. If we follow the gorge, we may yet find her along it.”

     

                “It is wishful thinking,” James sighed as he stood nearby, “and too dangerous to risk us all when we are so exposed. We attract unwanted attention, as is. Delays will only further encourage it.”

     

                “Then leave,” Kara curtly replied, raising her head and giving him a flat look.

     

                She pushed herself to her feet, bristling with anger, her emotions so raw. Waving a hand dismissively, she stooped to fetch her discarded sword and buckled the belt back on before flicking her fingers to draw the water out of her clothes, droplets splattering the ground as she stormed towards her horse. She scooped up her trident along the way, coated in dried black blood, and grabbed the pommel of her saddle before hoisting herself up. With a sullen look on her face, eyes glittering in the dark of the campfires that had sprung up in her absence at the makeshift camp, she cast a dismissive look around the gathered Fae.

     

                “You may depart with your soldiers and anyone else who wishes to go forth. But I will not abandon my wife. I have said the oaths, and they hold until I have confirmation that she is my wife no more. I will not settle for any proof other than her body in my arms.”

    Chapter 34

                Lena woke to the violence of cold water, her cheek pressed against the rough surface of stone as her lashes fluttered, the sound of rain pattering on rock rousing her a little more. She felt like she couldn’t move, shivering and limp, everything below the waist oddly numb as the churning river washed over her back. After a moment of dazed confusion, she pushed herself up, water running into her eyes and down her neck as she shifted on the flat rock jutting out over the rapids cascading away before her.

     

                Sitting up, managing to pull her legs up out of the water, huddling on the rock, she was a sorry sight. Soaked through, shockingly pale and battered, she scrambled to remember what had happened. She knew she’d fallen, or rather been dropped , but it had all happened so quickly. She’d dropped like a stone, a hundred feet down, hands clawing at thin air as stone jutted out of the cliff, answering her desperate terror but not fast enough for her to catch a handhold, and she’d hit the water hard. It was a long way down and her body felt bruised and battered as she took stock of things, but nothing felt broken. Or she was just too numb and cold to feel it just then.

     

                She’d hit the surface so hard that she’d blacked out for a moment, surfacing in the gloom as she splashed about, floundering. Lena couldn’t swim, could just about manage to claw at the water, frantically kicking her feet as she tipped her head back, water getting in her mouth as she drew in frantic breaths. It was so cold, the water seeping through her clothes, her cloak growing heavy as it weighed her down. She’d been fortunate enough to leave her sword buckled to her saddle while riding, or else that would’ve been another anchor dragging her down. As it was, furiously trying to keep her head above the water, she clawed for the broach fastening her cloak shut, tearing it free, dragging the cloak out from beneath her bow and quiver, still strapped to her back. 

     

                There had been nothing she could do about that whilst trying her hardest not to drown, water filling the quiver, the swift current dragging her away faster than she could try to tread water. She should’ve been counting her blessings that she was able to keep her head up, drawing in frantic lungfuls of air, the cold numbing as she quickly learnt to stop fighting the current. The only people who knew she was down there weren’t coming to save her, and Lena knew she could only fight to live for so long before wearing herself out. Resigning herself to her fate, too scared to even cry, she managed to get onto her back, the way she’d watched Kara float, trying to stop her body from sinking as she craned her neck up.

     

                It was cold and dark, what little sunlight hit the bottom of the gorge fading quickly, and Lena couldn’t see much, save for the dark rock closing in on either side. It was forty feet wide, the river flowing from someplace between two summits of the distant mountains, clear and frigid, babbling along rapidly with the smell of moss and wet rock filling her senses. So tired, unable to feel much of her body, vision furring at the edges as her mind reeled, her vertigo felt even though she couldn’t make out any shapes. Her mind started to drift in and out, mouthfuls of water coughed and sputtered back out as she jolted herself awake before unconsciousness could fully claim her. 

     

                She’d lost track of it all, her mind narrowing to the focus of breathing, her breaths coming hard, throat raw and aching, no sense of her fingers or toes or limbs as she drifted along, towed like a piece of driftwood. If anything capable of bearing her weight, offering a liferaft, swept by, Lena was oblivious to it, so cold that her lips turned a faint shade of blue, teeth chattering. With her Fae constitution, she had to wonder whether hypothermia was a problem. Still, there was little she could do about it, eyelids growing heavy, neck aching from the effort of keeping her face above the waterline.

     

                The last thing she remembered was the rapids, large rocks breaking through the water, churning the river an angry white as it tumbled down the staggered tiers. She hit the first rock hard, the breath expelled from her lungs as she smashed her legs into it, flung around and then went under as she was helplessly dragged down the rapids. Surfacing in a spray of water, arms wildly paddling, she swallowed a mouthful of water and choked it back up as she tried to figure out what was going on. The next rock hit her in the left shoulder, a dull throb of pain announcing itself as she was turned again, going backwards now, trying to realign herself in that starfish position, feet-first.  Lena didn’t know how many rocks she'd hit, disoriented and helpless, like a ragdoll amidst the current. The last one she remembered took her in the face, a blinding pain as everything dimmed. Now, crouched on a jutting rock, the remainder of the rapids cascading away from her, Lena could taste the coppery tang of blood at the back of her throat, which was raw as she drew in heaving breaths, her heart pounding unevenly.

     

                Her hair was plastered to her pallid cheeks and she looked around through a grey pre-dawn light, the visibility low as a layer of swirling mist hovered above the surface of the water, filling the gorge. She felt utterly alone amidst the seething water, unable to discern what lay ahead or behind, unsure what had happened or where she was, how many miles downriver she’d been swept. What was obvious to her then was she couldn’t stay there, needed to get up. She’d been tossed to the right side of the gorge, and with her muddled thoughts and the shock to her system, she wasn’t thinking with enough clarity to realise that she was on the wrong side. All that mattered to Lena was getting as far from the water as possible, her panic threatening to overwhelm her as she staggered to her feet, badly bruised, shaken and breathless. She was still able to move everything, hunched over as she hugged her arms to herself, rain sluicing down her face. The wind wasn’t so bad down there though, the high sides of the gorge protecting her from the worst. As she looked up, dread filled Lena as she took in a hundred feet of rock face that she needed to find a way up.

     

                Sinking back down to a crouch, Lena crawled to the edge of the rock, ten feet from the edge of the gorge, and stared at the part of the cliff that jutted out, a few smaller rocks creating the ledge of the rapids, barely big enough for her to stand on. Lena knew she had little chance of that, the stone slick enough for her to lose her footing and smash her head open on the rocks below as the water took her, and the best she could hope for was attempting to bridge the gap between each one and hold on with her hands. It was a daunting prospect though, and she sat for a while, a vacant look on her face as her body shook, eyes wide and glazed. Blood darkened her hairline and her cheek was bruised and scraped, a pinched look of worry on her face as she swallowed thickly. It was almost half an hour before she could convince herself to move, so convinced that Kara would find her and spare her the effort of rescuing herself. Eventually, she talked herself into doubtful thoughts of her wife leaving her behind, hearing about what had happened and knowing Lena couldn’t swim, leaving her for dead. She wondered if she’d mourn her.

     

                After feeling sorry for herself, Lena knew that she would be dead if she didn’t take action. Talking herself back into the conviction that her wife wouldn’t abandon her, that she would have the truth of the matter and perhaps rid them of Lillian’s presence for good as a result of that. Drawing in a few quick breaths, feeling a little unsteady, she slid to the side of the rock and eased her legs in, the water so cold it stung, keeping a tight grasp on the rock as she felt the rock beneath her feet and stretched her other arm out. It was shallow where she stood, the water up to her waist before it pitched over the edge of the ledge, but it was a powerful force trying to sweep her away, and Lena felt panic knife through her before her left hand grasped at the nearest rock, finding a hold.

     

                Crossing that ten feet to the side of the gorge felt like an eternity, going slowly but surely. She slipped on one of the rocks, leather splitting on a jagged edge, cutting her knee and scraping her palms. Choking on a sob, she felt her eyes sting with tears, frustrated, frightened and exhausted. No matter what she’d gone through before, she’d always had her wife there with her and Lena’s chest painfully ached as she longed for Kara’s presence, for her strong arms to pull her from the water. Reaching the wall, nestled in the corner of the jutting stone and the cliff face, Lena squeezed her eyes shut as she breathlessly sobbed, clinging to the stone with desperation. It wasn’t over yet though, water lapping at her heels and a hundred feet to scale, and she had to wait another ten minutes before she could steel herself to try. Drawing in deep breaths to calm herself, she studied the wall, palms pressed against the stone, muttering to herself as she tried to encourage the rock to obey her will, trying to feel the cracks, feel the substance of it beneath her hands. 

     

                As she pressed her fingers again, the stone seemed to shrink away, gouging a hole in the rough facade, and Lena’s heart raced in her chest as relief swept through her. Raising her arm, she tried again above her head, gouging another hole and trying to haul herself up. There was a little lip further up and Lena heaved with all of her strength, grateful for the months of sword fighting and archery that had built enough lean muscle to make it possible. It was still difficult though, feet scrabbling for purchase on the stone, little cracks sprouting weeds barely big enough to fit her fingertips. More than once, her hand or foot slipped and she dangled precariously, cleaving to the wall of the gorge. 

     

                Skinning her fingertips and palms, she pulled herself up with aching arms and shoulders, too afraid to look down at the dizzying drop back into the river. If she fell again, Lena was afraid she’d break herself on the rocks below, trying to keep it together, finding the threads of her courage to continue up and up, until the top was in sight, within reach. A cold sweat prickled her skin as she clambered the rest of the way up, desperate as she tried to gouge another handhold, the fragile grasp of her power flickering in and out, rain stinging her cheeks, the wind almost blowing her off.

     

                Clambering over the lip of the cliff, clawing fistfuls of grass and dirt as she dragged herself forward, Lena crawled a few feet from the edge before she shakily collapsed. Face pressed into the earth, the breath sawed in and out of her lungs, the taste of sweet sap, sharp pine and damp oak filling her senses as she lay in a sodden heap. Her clothes were completely soaked, her body battered and bleeding from a few cuts, and she was utterly alone, unsure how far downstream she was from the others. At that point, she thought she was on the right side of the gorge, her mind reeling from the ordeal, darkness creeping in on the edges until she was drifting, drifting and gone.

     

                Splayed on the edge of the gorge, the quiet forest around her, water roaring far below, Lena passed out where she’d crawled to and didn’t move again for hours. Exposed and as vulnerable as she was, it was not the wisest choice, but she’d had little say in the matter, her adrenaline and resolve deserting her the moment she felt the slightest prick of safety, everything slamming into her at once as she blacked out and slept like the dead. Wolves could have been set upon her and she wouldn’t have even stirred, a wet heap on the ground as she slept half the day away, through the dawn and noon and into the afternoon.

     

                Eventually, she stirred again. Cold and stiff, Lena struggled to move as she woke, just as confused but a little less scared this time as she slowly sat up, joints aching, body sore and raw. Kneeling on damp leaves, she wiped mud from her face and looked around. Trees surrounded her, roots sprawling along the ground, twisted brush and thick brambles in between wide trunks, a few of the trees fallen and grown over with moss and lichen. Tufts of sedge grass, mosses and ferns offered a thick, green sight with trails cutting through the darkness, winding through the trunks. Pushing herself to her feet, Lena felt for her dagger at her waist and felt the damp fletching of four arrows. The bow was still strung but she knew it would be useless, the sinew string wet, but Lena didn’t bother fussing with it then, trying to unstring it to dry out the sinew. She wasn’t so good with a bow yet that it would be of much use within the confines of the forest anyway, so she unsheathed her dagger and held it in a scraped hand, brushing damp hair out of her face and setting off what she thought was east.

     

                Heading a little further north as well, a safe distance from the edge of the gorge, she focused on where she placed her feet, trying to be quiet, if not quick in her state, and walked. It wasn’t long before her damp boots chafed against her feet, and she considered taking them off but was already wet and cold and didn’t want to risk losing any toes, plunging onwards uncomplaining as blistered formed. Alone and lost, Lena was determined to keep putting one foot in front of the other, stepping over roots, walking over wet grass and leaves, through bracken and brambles, hunger gnawing at her stomach, although she didn’t give much thought to food yet.

     

                By twilight, she had no idea how many miles she’d covered, quite sure her boots were wet with blood, but one thing that was blatantly obvious to her was that she was heading the wrong way. She’d occasionally cut back through the forest to the edge of the gorge to ensure she was following it truly and the sight of the dim sunset to the west had struck her with defeated dismay. Letting out a pitiful sob, Lena wanted to curl up into a ball and never move again. She was on the wrong side. Looking across the forty-foot gap, she wasn’t sure how she’d ever get across that.

     

                “Fuck, fuck, fuck,” she frantically whispered to herself, grabbing fistfuls of dirt as she clenched her teeth, eyes swimming with tears.

     

                She was cold, damp and hungry, hadn’t had a drop of water all day, and was exhausted. Deciding not to think about it just then, she chose to find a place to make camp for the night instead. It seemed a more pressing matter, the day darkening to night around her, the forest no longer a welcoming place as the shadows lengthened and the quiet rustling of the leaves and little things moving through the trees putting her on edge.

     

                A few metres back from the edge of the gorge, Lena found a fungus-riddled oak with thick roots, the tree leaning slightly, old and ivy-covered. Where two roots forked at the base of the trunk was a small hollow big enough for a person to curl up and she foraged through the underbrush while the light lingered, collecting a small pile of damp wood and leaves, found a handful of oyster mushrooms sprouting from the bark of a rotting log of beech wood, the toppled tree slowly decomposing and hollowed out by time. She cut them free, checking to make sure she was correct in identifying them, poisoning herself the only way things could get any worse right then, and bundled them in her torn tunic. As she’d wandered, she’d found a mossy rock with a slight depression on the top, where water had nestled from the rain that day, and Lena stooped to press her mouth to the water, the green taste of it cool down her throat as she sipped as much as she could before continuing on her way, finding a handful of sorrel as well and picking the leaves.

     

                It wasn’t much, but it gave her something to fixate on, setting her mushrooms and leaves aside, prioritising a fire for warmth before she ate. In the darkening gloom, shadows lengthening quickly, Lena didn’t stop to consider the dangers of a fire, of attracting unwanted attention, knowing she’d freeze without it. At the very least, the high canopy would mask the smoke, and if anything was close enough to smell it or see the glow of the flames, at least she’d die warm. Still, it was an effort to get the fire started, cursing her misfortune of being one of the Earthfolk instead of Firefolk as she desperately wished for a handful of flames. It took minutes of trying before she struck her dagger against a found stone at just the right angle and force to get the damp kindling smoking. It took a few minutes longer still before the smoke caught to flames, and then a careful process of feeding leaves and twigs to it until the hungry flames grew, the thicker pieces of wood she’d gathered slowly catching. 

     

                Once she had a merry, albeit small, fire going, Lena huddled close to it, warming her frozen hands as her lips trembled. The temperature dropped quickly, as though it was still midwinter, and she could see her breath hanging in the air before her as she tried to get warm, wishing for her cloak to draw around herself. The thorny brambles had snagged her tunic, and it had already been torn from her climb up the side of the gorge, and Lena felt the wind keenly through the holes, skin rippling with goosebumps as she slowly built the fire up. Toasting her mushrooms over the flames, she chewed the sorrel leaves, perhaps one of the worst meals on the road she’d had to date, but the lemony taste not unpleasant at least, and then ate the mushrooms too before curling up in her hollow and hoping sleep came for her quickly.

     

     

                “Sister, we must stop,” Alex insisted as night fell again, their party of sixteen traipsing through the forest, as they had been since the night before. 

     

                As if she didn’t hear her, Kara continued onwards, leading them along her chosen path. She hadn’t so much as stopped to eat, her horse plodding onwards even when the others lagged behind to dismount, stretching their legs and muttering amongst themselves before following after her, mostly at Alex’s urging. She wouldn’t let Kara go on alone, and she wouldn’t leave the others behind, James and his soldiers continuing on without them as they’d turned back to search for Kara. There had been a brief argument about it but in the end, those that weren’t soldiers were made to backtrack. Their party consisted of Kara, her sister and Kelly, Lillian and her hunters, Sam and Andrea, J’onn and M’gann and a handful of Lillian’s remaining Unseelie cohort. Tensions were high and a lack of sleep or a proper meal wasn’t helping.

     

                “Kara.”

     

                “You may rest if you desire to,” Kara quietly replied, shadows beneath her eyes, a dour look on her pale face and tense set to her shoulders as she stared straight ahead. “My path lies before me, though.”

     

                Spurring her horse forward to ride beside her sister, Alex stared at her with grave worry etched onto her elfin face. “You know I will not let you go alone, but the others need rest. As do I, as do you. They will not go any further this night.”

     

                “Then I shall leave them behind.”

     

                “We cannot leave Unseelie loose in the Court,” Alex fiercely whispered, scorn darkening her face.

     

                “I care not what happens to them. I must find her.”

     

                Reaching over, Alex grabbed the reins of Kara’s buckskin mare, forcing them both to a halt. Giving her a rare look of anger, Kara’s expression was furrowed with resentment, a warning in her low murmur. “Let go.”

     

                “I cannot. I will not let you bring harm to yourself in pursuit of her. Forgive me, but I love you too much to allow it.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, a lump caught in her throat and a hollow pit in her stomach, Kara looked at her sister with such a bleak ache in her eyes that Alex’s expression softened with pity. “If you truly love me, you will let me go. I beg of you.”

     

                “You know I truly do, but I will not let you go further without rest. You are in no condition to help her as you are; we may miss vital clues if we are all tired to the bone. Sister, please, rest a little while.”

     

                Doubt flickered in Kara’s eyes at the thought of missed clues, that perhaps she’d missed some sign of Lena below. They hadn’t slept that night, riding through it and all through the day as well, and it would be two nights gone without sleep if they didn’t pause now. What mistakes could she make if she continued in such a fashion? Seeing her sister waver, Alex seized the opportunity to talk her into stopping, a soothing tone and reasonable bargaining feeding into Kara’s uncertainty.

     

                “We shall stop no more than a handful of hours. It will not even be true night before we will be on our way but we will all feel refreshed for it. Something hot in our bellies and a moment to close our eyes. Then we shall all continue onwards together; many eyes and ears will benefit you.”

     

                Hesitating a moment longer, Kara slowly nodded and immediately swung herself out of the saddle. There was a palpable ripple of relief through their party as everyone else started to dismount, eager for a brief reprieve as they went to their tasks. Kara didn’t though, she just stalked off into the trees to be alone, and Alex allowed her the privacy, knowing she wouldn’t go far and would return soon. 

     

                She went far enough to not be heard, her quiet sobs catching in her chest as she covered her mouth, hand pressed against the trunk of a yew tree as she hung her head. Tears wet her cheeks and Kara allowed herself to feel the guilt, the fear and worry, her grief, all of it quickly rising to the surface the moment she was away from prying eyes. Crying until she’d exhausted herself, eyes bloodshot and cheeks splotchy, she sank down to the gnarled roots of the yew tree and sat a while, catching her breath, reining her emotions back in as she convinced herself it would all be okay.

     

                “She’s alive,” she whispered to herself, closing her eyes as she breathed slowly, trying to still her heartbeat. “She’s alive, she’s alive.”

     

                And it had to be true because she could say it, although Kara knew better than that how there were many ways to find loopholes in Fae. She had seen no body, and had no proof that her wife was dead, so she could believe in her gut that she was alive, right up until the point she held the proof in her arms. She just wanted a little more time to believe the impossible, to still have Lena in her life, to not have lost her. 

     

                And then there was a part of her mind she didn’t want to acknowledge that was clinging to the thought of Lena being alive because she hadn’t killed her yet. She would never recognise her feelings, would never allow herself to feel the true depths of them. Even then, knowing Lena was not dead by her hand, she couldn’t even entertain the idea that she loved Lena so it couldn’t be true that she was dead from a long fall into the water, because that would have been admitting to feelings that Kara had turned a blind eye to, ignored and dismissed with the easy explanation of familial love, and that would mean acknowledging that she was going to lose her anyway.

     

                Curled up between the roots of the yew, Kara sat with her head in her hands until she couldn’t keep the restlessness at bay any longer. It had been some hours, alone with her grief, and she climbed to her feet and retraced her steps back to the horses and the scattered bedrolls of their party. Shaking her sister awake, Alex glowering as she woke slowly, Kara straightened. “I must go on.”

     

                In the saddle before Alex had managed to rouse the rest of them, Kara was already setting off at a brisk pace. She hadn’t slept a wink and looked like it, desperate and tired and miserable, hunched in the saddle as she urged her horse onwards, knowing the horses needed their rest too but too much of an emotional wreck to be thinking clearly.  As she rode on, the others scrambling to catch up with her, tears pricked her eyes and her throat closed up, and she might’ve cried some more if she’d had a bit of privacy and enough energy to do so. As spent as she was, Kara urged them onwards, wilting a little more with each passing mile, her mood so black that any attempt at reasoning with her earned a sharp response, her voice unrecognisable to her own ears.

     

                Alex was miserable watching her sister’s torment but there was little she could do as she rode behind her, all through the night and the following day, until night fell again. It was agonisingly slow, following the gorge so they could look for her, which wasn’t always easy, the horses struggling at times, forced to stick to a walking pace with the densely packed trees. Kara was intent on a third night without rest by the looks of things, stubbornly continuing onwards in the dim glow of fire that Sam and Andrea conjured to light the way, the flames small and wavering with their exhaustion. She would have continued on if she wasn’t so tired that she couldn’t keep her eyes open anymore, swaying precariously in her saddle until she slumped sideways and fell, hitting the forest floor out cold. Relief swept through Alex as she reined her horse in and dismounted, going to her sister’s side and looking up at Kelly.

     

                “We’ll make camp here.”

     

     

                Waking to the foggy darkness of early morning, the forest eerie as she looked at the shadows of the trunks in the grey light, shivering near the cold ashes of her fire. She considered building it back up again but she knew the best way to get warm would be to start moving. It was just a matter of where. Sitting on her haunches for a few minutes, arms wrapped around her knees as she huddled for warmth, Lena considered her options and decided on the one that made the most sense. If she continued west, backtracking on the opposite side of the gorge, even if there was no bridge for her to cross over, she would eventually reach the sea. As much as she hated the sea, it was a guide for her, because if she reached the sea, she’d be able to find the Guardian, and if she found her way back there, she’d have help, would be able to find a new horse and supplies, something warm to wear, and then follow after Kara herself, perhaps beg for an escort. 

     

                Fortified by her decision, seeing the sense in it and deeming it the wisest course, Lena was off. She walked for hours on end without rest, pausing only whenever she found water, sipping droplets of dew off leaves or depressions in the ground, the grit of mud in her mouth, hungry and cold. Pushing through bracken tinged in shades of brown, patches of moss in green and amber, and crooked trees in every direction, she followed the edge of the gorge as the forest undulated before her, forcing her to pick her path carefully or risk breaking an ankle. Her ankle was already quite tender from the way she’d jumped off horseback in search of Kara, but that didn’t stop her. Lena set herself a gruelling pace, determined now, alternating between jogging and walking, the cold air painful in her chest.

     

                Miles passed by in that fashion and eventually, she could taste the brine from the distant sea on the edge of the breeze. It was comforting in a way she’d never expected from the sea, boosting her morale slightly, and she carried onwards throughout the day, dagger in hand, rain starting up but leaving her relatively sheltered beneath the canopy of the trees, and she walked until it started to get dark, following the winding path of a stream that struck a westerly path and had not yet joined up with the gorge. She’d found it three miles back and drank deeply from it, the cold making her teeth hurt, and had stuck to its side ever since, in case it was her only source of water. 

     

                Eventually, she repeated last night’s routine, collecting firewood and looking for food. Her campfire was built at the edge of the stream and Lena spotted a few flashes of silver in the water as the fading light caught the scales of little graylings still as the water passed around them. Lena’s fishing experience was limited to that one time with Kara, and she had no hook or rod even if she’d been adept at it, but after a few minutes of thinking she found a slender but sturdy branch and used the dried sinew from her bow to tie her dagger to the tip of the branch. It was a shitty spear but it was better than nothing as she crept to the riverbank, mindful of her shadow on the surface of the water, and patiently bided her time, striking twice and missing and then managing to spear a grayling a little further down the stream. 

     

                Her relief and triumph outweighed the guilt of killing the fish as she lifted the spear from the water, blood running pink off the grey scales, and carried it to the fire. Undoing her dagger from the branch, she made quick work of gutting the fish, removing the innards and head and making a crooked spit to hold it over the fire. Her stomach growled as the smell of the cooking fish filled the air and she felt a flicker of pride at her resourcefulness as she warmed her hands and tried to plan for tomorrow. She didn’t know how far she was from the sea, only that it had taken them a whole day of relatively non-stop riding from the border of the forest to where the boar had attacked, while she was still within the confines of it after two days of walking.

     

                She was so wrapped up in her thoughts that she almost missed the faint, pitiful keening. Sensitive ears pricked by the sudden disturbance to the quiet, she straightened, tense and alert, and waited a few moments before she heard it again. It was coming from somewhere downstream and Lena frowned, wariness winding through her, mindful of anything found within the forest. It wasn’t quite the dark of deep night yet but there was no moonlight or stars to see by and Lena had nothing but her dagger to arm herself with. Still, it would be better for her to have the jump on anything harmful, so she picked herself up to her feet, dagger clutched tightly in her hand, and crept ahead as quietly as possible. 

     

                It was obvious to her it wasn’t a human sound as she crept along the side of the stream, hunched low as it got louder. It was more of a whine, an occasional yelp, and she was cautious as she ducked through the branches of a weeping willow, so close now that she could hear it, even if she couldn’t see it. Behind a thick oak tree, the roots higher than her waist where the water had slowly eroded the earth covering them, Lena was momentarily stumped as she peered through the sedges and reeds. Then she heard the whimper again, closer than she’d thought.

     

                Peering over the root she stood behind, Lena looked down at the little bundle of grey. It was a wolf cub, soaking wet and desperately clawing at the roots and soft mud, unable to haul itself out, given how high the roots were. Lena realised it must have fallen in, hind legs submerged in the stream, and a pang of pity struck her. Its dark eyes met hers and it let out a high-pitched snarl, unthreatening as it bared its teeth in warning. Glancing around, suddenly struck with a sense of panic that its mother might be around, that she could be contending with something much bigger than she was, Lena couldn’t hear anything moving. After a moment, she figured a she-wolf would’ve rescued her cub if she’d known it was stuck in the stream, and Lena deliberated very briefly about it before she clambered on top of the root. 

     

                Reaching down as the cub raised its hackles, a feral little thing, fur slightly matted, Lena deduced it had been abandoned. It didn’t occur to her to kill the thing, to skin it and cook the meat for tomorrow, and despite the warning growls, she didn’t think it much of a threat. That didn’t stop the wolf from biting her though, snapping quickly, razor-sharp teeth slicing into her forearm as she reached for it. Letting out a shout of pain, Lena jerked her arm back, a few droplets of blood spilling, turning into little flower petals before they struck the surface of the water. With a scowl on her face, Lena considered leaving it but she felt her anger soften when she considered how scared it must have been. Clawing at the tree roots, gouging shallow lines in the wood, it let out another whine and Lena sighed, quicker this time as she snatched it up by the scruff of its neck.

     

                It snarled and twisted in her grasp, blood dropping from Lena’s bite wound on her arm as she held it aloft, frowning at the cub. Lifting it over the root, she quickly set it on the ground and it shied away, muzzle pulling back over its sharp teeth. Mouth flattening to a grim line at the hot pain in her arm, Lena shooed the cub with the hand clutching her dagger, trying to frighten it off. It was pitiful and wet, shivering as it hissed at her, and she rolled her eyes and backtracked to her camp, leaving nature to run its course. 

     

                The fish was starting to char on one side and she hurriedly crossed over to it, turning the spit, and slumped at the side of the fire. It was dark now, truly dark, all traces of sunlight faded, and she put her arm closer to the fire to inspect the bite. It wasn’t very big but they were deep. Moving to the stream, she rinsed her arm in the water and then tore some cloth from the hem of her tunic to bind the wound. Returning to the fire, she removed the fish from the spit and gingerly held it on the stick as she waited for it to cool. Ravenous, she could barely wait that long, picking pieces of white flesh from the slender bones, until she’d picked it clean. With a mouthful of water from the stream and a few more logs piled onto the fire to keep it burning throughout the night, Lena curled up on the dirt and fell asleep almost instantly.

     

                It was dark when she woke, disturbed by something. Her dagger was in her grasp and the fire was still burning, momentarily blinding her as her eyes tried to adjust, the brightness making it hard to see through the darkness. At the quiet snuffling, she managed to pinpoint what it was that had woken her up; the wolf cub. It was nosing through the innards of the fish that she’d tossed aside, not even considering that it might attract predators, and she watched it bolt down the heart and back away with a snarl. Raking a hand through her hair, Lena sighed and reached for the bones of the fish, tossing it towards the wolf. She watched it for a few minutes, not moving a muscle, and it eventually inched towards the offering, low to the floor, wary and nervous, before snatching it up and dragging it away a few feet. It must have deemed her not much of a threat because it laid down on its belly and started to gnaw at the bones while Lena watched, wide awake now. It moved on to the head and the remaining organs once it had licked the bones clean, and Lena watched it scamper off once it was done.

     

                Alone at her fire, alert and restless, she decided she couldn’t stay there any longer. She wasn’t sure whether it was because she’d slept already and now had the energy to continue, or because she was worried about what else might be attracted to the smell of blood, but she picked out a thick piece of wood from her little pile and set it into the fire to catch. Wishing for some pine resin and not wanting to sacrifice any more of her clothes, she made do with her flaming piece of wood as a torch and set off through the forest. 

     

                Following the stream, it wasn’t long before she came upon the corpse of a wolf. It was bigger than a normal wolf, but not quite the monstrously huge beasts she’d encountered before, leaving scars on her stomach and thigh. She’d been unsure whether it was alive at first but a gust of wind brought the stink of rot towards her and Lena inched closer to observe, taking in the telltale signs that the forest was starting to twist it, not only with its increasing size but the little button mushrooms sprouting amidst moulding fur. The blood on the ground was black as well, and she thought it must have been the she-wolf of the little cub. Leaving it untouched, she continued on her way through the mist.

     

                Walking all through the night, Lena followed the stream to its end. It was just after dawn, the sky a dull grey, and she found herself standing at the top of a narrow waterfall as the stream tumbled over the side of the gorge to join the river below. Over the last two days, she’d noticed the gorge narrowing, perhaps twenty feet wide now, and the forest sloping downwards, making the drop seventy feet. Still too far for comfort, but she was starting to consider how she could bridge that gap and get to the right side. She hadn’t come across a bridge yet and was starting to doubt that she ever would, but the trees were tall, their branches reaching out over the water. 

     

                Not for the first time, she considered climbing one of them to get a good look at her surroundings, but she had the idea then that if she could find two trees fanning out over the gorge, reaching for each other, she could possibly cross that way. It was risky, would be a hundred and seventy-foot drop down to the water, undoubtedly fatal, but it didn’t seem quite so impossible as she stood at the top of the waterfall, looking up at the leaning branches of a white ash tree a sycamore. They were towering trees, and she judged them to be about a hundred feet tall but couldn’t be sure of that. It could have been more for all Lena knew. But as she judged it, she made a rough estimation that the gap between their two canopies, the longest branches reaching for each other, could only be a few feet. It seemed a paltry distance, something she could cross with her eyes closed, by the pure feel of the trees themselves. 

     

                She was starting to panic a little now. Starting her third day alone, hungry and cold, bruised all over with a nasty bite on her arm, foraging for herbs along the way to help with pain or to give her something to chew on, her feet blistered and the wolf cub the only company she’d come across. She’d hoped perhaps there were Fae living nearby who could’ve offered her help but if there were any dwellings in the area, she hadn’t come across signs of them, not even the faintest tang of smoke on the wind. Lonely and knowing she was at risk of exposure to infection, the elements, or wild animals, if she continued as she was, with no resources and very little clothing, fear crept in.

     

                It was a risk, stupid and reckless, but she was getting desperate and knew that she would save herself another week of walking to the sea if she could just cut across the gorge. Surely the way it had gradually narrowed was a good sign that it would be fairly simple to cross it. If she wasn’t so afraid of the water, she might have tried to leap the twenty feet, relying on her Fae strength and speed to give her that little extra boost. But even then, Lena wasn’t the most athletic person and she highly doubted she’d manage a distance like that, half-Fae or not. 

     

                Looking back up at the white ash, she easily mapped out the handholds and after a brief moment of trying to reason with herself, she was scaling the trunk of it. Dagger sheathed at her waist, bow and quiver across her chest, she relied on her scraped palms and blistered feet to haul herself up, leather boots abandoned for the sake of feeling the bark beneath the soles of her feet, offering better grip. Moving slowly, mindful of how high she was going, Lena was soon sweating from the effort of climbing so high, her arms and shoulders aching and her stomach dropping as the wind buffeted her. Passing lower limbs, she continued higher through the tree, until she was so high and the branches were starting to thin, still sturdy enough to bear her weight but blown about by the wind as it grew stronger so high up. She wasn’t sheltered from the elements up there and stinging hail pelted her hands and cheeks as she wrapped her arms around the branch she was on and sat for a few minutes.

     

                Her hands shook and she swayed on the branch as she mustered up the courage to continue. It would be perhaps more dangerous climbing down so she had to continue, not wanting to think about how she’d have to climb down on the other side. Glancing over her shoulder, Lena looked down the length of the branch, ten feet long and perhaps as thick as her thigh towards the end, before it really narrowed, slender twigs branching off it, and she gritted her teeth and slowly turned. Straddling the branch, she grasped the wood tightly and shuffled along it, each foot making the branch sag slightly as she moved closer to the end of it. The branch of the sycamore on the opposite bank was further away than she’d anticipated, perhaps six feet, and her stomach swooped at the thought of bridging that gap. She had to try though, getting her feet beneath her, using the next branch overhead to balance herself, her knees almost buckling out of fear. 

     

                Desperate, wishing for her wife, hell, even for her mother , if only to not be alone, Lena had to try. Knowing she needed as much momentum as possible, she backed up along the branch and then decided to just do it. If she failed, she wouldn’t have to worry about that for much longer and hoped her heart gave out before she hit the water. It it worked, well, she’d worry about that when she made it to the other side. Drawing in a deep breath, she loosely held onto the branch to keep her steady and took a few wobbly, blundering steps down the length of the branch underfoot and threw herself into thin air. The branch of the sycamore was just before her and she reached for it, clawing at thin air as she missed it and fell.

     

                A ragged sound of defeat escaped her as the wind whistled around her, and Lena felt faint as her heart raced in her chest, hands still clawing at nothing, until she watched a branch move. She was sure it moved, that it responded to her desperate attempt to will it so, dipped the slender twigs at the end of it towards her as she fell alongside the canopy of the sycamore. Her hands grasped a fistful of leaves and spindly twigs, snapping them off, but the branch bowed with her weight and changed the trajectory of Lena’s fall as she swung inwards , now beneath the canopy. She was still falling though, slamming into the side of a branch as wide as her torso, scrambling for purchase before falling again, dropping five feet and hitting her back on the next branch, the air expelled from her lungs as she felt white hot pain in her ribs, cracking two of them before she fell again. Twigs scratched her face and Lena felt like she was in a game of pinball, tossed around as she fell twenty feet through the branches of the sycamore, before she hit a branch and rolled off to land on one two feet below, finally stopping her fall as she was winded. 

     

                Seeing black for a minute, Lena breathed raggedly, drawing in shallow lungfuls of air as she tasted blood at the back of her throat. Slowly, she pushed herself up and looked around, blood trickling from her nose as she dabbed at it, taking in the sturdy branch she sat on, one of the forks of a wider branch joining the trunk of the tree. Letting out a hoarse laugh of disbelief, Lena looked over the side of the branch and saw another sixty feet of descent before she reached the ground, but that felt like nothing as she revelled in the fact that she’d crossed the gorge. Now, she just had to find her wife.

     

     

                Kara woke to the grey of dusk and slowly pushed herself up, confused as blankets pooled around her waist and she took in the sight of the large campfire and a dozen people crowded around it. For a brief moment, she thought she’d been dreaming but then it all slammed back into her as she staggered to her feet, white-faced and livid. At the fireside, Alex caught sight of her on her feet and quickly set aside a bowl of stew as she scrambled up and crossed over to her sister. 

     

                “What-”

     

                “You fell from your horse,” Alex hastily started to explain. “Exhaustion got the better of you, sister, we had to stop.”

     

                “How long have I been asleep?

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Alex softly sighed. “It was at dusk you fell; it is dusk again.”

     

                “A day?” Kara exclaimed. “We have wasted a whole day? Why didn’t you wake me?”

     

                “You have not eaten or had a sip of water in days. Nor had you so much as closed your eyes. If you had seen reason and allowed for brief rests along the way, we would not have had to delay so long.”

     

                “You blame me? I am only doing what I must.”

     

                “No, I do not blame you, but you are not being reasonable , Kara. I understand-”

     

                “No, this you do not understand,” Kara sharply interrupted her. “You all may stay here or go onwards to your home; I will go alone from here so I am not delayed any further.”

     

                She angrily stooped to snatch up her sword and glanced around for her horse. As she spotted the mare, tied alongside Lena’s, she felt her sister’s hand on her shoulder, holding her in place. Shrugging it off, Kara shot her a warning look and Alex’s answering stare was pointed as her mouth thinned.

     

                “You are not going alone. You will sit and eat and we will continue together once we have finished.”

     

                “You would have me delay even longer? She is out there alone. I must-”

     

                Mournful, Alex reached out and cupped her sister’s face in her hands, so much pity and pain in her eyes as her shoulders sagged. “Kara … Kara, I hope she is out there, I wish it more than anything that she is well, that she has somehow prevailed, but …”

     

                Alex couldn’t say it, couldn’t break the fragile thread of hope her sister so desperately clung to. Kara knew exactly what she was getting at though, her anger burning hot to mask her panic as she jerked her face out of her sister’s grasp and then shoved her away for good measure, eyes pricking with tears.

     

                “She’s not dead,” Kara shouted, cheeks flaming as she gave her sister a wounded look. “She’s not dead. She can’t be because I haven’t-”

     

                Quickly closing her mouth, Kara swallowed the remainder of her words, yesterday’s thoughts - or was it the day before? - surfacing and dismissed as she refused to entertain them. But Alex knew her well enough to draw her own assumptions, opening her mouth to respond but quickly closing it as she heard a sound.

     

                There was a snapping off in the trees to the east, as if a branch had been broken, loud enough to be heard over the sound of their conversation, and they all quickly fell silent. Drawing her hunting knives free from their sheathes, Alex glanced at Kelly, who was on her feet with her strung bow in hand, already reaching for an arrow. Kara quietly unsheathed her sword and Sam and M’gann likewise armed themselves, everyone else warily preparing for another fight as they stuck to the campfire, knowing any beasts in the forest would be deterred by the threat of fire. 

     

                Picking her way silently across the carpet of leaves, Kara followed after her sister as the five of them moved in the direction of the sound. She could hear movement still, the sound of something trying to remain quiet as it moved towards them. Hoping it was a rabbit or fox, something that would skirt by them and continue on its way without any fuss, Kara silently moved with the others as they padded through the forest, fanning out slightly before Alex raised a hand to halt them. It was closer now, the sound of scuffing leaves breaking the silence, and Kara tightened her grasp on her sword as she held it at the ready, the air fraught with tension as whatever it was approached from behind a tree.

     

                And then the air left Kara’s lungs, sword spilling from her hand to the forest floor as she took in the sight of her wife stepping around the trunk of the dogwood. Lena stepped around it in a wary crouch and Kara’s knees almost buckled beneath her as she sagged with relief, taking in the tunic, which was little more than a rag, torn and crusted with blood and dirt, her dark hair a tangle of snarls and leaves, her green eyes wide and frightened, her face smeared with dirt and blood and little cuts and bruises. In her hand, she held her dagger at the ready, and as she processed the sight before her, it tumbled from her limp hand and she staggered forward.

     

                Kara moved quicker, catching her in her strong embrace before Lena could take another step, a torn sob catching at the back of her throat as she buried her face into the side of Lena’s neck. She couldn’t even speak, so weak with relief that she clung to Lena to keep herself standing, her wife feeling the same as she clutched fistfuls of Kara’s cloak in a white-knuckled grasp, as if scared she would vanish if she let her go.

     

                “You’re alive, you’re alive,” Kara whispered, her voice breaking before she let out a frayed laugh. 

     

                Pulling back, she carefully touched Lena’s cheeks, eyes flitting over her face as she reassured herself that she was okay before she kissed her. Kara had never kissed her like that before, so much desperation to it, as if she craved her, needed Lena like air. She could taste the loamy forest on her lips, wild, green and sweet and so wholly Lena, the knot of tension in her chest loosening.

     

                Taken by surprise, Lena forgot to kiss her back, her fists going slack in the folds of Kara’s cloak as she blinked. When she pulled back a moment later, Kara seemed to remember herself, reining in her self-control as her guard shot back up, cheeks turning pink as she remembered their audience, but she couldn’t bring herself to care that much, her hands anxiously fluttering around Lena, taking in the blood, the way she put most of her weight on her left ankle, barefoot and filthy. She looked feral and beautiful and Kara could’ve wept at the sight of her, giving Lena a tender smile.

     

                As she smiled at her wife, cradling her face in her hand, Kara watched as Lena seemed to register what had happened and what was happening. She drew in a sharp breath and her green eyes filled with tears as she flung herself at Kara for another hug, her voice small and uneven against the side of her neck as she let herself be vulnerable in the safety of her wife’s arms as Kara held her tightly.

     

                “I’ve missed you.”

    Chapter 35

                Lena wrapped her arms around herself as Kara guided her along, an arm tightly around her waist and Lena’s bow slung over her shoulder. Weak with relief, Lena was so tired now that she was safe, didn’t think she had the energy to go one more step, her bare feet filthy and frozen. It wasn’t far to where the rest of them were camped though, a dozen of them standing around a fire, tensed for danger. 

     

                Surprise crossed their faces at the sight of Lena, the tension bleeding out of shoulders and arms as their grasp on weapons went slack. It was quiet, the crackling of the fire and the soft snort of the horses cutting through the wind, and Lena’s gaze locked onto her mother’s. If Lillian was surprised to see her, she didn’t show it, but Lena’s exhaustion melted away as Kara led her towards the fire to warm her up. Instead of sinking to the ground, Lena continued onwards, shoulders taut now, her strides purposeful as she rounded the fire.

     

                Real fury passed Lena’s face, her expression darkening as her fine-boned features went hard, and she made a bee-line for her mother. The slap was quick and hard, the Queen’s eyes growing wide with shocked anger as she bristled, staggering back with a hand to her cheek. Drawing herself up to her full height as her pale eyes sharpened, she looked at Lena as if she couldn’t quite believe what she’d done. Around her, the Unseelie reached for the hilts of their weapons, but before they could unsheath them, Kara was in front of Lena, her own sword halfway out of its scabbard in a warning.

     

                “I would think twice before drawing steel on my wife if I were you,” she softly hissed, baring her teeth slightly.

     

                A few of them fell back, hands falling from the hilts but their lithe bodies coiled tight, just waiting for the tension to boil over so they could draw their weapons in full. Only Purity and Pestilence didn’t back down, to either side of the Queen and a foot in front, their hands still on their weapons as they stood, hackles raised. With a quick movement, Kara slammed her sword back into its sheath and thrust two hands out, the Fae hunters suddenly turning rigid.

     

                Surprise crossed their faces, eyes going wide, mouths parting in silent pleas as they seemed to teeter for a moment before they slammed to their knees on the forest floor and then were tossed sideways by a flick of Kara’s wrists. Breathing heavily, they lay where they had gone limp, the strings of Kara’s control cutting them loose, while Lena stared daggers at her mother over Kara’s shoulder.

     

                “I would advise you to keep your hounds on a tighter leash, Your Majesty,” Kara curtly spoke, “or else you will need to find yourself new hunters. Now, I will know the meaning behind this.”

     

                Glancing over her shoulder, she raised her eyebrows at her wife and Lena’s anger faltered for a moment, wounded disbelief flooding through her as her shoulders slumped slightly. “She’s the reason I fell,” Lena told her, voice breaking slightly.

     

                Scoffing, Lillian rolled her eyes and clicked her tongue. “You are quick to cast blame.”

     

                Looking back at the Queen, Kara’s voice was deathly quiet. “Is it true?”

     

                “I did not push her.”

     

                “Do not talk in circles around me , Your Majesty,” Kara warned her. “You are a long way from home and I will gladly drag you back to your son in chains. Is it true? ”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Lillian laughed. “Am I to blame for not reacting fast enough to use my ability to form a ledge for my daughter to catch herself on? Things happened quickly; I barely saved myself.”

     

                Lena let out a huff of wry amusement, shaking her head. “You saved yourself at the expense of me.”

     

                “Perhaps I am unaware, but I do not recall making any oaths to sacrifice myself for you. Perhaps you should have spent more time learning how to hone your powers, and then you might have saved yourself, instead of relying upon others,” Lillian haughtily replied. “Why don’t you tell your wife who is really to blame?”

     

                Kara gave Lena a perplexed look, half-turned towards her but unwilling to put her back to the Queen, and Lena’s expression darkened. “There is only one to blame and you and I both know it is you. Do you deny it?”

     

                “She is tired,” Lillian said to Kara, a faint smile at the corners of her mouth. “You should see that she is cared for before she continues to make accusations that cross the line.”

     

                “Don’t look at her ,” Lena snapped.  “Look at me . I am the one speaking to you. You made yourself a ledge and let me dangle over the edge. Admit it.”

     

                “Fine, I admit to that much,” her mother conceded. “But I did not drop you. You did not fall at my hand.”

     

                Lillian’s eyes darted to something behind Lena and Lena hesitated before turning. Her gaze landed on Sam’s ashen face, hazel eyes filled with panic. It became obvious to Lena that nothing had been said about Sam’s involvement and she was torn for a moment. Her relationship with the hunter was confusing and conflicting; she could never call her a friend on account of her murdering Lena’s mother, but Sam had guarded her well, had protected her right up until her mother’s words had gotten through to that other part of her that was Unseelie, that was obligated to obey the Queen. Sam, Lena could trust a little - Reign, she couldn’t.

     

                Swallowing tightly as she glanced back at her mother, Lena felt frustration fill her as she faltered. Knowing she’d have to throw Sam to the wolves to thwart her mother, and reluctant to do that, knowing it had been some shift within Sam that had made her let go, wrestling with her binding oaths, Lena cast Lillian a disdainful look of dismissal and turned away from her.

     

                “You are truly without a heart,” Kara stiffly told Lillian before she followed after her wife.

     

                Walking away, away from the fire and the simmering pot of stew, Lena angrily rubbed at her eyes. Her anger dissipated and she felt even more exhausted than she had before, trying to put some distance between herself and Lillian as she chafed at the unfairness of it. She wished Kara would run her mother through with her sword without any further explanations, but Lena knew it would end badly to act so impulsively.

     

                Catching up to her, Kara snagged Lena’s arm and turned her. Eyebrows furrowed in a sullen look, Lena met her gaze before her eyes flitted away, a muscle twitching in her jaw. Face softening, Kara gave her a searching look as she reached up to tenderly brush the backs of her fingers over Lena’s cheek.

     

                “What are you hiding from me?”

     

                “I- it’s nothing,” Lena heavily sighed, her mouth flattening with a grimace. “She just- I don’t like her being here. I wish we could be rid of her.”

     

                Kara’s shoulders drooped slightly as she smiled softly. Taking her wife’s hand, she led her further away, around the wide trunk of an elm tree. “Would it please you if I took her head for you?”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched with a smile as her wife’s words echoed her previous thought, and she willingly sank onto a gnarled root as Kara guided her down. “If you did that, then I’d be Queen, and that would be a whole different kind of problem.”

     

                “It is proving more difficult than anticipated to keep you alive, so perhaps we should make you Queen and weather the violence out of that eventuality now. Although, likewise, it is proving just as hard to kill you.”

     

                Throat growing tight, Lena’s eyes smarted as Kara sank to a crouch before her, a tautness to her features as she studied her wife with an anxious edge as if Lena might pass out at any moment. “You turned back,” Lena stated, her face furrowing.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Didn’t you think I was- I was dead?”

     

                Hesitating, Kara’s voice was hoarse and wavering when she quietly replied, looking up at the canopy. Lena could see her quick pulse at her throat. “Yes,” Kara whispered, finally admitting it aloud. “Yes, I thought you’d drowned, but … I refused to believe it. I had to turn back, to make for the sea, for I would not have accepted it unless I held your body in my arms and saw it with my own two eyes.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured.

     

                “I searched for you. As soon as I couldn’t find you- when they said you- you fell, I jumped in after you. It grew dark so quickly, I couldn’t find you, couldn’t hear you over the water. I- forgive me, I should have found you. You should not have had to endure whatever it was that transpired. As it is, I’m confused how we could have passed you without my knowing. Will you tell me what befell you?”

     

                “Oh, um … well, I can’t swim, you know that, and it didn’t take me long to realise I would drown if I kept trying to fight the water, so I turned on my back. I’ve seen you float like that and it- it worked, but the river took me. I was hoping I’d find … I don’t know, a log, a rock - I did end up finding a rock, but it was at the rapids. Tossed me about like a ragdoll. I, uh, I think I hit my head. I was unconscious anyway, and I guess the water flung me onto a rock. When I woke up, I knew I had to get up to the top, and I was closest to the northern wall of the gorge - pretty stupid of me to not realise that before, but I … wasn’t thinking clearly. I was … scared. I managed to mould some of the rock, tried not to look down or think too much about it, but I climbed up to the top. Thank God for all archery and sword-fighting, huh? I think I would’ve been too weak to make it ten feet up the side without the muscles I’ve built. Once I was up there, I passed out for a while and then started walking when I woke. I slept between the roots of a tree that night and made a little fire. Walked pretty much the entire next day and then did the same thing. The gorge narrowed the further west I went and eventually, I thought that I could- it was stupid, reckless, probably should’ve killed me, but … well, it worked. I climbed a tree that was leaning over the gorge, across from another one that leaned out over it. Once I was high enough, I jumped across. I swear the only thing that stopped me from falling to my death was the tree. It moved , gave me something to grab onto and fling myself towards the trunk. It … wasn’t fun. Then I just walked … until I got here.”

     

                Kara’s expression was solemn and after a moment, she sank to her knees, moving closer to Lena as she reached her hands up to cup her face. “Let me look at you. Are you hurt?”

     

                “Not badly,” Lena said with a small laugh.

     

                Her cuts and bruises were already healing, but by the faded sight of them, Kara could see how bad they’d been. Hands ghosting over Lena’s face and shoulders, she inspected every inch of her, Lena sheepishly telling her that she might’ve cracked a few ribs but was otherwise fine, her tender ankle still a little sore, but nothing worse than blood blisters and cuts on her bare feet. 

     

                “What happened to your shoes?” Kara asked, softly clicking her tongue as she picked up Lena’s feet, inspecting the soles of each of them.

     

                “I had to leave them behind when I climbed the tree. Didn’t want to slip off a branch.”

     

                “A wise idea, but your toes must be frozen. Here, come with me.”

     

                Lena took her hand and let Kara pull her to her feet as she stood, leading her further from their camp and pausing at the side of a small pond. There were a few of them dotted around, the dark surfaces glimmering slightly in the dim light, and it reminded Lena of the ones near Kara’s home in Argo, which she had used to take her back home so many months ago. Taking off her shoes, cloak and tunic and wading into the water, Kara wasn’t even knee-deep, and she made Lena sit on the edge, coaxing her to put her feet into the water. Sinking to a crouch, the water lapping at her chest, Kara gently washed Lena’s feet so she could get a better look at her soles, ensuring there were no specks of dirt or little thorns in the cuts or blisters, Lena wincing occasionally at the dull stab of pain as Kara drew out a sliver of wood or tiny stone with the pressure of the water. She washed her face and her hands too, Lena closing her eyes as she felt Kara’s fingers gently rinse away blood and dirt.

     

                Once she was reassured that Lena was clean enough, Kara climbed out of the water, drawing it from her clothes with a dismissive gesture before she used her shirt to dry off Lena’s feet and then gave her her boots to wear. She also made her wife swap tunics with her, Lena’s in poor condition and Kara not feeling the cold so keenly. Lastly, she draped her cloak around Lena’s shoulders and carefully fastened it.

     

                “There. Now, we shall get some food in you, and some tea, and then you will sleep as long as you wish,” Kara murmured, a small smile crossing her face as her blue eyes softened. “And when you wake, I shall bind our hands together so that you will never be parted from my side again, and your hand will become lost in mine and you will never be out of my sight.”

     

                Letting out a hoarse laugh, Lena’s chest felt tight at her words, as if she could hardly breathe. Stepping in, she wrapped her arms around Kara’s waist and felt her wife’s arms come around her shoulders, strong and possessive. Savouring her warmth as she held her tight, Lena let out a soft sigh as she remembered being lost earlier that day, wandering through the endless trees, feeling as if she was going in circles, as if the land was devouring her whole, ensuring she never returned home to her wife.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena rasped.

     

                “Do not apologise,” Kara mumbled into her hair. “It was not your fault, no matter what your mother says. I believe you to be unfailingly honest, even if you are hiding some of what transpired from me. I’m just … glad you’re safe. It was … the most frightened I have ever been in my life.”

     

                Lena knew it had to be true but she couldn’t stop herself from questioning that statement. “Weren’t you frightened when your parents died?”

     

                “I was, but that event had already come to pass. You … I wasn’t sure what had happened, and that frightened me, fearing the worst, the agonising search for you. That was more frightening than a letter delivered with word of what was already in the past. But … now you are here, and I am no longer frightened.”

     

                “I’m sorry for frightening you.”

     

                Kara drew back and let out a small laugh as she stroked the side of Lena’s face. “I have not known fear like this before; you may be the thing I fear most.”

     

                “I thought that was falling in love.”

     

                Dropping her hand, Kara’s face sobered and she gave Lena a faint smile. “Yes. Yes, you’re right. Come, we should get you warmed up near the fire.”

     

                Distracted by the promise of warmth, of food and sleep, Lena was all too willing to allow her wife to shepherd her back to the camp, forgetting to question how Kara had managed to lie about what she feared most if she already knew what her biggest fear was. Quiet with her preoccupied thoughts of doubt and stubborn objection, Kara refused to dwell on it as she walked barefoot through the forest with a tight hold on her wife’s hand.

     

                Back at the camp, a little cleaner and definitely warmer, Lena took in the second fire that had been started, a clear divide within their small group as tensions ran high. Sinking to the ground beside it, Lena let out a weary sigh and held her hand out towards the flames. She felt that she was being watched and looked up to find multiple sets of eyes staring at her.

     

                “What?”

     

                “You have an uncanny ability to survive,” Alex stated, mystified as her eyes narrowed and she shook her head. “It’s good, but I do not understand it. You must be beloved by the forest.”

     

                “It’s good to see you alive, is what she means to say,” Kelly said with a warm smile as she handed Lena a cup of tea.

     

                “Here,” Kara said, handing over a bowl filled with stew. “You must be starving after so many days of hunger.”

     

                Taking it, Lena’s eyebrows rose. “Oh, no, I- well, yes, I am hungry, but I did eat. Um … I found some mushrooms - I’m not an idiot, Alex, I made sure they were safe - and I caught a fish too.”

     

                “You caught a fish?” Andrea sceptically blurted out.

     

                “Yes, I did,” Lena softly replied with an arrogant tilt to her chin. 

     

                “You caught a fish?” Kara echoed, just as disbelieving, perhaps even more so after her attempt to teach Lena how to fish before. “How?”

     

                “With my dagger and a big stick, and a few failed attempts.”

     

                Spooning hot soup into her mouth, Lena would’ve sworn she’d never tasted anything so good and was sure it would’ve come out honestly. Ravenous, she was halfway through her bowl when Kara noticed the blood spotting the tunic she’d given to Lena, sure that she hadn’t gotten any blood on it herself, and didn’t remember seeing blood on her shirt when she’d taken her tunic off, but couldn’t be sure as she’d been too busy putting Lena’s torn one on.

     

                “Are you hurt?”

     

                “I already told you, I’m fine.”

     

                “There’s blood on your tunic. I’m certain there was no blood there before.”

     

                Glancing down at it, Lena blinked. “Oh. Right. Well, it’s not bad , there was just this wolf-”

     

                “You encountered a wolf?” Alex exclaimed.

     

                “A wolf cub. It was a feral little thing; it bit me on the arm when I saved it from drowning. Ungrateful creature. Anyway, it wasn’t serious.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Kara gripped her arm as her brows furrowed. “Why didn’t you show me this before?”

     

                “It doesn’t hurt much anymore. It did - they have very sharp teeth - but it stopped bleeding after a while. I thought I’d bandaged it well enough.”

     

                “You must have reopened the scabs when you were climbing.”

     

                “Or falling,” Lena snorted as she put her bowl down and let Kara roll up her sleeve and remove the bandage.

     

                Kelly rose to her feet and went to fetch some supplies from the nearby saddlebags, and Lena had little choice but to sit there and let them both fuss over her. The wound was bathed with hot, herbal water and then a poultice was smeared over the dotted bite marks before clean linen was used to bind it. Then Lena went back to her stew, finishing the lot of it and draining her tea. She was yawning by then, her eyelids heavy as her eyes prickled with exhaustion. Now that she was safe and fed, warmed by the fire and back at her wife’s side, Lena was realising just how much it had taken out of her to be walking through the forest alone on foot for the last couple of days. 

     

                Without much prompting, she lowered herself down to the packed earth and rested her head on her wife’s thigh, and Kara pulled a blanket over her and didn’t move an inch for the next few hours as Lena slept peacefully in her lap. Well-rested from her lengthy sleep, Kara stayed up half of the night, keeping watch as she slowly eased herself to put the fire at her back so her vision would be adjusted to the dark, running her fingers through Lena’s knotted hair as she listened to the quiet sounds of the forest. Eventually, J’onn woke and took over for her and Kara lowered herself to the forest floor beside Lena, her arm wrapping tightly around her wife’s waist as she burrowed beneath the blankets and breathed in that smell of pine and earth, and the faint tang of blood, clinging to Lena’s hair and skin. She slept peacefully with a weight off her shoulders but a pit in her stomach.

     

                Lena slept late, waking to the green light of the forest, her body heavy and stiff. The fire was built up and the others were already lingering over breakfast and more tea, a blanket of fog hugging the ground as the day failed to warm up. Before she could even fully sit up, her wife was there with a steaming cup, looking more rested and carefree after the torment of the last few days. Lena likewise felt better, the fear and uncertainty banished as the safety and reassurance of her wife and family took its place. 

     

                “Good morning.”

     

                “Morning,” Lena murmured as she dragged her hair out of her face and took the offered tea. “Thanks.”

     

                “Did you sleep well?”

     

                “Mm, I almost feel as if it was a dream. And you? You look more rested.”

     

                “Yes,” Kara softly smiled, “I had a good night of rest. Would you like some breakfast?”

     

                “I’ll do it,” Lena insisted, moving the blankets off her lap.

     

                Kara’s hand pressed down on her shoulder as her smile grew. “Allow me.”

     

                She was handed a bowl of hot porridge and ate it slowly, savouring the warmth of it as everyone else started to prepare to depart. Once she’d finished, Lena rinsed out her bowl and helped saddle the horses, finding her mare and stroking the velvety snout as she delighted in being reunited with the horse. Her belongings were untouched and she saw her sword buckled to the saddlebags as she’d left it, her bow and dried quiver now strapped to the saddle as well, a new bowstring and fletched feathers replacing what was lost or ruined. Taking stock of her things, Lena felt more in control as she tried to shake off the lingering feeling of being helpless and vulnerable to the forest.

     

                They were back in the saddle shortly afterwards, already days behind their anticipated schedule with limited supplies and the forest still clinging to winter. No one went without though, hunting and foraging whenever anyone felt like ranging off to scout the way, but Lena remained at her spot towards the back, quietly insisting to her wife that she wouldn’t ride in front of her mother, that she didn’t trust putting her back to Lillian. Kara brought up the rear with Sam and Andrea, and Lena could feel the Hunter’s eyes on her back, her stare wary and uncertain. Lena hadn’t had time to share words with her yet so the secret remained between the three - unless Sam had revealed the truth to Andrea as well.

     

                It was two days of riding to recover the ground lost over three days, the path easier as they moved away from the gorge, returning to the path they’d initially taken, which was not so steep or winding.
