At the rotting corpse of the boar, the flesh untouched by the animals of the forest, they followed the hoofprints of James and his soldiers, weaving between trees as the ground rose and then dipped back down. They all resumed the usual routine of riding all day, making brief stops at midday to eat and refill waterskins, riding until dark or until they reached some landmark that offered shelter.

     

                One night, they stopped beneath the overhang of a cliff, the keen edge of the wind dulled, another, they huddled in a hollow between two valleys, sheltered by a thicket of dogwood saplings and brambles. On one unfortunate evening, they camped on a grassy knoll that reached towards the sparse canopy sheltering it, making for a wet night as it rained from dusk until dawn, with nothing but a few tarps propped up with branches for shelter and no fire for warmth. The following day was a slog through mud, everything damp and a layer of frost blanketing the trees and grass. 

     

                Kara remained in good spirits despite it all, smiling often, singing just loud enough for Lena to hear her as they plodded along, identifying bird calls and mimicking them with uncanny ability, much to Lena’s delight. The forest grew wilder though, and eventually Kara stopped singing, stopped mimicking the birds, a certain tension palpable within their party - a different kind of tension to the usual distrust and contempt between the Courts. Kelly shot a deer one evening, showing Lena how to dress it, skinning the hide with swift precision and then carving the meat off the bones. There was enough to feed them for a few days, but the blood attracted a bear that night. It was gigantic and hungry from the winter, the forest twisting it into a hulking mass of mossy fur and rabid anger as it reared on its back legs, almost as tall as the trees, roaring loudly and carving deep gashes in trunks as it lashed. They had fire and their weapons, managing to fend it off without it claiming the deer, but it killed one of the horses before it was scared off, arrows bristling in its thick hide, black blood spotting the forest floor.

     

                They stayed awake most of the night, rebuilding the fire, resettling the horses as they coaxed them in closer, catching sight of eyes glowing in the dark as other creatures came to investigate. Some of them were ordinary foxes, slinking about low to the ground, but Lena caught sight of a pair of eyes higher than any normal animals should have been, unable to make out what it was before it retreated back into the darkness. The road from then on was more difficult, finding the paths too thick with brambles and underbrush, a landslide blocking the way through a narrow ravine, a thick fallen yew barring their path as they were forced to detour around it. Even when the way was relatively clear, the trees felt too close together, ivy and roots snagging on horses and cloaks and weapons, the sound of the trees rustling in the breeze feeling eerie, as if they were talking. The fog made it worse, thick in the places where the land dipped, and Lena stuck closely to the saddle in front of her, her heart beating quickly as she was permanently on edge.

     

                It no longer felt like a relief because she no longer felt particularly safe, although she knew it was better than being alone. The edges of the forest felt a safer place though, tamer and lighter, and halfway into their journey, it felt dark and ancient, filling Lena with that prickling feeling of being watched. Of course, she still felt that keen sense of peace to breathe in the damp moss and dirt, the smell of rain mingling with pine, so fresh and invigorating, but the whole time she felt tense, ready to flee. 

     

                Kara informed her that there weren’t many Fae out in those parts, too wild and unpredictable for any dwellings, save the occasional watch tower, unpopulated but offering a warm place to rest one night when they came upon one. This was in better shape than the crumbling ruins they’d rested in earlier on in their trip, tall and speckled with moss and ivy as it perched on the edge of a cliff. They left the horses below and carried their supplies up, resting within the damp walls as smoke from their fire filled the space. Moving on early the next morning, they continued onwards, the ground rising slightly the further east they went, the mountains growing closer every time they crested a valley or reached a knoll that gave them a glimpse through the trees. They were still so many miles away that Lena didn’t see how they were halfway to their destination, unsure of where Alex lived exactly but knowing it was at least close to the mountains. There wasn’t much else for her to do besides follow the horse in front and pitch in with cooking and maintaining their camp, so Lena went along with the plans made by others and dreamed of a proper bed and being warm and dry.

     

                Four days and many leagues later, they encountered their first Fae since parting ways with James and his soldiers. They were rangers guarding a bridge spanning the base of a waterfall, the trees on either side of the river manipulated into platforms and shelters with the help of Earthfolk powers, and Lena marvelled at the intricate woodwork as they were greeted by the rangers and welcomed up into the warmth of the dwelling on the southern side of the river. The shelters spanned levels and multiple trees, delicate bridges of woven branches growing together spanning the distance. She felt a prickle of envy at the craftsmanship of the place, thinking of her inability to do anything more than make a branch dip so she didn’t fall to her death. If she had a better grasp of her power, instead of the raw displays of pure strength, maybe she would’ve been able to manage the gentle task of weaving a bridge to span the gorge.

     

                “I thought you would have been seated by the fire,” Kara said as she stepped up beside Lena, nursing her own cup of tea. 

     

                Gesturing to the craftsmanship, Lena smiled wryly. “Just admiring the handiwork. How much effort goes into something like this?”

     

                “Oh, well, I’m sure a basic bridge takes relatively little effort. To make it look beautiful … considerably more.”

     

                “Ah, so, well above my means then.”

     

                “Do not exclude yourself yet. You must learn to walk before you run.”

     

                “Mhm, but I’m still crawling. How long until I even get to walk?”

     

                “You know, my grandfather was not very adept with bending water to his will,” Kara explained, “but he could summon snow with such ease. He could freeze the lake and make the most marvellous sculptures out of ice. Yet, he did not have the knack for making the little assistants I can make, and he could not slow the current of a river to stop. My point is, you may not move mountains, Lena, but you can bring the forest to life. I have said it to you before - you are life. The trees and plants, they reach for you, as if you are the sun helping them grow. Is that not something so- so wonderful?”

     

                “What use is making a rose bloom when someone’s trying to kill me?” Lena impatiently asked.

     

                “When someone is trying to kill you, your heightened emotions will manifest your powers spontaneously, as they have in the past. I’m sure of it.”

     

                “So, I’m supposed to rely on luck?”

     

                “No,” Kara said, raising a hand to gently squeeze Lena’s chin as she smiled. “You may rely on me also.”

     

                With a scathing sound at the back of her throat, Lena turned away from her wife, jamming her cold fingers into her armpits as she scowled at the bridge. Softly sighing, Kara stepped up behind her, pressing one palm over Lena’s stomach and the other over her heart.

     

                “Do not let your frustration get the better of you,” Kara murmured. “You will close yourself off from feeling if you do that. Here. Breathe, slowly. Feel your heart. Do not focus on what you cannot do but what you can. ”

     

                Lena felt her skin prickle as Kara’s mouth almost ghosted the side of her neck, closing her eyes as she felt her heart stumble. Her frustration dimmed slightly but she still felt annoyed, wanting to shrug her wife’s touch off, her envy evident as she brooded. 

     

                “You told me of what you did merely a week past,” Kara continued. “Moulding stone to climb up from the river, a tree branch moving to aid your fall. You can do it, Lena, you just take for granted that which is a small victory in pursuit of bigger displays of power. Do you think sinking my ancestral home beneath the waves was more triumphant because it was so blatantly destructive?”

     

                Her annoyance flared hotter and this time Lena did shrug her way out of Kara’s embrace, turning to face her as her mouth thinned, displeased. Green eyes surly, Lena folded her arms across her chest as she gritted her teeth.

     

                “I don’t take it for granted,” Lena defensively objected. “It’s just not enough.”

     

                “Enough for what? You expect mastery in months when it will take decades.”

     

                “It’s not enough to make up for what was taken from me. You don’t understand it. Your parents died and you had another family take you in, but you were still here, with people who understood you. You were still able to learn about what you could do, and live with people the same as you. That’s not what it was like for me when my mom died; I was with people who don’t even know this place exists. I didn’t get to learn what I could do, or be with people like me. I’ve lost out on so much , so yes, I’m impatient, but I have a lot to catch up on and I don’t want to wait decades to feel as if I belong here, like I’m not so much of an outsider.”

     

                Turning, she walked across the bridge as she sought a bit of space, aware that after all they’d been through, it seemed so trivial to complain about feeling left out. She could feel her cheeks warm as she sulked, hear her wife’s quiet footsteps following her across the bridge.

     

                “You may not like it, but you are an outsider. Until you have lived here long enough to know the ins and outs of our ways, the history, the politics, the families and forest, you will not be one of us. You are learning what you should have learnt as a child and you are with people like you now, so listen to me when I tell you it will come with time. Trying to force these things will only serve to frustrate you, when you should find joy in the learning, and satisfaction in the little victories. Be gentler to yourself, have more kindness and understanding for the ignorance forced upon you when you were taken from here and left alone.”

     

                “I am understanding,” Lena snapped. “You shouldn’t be so patronising.”

     

                Kara looked mildly surprised and concerned as she blinked, eyebrows rising slightly, perplexed. “Why are you so angry?”

     

                “Because- because I am. Every time I think that I’m fine, there’s something else that throws me for a loop. I survived in the forest for days by myself, and everyone thought I was dead, but I was fine . I kept myself alive with the things that I learned, but all of that could’ve been avoided if I could just … make a ledge. I wouldn’t have fallen if I could do that, and I can’t do that because she took me away from here and I don’t even know why. All I know is that she hated it here enough to take me away and then she fucking died and I was left all alone. I am angry - I’m angry at my mom. If she’d never left, maybe she’d be alive and I would’ve grown up here and been good at all of this. I would’ve felt like I belonged somewhere and known everything. It’s just- it’s hard to keep learning, to be nowhere close to knowing everything I should, when everything is trying its hardest to kill me without giving a shit whether I’m equipped to defend myself or not. And now she’s with us, and she only makes things worse, and I can’t help but think that maybe I’d be better at all of this if she hadn’t been my teacher.”

     

                “So then I’ll find you a new teacher. Once we reach the Mid Vale, we’ll find someone who can show you the proper way of it without your mother’s harsh methods. You are no longer alone, Lena, even if you were before. Your mother did what she thought best when she took you, even if it was not what was best in the end. I can understand your anger there; I am still often angry that my own mother and father left me behind and went to fight. How different my life would have been if they had lived. I understand it’s different for me, that I still had a family, that I was not taken from the only life I knew, for it to fade to nothing more than distant memories, but I feel your anger. Do not lose heart; it gets easier with time.”

     

                “Which part?”

     

                “All of it.”

     

                “Can you promise me that? I’m not sure I can handle it getting much harder than it is now. I’m tired.”

     

                “Yes,” Kara promised before hesitating, a tender smile softening her face. “Would you like to hear of my childhood? I was a clumsy child, believe it or not. In the water, I was very agile, very elegant and swift, but on two feet, I was not so graceful. Learning with a sword, it made it very difficult for me to be adept. I would often move too quickly and overbalance, or I would retreat too slowly and trip over my own feet. I was thinking too much, you see, too inside my head. So, when I speak of breathing slowly, of feeling your surroundings, it is because that is what I know. Meditation was very helpful for me. Do not think me patronising when I say you cannot force it, that you need to be gentler with yourself; I say it because I believe it will help if you work hard at it. Let your mind empty and the weight of your troubles will be easier to bear.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara cocked her head to the side, her smile growing. “Of course, there are other methods I have shown you before.”

     

                Lena gave her a droll look. “Are there? None come to mind.”

     

                “Indeed? Perhaps the lessons bear repeating.”

     

                “Maybe they do.”

     

                “Well, we have time to spare now if you would like to … go over things.”

     

                Shooting her a withering look, Lena rolled her eyes. “I’m not sure we have the time.”

     

                “Nonsense. It needn’t be a long lesson; a few minutes can be just as useful as many hours.”

     

                “Is that so? I’ve always thought longer lessons were more beneficial.”

                

                “Well, if you don’t believe me, I must insist on showing you now.”

     

                Kara plucked Lena’s cup from her hand and set both of them down before she grasped her wife’s waist and urged Lena the rest of the way across the bridge. The rangers were on the other side with the others, or across the bridge, so they were alone on the platform, ducking through a doorway and climbing a ladder up a level. Inside the confines of the small dwelling grown from the trunk of the tree, it was warm and dim and Lena found her back pressed up against the trunk growing through the middle of the room. Ducking her head, Kara kissed the side of Lena’s neck and softly laughed, her breath warm against Lena’s throat.

     

                “Now, if you would heed my previous lessons,” she murmured, “and breathe slowly , feel your heart.”

     

                Kissing her way down to the folds of Lena’s cloak, Kara hummed as she wove her fingers through Lena’s hair, urging her head back slightly. Lena’s heart hammered in her chest as her lashes fluttered, her hands knotting in Kara’s clothes, and she let out a sharp breath at the feeling of Kara’s mouth in the hollow at the base of her throat.

     

                “You are not following my instructions,” Kara lightly scolded her. “Take a deep breath in and slow your heart, clear your mind.”

     

                She started to kiss her way up the other side of Lena’s throat, a quiet huff of laughter making Lena’s stomach lurch. “I’m not sure this is the best method for me to clear my mind, to be honest.”

     

                “Oh, no, I assure you it is the best method, mostly because it is entirely distracting. How else would you learn to clear your mind of any distractions if you were not taught while being distracted?”

     

                “Well, you should know that … whatever lessons you teach me, I can demonstrate right back at you just as well.”

     

                Kara laughed, her mouth just below Lena’s ear. “I wouldn’t mind.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena turned her head, her nose touching Kara’s cheek, and Kara turned her face towards her, kissing her softly. “Go on, take my advice,” Kara gently urged her, serious now. “Clear your mind.”

     

                With a breathless laugh, Lena raised her eyebrows and Kara kissed her again. Lena could taste the rain on her, melting somewhat as she kissed her back, feeling her wife’s hands on her belt, dropping it to the floor as the sheathed dagger thudded on the wood, her cool fingers on her stomach. As Kara sank to her knees, she cupped the back of Lena’s thigh, gripping the leather leggings tightly, and pushed up her tunic to kiss her stomach. Trying to slow her breathing, Lena pressed one palm flat against the bark of the trunk as the other cupped the back of Kara’s head, and she couldn’t quite empty her mind, too wrapped up in the feeling of her wife’s lips on her stomach, the heat of her mouth teasing, the moment not nearly private enough for her liking, knowing that she could never be quiet enough for them to go unnoticed if she had her wife do the things she wanted her to. 

     

                Her whole body tense as she struggled for composure, desire low in her belly, Lena opened her eyes as Kara’s touch quickly vanished. She was standing close to Lena, fingers quickly rebuckling the belt around her waist, and she reached up beside Lena’s face and plucked something before stepping away, putting a good distance between them. Lena’s eyes dropped to the little white flower Kara twirled between her fingers, and she turned to eye the trunk of the oak tree, taking in the new green shoots and the little flowers that had seemingly sprouted and budded in a matter of minutes.

     

                “The key to clearing your mind, to not dwelling on your frustrations, is that you allow the positive emotions to shine through. Peace, happiness, confidence, enjoyment. Your ability at the moment is tied to explosive displays of negative emotions - fear, anger, sadness - but you cannot rely on your emotional state to enact your will.”

     

                Lena heard footsteps below then, her eyes shifting to the hole where the ladder was before she looked back up at Kara, who was studying the flower. “We shall work on your meditation technique. As I said, a few minutes is just as effective. Perhaps even more so; too long straddling the threshold of frustration can make one rather impatient.”

     

                Her wife’s smile was teasing and ever so slightly smug and Lena arched an eyebrow in warning before they both looked back to the ladder and watched as Andrea poked her head through the hole. She looked at them both for a moment, clearly having heard Kara’s supposed lecturing on meditation techniques, and raised her eyebrows.

     

                “We are to be moving onwards, if the two of you have finished with your lesson.”

     

                “Lena? Is your mind unburdened by your troubles?” Kara asked with feigned innocence, twirling the flower between her fingers as she cocked her head to the side.

     

                “Quite,” Lena curtly replied, moving towards the ladder. 

     

                Following Andrea down it, Lena pulled her cloak tightly around herself as she stepped outside, the cold air cooling her warm face as she paused to pick up their cups and followed her attendant back onto the other platform. Thanking the rangers for the tea, Lena filed after the rest of their party, making the long climb back down to the forest floor, finding the others already in the saddle, waiting to be off. Ahorse, she gripped her reins and glanced sideways at her wife as Kara sidled up next to her, hesitating before she reached over to hand Lena the flower she’d plucked, giving her a quick wink before she urged her horse forward.

     

                Trying to hide her smile, Lena shook her head and followed after her wife, after pocketing the flower, finding her maddening but enjoying the thrill of it. She found it hard to stay frustrated in the presence of Kara’s unfailing optimism, especially with her hands all over her, and Lena cursed the fact that they were still a week away from their destination and surrounded by far too many people for her liking. 

     

                She had to give Kara her laurels, her wife was rather good at keeping her hands to herself around other people’s prying eyes, but she fantasised about it a lot, watching her make tea, or the way her slender fingers deftly unbuckled the saddle from her horse, splayed over her thighs as she braced herself to stand. Lena almost chopped a finger off one night, dicing dried meat and letting her eyes wander to Kara’s hands as her wife shredded herbs for the stew they were making, distracting herself so much that she cut deep into the tip of her finger, the blood blowing away into petals as it dripped from the cut. She endured a worried lecture as Kara stitched the cut closed and Kelly applied a bandage, but from the look in her wife’s eyes, she knew Kara could feel the same smouldering tension between them, both of them wound tight as they waited patiently for the chance to be alone together. 

     

                That wasn’t the only tension within their party, moods growing sour with the limited fresh food, lack of proper beds and gruelling pace that was set. Lillian’s contemptuous comments and complaints were music to Lena’s ears, and she wouldn’t have minded if her mother’s horse stumbled off the side of a cliff, but at least Lena could be satisfied with the knowledge that Lillian was having more of a miserable time than she was. Not that it was much fun for Lena, the delightful return to the forest subdued a little more with each passing day, feeling exhausted and filthy, craving a hot bath and a proper meal. Still, after her brief stint wandering the forest, hungry and cold, Lena didn’t complain at all. 

     

                It was still a relief almost three weeks after setting out when they crested the Mid Vale, a stretch of green grass sloping downwards, dropped amidst the forest, in the foothills of the mountains. Trees surrounded them on all sides, birds flitting between branches and what were evidently early signs of spring visible in the budding wildflowers and new foliage sprouting all around. It was picturesque, a little blue lake deeper in the vale, a herd of red-tailed deer grazing in the distance, and Lena felt buoyed by the sight as they followed a narrow track down through the vale, to a set of stone doors carved into the face of the black stone geology of the vale.

     

                They came to a halt before them and Lena turned to Kara. “This is Alex’s home?”

     

                “Yes. The tunnel goes quite deep into the foothills, though, so we are not quite there yet. You see that ridge up there? We shall come up near there and look down upon the Mid Vale.”

     

                She pointed to the mountains hemming them in and Lena squinted up in that direction as she waited for the doors to open. The tunnel was dark as they all filed inside, but it was soon illuminated with a warm orange glow as Alex led the way with her hand wreathed in flames, her family close behind. Curious, Lena plodded along on horseback as they passed through precisely hewn stone, the tunnel sloping upwards through the darkness. It was a couple of miles up through the stone and Lena envisioned the weight of so much earth pressing down on them, trying to feel the structural integrity of the rock as the moved deeper into the foothills, until they were at the base of the mountains. They were still inside when they came to a stop inside a large entrance hall, illuminated with burning sconces as Alex brought them to a halt before a set of towering stone doors, open and beckoning them further inside. 

     

                Saddle-sore and weary, they all dismounted, the sound of the horses and overlapping voices filling the chamber, summoning a woman through the open doors. She had close-cropped hair and was wearing a burnt orange tunic, surprised to see them as she approached and bowed her head towards the four women.

     

                “Vasquez,” Alex warmly greeted her.

     

                “Welcome home. I had expected you days ago.”

     

                Unslinging her bow and quiver from her shoulder, Alex heavily sighed. “We encountered unforeseen trouble. It delayed us some.”

     

                “I will have food brought for your guests and the horses seen to.”

     

                Fetching her personal belongings, and Lena’s as well, Kara stepped up beside her wife as Vasquez hastily disappeared to make arrangements, and she pointedly cleared her throat.

     

                “Come, I will show you to my room. We will share quarters; I am no longer confident in your safety amongst present company. My sister will have no trouble procuring another bed. It shall be similar to our time in your mother’s Court after you were poisoned. Only, this time I will not let anyone who harms you leave this place alive.”

     

                Kara’s statement was loud and pointed, her gaze flinty as the wintry sea as her eyes dismissively swept around the dismounted party as she offered her arm to her wife. Lena stepped in closer and took it, her touch gentle on Kara’s sleeve as she looked up at her, a little wary of her wife’s motives.

     

                Leading them through the doors, Kara’s back was straight as she escorted her wife into her sister’s home, Alex and Kelly staying behind to organise the others. Curious about this new home she was in, Lena looked around with wonder, taking in dark stone carved into flames and smoke, sconces spaced evenly along the length of the tunnel they walked down, casting a homely glow over the chilly place. Leading them through a warren of tunnels, somewhat similar to Eliza’s halls but feeling denser, lacking the airy design of the Airfolk, Kara didn’t speak until she stopped outside a door and pushed it open.

     

                “This is my room,” she announced as she stepped inside, waited for Lena to come through and then shut it behind them. “There are no locks here; while your mother is present, I recommend caution.”

     

                “Do you really think she’d be so brazen to attack us here in your sister’s home? Especially once the rites are given. I mean, I’m not opposed to sharing quarters with you-”

     

                Kara let out a short laugh, flashing Lena a quick smile as she moved further into the open room with her armful of belongings. It was spacious, the stone walls adorned with tapestries, rugs thrown over the scrubbed stone floors, and through a doorway, Lena could see a four-poster bed draped with sheepskin and sheltered by a canopy. The hearth was empty but split apple wood was piled nearby in a wicker basket. A low chaise longue was before the fire, an armchair and a small table in the corner near a shuttered window, and a table was set on the opposite side of the room, two chairs set at it. Lena wanted to explore the bedroom to see what else was inside it, but studied the room she was in instead as Kara replied.

     

                “Oh, no, it was not out of concern for your safety that I insisted on you sharing quarters with me.”

     

                “But you said-”

     

                “I insinuated. They will infer from my honest words that you will share my room, and Alex will supply another bed, and I’m concerned for your safety, which are all true statements, but have been fitted together quite deceptively. No, I wanted you to share quarters with me for my own pleasure - and, yes, peace of mind about your safety, which is, of course, always paramount - but … I had gotten used to sleeping beside you, even on the forest floor. I hope- I hope I have not been rash in deciding for you, but I was rather hoping you’d share my bed with me while we’re here.”

     

                Lena was silent for a moment, surprised by the shy, vulnerable look on Kara’s face as she bit her lip and looked at her through her lashes. “Oh. Well, yes, that’s fine. You could’ve just said.”

     

                “But then they might get the wrong - or rather, right - impression.”

     

                Snorting, Lena rolled her eyes, “as long as we have a little privacy here, I’m sure we could have always employed plausible deniability anyway. I mean, as far as everyone else is aware, we’re merely a marriage of convenience for the sake of peace, and no one expected us to get along that well.”

     

                “That makes us all the more dangerous.”

     

                “Does it?”

     

                “Yes, of course. I would always have defended your life with my own out of obligation, but now I would defend it not only out of obligation but out of genuine affection. You cannot feign sincerity by definition of the word itself, so it is better to take precautions and have them believe I keep you at my side out of obligation still, so that other problems do not arise from the truth.”

     

                Lena’s shoulders slumped slightly as she gave her wife a pained look, aching and confused. “Kara … I don’t believe anyone thinks it’s out of obligation anymore. For either of us. I think … we’ve already revealed too much there.”

     

                Setting their belongings down on the table, Kara gave Lena a strangely fierce look, blue eyes bright in the dim room as her voice went slightly hoarse. “I have revealed nothing ; I alone know the truth of my circumstances. It is not for others to determine what is and is not, and I shall not divulge the secrets kept close to my heart. My life is already dictated by one prophecy; I will not let others use our marriage to dictate my actions.”

     

                Completely lost, Lena gave her wife a mystified look as she slowly shook her head. “I- what? Where’s all this coming from?”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Kara turned around and Lena didn’t see the ripple of panic, of pain that crossed her face. “Please ignore me, I am tired. It has been a difficult trip. For you most of all; you should rest.”

     

                “So should you.”

     

                “No. No, I must clear my head in the water. I will feel much better once my head is clear. I- forgive me my ramblings. I’m merely … frightened.”

     

                Lena walked towards her, her steps slow and cautious, and she laid her palm against her wife’s back. “Of what? It’s okay, you can tell me.”

     

                Kara’s expression was almost haggard as she turned, a wounded look in her eyes, confused and doubtful, a desperate, pleading edge there as well. “I do not wish to. I am still hoping I am mistaken, that my fears are unfounded. I will not share them with you unless I am certain; I do not wish to unnecessarily burden you with my troubles.”

     

                “It wouldn’t be a burden. God knows you’ve taken on my troubles enough times for me to at least help bear the weight of yours for a change,” Lena said with a crooked smile, trying to convince her.

     

                Picking up her hand, Kara kissed Lena’s knuckles and gave her a thin smile. “I thank you for the offer, but my troubles are too heavy. I would spare you the weight of them. They are for me alone to bear.”

     

                Pulling her hand back, Lena’s brow furrowed with annoyance as her stomach twisted with unease. It was plain that Kara was keeping something from her but she had no idea what, or when it had started, her wife’s sudden mood surprising to say the least. It only served to make Lena frustrated in turn, brushing past her as she was put out by the secrecy.

     

                “That’s not how marriage works,” Lena quietly rebuked her as she made for the bedroom. “At least not in one of genuine affection . When you decide you’re ready to share, I’ll be waiting to listen.”

    Chapter 36

                At the sudden coolness between them, Kara spent the first night in her quarters asleep on a low sofa in the main entrance chamber, barely any words swapped between her and Lena since the annoyed exchange. She’d taken her wife deeper into the mountain to the hot springs to bathe, sconces casting a soft orange glow over the water and damp black stone, staying close by as Lena’s fear of the water was evidently exacerbated by the dark cavern and passageways. She’d brought clean clothes for them as well and then led them to a small dining hall, a table laid for four as they ate with Alex and Kelly, leaving the others to dine together in the main hall or kitchen.

     

                Sleep was difficult to come by after she’d excused herself early, tired from travelling, eager for proper rest. Lena stayed to drink more wine and Kara pretended to be asleep when the heavy door quietly creaked open, hearing her footsteps pause before she softly sighed and continued on to the bedroom. Listening to the sound of the heavy quilt pulling back, the rustle of fabric and pillows as she got settled, Kara felt a twinge of dismay. She hadn’t planned on being so aloof, pushing Lena away for merely offering to listen and help. 

     

                Frustrated and weary, she struggled to drift off, and even when she did, she slept fitfully. Kara could sleep anywhere, many nights spent lying in the mud on the fringes of a battlefield forcing her to adjust, but a soft sofa after weeks of sleeping in the forest no longer felt comforting. She should have been in her bed, beside her wife, and perhaps if she wasn’t so intent on feeling sorry for herself, holding her pride, she might’ve crawled into bed anyway. Instead, Kara woke to the sound of the door opening, sitting upright as she watched Andrea step inside.

     

                “Oh, forgive the intrusion. I thought you would have been up at dawn.”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Kara cleared her throat, scratchy from sleep, as she climbed to her feet. “I thought to indulge myself in rest while I could,” Kara murmured, waving a hand dismissively. “It is no matter. You may have to wake her; I have not heard her stir.”

     

                Nodding, Andrea moved towards the bedroom as Kara motioned towards it. She considered making her way to breakfast but didn’t want to leave Lena to wander about, aimlessly searching for the dining hall, deciding to sit on the chaise longue again, running her palms over her thighs as she listened to Lena and Andrea’s quiet chatter from the bedroom. She emerged in yesterday’s clothing, reminding Kara that she would need to set aside some of her own for Lena to use until their belongings arrived upriver, and she rose to her feet, her expression impassive as a longing ache filled her chest.

     

                “Good morning,” she murmured.

     

                “Morning,” Lena coolly replied.

     

                Buckling on her belt, removing the sword and opting for a dagger, Kara gestured to the door. “Shall I escort you to breakfast?”

     

                Giving her an exasperated look, green eyes sullen and a thinning at the corners of her mouth, Lena moved towards her and took Kara’s arm. They walked through the quiet hallways in silence, Andrea trailing after them, observing their uncharacteristic stiffness as they feigned nonchalance, not looking at each other once.

     

                Sweeping into a large dining hall, tall pillars of basalt carved like flames, gilded with beaten copper to make it reflect a rosy glow, they joined the long table sitting alone amidst the echoing room. Five hearths were lit, two each on the left and right walls and one at the far end of the room, making the air toasty. The smell of food wafted towards them and Kara took a seat to Alex’s left, Lena beside her. The others were scattered along the length in their groups and Lena cast her mother a dark look as Kara watched her from the corner of her eye, reaching for the tea. It was a blackberry tea, steeped strong and dark, and she poured them both cups as usual, as if nothing was amiss.

     

                The fare so far inland was different to what they’d eaten on both coasts, and Kara relished the variety of early spring berries as she set some on her plate. There was fresh cream as well, bread baked with oats and nuts, slivers of freshly cooked hare and duck eggs, roasted tomatoes and potatoes and other hearty fare. The herbs they were cooked in were flavourful and a welcome difference from the winter seafood they’d subsided on for months. Not that Kara complained about that, enjoying the food on the coast while she could, but it was always nice to visit her sister’s halls and eat what the verdant valleys and mountain foothills provided.

     

                She lingered over breakfast for a long while, later than anyone else, near-empty platters keeping her company as she nursed another cup of tea, staining her lips purple. Lena had gone off with Kelly to learn, Alex’s stocked library holding a wealth of knowledge on healing for her to get through while they remained, so Kara was left to brood. After a while, she left the dining hall behind and wandered through the hallways, hands clasped behind her back, head bowed as she frowned, a look of consternation on her face as she rubbed her forehead, trying to quell her frustration. It was futile.

     

                Her appetite evaded her, so she missed the midday meal, making her way down to the hot springs and swimming through one of the deeper pools, narrow, twisting tunnels of stone connecting some of them. The water was warm and Kara enjoyed the darkness, feeling weightless as she dove to the bottom, letting the water bear her until she needed air. She could go a long time without surfacing so she dwelled beneath the water throughout the early afternoon.

     

                Drying off, she redressed and wandered the hallways again, running fingers through her long blonde hair, preoccupied with her thoughts until her sister waylaid her. They fell into conversation and she followed Alex all the way back to her rooms, grander than the ones gifted to Kara for her use, several chambers leading off the main living area. They dwelled there, Kara seeking some sort of comfort for a while, a reprieve from her mind, as she collapsed heavily on a sofa with a heaving sigh. It was silent for a moment before her sister spoke.

     

                “You have quarrelled with her,” Alex noted.

     

                With a quiet scoff, Kara’s mouth thinned. “I have not quarrelled ; she is merely sulking over unshared secrets.”

     

                “Secrets do not make for a good marriage.”

     

                “Neither does political convenience, so we have always had ill luck, then.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Alex gave her a withering look. “You are in a foul mood today.”

     

                “It has been a tiring few weeks,” Kara dismissively replied, “I am finally afforded the time to process what has transpired - forgive me if I am not in high spirits.”

     

                “I am sure your spirits would be higher if you were not quarrelling-”

     

                “We’re not quarrelling!”

     

                With a quick laugh, Alex raised her eyebrows with amusement, moving towards a table with a pitcher of wine. It was dark, made from cherries, and she poured them both glasses, extending one to her sister. Climbing to her feet and drifting closer, Kara took the offered glass and murmured her thanks, a brooding look on her face.

     

                “And what secrets are you withholding?” her sister asked.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara let out an exasperated sigh. “They are not for you to concern yourself with.”

     

                “Perhaps not, but I am allowed my curiosity.”

     

                “You will not find your curiosity sated,” Kara murmured. “I am in no mood for it today.”

     

                “Oh, you are in some sort of mood, certainly.”

     

                “Things are not progressing as anticipated. I find myself fearful of the future.”

     

                “We are quite safe here.”

     

                “For now. But I will not bring war to your doorstep; news from the frontlines does not bode well. We may yet have to meet him there.”

     

                “He seeks his mother, I am sure of it. Offer her up on a silver platter and see yourself with one less enemy and a Queen for a wife. It would benefit us all.”

     

                “And make her a greater target. No, I will not put Lena in the middle of it if I can avoid that. She has learned much, but she is no politician or ruler.”

     

                Alex deliberated, shrugging nonchalantly. “Yet.”

     

                “She does not wish to be, so I will not make her. Let her enjoy her flowers and learn her healing; she will be safe a while longer doing that. I will keep her out of harm’s way for as long as I can.”

     

                There was a long pause then, the room silent, the snapping of the fire filling the vaulted chamber. After a moment, Alex cleared her throat, a determined look on her face as she drummed her fingers on her glass, trying to go about it the right way.

     

                “I must ask-”

     

                “Don’t,” Kara softly cut her off, raising her glass to her lips.

     

                “Sister … I know you do not wish to pull on that thread, but … it is like the tide going out; no matter how slow it goes, it always does.”

     

                Kara’s face stiffened slightly, her anger rearing as she snapped back, “then I will stop the tides.”

     

                Her voice broke and her face flushed red as she abruptly turned away from her sister. Alex’s shoulders slumped as her mouth thinned. Pity cut through her, but there was frustration within Kara’s sister as well as she urged her to finally be honest with herself. Kara didn’t want to be honest with anyone.

     

                “It is not something you can stop, and I am sorry for that, but if you do not face your fears, you will live a small life, which you do not want.”

     

                Kara wouldn’t turn back around but Alex watched her intently, saw the fear she was trying to smother, fear she didn’t want her sister to see. Suddenly, Kara let out a breathless sob, her shoulders shaking as she curled in on herself, her face hidden in her hands. She continued to weep as Alex, surprised at the open display of emotion, steered her over to a low sofa, sitting beside her as she gently rubbed her back. She knew then that her sister had been holding it in for days, for weeks.

     

                Smoothing her hair back, Alex shushed her, and Kara squeezed her eyes shut as tears ran down her cheeks, trying to rein it all back in. It had been building inside her, exacerbated by Lena’s close brush with death, the agony of three days thinking she’d lost her, wrestling with the logic that she couldn’t have if she hadn’t killed Lena herself, of denying that she felt anything for Lena to come to the conclusion that she would kill her herself. It was so confusing, the weight of it building in Kara’s chest until she couldn’t keep it in any longer.

     

                “All will be well,” Alex murmured, a grim look on her face as she soothed her sister.

     

                “Don’t,” Kara choked out, her voice raw with pain.

     

                “You must give a voice to your fears, though. Else, it will have a power over you, growing stronger if you leave it unacknowledged.”

     

                “You know what it is.”

     

                “Yes, as do you, and you must speak it aloud, undeniably true.”

     

                Raising her head, tipping it back as she closed her eyes, looking so tired , Kara wiped her cheeks as she drew in a deep breath and sighed heavily. It took her a moment to speak, her throat tight around the lump of fear, and she couldn’t bring herself to look at Alex, as if ashamed she’d allowed herself to feel such things, knowing what her feelings would bring.

     

                “I have … something in my heart for her. I fear it will not go away, that it will only die when I do.”

     

                Lying to herself didn’t work anymore, because deep down she knew who it was she wanted. There was an ache inside her, but there was a certain sense of relief as well, to divulge the truth to her sister. Suddenly, she felt like she couldn’t say enough.

     

                “She is … the most beautifully tragic person I have met in all my days; I fear ever making her sad and can think of nothing but making her happy. I would … move mountains to be close to her; she is all the stars in my sky, the colour of my life.”

     

                She let out a breathless sob, fingers brushing away errant tears, a wretched expression on her face as she wallowed in her pre-emptive grief. “My heart is so full of her, I can hardly call it mine. If she asked me to love her now, I do not believe I would have the will to say no.”

     

                Alex softly sighed, smoothing a hand over Kara’s golden hair before she kissed her temple, guiding her sister’s head to her shoulder. With her sister’s arm around her shoulders, Kara wept quietly until she exhausted herself, her tears soaking the wool of Alex’s robe. Once she’d spent her tears, Kara drew in soft, hitching breaths until she had regained her usual composure.

     

                “I know this is not what you wished to happen, but I do not believe it will-”

     

                Shrugging out of her sister’s touch, Kara quickly rose to her feet, restlessly pacing as her anger spiked. “Do not tell me it will not come to pass.”

     

                “It may not come to pass for a long while, yet. You may have many happy years together, and you cannot know what will befall her in the end.”

     

                “Me. I will,” Kara loudly replied, her voice filling the vast chamber.

     

                “I do not think you capable of killing her with your own hand.”

     

                “By my hand or by my design, it matters not. I will still be at fault. No matter if her death comes from the sword in my hand or by a fall from horseback at my suggestion of a ride. Any ill that befalls her here is because I was too weak to send her away again.”

     

                “You are making a martyr of yourself.”

     

                “What do you know of it? You with your wife who loves you, who you are allowed to love, without threat of death delivered by your hand.”

     

                “My prophesied fate may have been different than yours, but that does not mean you are the only one who will ever face such a burden. I could die tomorrow; that would be a loss to my wife, as much as yours would be a loss to you. Do you not think our mother blames herself for my father’s death? That she does not hold the guilt of being unable to save him with her healing? Do you not think Kelly blames herself, holds that guilt of her lover dying in her arms? That has never stopped them from loving.”

     

                “It’s different. They did not know of what would come. Perhaps they would not have allowed themselves to love if they had known.”

     

                “Love is not a choice. Else, you would not feel this heartache, you would decide not to love her.”

     

                Scoffing, annoyed at Alex’s sound logic, frustrated at the whole thing, devastated by the knowledge of what would come, at an unknown point in time, Kara wrestled with her mixed emotions as she paced away. She was silent for a tense minute, Alex’s gaze tracking her movements, back and forth.

     

                “It matters not; I will end my own life before I end hers,” Kara said with such chilling, pragmatic certainty that Alex’s stomach dropped .

     

                “Do not speak of such things,” her sister warned her in a low voice.

     

                “Yes, I agree; we should not speak of this any longer. Please do not speak of this to her either,” Kara whispered, her voice wavering slightly. “I cannot bear for her to know- I do not wish for her to be afraid.”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Alex nodded and Kara felt some of the knotted worry in her stomach loosen, nodding in response before she hesitated, deliberated over saying something else, and then swept out of the room. The hallway beyond was warm, dark stone lit by a few small sconces, the hot springs deep within the mountain heating the floors as she passed through them, the humidity making the air seem thick as she breathed raggedly.

     

                Realising she was still holding the glass of wine, Kara knocked it back and walked the rest of the way back to her suite, pushing open the heavy doors and shutting them slowly so they didn’t bang. There was a hollow shakiness inside and she moved forward to the table, setting the glass down, her skin clammy and prickling from the heat of the lit fire, which never seemed to go out.

     

                She looked up at the flicker of movement from the corner of her eye, watching as Lena stepped into the doorway of the bedroom beyond. They looked at each other for a moment before Kara ducked her head back down, aware that her eyes must be bright and bloodshot, her cheeks splotchy, a general air of despair about her.

     

                Lena’s face slackened slightly with mild surprise, her mouth opening and closing before she haltingly spoke. “Are you okay?”

     

                Giving her a wan smile, Kara cleared her throat. “I am well.”

     

                “You’re upset.”

     

                “It shall pass.”

     

                “What happened?”

     

                “I was speaking with my sister. It is of little consequence.”

     

                A clouded look ran across Lena’s face. “Right.”

     

                Silence descended over the room and Kara licked her lips, wanting to cringe at the awkwardness. “I might rest before dinner.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena murmured, ducking her head as a strained smile crossed her face. “I’ll leave you to rest in peace.”

     

                She was gone before Kara could stop her, tell her she didn’t need to leave. Alone in her quarters, Kara bit back a groan as she wandered through to the bedroom and fell facedown on the mattress, wallowing in her misery.

     

     

                Following the distant sound of metal striking metal, Lena felt the heat before she even stepped foot inside the cavernous hall. There was the taste of metal in the air, like copper in her mouth, and everything was tinted in the fiery orange glow of the large lit forge. Taking in an assortment of tools, half-finished pieces of sculpted metal, tables scattered with rolls of parchment, oil cloths and chisels, barrels of water lined along one wall and a few heavy leather aprons on hooks. Alex was wearing one such apron, the sleeves of her shirt rolled up, and she methodically pounded a piece of steel as Lena approached, feeling the stifling heat down to the roots of her scalp.

     

                “What did you say to her?”

     

                “Hm?” Alex hummed, looking up, giving Lena a cursory glance before returning her attention to her work.

     

                “She’s upset. What did you say to her?”

     

                “Perhaps you should ask her yourself.”

     

                With a huff of impatience, Lena’s eyelids shuttered as she flexed her fingers. “She doesn’t want to talk to me.”

     

                Alex shrugged, raising the tongs to inspect the piece of metal pinched between them. Laying it back flat on the anvil, she tapped the hammer against the edge of the anvil and then rhythmically beat the piece of metal until the orange glow started to fade. 

     

                “My sister … is frustrating to understand. She is not the shallow pool I would like her to be; she keeps so much to herself that I fear I will keep swimming and never reach the bottom of her being. In that way, the two of you are similar.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes. “She’s like trying to draw blood from a stone.”

     

                “An apt expression.”

     

                “I’m supposed to be the stubborn one.”

     

                With a laugh, Alex moved to thrust the piece of steel into the fire again, reheating it as the edges slowly reddened, near-yellow when she pulled it out. “You are both stubborn. It is not necessarily a bad quality, although it does make it frustrating to convince either of you to do anything you do not wish to.”

     

                “Well, so far, she’s been pretty good at giving in. Or … you know, she’s been very eager to make me happy.”

     

                “And now she is making you un happy?”

     

                “No,” Lena mused as she watched Alex hammer the metal again. “Now, she is making me worry. Does she … talk to you about things?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Okay. That’s good. At least she’s talking to someone about it all.”

     

                “Here. Kelly usually helps, but you may make yourself useful while you’re here,” Alex said, gesturing to the bellows situated before the fire. “If you wouldn’t mind.”

     

                Warily moving over to them, feeling the intense heat of the fire, Lena pumped the bellows slowly, watching the fire rage higher. “Faster than that,” Alex instructed her.

     

                Picking up the pace, Lena watched her heat the metal in the roaring flames, feeling sweat prickle her face and back as the room became stifling. Licking her lips, she frowned. “Couldn’t you just make it hotter yourself?”

     

                Alex gave her a quick glance, one eyebrow slightly arched. “Yes, but it is not about speed , nor about ease. Some things are a labour of hard work and cannot be rushed. There is a balance to things, and it would remove the enjoyment and craftsmanship if I merely made crude knives as fast as I could. That is not the purpose of what I’m doing.”

     

                “I guess.”

     

                Hammering away for a moment, Alex moved back to the forge and reheated the metal as Lena continued to pump the bellows. With a smile, she raised her eyebrow higher. “You used to arrange flowers, yes? What is it about it you enjoyed? The art of the arrangements, or selling as many as possible?”

     

                Lena deliberated for a moment before she smiled. “Well, I was running a business, so … yeah, kind of selling as many flowers as possible. I get it though; I did always want to have a big plot of land to grow my own flowers. That would’ve taken time. A labour of love.”

     

                “Yes, a labour of love,” Alex agreed. 

     

                “You don’t really seem to do things the same way here, though. I mean … back home, everything is business, everything is capitalism-”

     

                “What’s that?”

     

                “I guess it’s like maximising your profits. You know, make things cheap, sell them high. Pay people less so you can make more.”

     

                “Oh. No, we make things for enjoyment and trade for what we need.”

     

                “Yeah, I like that. I think maybe if I hadn’t had to worry about making money to survive, maybe I would’ve taken the risk to grow my own flowers. No one really wants to trade flowers for anything useful though; I mean, I enjoy flowers, but they’re just a pretty thing to look at.”

     

                Hammering as she listened, Alex nodded and then set the hammer down, plunging the metal into a barrel of water. It hissed loudly, the surface bubbling until it slowed, and she pulled out the dull piece of metal, holding the tongs aloft as she eyed it in the glow of the forge. Lena slowed her pumping of the bellows and then Alex met her gaze.

     

                “Beauty should be treasured above all else. Nothing beautiful is ever useless.”

     

                “True. A girl’s got to eat, though.”

     

                “An easy enough feat when one can grow their own food at a touch.”

     

                “Something about the labour of hard work and ease and all of that?” Lena dryly said as she raised an eyebrow.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex laughed. “Food is another matter entirely, but even then, to wring a plant for all it’s worth is its own form of cruelty. To gently coax a bountiful harvest through the careful tending of plants is perhaps more akin to how we view it here. And when everyone is fed and no one goes hungry, we have more time for pretty things. When we are patient, trees bear fruit, but if you spend all winter blaming a tree for its barren branches, well … it will not make the tree fruit any faster but it will stoke your anger.”

     

                “Hm. This feels like we’re no longer talking about fruit,” Lena said with a thin smile.

     

                Alex gave her a droll look. “Do you wish to know what we talked about?”

     

                Lena floundered a moment, shifting uncomfortably. “Well, obviously, if she hasn’t told me about it then it’s probably something she wants to keep to herself.”

     

                “Some things, yes, but she was upset today after we spoke of our family and of some things between us that differ that she is not pleased with,” Alex slowly explained, eyeing the little knife she was making before moving over to the grindstone.

     

                Drifting after her, Lena watched as Alex pressed down on the pedal, the stone picking up the pace as it turned. She ground the edge of the short blade, sparks flying, and Lena watched with curiosity, unfamiliar with the process of forging. Once she’d finished the basic bevelling, Alex tossed the knife onto a work table and planted her hands on her hips.

     

                “It has been a long trip; she is weary. Allow her some time to properly rest and all will be well.”

     

                Nodding, Lena’s mouth thinned as she bowed her head. “I just- she’s nice. I don’t want to upset her.”

     

                “Lena,” Alex sighed, shaking her head as she picked up her newly forged knife, “you could take this and ram it into her stomach and she would still not be upset with you.”

     

                With a huff of laughter, Lena closed her eyes, a small smile on her lips. “I think even she has her limits.”

     

                “No, I am telling you. I mean it truthfully; she would rather die herself than cause you harm. So, do not fret so much. Her mood is not for anything you have done.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena whispered, some of her worry dimming. 

     

                She trusted Alex to be honest with her, to not be talking circles around Lena. And how could she? She said it wasn’t anything Lena had done; there was no way to misconstrue that. Running a hand over her face, Lena swallowed.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Alex gave her a small smile in return, brown eyes watchful but kind. “I like you, Lena; you are good for her, when I did not believe so before. But you have not yet known her a full turning of the seasons. It will come, with time, so you should not worry about what she keeps from you now. I am sure she will reveal all with time.”

     

                Cheeks dimpling with a shallow smile as she fiddled with the rings on her fingers, Lena nodded and lingered a moment longer before she slowly moved back towards the door. “I will leave you to your forging.”

     

                “You are welcome anytime, if you wish to learn,” Alex called after her.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Wandering back through the hallways, feeling relieved as the stifling heat dimmed, Lena craved fresh air, the smell of metal still clinging to her senses as she left the forge behind. As the hallways cooled, moving higher up through Alex’s home, the air cooled, the smell of stone replacing the steel and ash, but it still wasn’t the fresh air of the outdoors. She wished they were in Argo instead, the soaring tower of Kara’s lake home the one that Lena enjoyed the most, hating the lake but loving the trees encircling the tower and the breeze through the gauzy curtains. What she would’ve given to go back to last summer; perhaps she wouldn’t have left at all in the first place if she’d known how much she’d miss it.

     

                It was almost dinnertime and Lena found Kelly oiling her shield and hunting knives, the sword she carried, waxing the bowstring and polishing the wood. She looked up at Lena’s arrival but they didn’t speak, Lena taking a seat opposite her and watching her methodically care for her belongings, a whetstone filling the silence as she ran it over the edges of her weapons, using an oilcloth to polish it up afterwards. Lena watched closely, taking in the process so she could try and replicate it herself at a later time. 

     

                Once Kelly finished, she gathered up her things and tidied up, and Lena followed after her like a lost puppy, all the way to Alex and Kelly’s rooms, hovering on the threshold as she watched Kelly carefully stow her weapons. Smoothing out the skirts of her robe, Kelly turned to her and smiled once she’d finished, raising her eyebrows politely.

     

                “Shall we go to dinner?”

     

                They made their way to the small dining hall, a table set for four and only the two of them there. Taking their seats where they had the night before, Lena and Kelly opposite each other, Lena poured wine for them both into the pretty wineglasses, eyeing the design as they waited for their wives. After a few minutes, Kelly glanced at the stone platters, sitting on top of a length of stone resting on a pit of coals, keeping the fare hot.

     

                “We shall start without them.”

     

                There was boar and a variety of roasted root vegetables and leafy greens, Lena adding portions to her plate and sipping her wine in between mouthfuls. Alex joined them shortly but Kara didn’t arrive until they were halfway through, murmuring an apology as she took a seat. She looked as distracted as she had earlier but better rested, her cheek lined with the evidence of her lap. Little was said throughout dinner, a certain discomfort to the air as they all picked at their plates, eating slowly as they dragged it out, waiting for the tension to break. Alex and Kelly shared a few sideways glances that let Lena know they were somewhat aware of the confusing friction between the couple and she wondered what Kara had divulged.

     

                After dinner, the hour late enough for bed, she made her way back to their suite with Kara at her side, both of them tired and unsure how to bridge the sudden rift. It was silly, seemingly over nothing, but Lena was annoyed and Kara was silent, and neither of them knew how to circumvent that. As Lena started to shed her clothes, belt unbuckled, robe folded up, leggings tossed aside, she watched Kara through the open bedroom doors, arranging pillows into a comfortable fashion.

     

                Lips twitching with dismay, Lena hesitated before she softly cleared her throat. “You don’t have to sleep out there.”

     

                Looking up, Kara met her gaze, her blue eyes so sorrowful that Lena’s heart ached to see her so troubled, unsure what it was. Hesitating a moment, Kara meekly nodded and moved towards the bedroom, closing the doors behind herself, plunging them into darkness. Blindly moving towards the bed, Lena climbed in between the turned-down sheets, a pan of hot coals previously put between them at her feet to keep them warm, and she sank into the feather mattress as she listened to the sounds of Kara undressing before the mattress sagged beneath her weight. It was silent for a few minutes.

     

                “I’m sorry, I don’t mean to anger you.”

     

                “I’m not angry,” Lena replied. “I just- I have worked so hard to be honest with you about things, to open up the way I have never opened up to people - all the social workers, shrinks, foster parents - and it’s been hard but you- now you aren’t being honest with me. You can see why that might upset me that something’s bothering you and I have no idea what it is because you won’t be honest with me.”

     

                “You’d like to know what bothers me? Fine, I will tell you. It bothers me that we have had to run away. It bothers me that your brother could be anywhere, and that information is unknown to us. It bothers me that your mother is here, and that we cannot shake her off. It bothers me that I am so jealous of my sister’s marriage. It bothers me that there is a prophecy holding me back from my own happiness. And it bothers me that I cannot keep you safe.”

     

                Throat tight, Kara swallowed thickly, looking up at the dark ceiling as she listened to the sound of her heartbeat in her ears, too loud in the quiet of the room. She could hear Lena’s soft breaths too, her body tensed slightly as she anticipated her response.

     

                “That’s not what’s really bothering you, though, is it?”

     

                Silent for a moment, mouth turning down at the corners with dismay, Kara sighed. “No, it’s not.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena whispered, and Kara could hear the hurt in her voice, cleaving her chest to be the cause of it. “Thank you for being honest.”

     

                “I would tell you if I thought it would lessen the burden,” Kara whispered back as she rolled onto her side.

     

                In the pitch black of the room, she fumbled, reaching out to lightly brush her fingers over her wife’s cheek. Tears pricked her eyes, an ache in her chest at the mere thought of what her feelings meant, of how deep they ran, of how blind she had pretended to be for weeks - longer, perhaps. The thought of losing her made her throat close up painfully tight and she didn’t think she’d be able to finish her thought, drawing in a thin, shuddering breath.

     

                “I’m sorry,” she said, her voice strangled, rasping from the gut-wrenching, sickening dread that seized her. “I’m sorry for everything.”

     

                Rolling towards her, Lena reached up and pressed Kara’s warm palm firmly to her cheek. Kara heard her soft sigh as hot tears fell on her cheeks, unnoticed by Lena in the dark. “Don’t apologise. You’ve done nothing wrong.”

     

                “ Yet. But I’m sorry for everything I will do.”

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena murmured. “I would forgive you for anything.”

     

                Pulling her hand back, the warmth of her wife’s face lingering in her palm, Kara wiped her wet cheeks with shaky fingers. “Some things are unforgivable.”

     

                “Still, you’re my wife; you’re automatically forgiven. For everything except leaving me. Don’t do that.”

     

                Kara weakly chuckled, a pained smile crossing her face. She was glad Lena couldn’t see her expression in the dark. “I won’t.”

    Chapter 37

                Groggy when she awoke, Lena buried her face back into the pillows as she exhaled heavily, as if annoyed to be awake, although she was uncertain what had woken her. A moment later, she heard the door to their quarters creak shut and bolted upright in bed, her body taut with panic. Her sudden movement roused Kara, who reached beneath her pillow for a hidden dagger, suddenly awake in the dark. Lena couldn’t see her but she felt her wife lever herself onto her elbow, could imagine her golden waves tumbling about her shoulders as they listened to footsteps draw nearer. Throwing the blankets off, Lena bit back a curse.

     

                “There is no point; we are caught out now,” Kara softly sighed, reaching out to ghost her fingers over Lena’s shoulder, calming her.

     

                Grimacing down at her, Lena listened to Andrea hesitate on the other side of the door before throwing them open. With no windows or fires lit in the bedroom, it was pitch black until the doors were opened, the dimly lit living area seeming too bright as Lena scowled, blinking as her eyes watered slightly until they adjusted.

     

                “You fret over nothing, Your Highness,” Andrea drawled as she shook her head, sweeping into the room, fingers writhing with flames as she lit the sconces. “You are quite good at remaining secretive, however, I would be more discreet in front of other people if I had not intended to betray true feelings. Even if it was a kiss in a moment of relieved weakness that you were not dead.”

     

                Her eyes slid to Kara, who scoffed. “You will not speak a word of this to anyone.”

     

                “No. You have my trust and discretion - your wife has earned that.”

     

                Glancing at Lena, whose face clouded, Andrea’s stare was unwavering. She knew from that look that Sam had divulged the true nature of what had happened between mother and daughter at the edge of the cliff, and that Andrea was grateful that Lena hadn’t cast the blame on Sam. Lena considered, briefly, that perhaps Andrea didn’t trust Kara not to mete out just punishment for her lover’s actions, but even though she knew her wife had killed many people, she thought Kara so soft. She was kind, a little serious but warm and nice. Lena didn’t think of her as the threat that the Unseelie so clearly did.

     

                “Will you bathe now?” Andrea moved on.

     

                “No. No, I’d like to eat first. Perhaps practise my archery or sword fighting too.”

     

                “Sam will be more than willing to act as your partner. If your wife is otherwise indisposed.”

     

                “Yes,” Kara murmured, climbing out of bed. “I might be at that.”

     

                Annoyance flashed through Lena, and she scowled slightly, climbing out of bed as well. Her attendant arranged clothes for her at the foot of the bed and Lena changed into the soft leggings, billowing shirt and tunic, with a flowing robe over the top, belted at the waist with her dagger at her left side. Shaking back the cuffs of the robe, Lena slipped the assortment of rings picked out onto her fingers and then let Andrea comb out her hair, braiding little sections and weaving them together, adorning them with little gemstones and setting a circlet of leaves and flowers onto her brow.

     

                “Much better,” Andrea said with satisfaction as she stepped back to admire her handiwork. “Now, you are dressed fit for a Princess again.”

     

                “She does not need finery to be seen as such,” Kara murmured as she shrugged on a quilted jacket, a muted navy blue stitched with the ripples of a disturbed pond, drops of quartz like rain dimpling the surface. 

     

                She always opted for rather plain clothes in comparison to her wife, but they were still wonders of art to Lena, who enjoyed the blue tones of her wife’s wardrobes, of the little embroidered silver fish or patterns of waves worked into the designs. Even the simple garments of physical labour, or inner layers hidden beneath tunics, jackets, robes and cloaks, were all beautifully embroidered and Lena always thought her wife particularly beautiful in plainer clothes than the finery of necessary circumstances. Kara always looked more at ease in leggings and a loose shirt, salt staining the fabric and the sleeves rolled up over her wiry forearms. Perhaps it was because it made her more normal, less of a difference between them at such times, Lena always struck by how otherworldly her wife was on days such as MidWinter or their wedding day, truly a fae being from a dream.

     

                Lena would’ve told her wife as such, a murmured confession, weighted with the tension between them, of anticipation, waiting for her teasing touch, but things between them still seemed a little cool. She kept her words to herself, eyeing her wife with a grim thinness to the corners of her mouth as she felt annoyance flash through her again. 

     

                “Well, I am in need of some tea, and perhaps oatcakes and jam,” Kara said as she buckled on a dagger and tugged down the hem of her jacket. “If you will be joining me.”

     

                Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena smoothed a hand over her robe and stepped up beside her wife, reaching for her arm. Kara seemed to soften slightly, her blue gaze like the bottomless sea, tender as she cocked her head to the side.

     

                “You are always beautiful.”

     

                One side of her mouth curved into a smile and Lena did roll her eyes this time, tugging on Kara’s arm. Andrea scoffed behind them but followed them to breakfast, joining the others in the dark stone dining hall, lit fires casting a rosy glow over the dark chamber. Others were still absent, including Alex and Kelly, but they took their usual seats and started to fill their plates with the spread of food. 

     

                They barely said a word to each other, save for quiet thank yous whenever something was offered, a cup was refilled, and Lena felt discontent twist her stomach. She knew that she was being prickly, perhaps a bit unfair, and while the air had cleared somewhat last night, lying beside each other in the dark as they spoke their minds, there was still a part of her that couldn’t help but be annoyed that Kara was still withholding something. Of course, Lena didn’t think she was entitled to know all of Kara’s secrets, nor did she want to, but there was something about it that was affecting Kara’s moods, weighing heavily on her, and it was obvious for her wife to see. If it wasn’t affecting her so greatly, Lena would’ve been happy to let it go.

     

                They finished their breakfast in a stilted silence and she waited until Sam had finished eating before asking if she’d accompany her someplace where they could spar together. Vasquez, Alex’s Steward, guided her to an airy room they could use, the walls carved extensively and a few sconces lit for them, and Lena unbelted her dagger and removed her robe and tunic as she waited for Sam to come back with swords for them both. Removing her circlet for good measure, she stretched her muscles to ensure she’d warmed up properly and then accepted the sword once Sam had returned, Andrea waltzing in after her, a flagon of watered wine and a few cups in hand as she found a spot against the far wall and made herself comfortable. 

     

                They faced each other, waiting, until Lena struck out, finding her sword blocked with such speed that she’d barely seen Sam move. Shoving her backwards, Lena sent a slashing cut towards her ribs, which was parried, before Sam advanced on her, aiming for her neck, blocked by Lena, who was wide-eyed, heart racing. It suddenly struck her that it was perhaps very risky to spar with Sam, who could’ve lost control at any moment. She didn’t know what triggered it, only that those occasional moments where she’d thought her guard had been elsewhere, something vacant and tense about her, like a caged animal, hadn’t been her imagination.

     

                Kicking her in the shin, watching as Sam blinked in surprise, Lena shoved her away and Sam cocked her head to the side, moving in quickly to grab Lena’s wrist, immobilising her next swing, and then striking her across the mouth. Staggering backwards, Lena made a muffled sound of pain, cheeks flushing red as the coppery taste of blood filled her mouth. Swallowing the bloody saliva, Lena’s mouth twisted with annoyance and she moved in quickly, squaring her shoulders, batting Sam’s sword aside and then ramming her elbow into her chest. Stumbling back, guard open, Sam barely managed to right herself to duck past the cheap swipe Lena sent her way, scoring a shallow line across her leather jerkin. 

     

                Andrea let out a small laugh, pouring herself more wine as she watched, and Sam raised her eyebrows slightly. Split lip stinging, Lena grinned. With a huff of laughter, Sam tilted her head to the side and gave her a pointed look.

     

                “Do not get too cocky, Your Highness. That is a fault even the greatest swordsman cannot afford.”

     

                In a flurry of feinting moves, she slashed an angry bleeding wound across Lena’s upper arm as if to prove her point and Andrea clicked her tongue. “Please, leave her clothes alone. Lady Kara is spending a small fortune to keep her clothed, given Her Highness’ blatant disregard for her apparel.”

     

                “I actually take great care,” Lena defensively replied, “it’s not my fault everything here seems intent on attempting to kill me - or putting me in situations where I’m just as likely to die, besides.”

     

                Sam faltered slightly and Lena’s momentum drove her forward as she slashed at the guard’s thigh. The leather protected her some, but Lena still watched as her sword bit into Sam’s flesh, her mouth falling open and eyes widening as she quickly jerked the sword free. It wasn’t that deep, and it took a moment for blood to well up through the leathers, sliding down Sam’s leg. Drawing in a hitching gasp, Lena’s face whitened, her grip on her sword loosening as it clattered loudly to the stone floor.

     

                “I’m sorry,” she barely managed to get out before Sam’s hand shot out to wrap around her neck.

     

                Letting out a choked sound of surprise, Lena blinked, staring wide-eyed at the hard look on the fae woman’s face. It must have been some form of self-preservation, genuine harm tapping into the part of Sam that gave over to Reign, dangerous and threatening. Sam still had her sword in her hand, moving her arm, drawing it back as if to skewer Lena on it, but Lena couldn’t see that as she stared at Sam’s face and clawed at her hand, clutched tightly around her throat. 

     

                Then Andrea was at their side, all of it happening so fast, grasping the hunter’s arm, wresting the sword free and levelling it at her lover’s throat. “Let her go,” she quietly ordered her, voice fraught with tense panic.
