                Turning to look at her, Sam merely blinked, and Lena used her distracted attention to kick her in the thigh. Right over her new wound. Blood slicked the sole of Lena’s foot and Sam hissed with anger and pain, her leg buckling slightly, fingers digging in a little tighter.

     

                “Stop it,” Andrea snapped at Lena. “You’ll make her angry.”

     

                Lena’s face was starting to redden and she had a hawkish look on her face, indignant and slightly fearful, still trying to claw at Sam’s fingers as Andrea tried to convince her lover to let go. It was then that Kara showed up, whether drawn by the sound of harsh words and frantic heartbeats or by the curious desire to watch her wife spar, and it took her a moment to drink in the sight, the situation. It only took her a moment to verify that it wasn’t part of the sparring, and she moved quickly across the room with a livid look on her face.

     

                Grabbing Sam’s wrist, she squeezed tightly, almost tight enough to snap bones, and then followed up with a jab of the heel of her palm to her ribs to force the hunter to relinquish her hold on Lena’s throat. Fingers going slack, Lena was suddenly able to draw in a deep lungful of air, coughing on it as her hands rose to flutter around her tender neck as she doubled over. Still gripping Sam’s wrist, Kara drove her backwards, grasping her other arm as well, and Sam stared back at her with a hard look of anger, straining against Kara’s strength before she tipped her head back and smacked it into Kara’s nose. 

     

                Lena glanced up, still pink in the face, as she watched Kara let go of one of Sam’s arms and twist her other one behind her back, forcing it down at a painful angle before she all but wrestled Sam down to the stone floor. Andrea nervously watched at Lena’s side, a hand on the Princess’s back as she tried to ascertain that she was well while Kara dealt with her lover. Knee pressed into Sam’s back, hands pinned, Kara glanced over her shoulder, blue eyes bright with fury as blood coated her mouth and chin from her bleeding nose.

     

                “You,” she called out to Andrea, “come and calm her.”

     

                Andrea swiftly moved over to kneel beside Sam, smoothing a hand over her hair as Kara removed her knee from her back. Rising to her feet, Kara hurried over to Lena, gently cupping her chin, her fingers featherlight on her neck as she stared at the bruising skin with wide, worried eyes.

     

                “Let me see,” she murmured.

     

                “I’m alright,” Lena hoarsely insisted, gently jerking away from her touch.

     

                “What happened?”

     

                “I cut her.”

     

                “That is no justification for attacking a Princess in such a manner.”

     

                Lena hesitated, licking her lips, tasting blood as her eyes flitted up to Kara’s and then away. “She was not herself.”

     

                “Wha-”

     

                “She is … confused,” Andrea softly explained, shoulders slumping with weary defeat. “You know her well enough as Sam, but she is bound so tightly to Her Majesty that her arrival in the Seelie Court has had her … struggling since.”

     

                “I cut her. She thought I was a threat. That’s all,” Lena curtly explained, her voice rasping and thin.

     

                “That’s not all,” Kara murmured, glancing at Lena with bewildered surprise. “You have known of this.”

     

                Annoyance flashed through Lena, her mouth twisting as she quietly scoffed. “Yes. Of course I knew; it’s been obvious . If anyone else bothered to pay attention, they would’ve noticed it too. Could’ve helped- ”

     

                “There is no way to help her as long as the Queen remains here,” Andrea cut in. “One word from her lips, and Reign surfaces to do her bidding. It is … difficult for her to fight it, even if she wishes to. She would not intentionally harm anyone if she wasn’t trapped so, if she wasn’t forced; you know that, don’t you, Your Highness? You don’t blame her for her part-”

     

                Confused, Kara looked back to Lena. “What part?”

     

                Lena closed her eyes, grimacing as she suppressed a sigh. Opening her eyes again, she gave Andrea an irate glance, folding her arms over her chest, throat raw and the shallow cut on her arm stinging. It was silent for a moment and Andrea made a small sound of surprise, Sam now on her back, quiet and still but apparently herself, no one speaking for a moment.

     

                “Oh. I had thought you would have told her,” Andrea murmured.

     

                Kara was still looking at Lena, more confused but expectant as she waited patiently. A sigh passed Lena’s lips this time as she rubbed her brow, mouth a thin line as she stared at the stone floor.

     

                “My mother spoke truthfully when she said she didn’t drop me, but that was only a technicality. Sam had us both and was ordered to let me go. It’s as Andrea said - the Queen tells her to do something and her oaths take over Sam’s mind, forcing her to act as Reign, no matter how hard she tries to resist.”

     

                “You should have brought your concerns to me,” Kara tightly replied, rubbing her nose, which didn’t look broken and had stopped bleeding. “I would have helped her. None of this would have happened.”

     

                “Well, I didn’t know what you’d do,” Lena snapped, “and it’s not her fault. And I say that as someone who has no love for her, and very little reason to vouch for her, so …”

     

                Kara didn’t know what to say to that, a wounded look flickering in her eyes before she turned away, approaching Sam. Sinking to a crouch at her side, Kara pried apart the split leather of Sam’s leggings, humming as she eyed the gash.

     

                “It will need stitching. Lena will do it for you.”

     

                Eyes flitting to her wife’s back, Lena frowned slightly but didn’t say anything. Kara slipped out of the room and returned nearly ten minutes later with her arms full, sinking back to a crouch at Sam’s side. Sam was looking slightly pale, not necessarily from the small amount of blood welling up in the cut on her thigh, but from the whole ordeal. Laying everything out, Kara beckoned for Lena to join them and Sam worked her leggings down to bare her right thigh.

     

                Lena rinsed the gash out with the warm water Kara had fetched, and then slowly started to stitch it closed, a little clumsy with the needle but not as nervous as the time she’d stitched up her bleeding wife on a boat in the middle of the sea. Still, she felt guilt stab at her for injuring Sam, who remained quiet throughout, even if she did wince at the pain, and tried to be quick and careful. Pounding herbs into a paste, she then slathered the poultice over the crooked stitches and bandaged the wound loosely before sitting back, eyeing her handiwork.

     

                “My thanks,” Sam said after a moment, awkwardly clearing her throat. “And apologies.”

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena murmured.

     

                “Do not agitate it, Sam,” Kara said, climbing to her feet, looming over her, face clouded. “And perhaps no sparring until we can find a way to help ensure you are firmly yourself or Reign.”

     

                With a thin smile, Sam nodded and Kara met Lena’s eyes, jerking her head to the door. Following after her, arms folded over her chest like a sulking child, Lena felt tension in her shoulders as she trailed her wife through the hallways, Kara leading them down to the open chamber with the humid, damp smell of the hot springs. The main area was well-lit, stone pillars holding up the cavern’s ceiling, but Kara led them deeper, as she had last time, seeking out some privacy.

     

                Stripping off her clothes, Kara was a pale slip in the near-dark of the hotspring. Lena worked her way out of her layers, her dagger and robe forgotten about upstairs, discarding her clothes on the dry stone a safe distance from the edge. Her skin was ghostly in the dark, her hair in stark contrast, green eyes wide as she waited for her vision to adjust to the darkness. She could see the faint glimmer of light on the rippling surface of the ink-dark water and watched as it swallowed her wife’s pale legs, steam rising from the surface in a thin haze. Lena watched her, knowing how beautiful she would have looked, blonde hair unbound, otherworldly and infuriating but heartbreakingly handsome. Kara waded in deeper, soaking up to her shoulders, blonde hair fanning on the surface of the water for a moment before her head ducked under.

     

                Following after her a little slower, far warier, Lena sat on the cold edge of the rough stone as she dipped her legs in before the rest of her followed slowly. The water was pleasantly hot and the cut on her arm stung as she waded a little further away from the edge, the pool shallow enough that it didn’t even hit her shoulders if she stood to her full height. She met Kara’s gaze, the surface of the water rippling as it caught the dim light, and there was a moment of strange tension.

     

                “Why did you not tell me it was Sam?” Kara softly asked after a minute.

     

                Shrugging, Lena chewed her split lip, face rippling with pain as she forgot about it. “I didn’t want her to cop the blame.”

     

                “What did you think I’d do?”

     

                “I’m not sure. I don’t know if there’s … due processing here. It seems everyone kills as they please.”

     

                “You have studied our laws, you know that there are consequences, depending on the matter at hand.”

     

                “I just- I wouldn’t want you to get in trouble for behaving recklessly. And I don’t think it would be fair for Sam to suffer when- it was very obvious to me she was struggling with the orders my mother gave her. She didn’t want to do it; I could see it on her face.”

     

                “You are very forgiving, considering she killed your mother.”

     

                “I-” Lena faltered, eyelids shuttering as she swallowed thickly. “I don’t think I’ll ever be able to forgive that, but it was obviously something that she had little say in. I don’t think that’s right.”

     

                It fell silent for a moment and Lena felt exhausted. Her muscles burned pleasantly from her brief sparring but the emotional toll of the day was already more than she’d like to bear, and Lena felt tired, the hot water soothing her into a limp thing leaning back against the edge of the pool.

     

                “Will you come closer to me?” Kara whispered.

     

                Lena’s sore throat tightened and she looked down, still leaning back against the stone, feeling a little sullen. “Why?”

     

                “I want to feel your skin against mine.”

                

                “Do you? You’ve given me the opposite impression over the last few days.”

     

                Lena lifted her eyes at Kara’s weary sigh, unable to read her expression in the dark but feeling her pleading gaze. Face flushed and expression sullen, Lena ran a hand through her braided hair, the end of it soaked by the water as she slumped in the hot spring. She didn’t move as Kara moved towards her. Wet fingers slowly traced over Lena’s temples, cheeks, jaw, in a featherlight touch as Kara stood close to her, her breath warm on Lena’s lips as the sound of water filled the brief silence. 

     

                “That has not been my intended impression. I could not simply turn my back on you and leave you be. Even if I wished to. I am bound to stay with you, no matter how much it hurts you,” Kara murmured, her voice pained as her hands glided over Lena’s bruising throat.

     

                “It will be healed by tomorrow. It’s just … light bruising.”

     

                Kara’s hand slid over her shoulder and down to the shallow cut on Lena’s upper arm.

     

                “Little more than a scratch.”

     

                “You don’t understand,” Kara sighed. “Any mark upon you, be it a graze, a bruise, a scratch, is because of me. If I had not agreed to wed the elusive Unseelie Princess, you would not have been brought here to be hurt by me.”

     

                “But you haven’t hurt me. You’ve kept me safe.”

     

                “Not well enough at all. And it is as I say, a byproduct of my foolishness. I am … struggling to accept that, to bear the responsibility of your every hurt. It- it pains me. More than you can know.”

     

                “I came back,” Lena argued.

     

                “You wouldn’t have come back if you hadn’t come in the first place.”

                

                “Do we have to have this argument again? This isn’t some butterfly effect situation-”

     

                “What is that?”

     

                “I- you kill a butterfly and the whole world ends,” Lena flippantly explained, waving a dismissive hand.

     

                “How so?” Kara asked, amused as her voice softened.

     

                “It’s like a- a knock-on effect. Do you have dominos here? One thing leads to the next, to the next, to the next. Everything is a choice that has consequences, and this,” Lena gestured to her throat, “is a consequence of not speaking up about what’s going on with Sam. It’s no one’s fault, it’s merely what happened because I made a decision I thought was right. And I have to live with that, the same as everyone else, the same as you.”

     

                “My consequences are bigger.”

     

                Lena let out a rough laugh, her throat aching, and touched her forehead to Kara’s. “Well, that’s rather self-important of you.”

     

                “Wha- I’m thinking of you.”

     

                “Well, stop it. I’m more me than I’ve felt in my entire life, so maybe you should think about that, okay? I’ve learnt a lot, you know. I’ve even managed to survive three days alone in the forest, believe it or not, so, you know, I’m not so much of a lost cause as I used to be. I’m doing alright.”

     

                “I just walked in on you being strangled,” Kara softly exclaimed.

     

                With a scoff, Lena splashed water in her face, watching as Kara spluttered in surprise, wiping her eyes. “It’s all part of the learning curve, right? I won’t make that mistake again, so … problem solved. Don’t you think?”

     

                “You are a problem that I fear will never be solved,” Kara sighed, but Lena could tell that her broodiness had dissipated.

                

                “Ah, well, you’d be bored of me if I didn’t keep you on your toes.”

     

                “I could never grow bored of you.”

     

                “You’ll live an awfully long time; I’d never say never if I were you.”

     

                “I could live until the sun dies and the stars fade and you would still interest me as much as you have since the day we met. Of that I’m sure. You are too unpredictable, even in such a wild place.”

     

                “I think you’re confusing stupidity with unpredictability.”

     

                “You are far from stupid.”

     

                “Mm, well, I always feel like a complete idiot around you.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Because I want you to like me.”

     

                “I do.”

     

                “I know, but I think that’s only because I tried to make myself more likeable. I don’t think you’d like me so much if I was still a useless, sarcastic bitch all the time. I got over myself, eventually, but I don’t think you’d like me very much if we’d been married this long and were still at each other’s throats.”

     

                Standing close, her hands resting lightly on Lena’s waist, Kara hummed. “I liked you more than you give me credit for, but I will not say I’m not glad about how things are between us now. It’s much more pleasant to have you in my bed than to have you at my throat, as you say.”

     

                Her hands ghosted up Lena’s waist, and she cupped her face, leaning in slightly, her lips softly tracing over Lena’s mouth. Eyes closing, Lena let Kara kiss her, feeling her pulse quicken. She very quickly forgot about her sore throat and the tension between them of late, her whole body suffused with a keen ache for her wife as she thought about how long it had been since they’d been able to spend some time alone, undisturbed. At least, Lena hoped they wouldn’t be disturbed, thinking of the platform in the tree and the, admittedly thrilling, presence of others nearby, which had made it nigh on impossible for them to enjoy each other’s company the way that they would’ve liked.

     

                Kissing her with a little more fervour, Lena let her hands trace over Kara’s hot skin, nails digging shallow crescents into her back as she held her tightly. As Kara kissed her, lips bruising at the urgency, her fingers in her damp hair, tugging slightly, Lena felt the euphoric sense of relief wash through her as she banished any further anxious thoughts, feeling stupid as she realised that everything was fine, everything would be okay.

     

                Holding her against the edge of the pool, Kara tenderly kissed Lena’s bruised throat, her fingers cool and gentle, despite the rough calluses, and Lena tipped her head back, legs wrapped around her waist, feet in the warm water as she basked in her wife’s touch. It was exactly what she needed, a reminder of how easy it was between them, of how much she loved to be around Kara, how badly she wanted to be touched by her, wanted by her. The last few days were easily dismissed as Lena was laid back on the cold stone, legs over her wife’s shoulders, her only thought about how good it felt to have Kara’s lips kissing their way up her thighs.

     

                Afterwards, Kara’s forehead rested against Lena’s thigh as Lena’s breaths slowed, her skin flushed as the hazy satisfaction left her smiling with an arm flung over her face, she let out a breathless laugh, wishing that they could remain like that, tucked away from the world together. “God, you’re going to be the death of me.”

     

                She didn’t feel Kara stiffen, but she felt the absence of her touch as Kara lifted her head from Lena’s thigh, her hands dropping from her skin, shrugging Lena’s legs off her shoulders, limply splashing back into the water as Lena jolted with surprise. Pushing herself up slightly onto her elbows, blinking in surprise as she was pulled out of her blissful thoughts, Lena let out a confused laugh.

     

                Reaching for Kara, her fingers slipping over the wet skin of her chest, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Your turn?”

     

                Taking her hand, Kara removed it. “No.”

     

                With a small sound of protest, Lena’s expression furrowed. “Oh. Okay. You sure?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “I- sorry, just- am I missing something?”

     

                “What do you mean?”

     

                “You’re being very hot and cold.”

     

                “I was just giving you what you wanted; I was not asking for anything in return,” Kara shrugged.

     

                “What I wanted?” Lena spluttered. “I didn’t ask you to fuck me, so I don’t know why you’re acting like this was purely for my benefit.”

     

                Avoiding her gaze, Kara climbed out of the pool and stooped for her shirt, shrugging it on as Lena hurried to her feet. “I did not say that.”

     

                “What, so that’s it? You walk around here keeping everything to yourself and then decide we can have sex when it’s convenient for you, and then go straight back to avoiding me or avoiding talking about whatever it is that’s bothering you, even though you insist it’s not my fault? I’m not a toy. ”

     

                “No, indeed, you are a person who is not stupid and should know better than to make assumptions about how I’m feeling or behaving. You’re my wife by political arrangement; I’m not obligated to share my every thought with you.”

     

                Floundering at the rather cold and unexpected response, Lena watched Kara turn away and pick up her leggings, searching around for her other clothes. Seeing her cloak and jacket beneath Lena’s discarded tunic, Lena gathered them up as her eyes stung, feeling the heat moving up her neck as the breath hitched in her throat.

     

                “Asshole,” Lena snapped, throwing Kara’s clothes at her back.

     

                Surprised, a small sound escaping her as she turned and snagged her clothes before they fell to the ground, Kara was speechless for a moment as she stared at Lena with wide eyes. “Have I wronged you?”

     

                Cheeks flushing red, eyes bright with wounded tears as she clenched her teeth to keep her chin from wobbling, Lena’s anger dimmed as it was eclipsed by her fear, her sadness. “You’re leaving me.”

     

                “That’s absurd,” Kara softly replied, looking tired as her shoulders slumped. “I’m right here.”

     

                “Physically, but you- you’re pulling away - mentally. You won’t even talk to me anymore without behaving like … this. I’m not sure what happened, what I did-”

     

                “You didn’t do anything.”

                

                “Then what is it? Because I feel like I’m losing my fucking mind and I just- I want to help, and I’m trying to be understanding, but I don’t even know what the fucking problem is . It’s not right for you to do this, it’s not fair. Things have finally started to feel okay and now you-”

     

                Ducking her head, looking ashamed, Kara swallowed thickly. “You’re right. I’m sorry, it’s not intentional - but … they have only started to feel okay for you. ”

     

                Lena blinked, mouth opening and closing as she floundered for a moment. “Wha- I- well, what’s not okay? Just tell me that. Do you not want to be married to me anymore?”

     

                “No, it’s not that.”

     

                “Are you- are you tired of me?”

     

                “No, no, it’s not anything you have done. I’m- I’m merely … frightened.”

     

                “Frightened? Frightened of what?” A sickening thought struck Lena, her breath catching in her throat as she felt her stomach twist. “Have you met someone else? Have you- have you fallen for-”

     

                She couldn’t even finish her sentence, the small cavern deafeningly silent as they stood in the dimness, neither of them moving. Lena expected a scoffing dismissal from her wife but Kara remained silent for a long minute, each second making Lena’s body grow tenser as her heart thudded in her chest. Eventually, with a gravelly sigh, running a hand over her face, Kara replied.

                

                “Yes.”

     

                Lena’s stomach plummeted, shock slamming into her as she stared at her wife, speechless and disbelieving. Kara didn’t say anything else, didn’t tell her who or when, just met her wide eyes with a broken stare of her own, pre-emptive guilt and shame in the lines of her face. Pity overwhelmed any other feeling Lena was having and her expression crumpled, tense shoulders caving as she moved forward.

     

                “Oh, Kara,” she softly sighed, “I’m sorry.”

     

                She wanted to wrap her arms around her, hold her tightly, smooth her hair and comfort her, but the most she managed was touching Kara’s arm before her fingers slid off her skin and her hand hung limply at her side. With a weak smile, no longer meeting her gaze, Kara’s face rippled with pain.

     

                “You don’t have to be sorry,” she murmured.

     

                Lena didn’t know what to say, feeling sick, a heaviness in her chest as she pitied her wife, and other feelings that she hadn’t acknowledged yet. Reaching out, Kara touched Lena’s chin and her lips twitched with a ghost of a smile before her hand dropped away.

                

                “If my mind is brought to distraction, if you feel that I am not here , that is why. But it is not something I wish to speak about. It is not something I wish for you to help with; it is mine alone to manage.”

     

                “What else can I do?”

     

                Kara’s smile wavered, her eyes softly devastated, preemptively grieving the loss of the person she loved. “Nothing. Just … stay by my side, please.”

     

                “Always,” Lena mumbled before hesitating. “And what does this mean for us?”

     

                Letting out a choked laugh, Kara wrinkled her nose, cheeks shallowly dimpling, her eyes glassy with unshed tears. “You will always be my wife. Nothing will change.”

     

                Ducking her head in a nod, grimacing, Lena let out a soft sigh. She heard Kara swallow thickly, still clutching the remainder of her clothes, head bowed now as she didn’t look at Lena. “I would like to be alone for a moment.”

     

                “Of course,” Lena whispered, unmoving, feeling Kara’s lips brush over her cheek.

     

                Remaining rooted to the spot as her wife left, water drying on her skin, dark hair damp down her back, Lena waited until she couldn’t hear Kara’s footsteps anymore before letting out a ragged gasp of a breath. Sinking to the stone floor of the small cavern, Lena felt tears well up, and she didn’t know why she was upset, only that beneath the pity and empathy for her wife, there was a keen sense of heartbreak, of jealousy and longing that suffused her. 

     

                Breaking down into quiet sobs, the heels of her palms pressed into her eyes as tears wet her cheeks, Lena cried. Not because she thought that Kara loved her , but because she wished that she would.

    Chapter 38

                She didn’t go back to their room that night, missing dinner and wandering through the halls, poking in and out of rooms as she explored, trying to stamp down her feelings. Roaming freely, Lena realised the place was bigger than she’d originally thought, so many empty rooms tunnelling deeper into the foothills of the mountains, evidence of the few other fae who seemed to live and work there in the closed doors to living quarters or slight mess of belongings through open doors. She didn’t snoop but was curious about them, her rather narrow worldview restricted to those surrounding her and a season in the Unseelie Court, likewise tucked away for the most part. Lena had very little knowledge of how the fae lived in general.

     

                Stomach rumbling as she explored, she passed through rooms of stockpiled stores, of racks of weapons and armour, all sharp and well-oiled, large halls with rows of empty cots. Lena got lost, wandering the silent hallways as her bloodshot eyes and splotchy cheeks slowly faded, all evidence of her tears vanishing. Still, she couldn’t quite quell the frustration, the ache , and as the hour grew late and her eyes started to burn from tiredness, the crying spending her energy, she found herself in a room filled with healing supplies. Sinking to the cold stone floor, shelves were hewn into the walls surrounding her, crowded with glass jars and clay vessels, pestles and mortars, clusters of dried herbs and chests of cotton bandages, thin sinew and hooked needles. The smell was comforting, a mixture of earthy sweetness and bitterness, and Lena couldn’t see much once she’d shut the door on the dim torches in the hallway beyond, sitting alone in the dark as she rattled off lists of herbs and their properties in her mind until she drifted off.

     

                Waking hours later, cold and stiff, momentarily disoriented, she pushed herself to her feet. Lena had no concept of time within the dark confines of the mountain, unsure how long she’d been sleeping, but she woke in the same dismal mood she’d gone to sleep in and was opposed to the idea of finding her way back to their - Kara’s - quarters. It wasn’t out of any sort of blame Lena held towards her wife for falling in love with someone else, only that she felt some way about it and wasn’t sure she could stand in front of Kara with any sort of composure right then. It was a strange mixture of jealousy, jilted embarrassment and mournful resignation, as if she should’ve seen this coming, as if her marriage was about to end, despite what her wife said.  

     

                Resuming her aimless wandering, trying to soothe her wounded feelings while anxiously thinking of Kara, of how she was feeling, whether she should go to her, offer her what comfort she could. Lena wasn’t sure if that would make it worse; Kara had asked for space yesterday, and Lena wasn’t sure how long she needed. Instead, she walked and walked, bare feet scuffing over the stone floor, until she could smell manure in the still air, hear the soft snorts of the horses stabled near the entrance chamber and the sound of a cat chasing mice burrowing into the hay. Following the sound and smell, Lena reasoned that it was the perfect sort of company - they were living, breathing creatures but she wouldn’t feel obligated to talk and they wouldn’t intrude on her thoughts. 

     

                She hadn’t been there to help stable the horses after their arrival, so she was surprised by the sheer size of the stables, only two dozen stalls occupied and long rows of empty stalls disappearing into the dimly lit hall. Walking along the stalls, Lena found her mare quietly eating oats, tail swishing as her ears twitched at the sound of Lena’s footsteps. A smile quirked Lena’s lips as she leaned against the stone post of the stall, a rope fastened across the space to keep the horse inside. After a few minutes, Lena ducked under the rope and smoothed her hand along the flank of her mare, gliding up over her back and neck before she patted the mare’s nose. 

     

                Standing there a while, absentmindedly patting the horse as she brooded, Lena eventually went to fetch a brush to make better use of her time. Her horse was already well groomed, free of dust and dirt from travelling, bristly hair glossy and clean, but she gave her a good rubbing over and the mare finished with her oats and kept nosing Lena with soft snorts, eager for more gentle pats on her nose. The easy affection of the mare made Lena smile, some of her mood lightening as she leaned into her, warm and solid, and she didn’t move until she heard purposeful footsteps grow near.

     

                Brush in hand, she glanced over the stone wall, looking past the row of horses, and resumed brushing her mare as she ducked her head, a surliness stealing over her as she listened to footsteps approach.

     

                “There you are,” Kelly nonchalantly greeted her. “Kara was asking after you.”

     

                “Was she?” Lena indifferently replied.

     

                Humming as she hovered outside Lena’s stall, a heavy saddle in her arms, evidently on her way for a ride, Kelly studied her. Keeping her attention fixated on her repetitive brushing, Lena didn’t say anything else as she waited for her sister-in-law to speak or leave her be. Of course, Kelly opted for the former. 

     

                “You missed evening meal last night, and were not at breakfast this morning,” Kelly noted. “Have you eaten?”

     

                “No, I’m not-” Lena couldn’t finish her sentence, gritting her teeth with disgruntlement.

     

                Watching her, Kelly cocked her head to the side, neither of them speaking as Lena didn’t continue trying to wrap her tongue around the lie she’d tried to speak. Mouth turning down at the corners in a grimace, she cleared her throat and rounded her mare to tackle the other side, hoping to hide her disgruntled expression from view. Kelly continued to hover on the other side of the rope fence, letting the silence drag on for another agonising minute before she broke it. 

     

                “You are more downcast than you have been in weeks. Is something amiss?”

     

                Lena’s mouth thinned as she slowed in her motions before continuing again, brushing down the flank of the horse. “I’ll be fine. I just … have a lot on my mind.”

     

                “If you are looking for a listening ear, I will gladly lend mine.”

     

                “Thank you but I don’t want to talk about it right now.”

     

                “As you wish,” Kelly nodded, smoothing her palm over the velvety nose of Lena’s mare.

     

                They were silent for a moment and Lena tried not to look too brooding as she silently groomed the horse, stewing in her confusing emotions. She refused to try to make sense of them with any real honesty, not wanting to dive into the mess waiting for her if she gave up her ignorance. What good would it do? Lena had been hurt enough in her life; she didn’t need to add to her pain by trying to read into her unrequited feelings for her wife. Ignorance was better, would be preferable to the reckoning that would come of realising she was in love with Kara, the embarrassment of loving someone who loved someone else.

     

                “Come,” Kelly said with a small smile after the silence stretched on, her expression warm and understanding. “We shall take some air together.”

     

                “Hm?”

     

                “Saddle your horse. You are cooped up; it weighs on you, it is plain to see. I had planned to ride through the Vale, so you may join me.”

     

                Hesitating only momentarily, Lena nodded and ducked beneath the rope, moving through to the tack room, fetching a suitably sized saddle and carrying it back through. Kelly had moved to her horse’s stall and started saddling her own, both of them working in silence, although it took Lena a little longer to finish hers. She excused herself to quickly walk back to her shared quarters, warily sneaking inside and finding it empty as she hurriedly fetched her cloak and weapons, foregoing her boots when she couldn’t immediately place them in the tidied space. Pinning her cloak in place as she walked, bow, quiver and sword awkwardly bundled under her arm, Lena arrived back at the stables and deposited her armful of weapons before strapping them onto her body, stringing her bow and slinging them over her shoulder. 

     

                Kelly was already in the saddle and Lena swung up onto the back of her mare after leading her out of the stall. Letting Kelly lead on, they plodded out of the stables and turned down the hallway leading out into the vale spread out below. It was a mile of darkness and silence before the pinprick of light ahead made Lena’s heart soar. The smell of fresh air, untainted by the damp stone of the vents that brought it into the depths of the mountain, was so sweet as Lena perked up, the freshness of pine and grass, wood and sunshine carried on the breeze.

     

                When they emerged out of the open doors, Lena came to a stop, eyes closing as she breathed deeply, gratefully, her shoulders going slack as she felt the weak sunlight ghost over her cheeks and eyelids. It was still cool, despite being mid-morning by the position of the sun, and Lena basked in the freeing sensation of being out from under a mountain of stone. A little way ahead and off to her left, Kelly softly laughed and Lena opened her eyes, blinking at the brightness of daylight, taking in the cloudy pale blue sky and the stretch of trees and grass surrounding them, the snow-capped mountains to their backs.

     

                “The effect is immediate,” Kelly said with amusement. “You do not like to be kept indoors.”

     

                Lena let out a small laugh, her cheek dimpling with a grim smile. “I’m used to being indoors. Where I’m from, it’s all skyscrapers, just concrete and glass, and even the air isn’t that fresh. You’d think it wouldn’t bother me so much to stay inside when it’s all I’ve known, but … I think I’d hate to go back to that now. I think it would be a kind of … slow death.”

     

                “A captive animal does not know it’s held in a prison until it has been freed. It is natural that your soul aches for the trees after being given a taste of that home.”

     

                “Doesn’t it bother you? I mean, you spend so much of your time outdoors too, years , and she lives underneath a mountain. ”

     

                “Oh, well, this is not Alex’s home, as such. It is not her inheritance; her mother is a Lady, but her father was not of landed gentry, so until Eliza passes her halls onto Alex, she is without her own halls. This place is part of her duty, a reward from the Seelie Court for her prowess in war over these last years.”

     

                “So, what, she’s a Steward like J’onn? I thought that’s what Vasquez was.”

     

                “Vasquez is. Alex … well, she has been named Sentinel of the Vale, so her charge is to all who live within the Vale. It is a fortress, Lena. A garrison for our armies in retreat.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “She does not spend much time here, as she is serving the Court. As am I. We spend much of our time in border battles, or scouting, until late, so, yes, it bothers us both, but it is a necessity, out of everyone’s safety as much as Alex’s duty.”

     

                “So … is she like … a General or something?”

     

                Kelly laughed, “no, that’s Kara.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Your wife is our greatest living warrior, Lena. Surely you have seen her skill?”

     

                “Then why is she here? I mean, all of you … shouldn’t you be on the frontlines battling my brother?”

     

                “We have done as such for more than a decade, although it was not your brother orchestrating it then, but your mother as Queen of the Unseelie. Other things of greater importance have since drawn us away from the frontlines.”

     

                “What could be so important that your greatest warrior gets called away from a war?”

     

                Eyes sliding sideways as she smiled faintly, holding her reins in hand as they rode side by side down the sloping grass of the vale, Kelly raised her eyebrows slightly. “Her wife.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena’s mouth opened and closed as she was struck speechless for a moment, looking affronted. “Well, I- that’s not true. I’m not more important than making sure the Unseelie don’t slaughter the entirety of the Seelie Court.”

     

                “You are to her. And to any who hope for peace. Well, we all thought your marriage had earned us peace, but it is rather unfortunate your brother is not dead. If it were not for him, peace might have stood a while longer, and once you took your mother’s throne, it would have stood even longer. Alas, war is brewing as the skirmishes grow more frequent.”

     

                “Then go back. Surely you’re all needed back there to help?”

     

                “And would you stay behind if she went?”

     

                “I- well, no, obviously. I’d go with her.” 

     

                “And that would put you directly in the path of your brother, who would have your head. Kara will not risk putting you anywhere near him, if it can be avoided. So, she relegates herself to the rear of the fighting, knowing that she cannot leave you behind, that you will not stay behind. She has made her promises, for good or ill.”

     

                “You make me sound awfully selfish,” Lena murmured, somewhat surly. 

     

                Deliberating, head cocked to the side as a thoughtful look crossed her face, Kelly dubiously hummed. “No, I do not think it makes you selfish, as such. Of course, it would make it easier if you would agree to stay, but if I put myself in your place, I would find us in agreement; for me, it would be an almost physical pain to be away from Alex. I’m uncertain of how you would feel about it …”

     

                Her eyes slid sideways to Lena, judging her expression, waiting for her to give away some sign. Lena’s expression was impassive, or rather, her expression was as furrowed as usual, revealing nothing about what she was feeling. 

     

                “Well, that matters not,” Kelly continued a moment later, urging her horse ahead as they picked up the pace a little. “You shall not be left behind, but we shall not go any further east at present for that very reason. I hope that offers you some comfort.”

     

                “A little,” Lena admitted.

     

                They were deeper into the vale now, their horses trampling over long, waving grass as the wind swept through, trees sighing and a few red-tailed deer perking up, tense and watchful as they continued past. A few large clouds drifted overhead, the weak sunlight warmer than it had been in a while, and Lena basked in it, looking around at the beauty of the place. Behind them, mountain peaks pressed up against each other, and the sky felt unbelievably close and wide, stretching away from the mountains, cloudy blue to the east and south. The wind had a bite to it though, whistling down from the mountains with the smell of snow.

     

                Lena was just grateful for the clean air, no tang of salt on the breeze as they were too far from the sea, and she found it beautiful as they passed through golden fields and green meadows, beneath boughs of trees that had grown slightly crooked from the wind, branches bare in the early spring. Moving deeper into the shade of the forest, they encountered small pockets of water still rimed with ice, the temperature plummeting where the light couldn’t reach the forest floor, the canopy too high, the dimness making Lena feel a little uneasy as she followed on Kelly’s flank. Nothing stirred though, save the usual sounds of the forest, bird calls echoing through the trees and Lena’s breath hanging in the air before her as her mare plodded onwards.

     

                It was silent for the most part, neither of them talking for a while as they carried onwards, noon almost upon them before long, and Lena guided her horse down a stream bank and crossed the rocky shallows as she listened to the tinkling sound of running water. Her lungs ached from the cold and her fingers were red but she had no complaints, enjoying the peace, finding it pleasant to be trekking through the forest when it was for enjoyment instead of the harried race through the Court for their safety. With Kelly ahead of her and her own bow held in hand, Lena wasn’t worried for her safety, even if the dimness persisted, the trees growing taller as they blotted out all but the faintest hint of green light high above in the canopy.

     

                When passing by a tree of fairly ordinary height, Kelly stood in her stirrups as she passed beneath the branches, using the wind to help shake loose a few rosy apples she’d spotted, deftly snagging them as they fell down to her. Lena sidled past her and she turned at the sound of her name being called, eyebrows rising before surprise flashed across her face, an apple lobbed towards her. It arced overhead and she stood in her stirrups, reaching up to pluck it from the air and righting herself with a laugh. 

     

                “You have changed much of late,” Kelly noted as she observed her settle back on her saddle. “You are not the same woman I first met. That woman would barely speak, was frightened and helpless, but you have learnt much, even since returning from the Unseelie Court. You may have always had the beauty of the fae but it was plain to see you were not one of us, but now, you sit a horse well, are confident enough to stand in your stirrups, you have held your own in battle and wield a bow proficient enough, you speak our tongue and you laugh and help. It is good to see you have grown comfortable in yourself and it is good to consider you a friend, as well as family.”

     

                Hesitating as she bit into the apple she held but didn’t bite all the way through, tasting the juice on her tongue as she paused, still a little bitter, not quite ripe as it was a little too early in the season for that, Lena pulled her mouth free. Clearing her throat, she shrugged as she gestured vaguely with her apple. “I guess.”

     

                “And in seeing you as a friend, I hope you view me similarly, and that you might talk to me about anything you find yourself unable to talk to Kara about.”

     

                “Like …?” Lena hedged.

     

                Shoulders slumping slightly as she suppressed a sigh, Kelly briefly closed her eyes, grimacing. “Anything you wish to.”

     

                With a quiet snort, Lena rolled her eyes and shook her head, following Kelly along the shallow bed of a stream, ducking her head as they wove between drooping willows. Brushing a slender branch aside, her horse skirting around a clump of wild rosebushes as the sound of gently flowing water filled the beat of silence, Lena sighed.

     

                “You know, you’re starting to sound a lot like the shrinks they used to make me see when I was in the foster system. They were always trying to get me to talk about things, but they wouldn’t tell me what they wanted me to talk about, like it was some sort of … test. So, if you have something you’d like to ask me, Kelly, just ask.”

     

                Leading them further from the stream, they walked a path through tall grass, clusters of wildflowers, toadstools and bog myrtle liberally growing, everything so green and rich, moss and lichen covering every available surface, the smell of firs, smoke and the dampness of freshwater perfuming the air, Kelly didn’t speak. Lena thought that was the end of it for a moment, that her sister-in-law had either decided to mind her business or couldn’t pluck up the nerve to ask her what she so pressingly wanted Lena to divulge. But Kelly had always been frank and she pulled up short so that Lena could catch up to her, before nudging her horse to keep pace with Lena’s plodding mare.

     

                “I suppose I’m curious about the nature of your relationship with Kara,” her sister-in-law mused, head cocked to the side, chin angled up slightly as she spoke slowly, dark eyes searching the canopy overhead. She looked curious, more than anything, as if it was simply in her nature to want to know the answer to that. Lena couldn’t find herself to feel irritated, at any rate.

     

                Still, her answer was as dismissive as could be. “Well, the nature is she’s my wife.”

     

                “Very clever. You know what I am asking. If you will not answer, then say so.”

     

                “Has she- has she said anything to you?” Lena hedged, an anxious edge to her wary expression. “About- about her … prophecy?”

     

                “No,” Kelly slowly replied. “Although, she has spoken with her sister, so I am … aware of her circumstances.”

     

                “Oh. So, you know that she …?”

     

                Hesitating, Kelly glanced sideways at Lena. “What do you know?”

     

                “That she’s fallen in love.”

     

                “Ah. Yes, yes, I know that.”

     

                “I’m just- I’m worried about her,” Lena sighed with a pained look. 

     

                Her shoulders slumped and she looked over at Kelly, an ache in her gaze, the corners of her eyes creased with the strain of her worry. She came to a stop, her horse shifting beneath her as a gentle wind blew through the trees, and Kelly reined her own in as she glanced back at Lena, her expression briefly unreadable, a faint flicker of surprise in her dark eyes.

     

                “About her?”

     

                “Yes! Of course I’m worried about her. How could I not be? I mean, one of the first things I knew about her was how she never wanted to fall in love, how afraid of that she was. And now she has, and I feel sorry for her, but I don’t know how to help her.”

     

                “I don’t believe it’s something you can help with. I think understanding is perhaps the greatest gift you can give her at the moment.”

     

                “Of course I’m understanding. Well, I don’t understand what she’s going through, but I know it must be hard. Not that she wants to talk to me about it.”

     

                “Well … you are taking it remarkably well.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena ran a hand over her face, “how else am I supposed to take it? We were married out of mere convenience; she was always going to fall in love with someone, although she insists that it won’t change anything between us. I find that hard to believe though, even if I don’t know who I’ll have to fight for her attention.”

     

                Kelly blinked, her face suddenly grave as her horse softly whickered, picking up on her agitation. “She didn’t- she didn’t … tell you who?”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena smiled thinly, a little bitterly. “No. No, she didn’t. I don’t think she will. Maybe she’s trying to spare my feelings. It’s kind of her, but it won’t change anything, won’t make much of a difference.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                There was a beat of silence and Lena gave Kelly an apprehensive look. “Do you know who it is?”

     

                Hesitating momentarily, Kelly cleared her throat, a furrow between her eyebrows as her mouth thinned. “She has not told me.”

     

                “Oh. Yeah, I guess she probably doesn’t want anyone to know. You know as well as I do how she feels about … this.”

     

                “I suppose I just wondered how you felt.”

     

                Surprised by the forthright question, finally, Lena rubbed her brow as she swallowed drily. There was an ache in her chest and she had to swallow past the lump in her throat before she could respond, her voice a little raw, a little ragged. “How I feel doesn’t matter. She’s all I care about and I know she’s not taking it well. I just- I wish she would come to me with it.”

     

                Looking torn, Kelly agonised over the morality of telling Lena that Kara was in love with her, of revealing what wasn’t hers to tell, of keeping Kara’s secret for her, even to both women’s detriment. Watching the defeated slump of Lena’s shoulder, the rather despondent air about her, Kelly knew that as fond as she was of the Princess, she could never betray Kara’s trust. For all she believed that Lena returned Kara’s feelings - even if Lena was not so aware of them herself - it wasn’t Kelly’s place to ruin this semblance of peace the wives had created for themselves amidst so much uncertainty and trouble.

     

                With a resigned sigh, Kelly gestured to the wide trunk of an ancient, mossy tree as she stopped. “Here, let’s stop for a while.”

     

                Swinging down from her saddle, Kelly smoothed a hand over her horse’s back and left it to graze as Lena likewise dismounted. Still clutching her bow and the bitten apple in hand, she looked around, tall trees penning them in, the smell of the forest heady and sweet as she closed her eyes, bare feet burrowing into damp clover that reached past her ankles. 

     

                With a soft groan, Lena practically keeled over in it, the soft carpet pillowing her body as she spread her arms and legs wide, blinking up at the canopy, a dizzyingly far distance above her. She felt so small, so clueless. Running a hand over her face, she sighed and then turned her head as Kelly gracefully sat beside her with barely a sound, folding her legs and holding the apples she’d plucked in the hem of her cloak.

     

                “Eat up,” she ordered Lena, tossing her another apple.

     

                Snatching it out of the air, Lena pushed herself up onto her elbows and turned the other apple she’d bitten, finding the crescent her teeth had left in the rosy skin and taking a bite out of it. Chewing slowly, she basked in the fresh air and the freedom of being outdoors. Yes, it was a touch too cold and she was regretting not putting on shoes, but Lena wished it could be like that all the time. She felt a keen ache of longing for the forest, forgotten about until she was back amongst it. It was true that the relief had been immediate, but she still felt so keyed up, so tense with the weight of her troubles. Taking another bite, she sighed again, frowning as she made quick work of the rest of the apple before lobbing the core at the trunk of the nearest tree before flopping back down. The other apple was left in her lap and she closed her eyes, digging the heels of her hands into her eyes.

     

                “Come on,” Kelly gently coaxed her, climbing to her feet and dusting herself off. “You need to vent your frustration. Pick up your bow.”

     

                Dropping her hands, Lena cracked one eye open and stared up at Kelly. “It won’t help.”

     

                “You don’t know that until you try. Come, on your feet. You will practice archery, or I am willing to beat you bloody and bruised, which will not be as satisfying for you as target practice.”

     

                “Mm, that’s debatable. It would be more of a distraction, at least.”

     

                “You do not need distraction. What you need is the opposite of that, you need to focus. Come, I will not ask again.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, exasperated by the insistence, Lena pushed herself to her feet and picked up her discarded bow. Removing an arrow from her quiver, she fit it to the bowstring and lightly rested her fingers on the string, arching an eyebrow at Kelly. “Target?”

     

                Tapping her lip in thought, Kelly gestured to the knot of an oak tree barely visible past the trunks of other trees blocking the way, a distance of two hundred feet and a challenge for Lena’s middling skill. Still, she always felt she had something to prove and didn’t waver as she took up her stance, drawing the string back smoothly as she sighted the target, a narrow window of perhaps five feet afforded to her. It went slightly wide, striking the trunk of an elm tree a hundred feet in, ricocheting off the splintering bark and disappearing into the gloom.

     

                Mouth thinning with disgruntlement, Lena knocked another arrow, loosing again. This time she was going to hit the trunk, albeit too low for her target, but an unnatural gust of wind blew her arrow off course. With a stubborn just of her chin, shoulders squaring, Lena turned her accusing stare on Kelly. “You did that on purpose.”

     

                “You have to account for unforeseen circumstances. If this was a battle, your pause could have meant your death; the correct response would have been to shoot again, as quickly as possible.”

     

                Shooting again, Lena watched the arrow veer off its course but quickly had another arrow following on its flights, anticipating Kelly’s interference. Her arrow struck a little high and to the left of the whorled knoll marking the wide trunk. Kelly made a sound of approval and Lena continued to shoot until her quiver was empty, striking the trunk often, but always off her mark. She shattered a few more arrows on her wonky shots, but was relatively consistent. Enough so that after she’d crossed the long distance to the tree and fetched her arrows, salvaging others along the way, Kelly lightly tossed an apple in one hand, glancing from it to Lena with a thoughtful look on her face, before she tossed it up.

     

                “Loose.”

     

                Slow to process the order, Lena let out a sound of confusion and watched as the apple slowed, rotating as Kelly kept it airborne, before flinging it skywards again.

     

                “Again.”

     

                Spluttering, Lena knocked an arrow, drew it back and loosed it as she tried to judge the speed of the falling apple. She missed by a mile, her arrow lost in the foliage as the apple thunked to the ground. With a sigh, Kelly clicked her tongue, stooping to scoop it up again, backing away and then tossing it in a gentle arc. Trying again, Lena missed.

     

                “Come on, Lena, you can do better than that,” Kelly goaded her. “You’ve killed a moving target before.”

     

                Gritting her teeth as anger flickered through her, Lena knocked another arrow with a scoff. “It was a barely moving duck, not an apple flying at my head.”

     

                “People are much bigger targets - and slower .”

     

                It took another dozen attempts, and Kelly’s unfailingly encouraging coaching as Lena’s patience wore thin, before she managed to spear an apple with an arrow, seemingly by sheer luck. Still, Kelly was stoked, and Lena felt a prickle of satisfaction as well, listening to the other woman prattle off tips about factoring in speed and weight to determine how to aim accordingly. Lena’s mind was on other things, things she hadn’t been able to distract herself from while shooting, and perhaps that was Kelly’s intention from the beginning, but regardless, it worked as Lena couldn’t help but voice her train of thought.

     

                “Kelly, do you think you can love someone on sight? Like, don’t you think it’s a little superficial? Because I’ve been trying to figure it out, and I don’t think Kara was in love when we left your mother’s home, but the only people we’ve been around since we left were people she’s known a long time, your brother’s soldiers, my mother and her Unseelie, and those Rangers at the crossing,” Lena blurted out without pause. “I mean, I highly doubt she’d ever be able to fall in love with an Unseelie, just on account of my Court being responsible for orphaning her, and it seems like she knows pretty much everyone else at least decently enough to have had an inkling in the past, which leaves the Rangers, but … I don’t really buy it, you know? I don’t think you can fall in love at first sight. It’s- it’s shallow , and Kara’s not a shallow person. She’s … anything but that, but how do I convince her that she’s wrong? That just because she was … sucked in by a pretty face, it doesn’t make it love. She can’t just- she can’t just say she’s in love if she doesn’t even know the person.”

     

                “Well …” Kelly cautiously started, surprised by Lena’s tirade, “I- maybe she does know them. I won’t presume to know the depths of her feelings. But , it might interest you to know that I have been in love twice in my life-”

     

                “Yes, that too! You can love more than one person in a lifetime, so why is she so sure this is the person she’s going to kill?”

     

                “Again, I won’t presume to know how Kara feels on the matter, only that she must be sure to have admitted to her feelings. As I was saying, I have been in love twice, though, once as you describe it, where it was at first sight with Alex, and before that, with someone I had fought beside for years before realising the depth of my feelings. And Alex has loved twice too, in the opposite order, where it was at first sight the first time and then, secondly, took her a little longer to realise her feelings for me. Love … is never one thing . You may be correct in your assumption, but you could only be correct about it in regard to your feelings for … whoever you deign to love.”

     

                Rubbing her forehead as she sighed roughly, Lena’s mouth turned down slightly at the corners. “She’s just- she’s acting as if she’s signed the death warrant for someone she might not actually be in love with. It’s- it’s rash, it’s ridiculous.”

     

                Lena’s blustering objections petered off into silence and Kelly studied her for a moment, a tender look of understanding and pity on her face as her shoulders sloped. “You feel betrayed.”

     

                Gritting her teeth as she squeezed her eyes shut, Lena inhaled deeply through her nose, her mouth dry and her palms clammy around the smooth wood of her bow. She didn’t want to admit that Kelly was right, that Lena did feel betrayed, as if Kara had elbowed her out of the centre of her attention to make way for someone else, someone better , someone she loved.

     

                “You are jealous, too,” Kelly murmured. “You have denied it before but do you lo-”

     

                “No,” Lena snapped as her eyes shot open, two spots of colour flooding her cheeks as she angrily pointed a finger at Kelly. “Now you presume to know how I feel.”

     

                Stomping over to her horse, off grazing at the roots of a maple tree, Lena flung herself up into the saddle as the mare pressed her ears flat at the sudden agitation radiating from Lena. Settling comfortably, gathering up the reins, Lena’s face was red with embarrassment, anger and fear, and she wanted to bolt through the forest but was above such recklessness now. Instead, swallowing her pride and her wounded feelings, she waited for Kelly to wearily climb into the saddle to guide them.

     

                “Would you like to go home?”

     

                “Yes, please,” Lena stiffly replied, cringing internally at her churlish behaviour.

     

                Kelly just nodded, clicking her tongue as she urged her horse onwards. Lena wasn’t to know that she didn’t take them straight back the way they’d come, but in a circuitous loop back through the forest, prolonging the trip as they made further south first, Kelly trying to give Lena time to calm herself with even breaths of fresh air and the open outdoors around them. To take her straight back beneath the mountain, which was admittedly a reasonable distance away to let her vent some of her frustration in the hour and a bit it would take them to ride back, wouldn’t bode well for anyone. 

     

                Instead, she led them home in a roundabout way, skirting south of the vales spread out from the mountain foothills, and with the looming peaks of the mountains blotted out by the soaring trees, Lena was none the wiser. Stewing in her annoyance, her heart still somewhat pounding with the panic of Kelly touching far too close on her real feelings, still stubbornly denied as Lena stamped it down, Lena didn’t speak as they rode up inclines and down sloping earth, feeling far too tense and projecting that onto the forest. It was as if she was waiting for something to give, alert for danger as she sat rigidly in her saddle, only making the ride bumpier for herself, knowing her ass and her thighs wouldn’t thank her for it in the morning.

     

                Still, as they precariously picked their way down another slope, winding through trees, the sudden sound of a panicked cry made her stomach clench, and Kelly jerked up in her saddle, tense and alert as they both strained their ears. Voices pitched high with youth carried on the wind, their words inaudible but their distress evident, and Kelly spurred her horse onwards only a second before Lena scrambled to do the same. Trusting her horse to navigate her own way through the uneven terrain of the forest ground, Lena gripped her bow and the reins tightly in two fists, shoulders hunched as she ducked low in the event of a low hanging branch, charging through the forest as the voices grew louder. So did the sound of running water.

     

                She saw the flicker of dappled sunlight on water a moment before her mare broke through the treeline and onto a narrow sliver of a riverbank, a wide river cutting through the forest. Pulling up short, Lena’s head whipped around, trying to track the source of the voices, watching as Kelly swung down off her horse and plunged into the frigid water, where four fae children were struggling - or rather, three were struggling to haul in one limp one. Pale-faced with worry, Lena swiftly dismounted, although she couldn’t bring herself to step foot into the river. Instead, she anxiously wrung her hands and watched Kelly wade in. 

     

                It wasn’t particularly deep - Kelly was up to her thighs when she reached the children, and she was quite short - but the water moved swiftly, the three children soaked up to their chests, none of them older than ten, Lena guessed. It didn’t take long for Kelly to grab the limp form of the dark-haired boy from the other three children and their struggling forms, heaving him over her shoulder and grabbing handfuls of clothes as she towed them all towards the riverbank. Rocking on her heels as she toyed with her fingers, Lena reached forward as soon as Kely was close enough to the riverbank to hand off two of the kids to Lena, who gripped their sodden clothes and hauled them onto dry land. 

     

                They were both breathless and wide-eyed with fear, getting their feet beneath them as Kelly climbed out of the river with the other two, letting go of a redheaded girl and gently laying the boy down on the grass. Lena touched the shoulders of the two she’d grabbed and looked them over before determining they were fine and turning her attention to the boy that Kelly loomed over.

     

                “We need a Waterfolk, now,” Kelly ordered the wide-eyed children. “Go!”

     

                A little girl set off, bare feet quickly flattening the grass underfoot as she raced towards the trees, vanishing from sight a moment later. Lena took in the shockingly white pallor of the young boy’s face, deathly pale with bluish lips, his chest not moving. Dropping to her knees on the spongy grass of the riverside, Lena stared at the drowned form with wide eyes, dread pooling in her stomach.

     

                “Kelly, you need to help him.”

     

                Reaching out, Kelly pressed two fingers to the boy’s throat, a stern look of grim concentration on her face before her mouth thinned. “No pulse.”

     

                “Help him,” Lena insisted. “You’re a healer - do CPR!”

     

                “What?”

     

                Aghast, Lena stared at her for a moment with parted lips before she pushed herself up onto her knees and loomed over the boy. Hands over his chest, Lena started chest compressions, mumbling the vague tune of Stayin’ Alive that she’d learnt to keep time with at the First Aid course she’d done in her early twenties. Kelly let out a squawk of surprise as she watched her with consternation, and Lena shot her a panicked look.

     

                “What are you doing?” Kelly exclaimed. “You’ll break his chest.”

     

                “You need to give him air.”

     

                “His lungs are full of water.”

     

                “He’s not breathing. He needs air,” Lena ground out through gritted teeth as she continued her chest compressions. “Trust me.”

     

                Hesitating only briefly, Kelly worked the boy’s mouth open and funnelled air into his lungs in a far more effective method than mouth-to-mouth, Lena thought. Feeling sweat prickle her back as she continued her compressions while Kelly kept supplying fresh oxygen, Lena didn’t stop, even when minutes passed and her arms started to ache from the exertion, not until the boy suddenly gasped, eyelids fluttering, and retched up river water as he arched on the ground and she snatched her hands back. 

     

                Rolling him onto his side, Lena whacked his back as he continued to cough up water, his breaths sawing in and out with a hoarse rasp, chest heaving as he quietly groaned. Sinking onto the grass, spent, Lena breathed heavily as she wiped her face with a fistful of her cloak, Kelly staring at her with renewed interest, with shock .

     

                “What was that?”

     

                “What?”

     

                “He was- he was dead. He had no pulse, his heart was not beating.”

     

                “Don’t you … have CPR here?” Lena breathlessly asked, tipping her clammy face up as the breeze caressed her flushed cheeks.

     

                “Sepia? That’s a colour.”

     

                “Not sepia , CPR. It’s- well I can’t remember the acronym right now but it- it’s resuscitation, you know? Bringing someone back from the edge of death. You- you keep their heart beating for them and make sure they have air until … well, this.”

     

                Gesturing tiredly to the boy, who was looking a little frazzled as he weakly pushed himself up, hair plastered to his cheeks, which were reddening from the exertion of his coughing. Kelly gave Lena an even wider look of surprise while rubbing the boy’s back, murmuring gently to him as the sound of footsteps became audible on the wind.

     

                Two fae came running through the trees with the little girl lagging behind, their hair braided with polished river stones and threads of silver, their clothes in shades of blue and grey. They slowed at the sight of the boy sitting upright, the two other children warily standing nearby, clinging to each other with fear. The man looked around with confusion.

     

                “Who …?” he asked, trailing off.

     

                Kelly gestured to the sodden boy as she pushed herself to her feet. “He’s alright.”

     

                The woman drifted closer and sank to a crouch, her brow furrowed as she reached out a hand to touch his chest, cocking her head to the side before she looked up, deep blue eyes meeting Kelly’s gaze. 

     

                “The girl said he was drowning. There’s no water in his lungs.”

     

                “He had no pulse, drew no breath. Her Highness brought him back.”

     

                The woman’s attention turned to Lena, wariness and shock flashing across her face. “It wouldn’t be possible for her to be a Waterfolk.”

                

                “I’m not,” Lena wearily replied, climbing to her feet.

     

                “Then what Unseelie magic is this?”

     

                “It’s not magic, it’s science. Healing.”

     

                The man made a sound of objection at the back of his throat. “It’s not possible. Death is final; there is no coming back from it.”

     

                “He was … on the brink,” Lena tried to explain, rubbing her brow. “Just … take him to a proper healer; I’m not so good at that.”

     

                They both floundered for a moment and the woman helped the boy to his feet, smoothing his wet hair down. “We shall fetch his mother; come, Val.”

     

                “Your Highness,” the man said, giving Lena a shallow bow before he glanced at Kelly and nodded politely to her.

     

                They corralled the other children, all of them graceful and slight, almost cherubic in their etherealness, and Lena ran a hand through her snarled hair, yesterday’s braids coming undone, the front of her clothes damp and dirty. With a sigh, she wearily pushed herself to her feet and then reached a hand down to Kelly, who hadn’t moved. Glancing up at her, looking unnerved and apprehensive, Kelly took her hand and Lena hauled her up before picking up her discarded bow and making for her horse. 

     

                Back up in the saddle, Lena felt the adrenaline waning, leaving her feeling somewhat hollow - although that could’ve been from the little food she’d eaten in the last day - and her hands shook a little as she gripped her bow and the reins tightly. Kelly didn’t speak as she hauled herself up into her saddle and set off slowly, almost as if in a daze. Silence kept them company as they plodded along the river for a while, the sound of running water along their left, while the shade of the forest clung to their right, trees rustling and sighing, frogs croaking and fish splashing. It felt picturesque but Lena felt a little jittery, caught off guard by the close encounter with death. And it wasn’t as if she hadn’t seen her fair share of it by now, but it struck her that it was the first time she’d seen a child, and knew from her lessons how cherished they were, especially with a population that had severely dwindled over the last few centuries. But she’d saved him.

     

                They’d barely made it five miles, veering off to the right as they slipped back into the forest as Lena kept turning that fact over in her mind, before she let out a quick laugh. Kelly’s head sharply turned towards her and Lena laughed again, almost breathless as her face crumpled. Turning to meet Kelly’s bewildered gaze, she laughed again, shoulders shaking, unable to stop herself as she came to a halt. Closing her eyes, she tipped her head back as she inhaled deeply, the tension seeming to bleed out of her as she sagged where she sat, a serene look smoothing out the lines of her face as a smile curved the corners of her mouth.

     

                “Are you alright?” Kelly quietly asked.

     

                Nodding, her eyes still shut, pure relief spreading through her chest, elation radiating from her, Lena sighed heavily. “I really, really needed that. I really needed something good to happen today.”

     

                Kelly was silent for a second. “Open your eyes.”

     

                Where they’d just been, a patch of trees covered in lichen and moss, brambles and creeping plants, everything still rather bare in the early spring, was suddenly transformed. Blinking in surprise, Lena looked around at the vivid green of her surroundings, of the new shoots, new leaves, budding flowers and unripe berries that had sprouted where there had been nothing but the tiniest of buds. All around her, spring had been ushered in and her smile grew, delight buoying in her chest as she cocked her head to the side and then glanced at Kelly.

     

                “Huh. Well, I guess that’s good, isn’t it? I didn’t take out half of the forest with me.”

     

                A smile quirked Kelly’s lips and she nodded. “You have a knack for giving life.”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena murmured, her brow pinching into a bewildered furrow. “Maybe I do.”

     

                Shaking her head as her eyebrows rose and fell quickly, as if trying to shake off the confusion, but still dwelling in that feeling of lightness, Lena nudged her horse onwards as Kelly rode alongside her. They didn’t make it very far before Kelly spoke, her eyes trained on Lena for a few hundred feet before she broached the question that had been burning on the tip of her tongue since the riverside.

     

                “Lena? How … how did you do that?”

     

                “What, the trees? Your guess is as good as mine, I don’t-”

     

                “No, no, not- not the trees, the boy. He was- he was dead.”

     

                Lena looked at her with surprise, observing the mystified look of awe on her sister-in-law’s face as she tried to figure it out. “Oh. Well, it’s like I said, you just- you keep their heart beating for them until it restarts - if it restarts - and you just- well, you have to make sure they’re getting air too, otherwise they’ll just suffocate and their brain will die, um, and, well, their heart might not restart but it’s … well, it’s a way to give people a fighting chance, right? You- you don’t have that here? CPR? Is it called something else?”

     

                “I- no,” Kelly spluttered, “no, we don’t bring people back from the dead here.”

     

                “It’s not- I mean … if he was dead dead, no one could bring him back. It’s just- it’s science, it’s- I mean, I’m not a doctor, hell, I’d barely qualify as any sort of healer, unless it was like … a last resort. You’d probably have better luck-”

     

                “No, I’ve never brought someone back like that, I- and this is a common human thing to do?”

     

                “Yeah, at a hospital. It’s not like I’ve ever had to do it before, but I’m glad I went to that First Aid course. Never thought I’d need to put it into practice though.”

     

                “This is something they teach you?”

     

                “Yes, at a First Aid course. They teach you how to give CPR, do the Heimlich - um, that’s to help someone choking - wrap bandages, make a tourniquet, use an Epipen - that’s to help with allergies, you know, like peanuts or bee stings-”

     

                “Bee stings?”

     

                “Are bee allergies a thing here? God, this is so strange, I mean, you guys don’t have penicillin, I know that already, and your healing is like … centuries behind modern medicine, so I shouldn’t be surprised by how different it is but … how do you not know CPR? How am I able to save a kid’s life with a half-assed First Aid course knowledge and you’re this amazing healer and you don’t even know what that is? Isn’t that the strangest thing?”

     

                Looking uncomfortable, perhaps a little perturbed at Lena’s line of reasoning, about how Kelly should know things like that if she was truly a healer, especially if Lena knew it and she was all but rudimentary at it, Kelly hummed dubiously. “Yes, it is all … very strange.”

     

                With a soft snort, Lena rubbed her tired eyes and shook her head before they continued onwards. It was rather uneventful then, the only other disturbance aside from the birds flitting back and forth being an enormous deer slowly stepping through the trees, thirty feet tall and watching them with dark, liquid eyes from the gloomy depths of the forest. The day hadn’t warmed much and Lena shivered in her damp clothes, her breath still visible before her, mud drying on her feet, thistledown clinging to the hem of her cloak. She ached to be back beneath the mountain, if only for a bath, dry clothes and something hot to eat.

     

                By the time they reached the eastern vale, still miles away from Alex’s home, she felt stiff and some of her bewildered exuberance had dimmed. The sky had grown cloudier while they’d been in the forest, and Kelly commented that it was going to snow soon, smelling it on the wind as Lena stared at the dark clouds sweeping south from the mountains. Even as they rode the rest of the way home, there was a palpable shift in the air, the temperature plummeting, and they picked up the pace a little as the sunlight dimmed, still early afternoon but the day feeling surly and ominous, contrary like Lena’s emotions. 

     

                Trotting up the long corridor up to the entrance chamber, the chill emanated from the stone walls closing in around them and the shadows encroached, only evenly spaced torches lighting the way after hours of broad daylight and wide open fields, slopes and trees. Lena was already feeling the weight of so much stone closing in around her, but she’d had enough for one day, and comfort won over freedom as she walked her mare into the stables and slowly went through the motions of unsaddling her and rubbing her down, carefully tending to the horse before she tended to her own needs.

     

                She didn’t see Kara as she slipped back into their shared quarters, the fire in the hearth making it stiflingly warm, and she quickly found clean clothes for herself before making her way down through the mountain hallways to the hot springs.
