She only got lost three times and considered that acceptable, before she found the shallowest pool possible, unnerved by the wide springs and the unassuming surfaces that held depths beyond what she was comfortable with. Never letting go of the stone edge of the pool, and only submerging herself to wash her hair properly, Lena was quicker than she would’ve liked to be, wishing for a copper bathtub like the one in Krypton so she could relax in a tub of hot water without the overwhelming fear of drowning, and dried off and dressed before heading back up to her room.

     

                Dumping her dirty clothes there, she went off in search of food, finding J’onn and Alex in deep conversation in the kitchens when she arrived. They were drinking tea and Lena helped herself to a cup before fetching herself some soup from a slow-bubbling pot over one of the many fires. Alex made a few snide comments about her absence over the last day but Lena didn’t speak a word about what she’d been doing or what feelings she’d been wrestling with, and after finishing off her late lunch, Lena vanished to the well-stocked library to decipher a text on healing, filling pages with slightly wobbly glyphs. Her reading and writing were not so poor as they had been, and while she was slow, she was methodical and a fast learner and enjoyed the distraction after a perplexing day - few days, if she was honest. 

     

                As tiring as it had been, she didn’t stay up nearly as late as she’d hoped, eyes prickling with burning exhaustion as she sighed and rubbed at tired eyelids, smudging ink on the bridge of her nose. Tidying up after herself, she was at least grateful she’d missed dinner, but was nervous to head back to her shared quarters. She knew she was in dire need of her bed tonight though, back and shoulders aching from the storeroom floor last night, and while she could’ve snuck into one of the multitude of rooms housing cots for soldiers and refugees in the event of invasion, Lena didn’t want to spend a lonely night in a big, cold chamber.

     

                Instead, she plucked up the courage to push open the door to Kara’s quarters, barely even hesitating at the sound of a strong heartbeat audible within. She did note a slight uptick in the speed of it though, as Kara took notice of her arrival. Slipping inside, Lena slowed at the sight of her wife on a low sofa near the fire. Standing in the open doorway, Lena felt a heavy blow to her chest as she took in the white nightgown shrouding Kara’s lithe, muscled body, golden hair spilling around her shoulders and down her back, cheeks rosy and blue eyes mournfully wide and aching. She was devastatingly beautiful and Lena felt suddenly weak. It had only been a day but her eyes pricked with tears as the belated feeling of missing Kara slammed into her.

     

                Sitting there, staring at her in silence for a moment, Kara seemed to perk up and slump at the same time, and Lena didn’t know what to make of her welcome until her wife opened her arms, reaching for her with a plea in her ocean blue eyes.

     

                “Come to me, please.”

     

                Relief washed over Lena, even as her chest ached, and she couldn’t have said no to her even if she’d wanted to. It was like she’d been hoping Kara would say that, hurriedly closing the door and quickly going to her wife. Lena sank onto the sofa and into her wife’s embrace with a loosening in her chest, feeling as if she could breathe properly for the first time all day.

     

                They didn’t speak, and there was a palpable tension between them that remained unresolved, but for a few minutes, Lena let Kara hold her close and breathed in the smell of rain on her wife’s soft skin. The crackling of the fire filled the silence, and Lena’s eyelids fluttered as she closed her eyes, basking in the peace, thinking that nothing was more comforting than where she was right then. 

     

                Eventually, Kara softly spoke, her voice meek and uncertain, being very gentle with her wife. “I missed you.”

     

                Lena had settled into Kara’s embrace so fully that it was like she wanted to be engulfed by her, curling in on herself as she leaned into her wife’s side, her head in her lap. Looking up at her wife, Lena felt a lump painfully constrict her throat and it took a few attempts for her to swallow it down.

     

                “I missed you too.”

     

                Faltering, Kara’s face rippled with pain as she started to play with Lena’s hair, looking guilty and agonised. “I did not mean to upset you with- with what we spoke of. I hope you can forgive me.”

     

                Eyes closing, a thin smile, full of bitter agony, crossed Lena’s face. “There is nothing to be forgiven.”

                

                Kara didn’t respond and they lapsed back into silence for a few minutes, both of them breathing a little shallowly. Feeling exhaustion creep into the corners of her mind, Lena knew that she should go to bed but she was reluctant to move. She shouldn’t have craved being near her so much, especially after merely a day without being in her company, but there was a part of her that ached to be wanted, had wanted that ever since she was a child, and it was difficult for Lena to fill that need. With Kara’s arm draped over her, the other hand in her hair, her body so warm and solid beneath her, Lena felt the yearning inside her like an insatiable pit. She had never been any good at moderating the intensity of her feelings, and perhaps that was why it was so difficult for her to control her powers, but she couldn't see anything wrong with wanting to be held so tightly and for so long that she bruised.

     

                “I saved a boy today,” Lena murmured after a long while, her voice soft with hesitation and lingering bewilderment as she split the silence.

     

                Kara was still idly running her fingers through Lena’s hair when her wife turned her head in her lap to look up at her. Face furrowed slightly, Lena looked deep in thought as Kara hesitated in surprise, continuing to comb her fingers through her wife’s silken dark locks.

     

                “You saved a boy?”

     

                “He was drowning.”

     

                “I- you-”

     

                Smiling thinly, Lena’s eyes flitted down to Kara’s surprised expression. “I didn’t pull him out of the water - that was Kelly. There weren’t any Waterfolk around to remove the water from his lungs though, and he wasn’t breathing, no pulse. I never thought about how CPR might not be known here, even by your best healers. Strange, that, isn’t it? I did a First Aid course once, had to learn how to give CPR, and I wasn’t a doctor or anything, but now Kelly keeps looking at me like I can walk on water or something.”

     

                “Wait,” Kara said, her hand stilling in Lena’s hair as a wary edge crept into her confused expression, “you brought him back from death?”

     

                “I- sort of. I kept his heart beating for him until it restarted. I made Kelly give him air. It’s just … it’s CPR. It’s human medicine.”

     

                “I … do not understand.”

     

                She could hear Kara’s reluctance to admit that, but she looked so confused that all Lena could do was softly laugh, reaching up to touch her fingers to her wife’s soft cheek. “I’ll show you some other time. I think … I’d like to go to bed now.”

     

                “Okay,” Kara whispered as Lena sat up, ghosting her hand down her wife’s hair before she let her go.

     

                “Um … that spare bed you said we could put in here,” Lena haltingly spoke, raking a hand through her hair, trying not to offend her wife. “Is that offer still there?”

     

                A look of shock quickly passed Kara’s face, blinking in surprise, hurt quick to follow, and even quicker to be masked, although Lena still spotted it, and she stammered for a moment. “Oh, I- well, I- yes, yes, of course, if- if you wanted it.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, feeling a stab of guilt as she smiled tightly, Lena cleared her throat. “I think it would be for the best.”

     

                “Oh, uh … was there- was there a particular reason why?”

     

                Closing her eyes as she rubbed her hands over her face, Lena softly sighed. “It wouldn’t … feel right , with what you told me yesterday. You clearly … feel a particular way, so I’m just trying to respect that, and sleeping in a bed with you , and everything that’s happened between us, feels wrong.”

     

                “You are my wife. There is no one else who has more right to sleep in my bed.”

     

                “I know, but I thought you might prefer for me to sleep in my own bed from now on.”

     

                Kara smiled thinly, “I was aware of my feelings before I asked you to stay in my room, my bed. I have said before that I sleep better with you close by, assured of your safety. That has not changed. Unless it is for your own reasons that you wish to have your own bed. If so, I will see it done.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena shrugged slightly with an off-handed gesture. “I just don’t want you to feel uncomfortable.”

     

                With a quiet laugh, Kara reached out to cup Lena’s chin, smoothing her thumb over the side of her jaw. “I will not feel uncomfortable. Would it help if I promised to tell you if I ever felt as such? Yes? Good, then I promise to tell you, only if you promise to tell me.”

     

                At Lena’s reluctant smile tugging at the corners of her mouth, the eye roll and shallow nod, Kara smiled a little bigger and dropped her hand. Moving towards the bedroom, Lena dug out a nightdress and changed for bed before easing herself down onto the soft mattress, her aching body grateful for it as she pulled the blankets over herself. Closing the doors, blotting out the dim light of the fire beyond, Kara climbed into bed beside her and Lena felt her stomach jolt slightly, pulse quickening.

     

                Turning her head in the dark, she felt a flicker of comfort as she envisioned her wife lying beside her. Suffused with a deep ache for her, Lena fisted her hands in the sheets as she resisted the urge to shift left, to press up against her side. It was silent for a few minutes, the sounds of their soft breathing filling it, and Lena didn’t think she’d be able to fall asleep like that, as tense as she was, which was saying something, because she didn’t think she’d be able to make herself get out of bed, as exhausted as she was. 

     

                Five minutes must have passed before Kara quietly cleared her throat, a polite intrusion into Lena’s inner turmoil. “Lena?” she whispered, hesitating at the hummed acknowledgement. “Would it- would it be alright if you came closer, if I held you tonight? It has been … a difficult few days, and … I understand this may be the discomfort you were talking about, but … if it’s alright with you, I think I would take comfort in it. I just- the loneliness was keenly felt last night; I did not sleep well without you.”

     

                Her voice trembled as she spoke, shockingly vulnerable, almost as if she was on the verge of tears, and Lena’s throat felt tight as she drew in a shallow breath. She didn’t speak, she just felt the weak relief that swept through her, her desires echoed by Kara’s words, and shifted closer, rolling onto her side and slinging an arm across Kara’s stomach. Her wife let out a relieved breath and seemed to sink deeper into the mattress, a hand pressing against Lena’s back, her face pressed into the top of her head, lips barely brushing over dark locks in a kiss that wasn’t a kiss. And Lena felt similarly, the pounding of her wife’s heart louder as she rested her head in the crook of her neck and shoulder, breathing in the smell of freshwater that was so wholly Kara. She felt the rise and fall of her stomach beneath her palm, the delicious warmth of her solid body, and Lena’s lashes fluttered as she breathed quickly through parted lips, so close to Kara’s neck that she wanted to press her mouth to her pulse in a soft kiss.

     

                “Thank you,” Kara whispered, her grip tightening a fraction around Lena’s waist.

     

                “I’m sorry for not coming to bed last night,” Lena quietly apologised. “I felt that loneliness too, but I’m here now. Go to sleep. All will be well.”

    Chapter 39

                Waking well-rested, some of her troubles of the last few days dimming with the simple act of falling asleep in her wife’s arms, Lena didn’t move as she kept her head on Kara’s chest, listening to the thud of her heartbeat, the slow rise and fall of her chest with her even breaths. It was hard to worry when she was so comfortable, right where she wanted to be, just the two of them with the rest of the world blotted out, and yet, she was not Lena’s to have. She was her wife in name, and while they’d become friends, lovers, the family Lena had always wanted and never had, Kara loved another, and that was a bitter reminder. Still, she could pretend, for a little while, waking up in her wife’s bed, the warmth of her body warming Lena through, and she closed her eyes, reluctant to move until Kara awoke.

     

                She must have really had a bad sleep the night before last, because it had to have been almost another hour before she stirred, waking quietly. Her hand moved, ghosting over Lena’s hair as she smoothed it flat, her other arm tightening around her waist as she blinked back sleep and looked down at her wife’s face. Lena peered up at her through the dark, unable to make out anything but her face creasing with a soft smile nonetheless.

     

                “Good morning,” Kara rasped, her voice thick with sleep as she rubbed her face.

     

                “Morning,” Lena whispered, feeling a flicker of dismay, the peaceful morning coming to an end.

     

                She sat up, Kara’s hand sliding over her nightgown, as if trying to retain her hold on Lena, stretching sore muscles, her back and arms aching from the archery yesterday, the weight of the draw on her new bow heavier than the one she’d been gifted by Reign when leaving the Unseelie Court, and glanced down at Kara, sensing her watching her. With another small smile, Lena cocked her head to the side, eyes roaming over the shadow of her wife’s face.

     

                “What are you thinking about?”

     

                “You,” Kara murmured, reaching out to tug on the cotton of Lena’s nightgown.

     

                “And what about me?”

     

                “About how unfortunate it is that I am not one of the Firefolk, so I might set this room aflame so I can look upon you. And how unfortunate it is that I am not one of the Earthfolk, so I might make windows to wake up and set eyes on you at first light.”

     

                “Ah, well, I’d help with that but I think I might take a chunk out of the mountain if I start boring holes through the rock. And you would not be who you are if you weren’t of the Waterfolk, would you?”

                

                Humming, Kara let out a soft laugh, the backs of her fingers brushing over Lena’s cheeks. “Mm, you might like me more, though.”

     

                Stomach swooping, Lena’s breath hitched in her throat before she managed to get a response out. “No, I don’t think I would. I don’t think I could like you more than I already do.”

     

                And she couldn’t see her wife’s face in the dark, how Kara’s lips twitched with a bitter smile as she interpreted Lena’s words to mean that they would never be more than friends and lovers, when really, Lena was already so far gone in love, she just didn’t have a name for it yet. 

     

                “Come, let us ready ourselves for breakfast,” Kara murmured, the blankets rustling as she pushed them off her, jostling the mattress as Lena felt her get up. Their peaceful morning was over indeed. 

     

                She was half-dressed when Andrea arrived to assist, a fire in the hearth, courtesy of Kara’s nimble hands and some flint, and Lena was dressed in soft leather leggings, a brown shirt tucked in with a green knee-length coat split for riding over the top, a riot of flowers embroidered up each sleeve. Her foray outdoors yesterday had reminded her of how suffocating it could be inside for days at a time, and she was in the midst of musing aloud to Kara about her desire to go for a ride when her attendant arrived.

     

                Sitting patiently as Andrea braided her dark hair, a simple golden circlet set around her brow and the nephrite ring gifted by her wife on her finger, Lena brushed off any further finery. Made up with an ungodly amount of jewels and layered garments of increasingly elaborate embroidery and brocade just to drape herself over a chair and drink tea while she read was becoming somewhat tiresome, and Lena often thought it would be so much nicer to not be a Princess. In fact, when it had just been a few of them tucked away in Krypton, bundled up in winter layers with less concern for looks, Lena had preferred it. Even then, the clothes were always so beautifully made; she just thought the jewels and circlets were a bit excessive and envied Kara’s freedom to eschew them at her pleasure.

     

                “We shall go for a ride after breakfast,” Kara said to appease her, amusement in her blue eyes as she watched Lena shift with impatience while Andrea dabbed perfume oil at her throat and wrists, the finishing touch. “Just you and I.”

     

                “Are you sure?” Lena asked, her eyes flitting to Andrea. “I don’t mind if someone else accompanies me, if you … want some time to yourself.”

     

                “I will manage,” Kara smiled slightly. “I am in need of a swim in running water and some fresh air, I think.”

     

                Nodding, Lena rose from her stool as Andrea finished, glancing at her attendant. “Thank you. And what will you be doing today?”

     

                “Sam is busy, so I will find something to occupy myself with.”

     

                “You can come if you’d like.”

     

                With an amused smile, Andrea arched an eyebrow, her gaze flitting to Kara and back to Lena. “A gracious invitation but I am in need of better company than your inevitable squabbling, Your Highness.”

     

                Lena laughed, shrugging indifferently as she adjusted the dagger at her waist and then looked to Kara, raising her eyebrows in silent question. Bundling her cloak under one arm, her sword clutched in her other arm and Lena’s strung bow and quiver over her shoulder, Kara trailed her to the door, gesturing for her to exit first, and they made their way to breakfast. Lena couldn’t quite place it, but there was something awkward and bumbling about Kara’s behaviour, almost reminiscent of the early days of their marriage, when she didn’t know how to act around her. Except in a few months, they would’ve been married an entire year, had gone through so much together, only for the last few days to have pulled the rug out from under them with the knowledge of Kara’s love for another hanging over them.

     

                They both felt it, that palpable change between them, an almost nervousness, as if they didn’t know where the line was drawn anymore, after having crossed it so many times this past winter. Several times on their way to the cavernous dining hall, Lena glanced sideways at Kara to catch her wife already staring at her, both of them remaining silent as they exchanged raised eyebrows, wry looks and pink staining their cheeks as they played their coy game. It was almost a relief as they swept into the dining hall, the tension between them snapping as Lena let out a soft breath, Kara furtively glancing at her, a quick appraisal, before she led Lena over to her seat.

     

                Sinking onto it with a sense of relief, Lena met Kelly’s concerned gaze across from her, giving her a confused look and a quick smile as she held her cup while Kara started to pour tea for her. Quiet conversation filled the hall, the Unseelie at the opposite end, her mother sitting regally in the chair with the remains of her cohort around her, a few new arrivals, looking weary and travel-worn as they swapped news with Vasquez and a few of the others. Alex was reading over a letter at the head of the table, half-tuned into what her sister was saying, while Lena slowly ate her bowl of porridge and hung on Kara’s every word.

     

                It was all a series of numbers - whether that was sacks of grain and salt, injured, able-bodied fighters, fletched arrows or carrier birds - and Lena found it somewhat interesting, the amount of administration behind warfare. They kept their voices down, wary of the Queen at the other end of the, admittedly very long, table, and Lena tried to make sense of what was going on at the frontlines, what their current predicament was, and whether the fighting had progressed to either side of the river yet. As far as she was aware, for millennia, the bulk of the warfare hadn’t made it more than a mile into either of the Courts, only small forays like her brother’s attack at Krypton making it any further than that, and usually only attempted to assassinate key warriors or politicians in their tents.

     

                On her second cup of tea, she spread blackberry jam over warm bread, listening to them strategise positions of troops, and Lena was surprised to hear that there was no one united army front, that it was all spread out, each General with a few hundred - or thousand, depending on the severity of the current war climate - fighters spread out along the riverbank, fending off the Unseelie attacks. She wanted to ask questions, to understand why, but she didn’t think it was the appropriate time, too much riding on the intel and planned reactions to explain Warfare 101 to Lena. Instead, she viewed her wife in a new light with the information Kelly had provided her with yesterday, peeling a few boiled duck eggs, placing two on Kara’s plate as she continued to listen, filing the information away for later use.

     

                They finished their hushed conversation and Alex tucked away the letter, climbing to her feet and leaving without another word, her wife hesitating before she hurried after her with a cat in her arms, having found one in her lap at breakfast. Finishing off the dregs of her tea, Lena waited for Kara to finish eating before they both stood and took their leave as well, Kara buckling on her sword as Lena took her bow and quiver, slinging them over her shoulder. Walking down to the stables, they found their respective horses and Kara forewent a saddle considering the relative ease of their plans, while Lena wasn’t sure she’d even make it onto horseback without stirrups, let alone manage to stay on once they got moving. 

     

                Setting off at a gentle walk down the long tunnel to the open vale below the foothills, they came out into sunlight with the caress of a cold wind on their faces, breathing in the smell of grass, sun, trees and wind. Both of them seemed to perk up, like wilted flowers showered with sunshine, and they picked up the pace a little, still able to easily converse as Kara led them down a gentle path winding through slight trees that were slightly taller than they were on horseback, the vale like a little thin patch in the midst of the dense forest. 

     

                “Are we going to the river?” Lena asked as they trampled wildflowers and grass, soft mud giving way beneath hooves, thinking of the boy yesterday.

     

                “Yes, there are many lakes here, but the river is wilder, more invigorating. I may fish, or perhaps we will hunt for our supper.”

     

                “Alright, as long as you deal the killing blow. I feel bad for them, I don’t like it. It’s actually easier to kill a person.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara rested a hand on Lena’s thigh as their horses jostled for position at each other’s side. “My soft-hearted wife, however shall I unwrap you from lambswool and take you to war?”

     

                “I imagine you’d do everything in your power to keep me tucked away safely in a tower, General.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara murmured, glancing sideways at her as a delicate flush crept into her face. “And who did you hear that from?”

     

                “Kelly.”

     

                “Ah.”

     

                “I’m just wondering why I didn’t hear it from you.”

     

                “It did not seem important.”

     

                “It didn’t seem important? You’re their best fighter, and you’re going on a joyride through the forest with me.”

     

                “I am not the only General. I am merely General of the North, the representative for the Waterfolk, and have only held that title for the last half a decade. It was a position my cousin held, until his death, as was the assumption of him being our best warrior - he knew that I would beat him more often than not, and had every right to be General, but there can only be one per element and I did not want the burden of the responsibility back then. Lucy is the General of the South, of the Firefolk, James of the West and Airfolk, and Mon-El of the West and Earthfolk. They hold the line and have enveloped my bannermen into their armies in my absence.”

     

                Studying her, Lena hummed dubiously. “My wife, General of the Seelie Court, huh? Will you ever cease to surprise me?”

     

                “I should hope not. You might find me boring, in such a case.”

     

                “You don’t bore me. You’re a … comforting constant. I feel like a thousand years could pass and you’d still be just as dependable, just as obstinately noble and loyal. It’s a kind of stability I’ve always craved, I just- I never thought it would come about like this.”

     

                “I will endeavour to give you that stability for as long as I can,” Kara promised, her voice wavering slightly as a strangely subdued expression crossed her face, knuckles whitening in the hair of her horse. “Although, I am not confident it will be for very long.”

     

                “And why’s that? Was it to do with the letter Alex received this morning?”

     

                Mouth thinning, Kara shifted restlessly on horseback. “In part. Your brother is proving to be a rather efficient thorn, although it seems he has split the Unseelie Court in half, with those who bow to him and those who do not hold with traitors gone rogue. That puts us at a disadvantage, fighting two enemies instead of one.”

     

                “What did the letter say?”

     

                “They have taken our side of the river in Mon-El’s stretch of the border. Forces are to be taken from James and Lucy to help his counterassault. There is to be a reassignment of supplies in light of that. A few Councilmembers are calling for another Council meeting; as a member myself, I may be required to depart in the coming days to uphold my duty.”

     

                An anxious edge crept into Lena’s face. “How long would you be gone for?”

     

                “It is a week’s journey southwest of here, four days west of my home in Argo.”

     

                “And … where will I be?”

     

                Softly sighing, her shoulders slumping slightly as her mouth thinned at the corners, Kara gave her an amused look of resignation. “You know I would like for you to stay where it is safe, and there are many miles of the old forest between here and the grove where the Council meets - dangerous miles; the foothills here are not so dangerous, as the forest thins in the shadow of the mountain, but it will be dangerous where I intend to go, you must remember that - but I will not leave you behind if you wish to accompany me. In some regard, I believe it might help to bring my wife, for them to see proof of our commitment to bringing peace to fruition, even if the truce has been broken now, but … while I am able to civil with your mother and her ilk, I am not assured of my sister’s ability to do so, and Unseelie would not be welcome at the Council. I would need to ensure that no peril will come to either of our families while we are gone, but if I am assured of that, we shall go together.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena said with a small smile. “I’ll try my hardest not to get into any trouble on the way.”

     

                With an exasperated sigh, full of tender amusement, Kara gave her a droll smile. “My dear wife, you are incapable of such a feat. Trouble is drawn to you like flies to honey; I would be shocked if we travelled a fortnight through the forest without something troublesome befalling you.”

     

                “Hey, I came out of it alright last time.”

     

                “I believed you to be dead for three days,” Kara protested. “That is the epitome of trouble, some would say.”

     

                “Okay, yes, but at least I got out of it relatively unscathed. Just a few bumps and scrapes; it could’ve been a lot worse.”

     

                “Yes, and now I enable you to tempt fate once more, against my better judgement. That lambswool my sister insists I remove you from to toughen you up grows more enticing every day. I would like to wrap you up in it and keep you safe until the end of time.”

     

                “Well, you have more important things to worry about now,” Lena murmured, sobering slightly as she was reminded of Kara’s reality.

     

                “There is nothing more important than you.”

     

                Even though she said it truthfully, her voice soft and tender around the admission, Lena still had the knee-jerk reaction to quietly scoff and roll her eyes, dismissing her wife’s words as flattery. Kara didn’t press her point, not wanting to reveal too much, and they rode on at a gentle pace for another mile before they picked up speed, Lena laughing as she clung to her reins, chasing on Kara’s tail as her wife ducked low over the mane of her mare, outstripping Lena even without a saddle or reins. As accustomed as she’d grown to riding, she had not been raised to it like Kara, but she gave it her best shot, adrenaline coursing through her, her heart in her throat as her horse ran at breakneck speed, dodging trees and mossy boulders.

     

                Near the end of the vale, where the forest crowded in again, they slowed, the horses snorting as their flanks heaved, and Kara wheeled her mare around as she grinned. Lena reached her a moment later, her chest rising and falling quickly as she was jostled in the saddle, reining in her mare and affectionately patting the dappled neck.

     

                “I almost had you,” Lena insisted, even though Kara hadn’t said a word.

     

                “Perhaps,” her wife shrugged, “but almost is not enough. You either have me or you don’t.”

     

                With a sharp gleam of determination in her eyes, Lena swallowed thickly, her voice slightly rough as she kneed her mare forward. “I’ll have you, one day, one way or another. Just you wait and see.”

     

                Looking a little flushed as she made her own implications and tried to mask her longing, Kara laughed and reached out to cup Lena’s chin. “I am yours in any way you desire.”

     

                “Well, not any,” Lena said with a quirk of a brow, gently removing her chin from Kara’s warm grasp, uncertain about her wife’s open affection.

     

                It didn’t seem right for them to be as they’d once been, their lingering touches, the intimacy between them that had grown shockingly easy. None of that felt right when she knew that Kara’s heart had been given to someone else, and she was the other woman . Except she wasn’t even sure if that’s what she was, bound to her wife by unbreakable vows, made to be in each other’s lives no matter what. Even if there came a day when they hated each other, they would still be wed to each other. As it was, they didn’t hate each other, far from it, but that was just as complicated.

     

                “I have said any, so it must be so,” Kara insisted as she slipped into the shade of the trees.

     

                Following her, Lena felt the sudden cold of the forest, the tall canopy blotting out the sun as they forged deeper through the undergrowth and into pockets of darkness. She could still see her wife though, her eyes adjusting to the gloom, the green light filtering in high above their heads casting everything in an enchanting light as she breathed in the smell of pine, moss and dirt. Motes of pollen swirled overhead and Lena inhaled deeply, as if breathing in the forest, the sweet poison of it suffusing her.

     

                Broodingly humming, Lena didn’t respond to her as they picked their way through the trees. They rode through the trees for the better part of an hour with Lena in brooding silence, Kara attempting to make conversation with her on numerous occasions until she eventually slowed to glance back over her shoulder to make sense of her wife’s curt hums and sullen silence. 

     

                “What is it?”

     

                “It’s-“ Lena cut off, wanting to say it was nothing but getting choked off with the lie.

     

                “You may be honest,” Kara earnestly encouraged her.

     

                “And will you be honest?”

     

                Hesitating, surprise flashing across her face as she blinked, mouth opening and closing, Kara looked sheepish and flustered. “I always try to be as honest as I can with you.”

     

                Giving her a withering look, Lena smiled thinly. “That’s not the same thing.”

     

                “No, it is not.”

     

                She held Kara’s stare for a long minute, before her wife turned back around, her shoulders hunching slightly in a defensive, or perhaps guilty, manner. “I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with keeping secrets,” Lena called out, “I mean, that’s your business, but … I’d at least like to know why , if that’s okay.”

     

                Tipping her head back, Kara audibly exhaled, almost a sigh, and Lena could envision her with her eyes closed. “Some of my secrets may put other’s lives in jeopardy.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                “Okay?”

     

                “Yes, okay. If that’s your justification for it, then so be it. My curiosity isn’t more important than other people’s lives,” Lena curtly replied, somewhat annoyed but unable to be with such sound reasoning.

     

                Kara was quiet for a moment, the sounds of the forest filling the silence, before she cleared her throat. “Were you going to tell me that which you were trying to omit?”

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, Lena quietly exhaled, somewhat haughty as she straightened her shoulders, moving with her mare’s movements as they crested a short incline. “Um, no, probably not.”

     

                Bringing her horse to a stop with her knees, Kara dismounted in a fluid motion, grabbing the reins of Lena’s mare and halting her as well. Looking down at her, Lena arched an eyebrow as Kara reached up. “What are you doing?”

     

                “They have been cooped up in the stables; we shall go on foot and let them wander and graze awhile.”

     

                Removing her feet from the stirrups, Lena set her hands on Kara’s shoulders and let her bear her weight as she gently lifted her down. Feeling the dirt of the forest floor underfoot, Lena felt grounded, the feeling that she’d like the roots of the trees to ensnare her body and make her one with the forest filling her for a bizarre moment. Letting go of Kara, she turned to her mare, smoothing a hand down her snout before patting her back to move on with a quiet murmur, watching the horses trot off. 

     

                Taking her hand, Kara gently tugged her to keep going, and Lena shook her off a moment later, her hand tightening around the bow in her left hand, while she curled her right hand into a fist. Slowing, Kara gave her a bewildered look before she seemed to deflate, her expression aching as she reached for her wife.

     

                “Please do not be cross with me.”

     

                “I’m not,” Lena whispered, her smile tight and thin as she looked at the ground. “I’m entitled to my secrets, the same as you.”

     

                “Yes, but that is not what you are doing.”

     

                With a soft scoff, Lena continued onwards, trampling through ferns and over rotting foliage, damp and chilly underfoot, while Kara followed after her, confused and mildly panicked. She plucked at Lena’s cloak, trying to make her slow down, but Lena’s ire was growing, slowly stoked as she felt the ache in her chest, confused as well, her feelings for her wife, and their apparent unrequitedness, knotted up inside her.

     

                “Talk to me.”

     

                “You can’t have it both ways.”

     

                “How so?” Kara asked, her long legs keeping pace with Lena’s quick pace, annoyance spurring her on at a brisk walk.

     

                “You’re entitled to your secrets, that’s fine , but you can’t expect me to be honest with you. You can’t have your cake and eat it.”

     

                Face furrowing as she tried to puzzle out the meaning of Lena’s words, Kara floundered. “But- I don’t understand that expression.”

     

                “It means that you get out of this what you put into it,” Lena firmly explained, coming to a stop as she turned to face Kara, waving a hand around. “It’s hypocritical of you to expect something of me that you won’t give. Not when you can give it and are choosing not to.”

     

                “What? What is it you wish to know? I tire of our arguments. These last few days … you have not been yourself, and I admit that I, myself, have been otherwise preoccupied, but I do not like this rift between us. I only wish for things to be open, as they once were.”

     

                “Well, it can’t be. You made sure of that.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, jerking back slightly, Kara’s mouth opened and closed before she pressed her lips into a flat line, looking down, one hand on the hilt of her sword as she shifted from foot to foot. Her face was flushed with annoyance and her voice curt when she replied. “And what exactly have I done to have the blame laid at my feet?”

     

                “You dragged someone else into our marriage,” Lena quietly snapped.

     

                Her cheeks were flushed as well, eyes bright with hurt, anger eclipsing her wounded feelings, making her voice tremble. She had to feed into that anger, otherwise, Lena worried that she might start crying, a humiliating prospect, no matter how many times she’d cried in front of Kara. This was different, though. This was about the painful ache in her chest, the longing for her wife, the reality of heartache, even if she remained willfully ignorant of the depth of her feelings. How could it have been anything but painfully obvious though? 

     

                Shock flashed across Kara’s face, followed quickly by a ripple of guilt, looking ashamed as she cast her eyes everywhere but at her wife. “I have done no such thing.”

     

                “You have. You did the second you decided to love someone else.”

     

                “I have made no decisions . You think I would choose this? Knowing how long I have dreaded this eventuality, you think I would willingly decide to doom someone I love?” 

     

                “I- no, but-”

     

                “The only people in this marriage are the two of us. I have assured you of that numerous times, but you will not take me at my word, even though I have not lied. This is why I did not wish to tell you that I have fallen in love.”

     

                “What, because I might have feelings on the matter?”

     

                “And what feelings do you have at present? All that I can see is that you are behaving irrationally, blaming me because you cannot have your own way, because you believe you will have to share me. Is that it? You are jealous-”

     

                “Fuck you,” Lena softly snarled, her face reddening, from the tips of her ears down to her throat, the heat of discomfort flooding through her at how close her wife’s words struck.

     

                Abruptly turning, anger pulsing in her head, Lena rubbed her brow, her throat tight as her eyes stung. She knew that there was a kernel of truth to her wife’s words, that she was jealous, and yes, perhaps she was being irrational, but Lena didn’t have the words to describe why. All she knew was that the last few days, ever since Kara had dropped that bombshell on her, had left her frustrated and in a rather fragile emotional state.

     

                She barely made it a few steps before her wife snagged her arm, pulling her to a stop. Whirling around to yell at Kara some more, Lena didn’t anticipate the pleading look on her face, or the soft way Kara said her name, so tender and aching, and in that split-second pause, her wife had time to cup her face in her hands and kiss her. Briefly losing all sense, Lena dropped her bow to the ground and let Kara propel her backwards, until she hit the trunk of a tree, steadying herself as her knees went weak. But then her anger reared up again, her hands finding Kara’s waist before she roughly forced her back, her wife making a small sound of complaint as her lips were left chasing after Lena’s.

     

                “I’m not your whore,” Lena scornfully hissed.

     

                “My whore?” Kara spluttered, affronted. “No, you are not, you are my wife.”

     

                Lena let out a frayed laugh, pressing a hand to her forehead. “And where has that gotten me? You know what, I am jealous. For once - just once - it would be nice to come first, to- to be important to someone.”

     

                “You are important to me, you are the most important person in my life. How can you think otherwise?”

     

                Lips twitching with a bittersweet smile, Lena’s eyes closed as she sighed heavily. “Maybe now, but not for long. You’ll replace me soon, and I’ll have to step aside from someone else and be left alone again. And how can I begrudge you that?”

     

                Kara reached out to grip Lena’s upper arms, anguish crumpling her handsome features. “How can you still not understand? I speak as clear as day and yet you-” Cutting off, Kara looked down and let her go, “you are committed to thinking badly of me for something I have no control over, so I will spare us any further misconstrued words and ask what it is you wish to know. You would like honesty; I will give it to you at your own peril.”

     

                Her face was pale, a bitter look of anger and grief on her face, and Lena watched her throat bob, took in the tightening of Kara’s jaw, felt the warmth of her through the scant inches separating them as it made her stomach swoop. And truthfully, Lena didn’t want to know, didn’t want to put a name to the person Kara loved, didn’t want it to become any more real, any bigger, obstructing the easy manner of their marriage they’d fallen into. Except, it already had , and now she was just afraid that her jealousy would consume her, making her scornful, petty, desperate. She had to admit, she had enjoyed her wife doting on her, providing everything for her, trying to please her, to accommodate her, even amidst Lena’s rather prickly objections to any of Kara’s attempts. They’d gotten through it, and now she wished she’d been kinder, gentler perhaps, wondering if Kara might’ve loved her if she hadn’t been so awful at the beginning. She’d had good reason to be, of course, but now it felt like she’d ruined her chances at the start and was suffering the consequences of it now.

     

                Eyes filling with tears, spilling over to roll down her cheeks, Lena reached up to cup Kara’s cheek, urging her head up so their eyes met. She cocked her head to the side, gazing at her with aching green eyes, and smiled faintly. “I could never think badly of you. But keep your secrets; I do not wish for that which you won’t freely give.”

     

                Dropping her hand, she brushed past Kara as she stooped to pick up her dropped bow, hefting it in her hand and brushing off a few damp leaves clinging to the varnished wood. She heard Kara’s defeated sigh, the rustling of leaves as her wife turned, the plea in her voice as she spoke but a single word.

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “Go for your swim, Kara,” Lena roughly instructed her. “I’m tired of this conversation; I’d like some peace and quiet.”

     

                Her wife’s voice was meek and full of hurt as she quietly replied, somewhat apologetic and guilty. “As you wish. But I would have you come with me to the river, so that you are within my sight.”

     

                Nodding, Lena waited for Kara to set off through the trees, following after her, the silence between them weighted with tension. Birdsong drifted through the forest and the sound of their footsteps and the wind were the only other sounds, a few miles passing by in that fashion, Lena snagging her cloak on brambles and branches as they traipsed through the towering trees, until she eventually heard the sound of running water in the distance. It was another two miles of walking before she caught a glimmer of the dark surface of the wide river cutting through the trunks, the sound of running water louder now, a sweet dankness to the air.

     

                It was the same river she’d resuscitated the drowning boy yesterday, both days feeling so long that she would’ve believed more time had passed than a mere day, and she watched her wife unbuckle her sword belt and strip off a few layers before wading into the river. It was slightly deeper where they were, and it was past Kara’s waist as she let the flow of water rush around her, before she keeled over backwards, arms spread, and let it wash her away. Lena had to swallow the lump of fear in her throat, knowing no harm would come to her wife in the water, but hating and fearing it anyway; she had already lost someone she loved to the water, she didn’t want a repeat of it.

     

                To pass the time, she practised her archery, choosing a tree as her target and loosing arrow after arrow into the bark, scoring the trunk with little nicks and holes as she went to retrieve them and refill her quiver, before losing herself to the routine again. It was methodical, and she backed up after each quiver of arrows loosed at her target, making it harder for herself, the occasional gust of wind making her take stock of her aim, accounting for it when she angled her arm, her accuracy faltering slightly as the distance became greater. After she’d backed up too far for any sort of easy validation, her shots oftentimes going completely wide of the tree, she reduced it again, soothing her frustration with the relatively easy distance of fifty feet, nailing each shot and feeling a little better by the time she’d worn herself out.

     

                While Kara basked in the flowing waters of the river, studiously ignored by her wife, Lena flopped down onto the carpet of clover growing around the base of a cherry tree, exertion leaving her limp and aching as she closed her eyes. It didn’t take much for her to drift off, the droning of a few bees, the mildness of the day in her warm layers, the green smell of all things growing as spring awoke in the forest. She didn’t know how long she slept, only that when she opened her eyes again, the light was brighter and greener, the canopy overhead was thick with ripe cherries, and she couldn’t move her hands.

     

                Pushing herself up onto her elbows, Lena let out a sound of confusion as she looked down at her hands and wrists, ensnared by the thin roots of the clover, which had slowly stolen over her, growing thicker where she’d lain. It only took a small amount of effort for her to pull her hands free, breaking the fragile bonds, and she stared at her fingers, mud in the beds of her nails and grooves of her palms, feeling a little lightheaded as she blinked back her surprise. To her right, Kara sat in a hollow between two roots of the cherry tree, her blonde hair brassy with damp, wet clothes clinging to her body as she rested peacefully, some of the tension gone from her body. 

     

                “You have given much of yourself to the forest while you slept. The birds and squirrels will be grateful.”

     

                Humming, still annoyed with her wife but feeling a little out of sorts, as if she’d been sapped of all of her strength. It was a similar feeling to the aftermath of plunging Krypton into the sea, albeit to a lesser extent, growing cherries not nearly as taxing as ripping apart a limestone cliff face. It was only mild though, a slight dizziness, as if she’d skipped breakfast, growing cherries not requiring as much of her as her other feats with her powers, as few as they were. She hadn’t intended to hasten their ripening though, and must have let her guard down while sleeping in the forest, feeding into that part of herself that felt connected to it.

     

                Laying back down on the flattened clover, the shade of the cherry tree cool and damp, Lena stared up at the canopy of red fruit and breathed in the damp air, the river rushing past, birds flocking to the tree. It was still peaceful and she’d vented some of her anger, leaving her to bask in the simple act of being in the forest while her wife kept watch. With her eyes closed, she didn’t move a muscle as she heard Kara move, the rustling of leaves and creaking branches drifting down to her as her wife’s heartbeat moved upwards.

     

                Five minutes later, Kara’s feet thudded softly in the clover beside Lena, and she cracked open an eye to study her wife, who held her cloak bundled up. Sinking to a crouch, Kara opened the folds of fabric to reveal a pile of dark cherries plucked from the branches above. Glancing at Lena, their eyes met, and Kara plucked one by the stem, holding it out to her. Pushing herself up onto her elbows, Lena reached for it with murmured thanks and bit into the tart fruit, working the pit free and chewing. She could’ve devoured the entire pile, the perfect balance of sweet and tart, and they sat in silence for a couple of minutes as they ate, Lena sitting upright now, the lines of her lips quickly stained dark with the juice.

     

                “Come, there is somewhere I had planned to take you,” Kara eventually murmured, bundling up her cloak and the rest of the cherries.

     

                With a soft sigh, Lena picked herself up and grabbed her bow, trudging after her wife as Kara led them back through the trees. They walked another mile, Kara softly mimicking bird calls until the forest suddenly went quiet and she grabbed Lena’s arm, pulling them both into a crouch behind the large root of a hawthorn tree, Lena’s heart thumping in her chest as they listened to the distant groaning of the forest, a brisk wind sweeping through the trees, leaves raining down around them. 

     

                When the birdsong started back up again, Kara continued onwards and when Lena asked what that was, the only response she got from her wife was that it was simply the forest. In the early days of her stay in the forest, she’d seen the dead body strung up on large thorns, had been warned of the dangers, but she’d always attributed it to the creatures within the forest, but the hair-raising feeling of the trees, which always seemed serene to her, even with the ancient air about them as they towered over her, standing for a millennia or more, made her second-guess her assumption that the only thing to worry about in the forest were the things within it. She’d been warned, of course, but Lena wondered what the forest could actually do, so much of it alien to her, ominously unknown. All she knew was that it had its hooks in everyone in that realm, binding them tightly to it, and she thought back to the conversation many weeks ago about dying, and how they fed off the forest and the forest fed off their dead, a strange symbiotic relationship that she hadn’t thought too deeply about.

     

                Preoccupied by her trail of thought, Lena walked as if in a daze, paying little attention to her surroundings, until she heard the faint sound of laughter on the breeze. The dark green light of the forest seemed lighter ahead as Kara stepped over a rotting log covered in oyster mushrooms, and Lena was curious now, wondering where her wife had intended to bring her. Her answer was revealed ten minutes later, a glade at the end of another vale opening up before them as they reached the treeline. Wildflowers speckled the lush grass in a variety of pinks, purples and yellows and children ran about the glade, the reaching boughs of the trees shading it, while Lena took in the signs of trees moulded into the shapes of homes. There were maybe a dozen of them, and thrice that number of people milling about, while horses grazed freely.

     

                Lips parting, Lena looked around as she took in the small dwelling, finding a few homes hewn into the sloping stone of the bottom of the vale, while most looked like they were something out of a fairytale, doorways between roots, platforms in the canopy, woven branches bridging trees. It was beautiful, just like the huts at the bridge spanning the gorge on their way to the Mid Vale, and Lena took in the sight of ordinary people going about their lives. Not since she’d taken an arrow fleeing the Unseelie Court and wound up at a small dwelling had she seen regular people, and she’d been too feverish and wounded then to take much notice. Now, she watched as a man sat on a shaded root and hand-stitched a child’s jerkin, a woman gutted fish caught from the river and another read in the fork of a tree, while hounds ran about or basked in the sunlight and bees lazily trailed from flower to flower.

     

                Kara greeted them with familiarity, gesturing to Lena as she introduced her wife, and one of the women looked up from the arrows she was fletching in her lap, quickly climbing to her feet and crossing over to them. Lena looked somewhat startled at the woman's brisk approach, stiffening slightly until the woman dropped to her knees and reached for Lena’s hand, kissing her knuckles.

     

                “Thank you, thank you.”

     

                “Um …”

     

                “This is Val’s mother,” Kara murmured, “the boy from yesterday.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena looked down. “Oh. Oh, right. Is he … alright?”

     

                “He’s resting,” the woman said, her eyes glassy with tearful gratitude, slowly rising to her feet. “He has weak lungs, you see.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Lena didn’t know what to say, somewhat awkward at the gratitude, a little uncomfortable by the glances the other adults were giving her, as if she’d performed a miracle. She supposed to them she had , but it felt disingenuous to pretend that she had, and she felt like a fraud as she smiled weakly and shrugged.

     

                “My wife has also brought a cherry tree to early ripeness,” Kara interjected, hefting her cloak of cherries. “A gift for the children.”

     

                She walked forward as she spoke, calling out to the kids as she sank and spread her cloak out to reveal their bounty. A few of the children were sparring with wooden swords and they dropped them as they raced over to her, Kara laughing as they all crowded in, sinking cross-legged to the grass as they shared handfuls of cherries. A few of them were shy, taking a small handful and running back to their parents to hide behind them, and Lena smiled at how sweet they seemed, some of them perhaps two years old, tiny as they babbled in Fae, their laughter ringing through the glade. She watched as a few more appeared and soon found herself seated with a cup of blackberry cider amidst a group of adults, gentle conversation enveloping her as they all went about their day as they pleased.

     

              Sipping her cider, Lena just watched Kara, occasionally offering a hesitant answer to a question, sensing the wariness of the others, but her deed yesterday offered up some goodwill, despite being an Unseelie. As the children resumed their sparring, Kara found herself with a wooden sword in hand, entertaining them with her theatrical thrusts and parries as they ganged up on her, pantomiming getting stabbed as she trapped a girl’s thrust beneath her arm and staggered to a knee, letting a boy disarm her before she let out a loud laugh, the trio piling on top of her. 

     

                Chuckling as a tenderness filled her chest, Lena raised a cup to her lips and then hesitated at the sight of a rider on horseback emerging from the forest. It was Sam, and Lena’s brow creased with confusion as she watched her dismount, her expression brightening as she stepped forward, eyes fixated on someone else. Following her line of sight, Lena watched a girl of around twelve or thirteen streak towards the Hunter, barrelling into her for a tight hug. When she saw the girl’s face, it was a near-identical copy of Sam’s. It wouldn’t have been unreasonable to think she was Sam’s younger sister, but from the look on the Hunter’s face, Lena knew it was her daughter, watching with surprise and curiosity. 

     

                As if feeling her stare, Sam met Lena’s eyes a moment later and seemed to panic, locking her emotions away as the agonised joy visibly dimmed. Lena averted her gaze, not wanting to intrude, although it was plain she already had, and she turned her attention back to Kara. Watching her wife play with the children, Lena was struck by the thought that perhaps Kara wanted kids herself one day, that maybe she’d fallen in love with a man who would give her mini golden-haired copies of herself, with sea-blue eyes and an affinity for the water. What could Lena ever give her? She had nothing to offer but herself, and that wasn’t worth a lot in Lena’s eyes. She’d never even considered kids, and perhaps it was because she’d spent months without being surrounded by any, but even before getting dragged through to the Courts, she’d never once entertained that idea. What business did she have being a mother? She’d lost hers so young and spent the rest of her time growing up without one, so much instability as she’d moved from family to family, running away to shelters and then ending back up in the system. No one had ever wanted her, and so Lena had always known a child wouldn’t want her either. Somewhat bitter over her made-up scenarios, she decided that it was probably for the best that Kara had found someone else, someone whose childhood hadn’t been so turbulent. 

     

                Her cider tasted a little sour as she brooded, watching as Sam lifted her daughter onto her horse, smiling as she watched her ride around the glade, while Kara continued to spar with the children and Lena was left to sit on her root while the others talked and did their tasks for the day. After a while, Sam approached slowly, bit by bit, until she sank to a crouch a few feet away from Lena, hazel eyes still fixated on her daughter, drinking in the sight of her.

     

                “Your daughter?” Lena softly ventured after a few minutes.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You’ve never mentioned her before.”

     

                “You have not asked.”

     

                “How old is she?”

     

                “Twelve,” Sam murmured.

     

                “And she lives here? With- with her dad?”

     

                “Her father is dead. He was not involved . My oaths to the Queen bind me to the Unseelie Court, unless an emissary is needed, so my adoptive mother looks after her in my stead. I visit when I am able.”

     

                Lena was speechless for a moment, trying to find the words. “But I- we’ve been in the Seelie Court for months. Why didn’t you come here? You’re part of both Courts, right? You could’ve spent all that time with her-”

     

                “My oaths to the Queen bind me to you now. I am sworn to protect you as best I can; I am unable to defy those oaths for very long. The compulsion grows the longer I am parted from you. And Andrea would not be welcome as I am, and only half of me is welcome at that. Perhaps one day I will be free to raise my daughter, but I do not think me worthy of the task yet. I know what it is like to be loved badly and I would not make her suffer the same.” 

     

                “For what it’s worth, I think she would want you in her life. If I had the chance to have my mom around, I wouldn’t care what she was like, I’d just want her there. If I had someone who loved me, I’d want them to stay.”

     

                Turning to give Lena a bewildered look, head tilted to the side and hazel eyes mystified, Sam didn’t speak for a moment. “We don’t all have that luck. It is more complicated than that for me.”

     

                “It always is,” Lena murmured, her expression clouded as she watched her wife chase after a few of the kids with a little girl clinging to her back, the glade ringing with childish laughter as Lena felt a keen ache in her chest.

     

     

                The afternoon was dragging on by the time they reached the valley leading into the foothills of the mountain, the dark mouth of Alex’s home visible ahead as the trio rode towards it in companionable silence. Sam had ridden back with them, a buffer between the wives, although she didn’t speak, leaving the three of them in silence, and Kara was chafing at the frustration that had been building steadily over days. There was no easy solution in mind for her, and while she knew what the right thing to do was, it wasn’t quite so straightforward.

     

                She spotted her sister pacing near the mouth of the tunnel as they approached, horses plodding up the gentle incline of the foothills, and Kara raised a hand in greeting. Alex just stared back, her expression unreadable at that distance, and it wasn’t until they grew nearer that Kara could tell that her sister was visibly irate, a somewhat stiff set to her shoulders as she braced her hands on her hips, slowly walking back and forth along a stretch of grass as she waited for them to draw closer. Sam rode at the front and gave Alex nothing more than a questioning look, but rode into the tunnel when it became apparent that it was nothing to concern her with, and Lena slowly followed after her with Kara on her tail, raising her eyebrows at her sister. For a second, she thought perhaps Alex was just getting some fresh air to vent some of her frustration over this complicated war against two enemies, but no, she was there for Kara.

     

                “Sister, I must speak with you,” Alex brusquely waylaid her, stepping into her path with a rather severe look on her face as Kara pulled up short.

     

                Expression clouding, Kara glanced to Lena, who had reined in her horse as well, worry softening her face. Meeting Alex’s gaze, Kara raised her eyebrows slightly. “You may speak freely in front of Lena.”

     

                “I’m afraid I cannot. My words are for your ears only.”

     

                An anxious edge crept into Kara’s features and she swiftly dismounted, gesturing for Lena to continue through the tunnel after Sam. Accepting the dismissal in silence, still somewhat frosty, Lena urged her mare onwards, the sound of hooves clopping on hewn stone eventually petering off into silence. As Lena left them to it, Alex paced away from the entrance to her halls, and Kara nervously followed in her footsteps, wringing her hands.

     

                “What is it? What is amiss? Is mother-”

     

                She didn’t see the cuff to the side of her head coming, both of them too old for such childish clouts, and she let out an indignant squawk of protest, raising a hand to her reddening ear. Face darkening with a look of outrage, Kara bristled, drawing herself up tall as she met her sister’s hard stare.

     

                “And what have I done to deserve you boxing my ears?”

     

                “What have you done? What have you done? The transgression is that my sister is being disingenuous and a poor wife. Perhaps knocking some sense into you will help where words fail.”

     

                Alex smacked Kara’s arm and then her shoulder, her face furrowed with anger as she kept swatting her sister as Kara spluttered. “Stop this at once. This childishness is beneath you.”

     

                “As is your behaviour,” Alex retorted. “You are making a mockery of her. She has been honest about her fear that you will leave her, and yet you are letting her believe that you will leave her for another.”

     

                “I am doing no such thing,” Kara indignantly objected. “I have told Lena that I will not leave her, that she will always be my wife.”

     

                “And yet, you will not tell her the truth . You are harming both of you.”

     

                “Do not speak of what you don’t know.”

     

                “Then I will continue to speak of this, because I am more knowledgable than you think. Kelly spoke to me this morning of her ride with Lena yesterday. They spoke of you, and for a moment, Kelly thought you had been honest with her, was surprised by how well she was taking it, until she understood that you are purposely deceiving your wife. You have told her you are in love, and yet she does not know that it is her that you love. Tell me my wife is wrong in her assumption, because I do not want to believe that you are capable of such deception.”

     

                A muscle twitched in Kara’s jaw as she looked away, studying the clouds, the day growing overcast as it cooled. “Kelly is not wrong, but you-”

     

                Alex shoved Kara backwards, watching her sister stagger away before she reached out where she’d thrusted both palms against her chest and grabbed the front of her clothes this time, fire enveloping each fistful of material as her temper flared up. As the front of her jerkin started to char, fire eating through the delicate embroidery, Kara stared at her sister, aghast, and then drew water from the surrounding plants and ground before hitting Alex with a faceful, leaving her sister coughing and spluttering as her unlit hands smoked as water put out fire.

     

                “You are behaving boorishly,” Kara sulked.

     

                “You are. You are so … ignorant, Kara. She loves you! Are you truly so blind to her feelings? Has the salt air addled your brain?”

     

                “She loves me as I love you; I am the family she never had.”

     

                “Oh, don’t give me that excuse; she sees you as merely family but she will gladly go to your bed?”

     

                “She and I are friends . She has made her feelings on the matter clear to me. To me - not you.”

     

                “Has she? Because you told her you loved another and no one caught sight of her for an entire day and Kelly had to take her for a ride because she looked such a wreck, so miserable. I have heard this from my wife’s own lips.”

     

                “And if she loves me, why has she not told me?” Kara challenged. “Why am I the one who must be forthright and spoil everything?”

     

                “I will smack you again,” Alex warned her. “You may be taller and more powerful but I am your elder and your sister, and I am warning you.” Her voice softened then, pleading as she stared at Kara, reaching out a beseeching hand. “Do not take this burden onto yourself; give it to her. We are supposed to be burdened to each other, we are supposed to love . She is frightened to tell you the truth, but that does not make them any less real, mark my words. You will both be happier for it.”

     

                Turning away from her, Kara paced away a few steps, the smell of charred wool in the air as the front of her jerkin smouldered in ruins, two holes through the front of it. Running a hand over her face, she refused to entertain her sister’s perspective on the matter, of what her wife’s feelings could be. All that mattered to Kara was that she would kill Lena, and it didn’t matter whether their love was shared, because there was no happiness to be found together - at least not forever. Her main priority now was to let Lena live out the rest of her days without the cloud of fear that would come from knowing of her fate.

     

                With a solemn look on her face, Kara turned back around, agony written in the lines of her face. “I will not let the remainder of her days be clouded by fear of her death; that will not bring me happiness. I cannot do what you ask of me, but when she dies, I will embrace my death. To die will be a … kind of relief. I think my bones will rest easy beside hers, and there will be a sense of happiness in that.”

     

                There was a grim finality to Kara’s words, similar to those she’d spoken only days before, of killing herself before she’d ever kill her wife by her own hand. That didn’t mean she wouldn’t be to blame when Lena died, but she’d spoken aloud her refusal to do it at her own hand, and the compulsion of those words had lessened the guilt somewhat. But that did not mean she intended to outlive her wife by long, if at all. Her sister could run her through with one of her knives right now, a prospect Kara imaged Alex was currently entertaining, but the blame would still fall on her if Lena died in ten years time from an infection that she would not have suffered from if Kara had never let her stay. 

     

                There was silence for a few minutes, and Kara could see tears in her sister’s eyes, guilt striking her like an arrow to the chest, and she watched as Alex wrestled with her anger and pre-emptive grief, hardening herself against her feelings for her idiotic sister. Her voice was quiet and curt when she eventually spoke.

     

                “You have always been kind, and fair and honest, but now I do not recognise my sister. I never took you for a coward; how disappointing,” Alex regretfully murmured, her mouth twisting with dismay, a small amount of contempt, looking sad and defeated, before she drew in a deep breath and squared her shoulders. “I’ll have no part in this. You are not welcome in my home until you make this right.”

     

                “You aren’t suggesting-”

     

                “No, I am not suggesting, I am ordering ; I cannot tell her, as I have promised you I would keep it to myself, but either you tell her, or I will have Kelly tell her for you. You are being ridiculous and selfish and I will not let you step foot inside my halls until you have righted this.”

     

                Lips parting in surprise, Kara blinked as she stared at her sister, until a confused laugh worked its way up her tight throat, frayed and disbelieving. Alex looked almost ashamed to have spoken the words, knowing that they would both be compelled by the truth of them, that even though there was nothing blocking the open mouth of the tunnel, Kara could no more walk through it than if the stone doors had been sealed shut and barred her way. 

     

                Blanching slightly, Kara seemed shocked by her sister’s attempt to force her hand, and perhaps it was deserved, Alex’s heart almost certainly in the right place, but Kara wouldn’t stand to be made to do something she didn’t want to. Her surprise was quickly masked by her stubborn streak, the tips of her ears and cheeks pink as she jutted her chin forward, blue eyes cloudy like a storm.

     

                “So be it.”

     

                “Good, shall I fetch her?” 

     

                “No, I will not tell her,” Kara corrected Alex’s assumption, watching shock flash across her sister’s face.

     

                “Kara-”

     

                “ Oh , you can drink brine if you think I’m speaking to you right now,” Kara haughtily laughed, turning her back on Alex and walking off.

     

                Her sister knew better than to come after her then, and Kara traipsed across the vale as her horse roamed freely, grazing contentedly as Kara made for the little lake glistening in the sunlight at the end of the valley. She started a few grazing deer and rabbits as she stormed onwards, her long legs quickly covering ground as her cheeks burned furiously and her eyes smarted. By the time she reached the lake, clumsily fumbling with her sword belt as her vision blurred, Kara was drawing in shallow breaths through gritted teeth, sniffing as she tried to stamp down her pain.

     

                Wading into the water, scaring off the ducks and geese, the frogs in the reeds falling silent, Kara submerged herself and wallowed in the water for the next three hours, surfacing only when she needed air. It wasn’t until it was dark and she needed to start thinking about where to bed down for the night that she finally emerged, water streaming off her as she padded across the grass, picking the nearby sycamore tree she was fond of climbing on her usual visits to her sister’s hall, the trunk thick, no visible roots above ground, and the sturdy branches forking evenly off the trunk as they spread out and grew upwards in a rounded canopy. It was a nice tree, hardy and healthy, already bearing green leaves, and Kara decided she would sleep there tonight, a pitiful consolation to the comfort of a bed with her wife in it, but a necessary alternative.

     

                Still, even as she tried to convince herself of her nice home for the foreseeable future, knowing Alex wouldn’t be able to take back her words even if she wanted to, Kara felt wretched. Flopping down to the ground, soaked through as dusk crept in, mosquitoes and gnats thick in the air as frogs started to warble again and crickets made a racket, Kara drew her knees up to her chest and hid her face in her hands as she started to cry. She wasn’t prone to crying that often but felt like it was a far more common occurrence of late, her emotions all over the place, everything caught inside her, bottled up and ensnared by the dreaded prophecy. It was too much for her to sift through with any real effort, leaving her more melancholy and exhausted with each passing day.

     

                Crying her eyes out, oblivious to everything else, not even caring if the tree suddenly decided to turn on her, opening up the ground and wrapping her in its roots so it could feed on her body, Kara only had the energy to fixate on one thing - her wife. And almost as if she’d summoned her by mere thought, Kara heard the soft tread of footsteps on the grass, not quite able to be as silent as the rest of them, so unused to walking with the practised grace of those who’d spent decades in the forest. It could only have been Lena, and Kara’s shoulders tensed as she kept her head ducked down, trying to wipe her face on her damp sleeves, knowing her cheeks would be blotchy, her eyes red and sore. 

     

                “You should not be out here so late,” Kara murmured as Lena came to a stop a dozen feet away, uncertainty making her keep her distance.

     

                “I brought you dinner,” Lena softly replied, padding closer until she was at Kara’s side, sinking onto the damp grass at the base of the sycamore, a bundle of far more than food laid down before her. 

     

                Kara couldn’t look at her, turning her head aside, cheek resting on her forearms crossed over her knees. Sniffing, she closed her eyes, feeling the bite of the wind on her cheeks, and she drew in another soft, shuddering breath. Lena didn’t speak, but Kara felt her tilt her head to the side, the weight of it settling on her shoulder as her wife silently tried to comfort her. Eyes smarting with tears again, Kara quickly dashed her knuckles across them.

     

                “Thank you,” she managed to get out, gravelly and low. “You should return now.”

     

                “Alex said she has forbidden you from entering her home again but would not tell me why. She said I should ask you.”

     

                “My sister … my sister loves me, but it is a tough sort of love, and she is not always gentle with expressing her concern. She doesn’t think I’m being fair to you, and while I must agree with her, I am unable to rectify my mistake. I hope you can forgive me; I do not mean to hurt you, but I do not wish to speak of it.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena murmured, already tired from their earlier spat over secrets. They lapsed into silence for a moment and Kara sniffed again, so blue and fed up, letting out a soft sigh, before Lena lifted her head from Kara’s shoulder. “Look at me.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara raised her head, tipping it back as she sighed a little louder then, resigned and aching, before she lowered it again and turned to look at Lena. The tenderness of her wife’s concern made the corner of Kara’s mouth twitch with a ghost of a smile, and Lena reached out to brush her cool fingertips over Kara’s blotchy cheeks, softly tutting her tongue as she took in the redness of her wife’s eyes.

     

                “Whatever has you so upset … it will pass.”

     

                “Yes, it always does,” Kara agreed, eyelids shuttering as she drew in a shaky breath at the feeling of her wife’s fingers caressing her cheek. “I will be fine after some rest. Let me walk you back to the tunnel first, so I can know you are safely inside.”

     

                Lena let out a surprised scoff, her brow furrowing as her mouth thinned, and she quickly started to unpack the bundles before her, the food she’d brought Kara for dinner, as mentioned, but blankets, a roll of canvas, some rope, a canteen and a pot, her bow and quiver and a leather bedroll big enough for two. Her green eyes were peevish as she met Kara’s gaze, a little pouch of tea leaves in her hand as she hesitated.

     

                “Your sister might think she’s coming to my defence, but if she’s kicking you out, I’m coming with you.” Lena covered Kara’s hand with hers as they looked at each other, and Lena’s lips twitched with annoyance but her voice was gentle. “No matter how many times we argue or disagree, my place is at your side. Not even your sister can keep me away.”

    Chapter 40

                It was a damp night, the canvas tied to the tree and staked into the ground to create a lean-to against the wide trunk, offering some protection from the patter of rain that seemed endless, the wives huddled beneath it together as they talked quietly, swapping a skin of wine while Kara caught a fish and cooked it over a smoking fire that struggled to stay lit.
