Still, Lena didn’t regret her decision to come with her, growing rather introspective as the night wore on, the air cold as she shivered with a blanket and her cloak wrapped tightly around her shoulders, sitting with her conflicting emotions, Kara still not quite forgiven after their earlier argument, even though Lena couldn’t say why she was so upset by everything.

     

                It felt like an eternity before they bedded down for the night, the grass offering a somewhat softer bed than some others Lena had experienced, so it wasn’t all bad, and she was too tired to care much anyway. Feeling the warmth of her wife at her back, huddling together for warmth, Lena breathed in the smell of rain and woodsmoke as she shut her eyes and let sleep drag her under, the steady drumming of raindrops on the taut canvas a somewhat soothing melody. She slept soundly and deeply, waking as the sky started to lighten.

     

                It was still raining, heavier now, the canvas and grass sodden, and she fumbled behind her for Kara, finding the blankets cold, speaking of her long absence. Pushing herself up, breath visible in the air before her as she shivered slightly, Lena ducked her head outside of the lean-to and caught sight of her wife stretched out on the grass at the lakeside, arms and legs spread as she let the rain pummel her. Wondering if she should be concerned, still uncertain about her wife’s often strange behaviour, Lena ducked out from under the shelter and drifted towards the trees. She had her dagger at her waist and left her bow behind, intending to collect wood for a fire, and padded across sodden grass, numbing her toes as she moved past the treeline and into the dimness of the forest.

     

                It was colder there, in deep shadow, ice frosting over shrubs and bare bushes, a few spiderwebs spanning trunks beaded with dew and tiny droplets of ice as she ducked beneath them, stooping to pick up appropriate branches. Lena didn’t dare touch anything that wasn’t already on the ground, the hem of her cloak snagging on thorns and trailing through dirt as she stepped over roots and skirted around mossy rocks, the pile in her arm growing bigger. The air was so cold it felt like fire in her lungs, and she heard nothing but the birdsong and the rustling of leaves and bare branches as she went about her task, softly whistling as she went.

     

                She didn’t go too far, but she couldn’t see the lake or the sloping valley when she glanced back, the light dim as it filtered through the canopy. Still, Lena didn’t feel any danger as she stooped to pick up another thick branch, stepping on the lower part and bending the top to snap it in half, picking up both halves and adding them to her stack as she continued to whistle. Consumed by her task, she didn’t notice the way the forest fell silent, continuing her absentminded whistling, until something changed. It was a certain awareness , the hair-raising feeling at the back of her neck, running up her spine as she straightened, going still as she listened, hearing nothing. 

     

                Then she heard a hammering heartbeat and light footsteps turned clumsy in haste, rustling leaves on the ground as they approached, turning to watch her wife dart around a tree trunk, eyes wide and clothes soaked. She looked peeved, the tips of her ears parting her wet, blonde hair, cheeks a rosy pink as she seemed to emerge from the gloom. There was a panicked look in her blue eyes too as she hurried to Lena’s side.

     

                “You never whistle when the forest goes silent,” Kara roughly warned her, keeping her voice low as her eyes scanned the trees, taking Lena’s arm as she slowly started to tug her back the way they’d come.

     

                Letting out a confused sound of surprise, Lena clutched her armful of firewood to her chest as she staggered along, picking up speed as she got her feet under her. A fierce wind started up then, rushing through the trees with an eerie howl, making Lena’s skin rippled with goosebumps as she felt her stomach drop. There was a high-pitched screeching then, off to their right, Lena’s head whipping around as her breath caught in her throat, dropping some of the firewood as she was towed along by Kara, the wind getting stronger, almost angry.  

     

                “What was that?” Lena breathlessly asked as they ran along, Kara’s hand wrapped around hers now, moving quickly as they covered the hundred feet or so that Lena had ventured into the trees.

     

                Kara didn’t say anything until they burst through the treeline and out into the rain. Breathing heavily, her heart pounding, Lena came to a stop not far from their makeshift camp, dropping her armful of wood as she braced her hands on her knees, rain lashing down. After a moment, she straightened, brushing dark hair back as she rounded on her wife.

     

                “Don’t whistle when the trees are quiet,” Kara repeated, rubbing her brow.

     

                “I- what do you mean?”

     

                “You draw too much attention to yourself. Always. Any time you are amongst the trees … it is as if the forest pays especially close attention to you. Whether that be for good or ill. Yes, you will bring forth a tree full of ripe cherries, but you attract trouble too.”

     

                “It was just some wind.”

     

                “And yet, there is little wind here, away from the treeline. The forest is mercurial, it teases, it hunts, it provides. Do not whistle again.”

     

                “But- you always whistle,” Lena indignantly replied.

     

                A laugh escaped Kara, her panic diminishing now, and she started to pick up Lena’s dropped firewood. “I call to the birds, sing to the trees. Only when they are talking to me.”

     

                With a strained laugh, Lena gestured wildly. “Sure, why not? Now I have to worry about the fucking trees talking to me.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Kara gave her an admonishing look. “You should know better than most that trees, flowers, shrubs, all manner of plants, are living creatures too. Do flowers not flourish in your presence? As if you are the sun.”

     

                “That’s a manifestation of my latent powers.” 

     

                “Yes, but they are still alive. Much like the fish that are drawn to me and my power over water.”

     

                “Oh, so you talk to fish too?”

     

                A smile curled the corners of Kara’s lips and she gave her a withering glance. “Yes, but they are not very reciprocal, unfortunately.”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena started to help her pick up the firewood. “What was that noise?”

     

                “It sounded like a fox.”

     

                “A fox doing what, exactly?”

     

                “That is not the correct question; it is what was being done to it.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena’s face furrowing, she cocked her head to the side, apprehensive as she didn’t speak for a moment, letting the rain soak her throat as she cradled her firewood, now positively useless. “Can I see?”

     

                Pausing, Kara glanced to the trees, still waving from a strong wind, but that eerie howl silent now, and relented with a grimace and a nod. She set down the firewood in a neat pile and Lena followed suit before they walked back towards the trees, bearing left. Walking with care, trying to remain silent, unobtrusive as the wind occasionally whined, branches creaking and rain dripping down onto their heads and shoulders, they walked through the frosted forest until the trees parted to reveal a snarling mass of brambles with thorns as long as Lena’s arm, and a massive fox skewered by them. Black blood coated its fur, the orange a bright spot of colour in the darkness, and Lena stared at it with unease knotting her stomach.

     

                Kara reached for her hand, squeezing reassuringly before drawing her closer to the dead fox, hanging limply, pinned in place by the thorns. Looking up at it, a few feet higher than their heads, Lena watched black blood drip from the puncture wounds, soaking into the mud and leave-strewn ground. It didn’t so much as twitch, its body already growing stiff as it cooled, the blood still steaming slightly, and Lena took in the size of it. It would’ve been six feet tall on all fours, much larger than a common fox, and she took in the little button mushrooms and lichen growing over its fur. 

     

                “It’s a shame,” Lena murmured, eyebrows pinched together in a look of dismay.

     

                “It is the way of life.”

     

                They were silent for a moment, staring at the fox, before Lena softly sighed with regret. “We should cut it down-“

     

                “No,” Kara sharply cut her off with a surprised look at Lena’s suggestion. “Leave the forest be. It is not for us to meddle.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena nodded. After another second, Kara took her hand and tugged her away, and once they were far enough away, Lena turned back for a last glance and could’ve sworn the brambles of thorns were tightening around the fox’s body, as if ensnaring it further, a sentient creature absorbing its prey. Suppressing a shiver, Lena looked ahead and increased her pace slightly, thinking about it some more.

     

                “Can I ask why you don’t eat them? I mean … the wolves, the boar, there have been a few times we’ve seen animals that are huge , and it would feed a lot of people, but you always leave them alone. Even their pelts, which I’m sure would be nice and warm right about now while we’re camping outside.”

     

                “Any of the unnaturally big creatures you see aren’t suitable for eating. They’re … poisoned by the forest, I suppose is the best way to explain. That’s why their blood is black. They’re already dying before they’re killed by us in defence, or- well, the forest is claiming them, and will continue to until they die. Their meat is not fit for eating, and it is better to leave alone what the forest has claimed for itself.”

     

                “And what about people? Why aren’t you lot running around, twenty feet tall with mushrooms sprouting out of your skin?”

     

                Kara gave her a grim smile, “ah, well, it affects us differently. You can see it in the ways your brother has been twisted, in the way that Sam’s mind is torn in half. It is something not quite right.”

     

                “Was it always that way?”

     

                “No. There is none alive now who can tell us what it was like, but our written history speaks of times before the creatures were as such. The forest has always been a sweet poison though, that much has always been true.”

     

                “Isn’t there a cure?”

     

                “No. Or not yet. Unless your healing magic could be of some use.”

     

                “I doubt it,” Lena softly laughed. “And it’s not magic, it’s just science.”

     

                “I believe you promised me a demonstration,” Kara reminded her as they broke through the trees again, heading for their massive sycamore and the limited shelter it offered from the deluge of rain.

     

                The corners of her lips twitching slightly, Lena nodded. “I did. You’ll have to be my mannequin though, if you want a demonstration now.”

     

                “And what does that require of me?”

     

                With a soft snort, Lena rolled her eyes, taking her arm. “A mannequin is like a big human-shaped figure to demonstrate on. Come on, on your back. Play dead.”

     

                Willingly obliging, tossing her cloak back with a flourish as she grinned crookedly at Lena and sprawled on her back, Kara closed her eyes and then opened one again.

     

                “And what have I died of? A slit throat? An arrow to the heart?”

     

                “No,” Lena spluttered with laughter. “This won’t work for that. I told you, it’s not magic. I mean, it might help, but I sure wouldn’t be able to keep someone alive. At least, I highly doubt I could. You can be a drowning victim-“

     

                “I would never drown,” Kara indignantly replied.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena sighed. “Yes, I know that. You’re … the best swimmer to ever exist. Sure. But for the purpose of this demonstration- fine, you choked on a piece of food and you’re suffocating.”

     

                Kara chuckled, “that seems more probable.”

     

                “So, if you were choking, I’d do the Heimlich first, which is to get you to cough up whatever’s blocking the airway, right? But you were choking for a while and … you’re already unconscious, and- and your heart stopped, so now, my goal is to keep your heart pumping blood so your brain has oxygen. Air. If the brain doesn’t have air, it dies. So, you put your hands like this, and you compress.”

     

                She had her hands overlapped over Kara’s heart and demonstrated a compression. Face soft with amusement at the solemn look of attention on Kara’s face, Lena cleared her throat.

     

                “So, you keep doing that, and you have to do it at a particular rhythm. You know, like heartbeats.” Humming along to Stayin’ Alive, Lena continued her compressions, pressing lightly so she didn’t hurt Kara. “I’m doing it a bit light, but you’d want to do deeper compressions, so the heart is forced to pump, you see? But for kids and old people, you could accidentally break some ribs if you do it too hard, so you need to be careful. And then, you also have to keep oxygen flowing.”

     

                She loomed over her wife, ducking down as she inhaled deeply. Pressing her lips to Kara’s, she felt her wife’s mouth firm up beneath hers in a kiss, and Lena drew back with exasperation, giving Kara a stern look.

     

                “You’re supposed to be unresponsive.”

     

                “Of course.”

     

                “Anyway, so you inhale and then breathe into the person’s mouth to give them your air,” Lena said before she tried to demonstrate again.

     

                Kara kissed her again, hand cupping the side of Lena’s head, and Lena abruptly withdrew, turning her head aside as her face furrowed. There was a flash of irritation, her lips pressed together as she frowned at the trees.

     

                “Please stop doing that.”

     

                “Am I not allowed to kiss you?” Kara asked with surprise, pushing herself up onto her elbows.

     

                “Well, I’d prefer it if you didn’t right now,” Lena haltingly admitted. “It doesn’t seem fair - to either of us.”

     

                The flicker of hurt in Kara’s eyes was so well-masked that Lena didn’t catch it. “Oh. Well, of course. I apologise if I’ve been making you uncomfortable. That was not my intention at all, I- I would hate for you to feel-”

     

                “No, no, it’s fine, I just- it’s complicated, and I don’t want to make things harder for you. I don’t want there to be any confusion, either.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Um …” Lena floundered in the discomfort of the moment, hurriedly pushing herself to her feet, brushing off the skirts of her dress. “I’ll see if I can get the fire going.”

     

                Her voice wavered, embarrassingly so as she turned her back on Kara, cringing as her face reddened, and Lena quickly walked over to the pile of wet wood.  Sinking to a crouch, Lena rummaged through the stack for the driest pieces and started to arrange them in the way she’d been shown, fumbling with some flint as she tried to light the kindling. It took her the better part of ten minutes to even get it smoking, while Kara unpacked an assortment of items for tea and breakfast, tightening up the ropes holding their pitiful shelter taut as the rain continued to pour down. 

     

                Lena wished she’d waited for a less awkward time to make her discomfort known - perhaps when they weren’t forced into close proximity in the pouring rain of the outdoors - the tension palpable as they both silently went about their tasks. Kara fetched water once Lena had a decent-sized fire burning, smoke billowing from the wet wood, and they sat by the warmth of the fire as the small pot slowly came to a boil. Taking the pot off, Lena sprinkled some herbs into the pot and let it steep before filling two cups, while Kara cut an apple into pieces and tore a small loaf of bread in half. It was no worse than the food they’d had on the road, perhaps even better given its relative freshness, and they ate in silence.

     

                It continued to rain and they sipped a second cup of tea each before Kara went for a swim, while Lena practised her archery, unbothered by the rain, already soaked through. They passed most of the morning not ignoring each other, but talking very little and with overly polite tones when they did. She helped Kara set a snare for a few of the rabbits bounding about and foraged for some unripe strawberries along the fringes of the forest, watching them redden as she handled them, doubling in size before she plucked them from the plants. They still weren’t very big, at that, but she ate a couple and found the flavour better than any she’d ever had before coming to the forest, pleased with her harvest as she moved back to the fire, where Kara was already gutting and skinning a rabbit.

     

                Near lunchtime, Kelly came to check up on them, bringing more blankets, leather bedrolls and another sheet of canvas with some poles to hold the corners up, creating a canopy for them to sit beneath. She was apologetic and exasperated, talking quietly with Kara as Lena unpacked the bundle of dry clothes, eagerly changing into leather leggings, a shirt, tunic and surcoat split for riding. It was warm and more mobile than her dress, and even better, it was dry , even if she pulled her heavy, damp cloak back around her shoulders.

     

                Continuing to dig through the supplies, crouched amidst the saddlebags as she swiftly unpacked them - spare flint, plates, more tea leaves, fruit and cheese and wineskins - Lena glanced up with a length of coiled rope in her hands, the coarse hemp scratchy against her palms as she watched Kara reach up to cup Kelly’s cheek in hand. She couldn’t see her wife’s face properly, but she saw the slumped set of her shoulders, the way she meekly ducked her head, defeated, and felt a jolt of shocked understanding flit through her as her mouth fell open. Before she could even dissuade the thoughts from forming, Lena had leapt to the terrible conclusion that Kara’s difficulty in her feelings, and Alex’s anger surrounding it, was because of Kelly.

     

                Feeling shockingly pale, a little faint as she drew in shallow breaths, Lena looked down as she reeled from her revelation. It all made sense to her now, why Kara wouldn’t tell anyone, why Kelly didn’t even know who Kara had fallen for, why Kara might be embarrassed to admit that she loved her sister’s wife, why Alex had quarrelled and kicked her out, perhaps angry on Lena’s behalf too, both of them on either side of Kara’s feelings. Of course, Lena didn’t know just how wrong she was, but as she watched Kelly try to hug Kara, watched Kara weakly return it as she tried to shrug off her touch, as if she couldn’t bear to be hugged by the woman she loved, who didn’t love her in return, it felt so painfully familiar. It was how Lena had responded a little over an hour ago, withdrawing from Kara’s innocent kisses because she hated how Kara so readily gave her affection but couldn’t give her the love she craved. It only served to further convince her of her wife’s feelings for her sister-in-law, and Lena felt a cold anger seep through her, a stinging in her eyes as she tried to stamp down her hurt.

     

                As they spoke in quiet voices, Lena abandoned the saddlebags and moved over to Kelly’s bay roan filly, smoothing a hand down the young horse’s neck as she felt her restless energy from being cooped up inside. Listening to the rain drip from the branches overhead as the rain lightened to a steady patter, Lena basked in the comforting scent of horses, tanned leather and wet grass as she tried to expel some of the tension in her body, working hard to breathe slowly, deeply, convincing herself it would be alright. Clammy and pale-faced, Lena was struck with the sudden clarity that she loved Kara. The realisation wasn’t timely.

     

                She felt nauseous as she continued to stroke the horse, a dazed expression on her face as she felt as if she might pass out. Stilling, Lena knotted her fingers in the filly’s mane as she drew in painful breaths, her chest tight with panic, and she tried to muddle through her revelation, weak-kneed and agonised. It should’ve been painfully obvious to her, that she’d been jealous for quite some time, desperate for Kara’s love, oddly possessive of her wife, and yet Lena had blown off any attempt others had made to point out her behaviour. She’d never been in love before, never had anyone to love her, and so Lena didn’t know what she was looking for, had been willfully ignorant out of fear, but it had blindsided her now with how obvious it was.

     

                “Lena?”

     

                Startling at the sound of Kelly’s voice behind her right shoulder, Lena kept her eyes cast down as she turned slightly to glance back at her. “Hm?”

     

                Brow creasing with concern, Kelly cocked her head to the side. “Are you well?”

     

                “Me? Oh, um …”

     

                “You look as if you should sit. Come, let me see if something is amiss.”

     

                Lena opened and closed her mouth, intending to protest, but couldn’t make her voice work, her throat tight around them, her mouth horribly dry. Swallowing thickly, she was helpless to Kelly’s gentle hands grasping her arms and steering her over to the pile of blankets that had made up their bed last night. Urging her down, Kelly sank to a crouch before her and Lena’s gaze flitted past her to meet Kara’s eyes as her wife drew nearer, eyebrows raised a fraction, eyes wide with worry.

     

                “You look bone white,” Kelly murmured, frowning as she touched a hand to Lena’s brow. “Yet, you have no fever.”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena rasped.

     

                “Have you caught a chill? Does your chest ache? You should not be sleeping out here,” Kelly clicked her tongue, mouth thinning at the corners as she grimaced at her wife’s decision. 

                

                “I’m fine. It’s just-” she attempted to lie, to brush it off as something ordinary - missed breakfast or her period - but she couldn’t force the words out, her voice failing her. She tried for another angle, a half-truth. “I don’t like how everything is. Things are fragile enough without us all fighting.”

     

                “You do not need to worry yourself about these things,” Kara murmured, hands clasped behind her back as her shoulders lost some of their tension at the relief of Lena being fine.

     

                “Well, I am,” Lena curtly replied, a muscle twitching in her jaw.

     

                She couldn’t look at her. Her eyes started to sting, throat closing up, and she had to clench her teeth to stop her chin from wobbling. Feeling the heat start to creep into her cheeks, feeling churlish and stupid, Lena abruptly lurched to her feet, leaving Kelly kneeling, side-stepping Kara, unable to stay there any longer, playing the fool.

     

                “You two enjoy each other’s company. I’m not sitting in the rain all day.”

     

                Hurrying away, she trudged barefoot over the wet grass, the occasional patch of mud leaving her feet filthy as she drew up the hood of her cloak and staggered up the steep side of the valley. Horses milled about, grazing on the grassy slopes, and she was soon out of breath and soaked through again, her cheeks rosy from the cold as she continued her angry march up to the mouth of the tunnel, her heart hammering in her chest as she spiralled. Lena couldn’t help it; she’d jumped to conclusions and could feel the stability of the life she’d carved out in the forest starting to fall apart as a result of her own assumptions. 

     

                By the time she’d reached the mouth of the tunnel, she was blinking back tears, rubbing furiously at her eyes as she drew in shallow, hitching breaths. Slipping into the dark, she sniffed, frigid stone underfoot, and took a few minutes, hidden in the deep shadow of the entryway, to stamp down her devastation, the heartbreak she hadn’t even known she could feel. A few tears fell and she felt angry at herself as she scrubbed them away, wiping her face on damp sleeves, barely keeping it together as she was struck by this strange sadness. Lena knew what grief felt like but this was an entirely unfamiliar feeling and she didn’t know what to do about it.

     

                It all felt so wrong. Not that she loved Kara, and not that Kara loved someone else, but wrong that it was Kelly. Her sister’s wife. But of course, Lena couldn’t blame Kara for that either. She couldn’t blame her for not loving her back when Kelly was so much more accomplished in every conceivable way. She was an expert healer, she was skilled with a bow and several other weapons, she was smart and kind, a capable ranger and well-versed in the politics of Court - and she was beautiful too. Who wouldn’t want to love someone like that? Especially in comparison to a half-fae who’d been as helpless as a child when she’d been dragged there to marry Kara. Even now, eight months later, as far as she’d come, Lena felt inadequate in every comparable way. 

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, Lena rubbed her eyes, already red raw, and continued up the long tunnel. It was pitch black, the light of the tunnel fading behind her, and she felt weariness steal over her, the tunnel feeling endless, until she came out in that entrance chamber. Drawn to the horses first, Lena spent ten minutes stroking the flank of her mare as she reined in her emotions before she squared her shoulders and went to confront Alex.

     

                It took her the better part of an hour to locate her sister-in-law, her hair still damp and growing frizzy as she moved deeper into the humid halls beneath the mountain, wet clothes leaving a trail of water on the stone behind her until they’d dried off enough to just uncomfortably chafe on her search. Eventually, she found Alex in her forge, working alone in the room illuminated by the orange glow of fire. 

     

                Lena heard the sound of a hammer tolling first, the steady pounding beat alerting her to the presence of someone , at least, and she correctly assumed it would be Alex. When she wandered inside, a sorry sight as she shivered slightly, looking like she’d been dragged out of the lake outside, Alex glanced up from the piece of steel she was working on.

     

                “Sister.”

     

                Folding her arms over her chest, Lena drifted closer, her jaw clenched tightly shut as she breathed slowly through her nose, trying to retain her hard-won composure. She didn’t respond, even once she was close enough to Alex that she felt the fire of the forge strongly enough that it made her cheeks prickle with the heat.

     

                “You look as if you bear bad news. Is something amiss?”

     

                “I know the truth,” Lena rasped, so certain of her deduction that she was able to speak it truthfully.

     

                Alex did a double-take, her mouth opening and closing as her eyes widened, the hammer falling from limp fingers. “She told you?”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena let out a frayed laugh, pacing away from the forge as her eyes swam with tears. She wasn’t able to speak without the words coming out as an awful tremble. “No, no, I figured it out. I- I should’ve seen the signs earlier, really. It all makes sense now. I can- I can see why you were mad, why you kicked her out.”

     

                Letting out another laugh, Lena ran a hand over the snarled mess of her wind-blown hair. Bracing her hands against the edge of a worktable, she swallowed thickly. “And now I know why she didn’t want to tell me. Or anyone, for that matter.”

     

                “I’m sorry for what you’re going through.”

     

                Lena laughed again, wiping her face on her sleeve. Silent for a moment, her mouth turning down at the corners as her chin wobbled, she hung her head, stamping her feelings down before she turned around, raising her eyebrows as she met Alex’s surprisingly tender gaze.

     

                “And what about you?”

     

                “Me?”

     

                “Aren’t you sorry for yourself, too?”

     

                “Oh. Well, yes, I admit that I was hasty in my argument with my sister. I had thought she would tell you herself, and I’m sorry for my hand in forcing the truth to come to light.”

     

                Momentarily puzzled, Lena frowned, head cocked to the side as she took in Alex’s words, thinking that she was taking it remarkably well. Although, she could see some of Alex’s disapproval in her words, clearly unhappy with the situation.

     

                “But it is better for everyone involved that it has finally come to light. This secrecy … it benefited no one but Kara.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena agreed, looking down as she fiddled with her fingers. “But you’ll let her come back inside now?”

     

                She peeked up, a hopeful look on her face, watching as Alex faltered. “I do not believe it will be that simple. I had barred her from entering unless she told you herself. As you have uncovered the truth yourself, she will still be barred from my home. I assume you have not discussed it with her yet?”

     

                “No. I don’t think I want to.”

     

                “Oh. Yes, well, I understand why, of course.”

     

                “Of course,” Lena agreed with a thin smile, feeling exhaustion steal over her.

     

                “I hope that you do not blame her too much for it. It is not her fault-”

     

                “No. No, I don’t blame her. How could I? I just- I wish it was different.”

     

                Alex’s lips twitched with a sad smile, brown eyes aching as she held Lena’s stare. “As do I.”

     

                Lena jolted with the sickening realisation that it wasn’t just that Kara had fallen in love with Kelly, but that it meant she would kill her. She’d forgotten that key piece of information and it made her feel suddenly nauseous as her eyes widened, mouth falling open as her stomach turned. So focused on her own heartbreak, Lena had overlooked the most vital part of Kara’s prophecy, and she felt faint all over again as she tried to process the news. Eyes filling with fresh tears, a tremor in her hand, she turned away from Alex, the breath hitching in her chest. To her sister-in-law, it looked like she was struggling to come to terms with her own death. If they’d both been more forthright in their conversation, if everyone was more forthright, instead of dancing around truths to avoid tying themselves up in unbreakable promises or accidental oaths, they would’ve had things straightened out, leaving Lena to reckon with her own mortality, but she was left feeling sorry for everyone else instead of feeling sorry for herself.

     

                Hesitating with uncertainty, Alex pressed her lips together and then set down her tongs, before she crossed over to Lena and wrapped her in a hug. It was the arms of the wrong sister but it was the comfort Lena needed as she pressed her face into Alex’s shoulder, grateful to know that she understood how Lena was feeling, caught on the other side of it all. She didn’t know how Alex could keep it together so well though, knowing what would come of her wife at her sister’s hand.

     

                “All will be well,” Alex assured her, giving Lena’s back a rub. “We don’t know what events will transpire. It might not be for a millennia, it might not be as we think at all. It is frightening, I know, and it is not what any of us wanted, but we must go on, yes? We cannot live for the fear of tomorrow. You will get through this, as difficult as it is.”

     

                Pulling back, Lena nodded as she wiped at her damp eyes. “I just- I didn’t think it would happen like this.”

     

                “Our prophecies never come about as we think they will. Did I ever tell you of my own? No? I was told to beware of going west if I did not want to lose myself. Do you know what the meaning was? I would return changed because I went west and met Kelly, slowly fell in love with her, and returned better for it, losing my old self in the process.”

     

                “But how do you know that was it? What if you went west again and something bad happened?”

     

                Alex laughed, giving Lena’s shoulder a quick squeeze. “We have people who tell us of our prophecy; each person has one, even if they do not wish to know it. Nia is adept at telling them, you know, if you ever have an interest in knowing your own future. I think … perhaps it might be comforting for you. Once it has been told, a record is sent to the Council for safekeeping - it can only be told once, you see - and once it comes true , whatever event it may be, the ink fades. The words are still legible, but barely so, and I know that mine has faded. There is also … a sense of knowing . There is something in your chest that recognises the truth of the moment. You will not understand until you know what truth you are seeking.”

     

                Hesitating, Alex raised her eyebrows encouragingly. “Do you wish to know yours?”

     

                Chewing her lip, Lena shrugged, a clouded look on her face. “I don’t know. I don’t know if- if it’ll make much difference. I’m not going to get what I want.”

     

                “Perhaps not, but … it is always better to know.”

     

                “I don’t know, I thought that too, but … maybe now I think I might’ve preferred to not know. I don’t think I want to open that can of worms anymore.”

     

                “I don’t understand.”

     

                Lips twitching with a smile, Lena rubbed the back of her neck. “I don’t think I could bear finding out right now. There’s too much going on, and I’m not sure it would help. I’d rather not know what’s in store for me.”

     

                Nodding, Alex moved back over to her work table and picked up her tongs. “It is your decision. I can see that you have made it.”

     

                Nodding, running her hands over her arms as she kept them folded over her chest, Lena swallowed thickly, fear filling her chest. “What do we do now? In the meantime, I mean.”

     

                “You look as if you could do with a hot bath,” Alex murmured, not looking up from her work as she studied the piece of steel she’d been hammering. “And then you need to decide whether you want to go back outside with my sister or not.”

     

                Annoyance twisted Lena’s mouth and she quietly scoffed. “I’ll tell you the same thing I told her; my place is at my wife’s side. I understand you’re angry about the way she’s managed things, but I don’t think it was fair for you to do that. I mean, I get it, sort of, um … well, I think- it doesn’t matter, but I think you could’ve been a little kinder to her. It’s not easy for her, I know she doesn’t want it to be like this. I think this is probably the last thing she wanted to happen. And … I think you were right, and Kelly was right … about- about me. Um … I just don’t want her to get hurt, okay? I know you want that too, and I think … it’ll hurt us all, but I just- please promise that you’ll love her, no matter what. She’s going to need people who love her. She’d never- she’d never intentionally hurt someone she loves like that. I know she wouldn’t.”

     

                Alex stared at her for a long moment, the roar of the fire filling the cavernous room as the silence dragged on, until her expression softened. Mournful and solemn, Alex picked up her hammer, turning the polished wooden handle in her grasp, and hesitated before turning back to the forge.

     

                “Of course I’ll always love her. No matter what. She’s my sister; she would cut her own heart out if she thought it would make a difference.”

     

                “But it won’t,” Lena grimly murmured.

     

                Sighing, her shoulders sloping, Alex grimaced. “No. Not unless we’re mistaken.”

     

                Footsteps approached then and they both looked towards the door, watching as Kelly swept in, damp but smiling, her face softening with tender adoration as she looked to her wife, making a beeline for Alex. Lena watched Kelly cup her face and kiss her softly, had to look away at the jealousy that swept through her at the easy affection as Alex smoothed a hand over Kelly’s braids, smiling lovingly, at the anger for this tangled web that made everyone involved unhappy as she thought about how she loved Kara, and Kara loved Kelly, and Kelly loved Alex, and Alex’s wife was going to die. None of it was fair. Swallowing thickly, Lena rubbed her brow, her stomach knotted with unease.

     

                “Excuse me.”

     

                They gave her a bewildered glance, Lena’s moods always too confusing for them to understand, unsure what she was feeling, why she behaved as she did, but she didn’t explain herself, just made a swift exit. She took Alex’s advice and had a bath first though, wandering through the warren of hallways until she found herself in a vaguely familiar spot and managed to locate the hot springs from there, the caverns dark and humid as she found a small pool, feeling the steam caress her cheeks. Undressing in the dark, Lena rinsed off the mud and grass and dried herself as best as she could with her damp cloak before redressing in her still-wet clothes. 

     

                Feeling a little more put together as she wrung out the ends of her hair, she walked back through the hallways and made for the stables. There wasn’t anything she needed out of necessity, bringing supplies herself and more brought by Kelly, but she paused to let her mare out. Foregoing a saddle, not wanting to let the leather get ruined, left out in the rain for however long they were to camp outside, Lena hauled herself onto the mare’s bare back and guided them out of the stables and into the dark tunnel. She wasn’t used to riding bareback but managed well, all things considered, finding it more comfortable than her previous experiences with it, racing through the forest as she bounced about, clueless. It was still a little unnerving, slowly following the path down into the vale as she knotted her fingers in the mane and tried to hold herself steady with her knees clamped tightly, but Lena was not the same person she’d been when she’d first ridden a horse, so much changed since then. So much that she’d fallen in love without even meaning to, without even realising she had. 

     

                Arriving back at their makeshift camp hours later to find her wife sheltering beneath the wide-spreading canopy of the sycamore tree, Lena dismounted and sent her mare off to graze freely. She felt it would be a good idea to have a horse nearby, just in case. If Kara couldn’t get back inside, Lena didn’t want them to be trapped without resources if danger came their way. A very likely possibility. 

     

                Kara looked up at her arrival, fluidly rising to her feet, wringing her hands nervously as she took a step towards her and then halted, uncertainty written into the lines of her face. “Are you well?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena murmured, somewhat curt in her demeanour as she kept her eyes fixed on the grass, moving closer to the fire to help herself to some tea.

     

                Kara snagged her arm as she passed by, pulling her to a stop as she clicked her tongue, annoyance colouring her voice as she spoke. “I wish you would speak plainly. You are not fine, no matter how well you twist the truth to allow you to speak it so.”

     

                “What would you like me to say?” Lena asked, her voice hoarse.

     

                “Anything. As long as it is honest.”

     

                “I don’t think you’d like what I have to say very much.”

     

                “You can say anything. You have thorns, but I will gladly bleed if I am pricked by them. Nothing would make me turn away from you; you know that. I would sooner die myself than abandon you.”

     

                Lena scoffed quietly, hollow amusement crossing her face as she held Kara’s stare. They stared at each other, the rain a drizzle, water dripping from wet leaves as a certain stillness blanketed the vale. There was no wind now, faint bird calls filling the silence, and Lena breathed shallowly, her chapped lips parted as she felt the cold in her lungs, burning in her chest, amidst the horrible weight of her emotions. She felt like she was suffocating, the tightness of it almost painful, her voice wavering when she replied. 

     

                “Tell me who you have fallen in love with.”

     

                It hadn’t been what she’d wanted to say, but she couldn’t say what she wanted to. Even if she’d had longer to reckon with herself, to process her feelings properly, she still didn’t think she’d be able to tell Kara. Lena had never been good with her emotions, but she thought it would’ve been humiliating to tell her wife that she loved her, knowing that Kara was in love with someone else, with Kelly. Being alone with the misery of unrequited feelings was preferable. So Lena asked her, because if she couldn’t be honest herself, she at least wanted Kara to be honest with her.

     

                “Ah.”

     

                Kara let go of her arm, curling her hands into fists as she floundered for a moment, speechless. She looked agonised and Lena’s stare was unwavering as she waited impatiently, an eyebrow raised as she spread her hands. Pressing the heels of her palms into her eyes, Kara let out a soft groan.

     

                “Why is this something you wish to know?”

     

                “Don’t you think I have the right to?”

     

                “Perhaps. But … it won’t make you happy.”

     

                Shrugging, Lena smiled thinly. “I’m already unhappy . I’d rather be unhappy and hear it from your lips. At least- at least we could go back inside then. We wouldn’t be stuck out in the rain.”

     

                Truthfully, Lena didn’t mind the rain. It was wet and miserable and cold, but she enjoyed the fresh air, the wildness of the outdoors. She liked that it was just her and Kara, with no expectations, even if things were unravelling quicker than they could patch them up. It didn’t matter where they were together now, there would be no going back to how things had been. Not now that Lena had realised the true depth of her feelings, and not since Kara had fallen in love with someone else. 

     

                “You can go back inside, if that’s what you wish.”

     

                “What I wish is for you to be honest with me,” Lena hotly replied.

     

                “That honesty comes with a price. It is fraught with danger; I’m not sure I want to take that risk, even if it pleases you.”

     

                “Surely it’s not putting her life at risk for you to tell me who she is?”

     

                With a huff, Kara gave her a piercing look, blue eyes sad and irate as her mouth flattened with annoyance. “It is . If word spread of who she was, people might target her.”

     

                “Ah, so it is a she .”

     

                Lena tried to keep the jealousy out of her voice, verging into triumph instead, as if it pleased her that she’d been right in her assumption. Her lips twisted into a faintly bitter smile, and she watched Kara wince and avert her gaze, head tipped back and blue eyes fitting up to look at the canopy, the sky. Lena was seized with the sudden urge to kiss the length of her throat. 

     

                “Yes, it is,” Kara whispered, “but I will say no more of it now. I mean it when I say it would not be wise for me to share who it is. Not with anyone.”

     

                “But Alex knows.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara closed her eyes and sighed. “Yes, Alex knows, but it was in a moment of vulnerability that I confessed. It has perhaps made things more complicated now that my sister has involved herself.”

     

                “But she doesn’t know? This- this woman that you supposedly love. ”

     

                “No. I- I do not wish to tell her, because … I do not wish to frighten her with news of her death.”

     

                “Don’t you think that’s wrong? You’ll tell your sister, but she’s kept in the dark about it? It doesn’t just affect you, you know; it affects us all. And I’d want to know,” Lena said with sudden firmness, hugging her arms tightly to her chest as she clenched her jaw, staring straight at her wife, trying to reason with her. “If it was me, I’d want to know.”

     

                “You say that because I have not said it to you,” Kara murmured, her brow furrowing as she glanced at Lena and then away. “If I were to say that to you, you would feel differently. I think you would feel frightened to know that you were going to die, that I was going to kill you.”

     

                Lena waved a dismissive hand, her chest aching with longing. She could see that she was making Kara uncomfortable, perhaps pushing her too far, but Lena’s eyes were already stinging with tears, her voice wobbling as she forged onwards. “ She might, but I wouldn’t.”

     

                “And what makes you so certain?” Kara demanded.

     

                There was a divot between Kara’s eyebrows and a muscle twitched in her jaw as she looked at Lena again now, her gaze intense, her body brimming with tension. If Lena had been able to drag her eyes away from her wife, she might’ve noticed the way the surface of the lake rippled, the way the rain seemed to hover midair, Kara’s agitation radiating from her, affecting the water in the vicinity. Likewise, Lena was oblivious to the way the sycamore tree groaned, its branches dipping towards her, the forest stirred up, roots digging in a little deeper, tensing at the frustration that was bound to explode out of Lena.

     

                She could feel it, burning inside as she gritted her teeth, vision blurring as hot tears splashed onto her cheeks, her face flushing as her hurt made her too honest. Lena couldn’t have stopped herself from speaking even if she’d bitten her own tongue, the words already spilling out of her before she’d had time to think about the consequences of her honesty, before her mind had even registered what she was saying.

     

                “Because I would give anything for it to be me,” she hotly confessed, her voice breaking as she let out a pitiful laugh. “I’m- I’m so horribly jealous that it’s not. I hate that it’s not me.”

     

                Kara visibly whitened at Lena’s words, her mouth falling open as she stared at her, blue eyes wide with shock as her chest quickly rose and fell. Realising she’d said too much, mortified by what she’d said, Lena looked away, ducking her head down as they stood in silence for a moment. Tears slid down her cheeks, and she wiped them away with the cuff of her surcoat as the sound of hoofbeats approached. Still, Kara stepped closer, finally able to make her feet move as she stammered until she found her voice. She reached out for Lena’s arm, gently taking hold of her bicep, trying to meet her eye.

     

                “What-”

     

                “Kara!”

                Alex’s voice drifted over to them, and the corners of Kara’s mouth tightened. Shoulders tense, she didn’t look back at her sister’s approaching figure, thundering closer on horseback, Kelly close on her heels. Lena didn’t look up, steadfastly keeping her eyes on the grass, surreptitiously wiping her face.

     

                Riding bareback, Alex reined in her stallion, the horse rearing and stamping the waterlogged ground, while Kelly brought her filly to a stop behind her. Holding a scroll of paper in hand, Alex’s expression was serious as Kara half-turned to her, not quite looking at her sister, keeping her eyes trained on the sliver of Lena’s flushed face that was visible behind her curtain of hair.

     

                “A letter has arrived. From the Council.”

     

                “Give us a moment. Please.”

     

                Peering up, Lena felt a stab of panic as her eyes briefly met Kara’s before she looked back down. No one moved for a moment, and then Kelly cleared her throat, her filly shifting beneath her, attuned to the restlessness of her rider. 

     

                “It cannot wait.”

     

                Kara’s lips parted as she drew in a breath to respond, but then seemingly changed her mind at the last moment. Looking up through her lashes, Lena watched her close her mouth, lips thinning with dismay, before she nodded and turned to Kelly. Watching Kara cave the moment Kelly spoke of the urgency only served to reaffirm what Lena had already guessed, her heart sinking into her stomach as a pained look rippled across her face, the corners of her mouth twitching with the bitterest of smiles. 

     

                As Kara moved over to the horses, extending a hand for the letter Alex held, Lena turned and walked away from her, equal parts relieved and disappointed that it was the end of their conversation. With the moment over, she stamped down her feelings, wiping at her stinging eyes, and made herself scarce so she could nurse her wounded feelings in peace. Finding a little hawthorn tree at the fringe of the forest, Lena scrambled up the trunk, disappearing into the branches and nestling into a sturdy fork, where she closed her eyes and let her misery wash over her as she silently vowed not to speak of her feelings again

    Chapter 41

                Kara finished reading the letter Alex had handed her, her body tense with the anticipation of what came next. The instructions were clear, and she swallowed thickly, nodding as she scrunched the paper in her fist, hesitating as she looked off into the distance, her voice soft as she spoke.

     

                “Please fetch her down.”

     

                It was Kelly who went, hurrying towards the trees, where Lena had gone to nurse her feelings, and Kara felt a flicker of ire at her sister’s bad timing. There were things she had not yet said in response to her wife’s words, had not been given the chance to question what Lena had meant, a prickle of hope sparked in Kara’s chest, and so much fear twisting her stomach as she considered what that could mean, what would come next. 

     

                As she struggled between her feelings for her wife and her duty to the Court, Alex studied her face, her eyes narrowed ever so slightly, short hair ruffled by the wind as she took in the tightness at the corners of her sister’s mouth, the evident displeasure. Things were still tense between them, a palpable annoyance that was rare but not new, but it all stemmed from Alex’s desire to help. She hated to see her sister suffer and couldn’t keep her mouth shut, cocking her head to the side.

     

                “What did we interrupt?”

     

                “It is of no concern to you,” Kara murmured, rubbing her brow as she looked down, already running the numbers, mapping the route, the supplies. 

     

                Her mind quickly ran through it all, the familiarity of leadership that had been shirked once more shouldered as she felt dread suffuse her. She wasn’t sure how, but she thought it would be worse this time. War was never fun , but it had all felt so clear in the past, the Courts divided by the river, an army on either side. Now, she wasn’t sure where Lex was, who he was targeting, whether peace with the Unseelie could be brokered again to fight a common enemy, or if they even wanted Lex as their enemy or King.

     

                “You should know that she knows,” Alex said after a moment.

     

                Head jerking up, Kara met her sister’s gaze, raising her eyebrows in a questioning glance. “What do you mean?”

     

                “Lena. She knows . Knows the truth.”

     

                “No, she doesn’t.”

     

                Alex let out a huff of laughter. “I assure you, Kara, she does. I spoke with her when she came to my halls earlier; her words could not be misconstrued when she, herself, told me she figured it out.”

     

                A crease furrowed Kara’s brow as she shook her head. “No, she just- we were just speaking . That was not the impression given at all.”

     

                “Indeed, I doubt she would be honest with you when you haven’t been honest with her.”

     

                “And what do you know of our private conversations? If you had not interrupted, perhaps it would have offered more clarity.”

     

                “Don’t try to cast blame on me; we both know you have no intention of telling her. Even if you did, war is more important. You have squandered your time alone with her, so now you will either need the courage to tell her with prying eyes surrounding you or live with the knowledge that she may die never knowing that she has been loved. I hope it is not the latter - for her sake.”

     

                “And that is so easy for you to say,” Kara softly snapped. “Do you not think if it was that easy for me I would have done it already?”

     

                “I think you’re happy with your misery. I think you have let it dictate your life for too long, carrying it around with you, spending years waiting for it to happen. If I had known what I know now when we agreed to travel together to have our futures told, I would not have agreed, I would have stopped you-”

     

                Cheeks flushed and eyes bright with wounded anger, a muscle twitched in Kara’s jaw. “Stop it.”

     

                “And you did it to yourself . If you hadn’t carried this with you, let it shape your choices, you would not have put yourself in a position where you married her because you were scared to fall in love. It might have been someone else who took up that duty.”

     

                “Yes, that is typically how prophecies work,” Kara curtly replied. “No matter what, it was destined to happen.”

     

                “Yes, but you could have at least been happy.”

     

                “I am happy! It may not be what you wished for me, it may not make sense to you, but she makes me happy. Even at my lowest, even when I’m filled with so much fear, so much worry for her, I can never be anything but happy to be in her presence, to hear her voice and her laugh, and-”

     

                Cutting off, choked up as she looked down, tears blurring her vision, Kara swallowed thickly. Drawing in a shuddering breath, she closed her eyes. “Every moment with her is cherished - even our arguments - and I do not need her to know how much they mean to me for them to mean it.”

     

                Shrugging, Alex’s mouth twisted with disapproval. “What of her happiness?”

     

                “It is of paramount importance.”

     

                “Then act like it,” Alex softly snapped.

     

                “You-”

     

                Falling silent at the sound of footsteps approaching from behind, Kara pressed her mouth into a flat line. Her shoulders were tense, and as Kelly passed by her, she rested a hand on it, shrugged off by Kara, who turned, looking up at Lena. Her wife’s head was ducked down as she studiously avoided meeting Kara’s eye, her pale cheeks pink, and not just from the cold. Reaching out, Kara’s fingers brushed the back of Lena’s hand, and she tried not to wince when Lena moved it away, raising it to fiddle with her fingers.

     

                “We should make preparations,” Alex muttered before giving her sister a dismissive look. “You cannot enter - still - so you can pack up your camp. We shall meet you here as quickly as everyone can be mustered. If there is anything you need, let me know and I will have it brought to you.”

     

                “I need my sister on my side.”

     

                “That,” Alex haughtily replied as she started to walk off, “you already have.”

     

                With a soft groan, Kelly grabbed Alex’s sleeve and dragged her a few steps away, until she stumbled into motion, the hand between her wife’s shoulder blades urging her onwards. It left Kara alone with Lena, who was quick to hurry after the other two, panicked by the thought of being left behind with her wife, the thought of needing to continue that conversation, to explain herself.

     

                “Lena, a word,” Kara murmured, reaching for her, even though Lena was already beyond her reach.

     

                “I should pack,” Lena brushed her off, continuing after Alex and Kelly as Kara’s hand fell limply back to her side, her shoulders caving with defeat.

     

     

                Andrea helped Lena pack her things, her practicality cutting out all of Lena’s dresses and jewels, any finery left packed in a trunk in Alex’s halls, ill-suited to war and unnecessary luggage for the caravan. It left her with a pair of leather leggings, a wool shirt, a padded jacket and a leather surcoat over the top, made to change into it all, with a thick cloak fastened at the right shoulder over the top. She had two spare shirts and a few of her socks, which she bickered with Andrea over, making a case for their necessity until her attendant relented.

     

                “This will be more gruelling than traversing the forest,” Andrea warned her. “Your horse will carry your belongings, yes, but there is no end destination with clean clothes and a hot bath for you to freshen up with, no banquets of fine food. Allocate your space appropriately; I’d wager you’d rather have a cured ham in your bag than some socks.”

     

                “Well, how about you pack the ham and I’ll keep my socks,” Lena sniped, a little tense, a little worried, thinking about what came next, thinking about how this had happened at the most inopportune moment. 

     

                She’d seen her fair share of fighting already, more than a presumed human had ever thought she’d see in her lifetime, let alone by the time she was thirty , but war was a different matter altogether. Lena had watched war documentaries, had studied history at school, learnt the harrowing stories of WWI trenches, of the Civil War, vague recollections of Ancient Greek warfare, wondering what she was about to experience. Of course, their fighting was of a more primitive stance much akin to medieval history, with swords, spears and arrows instead of guns and bombs, but Lena had watched them throw around fire and water, wind and earth in their little skirmishes and ambushes as if it was natural, and she wondered how that would translate to a large scale war. She wasn’t equipped for that.

     

                Alex came to collect Kara’s things while Lena was finishing her own pack, rolling a blanket tightly as she watched her sister-in-law rifle through Kara’s belongings, setting aside the necessities, leaving an odd assortment scattered across the bed sheets. As she strapped her blanket to the top of her pack, Lena watched Alex nudge aside a few jewels - sapphires and emeralds bigger than Lena’s thumbnail - a few bent quills, a pretty shell and a creased handkerchief. Lena’s eyebrows shot up at the latter, recognising the clumsy stitching on it as she abandoned her own packing and reached out to snag it. 

     

                Alex cast her an indifferent glance and continued what she was doing as Lena unfolded the handkerchief, taking in the faded bloodstains, evidently scrubbed hard to remove, and the crooked waves she’d painstakingly embroidered. It was far from good, and she’d intended to give it to Kara, had even told her wife that, but had ruined it with Sam’s blood and left her guard with it. Except, here it was, amongst Kara’s things. As Lena frowned down at it, Alex finished stuffing all of Kara’s clothes into her pack and then looked about, finding the shell, slipping it into her pocket and then searching for something else.

     

                When she looked up, realising what Lena held in her hands, she let out a soft huff, taking it from her. “There it is.”

     

                “Why does she have that?”

     

                “This? She asked Kelly to ensure she had her handkerchief.”

     

                Stuffing it into her pocket, Alex grabbed Kara’s pack and jerked her chin to Lena. “Come. Bring your pack and weapons. Be ready to leave.”

     

                Lena had her dagger belted at her waist, no borrowed sword though, and her bow and quiver left at the makeshift camp beneath the sycamore. She followed on Alex’s heels, moving through the hallways and finding herself in one of the storerooms off the cavernous kitchen, where Vasquez and J’onn were in discussion, while a variety of kegs, sacks and crates were being carried out by the few Unseelie left in Lillian’s party, with M’gann, Sam and Andrea helping as well. Alex handed parcels of food to Lena, conversing quickly with her Steward as Lena lost track of the conversation, shoving everything into the remaining room in her pack, while Alex likewise filled hers and Kara’s to the brim. 

     

                Everyone moved with urgency, knowing their purpose or finding one, and Lena was once more surprised by their efficiency, trying to keep up with the flurry of activity. With her pack on her shoulder, looking around, feeling a little lost and overwhelmed, Lena jumped slightly as Alex grabbed her arm, palming Kara’s pack off to her. 

     

                “Go to the stables. Saddle your horse and go to Kara.”

     

                “My horse is outside.”

     

                “Well, saddle a horse and go find it. We must be ready to leave shortly.”

     

                Hesitating, fleeting terror filled her at the thought of being alone with her wife, embarrassment slamming into her as her cheeks started to redden at the mere thought , Lena floundered and then nodded, turning on her heel and rushing out of the kitchen before Alex could question her strange reaction. Getting turned around in the tunnels, she finally made her way to the stables, passing by others heading back towards the storerooms to pack up more, and found a sturdy stallion. 

     

                Taking a few minutes to smooth her hands over the horse’s neck, Lena started to saddle up, grabbing a thick blanket, the right-size saddle, checking all the straps and buckles, adjusting empty saddlebags, and getting the harness on as the stallion mare stayed still. She got another set for her mare and slung it over the horse’s flanks, hoping it wouldn’t be too much of an annoyance for him. The horse was more spirited than her placid mare, and the horse nudged her shoulder as Lena anxiously lingered in the stables, reaching up to idly pat his chestnut nose. 

     

                Kelly appeared a few minutes later, and Lena perked up, stepping out of her stall. “What do I do now?”

     

                “Oh, Lena. Um … here, take this,” she distractedly replied, reaching for a bulging sack. “It’s Kara’s armour.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, okay. Um, do I- do I need to pack tack? What’s going in the saddlebags?”

     

                “Just … take this and your packs and go. Everything will be distributed outside.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena softly exhaled, taking the sack and moving over to the stallion. He was a few hands taller than her mare, and she had to use the wooden post of the stall to brace one foot and boost herself up into the saddle. The packs had been clumsily tied on with the buckles of the saddle and a length of ropes, and Lena had to wedge the gigantic sack of armour in front of her, holding the reins with one hand to keep an arm around the bulk of it, knowing that Kara’s life would depend on the state of the armour. Lena imagined dropping it off the back of the horse, and denting a piece could very well be catastrophic.

     

                Urging the stallion out of the stall, Lena was jostled for space, side-stepping two Unseelie carrying sacks of flour, Sam with a barrel of wine, and then making for the entrance tunnel, the opposite way to everyone else. Setting a brisk pace down the dim tunnel, she came out into the sloping side of the valley in the foothills, taking sight of the small pile of packed belongings beneath the sycamore. Kara was pacing beneath the dripping branches, and her head jerked up at the distant flicker of movement as Lena stepped out of the tunnel. She paused her pacing, and Lena had to swallow the lump in her throat as she made herself continue across the distance separating them.

     

                “I have your armour,” Lena softly said as she approached, hefting the sack up and holding it out for Kara.

     

                Approaching, Kara took it from her with quiet thanks, sinking to the grass as she upended the sack, polished steel spilling out. Turning over each segment in her hands, Kara inspected her armour with close attention to the rivets and straps, before she set the breastplate and tassets back into the sack with her helmet. Lena dismounted, quickly unburdening the stallion of the two packs, as well as the second saddle, fishing the bridle and blankets out of the saddlebags, making another pile of items. 

     

                She shifted Kara’s closer to her, softly clearing her throat. “Alex has your shell - and handkerchief.”

     

                Kara’s eyes whipped up to meet Lena’s, mouth falling open in surprise before her cheeks reddened. She shut her mouth again and quickly looked back down, nodding as she offered no response. Feeling the awful tension thicken between them, Lena was silent for a moment, watching as Kara started to rifle through her pack for her travel clothes. 

     

                “Why do you have it?”

     

                Freezing, Kara was still for a moment before she slowly pulled out leather leggings, clearing her throat. “You said you made it for me.”

     

                “Yeah, but Sam had it.”

     

                “I asked her for it.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Because you made it for me.”

     

                “I- well, yeah, but-”

     

                “What did you mean? Earlier?” Kara asked, smoothly rising to her feet, her pants in hand, her expression unreadable.

     

                Opening her mouth as she drew in a quick breath, Lena hastily shut her mouth, casting her gaze down on the grass. After a brief pause, she abruptly turned, her stomach swooping with nerves. “I must fetch my horse.”

     

                She only got a few paces away before her wife snagged her wrist, pulling her back around. “Lena.”

     

                Stumbling slightly into her, a hand coming up to brace herself against Kara’s shoulder, Lena’s breath hitched in her throat, standing so close to her that she felt agony in her chest to be so close and not have her. She couldn’t help herself, her hand curling in Kara’s clothes as she crushed her lips against her wife’s, Kara’s mouth parted in surprise, unresponsive for a moment before she kissed her back. There was a desperate edge to Lena’s kiss, and she drowned in the feeling of it for a moment, forgetting herself, forgetting that merely a few hours ago, she was asking Kara not to kiss her. 

     

                And then she cut it off, shoving Kara away a little rougher than intended as her mouth opened and closed, red creeping up her neck and into her cheeks. Rubbing the palms of her hands over her face, she softly groaned, turning away as Kara was left stammering, eyes wide with surprise, unsure of what to do.

     

                “Lena-”

     

                “Don’t,” Lena softly pleaded, stalking off back towards the slopes of the valley, where her mare was grazing contentedly.

     

                “I know you spoke with Alex-”

     

                Panic shot through Lena, blanching as she stumbled midstride, her heart pounding as she swallowed thickly. Her hands were curled into fists to stop them from shaking, raising her voice as she refused to turn around and face her wife, avoiding any further conversation. “Just … leave me alone.”

     

                Frustrated, Kara threw her hands up, gritting her teeth, and then exhaled sharply. Gripping her leggings in a tight fist, she shook her head and then turned back to her belongings, wearily starting to strip off her clothes as she got changed.

     

                Further up the slopes, Lena listened to the wind and the trees, the nearby caw of birds, and whistled for her mare, the horse’s ears pricking at the sharp sound. As she neared, the mare raised her head and dutifully plodded towards Lena, softly whickering as she tossed her mane. Lena had had a few horses since she’d arrived in the forest, but she’d grown quite fond of this one, spending the most time in the saddle on the mare’s back, and she threw her arms around the mare’s neck, pressing her face into the bristly hair, the smell of damp grass letting her know she’d been rolling around, enjoying the open outdoors. 

     

                “Come on, girl,” Lena murmured, “let’s get you ready.”

     

                She had to go back towards Kara, who was doing up the clasps on her padded jacket, before for her coat of mail, rippling like molten silver as she worked it over her head and then picked up her leather surcoat, tying the front up. Lena felt nervous to be near her, fearing that Kara might try and question her again, which would lead to the all-too-familiar sting of rejection that Lena was used to, never loved, never wanted.

     

                But Kara remained mercifully silent, brimming with tension as she dressed herself, greaves and vambraces laced on, her sword buckled at her waist, while Lena saddled her horse, tightening the front cinch, strapping her pack down. Others started to arrive then, a cart loaded with supplies hitched up to one of the bigger draught horses, everyone already half-armoured, armed to the teeth with their weapons, and as Kara started to saddle her own horse, Lena fetched her belongings from the pile Kara had amassed from their deconstructed tent, slinging her quiver over her shoulder and gripping her bow. 

     

                The sky was already starting to darken a fraction, the beginnings of dusk settling in as the day slipped by quickly but felt agonisingly slow at the same time, and Lena tried to help where she could. Everyone else was well-versed in this, perhaps save Lillian, and Lena occasionally found herself standing awkwardly out of place beside her mother, trying to help but a little lost, while Lillian didn’t even offer at all. It wasn’t until everyone’s saddlebags were full to bursting and they had three carts piled high with supplies that they were ready to be off.

     

                Alex had a few of her fellow Firefolk there, including Vasquez, and a couple of faces Lena remembered from the nearby dwelling had appeared, word having been sent, so their numbers were slightly larger than when they’d arrived. She knew from travelling with James and his handful of soldiers that it would be slow-going, even slower now with the carts, and Lena wasn’t looking forward to it, rain clouds still on the horizon and night still ahead of them. 

     

                It surprised her, though, when she found out J’onn wasn’t coming. He smiled kindly at her as he explained his days of fighting were over, that he was a pacifist now, and would take Vasquez’s place as Steward for the time being. M’gann was going though, one of their best fighters, and Lena couldn’t comprehend how he could stand to be parted from her, not knowing her fate. She would walk into the middle of a battle with Kara just to keep her eyes on her and know she still lived. Lena knew how torturous it was to wait for the outcome of a battle, let alone a war. Still, he made his choice, giving her a slight bow and smiling as she hugged him and kissed his cheek. She’d miss the lessons on history and politics that their conversations usually devolved into over games of Stones, but she wished him well and let the others say their goodbyes.

     

                Up in the saddle, relegated to the middle, near the carts, she wound up next to Sam, who sought her out, reining her horse in beside Lena. Glancing over at her, distracted, tense and worried - about more than just war - Lena frowned slightly, her mouth turning down at the corners.

     

                “You know, I don’t need a constant guard, right? There are others around; you don’t have to ride with me. Where’s Andrea?”

     

                “Here,” her attendant answered from behind her.

     

                Looking over her shoulder, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Well, I’ll leave you two to it, then.”

     

                She nudged her horse forward, but they were already moving, a slow walk towards the forest, and she was forced to stay where she was, grimacing as she would’ve preferred her own company. No one was in high spirits, though, a certain restlessness plaguing the group as they trekked through the vale, and Lena stared at Kara’s back, her wife riding near the front of their party, deep in conversation with Alex and Kelly. The sight of her leaning in towards her sister-in-law made Lena’s chest hurt, and she was glad then that she had the length of a few others between them so she didn’t have to manage her expressions.

     

                “You have quarrelled again?” Andrea softly groaned as she picked up on Lena’s broodiness, rolling her eyes at the cutting glance Lena gave her.

     

                Cheeks turning pink, Lena felt a flicker of annoyance. “Not that it’s any of your business, but we haven’t quarrelled.”

     

                “You’re just ignoring each other? That is why she doesn’t ride with you.”

     

                “No. I- we aren’t joined at the hip. Is it so bad for me to want some space? From everyone.”

     

                Sam smiled faintly, glancing sideways at her, her lips barely moving as she spoke. “The lone wolf dies, but the pack survives, Princess. And you are surrounded by many enemies, even now.”

     

                Sharply turning her head to her, Lena’s expression was severe, a sudden spike of panic shooting through her. “What do you mean?”

     

                Their quiet conversation, barely above a murmur on account of the lack of privacy and sensitive hearing around them, despite the relatively spread out line of them, was ruined by Lena’s raised voice. Andrea softly hissed behind her, while Sam’s hand shot out to squeeze her knee in warning, exasperation in her hazel eyes as she grimaced.

     

                “You draw too much attention to yourself,” Andrea softly snapped. “And that makes you a dangerous target, is what she means. Even for supposed allies.”

     

                “Are you saying someone here is brave enough to attack me with my wife around?”

     

                “She is not infallible, and she is made vulnerable in her protection of you. Kill her, and a General and a Princess are lost. Your fate is tied to hers, and isolating yourself puts her at risk as much as it does you. Alone, you are easier to pick off.”

     

                “Then, unfortunately for my mother - I assume that’s who you’re warning me against? As if I need a warning after she tried to have you kill me before - I have more family than just my wife to guard my back.”

     

                “Exactly,” Sam murmured. “The pack survives . There are bigger things at play, things your eyes do not see, things your wife does not know. Do not underestimate anyone, least of all your allies.”

     

                “Like what? Speak plainly.”

     

                “I cannot. I am bound tightly with my oaths. I have said all that I can. Stay close to me, if not your family; I will guard you in your wife’s stead.”

     

                Rankling slightly on Kara’s behalf, Lena jerked her chin up in a haughty manner. “It’s not her job to guard me, and if it is, I’m sure she’s more than capable of guarding me well.”

     

                “Are you certain of that?”

     

                Lena let out a huff of laughter. “You think she would ever hurt me?”

     

                She missed the glance exchanged behind her back, the way Andrea opened her mouth and Sam shook her head slightly to silence her. It was common knowledge what Kara’s prophecy was, and so it was common knowledge to those who’d spent months around the married couple just who that prophecy was about. Even if Lena hadn’t realised it herself, even if Kara had only recently realised it, anyone else with eyes had realised. And that included Sam and Andrea, who kept their mouths shut in response to her question.

     

                Brooding, Lena stared longingly at her wife’s back as they rode along. Her companions remained silent, and everyone else whispered amongst themselves, a restless tension in the air as they made it into the cover of the forest, angling north-east. From what Lena had been told by Kelly, Kara had been ordered by the Council to return to her post on the riverbank, taking back her forces to help hold the line. Considering the north-eastern region of the Seelie Court was all Kara’s land, that was her position amongst the four Generals, so they angled north instead of directly east, towards the foothills of the mountains, on the doorstep of Eliza’s home once more.

     

                They didn’t make it more than a few miles by the time sunlight failed, full darkness beneath the canopy, the Firefolk lighting the way as they continued onwards, the temperature plummeting as the wind howled through the trees, and the sound of hooves trampling damp leaves filled the silence. There were a few moments that made Lena’s blood freeze - the chilling sound of a keening cry drifting through the trees, her shoulders practically up to her ears as she gripped the reins tightly, Sam whispering that it was just an elk making her relax somewhat, as well as the occasional howling of wolves, the snap of branches and flutter of wings making her heart thud in her chest - and she felt so cold, her breath visible before her, fingers numb around the leather reins, trying not to shiver. It felt endless, the biting wind working through her layers, and Lena already felt so drained from the emotional day.

     

                It wasn’t until midnight that they came to a stop, nothing to mark the spot as a special resting point, and she stiffly climbed out of the saddle.
