No tents were pitched, no tarps staked for shelters, they all just grabbed their bedrolls and blankets and lay where they could, a few fires lit and two guards staying up on first watch. Kara warily sought her out then, seeing where Lena lay her bedroll and setting hers down beside it. They didn’t say a word, just got beneath the blankets and faced away from each other. 

     

                Neither of them was awakened to take over the watch, so when they woke to the pre-dawn grey of the foggy morning, it was with Kara’s arm thrown over Lena’s waist, and Lena’s back pressed up against Kara’s chest. It wasn’t anything new, wasn’t something they hadn’t done before, long before they’d ever slept together, before they’d let things get so strained, but it was still somewhat awkward because of that strain. Waiting for Kara to move her arm, Lena slowly sat up and then pushed the blanket off herself, the cold like a knife in her lungs as she started to fold and roll the blanket and then the bedroll. A few others were already awake - the two on guard, Sam and Alex, M’gann and one of the Unseelie - and Lena walked over to one of the fires, sinking to a crouch as she extended her fingers towards the heat of the flames, a stinging in her cold palms.

     

                Some tea was coming to a boil over the fire, and Lena went over to her packed saddlebags, fishing out a cup. She helped herself to some tea and then hesitated, carrying it over to her wife in an attempt to ease some of the tension there. Kara was checking the hooves of her horse and glanced up at her approach, a flicker of surprise in her eyes, and again when Lena extended the steaming cup. Murmuring a thank you, she took a sip and then handed it back to Lena, their fingers brushing, doing something funny to Lena’s stomach as her chest spasmed. She put her mouth where Kara’s had been, taking a sip herself before handing it back. They drank the cup in peaceful silence, the fleeting brush of their fingers cutting cleanly through them both, although the other was oblivious to their inner turmoil, and Lena went to get them a second cup, repeating the process while they shared a loaf of bread and an apple procured from Kara’s saddlebags.

     

                They were back in the saddle soon after that, plodding north for a period, quiet conversation and then long stretches of silence between the group. Kara rode beside Lena then, behind Alex and Kelly, when neither of them was ranging ahead to scout the area. By the time it was midday, they were into the foothills, the pines reaching up, straight and scraggy from the winter, maples and yews growing everywhere they found room, and a few sloping hillsides of heather giving them a better view of the surroundings to the east. A deer startled them as it bounded from a thicket, Lena letting out a pitiful sound of protest as two arrows quickly took it down for fresh meat to bad out their supplies. They’d brought plenty with them, but that was to replenish the army's supplies too, so they took what they could reasonably use. She still shot Purity and Pestilence a filthy look when they went to claim the deer, the dark fletching matching their arrows.

     

                They briefly stopped then, Lillian’s hunters gutting the doe, blood staining the earth as they removed organs, cooking them over the fire Sam started, offering up the choice pieces to their Queen, while the others made do with the bread, soft cheese and berries. Still, Lena watched how everyone helped dress the doe, the way the hide was neatly cut away, how the meat was portioned, salted, packed away between them all, resources shared even with natural born enemies. She had to wonder again why there was any need for a war, why it was so difficult for them to be at peace, why her marriage to Kara hadn’t been the unifying peace they’d all hoped for, merely a brief truce. But their history was a bloody one that Lena only had the basic gist of, a sea of alliances and blood feuds too intricate and old for her to truly grasp, the majority of her life spent untethered to this place and these people.

     

                Deep in thought as she ate, trying to rationalise it all to herself, questioning so much with the more she knew, Lena didn’t speak much, lingering near Kara, while Sam hovered near her. She thought about her guard’s warnings as well, feeling the stress of trying to manage all of her emotions, everything that was going on. Lena felt woefully unequipped for any of it: love, danger, war, politicking. For the briefest moment, she wished she were back in her shop with her flowers, something familiar, something known to her, that she was good at, that wasn’t dangerous. The feeling passed quickly as she looked at her wife.

     

                Finishing her ration of food, Lena climbed back into the saddle, not feeling sore, more accustomed to it now, and fell back into line as they continued onwards. Alex’s garrison was two days from the river, but they were heading north as well, angling across the foothills, so it would be a longer trip for them. A week before they reached the stretch of river under Kara’s command, from what Kelly had told her. They didn’t stop again until well past nightfall, moving slowly through the forest, up hills or gorse, around treacherous slopes and down narrow gullies. They didn’t stop until the forest fell silent and one of the men who’d come from the nearby dwelling was taken, riding at the rear of the group, a frantic cry quickly silenced as a sudden panic swept through the group as everyone scattered. Before Lena could even process what the reason was, Kara was in the saddle behind her, having abandoned her own horse out of haste to reach her wife, her sword unsheathed in her hand as she breathed raggedly in Lena’s ear, their bodies flush as she hunched protectively over her. 

     

                The panic was short-lived, Kara urging them through the trees, Sam on their heels, all of them ducking branches as Lena was jostled uncomfortably, making it a few hundred feet until the forest seemed to sigh, a wind blowing through the trees, the branches groaning. Kara whistled, mimicking a wren, and Lena heard the answering response. Backtracking, their hearts racing, still on edge, they found their way close enough to where they’d been, a few of the others already returned, staring into the trees. Kara maneuvered them closer and Lena caught a glimpse of the man, hanging suspended by a web of vines that had snagged him from horseback, wrapped around his throat, his arms, legs and chest. From what Kara had told her, there was little to be done when the forest itself was in one of its mercurial moods, no beastly animal to fight off, merely the trees and the wind, the rivers and lakes.

     

                “Cut him down,” Lillian instructed her Hunters.

     

                “We do not cut them down here,” Kara objected. 

     

                Casting her daughter-in-law an amused look, Lillian arched an eyebrow. “You deny him a proper burial?”

     

                “He is for the forest, buried or not. It is not for us to meddle.”

     

                “Are you frightened, Lady Kara? You Seelie are a softer breed, no doubt about it.”

     

                “Regardless, you shall not interfere.”

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Lillian waved a hand dismissively. “Do as you please. I care not.”

     

                “We should keep moving,” Kelly murmured, appearing through the trees, releasing the tension in her bowstring as the threat passed.

     

                Nodding, Kara briefly rested her hand on Lena’s shoulder, her fingers digging in slightly as she squeezed, reassuring herself as much as Lena. Swinging down from the saddle, she whistled for her own horse and mounted, but stayed close to her wife. Sam likewise shadowed Lena, and everyone moved a little quicker, making it a few miles before they decided to call it a night. They were in a small glade, enough room for the score of them and their horses, with little room for comfort. The parcels of deer meat were removed from packs and cooked over the fire for their dinner, watered down wine passed around in skins as three fires were lit, the usual cliques forming around them, and Lena watched Kelly work sinew from the deer into a thin thread, sitting nearby, watching intently, asking questions, having a go as she learnt how under the healer’s instruction, knowing she might need to know how to make it to sew wounds closed one day.

     

                Within the hour, most of them were asleep then, and Lena felt a weariness in her bones as she finished off another mouthful of wine and huddled by the fire, her cloak wrapped tightly around her shoulders. Purity and Alex took the first watch, an unspoken rule that two Unseelie wouldn’t be left to stand guard alone, and one allowed in the first place in order to give the Seelie some rest, so Lena bedded down shortly after finishing with the sinew thread, assured of their safety for now. It felt like she’d barely closed her eyes when she was shaken awake a few hours later, blearily blinking back sleep as she squinted through the dark, the fires burnt down to embers. Rubbing her eyes, she hummed questioningly as she pushed herself up, Kara whispering to her.

     

                “It is our turn to take watch.”

     

                It had never been asked of Lena before, always the least skilled warrior, the softest of the group, so she was momentarily surprised to be woken in the middle of the night for her turn. Still, she was determined to do it and do it well, rising without complaint, crouching as she fetched her bow, pulling a rawhide bowstring from a pocket on her bags and stringing the bow before slinging her quiver across her back. Rubbing a hand over her face, still waking up, she looked around, the air cold in her lungs, and quietly padded to the southern end of their camp, leaving Kara to take the northern point.

     

                Clutching her bow tightly in one hand, an arrow fitted to the string, undrawn, Lena stared out into the darkness as she strained her ears, listening closely, never explicitly being told what to do but understanding the basics of keeping watch. Nothing moved as she picked out shadowed shapes in the faint moonlight, listening to the sigh of the trees. Somewhere in the vicinity of their camp, a black-faced owl hooted and then hooted again, the only sound to cut through the peace of the night as it momentarily frightened her, until Lena picked out the soft tread of footsteps not ten minutes later.

     

                She knew who it was; who else would it have been? Leaving her watchpoint at the northern end of the camp, Kara crept around the outskirts of the camp of sleeping companions, careful not to make too much noise and rouse them all to arms, as she made for her wife. Lena tried to ignore her, slowly circling further west of her point, trying to keep distance between the two of them, but she had to move so slowly to stay quiet that Kara inevitably caught up to her. Her hand was remarkably warm when it found Lena’s, tugging her into the trees.

     

                “I-” Lena started to resist, the single syllable too loud in the dark as Kara quickly clamped a hand over her wife’s mouth, softly hushing her.

     

                Lena reached up to yank her hand down, scowling as her cheeks warmed. “You’re supposed to be keeping watch.”

     

                “I must speak with you,” Kara whispered, her words hitching with desperation as she towed her wife further into the trees.

     

                “Not now.”

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “No. You can’t keep things from me whilst demanding the truth of me. Whatever you presume I meant … well, that’s your perception of it. It doesn’t mean it’s true. It doesn’t mean I have to explain myself.”

     

                “But if you would let me explain myself-“

     

                “Explain what? I already know. I know it all. I’m not fucking stupid, Kara,” Lena softly snapped, taking in Kara’s pale face as uncertainty flashed across her face.

     

                “No, I am the one who has been a fool. Perhaps I have become more used to removing heads than using my own. You say you know, then … will you not speak with me? I know you are upset, but … I feel I still must explain myself.”

     

                “Will you not take no for an answer?”

     

                Spluttering, ducking her head as she was appropriately chastened yet rankled at it all the same, Kara let out a quiet huff of frustration. “Of course I will. I just-“

     

                They were disturbed then by footsteps that weren’t quite loud, but definitely weren’t trying to be inaudible. They both looked back towards the camp as Alex came gracefully storming through the trees, grabbing them both by the fronts of the surcoats and jerking them towards her.

     

                “You’re supposed to be keeping watch , not arguing,” Alex hissed, keeping her voice low as the others slept on. 

     

                “We are not-” Kara couldn’t even finish speaking before she got choked up, mouth thinning as she tried a different avenue. “I just wish to speak in private with my wife, so if you can-”

     

                Alex silenced her with a cutting glance. “Save it. You forfeited the right to speak in private. What you wish does not come before ensuring the safety of all who travel with you. You have made your choice, sister, and now you must bear it.”

     

                Opening her mouth to retort, Kara was left floundering as Alex let go of her surcoat and turned her attention to Lena, blanking her sister. Letting go of Lena’s surcoat, Alex jerked her head to the camp, her eyes glimmering with annoyance - at both of them. “Back to bed with you.”

     

                “I-“

     

                “Now, Lena. I will take your watch and ensure our throats aren’t slit tonight because the two of you have made such a mess of things.”

     

                Shutting her mouth, resisting the urge to argue with Alex now too, Lena felt irritable as she crept back to her sleeping spot, Alex following after her without another word to her sister, continuing to the northern point of the camp as she forewent sleep to keep watch. Guilt needled Lena, and she felt adrenaline coursing through her as well, a tightness in her chest at how complicated it was all becoming. They were all going to be at each other’s throats soon, bickering and arguing as this little quartet fell apart over Kara’s feelings, and Lena had a bad feeling about walking into a war with everything such a mess. It was bound to end in disaster. 

     

                She slept very little then, stewing in her misery, worrying about the future, wondering if perhaps she should bite the bullet and just speak to Kara, lay it all out and be done with the torment. It had only been a couple of days of understanding her feelings and understanding Kara’s, even though she’d been feeling this way far longer than that, and Lena couldn’t imagine having to live with that weight in her chest, that stone in her stomach, as she was forced to pretend that she didn’t love her wife, driving a wedge between them to guard herself from inevitable heartbreak. 

     

                Lena was up before dawn had even broken, Kara sleeping beside her, a hand resting on Lena’s thigh, her blanket thrown over Lena for extra warmth. Throat tight, feeling guilty again, when all Kara had ever done was try to look after her, Lena eased herself out from beneath her wife’s touch and slinked off into the forest. The fog was thick, muffling the sounds of her footsteps, distorting the sounds of the forest slightly, uneasiness wending through her as she moved further from the camp, wanting some time to herself to think, to put some space between them. It was cold, but Lena could feel the weather warming, spring fully realising itself, each day warmer than the last, and she looked around at the patches of colour materialising as her movements made the fog swirl and ripple away from her. 

     

                Daffodils sprouted from the dirt in a patch there, red-capped mushrooms a little further, sprouting from the rotting bark of a mossy log, hollowed out with a sleeping fox nestled inside. She saw signs of a badger’s sett burrowing down between the roots of a hazel tree, and gathered blackberries from a plant, storing them in a pouch on her belt as they stained her fingers dark, some of them already gotten to by the birds. Plucking some wild garlic, chamomile and yarrow as she came upon them, Lena was enjoying the peace of her morning when it was disturbed. She hadn’t been paying much attention to her surroundings, but the quietest snap of a twig alerted her to the presence of another.

     

                Hand drifting to her dagger, uncertainty making her cautious, Lena silently jerked it free as she crouched slightly, knees bent, eyes scanning the trees for shadows looming out of the fog. But the fog was thick, and she couldn’t make out much, her footsteps muffled by damp leaves and soft earth as she crept to her left, for the trunk of an ash tree. A hand clapped over her mouth, the smell of ashes in her nose, the sharp edge of a hunting knife pressed to her throat, and Lena reacted before giving it much thought, attempting to stab her assailant in the waist, where it was soft, where it gave her more chance of puncturing an organ, bleeding quickly, but the hand covering her mouth caught her wrist, stopping her.

     

                “I told you you are easier to pick off alone,” Sam murmured, letting go of her and shoving her away. “And yet, you wander off anyway.”

     

                Heaving a relieved breath as she righted herself, turning, Lena reached up to touch her throat, unmarked but the ghost of the knife lingering, cold sweat making her feel clammy. “Sam.”

     

                “If I was your enemy, I could have slit your throat. Did you hear nothing of what I said?”

     

                Mouth twisting with annoyance, Lena’s eyes flitted away from the hunter. “I needed some space to think alone. What’s it to you, anyway?”

     

                “I am ordered to guard you. And I owe you a debt.”

     

                Raking a hand through her hair, Lena shot her a look of irritation. “Is it too much to ask that I might be allowed a little privacy? If it’s not her, it’s you. If it’s not you, it’s your infernal girlfriend, or- or my sister-in-laws. I’m suffocated by you all.”

     

                “Is it so unthinkable that you are cared for enough that you are sought out by so many to ensure that no harm befalls you? Whether that be physical harm or wounds to the heart?”

     

                “And what do you know of it?”

     

                “You think me so oblivious? Your feelings for her are plain to see. As are her feelings for-”

     

                “You knew? Why didn’t you tell me?”

     

                “It was not for me to say,” Sam said with confusion, her brow creasing. “I have great respect for Kara; she has helped me more than you can imagine, with my daughter and affliction. I would not willingly cause her distress because you were blind to the truth before your eyes.”

     

                “She said only Alex knew.”

     

                “And I imagine that is true, in the sense that she has only told her sister, but we all have eyes; I made use of mine.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena turned and marched back in the direction of their camp. “You’re all so- so … annoying,” she churlishly fumed, angered by her own stupidity once more.

     

                “I imagine you are feeling far more than annoyed by what you have uncovered. I cannot claim to understand, but that fear you are feeling … I know it well.”

     

                “I’m not-” Lena couldn’t force the words out, clenching her teeth as she looked down, a stinging in her eyes. Swallowing thickly, her voice softened. “I’m … hurt.”

     

                Pressing her fingertips to her eyelids, Lena huffed and then dropped her hands, opening her eyes to the sight of Kara standing ten feet away. Blanching as her mouth fell open, Lena’s white face quickly reddened. It took everything in her to keep her composure, to not lash out from her hurt at the presence of her wife seeking her out once more. Sam’s words rang in her ears, about how she had people who cared about her enough to make sure she was okay, and she knew logically that’s what Kara was doing, so she tried her best not to be angry. Still, she hated the thought of Kara pitying her.

     

                “We should get back to camp,” Lena muttered.

     

                Kara didn’t speak at all, not a single word, her face a mask of stiff agony as she walked beside Lena, reaching out to take her hand, holding it tightly as Lena limply let her. Sam followed behind, and they made it the hundred feet or so that Lena had wandered, everyone starting to rise now, the fires built up, food shared around. With her handful of berries, Lena shared them with Kara, Sam and Kelly as the four of them sat together, drinking tea to warm themselves before they were back in the saddle.

     

                They made hard east that day, the forest sloping down and then levelling out, the trees wide apart and monstrously tall, blotting out most of the light as the forest took on a dingy green tint. Lena felt tiny on horseback, picking her way across a carpet of pine needles, moss and leaves, watching sparrows swoop and flutter away. It was a nice day, the air cool but dry, ferns, brambles and hedges growing wild, flowers, herbs and root vegetables spotted as she silently quizzed herself on identifying the plants to pass the time. Kelly was scouting downriver, and Sam was shadowing the group at the rear, and by the time they’d almost hit the fringes of the war camp alongside the river, dusk was settling in and the sounds of fighting drifted towards them.

     

                Lena blinked, flinching slightly at the sounds of pain, of people dying, a faintly rotten smell in the air as blood and bodies warmed in the lingering heat of the day, the sound of clashing steel and shouted commands cutting through what had been relatively peaceful up until then. They’d stopped at midday and Lena had watched as armour was donned, buckles fastened as cloth was exchanged for mail, the movements of the group now a tinkling chime with every movement. She’d been left in her leathers, along with Andrea, Lillian and the Unseelie. Kara looked beautiful, every inch the General in her shining armour as she was suddenly in front of Lena, a solemn look on her face as she reached for her wife, cupping her cheek in her hand.

     

                “Stay away, at the top of the ridge; stay away from the fighting. Sam will protect you. Do you hear me?” she urgently spoke, already reining her horse in as it stepped backwards, putting some distance between them. “I will find you later.”

     

                Seized by a sudden terror, Lena felt pale and faint as she looked at her wife, so much left to say as the severity of the situation hit her. Her response was pitiful, falling short of her feelings. “Stay safe.”

     

                She wanted to reach for her, take her face in her hands and kiss her, ask to go with her, so afraid of being parted from her, but she simply said her two words and watched her wife leave her behind. 

     

                Sam sidled up beside her and took the reins of her horse, urging her away, back up the slope they’d just come down, a ridge of hawthorns and birches offering cover from any advancing enemies who might sneak through the camp. They weren’t alone - Andrea, Lillian, her Hunters and three other Unseelie were made to stay behind as well, remaining under Sam’s careful watch, none of the others trusted to get even close to the fighting. They might not be loyal to Lex, but they weren’t loyal to the Seelie, that much Kara was sure of, and clear arrangements had been made in preparation for what would happen once they reached the fighting.

     

                At the top of the ridge, Lena itched to climb out of her saddle, to pace back and forth and burn off some of her restless energy, but Sam wouldn’t let her. Likewise, her guard also made her withdraw from the edge of the ridge, the steep drop below offering a good vantage point but also making her an easy target for any archers within range. Lena fought her on it, wanting to keep an eye out for Kara’s returning figure, but her guard won, under clear instructions from Kara to keep her wife safe for her. Being left in the dark wasn’t easy, and even though she’d strung her bow, had it resting across her lap in case she had to defend herself, Lena wished she could have taken a more active participation in the fighting, if only to be glued to Kara’s side. So far, her efforts in battle left a lot desired, even if she’d been lucky enough to kill her share of fae. 

     

                So distracted by her worry for her wife, and the rest of her family, Lena was oblivious to their number decreasing by one, and because Sam and Andrea were too consumed with watching over Lena, they didn’t realise it either. It wasn’t until the distant sounds of battle slowly dwindled to nothing, over relatively fast as night started to fall, these little skirmishes relying on surprise attacks that didn’t last for very long, that anyone noticed. Approaching the edge of the ridge and staring through the gloom, a deep blue to the forest as figures approached, Lena made out the shadowed form of her wife. She couldn’t pick out Kara’s features, nor the colour of her hair, and she imagined there would be numerous Waterfolk fighters on horseback with a trident, but she knew it was Kara.

     

                Leaping from her saddle and staggering to the edge of the ridge, Lena left her bow hanging on the horn of her saddle and took the treacherous drop down to the ground below, small stones and crumbling dirt cascading down with her as she grabbed onto snaking roots and rocky outcroppings. For all her fear of heights, twenty feet down to the side of the ridge felt like nothing, staggering forward as she caught her balance at the bottom, watching as the shadowed, armoured figure dismounted and met her halfway.

     

                Drenched in blood, Kara looked fierce but otherwise fine, yet Lena still couldn’t help but practically fall onto her wife, hands running over red-stained steel, blood worked into the patterns of waves and scales. Covering Lena’s hand with her own, blood-crusted fingers squeezing gently with reassurance, Kara spoke, her voice a hoarse rasp.

     

                “It’s alright. Most of it is not mine.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena breathlessly murmured, “good.”

     

                She pulled her hand out from Kara’s and reached up to brush bloody hair out of her wife’s face, her worry dimming but still present as she sniffed and cleared her throat, trying to keep it under wraps. A moment later, she nodded, cupping Kara’s left cheek and leaning in to peck the corner of her mouth, a chaste kiss, a friendly kiss, barely even a kiss, letting her wife know that she cared, that she was glad she’d returned safely. Kara didn’t say anything, and Lena withdrew her hands, her eyes flitting to the others as they approached, all of them still alive, tired and bloody but alive.

     

                As the others came down from the ridge, there were two empty saddles - one was Lena’s - and as Kara looked at the group, she did a double-take, eyes flitting around as her keen eyesight pierced the darkness to make note of their missing party member. Her brow creasing as her face hardened, she took a step forward, cocking her head to the side as she stared at Lillian.

     

                “Where is Purity?”

    Chapter 42

                Lena, Sam and Andrea glanced around, then, surprised by the fact that they were missing one. Uneasiness wound through Lena, and she turned in a slow circle, something not feeling right about it. Sam’s warnings came back to her, and she looked to her guard, seeing something strained in her expression, that familiar eerie feeling that there was something just below the surface, something - Reign - trying to take over as the woman wrestled with it. Lena knew then that she must have known that one of her sisters was going to leave, but the question was whether Purity had the means to leave of her own free will or whether Lillian had made her. 

     

                The silence dragged on a second, and Lena shied closer to her wife as she looked at her mother, taking in the aloof look on Lillian’s face, as if she didn’t care at all. Something about it seemed too false, and she wasn’t the only one to leap to the same conclusion. Armour clanking as she turned to face Lillian, Kara frowned.

     

                “Where is your Hunter?”

     

                “I am uncertain where she is. It seems she’s slipped my leash.”

     

                Lillian’s lips twitched at the corners, eyes glimmering in the dark, and Kara quietly fumed, turning to her sister. “Search for her, please. I must meet with James, and I do not trust her to be left roaming freely through the camp.”

     

                Bloody and weary, Alex simply nodded, melting into the dark as Kelly followed after her. It left a rather tense group behind, and Kara looked at M’gann and the few others they’d added to their group, pinching the bridge of her nose as she softly huffed and then squared her shoulders, presenting a strong air in her bloody armour as she nodded more to herself than anyone else.

     

                “See that they are kept under close watch,” she murmured to M’gann, gesturing dismissively to the remaining Unseelie. “And see that my wife is guarded. We shall make camp here tonight while I am advised of our circumstances.”

     

                Hesitating, she glanced at Lena, a strained expression on her face, and reached out to briefly touch her arm. “Do not stray from the camp. Please.”

     

                Nodding, her mouth thinning, Lena covered Kara’s hand with her own before withdrawing it. Kara walked off into the trees, and Lena looked around as the others started fetching supplies. With some guarantee that they’d be there for at least the night, they made an effort to pitch proper shelters, poles and rope pulling canvas taut to create tents, all of them spread out and firewood collected to create a few fires. Lena helped with the firewood and started to make a stew, eyes flitting around as she watched everyone, taking in the quiet action. Lillian just stood there, watching, waiting for Pestilence to make her shelter for her. Their eyes briefly met, and she felt a shiver run down her spine.

     

                Brushing down her horse, and then Kara’s too, checking hooves for stones, rubbing dried mud out of their flanks and rinsing fetlocks, tails and manes, Lena set their saddlebags, saddles and reins into the tent Andrea pitched for her. Setting out bedrolls and blankets, Lena tried her best to help where she could, night falling as it started to rain, an hour turning into two, drinking water from her skin, having a bowl of stew and setting a pot of water over the fire to make tea as she dithered about. She helped Andrea make some dough, letting it rise by the warmth of the flour and then baking it in a covered pot borrowed from someone else, fresh bread ready for when her wife returned, for the others who were tired and bloody. One of the Seelie had a nasty cut, and she helped bathe it and apply a salve and bandage it tightly, trying not to wince at the gash in the man’s bicep. 

     

                It was another hour before Kara returned, alone, still in her bloody armour and silent as she entered the spread-out camp and found their tent. Lena had set her trident safely inside, and she watched from her spot at the fire as Kara worked a few pieces of her armour free, rummaging around in the dark for a few minutes and then pouring water from her skin into the bowl she’d scrounged up. With a rag, she started to clean her armour.

     

                Leaving her to her task, Lena sat silently with Sam and Andrea, sipping more tea, her eyes heavy as night dragged on. It was as quiet as it could be with hundreds of them scattered throughout the forest, along the riverbank, and Lena was confused by the seemingly disordered structure of the camp. The tents were spread out with a dozen feet between each one, small fires drawing small clusters, horses left to graze freely, and she questioned Sam on it. The response was that they didn’t want to damage the forest, that they didn’t crowd together and flatten flowers and shrubs, didn’t create large fires to scar the earth, didn’t march together and trample the ground to mud. It was bewildering to Lena; all she knew of warfare came from high school history and old movies, but she was sure there was supposed to be some sort of cohesive front for a strong defence, hell, even for a strong offence.

     

                Accepting the way things were there, as she’d grown accustomed to, she eventually roused herself. Fetching a bowl of stew and a cup of tea, she warily approved her shared tent, crouching before her wife and setting the bowl and cup down safely to Kara’s left. Polishing one of her greaves, Kara glanced up briefly, blue eyes clouded, a grim set to her mouth as her blonde hair spilt about her, matted and stained with blood, sweat and dirt.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Lena remained crouched before her, anxiously toying with her fingers as it took her a long minute to speak. “Are you okay?”

     

                Pausing, Kara swallowed thickly, the corners of her mouth turning down slightly. “I am well.”

     

                Softly sighing, Lena grimaced, reaching out to take the cloth from Kara’s hand. Her wife let her, and Lena dunked it in the water, wringing out as much as she could. “No, you’re not. You’re just good at twisting the truth.”

     

                Squeezing tightly, she shook off the rag and then reached up to cup Kara’s chin in her hand, pity knifing through her. The coppery smell of blood, dirt, water and sweat clung to her wife, and Lena slowly started to wipe her face clean. She had to rinse the cloth out twice before she’d managed to remove the dried blood from Kara’s cheeks and chin, her wife’s eyes closing as she let her tenderly wash her face without complaint.

     

                Clearing her throat, Lena wrung it out again and picked up Kara’s right hand, turning it over to wipe her palm clean. “You hate it.”

     

                “Of course I do,” Kara said as her shoulders caved with defeat. “I do not wish to kill my kin. This war … it is pointless. Our marriage was supposed to put an end to it.”

     

                “It still might.”

     

                “Might it? I can hear your heartbeat; you are frightened to be alone with me. As alone as we are right now.”

     

                Lena licked her lips, turning Kara’s hand in hers to wipe her nail beds, drawing in a shaky breath as her head thudded in her chest. “I’m not frightened.”

     

                She had also become adept at twisting the truth. While she wasn’t afraid , she was definitely nervous. And not least of all because there was something so very attractive about her wife in armour and blood, something that made Lena want to kiss her, hold her, even though it was the last thing she needed to bother Kara with right then. And that would have just complicated things that were already too complicated to bear. Instead, she didn’t explain herself any further, reaching for Kara’s other hand, wiping away more dried blood, doing what little she could to help her wife without crossing any lines, without betraying too much or asking for more than Kara could give her.

     

                Finishing, she dropped the rag into the bowl and gestured to the cooling stew and tea. “You should eat.”

     

                “Will you … stay?” Kara haltingly asked.

     

                Momentarily hesitating, Lena nodded, crawling further into the tent and turning, sitting beside Kara as it continued to rain, the canopy blocking out most of it, and pretending that everything was just fine. Reaching for the stew, Kara started to spoon it into her mouth, eating quickly and without her usual enthusiasm for food, and Lena hugged her knees to her chest, staring out at the firelit darkness.

     

                “What did James say?”

     

                “He’ll head south while we shift northwards. Forces will be shuffled along the line to evenly spread us. It’ll only be a few days of travelling north.”

     

                “Can I ask- I mean, I know I’m not exactly experienced in war, but … why does it all feel so … scattered? It doesn’t feel like we’re in a war camp right now.”

     

                “It is not how it’s done here.”

     

                “Yeah, Sam explained that, I just- no wonder neither side has won. You don’t have enough people fighting in any one area to overpower the other. All it would take is half of your army in one block, and you could probably cross the river and hold it.”

     

                “Holding the river is not our intention. It is not the Unseelie’s intention either. It is not a war to occupy land, it is a war for vengeance, of slaughtering each other until there is a fragile truce to recuperate. We do not fell trees and burn crops, or divert the river to create a drought; even the Unseelie would not dream of controlling the forest like that. It is merely … the destruction of our kind.”

     

                “How many of you are there?”

     

                “Once there were many. Hundreds of thousands spread throughout both Courts. Now, our best guess is tens of thousands. So much death, and for what?”

     

                “One day it’ll be over. Surely. It can’t go on forever.”

     

                “I’m unsure,” Kara murmured, frowning down at her stew. “Your world is one of constant warfare, is it not? Can there ever be peace amongst divided people?”

     

                Lena bit her lip, pausing before she reached out to rest a hand on Kara’s knee. “I don’t know, but we can try our best to make it happen.”

     

                Lips twitching with a faint smile, Kara nodded. She drank her tea and finished off the soup then, rubbing tired eyes and sighing. “It’s time for rest.”

     

                Heart aching for her wife, wishing to take all of her worries away, Lena watched Kara crawl further into the tent and get beneath the blankets. Following after her, Lena felt the hard press of Kara’s armour through her clothes, shifting back into her, feeling her wife ease herself closer, both of them silent as they moved into their usual sleeping position, neither of them speaking as they dwelled in the strained peace of their relationship. Drained and anxious, Lena found it hard to sleep, listening to the snap of the fire, the drum of raindrops on the tent, and a few minutes later, Kara draped her arm around her waist, her breath warm on the back of Lena’s neck.

     

                “Goodnight.”

     

                “Sweet dreams,” Lena murmured, everything else she had to say left unspoken.

     

     

                Three days later, they were miles north of where they’d met the war camp. Purity had been nowhere to be found, and they’d had to cut their losses as a portion of the camp was packed up, fae moving in small groups, at their own leisure, marching or riding north, leaving little evidence of their passing behind. It rained the entire three days they rode northwards, a constant downpour that was somewhat sheltered by the trees, but saturated them whenever they rode through the occasional glade, or along the exposed riverbank. No matter how carefully she dried her socks and soft shoes by the fire each night, Lena’s feet were always wet, especially in camp.

     

                They’d only set up their tents once more since the first night in the war camp, intending to stay there a few days as the frontline was maintained, as numbers gathered in small groups, holding each mile of the riverbank with a few dozen soldiers. There had been fighting every day so far, and after that initial battle upon their arrival, forced up onto the ridge, Lena had found herself with a borrowed coat of mail, a constant guard in Sam, and a desire to help. And thus, she found herself putting her somewhat amateur healing knowledge to good use.

     

                For days now, Lena had tended to the wounded and watched as injured fae limped or were carried back into camp, blood spilling out of them in petals, ash, water or swirling away into nothing, once the fighting had ended. Her hands never seemed to be rid of the blood, stained red no matter how much she rinsed them, trying to keep them clean, worrying about infections. And they shook like mad, all the time, while threading curved needles, while applying salves and pulling out arrowheads. It was nauseating at times, and Lena felt like crying, out of her depth, but committed to helping as much as she could.

     

                And that’s how she somehow found herself at the forefront of fae medicine. By the end of the third day, inspecting a red wound, the crooked stitches inflamed, she was cursing the lack of penicillin in the Courts, the fact that she couldn’t just apply some betadine and put a Band-Aid over it. But what was penicillin but just a strain of mould? And hadn’t she once read that Ancient Egyptians used mouldy bread to treat wounds when writing a school report? It was a desperate attempt to help, but she turned to Sam, her ever-present guard lurking nearby.

     

                “I need bread - mouldy bread.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Mouldy bread.”

     

                “I- well, I’m not to leave your side.”

     

                “Fetch someone. Anyone. His wound’s infected, I- I don’t know, it might help.”

     

                “Mouldy bread will help?”

     

                “Will you just do as I ask?” she snapped.

     

                There was a young fae girl, barely old enough to tag along with the camp, running messages, cooking meals, and Sam sent her running to scour the camp for mouldy bread at Lena’s request. It wasn’t very hard to find, fresh food a rarity, and any bread not eaten was quick to start growing mould with the damp. Grasping at straws, Lena created a poultice with the bread, applying the slightly dampened wedge with its mottled appearance to the thinly bandaged wound, before she bound it in place. 

     

                The next was the following morning, a feverish woman with a stump at her elbow, the wound starting to rot. Lena had to stop herself from gagging, tears in her eyes as she poured a warm tincture over the wound, taking in the blackened skin, feeling the breath hitch in her throat. She could smell the sweetness of it, turning her stomach, and she didn’t know what else to do. But she knew that maggots had been used to clean out rotting wounds, also in plentiful abundance within the camp of so much blood and death. Sending someone to pluck maggots off bodies that hadn’t yet been buried, she had to place them on the stump, the injured woman mumbling objections but too weak to resist, and Lena had to hope it was done in good faith. It seemed archaic to her, but it was very apparent that they were far from modern medicine, so even centuries-old methods seemed more promising to her than letting people die.

     

                After a day of tending to the wounded, and a long evening of the freshly injured having various cuts, stab wounds, dislocated joints and broken bones set, she was exhausted. Kelly had come to assist her every evening after the fighting stopped, and they walked back to their tents together, located as close to each other as the tents were pitched, and Lena trampled through shallow puddles, her damp cloak drawn tightly around herself as her breath misted in the air. 

     

                Kara wasn’t there, but Lena was sure of her safety; every day, as soon as the fighting stopped, she sought out her wife as Kara likewise sought her out. They hadn’t talked, that strange tension between them persisting, but they at least knew the other cared, and they were so desperately in love with the other that they had to know no harm had come to them. Lena had the worst end of the stick, with Kara in the thick of battle, the sight of her splattered with so much blood making Lena’s stomach lurch each time. And yet, the worst she’d sustained had been shallow cuts and bruises, a gash of two that Lena had stitched for her, forcing tea down her throat as her pulse raced with worry. Even a small cut could become infected.

     

                She’d already seen her wife that afternoon, the fighting ending not long after noon, leaving them to bury their dead, new trees or brambles and bushes sprouting where they were laid to rest. They couldn’t give any of the Waterfolk to the river because there were too many, and they had to drink from the flowing water, not wanting to pollute it with decomposing bodies. It was work for the Earthfolk, and Lena had watched once, her curiosity getting the better of her, wishing that she might’ve been able to do that for someone she loved, if it came to the worst. There were a few Unseelie dead they were left with too, and they were either exchanged at the river, handed back to members of their own Court, as the Seelie dead were likewise given back, or burned to ashes, no life coming from their bodies, if there was a blood feud owed to one of the Seelie on their side. The pyres burned further to the west, away from the camps, fiercely bright for a few minutes as the Firefolk quickly reduced them to cinders and let them scatter with the wind.

     

                They passed by a couple still burning, the faint, nauseating smell of burning flesh on the edge of the wind. It was a mercifully wet day, so the smell of pine needles and earth blotted out most of it, but Lena couldn’t adjust to the filth of the war camp. She was used to the elegance and finery of both Courts, different in their own ways but beautiful and refined, yet now she was subjected to the butchery of war in its full glory, even if the fae all looked regally beautiful in their wrought armour and embroidered surcoats. It was at total odds, and she thought that she might have liked to be back west again, tucked away somewhere peaceful with her wife.

     

                As she thought of Kara, she found herself back in their camp, fetching water to wash herself as she rinsed off blood and dirt, the faint bitterness of herbs on her hands. She’d washed as well as she could, changing her shirts, doing laundry when possible, but Lena felt dirty, in dire need of a bath, and she splashed water over her face and hair, trying to untangle it with her fingers, as she listened to footsteps and clinking armour approach. She didn’t have to look up to know it was her wife, done with her strategising for the day, Alex drifting off to spend time with her wife, while Kara sought out her own. Pouring the water out in the dirt, feeding the roots of a nearby tree, Lena turned as Kara spoke.

     

                “Why am I hearing you are treating wounds with maggots?”

     

                Lips twitching with a tired smile, Lena’s shoulders slumped. “Would you believe me if I said it was a healing method I saw in a medical TV show?”

     

                “One of your moving paintings told you maggots could heal amputations?”

     

                “No, it can help with infections. I think. I don’t know, I’m not a doctor. I thought it was worth a shot, though.”

     

                Kara gave her a bewildered look, somewhat dubious and disgusted by the idea, but merely shook her head. “First you stop death, then mouldy bread, now maggots. Whatever will you do next?”

     

                “Hm. Maybe leeches. I don’t know if you’ve discovered leeches yet.”

     

                Groaning, Kara looked even more concerned. “Leeches? Please elaborate.”

     

                With a soft laugh, Lena carried the empty bowl back to their tent, sinking onto their bedrolls as she tried to work her fingers through the knotted ends of her hair. “Well, they can be used to improve circulation. You know, make blood flow better. I’d feel less confident about that, though. Not that I’m really confident about the bread poultices or the maggots, but … well, it’s life or death. Anything is worth a shot, isn’t it?”

     

                “We heal remarkably fast,” Kara said as she rummaged through one of her bags. “Anything that might keep them alive an extra day or two while their body recovers is worth the attempt. As it is, the first man you used the bread poultice on has had his stitches removed today. Whether it was chance or successful healing, a man has lived where he might’ve died without your aid. Here, let me comb your hair for you; you look as if you have come crawling out of the forest itself.”

     

                Smiling slightly, Lena sat still as Kara combed her hair, something a little easier between them whenever things felt normal, when they spoke as they usually did, cared for each other without anything else clouding the moment. Feeling her wife’s fingers move gently over her hair with a carved comb, Lena closed her eyes, basking in the peaceful moment.

     

                “How long do you think we’ll be here?”

     

                “I cannot say. I would like to remain until I have your brother caught. It is only then that I will be confident of a possible truce, although that will depend on your mother’s cooperation. As our marriage is still intact, we could propose another break in the fighting, with the hope of true peace this time. Would that you had sworn the oaths yourself, so that we two might have spoken words that were ironclad, instead of the vague promises your mother and the Council promised each Court.”

     

                “Is our marriage not ironclad?”

     

                “Our marriage, yes, but the truce was deliberately vague. Neither Court would like to back itself into a corner, at the mercy of the other. We had imagined peace would hold a little longer than it did, though. Years, we had hoped for, so that we all might have children, and they would grow up safely, until the day they were called to war too. Instead, we may all slaughter each other to our last fae standing.”

     

                “I don’t think you would let that happen. You’re too merciful for that.”

     

                “I am not in charge.”

     

                “Well, maybe you should be. I mean, the Unseelie have a Queen. Maybe you got it wrong; maybe you should’ve stayed divided by your powers, with more control over your own people. Or, I don’t know, maybe the Courts should be united.”

     

                Kara let out a soft laugh, a finger brushing over the tip of Lena’s ear. “I think that was the intention of you. Heir to the throne, manipulated by the Seelie Court for the greater good. They would have had you dissolve the Unseelie monarchy, I am sure. It was never plotted in my presence, but I have not been to any Council meetings in some time.”

     

                “I would have done it if I’d become Queen, and that’s what they asked.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Well, I never wanted to be Queen anyway. And we both know I wouldn’t be very good at it.”

     

                “I have come to learn that you are very good at many things I once thought otherwise. You might’ve surprised us all if that day had ever occurred.”

     

                “Maybe. I guess we’ll never know; not unless we kill my brother before he kills me.”

     

                “He will not kill you. I will not let him,” Kara whispered, her voice softening as she leaned in slightly, sending a shiver down Lena’s spine as she imagined her wife’s lips so close to her ear.

                

                Closing her eyes, she lingered in the sensation a moment before clearing her throat, shifting forward, away from her wife. “Well, maybe not tonight. But I’m so tired that I might not notice if he snuck in here with a knife and killed me in my sleep. I think I might go to bed now.”

     

                “Alright,” Kara murmured, “I will leave you to rest. Sleep tight, my wife. And rest easy; no one will reach you while I am at your side.”

     

                Mouth hitching into a lopsided smile, Lena met her wife’s gaze and nodded. As Kara moved out of the tent, she bedded down, pulling her cloak around herself and piling her blanket on top, trying to stave off the chill of the night. As tired as she was, sleep was still hard to come by, though, and she woke many times throughout the night, once at the arrival of her wife, slipping into bed beside her as Lena shrank into her solid presence, seeking comfort, which was readily given. 

     

                Kara was up before Lena, and they ate breakfast by the fire, the warmth of porridge filling them, before the sound of horns interrupted. Bowl abandoned, Kara was on her feet in an instant, leaving Lena with her usual warning to stay away , Sam and Andrea left to watch her and the rest of the Unseelie, before she was whisked away to the fighting once more. Lena lost all appetite for her breakfast then as her stomach twisted itself into knots, and she climbed to her feet, heading towards the area reserved for the sick and injured. 

     

                The rest of her morning and much of the afternoon were spent treating what she could, although there was much she was inexperienced in. How was she supposed to treat strange rashes and chafing from the constant wetness of clothes and armour? How was she supposed to know whether a limb needed to be amputated? That was one thing she couldn’t do, leaving it for the other healers who were knowledgeable about such wounds, but the ragged screams of agony still filled the area as she worked on minor injuries. And while she was there, she showed a few of the healers CPR, explaining as simply as she could, no doctor to be able to fully explain the science behind it, but she’d managed to keep three fae alive with it so far, on the brink but alive all the same as their hearts started to beat a regular rhythm again.

     

                It was nearing dusk when the fighting stopped that day, the last hour of golden light filling the forest as Kara came through the trees, bloody and filthy and breathing raggedly. She’d broken the little finger on her right hand and had been hit by the solid swing of a hammer, a few rings of mail bent at her waist where they’d been smashed together, which they both presumed would be a mottled bruise tomorrow, but seemed otherwise unharmed, just run ragged from the ordeal. Grass and silt were caught in her armour, which had been drenched in river water as she’d wielded the flowing current to aid her attack, and Kara glistened slightly, hair damp and brassy as she drank from the skin Lena offered her.

     

                Before she could pause to wash, to clean her weapons and armour, the sound of hoofbeats coming from the southwest caught her attention, and although she was alert and tense, Kara didn’t draw her sword. The sight of a small party of vaguely familiar faces greeted them then, and Lena recognised the slight man in front as Querl, Kara’s friend and Steward at Argo in her absence. Close behind him was Nia, dressed in her armour, a silver whip coiled in her hand and a blue cloak falling from her shoulders as she reined her horse in, stepping in a small circle. They started to dismount, and Kara quickly hugged Nia, smiling with genuine delight at the arrival of more friendly faces. From what Lena could make out, they’d come with a couple of hundred from Argo’s surrounding dwellings, Kara’s retainers called to war at the pigeons she’d sent with letters, and it was obvious Kara was glad to have her own with her to hold the northern stretch of the river.

     

                “Querl!” Kara happily greeted him next, grasping his shoulders and then hugging him tightly. “It’s good to see you, my friend. We will have much to discuss. How fares Argo?”

     

                “Clear waters, until recent events dragged me away.”

     

                “Mm. Would that there was nothing more pressing than a nice, cold swim. Alas. And did you bring what I asked for?”

     

                “Of course. They finished not a moment before I departed, but it is exactly as requested. I shall have it fetched for you.”

     

                Nodding, she looked at Lena, their eyes meeting briefly, as Querl sent a man to do his bidding. They continued to converse quietly, skipping the pleasantries and diving straight into updates on the war front, Querl having gotten there days after them but already knowledgeable about the statistics as he rattled off figures. Listening with rapt attention, Kara had a stern look on her face as she stood covered in blood, unbothered and slightly feral looking, her stance casual as she gripped the pommel of her sword, eyes flitting around as she made vague sounds of acknowledgement at the back of her throat, prompting her Steward to continue. Her eyes kept landing on Lena, and Lena had to pretend that she wasn’t watching her, her heart in her throat as the sight of so much blood covering her wife made her feel uneasy, even if none of it was Kara’s.

     

                The leaves rustled nearby, and Sam prowled in a wide arc, keeping her usual watch over Lena, even though Kara had returned. Her slow steps always made Lena tense, feeling as if Reign was too close to the surface, as close to the border as they were, and she wished the hunter wasn’t beholden to oaths and orders so that she might be free from her supervision, but Kara had asked it of Sam herself, and despite her protectiveness over Lena, Sam was far more loyal to Lena. Hating the thick tension in the air, the faint tang of blood, death and smoke lingering, the sounds of the dying, Lena started to get restless, curling and uncurling her hands into fists as she felt her uneasiness prickle down her spine, the hairs on the back of her neck on end. She had the sudden feeling that she shouldn’t be there, that this was all so wrong.  

     

                But this was where Kara’s friends were making their camp alongside theirs, their belongings dumped in a pile, canvas ready to be pitched into shelters, the horses nibbling at green shoots on the ground as they grazed freely nearby. There were too many unknown people around these days that Lena kept thinking back to Sam’s warning, about trusting people, staying close to people who would protect her, and not trusting them either. Feeling off, her hands still faintly pink from the blood she’d washed off, the lines of her palms darker where it had dried in the creases and in her nail beds, Lena had to consider whether it was the right place for her to be, if she’d even done any good so far, or if perhaps she’d inflicted more harm by trying to help, in shock as she saw bodies split open, kneeling in pools of blood as people died.

     

                As she started to spiral, a tightness in her chest, running a hand through her hair as she frowned, the man returned with a pile of cloth bundles, split with another woman. They both set them down carefully, nodding deferentially to Kara as she thanked them, before vanishing back to their own business. Crouching, Kara started to sift through the bundles, a pleased look on her face as Lena watched her from the corner of her eye.

     

                “Lena,” Kara softly called to her, a little reserved, uncertainty colouring her voice.

     

                Hesitating, wondering if she could feign some greater task, worried that there weren’t enough people around to create that necessary buffer between them, considering the tone of her wife’s voice. Only Querl and Sam were in the immediate vicinity, and she worried that they might not be enough of a deterrent for Kara to start questioning her again, that she might ask them to give them some privacy, some unknowable emotion in her words as she looked at Lena. Relenting, Lena turned towards her, raising her eyebrows as she approached.

     

                “I have something for you.”

     

                Intrigued, Lena’s expression turned apprehensive as she watched her wife straighten with one of the bundles in hand, uncovering it to reveal polished steel. As Lena stepped up beside her, studying the object, she realised it was a helmet, wrought in the same fashion as Kara’s, but with leafy vines of ivy and flowers instead of waves and fish scales. Eyes quickly darting up to meet Kara’s, Lena cocked her head to the side slightly as her brow furrowed, realising that the strangeness to her wife’s behaviour had been excitement .

     

                “For me?”

     

                “A Princess should have armour,” Kara said with a certain firmness. “Especially in war.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena’s eyes dropped down to the other parcels, realising it must have been a full suit. Looking up at her again, her frown deepened as her mouth opened and closed. “You- you … got me armour?”

     

                “Come. Put it on.”

     

                Kara sank back to a crouch and started to unwrap the rest of them, glancing up at Lena and gesturing for her to start undressing. Looking around, she saw Querl retreating through the trees, Sam continuing her tense prowl of the area, and reached for the clasp of her broach. Shedding her quiver and cloak, Lena fumbled with the buckle of her belt, dropping it to the ground as Kara uncovered greaves, vambraces, pauldrons, tassets, and a gorget. Each piece was elegantly beautiful with vines of ivy and flowers, some wrought in filigree and others etched into the steel. Lena noticed that the flowers were predominantly lily of the valley, the curving stems and little bell flowers wrought with careful detail. 

     

                “Remove your surcoat, mail and jacket,” Kara instructed her, Lena quickly following her instruction.

     

                She was handed a deep green linen gambeson, the thin padding offering an extra layer of protection and making it so the armour wouldn’t chafe, while still remaining breathable. Then there was the chainmail hauberk, adjusting the light coat of shining steel rings as it fell halfway down her thighs. Kara had to help her with the breastplate next, her fingers nimble as she buckled the straps on the side, it all feeling so familiar to the few times she’d had Lena in armour before, but with an added layer of strain this time. Lena wanted to speak, and could sense that Kara likewise wanted to, but they both remained silent within earshot of Sam.

     

                “A cloak is no good for a fight, but this will keep you warm enough when you aren’t fighting,” Kara murmured as she shook out a deep green surcoat of soft leather, the edges trimmed in velvet with yet more lily of the valley patterns embroidered on top of the trim. She helped her into it, fastening the little silver clasps at the front as Lena stood rooted to the spot, letting her wife do it for her.

     

                Buckling on the pauldrons and the gorget, Kara reached for the vambraces, slipping one over Lena’s hand, snuggly fitting her forearm and laced tightly into place, and Lena watched Kara’s hands, the little nicks of old scars on her tanned fingers, the wiry strength of them, so capable and rough from use. She wanted to cover the back of it with her other hand, squeeze Kara’s fingers in a silent reassurance that all was well between them, even if it all felt so horribly hopeless. Instead, she let her wife continue her careful fastening of each piece onto Lena’s body, doing all she could to make sure she was as safe as could be. After the vambraces were the tassets, buckled onto the bottom of the breastplate, to cover Lena’s thighs, and then the greaves on her shins. There were light leather boots as well, the tops of the feet mailed, with a pair of mail-backed fingerless gloves for her hands, and it all felt so light, so perfectly suited for her , that Lena felt pleasure spread through her chest, even at such an awful time as that.

     

                There was a leaf-shaped shield to match the rest of it, slung across Lena’s back, and then Kara unwrapped a long, thin one that remained. It was a bundle of leather straps from what Lena could first see until the shape revealed itself to be a belt, tooled in the same silver ivy pattern adorning her armour, and attached to it, a smooth leather sheath with a sword inside it. Kara stepped in close, passing the belt behind Lena and then pulling it tight around her hips, working the end of the belt through the buckle and cinching it tight around her waist, before looping the long tongue of the belt back through itself and giving it a sharp tug to tighten the extra knot. Hesitating, Kara stooped to fetch the dagger she’d gifted Lena the better part of a year ago now, removing its small sheath from the belt and then standing close as she worked it onto Lena’s new belt.

     

                Taking a step back, Kara eyed her wife with a glimmer of satisfaction in her blue eyes, nodding as something akin to pride stole over her face. “There. Now you are perfect. A true Princess of the Earthfolk.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena murmured, looking down at herself, a smile on her lips. She looked up at her wife, and her smile grew, quickly followed by Kara’s own wide smile. For a moment, it felt as if everything between them vanished, and they were once again as they’d always been. She was Lena’s best friend, and Lena didn’t think she’d ever told her wife that, but for a moment, they weren’t troubled by the confusion of their feelings, at what was unsaid, it just felt like Lena was with her best friend, dressed up in her new armour and feeling bolder, braver for it. “It’s beautiful. I- really, thank you, Kara. I- well, I’m not entirely sure I’m worthy of it, but I think … the old version of me would never have been able to wear it and feel as if it was right to. But it feels right.”

     

                “The person you used to be was no less a fighter than you are now. You fought so hard for your survival throughout your adolescence; do not view your past self as weak or shameful. You have never been anything but strong, even in the face of so much adversity. I will need you to be strong a little while longer.”

     

                “I’m trying to be,” she whispered, unable to meet Kara’s gaze.

     

                “Draw your sword.”

     

                Lena hesitated before she gripped the pommel, realising there was a round piece of polished nephrite set into the pommel. Her favourite gemstone. She was slow to draw it as she processed that, the attention to detail, her favourite things worked into her armour, courtesy of her wife. Swallowing thickly, she drew the length of steel. It was the length of her arm and had a curving stem with lily of the valley etched down the length of it, a line of glyphs following the curve of it. Lena held the blade across her palm as she tried to read the writing, able to make out her name, make out Princess and sword.

     

                “What does it say?”

     

                “It says this sword belongs to Lena, Princess of the Unseelie, a rose amongst thorns, and life amongst death,” Kara murmured, running her fingertip along the glyphs. 

     

                With a half-hearted laugh, Lena sheathed the sword. “Ironic, don’t you think? To have that written on a sword used to kill people?”

     

                “It is no less true just because you have killed. Now, let me braid your hair out of your face so you’re not blinded by it if our camp is overrun and you are forced to fight.”

     

                Lena couldn’t object, moving to sit in front of a log at the fireside, while Kara fetched a comb. Her touch was gentle, working the comb through Lena’s tangled hair, working the knots free with as little pain as possible. It was soothing, and Lena closed her eyes, feeling her wife’s fingers in her hair, deftly braiding her dark locks into an intricate braid that would hold all day. She couldn’t have said when Sam left, but there was a change in the air, a subtle shift that stole over Lena’s body, that let her know they were alone. As alone as they could be with the various tents scattered throughout the trees, but alone enough. She felt Kara’s knuckle brush the tip of her right ear and drew in a soft breath, her stomach lurching, pulse quickening as her mouth went dry. Lena suddenly felt far too hot in her armour, a clamminess in her palms as she wished to be anywhere else, fearing what stupidity would befall her if she stayed there any longer with her wife, how much of a fool she’d make of herself and her unrequited feelings.

     

                “There,” Kara murmured, tugging on the bottom of Lena’s braid and then setting her hands on her wife’s shoulders.

     

                Sitting on the ground, leaning back against Kara’s knees, Lena suddenly felt so very tired. A sad expression crossed her face, pulling her brow taut as her mouth thinned, and she could feel the anticipation in the air. And yet, despite the recent imbalance between them, it felt so natural to be sitting alone with her wife, just the two of them to keep each other company. It was peaceful in a way Lena hadn’t found with anyone else, and her eyes pricked with tears as she tried to swallow.

     

                “I know you do not wish to speak with me alone,” Kara haltingly started to speak, breaking their fragile silence, “I have kept my words to myself for days now, but now that we are truly alone, I must ask you. I understand if you do not wish to answer, but I must ask it anyway; what did you mean?”

     

                Lena drew in a ragged breath, tasting the smoke of the fire. And still, the words caught at the back of her throat, a certain reluctance to her, her uncertainty weighing heavily on her shoulders. “I-” Lena cut off, ducking her head down, feeling the raw edges of her heart as she felt shockingly vulnerable. 

     

                Closing her mouth, she staggered to her feet, walking a few paces away, hearing the soft tinkling of her armour clinking, hearing Kara’s as well as she stood too. But Lena couldn’t go very far, late afternoon sunlight slanting through the trees as the wind stirred the short strands of hair at her hairline, branches swaying as the forest responded to her agitation. Still, it was tranquil, wild lupins growing in patches near the base of the trees, something beautiful growing in the midst of a war camp. 

     

                It felt like a moment of calm before the storm, and she turned, taking in the sight of her wife. Kara stood in a shaft of yellow sunlight, which bathed her hair and skin in yellow, despite the blood, like she’d been cast in gold. Motes of pollen swirled through the air, a few droning bees amidst the flies, and Lena’s lips parted at the sight of her. Her wife was beautiful, a fact she’d known from the moment she’d first laid eyes upon her, but it struck Lena anew with a sudden weakness, disbelief nagging at her as she wondered how she could not have known that she loved her. That she loved her for some time now, that she loved her in a way she hadn’t even been able to recognise, the feeling sneaking up on her until she hadn’t even known her heart had been stolen from her until it was too late.

     

                And as she struggled, Kara stepped in closer, reaching her hands out and taking Lena’s as she closed the distance between them. She half expected her wife to shake her off, but when Lena didn’t, Kara wondered what she was feeling then. As Lena stared at her, tears started to limn her waterline, and she let out a defeated sigh, her gaze softening at the tender look of concern on Kara’s face. Mouth set in a grim line, the corners curled with the faintest smile as she felt that old tug in her chest, the painful ache of longing, Lena leaned in a fraction.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Lena softly apologised, eyes stinging as her throat constricted around her words, voice wavering ever-so-slightly. “I’m sorry I came here and ruined your life. I’m sorry to make things difficult for you all the time. I didn’t mean to, I just- I wanted you to love me. I know you’re hurting, I know I’m so horribly selfish all the time, but I- even if it meant dying, I just wanted to be wanted by you. I want you so badly that it’s broken my heart to know that you love someone else. And I figured it out, and I’ve been trying to accept it with as much grace as I can, because I know it’s- well, it’s shit for everyone involved, but it just- it’s hard , it’s so hard. I want you to be happy, and I know you won’t be, because she’ll die and you’ll be lost in your grief, and I’m sorry to make things so awkward between us, because you’re my best friend, and I just- I didn’t mean to fall in love with you-”

     

                She was crying freely now, her face flushed, a look of regret for speaking so openly, but unable to stop the words that just kept spilling out of her, each one worse than the one before, every sentence more humiliating than what she’d already divulged days prior. And Kara was looking at her with something gentle in her eyes, and no small amount of shock and sadness on her face. 

     

                “What?” she murmured, quiet confusion creasing her face as Lena drew in a hitching breath.

     

                “I love you. I didn’t even know it was possible for me to love anyone . If I knew that I could , if I knew what it felt like , I would’ve known I was in love with you ages ago, because this feeling … God, I can’t remember the last time I didn’t feel this way. It’s- it’s been … months. It has to have been. And I was too fucking stupid to realise it, until you fell in love and I just- I felt sick with jealousy. But how could I fault you? I mean, she- she’s beautiful, she’s kind and smart, and I’m sorry she’s already in love with Alex, and that you don’t get to have your happy ending, but I don’t care if you’re not in love with me, if you’re in love with Kelly; I can’t keep it to myself any longer, because it’s just so- so tiring . I’m so tired.”

     

                Breaking off as she heaved another hitching breath, angrily wiping away her tears, Lena choked on a quiet sob as Kara stood before her, still holding one of her hands, blindsided by her wife’s bewildering confession. And as she tried to make sense of it, Kara’s chest filled with the warmth of amusement, of baffled delight and weak relief. It all felt so surreal that she couldn’t even feel any guilt or grief in the moment, buoyed by the knowledge that her wife loved her. Lena had gotten it all wrong, of course, but for a minute, Kara wasn’t weighed down by the burden of her prophecy; she was just so very, very happy.

     

                “Oh, you beautiful fool,” Kara laughed as she started to cry. Cupping Lena’s face in her hands, she kissed her cheeks, her brow, her chin, nose and lips, every inch of her she could as she laughed and laughed. “I’m not in love with Kelly; I’m in love with you. How could you think it could be anyone but you?”

     

                “What?” Lena mumbled, her turn to be confused now, her face pinched with doubt.

     

                “I have been yours since we met. I feel as if I was born that day, that perhaps I had known it then, as if I was born knowing you. You are so familiar to me that I would know you in darkness, I would know you blind. It is by you alone that I could be undone. I have never known what peace feels like, growing up in constant war, but I believe it may feel a lot like you.”

     

                And then Kara’s breathless rambling as tears ran down her cheeks turned into soft sobs as her face was wrenched with agony, the euphoria dimming as the torment rushed back in. And it was only then that Lena realised that she was going to die. She’d forgotten that for a brief moment, so blindsided by the fact that Kara loved her, that it wasn’t Kelly, or someone else, but her , that her feelings were returned. But now, she paled slightly as Kara apologised, her voice meek and pitiful as she continued to cup Lena’s face in her hands, desperate in her need for Lena to understand.

     

                “I’m sorry. I’m so sorry, please forgive me. I didn’t want it to be you, I never wanted to fall in love. I didn’t want to tell you, I didn’t want you to know. Everything I’ve done has been to keep you safe, so you wouldn’t be frightened. I’m sorry . ”

     

                But Lena had already said that she would have wanted it to be her, even knowing she was going to die, and she’d meant it then and still meant it now, even as she floundered for a moment, wrestling with her mortality. “It’s okay,” she whispered, reaching up to smooth a hand over Kara’s bloodstained hair, her wife quietly sobbing as they stood so close together, torn between the happiness and fear of what it all meant. “It’s okay, I know you didn’t want this to happen. But I’ll be alright, Kara. I won’t be frightened to die; it’ll- it’ll be a comfort to know that it’s by your hand, okay? I’m sorry to make you do it, but I’ll be okay, we’ll both be fine.”

     

                Shaking her head, looking pale with dread, more scared than Lena had ever seen her before, bottom lip quivering as tears rolled down her cheeks, Kara drew in a shuddering breath. Lena cut her off with a kiss, crushing their lips together, tasting salt, tasting old blood, not caring as she ran her hands over her wife’s hair, pressing herself as close to her as possible, silently cursing the bulkiness of armour for getting in the way. She wanted to feel Kara’s warmth, wanted to feel her arms around her, but she kissed her with urgency, heart pounding as adrenaline coursed through her. 

     

                Even though she said she’d want to know, that she wouldn’t be frightened to die, she was scared then . Lena couldn’t deny it. But it was Kara, and how could she ever feel afraid of her? The knowledge that her wife would kill her at some point wasn’t enough for Lena to give an inch , wanting to be as close to her as possible, wanting to drink her in, as limited as their time was. For all she knew, they might have another decade, another century together, but no amount of time would be long enough for her after realising the enormity of her feelings for her wife. But to kiss her then, safe within the knowledge that she was loved, a bliss she’d never felt, making fresh tears fall, was enough for Lena.

     

                They were interrupted by the sound of horns echoing through the forest, tearing them apart as the horses perked up, as distant shouts cut through the peaceful bubble they’d existed in for just a few minutes.
