And then Alex was tearing through the trees, a fierce look on her face as she hefted her twin hunting daggers, come to tear her sister away, Kelly flanking her, an arrow already nocked. They pulled up short at the sight of the two of them crying, standing nose to nose, clearly in the middle of something.

     

                Gently bumping Kara’s nose with her own, Lena stole a soft kiss. “Go.”

     

                “I-” Kara faltered.

     

                Wiping her tears for her, Lena nodded as she gave her a wavering smile, a shakiness filling her as she tried to be brave for her wife. Still, she cursed out her brother - or her mother, whichever of them was responsible for whichever enemy was attacking - for interrupting the moment, letting go of Kara and then pausing as her wife took her hand. Kara squeezed gently, faltering momentarily as her eyes flitted to her sister and then back to Lena. She tried again.

     

                “When you take your last breath, I will not outlive you for very long, I promise you that. And when we die, our bodies will be buried together, and we’ll grow into trees, and I’ll keep my leaves a little longer in autumn to keep you warm. I will rest easily beside you in death if I cannot have you long in life.”

     

                “Don’t say that,” Lena fiercely whispered, panic filling her as she gripped the sides of Kara’s neck, eyes widening with fear. “You can’t- no , I can live with dying - my life hasn’t been so- so great up until I met you, so I can die happy knowing that I got what I wanted before the end - but I can’t live with you dying. You have a family , you have a life , so much to live for. You can’t do that, please, promise me you won’t do that once I’m gone.”

     

                “I cannot,” Kara mumbled, “I have already said it, so I shall do it. And I will be happier for it, even though I wish it were different. Why would I care to live when you are gone? I wish that we have many years left together, that we might have more than an autumn, a winter and a spring, that we might have had an eternity to grow old together, but … in any life I might have lived, I would have wanted you as my wife. I’m sorry I did not tell you sooner.”

     

                Vision blurring as new tears welled up, Lena shook her head. “Just come back, okay?”

     

                Hesitating, Kara kissed her once more, not nearly long enough but full of her insistence, as if trying to push every ounce of her love into it, before she backed away, her eyes on Lena as she reached for her mailed gloves tucked into her sword belt. Alex grabbed Kara’s arm, her face pale and eyes wide with shock, understanding the implications of their conversation, that they had both been honest, perhaps too late, her voice low and firm as she tried to convince her sister to stay, sensing that it might not be wise for Kara to jump back into another skirmish in her current emotional state. But as devastated as she was by her dangerous love, she was filled with the comfort that Lena loved her back, and it instilled her with an urgency to end this now, to make the most of the time she had left with her wife.

     

                Lena watched her go, their eyes locked up until the last possible moment, before Kara vanished into the gloom of the forest, leaving her alone. Or rather, Lena thought she was alone, hearing footsteps and hoofbeats heading towards the river, until there was a soft, derisive laugh behind her. 

     

                Whirling around, Lena’s expression furrowed into a scowl as she took in the sight of her mother, tall and regal with a look of contemptuous amusement on her face. “Well, you are the fool after all. I had hoped for better.” Lillian clicked her tongue and sighed. “No matter, I will rid myself of you soon enough.”

     

                “Wha-” Lena started to exclaim, reaching for her new sword, sheathed at her waist and a desperate attempt to protect herself - from what , she didn’t know.

     

                She didn’t even get it more than two inches out of the scabbard before a hand was clapped over her mouth, strong fingers encircling her wrist, effectively immobilising her. Lena couldn’t shout for help, couldn’t draw her sword, couldn’t do anything but draw in frantic breaths through her nose. And then she smelled the familiar smoke and ashes of Sam, stiffening with surprise as she realised the guard’s warnings hadn’t been for anyone but herself. And Lena had been too blind to see it, the way Reign had been fighting for control the closer to the river they were, how she’d never been entirely gone, even on the most western coast of the Seelie Court, and that Lena should have known better than to put her safety in the hands of the woman who’d killed her mother. 

     

                Pestilence was there then, a rag in hand to gag her as Lena tried to bite her fingers, Sam - Reign - grabbing a fistful of her braid to stop her, and a length of hemp rope binding her wrists behind her back, the gloves and gambeson fortunately blocking any chafing. Unable to do anything but let out a muffled growl, glaring daggers at Lillian, Lena felt the cold edge of steel at her throat once more as Reign clapped a hand on her shoulder and held one of her hunting knives in the other hand, keeping Lena in check.

     

                “Bring her.”

    Chapter 43

                Bound and gagged on the back of a horse, Lena was helpless as she rattled about in her new armour, struggling despite her helplessness. It made no difference, but she still chafed her wrists raw where the rope settled into the gap between her vambraces and gloves, stubborn to the end. She was frightened, but her anger eclipsed that for the time being, until the sound of the river grew louder and she heard the splashing of the horses ahead of her walking into the shallow current. Only then was she seized with terror, unable to see anything but the underside of the horse, hands behind her back as she went still, afraid she would fall off and plunge straight into the frigid water. Reign rode in front of her, stiff-backed and cold as she urged the horse into the river, and Lena drew in frantic breaths, a panicked sound escaping her when cold water flecked her face as it churned around the horse’s legs.

     

                It was a wide section of the river, a mile upstream from the fighting, which was still dimly audible to the south, and Lena felt alone with her fear as her stiff body was painfully jostled. Eyes closed as her lips moved in a silent plea around her gag, she bit down on the rag and reached for her power, the power that was always there when her life was in danger, when there was some threat she instinctively needed to protect herself from. Halfway across, there was a faint tremor underfoot, and Reign sharply turned to look down at her, hissing in warning.

     

                “Stop it.”

     

                Unable to speak, Lena made a sound at the back of her throat, thrashing in panic as another tremor, stronger this time, made the surface of the river ripple. She wasn’t consciously doing it, still not having that fine a control over her abilities, but it didn’t stop Reign from reaching down to grab a fistful of her hair, braid clutched in her hand as she yanked Lena’s head up, neck at a painful angle as her back arched and she caught a glimpse of the sparkling river running towards them, trees hemming them in on either side.

     

                “I said stop it. Unless you wish to take a swim.”

     

                Lena stopped her thrashing, and as her panic dimmed, so did the tremors of the ground, the surface of the river returning to its usual glassiness after a few moments, and she swore around the gag in her mouth, the words muffled but her intent clear. A minute later, the horse was clambering up the riverbank, ungainly in the soft mud before firmer ground was underfoot. The rearguard, composed of Pestilence and one of Lillian’s Unseelie, worked their way up the bank, and the small group huddled in the shelter of the Unseelie Court for the first time in months. 

     

                There were seven of them, from what Lena had seen, dragged through the trees at knifepoint to waiting horses, and they’d all safely made it across the boundary of the river, which didn’t bode well for Lena. Any hopes of being rescued suddenly went out the window, and the fight in Lena fled as she lay limply splayed over the flanks of the horse, tears pricking her eyes. But she knew she couldn’t be killed; that right was reserved for her wife.

     

                That thought comforted her somewhat, and she stopped fighting, knowing that no matter what happened, she would come out of it alive. Or, at worst, if Kara found her, whether that was in hours, days or weeks, and her rescue attempt went awry, Lena would still die at her wife’s hands. It would be a kinder death, even if it was asking too much of her wife to bear the burden of it. Eyes closed as she focused on the sounds of the wind through leaves, trees seeming to sigh and sway, drawing in slow breaths through her nose as she calmed herself, focusing on the trees instead of the nearby sound of water. How badly she wished she could get off the horse and dig her hands and feet into the soft earth.

     

                “Purity.”

     

                Eyes snapping open, Lena felt a rush of anger again. This plan had been orchestrated with intention, not just out of sheer luck, and she had to wonder if the second wave attack had been timed precisely for her to be left alone, under the guard of a woman who was born of two Courts but loyal to one. Her blood pounded in her ears as she saw red, unable to even hear the conversation that was happening as she seethed, another tremor rippling through the trees. They seemed to groan, their roots digging in deeper, before it was counteracted. She wasn’t sure if it was her mother or Pestilence who brought the forest to heel, but it all went still, despite the anger radiating from Lena.

     

                “Deal with her,” Lillian dismissively instructed someone.

     

                Hearing the sound of a weapon being unsheathed, sending a thrill of fear through her once more, Lena started to struggle again but went limp as the hilt of a dagger slammed into her temple. It split the skin, blood ribboning across her face and brow as she hung upside down, knocking her out cold, and Reign sheathed her dagger again before urging her horse onwards. They left a trail of lilac petals in their wake as Lena’s blood dripped off her face and fluttered down to the forest floor.

     

                They continued through the forest, not far, barely a mile, urgency more important as whatever her mother had planned needed to be dealt with before Kara realised her wife was missing and came after them. It wasn’t long at all before the horses were reined in, the sound of fighting no longer audible, nothing save for the wind and trees and restless horses surrounding them. It was silent for a tense minute before everyone but Lillian dismounted, soft footsteps landing on a soft carpet of last autumn’s leaves. Lena had started to regain consciousness as they’d come to a stop, and she felt woozy and confused as she was suddenly heaved off the horse, no pretence of courtly deference to her then as she sagged in Reign’s hands. The Hunter was strong, but Lena was practically dead weight, groaning as a fierce headache pounded at her temples, her face sticky with blood and a nasty bruise already forming. Her feet dragged across the forest floor before her knees landed hard, her armour rattling from the movement as she swayed unsteadily.

     

                “Unbind her,” Lillian snapped her fingers.

     

                “Is that wise, Your Majesty?” Pestilence asked.

     

                Blinking slowly as she raised her head, Lena saw the hard look of warning on her mother’s face as she gave her Hunter a cutting look. “You question me? If you had finished the task set to you years ago, we would not be dealing with this now. See it done.”

     

                It was Reign who quickly obeyed, her long dagger in hand, sawing through the rough rope. Lena hunched over as her posture slumped, her shoulders aching from the way they had been awkwardly forced back, and she could feel the raw pain in her wrists as she braced her gloved hands against the ground.

     

                “Her gag too. I wish to speak with her.”

     

                Reign grabbed the back of the gag and dragged Lena’s head up, unknotting the rag and pulling it out of her mouth. Chest heaving as she drew in grateful breaths, her mouth dry from the gag, Lena was still for a moment, trying to get her bearings, before her hand shot to her sword. Before she could even get it more than an inch out of its scabbard, Reign had a hand firmly planted on the top of Lena’s head and her dagger at her throat once more.

     

                “Ah-ah,” she warned Lena, jerking her chin up a fraction.

     

                Feeling the bite of cold steel, stinging as it scored a thin line above her gorget, Lena quietly fumed, her mouth a hard line as she glared daggers up at Reign. At Sam, whom she’d grown to trust, even just a little, after everything that had happened when Lena’s mom had taken her from the Court, after being hunted down by the woman towering over her, the way she’d had her life ruined because of it. Even after all of that, Lena had started to trust her, had sympathy for the woman, who had been abused at Lillian’s hand for decades, perhaps longer, only to have fallen into the trap. 

     

                She wondered if that had been Lillian’s intention from the beginning, if she’d let Reign and Andrea flee the Unseelie Court under the guise of defection, or if it had just gotten out of hand, and she’d been too blind to see it. It had to be the latter, because Kara trusted Sam, but then, her wife had been too preoccupied with the torment of knowing she would kill her wife to even notice that Sam had slowly been slipping. Either way, Lena was angry and hurt, too, kicking herself for her own stupidity. 

     

                “Fuck you,” Lena tearfully snarled, poorly concealed betrayal in her eyes as she looked up. 

     

                Reign just blinked down at her, her expression impassive. There was no satisfaction derived from pooling the wool over Lena’s eyes, none of the kindness Sam had shown her, and the loyalty from being her constant shadow. She had so firmly slipped back into the other part of herself that she was unrecognisable to Lena as Sam. It made her even angrier, at the mercy of people who would gladly see her dead, not a single ally amongst them. Not even Andrea, who might’ve at least been persuaded, of sound mind, where her lover was not.

     

                Approaching, Lillian looked amused, smiling sharply as she cocked her head to the side. “Did you really think I was done with you? You foolishly fed me poison, orchestrated the removal of my hand, and fled my Court like a coward. Did you think I would not seek the vengeance I am owed?”  

     

                “You aren’t going to kill me,” Lena stiffly murmured.

     

                “You overestimate your worth to me. You are clever, but if you had any sense, you would have let your wife slaughter us all at Krypton. Especially after you were so lucky to escape my Court with your head attached the first time. You proved yourself a disappointment to the last.”

     

                Lillian clicked her tongue, reaching down to cup Lena’s cheek in the palm of her hand, stroking her cheek with a sharp nail. Lips twitching with hatred, Lena looked up at Lillian, her contempt palpable.

     

                “If you had any sense, you wouldn’t have brought me here. You wanted me to be your heir, and yet, you overlooked the fact that I wasn’t raised as you were. I am far more human than fae in my attitude and judgement, no matter how much of the forest is in my blood. And for that, I could only ever prove a disappointment to you.”

     

                Straightening, Lillian examined her a moment and then sighed as she drew her hand back and slapped her squarely across the face. A bright pain exploded across the right side of Lena’s face as her head whipped to the side, and it was only because Reign moved the dagger away from her neck with that unnatural fae speed that Lena was spared a slit throat. She bit her tongue, though, tasting blood in her mouth, and let out a frayed laugh 

     

                “See?” Lena rasped. “You know you can’t kill me. If I were that easy to kill, you would’ve done it already. But you know that I am hers alone to kill.”

     

                Stiffening, Lillian looked down on her, her haughtiness making her seem even taller, a derisive sneer twisting her mouth. “What I know is that you are prophesied to die here, on the banks of a river.”

     

                Lena blanched at her mother’s words, genuine surprise crossing her face. “How do you know that?” she hoarsely demanded. “I’ve never been to see the seers.”

     

                “Yes, you have. Why do you think your foolish mother took you and ran?”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena felt tears smart her eyes, a scowl furrowing her face as she worked hard to swallow the lump in her throat. “You’re lying.”

     

                “I cannot be lying, as you well know. That is your fate. By whose hand your death will come, it was not proclaimed. She may say she loves you, but it may be that she is destined to kill another whom she loves more . And say that you do meet your end at her hand, well … there is still pain I can inflict upon you without causing death. Do you think she will still think you beautiful with your face carved to pieces?”

     

                Lena felt a cold finger trail down her spine. Lillian’s tone was mild as she spoke, as if she were indifferent, but Lena didn’t doubt the sincerity. She wouldn’t put anything past her mother, not even torture, and she felt fear steal over her again, alone like a sheep amongst wolves. But she had teeth as well, and Lena wouldn’t go down without a fight.

     

                Hanging her head, shoulders curled and hands braced against the floor, she gritted her teeth and steeled herself. It was getting dark now, the edges of light blurring into night, a dimness to the green light of the forest as shadows lengthened and deepened, and she knew that the fighting could only go on for so long, that soon enough Kara would realise she was missing, that she’d come after her. While Lena hoped her wife would stay away, stay safe, she also knew there was no chance of that happening, so the least she could do was try to make it as easy as possible. 

     

                In the darkness, with the added layers of armour, she hoped the way her body tensed would go unnoticed, but as she shot to her feet, Reign planted a foot firmly in her back and kicked her forward, sprawling facedown in the dirt. Letting out a quiet grunt of pain at the jarring impact, Lena grasped at leaves and dirt as she struggled to catch her breath, winded, and felt the weight of Reign pinning her down. Angry, her cheeks stained red with it, Lena gritted her teeth as frustration washed over her.

     

                “Cowards,” she hissed, feeling the strong urge to punch something. “The whole lot of you. You think I’m a disappointment … but you still won’t face me. Where’s the honour in this?”

     

                Sinking to a crouch, Lillian reached out to trace a finger over the curve of Lena’s cheek. “I don’t care a whit for honour; I care about winning. And you will die, regardless, whether it is an honourable or dishonourable act.”

     

                “If you didn’t care for honour, you would do it yourself. But even you won’t stain your reputation by becoming a kinslayer, will you? You need someone else to do your dirty work for you.”

     

                Lillian chuckled, “Come, now. You would not kill me yourself either. You are too weak for that.”

     

                “Let me up and we’ll see who’s telling the truth.”

     

                Humming for a moment as she pretended to deliberate, Lillian smirked. “No, daughter, I do not think I will. But take comfort in the knowledge that your death will serve a purpose. You will be the catalyst for true peace once I rid myself of both children and seize both Courts for myself. You should be glad; is that not what you wanted?”

     

                Lena’s stomach lurched, and she tried to raise her head to look at her mother, her eyes wide with surprise. “You’re going to kill him?”

     

                “He is already dead to me. He has run from his crimes and his punishment. There is no greater shame; even you do not shame me as he does. It is unfortunate that you both have your father’s weak blood running through you, but it matters not. I will prevail where his line failed.”

     

                “Kill me if you must, but you won’t get away with this. Do you think she will let you do it uncontested? Even if you’re right, and I’m not the one she loves enough to kill, do you think she will let you live?”

     

                “Ah, but I heard her well, daughter. She will kill herself once you are dead. Two birds, one stone, as they say. I should thank her for making such a dramatic oath in the old tongue and ridding me of another problem. This is all turning out remarkably well for me, do you not think so?” Lillian laughed, giving Lena’s chin a painful squeeze before she stilled, head cocked to the side, listening, and rose to her feet.

     

                “Get her up,” Lillian ordered Reign, gesturing dismissively to Lena as her amusement faded.

     

                Staring out into the dimming forest, Lillian’s face was hawkish as a few others appeared in golden masks, dull in the shadows. Lex was there then, pushing forward, his face bare and scalp freshly shaved, making him look hard as Lena was hauled to her feet to look at him. Reign kept the edge of her dagger pressed firmly into Lena’s jugular, dragging her back to stand with the others as Lillian stepped forward to greet her son.

     

                “Mother,” Lex smoothly greeted her. “I am glad to see you.”

     

                “Is that so? You have run me out of my own Court. Or am I mistaken in that assumption?”

     

                He flashed his teeth in a sharp smile, and Lena felt her whole body tense. Caught between both of them, Lena trusted the sly manipulation of her mother more than her brother’s cunning unpredictability. He would hurt her, yes, but she couldn’t see what he had planned, and that unknown made her blood run cold. She would pick the devil she knew, if it came to it, but she didn’t think she had much say in what happened next. Still, her mind scrambled for a way to twist this meeting to her advantage, to pit mother and son against each other, to save herself.

                

                “You are not mistaken, but I merely intended to claim that which is rightfully mine. I am King, no?”

     

                “No, you are not,” Lillian haughtily objected. “Nor are you my heir.”

     

                His eyes darted to Lena and he cocked his head to the side, smiling softly. “And yet, you bring your heir here to sacrifice her for your own ambitions.” 

     

                “And you. You come here to see your sister dead, so that one day you may take what she lawfully should have inherited. You are no better than I - you are truly my son.”

     

                “And what of me? You say that I am not your heir. What are your intentions for me?”

     

                “I will make you my heir once she is dead, but I will not give up my crown.”

     

                “It is mine by birthright.”

     

                “You spurned it the moment you went rogue. I will not give it up to see you wreak havoc across both Courts. At least my ploy for power will see peace come to fruition.”

     

                “So long as they bow to you. How many will you slaughter if they do not?”

     

                Lillian’s lips twitched with impatient amusement. “Fewer than you will for pleasure.”

     

                “Do you think me foolish enough to believe that you will let me walk away from here unharmed?”

     

                “I cannot harm you; you are my blood.”

     

                “You cannot harm her, and she is not of your blood. She is your daughter all the same, so you cannot kill her, but that does not mean she will not die here. You needn’t dirty your hands to see it done. Which one of your Hunters will gut me? Hm? Which one has been tasked with the honour?”

     

                “She dies to placate you. I had thought to make further use of her and her wife, before ridding myself of her, but it is for you that I have dragged her here to spill her blood. The threat she poses to your inheritance will be put to an end; the threat you pose to the Courts will be dealt with after that. There are agreements we may come to, but you will not walk out of this with a crown.”

     

                He was angry now, his face reddening as he scowled at their mother. “You condemn me with your words. You deny me what is mine by speaking it as such. What reason do I have to stay my hand now? I could cut you down where you stand. I am already cast out from the Courts; I have no qualms about committing regicide or matricide.”

     

                Raising her chin, looking down at her son as if he were beneath her, which Lillian probably did think, after everything that had transpired, her lip curled slightly with contempt. “You will not kill me, because I am destined to die staring life in the face. You are not life, you are death. And you are destined to never be King.”

     

                Taking a step forward, fuming, his eyes gleaming dangerously in his hard face, Lex opened his mouth to speak, but Lillian raised a hand to silence him. “I tire of this. We are close enough to the river for it to be true; let us slit her throat and be rid of one problem.”

     

                Lena had remained silent throughout, waiting to see how she could manipulate what happened next, but the breath caught in her throat at the sudden shift, as time ran out. Feeling faint with panic, with dread, she felt her knees buckle slightly. Only Reign’s hand fisted in the collar of her leather surcoat kept Lena on her feet, the keen edge of the dagger at her throat, sweating in her armour as she stammered wordlessly, her heart pounding in her chest. There was no way out of this, and Kara was not there, and Lena was torn between relief that Kara would be spared the guilt of killing her and devastation that perhaps Lillian was right, and she was not loved as much as Kara thought.

                

                “Please,” Lena whispered, her voice fraught with desperation, as Lillian turned around, walking towards her people.

     

                Eyes filling with tears as she gritted her teeth, throat painfully bobbing and stinging as the edge of the dagger cut her skin, Lena tried to plead for her life. Her voice was barely audible, though, as breathless and scared as she was, and her eyes met Lillian’s as the Queen approached and stopped before her. With a quick jerk of her chin, her eyes never left Lena’s face.

     

                “Do it,” she ordered Reign.

     

                Tears slid down Lena’s cheeks as she raised her chin, defiant to the end, and she closed her eyes too. Her last memory wouldn’t be the sight of her mother, it would be the sound of the wind in the trees, the smell of dirt and rain, and the thought of her wife. Her wife, whom she hadn’t had time to openly love, hadn’t had time to spend a year with yet. And while she could easily accept that perhaps she wasn’t the love of Kara’s life, she hoped that Kara would know that she had been Lena’s, and even though she hadn’t known it, hadn’t been able to show it all that well in the last few days when she had known it, it was no small thing to Lena.

     

                And then the blade sang in the evening air, and the sensation she felt wasn’t white-hot pain but the shocking splatter of warm blood on her cheeks. Confused for a moment, her face furrowing, Lena’s eyelids fluttered open and her eyes flew wide with horror as she watched Lillian stagger, her hand at her throat, her stump too, trying to stem the torrent of blood gouting from her slit throat. Mouth open, Lena couldn’t speak, couldn’t make a sound as she tried to process what had happened, as panic shot through the assembled group.

     

                “Run,” Reign firmly ordered her, the word sudden and low as she was beside Lena then.

     

                Glancing at her, Lena blanched at the sight of the dagger coated red and realised it had been her. And one look at her face, at the way it was screwed up, how she seemed to roll her shoulders, stretch out her neck, let Lena know it wasn’t Reign, it was Sam. Sam, who was fighting hard against the control of the Unseelie Court, against her Queen’s orders, who had taken her opportunity to free herself and her sisters from Lillian’s control, had repaid the debt she owed Lena by slitting the throat of the woman who had orchestrated Elizabeth’s death.

     

                Struggling to comprehend what was happening, pale and panicked as she drew in shallow breaths, Lena didn’t move as she watched the fighting start. Sam had a sword in hand, and Purity and Pestilence - although they weren’t the Hunters Lena knew, and she didn’t know their real names - flanked her with their own weapons, engaging Lex’s Rogues with dangerous efficiency. And Lillian was on her knees, eyes wide, mouth opening and closing as she made a pitiful sound at the back of her throat.

     

                It surprised Lena how much pity she felt her her mother then. She hated her, of course, and had from the moment she’d met her, and Lillian deserved her death, if only as revenge for having Lena’s mother killed, but Lena was nothing if not merciful. It was what set her apart from the fae, both Seelie and Unseelie, and what had made it so difficult for her to adapt at the start. She didn’t have the stomach for death, didn’t like it, and she didn’t care if it made her weak to show compassion for the woman who’d kidnapped, threatened and sold her off to supposed enemies for her own gain; that was just who Lena was.

     

                “It’s alright,” Lena rasped in English, unable to find a truth to comfort Lillian as she dropped to her knees, reaching out to cover her mother’s hands with her own. “It’s alright, it’ll be okay, I’ll help you. Let me help you. You can’t die. Please. I don’t want to be Queen, you can’t die.”

     

                She couldn’t help but babble, tears of fear on her cheeks as her gloves were stained red, as the life drained out of Lillian, petals scattered around her and blood dripping down Lena’s breastplate as she died. It was a quick death, all things considered, her carotid artery cut, but it still felt agonisingly slow as she clawed at Lena’s surcoat, her blue eyes wide beneath severe eyebrows, drawn together in bewilderment as she choked on her own blood, lips stained red. 

     

                As she sagged, Lena lowered her to the floor, confused and helpless, Lillian’s eyes locked onto hers, and she watched in shock as she took her last breath. It was unexpected, it was gruesome and painful, and Lena was left reeling as she pulled her hands away from Lillian’s throat, staring down at them as they shook, feeling nauseous and dizzy. And the others were still slaughtering each other, although she couldn’t have said what was happening, her mind narrowed to the death of the Queen, and it wasn’t until someone grabbed a fistful of Lena’s surcoat and dragged her to her feet that she was slapped back to reality, struggling to free herself. But it was just Sam, bloody and frantic, her hazel eyes lucid and desperate.

     

                “Run,” Sam snarled as she pushed Lena away.

     

                Stumbling, shocked as her mother’s blood stained her gloves and armour as she trembled slightly, Lena stared at Sam with wide eyes set in her pale face, before she managed to get her feet to work. Without any further encouragement, Lena turned and ran as fast as she could, ran for her life, as the forest blurred past her. She ran and ran, and didn’t stop until she reached the river.

    Chapter 44

                Lena ran and ran until she reached the river. Only then did she stop, rather abruptly as she realised that there was no way she could cross it, her stomach sinking with dread as she stood on the sloping banks, dirt giving way to reeds as the river churned, dark and glistening as darkness encroached on the forest, pink-tinged wisps of cloud fading into the deepening blue above as the sunlight quickly waned. Drawing in quick, sharp breaths, Lena looked around with wild eyes, sweating in her armour, which was light , but would’ve weighed her down even if she did know how to swim. But Lena had been afraid of water for as long as she could remember, murky memories of a dank lake, soft silt underfoot as she struggled to swim up, up, up, her mother’s hands pushing her ahead, making sure she was safe before the Hunters caught up.  

     

                Now, standing as close to the edge as she could bear, Lena pressed her palm against the rough bark of a tree as she scrambled for a plan. There were bridges, she knew that much, but she didn’t know where, or how far away she was, or whether they were in the thick of the fighting. She had a sword and dagger with her, but that didn’t inspire much confidence in her when she thought about how she was in enemy territory and not nearly as adept at swordfighting as she’d need to be to fight her way across an occupied bridge. But she couldn’t stay there, had to keep moving, because she didn’t know how Sam would hold out against her brother’s band of Rogues, or whether her fellow Hunters would stand by her side. There were too many unknown factors for Lena to be able to plan accordingly, and she ran a hand over her braided hair, the stickiness of blood on her palm as she ghosted over where she’d been struck.

     

                Drawing in a shaky breath, which was more of a breathless, hitching sob, Lena fell back against the tree, thinking hard. The river was too wide for her to try and encourage the branches of trees on opposing banks to bridge the gap as she had with the gorge, and it was too deep for her to brave wading knee-deep through the strong current. There were no logs for her to drape herself across and paddle along on, and she wasn’t frightened enough to seize control of her power and form stepping stones from the riverbed - even that would’ve been a stretch for her to brave too, but she thought she could’ve managed it then, push come to shove.

     

                But Lena was smart, resourceful enough to make it through a difficult childhood, and through a difficult adulthood too, which only seemed to get worse the longer she spent in the Courts, but she wouldn’t go down without a fight. One thing about Lena was that she never gave up, even to the point of her own embarrassment, weaker than the others, unskilled and clumsy by their standards. But she would never know when to give up, not until she physically couldn’t, and even then, she’d still try . Drawing in a few quick breaths to steel herself, Lena pushed off the tree and ran south, towards the fighting.

     

                Following the riverbank, she ran as fast as she could, sweating as an ache formed in her chest, each breath sawing in and out, the last few traces of peach leaving the sky as darkness fully set in. She had to rely on her sharp vision to make out the detail of things, still able to see the deep colours of leaves, trunks and water, making far too much noise as she ran, unsure how far away she was, where the others were behind her. Her only thought was to head towards the fighting, towards Kara . 

     

                But one thing Lena didn’t factor in was her wife noticing she’d disappeared so soon. She thought in a few hours , perhaps, when the fighting had stopped and Kara couldn’t find her anywhere in the camp, when she saw Lena’s new helmet abandoned on the ground, and none of the Unseelie present. Of course, Lena had forgotten that Andrea wasn’t with them, that Andrea was wholly herself and had left the Unseelie Court, staying by Lena’s side of her own free will. Lena wasn’t to know that she’d watched the whole thing happen from the shadows of the forest and gone straight for Kara as soon as Lena had been carried off on horseback. Perhaps Andrea had ulterior motives in her love for Sam, wanting to see her safe, too, but it helped all the same. Yet, Lena didn’t know any of that was happening on the opposite bank of the river as she ran until exhaustion set in. 

     

                She must have run back to the river at a north-westerly angle, because it was further along the riverbank than she remembered going, although they had been on horseback. Still, she eventually heard the sounds of the battle on the wind, somewhat muffled but audible as she came to a stop. Leaning against a tree, she tried to catch her breath, wondering how close she should risk getting, if perhaps she should climb a tree now and wait it out. The river was still deep where she was, not quite the shallow ford where the fighting was occurring, but if she waited long enough, and everyone went to bed, she might be able to sneak across the river.

     

                As she was deliberating over what to do next, Lena caught a flash from the corner of her eye, something catching the moonlight on the other side of the river. Straightening, her body tense but hopeful, she stepped closer to the glimmering surface of the river, narrowing her eyes. Then she caught sight of it again, silvery and bright against the darkness of the forest, pausing and sinking low to the ground. And Lena would’ve known her anywhere, by the vaguest shadow of her figure, her heart leaping in her chest with weak relief as tears pricked her eyes, watching Kara check some tracks she was following.

     

                “Kara!”

     

                Her wife’s head jerked up, and she fluidly rose to her feet. While Lena couldn’t see her expression in the dark and from such a distance, she could sense her relief and her worry, lunging forward, stepping into the river, her voice carrying softer than Lena’s shout.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                Smiling, her shoulders slumping, her knees feeling so weak that she could’ve sunk to the riverbank right there, peace replacing her worry. But forty feet still separated them, and Lena wasn’t going to swim across it. Knowing that, moving with urgency, as if sensing that they weren’t actually safe yet, Kara fought against the natural current of the river, bringing a portion of it to a stop as a tall wall of water rose at her hand. It was like watching the sea part, except the river that had already passed her by continued to flow, filling in the gaps as it evened out the water level, leaving Kara shin-deep in river water, silt and algae, straining with the effort of holding back an entire river. 

     

                And Lena was too engrossed in watching her that she didn’t hear the sound of footsteps approaching from behind, didn’t hear the sound of a bowstring being drawn back, and only heard the sound of the arrow loosing when it was too late. Lena was still looking at Kara, watching her part the river so Lena could walk across, so she could walk to Lena, when the arrow hit. Fully armoured, there were few weak spots, but the archer aimed true and caught Kara just below the armpit, punching through steel mail and making her pause.

     

                The scream that tore out of Lena was unlike any sound she’d ever made, her hand clapping over her mouth as she staggered back, hitting the trunk behind as dread suffused her. She felt a sudden coldness steal over her, throat scraped raw as tears sprang to her eyes, and she watched as the wall of water wavered slightly, breaking momentarily before Kara stubbornly held it at bay. Fear seized Lena’s heart, squeezed tightly in her chest, and she lurched forward, her legs unable to bear her weight as she collapsed to her knees in the grass and mud, ripping up fistfuls as she frantically crawled forward, towards the murky edge of the river, watching as Kara lengthened the wall of water, ten feet stretched to twenty, to thirty, but not enough to span the entire width of the river. 

     

                Looking to her right, Lena watched as churning black water forced its way through the ten-foot gap that Kara hadn’t managed to keep at bay, the banks of the river starting to swell as her wife effectively built a dam. Kara seemed unphased by the arrow, having suffered worse and her mail taking the brunt of the force, but it was an injury all the same, and the next arrow made her falter as it took her in the side, in the gap where her chestplate met, punching through mail and the soft flesh above the waist as she let out a ragged sound of pain. That made Kara stop, and Lena could see the slow surprise as her wife looked down, her wall of water failing somewhat as it dipped, the level of the river rising to Kara’s knees as she staggered.

     

                Lena’s face was wet with tears, and she turned, anger making her face hard as her eyes scanned the trees, trying to find the archer. But they were slightly further downstream and deeper in the trees, and Lena couldn’t see them where they hid in the dark, although her hand went to her sheathed dagger, ready to slit their throat at the first sign of them. And the whole time, her voice was stolen from her, and she could do nothing but silently scream at Kara to go, to get out of the water, to run. Lena would be fine; she was going to die by Kara’s hand one day.

     

                But that wasn’t what her prophecy said. Not according to Lillian. Lena was going to die on the banks of a river, perhaps the one she stood beside now, perhaps a different one altogether. How was she to know? But when the third arrow glanced off Kara’s chestplate, skittering across steel and vanishing into darkness, and the fourth one took her in the thigh, below her tassets and above her greaves, when Kara buckled, sinking to her knees, the water lapping at her waist as she raised her head and stared straight ahead at her wife, Lena wasn’t thinking of herself. Watching as the full force of the river slammed down on Kara, Lena scrambled to the edge of the river, unaware of her breathless sobs, of the tears running down her cheeks, unaware of anything except the fact that the river had come down on Kara and Lena couldn’t see her in the churning froth of water as the river surged downstream uninterrupted.

     

                It was Kara , though, and Kara was a good swimmer. But she was hurt, and the pressure of that much water might’ve knocked her out cold, and if there was one thing that could make Lena get into a moving body of water, it was her wife’s safety, her wife’s life . She couldn’t even feel her terror properly, eclipsed by her desperation, the tight grip of urgency, and then she was in the water, up to her thighs, the current strong and quick as it tugged at her. Her body went numb from the searing cold of it, her limbs heavy as she waded forward, sobbing softly to herself as she submerged herself up to her waist, then deeper as she moved away from the bank. Her foot slipped, and she went under, the green taste of the river filling her mouth as she struggled to right herself, weighed down by her armour.

     

                She couldn’t swim, but Lena wouldn’t stop fighting, and as she fought, her fear turned into anger. Anger towards herself, for not being able to swim, for not being strong enough, her head going under and under, choking on water as she clawed at the river, anger at her mother for taking her across it in the first place, anger at her father for being one of the Earthfolk, making it impossible for her to command the river to stop. But in that anger and blind terror, she felt the riverbed beneath her, the earth and stone, and all of her frustration bubbled out of her as the surface of the river shuddered, as the riverbed split, everything shaking as sharp rocks jutted up through the water, turning it to white froth as it churned about them. Clinging to the first rock, cutting her fingertips as she held on tightly, Lena felt weak and limp as her strength was sapped away, without her even meaning to, on pure instinct alone as she created a stretch of rapids, changing the structure of the river in her desperate attempt to cross it and get to her wife.

     

                And there , Kara’s limp form splayed on a flat, jutting rock. Lena had to let go of the stone she clung to, letting the river wash her downstream before she smashed into another piece of rock, rattled around in her armour as she bruised and battered herself. There were more arrows too, aimed at her this time, one shallowly scoring the side of her neck, another punching through the mail of her bicep, not even felt as Lena kept moving. If she just kept moving, everything would be okay. If she could get to Kara, things would be fine. If she could get to Kara, if she could get her wife to safety, Lena would gladly bleed out on the riverbank, the right side of it, and die happy, filled with relief, with a sense of peace. But she would not die crossing the river, she would not die for Kara before she even reached her. 

     

                It was slower than she would’ve liked, but was all happening frighteningly fast, merely a handful of minutes since she’d spotted her wife tracking her on the opposite shore, and as she clambered over newly formed rocks, water heaving around her as the river turned furious, splashing over rapids that hadn’t existed until she’d stepped foot into it, Lena passed the halfway mark, then two-thirds. Then Kara was merely a few feet away from her, weakly swimming towards Lena, pierced with arrows and still fighting to save her. But this time, Lena would save her , from the water Kara had insisted she would never drown in. Weak and breathlessly pleading for strength, Kara paddled closer, until Lena had her arms around her, bearing her wife’s weight, the stronger of them now, and managed to stand. The ground sloped up there, ten feet to the riverbank, and Lena was up to her chest as she hauled Kara with her, still softly sobbing as she gritted her teeth and pulled, the water level dropping, until she was knee-deep in the weeds, dragging Kara up onto soft mud and clawing out after her.

     

                The sky above was a deep blue, still too early for most stars, and Lena drew in frantic breaths as she didn’t stop there, dragging Kara behind a bush and then dropping to her knees with a tearful cry. Lips parted, turning up at the corners in a listless smile, Kara’s lashes fluttered as she drew in a wheezing breath, a rasping laugh catching at the back of her throat. She raised a hand, smoothing her fingertips over Lena’s wet face, water running off them both and pooling beneath them as Lena quietly sobbed.

     

                “It’s okay, you’re okay,” she tearfully insisted, her hands nervously fluttering around her wife, taking in the scratched armour, dried blood in the filigree grooves of waves and scales, three arrows piercing the right side of her body, the fletching of one snapped off, another hanging by a few splinters.

     

                “You must … go, Lena,” Kara told her, her breath laboured, blood frothing out of her wounds like pink sea foam. “Leave me. Leave me … here, while there’s still- still … hope for you.”

     

                “Don’t say that. Don’t- don’t you say that. My place is with you; I’m not leaving you. You can’t make me leave. Please. ”

     

                Eyelids sliding closed, Kara smiled, her teeth stained red with blood as she made a sound at the back of her throat. “All will be well. Find Alex; she will … keep you safe.”

     

                “No,” Lena hoarsely objected, feeling cold all over again as her eyes ran over her wife’s body, the plated armour hiding the injuries beneath. She needed help, she needed healing. “It’ll be okay, do you hear me? Kelly … we’ll get Kelly to help. She’ll heal you.”

     

                Lena was already scrabbling at the closures of Kara’s armour, the buckles tricky with her shaking fingers, but she managed to undo the gorget and started working on the chestplate, two arrows sticking through the gaps as she tried to undo the straps. And the whole time, she breathlessly babbled, while Kara weakly shook her head, water slowly spilling out of her, which was actually her blood, seeping out around the arrowheads. And then there were footsteps, and Alex was there first, tearing through the trees, pulling up short as her face went deathly pale.

     

                She sank to her knees at Kara’s side with a small cry of grief, reaching out slowly to take her sister’s hand in her own, confusion and grief flitting across her face before it hardened into grim acceptance as her eyes glossed over with tears. There seemed to be some unspoken exchange between them, one that Lena was oblivious to as she fumbled with the buckles, trying to remove the armour as Kara softly tried to get her to stop.

     

                “Lena. My Lena. All will … be well. Let me … die here, near the- the water, under … the trees. I’ll go … happily, for you still … live.”

     

                “No,” Lena softly snarled, finally working the breastplate free, dragging it aside, Kara’s face spasming with pain as her thin breath caught in her chest. “No, you will not leave me. You can’t leave me, you- you can’t die. It’ll kill me.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara let out a strained laugh, choking on a sob as she tilted her head slightly, looking up at her wife with a wavering smile on her lips as tears leaked from the corners of her eyes. “So that is … my fate. After so- so much … effort to convince you that I did not … love you, I shall die in your arms, instead of you in mine. After all of it… you’re safe .”

     

                Kelly was there then, her dark eyes wide as her lips parted, and Lena wept freely as she knelt at Kara’s side, her fingers and gloves slick with blood where she tried to tamp down the arrow wounds. And Kara was crying freely then too, unable to hold back her tears as Lena sobbed over her, unsure what to do, how to fix her.

     

                “Don’t say that. Don’t say that. Don’t you dare leave me, not when I- not when I just got you. I love you, I love you . You can’t leave me, please. Kelly? Kelly, you have to- you have to help her, you have to-”

     

                And Kelly, who was quietly devastated, her face wrenched with grief, knelt beside Kara’s torso and inspected the wounds, if only to ease Lena’s desperate pleas as she sobbed over her wife. Giving her care over to her sister-in-law, Lena took Kara’s head in her hands and gently lifted it into her lap, crying as she wiped her bloody golden hair out of her face, wiping tears with wet, bloody fingers, leaning down to press her brow to Kara’s, wracked with so much agony that she could hardly feel anything else.

     

                “Hush,” Kara softly shushed her, blood on her lips now, her lung punctured, her face shockingly pale. “It is … no great thing … to die, not when I- I have known love. Forgive me … I did not mean to- to kill you in such a way.”

     

                “No, no, no,” Lena sobbed into Kara’s hair, kissing her over and over again, on her cheeks and brow, her hair and nose and eyelids, her lips and temples, as if in doing so, she could make her whole again, heal her wounds as if they’d never been there. “Don’t do this. Please. Please stay. You- you promised you’d never leave me. You promised. You don’t know h-how much it’ll kill me if you go.”

     

                Kara reached up to touch her hand to Lena’s cheek, her fingers cold and clumsy, her voice a breathless gasp as tears ran down her temples. “I’m sorry. I’m so … sorry.”

     

                Lena raised her head then, straightening up slightly as she looked down, staring at Kara’s face, watching as the taut look of pain softened into relief, a ghost of a smile on her lips as her blue eyes stared into Lena’s. And then her lashes fluttered and a soft, dreadful sigh slipped through her parted lips as her hand fell limply from Lena’s cheek. And then nothing. 

     

                It took Lena a long, terrible second, the length of a heartbeat that never came, to realise that she was dead. Her wife was dead in her lap, and she couldn’t quite comprehend it, taking in the peaceful look on Kara’s face as she knelt there, waiting for her to take a breath, to open her eyes. Lena loved her eyes, the colour of the sea on a clear day, a colour she would have happily drowned in, but they stayed closed, her chest still.

     

                There were sounds of raised voices then, on the other side of the river, of splashing water and the hiss of arrows, and Lena had barely comprehended what had happened before arms were around her, dragging her away. She was hauled to her feet, Kara’s head slipping from her lap, thumping softly to the leaf-strewn floor of the forest, and Lena was yelling, fighting, struggling, her eyes glued to her wife’s face as Kelly looked up, looked past Lena, her hands still pressed to Kara’s wounds. And Lena was dimly aware that it was Alex dragging her away, Alex she was fighting against, and she couldn’t understand why Alex was leaving her sister, why she was taking Lena away from her wife, ignoring Lena’s pleading sobs, ignoring her broken insults, her grip so tight around her that even when Lena clawed at her hands and cheeks, scratching at any skin, biting her fingers, feral and desperate, Alex still didn’t let her go. Because Alex had made a promise to her sister a long time ago that if anything ever happened to Kara, she would take Lena and go. And Lena didn’t know just how far she would be taken, even an inch from her wife too much to bear as she was rocked with the sudden blow of grief, so unexpected because it should’ve been her. 

     

                She fought the entire time, right up to the moment that Alex stepped into the deep shadows of a hawthorn tree and dragged her with her, through the shadows and out into a dingy park, the sounds of sirens, cars and a noisy city washing over them, the choking smell and taste of polluted air catching at the back of their throats as Alex wrestled Lena to the dirt, pinning her to the ground with a hand over Lena’s mouth, muffling her incoherent yelling as they both cried. Eventually, Lena finally passed out from sheer exhaustion, and as Alex finally slackened her grip on her, pushing herself up, removing her knee from Lena’s back, she heard the sound of her sister’s name fall from Lena’s lips in a soft, broken plea before she finally fell quiet.

    Chapter 45

                The light was all wrong when Lena came to, the taste of the air acrid, the smell catching at the back of her throat as her ears were assaulted by the noise. And it hit her immediately, no confusion, no moment of forgetfulness; Lena regained consciousness to the agonising pain of loss. Breath hitching, she tried to move, finding herself immobilised, but she could feel the bindings, was aware of her surroundings as she’d only ever been at her most emotional. But the intensity of her grief right then eclipsed any moments of fear, panic, or desire that had opened the gates to her powers in the past, so it was an easy thing for Lena to simply push away the roots that had ensnared her, called by the raw agony of losing her wife, holding her together as she’d cried herself to sleep.

     

                As the roots were pushed away, snaking back down into dry earth, Lena blinked against the grey light, breathing in the smell of the dusty ground, her cheek pressed against it as she lay there for a few moments, dazed. Blinking slowly, drawing in shallow, gasping breaths, she weakly pushed herself up, her armour rattling, and looked around. The ground was torn up and cracked, gaping fissures in the hard-packed dirt radiating from where she’d lain, the unearthed roots of the hawthorn trees circling them, trunks leaning precariously from the small crater she’d made amidst them.

     

                Sitting up, she felt weak and hollow, blood and dirt covering her, a stiffness to her joints as she blinked, swallowing thickly. Her throat was horribly dry, and she was trying to make sense of it all with a strange vacancy in the pit of her stomach, leaving her expression blank, as if she had no clue what had happened. But Lena remembered it all, every painful second of it, the memories seeming to drag on for an age, each moment shockingly clear in her mind, every minute act, from the sound of the first arrow punching through Kara’s mail, to the sound of her rattling breaths, to the feeling of her hot blood on Lena’s fingers. To the way it felt to claw at her sister-in-law’s cheeks, skin under her nails as she fought, feral and desperate to hold Kara’s body in her arms and die beside her on the river, as intended. But it was already a kind of death to have lost her, Lena’s chest feeling as if it had been split open, a physical blow that made her heart race, painful to breathe.

     

                Her eyes landed on Alex then, curled up in between two roots at the base of a hawthorn. She looked as if she hadn’t slept a wink, not in weeks , dark shadows beneath her eyes, her face hollowed with grief, brown eyes unseeing, and the parallel lines of Lena’s nails raking her bloody face. As Lena sat up, Alex looked at her, but neither of them spoke, the sound of passing cars, honking horns and sirens filling the silence, but Lena felt her anger slowly stoked to life, the agony in her chest as she let out a breathless gasp, bowing over as she clutched fistfuls of dirt in her gloved hands. Then she looked down at them, her fingers trembling, dried blood - Kara’s blood - staining the leather and her fingers, and Lena felt bile claw up her throat as a broken sob worked free.

     

                Lurching to her feet, unsteady and suddenly seized by a manic urge, Lena scrambled up the sloped sides of the shallow crater and threw herself towards a hawthorn tree, her fingertips scraping bark, before an arm was around her throat, dragging her away. And then the anger burned hot, tears blurring her eyes, and Lena fought against Alex’s tight grasp, softly snarling as she tried to haul them both towards the trees, desperate and determined. She was the same height as Alex, but she didn’t have the wiry strength of years of fighting, her body still soft and unused to handling the weight of weapons in long wars, so it was futile, but that didn’t stop Lena.

     

                Not until she was breathlessly sobbing, her body going slack to dead weight as Alex dragged her backwards and suddenly found Lena compromising. Overbalancing at the edge of the shallow crater, Alex staggered over the lip and took Lena down with her, the two of them landing in a heap of rattling armour, briefly winded as they blinked back stars. And then Lena was trying again, grasping at loose dirt, crawling on hands and knees, until hands grabbed her ankle and dragged her back down. Kicking out, Lena caught the edge of Alex’s jaw with her boot, hearing the muted grunt of pain but not caring, while Alex kept a tight grip on her ankle, clawing her way up Lena’s body, grabbing her surcoat and then her sword belt, until she got her arms around her, dodging Lena’s elbow aimed at her face.

     

                “Stop it,” Alex rasped, “stop it.”

     

                “Let go.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Alex wrestled with her, getting Lena onto her back, a knee pinned to her chest while her hands pinned her arms, while Lena looked up at her, feeling sick and dizzy, her chest quickly rising and falling. Her dark hair had come partially loose from her braid, and tears cut through the dust on her cheeks as she softly sobbed, feebly trying to resist, and Alex let go of her wrists to grab the front of her soiled surcoat, sharply shaking her, just once.

     

                “You can’t go back. I promised her I’d take you and leave if anything happened to her. Do you understand?”

     

                Lena weakly shook her head, her arms still splayed as her chin wobbled. After a moment, Alex climbed off her, raking a hand through her hair, wincing as she rolled her shoulder and then reached down to offer Lena a hand. Yanking her to her feet, Alex looked at her through a film of tears, her expression agonised as she mourned the loss of her sister as deeply as Lena did, perhaps even more so, because she’d known her for years, for so long that Lena would later be jealous of all the memories Alex had with her. Reaching up, Alex cupped Lena’s cheek in her hand, gentle and regretful as her bottom lip trembled.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                Lena batted her hand aside, anger flashing through her, and she slapped Alex, pushed her away as she advanced on her, breaking down as tears ran down her cheeks, her voice hoarse with anguish. “This is your fault. You took me away. Why did you bring me here? Take me back. Take me back to her. Please. I can help her, I can-”

     

                Cheek reddening, Alex looked guilty, looked ashamed as she cautiously approached Lena, reaching out for her like she was a rabid dog, ready to bite. She was crying too, but silently, none of the ragged sobs that Lena couldn’t swallow, none of the raw, gut-wrenching sounds of desperate confusion. Placing a hand on the pauldron covering Lena’s shoulder, Alex swallowed thickly.

     

                “She’s dead, Lena. There’s nothing you can do for her now.”

     

                Covering her face with her hands, Lena sank to her haunches as a pitiful whimper escaped her. “No, no, no. No, she can’t be. She can’t- she can’t leave me like this. Please.”

     

                She started to panic then, her breaths coming quick as dread set in, a cold feeling, the reality getting to her, and Lena clapped her hands over her mouth, her erratic pulse loud in her ears as the ground started to tremble. It intensified as she let her emotions run wild, pouring out of her and into the earth, and Alex had to grab her arm, shaking her as she dragged Lena to her feet.

     

                “Stop it. You can’t do that here; you’ll bring the city down. Stop.”

     

                Except, Lena didn’t know how to stop it, her haywire emotions making it uncontrollable in a way it had never been before. She’d intuitively wielded her powers before, even a big enough display to drag Krypton into the sea, but it had never been controllable in a way she could command it at her will. Except now, unable to stop the power from spilling out of her, agony fuelling it, breaking through that emotional block that had tied the two together, as she grabbed Alex’s wrist and felt the roots beneath the dirt as they snaked out of the ground, winding up her sister-in-law’s legs, creeping up her thighs as they lashed her in place.

     

                Looking down, Alex’s mouth opened and closed for a moment, and she struggled, trying to move her feet, but found them bound fast. She was still holding Lena’s arm, and gave her a warning look, but Lena was gripping her wrist too, and squeezed tightly as she drew back, until Alex was leaning forward, until she couldn’t go any further without risking a snapped femur. Forced to let go, Alex looked livid, her eyes still pitifully bloodshot but her expression hardening now, bristling at the fact that her charge, who had never been much of a threat, overpowered her.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “I have to go. You’ve upheld your promise to her, you took me from there, but I will not have my choice taken from me. I will not be taken from her, not by her will or anyone else's.”

     

                It might’ve been more bearable to have been taken from Kara’s side if Lena had made that decision herself, but then, she never would have left her there. Lena would have let herself be riddled with arrows as well before she left Kara behind, before she left her body to linger on the riverside until someone buried her. She was of the water, of the lake and rivers and seas, and she didn’t deserve to be buried in the damp earth, to become a tree. It felt like the most important thing in the world to her then that she might get back to her, take her to Krypton and send her off into the sea, to feed the fish and let her bones rest in the sand. She didn’t care if Alex came or not, or whether she would let her; Lena would go anyway.  

     

                Scampering up the crater again, quickly as she listened to Alex quietly curse, the smell of smoke, of burning wood, suddenly filling the air, a palpable pain radiating from the hawthorn trees as Lena’s stomach lurched, she turned. Alex’s hands were writhed in flames as she burned away the roots, and Lena blanched, flinching, as that reaction radiated through her and into the ground, watching as the roots recoiled, loosening. Killing the fire in her hands, Alex gave Lena an irate look as she freed her legs, and Lena’s eyes widened a fraction before she turned. Reaching out, Lena pressed her palms to the hawthorn, eyes shut, and willed it to let her through, with every fibre of her being, until she seemed to pitch forward.

     

                Stumbling into empty air, Lena was hit with the thick smell of the forest, dizzyingly sweet and fresh as she pitched straight towards the ground, grunting at the impact as she sprawled on the soft carpet of leaves. But there was no sound of running water, and as she pushed herself to her knees, Lena frowned, her head whipping around as she turned in frantic circles, not recognising her surroundings. It was the forest, most definitely, but it wasn’t anywhere close to the river dividing the Courts, no sounds of fighting drifting on the wind, no smell of blood or smoke. Nothing . 

     

                It was perfectly peaceful, and warm. It was warmer than it ought to be, early spring still carrying a chill to the air, frost in the mornings, and the wetness of dew in the deep shadow of the forest, yet it was warm. Too warm in the layers of Lena’s armour and clothes, breathing quickly, panic thrumming through her as she realised she had no clue where she was. She already knew very little about the layout of the forest, having seen no aerial maps to accurately show the entirety of it, and while she vaguely knew which direction and how many days the locations she’d been to were from each other, Lena hadn’t had to navigate the way herself. The best she’d managed was trekking through the forest after falling into the gorge, and that had only been possible because she’d known it would lead back to the coast, where she’d be able to find the Guardian, at least.

     

                Alone, somewhere in the forest, with no way of knowing how far she was from civilisation, no supplies to help, no clue which direction the sun was coming from, Lena let out a choked sound of helplessness. It was too much to bear then, and she collapsed to her knees, sobbing into her hands as the sound of droning bees and birds singing through the trees surrounded her. Her hands gripped fistfuls of leaves and haws, the little red fruit from hawthorn trees that fruited in the summer, when the hawthorns had held early spring white flowers when she’d left. Raising her handfuls of haws and leaves to her face, she cried her eyes out, that sickening realisation that she’d been gone a lot longer than the handful of hours she’d been unconscious for, making her chest ache even more. Lena felt delirious with the agony of it, and all the strength fled her then.

     

                Crying until she was too exhausted to continue, Lena slumped to the forest floor, balled up in the roots of the hawthorn tree she’d fallen through, and stared vacantly into the forest, wide trees growing impossibly tall, shafts of bright sunlight spilling through the high canopy, tinting everything in a yellowish-green hue. The warmth of summer was present in the flourishing plants that filled her vision, of bushes laden with berries as birds picked them, of bees pollinating wild lavender and bluebells, chamomile, sage and thyme, while squirrels and dormice scurried up trees to pick hazelnuts and walnuts. The whole forest was alive , and Lena’s grief poured out of her, helping it flourish even more, apples, pears and cherries ripening, wildflowers growing rampant, feeding off her, even as she fell unconscious, dizzy and desolate.

     

                She woke again but didn’t move, the forest dark and cold now, her knees drawn to her chest as she shivered. Glowing eyes occasionally cut through the black, but they were close to the ground, merely ordinary foxes, rabbits or badgers, and even if they hadn’t been, even if something came lumbering through the forest to tear her to shreds, Lena wouldn’t have moved an inch. Instead, she slept again, and slept and slept, and wished she could sleep forever. In between bouts of wakefulness, Lena caught glimpses of the forest, of the blue-green of early morning or dusk, the golden-tinted green just before sunset, the blackness of night and brightness of midday, never quite knowing which one it was, or how long she slept for, curled up with her cheek pressed to the dirt and leaves as the roots crept around her, the hawthorn tree seeming to accommodate her presence, almost protective, a little hovel at the base of its trunk sheltering her from the forest.

     

                Lena wasn’t sure how much time had passed when she heard the thud of something heavy thudding to the ground, jerking her awake, her eyelids fluttering, head rising slightly off the ground. Her body was stiff with disuse, having remained curled up in her armour for who knew how long, and she didn’t make any attempt to draw a weapon, to protect herself against whatever was out there. The sound of a few staggering footsteps on the slippery carpet of leaves, coupled with the quiet swearing of a familiar voice, made her relax, her quick pulse settling, even though she still didn’t move.

     

                Alex stumbled out of a deep shadow days after Lena with a peeved look on her face as she heard the sound of Lena’s heartbeat and tracked her down to the base of the hawthorn. Sinking to a crouch, bracing a hand against one of the thick, gnarled roots, Alex’s mouth was a flat line of annoyance as she looked down at Lena.

     

                “That,” she tightly muttered, “was very foolish.”

     

                Eyes closing, Lena exhaled softly. “Leave me alone.”

     

                “How long have you been here?”

     

                “I don’t know.”

     

                “I stepped through immediately after you did; how long has it been?”

     

                “It doesn’t matter,” Lena murmured, “it’s already summer.”

     

                Looking around the forest, Alex quietly cursed, hesitating before she pushed herself to her feet. She pressed a palm to the trunk of the hawthorn, looking up at the ripe haws, turning to take in the vivid greenery of the forest in full bloom, flowers, ivy, herbs and fruit in every direction, swearing again. Lena remained where she was, so devoid of any will to live, any motivation to pick herself up, and caught a flicker of movement as Alex started to climb the hawthorn, the squat trunk and spreading branches spanning a wide circle of the forest, ample hand and footholds for her to climb up high. Leaves and haws rained down, and Lena closed her eyes, ignoring her sister-in-law as she nursed the raw pain in her chest, trying to fall asleep again so she could see Kara sooner, so she could blot out the rest and pretend it hadn’t happened. 

     

                It was a few minutes before she heard the sound of rustling branches, Alex landing in front of her with a soft thud, bent knees and rattling armour, before she straightened and raked a hand through her hair.                 “I cannot see anything but trees. I would imagine we are somewhere south, away from the northern mountains, but I cannot ascertain where , and I’m unsure whether the sun is setting or rising.                 Lena didn’t respond, and Alex looked down at her with an unreadable look on her face, trying to put up a brave front, although there was a strained quality to her expression. Clearing her throat, hands planted on her waist, she grimaced at her sister-in-law’s limp form curled amongst the roots of the hawthorn tree.

     

                “Well, I’ll fetch some firewood; you start foraging for our dinner.”

     

                Unmoving, Lena closed her eyes, turning her face into the dirt more, as if trying to hide from Alex and the world. She didn’t care about a fire, she didn’t care about satiating the gnawing hunger in her stomach. Lena was content to stay exactly where she was and let the world pass her by, until she starved or was hunted down by something bigger than her. But Alex wasn’t.

     

                “Get up.”

     

                “Just … go. Leave me alone,” Lena murmured.

     

                She had a banging headache and felt dizzy and weak, dehydration making her limp and sluggish, her throat dry and hoarse, a pain in her arm where the arrow had pierced her mail and shallowly scored her skin. Lena didn’t even have the energy to fight with Alex, had spent all of it before she’d come through the tree and spent a couple of days curled up exactly where she was right then. Lena just wanted to sleep now, to blot out the rest, because at least if she was asleep, dreaming about Kara, she didn’t have to think about how it felt to hold and look at her dead body.                 After a few moments of silence, Alex walked away, and Lena felt relief sweep through her, eyes closing as her face furrowed against the dull pain radiating from the middle of her face, hoping to sleep now. Alex dropped to her knees at Lena’s side, and Lena’s heavy eyelids parted to find that the forest was darker; it was definitely sunset. Looming over her, Alex cupped Lena’s head and forcefully turned it, before she raised the rounded pauldron from her shoulder to Lena’s lips. Struggling, Lena felt the dull clink of metal against her teeth as cool water was forced through her lips, down her throat. Spluttering, choking on it, Lena pushed herself up onto her elbows, water spilling down her chin and dotting her filthy surcoat as she coughed, batting the pauldron away with a scowl on her face.

     

                Wiping her chin with a dirty hand, she coughed again, scowling as she tried to catch her breath. “What’re you doing?”

     

                “You have been here for days. You need to drink some water,” Alex pragmatically replied.

     

                “Oh, will you just fuck off?”

     

                “I promised her I’d look after you.”

     

                “I don’t care. I don’t care what you promised; you shouldn’t have taken me from her. I could’ve helped her.”

     

                “Her heart stopped, Lena.”

     

                “Barely. We could’ve- we could’ve brought her with us . We could’ve- there are hospitals. They could’ve made her better,” Lena pitifully argued, fresh tears spilling down her cheeks as she drew in a shuddering breath, growing angry then. “They could’ve saved her. It wasn’t- it wasn’t that bad. If you had real doctors here, she wouldn’t-”

     

                “Don’t do this to yourself,” Alex softly sighed. “Don’t go down this line of thought; it helps no one.”

     

                Thumbs pressing into her eyes as she let out a small sob, Lena shook her head. “You should’ve saved her first.”

     

                “Don’t you think I wish I had? I am trying to hold myself together to keep you safe for her, but I just lost my sister, Lena. I understand that you- … you lost your wife, but you didn’t even have a full turning of the seasons with her. I’m sorry for that, I am, but I have known her for years. We were children together, and I- I made a promise to her, and I had to leave my wife behind to hold it, and I was prepared to do that for years . That is what Kara wanted. She didn’t want to go to your world, to be subjected to your- your magic healers, away from the sea and the trees; that is not how she wanted to die. I did what my sister wanted.”

     

                Alex was crying then, quietly breaking down, sharp exhales masking the sobs she wouldn’t let escape her, soft gasps as the breath hitched in her throat, and Lena felt pity knife through her, but she felt angry too. 

     

                “I don’t care,” she murmured, wiping her cheek. “It was supposed to be me.”

     

                “No,” Alex whispered, ducking her head down as her chin wobbled. “No, it wasn’t. It never was. She understood that … at the end.”

     

                “I understood her, too; that she didn’t want to live after I passed.”

     

                Alex’s shoulders slumped, and she raised her head again just as Lena jerked her dagger free and stabbed it towards her own throat. Eyes flying wide, Alex was still quicker, still stronger, and she grabbed Lena’s arm, driving the dagger aside as she softly snarled, bending Lena’s wrist until it was painful, until she had to let go. Letting out a gasp of pain, Lena loosened her grasp and let Alex yank it from her hand, shoving her back against the gnarled root with a scathing sound.

     

                “Don’t,” Alex sharply warned her.

     

                Lena nicked herself, though, a stinging at her throat as she reached up to touch the slow-bleeding wound, too dehydrated for more than a sluggish few drops to squeeze out. Scowling, her cheeks flaming, Lena kicked Alex’s foot as her sister-in-law dragged Lena’s sword from its scabbard for good measure, unwilling to take any chances. A breathless sob escaped Lena, and she grabbed a fistful of her surcoat to wipe her face, her cheeks blotchy and dirty, eyes red raw, the grief so fresh, as if minutes had passed, still not comprehended as real because she’d spent most of the days since asleep.

     

                More tears welled up, and Lena drew in a deep, shuddering breath, exhaling sharply as she sagged where she sat, slumped with agony. “I left her. I left her, and now … I can’t even bury her properly. It’s too late.”

     

                “It’s alright. Calm yourself.”

     

                But it wasn’t alright, and Lena could feel the frayed edges of her composure unravelling again, the suffocating weight of the loss unbearable. “No, no, I- it should’ve been me. It would’ve been okay if it were me. ”
