                “No, it wouldn’t have,” Alex gently interrupted her rambling cries. “But … it doesn’t have to be in vain. My sister … my sister died happy knowing you were alive, safe. All she wanted, her whole life, was peace. You can still fight for that, you can still help … make her wish come true. It was supposed to be the two of you, but you can do it, you’re still the Unseelie Princess, so you can plead my sister’s cause to your mother and-”

     

                Lena flinched, the shocking reminder that her mother was dead cutting through the fog of grief. She’d forgotten, amidst so much pain, so much having happened so suddenly, and she floundered for a moment, eyes wide and tearful as she numbly shook her head.

     

                “No, no, my mother’s dead.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Sam,” Lena rasped, running a trembling hand over her face. “Sam cut her throat, I- she died in my arms, right before-”

     

                Her throat closed up, cutting her off, and Lena hung her head. Swallowing thickly, she opened her mouth, lips trembling, and sniffed, clearing her throat as she tried to forge ahead.

     

                “She was going to kill me. For my brother. Then … she was going to cross him. At some point. Take both Courts for herself, unify them under her control. She made Reign- but Sam broke through. She made me run. I-”

     

                Falling silent, her face grey beneath the blood and dirt, Lena tipped her head back, eyes closed as pain spasmed across her face. Better to have had her throat slit by Reign, bled out across the river, than to have had to watch Kara fall to arrows on the opposite bank. That had been more frightening than water ever had, because Lena had only ever feared water because of the loss of a loved one, and she’d thought this time, she’d get there in time if she braved the current. Alex stared at her in stunned silence, too, for a moment, her jaw slack as she took a moment to absorb that news.

     

                “Then you’re-”

     

                “No,” Lena firmly cut her off.

     

                “Yes. Yes, you are . Your brother isn’t fit to be King, has turned his back on the Courts, has forsaken the natural order of things, so he will not be accepted. That makes you Queen.”

     

                Mouth set in a hard line, contempt filling her at the idea of the thing she’d never wanted, the thing she’d scorned since she’d arrived, no Princess and certainly no Queen, Lena didn’t respond. Yet, it was true. There was nothing she could do to change that fact, just as there was nothing she could do to change the fact that her wife was dead. They’d had an hour, at most, with the knowledge that they’d loved each other. A mere hour. The pain of that knowledge cut cleanly through her chest, a bleak feeling filling her, and Lena knew that Alex was right; Lena couldn’t let Kara’s death be in vain.

     

                Sitting in silence for a few minutes, the evening growing darker, although it must have already been late, deep into the throes of summer, Lena eventually pushed herself to her feet. Wiping her face on her sleeve, Lena set off without a word, and Alex scurried to her feet, taking a few steps after her, wary and concerned, but stopped when Lena sank to a crouch at a nearby strawberry plant. The size of them had nearly doubled as everything within the nearby vicinity had fed on her power, sapping what strength she had, and Lena bundled them into her bunched-up surcoat before moving onto another plant. Her shield ended up bearing everything she foraged for, the leather strap worked over her head and carried like a platter as she found mushrooms, unable to identify them in the gloom, climbed the apple, pear and cherry trees she’d spied, stole a few eggs from high up nests too, and then snared a rabbit with a root as it had hopped along, nibbling at walnuts that had dropped from the tree she was foraging at. 

     

                There were a few herbs as well, and some root vegetables, enough for two to satiate their hunger for the night, and for breakfast too, and she carried her shield back to the divot amidst the roots, where Alex had piled some firewood. Her sister-in-law was nowhere to be found, Lena’s sword and dagger taken with her, so Lena sat down and hugged her knees to her chest as the forest grew dark and cold, until Alex returned ten minutes later, two pauldrons filled with water now as she tried not to spill any. She set them down safely out of the way, surveying what Lena had foraged as she reached for the firewood, and soon had a small fire burning. It wasn’t very big, and she lit it close to the sloping basin amidst the roots, hoping to hide it from prying eyes, so that they might go unnoticed within the forest. But Lena had lain there for a couple of days at least, and nothing had disturbed her there, her grief seeming to satiate the trees, at least, encouraging little creatures to come closer, to feast on the flourishing plants.

     

                Still, they were small, infinitesimal things to the vastness of the forest, and Lena felt daunted by the towering trees as the two of them huddled around the fire. Alex skinned and gutted the rabbit, shoving herbs inside it and skewering it to make a spit. The smell of cooking meat filled the air, and they picked at the fruit and nuts, Alex squinting at the mushrooms, bruising them and deciding they were fine. It was silent for a time, and Lena warmed her hands as she stared into the flames, occasionally taking a sip of water, until the pauldron was empty, her headache somewhat alleviated. Splitting the rabbit, Alex gave Lena her portion, and she wolfed that down too, her fingers covered in grease as she thought deeply, going through the motions with a drawn look on her face. Alex made her drink the rest of her water too, before she banked the fire down to embers and told Lena to get some rest.

     

                Curling up amidst the roots, much like she had since she’d come back through to the forest, Lena closed her eyes and tried to fall asleep, until she finally did. She woke sweating and crying out into the darkness at some point, the darkness completely enveloping her, the embers of the fire cold, and Lena was quickly silenced by a hand clamped over her mouth, stifling the noise, Alex softly hissing. Swallowing the rest of her shout, Lena let out a breathless sob, her cheeks wet again, and she heard the rasp of metal as Alex crouched beside her, little more than a shadow, waiting, listening intently. 

     

                It was then that Lena realised the forest was completely quiet. Just like that time it had been when Kara warned her against whistling to it, that eerie feeling of nothing moving, not even the wind, all of the hairs on Lena’s body standing on end. She remembered the fae who’d been snagged on their way to the river, his body hanging amidst the thorns that had pierced his body, feeding the forest, and her pulse spiked at the thought of either of them being ripped apart like that, some malevolent force within the forest killing them, while they couldn’t fight it.

     

                As if reading her mind, the wind suddenly started to howl through the trees, which groaned and swayed, an eerie rustling that sounded as if they were talking, and Lena felt her stomach lurch with dread. But she could feel it, the anger, the pain, her own feelings so raw and exposed that it seemed like a lightning rod for the forest to feed off of, and she could feel it too, a shock to her system as she recognised the familiarity of it. It felt the same as she did, a deep sense of grief, and Lena closed her eyes as she pressed her palm to one of the thick hawthorn roots, her body slumping with weary understanding as she pressed her cheek to it as well.

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena whispered, an ache in her chest as she felt what it felt, felt the grief, the rage, and felt it take hers too. “It’s okay. Hush now. I won’t hurt you.”

     

                “What are you doing?” Alex quietly hissed, her eyes wide with panic as the forest raged, the wind intensifying, buffeting the branches overhead, the patter of fruit, nuts, and budding flowers raining to the floor, adding to the maelstrom.

     

                Tenderly stroking her fingers over the root, Lena let out a forceful breath, not feeling the tears on the cheeks, but so deeply entrenched in her misery that she felt a kindred spirit in her surroundings, her wide open emotions making it so easy for her to feel everything around her, as if the forest was an extension of herself. It was dizzying, disorienting, and Lena gave herself to it, the forest quietening, dimming, coaxed back to sleep as it fed off of what she so readily gave, trees straightening, plants flourishing, flowers blooming in the dark. 

     

                “What are you doing?” Alex repeated, not so panicked now, but bewildered and a little frightened.

     

                Lena was already slipping into unconsciousness, though, too much of her energy sapped as she soothed the forest, not even sure what she was doing, just feeding into the familiar feelings that had radiated from around her. She passed out with her hand and cheek still pressed to the root, her body going limp as a weary sigh slipped past her lips, and didn’t wake up again until it was broad daylight, perhaps a little later than was ideal, already midmorning, a portion of the day wasted as she slept and slept, much as she had for days. And yet, Lena was still so tired.

     

                Alex was sitting on one of the roots when Lena woke, eyelashes fluttering against the sunlight as she pushed herself up, and she glanced over at her. Running a hand over her face, a headache pulsing at her temples, Lena cleared her dry throat, looking around. Everything was greener, fuller, and she frowned as she took in the abundance of life surrounding them, butterflies and bees dawdling past, shafts of sunlight highlighting the intoxicating amount of pollen in the air, each breath drawing in more of the forest, binding them to it.

     

                “What did you do?” Alex asked after a long minute.

     

                Looking at her, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction, confused. “What do you mean?”

     

                “What did you do? Last night. We- the forest went silent . That’s never a good sign.”

     

                “I know.”

     

                “So, how did you stop it?”

     

                Face creasing with confusion, Lena tilted her head to the side. “I didn’t.”

     

                “Yes, you did.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, seeming disturbed now as she tried to think, Lena shrugged. She didn’t have a good enough answer to know what she’d done, if she’d even done anything. “I don’t know,” she mumbled, “I just- I could feel it. It was in pain, it was angry. It felt like …”

     

                “It felt the same way you do,” Alex sighed, a flicker of sorrow passing her face.

     

                The breath caught in Lena’s chest, and she painfully swallowed, looking down. She felt too tired to cry any more, but she didn’t understand how Alex was keeping it together so well, but then one look at her showed the shadows beneath her eyes, the taut look of grief on her face, and Lena realised she was just repressing it all. Focusing on keeping them alive, safe and healthy, Alex didn’t seem to have time to think about anything else, two pheasants at her feet, half-plucked already, and the pauldrons refilled with more water as the small fire burned.

     

                Lena took a sip and then went to gather a few handfuls of anything edible that had grown wild in the night, coming back with a different variety of mushrooms, Alex tossing out two poisonous ones, and some carrots and mint. There was still enough fruit on her shield to see them through breakfast, as well as the uneaten eggs, Lena sceptically watching Alex break a hole into the top of one and swallow it raw before she followed suit, understanding it was more important to eat than to worry about what one was eating. 

     

                Alex had both pheasants roasting, their organs frying on a relatively flat stone she’d found, and was cracking walnut shells open when she cleared her throat. “I’ve ascertained the direction of the sunrise. If we head north-east, we shall reach the river near where we left off. Depending on how much time has passed … well, we can always find our way to my mother’s halls if need be.”

     

                Stomach sinking with that reminder that it was summer, that they had left in spring and returned hours later from the human world, with no clue how much time had passed here. Lena hoped it had only been a couple of months, merely at the start of summer - they wouldn’t have lost too much time then. But what did it matter anyway? There was no one waiting for her. The least she could do was get Alex back to Kelly, though, hoping it hadn’t been years for Kelly, hoping that the fighting hadn’t taken her too. Then, Lena would be able to walk off into the forest and keep going until she succumbed. To what, she wasn’t quite sure; she’d even gladly drown herself now, give her body to the fishes, where her wife hadn’t been afforded that right.

     

                Lena sipped some more water and picked at the food, not saying anything as Alex wrapped the untouched pheasants in large leaves, split the cooked organs between herself and Lena, who ate them with little relish but did force them down, and then clenched her fist to quench the fire. They had little supplies, save weapons and their small amount of food now, and they both drank the water in Alex’s pauldrons, hydrating at least a little before they set off. 

     

                Following after her, her shield strapped to her back, but her weapons still in Alex’s possession, Lena didn’t feel that she had much say in the matter. If she’d kicked up a fuss and tried to remain, she imagined Alex would simply fashion some rope out of vines and drag Lena behind her if she had to. Having spent her entire life there, venturing through the forest, through all manner of danger beyond war, Alex set off with confidence, her tread so light that her footsteps were silent, and Lena was left to tail her with less grace, not quite able to walk with the same quietness, although she had gotten better, placing her footsteps with care.

     

                They covered a few miles, stopping at a thin stream of water, barely more than a moving trickle but clear and cold as they drank deeply, before continuing onwards. Her boots were still somewhat damp, despite the days since she’d crossed the river, and Lena’s feet started to blister, each step pinching and painful, but she didn’t complain, the pain nothing to the invisible one inside her. Putting one foot in front of the other, Lena kept walking, as if in a daze, unable to really think about anything, all of it blotted out by the all-consuming weight of her grief, bleeding out of her as the forest took and took, until flowers were blooming in her wake, everything vibrant with life, the whole forest seeming to sigh with contentment as she stumbled onwards.

     

                Giving so much of herself, though, Lena was exhausted. It sapped her strength without her even meaning to let it, no control over the wide-open floodgates that had been so tightly locked before. Usually, Lena’s bursts of emotions were short-lived, bouts of anger, or fear, or any emotion that elicited a strong enough reaction, before it guttered seconds or minutes later. But this, her grief, was constant.

     

                By the time dusk started to fall, they’d traversed miles of the forest, yet their surroundings hadn’t changed much. Lena could barely stay standing, swaying unsteadily as she staggered up a sloping incline. Before she could crest the top of it, her vision swimming as everything pitched, she dropped to her knees, clammy and exhausted, slipping down a little, leaves scattering as she curled in on herself, her fingers shaking, head aching. Leaves rustled as Alex backtracked, gently picking Lena up, setting her back on unsteady legs and dragging her arm around her shoulder.

     

                “Come on,” Alex murmured, “we can go a little further yet.”

     

                Bearing some of her weight, Alex led Lena onwards, until it was almost too dark to see, that hour after sunset when the forest was a deep navy. They could make out little more than shadows, and Lena knew it was late, only a couple of hours off midnight, and she was eager to rest when Alex brought them to a stop. Sinking heavily to the floor, Lena found herself hidden behind some overgrown bushes, her back to a packed dirt wall, roots of the elm tree above visible through the earth. It provided them with a little bit of shelter, the bushes pressing them in close, the space narrow and not particularly long, and Alex flopped down beside her.

     

                She didn’t start a fire that night, not enough room for one, but she turned her left hand palm up and conjured a ball of heat, casting an orange glow over them as she unwrapped the parcel of leaves with her right hand. They split one of the pheasants between them, in between bites of raw carrots and the handful of hazelnuts and cherries leftover. Then, dizzy and weak, a shakiness inside her, Lena leaned back against the wall of dirt behind her, her eyelids sliding shut, her misery coming back to remind her of what she’d lost - as if she could forget.

     

                “You need to stop doing that.”

     

                Lena opened her eyes as Alex quietly spoke, her voice hoarse with tiredness. Looking at her sister-in-law, Lena followed her line of sight to the bushes. In the handful of flames Alex held, Lena could see that the row of green bushes was heavily burdened with ripe blackcurrants, the little berries growing in size as they watched, growing in number as little budding ones fruited. Then, Lena realised it was coming from her , that more of her strength was being fed to the forest, making her tired.

     

                “I don’t know how,” she whispered.

     

                “You give too much of your strength. Too much life to the forest. You must stop, or else you’ll not have the strength for what comes next.”

     

                “What comes next?”

     

                “Peace. Won by the throne-”

     

                “No. No, I already told you-”

     

                “Then you will let us continue to slaughter each other?”

     

                “She never believed I could be Queen, okay? She knew it then, and I know it now. They’ll make sure I don’t last a day -”

     

                “I will help you.”

     

                “It’ll be pointless.”

     

                “Then, what is it you wish? If it is not peace, then you are content to let us kill each other to the last man? That is not what she wanted.”

     

                “No,” Lena softly agreed.

     

                “So, what is it you want?”

     

                Anger grew in her chest, and Lena swallowed thickly, her face spasming with her agony. She kept thinking about the arrows, punching into Kara as she tried to get to Lena, the blood on her lips, the blood spilling out of her, welling up and then turning to water as it dripped off her, her teeth painted red as she smiled through the pain, her voice weak but relieved. None of it would’ve happened if not for Lex. To a certain extent, Lillian, too, but she was already dead, and even though Lena had panicked at the time, she was glad she’d already paid for what she’d done. But Lex was still alive, and that burning anger made Lena’s vision dim, her rage so cold that she couldn’t speak past the lump in her throat for a long minute.

     

                “Revenge,” she eventually whispered, realising her eyes were wet and burning.

     

                Alex stared at her for a moment, considering her words, and then nodded. “Then I will help you get it.”

     

                Looking at her, surprised by her acceptance, expecting the honourable objection that she might’ve gotten from Kara, had she suggested the same, Lena blinked. Swallowing thickly, Alex curled her fingers in, extinguishing the flame in her palm and plunging them into darkness, before she softly sighed, shifting from her crouched position.

     

                “Get some sleep.”

     

                It took Lena a moment to make herself move, already so spent, but she shifted onto her side and drew her legs up, curled into a ball with the bushes blotting out the gentle breeze. The night was cool without a fire, but they managed just fine, neither of them up to the task of taking watch, and the forest seemed harmless, satiated by Lena’s constant tithe of energy, although neither of them knew what to make of that. Too tired to even fear anything bad happening in the night, Lena was asleep in moments, sinking into it with relief as she hoped for dreams of Kara. 

     

                Shaken awake early, Lena felt more rested, if not quite strong. They ate as many blackcurrants as possible, their lips and fingertips stained purple, and they had to go without water, hoping to find some as they walked. They still had one pheasant left, though, so dinner would be sorted, at least, although that didn’t seem a pressing matter in Lena’s mind. Continuing their trek through the forest, Lena’s energy waned throughout the day, even with the foraging they did along the way, the abundance of wild food theirs for the taking giving them energy, the fresh streams or brooks whetting their thirst, but it was either keep walking or sit down and refuse to get back up. Even thoughts of revenge didn’t motivate her; there was merely nothing better to do than follow Alex, and she didn’t think she had much say in the matter.

     

                Days passed by, so much of the forest traversed, and Lena wished for something to drink, something hard, something numbing. The most they managed was water, following a wandering river for the last four days now, a source of water and occasionally food, Alex not so adept at fishing as her sister had been. They spoke very little, Alex growing exasperated by the wake of life Lena left behind them, her strength waning by each afternoon, until she couldn’t stand, until the weight dropped off her, grief hollowing out her face, her armour clattering as she stumbled about. They were both filthy and exhausted, and Lena willed something to come and eat them, or for her brother to find them. But they saw no one, and when a large bear stumbled upon them, it seemed more curious than anything, snuffling in their direction, lumbering towards them as moss and mushrooms and ivy grew over it, the strangeness of the beasts in the forest now seeming so ordinary, anger that had taken root inside innocent animals and made them grow big and furious, now soothed by the kindred feeling radiating from Lena.

     

                It walked off, its curiosity satisfied, and Alex, sweating as she panted, weapons in hand, glanced at Lena with a perturbed furrow on her face. She didn’t know how, but she knew this strangeness could be attributed to Lena, the same way the temper of the forest had been mollified. Neither of them had any way to explain what was happening, except that Lena, who had never been able to direct her power at will, now seemed to feel the forest on a deeper level than was normal, all the pain in her heart bared, the forest calling to her, as if she was one of its creatures. They didn’t have the time then to acknowledge what was happening, that she was dangerously close to giving too much of herself, that the power could burn right through her, taking every scrap of energy and leaving her heart to give out, not enough strength in her body to keep it beating. 

     

                But she went on, two weeks passing by, both of them filthy but obstinate, walking onwards, Lena’s feet bleeding and blistered, unused to so much walking, especially in full armour, and Alex very sure of herself, even though Lena caught flickers of doubt in her eyes. They hadn’t seen any mountains yet, heading north-easterly, and there was no sign of the river either. When they found old ruins one evening, making an early camp, even indulging in the luxury of a fire for the brown trout Alex had caught with her bare hands, Lena ventured the question that had been nagging at the back of her mind for days now.

     

                “You don’t know where we are, do you? You’ve never seen these ruins before. You’ve never been to this place.”

     

                She’d watched Alex poke around upon their arrival, finding nothing but large spiderwebs spanning the crumbling ruins, making Lena shiver as she thought about the size of the spiders that had spun them. Her sister-in-law hadn’t said a word, but Lena had caught the doubtful edge to her face, the worry in her brown eyes as her handful of flames had illuminated her hard features.

     

                Even now, Alex looked a little uneasy, leaning back against moss-covered stones, the smell of the fish cooking filling the ruins as the firewood snapped and crackled, a faint trail of smoke rising skywards. She didn’t look at Lena for a long moment, her mouth a flat line, but then she met her gaze and let out a soft sigh.

     

                “No, I do not. No, I have not.”

     

                “What does that mean?”

     

                “It means … either I am not so well-travelled as I’d thought, which I find hard to believe, for the forest is wild and vast, but I am certain I have explored all of the Seelie Court in my years, or …”

     

                “Or, this isn’t the Seelie Court,” Lena finished for her.

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Alex stiffly nodded. Shifting, she used a stick to turn the fish, one side of it charring in the flames. “There is only one way to be sure. We continue east; either we reach the river, or we reach the sea.”

     

                “What happens if it’s the sea?”

     

                “Then we backtrack. There must be dwellings; we will find our way back to the seat of the royals and instate you as Queen. I am certain that even Unseelie have morals and will aid us in returning you to your family’s home.”

     

                “And what if they try to slit my throat instead? You forget that my brother lived in these wild parts for years , undetected. He very likely has allies in these parts.”

     

                “Well, I shall slit their throats first.”

     

                Letting out a quiet huff of laughter, Lena smiled faintly. It was the first time she’d laughed in weeks, and it brought stinging tears to her eyes, the sound dying in her throat. Sensing the shift in her mood, Alex didn’t say anything else, just checked the fish and let Lena dwell on her grief. Almost three weeks had passed since she’d come back through the trees, and it still didn’t make a bit of sense to her. Kara couldn’t be gone. Kara had come into her life in such a traumatic way and had stayed throughout the better part of a year, irritating her, lecturing her, protecting her, befriending her, loving her. They hadn’t had enough time. They hadn’t even had a year. Not even a full hour to love each other honestly. 

     

                Lillian had ripped apart Lena’s life three times now; the first when she’d hunted down Elizabeth, letting Lena slip away, and then again when she’d arranged a marriage and dragged Lena back, only to do it again, her final act resulting in the death of Lena’s wife. And that was the worst one, because Lena’s life had been bland, monotonous, lonely, until she’d met Kara, until she’d come back and stayed, the forest in her lungs, in her blood, like some sort of drug calling her home. And now, it felt as if she’d been split in half, and nothing could stitch her back together, the pain of that loss still so fresh, so raw, and all because her mother had double-crossed them, had dogwalked Lena straight into a trap she’d been warned against, too trusting of the Hunters who’d shown their loyalties time and time again, leading them straight back to the border, where the pull of Lillian’s control had only grown stronger. Really, it was her own fault; she should have agreed with Alex and let her take Lillian’s head, no matter Kara’s objection to the act. 

     

                It was too late for that now, but she’d have her revenge. Not against Lillian - a slit throat would have to do, and it was a small comfort at that - but she would hunt Lex through the forest, let any number of people die, until she found her brother and made him pay. It didn’t matter that the arrows hadn’t come from his hand, that he hadn’t nocked the arrow and pulled back the bowstring. All of this was a result of his actions, of his power-hungry attempt to seize power for himself, at the cost of anyone who stood in his way, including his own family. And Lena didn’t care one bit about what names she’d be branded with for killing her own brother; she would have her revenge. She wasn’t sadistic, knew she wouldn’t have it in her to make him suffer, no torture or drawn-out death as punishment for these weeks of agony she’d been subjected to, but his simple death would suffice.

     

                First, she needed a crown and a throne, though, which she chafed at the idea of. She knew Alex was right, though, knew it was the quickest way for Lena to get what she wanted, to amass an army to go after Lex, to bring him to her. She didn’t think of any long-term ramifications of that, didn’t think of how to keep her throne once she’d attained it, or what they would do to her after ending her brother’s life, branded a kinslayer and deposed. Lena didn’t care what happened then, would kill herself quickly, if it meant she’d be buried beside her wife, their bones feeding the trees planted over them. But that would have to wait until her revenge had been fulfilled.

     

                It took them a couple more days of walking before they got their first whiff of salt air. They must have walked through the wildest, most remote parts of the Unseelie Court, uninhabited as far as they’d noticed, until they finally reached the eastern coast of the forest at sunset, three weeks after setting out. Lena felt bitterness fill her, frustration mingling with the disappointment of realising they’d gone the wrong way, that she’d brought herself through to the wrong Court. And Alex had been seeking her out, had come through after her days later, not knowing that Lena’s grief-stricken thoughts hadn’t been able to hone in on the place they’d left from. 

     

                A few more miles, and they reached the edge of their world, the forest abruptly ending as the trees fell away to sheer slate cliffs, glittering waves stretching away as far as Lena could see. It was heart-wrenching, the sight of the swell, the smell of the brine, the loud crash of the waves. All Lena could think of was how Kara would love it, that her wife would’ve leapt off the edge of the cliff, the fifty-foot drop exhilarating before the waves cushioned her fall. Instead, Lena stayed five feet back, feeling the grasping wind trying to blow her off the edge, pine needles shifting underfoot as she pressed up against a trunk.

     

                “Shit. We really are in the Unseelie Court,” Alex swore, shading her eyes as she stared out at the blinding brightness of the writhing sea.

     

                It was strange to see the open sky, a few wisps of clouds trailing along, but so much blue. The smell of pine and salt mingled, fresh and invigorating, but Lena only felt sick. Her grief was a hard pressure in her chest, and she drew in a few shallow breaths as she tried to quell the urge to cry, to break down. Slowly sinking down the trunk of the tree, the wind in her face, the balmy day cooled by the coast, Lena let out a hitching breath.

     

                “What do we do now?”

     

                “We follow the coast until we find people.”

     

                “What if there aren’t any?”

     

                “There will be. Most must have been called to the river, to fight. But there will be dwellings. There are always children and the elderly, the injured, and the coast provides well.”

     

                With little more to say on the matter, Alex started leading them north, following the cliffs. They walked for two days, struggling for water, feeling the effects of dehydration by noon on the third day, their heads hurting, their limbs heavy as they slowly plodded along, following the rugged coastline. The sound of a shout finally caught their attention, and Alex eagerly stepped up to the edge of the slate cliffs, letting out a ragged sound of relief as she saw the curve of a brown beach along the base of the cliffs below, following the coastline for at least a mile. A woman was using the waves to push a small skiff onto the beach, while a fisherman on board of the little wooden boat braced themselves against the narrow mast as they held the rudder fast, a small triangular sail hoisted and angled so it didn’t catch the wind, similar skiffs already beached, which other fae worked on the hulls.

     

                Eyeing the sloping cliff face, Alex saw the treacherous path etched into the side of it, two hundred yards away, patchy grass and moss in the grooves of the slate. The cliffs were only thirty feet high there, small outcroppings jutting into the sea, creating narrow gullies into the small bay, and as Lena braved taking a daring look, she saw there were a few dark mouths burrowing into the cliffs, seeming like natural gaps in the layers of slate. Getting a second wind of energy, Alex led them onwards, to that narrow path, tiny pieces of slate skittering free as she hurried down, sure-footed and quick, while Lena kept squeezing her eyes shut, her fingertips scrabbling at the slate, until the skin was rubbed raw, each step making her stomach lurch as vertigo hit her. The switchbacks and uneven footing made it worse, but she managed to make her way down to the beach, the brown sand studded with smooth pebbles that far up the shore, and she stumbled after Alex, weak-kneed with relief.

     

                That relief was relatively short-lived, though, Alex calling out as she waved a hand to get the attention of the man and woman. Others were drawn by the sound of her shouts, a few children sitting high up on the outcropping of rocks as they played, climbing after each other, a few of the elderly fishing from lower down with nets or rods, while more ducked out of the cliffs, through the dark mouths of deeper caves that Lena had spied. And it didn’t take long for them to assess that the two women who’d stumbled onto their beach weren’t Unseelie, long knives, tridents and axes hefted as the beach grew tense, eyes flitting around, as if expecting more, as if expecting an army.

     

                “Unless my eyes deceive me, that is Seelie armour,” a woman called out, jerking her chin towards them both as she gripped the handle of her axe. “And you are trespassing a long way from home.”

     

                “Halt!” Alex called out, one hand on the pommel of Lena’s sword, still at her waist, the other hand raised in defence. “We bear you no ill will; we have returned from the human realm and have been led astray. We require assistance-”

     

                A man spat into the sand, a derisive look on his face as he twirled his long knife in his fingers. “We’re happy to oblige with a quick gutting. A Seelie isn’t worth more than that.”

     

                “The Queen,” Lena croaked, trying to clear the dryness in her throat, her eyelids shuttering as she staggered forward, brushing past Alex. “The Queen’s dead.”

     

                “We know,” the woman flatly replied. “We may be so far from the river, but word still reaches the eastern shores.”

     

                “How long has it been?”

     

                “Near-on half a turning of the seasons, now. We are at the tail-end of summer.”

     

                Half a year. Lena’s stomach dropped. Would Kara’s body be no more than bones now? Had the forest stripped her of her lithe muscle, her tanned skin with its constellations of freckles, her laughing blue eyes and golden hair. Lena felt sick. That feeling in her chest compressed, anger filling her, making the beach tremble, loose slate raining down from the cliffs, and Lena was filled with the burning urge for her revenge.

     

                “Then you will know her son was banished, branded a Rogue and unfit to rule.”

     

                “Of course.”

     

                “Which means that I am her heir,” Lena said, pulling herself together, drawing herself up tall as she raised her chin and faced the encroaching Unseelie as they grew wary at the trembling earth. “My name is Lena, Queen of the Unseelie, and you owe me your fealty.”

    Chapter 46

                Waist-deep in the sea, stripped to her underclothes as the late summer sun beat down on her, Lena ran her fingers through the surface of the water, the smell of brine enveloping her as gentle waves rocked her. Sand shifted underfoot, and she squinted her eyes at the horizon, thinking about how easy it would be to keep going until the sea took her. Lena still couldn’t swim, but she was no longer afraid of any body of water; instead, it brought hope. Perhaps if she let the sea take her, her bones would rest at the bottom of it, fed to the fish, and in some way, she would find her way back to Kara, who’d been given to the earth. It wouldn’t be the burials either of them should have received, but she’d be in the water, and her wife would be in the earth, and they’d both have that little bit of each other in death, if they couldn’t in life.

     

                The one flaw in her plan was the woman shin-deep in the surf, behind Lena’s right, watching her closely with distrust in her eyes as she pretended to idly carve a piece of driftwood. Alex hadn’t let her out of her sight since they’d made it to that sliver of beach along the far eastern shore, or for the month before that, not since she’d followed Lena back into the forest, quietly fuming at her ruining the plans Kara had made Alex promise to uphold. It was starting to get somewhat annoying, two days on the beach, the Unseelie deferential to her but wary all the same, their new half-fae Queen looking haunted and a little feral. 

     

                She looked a right sight better than she had . They’d stripped off their armour and clothes to wash in the sea, sand scouring away weeks of sweat, old blood and dirt, lank hair rinsed clean and their dirty garments wrung out and left to dry over rocks, while the Seafolk had given them dry robes to wear. They’d eaten a few warm meals, fresh bread and stews of clams and crabs, a welcome change from the foraged fruits and herbs and whatever they managed to snare along the way. They’d even been shown to quarters inside the cliff, separate rooms offered up with pallets, blankets and pillows, but Lena had refused to sleep in there last night, making her bed on the dry sand at the top of the beach, staying near the sea so she could be near the lapping waves. She’d strangely slept soundlessly and dreamt of being in Krypton, in Kara’s room overlooking the sea, in her bed, the smell of salt and water suffusing her pillows, the sound of her voice whispering in the dark as Lena stayed all night, entangled in her warmth.

     

                Waking early with the dawn, the beach blue and cool, Lena had felt a pain in her chest, finding it hard to breathe. The nauseating memory of holding Kara’s body in her arms wormed its way through everything else. She couldn’t understand it. How could her wife be dead? Only an hour before that, they’d been professing their love to each other; they should’ve had years . Rising, she hadn’t said a word all day, sitting on the wet sand as waves lapped over her feet, the sun coming up, the Unseelie going about their daily lives as they fixed boats and nets, carved new axe handles, fished, gutted fish, made bread and went up to the forest to forage. They approached her a few times, bringing breakfast, bringing tea and water, and Lena didn’t acknowledge them, staring off into the horizon as the day warmed, a mild breeze blowing in.

     

                It was late afternoon now, and Alex had failed to get her out of the water to eat the food brought for her. The skin of Lena’s feet had pruned, and her brow had been furrowed for hours against the glare of sunshine, the sky cloudless, the itchy feeling of a sunburn over the bridge of her nose, her chest and shoulders, ensuring Lena would regret it later, but she remained in the sea anyway, hoping for answers, for some sort of revelation. But there was no rationalising her grief, her loss. After a month, it was still just an endless pit of despair.

     

                Blowing wood shavings off her carving, Alex smoothed a thumb over the length of wood and then softly sighed. “Will you remain here all day, or would you like to seek some shade?”

     

                Lena didn’t respond, staring blankly ahead, as if she hadn’t heard her, as if Alex hadn’t spoken at all. The sound of the waves breaking on the shore filled the silence, a few seabirds crying out as they fought over the entrails of fish being gutted by a few fae further down the beach. Closing her eyes, she breathed deeply, salt air scouring her lungs, trying to forget, trying to force her mind outside of her body.

     

                “You will make yourself sunsick,” Alex cautioned her, “and you should drink some water.”

     

                Opening her eyes again, Lena stared out at the blue-green waters, serene and sparkling as gentle waves rolled in, their size diminishing as they reached where she stood. She wasn’t frightened that they would tow her out, the sand shifting around her feet until she was ankle-deep in it, the spray of water flecking her cheeks and arms from the force of the breaking waves. It was strange not to fear anything anymore, a certain numbness to her as she waited patiently for a way out of her life. 

     

                “Do you hear me?” Alex continued. “Your revenge will be short-lived if you perish from thirst before we even make it to the river. Your brother will be glad of your foolishness, that much is sure.”

     

                “I would be glad of my death, too,” Lena murmured, her first response in hours , her voice scratchy and low.

     

                She heard Alex wade towards her at an angle, braving the sea as it soaked into her clothes, until she was at Lena’s side. Lena didn’t glance at her, just stared ahead, trapped in the prison of her own mind, her own misery. Grabbing her arm, Alex tugged on it, her brow furrowed together in a stern look of annoyance.

     

                “Come away, now, Lena.”

     

                “You should return to your wife. My revenge … it is very far away from me. I don’t have the means to achieve it. In fact, I never said I would seek it, only that it was what I wanted.”

     

                “Then why have you followed me here?” Alex challenged her.

     

                Shrugging slightly, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners. “There was nothing else for me to do. You wouldn’t let me die.”

     

                “Indeed, I will not abandon you while you still draw breath. I made my promises.”

     

                Eyes sliding sideways, Lena clenched her jaw, anger filling her. “Then I will relieve you of your promises and we shall both be happier for it.”

     

                “You-”

     

                She lunged at Alex, her hand ensnaring her right wrist, the one holding the little carving knife. Then Lena grabbed for the knife, getting her hand around the short blade, the bite of it digging into the soft flesh of her palm white-hot as it cut through the haze of nothing, and Alex let out a hiss of warning, trying to pull the knife away as she dropped the piece of wood she’d been carving and grabbed Lena’s wrist just as tightly. The pain of the small bones being squeezed made Lena quietly gasp, and she uncurled her fingers, blood running down her cut palm and pale forearm, dripping off her skin and drifting down to the surface of the water in pale petals.

     

                She still had hold of Alex’s wrist, though, and hooked her foot behind her sister-in-law’s leg, tipping her off-balance. Stumbling back, sagging to the water, Alex dragged Lena with her until they were both kneeling in the water, waves crashing over them, sand shifting beneath them as they struggled. Choking on saltwater, Lena was momentarily disoriented, pushing herself up and then collapsing as another wave struck her, while Alex staggered to her feet and hauled Lena up, dragging her back towards the beach.

     

                Pulling up short, Alex scoffed, and Lena raised her head to find a few of the Unseelie closing in on them, trident, axes and knives hefted as they aimed them at Alex. “She has nothing to fear from me,” Alex bit out, “she is her own worst enemy.”

     

                Grabbing the back of Lena’s sodden shift, she dragged her to her feet and snatched her hand up, clicking her tongue as she stared at the gash across the Queen’s palm. “You will need to do better than that if you wish to kill yourself, Lena.”

     

                Cheeks reddening, Lena yanked her hand back, quietly fuming as she curled her fingers over the wound, blood seeping through her fingers. Drawing in quick breaths, Alex raked her hair out of her face and gestured dismissively towards Lena.

     

                “Is there a healer here to help Her Majesty? She is in need of more than a few stitches; perhaps one might be able to knock some sense into her as well.”

     

                Lena shot her a venomous look, jaw clenched, and watched as Alex cleaned off her knife on her clothes, leaving a faint pink smudge on the hem of her soaking white shirt. One of the young women haltingly approached, extending a hand towards Lena, treating her like a skittish animal as she tried to herd her out of the water.

     

                “Your Majesty? We should have your hand seen to.”

     

                Eyes moving to the woman, Lena didn’t move. But then the pain in her hand grew too great to be ignored, the salt in it making her hand feel like the skin was being flayed from her palm. Glancing down, Lena took in her trembling hand and swallowed thickly, taking a step forward and then trudging out of the sea, leaving footsteps gouged into the wet sand as she traipsed up the beach. The Unseelie woman followed after her, as did Alex, pushing aside a man’s trident, giving a different woman a look of warning, and Lena flopped to the sand at the base of the slate cliffs, water drying on her skin as her hair dripped onto the dry sand. 

     

                The Unseelie had been deferential since she’d revealed her identity, but somewhat reserved, not knowing her at all, unsure how to approach this woman who had barely said a word to anyone , and looked a wreck. Even now, they all dispersed, casting bewildered glances at her, while a few attempted to help, fetching clean rainwater in a bowl, herbs and bandages, an old sail rigged as a lean-to when she silently refused to move inside at their urging. Alex crossed her arms over her chest and protectively stood nearby, just beyond the shade of the sail, while Lena let the young woman who’d tried to coax her out of the sea tend to the gash on her palm.

     

                She manipulated the water to clean out the wound, rinsing out sand that had gotten trapped in it and then informing Lena it would hurt, before she started to stitch the edges closed. Stiffening, her eyelids fluttering shut as her face went taut, Lena didn’t make a sound as she felt the dull pain of the curved hook pushing through her flesh. In and out, a neat row of stitches lined her palm, and the woman used a pestle and mortar to grind herbs together with honey. The astringent smell of herbs washed over Lena, and she opened her eyes, staring down at the mixture.

     

                “What are you using?”

     

                “Yarrow, comfrey, garlic, chamomile and honey, Your Majesty. Yarrow is to-”

     

                “Stop the bleeding. Yes. A good choice.”

     

                “Thank you, Your Majesty.”

     

                A ripple of pain crossed Lena’s face as the woman started smearing the mixture across her palm, covering the row of stitches with the salve. She cleared her dry throat, feeling uncomfortable as she shifted on the dry sand. 

     

                “You don’t have to call me that.”

     

                “But you are Queen, Your Majesty.”

     

                “I don’t want to be,” Lena tightly replied.

     

                A young boy, perhaps twelve in age, brought a steaming cup over to her, ducking beneath the sail, his hand shaking slightly. Lena eyed in and then glanced at him, his dark eyes wide and wary, and she cocked her head to the side, a headache pounding at her temples. Her throat felt scratchy, but she was wary, still.

     

                “It is willow bark tea, Your Majesty,” the woman murmured, and Lena took the cup, quietly thanking the boy before she took a sip. She took an even greater swig, hoping the pain would recede somewhat, and the woman hesitantly continued. “Perhaps because you do not wish to be, you will be a good Queen.”

     

                Letting out a hoarse laugh, Lena peeled open her eyes, glancing at the woman as a reluctant smile twitched the corners of her mouth. “Do you mean that my mother was a bad Queen for being power-hungry?”

     

                “I couldn’t say, Your Majesty. We were never graced with her presence, nor that of your father. We are quite removed from the smaller intricacies of politics, so far east.”

     

                “I think that’s best for you all,” Lena sighed. “And better if it stays that way.”

     

                “Mm. But you will not stay long, will you?”

     

                Lena had no answer for that. Now that she was somewhere relatively safe, resources and comfort awaiting her, instead of the exposure of the wild forest and her hunger and thirst reliant on what she could find along the way, Lena wasn’t sure what came next. It would be ideal to stay there awhile, waiting for her death, which would occur at some point, if not in the immediate future under Alex’s watchful gaze. But she didn’t feel motivated to do anything now, not even seek out revenge. They’d spent a month walking through the forest, and she just wanted to sleep now.

     

                She fell asleep on the sand and woke in a stone room wrought into the slate cliffs, a few beeswax candles illuminating the space. The pallet she was on was soft, and her body felt heavy, her right hand aching as she glanced at the bandaged lump on top of the woven blankets. The smell of salt was strong in the air, as well as the dampness of stone, and she glanced about, finding Alex sitting on the edge of another pallet, the quiet rasp of a whetstone over the edge of her blade filling the room. 

     

                Their eyes met, but they didn’t speak. Lena felt angry, no matter how unfair it was to feel so, and Alex was annoyed, neither of them having the time to process their grief, too preoccupied with being at each other’s throats as Lena wished Alex would leave her there and go back to Kelly, while Alex hoped for more of Lena’s fight to surface. They were both too stubborn to cave to the other’s whims, and while Lena might’ve had the upper hand with the Unseelie, the new Queen able to ask anything of them if she wished, she inspired no such loyalty or deference in Alex, who’d grown up with a democratic Council and didn’t pander to Lena in the slightest.

     

                It was a slow week of very little said between them, Lena sleeping a lot, waking to eat and then sleeping some more, her skin red and peeling as she healed quickly from her sunburn, water staving off further dehydration, and herbal teas easing the pain in her hands. Her stitches came out at the end of the week, and she spent more time on the beach, in the shallows, watching the Unseelie go about their daily lives. It was a more genuine insight to how they lived in the Courts than she’d seen elsewhere, and she watched without intruding, sipping drinks and staring out at the sea, the sail kept up for shade as she often slumbered on the sand, the smell of salt and the hissing of water on sand oddly comforting, reminding her of her wife.

     

                After that week, she wasn’t so tired, and she waded out into the water, the shock of cold making her gasp, gritting her teeth as she forged forwards, chest-deep and reckless. Alex was behind her, on the shore, watching, Lena’s sword belted at her waist, not a single sharp object allowed within the Queen’s vicinity, so no physical harm would come to Lena. There was nothing she could do about the mental, though. She’d never felt a loss like it before, not even the murky memories of her mother, which had haunted her childhood and followed her into adulthood. The fear of that paled in comparison to the fresh agony of grieving for her wife.

     

                And as if she’d opened the floodgates on her pain once more, although it had never truly closed, Lena was slammed with the full weight of her loss, her pain, her misery. As she relived it all again, her mind clearer than it had been in weeks, so much of that month spent not really thinking much at all, just existing as she put one foot in front of the other or slept as she wallowed in that constant, familiar pit of grief, she broke. Chest-deep in the water, she hunched her shoulders and buried her face in her hands as she wept, an endless stream of tears, of loud, gut-wrenching sobs heard by all on the beach, but she couldn’t stop, and it didn’t make her feel any better, a chasm in her chest that she could never fill.

     

                Arms came around her, Alex bracing Lena against her chest as she quietly tried to comfort her, her voice wavering too, thick with tears as she tried to mask her own grief for her sister. She was better at it than Lena was, and her stoicism only made Lena angry. Struggling in her grasp, she shoved Alex away, drawing in hitching breaths as she waded away, almost too deep for her to keep walking, hoping that it was deep enough to make her struggle to keep her head above the gently rocking waves, so she might wear herself out and go under. Of course, Alex wouldn’t let that happen; Alex didn’t care what Lena wanted.

     

                Those angry thoughts made Lena struggle towards the shore, water sluicing off her borrowed shift as she stormed across the sand, dashing the backs of her hands over her eyes, her face crumpled with sadness. Angry, the ground trembling slightly, Lena made for that narrow path up the slate cliffs, walking the length of the beach and then scrambling up it, feeling the way the earth shifted, tiny bits of slate raining down as her uncontrolled power fed into her surroundings. She managed to make it to the top, sinking to her knees as she clutched at fistfuls of pine needles and leaves, loamy earth and the sounds and taste of the forest filling her senses. Closing her eyes, Lena let out a forceful breath, and the forest seemed to exhale with her, settling down as her energy fled her.

     

                She didn’t move further than the edge of the cliff, and she put her back to a towering pine, rough bark beneath the thin linen of her shift, breathing in the heady smell as she watched the sun flickering in the needles. Closing her eyes, she listened to the waves crashing against the shore below, and it could’ve been Krypton, save for the fresh smell of pine that was so wrong. She braced herself for a fresh wash of pain, knees drawn to her chest as she clenched her jaw. It would’ve been less painful for her to climb to her feet and step over the edge of the cliffs, but she was unsure whether it would do much, given how quickly the fae healed, made of hardier stock than an ordinary human. Based on how quickly she’d always healed from her injuries, especially the ones she’d acquired in the Courts, which should have been fatal, or at least debilitating, Lena was quite certain she’d inherited her father’s genes on that matter. Dropping thirty feet to the dry sand below might break both legs, perhaps her spine, but she was left with the disappointing notion that she’d survive it to endure weeks of bed rest until she recovered.

     

                And then there was Alex. And there was only one thing Lena thought might get her sister-in-law to stop shadowing her everywhere, watching her like a hawk, stewing in angry silence as Lena’s unwillingness to do anything disappointed her. Rubbing at the peeling bridge of her nose, Lena considered her options. They were slim, at that, but she didn’t know these people, these Unseelie who were technically now her subjects, and she knew she couldn’t stay there. Not forever. But wherever she went, Alex would come with her, so it seemed like the logical option to go back to the Seelie Court, turn her over to her wife and then slip away. The problem with that was the two warfronts, which would make it nigh on impossible for them to safely cross. But there was a simple solution to that, one she didn’t want to make, but she felt the only way to get what she wanted was to give Alex what she wanted first. So, Lena decided not to die just yet.

     

                When wary footsteps on stone reached her ears, she opened her eyes and could just see the top of Alex’s head from where she was sitting against the base of the pine tree. As she walked further up the path, her brows, then her eyes visible over the lip of the cliff edge, Alex stopped as their eyes met. Staring at her for a few moments, Lena wearily pushed herself to her feet, brushing pine needles off the back of her clothes, and walked back towards the start of the path. Leaning against the uneven layers of slate, Alex watched her approach in silence, and Lena cleared her throat, raking salty locks of hair back as she avoided meeting her gaze.

     

                “We’ll leave tomorrow.”

     

                Nodding, arms folded over her chest, Alex pushed off the slate, straightening up. “To go where?”

     

                “To the seat of the Unseelie Court,” Lena unhappily informed her.

     

                While she still wasn’t looking at her, she caught the flicker of surprise that crossed Alex’s face from the corner of her eyes. Brushing past her, heedless of the drop off the edge of the narrow path, Lena started her way back down to the beach, plodding along with slumped shoulders and the weight of the world seemingly carried by her. She went back into the room offered up to them, lying down on the bed in her wet clothes as she closed her eyes and tried her hardest to sleep, the new scar on her palm itchy after the stitches had been taken out, and she almost considered going to find that young woman who’d healed her to ask for a tea to help her sleep, but wanted to nurse her wounds in private.

     

                Alex brought dinner in for her, a piece of fish cooked over a fire, crab meat and little cockles, seaweed bread and a salty broth with onions and potatoes in it. There was some wine too, and Lena downed a glass before she started to eat, mostly to give herself the energy for tomorrow, although she hadn’t planned a single thing. That seemed like an oversight, but she wasn’t in the right frame of mind to be thinking about anything, so she would simply pick a direction and walk until they figured things out along the way.

     

                Rising early, as they all did, she stripped off her borrowed shift and hesitated before folding it with care and leaving it at the foot of the bed, straightening out the sheets as well, grateful for the help they’d been given, the kindness shown to them by strangers, and enemies in Alex’s case. Changing into the clothes she’d cleaned in the sea, she put everything on layer by layer, fumbling with her armour as she tried to recall Kara’s instructions, so long ago now, never thinking she would have to do it herself. The buckles were tricky, and her eyes smarted with tears as she grew frustrated, but she managed it, or thought that she’d done it all correctly, at least. The surcoat went over the top of the breastplate, and she itched for the familiar weight of her belt, sheathed sword and dagger hanging from it, but they were still safely in Alex’s possession, and she didn’t think her sudden agreement to take up her mantle as Queen was likely to let Alex’s judgement lapse so easily.

     

                Her sister-in-law was already up and out on the beach, and by the time Lena emerged, dressed in her armour, shield slung over her back, her hair loose instead of braided, unable to bear thinking of her fingers going about the task that Kara had so lovingly done for her on a few occasions, Alex was packing items into two packs. Apparently, she was a better planner than Lena was, had clearly begged for provisions to see them on their way, or perhaps they were given freely by the Unseelie. At least they would have a cook pot and waterskins this time, a blanket as the nights grew cooler, and salted and dried foods to see them through days when food was scarce.

     

                “We will take you as far as Cadmus,” a man was saying, hefting a coil of rope, blue eyes a little hard in his suntanned face, perhaps resentful to be aiding a Seelie. But Lena was still Queen, so help was given regardless of feelings on the matter. “They will have horses on the plains; it will be a quicker route than following the coast to the northern estuary, where the border begins.”

     

                Nodding, Alex did up one of the packs and then tucked a linen-wrapped bundle into the top of the other before tying that one off too. “Thank you.”

     

                “Your Majesty, you should eat before you depart,” the familiar young woman appeared at Lena’s elbow, holding a cup of tea out towards her.

     

                Thanking her, Lena moved over to a large fire, driftwood flickering blue and green as the salt changed the colour of the flames, and accepted a bowl of porridge. It struck her again how ordinary these people were, how they were the same as the Seelie, how their main concerns were providing for each other, staying safe. Spooning oats into her mouth, Lena glanced at the young woman and softly cleared her throat.

     

                “What’s your name?”

     

                “Jess, Your Majesty.”

     

                Ducking her head in acknowledgement, Lena hesitated, spoon halfway to her mouth before she quietly replied. “I’m Lena.”

     

                Jess gave her a quick smile, frowning slightly with amusement as Lena introduced herself, as if she didn’t know who she was, hadn’t spent a week attending to her. They ate their breakfast in silence after that, Alex joining them, and Lena watched as one of the little skiffs was readied for sailing.

     

                “Once I’m back, is there anything you need out here that I can give you in return for your help?” Lena awkwardly asked as she sipped her cooling tea.

     

                “There’s only one thing any of us wants,” Jess murmured, her dark eyes distant and thoughtful. “For our families to come home, so that parents might see their children return safely, and children might grow up with their parents alive.”

     

                “It’s my intention to end the fighting. For good.”

     

                “Then, you would be the first to achieve it.”

     

                “I’ll be the first of many, I’d assume. Unless my ignorance of our history has made me overlook another bastard-born, half-fae Queen, raised in the human realm and married to a Seelie.”

     

                “I believe your assumptions are correct.” 

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena smiled, the ache in her chest differing from its usual agony of loss as it softened with the reminder of how her marriage had turned out, how happy they’d made each other, how frustrated they had been, angry at times and tender at others, all the things that had amounted to the love they’d felt. It had never been easy, it had been the most agonisingly slow dance around their true feelings, but it had never been love all the same.

     

                Draining the rest of her tea, Lena reached for a pot kept near the edge of the fire to stay warm and made to refill it, four of the Unseelie rushing to help her, until she gave up with exasperation, rubbing her tired eyes, feeling frustrated. Sipping her new cup of tea, the heat spreading through her, she stared out at the sunrise, the sky mottled pink and lilac as a few clouds drifted across the horizon. It looked to be a fine day, the air cool but warming as the sun crept higher, and she watched as a few of the Waterfolk drew waves in to help unbeach the skiff, pushing it out into the shallows.

     

                “We should be off,” Alex murmured, standing, dusting sand off her armour.

     

                Following suit, a little unsteady after a week without the weight of her armour, Lena glanced around at everyone present, feeling somewhat awkward. “Thank you for your help. It won’t be forgotten.”

     

                Drawing away, unsure how to say goodbye to these kind strangers, she turned and strode towards the little boat, a triangular sail hoisted, packs nestled beneath benches, and the man - Corben, she’d heard someone refer to him as - moving back and forth with ease. Jess joined them, and Lena waded into the surf, white foam soaking her feet - she’d left her boots off, for now - and took Alex’s hand as she helped her into the boat. The four of them settled in the boat, and those who’d helped ready it motioned back and forth, encouraging the sea to come in and out in a nauseating rocking motion, until the skiff was free of the shallows and Corben steered with the tiller.

     

                The boat didn’t seem seaworthy to Lena, too small to battle against the waves, and she felt queasy as she sat on a bench, clutching the side of the narrow skiff in a white-knuckled grasp as it pitched and swayed. Wind in the sails, they skirted around the outcropping of rocks and headed north, and Corben stayed close to the coastline, which Lena was grateful for, eyes closed as she breathed shallowly. She might not have been afraid to fall in and drown anymore, but the motion still tied her stomach into knots. Fortunately, she managed to keep her breakfast down and soon grew accustomed to being onboard a boat again, although this one was far smaller than the one they’d fled Krypton in, and that one hadn’t been that big either.

     

                The first hour passed as the sun fully rose, the sky turning blue, and Lena was miserable beneath the sun, exposed and baking in her armour. She hadn’t blinked at spending an entire day in the sea, burning until her skin had been red raw and peeling, but this was a different kind of misery, and she hadn’t willingly chosen it either. Not speaking, the sea air buffeting her face, tangling her unbound hair, she squinted against the brightness and bore it with little more than a sullen look on her face. And that sullen look turned mournful as she thought about how much Kara would’ve loved it, and with that came the regret that Lena have never indulged her in such things, that perhaps she would’ve liked a day on the water with her wife, showing her the sea and coves where she’d grown up swimming and fishing. Well, it was too late for that now.

     

                She ended up dozing off, sitting in the bottom of the boat, leaning back against the mast, and was roused near lunchtime, Alex bidding her drink some water, although Lena didn’t eat anything, unsure whether her stomach could handle it. They briefly stopped off in a small cove, tiny pebbles making up the shore, stretching legs, having a bathroom break, Jess spearing a few silver fish in the shallows with a slender trident, Alex quickly cooking them over nothing but her flaming hands, the four of them sharing them as they milled about on the beach in awkward silence. Washing her hands off in the water, Lena trudged back to the skiff and clambered back in, sinking back to the floor of the boat and curling up small as she settled in for their ongoing trip.

     

                It was a full day of sailing, the sunlight failing as the sky purpled and darkened, stars winking into existence, the moon full and close as it shone on the surface of the sea. Corben kept sailing onwards, and Lena felt queasy again, unable to make out the size of the waves, which had roughened, but they made the trip safely, firelight in the distance growing larger as they approached Cadmus late in the night, midnight almost upon them. By moonlight, they ran aground on the wet sand of a long stretch of beach, near enough to the dotted fires that they heard a few shouts go up and were met on the beach by the time the sail had been lowered and they’d disembarked.

     

                Feeling the ground pitch beneath her as she adjusted to being on land again, Lena raked her hair out of her face, watching the shadowed figures draw nearer as a few night owls approached. Jess called out a greeting, alerting them to where they hailed from, but she didn’t introduce Lena until they were much closer. Tired, dry-eyed and wind burnt, Lena was brooding and a little cold as the beach turned into soft grass, a pack hefted over her shoulder, like Alex and Jess, and she was unassuming, until their attention was purposely drawn to her.

     

                “You’re in the presence of our new Queen,” Jess informed the few who’d come to greet them. “Lena, of the Unseelie.”

     

                There was a moment of silent confusion, and a man with hair of middling length and a neat beard covering his mouth and jaw peered closely at her, before he blinked and sketched an elegant bow towards her. “Your Majesty, you are a long way from home.”

     

                “I intend to journey back there,” Lena wryly replied.

     

                “Corben has sailed us here with the intention of riding the rest of the way to claim Her Majesty’s throne. If you will permit us horses and supplies,” Jess explained.

     

                “Our loyalty demands it of us,” the man proudly declared, ducking his head as he gestured. “We will have shelter for you this night, Your Majesty. I am Jack, of the Airfolk. My tent is yours, if you should wish it.”

     

                He was a smooth talker, but his flattery fell short, Lena not one to soften to charm, and she cast him a faintly amused glance as he walked a step behind her. It was uncomfortable to be treated as such, being a Princess only affording her some deference, and she didn’t know what to say as she took in this man with his loose-fitting pants and tunic in shades of grey and white. He directed them to a few large tents erected on a vast stretch of grassy plains, studded with wildflowers and rolling hills. Except, as she approached the tents, she realised each mound in the distance had actually been partially dug out, dark holes burrowing into the hills, reminding her of little hobbit holes. She looked around with interest as the scattered campfires illuminated the dwelling, a clear divide between the nearby tents and the man-made hills in the distance.

     

                “They live beneath the hills?” Lena asked, glancing back at Jack.

     

                “Yes, Your Majesty. As I’m sure you know, there are more Earthfolk in the Unseelie Court than the other elements, but we have a population of Airfolk here too. We find the wind off the sea and the open plains an amenable place for our tents, so we share this stretch of land with the Earthfolk who prefer to live beneath the hills, a little further from the coast.”

     

                She hummed in acknowledgement, eyeing the domed tents in the immediate vicinity. Others were appearing now, coming out of tents, while in the distance, she saw shadowed figures appear out of the ground, converging on the Airfolk settlement as a young man who’d been amongst the small group greeting them ran towards the hills, spreading the word. Apprehensive, Lena’s pace slowed, and she could feel the tension radiating from Alex behind her right shoulder as they were fully surrounded by Unseelie again. But they were just ordinary people, as Lena had seen, more ordinary than the two outsiders they welcomed into their midst, and she let herself be led over to a large fire, Jack calling for a chair, despite the others who had been sitting cross legged on the grass, leaping to their feet at her arrival. 

     

                Lena sank to the grass before one could be procured for her, trying to retain her grace in her armour, and the others slowly eased themselves back down to the grass, staring at her with wary surprise. In short order, food and wine were brought to them, the rites of hospitality once more satisfied before anyone could properly relax, and even then, they all hovered about her, barely anyone speaking, most of them roused from sleep at her arrival. It was awkward and uncomfortable as Lena sipped her tea and felt their eyes trained on her face, observing her, taking in the measure of her.

     

                “I’d like to sleep,” she murmured after draining her cup, glancing at Jack, who knelt to her left.

     

                Leaping to his feet, he offered a hand, but Lena pushed herself to her feet unaided, reaching for her back, insisting that she could carry her belongings herself. Everyone else stood as well, and she felt vaguely embarrassed as she cleared her throat, softly bidding them all goodnight. She followed after Jack, Alex on her heels, and he hesitated, glancing down at her.

     

                “Would you prefer to sleep below ground, Your Majesty? We can arrange-”

     

                “A tent is fine.”

     

                Nodding, he led them to one of the domes, canvas stretched taut over curved willow switches and staked to the ground, and pulled back the flap to let them inside. The wind was blotted out and the space was warm, a stone basin holding the embers of a fire, and there was the clutter of an ordinary life - a robe draped over the back of a wooden chair, rumpled bed sheets where it hadn’t been made that morning, a few books and scrolls on a table with an assortment of beeswax, candles and honeycomb. There were a few shut chests as well, hiding the rest of the man’s life, and Lena felt a prickle of guilt for usurping his home for the night.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “I understand the circumstances of your marriage, but I hope that you will not be opposed to sharing a bed for one night. Unless things are not amicable, in which case, I will find suitable accommodations for your wife.”

     

                There was a beat of silence, Lena glancing sideways at Alex, who looked at her, both of them similarly aghast at the suggestion, before Lena quietly replied. “She’s not my wife.”

     

                “I- oh. Forgive me, I assumed …”

     

                “She’s her sister.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “One bed will be fine,” Alex curtly replied, trying to put an end to the awkward encounter.

     

                Unsure what to say, Jack hovered for a moment and then sketched a shallow bow towards Lena before slipping back out into the night. Letting her pack fall off her shoulder, thumping to the woven reed mats underfoot, Lena let out a weary sigh, tired from a long day. She started to take off her armour, fumbling with the buckles of the gorget, and Alex quietly cautioned her as she started to do the same.

     

                “Remove your breastplate, tassets and gorget only. Keep the rest on; there are more Unseelie here than there were at the beach. It would not be wise to leave ourselves completely vulnerable.”

     

                “They just seem like people,” Lena murmured.

     

                “They are,” Alex conceded. “But I would be wary of sleeping amongst a hundred unknown Seelie, too. These are not safe times.”

     

                “Have there ever been safe times?”

     

                With a small huff of laughter, Alex gave her a wry smile. “Long before our time, and even long before the time of our grandparents. But that does not mean those days can’t come again.”

     

                “I don’t think it’ll be as simple as killing my brother.”

     

                “No, but it will be a start. And revenge will satisfy us both, at least.”

     

                “Not nearly enough. Not even if I killed him and every single Rogue, every person who’s ever aided him. Not even if I could bring them all back to kill them all over again.”

     

                “But it will be a start.”

     

                Running a hand over her tired face, tense and annoyed, Lena dropped her breastplate to the floor, the tassets still attached to it, keeping the rest of her armour on, and turned to the bed. “I’m tired.”

     

                “Pass me a pillow; I will make do with the floor and a blanket,” Alex murmured.

     

                Taking a pillow from the bed and one of the thick wool blankets as well, she handed them over and then climbed into bed, drawing the remaining blankets up over herself. Shutting her eyes, dead tired but tense, Lena found sleep hard to come by. Eventually, she drifted off, but she didn’t feel well-rested when she woke shortly after dawn, the sun still rising. Alex was already up, her armour donned again, and Lena stared up at the ceiling of the domed tent as she tried to dwell in sleep a little while longer. 

     

                Sighing, she made herself get up a few minutes later, straightening out the blankets, struggling with her armour to buckle everything back on, working her surcoat over the top, and snagged Alex’s pillow and blanket as well to finish making the bed. Glancing at Alex, Lena didn’t know what to say. She’d come to know her sister-in-law fairly well, trusted her almost as much as she trusted Kara, but there was this strain between them now, both changed by their shared grief, and Lena wasn’t quite sure how to be the person Alex wanted her to be. She was a strong woman, but this wasn’t about strength; it was asking Lena to find the will to live without her heart.

     

                “We should get going,” Lena murmured after a few moments.

     

                The quicker they were off, the quicker this would all be over. Reaching for her shield and her pack, Lena stepped out of the tent.
