The plains were covered in a thin layer of mist, lying low over the long grass, and she felt a bite to the air blowing in off the sea, taking a moment to breathe in what could be her last few lungfuls of salt-tinged air, and she was almost immediately accosted by Jack, getting a good look of his features in the light of dawn.

     

                “Your Majesty,” he dipped his head in a polite bow. “We have food if you would like to break your fast. There is also a steam tent, if you would like to-”

     

                “We intend to leave as quickly as possible.”

     

                “Then I must ask quickly if you will permit me to guide you.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena glanced over her shoulder at Kelly, who nodded slightly, before she relented, looking back at the man. They did need a guide, neither of them having traversed the Unseelie Court, or in ownership of maps that might’ve helped, so Lena supposed she should take him up on it if he was willingly offering. 

     

                “If you’d like.”

     

                Perking up slightly, pleased that she’d agreed, he ducked his head and then gestured for her to walk ahead of him. He spoke animatedly of the Airfolk camp, the domed tents arranged in orderly circles around central fires, and she watched the people gathered around them, eating breakfast, embroidering linen garments, scutching flax fibres, and harvesting honey from frames taken from nearby hidden hives. As she studied the camp, Lena looked past it and realised that what she’d assumed were wildflowers in the dim light of the campfires upon their arrival were actually late-blooming flax flowers that hadn’t yet been harvested. Looking around, she assumed that a large portion of the plains was given over to the flowers, and perhaps they tended bees to pollinate the plants and provide honey, providing for the fae as they were looked after by them in turn. 

     

                Despite the earliness of the day, the sky was clear as the horizon brightened, and while there was still the coolness of the night in the air, it promised a mild day. Sitting by a crackling fire, Lena was served breakfast, an array of food set before her on multiple trays, the hospitality overwhelming, making her wish she was back inside the tent, or back at the beach, hidden in a cave where they wouldn’t bother her. It seemed that anyone who knew who she was was now bound to overcompensate to please her as best as they could. Adding some walnuts and honey to a bowl of porridge, Lena selected a flaxseed tea and a little bowl of berries, and then dragged one of the trays towards Alex and the other towards Jess so the rest of the food wouldn’t be wasted.

     

                Eating her rather plain meal and enjoying her tea, Lena was silent, and she felt uncomfortable being watched, her eyes darting about, trying not to meet the stares of anyone looking at her. That was nigh on impossible, so she kept her eyes on her food for the most part, ignoring Alex’s words, said under her breath.

     

                “You might try endearing them to you, you know. You won’t inspire much loyalty by ignoring them.”

     

                But Lena didn’t particularly care for loyalty, and these were not the folk who needed to heed her orders. It would be those tucked away in her mother’s warren, politicking and aiding her brother, whom she needed to assert her command over, and they were just as likely to cut her throat as to obey. She wouldn’t mind if that happened, but she’d like to attain peace first, if possible.

     

                Finishing her meal, she set her empty cup and bowl on one of the trays and then climbed to her feet, biting back a sigh at the flurry of activity as everyone else rose too. Stooping to heft her pack, Lena grimaced slightly and cast a quick look around the group.

     

                “Thank you,” she awkwardly said to no one. “Your help is appreciated and won’t be forgotten. If you, um, if you need anything … send word. I’ll try my best.”

     

                “A rousing speech,” Alex muttered, her own pack on her shoulder as she stood to Lena’s right.

     

                Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena glanced at Jack and gave him an expectant look. He led the way to the stretch of green between the Airfolk camp and the scattered mounds of the Earthfolk in the near distance, four horses nibbling at the grass with blankets and linen pannier bags across their backs. They didn’t have saddles or bridles, and Jack was apologetic as he informed them, but helped divvy up their supplies into each side of the panniers before he offered to boost Lena into the saddle. Without stirrups and in armour, she was uncertain of her capability to get ahorse without help, but a glance from Alex confirmed her thought that she should do it alone, to show her competence, if nothing else, watching eyes behind them and ahead as the Earthfolk started to appear to catch a glimpse of her.

     

                Waving aside his assistance, Lena gripped a handful of the horse’s mane, set a hand on its back to brace herself, and then hauled herself up with a little less grace than she would’ve liked. Shifting so she was comfortable, she smoothed the neck of the horse. It was smaller than the slenderly built horses she’d ridden through the forest, with long feathering on its fetlocks, and piebald colouring. Alex needed no assistance, but Lena was surprised when Jack helped boost Jess onto the back of one of the two remaining horses, frowning as she stared at the young woman, whose face was pinched with unease.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “If you’ll permit it, Your Majesty, I wish to accompany you as well.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “I have not had the privilege of leaving home much, beyond the occasional ranging trip into the forest above the cliffs, or similar trading trips to visit the settlements here. I’m an accomplished fighter, as we are all trained to be, but my parents bid me stay out of the war as long as I can. I thought … perhaps I might seek adventure this way, safely, instead.”

     

                Considering it for a second, Lena softly sighed. “I can’t promise it will be safe at all, but you can come if you really want to.”

     

                Ignoring the gratitude from the young woman, Lena watched Jack mount his horse and grip its mane before urging it onwards. With a backwards glance at the gathered Airfolk, Lena ducked her head in silent thanks to the group that had come to see them off and then followed after Jack, Jess falling in behind her, and Alex bringing up the rear. Jack led them straight into the heart of the Earthfolk settlement, winding between the mounds of grass-covered dirt as Lena studied the homes with interest. The Earthfolk who were waiting to catch a glimpse of her nodded deferentially, and she apprehensively returned them, even pausing when a little girl ran up to her horse and held a little white daisy up to her. Smiling, Lena leaned down and took it from her, hesitating before she worked it behind her short-tipped ear, softly thanking the girl and then moving on.

     

                They left the Earthfolk settlement behind and made for the trees in the distance, the towering trees of the forest beckoning them, and Lena was eager to be within their shade but it was a few miles of riding before they achieved that. The cool smell of rotting foliage washed over her with relief, and she breathed deeply, feeling the forest around her, the trees groaning slightly as their leaves rustled, although there was no breeze. It seemed the others noticed it too, because there was a tense pause, as if expecting some sort of attack, before they forged onwards, deeper past the shorter, tightly packed trees, until they grew bigger and further apart, needing more space for their thick trunks and wide spreading roots and canopy.

     

                That first day, no one said much, miles passing by as they traversed dense ferns, brambles and bushes, up sloping inclines, through narrow ravines, and across slow-trickling brooks and streams. Riding through to dusk, they were eaten alive by mosquitoes, the dampness of the forest providing ample breeding ground for them throughout the summer. Finally, they stopped for the night, and Alex made a fire, while Lena tended to their horses, Jess took their waterskins to find a source to refill them from, and Jack started to pluck a pheasant he’d shot with his bow as they’d ridden along. Their stores had been replenished as well, so they had fresh loaves of bread for the time being, and a hearty stew was made with some of the food they had with them, as well as a few root vegetables Lena managed to identify once she’d finished with the horses.

     

                In the darkness of night, they all ate their stew with their bread, sipped some tea and then went to sleep with a familiarity that Lena was grateful for. It was like a return to the routine of her life since they’d fled Krypton, brief periods of time where she’d stayed somewhere for a stretch of days, before ultimately ending up travelling through the forest again. The week she’d spent on the coast had helped her recover from that hard month of walking with no supplies, but she felt a little sore after a day of riding without a saddle. Falling asleep fast, Lena slept soundly and dreamt of her wife.

     

                Jolting awake to the pitch black, Lena sat up, feeling the forest floor trembling beneath her, and she realised her cheeks were wet, her chest heaving as she tried to catch her breath, and Alex had been the reason she’d awoken. She’d shaken Lena awake, her pale face grim with understanding, etched with unspoken grief, and Lena ran a hand over her face, drawing in quiet gasps as she felt the forest around her. Roots had snaked over her as she’d slept, called to her power, and her legs were still partially bound as she struggled to free herself, her mind still full of the hazy memory of Kara. She couldn’t remember the particulars of the dream, but she’d been there; she was always there.

     

                Curled up, face in her hands as she gathered herself, Lena took a minute before she could speak, her voice hoarse and small when she looked at her sister-in-law. “I’ll take over your watch.”

     

                Hesitating, Alex nodded, and Lena extended a hand for her sword. Considering it for a moment, Alex shook her head, her mouth a hard line, and she drew away from Lena, arranging her blankets nearby. “Wake me if you hear anything.”

     

                Swallowing her frustration, Lena drew her blanket around her shoulders as she leaned back against the wide trunk of a sycamore, feeling cold as her chest ached. She realised two pairs of eyes were looking at her from where they’d made their beds across the fire from her, and Lena felt embarrassment wash over her as she averted her gaze.

     

                “I will take watch, Your Majesty,” Jack whispered after a moment, already reaching for his bow.

     

                “No,” Lena tersely replied, rubbing at her eyes. “No, I will do it myself. Thank you.”

     

                He seemed perplexed by that notion, and she was reminded that the Unseelie Court were quite traditional in their values, compared to the Seelie Court, where being clueless of her heritage had granted her more grace than being a Princess. It had been expected of her that she assist, that she learn their ways, adapt to them, and make herself useful. Lena had gotten used to that and had forgotten that in her mother’s halls, Lillian had them all at her beck and call. Of course, Lena hadn’t quite been afforded that in the Unseelie Court either, but that had been at Lillian’s instruction as well, treating her as more of a political prisoner than a daughter.

     

                Still, she’d expressed her desire to keep watch, so her decision was indulged, and everyone went to bed with no further questions about the disruption. It wasn’t long until dawn anyway, the sunrise still relatively early as late summer hadn’t quite given over to autumn yet, and nothing disturbed her as the forest seemed lulled by her presence. Lena quietly started to make some tea as the darkness alleviated slightly, and by the time the others rose, she’d built up the fire and the pot over it was bubbling. 

     

                Eating a quick breakfast with their tea, they broke camp and were off again, the day bleeding into night again, where Lena woke with her usual nightmares, although she hadn’t cried out that time or woke in tears, despite the forest reacting to her. In their wake, everything bloomed, a second wind sweeping through the forest as early summer fruits budded and ripened all over again, and Jack and Jess were utterly bewildered by it. Alex wasn’t happy at all, Lena’s powers still rushing out of her without any real attempt to put a stopper on her grief, and it left Lena exhausted every day, but at least she wasn’t travelling by foot this time and could just sway as she sagged on horseback. 

     

                Three days passed by, each one much like the day before, except the temperature plummeted as they forged deeper into the wild forest. They encountered a boar at one point, ordinary in size but still fierce, and they managed to flee without needing to kill it and waste meat, and they had a close miss with a bear cub and its mother, the roars shaking the forest as it echoed through the trees, the smell of singed hair clinging to them for a while after as Alex covered them. None of them were injured, fortunately, and they soon entered a series of deep valleys, small rifts and gaps between their forested, sloping sides, creating narrow vales where the sun never touched the bottom. The wind would tear through them with a savagery that was only dimmed by Jack’s efforts, but the chill of it still bit at their exposed skin and made them feel as it they were going to be swept off horseback, a potentially fatal fall always a risk as they sometimes skirted along passes high up the side of a valley, nothing but bare rock sloping down to narrow rivers and clusters of cedars below. 

     

                It took them just over a week of travelling to cover the distance, enduring rain and storms in the areas where they were closer to the canopy, where it thinned slightly for them to catch glimpses of the sky and suffer the dampness of it. On their final day, Lena shivered as the cold sapped the heat from her bones, desperate for a fire and soaking wet in her armour as thunder rumbled and lightning flickered through gaps in the canopy. It wasn’t the way she’d anticipated making her return, hadn’t even thought she’d ever find her way back there, but it was near dusk, the storm passing hours before but leaving them miserable for the rest of their journey, when they passed the boundary of the Unseelie Court, stone archways and artfully sculpted trees looming out of the dim forest as lit lamps hung through the trees to light the way.

     

                It hit her with a sense of deja vu, the smell of standing water on the wind, the sound of the rippling pond she knew she’d find there getting louder as they plodded through the trees, Jack now relegated to the back with Jess, as Alex rode on Lena’s tail, curious but alert. Figures materalised, recognising her by sight after her autumn spent at the Court last year, and she garnered an entourage as Lena rode her piebald horse through the trees, until she reached the wide pond, water lilies holding small lit candles as they drifted across the surface with the current, the warbling of frogs in the reeds, the hoot of an owl in the large oak tree growing from the centre of it all. Its roots jutted over the water as she remembered, creating small grottoes for ducks and geese splashing about and eating the algae on the surface. The first time she’d been there, she hadn’t noticed the throne nestled amidst the thick roots of the sprawling oak, and when she had, it had been occupied by her mother. This time, it was empty.

     

                Reaching the edge of the pond, where the roots snaked and wove a path to the throne, Lena dismounted from her horse and gripped the pommel of her sword. She’d asked Alex for it back that morning, and her sister-in-law hadn’t questioned why, and although it wasn’t quite the finery she would’ve hoped for in an ideal world, dressed in her armour, her surcoat wet and dirty, her long hair hanging in damp ropes, Lena had never felt more deserving of wearing it. Still, her heart was pounding like mad, her sensitive hearing picking up the soft footfalls of her growing audience.

     

                Walking along the path the roots made, a few white butterflies flittered around her, settling on her arms, shoulders, hands and hair as the forest started to bloom, wisteria, lupins and jasmine filling the air with the sweet smell of their perfumes, catkins on the oak tree cascading from the branches so late in the year. Lena approached the throne, carved out of the tree itself by some skilful manipulation of the trunk, and turned, removing her sword from its scabbard and then sitting and resting the blade across her knees. It was a tense minute, her emotions erratic and bared to the forest as it fed on her, and she watched the small crowd stir slightly as the fae started to kneel before their new Queen without a word passing her lips.

    Chapter 47

                Bending over a piece of parchment held flat on the desk, Lena slowly scratched the quill over the page, pausing to dip it into the inkwell, a line of candles stuttering as they melted and pooled on the wood. Her dark hair hung in long, damp tendrils around her face and shoulders, her pale skin flushed a delicate pink from a much-needed bath in the hot springs below ground. Wrapped in a clean bedrobe, belted tightly shut at the waist, Lena looked small and unassuming, but there was a serious look on her face as she copied the elegant, swirling glyphs Alex had copied out for her as she’d orated them.

     

                The room was empty, save Alex, who lingered against an earthen wall, warming her hands over a lit brazier and still dressed in her armour, dirt and blood on her hands and face, caught in a few strands of her hair. She’d refused to bathe when Lena had, lurking inside the steaming room as she firmly insisted that she wouldn’t let her attention lapse in such a dangerous place. Lena didn’t object, knew that Alex was right, that they couldn’t let their guards down, but it did pose the question of what they were going to do. Alex couldn’t stand guard over her day and night, needed her own rest, her own time to care for herself, but their circle of trusted people had been reduced to two. If Kelly had been there, if Kara had been there, it would’ve been easier.

     

                Hunched over her task, dark ink staining her freshly washed fingertips from the repetitive effort of writing her letters, the wide desk strewn with crumpled pieces of parchment from the multitude of drafts and mistakes, Lena finished off the last of them with a flourishing signature. It had been mindless in a way, as if she were practising her penmanship, copying the glyphs Alex had written for her and melting wax to press in the seal she’d found on her mother’s desk. Raising the small spoon of softened wax, Lena dribbled the remains of it onto the folded seam of the letter and lifted the golden seal, pressing it into the plum coloured wax and holding it firm until it cooled.

     

                Gathering up five letters in her hands, Lena walked over to the doors to the chamber and opened one half, poking her head out. Jack was standing outside, his back straight, a long hunting knife in his hands as his dark eyes watched the hallway. Lena had tried to convince him to go when she’d sequestered herself inside her mother’s office, but he’d firmly insisted on remaining at the door. A first line of defence, she supposed. She assumed he’d be a safe bet to carry out her wishes, though, and he turned as she opened the door, giving her a shallow bow as he smiled.

     

                “Your Majesty.”

     

                A lick of irritation ran through Lena at the title, but she pushed it aside, holding the letters out to him. “Can you send riders with these, please. These three, to whomever is commanding our forces along the river. These two, to the Seelie Court. Perhaps a raven for that; I don’t think they’ll allow an envoy at this time.”

     

                “Of course, Your Majesty. I would be honoured to deliver them myself-”

     

                “No,” she cut him off, her voice a low murmur as she frowned slightly. “No, I’d prefer to have you here. There are very few I can trust to stand watch, and I fear I don’t have many friends here.”

     

                He seemed pleased that she wanted him to stay, assuring her that he’d see it done, before she slipped back inside and shut the door, falling back against it. Alex looked up from the brazier, her hands held dangerously close over the flames, and raised her eyebrows. Rubbing her tired eyes, the day a blur that she hadn’t had time to comprehend, Lena let out a weary sigh. It had been a long morning, sitting on the throne with that sword across her knees, the forest warming as green light illuminated heady pollen, ducks, geese and songbirds clamouring in the grottoes and pools of water, everything so alive, so ripe and vibrant as the Unseelie paid homage to her, kneeling and swearing tight oaths that Alex had come up with, tweaked by Lena. Her sister-in-law was a menacing guard, standing beneath the trees with suspicion and contempt on her face as she dared anyone to make a wrong move. Lena was grateful to have her.

     

                But now, watching as Alex paced before the brazier, limned in orange light from the warmth of the flames, Lena realised there was more to her displeasure than merely being in the Unseelie Court. “You’re angry with me,” Lena noted, cocking her head to the side, feeling a knot in her neck from the hard journey. “Why?” 

     

                Alex abruptly stopped, giving her an annoyed look. The warm glow of light illuminated the sharp planes of her profile as her mouth turned down at the corners, and her voice was exasperated as she replied. “I’m not angry at you; I simply don’t know what to make of it, of you.”

     

                “Why, because I’m recalling my army? I thought you’d be happy about that, at least. It assures your friends and family of their safety.”

     

                “No, because of what you didn’t do,” Alex said with more vehemence, rubbing her bottom lip as her delicate features creased with worry. “You can recall your army, but that will not root out the cause of this. There are Generals, soldiers, and ordinary folk who will not be pleased by your decision. You are inviting chaos home, and you risk your life without mitigating the risk of such a decision.”

     

                “What would you have me do? Would it have been better if I’d removed their heads first, without giving them the opportunity to declare their loyalty?”

     

                “Only a fool would think differently.” 

     

                Lena was unruffled as she shrugged. “I think differently.”

     

                Upon entering the room, there had been a brief panic of everyone trying to attend to her, the servants that had moved silently through the halls under Lillian’s reign rushing about to try and meet Lena’s needs with the same nervous urgency. It had taken Lena allowing two women to bring a spread of food for everyone to leave her alone, and she’d sent Jess off with them at Alex’s insistence. They’d returned and left a platter of sliced meat, fruits and cheeses, and a loaf of bread, which was still warm. A pitcher of blackberry wine and two goblets had accompanied the food, and Lena was glad for the rather simple fare, although she hadn’t eaten a bite yet. Alex had smacked her hand away from the pitcher of wine earlier, and then called Jess over, plying her with a plate filled with everything and a cup of wine, bidding her eat. It wasn’t until Jess had apprehensively had a bite of everything, and a sip of wine too, that Alex was satisfied, keeping the young woman inside the room for half an hour before she vocally declared her relief that it wasn’t poisoned and sent her off. There had been a heated debate, with Lena firmly objecting to using the young woman as a poison tester for her, while Alex had deemed it necessary, and Jess, before she’d left, had meekly assured Lena that she’d known her intention before taking a bite and hadn’t minded.

     

                Now, Lena gravitated towards it, hunger gnawing at her stomach as her nerves finally abated. Jess had left the barely-touched goblet of wine behind, and Lena refilled it, and the empty one for Alex, and handed it out to her. Taking it with a grim look on her face, Alex sighed and then knocked back half. Taking a measured sip from her own cup, Lena turned her attention back to the food. The only thing that had kept her hungry these weeks had been the way she bled all her energy into the earth, into the roots and bones of the forest, and it had carved away at her body, bit by bit, her grief leaving her not nearly ravenous enough to offset the taxing demand on her body, and her lips were chapped, cheeks hollowed and eyes ringed by dark shadows as she plucked a ripe cherry from the platter. 

     

                Chewing on it slowly, removing the pit, Lena’s expression was dour. She hated the way it all was; her grief felt like a bad dream that she couldn’t wake up from. This was the only way forward for her, despite what Alex thought. They were united on the topic of peace, but how they attained that seemed to differ. While Alex thought more bloodshed might put an end to it, once Lena had ferreted out unloyal or dissatisfied Unseelie and killed her brother, Lena thought about Kara, and what path she would take if she’d been able to. She knew her late wife would’ve chosen to believe the best in people, only taking lives out of self-defence and necessity, not as a precaution. 

     

                “You think I don’t want to make everyone involved suffer? Even for the act of being on the riverbank, being the reason why we were there. I do,” Lena said after a long moment of silence, turning back to the platter, helping herself to bread and piling shaved meat onto it. Taking a rough bite, she chewed angrily and swallowed before glancing at Alex. “It’s not what she would want, though. I- that thing between us … we never got the chance to find out what it could’ve been, but I know what she wanted from life. So, I can try my best to give it to her in death.”

     

                Letting out a long sigh, draining the rest of her wine and moving over to the table to refill her goblet, Alex briefly laid a hand on Lena’s shoulder, a heavy, reassuring weight. It was cold comfort, though.

     

                “She loved you, Lena. You were the only person she loved in that way. In private, she often told me how- how happy you made her, as … frustrated as she was to hold her love a secret. She would’ve been … happy to spend a long life with you. I know that much.”

     

                A small sound escaped Lena, almost breaking her composure as she ducked her head down, saying nothing. Her cheeks were rosy and her eyes were glassy with tears, though. She couldn’t bring herself to look at Alex, but she could feel her eyes on her, knew the deep well of concern she’d find in them. Her eyes stung with tears as she kept her gaze down.

     

                “I also know that you … you are a pot on a slow boil. You have been angry since … the moment I met you. And now, you grieve with no idea how, and you seek revenge without direction. I understand that you don’t want to spill blood if you do not have to, but I urge you to take my advice and take precautions. You must have them bind themselves tighter to you with oaths they cannot break; you must have every entrance to this place guarded, sentries in the forest watching.

     

                “I won’t make them prisoners to me. I don’t wish to be my mother. That won’t help me defeat my brother, it will just- it’ll make them resent me. I know it, because I resented her for binding me to- to her with wedding vows.”

     

                “He will come for you.”

     

                Raising her head, Lena’s gaze was hard, and her voice was brittle as she replied. “Not if I come for him first.”

     

                Scoffing, Alex ran a hand through her hair and raised her eyebrow expectantly. “So, what plan do you have?”

     

                Taking another bite, Lena chewed thoughtfully and spoke slowly when she responded. “The plan? The plan is … we rest, and we recover. And when my army returns … well, I’ll think of what to do next, then.”

     

                Swallowing a groan, Alex rubbed her eyes and gave Lena an exasperated look. “You’re more trouble than I’d bargained for. I should knock you senseless and carry you back to the Seelie Court.”

     

                “If you wish,” Lena indifferently shrugged, taking a sip of wine and then finishing off her bite to eat.

     

                There was more, but she suddenly felt so weary, so heavy with exhaustion. She just wanted to sleep now, despite how early in the day it still was, and while Lena knew she had that luxury, she was reluctant to. Mostly, it was because she knew she’d either have to brave going to the quarters she’d shared with Kara, or find ones she hadn’t. Both were painful prospects. Biting her bottom lip, a wary edge crept into Lena’s features as she dithered, trying to prolong the moment of relative peace, although she would never know such a thing again. Alex watched her, a pained look of understanding on her face, of a similar grief, and a flicker of guilt as well, for not stopping it from happening, for encouraging her sister to court Lena, for leaving Kara’s body behind to hold to her promise. 

     

                With a soft sigh, Alex reached out to pinch Lena’s goblet, setting it firmly on the table with the rest of the uneaten food. “Come. You should rest.”

     

                “You should rest,” Lena shot back, her eyes flitting over Alex. “And you should wash first.”

     

                Humming in vague agreement, Alex ran a hand over her face, the sweat and dirt accumulated since leaving the beach, and grimaced. “I think we need to sort out security first.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena sighed. “Just go in the bath. I’ll stay inside the chamber with you, and, if you’ll permit me, I’ll have my dagger in hand, on the off chance someone barges in to cut my throat.”

     

                “It’s not the off chance.”

     

                “Well, for the record, not that many people tried to kill me while I was here.”

     

                “Your mother was Queen at that time. I’m sure the threat of what she would do was enough of a deterrence for all but the most foolhardy. You’ve yet to show your teeth to them; they’ll bite to test your limits. Be sure of that.”

     

                Humming in distracted agreement, Lena moved towards the door, reaching for the handle. Alex’s sharp cry of warning made her stop, and she was nudged aside, listening to the annoyed mutters about how someone could be outside the door. They bickered back and forth the entire way to the baths, with Lena insisting that her hearing was keen enough to hear someone on the other side of a door, or footsteps approaching, and Alex insisting that Lena needed to be cautious, be well-guarded. As if to prove her point, Alex held a long blade in hand and cupped flames in the palm of the other, bristling with anticipation.

     

                As if to prove her point, Lena made it to the bathing rooms unscathed and impatiently waited for Alex to pick the room with the correct temperature for her. Naturally, she chose the hottest one, the steam so thick that as Lena had the long knife pressed into her palm, she didn’t think anyone would be able to spot her in the room. Retreating to a corner, she felt her skin prickle with condensation and sweat as Alex stripped off her armour, the sound muffled in the steam, and splashed into the water.

     

                “It might do for us to share quarters for the time being,” Alex proposed from the hot spring.

     

                Scoffing, Lena’s mouth flattened. “I’m not sharing a bed with you. It’ll be fine. You’re starting to sound paranoid; you’re starting to sound like-”

     

                She almost said her name. It choked her up, getting caught at the back of her throat, and Lena shut her mouth. The silence inside the room was heavy, the sound of water filling it as Alex scrubbed herself clean from within the steam drifting from the surface of the deep pool. Eyes prickling, a building pressure up the back of her nose, Lena struggled to swallow past the sudden tightness in her throat.

     

                “I enact her will in her stead,” Alex softly sighed, her quiet words carrying in the relative silence. “She wouldn’t let you stray from her sight if she were here.”

     

                Feeling a lick of anger, her pain as fresh as the day she’d lost her, Lena drew in a shaky breath. “But she’s not. And I can’t- it’s all so … suffocating.”

     

                Climbing out of the water, Alex dressed in her dirty clothes and donned her mail again as a precaution, although she bundled most of her armour into her ragged cloak. The steam parted as she approached Lena, taking back her knife and giving her a tired look.

     

                “Yes, I imagine it is.”

     

                Turning, she walked over to the doors, pausing a second to listen, before stepping outside. With little choice but to follow after her, Lena wandered through the hallways, almost aimlessly, although she did know the way. With Alex at her side, she almost subconsciously brought them to the quarters she’d shared with Kara. Standing outside the door, indistinguishable from any others, but theirs all the same, Lena’s pulse raced as she stared at the wood, at the way the roots formed the archway of the frame, thinking about what lay beyond it. Theoretically, it was just a room. They’d barely been friendly, then, but the thought of walking into a suite where they’d had rooms across from each other made her chest ache.

     

                After a few minutes, antsy and wary, Alex moved to the door directly across from that one and threw it open. Sticking her head inside, she nodded to herself and then turned, grabbing Lena’s arm and hauling her across the threshold, before she shut the door behind them. Looking around the place, Lena felt a sense of relief, although the rooms were nearly identical in layout and furnished similarly. But she’d never been inside that room, had never lived there with Kara, and that made all the difference.

     

                Turning to the door, Lena could feel what she’d failed to do all those months ago, pressing her palm to the wood and feeling the roots shift beneath her touch, everything still pouring out of her, affecting the earth and plants around her. The roots moved to make it so no one could open the door without breaking it down, and surely they’d hear that and be able to prepare for an attack. Alex had also picked a room without a small window at ceiling height to allow for airflow, leaving the room dark and smelling heavily of earth, but offering no way in, aside from the door.

     

                “Sleep,” Alex ordered her, moving through the sitting room with a palmful of fire and peering into one room, finding a desk and a divan, and then a bed in the room next door, gesturing her into it.

     

                Stepping into the room, Lena made straight for the bed and climbed onto it, the blankets cool as she dragged them back and then covered herself up. It wasn’t even dusk yet, but the room was pleasantly dark, the glow of Alex’s cupped flames the only source of light, and she could’ve slept. Lena thought she’d find it rather easy. But then Alex extinguished the flames and ordered her to come and help her, Lena stumbling out of bed, her eyes trying to pierce the darkness, making out the shadows of her sister-in-law as she struggled to shift a heavy vanity.

     

                “What’re you doing?”

     

                “Barricading the door,” Alex stated, as if that should’ve been obvious.

     

                “You can’t barricade us in. How will you get out?”

     

                “I’m sleeping in here. There’s a divan at the foot of the bed; that will do nicely.”

     

                “You’re not sleeping in here. Go find your own room.”

     

                “No, now lift.”

     

                Roughly sighing, Lena heaved against the vanity and the two of them managed to drag and carry the heavy piece over to the door, wedged up against the wood. Then, Alex illuminated the room again and stole a pillow from the bed before dragging the divan away from the bed and making a bed for herself. Climbing back beneath the blankets, Lena sighed again, flat on her back as she looked up at the ceiling, the room going dark as Alex extinguished her flames. The silence was thick for a few minutes, but Lena knew she wasn’t asleep yet. There was a lump in her throat, and she couldn’t stop herself from speaking, the weight of her unshared thoughts unbearable. 

                

                “I miss her snoring.”

     

                With a soft sigh, Alex shifted on the divan, and Lena could hear the regret in her voice. “There are a great many things I miss about her.”

     

                “You know, last time I was here, we didn’t get on that well. I wish- I wish I hadn’t spent so much of our time together complaining, or blaming her for it. Um … we used to argue all the time, and … I would give anything to argue with her again, but I just- I regret it so much. We could’ve had more time together if I hadn’t been so awful. I was so- so ungrateful, and she took it with far more patience than I deserved.”

                

                Her eyes were stinging with tears now, that cavernous feeling of her endless grief in her chest filling her with pain. Working hard to swallow, her voice low and rough, Lena drew in shallow, ragged breaths. “I just- I miss her. I miss her so much. When will it end?”

     

                “I don’t think it ever does,” Alex softly replied.

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena drew in a shaky breath and pressed the heels of her palms to her eyes for a long moment before she dropped them and rolled over. Without another word, she pressed her face into the pillows and wished they smelled like salt and sea. Her sleep was fitful, but she slept long, indulging in a soft mattress and four walls around her after nights of sleeping on the forest floor. She didn’t feel well-rested when she woke, a heaviness to her limbs as her eyes peeled open to the darkness of the bedroom. At the sound of her stirring, she heard Alex move.

     

                “Are you awake?”

     

                Humming vaguely, Lena sat upright and rubbed her eyes. She could’ve done with a few more hours, her eyes prickling and her shoulders slumped, but Alex was on her feet, asking her to help shift the vanity away from the door again. Disgruntled, Lena helped drag it away, just enough for them to slip through so they wouldn’t have to repeat it all again come bedtime, and trailed her to the front door. Despite the relative ease of feeling the world around her now, everything at her beck and call, Lena was still a little muddled as she tried to remove the roots, taking a few minutes to coax the roots away, before Alex insisted on preceding her out of the room, knife in hand.

     

                “Which way to breakfast?” Alex asked, head turning back and forth as she cleared the hallway.

     

                Lena set off, her guard following at her side, and led them through the hallways to the large room where she’d spent every morning dining with Lillian and Kara, ravens flapping about as they were fed slivers of raw meat, the silence or snide conversation grating against Lena’s nerves. She passed by a few servants, all of them bowing and retreating to the shadows, armfuls of firewood or clean sheets as they went about their tasks, and Alex watched them like a hawk. 

     

                When they found their way to the dining hall, they found it empty of people and food, the table bare, the chairs all neatly pushed in. Stepping back out of it, Alex was looking about for a servant, when a handful of them appeared, slightly breathless, deferential as they bowed their heads and carried an assortment of food, drink and servingware into the room. Apparently, whispers still spread just as fast, the unseen servants scurrying about to do her bidding without being asked - and this time, it was her bidding, and not that of her mother’s. Despite being a Princess, she hadn’t been afforded the full power of that, at Lillian’s mercy, until she’d left.

     

                She hesitated before taking the large seat at the head of the table, the one Lillian had always occupied. It seemed imperative that she entrench herself in everyone’s mind as Queen, so there could be no doubting her authority, of the role she played in the Unseelie Court. It seemed they responded better to strength than humility, so she took her seat, with Alex at her right hand, and let them continue to lay the table with the spread of food. Lena was still wearing her dressing gown, no clothes at hand to get changed into, and she slumped in the large chair, clutching the arms of it as she watched them come and go without a word. They left the doors open, and Lena sighed once the two of them were alone, leaning forward and reaching for a pitcher of water and pouring a cupful.

     

                When she went to take a sip, Alex let out a sharp sound of warning, scowling at her as she snatched the cup and took a sip. Rolling the taste around her mouth, she nodded and set it down as Lena spluttered. “What if that had been poison?”

     

                “Then I would have saved your life.”

     

                “Well, I’d rather innocent people not die for me.”

     

                Alex gave her a thin smile. “Fret not, I’m not that innocent.”

     

                “It’s not funny. What if you’d died? Do you think I’d be glad that I was alive?”

     

                “I would hope so.”

     

                As they bickered, Alex started to take a piece of everything on display, taking small bites as Lena fumed. When she tried to follow suit, her hands were slapped away again, and she huffed, throwing her hands up in a helpless gesture of annoyance. It was then that she realised Alex was acting as her poison tester that morning, for lack of another person available, and she was already too far into it for Lena to stop her. Although she hoped that if she was poisoned by it, Lena could remedy it fast enough to save her.

     

                But after ten minutes, nothing was amiss, so Alex let her have some breakfast. Helping herself to food, if only for the strength to keep going, to not drain herself completely, Lena slathered bread with butter and jam, ate an assortment of fresh fruit and helped herself to a cup of tea. Kara wasn’t there to peel her boiled eggs for her, so Lena did that task herself with a lump caught in her throat. Alex didn’t pester her with questions, so breakfast was a rather quiet affair, the servants occasionally coming and going to take platters, bring fresh tea and water, and another loaf of bread, still steaming from the kitchen ovens.

     

                A woman was swapping out another pot of tea, filling Lena’s empty cup and then setting the pot down in front of her, before she continued to clear away an empty teapot. Lena reached for her tea and caught a whiff of it as she half-raised it to her lips, the smell of something faintly bitter and woody hitting her nose. Hesitating as her stomach turned, sickening familiarity making her clam up, Lena set her cup down and cleared her throat, gesturing to her plate.

     

                “You may take this as well.”

     

                The woman glanced over to her and ducked her head, straying closer and reaching out to take it as Lena picked up a sharp knife, as if to add it to her plate. Instead, as the young woman’s hand reached out, Lena slammed the knife through the back of it and deep into the wooden table. A hoarse shout of agony escaped the woman as she dropped the empty teapot, the dregs splattering over the floor as the crockery shattered, blood seeping from the through-and-through wound as Alex shot to her feet, alarmed, confused. 

     

                Lena let go of the knife pinning the servant’s hand to the table and grabbed her other wrist and a fistful of her hair, forcing her head back. The woman bared her teeth, and Lena’s face was hard with anger and a small bit of panic, too, a little bit of fear. “I might not be the most proficient in poisons, but the smell of Dar-Essa isn’t one I’m likely to forget anytime soon. A grave mistake on your part to have picked the one poison I’m well acquainted with to put in my tea.”

     

                Alex was behind the woman then, her long knife pressed to the underside of her jaw, the keen edge drawing a few beads of blood as she silently fumed. She looked doubly annoyed that Lena had been about to take a sip of untested tea, but she kept her chastising to herself for the time being. Letting go of the woman’s hair but keeping a firm grasp on her right wrist, feeling the small bones grind against each other, Lena’s eyes ran over her face. She didn’t recognise her.

     

                “What’s your name?”

     

                The woman didn’t respond, breathing quickly through parted lips as she looked at Lena with wide eyes, full of fear. Alex adjusted the angle of the knife against her throat as she spoke in a low voice.

     

                “Her Majesty asked you a question.”

     

                Still, no response was forthcoming. Lena let out a huff of laughter, the corners of her mouth quirked into a smile as she studied the woman’s face. For a long minute, her heartbeat filled her ears, and Lena tried to school it into a calm drum as she reminded herself that she had the upper hand in the situation. Softly clearing her throat, Lena then sighed heavily.

     

                “My sister, here, believes that in search of peace, I must shed a little more blood to achieve it. That is not my wish, but if you aren’t quick to speak, my patience will wear thin, and you will find yourself the first to have your blood spilt. If you tell me what I wish to know, I may be lenient.”

     

                “You lie. You’re going to kill me anyway,” the woman rasped.

     

                “No, I’m not. That will depend on your compliance. Now, what is your name?”

     

                “Alanna.”

     

                “Alanna. Right. And who instructed you to poison my tea?”

     

                Licking her lips, the young woman masked a wince of pain as she swallowed, the knife pressing firmly against her larynx. A bead of blood rolled down her neck. “I do not know their name. I was merely given the flowers by someone I met in the forest.”

     

                “Met them where?”

     

                “In a valley to the south-east. Where the rowan tree grove hides the bones of the last Seelie invasion.”

     

                “What did they look like?”

     

                “I- I don’t know. They never took their mask off.”

     

                It confirmed what Lena already knew. It was unlikely it was her brother - she thought he might come directly to her if she was so close within reach - but one of his lackeys with a golden mask. She thought it likely they’d shaved their head, too, done with the Courts, following his new creed of bleeding their kind until he had total control. 

     

                “When was this?”

     

                “Last autumn,” the woman rasped.

     

                “Last autumn?”

     

                “Yes. When you left for the Seelie Court. I was- I was ordered to … do it if you ever returned.”

     

                Alex scoffed, her brow furrowed as a muscle twitched in her jaw. “What oaths did you swear?”

     

                “None. I was promised-”

     

                “What?” Alex demanded.

     

                “I was promised … power. Wealth. Status.”

     

                “Greed is against our ethos,” Alex softly snarled. “If that is what you wished for, there were other ways to attain it, without harming your Queen. If you had but told her, come to her with this information, you would have been rewarded for your loyalty. Instead, it has cost you your life, without the satisfaction of sated greed.”

     

                Lena still had hold of the woman’s wrist, her other hand gripping the knife to keep it pinned, so she was slow to react as Alex cut Alanna’s throat. Blood was hot and thick as it sprayed the front of Lena’s dressing gown in what was an increasingly familiar act, making her stiffen at the warm flecks striking her cheeks. Anger flashed through her as the woman gurgled, choking on her own blood as she sagged. Wrenching the knife from her hand and letting go of her wrist, Lena turned her ire on Alex.

     

                “Why did you do that?” she flatly asked, green eyes flashing with annoyance. “I told her I’d let her live.”

     

                “No, you did not specify that exactly. And I did not promise her anything. A fortunate thing, at that, as it would not be wise to let your brother’s spies live. Or have you listened to nothing I have said? Here. Quickly.”

     

                Alex grabbed Lena’s arm and tugged her closer, pressing her hand to Alanna’s throat, then grabbed her other arm and knocked the knife out of it, so that Lena was essentially putting pressure on the fatal wound. It wasn’t to attempt to save her, though; Alex was more concerned with Lena’s hands staining red. Satisfied, she brushed Lena’s hands aside and then pushed her long knife into her palm, before reaching down to grab a fistful of Alanna’s dress and dragging her out of the room.

     

                “What are you doing?” Lena hissed, hurrying after her, furtively looking about, as if she might be found guilty, complicit.

     

                “What is necessary,” Alex softly snapped, glancing over her shoulder, before she impatiently gestured ahead. “Now, you walk us outside and we will let them see you covered in blood with a dead spy at your feet, and we will burn her body, as is done to those without honour. It will be an effective message; it will show your strength.”

     

                “This is not where my strength lies. I hate killing people, you know that I do.”

     

                “Yes, yes, your strengths are in other qualities, but they will not see the merit in flowers and healing. You cannot win a war with love and mercy.”

     

                “Wha- I- yes. Yes, I think you can win a war with mercy.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively as she trailed after Lena with the dead body towed behind her, Alex sighed. “You can rule with mercy. To rule, you must first win. And to win, you must defeat your enemies. Now, you can have others do that for you, but it is always best for them to believe that you are capable of it yourself. Then, they may not be so bold moving forward.”

     

                “She was hardly fucking bold. She slipped poison into my tea.”

     

                “A coward, as well as foolish.”

     

                “I won’t kill everyone who disagrees with me.”

     

                “A prospect I am most grateful for,” Alex said with a fleeting smile.

     

                Scoffing, Lena continued to march through the warren of hallways, until she led them out into the early morning. The forest was cool, trees rustling and groaning as they fed on her power, and she followed a rugged, mossy path as night blurred into day, the light still holding a bluish quality to it. Everything was damp and cool, dew speckling the vivid green of ferns, ivy and leaves, birdcalls coming from the dappling shade of the canopy as birds flitted between branches. There was a sweetness to the fresh air, flowers and berries tasted on her tongue as she drew in deep lungfuls, trying to keep her breakfast down as she trampled across leaves and needles, the heady perfume of late summer apples softening as the season passed, making her feel slightly nauseous. 

     

                There were few about, and Lena hoped she didn’t look as wretched as she felt, biting the inside of her lip as she kept walking, wondering when Alex would tell her to stop. She tasted blood in her mouth, biting too deep, and she had to clench both hands into fists to stop them from shaking from her close brush with death, the knife clutched tightly in her grasp. A couple of early risers slipped away, and then reappeared, a few more gathering with them, eyes watching from the shadows as she walked through the quiet forest at early morning. Bees droned, cherries hung densely on branches, alongside trees of pears and hazelnuts, everything blooming as anger, fear, and grief radiated from her, everything answering her beckoning call. Including the forest floor, trembling slightly beneath each footstep, summoning more and more, as they came to see what the disturbance was.

     

                It was merely their new Queen, painted in blood up to her wrists with a dead woman dragged after her by a fierce-looking guard. Making for the lake, for the throne, thinking it a good place to enact her punishment, to create a spectacle, Lena followed the sound of trickling water from the lapping lake, a peaceful sanctuary soon to be sullied by death. Only a dozen people were around to trail them there, curious whispers pricking Lena’s ears, and she walked along the roots of the tree to sit on her new throne as Alex arranged Alanna on the ground at the edge of the lake. 

     

                Alex gave her a slight nod, and Lena raised her chin a fraction, drawing in a breath as she steeled herself, raising her voice so it would carry just a little. With a nod, she gestured for Alex to continue, speaking as her sister-in-law set both hands aflame and denied the would-be-assassin an honourable burial as she drove home her warning for the Unseelie to spread.

    Chapter 48

                Taking Alex’s advice, Lena took more precautions. The servants were all questioned by Alex, two put into the dungeons, and Jack freely spoke binding oaths that made them willing to entrust Lena’s safety to him, building her personal guards to two. Jess became a second shadow as well, following Lena everywhere, insisting on testing her food, fetching dresses and jewels from her old quarters, Lena feeling a sense of deja vu at being in the Unseelie Court at the turning of the seasons, late summer indistinguishable from early autumn, recalling her memory to this time last year. But last year, Kara had been there with her, and Lena hadn’t had to worry about the running of a Court, although nothing much had changed about the possibility of death, she supposed.

     

                They spent that night inside, holed up in her mother’s office once more, a lit brazier and candlelight illuminating the dark space as Lena and Alex pored over maps of the Unseelie Court, getting their bearings, understanding the layout of the terrain, and the size of it. It was half the size of the Seelie Court, which they’d suspected from their travels, so much quicker to almost reach the river from the coast, but it helped them take stock of things. Jack wasn’t very knowledgeable about the military tactics employed by the Unseelie, but Alex was able to pinpoint a few key holding points where she’d skirmished with them over the decades. Jess kept their goblets filled, fetched dinner with her own hands, and offered up information that had slowly reached the coast over the years, news and rumours of movements of their forces, where fights had taken place, and suspected numbers. It wasn’t enough, but it was a start.

     

                It was late when they all retired, and Lena bid them both retire in her suite, Jack taking the sofa in the open sitting area, Jess taking the other bedroom, and Lena resigning herself to Alex sleeping on the divan once more as she barricaded them inside. While she didn’t know the other two that well at all, she knew them better than the few who remained behind, any familiar faces she might’ve recalled from her last stay were nowhere to be seen, so Lena was more inclined to rely on them. She had very few friends, even in the Seelie Court, and she could feel the net drawing in tighter.

     

                Waking early to the sheets tangled around her legs, feeling hot in the confines of the dark room, the smell of earth making her feel like she was in a grave, she kicked them off in frustration. Running a hand over her clammy face, her heart racing, she tried to shake off the lingering memory of her dreams of Kara. Squeezing her eyes shut, Lena pressed her fingertips to her eyelids and breathed slowly through her mouth. She heard the sound of Alex shifting then, her voice thick with sleep as she spoke.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena unhappily replied, rubbing her brow. “My mind … wanders.”

     

                Lying back against the pillows, she let out a weary sigh, feeling exhausted again, unable to get comfortable. She wasn’t sure what time it was, but she didn’t get out of bed, somehow finding her way back to sleep for a while longer, recovering from the forest draining so much of her strength. The next time she woke, her eyelids felt heavier, aching for more sleep, but she could tell by the sound of Alex’s breathing that she wasn’t asleep, so Lena got up, both of them shifting the vanity away from the door. 

     

                They emerged to the sight of Jack and Jess waiting patiently in the sitting room. Breakfast had already been arranged, and Jess was sipping a cup of tea, while Jack was absentmindedly keeping the pit of a cherry spinning in a little vortex of wind in his cupped palm. They looked over at the door as Lena followed Alex out of the bedroom, both hurrying to their feet, while Lena just exasperatedly waved a hand at them, a silent order for them to be at ease. They seemed to think she was authoritative, but she felt so small, so uncertain, and she didn’t have the patience or energy to act that part, with all the deference and respect it came with.

     

                Crossing over to the laid table, Lena dropped onto a seat and sighed, glancing at the teapot, which was still faintly steaming. Pouring herself a cup, she took a sip, the tea warm but not particularly hot, and then tipped her head back, eyes closing. The only sound in the room was the chair across from her being dragged out as Alex joined her at the round dining table set towards the back of the sitting area, and they dwelled in silence for a minute before Jack hesitantly cleared his throat.

     

                “Forgive me, Your Majesty, but you ought to know that General Rhea has returned from the border. A messenger arrived this morning to advise you that she waits at your leisure for you to receive her.”

     

                Straightening up, Lena glanced at him, her shoulders slumping with exhaustion, her face equally as drawn. “General Rhea. Right. And who is that?”

     

                “The nearest of your three Generals, from what I gathered. Her forces return at a slower pace in her wake.”

     

                “From my time amongst the servants this morning, the Court gossip is that she is Seelie by birth, and defected half a century ago,” Jess quietly provided.

     

                Alex groaned, slapping her palm on the table. “I know of her, although we never met. She is Mon-El’s mother,” Alex told Lena. “A frightening woman, or so I am told. Power hungry and not satisfied with the democracy of our own Seelie Council.”

     

                “And, what, she thought she’d have more power serving a monarch instead,” Lena scoffed.

     

                “So it would seem. Admittedly, she was not incorrect in that belief; she was not a General in the Seelie Court, but has become so here.”

     

                “And why am I supposed to receive her?”

     

                “Well, given that you are Queen now, and she your subject, admittedly a rather important one, I suppose she would like an explanation, perhaps new orders, or gratitude, even.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena grimaced and picked up her cup of tea again, taking another sip. “I don’t have any orders.”

     

                “Then focus on explaining, and thanking her. Do not slight your Generals; they will have more sway over soldiers than you do. A coup is all we need now.”

     

                Lips twitching slightly, Lena felt a pang of pain in her chest. “I have been warned away from coups. Although that warning was more against committing them myself. I’ll try my hardest not to offend anyone, but I make no promises.”

     

                “Then we should make sure you’re appropriately armoured,” Alex scoffed. “Just in case she decides regicide would be a better use of her talents.”

     

                “I don’t think that’s a good idea. I mean, she’s a General, being recalled by her new Queen. If you don’t want me to slight her, I think showing up in armour when I’m blatantly not a warrior might be a bad way to go about that. If there’s one thing I know about Unseelie, it’s their pride.”

     

                “I hope you include yourself in that. And you have seen battle, have killed; I think that would qualify you to wear armour.”

     

                “I don’t think she will think the same.”

     

                Waving a dismissive hand, Alex sighed. “Fine, then you will just wear your mail. At the very least, if she tries to stick a knife in your side, it will be harder for her to do it.”

     

                “Fine.”

     

                Jess had climbed to her feet at the first mention of armour and returned with an armful of Lena’s from where she’d taken it after it had been shed for a bath. All of it was clean and polished, and her new attendant started to lay everything out on the sofa, while Lena watched her and bit into a strawberry. She finished her bite and then softly sighed before climbing to her feet, crossing over to the sofa to pick up her chainmail, the scratched and scuffed leather surcoat, and the washed gambeson for some padding. Retreating to her room, taking a lit candle with her, Lena changed in the dark, keeping on the leggings and billowing shirt she was wearing beneath her dressing gown. Her sword was next to the divan, and she unbuckled it from the belt, keeping only the dagger attached, before she belted it around her waist.

     

                Exiting the bedroom, Lena met Alex’s gaze and raised her eyebrows. Sighing as she rubbed her brow, Alex gestured to Jess without looking at the young woman. “Will you attend to her hair, please. Anything will be an improvement.”

     

                Scowling, Lena teased her fingers through the dark, tangled waves as Jess hurried to her feet. Letting the young woman coax her through to the room she’d taken, Lena found herself sitting at the vanity as Jess fetched a comb from her packed bag and started to neaten up the tangled knots of her hair for her. Neatly braiding a few sections with deft fingers, she stepped away, and Lena rose from the low bench, returning to the main sitting area of the suite and spreading her arms exasperatedly.

     

                “Satisfied?”

     

                “You will suffice. Come. You should not keep her waiting long. It is unseemly.”

     

                “I thought Queens did what they pleased,” Lena grumbled, smoothing a hand over the embroidered surcoat, her fingers finding the little stitched lily of the valley flowers and thinking of her wife, as she always was.

     

                “They do. That does not mean it isn’t unseemly to be seen as self-important and inconsiderate. If you wish to change the perception of what it is to be Queen of the Unseelie, I should start there if I were you.”

                

                “Well, thanks to you, their perception is that I kill people and burn their bodies.”

     

                “That was necessary, and she was a traitor. And you have recalled your armies; that is a display of peace that cannot be denied.”

     

                “They might think me very stupid for it.”

     

                “Yes, I suspect many will.”

     

                “You’re not very good at this comforting or reassuring thing.”

     

                “I can be, but I don’t find it necessary at present,” Alex off-handedly replied as she kept pace with Lena, both of them walking down the hallway, with Jess and Jack in their wake. “Where are we going?”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured, her face crumpling. “I don’t know, actually. Um … Jess? Where did they put her?”

     

                “She is waiting at your throne, Your Majesty.”

     

                “Right. Of course,” Lena murmured, setting her shoulders and nodding. Then her shoulders went slightly slack, and she came to a stop, glancing over her shoulder. “Actually, could you fetch her for me? Bring her to the room with mosaics. Do you know it?”

     

                “I do, Your Majesty. I will bring her right away.”

     

                Her attendant sped off, and Lena rubbed her brow before she set off again. Navigating through the warren of passageways, she made for the chamber where she’d spent countless hours being trained in sword fighting. Jack took up a guard position outside of the double doors, and Alex shut them behind the two of them and started to prowl around the circular chamber, studying the mosaics as Lena waited patiently with her hands clasped behind her back. She kept her back to the door, standing in the middle of the room with her eyes closed, memories flooding in.

     

                That was the worst part about being back there. Out in the forest, or on the coast, Lena only had to contend with the agony of her grief, nothing familiar in the places she was passing through for the first time. But at the seat of the Unseelie Court, they’d spent an entire autumn together, passing through numerous rooms of the place as Lena was given a rather thorough education and made to sit down for breakfasts and dinners with her mother and her wife, went on bracing walks through the forest, climbing trees together or just enjoying the vivid greenery. Kara was in all of it, in everything, to the point where Lena couldn’t move an inch within those halls without being reminded of the memories, on top of the suffocating grief. It was numbing, in a sense, too much for her to process as she existed in a haze of painful misery. It was locked behind a rather impassive expression most of the time, but it bled out of her, the rich vibrance of the forest a sure sign of it, as her powers fed it all and brought new life back to that which should have been winding down for the autumn and winter months.

     

                Five minutes passed before the doors opened behind her, and Lena shook off the ghosts of memories, her eyes snapping open as she turned. Her first glimpse of Rhea revealed a tall, intimidating woman in scratched but gleaming armour wrought with thorns. A maroon cloak fell from her shoulders as she walked into the room with a smile on her lips, dark eyes assessing. There was something about her that reminded Lena of Lillian, and she knew that Alex had been right; she didn’t want to slight this woman.

     

                “General Rhea,” Lena quietly greeted her, bare feet moving a step forward.

     

                The doors shut behind the General, who offered her a quick bow of her head, “Your Majesty.”

     

                “Thank you for your patience, and your swift return. I had not expected you so soon.”

     

                “I admit, I was surprised to hear that we had a new Queen. It seemed prudent to return and see for myself.”

     

                “And are you satisfied that I am the true heir of my mother?” Lena spread her hands slightly, as if encouraging her to take her measure.

     

                Rhea’s dark gaze flitted over her. “Yes, I believe you to be so. I have laid eyes on your father’s lover before; you are made in her image.”

     

                Lena kept her expression neutral as this woman pointed out the circumstances of her birth. It wasn’t a secret, of course, but most weren’t so brazen as to say it unless she was being insulted. She wasn’t sure if that was the case, didn’t know what to make of this woman yet. 

     

                “There is something of Lillian in me as well,” Lena replied. “And I’m hoping my mother’s judgment was sound when appointing you as one of her Generals, and that my trust in you will also be sound.”

     

                “I am loyal to my ruler,” Rhea smoothly said, bowing her head slightly. “My soldiers retreat from the river, as you requested. They await further orders - as do I.”

     

                “They should return to their homes.”

     

                “Are those my orders, Your Majesty?”

     

                “I- well, I’m asking , not ordering. But … there’s a place I would like to go to; if you could take me there, I would appreciate it.”

     

                “If that is your will, then I will guide you.”

     

                Nodding, Lena rubbed her brow and then dropped her hand, making her raise her chin a fraction, squaring her shoulders, trying not to look so bowed beneath her grief, her worries. “Thank you. We’ll leave as soon as you’re rested enough.”

     

                “May I ask where you intend to go?”

     

                “There’s a valley of rowan trees, where we battled the Seelie the last time they crossed the river in force. That’s where I wish to go.”

     

                “I know it. And how many companies will be required?”

     

                “None. A small party will suffice. It will be us, my sister, and the two outside. Perhaps no more than five of your best, if you think it wise.”

     

                “Your wife will not be joining us?” Rhea asked, her eyes scanning the room, as if she might’ve overlooked Kara.

     

                A lump rose in Lena’s throat, and she blinked in surprise, her lips parting as she drew in a short breath. “My wife is dead.”

     

                A scathing scoff worked up Rhea’s throat as she raised her eyebrows, speaking before she thought. “I very much doubt that the General of the North has died, and word has not reached me. It is more likely that she has found some puddle to crawl into to lick her wounds.”

     

                Lena felt anger pulse through her, white-hot, and heard the sound of Alex’s footsteps storming towards them. She held a hand up to stop her without looking, her eyes glued to the General’s face. “I suggest you watch your tongue when you speak about my late wife. I am forgiving about many things, but speaking ill of her is not one of them.”

     

                Bristling at being chastened by the young Queen, Rhea jutted her chin forward. She didn’t apologise, no bowing or scraping from her, and Lena respected that a little, even if she found she didn’t particularly like the woman. There was something about that woman that made Lena think Alex had been right to force her into chainmail, although her words had only been compliant so far. 

     

                “As it is, I watched her die with my own eyes and held her in my arms. If word has not reached you … well, there was no Unseelie about at the time.”

     

                “It is as you say,” Rhea easily agreed. “We will leave with the dawn, if that pleases you.”

     

                “You don’t wish to stay and rest a couple of days first?”

     

                “I am not in need of rest, Your Majesty. A poor General I would be, to have worn myself out from not half a day’s travel.”

     

                “Then dawn it is. Thank you.”

     

                Inclining her head, Rhea’s gaze flitted to Alex, who hung back behind Lena’s right shoulder, and then back to Lena. “Your Majesty.”

     

                Walking over to the door, jerking open one half, Rhea left, closing the door behind her. They listened to her footsteps retreat, and Lena rounded on Alex, closing her eyes momentarily as she sighed heavily. Gesturing helplessly, she shook her head. “That could have gone better.”

     

                “A loathsome woman,” Alex scoffed, a dark look on her face. “I’m sure the Seelie Court were glad to see the back of her. A pity we’re too honourable to have put a knife in it as she departed.”

     

                “She wasn’t so bad. It just … could’ve gone better. Could’ve been worse, too.”

     

                “I suppose it could, at that.”

     

                “Come,” Lena sighed. “We need to prepare to leave in the morning. I was hoping she’d say she needed a bit longer, but … well, maybe it’s better to get it over and done with.”

     

                “What do you hope to achieve with this?”

     

                “I don’t know. Answers? Maybe someone will be there.”

     

                Alex trailed her out of the room, Jack and Jess perking up and falling into step behind them as Lena swept out of the chamber. “You should not have allowed her to bring five of her own. It leaves us outnumbered. Perhaps one to four, unless we are certain in our trust of your new companions.”

     

                She turned to glance at both of them, walking backwards for a few steps as she gave them scrutinising glances. Jack and Jess both seemed mildly surprised but not offended, and Lena scoffed, rolling her eyes as she grabbed Alex’s arm and turned her back around.

     

                “I can’t see daggers in the dark at every opportunity. Besides, they’ve had plenty of opportunities to kill us and they haven’t.”

     

                “Yet,” Alex mused, glancing over her shoulder to arch an eyebrow at Jack, who gave her a charming grin. “Perhaps that is because they knew they would be outmatched. By me - you’re still somewhat abysmal with a sword. I’m unsure why she went through the pains of having one made for you.”

     

                “For appearances. Obviously. We all know I’m better with a bow when it comes to it.”

     

                “Well, let us hope it doesn’t come to it. I don’t like our chances very much. We shall all have to watch our backs.”

     

                “When do we ever not have to?”

     

                “Yes, it does rather seem like that,” Alex murmured with a troubled look on her face as she rubbed her chin. “We shall find you a bow to take tomorrow, though. When it comes to it, if you can put an arrow in even just one of them, that will help even the odds.”

     

                Humming in agreement, running her thumb over her fingertips. She’d lost her calluses over the last six weeks, but she could still feel the weight of a bow in her hand, the weight of the string being drawn back, the way a quiver would hang across her back, full of arrows. Lena would feel more comfortable with a bow as well, regardless of whether Alex would trust her to have a sword at her side longer than half an hour anyway. The dagger she was currently wearing was already being closely watched. 

     

                Returning to their suite, Lena flopped down on the chair she’d recently vacated and reached for the cold tea, hesitating and then holding the pot out to Alex. “Would you mind?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex took the teapot from her and cradled it in her palms, heat radiating from them until steam curled from the spout. She set it down on the table, and Lena quietly thanked her, pouring a cup for herself and then Alex, holding the teapot aloft for the other two, who shifted uneasily, exchanging glances as they frowned. Rolling her eyes again, Lena just set the teapot down.

     

                “You two don’t have to stand there all the time. You can just … sit, go do something … explore or whatever. Or, you can have a cup of tea. I don’t bite.”

     

                “It wouldn’t be appropriate, Your Majesty,” Jess quietly ventured.

     

                “If it’s what I’m ordering, then how could it not be appropriate? You came with me to see more of the Court; go and enjoy your day. Tomorrow could be fraught with danger. Or one of Rhea’s soldiers could cut you down. Depending on how trustworthy she is. I’d hate to think your last day was spent standing silently in the corner, waiting for me to tell you what to do.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Jess looked a little uncertain, as if she couldn’t tell if Lena was joking or not. “Um … thank you, Your Majesty.”

     

                “Could you just call me Lena, please?”

     

                “I’m afraid not, Your Majesty.”

     

                Alex snorted, climbing to her feet and crossing the room. She gently took Jess’ arm and then beckoned for Jack to follow her, opened the door and pressed them both out into the hallway before shutting the door in their face. “Off with you both. If you want to be helpful, you can bring us food at noon, but otherwise, don’t come back until evening mealtime,” she called through the doors.

     

                Lena gave her a reproving look but felt a flicker of relief. “You could’ve let them stay if they didn’t want to go.”

     

                “But you didn’t want them to, so now they’re gone. You might unwind and speak plainly now that we’re alone.”

     

                “I’m not keeping anything hidden.”

     

                “No, but you have yet to explain what you hope to achieve with this.”

     

                “I told you - answers.”

     

                “What answers? Where your brother is? He will be too smart to sit around in one place. He hid for years without being discovered, secretly sowing discord with his Rogues, attacking people in the forest. He will not be found by asking one of his captured masked men. And will you have the stomach to do what needs to be done to get answers from them, regardless of what information they have?”

     

                “He’ll be around here somewhere,” Lena darkly murmured, taking a sip of her tea. “He will want my throne for himself, now that he hears I’ve come back. While I was gone, he could’ve stayed away, carrying out his plans while still calling himself King, but now he’ll need to come back and remove me. That’s what happened last time, when I was brought here as heir; he tried to have me kill our mother so he could kill me in turn and be free to take the throne.
