He’s been masquerading as King in all but name since she fled the Unseelie Court; I wouldn’t be surprised if half of the Court has been promised something in exchange for their loyalty to him. That I haven’t been killed yet is surprising.”

     

                “Not for a lack of trying,” Alex curtly pointed out.

     

                “No,” Lena rubbed her brow, a faint headache at her temples. She felt wretched, stress squeezing in alongside her grief, eclipsed by it but still adding to her general malaise. “I think that was merely a test, though. He likely didn’t expect it to work, and it was more of a precaution in case I did show up here. The next attempt will be well-plotted, I’m sure.”

     

                Sitting back down, Alex reached for her tea and drained half of the cup, humming disconcertingly. “I agree.”

     

                “No point worrying about that yet. We should focus on tomorrow.”

     

                “One thing, Lena; if it comes to it, your grief will be the best weapon you have, so if you must, you split the ground open and let it swallow us all whole. Your power will radiate from you, so you should be on the edge of it and be fine, but if I am amongst them, if Jack and Jess are - I know you feel obligated to care for them, and that is well and good, very noble - you must let us fall to save yourself. You have called back your army; you are the keeper of this new peace. You cannot die.”

     

                Fixing her with a piercing stare, Lena swallowed thickly. “I’m sorry, I won’t do that. If you don’t care about your own safety, then consider it for my own well-being; I can’t lose anyone else. I can’t lose you. ”

     

                “I’m no replacement for my sister,” Alex said, her eyes glassy as Lena watched her throat bob with difficulty.

     

                “I know,” she hoarsely replied. “You’re not a replacement; you’re my sister. The rest of my family. I wish Kelly were here, too. And your mother. It wouldn’t be more bearable, but … we wouldn’t be so alone.”

     

                “I wish they were here too. We’ll make it back to them once this is all over.”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched with a ghost of a smile. “That’s very optimistic.”

     

                “I will do what my sister would’ve in her stead.”

     

                Nodding slightly, Lena’s eyes prickled, and she reached for her cup of tea, taking another sip as she tried to wash down the lump in her throat. It was so unbearably difficult without Kara that she could barely stand to even mention that she was gone, the memories, the thoughts, the ache in her chest, all of it so painful. How was she supposed to keep going, keep shouldering the burden of her loss? It was debilitating; Lena could’ve slept and slept, until the end of time, until the forest sapped her of everything she was made of, until she was nothing more than bones. It was so tiring. And yet, she had to keep going. She had to do what Kara wanted, and only then could she rest.

     

                The rest of the day, she brooded and paced, self-confined to her quarters, and then made an effort to pack her things up, which had mostly been unpacked anyway. Jess had fetched her dresses, circlets and jewellery, the fine things her mother had ordered her dolled up in, as well as the simpler training gear, still beautiful but sturdier, more suited to traversing the forest. Fetching clothes for the morning, she laid it all out on the end of her bed, a lit brazier chasing away the dark and damp chill, and wasn’t disturbed, save for noon, when fresh food was carried in by Jess, who then vanished again, performing the same service at dinnertime. 

     

                No one was very talkative, and they made for a rather strange quartet, so everyone went to bed relatively early. Lena was shaken awake by Alex and blearily changed into the clothes she’d left out, before she started to buckle herself into her armour. Whatever Rhea thought, it would be stupid to wander through the forest vulnerable and an easy target. She belted on her dagger and hesitated at the sight of her sword leaning against the wall beside the divan Alex had vacated, before she belted it on anyway. That was her sword, made for her by her wife, and Lena would take it with her, even if she couldn’t use it well. Besides, it would be easier to kill herself with a dagger than a sword, and Alex would watch her like a hawk for that.

     

                Dressed, after Alex had helped her with a few of the trickier clasps and pieces of armour, Lena fastened an old cloak around her shoulders for extra warmth, and then slung her shield across her back, fussing with the fall of the cloak. Walking out of the room, she found Jack already up and dressed, giving her a neat bow.

     

                “Your Majesty. Jess has gone to fetch food to break your fast.”

     

                “Thank you. Come, sit for a moment.”

     

                She gestured to the table, and he hesitated before heeding her command, apprehensively sinking onto a chair once Lena was settled on hers. She could hear Alex moving about in the bedroom, donning sharpened hunting knives, cinching straps tight on her own armour. Clearing her throat, Lena looked at Jack, her stare appraising, assessing.

     

                “You don’t have to come today if you don’t want to.”

     

                “I would like to, Your Majesty.”

     

                “Was your life not full of enough danger for you?”

     

                “My life is quite fulfilling. I enjoyed spending time with my bees, but I would like to help bring about peace, Your Majesty. I believe in your cause; I would like to ensure your safety while you accomplish it.”

     

                “Is that what you want to do with your time? Guard me?”

     

                “It’s a worthy cause.”

     

                “It’s a shit job,” she said with a small laugh. “Practically every other person wants to kill me, you know.”

     

                He smiled, genuine warmth touching his eyes, and he dipped his chin in acknowledgement. “I have learned of that from rumours and whispers, and your sister’s stories. I suppose I will just have to be better at killing than they are. Considering you are still breathing, I shouldn’t think I need to be that good.”

     

                A ghost of a smile touched Lena’s lips, and she arched an eyebrow. “I’m not so helpless, either. I don’t enjoy it very much, but I’ve had to act in self-defence.”

     

                “It is good that you don’t enjoy it. We might have more peace because of it.”

     

                “That will depend on everyone else, as well.”

     

                Jess appeared then, her arms full as she awkwardly shouldered the doors open. Lena and Jack both rose to their feet and moved to help her, her guard beating her to it and relieving the young woman of a few wrapped bundles. There was a bow and a full quiver slung over Jess’s shoulder as well, and she slipped them off once she’d set down the laden tray she’d managed to balance. Turning to Lena, she extended them both, giving her a small smile.

     

                “I fetched these for you, Your Majesty. As you said, you prefer a bow.”

     

                A flicker of surprise shot through Lena, and she glanced at the young woman, reaching out to take them. “Thank you. That’s really thoughtful.”

     

                Setting the bow and quiver against the side of the sofa, Lena sat back down and beckoned Jess over. “Come. We should eat; dawn won’t be far off, and I don’t think we should keep General Rhea waiting.”

     

                “You’re the Queen, Your Majesty; we all wait at your leisure.”

     

                “I find that rude. And I’m too impatient, myself, so … come and sit. Quickly.”

     

                Alex appeared then, and the four of them sat at the table, the food brought for Lena and Alex split between the four of them at Lena’s insistence. She wasn’t hungry anyway, despite the way her body needed it, craved sugar and energy to keep the hollow shakiness within her at bay. Spooning porridge into her mouth, sipping tea, Lena ate quickly, eager to be off, for this to be over. The sooner she found her brother and dealt with him, the sooner she could put an end to this interminable misery.

     

                Just as keen, Alex knocked back her tea as soon as Lena was finished, and out of deference, Jack and Jess were magically finished at the same time, despite their still being food on their plates and tea cooling in their cups. Resisting the urge to insist they finish, Lena just slung her bow and quiver over her back and moved towards the doors, Alex cutting in front of her to go first, while the other two followed.

     

                The four of them walked through the hallways and out into the darkness of early morning. The first fingers of dawn were yet to pierce the canopy overhead, and Lena’s skin prickled within the shell of her armour from the chill air. Rhea was waiting for them, armoured and standing tall in the open space between towering trees. At their appearance, she gave Lena a curt bow of her head and waited for them to reach where she stood before she turned and walked half a step behind Lena as she led them off.

     

                “I have asked horses to be readied for us; my soldiers are seeing to it as we speak.”

     

                Lena inclined her head, “thank you.”

     

                “It is not so far; we will be back by nightfall, depending on your purpose there.”

     

                “I’m hoping it will be a longer trip than that.”

     

                “Very good. I had my soldiers' ready provisions, as a precaution.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Rhea smiled faintly as Lena half-turned to keep glancing at her when she spoke. “You insist there is much of Lillian in you, but you are unlike your mother in many ways; I cannot recall a time she thanked me for doing my duty.”

     

                “I think there are a great many things I hope to be better at than she was. Peace, for one.”

     

                “Ah. So, you do intend to keep us away from the border, to send us all home again.”

     

                “Wouldn’t that be a good thing?”

     

                “In a sense. But it will remove our line of defence. It is a great deal of trust to put in the Seelie to not breach our borders.”

     

                “Then it’s fortunate I do trust them. It’ll be no difference to the truce my marriage brought about. Although hopefully this one will last longer than half a year.”

     

                “You have a lot of confidence in your choice.”

     

                “I have no other choice.”

     

                “There is always another choice.”

     

                “Not in this. Not for me. I have to do it.”

     

                “Well …”

     

                Rhea didn’t say anything else, and Lena was uncertain of whether the General agreed with her or not, whether it offended her to be made superfluous to Lena’s plans. If there was no need for forces gathered along the river, ready to swap blows with the Seelie, what was the purpose of a General? They were silent the rest of the way to the structure grown out of the massive willows, the drooping branches woven together to create a circular enclosure, the smell of manure and the whickering of horses greeting them. Between parted branches, Lena glimpsed a soldier cinching a saddle tighter around a roan horse, quiet voices conversing within, and then another soldier led out a white stallion, ready to go. The soldier noticed them and his eyes ran over the group, trying to assess who his new Queen was, before taking in the way everyone was ever-so-slightly standing behind Lena and sketching her a quick bow.

     

                He let go of the reins and disappeared back through the gap, reemerging a minute later with a mare that looked almost completely black in the dark, but was slightly dappled a dark grey over the flanks. The soldier led the mare over to Lena and bowed his head again, holding the reins steady as Lena smoothed a hand over the horse’s velvety nose, letting her grow used to her before she hauled herself up into the saddle, her armour rattling as she seated herself and got as comfortable as she could. The other four soldiers were appearing now, bringing the other horses, everyone sizing themselves up accordingly, and Alex wedged herself tightly beside Lena, eyes restlessly darting around. It was obvious she was on edge, holding no trust for these Unseelie.

     

                When they set off, Rhea took the lead, one of her soldiers at her side, then another two, followed by Lena and Alex, with Jack and Jess at their backs, lesser threats in Lena’s eyes, and then two more Unseelie soldiers bringing up the rear. Their party of ten moved slowly through the trees, listening for anything stalking them, hunting them quietly through the forest, of any dangers lurking about, the other three in their group of the Earthfolk keeping track of the minute changes in the forest, of any approaching footsteps felt through the ground. 

     

                An hour passed, the miles going slowly as the forest went on, relatively unchanging as they angled south-west through the towering trees, across the occasional stream, down slopes and up inclines, skirting along the tops of sudden twisting ravines, along the bottom of mossy cliffs, picking their way around large chunks of stone, over snaking roots. The forest brightened somewhat, the air still holding a chill, everything dewy and damp, making the air smell earthier, greener, and Lena was somewhat relieved to be back out under the endless canopy. It was easier than being cooped up inside, wondering who might slip poison into her food or drinks next, who might shoot an arrow into her heart, cut her throat, or drown her in the hot springs. 

     

                Another hour passed by, and Lena sensed the building tension in their group, but it was Alex who spoke up, more attuned to these unspoken signals passed between soldiers so in sync, so comfortable around each other that a glance could convey much. Straightening a little in her saddle, Alex softly cleared her throat and leaned forward, as if speaking directly to Rhea, although her question was posed to them all.

     

                “What is it?”

     

                Rhea turned slightly in her saddle, although she didn’t turn her gaze from the forest. “Nothing.”

     

                “You have all grown tenser with each passing mile; I cannot find a reason for it, as there seems to be no danger, so what is the reason for your behaviour? If you mean to betray-”

     

                “We are tense precisely because there is no danger,” Rhea cut her off, drawing her horse to a halt, twisting around to give Alex a hard stare. “The forest … it is calm. Not quiet, but there is a peace to it that is rare, unusual. It is … placated.”

     

                Alex scowled at Lena, who shifted uncomfortably in her saddle as she avoided her gaze. Even as they paused for a moment, the forest around them flourished beyond the stretching of branches and roots, of straightening trunks and stems, seemingly emboldened by her passing. As they lingered, the leaves turned greener, canopies fuller, late summer fruits ripening. It was all because of her, because she couldn’t close off her emotions, dim the intensity of them, let it seep from her in a constant flow of grief. Even numbed to the intensity of it, used to the way it suffocated, overwhelmed her, Lena knew it was bigger than she could cope with, had to compartmentalise it to function, but the part that she let herself acknowledge was unbearable enough that she didn’t think she could feel anything else. 

     

                And yet, she had made the forest calm, her grief feeding it, taming it, like she was a lullaby sending it to sleep. She didn’t like that thought, but she felt helpless to stop herself from doing it. The hairs on her arms and the back of her neck stood up, and she glanced around uneasily, with the sudden feeling that she was being watched, that the forest was pressing in closely around her. Lena had never felt like that outdoors; it had always been freeing, soothing, but she suddenly felt exposed, under a microscope as she was fed on. Her pulse quickened, and she looked at Alex, whose annoyance quickly melted to concern.

     

                “What is it?”

     

                Shaking her head, Lena opened and closed her mouth, her jaw tightening. “I don’t know.”

     

                “We should not linger,” Rhea said, urging her horse onwards. “All is calm now, but the forest has a will of its own.”

     

                They all knew that well enough and were quick to continue. Uncomplaining and watchful, Lena couldn’t shake that brief feeling of eyes in the forest, something unseen keeping watch over her. Despite the mild day, green light filtering down, birds flitting back and forth, squirrels chittering, rabbits and mice scurrying through the carpet of leaves, Lena felt uneasy. It wasn’t the first time she’d had that feeling, but now that she’d been reminded of it, she couldn’t shake her troubled thoughts, eyes darting about, as if she’d see some figure between the trunks, some danger the others hadn’t sensed. A headache was forming behind her eyes, and she rubbed the tender spot as she hunched slightly in the saddle, her eyelids heavy, her body leaden as she felt suddenly weary.

     

                The morning passed slowly, taking an age to reach noon, to reach the place where the ground began to slope downward into a shallow valley. Despite the day brightening, warming, the floor of the valley was covered in a dense mist, obscuring what was hidden at the bottom as they crept down into it, single file now, through gnarled rowan trees covered in moss. Lena could hardly see Rhea, two horses ahead, and while her eyes were quick to adjust to the darkness, the wall of white was impenetrable, everything turned to eerie, looming shadows. 

     

                “We should leave the horses here,” Rhea said as the fog thickened. “It will not be safe for them deeper in the valley; they might easily go lame.”

     

                The General swiftly dismounted, and the others followed, Lena easing herself down with them as their armour rattled in the muffled silence. Alex stepped in close to Lena, her eyes darting around, her skin seeming ghostly in the pale gloominess, and she was already wielding a long knife in her hand, a restless tension in her wiry body. She didn’t look at Lena as she spoke, her voice a low murmur that was still audible to the rest.

     

                “I do not like it here; be wary.”

     

                Nodding, Lena slipped her bow off her back, the string taut but likely to get damp in the misty air if they lingered too long there. Silently removing an arrow from her quiver, Lena fitted the fletching to the string, holding the arrow securely in place, thumbing the stiff feather as she felt her throat go slightly dry. Leaving the horses behind, they set off on foot, the group fanning out slightly, Lena nestled somewhere in the middle with Alex on one side, Rhea on the other.

     

                “What is it you seek here?” the General quietly asked.

     

                “I’m not sure,” Lena breathed, her eyes watching the ghostly trees, mist swirling around her as they stirred up the air, the taste of something rotten getting caught at the back of her throat. The urge to vomit crept up her throat, and she worked to swallow hard. “But we’ll see.”

     

                “It is not a place to linger long,” Rhea warned her. “It is a battlefield. A few years have passed, but the forest is not done with them yet.”

     

                Lena gave her a sharp look but didn’t reply. They walked onwards, the rest of them almost wraithlike in their silence as they moved like shadows, while Lena tried her hardest but felt so noisy, her breath, her armour, her footsteps all seeming too loud to her ears. She would frighten off anyone there - if there was anyone there. Going deeper, the forest darkened, despite it being distinctly day. The rowans grew dense, the mist so oppressive that each breath felt like a mouthful, what light reached the floor of the valley dimming to almost nothing. Lena’s skin was crawling now, and she couldn’t see past her own nose, her breaths sharp and quick as she lost track of the others, had to extend a hand to blindly feel her way through the trees.

     

                A cold finger of panic trailed down her spine, and Lena turned in a slow circle, feeling as if she was being watched again, her fingertips tingling as her heart thudded. She couldn’t see Alex, and she couldn’t make her voice work, wanting to call out for her, but she knew that was a bad idea anyway. If she couldn’t see anyone, they couldn’t see her, and Lena was starting to think it had been a bad idea to come there with so few of them. Pushing onwards, she swallowed the prickle of fear in her chest and forged forward. Then she came to a stop.

     

                Through the wall of fog, she saw a shadow. It was just vaguely distinct against the blank whiteness of the valley floor, rowans twisting at strange angles, furred with moss and splattered with lichen, and the breath hitched in her throat. Rushing forward, Lena clutched her bow tightly in her fist, an arrow still pressed to the grip, nocked to the bowstring, and she lurched about with confusion, the ground sloping away from her as trees loomed out of the gloom, pulling her up short, making her stumble as she narrowly avoided running face-first into them. And around her, the forest was alive, wild and voracious, the branches and roots snaking and reaching, grasping at her as she rushed past, in pursuit of something , snagging on her hair and screeching over polished steel.

     

                She couldn’t see the shape anymore, but something was moving; she was sure of it. Lena didn’t know what to make of it, a desperate urge for it to be one of the masked fae seizing her, urging her onwards alone, undoubtedly outmatched but stubborn, angry, grieving all the same. Moving quickly, her feet crunching over damp leaves, Lena tore through brambles of thorns, so sharp they scraped her cheeks and scratched her armour, tearing her cloak and scoring her leather surcoat. Face scratched red, bleeding where the points had gouged too deep, she pushed herself through, her descent reckless, catching herself on a jagged jut of stone, sending her to the floor, rolling a short way as she snapped the arrow she’d nocked and ended up winded in a heap. 

     

                On her feet again, a few arrows short where they’d spilt out of the quiver, Lena kept going and only came to a stop when she suddenly realised she was standing in water. It was cold and slippery with algae, her feet sinking to her ankles in mud as she drew in panicked breaths, that odour of rot growing stronger as she turned, dragging her feet free, trying to make out anything in the gloomy mist. Voices shouted, muffled and distant, and she tried to move, her feet squelching through the mud, shin deep in a stagnant pool of water, swaddled by mist as she staggered onwards. Her feet kept snagging on things, on branches submerged in the shallow water, snapping under her feet, and she couldn’t see where she was going, but her skin was prickling like mad, that feeling of being watched so intense that she was starting to panic as she walked onwards through the mud, the detritus that had accumulated on the valley floor, in that pool of water, the smell so rank that she barely dared to breathe through her nose.

     

                Walking onwards, Lena walked straight into something warm and solid, something that smelled damp, like wet dog, and something very much alive. Rebounding off it, a soft grunt of surprise escaping her, she staggered back, feet splashing, and looked up as she tried to right herself. Up into the muzzle of a wolf, the mist parting around a dark nose, sniffing at her as dark eyes watched her. She couldn’t even scream, her stomach plummeting as she staggered back further, the wolf ten feet tall as it loomed over her, and then caught her foot in something and went down in a clattering of armour, snapping twigs and splashing water.

     

                Splayed in the mud and water, trapped, Lena looked up with eyes wide with fear as she struggled to stand again, the armour cumbersome, and whatever she was caught in making it harder. She didn’t want to tear her eyes away from the creature, finding it a little gangly, as if only half-grown, skittish as it drew itself lower to the ground, ears flattening against its skull. Dragging her eyes down to whatever her bow had snagged itself on as well, Lena’s stomach lurched as she realised what she’d thought were fallen branches, small twigs snapped under her feet as she’d waded through the shallow pool of water, were actually bones. So many of them, mist gathering on the surface of the water, obscuring the skeletons that lay partially submerged, except now she was down in the water with them , taking in the decomposed bodies, only scraps of flesh and hair remaining on the bleached bones of fallen warriors.

     

                It seemed stupid to be troubled by the sight of bones after treating all manner of wounds on the battleground, but Lena couldn’t stop the yelp of panic that escaped her, swallowed up by the mist. The young wolf was startled by the sound, shrinking back slightly, dark eyes watching her, muzzle parting over sharp teeth, nose twitching as it sniffed, then drew in closer. Trying to free her bow with more urgency, her heart pounding in her chest, Lena felt cold fear slide through her as she found it tangled up in a half-splintered ribcage, and yanked her dagger free instead, her hand remaining steady. A small mercy. 

     

                Holding the dagger tightly in one fist, she drew in short, sharp breaths, her heart beating so fast and hard in her chest that it was almost painful. Kicking mud and water, Lena dragged herself backwards on her elbows, water seeping into her through the gaps in her armour, frigid and dank, and she gasped at the cold that seeped into her bones. Escape was awkward and bulky in her armour, her shield and quiver still strapped to her back, making it hard to manoeuvre herself, her cloak bunching up and getting caught on bare bones, and all Lena could do was inch away as the wolf inched closer. The entire time, she waited for those sharp teeth, as long as her forearm, to snap shut around, to cut through steel with ease, and considering how badly she wanted her suffering to end, she didn’t want it to end before she’d killed her brother first.

     

                She was by no means adept at controlling the earth, but in similar life-threatening situations, when she’d finally tapped into it through fear, adrenaline, any strong emotion, it had come to her in her times of need ever since. Except this time. Lena had gotten used to feeling the forest, the earth, the plants and trees, since the loss of her wife had split her chest wide open and let her pain rush out of her, but now, when she needed it, she couldn’t feel it. Or rather, she could feel it, a certain awareness filling her, as it had for months and months, but any grasp on it was impossible. Control evaded her, much as it always had. And Lena didn’t know why the forest wouldn’t help her, why it felt so beyond her reach, despite weeks of feeding on her, so sensitive to her emotions, but she was left helpless, splayed in the water as the wolf inched closer.

     

                Closing her eyes, her jaw clenched tightly shut to stop her chin from wobbling, Lena turned her head aside and felt the warm breath of the creature on her cheek as it moved in closer. Gripping her dagger even tighter, until her knuckles were white inside her mail-backed gloves, she readied herself to plunge it into the wolf’s jugular, a last, pitiful effort to kill it before it killed her. Even if she managed that, she thought she might go down with it, the beast collapsing on top of her, if it didn’t grab her and shake her until the force rattled her to death. But it didn’t snap at her, it just sniffed, and then again, until she felt the wet press of its nose right into the apple of her cheek, flinching as she swallowed the lump in her throat. And then the slightly rasping wetness of its tongue over her bleeding scratches from the thorns.

     

                Eyelids fluttering, Lena opened her eyes and moved her head ever so slightly, so she was glancing at the wolf through the dim light of the misty valley. She felt that prickling feeling again, and her brow creased into a frown as she looked at it, taking in the dark eyes, an almost silvery sheen to them in the low light as they winked in the darkness, and she felt confused. The wolf bumped her with its snout again and then nipped at her right arm, the one still holding her dagger in hand. Jolting, Lena dropped her dagger as the breath rushed out of her, and she felt alarm shoot through her, the wolf snapping its teeth, letting out a forceful breath and sinking a little lower, almost expectant.

     

                Then its ears pricked up and it drew to its full height, turning tail and shooting off into the mist, leaving tendrils swirling around in its wake, closing back over the path it had taken through the valley. The tension bled out of Lena, and she splayed in the water as she drew in ragged breaths, covered in a cold sweat as she stared up at the thick shroud of whiteness overhead, swallowed up by the mist as she tried to make sense of what had just happened, and how she’d survived it. Wolves had attacked her numerous times since she’d come to the forest, and yet, this one had been practically docile, like a pup. Something snagged in Lena’s mind, a thought returning to her, of that wolf cub she’d saved, the one that had bitten her arm. It didn’t seem possible, but with those dark eyes and the grey pelt, it could’ve been the very same one.

     

                Ripped out of her thoughts a moment later, Lena was suddenly seized. A hand grasped the shoulder of her cloak, and Lena let out a hoarse shout as she thrashed, and then suddenly found herself dragged to her feet, bow torn from her grasp, feet sinking into mud. Blinking in surprise, Lena breathlessly found herself staring at Rhea, who held her sword in hand and was looking at her with inscrutable brown eyes. Water poured from the gaps in Lena’s armour, the sodden hem of her cloak trickling with it, and Rhea reached out to pluck a limp patch of algae from Lena’s pauldron.

     

                “Are you well?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena rasped, catching her breath as she shook water off her hands.

     

                Her attention turned to her bow, stooping to work it free from the ghostly fingers of ribs, and then she fumbled through the cloudy water for her dagger, stirring up more mud as she grasped about. Coming up empty-handed, feeling a little more urgent now, the dagger the first gift Kara had ever given her, Lena straightened and looked down into the murky water as she tried to spot it, and then saw a flash of steel in Rhea’s hands. Her head jerked to the General, who was holding Lena’s dagger, and her stomach lurched, eyes darting up to meet Rhea’s piercing stare.

     

                Lena briefly wondered whether she should try and run or if it would be better to at least raise her chin and bear it head-on, but barely a moment passed between them before Rhea flipped the dagger and caught it by the tip, extending the hilt to Lena. Warily taking it, Lena closed her fingers around the hilt and swallowed, her throat bobbing as she sheathed it at her waist.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “You should not wander alone,” Rhea replied, her eyes flitting about. “Who knows what could befall you.”

     

                “A wolf,” Lena curtly replied, swiping a hand over her face, a muscle twitching in her jaw.

     

                “A wolf?”

     

                “It must’ve heard you coming; it ran off.”

     

                Rhea seemed on edge now, glancing around, and she levelled her sword at shoulder height, settling into a rooted stance with the tip ready to thrust forward at the sound of something splashing towards them. Slipping one of her few remaining arrows from her quiver, Lena fitted it to the bowstring, damp now, and nocked, drawing back the string a little as her stomach sank. The splashing grew louder, and they couldn’t be sure of the exact direction within the muffling confines of the mist, but a moment later, a voice was added to the sounds.

     

                “Lena!”

     

                Relief shot through her, recognising the shout as belonging to Alex, and Lena started sloshing through water in the general direction of her sister-in-law’s voice. “Here!”

     

                It took five minutes of fumbling about, the General following slowly in her wake, before Alex appeared out of the mist, a little scratched up, her hair damp from the air, and her face stiff with worry. Her shoulders slumped at the sight of the Queen, and she moved towards Lena, briefly cupping her face as she nodded, the severe expression softening a little as she was likewise relieved.

     

                “You should not have gone wandering from my side,” Alex softly scolded her. “I have sworn to keep you safe; you make it a difficult task.”

     

                “I got lost. The mist, it was too thick,” Lena helplessly explained. “I’m fine, though.”

     

                “Fine? What mess have you waded into this time? You are soaked and look as if you have gone crawling through mud.”

     

                A prickle of annoyance needled her, and Lena looked down at herself, trying to flick water and mud off her hands and arms. “I’m fine.”

     

                Rhea sheathed her sword as she spoke up. “I found her ensnared by some bones. She said there was a wolf-”

     

                “A wolf?”

     

                “I will have two of mine scout ahead and behind to ensure it doesn’t attack.”

     

                “Leave it be,” Lena wearily sighed. “It didn’t do anything but lick my cheek. It could have attacked me - I know how fast and vicious they can be - but it was young, wary. Perhaps it hasn’t learnt to be afraid of us yet.”

     

                “It puts us all at risk not to take precautions. It could be anywhere in this fog.”

     

                “I assure you, it is of no harm to us.”

     

                Rhea closed her mouth, lips twitching with dissatisfaction, with derision, although she never said a word. Closing her eyes, Lena shook her head, suppressed a sigh and then set off, eager to be away from the grave of bones and armour, picked clean by all manner of life within the forest in the years since the battle there. It didn’t feel right to disturb the dead as they were.

     

                They kicked their way through mud, water and bones the rest of the way back to the sloping sides of the valley, water in Lena’s boots as she stepped out onto wet leaves, soggy underfoot. The three of them moved through the trees like wraiths, water steadily dripping from Lena as she trudged along, tired and irate, defeated by the pointless trip there. Silent, a lump caught in her throat, she held her bow tightly, an arrow still nocked, just in case, but they went about unharmed, any shadows she saw materialising into the shapes of gnarled trees as they drew nearer. The forest revealed nothing else to her, and her sharp ears picked up nothing as they drew up the sloping side of the valley.

     

                The sound of a twig snapping brought them all to a tense halt halfway up, but the soft bird whistle, mimicked by Rhea, revealed one of the soldiers, and Jess at the woman’s side, her trident clutched in her hands. Dipping her chin as she lowered her eyes, Jess reached a hand towards Lena and crooked her fingers, drawing the moisture out of Lena’s clothes, a ribbon of water glimmering in the foggy air, before she scattered it to the ground. That simple act of kindness was too much for Lena, standing in her dry but dirty clothes and armour, thinking about the times that Kara had done that very same thing for her.

     

                Suddenly, there was a burning pressure behind her eyes, and Lena blinked rapidly as she ducked her head, throat tightening as something caved in her chest. She wanted her wife. She wanted Kara at her side, to hold her hand, to hear her soft, reassuring words, to keep her safe. It was so unfair, and Lena’s grief split her in half as she let out a quiet, forceful breath, her vision blurring, even as she tried to dispel the tears.

     

                “We should keep moving,” Rhea said. “Stay close this time; Her Majesty saw wolves.”

     

                “No. No, I’m done here. Let’s go,” Lena murmured with a weary, disappointed anger, her head down, eyes fiercely stinging as she pushed onwards.

     

                They all fell into step with her, walking further up the valley, Rhea signalling to the others, hidden and scattered throughout the fog, with bird calls. By the time they heard the soft whickering of the horses, where the fog started to thin, two of the others were already converging on the place. Lena was up in her saddle in an instant, arrow slotted back into her quiver, strung bow across her back, and she held the reins in a tight fist, eager to be off, keeping her head bowed as she swallowed and swallowed, but was never able to stifle her grief.

     

                It took a while to get all ten of them on horseback, and Lena didn’t waste a second after that, spurring her horse into motion, the mare eager to get away from the lingering smell of decay, while the others all trotted after her, jostling for position. The ride back was stiff and silent, the miles passing by as a pall was cast over the group, a certain restlessness to Rhea and her soldiers at their seemingly wasted time, while Lena was too consumed by the tide of grief that had swept her away from the numb front she’d been cultivating to get through each day to even care.

     

                The forest was getting dark by the time they arrived back safely, and she dismounted her horse and strode off without a word, feeling overwhelmed by the sheer size of the forest, the magnitude of the task ahead of her, every inch of it needing to be scoured to find her brother. It felt impossible, and she was tired and cold, in the depths of her misery once more as she trudged through the trees, past fae sitting outside embroidering, playing stones, drinking wine or playing wind instruments, ignoring them as they rose to their feet at her passing. Drawing in shallow, even breaths as she tried to stamp down her feelings, Lena walked back below ground, following the steps into the burrow of passageways and rooms, and walked without thinking.

     

                It wasn’t to her new suite that she went, but the old one, directly across from it. The suite she’d shared with Kara. Defeated, Lena just wanted her, and she couldn’t have that, but her mind longed for the closest thing she could get to: a room where she’d lived, a bed where she’d slept, a desk where she’d read books, written letters. Walking straight inside, she didn’t even have time to doubt her actions, crossing the threshold and moving through to the study first, the bedroom feeling unbearable to be inside right then. But even going into the study, cold and empty, untouched since it had been tidied up after they’d left, was too much.

     

                Not a thing was out of place; the desk was made up with empty goblets and a pitcher for water or wine, a pot with cut quills, and two empty inkwells sitting on a silver tray. In the desk drawers, she’d find ink and parchment, wax to seal letters, a knife to open them, but any of the clutter they’d left behind had been tidied up, thrown away. There were no books Kara had been reading left waiting for her on the desk, no ashes in the brazier from the last fire she’d lit in there. It was a cold, lifeless room, and Lena felt so far away from her wife as she stood in the middle of the study.

     

                She felt a hot wash of rage, slamming her hands on the desk and then sweeping everything off it in a fit of anger. It wasn’t as satisfying as she would’ve liked, the goblets, pitcher and tray all made of silver, and everything else paper and parchment. Lena wanted to break something. It shocked her, the intensity of her desire to smash something, to put her fist through a pane of glass, to shatter a mirror or a mug. Yet, she was in a place of relative sturdiness, everything finely made and made to last, and the best she managed was tossing an empty clay inkwell to the floor to crack into pieces.

     

                “Fuck.”

     

                Her tears welled up then, and she couldn’t stop them now, fumbling for her bow, the quiver and shield, shedding them, tossing them angrily to the floor. Clawing at the broach pinning her cloak around her shoulders, she undid the clasp and wadded up the heavy wool into a ball, throwing it to the ground as well as she quietly sobbed.

     

                “This isn’t the end,” Alex softly insisted from the doorway. “We’ll find him. I won’t stop until we have our revenge for what he did to her.”

     

                “Please, leave me alone. Just this once, leave me alone. I don’t want to talk to you. I don’t want to be around anyone. I just- I want to be alone.”

     

                “No, that isn’t what you want. You want her.”

     

                The air fled Lena’s lungs, and she buried her face in her hands as she hunched her shoulders, a sob catching in her throat. “Don’t.”

     

                “It’s alright, Lena-”

     

                “Leave me alone.”

     

                “You know I can’t do that.”

     

                “I don’t care! I don’t care what you promised her. You should’ve let me die. You should’ve let me do it,” Lena shouted at her, whirling around. 

     

                Her wet cheeks were flushed red with anger, and she dashed tears away, her chin wobbling as she scowled at Alex. Then she fumbled with the belt around her waist, sword and dagger attached, and undid the buckle, bundling it all up and thrusting it at Alex, pressing them to her chest. Angrily wiping her face on her arm, the cold brush of steel doing little to dry her tears, Lena sniffed and gestured dismissively to the weapons.

     

                “There. You have my weapons. I can’t hurt myself with them, so leave me be. Please. I know you mean well, I just- let me be alone in my grief.”

     

                Alex’s eyes were bright with tears as she stood in front of Lena, of a height with her, and reflected her pain back to her in her agonised gaze. “You are not alone in your grief,” Alex murmured, swallowing thickly. “But I will leave you to your pain for now.”

     

                A ragged sound of relief came out of Lena, and she turned around again, moving to the desk, bracing herself against the edge of it with one hand, she covered her mouth and closed her eyes. Alex’s light footsteps slipped away, and Lena softly cried as she leaned heavily on the desk, angry and hurt, and so lost. She wasn’t sure why it was hitting her so hard then, her grief no bigger or smaller than it had been the day before, but she supposed that was how it worked - there was no rhyme or reason to how it hurt, when it would strike.

     

                “You wish to find your brother. That was the purpose of our trip?”

     

                Lena whirled around at the sound of Rhea’s voice from the doorway, backing up against the desk as her heart thundered and alarm crossed her features. She’d thought she was alone, that no one else had come in after Alex had left, but her General was light on her feet, it seemed. Wiping her cheeks, sniffing as she ducked her head, trying to hide her tears, Lena nodded. She couldn’t speak, her throat so tight, a lump caught in it, but Rhea simply stepped inside, clicking her tongue as she approached.

     

                “Sweet girl,” Rhea softly sighed, reaching out to cup Lena’s chin, urging her head up. “You should have told me. I am your General; I will see it done, I will find him for you.”

     

                Face softening with surprise as her eyebrows lifted, Lena’s lips parted as she stared at her General. It took her a moment to speak. “Really?”

     

                Lips curving into a sharp smile, Rhea wiped her tears away for her. “You are Queen; if that is your wish, you need only ask.”

    Chapter 49

                Despite her initial reservations, Lena had little choice but to trust Rhea in the following days. After all, she’d promised to find Lex, had said it in Fae, so there could be no misconstruing her words, so Lena was comfortable in their aligned interests, at least. Alex, less so, arguing with Lena behind the closed door of their shared bedroom or Lillian’s study, which Lena had commandeered now. She didn’t trust Rhea at all, unwilling to even concede that she must have been honest about her intentions to find Lex, or she would never have said it, could never have gotten the lie out. Claiming that Lena was naive, that she wasn’t suited to the intricate politics of the Courts, Alex was stubborn in her insistence that they couldn’t trust the General, nor the influx of soldiers returning from the riverbank. Lena was likewise irate as she accused Alex of being biased, of letting her opinion of the millennia-long feuding between the Courts cloud her judgment.

     

                Ordinarily, Lena would’ve stormed off, holed herself up somewhere to sulk and brood over the frustrating scenario, but in a Court she admittedly was unsafe in, with only her sister-in-law to rely on and truly trust, she was stuck alongside Alex. The two of them were quite similar in their stubbornness, their belief that they were right, and their shared grief, so it made things tense between them as they were forced into close proximity, with Alex having to go along with Lena’s plans. She couldn’t leave her behind, no matter how unhappy she was, how little she trusted Rhea, so Alex was left keeping a close eye on her, a most attentive guard, holding to her promises to her sister with the utmost devotion, in her memory. 

     

                And Lena felt so helpless, Rhea insisting she remain behind, leaving a few select soldiers in charge of protecting Lena, while she took only a handful with her as well. Alex cautioned Lena against that too, unwilling to trust soldiers picked by someone she also didn’t trust, trying to talk Lena into picking her own from the Unseelie who’d remained behind, who weren’t under the command of another, although, ultimately, their command was under Lena. It was how Lena tried to placate her, reasoning that they would obey her as their Queen, even if Rhea was their General. Still, even she had to admit that it made her uneasy to have them shadowing her, along with Jack and Alex. 

     

                She’d taken it upon herself to go and walk amongst the other soldiers, though, trying to make herself useful while she waited, tending to the injured as she stitched up gaping wounds, applied poultices, bandages, brewed teas and stained her armour and surcoat with more blood. None of that mattered, only that she might help alleviate the pain of a few more people, save a few more lives, after so much bloodshed and suffering. They all looked at her like she’d gone mad, toiling alongside other healers beneath a Queen, but no one said a word, letting her do as she pleased, because she was their Queen, even if they didn’t know what to make of her. It was good work, tiring and long, and something Lena was good at, despite her limited practical training, but where she lapsed, the trained healers filled in, and her knowledge of plants more than made up for her shortcomings as she spent her spare time wandering the fringes of the seat of the Unseelie Court, plucking chamomile, yarrow, wild garlic and comfrey, anything that could be used as it sprouted around her, feeding on the constant river of grief. No amount of exhaustion could stop that, only banish it to the back of her mind for a time.

     

                At it again, kneeling in the damp earth and leaves at the tents and shelters erected throughout the trees at the fringes of the dwelling, Lena was placing maggots onto an infected abdominal wound with bloody hands, arguing with one of the healers, who seemed horrified by her methods, when the sound of horses and shouts reached them. Remaining knelt in the dirt, Alex, Jack and Jess all hovering about, watching over her, while her other guards milled about, stiff and silent, Lena continued to place the maggots she’d had brought to her. The man she was tending to was pale and feverish, and she’d had to give him a strong tea to knock him out, the infection and pain sapping his strength. He slept now, and she didn’t think the wound was too bad, hoping the maggots would break down the worst of the infected tissue so it could start healing properly. Rhea found her there ten minutes later, muddy and tall in her armour as she stepped through the soldiers to stand over Lena.

     

                “Rhea,” Lena said with desperation, hurrying to her feet, eyes wide and hopeful. “Any news?”

     

                “Your Majesty,” Rhea replied with a curt bow of her head. “Nothing of importance. With soldiers returning home, there is much disturbance in the forest. It is making it rather hard to conduct my task. It may interest you to know that I crossed paths with Rama Khan several days past; he is your General-”

     

                “I’m familiar. Thank you.”

     

                Bristling a little as Lena cut her off, Rhea’s mouth tightened at the corners, and she appraised Lena and the man she’d been kneeling beside. “You have been keeping busy in my absence. I had not known you were a healer.”

     

                “Not much of one, but I’m trying to learn, and making myself useful with what I know,” Lena replied with a thin smile.

     

                “She was placing maggots in his abdomen, General,” one of the soldiers piped up.

     

                He was one of the ones left behind to guard Lena, and she shot him a disgruntled look, taking the cloth Jess held out to her to wipe her bloody hands. “Yes, I was,” Lena curtly replied, looking down as she tried to work the blood out of the grooves of her palms and knuckles. “It’s a method to clean infected wounds, used for centuries in my world. Until better methods were created. It seems maggots aren’t in use here, yet, based on the reactions from both this Court and the Seelie.”

     

                She looked up and gave Rhea another thin smile, taking in the faint look of disgust and apprehension. “And you believe your human methods are better? I have visited your world for a time in my youth; a noisy and polluted place, with too much iron for me to enjoy it. I did not think it superior to our world, here, in any conceivable way, but I did not know their healing practices included maggots.”

     

                “Fortunately, my sister has knowledge of their practices,” Alex replied with a little steel in her voice, and a little bit of pride, too. “She has applied it to wounded soldiers in the Seelie Court, and infected wounds that should have been fatal recovered well from the method. I would not disregard your Queen so quickly; she may surprise you yet, General.”

     

                “Her Majesty already surprises me,” Rhea smoothly responded, hands clasped behind her back. “I am sure she will continue to surprise me, as well. I hope I may surprise her in return. Not all Unseelie are the same.”

     

                Lena pulled her gloves from her belt and worked one on, and then the other, before speaking. “I already know that. I don’t discount your value just because you defected to this Court. It’s my Court as well, even if I was taken from here at a young age.”

     

                “Of course, Your Majesty. As Queen, it belongs to you, regardless of your upbringing,” Rhea easily conceded.

     

                “Shall we return to my halls to discuss your travels?” Lena suggested, changing the topic as she gestured in the direction of her warren of rooms and tunnels. “Perhaps over tea - or wine if you would prefer.”

     

                “If it pleases you.”

     

                Lena turned to Jess and asked her to go ahead and prepare something to eat and drink for Rhea, before they followed at a slower pace, Rhea half a step behind Lena on her left, Alex on her right, and the soldiers fanned out behind them. It was a silent and tense return, no niceties forthcoming from Rhea, with Lena giving up on her politeness after asking after her well-being and being given a brusque answer. They walked the remaining distance without further attempts at conversation until they reached Lena’s study, and she shut herself inside with Alex and Rhea.

     

                Rounding the large desk, Lena eased herself down onto the chair behind it, her aching body grateful for the rest after hours of tending to the sick and injured. They dwelled in silence, both women standing across the desk, with a wide gap between them, before Lena blinked in surprise, gesturing to a comfortable chair in the corner.

     

                “Please, sit. Bring it a little closer; Jess will be back with a tray soon.”

     

                “The General may have it. I’ll stand,” Alex said, her arms crossed over her chest as she leaned against the wall beside the door, her eyes fixed on Rhea.

     

                Taking the chair and dragging it over to the desk, Rhea settled onto it, the desk between her and Lena. Studying the maps still spread across the desk, Lena ran her fingers over the parchment and thought for a moment, the room quiet, broken only by the sound of Alex’s footsteps a moment later, approaching the brazier against the right wall. She lit the coals, the warmth immediately palpable, before taking up a position beside it. It wasn’t lost on Lena, and she doubted on Rhea, either, that it put Alex within closer reach of Lena - and the General.

     

                A minute later, one half of the doors opened and Jess came inside with a laden tray, crossing over to the desk and setting it down. She gave Lena a quick curtsy, dark eyes darting to Rhea and Alex, before she backed away and quickly left them to it. She’d brought tea and wine, including fresh bread with a few preserves, and little cakes, cheeses and thin cuts of meat. Climbing to her feet, Lena started to pour a cup of wine from the silver jug, filling three of them, and then a cup of tea as well. The latter she put in front of herself, before picking up a wine and rounding the desk, crossing over to Alex and handing it over with a pointed look to play nice. Grimacing, Alex took a sip of her wine and remained silently glued to the wall.

     

                “I hadn’t expected you back so soon,” Lena said as she crossed back over to her desk, reclaiming her seat. 

     

                As she started to add honey and cream to her tea, Rhea sipped her wine, leaning back against the chair and taking her time to respond. “It was proving futile.”

     

                “Futile?” Lena echoed, her hopes dashed as quickly as that.

     

                “We were wandering aimlessly and encountering too many soldiers to move with stealth. No doubt there were a few Rogues scattered throughout the trees, watching us and them. It made it difficult to ascertain, though, and we caught no sight of them.”

     

                “So, what now?”

     

                With a soft sigh, Rhea took another sip of wine and pushed herself to her feet. Alex tensed slightly, straightening from her lounging position, but made no further movement. Looming over the desk, Rhea plucked a quill from a clay pot and then unstoppered a vial of red ink. Dipping the nib of the quill into it, she started to draw on the map.

     

                “Our search area concluded this region. We followed this route, so we can be confident that he is not present here.”

     

                “Is that your plan?” Alex scoffed. “To search the entire forest, bit by bit?”

     

                “It may be our only option.”

                

                “A time-consuming one.”

     

                “I can’t afford to wait that long,” Lena interjected, a furrow between her eyebrows.

     

                She couldn’t say it was because she didn’t want to be alive much longer, that she wanted him gone to eliminate the threat of him creating a new war, before she killed herself. Instead, she played on her safety, which was a very real concern, and only because it was likely he would have her killed before she dealt with him and made a true peace.

     

                “Every day he’s walking about freely is another day he might attack.”

     

                “If my methods are not satisfactory to you-”

     

                Lena cut Rhea off, trying to be as polite about it as she could be, not wanting to offend the woman. She was under no delusions that she was safe around anyone, save Alex, and was conscious that a wrong word might land her with a knife in her side, just for the sake of ridding the Court of an easy target. Trying to choose her words carefully, Lena sat forward in her seat, reaching for her cup of tea.

     

                “No, no, that’s not it at all, it’s just the luxury of time that we don’t have. But … we have newly returned soldiers; what if they helped with the search? We could cover ground more quickly that way.”

     

                “You’d like to utilise your army as a hunting party?” Rhea slowly summarised, clearly displeased.

     

                “Yes. Well, only the ones who want to. It might give them something to do if they don’t want to go home or sit idly. I wouldn’t force them to, but … it would help. Don’t you think so?”

     

                “It might hasten the process, yes. However, I don’t believe it would be fruitful. We will alert him to your intentions, and will likely lose many valuable soldiers in the process. You are new to the forest, so you might not understand the viciousness of those like your brother. They have shirked all moral responsibility in favour of brutality.”

     

                Trying not to let herself rankle at the condescension, Lena smiled tightly and took a sip of tea. “I am aware, yes, and understand it perfectly. He’s an evil man; there’s no plainer way to say it. I’ve run into him before, I’ve seen firsthand what he’s capable of, and been manipulated by him as well. It’s why I want this done quickly. No fuss, no mess. I’ll even settle for someone else bringing me his head, if it comes to it, although I’d like him alive.”

     

                There was a brief pause, Rhea watching her intently with dark eyes, before she spoke. “You mean to kill him yourself, Your Majesty?”

     

                “I’d like to - I think - but I don’t think I’m in a position to do that. Apparently.”

     

                “It would be unwise if you were hoping to remain Queen.”

     

                “So, I shall do it for her,” Alex declared, her face hard, her eyes swimming with anger and hatred and grief. “I am owed my revenge, too, for what he did to my sister.”

     

                “We are all owed revenge for the loss of someone,” Rhea smoothly countered.

     

                “Will your son be owed revenge for the loss of his mother?”

     

                Wearily sighing, Lena set down her cup and gave her sister a withering look. “Alex.”

     

                Gesturing dismissively with her cup of wine, Alex scowled. “She talks of shirking moral responsibility when she left her son and husband behind in favour of power with the Unseelie.”

     

                “A sacrifice, but one I do not regret,” Rhea shrugged. “Many things must be sacrificed for power. For peace, too, it would seem. It does not make the sacrifice less painful to bear, but knowing it is necessary may be a balm.”

     

                “You mean I should be comforted by the knowledge that my wife died to bring about peace?” Lena asked, anger spiking through her.

     

                “Perhaps. A cold comfort it may be, but a comfort all the same.”

     

                “Peace could’ve been bought without her blood being spilt.”

     

                “But it was not.”

     

                Feeling the tips of her ears redden in the ensuing silence, Lena clenched her jaw and swallowed thickly as she laid her hands flat on the map, dropping her gaze to it. “We are off topic.”

     

                Rubbing the tender spot at her temple, Lena picked up her tea and drained the rest of the cup before she set it down heavy-handedly. Leaning back in her chair, she considered it for a moment, all of the longing in her chest, the pain of her loss, the impatience and anger, and a hundred other emotions and opinions, and closed her eyes, cupping her face in a hand for a brief moment, before she sighed.

     

                “You will go to the wildest section of the forest. Wherever it’s most secluded, most dangerous, and you will search for him there. He’s not stupid; he’ll be somewhere out of the way, where they won’t be easily found. Otherwise, we would’ve heard whispers and rumours of his whereabouts over the years when he was supposedly dead.”

     

                “There are many such places,” Rhea reasoned.

     

                “We’ll tick them off, one by one.”

     

                “Have we considered he may not be hiding in the Unseelie Court?” Alex asked.

     

                Lena waved aside her opinion, “we have to assume he is, for now. We can’t mount a search into the Seelie Court without opposition, even though I won’t allow for any bloodshed. Not until we’ve exhausted our efforts here, at least.”

     

                “I won’t disagree with you there. I think it best to keep Unseelie out of my home at all costs. I think we should send messages, though. The Council could initiate their own search at the same time, drawing the net tighter around him.”

     

                “Yes, that would be a good idea. I’ll leave it to you to write them up; I don’t want to mess up the wording and have them fording the river again at a perceived threat.”

     

                Steering the conversation back to her own task, as if annoyed that she might be overruled, overshadowed, Rhea cleared her throat and raised her eyebrows in polite inquisition. “If we are successful in finding him, what would you have me do?”

     

                “Ideally, you wouldn’t be discovered, so I’d have you come and fetch me and bring me to him. Failing that, I’d rather have him dead, either way. I want them all to be held accountable for turning their backs on the Court, for fanning the flames of war. We’ll go there and oust them with the army, then.”

     

                “As it pleases you, Your Majesty.”

     

                Suppressing a sigh, Lena rubbed her eyes and dropped her hand from her face, fixing her General with a strained look. “Do you think it’s a good plan?”

     

                Hesitating slightly, Rhea took a slow sip of wine and then cleared her throat. “It is as good a plan as we have. I have an idea of where to start, so, indeed, I will start there. At any rate, I vowed I would find him for you, so I must see it done.”

     

                “Thank you,” Lena mumbled. “I know I’m not what you’d hope for in a Queen. I don’t want you to think that I’m unappreciative, I just- I want it done quickly, and you seem to be my best shot at that.”

     

                “I’m pleased by your trust in me. Now, I must prove myself worthy.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “I will take my leave now, unless Your Majesty has further need of me?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction. “You’re leaving already?”

     

                “I do not believe in wasting time on socialising and leisure. I have a task; I will see it done in a timely fashion. Pleasure may come after I have achieved my goal,” Rhea haughtily replied, rising from her seat, setting down her wine and giving Lena a short bow. “Your Majesty.”

     

                Lena didn’t stand, which she thought might’ve been rude of her, perhaps not the Queenly thing to do in front of her new General, but she was tired and contemplative, comfortable in her wide chair as she propped her chin up in her hand. Absentmindedly nodding to her, Lena lingered in her thoughts, her worry eating her up, insides twisting with discontent as she was filled with a weary restlessness. She wouldn’t argue for Rhea to stay and plot out a better plan, not if it meant it would be over and done with quicker. She didn’t even ask how long she would be gone this time, too impatient to be curious, to be thorough.

     

                Sweeping out of the room, Rhea left without another word, and Lena let out a breath. While she had to rely on the other woman, she felt tense around her, trying to perform well and failing abysmally at that. It was easier to be around Alex, whom she could admit her shortcomings to, who would argue with her in an honest fashion, instead of talking circles around her in Fae. There was something freeing in that, and while they were in disagreement over many things lately, it was refreshing to have a friend with her. 

     

                They gave it a minute before Alex moved from her position to the vacated chair. She collapsed onto it, roughly exhaling, tucking her hair behind her pointed ears, and drained the rest of her wine. Setting her silver goblet on the arm of the chair, she tapped her finger against it, lips pressed into a flat line.

     

                “I don’t trust her,” she eventually stated.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena sat forward in the chair, reaching for the jug of wine and pushing herself up slightly to extend it to Alex. “I know you don’t.”

     

                “I wish you would take my advice.”

     

                Filling her goblet and then setting it down, sinking back onto her chair and reaching for her own wine, Lena grimaced. “And what advice would that be? Beheading? Jail?”

     

                “Tighter vows, for a start, but jail would be wise. Not a cell , but perhaps detain her in a room here, until you’re sure.”

     

                “And when I was sure, what reason would she have to obey me then, after that?”

     

                “Well, the tighter vows, of course.”

     

                “Of course,” Lena scoffed, swallowing a large mouthful of wine. Rolling the taste around her mouth, she was silent for a second before she sighed, rubbing her eyes. “She’s already sworn to find him for me.”

     

                “Yes, so you’ve told me.”

     

                “So … we’ll just wait and see if she does.”

     

                “And what do you intend to do until then?”

     

                Rubbing her chin as she hummed, Lena considered the question. “I’ll help heal the soldiers, and if there’s time for anything else after that, well … we’ll see.”

     

     

                It was another week before Rhea returned again. Lena had kept herself busy as planned, instructing every spare room in her halls to be repurposed for soldiers to convalesce in, if they weren’t fit to travel home, or didn’t wish to return home. It filled the place up, and put the variety of messengers, healers, squires and the like to work, assisting the servants in between their other tasks. Alex had Lena locked up behind a closed door as much as possible, not trusting anyone, not even the earthen walls between each room, insisting that any Earthfolk could part the dirt and stroll into Lena’s room if they wanted to hurt her. She was right, of course, but Lena didn’t want to be reminded of the constant threat on her life, didn’t want to go back to being cooped up inside all of the time. She craved the outdoors, the fresh air and trees, but not as much as she craved her wife.

     

                She slept less and less with each passing day, staring at the dark ceiling at night, thinking of Kara, trying not to cry, unsure if she even could cry anymore, her emotions so dulled that she existed in a constant state of misery. And she was so tired, because even when she did sleep, it wasn’t enough to offset the amount of energy she expended, pouring into the walls of the halls, until she was overwhelmed by her awareness of the place. She knew how many people were in each room at all times, felt their footsteps through the root systems and the very dirt she stood on, her senses constantly flooded by the feeling of them, as if they were walking through the bones of her body. It was too much, it was exhausting, but she couldn’t switch it off, just had to adjust to the newfound feeling of being one with the forest, growing into her powers as an extension of her grief. It seemed sick that this was how she grasped the ability to use it at her will, but she never did, never revealed that she could do anything with it, and wasn’t even sure what she could do beyond feeding the forest her life force. Even that seemed wrong, toying with the seasons in the way she’d been cautioned against at the very beginning, disrupting the natural order of summer fading into autumn. But Lena couldn’t help it.

     

                The only distraction from the feeling of too many vibrations through the ground was tending to the soldiers, and it was something that benefited her on multiple fronts. Most importantly, she was able to help tend to wounds and help ease the suffering of so many people, toiling away at bedsides, and visiting those still camped outside to dole out teas and tinctures, change bandages and the like, but it also endeared her to them a little too. They didn’t know her at all and had been called back from the frontlines by her, left to twiddle their thumbs in the meantime, while they waited to go home, but she’d put an end to the likelihood that they were going to be cut down in battle. And now, she was helping heal them with her own hands, rather solemn, and brusque when she spoke, but kind to these strangers as she told them they’d be fine, or told them their wounds were looking better. They all healed quickly, of course, so they knew that her words were truthful, or at the very least, they weren’t going to die, past the stage of immediate danger of infection and the like. It was good work for Lena to do, as well, wearing her out in the hopes that she’d sleep later that night, although she rarely did, but she enjoyed it all the same, with no ulterior motives, but of great benefit to herself, all the same.

     

                “The maggots have done their job well, Hector,” she informed the man she’d been treating with them the last time Rhea had shown up again.

     

                “I cannot deny it, Your Majesty, I was revolted when I woke to hear of what you had done to me. But I live because of it, so I find myself in your debt,” he said, his tanned face lined with age, hair cropped short.

     

                He was a seasoned fighter, and while she didn’t like to ask his age, he had to be centuries older than her, which was a little disconcerting, but perhaps went in her favour. To many of them, she was barely older than a child, and many of the soldiers had likewise put themselves in her debt, marvelling over her strange techniques, bread poultices and leeches working wonders on other wounds, so adept at healing at her age, bringing her human methods to the Courts. They were all sceptical, of course, but they found her fascinating all the same. A half-fae Queen, who was kind and laboured over their wounds herself, was a novelty to them, her methods aside. Not all of them warmed to her so quickly, but she tried her best, not wanting to rely on soldiers who didn’t know the first thing about her to defend her, if it came to it. She couldn’t say she’d lay her life down for a stranger, depending on the circumstance, so she didn’t think it was fair for her to ask that of them. At least this way, they might be loyal to her, not just to the crown that had been fashioned for her.

     

                It had been Alex’s hands that had wrought the silver circlet, using flame-wreathed fingers to twist the thorns - her mother’s emblem - into swirling vines, creating something far more elegant and softer for Lena. It was nestled amongst her dark hair now, but the importance of it was somewhat minimised by Lena’s dishevelment. She’d been at it all morning, dressed in her armour once more, the green leather surcoat irrevocably stained with blood by now, and she looked less like a Queen or healer, and more like a battle-weary soldier. None of them seemed to mind that she wasn’t the latter, and she felt it allowed her to blend in a bit more, even if the group of guards made her stick out like a sore thumb. Even now, Jack was standing at the foot of Hector’s bed, his eyes scanning the room, hand on the hilt of his sword.

     

                “I’m glad to do it,” Lena assured the wounded man. “Less glad to have to use such … unusual methods, but I think a life is worth more than any reservations about it, don’t you think?”

     

                “I find myself unable to argue with you, Your Majesty.”

     

                “My sister does not have that problem,” Lena wryly replied, her eyes flitting over to Alex, who leaned against the wall beside the door, twirling a knife in her hands, a silent warning as much as an impatient habit.

     

                “You keep her here against her wishes?” Hector asked, wincing slightly as Lena slathered a new salve over the wound, which had been stitched up after the maggots had made themselves useful. The slightly crooked row of stitches she’d given him was a little pink but not inflamed.

     

                “No, she stays against mine,” Lena said with a humourless smile, thin and quick. “The cause of much strife, but she has promised to keep me safe.”

     

                “I would like to make the same promise, once I’m healed.”

     

                “You should focus on resting.”

     

                “I will, Your Majesty, but I would rest easier if I knew I would have a worthy purpose once I’m healed.”

     

                She smiled again, a faint twitch of her lips. “And that worthy purpose is shadowing me everywhere I go?”

     

                “It would be, yes. I am indebted to you; I would pay that debt with my life in your service.”

     

                “Are you a good fighter?” Lena asked, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “Yes, I believe so. This,” he gestured to his abdomen, “was taken in a duel with two Waterfolk Seelie. I am Airfolk, so it was not on equal footing that I found myself.”

     

                “Rest up. I’ll consider your offer once you’re up and about.”

     

                He thanked her, and she moved on to another bed as a healer moved in to dress his wound, making her way to every bed in turn, requesting water or tea for those who’d already been tended to, making polite conversation for a few minutes before moving on. Finishing off in that room, she went through to another one, likewise brimming with soldiers, a woman with two broken legs propped up on pillows as she told a story that made those nearby laugh. Those who noticed her when she walked in stood, or attempted to stand, and Lena quickly waved them back down onto their cots or piles of blankets, everyone crammed in together like sardines. It wasn’t optimal, and she’d tried to take a camp bed in the study for herself, to free up two beds and the sofa in her suite, but even Jess had piped up to talk her out of it, insisting it wouldn’t be proper.

     

                “Look, Your Majesty!” a girl said, holding up her left hand and wiggling her fingers.

     

                Lena crossed over to her, smiling slightly as she sank onto the foot of her bed. She looked to be about nineteen, too young to have been fighting, even though she’d insisted she was when Lena had told her so three days prior, when she’d placed leeches on the tips and backs of the girl’s fingers. Unable to remember her name, Lena remembered her face well enough, the easy way she’d accepted Lena’s decision to use leeches to help increase the blood flow to her extremities, after a deep cut across the top of her palm had almost severed all of her fingers in one blow. Lena hadn’t been sure about the extent of nerve damage or whether the veins and arteries had been fully severed, but she’d stitched the wound together all the same, hoping for her best. The fingers had been a bloodless white, almost waxy to the look when she’d checked on the girl hours later, so she’d insisted on leeches, coaching a healer on how to swap them out, how long to leave them on for, and what to look out for. The girl’s fingers were now pink and moving, much to Lena’s relief and delight.

     

                “You’re healing well, it seems.”

     

                “Your leeches worked. I thought I might keep one of them,” she grinned, pointed ears parting red hair as she looked over the side of her cot, picking up a clay cup. “Look! She’s gotten so big from all the blood.”

     

                “Oh, um … that’s nice,” Lena apprehensively replied. “I’m glad to see you’re doing better.”

     

                “Much. Thank you, Your Majesty.”

     

                Nodding, Lena gave the girl’s knee a quick pat. “I’m sure you’ll be climbing trees again in no time, but I’ll leave you to rest. And try not to use your hand - at least not until the stitches come out.”

     

                Eagerly agreeing, cradling her cup with the leech between the palms, the girl reclined against her pillows as Lena moved on. She had several similar conversations with others, spent ten minutes bathing the forehead of a man who’d taken a blow to the head and hadn’t woken up yet, and promised another she’d have paper brought so he could write a message for his family. It was draining work, her emotions already so depleted by her grief that it took all of her effort to dole out thin smiles, converse with these people, who were supposed to be her subjects, who were mostly polite and deferential, and grateful, at least, but whom she felt very little towards. Alex put a stop to it after she finished in that room, almost lunchtime, with her at it since dawn that morning.

     

                “Jess has fetched food for the midday meal,” Alex informed her, snagging Lena’s arm as the Queen made for another room and was brought up short. “You should eat, rest a moment.”
