                Rubbing her tired eyes, glad for the lack of mirrors so she didn’t have to concern herself with how worn out she looked, Lena softly sighed. “Just for a moment.”

     

                Nodding, Alex shepherded her back through the hallways with Jack, her other guards posted at every entrance to the warren of rooms, while only the servants, messengers and squires walked the hallways. They all stopped to bow or curtsy as she passed them by, nodding in return as she took in the stacks of clean sheets, trays full of food, armfuls of dirty bandages and jugs of clean water, going about their business without complaint of the changes to their usual duties, and Lena was soon shut inside the study with a wash of relief. She invited Jack inside as well, Jess already there with a laden tray, and she sat gratefully in her seat, too tired to even serve herself for a few minutes.

     

                “You must sleep more,” Alex chided her, pouring tea from the pot for them all, making use of the two silver goblets for the wine to scrounge up four cups. 

     

                She set a teacup in front of Lena and then extended a goblet and a cup to the other two of their party, before claiming a goblet for herself and settling into the other chair in the room. Trying to run a hand through her hair, the movement halted by the circlet around her brow, Lena grimaced and let her hand drop uselessly to her lap. 

     

                “Telling me I must doesn’t make the act any easier.”

     

                “You should brew yourself one of those teas you’re always making for everyone. In fact, I could brew one for you myself; my mother gave me as much training as she gave- gave my sister.”

     

                “I don’t want to sleep. I have more important things to worry about.”

     

                “You are wearing yourself thin. If anyone tried to duel you now, you wouldn’t offer much of an opponent.”

     

                Lips twitching at the corners, Lena gave Alex a droll look. “I wouldn’t offer much of an opponent at the best of times.”

     

                “I admit you’re doing a fine job of wooing your people, so I suppose there is some good to come out of you running yourself ragged.”

     

                “I’m not trying to woo anyone,” Lena scoffed. “I’m trying to leave as few bodies behind as possible.”

     

                “Behind what?” Alex asked, fixing Lena with a hard stare.

     

                “It’s nothing important,” Lena waved a hand dismissively, straightening in her chair as she took a swig of tea and then reached for the top drawer of the desk. “I just find it highly unlikely I’ll stay in the Unseelie Court forever. I don’t want them to die , but I’d like to leave behind good people who might be more open-minded.”

     

                “Open-minded about what?”

     

                Pulling out a roll of parchment, Lena cleared her throat as she tried to flatten it out before handing it over to Alex. Sipping her tea and gesturing for the others to come and get something to eat, Lena let her sister-in-law read over the document she’d clumsily written and rewritten a dozen times, trying to word it correctly, trying to make it airtight. It was brief, and Alex lowered the parchment to her lap and gave her a look that bordered on anger, eyes sharpening as she pursed her lips slightly.

     

                “Why would you do such a thing?”

     

                “I need an heir,” Lena mumbled, shrugging.

     

                “Yes, but not me,” Alex spluttered, sitting rigidly in her chair.

     

                “Then who? My brother? I want him dead, and even if I die before he does, like hell am I letting it go to him. He’s not entitled to it anyway, and my mother said his fate was never to be King, so that works out well. I have no other family that I’m aware of - should it go to some distant cousin I’ve never met? Is there a distant cousin?”

     

                She turned her attention to Jack and Jess, the former sharing a glance with the latter. Eating his mouthful of fruit cake and clearing his throat, Jack gave Lena a wavering smile. “I believe your mother … dealt with any other potential heirs in your father’s line when she assumed the throne. Her own line, too, I believe. That was the reason for your retrieval, as rumour has it.”

     

                “Mm, that makes sense,” Lena hummed, nodding before returning her attention to Alex. “See? So, I need an heir, and you’re the only person I can trust and-”

     

                Alex’s face was pale and flushed at the same time, on her feet as she threw the parchment onto the table, eyes wide with disbelief and fear. “They will kill me.”

     

                “I- not if you’re the heir. I mean, they’ve tried to kill me, yes, but that was mostly my brother’s doing, because he wants this for himself. They might … leave you alone. Or … well, you’d be able to do whatever you wanted to help unify the Courts, or whatever, so-”

     

                She cut off at the sound of multiple sets of footsteps and rattling armour coming down the hallway, her attention drawn to the door, and she cocked her head to the side at a knock. Rarely was she summoned, a reclusive Queen if she wasn’t with the soldiers, the nobility doing as they pleased, with little input from her, and her brow furrowed delicately at the intrusion. Jack jerked a dagger free from his belt and moved to answer the knock at a nod from Lena, while Alex held a palmful of fire in her right hand, in anticipation of trouble.

     

                “General Rhea would like to see Her Majesty the Queen,” a woman loudly proclaimed as Jack opened the door a crack.

     

                “Rhea is back?” Lena said as she straightened, setting her tea down.

     

                Jack stepped aside, holding the door open as Rhea swept in, barely a hair out of place as she stood tall and regal, dipping her head to Lena. “I hope I am not interrupting.”

     

                “No, no,” Lena sighed, gesturing for Jack to close the door. “It’s actually good timing; we were just discussing the line of succession.”

     

                “Lena,” Alex harshly ground out, extinguishing her palmful of flames and giving her a cutting glance.

     

                “Yes, you’re not happy, I understand that, but I have no other choice, okay? I’m not asking you to stay; I want you to go back to Kelly so badly.”

     

                Glancing at Rhea, Alex gave Lena a pointed look. “We should discuss this in private.”

     

                “No, it’s good that she’s here. She can be a witness to my will; all of you can, so there can be no doubting my will when- if -”

     

                “No,” Alex snapped. “No, I won’t let you speak of such things. I won’t let you ruin my future by burdening me with this. I want no part in it.”

     

                Exhaling roughly as she propped her elbows on the desk and put her head in her hands, Lena fought to control her temper. “Alex-”

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “Your Majesty,” Rhea interjected, wary and confused. “Perhaps you should advise your sister to leave, and I can assist with this.”

     

                “No, she needs to stay.”

     

                “As you wish. Might I be informed of what you would like me to sign as a witness for? As I understand it, you have no living family to pass your title to - unless you have a child in your realm that we are ignorant of.”

     

                “No, there’s no child. But I do have living family. I have a sister, made so by your laws here.”

     

                Her eyes shifted to Alex’s face, the pleading look in her eyes as she tried to caution Lena against her decision. But Lena felt like she had no other choice, because she didn’t have any blood-related heirs, no one to assume the role of the monarch if she died, and she couldn’t make peace and then kill herself, plunging the Unseelie back into a succession war and further war with the Seelie. Alex would keep the peace in her stead, could bring Kelly to the Unseelie Court, create a lasting peace with the Seelie and forge a friendship between both Courts, as Kara and Lena’s marriage was supposed to. Lena would kill her brother, or die trying, and then she would leave it all in the hands of her sister, who would make a far better Queen than she would, who would understand things better, wouldn’t be such an easy target or a weak link in the hierarchy of things. 

     

                Lena watched as understanding dawned in Rhea’s eyes, disbelief and affront crossing her face before she schooled her expression into something hard but more neutral. “Your Majesty,” she started, floundering wordlessly for a moment before forging on. “You cannot mean to make her your heir. She is not from this Court; she will never be accepted. I must caution you to rethink your decision.”

     

                “I find myself in agreement with the General,” Alex said with annoyance.

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena let out a short breath, reaching for the parchment, which had rolled itself up again. “I may not be politically savvy, I may not be a particularly good Queen, I may not even be that good at healing, or anything you think is worthwhile here, in both Courts, but I am smart. And I know right from wrong, and this is the right decision. This is what peace looks like - this is how we ensure that war doesn’t break out again.”

     

                “This is how you instigate a war,” Rhea tried to reason with her.

     

                “And that’s why I would like you to be a witness to my decision, so that your signature can hold some weight, when- if the time comes. They’ll be more accepting of it if you’ve signed in solidarity with me.”

     

                She watched as Rhea hesitated, briefly considering that her General might outright disagree with her, object to being used in such a fashion, but much to her surprise, and Alex’s, by the look of shock on her face, Rhea nodded after a long, silent pause. Blinking in surprise, Lena perked up in her seat, emboldened by the agreement, and fished out a quill, uncapping an inkwell and nudging it closer to Rhea. Taking the quill from her, dipping the nib into the ink, Rhea read over what Lena had written and hesitated, only momentarily, before signing her name in whirling glyphs.

     

                Handing the quill back to Lena, she stepped away from the desk, and Lena beckoned Jack forward. He signed his name without complaint, quickly followed by Jess, before Lena held the quill out to Alex. Face furrowed with discontent, her mouth a flat line as worry clouded her gaze, Alex reluctantly approached and slowly took the quill. Lena watched her throat bob as she swallowed thickly, before adding her name to the bottom of the document. A prickle of relief washed through Lena, and she felt pleased as she took the document, scattering fine sand over the ink to dry it, before she rolled it back up and put it in her desk drawer for safekeeping.

     

                “Thank you all. Now, what news do you have for me? Will you take some wine while we talk?”

     

                “No, thank you,” Rhea curtly replied, holding a hand up in rejection as she remained standing. “I have nothing of importance to report back to you. We scouted two areas of the like you requested I search, and came up empty-handed. No signs at all. I lost three of my number; two to a rather large bear, and one to the forest itself. I will be off immediately, once we have filled their vacancies and replenished our provisions. They are readying fresh horses as we speak. I only sought to keep you up to date on my movements.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena nodded, dismay flooding her. “Thank you. Really. I appreciate your efforts.”

     

                Nodding, Rhea gave her a faint bow before turning and walking to the door. Leaving without further conversation, although Lena was sure she could’ve at least provided more information, other than three people had died and she’d come back with nothing to show for it, Rhea shut the door behind herself and left the four of them to it. Reaching for the bread, Lena sighed as she grabbed a slice, placed some ham on top and folded it in half. Taking a glum bite of her makeshift sandwich, she chewed slowly and swallowed, the other three staring back at her.

     

                “I don’t think she was pleased.”

     

                “Jess, Jack, could you leave us? Please,” Alex requested without looking in their direction.

     

                Biting back a groan, Lena rubbed her eyes with the back of her hand and took another bite of her sandwich, while her guard and attendant made themselves scarce. Swallowing her bite, she set her sandwich down as the door clicked shut, and Alex didn’t even wait for the sound of retreating footsteps before she spoke.

     

                “What the fuck?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena took a swig of tea. “I understand you might think it was the wrong decision-”

     

                “It was a foolish decision.”

     

                “It wasn’t! You’re the person I trust most now that she’s gone. You’re the only person I can trust with this task. I’m sorry to do it, I know I should’ve asked, but I need you to be my heir.”

     

                “Why?” Alex demanded, stalking closer, gripping the back of the chair across from Lena. 

     

                “Because who else?” Lena countered, gesturing helplessly. “I can’t pick anyone from here. They don’t care about the sacrifices it’s taken to get to where we are right now, and they’re not going to do what needs to be done to create a lasting peace. You do; you will. And Kelly will as well-”

     

                “You think I’m going to invite my wife here? Are you mad? They’ll gut her right after me.”

     

                “You don’t have to live here. Abolish the throne for good, if you like. Make a Council here, or unify both Courts into the Seelie Court. I already told you, you can do whatever you want, when it comes to it.”

     

                “Stop it,” Alex hissed, definitely angry now, her cheeks red, eyes bright as she pointed a warning finger at Lena. “Stop this when . I know what you mean to do; do you think me a fool? Do you not think I am a step ahead of you already? That you have made a mistake in choosing me to be your heir? That would require me to be alive when you no longer are, but I will be cut down in defence of you before anyone else ever takes your life. Do you understand? I will not be your heir; I have a promise to uphold, and I intend to. And now you have angered your General over nothing. ”

     

                “Angered?” Lena scoffed. “She signed it.”

     

                “She is angry. She might have signed your piece of paper, but I can assure you, it will never see the light of day if you die. She will make sure of that.”

     

                Flushing, Lena’s mouth thinned at the corners with annoyance, and she could feel her haughtiness settling in, too tired and irate for this conversation. “Well, you’re certainly sure of a lot.”

     

                “Lena-” Alex started, and then cut off, shutting her mouth as her lips thinned. She waved dismissively in her direction. “Do what you please. It seems you always do, regardless of what advice I give you.”

     

                Feeling a little bubble of shame within her, Lena swallowed thickly, her eyes stinging as her words came out hoarse. “I’m sorry. I’m just trying to do what’s best for everyone.”

     

                “This is not what’s best for everyone,” Alex snapped, releasing her grip on the back of the chair and rounding the desk. She loomed over Lena and reached down to yank free the dagger at her waist, holding it in a fist as she gave her a frustrated look. “It is not best for me.”

     

                Stalking towards the door, she jerked it open and slammed it shut behind herself. Banging her fist on the desk, Lena silently cursed as she put her head in her hands again, breathing roughly as she closed her eyes. Her insides were knotted, and she felt as frustrated as her sister had been, slamming her fist down on the desk as she had no outlet for it all. Alone, Lena slumped in the chair and breathed slowly, trying to compose herself. She could hear the sound of presumably Jack on the other side of the door, and couldn’t allow herself to fall apart within earshot of someone else. For the first time in a while, Lena made a conscious effort to reach out for that power lurking in her veins, rising from her seat as she fixated on the wall opposite the door and pushed against the earth.

     

                It caved beneath her will, packed dirt and stone parting as she pushed through to the room on the other side of the shared, thick wall. It was a simple thing to seal the wall back up behind her, and she felt her heart race in her chest at this secret escape, this bout of freedom. There were no guards around her, no one to stop her, and she felt that restless energy take over her legs as she hurried out of the room she was in - nothing more than a storeroom, by the casks and crates - and into the first door she saw on the opposite side of the hallway. That one was similarly stocked with bolts of fabric, with rolls of leather and shelves full of spools of thread, skeins of yarn. The back wall was free of shelving, and Lena shifted a few large rolls of velvet to leave enough space to work herself through to the empty room on the other side of the wall.

     

                In that fashion, she stole out of her home like a thief, room to room, until she reached the final wall, felt the unending earth beyond where her hands were splayed flat against it. Eyes closed, she pushed the earth up, boring a hole through to the surface, green-tinted sunlight and fresh air hitting her cheeks as soil and leaves rained down on her. Widening the hole, Lena carved a tunnel out and crawled through, packed earth giving way to damp earth, smearing her armour as she dragged herself through, filthy hands clawing her up and through, until she came out the other side. Filling the tunnel back up, Lena climbed to her feet and tried to wipe off as much of the mud as she could, only serving to leave streaks of it across her cheeks by the time she was done. 

     

                Walking away from the mound with the trees growing over it, Lena drew in deep lungfuls of cool forest air, listening to the sound of the leaves rustling as she closed her eyes, basking in it. She could feel it all, down to the smallest plant, the smallest clump of dirt, and she felt her skin tingle from that awareness as she stood there for a moment. It wasn’t the wisest decision for her to walk unarmed and unattended through the forest, even within the relatively safe confines of the dwelling, too many lights and people congregated there for animals to venture further than the fringes of the boundary, but Lena needed space. Space and freedom, the best she could hope for to nurse her grief, to give in, just for a moment, and acknowledge it in its entirety, instead of letting it numbly pervade her body.

     

                She walked aimlessly, no one nearby to notice her, and Lena felt the tightness in her chest recede a little, making it easier to breathe, until it was too easy, and they came quick and fast. Finding herself in a small meadow of lush grass and wildflowers amidst a copse of yew trees, Lena sank to her knees in the grass as she started to cry. Quiet, muddy hands covering her mouth, tears stung her eyes and dripped into her lap as she rocked herself slowly, her misery so all-encompassing that she was scarcely aware of anything else. She wouldn’t have moved a muscle if someone had attacked her then.

     

                Wilting into a heap on the grass, Lena quietly cried herself to sleep, surrounded by the forest as the wildflowers grew in abundance while she slept, oblivious to the effects she was having. Exhausted, she slept the afternoon away, waking with a jolt to the failing light of evening. Filled with that apprehensive sense that she was being watched, Lena pushed herself up into a sitting position, rubbing her bleary eyes as her skin prickled with goosebumps, and looked around at the changed meadow. Bees droned as they ambled from flower to flower, songbirds fluttering between the lower branches of the yew trees, nesting in the higher ones, and Lena felt the hairs on the back of her neck stand on end.

     

                It filled her with that notion of being watched again, although she looked around and saw nothing. She felt nothing, too, at the fringes of their little community, the seat of the Unseelie power, alone and not quite so safe as she’d thought when she’d walked away from the burrow of rooms and hallways. That was a safe hiding spot; that was somewhere they’d have to search every room to find her in. As she picked herself up and hurried back the way she’d come from, that thought struck her, and then struck her anew as she came to a sudden halt. Blinking slowly as the thought grew in her mind, more convincing with each passing second, Lena stood amidst a snarling mass of blackberry bushes and let herself be convinced.

     

                With more urgency, redoubling her efforts as she all but ran back to the burrow of her home, Lena caught the guards stationed at the closest door off guard, the mound of dirt overgrown with grass and plants guarded at every entrance, yet her arrival out of thin air with no guards made them scramble with surprise. Feet pounding down the few short steps into the hallway, the smell of earth and stone replacing the freshness of trees and moss, Lena was escorted by one of the guards, while the other retained his post. The woman kept pace with Lena’s hurried steps as she wound her way back through to the study, confusion and panic flitting across Jack’s face as he turned his head to look at the shut door, then back to Lena, who was striding towards him.

     

                “Your Majesty-”

     

                “I slipped away on purpose; don’t beat yourself up about it,” she cut him off, opening the door and stepping inside. “Will you fetch Alex, please?”

     

                He hesitated and nodded, instructing the soldier to stand guard in his absence. Shutting the door behind herself, Lena crossed the room and braced her dirty hands on the desk as she loomed over the map spread out across the surface of it, weighed down at intervals with heavy objects lying around. Her eyes scanned it, and she lightly skimmed a fingertip over the thick parchment inked with a topological approximation of the entire Unseelie Court. The coastline, every river, lake, stream, valley and mountain mapped out for her eyes. Anxiously chewing on her lip, she tried to rationalise it to herself, tried to come up with a compelling argument to make her sister listen to her, be on her side again. Lena was confident that she was at least onto something.

     

                The door opened a few minutes later, while she was deep into her spiralling theory, and Lena’s head jerked up, heart hammering in her chest as she looked at Alex’s disgruntled presence and found herself floundering, throat tight, renewed desperation filling her. Jack made to leave them to it, but Lena made a sound of objection as he started to back out, gesturing him inside. He’d dismissed the woman guarding the door and shut it behind himself, the three of them able to manage anyone who showed up unexpectedly.

     

                “I think I might be onto something. Maybe. I’m not sure, it just- it makes sense.”

     

                “What does?” Alex asked, all of the annoyance between them forgotten about in the moment.

     

                “Where he’s hiding . He needs more than one way out; they need to be able to travel the forest without being seen.”

     

                “Well, yes, that seems to be the problem with finding him. We cannot track what leaves no trace.”

     

                “Yes, exactly, but they’re getting around somehow. They’re staying somewhere. Somewhere no one will go.”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Alex let out a soft sigh. “Speak plainly, please. I haven’t the patience today. It has been trying enough already.”

     

                “Tunnels,” Lena proclaimed.

     

                “Tunnels?” Alex sceptically echoed, drawing closer to the map. Her eyes scanned over the lines of different coloured ink as her brow furrowed. 

     

                “Think about it. He’d be belowground, they could all move around easily, and no one would know they were there. He’s Earthfolk; most of the Unseelie are. It wouldn’t be that hard to tunnel underground. I did it earlier, and I’m hopeless at best, and still, no one noticed I was gone all afternoon.”

     

                Alex gave her a tight-lipped look of admonishment before glancing over at Jack to give him the same look, while he gingerly shifted from foot to foot, murmuring apologies.

     

                “And where would these tunnels be?” Alex asked.

     

                “Well … I don’t know that . But once Rhea returns, we could get her to scout the area with that in mind, see what her powers pick up underfoot. She might come across a lead.”

     

                “Have you considered the mines, Your Majesty?” Jack hesitantly ventured, meekly raising a hand as he intruded on their conversation.

     

                Lena’s eyes darted to him, and she cocked her head to the side. “The mines?”

     

                He moved over to the desk, his finger running along the mountain ridge spanning virtually the entire length of the Unseelie Court, from north to south. They’d passed through one of the lowest passes of it on their trip from the coast, but it had seemed an ordinary mountain range to Lena, no one else about, nothing unusual about it at all.

     

                “There are mines there?”

     

                “Of course. Well, we have many places we mine for ore and jewels, but this would seem the most logical to me, if you were seeking tunnels.”

     

                “The entire range is a mine?”

     

                “We have existed for millennia; our mining has been extensive over that time. Our love of finery has made many go seeking their own treasures. Over time, tunnels have spread throughout it, I have no doubt.”

     

                “But surely it is still being mined? Others would’ve realised,” Alex tried to reason.

     

                Jack nodded as he considered her doubts. “Yes, it is still being mined, although, with the constant war with the Seelie, there aren’t many who would have had time for it. Many sections will have collapsed, or been abandoned, so it would make it fairly easy for people to dwell there unnoticed.”

     

                “He was presumed dead for years,” Lena mused. “Could he have hidden there that long and gotten away with it?”

     

                “He has hidden somewhere and gotten away with it,” Alex sourly replied. “An abandoned section of the mine is as good a place as any. Better, perhaps, with less risk of being taken by the forest or its creatures.”

     

                Glancing up at Jack, Lena gestured for him to come closer, waving a hand at the map. “The valley we went to the other week, where is that?”

     

                He tapped a spot on the map, and she nodded, mouth a flat line as she studied the distance to the mountains from that point. “Where’s the nearest mine entrance there?”

     

                Jack tapped another spot, murmuring that he wasn’t quite sure, but he thought it was there. Humming to herself, Lena picked up a quill and dipped it into the open inkwell, freehanding a line from point to point, until she’d created a triangle. Her residence, the mine entrance and the valley. Tapping her chin with the end of the feather, she considered it.

     

                “They’re all within a day’s ride of each other.”

     

                “Should I send a rider to General Rhea with this information, Your Majesty?” Jack asked.

     

                Her eyes met Alex’s, and she saw the flicker of wariness there. She hadn’t trusted her enough lately, or had disagreed with her too much, and Lena didn’t like these cracks in their relationship, the only friend she had with her, the only family, so she hesitated. Swallowing, her mouth thinned, and she was silent for a moment before drawing in a deep breath.

     

                “No,” she murmured, pausing before continuing. “I shall go myself.”

     

                Alex seemed to straighten where she stood, her relief filling her, making her look more determined instead of weak. “I’ll find Jess and ask her to make arrangements. Jack, pick six trusted soldiers to come with us. And you,” she turned her attention to Lena, her face clouding with annoyance. “You should get some rest.”

     

                “Rest? No, we leave now. I want this over with.”

     

                “You have barely slept-”

     

                “I’ll manage. Depending on what we find, I’ll sleep when we get there.”

     

                Torn between insisting she take care of herself first and wanting her revenge as much as Lena did, Alex eventually relented. Nodding, she looked at Jack and jerked her chin towards him. He dipped his head and backed away to the door before leaving and closing it behind himself. Swallowing a groan, pleased to have a solid trail but too tired to deal with the consequences of that, Lena sat heavily in her seat.

     

                “Why didn’t you want to send a rider?” Alex asked, easing herself down onto the chair across from her.

     

                Giving her a weary look, Lena sighed and grimaced. “Because we have something more solid to follow, and much like with the valley, I’d like to go myself. She can continue to conduct her own search, with no probable leads, and if she finds something, she can send word or bring him back. But I found this myself - well, with help, but still - and I don’t trust anyone more than I trust myself and you.”

     

                Accepting her reasoning, Alex nodded. They lapsed into silence for a moment, and Lena swallowed the lump in her throat as she stared at the map on the desk between them, guilty and ashamed for a moment. “I’m sorry. I know I haven’t listened to you as much as I should’ve. And I didn’t mean to twist your arm with the whole heir thing, but I hope you can see I didn’t really have any other options. But I’ll burn the document if you want me to. I just- your loyalty is all I have, and I could never deny your sacrifice. I’m sorry that you’re here, that you’re kept away from Kelly and your mother, but … I wouldn’t have made it this far without you.”

     

                Sighing, raking her hair back, Alex closed her eyes and shook her head slightly. “Do not think I have forgotten to be angry about it, but no, you cannot burn it. I do not wish to be your heir, but I understand your intention and why you have little choice but to make it me. But I had forgotten that I must put duty above my own desires, as you have since you arrived in our realm. As you do now, playing the part of Queen, when all you wish is to be alone with your grief.”

     

                Mouth curving with a small, regretful smile, Lena hummed in agreement. “I hope you know that if things were different, I would never put you in this position. I’m so grateful to you for all of your help, it just- this isn’t the way any of it was supposed to happen. But you’ll make a good Queen.”

     

                Alex’s gaze was piercing as Lena raised her eyes to meet her stare. “I might have, yes, but I still hold by my word that I will fall in your defence before I let harm befall you.”

     

                “I always wished I had siblings,” Lena said after a moment, a flicker of fond amusement crossing her face. “I would have liked to have had a sister like you when I grew up.”

     

                “You have me now,” Alex sighed, climbing to her feet. “I wish you had her, too.”

     

                The shadow of grief that never truly lifted, hadn’t budged in months now, descended over them once more, and Lena nodded, a little curt as her throat tightened with the reminder. Not that she ever forgot, she just preferred to talk about something else. Pushing herself to her feet, Lena trailed after Alex, both of them stepping out into the hallway, making for their suite, where they found Jess stowing parcels of food into packs. Donning her cloak, Lena fetched her shield, her bow and quiver, and belted on her sword, before asking Alex for her dagger back. Relenting, only because they would be in the wilderness, under threat of attack, Alex procured it and handed it to her, the blade quickly sheathed on Lena’s opposite hip as she armed herself as well as she could.

     

                As ready as they could be on such short notice, they left the suite and went above ground to track down Jack, making for the willow trees where the horses were stabled and setting about saddling ten of them in silence. Jack showed up with a few soldiers in tow, informing Lena that the others were coming, and the two women and the man who had followed him watched her continue to saddle a stallion with wary surprise. She looked up once she’d finished with the front cinch, smiling as the horse tried to nibble at the brooch pinning her cloak in place, and she raised her eyebrows at the sight of a recently familiar face stepping inside, dressed in armour.

     

                “Hector,” she said with surprise.

     

                “Your Majesty.”

     

                “Are you healed well enough to accompany us?”

     

                “I am, Your Majesty. Thanks to your care.”

     

                “He insisted when he overheard, Your Majesty,” Jack explained.

     

                “I intend to repay my debt,” Hector said with a bow of his head.

     

                Smiling faintly, Lena nodded and patted the horse’s neck, before moving towards one sized more appropriately for her. “We should be off.”

     

                They all claimed a mount and settled into their saddles, and Alex put herself beside Lena, as usual, murmuring a low warning for her to stay close. It didn’t matter that she’d asked Jack to pick people he trusted, only that they were two amongst eight Unseelie, with Lena discounted as one in her sister’s eyes by the nature of her upbringing in the human realm. The rest of their party settled into order as they set off through the forest, dusk making everything blue and smudged as the warmth of the day started to fade.

     

                The first hour was leisurely, although they kept a brisk pace, but things grew wilder after that, the miles of relatively flat and open forest giving way to narrow gullies, uneven hillocks and thick brambles. As it darkened, they all grew warier as well, everyone with a weapon in hand - Lena had her bow fitted with an arrow and clutched in her left hand, ready to aim, draw and loose if needed - and more than once, the hoot of an owl or the sudden flap of bats swooping overhead made them all tense as they readied for a fight. Lena could feel the forest around them, though, and she knew they were alone. Knowing that didn’t make her less tense, though, her stomach in knots as she was filled with a desperate urge to be right, for this to be it. She’d waited long enough; the weeks that Rhea had been assisting, leaving Lena restless and impatient. Now, she was hopeful, even if it was mixed with her weary despair, but it wasn’t as if she had much else to pile her hope onto.

     

                Midnight came and went, and they continued through the forest, everything calm, nothing coming to hurt them, although Lena’s skin hadn’t stopped prickling since they’d left. Perhaps that lent to the tautness of her body, to the knot of unease that had the hairs on her body standing on end. Either way, she kept silent about it, nothing close enough in her awareness to tip her off to an ambush, an attack, but her muscles were aching from the stubborn tension in her body as they carried on. The forest grew colder as well, tendrils of mist making the air damp and close as they trekked through shallow valleys once they’d reached the beginnings of the foothills, and Lena could taste the pine on the air, the mud and ice. The mountains were hidden from them, the trees still crowding thickly on the foothills, in the valleys, but she could feel their oppressive presence, looming before her in unfathomable piles of rock and dirt.

     

                The blackness of night lightened to the navy of pre-dawn by the time they came to a stop. She had very little clue where they were, save for the spot pointed to on a map, and they were greeted by nothing. Jack and Hector dismounted, moving towards the dark mouth of the mine shaft entrance. It was cavernous, twenty feet tall and wide enough for four to ride abreast, but it offered them nothing by appearance. Closing her eyes, Lena reached out, feeling the emptiness of the shaft, of the branching tunnels, where rock had been excavated. There were no vibrations of anyone’s footsteps within them, or at least not close enough for her to sense them, and she suddenly doubted herself. It had been a mistake, a fanciful idea that had been born from her desperation, from the urge to be right.

     

                “Your Majesty,” Jack murmured, stepping up beside her and looking up. “Four of us will go in and see if there are signs of disturbance. Footsteps within the dust, and the like. I will take our Firefolk and Earthfolk, so we may see and feel what lies ahead and below.”

     

                Nodding, her face pale in the darkness of pre-dawn, Lena’s mouth thinned. “Take no risks. Please. I won’t have anyone die by putting a foot wrong or bringing down the mountain on top of everyone. Try to be quick as well; I have the feeling we’re being watched, and I don’t fancy sitting here in broad daylight like sitting ducks.”

     

                He nodded deferentially, and Lena was left with the other five of their party, including Alex and Jess. Dismounting as the four disappeared into the mine, Lena walked off her stiffness in the small clearing at the mouth of it, the freshness of pines filling the air as the coniferous trees crowded in close, the horses scuffing up needles as they sniffed around for something to graze on. The six of them that remained behind split an early breakfast from the provisions Jess had packed, and Alex boiled water for tea, Lena sipping hers from where she sat on a jutting piece of rock beside the entrance of the mine.

     

                The sun had started to rise by the time Jack returned, dust in his hair, ageing him decades, the other three following after him. They were all unharmed and defeated, empty-handed from their search. Dark eyes soft with sadness, Jack sketched her a quick bow as he apologised for their failure, and Lena just smiled slightly.

     

                She refilled her empty cup with more tea from the pot Alex had kept hot and held it out to him, giving his armoured shoulder a quick pat. “It was a long shot, Jack. Thank you, anyway. You’ve crossed one thing off our list.”

     

                Giving the newly returned some time to rest, the forest brightened as unhindered sunlight filled the small clearing they stood in, while they basked in the warmth of it, Lena moved over to Alex. “We should start our return.”

     

                “Return?” she repeated with surprise.

     

                “It was a waste of time,” Lena grimaced, scuffing her foot across the rocky ground.

     

                “No. Not yet, at any rate. You heard Jack; these mountains span virtually the entire Court. This is but one entrance - the nearest one - and the next is not half a day’s ride from here. If no one is here, they may yet be at another.”

     

                “We aren’t equipped well enough for a widespread search. This Court might be smaller than the Seelie Court, but it’ll take us weeks , months , even, to search every entrance to the mine.”

     

                “Then they will be months well-spent.”

     

                “And what if we come up with nothing?”

     

                “Then we know where he is not,” Alex said with surety. “And Rhea will be searching other areas. We will cover more ground if two groups are working towards it. I believe she should have listened to you and enlisted the help of more soldiers.”

     

                “Well … we’ll see how we go. We might still have to go that far. Although she was probably right that it would tip him off if too many people were searching the forest for him.”

     

                Alex’s head sharply turned towards her, and she pushed off the wall, quickly crossing over to Jack. “When you sought out trusted soldiers to accompany us, how many did you ask? Who knew of our plan?”

     

                Mouth opening and closing at Alex’s demanding tone, Jack frowned as he glanced at the soldiers and then Lena. “I visited those who had recovered well enough to be considered and asked for volunteers. For anyone who would like to repay their debt to Her Majesty for tending to their wounds.”

     

                “And there were others around?”

     

                “Yes. They were in the camp.”

     

                “And who is in charge of the army while Rhea’s absent? Was there someone there who reports to her?”

     

                “Yes, she has a Captain.”

     

                “And you spoke to this Captain? You told her where we were going?”

     

                He seemed confused now, or wary, perhaps, shifting uneasily. “I- yes, I asked her to come. She objected. She said it would be best for her to remain, that Her Majesty would not like her company - she did not like her company last time they were acquainted.”

     

                That made Lena stiffen, more alert now. “What was the Captain’s name?”

     

                “Veronica, Your Majesty. She would have been at Court when you were last-”

     

                “I know her,” Lena cut him off, old anger resurfacing, an uneasy twisting feeling in her stomach as her throat tightened. She glanced at Alex, who looked at her and read her expression, nothing more having to be said.

     

                Alex swore after a moment, lunging for her horse, dragging herself onto the saddle as the others all scrambled to follow suit, Lena likewise following. Jack was the slowest to react, hurrying to mount up and follow after them, dodging past Jess to keep pace behind Lena and Alex.

     

                “Your Majesty, what-”

     

                “We have been given away,” Alex fumed.

     

                “I beg pardon, I-”

     

                “It’s not your fault, Jack,” Lena shouted over the wind and the distance between them, clinging to her horse for dear life with a sinking feeling in her chest and stomach, that cold dread pervading her. “My trust was misplaced. We were made the moment I asked General Rhea to find my brother for me.”

     

                He frowned, opening his mouth to reply as they all rode at breakneck speed through the trees, backtracking as quickly as possible, with little concentration given to their surroundings. Before he could say a word, the ground in front of them burst apart, the rider ahead thrown from their horse, Alex managing to cling to the mane of her stallion as it reared, while Lena’s mare skidded, hooves slipping over pine needles and leaves as she came to a treacherous stop. Bow clasped tightly in her hand, an arrow nocked again the moment she’d been in her saddle, Lena had it raised and drawn the moment she’d been brought to a halt, throat dry as she watched an armoured figure slowly sidle into view on horseback.

     

                Rhea had her sword balanced across her knees, the remainder of her party slipping out of the cover of the trees to form a wide arc, hemming Lena’s party in together. With a smile that didn’t quite reach her eyes, Rhea let out a quick laugh. 

     

                “Clever girl.”

    Chapter 50

                “I really wanted to think better of you,” Lena said with contempt, giving Rhea a dismissive once-over. “But you have proven my sister correct, instead. What a shame. I would have given you anything you asked of me if you had done this task for me. I would have been in your debt. Instead, you betray me.”

     

                “You betray yourself,” Rhea harshly replied, her face twisting with derision. “I could have overlooked a half-fae Queen, given your father’s blood, your claim to the Unseelie throne. I could have used your ignorance to my advantage, I admit it. Ending a war you had lost your wife to, I could understand. But I could never accept you making that Seelie your heir. You all but signed your death warrant with that grievous mistake.”

     

                “And what of your promises to me?”

     

                With a smug laugh, Rhea smiled. “I promised nothing more than finding your brother. I have found him. And I have brought him to you.”

     

                “And he will make a better King? You would rather pledge your allegiance to the man who has killed his own people, has spilt so much blood that the forest is angry?”

     

                “No, he will be as dead as you when I am done. It is time a new family sat on the Unseelie throne. A Queen deserving of it, without the squabbles of families and owed inheritances.”

     

                Lena scoffed, a smile curling the corners of her mouth. “And I presume that will be you? Have you forgotten you’re from the Seelie Court? Or doesn’t it matter to you when you’re the one on the throne?”

     

                “It matters less when I have spent nigh on a century earning the trust of the Unseelie, leading the armies, knowing the soldiers. I may be Seelie, but I am no foreigner to these parts.”

     

                “So … a coup it is then. Well, get on with it. I’ll come with you if you let my sister go. Let them all go. Your quarrel is with me.”

     

                Alex sharply glanced at Lena with a scowl on her face, and jerked on her horse’s reins, making it steer into Lena, before she stretched and smacked the rump of Lena’s mare. “Go.”

     

                “Alex,” Lena snapped as her horse lurched forward, bringing her towards Rhea and her soldiers, before a blast of air buffeted them.

     

                The mare reared, and Lena was still holding her bow, the nocked arrow rocketing up into the canopy as she was thrown from horseback. Dumped to the forest floor in a heap of armour, Lena felt the brunt of the impact in every fibre of her being, the breath fleeing her as she blinked back black spots. Gasping for air, unable to make her vision focus, she was filled with the sudden clarity of agonising pain. And it wasn’t coming from her, no broken bones begging to be noticed, but from the trees. Eyelids fluttering, Lena drew in a wheezing breath of panic.

     

                “The trees. The trees.”

     

                She couldn’t sit up, had to roll over onto her stomach, aware of trampling hooves, of shouts and ringing steel, and pushed herself up onto all fours. Back to the General, she hurriedly staggered to her feet and whirled around, blinking as she found someone bearing down on her. Someone wearing a gold mask. Raising her left arm defensively, Lena caught the sword swing in the wood of the bow, narrowly missing her fingers, and reached up to grip the other side of the bow, trying to push back against the masked fae. Instead, she was overpowered back down to the ground, and jerked her head aside as the blade finished splintering the bow and scraped over the steel of her breastplate, sparks skittering over her left pauldron as the blade was turned aside. A snarl of anger at her broken bow, Lena wrapped the limp bowstring around the fae’s sword arm and jerked their wrist aside, before she unsheathed her dagger.

     

                The fae was scrabbling at her neck, sitting squarely on her lap to keep her pinned, and Lena managed to dispatch them with a quick thrust of the dagger through the bottom of their jaw. She could see the glimpse of steel through the mouth parting in shock, the fae sagging on top of her, and she wrenched the dagger free before pushing the fae off her and climbing to her feet. Moving her dagger to her left hand, Lena unsheathed her sword, the weight of it heavy in her shaking arms, and she tried to grip dagger and sword in two hands, drawing the sword high overhead, before heaving it down with all her strength, splitting the fae’s head, steel cutting through soft gold and the shaved skull. Brain matter splattered from the open mess of the skull, and Lena drew in a heaving breath, separating dagger and sword into the appropriate hands as she looked around, wild-eyed at the unfolding chaos. One thing she’d learnt was that real-life battles were more chaotic and clumsy than movies had made them seem, with a lot of hacking and stabbing and brute force rather than the elegance of duels she’d been trained by.

     

                Multiple trees were burning, and she felt their pain keenly, almost blinding in the intensity of it, and she tried to blot it out, tried to dim the forest. Instead, she poured her grief into it, and as she stalked towards one of Rhea’s soldiers, knowing she was far outmatched by any vetted soldier there, Lena was vaguely aware of new green bark growing over blackened sections sloughing off the trunks. Fortunately, she caught the man by surprise, his back to her as she made for him, and perhaps it wasn’t the most noble way to fight, and maybe there wasn’t such a thing, but she swung her sword at his unhelmed face. He turned into it, made aware of her presence, and she caught his jaw, splitting it in half. Staggering backwards, wide-eyed, he dropped his sword as he raised his cupped hands to his face, blood pooling into his palms as he made a wordless sound, almost pitiful. It didn’t stop her from quickly hacking into the side of his neck, felling him with a flicker of guilt spared for the man.

     

                Dodging a rearing horse, reaching a hand out to try and soothe the animal, feeling sorry for them, caught up in it all as fire and air were exchanged, no water nearby for the Waterfolk, and the earth oddly still, despite most of the Unseelie being Earthfolk, including Lena. There was not even the slightest tremble underfoot, and she felt uneasy, uncertain, as she shied back from a Rogue and then shoved them away, right into the trident, wielded by Jess, the young woman agitated and bloody, this more battle than she’d ever seen before, even less experienced than Lena. Ushering her behind her, Lena tried to swallow the dryness in her throat as she looked around, teeth clenched, shoulders set.

     

                And then she saw Rhea, engaged with two fae. One was Hector, the other a masked Rogue, all three of them fighting each other, and Lena briefly saw red. Forging towards her, Lena watched Hector kick the masked figure’s knee, making them stumble, but he had to dodge a swing from Rhea before he could dispatch the Rogue. Lena stormed towards her, her green eyes flinty as she sheathed her dagger and clutched her sword tightly in two hands.

     

                “Rhea!” she barked, drawing the General's attention.

     

                Head jerking in her direction, Rhea blundered slightly by letting her attention lapse, and Lena watched Hector stab at the gap in her armpit, only protected by mail. Snapped back to the moment, Rhea wedged his sword between her arm and chest, and Hector had to let go of his weapon to stagger away from her, right into the well-placed thrust of the Rogue’s spear. Lena let out a sound of outrage as she watched the older man sag to his knees, and the forest responded. It responded to her only, roots sprouting from the ground in an explosion of dirt, encircling the ankles of the Rogue, quickly creeping up calves and shins and dragging the Rogue. The same happened to Rhea, who tried to hack away at them when they wouldn’t respond to her power.

     

                Barrelling into the General a moment later, the impact dragged them both down to the ground in something more akin to a brawl than a proper duel. Lena lost her grip on her sword as she felt the roots continue to wrap around Rhea. Now that she was pressed into the dirt, they wrapped around her arms, creeping across her breastplate, binding her by Lena’s rage alone. She didn’t go down easily, though, struggling beneath Lena, although she seemed confused as to why the roots wouldn’t obey her. If it came to a battle of power, Lena hadn’t anticipated she’d win, but the roots continued to wrap around her as she helplessly struggled with Lena’s hands wrapped around her throat. Reaching for her waist, Lena yanked her razor-sharp dagger from its sheath and straddled Rhea, pressing the edge to her throat, making the General still.

     

                “You should have stayed loyal,” Lena said with regret.

     

                “Your Majesty,” Rhea rasped, her face pale now, dark eyes widening. “I only want what is best for the Court. Perhaps I have been remiss in thinking that was not you. I will help you kill your brother-”

     

                Lena cut her off, her voice sharp and firm. “No. No, I gave you your chance, and you betrayed me, killed people of your Court. There won’t be any other chances, and I’m not as soft as you think I am.”

     

                “Then fight me. I am a General; fight me if you think I deserve to die for my treachery.”

     

                A small huff of laughter worked its way past Lena’s lips, and she gave the General a derisive look of amusement. “I am not as foolish as you think I am, either. No, I will kill you now, in the dirt, while I can be sure I’ll win. That is what will be best for the Court, I am sure of it.”

     

                Opening her mouth to protest, to plead or beg, Rhea was silenced by the quick jerk of the dagger across her throat as Lena slit it. Blood spurted from her jugular, deep red and spilling quickly, soaking into the ground and staining it black, until the river was only a few droplets, which turned into burgundy petals as they dripped off the side of her neck and landed in the blood. The ground eagerly drank it up, and Lena didn’t move off her until she was sure she was dead, unwilling to risk another enemy walking around freely. Even then, she sat on her corpse, drawing in heaving breaths, until a hand clapped down on her shoulder, grabbing a fistful of her cloak.

     

                Whirling around, thrusting her dagger towards the attacker’s thigh, the blade was fended off by a long hunting knife, and Lena looked up as Alex dragged her to her feet. Blinking, Lena’s shoulders slumped with relief, and she sheathed her dagger and stooped to pick up her sword, breathing in the heavy smell of blood, bile creeping into her mouth as she stepped over Rhea and looked around at the others still fighting. There were many dead littering the ground, and Lena watched Jack send two arrows in quick succession into a Rogue, evening the odds a little more. Jess was trying to help Hector rise to his feet, and Lena hoped he wasn’t badly injured, that perhaps he’d recover, that she might tend to it later, once they were safe. 

     

                For now, she had bigger priorities. Primarily, the smoke that was filling the air, a great swathe of forest burning, the fighting causing so much damage. And where the fire hadn’t wrought destruction, the wind the Airfolk had whipped about had snapped branches and dragged leaves and needles from them. The entire area had not gone unscathed, and Lena could feel the pain of the forest. No one else seemed to, none of the Earthfolk affected by the agony that seemed to radiate from the trees, a silent scream, but then, they couldn’t move a leaf, couldn’t do a thing with the earth of the plants, and they still didn’t know it was because Lena had the forest in the palm of her hand, while the forest held her in its palm as well.

     

                “The trees,” Lena said as she grabbed Alex’s arm. “You need to help them.”

     

                “Never mind that,” Alex fumed, her face taut with worry as she hauled Lena along, yanking her back a step and angrily sending a small knife hilt-over-tip into the neck of an armoured woman coming at them, before forging onwards.

     

                She was making for a horse. Not Lena’s mare, but a chestnut stallion, a little too tall for Lena, but skittishly caught in the middle of the fighting and the nearest option. Grabbing the reins, Alex steadied the stallion and gestured impatiently for Lena to mount. But Lena was too preoccupied with the dwindling fight, the stragglers still going at it, only Jack, Jess and an unnamed woman remaining of their party - sans herself and Alex. She was unsure how Hector was faring, if he still had a fighting chance, but she felt a stab of guilt to be fleeing. Every part of her objected to that, and yet, as she stood rooted to the spot for a moment, Alex started to force her up into the saddle, practically lifting Lena off the ground as she started to push her up against her will.

     

                Awkwardly clambering onto the saddle, wriggling on her stomach as she mounted up in a less-than-graceful manner, Lena managed to get herself properly seated. Looking down at her sister, she opened her mouth and was cut off by a repetition of Alex’s earlier act, a quick slap to the stallion’s rump, forcing Lena to lunge for a fistful of his mane to keep herself seated. Panic knifed through her at the thought of losing Alex, of leaving her behind to dispatch the rest, and it was a deeper panic than she’d felt in months now, not since Kara had died. To lose all she had left was more than she could bear, and she was angry that Alex was bound by her oaths to Kara to protect Lena with her life. Lena didn’t want that; Lena wanted her to survive her, to be Queen in her stead so she might find peace beneath the ground, a part of her perhaps finding its way back to Kara in the earth that they would both be buried in.

     

                The stallion wove between trees as Lena turned, trying to look behind her, her feet not in the too-long stirrups, leaving her unable to safely seat herself to guide the horse, to wheel him back around and go back. It didn’t stop her from trying, thundering thirty feet away as the sound of fighting dimmed behind her, her attention dragged forward again to be faced with a shocking sight.

     

                It was undoubtedly him. She didn’t know her brother well at all, but she knew him by sight, even with that gold mask on his face. He was leaning against the trunk of a hawthorn tree, toying with a knife, and she managed to rein the stallion in, hooves skidding over leaves and needles. He was still twenty feet away from her, but she knew he was watching her, taking in the armour, the circlet crown around her brow, something different about her compared to the last time they’d been face-to-face. He wouldn’t have known what it was, but it was her lack of fear. It was simple, really; Lena wasn’t afraid to die.

     

                “Lex,” she softly breathed, and it carried in the quiet stillness of the forest, nothing moving around her. 

     

                There was a roar in her ears, pulse racing as her vision dimmed, and Lena barely acknowledged that hair-raising feeling of being watched, her skin pricking with goosebumps as she spurred the stallion onwards. Her brother turned and ran then, all pretence of nonchalance vanishing as he set off quickly, but she was on horseback, and the forest answered to her. The ground before her rippled ahead, violently trembling, the earth churning as it chased after her brother while Lena rode him down, the distance between them shrinking, until she was so close that the stallion could almost trample him underfoot.

     

                Instead, roots erupted from the ground and ensnared him, tripping him up as he went sprawling. Bringing the horse in a tight circle around him, Lena looked down at Lex as she watched him struggle, writhing as he spat curses through gritted teeth. She waited until he was tightly bound and then dismounted, her feet firmly landing on the carpet of leaves and needles underfoot, a crook of her fingers making the roots jerk him up onto his knees, like he was a puppet. Stepping in close to him, Lena reached out with her left hand to remove his golden mask, tossing it aside as she took in the cruel set of her brother’s face, the smirk on his lips, eyes bright with amusement. 

     

                “Your Majesty,” he mockingly greeted her.

     

                “Don’t you dare speak to me,” Lena snapped. “Not after what you did.”

     

                He laughed, the sound light and relaxed, as if he wasn’t kneeling before her, sword in her hand, completely at her mercy. “You sound angry, but I can smell your fear.”

     

                “I’m not afraid of you. I’m going to kill you.”

     

                “You cannot; it would make you a kinslayer.”

     

                “I don’t care.”

     

                He looked surprised, as if he’d thought she’d stay her hand because of it. But Lena didn’t intend to outlive him for very long and would bear that sin if it meant taking him out before she went. It mattered very little to her, and he was only her brother by blood, a technicality, not by want of family. Lex’s expression turned scornful, and he spat at her feet as he struggled.

     

                “Will you not fight me fairly? I am a King; I deserve an honourable death.”

     

                “You aren’t a King,” Lena murmured, “and you’re entitled to a death, but not an honourable one. You have not conducted yourself honourably, so you will die a dishonourable death, and my sister will burn your body to ashes to deny you an honourable burial, as well.”

     

                She looked into his dark eyes, so different to her own, nothing about them similar, and didn’t flinch. And then something scored a hot line across the side of her neck, an arrow buzzing past, just skimming her as she felt the sting of the cut. Whirling around, Lena blinked at the sight of a masked man dropping from the low branch of a tree with a bow in hand, lazily pulling another arrow from the sheath on his back and sketching her a playful bow before nocking and fitting it to the bowstring.

     

                “Now, that was a poor aim,” he clicked his tongue. “Please do stand still for this one; I fear my aim is not what it once was.”

     

                He loosed the other arrow at her, and Lena threw herself sideways, anger hot in her veins again as she shot an arm out towards the man, roots wrapping around his ankles and creeping up his legs. Coming at him from his left side, Lena hacked at the side of his neck, the blade getting stuck halfway, the swing not having enough strength behind it to behead him, and Lena planted her foot against his bound legs to jerk it free. The leaves rustled then, a quiet warning that she didn’t heed until a throwing knife punctured the back of her surcoat and breastplate, making her stumble forward a step from the impact, although the short blade hadn’t managed to pierce mail and gambeson. Turning, Lena was already lashing out with her sword, driving a woman backwards as she stepped away from the swing.

     

                She had another throwing knife in her hand, tossing it at Lena’s neck as she scurried backwards, briefly distracting Lena as she ducked, keeping her balance, and then dashed in. Still straightening back up, Lena didn’t have time to bat her away before the woman was inside her guard, another of those little throwing knives jammed in her side, in between the edges of her breastplate, the close-up force of it piercing the mail and gambeson too. A pitiful sound escaped Lena, pain radiating through her side, and she elbowed the woman in the sternum, slamming the pommel of her sword into her shoulder to create more space between them.

     

                “Kill her, Nyxly,” Lex ordered her, still tightly bound.

     

                Lena wouldn’t let him go; she wouldn’t let this woman escape, either. A soft snarl escaped her, and the ground exploded around Nyxly, trapping her as it had trapped Lex, as it had trapped the other dead man. The woman let out a cry of surprise, and Lena watched her panic for a moment, confused as she tried to will the roots to let her go. Advancing on her, Lena didn’t feel a single ounce of mercy as she gripped her sword in both hands and shoved the sword right through Nyxly’s abdomen. The woman choked on her surprise, eyes wide as she gasped, held fast by the forest as blood filled her mouth, spilt over her lips, and she died quickly.

     

                Turning her attention to her brother, Lena let out a broken laugh. The forest was silent again, no wind through the branches, no lilting birdsong. It was dead quiet, dangerously so, and Lena walked over to Lex with weary relief, a little knife in her side and a slight tremor in her hand, but the knowledge that it was done. In a moment, it would all be over, her revenge complete.

     

                “You still don’t understand, do you?” she asked him, standing over him as he was left kneeling, tightly bound. “You can’t control the forest; it won’t answer to you. It answers to me. I feed it and it feeds me, the way it was always meant to be. You’ve all ignored it for so long, the anger and pain you’ve caused it with these unnecessary wars. No one listened anymore, no one fed it, except to feed themselves. You’ve all been blind, and that is your downfall, as much as the murder of my wife.”

     

                “Murder?” Lex scoffed, “I did not touch your wife.”

     

                “Not directly. Just as I’m not going to touch you. But you’ll be dead, the same as her.”

     

                She spoke slowly, clearly, the forest still, waiting patiently. And then she whistled to the quiet forest, ignoring the warning Kara had given her months ago, ignoring the prickling sense of unease, of being watched. Lena thought she knew what came next, had guessed as much, and the answer was unsurprising as she felt the vibrations through the earth, the forest shaking as the wind picked back up, a terrible scream that snapped branches and whipped up fallen leaves, the hairs on Lena’s arms and neck standing on end as she felt something approaching behind her. 

     

                Remaining rooted to the spot as the strange musk of the forest and wet dog enveloped her senses, Lena turned her head left and up, reaching up to lay a hand on the muzzle of the gigantic wolf as it crouched low over her shoulder, tense and quiet. Feeling wiry fur under her fingers, Lena swallowed thickly, turning her gaze back to her brother, whose face was slack with disbelief and dread. He couldn’t even speak, no amusement on his face, and Lena stepped aside. As soon as she did, the wolf’s muzzle peeled back over sharp teeth, and a growl started in its chest, a low rumble that grew louder until it was snarling in her brother’s face.

     

                “Take him.”

     

                She didn’t have to say more than that, the wolf knowing what she wanted, or perhaps just giving into animal instinct, which just so aligned with what she wanted too. Lena couldn’t say why it hadn’t attacked her last time, although she suspected it was that same wolf cub she’d rescued so long ago, and why it didn’t attack her now, but she was grateful that it felt no such reservations for her brother. It lunged for Lex, mouth open, and tore him free of the roots, shaking him like a ragdoll as his blood rained down, little green petals drifting down to the forest floor, before the wolf dashed off with his body clamped in its jaws.

     

                As soon as the wolf was gone, Lena let out a gasping breath of fear and confusion, relief and shock, drawing in frantic breaths as she shook all over. And then a sob worked its way up her throat, eyes stinging with tears as she collapsed to her knees, her face in her hands. And that constant wave of grief continued to pour out of her with a certain lightness to it now, the end so near, and Lena dashed a fist across her face and sniffed, before she reached down for the little knife in her side and pulled it out. It hurt like hell, and blood welled up as she tossed the knife aside, pressing her hands to her side as she blinked, in a daze.

     

                And then there was a slight bump in her plan, Alex’s voice carrying towards her. She’d gotten turned about in the fighting, in the binding of her brother, so Lena was facing the way she’d come, her horse scared off somewhere by the wolf, and she watched Alex run towards her. A sob worked its way up her throat, guilt forcing a lump in her throat as she watched the distant figure calling her name race as fast as she could to help her. But Lena didn’t want any help, was beyond that now, was glad that she was. It didn’t lessen her guilt, though, because she knew she was leaving behind a sister she’d grown to love, who’d sacrificed so much to keep her safe, and Lena was thanking her with a throne she’d never wanted and a target on her back by half of the Unseelie Court.

     

                The forest was quiet again, that feeling stealing over Lena, and she felt weak with relief as she closed her eyes, a smile on the corners of her lips as she heard Alex shout her name again, fraught with panic. Eyes opening, glassy with tears, Lena looked at her, thirty feet between them, and gave her a pleading look of understanding as she moved her hands away from her bleeding side, unstaunched and slowly pumping out her life. Swallowing past the tightness in her throat, she softly called out to Alex.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Lena!” Alex sharply called, redoubling her efforts, twenty feet away now, battered and bruised, bleeding a little but loyal to the end.

     

                And then Lena whistled to the silent forest, feeling the ground shudder with the quick footfalls of clumsily big paws, and the monstrously big wolf cub bounded back through the trees, licking a bloody muzzle clean. Kneeling in front of her sword, watching her sister skid to a pause, aghast and small before the wolf, Lena smiled faintly, at peace with her ending, and held her arm out to the wolf, which was sniffing towards her, nosing the bloody palm held out to it.

     

                “Take me,” she rasped.

     

                And the wolf did.

    Chapter 51

                Miles and miles away, almost to the boundary of the river, dusk falling anew over the forest, a whole day since she’d left the seat of her Court, Lena was gently set down by the wolf, groaning as it pressed its nose into her cheek, sniffing loudly. Forcing her eyelids open, aware that she must’ve passed out at some point, whether out of relief or shock, she wasn’t sure, Lena stared up at the wolf and pushed its muzzle away from her. Then came its tongue, rasping and wet as it started to lick her bloody palm, and an even louder groan slipped out of her.

     

                Her hand moved to her side, the dull ache of pain there. It wasn’t good, but she’d thought she’d be dead already. Blinking as she came around, feeling warm in her battered armour, a headache pounding behind her eyes, Lena was filled with a sudden rush of anger. Pushing herself up onto her elbows, she caught a glimpse of the purplish-blue of dusk, the trees turning inky black against the sky, and heard the melody of running water rushing past nearby. Sitting up, Lena drew in a ragged breath, the pain in her side flaring white-hot, and tried to take stock of things. Disappointingly, she was still very much alive. For the time being, which was easily changed.

     

                Gritting her teeth against the pain, Lena turned onto all fours and pushed herself up, a slow, agonising act, before she got her feet under her, staggering about for a moment. The wound in her side was still slowly bleeding, and that was the downside of such small, poorly placed knives. It would kill her, eventually, but more likely from infection than the rush of blood loss needed to stop her heart. And as Lena fumbled for her sword belt, she realised she’d left her sword behind, and was missing her dagger as well, which left her shit out of luck to finish the job herself.

     

                Anger filled her, frustration at the situation, and she whirled on the wolf, which was crouched slightly, apprehensive and tensed, but almost playfully watchful. Tears stinging her eyes, Lena took a lurching step towards it, spreading her arms wide as the wolf blinked, liquid dark eyes holding the light of the forest, like little stars, and it snuffled in her direction. Impatient and annoyed, Lena beat a hand against her chest, the leather of her surcoat muffling the rattling metal as she tried to egg it on.

     

                “Kill me, you stupid wolf!” Lena demanded.

     

                Its head darted forward to nip at her right arm, the one bitten by the cub when she’d rescued it. At least she thought it was the same one. Yanking her arm away as another wave of frustration swept through her, Lena huffed and kicked some leaves in its direction.

     

                “Yes! I know it’s you! Now, eat me. Please.”

     

                The wolf just snapped at her again, teeth clicking together, but otherwise, it just watched her, unmoving. It was almost puppyish, but there was a stillness, a tension to it that left her unable to mistake it for a harmless dog. She just wished it would behave normally, like the other wolves she’d encountered. Lena could do with sharp claws raking across her stomach right about then, but it seemed pointless to strip off her armour when the wolf was almost dense in its refusal to hurt her. It should’ve been easy, the easiest thing in the world, after a year of everything and anything trying to kill her, and yet, when she was finally ready to die, no one was around to deliver it.

     

                “Fuck,” she swore, kicking up another pile of leaves.

     

                Running a shaking hand through her hair, she felt a hollow pit inside her, dizzy with pain and blood loss, and unsteadily started to pace. To add to her ire, the wolf darted forward to snag the hem of her cloak as she walked away from it, and Lena was embroiled in a brief game of tug-of-war before she stormed towards the wolf and was dragged down to the ground as it scuttled backwards, still clutching the cloak in its jaw. 

     

                Tearing herself free with the rip of cloth, staggering forward a few steps as she was suddenly freed, Lena silently fumed, her change in circumstances almost laughable as she found herself warring with an oversized wolf cub. Not in the mood for it, almost single-minded in her pursuit of death, Lena considered her other options and then found her pointed ears pricking at the sound of running water. That would do nicely.

     

                Setting off towards it, unbalanced and light-headed, Lena had to lean against the trunks periodically to catch her breath, keep herself upright, leaving a trail of petals in her wake from the steady drip, drip, drip of her blood drifting down to the forest floor. Reaching the banks of the wide river, unrecognisable from the spot where she’d watched her wife die, because Lena was sure she would have known that spot, felt it in the air, in the heaviness of the loss of life if it was nearby, Lena sank to her knees in a rattle of armour. Leaning forward, the fast water of the wide river rushing past her, she slipped her hand in, a silly, inconsequential thing to check, and found it frigid as she let it wash over her skin, her bloody hand and split knuckles numbed by the cold.

     

                It didn’t stop her from shifting, swinging her legs around and slipping into the river. Her foot slipped on a rock gone slick with algae, and she went in fast, submerged beneath the churning surface as she got a mouthful of water, swept away by the current. It was a natural survival instinct that her feet scrabbled for purchase on the pebbled bottom of the river, kicking up silt and mud as she got her feet under her and stood, water rushing off her as she broke the surface, waist-deep as she drew in heaving breaths of shock from the intensity of the cold. 

     

                Gasping and spluttering for a moment, slowly slipping with the river’s current as silt shifted underfoot, Lena realised her mistake and quickly dropped, letting the swift waters take her as she sank in her heavy armour. Head going under, she closed her eyes and exhaled a stream of bubbles, until she had no air in her lungs, until they were painfully aching, the cold making her stiff and numb, a painful pressure in her head. And then she was snatched up and skimmed along the surface of the river, choking on fresh air as the wolf snatched up a mouthful of her cloak and dragged her along. The swift-moving waters were no trouble for the size of it, lightly trotting to the opposite bank and dragging her up onto wet mud and weeds as she found herself back in the Seelie Court.

     

                Resigned to her lot, exhausted and thwarted again, Lena was limp as the wolf continued onwards, dragging her along by her cloak as Lena was jostled about over the uneven ground, sliding along over leaves and needles and every rock and bump possible. Rattled about, Lena listlessly breathed as she was helpless to stop the wolf from dragging her, or to find some other way to kill herself, anyway, so she just let it happen, an unending, jarring and bruising trip through the forest as miles passed by and the last few fingers of pink sunlight stopped filtering through the trees, a true darkness settling in as everything turned cold and dark.

     

                She was shivering in her sodden clothes and armour, teeth rattling, the pain in her side a constant, dull ache, and she thought it might end soon. Eventually, it had to end, and she silently prayed that it would be over quickly, that her suffering would be finished, and her wife would be with her once more. Bouncing over the uneven ground, the sound of the wind in the trees, of owls hooting and things scurrying through the undergrowth, Lena fell into a stupor, or might have passed out again at some point. At any rate, she came around again in a heap on the forest floor, darkness enveloping her, curled in on herself as her breath misted in the dark, invisible to her eyes but the cold keenly felt. 

     

                Remaining huddled where she lay, Lena closed her eyes and shivered violently as she willed herself to die, or to slip into unconsciousness at least, with very little luck.
