It wasn’t until the darkness became a faint purplish from a dawn she couldn’t see through the canopy that Lena made herself move. If nothing was going to come and snap her up in the middle of the night, she would need to find her own death. Stiffly pushing herself to her feet, pain radiating from her waist, Lena was left breathless and sweating as she stood in the lavender dawn of the forest and swayed unsteadily for a moment.

     

                She didn’t know where to go, where she was, and she couldn’t hear anyone about, not even that useless wolf. All she wanted was to go somewhere peaceful and die, somewhere she could be with Kara, a comforting presence to pass away with. And she was back in the Seelie Court, although she didn’t know where, so Lena’s thoughts naturally went to Argo. She’d plunged Krypton into the sea, but that hadn’t been her first home there. It had been that tower in the lake, prickly and untrusting, not yet in love with her wife, not yet friends with her. That had been her first home, surrounded by water, and Lena wished she were there now, amidst Kara’s things.

     

                The trees seemed to groan around her as she was filled with desperate defeat, and Lena thought she was imagining things at first. But then they were groaning as they moved, a phantom wind sighing through their branches as they rustled and moved, gently caressing her as it blew south-westerly. Pausing, wondering if she’d gone mad or if the forest was helping her, Lena blinked dumbly and then decided she had nothing to lose, and it was as good a direction as any. Setting off through the trees, the sighing wind ruffling leaves ahead of her, keeping her on path as the boughs dipped and swayed in the same direction, Lena walked.

     

                It wasn’t particularly fun, hunger gnawing her stomach on top of the thirst in her throat, the pain in her side, the chill and exhaustion in her bones. Perhaps that would make death all the sweeter, to be done with the discomfort of life, but either way, she didn’t care. She would drop while she walked, or she’d make it to some destination and drop there. It was just a relief that she was alone, no fiercely protective sister to guard her every movement, and Lena drew in breathless gasps of sobs as she stumbled onwards for what felt like forever, the forest growing lighter, bit by bit, until everything was a golden green, sweet and heady with life, brought about by her passing through. The wolf was gone, and she didn’t question where to, or when it had let her go and left her alone, and she didn’t get that prickling feeling of being watched again until lunchtime.

     

                She was walking through a particularly dense patch of ferns, shoulder-high in some places, when she had that sensation raising the hairs on the back of her neck, and had just enough time to acknowledge the trembling underfoot that signalled approaching footfalls, before the wolf tore through the ferns. It was little more than a grey blur, a shower of leaves and dirt spraying from its forceful paws as it ripped everything up in its haste, before it leapt at her. It hit her right between the shoulder blades, sending her to the ground with a heavy thud and a wheezing cough as the breath was forced from her lungs. Blinking back black spots as she lay there, the taste of blood in her mouth from where she’d bitten her tongue, cheek pressed into dirt, Lena let out a groan, pain everywhere from the jostling impact, but slowly fading as she took stock of it all.

     

                The wolf sniffed her, wet nose pressed into her cheek, and she flinched, her pale face furrowing with irritation. She wasn’t in the mood for it, tired, thirsty, foot sore and hungry. Even if she didn’t have a little stab wound in her side, she wouldn’t be in the mood for it, but that certainly didn’t help. It had stopped bleeding, she assumed during the night, and the gambeson had helped soak up most of the blood anyway, but she could feel it seeping wetly again and knew it needed stitching closed, knew that it needed to be cleaned out, or would grow infected. But then Lena wanted that, wouldn’t have minded being feverish and blood poisoned if it helped speed things along, not quite the clean death she’d envisioned, but a death all the same. For the time being, she had a monstrously big wolf cub crouched over her, a paw on either side as it hunched, head ducked down, and Lena still held onto a sliver of hope that the wolf would open its jaws and snap her up in one bite. Was that too much to ask for?

     

                Dragging herself forward on her elbows, leaving a furrow behind her in the dirt, Lena got onto her knees and staggered to her feet before whirling around. Angry, teary-eyed with her frustrated desperation, she raised her arms and yelled at it, trying to get it to go away. It jerked back a step at the sudden loudness, ears flat to its skull, but it didn’t run, didn’t attack, just remained crouched with a predatory stillness to it, dark eyes watchful. Stooping, Lena picked up a small pebble and threw it at the wolf, the size of it pitifully small as she lobbed it towards its snout, so small she was unable to even see where it bounced off, as harmless as a fly and less annoying at that. Gritting her teeth, she grabbed more, flinging handfuls of dirt towards it, until her frustration bled out of her and set the forest trembling.

     

                The wolf seemed more wary about that, ears pricking up, and Lena was left panting and weak by the time the wolf slunk backwards and the trembling petered off to nothing. Turning, Lena continued on the way the forest had been guiding her, heedless of the wolf, slipping into that almost meditative state of pain, putting one foot in front of the other as she plodded onwards, slowly bleeding. Except, the wolf trailed after her, fifty feet away perhaps, and then off to her left, but it was very much there, following her, no matter how badly Lena willed it to go away. Ignoring it, she continued to walk, all through the afternoon and into the evening, the light failing as night fell, a few hours short of midnight and leaving Lena with very little to go by, the moon obscured by the canopy. Her wet boots had chafed her feet raw, and she had blisters everywhere, each step an uncomfortable pain that she tried to stamp down, but with little light to go by, she finally gave her feet a rest, coming to a stop right where she was and sinking to her knees.

     

                Heavy eyelids closing, she fell asleep quickly, dreaming of her wife. There was no comfort in the act of sleep, no relief from her exhaustion, but there was in the dreaming. Still, she woke to the damp forest, mist shrouding her, wet cheeks, and felt that chasm in her chest. Her grief hadn’t ended with killing her brother, and she knew there was only one way to make it stop, but it was taking a lot longer than she’d anticipated. Even worse, when Lena sat up, raking tangled hair out of her face, she saw the faint glow of the wolf’s eyes through the gloom of the forest, swallowing a groan as she found her new companion half-hidden behind the large roots of an elm tree, watching her where it had lain down at some point in the night. Ignoring it, Lena climbed to her feet with the intention of being on her way, her face almost greyish in pallor now, a waxy sheen to it, and her feet were raw, to say nothing of the pain in her side, making her stumble and then collapse back down again, unable to get her legs beneath her when she tried to get up. She tried once more, breathless and limp, making it to her feet that time and then buckling almost immediately, collapsing again in a clatter of armour.

     

                She wasn’t sure if it was luck or misfortune, but the wolf rose to its feet then and warily approached, nudging her with its nose, before it delicately snatched her up in its jaws, nipping the woollen cloak and leather surcoat as she dangled limply from it like a cub being carried. It set off through the forest with her hanging like that, and she was helpless to stop it, feverish, with a banging headache behind her eyes, and a complete and utter will to live anyway. Eyes closed, unsure if it was even taking her in the same direction she’d been following - although she did think she could feel the wind ruffling her hair, but that could’ve just been residual disturbances of the wolf’s brisk trotting through the forest - Lena didn’t resist at all. It was uncomfortable, hanging like that, gravity dragging the weight of her down, and she found it impossible to pass out, but the wolf didn’t seem to care in the slightest. 

     

                After about a couple of hours of her arms and legs just dangling like that, she tired of it and started to wriggle. They’d covered more miles than she could’ve on her own two feet in a whole day, and they hadn’t seen a single soul, nothing but the sound of the forest and its creatures falling on her ears, and Lena supposed the wolf wasn’t stupid enough to get close to any fae they might’ve stumbled upon naturally, but she really wished they had. She could’ve used some help right about now. Not to kill the wolf, not to heal herself, but to direct her to Argo with the fastest horse available. Instead, she writhed and twisted until the wolf growled in frustration, the sound freezing Lena’s blood, and was almost gently deposited back into a heap between the wolf’s front paws.

     

                “Will you … go,” Lena rasped, her throat dry and voice hoarse.

     

                On her back, bright morning creating a halo around the wolf’s head, she looked up at it, and a long, low groan escaped her as its tongue licked at the front of her surcoat, then her chin, the force of it jerking her head up, pressed firmly into the dirt. Sighing, she grimaced, eyes closing, and reached up with a leaden arm to weakly try and swat it away.

     

                “Go. Please. I’m trying to die.”

     

                It didn’t go. It just backed away twenty feet and sank to its stomach, paws stretched before it as it watched her, while the forest started to feed off of her, flowers and fruits sprouting, birds suddenly flitting through the branches, a myriad of breeds as they were called to the sweet berries, while squirrels and mice came for the nuts, bees to the flowers. It was less than peaceful, and Lena was utterly exasperated as she stared up, the world spinning, the forest still blowing south-westerly, coaxing her onwards. 

     

                Staying on the forest floor until the sunlight seemed to be filtering down from directly overhead, Lena sat up, sudden vertigo making her hunch over, hands covering her eyes until the sensation passed, before she climbed to her feet. Unsteadily lurching towards the wolf, which rose to a crouch, ears pricked and wary tension in its shoulders, Lena extended a hand, whistling softly through cracked lips.

     

                “Here.”

     

                Warily approaching, a hand extended towards it, Lena clicked her tongue, trying to coax it closer, but it was a wild animal, as docile as it had been towards her so far. She hadn’t forgotten that it had torn her brother apart and come back with blood staining its muzzle. Still, she walked towards it, lurching and tired.

     

                “Come on,” she softly called, rubbing her thumb and fingers together, trying to entice it towards her.

     

                It just blinked those big, dark eyes at her and didn’t move, save to sink back down to its belly. The musky smell of the forest hit her as she drew closer, catching sight of the little patches of moss growing amidst grey fur, like a parasite overtaking its host. That’s what she suspected happened to all these animals, the forest getting in them, making them grow bigger than was normal, taking over their body with moss and vines and mushrooms, feeding off it as the animal fed off the forest, until the animal died and fed the forest some more. Pity stabbed through her, but she didn’t have time for that, shifting closer, bathed in warm light filtering through the canopy of yellow leaves as pale bark sloughed off the trunks of the trees surrounding them. It was odd, the whole thing surreal, and Lena was struck with the questioning thought of whether she was already dead or not. But she had to believe that death wouldn’t hurt like her ongoing painful grief.

     

                The wolf turned its head and sniffed at her as she approached its left side, and Lena felt pale and shaky as she reached a hand out to sink her palm into the wiry fluff of fur on its leg. Burying her hand in it, a lump in her throat, she felt the growl before it became audible, a low warning building in the wolf’s chest. She shushed it, reaching with her other hand, until she had two fistfuls of fur, the wolf still softly growling, and then she started to climb it. It turned its head to watch her, showing its teeth as it continued to growl, while Lena continued to hush it, climbing hand over hand, feet braced against its leg, until she reached the shoulder. It was like mounting a very, very large horse without a saddle, wiggling awkwardly on her stomach as she moved to the spot at the base of the wolf’s neck, wide and not quite as appropriate for riding as a horse was. She supposed that would be why the fae had never tried to tame the wolves to ride them, as far as she knew.

     

                Settling in as best as she could, she gripped fistfuls of fur across the wolf’s shoulders, and it stopped growling then, head laid down between its paws, and Lena was faced with a new challenge. Gently tugging the fur, she clicked her tongue, trying to coax it into moving as the forest stirred around her, that breeze created by moving branches swaying in a southerly direction, guiding her, but the wolf didn’t move. For five minutes, Lena tried to make it get up, but it didn’t seem to want to, no matter how much she whistled, patted its back, dug her heels into its ribs, until it decided to move itself.

     

                She’d all but given up when it suddenly lurched into motion, rising to its feet, rising and rising as Lena let out a panicked yelp, shifting on its back as she hurried to grab its fur, trying not to pull it out, although she wondered if the wolf even felt her there. Head tipped back, it let out a chilling howl, deafening in her ears as her body rippled with goosebumps, and she shuddered from the sound of it. Then, the wolf set off at a quick trot, nose twitching as it craned its head back, and Lena had to squeeze her eyes shut, a twenty-foot drop awaiting her below. It might not have been such a bad thing, but only if the drop killed her. Unfortunately, Lena didn’t think twenty feet to a forest floor of damp leaves would do more than break a few bones. Instead, she remained on the wolf’s back somehow, even as it picked up speed, loping through the trees, bringing Lena up amidst some of the lower branches as she pressed herself flat to the wolf’s back to make sure one didn’t take her out, eyes tightly shut out of fear of heights.

     

                The motion of its gait was quickly familiar, though, not so dissimilar to a horse as to leave her jostled about, and while she couldn’t steer the wolf, at least they were moving. Perhaps when they stopped, it would be hungry enough to finally eat her, or maybe it would slip away to hunt. For now, she just had to hold on for dear life, which was growing harder as her tightly knotted fingers grew stiff and she started to feel faint, that waxy sheen on her face growing even greyer, sweat dampening her hairline, even as the wind whipped it dry. It was how she passed the rest of the afternoon and into the night, a far more pleasant experience than the bone-rattling and bruising trip of being dragged along by her cloak 

     

                Cold and stiff as she clung to the back of the wolf, Lena was oblivious to it all, save for the motion of the wolf, slipping in and out of light sleeps until she was suddenly aware of her surroundings again, the sudden halt of movement. Blearily blinking as she pushed herself up, she scrambled for balance as she almost lurched off its back as the wolf sank down to its belly and stretched out, tongue lolling. It was pitch black, and Lena couldn’t see much, even with her sharp vision, but it was apparent they weren’t going any further that night. She couldn’t stay up there, so she made her stiff limbs move and practically fell off the side of the animal, clutching at fistfuls of fur as her weak arms refused to lend her anything strength. Annoyed by the yanking on its leg, the wolf turned its head to snap at her, but she was already collapsing into a heap, glad that the height of the fall had been considerably lowered by its lying down. Still, a ten-foot drop wasn’t any more pleasant, and she knew new bruises would be forming over ones accumulated over the last few days, coughing and groaning as she tried to catch her breath.

     

                Once she’d gotten past it, her dry mouth coppery with the taste of blood, she let out a ragged breath and crawled through the dirt to press herself up against the belly of the wolf for warmth. Her clothes still hadn’t dried, a lingering dampness leaving her cold and shivering as the forest cooled, but buried into the side of the wolf was a lot warmer, and it didn’t seem to mind so much, getting comfortable again as Lena closed her eyes and breathed in the animal smell of its fur and tried to sleep. It wasn’t that hard; she hadn’t eaten or drunk anything since before the fighting had unfolded, had been slowly bleeding on and off, and now it had been days - two? Or was she into the third? She was having a hard time keeping it all straight in her head - and it was taking its toll. Dehydrated and hungry, she didn’t so much as fall asleep but passed out.

     

                The forest was blue and cold when she opened her eyes, not quite light but dawn not far off, and Lena lay there for a moment, listening to the noise of the forest. Noticeably, the wolf was absent, its warmth gone, and Lena lay there for a few minutes before getting on with it. Dragging herself up on her own two feet, she closed her eyes and her lips silently moved in a plea to the forest to help her. It wasn’t so much the words, but the desperation that poured out of her that moved the trees, their branches swaying towards the direction she wanted, her intention guiding them as their movements guided her. Setting off, Lena made slow progress, hot in her armour, everything a little fuzzy, a little dim. But there was still pain, and a hell of a lot of it. It forced her onwards, more motivating than anything else had been, even her revenge.

     

                And she didn’t have to go far, oblivious to the distance the wolf had covered, leading her almost to the very shores of the lake. She was a few miles shy, and she reached the shore as a dazzling sunrise painted the sky pink, orange and lilac, reflected back on the glassy surface of the endless stretch of water. And there, not too far from the shore, although she’d come at it from the wrong angle, was the tower, pale stone elegantly wrought into a hundred feet of pillars and archways rising from the surface of the lake. It stole the breath from her, a wordless cry slipping past her cracked lips as her vision blurred with tears. Her grief rose up with a vengeance, a pain like she hadn’t known before, and she followed the curve of the shore, staggering the remaining mile of coastline to the hidden stepping stones leading out to the tower.

     

                Lena had been terrified last time she’d been there, her fear of water making it virtually impossible for her to leave, unwilling to set foot in it, but as she came to the shoreline, the looming tower so close now, she wasn’t afraid at all. Perhaps this would be a fitting death for her, to drown herself in the lake of her wife’s home, where Kara had spent countless hours swimming and fishing, as much of the lake as the water was. Chin wobbling, her pain obliterating everything else, Lena walked out onto the first stepping stone, water lapping up to her ankles as she kept her eyes forward, blinking past her tears as she felt the burning urge to be inside her wife’s home for a moment, just a brief moment before she died, to feel close to her again, maybe run her hands over her bedsheets, the spines of her books, the strings of her harp. For a minute, she could imagine Kara was out for a swim, or rowing her boat around the lake, like she had so many days when they’d lived here. For a minute, the pain might go away.

     

                Walking from stepping stone to stepping stone, the water cold, numbing her feet and shins as it grew deeper, Lena walked up to the tower, the detail of the carved pillars and archways coming into focus, the gauzy curtains billowing in the wind, and she breathed in the smell of fresh water, so wholly her wife. It felt like coming home for the first time in months. One foot in front of the other, she walked right up to the circular stone floor of the ground floor of the tower, partially submerged underwater with that pale, leafless tree growing from the centre, the gnarled roots peeking up through the surface as water softly lapped against the smooth trunk, and the bottom steps of the circular staircase vanished upstairs.

     

                Coming to a pause in front of it, Lena let out a choked sound of raw agony and reached out to press her palm against the pale trunk of the tree. She stood like that for a moment before she sagged to her knees, sobbing amidst the roots, slumping sideways as she curled up into a ball, letting the water seep into her clothes and armour, a little pink at her side as it rinsed away new and old blood, and she cried and cried, tears wetting her cheeks as she fell apart, bawling her eyes out as she gave up. And as she cried, her grief had nowhere to go but into the pale, skeletal tree, and as she cried, staring through her tears at the painting of a sunrise above the forest, Lena thought it would be the last thing she ever saw, and a smile dimpled her cheeks as the lines of grief eased around her eyes. And as she let out a heavy, resigned sigh, the tree bloomed with silvery grey leaves for the first time in millennia, and Lena closed her eyes and waited to die.

    Chapter 52

    Chapter Notes

    soz for the lack of updates, it's not abandoned!! i had some personal stuff going on so had to take a break

                Lena’s eyes cracked open to a glaring brightness, her eyelids slowly peeling back as she woke slowly, taking a few moments to realise she was staring up at the high ribbed ceiling, the pale grey stone wrought in swirling motifs of waves. She knew that ceiling, the arches and pillars, the gauzy curtains letting in cool air, and she was dimly aware of the soft mattress beneath her, the bed she’d spent so many nights in. And then she was aware of a nearby heartbeat, and was filled with euphoric joy as she fully awoke, pushing herself up too fast in her haste.

     

                Residual pain knifed through her side as she managed to get up onto her elbows and then sag. A driftwood chair pulled up to the side of her bed squeaked and scraped over the stone floor as a figure rose, and hands reached out to gently push her back down against the pillows. Lena’s joy plummeted, her stomach sinking with dread as she looked up at Alex and realised she’d been mistaken. For a moment, in that brief second between sleep and consciousness, she’d seen the ceiling, heard the heartbeat, and thought that she was with Kara, that she’d died too. By the withering look her sister-in-law gave her, she hadn’t been far off that reality.

     

                Sitting back on her chair, dark circles beneath her eyes that spoke of exhaustion, her thin face leaner and shadowed with grief and worry, misery and irritation, Alex folded her arms over her stained, travel-worn clothes. Her expression wasn’t so hard as it should have been, only grim and stressed as Lena cast her a cursive glance and then looked up at the ceiling. There was a lump in her throat, and she could feel the building pressure behind her eyes, the threat of tears, the constriction in her chest as she verged on quiet, breathless sobs.

     

                “You led me on a merry chase through the forest,” Alex broke the silence, her voice soft and pitched with forced levity. “Fortunately, I am an accomplished tracker, so I found you in time. I haven’t the skill of my mother, wife or sister with wounds, but I was able to treat your injuries and stave off infection. It has been a long four days, fraught with fevers, chills and the beginnings of blood poisoning, but the threat has passed. In part, that is thanks to you and your maggots.”

     

                Lena could hear her heartbeat pounding in her ears, strong and even, loud, as she felt the blood pulse in her head. Anger swept through her, unjust perhaps, but felt all the same, and her vision blurred. Closing her eyes, a tear ran from the corner, down her temple and into her greasy hair. She couldn’t speak, the lump in her throat hard to get down as she blinked away her tears as the silence dragged on, and stared up at the ceiling as the tension built, Alex waiting for some sort of response.

     

                “You will recover to full health,” Alex concluded after Lena remained silent. “You are lucky.”

     

                That earned a scoff in response, derision twisting Lena’s mouth as the anger within her burned hotter. She hated her for a moment. Just for a moment, and unfairly so, considering her life had been saved, but that was exactly why she hated her, and it was easy to rationalise that feeling to herself. 

     

                “Lucky?” Lena breathlessly choked out. “You’ve taken from me the only thing left that I wanted.”

     

                “I have kept my promise.”

     

                “Why are you here?” Lena sharply asked, struggling up again, angrily swiping the back of her hand across her wet cheeks as more tears fell. “You shouldn’t have come after me. It was done. It was finished.”

     

                “Because you were left in my care by my sister, and therefore, are my responsibility.”

     

                “No, I’m not. Stop it. Stop it. You have a life, you have a wife; you were supposed to go back to her. You were supposed to fix what I can’t. I didn’t want to be Queen; I just wanted to die, and you took that from me.”

     

                Alex swallowed, a strained look on her face, but no guilt in her clear gaze. “You will not make me regret my actions. I only hope that one day you will see that I did what was right, and that you will not resent me so for doing it.”

     

                Choking on a laugh as she palmed away more tears, more of them silently sliding down her cheeks now as she sniffed, a furrow between her brows, Lena shook her head, bewildered and disbelieving. “Hope as much as you like; it won’t stop me from getting what I want.”

     

                “By all means, try it again,” Alex suggested in a somewhat brittle tone. “You will find not a single blade here that is not closely guarded by me. You will find me a strong enough swimmer to keep you from drowning. You will find no rafters to hang a rope. You will not be out of my sight long enough to harm yourself in any way you can conceive of. If that angers you, I am sorry, but I will not let you do this. But I will remain with you and see you through your grief as best as I can, though, even if it is on the receiving end of any curses you may hurl at me. You may hate me for it, but you will live.”

     

                “Her dying was the death of my heart; why would I care to live when she’s gone?” Lena scornfully asked.

     

                “Because she wished you to. If you cannot live for yourself, then live for her.”

     

                Lena stewed in the frustration that drowned her, her hands trembling as she ripped the blankets off her and staggered out of bed, a quiet gasp escaping her at the weakness in her limbs, feeling faint as her face paled. Her hand went to her side, where she’d been stabbed, albeit not very deeply, and she struggled to swallow.

     

                “You should rest. You have slept the last four days since I found you, but the fever and infection will have taken their toll,” Alex murmured.

     

                Instead of getting back into bed, as defiant as ever, Lena stood in the thin chemise she’d been changed into, her armour elsewhere, as her chest quickly rose and fell, heaving with her shallow breaths of anger. And then a gauzy curtain ballooned inwards with a gust of wind, the sheer fabric parting slightly to ruffle Lena’s unbound hair, and she felt her stomach swoop with the knowledge of how high up they were. Below, they were surrounded by water, a vast lake with a strong undercurrent, and Lena was only a few steps away from the open archway. It would be a simple thing to step through the curtain, and the idea took root, a last, desperate attempt.

     

                Studying her face, Alex read her thoughts in the glint of defiance in Lena’s eyes as they flitted to the archway, in the set of her mouth and jaw, the tensed muscles of her legs and shoulders. With a grim sigh, Alex gestured dismissively. “You are welcome to try it, although I will save you the trouble and tell you now it will not work. We are thirty feet up, would you say? Not nearly high enough for you to suffer more than being mildly winded for a moment. Yes, you could argue you are incapable of swimming and would soon drown, but I will remind you again that I am a strong swimmer and will pull you out before you reach that eventuality. You know how I try to avoid the cold and wet when the weather is cool, so I would prefer it if you didn’t-”

     

                She was still talking when Lena darted towards the archway. In a few steps, barging through sheer fabric, there was only open air, and a thirty-foot drop to the sparkling surface of the lake. It was a quick drop, Lena’s stomach plummeting with fear, adrenaline coursing through her in the seconds it took for gravity to slam her into the surface, driving the air from her lungs, as Alex had predicted. The intensity of the cold, even in late summer, made her skin feel numb almost immediately, and she thrashed about as instinct took over, but she was such a poor swimmer that her head never broke the surface. Adjusting quickly, Lena opened her mouth and sucked in some water right as a hand grabbed her arm, and she was hauled back to the surface. Struggling as she coughed and spluttered, gasping for air as she simultaneously fought to sink back beneath the surface and drown herself, Lena was towed back towards the tower, helpless in Alex’s strong embrace.

     

                Clambering onto the drowned ground floor with the flourishing pale tree, Alex grabbed a fistful of Lena’s sodden chemise and dragged her after her, wading through shin-deep water as Lena’s feet scrabbled for purchase on softly worn stone, splashing as she sputtered water and clawed at Alex’s leather leggings. Towing her to the staircase, Alex dragged Lena up a few steps and then flopped down on dry stone, letting go of Lena as she caught her breath. Splayed limply at her feet, her own legs still half-submerged in the water flooding the ground floor, Lena drew in ragged breaths, her throat scraped raw from her coughing, and promptly burst into tears.

     

                With a wretched sigh, Alex slithered down a few steps and gathered Lena into her lap, tears in her brown eyes as she patted her sister-in-law’s wet hair and let her sob into her lap. “I am sorry,” Alex unevenly rasped. “I know the pain you feel, but I cannot give you the relief you seek from it. I care for you, sister, even if that means I must let you linger in pain.”

     

                “Please,” Lena pitifully begged, her face pressed into the leather of Alex’s pants as she clutched fistfuls of wet cotton. “You have … already done so much for me, but I ask that you do this one thing and end my agony.”

     

                “I cannot. Even if I had not vowed to care for you in my sister’s stead, I would not be able to end the life of one of my family. You may be angry with me, and I will not blame you for that, but one day … one day, this pain will be smaller, and you will have a future ahead of you. You love her, as I do, albeit differently, but you are more than your marriage; you will have a life after this.”

     

                Tearing herself away, tear-stained face pink with anger as her face furrowed, Lena scoffed contemptuously. “Fuck you.”

     

                Staggering to her feet, splashing in the shallow water covering the bottom few steps, Lena hurried down, then, the hem of her chemise swirling about her shins as she waded through the water. Shoulders set, her mouth a flat line as she tried to stop her chin from wobbling, Lena dashed tears away and splashed her way through the open chamber, making for the stepping stones leading to the distant shore.

     

                “Lena,” Alex called after her, wearily rising to her feet.

     

                Forging onwards, ignoring the calls, Lena reached the first stepping stone and stepped across the gap, deep, dark water separating them beneath the rippling surface. Alex quickly caught up with her, ruffling her choppy hair with frustration as she stood at the lip of the tower, while Lena made for the next stepping stone.

     

                “You should be resting. Come, let me help you to bed and then-”

     

                “I don’t want to go to bed,” Lena whirled around and hoarsely shouted at her. “You’ve done enough. Leave me alone now.”

     

                “No.”

     

                Turning back around, her head spinning, shivers wracking her as her chemise clung to her wet skin, Lena had to fight to stop her teeth from chattering. “You know, you can’t watch me forever. It doesn’t matter how long it takes - a month, a year, a decade - I won’t stop trying to be with her.”

     

                “That is all well and good for you to try,” Alex curtly replied, “but you cannot leave.”

     

                Scoffing as she hopped to the next submerged stone with a small splash, Lena suddenly halted at the sight of a few soldiers in gleaming steel armour, the sun glinting off the sharp tips of their spears. Brow creasing, Lena squinted in their direction, holding a hand up to shield her eyes as she tried to make out their faces, wondering if perhaps Jack and Jess had made the trip with Alex. They were all unfamiliar to her, though, and Lena took another step before she was pulled to a halt by Alex’s tight grasp around her upper arm.

     

                “Let me go,” Lena bit out, trying to pull herself free but too weak.

     

                “They won’t let you leave,” Alex spoke over her.

     

                Her grasp went loose as Lena jerked herself free and stumbled through the water of the stepping stone, stopping before she fell over the edge, and turned to look at Alex with confusion. Wariness flickered in her eyes, and she grasped fistfuls of her wet chemise as she gave her sister-in-law a stubborn jerk of her chin.

     

                “What are you talking about? They’re here to guard me, aren’t they?”

     

                “Yes. They are here to keep you safe, and to keep you here.”

     

                Spluttering, Lena looked indignant as she scowled. “What do you mean?”

     

                “I believe the correct term for you would be political prisoner.”

     

                “Prisoner? But I- I’m Queen of the Unseelie.”

     

                “Yes. That is precisely why the Council saw fit to put you under guard here. You are our biggest enemy, our greatest threat to peace.”

     

                “Me?” Lena spluttered. “I’m the reason we have peace.”

     

                “Yes, well, I know that, but without the security of an arranged marriage, they find you a risk. They will not let you leave. Trust me. I have already argued against it in your stead, with little success.”

     

                Swallowing, Lena felt the urge to argue claw up the back of her throat and had to bite her tongue to stop herself from lashing out. Dry-eyed now, she cleared her throat, a muscle twitching in her jaw, her emotions pitching to extremes in the disorientation of waking up again. 

     

                “And how did they know to find me here?”

     

                “I sent letters. To my mother and Kelly, as well. So far, they have yet to show up, but the nearest members of the Council have gathered with a retinue of guards to ensure you are kept here.”

     

                “They will not keep me here,” Lena firmly told her.

     

                Alex helplessly shrugged, a strained look on her face as she rubbed her brow. “You are in no position to try and leave now. You should rest; we will find a way out of this once you have recovered and we have discussed it further.”

     

                “I don’t need your help. I need- I need-”

     

                Lena’s throat closed up, and she let out a breathless gasp, hitching in her throat as she pressed a hand to the ache in her side, her eyes stinging again. She needed Kara. She needed the comfort of her company, her reassuring presence, the way she was still so gentle in her stubbornness, could talk Lena through anything, even their different opinions. What she would’ve given to hold her again, even just once, just one more day, one more hour. There was so much they hadn’t talked about, things she still needed to say, but that opportunity was long gone. It was unfair to have that sort of happiness for a moment before it had all gone so horribly wrong.

     

                Anger filled her, and she stormed back towards the tower, skirting past Alex as she splashed her way across the stepping stones, finding herself breathless as her vision dimmed. Dizzy and pale, she staggered towards the stairs and had to practically crawl up them as she pushed her healing body too far. By the time she reached her floor, she had no choice but to let Alex help her to the bed, sweating and grey-faced as she drew in painful breaths, a trembling hand pressed to her side.

     

                Stripping off her sodden shift, letting it splat to the stone floor, Lena collapsed back into bed, wrapping herself in the thick quilt as she shivered, eyes squeezed shut. Moving over to the carved screen hiding the tub, Alex fetched her a towel and then a clean chemise from the wooden chest with a few items of Lena’s clothing that had been left behind. Lena didn’t so much as glance up at her as she crossed over to her bedside and stood over her, choosing to keep her eyes screwed shut, as if that would make Alex go away.

     

                “Dry yourself off and let me change your bandages.”

     

                “Go away.”

     

                “No, I will not. I should - you are almost being ungrateful enough for me to leave you to your fate - but I think that would make you happy, so you are stuck with me instead. Now, I tire of your antics; dry off and let me tend to your wound, before you do irreparable damage out of sheer stupidity.”

     

                Lena opened her eyes at the weight of the towel flopping onto her lap, and she remained still for a moment longer before letting out a listless sigh and pushing herself up. The blankets had dried off some of the wetness, damp sheets sticking to her skin as she pushed herself up, and Lena snagged the towel and started to wring as much water out of her dripping hair as she could, while Alex moved about the room, snatching up objects scattered across the table. Abandoning the towel, Lena shivered her way into the chemise, wishing for something thicker as she hugged her arms to herself. Setting her armful of items down on the chair and dragging it closer to the bed, Alex sank onto the edge of the mattress and gestured to Lena.

     

                “Let me see.”

     

                “I’m fine,” Lena rasped, tugging the blankets up higher.

     

                “My patience wears thin. You will do as I say, whether it is by choice or force. I do not wish to baby you, but if you insist on behaving childishly, I will have no choice, so let us make it easier for each other-”

     

                Lena scoffed and ripped the blankets back, sitting up straighter and swinging her legs out of bed. “You’re getting on my last nerve now.”

     

                Alex reached out to stop her, and Lena batted her hand aside with a disgruntled look. Raising her eyebrows, Alex grimaced. “Is that how you wish it to be? Fine.”

     

                She reached out for Lena again, and Lena snagged her wrist, scowling, but was too slow to stop Alex from jabbing her in her solar plexus, winding her. Then, Alex followed up with a jab to her wounded side, making Lena’s vision dim as she let out a strangled cry of pain, knees buckling. Pushing her back down to the mattress, having remained seated on the edge of the bed the entire time, Alex sighed.

     

                “See? You should not be out of bed. Now, sit still.”

     

                Still struggling to breathe, her face clammy and white, Lena lay limply against the pillows and let Alex ruck up her chemise and cut away the wet bandages. Staring up at the ceiling, her vision swimming, Lena felt detached from her body as she helplessly let Alex clean her side. The stitches were bleeding slightly from her constant agitation of the wound, and the days it was left untreated and had grown infected left it unhealed for longer than her wounds usually persisted, although it was no longer red at the edges, and her sister was careful as she gently bathed the stitches. The fragrant smell of herbs became bitter as Alex pounded them together with a pestle and mortar, mixing in honey as Lena took note of what she was using, remaining silent as she found nothing objectionable.

     

                For all of her ire, Alex was kind and gentle as she tended to her, and Lena’s eyes stung. She’d apparently been out of it for four days after Alex had found her, and she was unsure how long it had taken her to find her as well, and she could only imagine she had barely left Lena’s side since, tending to her similarly through that time. She started to cry, not a peep out of her as tears welled up and ran down her temples, wiped away as more chased after them, and Alex said nothing, diligently smearing the paste over the wound, sticking a square of linen over it and leaving it unbandaged. Tidying away the paraphernalia, she moved from the bed to the chair, while Lena felt shame sting her cheeks. But she couldn’t feel grateful towards her, because she didn’t want to be saved.

     

                “I miss her too,” Alex said after a long silence, her voice wobbling and halting. “I miss my sister. And I miss my wife. And my mother. You are all I have in the world at present; I am sorry for being poor company, but … you are all that is keeping me going. Else, I fear I would fall apart, too.”

     

                Lena’s eyes slid sideways to look at her, and she saw tears swimming in Alex’s eyes too, the loss of her sister creeping back up on her after spending so long stifling her grief as she focused on keeping them both safe. Another stab of guilt knifed Lena as she considered how solely consumed with grief she’d been, leaving no room for Alex to process the loss of Kara as well, but she felt so debilitated by it that she didn’t have the energy to try and make space within her own grief. She couldn’t find the energy to stop grieving either.

     

                With a heavy sigh, Alex gave Lena’s leg a pat over the top of the blankets. “I will make you some tea, and then you should sleep.”

     

                “You need it more than I do,” Lena mumbled, staring up at the ribbed ceiling.

     

                “Yes, I do, but it is not an opportune time for me to rest. That will have to wait.”

     

                “For what?”

     

                Alex shifted uncomfortably on her chair, a troubled look crossing her face. “I have yet to hear from Kelly or my mother. There has been no response to my letters from them, and no sign, either. The four Councilmembers are the only response I have received, but they will not speak with me.”

     

                “What did you say in your letters?”

     

                “That I was here with you. That your brother is dead. That you were injured and recovering. I had hoped to at least have my wife with me through this ordeal.”

     

                The worry in her voice gnawed at Lena, and she swallowed past the tightness in her throat. “I’m sure she’s fine. She would’ve gotten away after we left them. Maybe she’s just- she hasn’t been at any of the locations you sent letters to.”

     

                “And my mother? She would surely have been in her halls in the mountains.”

     

                “Days north of here, isn’t it? Maybe she left to join us without sending word.”

     

                “No, she would have responded before leaving.”

     

                “Maybe the birds didn’t reach her.”

     

                “Perhaps not, but they have delivered letters in winter months, when the mountain passes are closed from the snow. It is either bad luck or intentional sabotage.”

     

                “Well … we have a streak of bad luck,” Lena murmured, rubbing her sore eyes, tired and defeated.

     

                “We do indeed,” Alex agreed with a sigh. “I will fetch some tea.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, she made for the open staircase spiralling around the tower and stepped onto the smoothly worn stone before pausing and giving Lena a warning glance. “Do not even think about throwing yourself from the tower again. I will drag you back out, and I shall bind you, wrist and ankle, to the bed next time. It will leave me in a foul mood, though, and my mood is already low enough.”

     

                Eyelids shuttering, the ghost of a smile touched the corners of Lena’s lips. “Fine. I won’t.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “I should be thanking you.”

     

                Alex let out a soft chuckle. “But you are not grateful, are you? You are not grateful, because you wish you were dead, and I have kept you from that.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena quietly agreed, a lump rising to her throat again.

     

                “Just as you will not thank me, I will not apologise. We shall be even in that.”

     

                She started to make her way downstairs but paused as Lena quietly spoke. “I’m sorry.”

     

                No response was forthcoming, and Lena listened to her footsteps continue on the stone steps, disappearing from her hearing and then returning five minutes later. Holding a tray, Alex moved over to her bedside and set it down on the mattress, picking up a steaming bowl and holding it out to Lena.

     

                “It is little better than what we had eaten on the road; Querl brought most of Argo’s food stores with him to the river, and I am not so efficient without my sister’s water assistants to help, but it is hot and filling.”

     

                Lena considered objecting, taking the route of starvation instead, but that would be long and tiresome, and Alex would undoubtedly find a way to force food down her throat before it got to that point, so Lena relented. Perhaps she was just feeling sheepish after the ordeal she’d put her sister-in-law through, or maybe she was just clinging to a quick death in the near future, once she’d slipped Alex’s attention, but either way, she eased herself up against the pillows and took the bowl.

     

                Alex seemed to visibly relax as the tension bled out of her, relieved that Lena started eating without argument, and she picked up one of the cups on the tray and sipped some tea while Lena spooned stew into her mouth. It was her first proper meal in a week, perhaps longer, and despite Alex’s opinion on it, it was heavenly to Lena, as much as she resented feeding herself. She emptied the bowl and then set it down on the tray, picking up the tea, inhaling the smell of herbs that Alex had used to brew it, soothing and warm. Draining it quickly, the heat of it and the stew warming her through, and her eyelids grew heavy by the time she finished. It made her wonder whether Alex had brewed hers with a few extra herbs, or whether she was just that tired, despite her four days of uninterrupted sleep. Either way, Lena wasn’t conscious for much longer, asleep before she knew it.

     

                Waking to darkness, she felt lethargic as she rubbed her eyes, her mind fuzzy, her body heavy. Moonlight filtered in through the curtains, and Lena made out the sleeping figure at her bedside, arms crossed over her stomach, chin to her chest. Alex didn’t stir at all as Lena sat up, easing the blankets back and slipping out of bed. Her bare feet were quiet on the stone floor, and she almost considered waking her sister and sending her off to a proper bed, but that would just open a can of worms with her following Lena about like her personal shadow, instead of properly resting. Even if it was in a chair, at least she was getting some sleep, so Lena left her there, tiptoeing across the room and silently padding downstairs.

     

                Around and around she went, until she reached the bottom few steps, submerged in frigid water. It was like a sheet of glass in the stillness of the night, and Lena stared at the patterns of light shimmering on the surface as moonlight slanted in through the open archways. Slowly, she descended the last few steps, the water so cold that it burned, made her feet go numb, but Lena continued, soaking the hem of her dry chemise as she waded in further. She didn’t know what she was doing, why she’d gotten out of bed to go downstairs. It wasn’t to kill herself, oddly enough. Instead, she walked through the flooded chamber to that pale tree, a few fallen leaves floating on the surface of the water, and pressed her palm to the smooth bark. Sinking to her knees, stone hard beneath her, water soaking her through once more, Lena curled up amongst the roots and closed her eyes, pressing her cheek to the cold bark as she let out a soft sigh. 

     

                It was comforting, a piece of life amidst the cold loneliness of the water, and she poured herself into the tree without intending to, as she had the bad habit of doing, and remained curled up there despite the pain of the water as the chill worked its way into her bones. As she sat there, time slipping past, the sky lightened from black to navy, to indigo as dawn broke over the expanse of the lake. At the sound of footsteps hurrying down the stone steps, growing louder over the peaceful lapping of the lake, the wind in the trees, Lena peeled her eyelids open and stared out at the stretch of towering trees on the shore, the dark water reaching their roots, and she felt a pang of longing to stand in their shade, the wind only bringing a whiff of the rich greenness.

     

                There was little chance of that happening; the guards were somewhere in the trees, no doubt keeping watch throughout the night, and Lena didn’t have the motivation to try and get around them. What was she going to do, row a boat across the lake? Admittedly, it wasn’t a bad option, but she thought that might draw attention to herself, either by Alex or the guards, so it would inevitably be futile anyway. Alex was already coming to find her anyway, her footsteps quick as she rushed down through the tower. Lena was looking at the empty steps, waiting, and watched as Alex came into view and abruptly stopped.

     

                Dishevelled, Alex blinked owlishly as she roughly raked a hand through her hair, a troubled look clouding her face, even as her shoulders slumped with relief. Her voice was gravelly as she spoke. “I expected to find your body floating in the lake.”

     

                “No. Not this morning, at least. You needed your rest.”

     

                A strangled laugh escaped Alex, and she waded through the water as she descended the last few steps and slowly approached Lena. Sinking to a crouch near her, Alex reached out to pat Lena’s shoulder. “You are a strange woman, and I am unsure where we are going, or what will happen next, but I am glad to have you with me.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena wearily sighed, eyelids closing as she exhaled, shivering where she remained curled up. “I am glad to have you with me as well. As ungrateful as I am.”

     

                A small smile curved Alex’s lips, and she rose to her feet, water sloshing around her shins. “Your lips look almost purple. How long have you been down here?”

     

                “Long enough to watch the sunrise.”

     

                “Let us get you warm and dry; you will catch a chill otherwise.”

     

                Lena didn’t have the energy to object, to say she didn’t care about what befell her, that she would’ve been quite content to remain curled up there forever, as she’d intended before Alex had tracked her down and saved her from her fate. Maybe she felt guilty for worrying her too, but either way, she made her stiff limbs unfold and let Alex help her to her feet. Her chemise and the linen were soaked again, and she hugged her arms to herself as she slowly plodded up each step.

     

                Back on her floor, in her open room, Lena pressed a hand to her side as she stooped to fish something dry out of the chest, finding nothing but a few dresses unsuitable for anything but lounging about. With a quiet sigh, she turned and left a trail of water in her wake as she made her way to Kara’s floor, where her room was, with her things, where they’d lived separately at the time. It wasn’t unfamiliar to Lena, but it wasn’t quite the same as walking into the room they’d shared together, and yet, it hurt almost as much, seeing Kara’s books, her inkpots and quills on the desk, her harp, blankets she’d wrapped herself in, the bed she’d slept in. It was all so personal, so her, and Lena swallowed a sob, making for the large wooden chest with some things Kara had left behind.

     

                Shedding her chemise, Lena swapped it for a deep blue robe of crushed velvet, like the sky as the blue hour tipped towards black. It was heavily embroidered with silver fish, swimming up each sleeve and in a spiral on the back, and she hugged the flowing fabric to herself, breathing in the faint smell of rain and salt, of sage and woodsmoke where it had been washed. Agony split her anew, and Lena stumbled over to Kara’s bed and tumbled onto the covers, curling herself up into a small ball. She felt Alex watching her, and squeezed her eyes shut, swallowing thickly, even though she didn’t cry.

     

                “I’d like to be alone, please.”

     

                Alex didn’t move an inch, and Lena let out a frustrated huff. Her hands balled up in the crushed velvet of the robe, and she gritted her teeth for a moment before continuing, a little tersely.

     

                “I won’t do anything to hurt myself this morning, you have my word. Go and sleep in a proper bed; you don’t need to watch over me. I’ll be okay by myself.”

     

                Still, Alex hesitated before relenting, taking Lena at her word. She’d said it, so it had to be true, even if it only applied until midday. That still gave Lena some time alone to nurse her wounds for the next few hours, and give Alex a much-needed break, too. Listening to the quiet scuff of retreating footsteps, Lena let out a breath, her body sinking into the mattress as the tension bled out of her. Remaining there for the rest of the morning, she didn’t so much as sleep but slipped in and out of a stupor, thinking of nothing at all, so numb to everything. 

     

                It was the distant sound of raised voices that roused her. Climbing to her feet, she padded over to the archway, parting the gauzy curtains and looking out towards the shore, not looking down at the long drop below her. The guards were gathered in a loose group near where the stepping stones started, and ankle deep in the water, on the first stepping stone, stood Alex. By her gesturing and the indecipherable sound of her raised voice, she was arguing with the guards. Lena watched her for a moment before her curiosity got the better of her and she crossed over to the stairs and hurried down to the ground floor, gathering up fistfuls of the hem of her long robe and wading through the chamber, hopping from stepping stone to stepping stone with haste.

     

                “No, no,” she made out Alex’s vehement objections as she drew nearer, “you misunderstand me; I am not asking, I am telling you. You will not keep me here when I have a wife I must return to.”

     

                “You can leave. She cannot.”

     

                “And as I have told you, I am bound to keep her safe, so I cannot leave without her.”

     

                “The Council have instructed us not to let her leave.”

     

                “Then I will speak to the Councilmembers here now,” Alex demanded.

     

                The exasperated soldier sighed and rolled his eyes, leaning casually on his spear, bored by his charge. “You are not at liberty to make demands of them.”

     

                “I am,” Lena softly called out, drawing their attention to her as she bridged the gap between them, standing on the same stepping stone as Alex and stopping at her shoulder. “I am Queen of the Unseelie and the peace between our Courts hinges on my word; fetch them for me.”

     

                There was a momentary unease amongst the assembled soldiers, as if they wanted to dismiss her request but didn’t want to be the one to say it, to risk plunging them back into another war, when the last one had been over for barely a month. When no one was brave enough to vocally object, the one who’d been speaking to Alex cleared his throat and gestured to one of the soldiers flanking him, sending the woman off into the trees without a word. Folding her arms over her chest, wearing nothing but her wife’s flowing robe, her face drawn and pale, her body feeling heavy, Lena waited impatiently. No one spoke, not even her to Alex or vice versa, and they were left listening to the lapping water and the wind through the trees.

     

                It felt like an hour before the sound of hoofbeats treading on the forest floor pricked their ears, and Lena was in desperate need of sitting down, already irritable and light-headed before they’d even gotten to their meeting. Still, she remained, uncomplaining, looking as far from a Queen as she could get, and watched as four horses stepped out of the treeline with two women and two men a-horse, resplendent in embroidered robes and pristine armour, and no shortage of velvet, gold and silver, precious gemstones and embellishment between them. Two of them she judged to be Airfolk - the dark-haired woman and the man with greying hair - and the blonde woman Waterfolk, while the dark-haired man Firefolk, by the colour of their clothes.

     

                At their arrival, Lena straightened, shoulders back, and closed the distance to the shore, soft mud under her bare feet as the soldiers retreated to the treeline, spread out in a crescent behind the four Councilmembers. Dismounting, the Councilmembers gracefully approached, and Lena raised her chin a fraction beneath their scrutinising stares, assessing her, taking her measure. Whatever they made of her, she hoped she could set the record straight once they got to talking.

     

                “These are Councillors Maxwell, Olivia, Morgan and Cat,” Alex introduced them as she stood at Lena’s right shoulder. “And this is Queen Lena, of the Unseelie.”

     

                Giving them what she hoped was a dignified dip of her head, Lena clasped her hands behind her back. “Thank you for coming.”

     

                “We did not think we had much of a say,” Morgan drawled with a crooked smile, dark eyes glimmering with amusement. “We were led to believe it was a matter of peace.”

     

                “In a sense,” Lena agreed. “I think we can all agree that peace would be preferable.”

     

                “Of course,” Olivia agreed, “and we have no intention of jeopardising that, unless we are left with no other choice. I speak on behalf of all members of the Council, including those who are unable to be present, when I say that we are thankful you withdrew your forces across the river.”

     

                Lena smiled thinly. “War has never been my intention. I would prefer not to resort to it again, unless I’m left with no other choice, as well, so we are agreed on that. So, I must ask why I’m being kept here against my will.”

     

                “It is for your protection,” Maxwell said, brushing invisible lint off his neatly trimmed surcoat. 

     

                “Oh, I’m sure that’s part of it. As well as my cooperation.”

     

                “The truth of the matter is,” Cat sighed, hands on her hips, giving Lena a droll look, “you’re our greatest threat, our greatest enemy, whether you intend to be, or not. Now, we know you agreed to marry Lady Kara to bring about an era of peace, but-”

     

                “Yes, I did. Also against my will, might I add, but I was committed to that, at great personal sacrifice, too. Unfortunately, many things went wrong there, and I never wanted to be Queen, but here I am,” Lena said, spreading her arms, before letting them fall limply to her sides. “Now, I intend to honour my wife’s wishes as best as I can.”

     

                “That is all well and good, but that does not appease the Council much,” Morgan scoffed. “What reassurance is that to us? What is to stop you from deciding you no longer wish to honour her wishes?”

     

                “Why would I, when she sacrificed everything in the hopes of achieving a lasting peace one day?”

     

                “Yes, we are very much aware of what Lady Kara sacrificed,” Maxwell curtly replied. “As you know, the decision to wed you two together was made by the Council. We were involved in that process as much as she was.”

     

                “Yes, I am aware of that fact. So, you know how important it was to her, and why it’s important to me to honour it in her absence.”

     

                With a snort, Morgan raised his eyebrows. “So, it will only last as long as you are separated, you mean?”

     

                “Well, I can’t speak for anyone else who succeeds me on the throne,” Lena carefully replied, a furrow between her eyebrows. “But if it’s any consolation, I’ve named my sister as my heir. I’m sure Alex will be as devoted to keeping the peace as I am, if not more. Is that not reason enough to believe me?”

     

                “You’ve named your sister as heir?” Cat asked in surprise, blue eyes wary. “Over your wife.”

     

                Lena’s voice was curt as she shifted with annoyance, a prickle of anger within her at the dismissive air of the four of them, their lack of empathy for her, or respect for their fallen Councilmember. “Of course, I would’ve picked my wife if she hadn’t died on the banks of the river. I thought her sister was a trustworthy alternative.”

     

                “Died?” Cat scoffed, rolling her eyes. “It was hardly fatal.”

     

                “Her heart stopped while I held her; how else would you describe it?”

     

                There was an exchanged glance between the Councilmembers, but no one was forthcoming with what that glance meant. Alex’s brow creased as she looked from one to the other with wariness in her eyes, while Lena clenched her jaw, her patience wearing thin as she rubbed her brow, an ache at her temples. 

     

                “When was this?” Olivia asked.

     

                “When- months ago,” Alex huffed, disbelief on her face. “You mean to tell us you have not heard? It was barely spring; word does not take that long to travel, especially when it is concerning the General of the North falling in battle.”

     

                They all swapped looks again, an uncomfortable pause, before Morgan gave them a shrewd look. “Yes, well … accounts can … vary. So, this promise of peace is in honour of Lady Kara? Because you are separated?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena whispered, a lump in her throat. “Yes, of course it’s in her honour. I want peace too, so no one else has to experience this pain, this- this grief, but even if I didn’t want it, I would do it in her honour. I would do anything for her.”

     

                “Anything?” he pressed. “That is a tall order. Surely there are some things you would not have done. If she had asked you to abdicate, to abolish the Unseelie monarchy, would you have done so?”

     

                “If it brought her back. She would never have asked that of me, but if it could bring her back, I would do it in a heartbeat. I would give anything to have her back. Even for a moment.”

     

                “You will give up the Unseelie throne, relieve the Court of a ruling monarchy in exchange for your wife?”

     

                “Yes. Yes, of course I would. I would give my own life in exchange for hers. I wish it had been me - it should’ve been.”

     

                There was that strange silence again, and Lena’s eyes were stinging as she pressed her mouth into a flat line, watching as Cat gave Morgan a bewildered look, somewhat annoyed and disapproving. It was she who turned to look at Lena, an eyebrow arched as the corners of her mouth curved with amusement.

     

                “She is not dead. Why is everyone acting as if it were so?”

     

                “She is,” Lena insisted. “You say she is not because you weren’t there, but I’m telling you-”

     

                “Then you are mistaken,” Cat cut her off, “unless she has passed very recently, Lady Kara is very much alive.”

     

                “You’re lying,” Lena accused her, although Cat couldn’t have been, or she wouldn’t have gotten the words out.

     

                Alex stepped forward then, her face pinched with confusion, and cocked her head to the side. “What do you mean, she’s alive?”

     

                “We have seen her recently,” Olivia replied.

     

                “When? When was the last time you saw her?”

     

                Olivia hesitated, licking her lips as she glanced at her fellow Councilmembers, before she spoke. “A week ago.”

     

                “That’s not possible,” Lena whispered, wariness in her eyes. 

     

                She wouldn’t allow herself to entertain the thought, to even think for a second that what she said was true. Hope was futile and would only bring more pain once they straightened out this miscommunication. Perhaps they’d thought it was someone else, maybe they’d visited the site where their General of the North had been laid to rest, out of respect. Any number of things could be true, but not that Kara was alive. Not when Lena had felt her body go slack, and heard her heart stop beating.

     

                “It should not have been,” Cat agreed, “but we heard of her injuries, heard that she had survived, against all odds, and have laid eyes on her ourselves. Whatever may have happened, she did not die on the riverbank in spring.”

     

                “And now, she is brought back to you,” Morgan said with a pleased smile, clapping his hands, “and you will give up your throne, as you have promised to.”

     

                “Wait, what?”

     

                “Your wife,” he clarified. “She passed this way a week past, along with a few companions. And now, we shall have the Unseelie Court in our hands. Finally. A good outcome for all, do you not agree?”

     

                Rubbing her brow, confused, frustrated, wary, Lena was having a hard time keeping up with what they were saying, the things that should’ve been impossible for them to say without it being a lie. But the fact that they were all saying they’d seen Kara had to be true, or else they would’ve gotten choked up on the words. But how was that possible? How were they twisting it in their favour?

     

                “No, I- that’s not- that’s not … possible. You can’t- you can’t say that when it’s a lie. You shouldn’t be able to-”

     

                “You have been misled,” Cat sighed, a little more patient and kinder now. “She never was dead; you are only able to say so because you believed it, and thus, it was true to you. And you have promised to abolish the monarchy in exchange for having her back. That was a foolish promise to make without confirming for yourself that she could not be brought back.”

     

                Ignoring that part of it, too focused on the part about Kara, starting to feel hopeful now, despite her warnings to herself, Lena shook her head. Her face was even paler, if that was possible, her pulse racing as her chest rose and fell with quick, shallow breaths.

     

                “She’s alive?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You saw her?”

     

                “I spoke with her myself,” Cat confirmed.

     

                “As did I,” supplied Olivia.

     

                A small sound escaped Lena, more of a whimper than anything, as she cupped her brow, tipping her head back. Taking a moment to process that possibility, she swallowed thickly and allowed herself to believe it. Still, she would have to see it for herself to know for sure. “Where is she?”

     

                “It matters not,” Morgan coolly interjected. “You cannot go to her; you are in our custody.”

     

                Anger flashed through Lena, and she lowered her head to stare at him, her face hard, eyes flat with a warning he didn’t heed. “You will tell me where she is. “

     

                The ground trembled slightly, and the assembled Councilmembers and soldiers exchanged uneasy glances, the horses shifting restlessly further in the shadows of the trees, while the lake rippled from the disturbance. Hands balled into fists, Lena took a step forward, not exactly threatening, but determined, desperate.

     

                “You will not leave this place,” Maxwell declared, as the soldiers all unsheathed their swords, gripped spears tighter, and angled tridents in her direction. 

     

                “I demand you tell me,” Lena insisted. “You won’t keep me here. You can’t; I’m not under your jurisdiction, and it will be in your best interest to let me go without a fight.”

     

                He laughed, raising his eyebrows in surprise as he smiled, his stance casual as he spread his hands helplessly. “I’m afraid you are outnumbered.”

     

                “In the name of peace, I suggest you tell her,” Alex quietly threatened, stepping forward, the forest still and silent beyond them all.

     

                “She is one woman,” Morgan scoffed, rolling his eyes as he grinned. “A rather unimpressive Queen, at that.”

     

                Alex smiled thinly. “Then you do not know who you are dealing with.”

     

                The ground was suddenly torn open, soil and mud churning up as roots erupted from the dirt and quickly ensnared them all. Every soldier and Councilmember. Lena didn’t even have to move, the forest so attuned to her every emotion that it leapt to help, knowing her intentions without her even having to think it. They were all thoroughly bound within moments, startled shouts and curses overlapping as they found themselves unable to move their legs. They still had use of their arms, although the roots were slowly creeping upwards, but short of throwing a spear at her, Lena was out of arms’ reach, rendering the soldiers useless.

     

                “Where is she?” she quietly snarled, green eyes flashing a warning.

     

                The snarl was echoed by the deep rumble within the confines of the trees, a hulking shadow lurking within, grey fur visible as her wolf cub slunk through the towering trunks. Watching as Morgan and Maxwell paled, fear in their eyes, struggling against their bonds as they found their arms bound now, Lena clicked her tongue in warning as she took a step closer to the women. In front of Cat and Olivia, Lena looked from one to the other, her stare piercing and almost manic, the sheer desperation within her leaving her reckless and determined, and spoke quietly. It was less of a demand this time and more of a plea.

     

                “Where is she?”

     

                “She went to the Unseelie Court in search of you,” Cat sighed. “That is all I know.”

     

                Swallowing thickly, Lena nodded. “Thank you.”

     

                With a breathless laugh, Morgan gave her a contemptuous look. “Do not thank us; we will not let you leave.”

     

                Lena was already moving, rushing between them and plunging straight into the trees as she let out an amused scoff. “Try to stop me. I dare you.”

     

                And then she felt the blinding pain of being burnt as Maxwell, as well as two Firefolk amongst the assembled guards, started to burn their way free of their bindings. Hesitating, wincing at the feeling, as if it were her own skin, Lena’s concentration lapsed, and the roots loosened, shrinking back into the ground like wounded animals, allowing them all to escape with varying success. Buffeted by the strong wind of an Airfolk soldier, Lena felt her stomach drop as she staggered, almost slipping on a patch of leaves, before catching herself, but turned to find Alex separated from her by a dozen soldiers and the four Councilmembers. 

     

                While she wanted to hunt for Kara more than anything, while her heart pounded at the sliver of hope that her wife was alive somewhere in the Unseelie Court, Lena couldn’t leave Alex behind in good conscience. Not after everything she’d done for her, everything they’d been through together, but there was no conceivable way Lena could keep them all trapped long enough to get away without the forest being harmed, or without killing them all. She didn’t want to take it that far; that wasn’t what Kara would want, even if it meant reuniting with her quicker. Knowing that too, Alex unsheathed two long hunting knives and met her eyes across the distance separating them. With a nod, Alex hefted the hilts of her knives in her hands, a stubborn set to her jaw, determined to delay the soldiers for as long as she could to give Lena a chance to get away, even if it meant defying the Council of her own Court, even if it meant getting hurt. Still, Lena hesitated a moment longer.

     

                “Go, Lena,” Alex called to her, giving her another reassuring nod. “Find her!”

    Chapter 53

                Never much of an athlete, Lena would’ve believed she could have run in the Olympics with how fast she tore through the trees, never having run so fast in her life - not even to save her own life. Weaponless, not even a little knife to protect herself with, Lena felt brambles and branches of wildly growing bushes snag in her hair and scratch her cheeks, her bare legs as the robe flapped around them. She didn’t slow for a second, even when her lungs burned and she got a stitch in her side, face reddening from the exertion as her heart pounded. It was surely sheer adrenaline that kept her going, making her unable to feel the pain in her side, the weakness in her limbs, too focused on that desperate hope as she put one foot in front of the other, streaking through the forest alone.

     

                Except, she wasn’t alone, because she had the vague awareness that her skin was prickling, that she was being watched, even if she didn’t have the time to acknowledge it. It was the wolf, she was sure of it. Somewhere nearby, adeptly camouflaged amongst the underbrush, the wolf was keeping pace, tagging along as Lena’s desperation poured out of her, the attention of the forest honing in on her once more. Nothing could have hurt her then, though, not every creature in the forest combined, nor every soldier, because Kara was alive and she would find her. Whether she had to crawl to her in the end, it didn’t matter, but Lena would stop at nothing, even if it was only chasing after a sliver of hope. 

     

                It hadn’t crossed her mind yet that she had no idea where she was going. She’d just picked a direction and run as fast as she could, knowing she just had to reach the river. But the forest was vast, on both sides of the river, and she didn’t know enough to guide herself through it, but that didn’t seem important yet. She’d only gone a few miles, and when she’d made that trip on horseback, from Argo to her mother’s home in the Unseelie Court, it had taken the better part of a day. On foot, it would take days, possibly a week, and that was if she wasn’t led astray by her poor navigation. For now, she was more focused on covering ground, heading somewhat eastwards.

     

                Her pace slowed a little, cardio not exactly her strong suit, but she persisted, her bare feet not quite callused enough to not feel the little stones, the sharp pieces of broken twigs and thorns that cut up her soles. It was dim within the confines of the forest, the thick trunks crowding in together, ferns and brambles as tall as she was making it difficult in some places for her to keep up her dogged pace, but Lena pushed through them unperturbed, her robe catching and tearing, until it was only loosely tied around her waist, slipping down her shoulders as she drew in ragged breaths, already sweating and dirty.

     

                Running until her legs were wobbly, until she was practically staggering along, slipping a few times and only just managing to catch her balance, Lena had to stop. Hand out, fumbling, she braced herself against the trunk of an elm tree, chest heaving as sweat ran down her face, soaking into the velvet and the leaves underfoot. The stitches in her side had reopened, and she could feel the wetness of blood on her side, along with slick sweat, her lungs burning as she drew in frantic breaths, all but collapsing against the trunk. Lena didn’t know how long she’d been running for, but it felt like an eternity, with nothing much changing in the landscape, the rolling forest, with its slopes and dips, mossy boulders and puddles of stagnant water, trickling streams and rank upon rank of trees. She could’ve been walking in circles for all she knew, and she was starting to feel that desperation dip down into bleak helplessness, losing steam now that she’d been forced to stop. That didn’t mean that she would stop, though, but it wasn’t as nearly straightforward as she’d hoped.

     

                “Fuck,” she gasped, forehead pressed to the elm’s trunk, sweat wetting the bark as her chest tightened with panic.

     

                So far, Alex hadn’t caught up with her, and Lena didn’t know what to do.
