She could spend an eternity scouring the forest for Kara without ever finding her, could starve herself to death, drive herself mad in her aimless wandering, but still, she would search. Lena didn’t have it in her to give up, even when she’d wanted to, and had been forced to endure by Alex’s maddening insistence, and now that she had hope, she wouldn’t give up. Tired, perhaps more tired than she’d been in her life, the last week catching up with her, Lena pushed herself up straight, her palms pressed against the trunk of the elm, tears in her eyes as the sweat dried somewhat on her dirty face.

     

                Tipping her head back, Lena looked up at the canopy spreading wide overhead, standing in the deep shadow of the ancient tree, and she let out a forceful breath. Tears spilt over, and her chin wobbled as she pressed her palms flat to the rough bark, a deep ache in her chest as she was filled with longing.

     

                “Please. Please help me find her,” she rasped, resorting to begging, just in case they could help, in case they could feel her intentions, just as it had seemed on the way to Argo, when she was just as lost.

     

                A deep groan filled the quiet forest, echoing around her, as if the trees were talking to each other, and Lena went weak at the knees, palms grazing down the trunk as she sank to the ground. Nestled amongst the roots, breathing in the smell of damp soil, of rotting leaves and over-ripe apples, fresh pine and pollen, she let out a choked sob, trying to keep it together as minutes slipped by and tears continued to slide down her cheeks. The wind continued to ghost through the forest, rustling leaves and branches, swirling debris on the floor about, and Lena wiped her grimy face on torn sleeves, her face mournful and pleading as she stared up, so small in comparison to the width of the trunk, just a tiny, insignificant part of the forest. But she was insignificant in the way bees were, or tiny minnows, just a little part of a greater ecosystem, and not so unimportant to the trees as she thought. 

     

                Whether it was because she gave so much of herself in her begging, or whether the forest was just that enamoured with her, Lena would never know, but despite the constant south-westerly breeze, the branches of the elm seemed to bend and point north-easterly. It was not just the elm, but the others too, the trees groaning as they all leaned in the same direction, in opposition to the wind. Eyes widening a fraction, a frayed sound of disbelief escaping her parted lips, as if surprised that it worked, vindicated that she hadn’t been crazy last time, that the trees had helped, Lena hoarsely laughed.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena breathlessly whispered, heart pounding as fresh hope filled her.

     

                She leaned in and kissed the trunk, patting the rough bark with grateful affection, before she made herself stand, legs aching and weak beneath her, but forced to bear her weight as sheer stubbornness kept her going. Palm pressed against the trunk a moment longer, Lena drew in a deep breath and set her shoulders.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Stumbling off in the direction they were pointing, scuffing up leaves and dried bark, stubbing her toe on a rock, Lena drew in panicked breaths, impatient and frantic in her urgency. Making it a hundred yards, something big leapt at her, and she skidded on a patch of leaves and fell into a wild-growing patch of nettles, hissing and spitting curses as she watched the hulking wolf cub crouch nearby, those eyes watching her closely, unblinking. Body going slack in the nettles, Lena let out a ragged sound of relief, closing her eyes as she clapped a hand to her brow, trying to still her racing pulse. She took a moment to gather herself before she picked herself up, working nettles out of her tangled hair, roughly yanking the hem of her robe free, little burs caught in the velvet.

     

                Panting, chest quickly rising and falling, she scowled at the wolf. They stared at each other for a moment, and the wolf crawled forward on its belly, a soundless huff escaping it as it snapped its teeth. Scoffing, Lena dragged her robe tighter around herself and hurried off, damp, dirty and shivering, and made it three steps before she was jerked backwards, teeth nipping at the shoulder of her robe. She went sprawling to the ground again, winded and angry, having very little patience for the wolf’s antics now. It was all well and good for it to be fond of her, to trot along in the shadows, but she had to find her wife.

     

                Pressing its nose into her shoulder, it sniffed and prodded her, snapping its teeth again as it sank to the ground, making itself as low as possible. When Lena did nothing except sit up, rubbing her elbow, which had slammed into a hidden rock, the wolf softly whined and inched closer. It took her a minute to realise it was trying to get her to climb on its back, as she had on her way to Argo, hauling herself up onto the skittish wolf’s back with a little coaxing and soothing. It had taken her to the lake, had known her intention as much as the forest had, she was sure of it, and it was a quicker way to pass the miles.

     

                Scrambling to her feet, Lena let out a tired sound of gratitude, stepping into the wolf, burying her hands in its fur. “Oh, you beautiful creature,” she murmured into the soft topcoat of fur, the musky smell of wet dog in her nose.

     

                Gripping fistfuls of the wiry undercoat, Lena somehow found the strength to pull herself up, bare feet scrabbling for purchase as she dragged herself, hand over hand, up onto its back. Flopping limply over its back, she barely had time to make herself secure before the wolf took off, running through the trees in the same direction their branches leaned in. Shifting precariously on its back, managing to get her head up slightly, Lena watched the trunks blur together on either side of them, the wolf dodging past them, deftly weaving through the trees as it crossed the total distance Lena had covered in a handful of minutes. Watching the forest smear into a streak of brown and green, Lena’s hope was renewed, and she was tense with expectation, with that strong desire for it to be true, her lips moving in a silent prayer as the miles passed by.

     

                After that, she was lulled by the rhythm of the wolf’s body shifting beneath her, her eyes staring blankly ahead as her mind ran through the endless possibilities of what she’d encounter next. When she narrowed it down, though, there were only two outcomes: Kara was alive, or she was dead. If it were the latter, nothing would change, life continuing on as it had for the last couple of months, but Lena’s raised hopes would be dashed to pieces, and she didn’t think she could bear that. One good thing was that she was alone with the wolf; weaponless, yes, but alone. At the very least, she’d been able to slip Alex’s overprotective presence, but that was fraught with danger if Lena found herself defeated again. There would be no one to stop her, and she was glad.

     

                As if thinking of her had summoned her, Lena let out a small sound of panic and gripped the wolf’s fur tighter as it suddenly veered off to the left, picking up the pace as it chased down the sound of hoofbeats. Catching up quickly, the wolf bounded in front of the horse, charging eastwards, approaching from a different angle than they, with Alex bent low over the stallion’s neck. At the sight of the wolf charging towards them, the horse reared, a hysterical whinny escaping it as it kicked its legs, while Alex let out a panicked shout, clutching at handfuls of the mane to remain seated. She ended up falling from the saddle, rolling and coming up in a low crouch with a knife in hand, wide eyes trained on the wolf, ready to die fighting, at least.

     

                “Wait!” Lena called out, the wolf skidding to a stop at the unfolding chaos, hackles raised, head low. “It’s me! It’s me!”

     

                Alex straightened, her horse bolting, and Lena half-slid, half-fell off the wolf, landing with a heavy thump on the densely leafed floor of the forest. Knocking the air from her lungs, Lena pressed a hand to her sternum as she staggered up, looking a right mess as Alex gave her a mildly alarmed look.

     

                “What are you doing?”

     

                “Fell a few times. I was running,” Lena wheezed.

     

                “I- you were riding it!”

     

                Catching her breath, a spasm of pain crossing her face as her hand moved from her sternum to her waist, the velvet wet where it clung to her ripped stitches, Lena nodded dismissively. “It was quicker than running, and it insisted.”

     

                “It- of course. Yes, why not? I should not bother questioning you; you do everything the wrong way and somehow endure.”

     

                “We can puzzle it out later; let’s go,” Lena brusquely replied.

     

                Alex spread her arms helplessly, looking around. “My horse has bolted, in case you have not noticed. It took me an age to catch it, once I had escaped, and now we shall be walking for a fortnight with the state you are in.”

     

                Jerking her thumb over her shoulder, Lena shrugged one shoulder, “we’ll take the wolf.”

     

                “Absolutely not. It is a wild animal.”

     

                “Suit yourself, but I intend to find my wife now, not in a fortnight.”

     

                “You do not even know the way! You were coming from the south.”

     

                “The forest is guiding me.”

     

                “Oh,” Alex said with a slightly hysterical laugh, “of course it is! While you are at it, could you perhaps communicate with the forest and ask it to find my horse, then?”

     

                Lena was already making for the wolf, which had skulked away into the shadows, a mass of grey and two bright eyes in the fading light of the forest, and she softly clicked her tongue, rubbing thumb and fingers together as she tried to entice it forward like an alleycat. 

     

                “That will not-” Alex started with a rough sigh, and abruptly cut off as the wolf shifted forward, belly low to the ground, nose twitching.

     

                Slowly approaching, her hand held out, Lena made soothing sounds as she crept closer. The wolf likewise slowly approached her, dark eyes big and watchful, whole body tensed to spring, until her hand buried in the short fur of its muzzle, seeming impossibly small in comparison to its bulk. Scratching it beneath the chin as it hunched over, chin lifted slightly for her, Lena glanced over her shoulder at Alex, who was apprehensively watching her, a knife still in hand.

     

                “Come on, it’s harmless. You don’t need to be afraid.”

     

                “It is not fear that I feel, but they are dangerous, Lena. You know as well as the rest of us; you were nearly gutted by one on only your second day within the Courts.”

     

                “I think it’s the one I saved from the river,” Lena continued to explain, “so it likes me. I think it’s a he. He’s gotten a lot bigger, anyway. The forest has gotten to him.”

     

                “Then it is best if you leave him to the forest.”

     

                “I’m not keeping him as a pet, but he’s rather useful. Especially when we’re in a rush.”

     

                Without further ado, reassured that the wolf was placid enough to let her ride him again, Lena smoothed her hand along the wolf’s jaw, the underside of its neck, then along its left foreleg, before she knotted her fingers in its fur. Hauling herself up onto its back, Lena got comfortable, trying to tug the robe around her bare legs as she was reminded of her dishevelled appearance, and beckoned impatiently to Alex. With mumbled curses and complaints, Alex sheathed her knife and stomped over to Lena, the wolf shying away, muzzle pulling back over his teeth as a quiet snarl rumbled in his chest.

     

                Alex looked indignant at the wolf’s reaction, her eyes sharply jerking up to Lena. Patting the scruff of its neck, Lena clicked her tongue and shushed the wolf. “She’s a friend.”

     

                Snorting, the wolf let out a grumbling whine but didn’t object as Alex warily approached and then scurried up its back with more agility than Lena’s clumsy mounting. Scooting up behind her, still grumbling, Alex grabbed a fistful of velvet to keep herself steady behind Lena, and without a signal, the wolf started to move.

     

                “This is less efficient than a horse.”

     

                “Quicker, though,” Lena insisted. “And we need to be quick. I need- I need to know. I can’t-”

     

                “I know,” Alex murmured, giving her a pat on the shoulder. 

     

                Swallowing the lump in her throat, Lena nodded, as if reassuring herself, too, and focused on remaining on the wolf’s back as its lurching gait evened out, the wind in her face as her eyes streamed.

     

                “Well, it is quicker, I will admit to that,” Alex said over the wind rushing in their ears. “But how does it know where to go?”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena called back, “it just- it knows what I want, or the forest does. I’m a bit iffy on the details of communicating with trees, but they seem to like me, or they haven’t killed me yet, at least. Either way … it’s useful.”

     

                Alex made a noncommittal sound at the back of her throat, which may have been in agreement, and they lapsed into silence then. As fast as the wolf was, it was still a vast distance to cover, and the light faded until the forest was cold and blue with dusk, both women shivering slightly, ill-equipped for travel, but they covered miles and miles before the wolf slowed. By that point, trotting through the trees, high up near the lower branches of the canopy, frequently having to duck, they could hear running water. Lena’s heart thudded in her chest, eagerness filling her at the thought of being so close to the Unseelie Court. As soon as they crossed over, she would be able to search to her heart’s content, under her own jurisdiction - although, she wouldn’t put it past her people to stage another coup, and she was past caring - and Lena was desperate to reach the bridge.

     

                Coming to a complete stop, the wolf eased himself down to the ground, stretching out, panting slightly as the forest darkened around them. Sitting on its back, both women were silent for a moment before Lena gave the wolf’s neck a quick pat, digging her heels into its shoulders.

     

                “Hey! We’re not there yet. You need to keep going.”

     

                Ignoring her, or just not understanding her at all, because it was a wolf, the cub just lowered his head onto his paws, leaving them sitting on him, thirteen feet in the air. It wasn’t a long drop by any means, but just long enough to make Lena apprehensive as she peered over the side of it.

     

                Alex let out a frustrated huff. “See? This would not be happening if we had ridden horses.”

     

                “We’ll have to go on foot,” Lena murmured, wriggling until she was at the shoulder of the wolf, able to angle herself to drop down to the ground.

     

                Without waiting for her, the sound of running water loud in her ears, Lena climbed down, hitting the ground with a jar to her ankles, although it was unimportant as Lena continued in the direction of the river. Still on top of the wolf, Alex let out a sound of complaint, annoyed by the delay, by the possibility of spending a week scouring the forest on foot, probably trekking it back to Lena’s halls to fetch horses and resume their search. It was an inconvenient delay because of the whims of a wolf she was already sceptical about at best.

     

                As Lena moved through the wide trees, towards the sound of water trickling by, her skin prickled with a strange sensation. She heard a low growl behind her as the wolf raised its head, turning to watch it turn slightly towards Alex, muzzle pulled back over sharp teeth, snapping in her direction. In a hurry, Alex was sliding off its back, swearing and stomping towards Lena, who shushed her as she strained her ears, sure that she’d heard something. Her skin prickled with unease, and she wished she had her bow with her, hell, even a dagger, but her powers would suffice, no matter how wild it ran with her erratic emotions.

     

                “What is it?” Alex breathed, knives in her hand, eyes darting around, body tense.

     

                They were silent for a minute, nothing but the sighing wind through the branches, the sound of the river, and the soft hooting of an owl nearby as night blanketed the forest, drawing forth mice and rabbits, foxes stirring in their dens. It was peaceful, ordinary, and Lena let out a sigh.

     

                “Nothing,” she murmured. “I … thought I heard something.”

     

                Nodding, giving the wolf an irritated glance, Alex padded a short way ahead of Lena, head cocked to the side, a stern look on her face. Lena trampled closer with a little less grace, snapping a twig underfoot, rustling leaves, about as unintrusive as a vole but still audible compared to her sister-in-law, and Alex hissed to make her stop. Freezing, Lena cocked her head, ears straining, her body going tense again as she wondered if there was danger she’d missed. And there, faintly, she could hear the soft sound of trampling feet, coming from what, she didn’t know. 

     

                Exchanging a glance with Alex, she took the knife that was held out to her, the feel of the grip unfamiliar in her palm, hefting the weight of it as she tried to get its measure. It would do well enough if it came to it. Alex silently beckoned her and pointed behind her for Lena to follow on her heels, and the two of them slipped from trunk to trunk, darting across the wide gaps between trees, stepping around ferns and bushes as quietly as they could as they neared the river, listening to the distant thundering grow louder. Very quickly, it was distinguishable as a stampede.

     

                “Horses,” Alex stated the obvious, her voice barely a breath.

     

                Stomach lurching, heart racing as she found herself firmly caught between fight or flight, wondering whether the Unseelie had taken it upon themselves to send a retinue, whether it was someone who’d tried to assume her throne and wage war again, or whether it was merely scouts along the border. Alex continued to creep north-easterly, drawing closer to the river, merely a hundred feet away from them now, the soothing trickling of it growing louder, a certain dampness to the air, the sound of ducks quacking and splashing in the rustling reeds on the banks adding to the din. 

     

                Through the gloom, they slipped through the trees like shadows until they could see water shimmering in the near distance. Holding a hand out to keep Lena at bay as they drew closer to the riverbank, which wasn’t that wide where they were, perhaps twenty feet at most, Alex crouched and slowly inched into the tall reeds, using them for cover as the silver moon slipped down through towering trees. They were so tall there, taller than the redwoods Lena had seen back home, that the trees on opposite banks touched over the river, canopies tangling together to create a lattice over the river, letting in dappled moonlight. 

     

                It was cold, too, and Lena hugged her arms to herself as she hung back in the shade of a beech tree, listening to the sound of approaching horses grow louder, and then abruptly stop. It was definitely to the north-west of them, on the opposite side of the riverbank, and Lena wondered if it was shallow enough for the Unseelie to ford the river if they desired, if they spotted them. There was the sound of harnesses jingling, the murmur of quiet voices, snorting horses and the soft thud of dismounting bodies.

     

                Lena closed her eyes, a bitterness filling her, and she listened as barely heard footsteps tiptoed back to her a few minutes later. Opening her eyes as Alex crept around the tree to join her, Lena watched her straighten up, leaning in close as she kept her voice down.

     

                “No more than a dozen. Soldiers, by the look of things. I caught moonlight on their armour and weapons.”

     

                “Fuck,” Lena swore, knowing they couldn’t face those odds if it came to it. Not in a serious fight. And she looked far from a Queen right then, even if that meant enough to make them stop if they were spoiling for a fight. 

     

                Shushing her with more urgency this time, Alex gave her a cutting glance. Pressing her lips together, Lena felt anger flash through her at their predicament, running off at the word of Councilmembers who were most definitely adept at twisting the truth, letting herself believe that the wolf was taking her straight to Kara, only to find a group of soldiers as the latest roadblock in her futile pursuit of hope. And it was cold too, Lena’s toes numb, the soles of her feet tender and bruised, nothing but a torn and muddied robe on as she belted it a little tighter, still clutching Alex’s long knife. She was lightheaded from low blood sugar, low blood pressure, low everything. Her sole meal in days was nothing to the enormity of her appetite, and despite the amount of sleeping she’d done over the last four days, she was exhausted. She, quite simply, didn’t have the will to continue.

     

                Sinking to the floor, pale legs splayed before her, Lena dropped the knife to her lap and buried her face in her grazed palms. The ground started to tremble beneath her as she let her emotions well up and spill out of her, and Lena thought she might burst into tears at any moment. She would’ve thought things couldn’t get any worse, except a few minutes later, it started to rain. 

     

                “Perfect,” Alex muttered through gritted teeth, glancing up at the canopy as rain dripped through the gaps.

     

                Miserable and wet, the two of them huddled at the base of the beech tree as the rain grew heavier, both of them tired but too alert to sleep, aware of the dangers of the forest and the soldiers camped out on the opposite bank. They’d gone too far to see the wolf, if it was still there, and Lena wasn’t sure whether to count on its help once more, mindful of the fact that it wasn’t a pet at her beck and call, but she hoped it was lurking nearby, sleeping perhaps, and curious enough about her to come at the first sign of trouble. She wasn’t sure whether to feel comforted by that hopeful thought or not, the rain pouring through the trees, almost torrential now, practically unheard of within the confines of the forest, and she raked damp hair out of her face, cursing everything she could put even the slightest shred of blame on for winding up in such a ridiculous situation. And she didn’t even know if it would all be worth it in the end, wasn’t even sure if Kara was alive or if they were just chasing after a ghost.

     

                They heard a shout almost an hour later, the rain still coming down, the darkness almost complete, their sharp vision able to differentiate the shades of grey as heavy clouds blotted out the little moonlight that had been filtering through the branches. They both tensed at the sound of it, wondering what might have befallen those on the opposite riverbank, but they didn’t do more than share a look, no panicked yells or terrified screams following. Shifting restlessly, Lena tried to get comfortable with a root in her back, knowing that they weren’t likely to go any further that night, wishing they could’ve lit a fire but not wanting to risk anyone seeing the glow of it or catching a whiff of smoke, which wasn’t probably anymore, considering the sudden deluge.  

     

                They’d just lulled themselves back into their grim stupor when there was another shout, closer this time. It must have been almost parallel with them, just on the opposite bank, and Alex sat up straighter, wide-eyed and pointed ears pricked as her face creased with apprehension. The rain was loud, but their hearing was keen enough for them to make out a raised voice, even if they couldn’t decipher the words. And while Lena tuned it out, Alex shot to her feet.

     

                “Kelly.”

     

                Head jerking to look up at her, Lena scrambled to her feet as Alex ran towards the riverbank, no attempt to remain concealed now, even if she was wrong in her assumption. Dashing after her, her stomach swooping with nervous anticipation, knowing that if Kelly was there, that would be where Kara was, Lena felt nauseous. This was it, the final shreds of her hope, and she felt sick with her desperation, clammy and lightheaded as she stumbled and staggered in her sister’s wake. Alex was already at the riverbank, wading ankle-deep into mud as she pushed reeds aside.

     

                “Kelly?”

     

                Her shout was slightly muffled by the rain, but it silenced the raised voice across the river, leaving them listening to the lashing rain as the forest otherwise went still around them. It was like the wind died, the trees all swaying back upright, a sense of relief pervading the area, as if their job was done. Lena’s heart was thumping in her chest, which grew tighter with each shallow breath, until she felt as if she was on the verge of a panic attack, about to break down any second now. And nothing. No response, only the tense anticipation, and the faint flicker of shadows moving across the river, barely noticeable through the sheeting rain. 

     

                “Alex?”

     

                A jolt ran through Lena at the faintest, confused shout, just able to make out Alex’s name, Kelly’s voice. She heard the hoarse cry of relief that Alex let out, forging further into the reeds, the splash of water as her feet slipped into the river, the yelp of alarm at how deep, how cold and swift it was, despite the deceptively calm surface. 

     

                “The bridge!” came Kelly’s laughing shout, elated and urgent.

     

                “Bridge?” Alex muttered to herself, clambering back up the bank, clutching at reeds, at plants and weeds. “We are near a bridge. That damned wolf was right.”

     

                Lena was left standing there dumbly, her mind reeling as she watched Alex run off, following the river north. Blinking, fear gripping her heart, Lena’s mouth opened and closed, her chin wobbling as she tried to make her voice work. When she did, the words came out feeble, cracking as her throat went dry.

     

                “Kara? Is she with you?”

     

                No response was forthcoming, not that they would’ve heard her anyway, and it wasn’t until a sudden gust of wind rushing up from the south hit her with enough force to stumble off balance, that Lena made her feet move. And then she couldn’t run fast enough, the dull pain in her side nothing to contend with as she ran, ran as if her life depended on it, already crying, regardless of what awaited her around the bend in the river. And then she saw the bridge, flat and low, barely two feet above the surface of the river, and while she couldn’t make out the details, Lena knew it would be littered with rust coloured leaves and furred with moss. And on either side of the river, tall pillars of pale, broken stone arranged in semi-circles, the ancient remains of a covered walkway spanning the river, an old waypoint from before the Courts had split. 

     

                She knew this place. She had been there before, an eternity ago. It was all familiar - the bridge, the pillars, this bend in the river, the soaring trees - even the woman on the opposite bank. Even in darkness, in the pouring rain, with poor visibility, Lena knew her. This was where they’d first met, standing on opposite banks to where they had been that day, their bloody hands clasped, marriage vows binding the two strangers together. Lena hadn’t known what she’d gotten herself into then, dressed up like a doll in more finery than she’d ever owned, but she’d thought Kara was the most beautiful person she’d ever seen. Standing there, rain sluicing down her ghostly face as she stared at her wife, back from the dead, Lena still thought she was the most beautiful person she’d ever seen.

     

                Alex was already across the river, had already met her wife halfway, had run to her sister, and her mother, who was part of their company, and Lena was left alone on the opposite side to them, watching as Kara looked around for her, as Alex gestured back across the bridge. In a daze, Lena drifted out of the treeline, through the pillars, towards the start of the bridge, mud and wet grass underfoot as she stared across the short expanse of stone stretching across the river, wariness on her face as her eyes smarted with tears. Kara had rushed towards the bridge at her sister’s gesture and pulled up short a few steps onto the slick stone at the sight of Lena.

     

                Chin wobbling, tears tracing down her cheeks, Lena cocked her head to the side and stared at her as Kara continued, slower now, cautious, even though the lines of her body were taut with barely restrained urgency. The rain stopped as she approached, the clouds dispelling as her wife’s depressed mood abated, taking the poor weather with it. Moonlight started to filter back down through the woven canopy overhead, and Lena could make out her face now. She was crying too, but a wide smile split her face, teary eyes creased at the corners, and she reached a hand out towards Lena, waiting almost in the middle of the bridge.

     

                “Lena,” Kara softly called to her. “Come to me.”

     

                The sound of her voice almost split Lena in half, and she let out a ragged sound of confused relief, lurching into motion again. Soaking wet, filthy and barely able to stand, Lena hadn’t envisioned this to be the reunion she had with her wife - although, she hadn’t really anticipated any sort of reunion where they were both alive, and she had never been a believer in any sort of afterlife, either - and she drew up short again, a third of the way across. Haggard, with dark circles beneath her eyes, breathless sobs leaving her chest heaving, she was a sorry sight, her grief evident in the thinness of her haunted face, and she suddenly wondered if she’d gone mad, doubting herself and her sanity. Or was she dead? Lena didn’t trust her own eyes and ears. Was it some sort of trick of the mind? Was this what her death looked like? If it was, she had no complaints.

     

                “Is this a dream?” Lena haltingly whispered, tasting her tears as Alex’s knife slipped from numb fingers and clattered to the bridge underfoot. “Am I- am I dead?”

     

                “No,” Kara said, her smile growing a fraction, letting out a choked laugh. “All is well.”

     

                Taking another step closer, uncertain, shaking her head slightly as she tried to wrap her head around it, almost manic in her hunt for her wife that she hadn’t taken the time to puzzle out how it would be possible, only wanting it to somehow be, Lena’s brow furrowed.

     

                “But … I watched you die,” she unevenly said, her voice breaking, the words verging on a sob as her emotions overwhelmed her.

     

                Even on the bridge, she could feel the tremors radiating through the ground, raindrops and leaves shaken loose as the trees shuddered at the output of power funnelling out of Lena. It was so overwhelming, so disorienting, surreal. She didn’t know what to think, what to believe; she knew what she wanted to believe, but that didn’t make it the truth.

     

                “I was badly hurt,” Kara patiently explained, keeping her distance, giving Lena the time and space to process it, her wife so visibly unstable, even though she never dropped that outstretched hand. “But now I am recovered. I came looking for you as soon as I was well enough; forgive me, it took longer than expected.”

     

                Choking on another sob, barely able to see through her tears, Lena took another step closer, confused, disbelieving, but soothed. Just listening to her talk, letting herself be comforted by the familiar balm of her wife’s voice, something loosened in her chest, some knot of grief coming undone after months, the tension bleeding out of her. And whether it was real or some figment of her imagination, Lena didn’t have it within her to care, letting out a wounded sound of blatant longing, needing her wife, in any capacity, and bridging the few feet separating them with quick steps, throwing herself at Kara as she broke down into sobs.

     

                Arms coming around her, Kara let out a forceful breath into Lena’s wet hair, holding her tightly, holding her upright as Lena’s knees gave out beneath her weight. Kara was still crying, too, but in quiet, breathless gasps in comparison to the loud, gut-wrenching sobs coming out of Lena as she buried her face in her wife’s shoulder and shook from the force of them, desperate hands clutching at Kara’s cloak, her armour, her hair. Kara gently shushed her, but it only made Lena cry harder, feeling her hand smooth over her wet hair, the solid feeling of her in familiar armour as she kept Lena upright, breathing in the smell of her, so achingly familiar that it was like whiplash. As if laying hands on her had convinced Lena that she was real, she couldn’t stop crying, but her sobs morphed into laughter, the fear, the wariness turning into elation, wonder, unbridled joy. She still couldn’t stop crying, everything still a little muddied by the shadow of her grief, but the trembling subsided, while the forest flourished, feeding off her. 

     

                Finally gathering some sense of composure, enough to unwind her arms from around Kara’s neck, Lena pulled back slightly, giving her a clumsy kiss, hitting the side of her mouth, and then peppering her wet cheeks with more kisses in between her laughter. Kara was laughing, too, her hands running over Lena, warm, calloused fingers brushing her cheeks, through tangled hair, over wet velvet and bruised skin, and all around them, the forest fruited with summer flowers, winter berries, autumn apples and new spring growth, a riot of life as it sapped the outpouring of joy radiating from Lena.

     

                “You’re alive,” Lena whispered, her eyes roving over Kara’s face with awe, with disbelief. 

     

                She felt faint, a tightness in her chest, the notion that she couldn’t quite catch her breath properly, vision dimming at the edges as she stood, weak-kneed, in front of her wife. Her very much alive wife. Unable to stop the breathless laughter working up her throat, Lena’s cheeks dimpled as she smiled through her tears, cupping Kara’s face in her hands as she stared at her with wonder.

     

                “You’re alive,” she murmured, leaning in to touch her forehead to her wife’s, right before she let out a listless sigh, lips ghosting over Kara’s mouth, and passed out in her arms.

    Chapter 54

                Dark hair scattered across the cushions, Lena restlessly squirmed on the bed, a pucker between her eyebrows as her lips wordlessly moved, and she woke a moment later with a start. Mind still in the clutches of sleep, she was confused as she let out a rough exhale, rolling onto her side, looking at the wall through heavy eyelids as she heard the firm heartbeat on the other side of the bed, the sound of someone moving. The smell of damp earth was familiar to her, and there was a pit in her stomach as Lena buried her face into the pillows, dimly aware she was back at her Court.

     

                “I’m fine, Alex,” she sleepily mumbled. “I was just dreaming.”

     

                “Good dreams, I hope.”

     

                Her eyelids flew open at the sound of her wife’s voice, and Lena pushed herself up, all memory of sleep forgotten now. But not the dreams she’d had. Dreams of Kara, of finding her on the same bridge where they were married. Sitting up as she turned towards her, Lena made out her wife’s features in the darkness of the room, the long hair spilling past her shoulders, the curve of her lips, the slope of her nose, the robe that was undoubtedly some shade of blue. Kara looked like any of the numerous other times Lena had been with her at night. 

     

                “A dream within a dream, within a dream,” Lena murmured, her eyes stinging with tears as she stared at her, a wavering smile growing on her lips. “If you are the object of my dreams, I hope I never wake.”

     

                Kara stood and sank onto the edge of the bed, the mattress jostling at the weight of her, a look of concern and apprehension on her face as she reached a hand across the blankets. “I am not a dream.”

     

                Lena let out a choked laugh, clumsy fingers wiping away an errant tear. “Then you are a figment of my imagination. It all seems so real.”

     

                Moving further across the bed, Kara knelt near her and reached out to take her hand. She pressed Lena’s palm to her chest, and Lena frowned as she felt the steady beat of her heart beneath it, felt the solid warmth.

     

                “I am real.”

     

                “No,” Lena whispered with a sad smile, eyes glassy as she looked at Kara’s face. “You died.”

     

                “For a moment.”

     

                Lowering Lena’s hand back down to her lap, Kara shed her robe, a ghostly white shirt beneath it, and then hurriedly shed that too. Her skin was pale in the dark, and Lena could see the absence of the wounds she should’ve had, no blood, no arrows piercing her. Frowning, confused, Lena tentatively reached out to touch her. Kara didn’t move an inch, letting her wife explore the bare expanse of skin as Lena’s fingers ran over the places she’d watched the arrows puncture steel. She knew them by heart, as if they’d struck her own body.

     

                The room was starting to lighten; dawn ushered in through the slit of a window near the ceiling. It made it easier for Lena to see, the minutes passing by, her fingers running over the shiny, circular scars at Kara’s waist, her ribs. Like burns. Kneeling still, Kara watched Lena with a burning intensity, her lips parted as she shallowly breathed, hair spilling around her shoulders, and Lena kept looking up, meeting her eyes, as if reassuring herself that it was her, that the dream hadn’t morphed into something else. The furrow between her eyebrows deepened, and she withdrew her touch, burying her face in her hands, which trembled, as she squeezed her eyes shut.

     

                “You’re not real,” she whispered to herself. “You’ll be gone again when I open my eyes, when I wake up.”

     

                Reaching out, Kara cupped the sides of Lena’s head, trying to urge her to look up. Lena kept her head ducked down, resisting the gentle touch of her wife as she drew in shaky breaths, her palms growing wet as she silently cried. Softly shushing her, Kara ran her hands down to Lena’s shoulders, gripping her firmly, ducking her head down as she tried to make her listen.

     

                “Lena. Lena, open your eyes. I am here; I have not left you.”

     

                “No, no, no, you’re not real.”

     

                “Open your eyes, my love.”

     

                Letting out a soft whimper, afraid to look, unable to bear the disappointment, the renewed grief, Lena drew in a shaky breath, the sound thick with her tears. Licking her lips, she raised her head a fraction, eyelids parting as she peered through wet lashes spiked together, and caught sight of thighs clad in soft leggings. Raising her head a little more, her eyes travelled over smooth skin, nicked with the occasional scar, familiar to her, save for the new shiny ones, small and round, where arrows had pierced the skin. Up, until she met Kara’s eyes, able to make out a dark shade of blue as the morning continued to dawn, a light in them that she had thought had been lost forever. Lips curved into a small smile, face wrought with a silent plea for forgiveness, Kara swallowed thickly. 

     

                “See? I am here.”

     

                “Have I- have I died?” Lena asked, wiping her face on her chemise as more tears wet her cheeks. “Is this what death is?”

     

                “No, this is what life is.”

     

                “But you died,” Lena repeated, her voice breaking as she sniffed.

     

                “Yes, but I was brought back. I did not go very far into death. Listen to me; I am not lying, you know that I could not.”

     

                “Have I gone mad?”

     

                Kara let out a small laugh at that, reaching out to press the backs of her fingers to Lena’s cheek, catching a stray tear. “No, you have not gone mad.”

     

                Face crumpling with anguish, with confusion, unable to let herself hope, Lena shook her head. Then she looked around the room and realised that it was their suite, the one they’d taken over after she’d been poisoned. Lena had refused to sleep there, had only entered that space once since Kara had died, and she rubbed her brow as her green eyes clouded over. Scrambling off the bed, she staggered slightly, her other hand going to her waist as she let out a surprised gasp.

     

                “Careful,” Kara cautioned her, extending her hands, trying to calm her like a wild animal. “You are injured.”

     

                Frown deepening, Lena gripped a fistful of her chemise. Hurriedly bunching up the fabric, she found clean bandages wrapped around her middle, over the place she’d been stabbed. But that had been a dream, hadn’t it? Her pulse raced as she tried to puzzle through it. Was her brother alive? She could’ve sworn she’d killed him - the wolf had killed him. And the wolf had taken her to Argo, where she’d tried to kill herself. Twice. Alex had stopped her both times. But had that been a dream, too? She remembered waking up there, she remembered meeting the Councilmembers, running, running so fast she reopened her stitches. And the wolf had found her again, had taken her to the river. To Kara.

     

                Letting out a slightly hysterical laugh, Lena let go of her chemise and grabbed a fistful of dark hair as she slumped back against the earthen wall, tears running down her cheeks. Her pulse was racing, skin clammy as her chemise stuck to her back, her chest, and she wiped her sleeve over her face, sniffing as she tried to figure out what was real and what wasn’t. Kara moved over to her side of the bed, shifting so that she was sitting on the edge instead of kneeling, working her shirt back over her head as she patiently waited for Lena to speak, not wanting to spook her further, seeing how fragile she was and keeping her distance. 

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena whispered. “I don’t know what’s real and what’s not. How do I know? How do I know if I’ve gone mad? I’ve felt mad for months without you. I miss you. I miss you; I’ve imagined you everywhere.”

     

                “Was I ever really there?” Kara asked.

     

                Considering the question, Lena cocked her head to the side and then slowly shook it. “No. No, you never came.”

     

                “Yes, because that wasn’t real. But I am here now.”

     

                Feeling even more confused, Lena rubbed at her eyes and drew in a shuddering breath. “Then I- I must be mad. I’ve gone- I’ve gone crazy. That’s why I can see you. Oh, God. Oh, God. This is- what the fuck. What- Alex. I need … Alex.”

     

                She pushed off the wall and strode towards the door, throwing it open as Kara scrambled after her. “Lena, all is well. Come back to bed, my love. You should rest; I will send for my sister, and she can explain.”

     

                Snagging Lena’s arm, she tried to pull her to a stop, but Lena yanked herself free, almost tripping over her feet as her chest rose and fell, her breath coming quicker now, wordless sounds of pain, of panic working up her throat. Trembling, sweating profusely, Lena made a beeline for the door to the suite and threw it open, ignoring Kara’s gentle voice behind her. The guards on either side of the door startled slightly at the sudden appearance of her, and her state of dishevelment, and Lena paused at the sight of them.

     

                “Jack,” she said, blinking as her shoulders caved with relief. “Are you dead, too?”

     

                He floundered for a moment, bewilderment in his dark eyes. “No, Your Majesty.”

     

                “Oh. There’s a- a ghost. A ghost inside,” she said, her voice shaking, eyes wide and manic.

     

                “A … ghost?”

     

                Reaching for him, she grabbed his surcoat with an air of desperation about her, clinging to him as she tried to explain. “My wife. My wife’s spirit is in my room.”

     

                His eyes flitted to Kara, who stood in the doorway, face crumpled with anguish as she slowly reached for Lena. Hands cradling her wife’s waist, Kara tried to draw her away, reaching up to gently pry her fingers off Jack’s surcoat.

     

                “Come,” Kara murmured, working Lena’s hand loose, her other hand smoothing up her ribs, up to her arm and down to her wrist, to pry the other one free, too. “Let me put you to bed.”

     

                Lena’s whole body went limp, and she sagged in Kara’s grasp, down to the earthen floor, curling in on herself as she started to sob. Kara sank with her, hands still encircling her wife’s wrists, and she moved Lena’s long hair off her neck, pressed her brow to the back of her head as she quietly shushed her. Chest heaving with the effort of her sobs, Lena hung her head as she broke down, unable to stop herself.

     

                Dimly aware of voices, of strong arms lifting her, the smell of rain and salt enveloping her senses, Lena leaned into her wife’s shoulder and continued to cry. She couldn’t make herself stop after that, aware that she was being laid down on the bed, her hands clutching fistfuls of Kara’s shirt, repeatedly begging her not to go, to stay with her, even as her wife climbed onto the bed beside her and wrapped her in her embrace. Head on her chest, listening to the familiar sound of her heartbeat, Lena cried and cried until the front of Kara’s shirt was sodden from her tears, and then she cried some more.

     

                She was still crying when Alex appeared in the doorway, albeit quieter, exhausting herself quickly, and she stared at her with bloodshot eyes, drawing in hitching breaths as she kept her fingers knotted in the fabric of Kara’s shirt. Tears slid soundlessly over the bridge of Lena’s nose, dripping onto the wet cotton, and she blinked slowly, feeling Kara’s fingers in her hair, feeling the raw pain in her chest.

     

                Apprehensive, seeming confused by the sight before her, Alex’s eyebrows drew together as she hovered on the threshold of the room. “It is good to see you awake,” she slowly said.

     

                “Alex,” Lena whispered, her grip on her wife tightening. “Alex, I think I’ve gone mad.”

     

                Looking from Lena to Kara, Alex’s wariness deepened into pure bewilderment. Mouth opening and closing, she cleared her throat and walked further into the room, cocking her head to the side. “Why do you say that?”

     

                “She does not believe that I am real,” Kara murmured, tenderly smoothing away tears as she looked up at her sister with agony.

     

                Letting out a laugh, Alex’s face rippled with amusement, and she smiled. Her eyes moved back to Lena’s face, and she crossed the rest of the space to the bed and knelt beside it, reaching out to touch the back of Lena’s hand. Lips pressed into a line, the corners quirked up slightly, Alex gave her a firm nod.

     

                “You are mad? Very well, I am mad, too, then, because I see her as well.”

     

                Blinking, Lena drew in a hitching breath, her voice gravelly as she spoke. “You can see her?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “I don’t understand. She died. Did we die?”

     

                “No. No, we did not die. She did not die, either. Do you remember the Council? They spoke truly, and we went to the bridge. Do you remember that? You tore open your wound again and passed out. We have brought you back to your Court to recover here. It has been a little over a day.”

     

                “But we saw her.”

     

                “Yes, we saw her die. Just as Kelly saw that boy at the river die. My wife has told me of what transpired; she saved Kara’s life, brought her back, as you brought back that boy.”

     

                “Is that true?” Lena asked in a small voice, her chest hitching with breathless sobs.

     

                “Yes,” Alex firmly replied. “If you do not believe me, then I will prove it.”

     

                “How?”

     

                “Give me your finger.” Alex took Lena’s hand in hers and turned it over in her grasp, jerking free her dagger and fixing her sister-in-law with a serious look. “You cannot feel pain in a dream.”

     

                Nodding as much as the position she lay in allowed, Lena sniffled and watched as Alex gripped her finger, pressing the sharpened point of the dagger into the tip. Wincing at the sting of the cut, Lena watched blood well up and jerked her hand back, frowning as she eyed her finger. A bead of red blood clung to the skin, and she smoothed her thumb over it, smearing it across the whorls of her fingertips, watching another bead well up in its stead.

     

                Slowly sitting up, Lena looked at her finger with a look of sheer bewilderment on her face. She looked up at a flicker of movement in the doorway and blinked in surprise at the sight of Kelly. Holding a steaming cup in her hand, Kelly stepped into the room and handed the cup off to Alex, who held it out to Lena.

     

                “Here, drink this. It will help.”

     

                Lena drained most of the cup in one long gulp, her hand trembling slightly, and frowned as she lowered it, the strongly steeped taste of valerian root bitter to the taste. Coughing as a sob hitched in her throat, Lena gasped for air, her face crumpling as she looked into the cup and then looked up again. Taking the cup from her, Alex climbed to her feet and gestured to Kelly, who gave Lena a kind smile as she took her wife’s spot, and reached out to cup the back of Lena’s head, before she cut off the air in her lungs.

     

                Mouth soundlessly opening and closing for a moment, Lena was too distressed to properly understand what was happening, but it didn’t take long for her body to go limp. Cradling her head, Kelly helped lower her back down onto the bed, at Kara’s side, allowing air back into her lungs and hoping the valerian root worked quickly to help her sleep. The three women were silent as a few minutes passed by, waiting for Lena to wake as they watched her chest slowly rise and fall, until it became apparent that she was sleeping soundly.

     

     

                The next time she woke, it was to a bright room and a fresh breeze sweeping in through the narrow window. The smell of the forest in late summer, of green plants warmed by the sun, was sweet as Lena drew in a deep breath, stirring slowly as she kicked at the blankets covering her, a heaviness to her limbs and a bitter taste caught at the back of her throat. Grumbling, she rubbed her tired eyes and blinked up at the earthen ceiling, taking in the sight of thick roots arcing overhead like it was vaulted. Blinking slowly, Lena was aware of another heartbeat in the room, and her stomach jolted with the memory of a dream. Had it been a dream? She’d cried so hard she’d given herself a headache, and she looked at her finger, bearing the tiniest scab and the faint redness of old blood, her sharp senses able to pick up on the barely noticeable tang of copper.

     

                Closing her eyes again, Lena pressed her fingertips to her eyelids and drew in a trembling breath, steadying herself. “Am I awake?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara quietly responded from the chaise longue across from the foot of the bed, where she sat, watching Lena as if she were a cold drink of water before a parched woman.

     

                Fingertips still pressed to her eyelids, Lena swallowed thickly, her voice hoarse with fear as she continued. “Are you real?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Prove it to me. Tell me what happened.”

     

                “May I sit on the bed with you while I explain?” Kara asked, sounding desperate, pained to be so far away from her when all she wanted to do was hold her.

     

                Lena dipped her head in a nod, her chin wobbling as she kept her hands over her face. She felt the foot of the bed shift, jostling her slightly, similar to earlier, or to the dream she’d been having, depending on whether she believed she’d gone mad or not. Her next breath was a long shudder, and her voice hitched, cracking as she spoke.

     

                “I can’t look at you. I can’t look at you unless I know-”

     

                “Okay,” Kara whispered. “Keep your eyes closed and listen, and I will tell you what came to be.”

     

                Nodding again, her lips quivering as she pressed her mouth into a flat line, Lena lay in the middle of the bed, twisted in the blankets, and didn’t speak. It took a minute for Kara to speak, the sound of birds outside and the snap of the fire guttering in the brazier as a gust of wind blew in stronger. Clearing her throat, Kara sat cross-legged, hands clasped tightly in her lap, and slowly began to speak, her voice soft and lilting, heartachingly familiar to Lena, who had to struggle not to immediately dissolve into tears as a pang of longing struck her again.

     

                “I was struck three times - you know this - and you pulled me from the river. Kelly was still removing my armour when my heart stopped; I was bleeding too much around the wounds, but the arrows staunched the worst of it, as well as my gambeson and shirt. I was fortunate. It gave Kelly time to remove my breastplate so she could do what you had done to that boy, do what you had shown me. She kept the air flowing in and out of my lungs, as you’d instructed. I was not conscious of it, but Kelly informed me that when you left, when my sister pulled you through to the human realm, your power had bled out of you. You broke the riverbank; I was back in the water. My blood … you know it turns to water when it spills out of me; the water is healing to me in return, much like the earth would be for you.”

     

                “The water healed you?”

     

                “In part.”

     

                “How?”

     

                “I have told you before, but there is a certain magic in us that comes from the element that we each have control over, and in turn, we give back to them, are part of the cycle. It cannot help when death comes quickly, but the arrows … they staunched much of my blood. Andrea was there. She helped Kelly remove them, one by one, and used fire to burn the wound closed. That is why my scars are like that; they burnt them to stem the blood flow. Kelly did not stop the, um … compressions? The air flow. She said you were very firm that you should not stop the air flow.”

     

                “But you were losing blood. It was- it was all over me.”

     

                “Yes, but it was not very fast. You know how quickly we heal; beating my heart for me and helping me breathe bought my body enough time to start healing itself. There was a hole in my lung, we believe, but no bigger than a small nick, so it was able to close quickly, and the water helped replenish my blood and the burns to scar. Kelly said they kept me in the water for a whole day. My heart was able to beat by itself, but it was weak, and I did not stir. The fighting went on, but I was kept safe, and your brother did not ford the river. After that day, they pulled me from the river and retreated with me. I was heavily bandaged, given many teas to help my heart strength, and did not stir for a week.”

     

                “That’s not possible.”

     

                “Before you, it would not have been,” Kara agreed, a small smile on her lips as her gaze softened. “But it seems that I was right; you have a knack for life. I live because of you. Because of the healing you brought here.”

     

                “No,” Lena objected.

     

                “Yes. I was taken to my mother’s halls when I awoke. They had to get a wagon up through the passes,” Kara said with a snort of laughter, “and I rested there for the better part of a month, until I was well enough to travel. I came for you, then.”

     

                “You came for me?”

     

                “Did you think I would not seek you out at once? Alex and I had an agreed-upon meeting place in the human realm. It took some time for us to reach it, but it was immediately apparent you had never arrived there. We returned to the Court to find most of the summer had passed in our absence. I feared it might have been years, but even the months I lost with you pained me. I thought of nothing but how you were faring throughout this. I do not think it is arrogant of me to say that you would have been mourning the loss of me, is it?”

     

                Lena choked on a laugh, her eyes stinging with tears as she kept them closed, her chest aching. “No. Not at all.”

     

                “We returned a little over a week ago. I came to the Unseelie Court immediately upon word of your crowning, only to find that we had missed you. In our search, we came upon those few who had accompanied you, and they spoke of your brother’s death, and the death of your General, and how you had vanished. My sister had left them behind - there was an injured man with them.”

     

                “What was his name?”

     

                “Hector.”

     

                Lena swallowed thickly, her stomach swooping. But then, if she was hallucinating this whole thing, wouldn’t Kara be able to give her the answers she wanted? She wasn’t convinced. Kara continued after a brief silence, when it became apparent Lena wasn’t going to continue.

     

                “We were on our way back to the Seelie Court when you found us.”

     

                There was a beat of silence again, Lena trying to rationalise it to herself, that it was possible for that to have happened, that Kara might’ve been saved. She wasn’t a doctor, barely a healer, but she was fairly confident a human couldn’t have survived three arrows to their torso. And yet, Kara was far from human. Even Lena had survived injuries that should’ve been fatal. She had scars from a monstrously huge wolf on her abdomen and thigh; she’d been stabbed, and her body had tried to heal her so quickly that she hadn’t bled out in the days she’d staggered through the forest. None of that should’ve been possible. And she’d seen where the arrows had struck Kara, had seen the scars now, too, and only one of them had been fatal, had been grave enough to kill her so fast. Was CPR really enough to stave off death long enough for her body to undo the worst of the damage?

     

                “Alex tells me-” Kara started, before she faltered, her voice rough with pain. “Alex tells me you have not been well, that you no longer wished to live.”

     

                “Why would I want to live without you?”

     

                Shifting closer to her on the bed, drawn nearer, as if it hurt to be even a few feet away. “Forgive me for causing you so much harm.”

     

                “It wasn’t you.”

     

                “In part, it was. I only wish you knew of my fate sooner. More time has passed than I can bear to think of, and I did not suffer half as much as you did.”

     

                “I’ve relived that moment over and over, trying to figure out how I could’ve saved you. I dream of it every time I close my eyes, or … I dream of when we were happy. How could you not have known I loved you then? We deserved more time together.”

     

                “We shall have it now. You have brought about peace; we will have all the time in the world together.”

     

                “It’s too late,” Lena whispered. “Too late for us.”

     

                “No, you are wrong. I will prove it to you, prove that this is not a dream.”

     

                “How?”

     

                “It is possible to lie in a dream, so if you can lie, this is not real. Choose a small one that you know is not true. Think of a lie. Think about how the sky is red.”

     

                Eyes still closed, Lena did as she was told, thinking the lie, and waited for Kara to continue. She’d shifted a little closer, sitting cross-legged beside Lena’s stretched-out legs as she studied her face.

     

                “Now, say the sky is red.”

     

                “The sky is-”

     

                Throat closing up, Lena was cut off, unable to get the lie past her lips. It was a familiar sensation, no end to the small lies she’d attempted over the last year, trying to circumnavigate the binding language of the fae and learning to do it in a smarter way. She couldn’t get the words out now, though, couldn’t have lied to save her life, because she was very much awake.

     

                Dropping her hands from her face, Lena drew in a shaky breath but still wouldn’t open her eyes. “Now you say it.”

     

                “The sky is-”

     

                Kara’s voice cut off as she struggled with the lie, unable to get it out. Clearing her throat, she shook her head. Lena still wouldn’t look at her, and she felt her heart race in her chest, that flicker of hope again. Drawing in a quick, hitching breath, she swallowed and then made herself open her eyes, so she could watch Kara struggle, so she could be sure she was trying to lie, so she could know, without a doubt, that she was being honest. Pushing herself up onto her elbows, Lena looked up at her and felt her stomach swoop at how real she looked.

     

                “Tell me you’re dead.”

     

                “I’m-”

     

                She watched Kara flounder, mouth opening and closing without a further sound, her pulse picking up as the tendons in her neck strained with the effort to lie. Chest quickly rising and falling, Kara swallowed, her blue eyes earnest as she kept her unwavering gaze on Lena’s.

     

                “Tell me you’re alive,” Lena commanded her.

     

                Kara’s lips quirked up at the corners, and her eyes held a tender look as she tentatively reached out. Eyes dropping to the extended hand, Lena sat upright and slipped her hand in Kara’s, feeling the familiar roughness of her calloused palms, the warmth and strength of her fingers.

     

                “I’m alive,” Kara softly told her without even the slightest bit of a struggle.

     

                “You’re alive?” Lena asked, her brow creasing, a note of doubt in her voice, before she spoke it again, a statement this time, instead of a question. She didn’t struggle at all, wanting to believe it. “You’re alive.”

     

                “I’m alive. And I love you.”

     

                Nodding, Lena pressed her mouth into a flat line, trying to convince herself, trying to get her belief across the line. Her eyes filled with tears as she ducked her head and let out a choked sob, pressing the heels of her palms into her eyes as she started to cry. So overwhelmed, she didn’t know how to react, other than to break down again. 

     

                After a moment, she dropped her hands from her face and threw herself at Kara, her wife letting out a quiet grunt as she was slightly winded, before she let out a hoarse laugh, an arm wrapping around Lena as she propped herself up on the other elbow. Clutching fistfuls of Kara’s robe, the same robe she’d worn in what Lena had thought was her last dream - another hint it was all real - Lena choked on a sob as she tried to laugh as well, until she was breathless with it, her relief so intense that she felt faint, feeling Kara shaking with laughter beneath her as she held Lena close.

     

                They didn’t speak, they just laughed and cried, Kara cradling the back of Lena’s head, thumb smoothing over her hair, until they were both out of breath. Sniffing, Kara wiped her face on the sleeve of her robe and sat up, moving Lena with her. Her voice was rough with her tears as she spoke. “Let me look at you, my heart.”

     

                Making herself unclench her fists from Kara’s clothes, Lena let herself be held at arm’s length, raising her head to let her wife look at her blotchy face. Kara’s face was likewise tear-stained, her eyes red from crying, but her smile was radiant as she cupped Lena’s face in her palms and laughed again. 

     

                “I have been unable to recall how beautiful you are,” Kara murmured, touching her forehead to Lena’s, their noses gently bumping.

     

                Fingers running over her wife’s arms and shoulders, Lena drew in quick breaths, and then started to kiss her, clumsily peppering her wife’s face with them, desperate and manic as she clutched the shoulders of Kara’s robes so tightly it turned her knuckles white. In between stuttering laughter and broken sobs of pure relief, Lena kissed every inch of Kara’s face she could reach, hearing her wife’s laughter in response as she firmly held Lena’s waist in her hands, holding her before her. Still clutching the robe, Lena’s hands shook as she started to drag it down, her fixation changing trajectory as she grabbed a fistful of Kara’s shirt and yanked it up. Obliging, shedding her clothes once more, Kara shifted back onto her elbows again, legs splayed either side of Lena as she let her see her scars.

     

                Lips and chin quivering, Lena looked at them, truly looked this time, her eyes wide with concern, filled with the memory of the arrows, and she reached out to slowly press her cool fingers to the one on Kara’s chest. It was smooth beneath her fingertips, the shininess of the burn making it pale against the faded tan of her wife’s skin. She looked up at Kara’s face, gauging her reaction to the scar being touched, and found her studying Lena intently, giving her a quick smile, balancing on one elbow so she could reach out and tuck Lena’s hair behind her ear. Swallowing the dryness in her throat, Lena’s fingers brushed a path to the other two, Kara having to raise her arm for the one that had struck the side of her ribs, and Lena drew in a shaky breath.

     

                “Do they hurt?”

     

                “Not anymore. Not for some time, now.”

     

                Nodding, Lena blinked away the burning behind her eyes. “I don’t know how this is possible,” she whispered, looking up again.

     

                Kara watched her expression shift to bewilderment, and smiled as she reached out to stroke the curve of Lena’s cheekbone. “It is quite simple; I could accept dying, but I could not accept putting you through it. You needed someone to stay and love you.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena sniffed and shook her head, cheeks dimpling with a hidden smile as she pressed her lips into a flat line. “That doesn’t explain how it’s possible. You should’ve died.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Throwing herself on top of Kara again, Lena got her arms around her neck, holding her as tightly as she could, until she felt as if she might break her wife’s ribs. Kissing the side of her neck, breathing in the smell of rain and salt, Lena let out another sobbing laugh.

     

                “I love you. I love you; I didn’t think I’d get to say it again. I thought that was all the time we were going to have. Most of it wasted on- on … us being so stupid.”

     

                Her skin rippled at the sound of Kara’s soft laughter reverberating through her chest, and Lena pressed her face into the crook of her neck and shoulder as she let herself be soothed by her wife tenderly stroking her hair. “We were rather foolish, were we not? But fret not; I will always be by your side. Unless I am standing in front of you to keep you from harm.”

     

                “I think we might be safe now,” Lena whispered. “My brother is dead. I had him killed.”

     

                “Yes, by a very large wolf, I believe. Your loyal subjects found his remains a league from the fighting and burned him to ashes. They could not disappoint their Queen by letting him escape again, if by some chance he had survived the wolf. They could not let your supposed sacrifice be in vain.”

     

                “It didn’t really go the way I planned,” Lena meekly laughed.

     

                “My sister is under the impression you were hoping the wolf would kill you, too.” Wincing at the disapproval in Kara’s voice, Lena hid her face deeper into her neck, making Kara chuckle softly. “You cannot hide from the truth; I would like to know why you did such a thing.”

     

                “I already told you; why would I want to live without you?”

     

                “Because you are a person, with a life full of unlived potential. In a millennium, I might have been a distant memory of someone you loved for less than a turning of the seasons.”

     

                Pushing herself up, Lena felt a flash of anger, her face hardening. “Don’t say that. Never say that. You’ve given me so much; it wasn’t much of a life until I met you. I might’ve tried really hard not to fall in love with you, but it’s- it’s not some … fling, okay?”

     

                “I believe you,” Kara murmured, brushing Lena’s hair back and then pushing herself up to chastely kiss her, pausing and smiling at the ability to do so, and then kissing her again, lingering a little longer as she savoured it. “But I would not have wanted you to mourn me forever.”

     

                “Well, I wasn’t planning on mourning you for long at all,” Lena weakly replied with a wavering smile, wiping her stinging eyes.

     

                “I am gladder than I have ever been that I was placed in the path of my sister, to grow up with her, love and trust her as I do, so that she might one day stop you from something that would have broken my heart nearly as much as if I had killed you myself,” Kara solemnly whispered, a brooding look on her face as she stared up at Lena with a divot between her eyebrows, blue eyes overcast.

     

                “I’m glad as well. It wasn’t for a lack of trying that I’m still here; it was her sheer stubbornness alone. It might surpass mine.”

     

                “I would not think that possible, but I am glad. So very, very glad. If I had returned and found you … gone,” Kara said, her voice cracking at the thought. She shook her head and drew in a deep breath, as if needing to steady herself. “I would have done as you had. I made a vow when I knew it was you that I loved, that I would follow you into death quickly. I thought it would be at my hand, but even if it was not, I do not believe I am capable of surviving in a world without you in it.”

     

                “Believe me, it’s not nice. But then … you believe the prophecy was false? You don’t- you don’t think that you’re going to … kill me anymore?”

     

                “No, I felt it became true when I looked upon you on the riverbank, when the knowledge that I would die killed something within you.” Kara paused and then grimaced. “I also had Nia check the records; she tells me my prophecy has faded, and I am inclined to trust her words, so it is certain proof that my fate has been fulfilled. I will not raise a hand to you in anything but kindness.”

     

                “My prophecy,” Lena started, her throat closing up and giving her pause. She swallowed and tried again. “I found out what my prophecy was. My mother … she told me across the river that I would die on the riverbank. I think … our prophecies came true at the same time. Watching you die … yes, something inside me died.”

     

                “Forgive me for making you suffer so. Will a lifetime of atonement, of nothing short of devotion to you, make amends?”

     

                Kara asked it so seriously that Lena could only laugh, hovering over her as she cupped her wife’s face in her desperate grasp and kissed her firmly, a shakiness in her chest as she still hardly dared to believe she was there. Drawing back, Lena gave her three quick kisses and rested her brow against Lena’s, still holding her face in her hands, unable to make herself let go of her out of fear she might vanish again. With a smile in her voice, she whispered her words against Kara’s mouth and felt her grief abate for the first time since that spring.

     

                “Leave me again at your peril.”

    Chapter 55

                Lena woke to a blue room, unsure whether it was dusk or dawn, lurching upright as she came to all at once, chest heaving, the fog of sleep immediately shaken off as she clutched at the front of her chemise. It was damp with sweat, plastered to her skin, and she looked to her left, a ragged sound of relief escaping her as her body sagged with relief at the sight of her wife. Kara was already awake, stirring at Lena’s restlessness, but she kept her hands to herself, blue eyes clouded with wariness, an ache in them too. With a hoarse laugh, Lena wiped her clammy face on her sleeve and then reached out to touch Kara’s cheek.

     

                “A dream. It was just a dream.”

     

                Covering her hand with her own, Kara smiled faintly. “Yes. I am here.”

     

                More tension bled out of her as Lena sank back into the pillows, shuffling closer to Kara, grabbing fistfuls of her shirt as she pressed her face into her stomach. Lowering herself back down, Kara pressed a hand to Lena’s back and stroked her hair, her fingers light and soothing.

     

                “Good morning, my heart,” she murmured to Lena, a tenderness in her voice that made Lena’s eyes sting with tears.

     

                Moving up the bed, her head now firmly on Kara’s chest, Lena drew in a shuddering breath, wiping her eyes as she swallowed thickly. “I thought-”

     

                “I know,” Kara whispered, dipping her chin to press a kiss to Lena’s hair. “Fret not, all is well now.”

     

                With another hoarse laugh, Lena buried her face into Kara’s shirt and breathed in the scent of saltwater, exhaling forcefully as she relaxed. “I think it will take me a while before I believe it. I can hardly believe you’re here.”

     

                Softly chuckling, Kara continued to stroke Lena’s hair. “I will endeavour to make sure all is well, and that I do not stray too far from your side. Perhaps I should bind our hands together, so that we may never be parted again.”

     

                “I wouldn’t be opposed,” Lena murmured with a weak smile.

     

                She felt so tired, the emotional toll of the last few days so draining that even the amount of sleep she’d had wasn’t enough to offset it. Lena hadn’t eaten either, bedridden from her injury, and then her bout of mania, and her stomach growled as if to make the point. With a quiet laugh, Kara lifted her head.

     

                “You must be ravenous. I shall have to remedy that,” she said as she sat up, cradling Lena with her movement. “Shall I bring you a tray?”

     

                Sitting upright, Lena stretched her arms, her waist twinging slightly, and felt her muscles pleasantly ache. She’d spent too long in bed and needed to stretch her legs, needed to wash. Eyes creasing at the corners, Lena reached out to touch Kara’s chin, a thrill shooting through her that her wife was alive, and another at the fact that Kara loved her, that nothing was stopping them from being together. They hadn’t had the chance to experience that yet, the confession leading into Kara’s supposed death, with no time for them to figure out what could have been. But now, nothing was stopping Lena from leaning in and pressing a lingering kiss to Kara’s mouth, lips soft and familiar beneath her own.

     

                Drawing back, pulse racing, breathing a little shallow, Lena traced the line of her jaw and smiled, the corners of her lips twitching. “I think I’d like to get out of bed. And I should probably wash; it’s been so long I can smell myself.”

     

                Ducking her head down, Kara pressed her face into the side of Lena’s neck and hummed. “I have missed the smell of you.”

     

                Laughing as she squirmed, the feeling of Kara’s breath on her neck ticklish, Lena felt a warmth spread through her chest and turned in her wife’s embrace, wrapping her arms around her, holding her close. She felt Kara’s arms tighten around her and let out a contented sigh, the two of them wrapped up in each other for a moment before Lena pulled away.

     

                “Let’s go to the baths.”

     

                Catching her hand, Kara pressed a kiss to her knuckles, “as it pleases you, Your Majesty.”

     

                With a scoff, Lena rolled her eyes and moved to the edge of the bed, tugging Kara’s hand to bring her with her. “We will need to talk about that soon.”

     

                “In good time,” Kara assured her as she got out of bed.

     

                She didn’t drop Lena’s hand, pausing to pick up a brocade robe and snag her sword belt, before letting her wife tow her through the room. At the doors, Lena opened one half and stepped into the hallway, finding a guard on either side of the door as both of them bowed their heads at the sight of her. Lena blinked at the sight of the older one, surprised but also a little relieved, another truth before her eyes.

     

                “Hector.”

     

                “Your Majesty.”

     

                “You’re well? You’ve recovered from your injury?”

     

                “With barely a scar to show for it, Your Majesty.”

     

                Smiling, Lena nodded, “good, I’m glad.”

     

                He nodded, and she reached out to touch his arm and looked at the other guard, “please, both of you, rest for the day. I will be well protected with my wife.”

     

                “Your Majesty,” they both murmured, bowing their heads again.

     

                Squeezing Kara’s hand, Lena continued, walking through familiar hallways as she led them to the baths.
