Making her way to the bathing room that she’d claimed for her use, Lena shut the door after Kara slipped inside and turned to her wife, relinquishing her hold on her hand to start undressing her. Kissing her, Lena let her hands slide over warm skin, the steam of the room making her sweat, and she pulled off Kara’s shirt, her wife forced to drop the bundle in her arms as she laughed against Lena’s mouth.

     

                Kara started undressing her too, a little gentler, and unwound the bandages around Lena’s waist, pulling away as she circled the stitches with her thumb. Ducking her head to take a look at the wound, Kara hunched over to press a kiss just above it, satisfied that it was healing well after all Lena had done to make it worse. Shedding the rest of her clothes, Lena moved towards the steaming pool of water and slipped in, the heat making her skin prickle as she sank up to her neck, watching Kara shed her leggings and pad towards her. Slipping in, Kara immediately submerged herself, kicking off as she swam two strokes away and then turned and swam back to Kara. Popping up, water sluicing down her face, she smiled and moved in closer, water eddying about her, and pressed Lena into the cold edge of the pool. Rough stone against her back, Lena met Kara’s kiss halfway, and couldn’t stop herself from smiling into it, raising her hand to tangle her fingers in Kara’s silken hair, softly moaning into her mouth.

     

                “Have you missed me, wife?” Kara lightly asked, amusement sparkling in her eyes as she drew back.

     

                “More than you can imagine.”

     

                “I think I can imagine it, although I had the hope of our reunion to tide me over.”

     

                “Mm,” Lena murmured, softly bumping her nose against Kara’s. “I didn’t. It felt like having my heart ripped from my chest.”

     

                Kissing the side of her neck, Kara hummed in agreement. “I will not pretend our agonies were the same, but I have felt half a person these months without you.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena sighed, “yes, that’s how it felt. You can’t leave me like that again. Promise me. I wouldn’t survive it again.”

     

                “I will not stop you from accompanying me wherever I may go.”

     

                “Even into death?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara defeatedly sighed. “If that is what you wish, then I will not stop you, even then.”

     

                Arms over Kara’s shoulders, fingers loosely laced behind her neck, Lena smiled. “Good.”

     

                “And you must promise to allow me the same.”

     

                Hesitating, delicately biting her bottom lip, Lena met Kara’s pointed stare as she replied in English. “Okay.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara raised an eyebrow. “In Fae, please.”

     

                “Fine. I will not stop you from accompanying me wherever I may go, either.”

     

                “Good,” Kara echoed, giving her a chaste kiss. “But, we are alive for now, so let us live a while yet.”

     

                Smiling, although there was a shadow of worry in her eyes, as if doubting herself once more, her sanity, Lena kissed her slowly, her hands trailing down Kara’s wet skin, beneath the water, before her wife stopped her. Very stern with her insistence that Lena needed to recover from her injury and regain her strength, Kara untangled herself from Lena’s touch and made her wife soak in the heat of the water as she fetched soap. Lena was still as she let Kara wash her, lathering soap on her skin, on her best behaviour as she kept her hands to herself, eyelashes fluttering as her wife pressed gentle kisses to her neck, shoulders, arms. After her hair had been washed, she ducked under the surface and rinsed the suds away, before she washed Kara in return, her touch light and teasing, enjoying the pointed looks Kara gave her, the flutter of her pulse over ticklish spots, chasing her touches up with innocent kisses.

     

                Climbing out of the pool, Kara carefully lifted Lena out and wrapped her in a towel, gently drying her off and then fetching her worn clothes. They hadn’t brought anything clean with them, and they both redressed, Lena’s bandages left off, the wound already scabbed over and starting to scar, before Kara buckled on her belt and then took her wife’s hand. Leading them outside, Kara looped Lena’s hand through the crook of her arm and squeezed her hand.

     

                “Let us see to your hunger.”

     

                Knowing her wife was surely hungry as well, Lena nodded and pulled Kara closer, so they were pressed together as they walked down the hallway. Kara led them to the dining room, where they had spent so many mornings with Lillian, and the sound of voices drifted towards them through the open doors as they approached. Stepping into the wide doorway, Lena stopped as she found the rest of Kara’s family seated at the table, the three women turning their attention to her.

     

                Alex was on her feet first, turning to face them, a small smile playing on her lips as she stared at Lena. “She wakes.”

     

                Removing her arm from the crook of Kara’s elbow, Lena crossed the few steps between herself and her sister-in-law and threw her arms around Alex. Hugging her tightly, Lena’s face furrowed with the intensity of her gratitude, and after a moment, Alex hugged her back, giving her back a gentle pat. Pulling away, Lena’s eyes were bright with tears, and she gripped the front of Alex’s leather surcoat, letting out a strained laugh.

     

                “I didn’t believe you when you said I would be grateful one day, but thank you. I wouldn’t have made it through these last months without you. I am in your debt.”

     

                Cupping Lena’s neck, Alex gave her a wry smile, “I am glad to see you have regained your sanity. Now, you may pay that debt and remove me as your heir.”

     

                With another choked laugh, Lena nodded, “very soon, I promise.”

     

                Kissing her cheek, Alex patted her shoulder, and Lena turned her attention to the other two women. Kelly was seated beside Alex and rose to her feet as Lena met her dark gaze, opening her arms as Lena stepped towards her. Giving her a hug that was gentler than the one she’d given Alex, but no less grateful, Lena let out a relieved sigh.

     

                “Thank you,” she murmured. “Thank you for saving her. Thank you for staying by her side.”

     

                “I have you to thank for bringing your healing methods here with you,” Kelly replied, a note of amusement in her voice. “I am relieved I was able to stave off a tragedy, and am glad that we are all together once more. We shall talk more later. I imagine you have questions.”

     

                Drawing back, Lena blinked rapidly, a hoarse laugh catching in her throat. “Plenty.”

     

                Smiling, Kelly nodded and sank back onto her chair, while Lena’s gaze moved to Eliza, standing on the other side of the table. Rounding the large chair at the head, Lena met Eliza halfway as she reached out for a hug, the gentleness of her mother-in-law leaving her aching as she thought of Lillian and Rhea, the sting of their actions, their betrayals. Glad to see everyone alive and well, Lena felt almost dizzy as she tried to process them all being together in the Unseelie Court, sinking onto her chair as she looked to Kara, watching her take the seat to the right of Lena. 

     

                The table was already set with a spread of food, the others halfway through breakfast, and the five of them sat together at the far end, Kara reaching for the pot of tea closest to her and lifting the lid to peek inside before she filled a cup for Lena and then for herself. As Lena watched her do so, her eyes prickled with tears, and her throat closed up, a tightness in her chest as her breath turned shallow. Hunching over, Lena buried her face in her palms and let out a strangled laugh, feeling the light touch of Kara’s hand against her shoulder.

     

                “What is it?”

     

                Raising her head, Lena gave her a tearful smile, her shoulders slumping and her eyes achingly tender. “I’ve missed you pouring my tea.”

     

                There was a ripple of quiet laughter from the other four women, and Lena felt her cheeks warm, laughing as well as she gestured helplessly. Stroking her cheek, Kara gave her a warm smile, adoration in her blue eyes, and nudged the cup of tea closer to her.

     

                “I have missed pouring it for you.”

                

                Leaning into her touch, Lena’s face softened. “I’ve missed a lot of things.”

     

                “Then it is fortunate we will have time to spend on those things.”

     

                Lena picked up her tea as Kara dropped her hand from her cheek, taking a sip and smiling sweetly at her wife. Fingers brushing the sleeve of the robe Lena was wearing, Kara returned her smile, eyes crinkling at the corners, and picked up her own tea. They weren’t very talkative throughout breakfast, but Lena basked in their company, in the attentiveness of her wife as Kara deftly cut open figs and sliced up a pear for Lena, watching the way she ate, the curve of her neck, her capable hands, the dimples in her cheeks as she seemed incapable of not smiling. Lena could barely stand to take her eyes off her, a part of her still afraid Kara might vanish if she did, but she was very real and very much alive, the sound of her laughter sending Lena’s heart racing as she delighted in the sound.

     

                She was on her third cup of tea when Kara started to question her about what had happened in her absence, hearing most of it from Alex already, but wanting to fill in the gaps, the things that had happened when Alex hadn’t been glued to her wife like a second shadow. The other three listened intently too, Alex occasionally correcting Lena or reminding her of things, adding to the story as she peeled the skin from a green apple and lounged in her chair, looking at ease in the Unseelie Court. It felt strange to have them there, stranger to be recounting her tale to her wife, who should’ve been dead and buried for months now.

     

                “The wolf,” Lena sighed, shaking her head with a divot between her dark brows. “I don’t know why - I can only assume it’s the cub that I saved; it kept nipping my arm, where it bit me there - but it stayed nearby. I’m glad it did. Saved my ass a few times, and helped with a few problems.”

     

                “Of course you would manage to acquire a pet wolf,” Alex scoffed. “How you still live is beyond me, with your reckless impulsivity.”

     

                “Well, it’s hardly a pet. I’m not planning on keeping it as a guard dog, but it’s good to know it’s out there and will come if I whistle. Or maybe it’s had enough, now. I just hope no one attacks it; it’s a harmless thing.”

     

                “Harmless?” Kelly laughed, arching an eyebrow. “It savaged your brother.”

     

                “It also let us ride it to the bridge. And if anything, killing my brother should be a point in its favour.”

     

                “I wish I got to ride it,” Kara grimaced, a longing in her voice.

     

                Touching the back of her hand, Lena smiled, “well, I’ll see if it still likes me enough to take us both.”

     

                “It’s a wild animal,” Alex spluttered. “You just said you will not be making a pet of it.”

     

                “I won’t be,” Lena shrugged, “but I think he likes me.”

     

                “Mm, I fear he is not as fond of me.”

     

                “Perhaps you need to make a royal decree that no one should harm it,” Kara suggested.

     

                “Well … I’m not sure I’m in a position to make any royal decrees,” Lena hedged.

     

                “How so?”

     

                Clearing her throat, she set her cup down and winced slightly, meeting Kara’s bewildered gaze and giving her a sheepish smile. “There are some other people who should be present for this conversation.”

     

     

                In a large room bare of any furniture, Lena sat rigidly in a chair that had been dragged in for her by her wife, her family all bringing one for themselves and arranging them in a half moon on the mosaic floor. Staring at the floral and thorn pattern beautifully wrought by the tiny tiles, Lena waited patiently for the others to arrive, no explanation given yet, as she didn’t want to repeat herself, and didn’t want to be talked out of her decision. She wasn’t sure she had much of a decision.

     

                A flicker of nervousness shot through Lena as she restlessly waited, tapping a finger on the arm of the chair, until Kara reached across the tiny gap between their chairs to cover her hand with her own. Glancing up, Lena’s brooding expression smoothed out into a warm smile, and she could read the apprehension in Kara’s eyes, almost concerned, but she hadn’t asked Lena any further questions, patiently waiting until her wife was ready. Lena wished the others would arrive quicker, but so far, only Jack, Jess and Querl had arrived. It was the first time Lena had properly seen them - in months for Querl, days for the other two - and her lips curved with a smile, nodding politely at the three of them, before asking them to add the chairs they’d been instructed to bring with them to the half moon.

     

                Within the next ten minutes, almost everyone else had trickled in, and the same moment of reunion repeated with each familiar face. There were still two missing when Andrea arrived with Sam in tow, both of them bowing their heads deferentially to Lena, curious glints in their eyes, as if surprised she still lived, eager to know what had transpired. They placed their chairs amongst the nearly completed circle, and Lena impatiently stared at the open doorway for a few minutes before breaking the tense silence as she directed her question to Sam.

     

                “Sam, where are your sisters?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Sam’s lips parted, and her eyes darted about before she licked her lips and cleared her throat. “Dead, Your Majesty.”

     

                Lena likewise blinked in surprise. “Oh. Well … that’s no good. Um …”

     

                “Forgive me, Your Majesty, I was unaware when I went to fetch them,” Jack murmured.

     

                She waved aside his apologies and grimaced, her brow furrowing as she propped her elbow on the arm of her chair and her chin in her palm. Thinking for a second, Lena hummed dubiously. “Well … that’s put a hole in the plan.”

     

                Turning to her wife, Lena hesitated, and then looked back at Sam, and then Andrea. “You’re both from here; are there any other Earthfolk and Waterfolk you trust?”

     

                They exchanged a glance, looking confused, before turning back to her. “How trustworthy do they need to be?” Andrea asked.

     

                “Extremely.”

     

                “And they have to be loyal to you. That might be a bigger problem.”

     

                “Not necessarily to me. To peace, yes. That will be necessary.”

     

                “There is always Rama Khan,” Sam suggested. “He was one of your Generals.”

     

                The name was familiar to Lena, although she’d never set eyes on the man before. She was silent for a moment, lips thinning, before she nodded. “He’s Earthfolk, isn’t he?”

     

                At the nod from Sam, Lena considered it for a moment longer. “And he would see the necessity for peace?”

     

                “He has always been quietly vocal about the damage done to the forest by the constant warfare. He is centuries old, a seasoned warrior. I believe he would see the wisdom in your decision. Did he not retreat with your army upon your command?”

     

                “And William is a well-known Waterfolk Unseelie,” Andrea chimed in. “My family have long been acquainted with him. He is not a warrior, has no taste for bloodshed, is more scholarly in personality. He might be to your liking.”

     

                “You would personally vouch for him?”

     

                Hesitating momentarily, Andrea nodded. “I would.”

     

                “Jack, fetch them both, please.”

     

                He stood and immediately walked towards the doors, vanishing from sight. After a long beat of silence, Lena cleared her throat and smiled wanly. “If anyone would like to take a break while we wait, feel free.”

     

                “Should we not begin?” Kara asked, reaching to lightly touch the back of Lena’s hand.

     

                “Not yet. It’ll be better if I do it all in one go.”

     

                “As you wish.”

     

                The others all started to quietly talk amongst themselves, Alex getting up to pace back and forth, a tense set to her shoulders, while Sam kept giving Lena anxious glances, a wariness to her expression. After a few minutes, Kara turned to Lena again and smiled, running her fingers over the back of Lena’s hand, drawing her attention to her.

     

                “I have a gift for you, once we are finished here.”

     

                “A gift?” Lena echoed, raising her eyebrows slightly. “You being here is enough of a gift.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, although she flushed with delight, Kara’s cheeks dimpled. “Well, it is a small gift. It is nothing extravagant, but I hope you will be pleased by it, all the same.”

     

                “If it’s from you, I’ll love it.”

     

                “I hope that you do. I strive to make you happy. In all things.”

     

                Lena’s stomach fluttered as her heart soared in her chest, pink creeping up her neck and into the tips of her ears as she toyed with her wife’s fingers. She did not need to feel so self-conscious over her wife trying to please her, over the implications behind her words, but this was all so new to Lena. Before, they’d both been firmly in denial, and now everyone knew, but they hadn’t had the time together for it to feel so natural between them, and while they’d gotten comfortable with each other while skirting around their feelings, there was a difference now, with their honesty. Still, Lena could hide the fact that she was smitten, and a little smug too, her hand in Kara’s as she basked in the overwhelming relief that her wife was alive and well. She could’ve started crying again.

     

                Another ten minutes passed by, and Kara climbed to her feet, Lena’s hand still in hers. “Come, let me give you your gift now, while we wait for Jack to track down your subjects for you. I find myself restless sitting here.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, Lena looped her arm through Kara’s and let her guide her through the hallways of the seat of the Unseelie Court. It felt so similar to their days when Lena had been toted about from lesson to lesson, with Kara accompanying her out of boredom and to keep an eye on her, both of their safety at risk in such a harsh Court. With a soft sigh, Lena leaned into Kara with a tender smile on her lips.

     

                “Did you ever think we would be back here like this?”

     

                “In a sense,” Kara replied, reaching up to softly pinch her chin, her eyes creasing with amusement. “When Sam told me she had slain your mother, I knew you would need to return to be Queen here. And I would follow you anywhere, even if I will miss my home at times. I imagine we will return for diplomatic meetings, so I will treasure those moments when they arise.”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena drew back slightly, frowning up at her wife. “I- you’re planning on staying here?”

     

                “We are married,” Kara slowly replied, looking perplexed. “My heart is yours, as is my sword and my life. If the cost of remaining at your side is my lake and all my rivers and seas, then it is a cost I willingly pay.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Lena stared at her for a moment before increasing their pace. Kara easily kept up with her and remained silent, navigating her way to the suite that had shared for a time, a few servants bowing and hurrying about their duties as they swept through the earthen passageways until Lena ushered Kara into the suite and shut the doors. Rounding on her, looking a little flushed, Lena floundered for a moment longer before reaching up to cup Kara’s face in her hands, giving her an aching, searching look.

     

                “I wanted to do this in one go, but … we’re not staying here. Well, we’ll have to sometimes, I guess. But … I don’t want to be Queen. I never did.”

     

                “That is why you will make a good ruler.”

     

                “Kara,” Lena curtly said before cutting off and sighing. Her shoulders sagged, and she gave her wife a tender smile. “This meeting is for me to make other arrangements. I’m not abdicating, but … abolishing, rather.”

     

                “No,” Kara murmured, her expression furrowing. “No, you cannot. You will cause a civil war amongst the Unseelie if you leave it leaderless.”

     

                “Not leaderless,” Lena corrected her. “Unified.”

     

                Expression blank, Kara was silent for a moment. “You meant to unite the Courts? Make Seelie and Unseelie into one?”

     

                “After a fashion.”

     

                Speechless, a range of emotions passed over Kara’s face before she replied. “They will revolt.”

     

                “No.”

     

                “Lena-”

     

                With a small huff, Lena leaned in and pecked her on the lips, giving her a quick grin as she pulled back. “Please be quiet, and let me explain.”

     

                Obeying, Kara took her hand and led them over to the sofa, sitting together as their knees touched and their hands lay in their laps, fingers entwined. Drawing in a deep breath, Lena cleared her throat and started to lay out her plan.

     

                “The Seelie Court has been so effective because of the Council. Now, after my encounter with some of those Councilmembers, I think better people could have been chosen, but the fact remains that the onus is not on one person to make a decision. Everyone on the Council gets a vote. I’m not sure how it’s done in your Court, but I believe if there are vows that are worded correctly, we could erase the risk of corruption by ensuring Councilmembers cannot be bribed, have to make decisions in the best interest of the Court, etcetera. Regardless, I think democracy is much better than a monarchy, and I’ll gladly set aside the throne to make an Unseelie Council. Now, I’m not naïve enough to think that the Courts will willingly be united into one, but in my world, they’re called parties. Typically, there are two major parties, so in this sense, the Seelie and Unseelie will be two parties. You have twelve Councilmembers, so the Unseelie shall have twelve Councilmembers, and both Councils will make decisions for the Courts together. Everything will be put to a vote; there will be no need for war or a closed border. Fae may come and go as they please, unharmed, and trade can flow across the river. Everyone benefits.”

     

                “It will be no easy feat,” Kara quietly replied.

     

                “But it is a good idea, and a fair chance at true peace. You know that one person should not decide the fate of a Court full of people. Yes, I may have good intentions, but you know as well as I that I can make wrong decisions, and despite our marriage tying both Courts together, that could doom a lot of people.”

     

                “The Unseelie may not be as agreeable to this as I am, though.”

     

                “I will pick the Councilmembers. And not all of them will be Unseelie.”

     

                Kara blinked in surprise, arching an eyebrow. “Surely, that is one way to ensure the Unseelie do not agree with you.”

     

                “I will make them agree. I can be quite persuasive, you know,” Lena said with a crooked smile.

     

                “Yes, I am well aware. You tricked me into giving you my heart when I was firmly set against that very thing,” Kara wryly replied, her cheeks dimpling with amusement. “Very well, I am persuaded into supporting your quest for democracy, as well. Now, save the rest for the meeting and let me give you your gift.”

     

                Letting go of Lena’s hands, Kara rose to her feet and moved into the bedroom, where Lena could hear her rummaging through her bags. A minute later, she returned with her hands hidden behind her back and an impish look of delight on her face as she approached.

     

                “Close your eyes.”

     

                Obeying, amusement in the corners of her mouth, Lena patiently waited until she felt the weight of something placed in her lap. When Kara told her to open her eyes, she looked down to find a book with a familiar title embossed on the clothbound cover. Tears pricked Lena’s eyes as she looked up, her hands firmly clasping the book as she struggled to speak for a moment.

     

                “Wha-”

     

                “Finding you was of utmost importance,” Kara almost breathlessly cut her off, kneeling before Lena with a bright intensity to her eyes. “But I could not help but make one stop while we waited in hope that you would show up with my sister. I had to bring back a piece of home for you.”

     

                Lena raised the copy of The Secret Garden to her chest and pressed it to her heart as twin tears rolled down her cheeks, her lips pressed together as she smiled. “You remembered,” she whispered. 

     

                “I have remembered all that you have told me.”

     

                “Thank you. I’ll treasure it forever.”

     

                She leaned forward, moving one hand to cup Kara’s cheek so she could kiss her softly, trying to push all of her gratitude, all of her happiness, into it. Pulling back, Lena laughed and wiped her cheeks, turning her attention to the book as she turned the copy over in her hands. Green cloth beautifully toolled in gold leaf, it was a better copy than the tattered paperback she had owned herself, and she fondly ran her fingers over the cover.

     

                “I tried my best to keep it in good condition through my travels, but I read it myself several times while waiting for you.”

     

                “How long did you wait?” Lena asked, raising her head.

     

                “Two months.”

     

                A flash of shock crossed her face, and she blinked as she stared at Kara for a moment. “So long?”

     

                “Yes. I had to be sure. I was confident my sister would do as I asked and bring you there. I had not accounted for your stubbornness.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena leaned forward to bury her face in Kara’s shoulder. “A grave oversight on your behalf.”

     

                “Quite,” Kara smiled, stroking Lena’s hair. “One I shall try not to make again.”

     

                “I’ve missed you,” Lena softly sighed, her eyes closed, a peaceful look on her face.

     

                As long as she’d slept recently, oblivious to the world or thinking herself mad, there were still shadows beneath her eyes, evidence of months of exhaustion and grief that weren’t so quick to fade. It was all catching up to her now, soothed by her wife’s presence and leaving her able to feel her emotions, rather than trying her hardest to suppress her grief in her pursuit of revenge. It would take some time for Lena to adjust to this reality again, but she was content to just sit and bask in the comfort of her wife’s embrace, that solid warmth beneath her, for a while. The rest of it would follow.

     

                “I have missed you, too. It has made me realise how foolish I was for lying about my feelings for you for so long.”

     

                “That long, was it?” Lena asked with amusement, lifting her head off Kara’s shoulder to look at her. “How long exactly?”

     

                Smiling, Kara lightly touched Lena’s cheek. “Well, there are several moments. It is not so clear-cut. At first, I was lying to myself; I remember a time when I could not say in Fae that I loved you, and had to say it in English. Even before that, you wished to accompany me to battle, and I did not want you to go. More than an ordinary wish to preserve life, I did not want you to go. I told you later that my eyes could not help but search for you - it was true then, as it is still true. And before even then, I tried to flatter you with compliments, many of which you did not take well. I tried to shower you with gifts that you did not need or seem to care much for, and much of it I explained to myself as attempts to encourage a cordial marriage between us. In hindsight, I cannot be sure exactly when it began, but I know when I could not deny it to myself anymore.”

     

                Kara let out a soft laugh, leaning in to kiss Lena’s temple, her hand cupping the side of her face. Lena’s eyelids fluttered as she smiled slightly, a warmth spreading through her chest. With a contented sigh, Kara drew back and laughed again.

     

                “You must know when I speak of. You fell - or, rather, were dropped - and I searched for you for three days, to the point of exhaustion. Everyone else was of little faith, but I could not admit how I knew for certain that you must have lived. You must have because I had not killed you, and I was to kill the one I loved. Even then, I doubted ever so slightly that you lived, because I let you stay in the Courts, so any ill that befell you was still my fault. Alex knew, of course. It was undeniable, yet I could not speak the truth aloud. It left me reeling, wracked with guilt, for I knew what I would do, and yet, you had not asked me to do it to you; you did not love me in return. I knew that there was attraction - how could we have lain together so often without that? - and friendship had bloomed, but I had thought of myself as nothing more than family to you. That stability that you had been denied in childhood. I did not imagine you would have returned my feelings. And then you told me in a sense, and it was at the most inopportune moment - I could have strangled my sister for interrupting - and I did not get to tell you how wrong you were, that it was not Kelly I loved, until right before disaster struck. As it so often has where we have been concerned.”

     

                “I’ve regretted how much time we wasted since then,” Lena whispered, lightly tracing her fingertip over the shape of Kara’s mouth.

     

                “We shall not waste any more,” Kara promised, catching Lena’s hand and kissing the pad of her fingertip.

     

                Leaning in, Lena gave her a quick kiss, and Kara caught her other wrist, pulling her in closer and holding her in place as she kissed her back slowly. Smiling into it, Lena went limp, half-splayed on top of her, and knotted her fingers in the fabric of Kara’s shirt. Humming against her lips, Kara broke off the kiss enough to mumble against Lena’s mouth.

     

                “Mm, yes, I have missed you very much.”

     

                With a louder laugh, Lena bumped her nose against Kara’s, and her wife laughed as well, relinquishing her hold on Lena’s wrists to hold her waist instead. A knock on the door interrupted them a moment later, and Kara straightened, bringing Lena with her. Head cocked to the side, she listened intently before a brusque knock sounded again.

     

                “We are waiting for you,” Alex’s curt voice came through the wood, rather muffled and disgruntled. “If you care to grace us with your presence.”

     

                Pushing herself up, Lena ran a hand over her robe and then cinched the belt tighter, running her fingers through her hair as Kara crossed over to the door and jerked it open. “I was giving Lena a gift.”

     

                With a grimace and a dismissive glance, Alex rolled her eyes. “Please do not speak of this any further to me. I have no interest in what you were partaking in behind closed doors.”

     

                Giving her a withering look, Kara sighed and held her arm out for Lena to take as she approached. “It was a book, sister. From the human realm.”

     

                Alex’s face crumpled. “Oh. Well … that is quite boring.”

     

                “It was perfect,” Lena corrected her, giving Kara’s cheek a kiss. “Shall we?”

     

                The three of them retraced the path to the hall where the others were assembled, everyone seated, until Lena swept in and the Unseelie climbed to their feet, waiting patiently for her to be seated. With a sigh, Lena settled in and then leaned forward in her seat, hands laced together as she looked around at them all.

     

                “Thank you for coming,” she awkwardly started. “I’m sure you’re all curious. I’ll not beat around the bush; I wish to establish an Unseelie Council to replace myself as Queen.”

     

                There was a stunned moment of silence before Alex leaned forward, apprehension on her face as she cleared her throat. “I beg your pardon. You wish to give up your throne?”

     

                “You know that I do,” Lena tutted, rolling her eyes. “I don’t believe one ruler should dictate a nation of people. The Seelie have the right of it, even if some of their chosen representatives are … somewhat lacking. Either way, establishing an Unseelie Court will bring us one step closer to peace. To unification.”

     

                “What has that to do with me?” Andrea asked, her eyes full of suspicion.

     

                “I need three of each element. I will represent one of the Earthfolk, along with Rama Khan and Hector. Waterfolk will consist of Jess, Querl and William. Airfolk of Jack, Kelly and Eliza. And Firefolk of Sam, Andrea and Alex.”

     

                There was a brief moment of silence before multiple voices started to overlap, almost everyone present speaking over each other in their surprise and confusion. Lena softly sighed and clenched a fist, the mosaic floor of the hall trembling as she disturbed the earth underfoot. They all quietened one by one, remaining seated and looked at her with varying expressions. Holding up a hand, Lena’s mouth thinned as she shifted on her chair.

     

                “I will take your questions one by one.”

     

                “I have a question,” Alex curtly spoke, “have you truly lost your mind?”

     

                Giving her a droll look, Lena smiled faintly. “You didn’t want to be my heir; this is my solution. You have no Halls of your own until you inherit from your mother. You are Sentinel of the Seelie, and now you will be a Councilmember of the Unseelie. It will help to unify our Courts.”

     

                “They will slit my throat and drag my body through the streets.”

     

                “You’re being dramatic. I need people I trust. I need people who will do what they have to for the good of all people and the forest.”

     

                “With respect, Your Majesty,” William spoke up, “you and I have never met.”

     

                “Yet, your character has been deemed worthy by someone I do trust. That is good enough for me.”

     

                “We should have been consulted first,” Eliza quietly interrupted. “Those of us from the Seelie Court have other affairs that require our attention.”

     

                “I understand that. The Seelie Council is scattered throughout your Court; the Unseelie Court is even smaller, so when meetings are required, it will make for shorter trips. A week at most is not so long a journey when peace is at stake. I thought- well … I was hoping you might understand.” Lena’s shoulders slumped as she gave her mother-in-law a pleading look, sheepish but hopeful. “I’m not telling anyone they have to do it, but … surely you all understand how important this is. Can see how much this would change things. For good.”

     

                It was quiet for a second before someone spoke. “I do.”

     

                Lena turned to look at Kelly, blinking and then smiling, her face softening with relief, with gratitude. “You will join me?”

     

                “I cannot say I will be accepted here when I am from another Court, but if you aim to unify both Courts through two Councils, then I am with you. Of course I must be. I will not uproot my life to move here, though. It is as our mother says, we all have our lives and affairs, too.”

     

                “Your Majesty, I do not think myself qualified-” Jack started once Kelly finished speaking.

     

                Waving aside his concerns, Lena’s brow furrowed. “I’m not looking for qualified people, Jack. I’m looking for good people who are willing to try, who can convince others to believe in what I’m proposing. This will only work if we’re all committed to trying. There will be uprisings, attempted coups, all sorts of things that I’m not quite sure I’m prepared to deal with, but I’m surrounded by some of the most experienced Generals on both sides of the river, by politically minded individuals, and loyal friends. We all have our strengths and weaknesses, but together, I believe we can make this happen. It would mean a true peace, lasting for longer than the mere months you’ve had in the past. Now, I know I’m an outsider here, I know I don’t have the experience or skill, but I’ve inherited a throne that is very clearly doomed. It hasn’t taken me very long to figure that out.”

     

                Then Andrea opened her mouth, and Lena suppressed a sigh, settling back in her chair as what followed was an hours-long meeting, where everyone kept raising points, changed sides, deliberated over Lena’s plans, poked holes in said plans, helped plot better plans, and then objected to the idea of a Council in the first place. Kara, while not intending to be on the Unseelie Council, with her own seat already secured on the Seelie one, was very vocal, and heated at times, in Lena’s defence as she tried to plead with her family and Querl, convincing them to see the reason in Lena’s idea.

     

                It was past noon by the time they’d exhausted all topics of conversation, no more points to argue but plenty to think about, and Lena wearily told them all she’d await their answers at the end of the week. They were all sworn to secrecy before trailing out of the room, until only Kara’s family, Andrea and Sam remained. The latter lingered with a clouded look on her face as she anxiously fiddled with the pommel of the sword belted at her waist. She whispered something to Andrea and then strayed a few steps towards Lena.

     

                “Might I speak with you privately for a moment, Your Majesty?”

     

                Lena glanced at her with mild surprise, head tilting to the side, and nodded, glancing at Kara, who picked up her hand and pressed a kiss to her knuckles. “I will wait for you in the dining hall with a fresh cup of tea for you.”

     

                Giving her a tender smile, Lena squeezed Kara’s hand before letting go and watched her wife quietly shepherd the rest of her family out of the hall. The doors were shut behind them, leaving Sam alone with Lena. For a moment, Lena had the briefest thought that she was unarmed with her mother’s old Hunter, but she pushed it aside and climbed to her feet.

     

                “Something on your mind?”

     

                “Why have you picked me?” Sam asked, hazel eyes perplexed beneath sternly drawn eyebrows.

     

                “Were you not paying attention?” Lena lightly teased, arching an eyebrow.

     

                Sam’s grave expression didn’t soften, the corners of her mouth thinning as she kept her gaze on Lena. “I killed your mother.”

     

                “After a fashion, yes, I am aware of that fact.”

     

                “Yet, you would entrust a seat on the Unseelie Council to me.”

     

                “Yes, I would, funnily enough. I do trust you. I might not forgive you, but you were bound by your oaths. And yet, you killed Lillian. You killed her to save me.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “I swore to be your guard, to protect you. Her control over me had lapsed somewhat during the months I was with you. Enough for me to slip the leash for a moment and cut her throat.”

     

                “Why?”

     

                “I helped take your mother’s life; it was only fitting that I helped save her daughter’s.”

     

                “You swore to repay that debt one day,” Lena reminded her. “And Andrea saved the life of the person I love most … much as she loves you. I consider your debt repaid - in part, thanks to her. Thank you.”

     

                Blinking, as if surprised that she should be thanked for it, Sam opened and closed her mouth. “A life for a life, then?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “And the Council?”

     

                “We are not quite friends,” Lena slowly spoke, a deeply thoughtful look on her face as she tilted her head to the side again, observing her. “But you have been a close companion for months. I do trust you to put the best interests of the Court first. I think … perhaps you know better than most how bad it can be for one person to have absolute control. And I think coming from both Courts, you can bridge that divide, too, given time. Ultimately, you’re one of the best people for the job. That’s all there is to it.”

     

                “And what will you require of me?” Sam warily asked.

     

                “Require of you?” Lena softly snorted, her brow furrowing. She smiled, her cheeks shallowly dimpling. “To be free. Go home, watch your daughter grow up. I know what it’s like to grow up without a mother, to wish she were there for it. Give her what you denied me. And do me the kindness of taking me up on the offer of joining my Council. It is an offer - not an order.”

     

                “It seems too good to be true.”

     

                “It’s true. Perhaps it’s time for something good to happen to you.”

     

                “And what shall I call you, then, if you are no longer my Queen, and I, no longer your Hunter?”

     

                With a smile, Lena held out a hand, the other woman slowly taking it. “Just Lena will do.”

    Chapter 56

                Despite giving everyone until the end of the week to give her their answer, Lena insisted on leaving the next day. She was pale-faced and exhausted, still recovering from the emotional toll of the last few days, all of her shock, grief and confusion catching up with her at once, and the irritated wound in her side that she’d done everything she could to ensure it healed poorly, but she insisted, nonetheless. Kara wasn’t very pleased about it, the two of them bickering in their old, familiar way, much to the amusement and relief of those who knew them best, who had endured many similar spats with them before, but it was futile, trying to argue with her stubborn wife.

     

                Lena insisted they’d go slowly, the letters already sent by raven and pigeon, and enough yeses by the end of the meeting she’d called to instil her with confidence that her idea would work. She wasn’t doing it because she’d been made to by the twisted words binding her in a promise - Kara hadn’t exactly been returned to her; she’d never truly been taken in the first place - but because Lena had never intended to keep the throne in the first place. It was the thing that had gotten her mother killed, which had led to her living most of her life oblivious to who she really was and what ran through her blood. It had been the thing she’d never wanted, but had been subjected to for a marriage out of mere convenience. If they were to have peace between the Courts, Lena intended to see it done properly, with something more lasting.

     

                Still, it took longer to depart than Lena had hoped, the morning dragging on as preparations were made. Kara was to blame for most of the delay, insisting on a full retinue of soldiers and proper arrangements for Lena’s safety, arguing that she was still Queen until she formally abdicated and, thus, needed to be kept safe. Part of that entailed Lena lying down in one of the healing rooms, shirt rucked up around her ribs, leggings jerked down, to expose the wound in her side as her mother-in-law pored over her and her wife looked over her shoulder, wringing her hands.

     

                “Well, I must say, it is healing well enough, considering all you did to ensure it healed poorly,” Eliza said with dissatisfaction, giving Lena a stern look.

     

                “See? Nothing to worry about,” Lena told Kara with a quick grin.

     

                “I said it is healing well enough,” Eliza repeated, “not that it is healing well. It has been reopened too many times for a clean scar. You are lucky the infection has retreated.”

     

                “But it is still present?” Kara anxiously asked.

     

                “There is some inflammation around the stitches-”

     

                Seizing her mother’s words, Kara cut her off as she jumped in. “So, she should not be travelling.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena rolled her eyes. “You cannot wrap me in lambswool anymore. I survived months without you; I’m not so useless anymore.”

     

                “You have never been useless, only precious,” Kara softly rebuked her, blue eyes tender beneath broodingly furrowed eyebrows.

     

                Smiling lopsidedly, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction as she reclined with one arm folded beneath her head, her attention split between Eliza’s gently prodding fingers and her wife’s nervous expression. “I’m fine, Kara,” she insisted, not for the first time, reaching down to poke her side. “See?”

     

                Eliza clicked her tongue and batted Lena’s hand aside with a pointed glance, “you will undo my good work if you keep that up. And you are not fine, you are recovering from extreme blood loss and emotional turmoil. I would advise some more bedrest-”

     

                “See!” Kara exclaimed with relieved triumph.

     

                “But,” Eliza continued, straightening as she turned to her daughter, silencing her before she could lecture Lena further. “You are fit enough to travel, if that is your will. At a slow pace.”

     

                “I will arrange a wagon,” Kara spoke aloud.

     

                Scoffing, Lena’s face crumpled. “I will not ride to a Council meeting in the Seelie Court in a wagon. That’s not the picture of strength and determination I’d like to bring to a meeting about the abdication of the throne and creation of a joint Council. It will breed rumours of weakness and prime the Unseelie Court to be attacked, to be annexed. That won’t result in peace.”

     

                “I’m inclined to agree with her,” Eliza quietly replied, glancing sideways at her daughter. “We are a hard people, regardless of which side of the river we reside on, and it will not aid her to be seen as soft when she is proposing an alliance that will hopefully stand the test of time.”

     

                Sighing, shoulders slumping, Kara grimaced. “Yes, I know. It does not mean I have to be happy about it.”

     

                “Be happy you did not have to think me dead for months,” Lena said with a wry smile.

     

                “No, only fear that something ill had befallen you that I was too late to save you from,” Kara grumbled.

     

                “Oh, ye of little faith,” Lena laughed as Eliza moved away from the bed and started pulling things from the shelves lining the walls.

     

                “It was not you I had no faith in, but your enemies were numerous.”

     

                “And now there are fewer of them. I have gotten quite good at killing; you will be proud.”

     

                “It is not your ability to kill that makes me proud. Your compassion and empathy are more laudable qualities. But, I am proud of you in all that you do, even if it is meting out justice or defending yourself.”

     

                “Then be proud of my resilience when I ride on horseback while recovering from a small, really minor, injury.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara folded her arms over her chest. “A stab wound is not minor.”

     

                “You may chastise her more after I have finished here,” Eliza called over her shoulder, “I am in need of her mind, for now. I shall quiz you on how your education has progressed since I departed from Krypton, Lena. How would you best treat your wound?”

     

                Stifling a groan, Lena relaxed on her bent arm as she ran through the healing she’d doled out since leaving Krypton. It had been months since she’d been under Eliza’s tutelage, and she’d forgotten the rhythm of her questions, the follow-ups, the elaborations. But she had continued to learn in their time apart, and Lena rattled off herbs as Eliza plucked them from the shelves and pulverised them with a pestle and mortar, creating a paste to slather over the healing wound. Eliza was also interested in the rather medieval healing methods Lena had brought into use, combining snippets she’d read in old books with uses for plants with things she’d seen in documentaries or TV medical dramas, melding fact with fiction in a desperate attempt to help dying fae. Insisting that Lena would have to show her in detail at a later time, Eliza slathered the paste over the stitched wound and applied a thin piece of linen to it before wrapping a bandage around Lena’s waist to hold it firmly in place while she rode.

     

                Climbing off the table, Lena tucked her shirt into her leggings and gave Kara a quick smile, thanking Eliza before she strode out of the room to continue her preparations to leave. Falling into step beside her, Kara escorted her down the hallway and back to their suite, taking Lena’s arm to loop it through hers. Back in their suite, Lena found Jess packing her bags and Andrea fussing over clothes, and quietly scoffed as she rolled her eyes.

     

                “As fellow Councilmembers, it’s not really appropriate for you both to be packing my bags for me anymore.”

     

                “Until you formally abdicate and establish a Council, we remain your attendants, Your Majesty,” Andrea curtly replied. “If proven successful in your plans, I will gladly stop bowing and scraping.”

     

                She gave Lena a quick grin, and Lena laughed. “What have you laid out for me?”

     

                “A new surcoat in the fashion of your old - green velvet this time, so it is more formal - and new leggings. I opted for thick wool for comfort while your injury … persists. The seamstresses have finished a new shirt this morning; you might consider a different colour other than white, given how quickly you ruin them with blood and dirt. The weather is mild, but if you require shoes, I can arrange some-”

     

                “No shoes,” Lena interrupted, “thank you. And my armour? Has it been polished?”

     

                “Yes, Your Majesty,” Jess replied. “I saw to it myself while you were bed-bound.”

     

                “Good. I’ll wear that, too.”

     

                “That much weight will not help you keep up your strength,” Kara murmured behind her.

     

                Reaching back, Lena fumbled for her hand and squeezed gently, placating but also a slight warning. “My strength is fine. There was a time you would’ve killed for me to be wrapped in steel at all times. I’m sure it would’ve saved you a few headaches.”

     

                “If you are fine, then I will dress you in it myself.”

     

                “I know my way around a suit of armour these days,” Lena replied with amusement, feeling Kara’s fingertips press against her spine.

     

                “I do not doubt it, but I would like to ensure each buckle is securely fastened. You are right; your physical safety is of paramount importance to me, whatever else might ail you.”

     

                “Whatever else being nothing.”

     

                “Of course, it is as you say,” Kara dismissively agreed, putting her hands on Lena’s shoulders and kissing the back of her head. Her eyes flitted to Andrea and Jess and she stepped around Lena. “You may leave us if everything is ready; you will have your own bags to finish packing, I’ll warrant.”

     

                They both gave Lena shallow curtsies and exited the room, leaving her alone with Kara. Lena was rooted to the spot as Kara’s hands slipped from her shoulders and she moved away from her, and she felt a nervous swoop in her stomach. She wasn’t sure why, but things felt a little off, or perhaps she was just unused to her wife. Or the knowledge that she openly loved her, feeling oddly bare to her after more than a year of marriage. They had never been so open with each other, no secrets left to uncover, and the thought of how little time they’d had to adjust was obvious in the moment.

     

                “I’m fine, you know,” Lena quietly insisted as she heard the hiss of chainmail as Kara moved it aside to pick up the padded gambeson for Lena to put on beneath her armour.

     

                She was already stripping off her clothes to change into the leggings and shirt laid out for her, picking up the soft leggings and shoving a foot into one leg hole. Kara softly sighed as she approached, and Lena got her other foot in, shimmying the leggings up her calves and thighs before she straightened and turned to look at Kara. Her wife was giving her an exasperated look, and Lena smiled crookedly as she laced the leggings and snatched up her new shirt, billowing fabric going over her head before she tucked the hem into her leggings.

     

                “You say that you are, but I wish you would allow yourself the proper time to recover. Not just from your injury, but all that you endured. Things are moving very quickly.”

     

                Lena let out a quiet laugh, “you know, I was just thinking how little time we’ve had to adjust to everything that’s changed between us. You read my mind.”

     

                “I think not only of what has changed between us, but the lingering grief, the shock of my return. The emotional toll of it all has been taxing on me; I cannot imagine how it has affected you. I see it in my sister, too. These months of ignorance have not been kind to either of you.”

     

                Reaching out, Lena pinched Kara’s chin between thumb and forefinger and stole a quick kiss. “I am perfectly well, wife. What have I to complain about?”

     

                “I imagine you could find one or two things,” Kara murmured, her lips twitching slightly, although her blue eyes remained full of concern.

     

                With a sigh, Lena took the gambeson from her and started to don it, her mouth flattening. “Will you tell me what the real problem is?”

     

                “Truthfully?” Kara apprehensively said, hesitating a moment as Lena waited patiently, tying the front of the gambeson closed. “I am afraid. I know it was I who left, in some way, I who made Alex take you, but … I have only just gotten you back. I fear what might happen if we leave these walls. It is not that I doubt your plan, only that I cannot account for the actions of others. It would kill me to lose you once more so soon after finding you back in my arms.”

     

                “A simple solution then,” Lena replied, her brusqueness softening in light of her wife’s honesty, reaching out to take both of Kara’s hands in hers, before raising them to her lips so she could kiss the knuckles of both. “We shall not lose each other.”

     

                Kara let out a quick laugh, the tense set of her shoulders loosening as she exhaled slowly. After a moment, she dipped her chin in a quick nod. “Yes, I suppose we could always aim for that.”

     

                Smiling, Lena kissed her slowly and then gave Kara’s arm a quick pat to send her off to fetch the chainmail. She was still as she let Kara dress her in each piece of the armour, the weight of it familiar to Lena after so many months of wearing it, even if it did add a few extra pounds to burden her body with. Of course, she would never admit to that in front of Kara, knowing that her wife would only fret that Lena was adding too much stress to her injured body. Instead, as Kara finished with the vambraces, Lena smiled at her and picked up the surcoat, the final layer over her ornately wrought armour, Lena thinking it a pity to hide most of the craftsmanship. Ivy was embroidered around the edges of the velvet surcoat in gold, and Lena smoothed her hands over the folds of fabric before reaching for her sword belt and buckling it around her waist. 

     

                “How do I look?” she asked her wife, a playful smile on her lips.

     

                Kara pursed her lips as she gave her a slow once-over. “You look … hot?”

     

                With a snort of laughter, Lena swatted her arm and rolled her eyes. “That would be the only slang you remember.”

     

                Grinning, looking pleased with herself for correctly applying it to her wife, Kara turned and moved over to her packed bags, which had remained there since her arrival at Lena’s home. “You are missing something, though.”

     

                “Oh?”

     

                “I have carried this with me these past months without you,” Kara said, rummaging around and pulling something shiny and bulky from her pack, before she straightened and held it between her palms. Lena recognised it immediately, despite having lost possession of it almost immediately after acquiring it, and let out a small laugh at the sight of her helmet. “And now that I am able to return it to you, I find it unbearable to cover so much of your face with it.”

     

                “In that case,” Lena said, closing the gap between them to take the helmet from Kara’s hands, “I shall carry it with me. I would hate for you to endure something unbearable.”

     

                Kara grinned and leaned in to kiss Lena, gently cupping her chin before pulling back. “And now I should change, or else we will still be here come nightfall. While I am not opposed to that, you will be very annoyed, and I would hate for you to endure that.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena turned and walked over to the chaise, taking a seat. “Be quick about it then.”

     

                She watched as Kara started to pull on well-worn undergarments to protect her from chafing armour, and then slowly added the layers of scratched steel piece by piece. When she buckled on her breastplate, Lena clicked her tongue in reproval, straightening on her seat and climbing to her feet. She walked over to her wife and reached out to touch a fingertip to the rent steel, holes puncturing the scale and wave patterns engraved and filigreed on that piece of armour.

     

                “You have not had this mended yet?”

     

                “It was not the most pressing matter on my mind once I had recovered from my wound,” Kara said with a crooked smile.

     

                “You can’t walk around with holes in your armour. I’m going to guess there are holes in your mail as well, then?” At Kara’s sheepish expression, Lena huffed. “And you speak of my safety?”

     

                “I will ask my sister to mend it for me as soon as practical,” Kara promised.

     

                “That shall have to do.”

     

                Amused, Kara smiled again as she glanced at Lena, holding her gorget in her hands as she raised it up to her neck to start fastening it in place. “It might not be a comforting notion, but armour did not stop me from being impaled by arrows. But even hole-riddled armour is better than none, so it will suffice.”

     

                “You will be the death of me,” Lena grumbled.

     

                Kara let out a bark of laughter, head tipping back as the sound filled the room, and she positively beamed at Lena, eyes creasing at the corners. “Not anymore.”

     

                Giving her a small smile, pleased and adoring, Lena’s eyelids shuttered with exasperation. “Finish getting ready.”

     

                “As Your Majesty commands,” Kara murmured with a slightly mocking bow.

     

                Lena wrinkled her nose and retreated back to the chaise, thinking about how strange it was that she had not been Queen when they’d been parted. So much had changed, and yet, there was a carefree lightness between them now. The worst was over; nothing could ever be worse than that had been.

     

                Five minutes later, Kara was ready, their packs were tightly fastened, and the two of them were walking through the hallways to the assembled group outside, horses stamping and snorting as they flicked their tails impatiently. There were a dozen guards to accompany the twelve potential Unseelie Councilmembers and Kara’s family and friends, and everyone was outfitted in armour and finery, a nervous tension hanging over the group. As soon as the last pack was fastened to the horses, they all mounted up, half of the guards preceding the procession, and the other half at the rear. Lena found herself at the front of her party, riding on the heels of the guard in front of her as Kara rode at her side, and she glanced sideways at her wife, taking in Kara’s slack shoulders, an unfamiliar air of ease about her.

     

                Setting off in two columns, they rode at a slow pace through the trees, the forest calm and peaceful around them as an autumn chill pervaded the day, a light fog and a certain dampness to the air making them all a little stiff in the saddle. Lena had the sneaking suspicion that Kara had asked for them to keep such a slow pace to not agitate Lena’s restitched wound, and while it felt snail-like, she was content to let her wife have this one thing, and, truthfully, she was a little wary about reopening the wound again if they went too fast. 

     

                It was quiet and calm as they rode along on horseback, the jingle of armour and harnesses, the soft scrape of hooves over a thick carpet of pine needles as shafts of green-tinged sunlight filtered through the canopy. Bees droned, and birds flitted from branch to branch, calling to each other as the forest was filled with the sound of birdsong, and somewhere close by, to the south of them, Lena could feel the forest floor, the gentle vibrations of the quiet footfalls of a large beast tracking them. It was the wolf, she was sure. The thought made her smile as she held her reins loosely, the wind tugging at the ends of her unbound hair as she scanned the trees but found no sign of her companion.

     

                With their late start, they didn’t reach the river until nightfall, the forest a deep navy, only their keen eyesight letting the procession of fae pick their way through the forest without light. They heard the river before they saw it, though, and after conferring with her sister, Kara suggested they camp there for the night and continue onwards at dawn. Eager to agree, feeling a little battered from hours of riding, Lena swung down from her saddle and smoothed the side of her horse’s neck as she looked around. They’d stopped in a stretch of forest where the trees were spaced far apart enough for their band of thirty to scatter in small groups between trunks, but stay within range.

     

                Tasks were divided up, and Kara took the task of fetching water, naturally, which meant Lena went with her. Threading her fingers through her wife’s, Kara slowly walked alongside her wife, swinging their hands slightly as Lena fought back a smile, pine needles soft and fragrant underfoot as she followed the weaving path through the trees. It couldn’t have been more than a hundred metres before they reached the river, the thick canopy giving way to a narrow river of star-speckled darkness overhead as Lena looked up. She couldn’t see the moon, but the stars brightened the night, and her skin prickled at the sound of running water. For a moment, she was afraid to look at the river, the dark surface glistening in the starlight as it rippled from the current and the cool wind.

     

                When she looked at it, she suppressed a shiver, thinking about all the times she’d been on the banks of that river. Last time, it had been to reunite with her wife, whom she’d thought was dead, and the time before that, it had been to cross it to end her life. Before that, it had been running from her slaughtered mother and bloodthirsty brother, running towards her wife, only to watch arrow after arrow puncture Kara’s armour. It had been the moment that Lena’s fear of water had diminished, the fear of losing someone she loved taking over. Perhaps that had always been her biggest fear. Either way, it had been enough to spur Lena onwards, into the frigid, fast-moving current of the river, struggling to swim towards Kara, to save her.

     

                “You crossed the river for me,” Kara murmured, intruding on Lena’s thoughts.

     

                Looking away from the dark river, Lena’s face rippled with a strained expression of conflicting emotions before she met Kara’s gaze. “I would cross oceans for you.”

     

                Still holding her wife’s hand, Kara gently squeezed it and leaned in to kiss her. They were quiet as they stood there, side-by-side, looking at the river as they enjoyed the quiet night, the sound of a hooting owl in the distance, the sound of crunching pine needles under soft footsteps in the forest behind them, and Lena felt happy to be there, beside the river. It didn’t fill her with fear anymore, even though she didn’t think she’d like to step foot in it, and she felt reassured by her wife’s solid presence at her side, knowing that last time, Kara had tried to keep the whole river at bay for her. Lena would always be safe by her side.

     

                “Are you two going to stand there all night, staring at each other all moony-eyed, or will we have water for tea tonight?” Alex’s voice drifted from the trees behind them.

     

                They both glanced over their shoulders, half-turning, and spotted her ferreting out suitable firewood, a bundle already tucked under her arms. Kara cracked a smile and scoffed, and Lena fought a smile, leaning in to give her wife a quick kiss before letting go of her hand. Reaching out towards the river, Kara directed two ribbons of water to rise from it and manipulated them into two suspended globes, giving Lena a quick look before she set off back towards camp with their water. Lena lingered a moment longer on the banks, staring after her wife, while her sister foraged through the underbrush for more firewood.

     

                “Coming?” Alex asked after a minute, and Lena blinked, shaking her head slightly as her eyes moved to Alex.

     

                “Yes, I was- it just … doesn’t feel real. Still.”

     

                With a snort of amusement as Lena walked towards her, Alex shifted her armload of firewood and reached out to flick Lena in the middle of her brow. Scowling as she made a complaintive sound, Lena batted her hand away and rubbed the spot, and Alex laughed.

     

                “It is real.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena fondly slapped her arm and then took half of the firewood from her, trailing her back through the trees to their scattered camp. In short order, they had a few campfires going, a stew bubbling over the flames, and cups of steaming tea in their hands as they all sat in small groups. Lena was sitting cross-legged, with Kara stretched out, leaning against her, bickering with her sister as they laughed. It made Lena feel warm, a deep gratitude in her chest as she realised how much she’d missed this.

     

                They’d spent so many nights much the same, lounging about a campfire in the forest, eating pretty poor food that they’d grown tired of days before, drinking tea and stretching out on a bed of leaves as they huddled beneath their blankets. It had never been comfortable, and sometimes it had been wet and freezing cold, but Lena had forgotten how much she’d missed it. The familiarity of it made her heart swell in her chest, so much emotion inside her that she could’ve exploded. At the centre of it all, she was just so happy.

     

                As everyone went to bed, two guards kept watch over them, even though Lena could feel the stillness of the forest at peace, she stretched out alongside her wife, their bodies fitting together as Kara lay pressed up against her back. It was a shame they were wearing armour because Lena wanted to feel the warmth of her, feel the touch of Kara’s hand across her waist, but it was enough to know she was beside her. After so many nights apart, thinking she would never sleep beside her wife again, that was no small comfort.

     

                They rose before dawn, the forest damp and misty, and before crossing the river, the soldiers bearing the Unseelie standard on their spear shafts attached smaller white banners below the standard, signalling their peaceful intentions. Crossing the bridge Lena had first met Kara on, they rode into the Seelie Court and turned south-westerly, deep into thick forest and treacherous slopes. It rained most of that second day, a fine drizzle that left the Firefolk rather miserable, although Lena wasn’t enjoying it much either, but they rode on until dark, their pace not much quicker than the day before, despite Lena’s growing impatience.

     

                It took them two weeks to arrive at the seat of the Seelie Court, moving through the forest without trouble. They’d passed by many Seelie in that time, and many creatures, but the white banners, their Seelie companions' explanations, and the way Lena soothed the forest made for easy passage, even if there were a few contemptuous looks and tightened grips on swords as the Seelie fought the urge to slay their enemies. The tension built with each passing day, and despite Lena’s wound fully healing by the end of the first week, they still made slower progress than she would’ve liked throughout the second week, skirting round swathes of boggy forest and the ever-changing land, with its valleys and canyons, hills and cliffs, a familiar headache from the last time they’d journeyed across the Seelie Court. 

     

                Their destination was more southerly this time, though, and not coastal, and while she would have been hard pressed to identify anything even if they had been heading back towards Kelly’s mother’s home, Lena found herself in unfamiliar territory, the knowledge that she’d never passed this way before leaving her a little apprehensive. Still, they reached their journey’s end without issue, Kara quietly informing Lena that they were at the fringes of it as they passed into a grove of towering rowan trees. Even if her wife hadn’t told her, Lena knew they had reached the Council’s meeting place when a soldier in gold-trimmed steel armour stepped out from behind a trunk, a spear held tightly in two hands as it was levelled at them. After a moment, the soldiers straightened, grinding the butt of the spear into the dirt as her eyes landed on Kara, before she pressed a hand to her chest and gave Kara a slight bow.

     

                “Lady Kara. They are expecting you.”

                

                “Then we shan’t keep them waiting any longer,” Kara replied, giving her a courteous nod before urging her horse onwards, Lena spurring hers on a split-second later.

     

                Only the twelve of Lena’s chosen council, in addition to Kara, went onwards; the rest were left behind with the pack horses and soldiers, and Lena silently prayed they wouldn’t cause any trouble. It would be all she needed to try and sell this new plan of peace to her would-be-enemies, only to have a few hotheaded soldiers start feuding during her attempt. Glancing back over her shoulder, she gave the group a once-over, her stomach knotting with worry, before she turned her attention back to the way forward, her horse trotting on the heels of Kara’s as her wife led them to the Council.

     

                When Kara stopped, Lena reined her mare in and dismounted as well, the rest of her makeshift Council coming to a halt behind them. While they were all dismounting, Kara reached for Lena’s hand, snagging her attention, and Lena stared at her with apprehension, biting her bottom lip. Reaching up, Kara gently swiped her thumb over Lena’s mouth to get her to stop, and gave her an unwavering look as she squeezed her hand.

     

                “You will do well.”

     

                Lena let out a quiet bark of laughter, half choked with fear, and she squeezed her wife’s hand in return, trying to resist the urge to fix her hair, knowing it was snarled from the wind, and not nearly clean enough, despite the hasty bath in a shallow stream that morning. She’d hoped to look more presentable, less travel-worn, but she supposed it might add to the hardy air she was trying to cultivate for herself, instead of prissy and haughty, as they expected of an Unseelie Queen. She had to thank Lillian for that, and Lena imagined half of her battle would be undoing these preconceptions the Seelie Council had of her. The other half would probably be undoing the damage of fighting four Councilmembers only weeks prior and slipping free of their imprisonment. There wasn’t much she could do about that, though, and Lena couldn’t bring herself to care anyway; it had led her straight back to her wife.

     

                On foot now, they walked the last fifty metres through the trees, the wind sighing, the tree branches swaying in the direction they were going, as if the forest was guiding Lena onwards. Reaching out, her fingertips brushed over mossy rowan trunks as she concentrated on her gratitude, trying to push the sensation into the trees. She thought they must have already known she was grateful for the help of the forest, for all it had done, and how it had kept her safe these past months. It was an encouraging thought, and she straightened her spine and held her head high as they reached the edge of a clearing, twelve chairs arranged in a circle beneath the sparse canopy overhead as green sunlight filtered down. The eleven Councilmembers gathered there were already seated in silence, any conversation halting the moment they’d picked up on footsteps in the distance, and Lena paused slightly, before Kara’s grip on her hand kept her stumbling forward.

     

                “My apologies for the delay,” Kara called out as she loped towards the circle of chairs, towing Lena with her. 

     

                “We have waited here half the day,” Maxwell complained.

     

                He shot Lena a dark look, evidently still clinging to his resentment over what had transpired a few weeks ago. She didn’t waver, though, just let Kara steer her towards the single empty chair. It was carved with water motifs, in between a chair with a Firefolk and Airfolk, and an Earthfolk a seat further. The pattern repeated three times, bringing their number to twelve.

     

                Kara paid him no mind, pausing behind her chair and holding Lena’s hand aloft as she gently urged her to step between the chairs and take her seat. “We had anticipated an earlier arrival, but travel was slow-going.”

     

                Taking a seat on the stone chair, worn with time, Lena’s armour scraped over stone as she made herself comfortable, watching the ripple of surprise, the way a few straightened, brimming with tension as they frowned. Kara stood behind Lena, reaching down to put a hand on her shoulder as her eyes darted from face to face, gauging the responses of her fellow Councilmembers.

     

                “You let her sit in your place at our Council? She, who is Unseelie?” Morgan scoffed.

     

                “She is my wife.”

     

                “A farce of a marriage,” he waved a dismissive hand.

     

                “Perhaps in its origins, but that is not so, and has not been so for quite some time. I would sooner let all the rivers, seas and lakes in both Courts run dry before I would stop loving her,” Kara stated with a stubborn jut of her chin, staring down her fellow Councilmembers.

     

                “I am not here as your enemy,” Lena quietly cut in. “I am here as an ally. I may be Unseelie by blood, but I am here to create a lasting peace between our Courts. To unify us, in a sense.”

     

                “You should be here as a prisoner,” Morgan said, pushing himself to his feet. 

     

                He rose fluidly, the quick motion making Kara pull her hand from Lena’s shoulder and fall to the hilt of her sword. The scrape of a foot of steel unsheathing rang out in the quiet of the forest as Kara slipped into a fighter’s stance, jaw set with stubborn determination as her eyes darted around quickly, taking note of the hands that fell to weapons. Lena’s stomach jolted at the thought of bloodshed here, so close to the end, so near to peace, and she held her hand up, a warning to her wife to rein in her leap to action. 

     

                “Peace.”

     

                After a tense minute, Kara slowly sheathed her sword and set her hand back on Lena’s shoulder, retaining her protective stance behind her chair.

     

                Morgan forged onwards, taking a step towards Lena’s chair, and she could feel Kara’s hackles rise at his approach, although she didn’t reach for her sword again. He didn’t take more than that step, though, the low growl of the wolf somewhere in the trees giving him pause. “Several of my guards were injured in your escape-”

     

                “Injured by me,” Alex called out as she stepped forward. “A Seelie. And I will answer for my crimes, if you will answer for yours. She was not yours to take prisoner against her will - she is Queen and had pulled back her army in a show of good faith. You kept her there unlawfully.”

     

                A woman, a stranger to Lena, piped up, giving her a contemptuous look. “It was not unlawful; a foreign sovereign trespassing-”

     

                “She was not trespassing,” Kara cut her off, sounding peeved as she clicked her tongue. “Come now, Selena, you were here when the marriage deal was made - we all were. My wife was to spend every summer and winter in the Seelie Court, and I was to spend every spring and autumn in the Unseelie Court. We were also to have free travel between Courts as political ambassadors, and protected under such positions, so long as a truce stood between our Courts.”

     

                “A truce that was violated when you cut the hand off her mother,” Selena retorted.
