                “And a truce that was reinstated when the new Queen sent messages here declaring a new truce and pulled her army back from the river.”

     

                “A truce that I intend to keep,” Lena softly said, hands folded in her lap.

     

                There was a beat of silence, all eyes on her, the sound of the wind through the trees, and Lena met their stares with a level gaze. She didn’t waver beneath them, looking from person to person as the silence dragged on, until someone cleared their throat. Her eyes doubled back to a familiar woman, and Lena politely raised her eyebrows.

     

                “How do you propose that?” Olivia asked, shifting forward in her seat, hands laced together and elbows on her thighs as she stared intently at Lena.

     

                Kara had advised her that she was one of the more diplomatic Councilmembers, a critical thinker of rational mind, instead of hotheaded and grudging, like the two men Lena had already had the misfortune of running into.

     

                “The Seelie Court is a democracy; I think a Council has far more merit to it than a monarchy.”

     

                There was a ripple of surprise, a few exchanged looks, and a few of the fae straightened in their seats. Cat lounged in her chair, legs crossed and chin propped up in her palm as she pursed her lips, giving Lena a shrewd look.

     

                “You said before you would give anything to have your wife back. When it was posed to you that you would give up your crown, you readily agreed. You are merely here to uphold that promise, unless I am mistaken.”

     

                “You are mistaken,” Lena said with a thin smile, her hands moving to grip the arms of the stone chair. “In a sense. I was never bound by that promise because my wife was never taken from me. She had been alive for months by that point, in the human realm, so had already been returned to me. But that does not change my belief that a monarchy is only self-serving and prone to uprisings.”

     

                Hesitating, Lena’s smile turned wry, and she arched an eyebrow slightly. “I might not be the most ideal Queen, and my knowledge mostly comes from what I know of human history, but I’m still certain I could do without a coup. I’m sure you will agree that peace is preferable to war. I intend to forge a peace that stands for longer than a season or a year. One that stands for aeons.”

     

                “So, what is it you propose?” a man in grey Airfolk robes asked, sitting straight in his chair, fingers laced together in his lap as he watched her apprehensively. 

     

                “A Council, much like this one. I have already chosen representatives. They have accompanied me here today. Some are Seelie in birth, but are committed to peace between Courts, and I believe they will have honourable intentions when making decisions for the Unseelie Court.”

     

                The man nodded thoughtfully, silence falling over the circle again, until Maxwell scoffed, gesturing towards the man with a disbelieving look on his face. “Surely you do not believe a word she says, Jul-Us.”

     

                “How am I to doubt them when she speaks truly in our tongue?” Jul-Us reasoned.

     

                “I speak truly,” Lena stated, although it was obvious anyway, the whole conversation held in Fae. “I am not here to deceive anyone. I am not here to twist words, to gain an advantage for myself and my people. I am here on behalf of the forest.”

     

                “The forest?” Morgan snorted.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “We journeyed here from the Unseelie Court without a whisper of trouble,” Kara announced. “We have come with a wolf in our midst. My wife has ridden him, even. Has anyone here managed such a feat? No? Has anyone journeyed through the forest unharmed, with no sight of trouble, from the creatures or the trees themselves? From the rivers and lakes, the earth, marshes, and mountains? From the wind, from fire and rain? There is a reason for that.”

     

                “What reason?” an unknown fae demanded, haughtily raising her chin.

     

                “The simple explanation is that you have treated your home poorly,” Lena softly replied, a look of dismay on her face. “The ground has been soaked with blood, the rivers have run red with it, the lakes have been polluted with bodies. Trees and earth have been scorched by fire. The very blood in your veins has been poisoning the magic within it. If you do not believe me, listen to the elements. They are angry at their mistreatment - on both sides of the river.”

     

                They all seemed shocked for a moment that she would say such a thing to them. She, who had been born there but was only half of them, and had been raised away from the Courts. It had been easier for her to see what was right before their noses, where they had been steeped in bloodshed for so many centuries and generations that they didn’t know any difference. They should have known better, though.

     

                “Then it is the blame of the Unseelie,” Maxwell dismissively replied, waving a hand.

     

                “It is the blame of us all,” Kara snapped back. “It is the responsibility of all to undo this harm, as well.”

     

                “And how do you propose we do that?”

     

                Kara’s lips curved in a smile as she raised her hand from Lena’s shoulder and tenderly touched her wife’s cheek, looking down at her from behind the chair back. “Listen to my wife.”

     

                “And what do you propose, Your Majesty?” he mockingly asked.

     

                “It is as I say - there must be peace between our Courts. A Council for each, yes, but more than that. We must make decisions for both Courts together. I propose a Council for each Court, of twelve each - three of each element - as you have done here in the Seelie Court. However, both Councils will meet together for their meetings. All twenty-four Councilmembers. Decisions will be made for the entire realm, not just their respective Courts. It will give a voice to both parties, and it will make for fair, unprejudiced and unbiased decisions. How is that not in the best interest of all?”

     

                “It is … ambitious,” Olivia hedged.

     

                “But is it possible?” Cat mused.

     

                “It will take time,” Lena conceded. “I am not naïve enough to think it will happen overnight. It will very well take years to undo the harm, and I imagine decades before there is any sort of trust between the ordinary folk of the Courts. I would hope that all present would be more committed to trusting each other than ordinary folk, though.”

     

                There were a few scoffs and a smattering of laughter, at Lena’s expense, and she felt her face flush as she gripped the stone arms of the chair, her expression hard with the stubborn set of her jaw and her piercing stare beneath strong brows. After a moment, their amusement petered out in response to her stony silence, and that of those assembled behind them, and Lena cleared her throat, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “Shall we begin negotiations?”

    Chapter 57

                “It’s starting to frustrate me,” Lena grumbled, her arms folded over her chest as she kept her eyes closed to the low roof of the tarpaulin stretched over a low branch, which had made up their lodgings for the last ten days. “How long will it take?”

     

                Stretched out behind her wife, with Lena’s head in her lap, Kara hummed with amusement. She looked the picture of ease, leaning back on one elbow, legs crossed at the ankles as she idly ran silken locks of her wife’s hair through her fingers, content to lie there all day, breathing in that mossy, forest smell of her as they awaited the decision of the council. They’d been deliberating for ten days, occasionally requesting the presence of Kara or Lena, usually both, to discuss a point, but otherwise taking their time. It was getting the better of Lena’s patience, though.

     

                “It will take as long as it takes.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena’s mouth thinned. “Surely it cannot be such a difficult decision to make.”

     

                “You are impatient. It serves to prove your point; if it were up to one person - you - the decision would have already been made by now. Whether it was the right decision or not. The Council will come to the right decision amongst themselves, I am certain.”

     

                “You’re part of it; shouldn’t you have a say?”

     

                “Ah, well, they already know what my vote will be when the time comes. It is not for me to make their minds up for them.”

     

                Lena clicked her tongue in mock annoyance and then smiled slightly, her eyes still shut. “You could at least threaten a few of them for me. Bully them into siding with us.”

     

                “I will leave that as a last resort,” Kara whispered conspiratorially, letting her fingertips graze along the curve of Lena’s ear, up to the short point of her ears.

     

                Suppressing a shiver as her skin prickled with goosebumps, Lena shifted restlessly on the tent floor, her folded arms uncrossing as she let her hands fall to her sides in fists. She felt a flicker of frustration and let out a huff of laughter. As if reading her mind, Kara’s lips twitched with amusement. 

     

                “I wish we were elsewhere, in a meadow, perhaps, braiding flowers into your hair and kissing your bare skin,” Kara murmured, her fingers returning to tenderly stroking Lena’s dark hair as she stared at her in wonder.

     

                “Mm, that would be nice,” Lena hummed, opening her eyes as she looked up at her wife. “It’s strange to think about how much I miss those quieter moments, before everything went to shit, when so much of it was spent slogging our way through danger. Even stranger to think about how different things were between us then, compared to now, and how … I don’t know, it feels strange that my heart is wide open to you, but we’ve barely laid a finger on each other, which is the complete opposite of how it was before.”

     

                Kara laughed and smoothed her thumb over the divot that appeared between Lena’s furrowed eyebrows. “Yes, it is rather different now, is it not? I shall remedy it as soon as we are elsewhere.” 

     

                With a quiet snort of laughter, Lena rolled her eyes and then pushed herself up onto her elbows, staring through the opening of the tent. “These past months, I’ve been very grateful to your sister for staying by my side and keeping me alive, despite my best efforts, but I could do with her being a little further away right now. Just out of sight - and earshot.”

     

                Palm smoothing from the crown of Lena’s head down to her lower back, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners as she leaned in and kissed Lena’s brow. “I shall take you somewhere alone once this business has been dealt with. It should not take much longer, now.”

     

                “Oh? And where will you take me?”

     

                “I will take you home.”

     

                “And where is home?”

     

                “Wherever you would like it to be.”

     

                Lena smiled ruefully, “well, it couldn’t be Krypton.”

     

                “I would rebuild it with my bare hands if that was where you wanted our home to be. Although I would not believe you if you said it was. There aren’t enough trees, and you do not like the ocean.”

     

                “There isn’t enough water for you at my home in the Unseelie Court.”

     

                “We will have to divide our time between both Courts, regardless of where we live. There is enough water there to satisfy me, and we will not be so confined this time, I should think. If that is home to you, then it will be our home when we are not called to the Seelie Court.”

     

                “You have been my home since I came here,” Lena replied, catching Kara’s hand in hers, smoothing her thumb across her wife’s knuckles as she stared at their hands for a moment and then looked up to smile at her. “But when you were gone, and I had lost my home, the place I went to to feel close to you again was Argo.”

     

                “Argo,” Kara hummed, her face delicately furrowing as she considered it. “It is surrounded by a lot of water.”

     

                “I don’t think I’m afraid of it in the same way anymore. And it’s surrounded by trees, too. The whole forest. It’s a good middle ground, and we can go to my home for the winter. The lake will have frozen over then, anyway.”

     

                “We have not lived there in a long time,” Kara mused, “so much has changed since then. You would barely speak to me when we were at Argo.”

     

                “Now, I think if I had to go a day without speaking to you, I would feel as if I’d lost part of myself,” Lena murmured, amusement colouring her voice.

     

                “Aye, it would feel as such to me as well. It did, in fact, when we were parted. I had not known what I was missing out on before I met you, as opposed to love as I had been, and now I have also seen what life is like without you in it since meeting you, and I wish to never know it again. How remarkable it is for one person to leave such a lasting impression on my heart; I had resented the mere idea of that, right up until that moment on the riverbank. For those precious few moments before my heart stopped, I knew a peace that had been lost to memories of my childhood, before the prophecy had filled me with fear.”

     

                “You need never be afraid again,” Lena promised, reaching for Kara’s hand and bringing it to her mouth, placing a lingering kiss on her palm as she stared at her through her lashes.

     

                Cheeks shallowly dimpling as her gaze softened, Kara hummed in agreement. “I will always fear that. But I am comforted in the knowledge that I will follow you until the end, to whatever end that may be. And I will be buried beside you, and the Court will take our bones, but history will not forget us; our names will be spoken in sentences together for all time, and in that, we shall never truly be parted. What is there to fear in that?”

     

                “You really think they’ll remember us?” Lena asked, a little sceptical as she grinned lopsidedly.

     

                “Undoubtedly,” Kara firmly insisted, with an earnestness to her features. “The final monarch of the Courts? Our lives are long, our memories even longer, and they will record your abolition in the annals, besides.”

     

                “Mm, depending on whether the abolition comes to fruition.”

     

                “Ah, you fret over nothing. Believe me in this - they will make the right decision.”

     

                “Anything to see the Unseelie throne empty, huh?”

     

                Kara laughed, shrugging a little sheepishly. “I would not be surprised if that was the ulterior motive of more than one on the Council.”

     

                “If it gets me what I want, then so be it. I can charm them into cooperating with me, I’m sure. It worked well enough on you.”

     

                Tipping her head back, Kara let out a loud laugh. “You charmed me into cooperation? A most amusing jest; it would have been easier to squeeze water from a stone than get you to cooperate. At least for a time. I have met mountains less stubborn than you.”

     

                “Is that any way to speak to your wife?” Lena clicked her tongue and swatted Kara’s arm.

     

                “I am in agreement with my sister,” Alex’s voice drifted towards them, and Lena softly groaned, ducking her head to peer beneath the tarpaulin, catching sight of Alex’s legs as she crossed over to their tent. Stopping at the side of the makeshift tent, Alex stooped to arch an eyebrow at Lena. “I heard that.”

     

                “Have I not suffered enough already? Now you come to torment me further.”

     

                “I have not said my reasoning for coming,” Alex started to patiently defend herself.

     

                Kara let out another loud laugh, and Lena gave Alex a withering look. “You don’t need to.”

     

                Letting out an exasperated sigh, Alex straightened up, so Lena was left staring at her shins. “Well, if you already know why I’m here, best you hurry and get out of your tent before I cut the tarp down on top of you. It will make it a swift fight if you are left ensnared.”

     

                Grumbling under her breath, Lena started to crawl out of the tent and just straightened up, complaining, when one of Alex’s knives raked the shallowest scratch across her throat. “I’m still recovering from yesterday’s bruises- hey!”

     

                Staggering back a step, Lena momentarily floundered for balance as she almost fell onto the tarp and brought it down on top of Kara. Scowling at Alex, she reached up to touch her fingertips to the stinging scratch. “Do you have to do this every time? One day you might actually hurt me.”

     

                “If I intended to hurt you, you would be hurt. Now, the fight has already begun, and you have yet to draw your weapon. Until you learn that lesson, I will continue to catch you off guard.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena drew her sword and rolled her eyes before lunging towards Alex, watching her carefully retreat a few steps, giving Lena more space to move without collapsing her temporary home. She lashed out again, a clumsy strike to give her an extra few feet, but Alex didn’t fall for it, deflecting Lena’s blade with one of her long hunting knives and then stepping inside her guard with the other one, aiming for the gap in the side of Lena’s breastplate. Turning her torso, Lena reached for Alex’s wrist and managed to get the sharp edge of her sword between them, although she couldn’t do much more than that with Alex so close to her. Grinning, her sister-in-law dropped the knife in her left hand and gripped Lena’s right wrist tightly, squeezing the small bones in her hand until she let out a quiet gasp and let go of her sword. Then, Alex wrapped her in a bear hug, heaving her off her feet as Lena let out a squawk of protest, and was slammed down to the forest floor, blinking back dizzying black spots as she groaned.

     

                “Gentle with her,” Kara lightly chided her sister, peeling an apple with a knife as she watched the two of them fight.

     

                Alex laughed, and Lena swore at her, somewhat breathlessly as she found herself winded, staring up at the distant canopy overhead. Stooping to pick up her dropped knife, Alex teasingly called to her. “Quickly, Your Majesty, on your feet or you will be surrendering once more. Come, fetch your sword before I put my knife to your throat.”

     

                Scowling as she rolled over, Lena got her hands under her and pushed herself up to her knees, hearing Alex’s quiet footsteps behind her, and then turned and threw herself at her sister’s legs before Alex could step back. With a yelp of surprise, Alex went down under Lena’s tackle, and there was a smattering of laughter from the onlookers in the surrounding tents, Kara’s loudest of all, and Lena crawled her way up to Alex’s chest, kneeling heavily on it as she jerked her dagger free from her belt and grinned.

     

                “Do you-”

     

                With a quick yank of a fistful of Lena’s hair, making her grit her teeth and stifle a curse, Alex had her off her and sat on Lena’s breastplate with the dagger she’d just taken from her in her hand. Looking pleased with herself, doubly so in light of Lena’s frustration, Alex chuckled, enjoying herself immensely as she wound up her sister. And Lena couldn’t truly be annoyed, because there was a lightheartedness to their antics that had been missing for so long, but brought back to them with the return of one they both loved dearly.

     

                With a sigh, Alex idly twirled the dagger in her hand and gave Lena an exasperated look, brown eyes glimmering with mirth. “One day, I am certain you will beat me, but it is not this-”

     

                The ground exploded around them then, and Lena had Alex wrapped in roots before she could even finish her sentence. With a yelp of surprise, Alex was hauled off Lena, feet scuffling against the ground as she squirmed in her constraints, and Lena picked herself up, armour clinking, body aching, and dusted her hands off as she beamed at Alex. They were of a height, but Lena had the roots lift Alex a few inches higher, watching her face furrow with annoyance as her bare feet scrabbled for purchase and found none, and Lena chuckled as she reached up to give her sister’s face a fond pat.

     

                “Shall we say I won this one?”

     

                “You cheat!” Alex objected, spluttering.

     

                “I didn’t cheat; you’re just used to fighting me without my powers and assumed I wouldn’t use that to my advantage. A lapse of judgment on your part. I’m sure you won’t make it again.”

     

                She commanded the roots to let Alex go, her sister landing in a slight crouch as she gave Lena a grim look and then laughed, straightening. “Well fought, then. I have learned a lesson here - well-needed, I think, for one should never underestimate their opponent.”

     

                “And I’m sure you’ll knock me on my ass tomorrow, with no more tricks up my sleeves, so all will be right in the world.”

     

                ‘Tomorrow? Think again, sister. Pick up your sword,” Alex ordered her, fetching her knives as Lena loudly groaned and then obeyed.

     

                After two more bouts, where Lena was sure her sister was about to boil her inside her armour, dodging flames and squawking indignantly at the whiff of singed hair or cotton as Alex swiped too close to her surcoat, Kara and Kelly joined in, bringing all four elements into the mix as they all moved with varying grace, battering each other and wielding their powers. It wasn’t long before the ground was churned to mud, and the fierce wind Kelly brought against them left them all flailing and slipping to the ground, until they were all breathlessly laughing, practically brawling now, weapons lost and more ungainly tactics employed. Lena couldn’t catch her breath as she laughed while Kelly had her in a headlock, watching Kara press Alex’s face into the mud with her arm twisted behind her back, only to be yanked into a puddle of muddy water by a little root that Lena had manoeuvred around her ankle. 

     

                All four of them were filthy and laughing when a rider on horseback appeared, the sound of hooves trotting on the leaf-strewn ground making them pause as they slowly pushed themselves up. It was one of the Seelie guards from the perimeter of the Council’s meeting place, and Lena quickly climbed to her feet, mud caked onto her armour and dirty water streaming off it. Wiping a muddy hand over her face, which only served to smear more mud across it, she cleared her voice.

     

                “What news?”

     

                “The Council would like to confer with you on a few matters,” the man said, giving them all a once-over. “At your earliest convenience.”

     

                Without anything further, he pulled his horse around in a tight circle and trotted off the way he’d come, and Lena quietly cursed, raking her fingers through her muddy hair. “I’ve been waiting all day, and now they choose to summon me, when I’m in such a state.”

     

                “They can wait,” Kara soothingly assured her.

     

                “No, I don’t want to wear their patience thin. They already think very little of me, being Unseelie, and half at that.”

     

                “They knew that when we agreed for me to wed you.”

     

                “Yes, but they were under the impression I had been raised here at that time. They’ll think me childish to come covered in dirt, now, but at least I’ll be on time.”

     

                “One moment,” Kara insisted, turning around and hurriedly glancing about, before she settled on the muddy pool she’d recently been wallowing in, funnelled a large wave of water up from the puddle, and doused her wife in it.

     

                Spluttering as brown water sluiced down her, Lena gave Kara a grim look as she wiped silt from her eyes. Freezing, Kara looked mildly panicked as she stared at Lena, her eyes shockingly blue in her mud-streaked face. 

     

                “Forgive me, I thought that would be more successful than it was.”

     

                “You look like a drowned rat,” Alex supplied, lips twitching with a smile.

     

                Scoffing, Lena waved a dismissive hand at her and let the earth shift under her feet, making her keel over backwards and sink into the same puddle Kara had tried to wash her off with. Spitting water as she sat up, Alex complained as Kara and Kelly chuckled, and Lena looked a little less concerned as the corners of her mouth curved up. Wiping her hands on her soiled surcoat and trying her best to work her fingers through the tangled mess of hair, Lena strode towards the gap in the trees and went to meet the Council.

     

                Kara’s hurried footsteps chased after her, and Lena paused at the sight of a spotless white handkerchief emerging from the cuff of her wife’s robe. It had clumsy waves embroidered around the edge, and Lena’s expression softened as she was pulled to a stop, her eyelids closing as she let Kara tenderly wipe away as much mud as she could. Handkerchief vanishing back up her sleeve, Kara took Lena’s chin between thumb and forefinger and kissed her softly.

     

                “You are beautiful no matter how you come before them. And more importantly, you are still yourself, no matter how you look.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara slipped her hand into Lena’s and led her onwards, seemingly content to stand before her fellow Councilmembers with a layer of mud coating her. The forest was calm, bees, birds, squirrels and mice filling the quiet of rustling leaves and sighing branches, and Lena stared upwards as she walked along. She hadn’t heard the forest go quiet since before she’d left the Unseelie Court prior to reuniting with Kara, and watching the pale green shafts of sunlight filter through the high canopy overhead, she felt as if she was in a different world, one not quite so dangerous as the wild parts of the old forest had felt before. The sense of foreboding was gone, and she had to wonder if part of it was because there were no creatures about to make her skin prickle - although, she knew her wolf was out there somewhere, probably close enough for her to whistle for him - or whether she’s imparted so much of her energy into the forest that word had spread throughout the trees, knew her as a friend and made wherever she stepped foot safe instead of dangerous.

     

                “What are you thinking of?” Kara gently intruded.

     

                Shaking her head, Lena kept staring up at the trees as she frowned slightly. “Nothing much, I just- just think of how many thousands of years of stories these trees hold. They’ve seen and felt so much in their lifetimes. No wonder the forest has been so angry.”

     

                Eyes quickly darting up, Kara pondered that for a second before she nodded in agreement. “Not anymore. Not if you have anything to say about it. Peace flows like a river.”

     

                Lowering her eyes to her wife’s face, Lena’s gaze was thoughtful as she considered that. “Yes. Yes, I suppose it does. It has flowed from me for quite some time now; I have to believe that is the way to solve this anger, this danger. I have wanted peace for so long that perhaps the trees have listened to my intentions flow from me.”

     

                “I have no doubt about it.”

     

                “Do you not? Why are you so quick to believe my theory?”

     

                “Because you have brought peace to me, and are we so different from the trees, really?”

     

                “We’re all alive, in different ways,” Lena agreed.

     

                “And we all crave peace so we may continue to live. The trees are on your side, as much as I am. I am certain.”

     

                Lena’s smile made a dimple in her cheek as she glanced sideways at Kara and squeezed her hand in silent gratitude. If her wife believed in her so wholeheartedly, how could she not have the courage to believe in herself just as much? She had to at least try to convince the Council that peace was in the best interest of everyone, including the forest. Whether they agreed with her was not her decision to make, but Lena was rather stubborn, and she wouldn’t give up, no matter how long it took. She thought perhaps there was some truth to Kara’s opinion that she was more stubborn than a mountain.

     

                Onwards they walked, two miles through the hush of the forest, autumn in full swing as russet leaves fell around them, berries and plums ripening on trees and bushes as the animals picked at them, and Lena found herself appreciating the forest even more. She hadn’t loved it enough last autumn, had still been so bitter and resentful, but with a full turning of the seasons under her belt now, she couldn’t imagine a life anywhere else. Her old life felt a distant memory, a dream of some other person, and she felt as if she’d always lived there, amongst the ancient trees and gigantic creatures. She was finally living the life she always should’ve been, if things had been different, if her mom had never taken her and run. It was with a pang of bittersweet sadness that Lena thought about what could’ve been if they’d stayed, if Elizabeth had never found out Lena’s fate and tried to save her, if Lillian had only made her Hunters bring them back.

     

                Sensing the sudden sombreness that swept over Lena, Kara cocked her head to the side and squeezed her hand. “What troubles you?”

     

                “I’m thinking of my mom.”

     

                “She would be proud of you.”

     

                “You think so? She never wanted me to live here; she ran to keep me safe.”

     

                “That does not mean she would not be proud of the woman you are. I never knew her, of course, but I cannot imagine she would not be pleased that you are attempting to bring peace to the Courts. Who would not be proud of such a feat?”

     

                Lips twitching slightly, Lena shrugged. “I imagine there are a fair few people.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Kara rolled her eyes. “Pay them no heed. They go against the natural order of things to behave as such. We are meant to live together, to help one another, to tend to the forest and its creatures with no hatred in our hearts. We will all be better for it.”

     

                “Will you tell them that at the meeting?” Lena asked, a plea in her voice as she fretted over facing the Council.

     

                Pausing, Kara raised a hand and pressed it to Lena’s dirty cheek, a confident smile on her lips. “I will not have to. You will tell them yourself, and they will believe you.”

     

                Drawing in a deep breath, shoulders squared, Lena slowly exhaled and nodded. “Yes, you’re right. I can do this. I am my mother’s daughter - both of them - and I will stand up for what’s right and make them see sense. I won’t take no for an answer.”

     

                “My stubborn wife, how I love you with all my heart,” Kara fondly sighed, as if Lena had charmed her all over again.

     

                They didn’t speak as they walked the last few hundred feet through the trees, passing by the guards spread across the perimeter, not wanting to be overhead. Lena didn’t think it would do much for their opinion of her if they overheard her voicing her doubts. As they drew closer, she slipped her hand from Kara’s and took her arm instead, drawing her tighter to her side, and Kara kissed the side of her head and let herself be towed along. A glimpse of chairs and seated fae came into view past the trunk of a rowan tree, and they walked to the circle in silence and were greeted with silence as well.

     

                Lena indicated for Kara to take her seat this time, a rightful Councilmember, although she looked far from the regal Lady whom she’d wed on the bridge a year past, even muddier than Lena was, but unconcerned with her appearance as she settled herself on the stone chair and crossed an ankle over her knee.                 Cat arched an eyebrow as she gave Lena a once-over glance. “I know you Earthfolk have a penchant for dirt, but I did not think you bathed in it.”

     

                “The hot springs of my home are sorely missed,” Lena wryly replied, “but I have my wife to thank for ensuring I have a muddy pool to roll around in.”

     

                “A lesson in melee,” Kara explained, holding a hand out towards Lena. Slipping her hand in her wife’s, Lena smiled faintly as Kara kissed her knuckles and then held her hand in both of hers. “My wife is becoming quite the warrior. Fortunately for us, we shall hopefully be spared her wrath on the battlefield. Am I to understand you have come to a decision?”

     

                “Not yet,” Selena coyly replied, her eyes flitting between the pair.

     

                “There is no rush,” Olivia idly replied, tapping the arm of her seat. “We would like clarification on a few matters before we reconvene to discuss the matter further.”

     

                “What might I clarify for you?” Lena exasperatedly asked, giving the Councilwoman a tight smile.

     

                “We are sceptical of your intentions,” Maxwell stated, shifting in his seat, looking a little too self-satisfied for Lena’s liking.

     

                “My intentions have been plainly stated.”

     

                “Yes, we have heard enough of your platitudes of peace,” Morgan huffed, a dismissive flick of his hand making Lena stiffen. “That does not make it so. Were you not wed to our General to bring about peace? How did that fare? It did not last half a year.”

     

                “That was not a promise I made,” Lena haughtily replied. “But when I make a promise, I keep it.”

     

                “And what promise do you make?”

     

                “I promise that if you agree to a joint Council with the Unseelie, we will make decisions for both Courts together. That I will not instigate any wars, and will abolish my throne in favour of an Unseelie Council being formed.” There was a beat of silence, and Lena felt her frustration grow. “You have the advantage here. I intend to make several Seelie Court members part of my Unseelie Council. It puts my people at a disadvantage, but I believe I have picked my Councilmembers well, and they will do the honourable thing and vote wisely and considerately for the sake of the Unseelie, and not just in the interests of the Seelie Court. We will be able to align our interests if both Councils work together, though.”

     

                “What do you know of Seelie interests?” Morgan scornfully asked.

     

                “I know enough from my wife,” Lena replied, gesturing to Kara. “I know enough to not lay the blame of millennia of warfare on just one Court. I understand there is history I am ignorant of, but it has affected me the same as it has affected all within both Courts, and I put the blame on both Courts. This- this equivalent retaliation must come to an end. Else, it will destroy both Courts.”

     

                “You seem awfully confident in that assumption,” Maxwell said with a condescending smile.

     

                “I am confident, actually,” Lena replied, finding her bravado. “My wife spoke to you of the dangers in the forest. That was not always so, is that not correct? I have confessed that there is history I am ignorant of, but that does not mean my time here has been spent idly. I have learnt to read Fae, and have been educated as best as I could be in between my other crucial lessons on survival. My wife spoke truly of our passage through the Courts to come here; we encountered no trouble. We have encountered no trouble since arriving, either.”

     

                “I fail to see the relevance,” Selena remarked, seeming bored.

     

                “The relevance is that we have encountered much trouble in the past. I bear numerous scars from that trouble.”

     

                “How clumsy of you,” Morgan drawled.

     

                Shooting him a venomous look, her disdain for him stronger than her opinions on the other Councilmembers, Lena paused for a moment, a muscle twitching in her jaw, before continuing. “I was unable to use my powers, you see. There was a- well, I’m unsure how to explain it. It was not a tangible connection for me, the way it seemed so effortless for everyone else. I believe that was linked to my being raised in the human realm, cut off from the forest. Upon my return, I experienced sporadic success with using my powers; however, they were usually in moments of peril or desperation. Emotionally fuelled, if you will. Under the presumption of my wife's demise, that block was undone, and a constant flow of strong emotion poured out of me. Out of me and into the forest. And ever since, I have been able to feel the forest around me. It is very responsive, as some of you have experienced.”

     

                “I still fail to see the relevance,” Selena impatiently huffed, eyelids shuttering as she grimaced.

     

                “Since that day, the forest has been peaceful. Not quiet, but peaceful. I gave so much of myself, so much energy, that I was in a near-permanent state of exhaustion, and might’ve died if I’d been left alone to go so far. In expending so much of my energy, giving so much of myself to the forest, it … soothed the trees. The anger they harbour, the pain from long years of warfare, the ground and roots drinking so much blood, holding the bones of thousands of dead, has been lessened by allowing the forest to thrive. Of course, I am but one woman, and the forest seems endless, but it is ancient, and has memories beyond what any of us can recall. It has been hungry for revenge against us. We have not treated the forest kindly, nor the rivers and lakes. My wife spoke of this last time, told you of the atrocities wrought against nature in the name of blood feuds between Courts. It is time that the energy spent killing each other with the very elements we have been abusing was put to better use. The elements are not ours for the taking, and it has been a gross misuse of the power bestowed upon us that we have seized control and used it to cause harm, when the intention of it was to help, to provide for ourselves and tend the forest. I am not innocent of that either; when my emotions ran high, and I was desperate or frightened, I was able to breach that block and seize control of the earth to help me, against its will, but now … I need only ask, and the earth, the trees, the plants … they willingly help me. We help each other; there is no taking advantage now. That is the true meaning of symbiosis, of living off each other to stay alive. Until we stop this war, until there is true peace, we will not be able to undo the harm done to the Courts.”

     

                “How can we know your theory is correct?” Olivia asked.

     

                Biting back an impatient huff, Lena looked at Kara and then back to Olivia, and then to every Councilmember assembled. Then, she whistled, hoping her assumption that her guardian was lingering within earshot. It wasn’t long before she felt the tremor underfoot, turning to look in the direction of it, waiting calmly for the wolf to appear. At a few panicked shouts, the sound of metal ringing out, and the footsteps of soldiers rushing to answer the cries of alarm, Lena felt her heart lurch in her chest.

     

                “Do not harm him!” she called out, her voice ringing through the trees.

     

                A low growl echoed in response, and she heard the quiet rasp of weapons drawn, turning to find every Councilmember on their feet, most of them holding swords, knives, spears or tridents in hand. One of the Airfolk was quietly stringing their bow, and Lena frowned.

     

                “Sheath your weapons,” she indignantly scolded them all. “Now.”

     

                There was another growl, before she caught a glint of the wolf’s eyes closer to the ground than they should’ve been as it shrank to the ground, warily creeping forward to answer her call. Relief shot through her to see that it was fine, and half a dozen guards materialised between the trunks of the rowan trees, pointing their weapons at the wolf as they gave it a wide berth, looking pale with uncertainty. Holding a hand up to keep them all at bay, Lena walked forward, a faint smile on her lips. She reached out with her other hand and clicked her tongue, coaxing the wolf forward.

     

                “Come. All is well.”

     

                It straightened slightly, the shadowed mass rising into a hulking mass of fur and clumsy feet as it skulked towards her, trusting. Moving through the trees as the Council gathered together behind her, weapons held loosely in hand, Lena slowly approached the wolf and held her hand out, watching it creep closer and lower its head, until its wet snout pressed into her palm.

     

                “There,” Lena murmured, pleased with herself as she rubbed the wolf’s muzzle, grinning. “You’re a friend, you needn’t fear.”

     

                “What is this?” Cat sceptically asked.

     

                “I told you before, she has tamed the wild,” Kara proudly declared. “Perhaps we all might have such success if we follow her lead.”

     

                “He is not tamed,” Lena corrected, “he is still quite wild, but we trust each other. I have cared for him, and he has cared for me.”

     

                “One tame wolf does not make for a successful plan,” Morgan scoffed.

     

                “I am inclined to disagree,” Jul-Us slowly replied, his dark eyes turning to Lena as she glanced back over her shoulder. “When has anyone here managed to befriend a wild creature? Let alone ride one, if Lady Kara is to be believed. I would like to know more.”

     

                Shoulders slumping with relief, Lena let a slow smile spread across her face as she turned back to the wolf, knowing she’d won. It wasn’t an easy win, and by no means was it quick, but the rest of the day was spent talking to the Council, the wolf flopping to the ground at the base of the rowan tree behind Kara’s seat, a quiet but powerful reminder of how Lena had managed to charm the forest and its inhabitants to her side, and Lena talked until her voice was hoarse, trying to explain it all properly. There were parts of it she didn’t know herself, could only surmise through common sense, but she was talking about magic, something that shouldn’t have even been possible, and yet, it was as normal as the air they breathed in the Courts. 

     

                Dusk was settling when the assembled Council finally fell silent. The air was cool and damp, and Lena was desperate to wash the mud off her skin and change into something clean, her once-damp clothes badly chafing as the hours had passed and she’d dried off, and she was hungry, too. But the waiting was worth it, as they all exchanged glances, some reluctantly, and nodded.

     

                “Very well,” Cat sighed with a theatrical eye roll, “we are all in agreement. We shall support this joint Council, so long as it aligns with the interests of the Seelie Court.”

     

                “In the case that it does not, we shall vote again to revert to our independent Council,” Olivia declared with a decisive nod.

     

                “Good,” Lena said, her stomach swooping with elation as she tried not to show how relieved she was. “Then I should return to the Unseelie Court at once; I have a throne to abolish.”

    Chapter 58

                The return trip to the Unseelie Court was slightly quicker, retracing the path they’d taken with plans to meet the Seelie Council at the river once Lena had abolished her throne. She felt conflicted about her decision, hopeful that it was the right one, but a small voice at the back of her mind fretting that it wasn’t, that she would be placing the fate of the Unseelie Court in the hands of others who might find a way to exploit her decision, but she knew in her heart that this was a better way. It was less of a burden for her to shoulder as well, no longer solely up to her to uphold the peace of the Unseelie Court, as it had been when she’d been married off to a stranger with no say in the matter and no knowledge of where, who or what she was. In a sense, it felt like a full circle moment, back to the beginnings of a peace treaty, with a little more experience and understanding under her belt to know what she was doing this time around.

     

                They’d been gone a month before they’d even made the return trip, and autumn was well on its way to winter as they trekked back towards the Unseelie Court, and they had to delay one morning for Midautumn rites. Lena went first, autumn, the season of the Earthfolk, and she was their rightful Queen for a little while longer, and she cut her palm and let her blood splatter onto the fire in a shower of petals before offering up a pear to the flames. It was nothing so grand as the Midwinter celebrations at Krypton, and she’d missed every other solstice since then, but it was reminiscent of that first Midautumn shared with Kara, simple but meaningful.

     

                The fortnight it took for them to return was uneventful otherwise, passing through long miles of towering oaks, pines and leatherleafs, skirting around thickets of vine-woven brush as squirrels, thrushes and finches darted everywhere. Given Lena’s warnings about treating the forest kindly, they were careful now, all of them giving what energy they could to their chosen elements, sating the restless energies until the forest was almost docile. They were rewarded with deer and rabbits; those more adept at hunting caught enough to feed their small host, and tiny streams kept them and their horses watered as they moved through the forest. If the Seelie Councilmembers had been sceptical of her honesty, their peaceful trip to the wide river dividing the Courts was convincing enough to soften their doubts, if not entirely. 

     

                Upon reaching the river, the Seelie Council, sans Kara, remained on their side, while Lena’s party continued onwards across the bridge, the horses trotting along the low, flat stones over churning dark water as they entered back into her realm. She would return within the next day to confirm her success and formalise their new arrangement, but the Seelie rejected her suggestion that they accompany her to the seat of the Unseelie Court and witness it for themselves. Lena had thought they might be interested in seeing the Court of their enemies, but she supposed a tenuous peace, at best, was not convincing enough for them to risk their lives and that of the entire Seelie governing body. Lena could hardly argue against their caution and deigned to prove the sincerity of her intentions, of her goals of peace, by sending a host of Unseelie with whatever finery and supplies that could be arranged quickly to make the Seelie camp more homely while they waited for her to join them and discuss things further.

     

                Still, it was hours of riding, almost half of the day, before the retinue reined their horses in and walked them through the hushed peace of the Unseelie dwelling. The sound of strings and flutes quietly added to the calming ambience of the forest at dusk, the green tint darkening as sunlight failed, and leaves softly drifted down from the high canopy to be crunched under the hooves of their horses as they slowly filed through the mixture of stone and living tree dwellings. Those of her people she passed by gracefully bowed or curtsied, a few refusing to give more than a polite nod of deference, and Lena smiled kindly to them as she acknowledged them all in return, sitting her horse well as she looked every inch the Queen, now as she made her way to the throne to give it all up.

     

                The closer she got to her destination, the better Lena felt about it, the more sure she was in her decision. Instead of doubt, there was just an overwhelming sense of relief. How could she be making the wrong call if the thought of the end in sight made her feel that way? Jack and Hector had ridden at the head of their retinue as an advanced guard, and they reined their horses in at a wide gap in the trees, the air already smelling damp and the sound of lapping water just audible to their sensitive hearing. Reining in her horse, giving its neck a grateful pat, Lena swung down off her horse and let out a forceful breath, her shoulders still holding onto the tension in her body, but the determination to end it filled her. She adjusted the velvet surcoat she was wearing and turned, smiling as her eyes fell on Kara.

     

                “I know your mind is set,” Kara said, blue eyes intense and determined, as set on Lena’s path as her wife was, “but now is your last chance to change it, to stop what you have set in motion.”

     

                With a quiet huff of laughter, Lena reached out and cupped Kara’s chin in her hand, her nose wrinkling as she smiled. “No. I will not disrespect those who have stood with me since I proposed the idea, or go against the Unseelie Council once I have gained their support. It is not for me to undo what good my actions have done.”

     

                Nodding, Kara’s lips curved with a smile. “Good.”

     

                “You do not want me to change my mind?”

     

                “It is not that, although you know I am on your side in this, and most things. I just wished for you to know, without a shadow of a doubt, that you wanted to do this. So that you cannot look back upon this moment with regret and feel you had made your decision in haste.”

     

                “Haste?” Lena snorted, rolling her eyes. “With how long it took the Seelie to get on board with my plan, I’ve had plenty of opportunities to change my mind. It is set.”

     

                “Much like a mountain,” Kara murmured with a teasing glint in her eyes.

     

                The others were all dismounting now, horses whickering and nosing the ground for something to eat as they were left grouped together, and Lena looked around at her chosen Council. The soldiers who’d accompanied them were already reaching for bridles, coaxing horses into motion again with the soft click of their tongues, and Lena smiled as her Councilmembers looked to her.

     

                “I am famished,” Kara groaned, stretching out her muscles. “Shall we dine and bathe?”

     

                Her question was posed to Lena, who turned to look at her and hesitated. She would’ve liked something fresh to eat as well, and imagined the kitchens already in a frenzy to whip up something worthy of a Queen, a lingering sense of panic from Lillian’s days of ruling, and she would’ve killed for a nice hot bath, sure there was dirt in places she hadn’t been able to properly wash in over a month, but she still hesitated. There was a conflicting expression warring on her face, and she let out a small huff, shrugging helplessly as she gave her wife a pained look.

     

                “I wish this to be the last day the Unseelie has a Queen.”

     

                “It is barely dusk,” Andrea reasoned. “We shall have you a mere Lady by midnight, but you should allow me time to make you ready.”

     

                “You’re to be a Councilmember, not my attendant.”

     

                Andrea gave her a haughty look and smiled slightly. “One last time. For old time’s sake, no?”

     

                “You are making a statement,” Kelly agreed. “One should look one's best in such cases. As should the rest of us. What a filthy rabble we make; it is hardly the impression we wish to give the Court. We should look competent at the very least.”

     

                Nodding in agreement, Lena’s mouth thinned. “Alright. I see the wisdom in that. Before midnight, though. It has to happen before then.”

     

                “It will give me time to make the rounds, Your Majesty,” Hector assured her.

     

                “The rounds?”

     

                “I am sure there are many folk here who would like to witness this moment. They may not agree with your intention, but it is history in the making. The like that has not been seen in the Unseelie Court before.”

     

                “Oh. I suppose. You will all join me for dinner, then. After we are more presentable. The first feast of the first Unseelie Council.”

     

                There was a ripple of agreement, and Lena turned, holding her hand out as she started to walk off, her wife falling into step beside her and taking her hand. Raising their entwined fingers, Kara kissed the back of Lena’s hand as she gazed at her. Glancing sideways, Lena smiled faintly and squeezed her hand, the sound of footsteps following after them as she led the way into the underground halls of her home. The thought crossed her mind whether she was still entitled to call it her home, inheriting it as the new Queen, a title she was due to give up in a few hours, and she wondered how many other homes she had scattered throughout the Unseelie Court that she was ignorant of. There were a few, she knew that much; she’d requested that Rhea search them all as part of her hunt for Lex, to no avail. 

     

                Preoccupied, Lena led Kara straight to the pools deeper beneath the ground, into the rockbed beneath the dirt, the humidity and damp stone smell reaching them before they made it into the warren of hallways. Making for what had unequivocally become Lena’s bath, she pushed the doors open and stepped into the room, the air almost tangible against her cheeks as it immediately made her feel clammy all over. It was more of an ordeal this time, removing bulkier pieces of armour, allowing Kara to assist as if she were her squire, before she returned the favour for her wife, leaving two piles of battered steel and then shedding layers of wool, cotton and velvet.

     

                Slipping into the water, Lena softly hissed at the stinging heat, her muscles loosening as the warmth washed over her, and she fully submerged herself for a moment before surfacing in time to watch Kara gracefully dive into the shallow pool without a splash. She was a dark shadow beneath the surface, gliding the length of the pool before she surfaced, hair dulled to brass and plastered to her head as she turned and grinned at Lena, in her element. Expression softening with a smile, Lena leaned back against the edge of the stone pool, legs stretched as far as they could so she could stay submerged up to her neck, letting the warm water soothe her aches and pains. Swimming back over to her, Kara kissed Lena’s shoulder and reached past her, to the washcloth and bar of soap she’d grabbed from a stocked shelf before diving in.            

     

                Remaining where she was, Lena closed her eyes as Kara pressed the washcloth to her cheek, wiping away days of grime, the sweat and dust of their travels caught in her pores and the fine lines of her face. She had to straighten up bit by bit as Kara soaped up the washcloth and scrubbed Lena’s throat, her shoulders and collarbones, washing every bit of Lena with careful consideration and manipulating the water to rinse the suds off as she went. Lastly, she washed Lena’s hair for her, her fingertips pressing into Lena’s scalp as she slowly massaged the soap into her roots. Luxuriating in the sensation, Lena closed her eyes and tried to fight the buoyancy of the water until Kara finished, and she rinsed her hair off. Then, Lena returned the favour, indulging herself in the task as much as it was for Kara’s benefit, enjoying the small kisses she placed on her wife’s throat, her collarbones and sternum, her shoulder blades and hips as she slowly made her way down her body. Kara let out a small huff of laughter as Lena’s mouth wandered before coaxing her back up.

     

                “You will need to wait a little while yet for that if you wish this to be the last day the Unseelie has a Queen. We have been apart for so long, and I have waited longer yet to touch you, and I do not intend to rush after so much waiting.”

     

                With a click of her tongue and feigned exasperation as she rolled her eyes, Lena’s cheek dimpled as she gave her a coy look. “Very well. But you shall need to take me home as soon as our business is done; it is agony not to have you all to myself. I’m selfish, I can’t help myself.”

     

                Chuckling, Kara leaned in and gave her a firm kiss. “If you are selfish, then so am I. If it were up to me, I would damn the whole idea of this Council and lock you inside this room with me for a week, but I fear a week without your guidance would result in another war, and we cannot have that.”

     

                “It would almost be worth it,” Lena wistfully replied, giving her a wry look. “Let me wash your hair, and then we’ll eat.”

     

                Obeying, Kara ducked down in the water and let Lena start massaging soap into her scalp, before rinsing her hair and climbing out. They dressed in their undergarments and donned their cloaks, leaving their armour behind to deal with later, but taking their swords with them, and then padded barefoot back to their quarters. Andrea had been busy while Lena was bathing, a pile of varying fabrics in shades of green and brown piled onto the chaise at the foot of the bed, and she’d only just changed into her clean undergarments when Andrea bustled in, clean and neatly dressed in new clothes.

     

                “You took your time,” Andrea noted, “dinner is ready, by the rush in the hallways. Let me get you dressed.”

     

                Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena allowed Andrea to ferret out the layers for her: soft leggings first and a clean cotton shirt, then a long tunic that fell to her shins. Over that went her old leather surcoat, cleaned and conditioned until the leather was soft, the stitching and embroidery repaired, with her sword belt cinched around her waist. Andrea held up a voluminous velvet robe in a deep shade of emerald, and held her into that as well, the sleeves slashed to the elbows so the heavy fabric fell away from her, more embroidered along the edges of it, before she made Lena sit and started on her hair. Drying it off with her fire, and then braiding and twisting sections with silver and gemstones, Andrea tamed her hair and finished it off with the silver circlet Lena had been wearing of late, trying to look every inch the fae Queen, and slid a few rings onto her fingers for good measure. One of them was the ring Kara had gifted Lena, treasured and never off her finger for long.

     

                Once she was deemed presentable, Lena was ushered out of the room, finding her wife running a whetstone along the edge of her sword as she patiently waited, already resplendent in robes of navy and stone grey. Lena never tired of the way the shades brought out the deep blue of her wife’s eyes, and she felt herself melt a little as Kara’s attention immediately turned to her, a brightening of her eyes as she stood and sheathed her sword at her waist in one smooth motion. Extending a hand, Kara waited for Lena to meet her before lacing their fingers together and leading her to the door. Andrea followed in their wake, and Sam peeled out of the shadows, ditching her leathers for the maroon she wore more often, now that she was no longer a Hunter bound to Lillian. The four of them walked to the dining hall, already half-full of those invited, and Lena took her seat at the head of the table and let Kara pour her some of the mulled cider steaming in a jug.

     

                William and Rama Khan were the last two to arrive, politely nodding to her before taking their seats, and Lena reached for her cup and softly cleared her throat, hesitating slightly as her brow furrowed with deep thought. “I just wanted to thank you all. None of this has been lightly decided, and I know it’s taken much convincing for some of you to accept what I’m offering, but I’m grateful. I hope it will be successful, and I’m happy to have so many friends - and a few strangers - to pave the way forward. Thank you.”

     

                She raised her cup slightly as her eyes ran around the table, a fleeting smile on her lips, and took a sip of her mulled cider. There were raised cups in her direction as well, and she nodded as her eyes nervously darted about, so close to the end of it all and a little worried that someone would back out, that they all secretly thought she was making a foolish mistake, but everyone seemed at ease. Dishes were being passed along, cups refilled, and Lena served herself and Kara some duck and a small serving of greens, her appetite evading her as she picked at her meal. She switched it out for a bowl of stew after a few bites, managing to get down most of the broth, even if she left limp vegetables behind, and didn’t dare drink more than a single cup of mulled cider, even when the blackberry wine came out. Pies and honey cakes were laid out for dessert, and with some coaxing from Kara, she had half a slice of cherry pie with thick cream, and finished it off with a cup of tea, leaning back in her chair as she brooded somewhat and waited for everyone to finish their meal.

     

                It went on for a couple of hours, and Lena indulged them in this reprieve from travel, in good food and drink, somewhere comfortable and warm after weeks of rain and mud. With a few lit braziers around, warming the room and casting a cosy glow, she found herself content to be there as well, no matter what happened next, but she was still set on having it all done and dusted by midnight. When the leftovers had been whisked away and empty plates removed, there was a final round of wine and tea before she climbed to her feet, feeling a flutter in her stomach before she set her shoulders and gripped the pommel of her sword.

     

                “It is time.”

     

                Kara was on her feet in a heartbeat, taking Lena’s other hand and leaning in to give her a chaste kiss. “All will be well.”

     

                Nodding, Lena stepped out from behind the table and made for the door with her wife at her side, hand-in-hand, and they led the procession from the room, making their way down the wide hallway and up through to the surface. Soldiers and servants followed in their wake, until it seemed like the whole place had been emptied of people, and as she walked the familiar path to the lake, with the gigantic tree and its gnarled roots and the throne set into it, it felt as if every Unseelie within a mile of the Queen’s seat had gotten wind of Hector’s summons. Her skin prickled at the feeling of so many eyes on her, and she walked towards the massive tree, smoothly worn bark underfoot as she stepped lightly along a root, until she reached the throne.

     

                Staring at it, Lena was still for a moment. She didn’t even take a seat, no final moment on it as Queen. Briefly, she wondered what to do about it, but she knew what needed to be done and slowly reached out a hand, laying her palm flat against the back of the seat, where the trunk had been shaped into a throne for her forebearers. It was strange to think she didn’t even know who had made it, who had kept the Unseelie Court for themselves after the Seelie Court had united into the Council. How many rulers had sat on that throne? She knew one thing: she would be the last.

     

                With a slow ripple, the wood started to move beneath her palm, and her audience was quiet as she poured as much of her energy as she could into the ancient tree, putting her will into it as it slowly shaped itself to her intentions. It took the old tree a few minutes to move its massive trunk and thick roots, but eventually, the throne was closed over as roots twisted over it and old bark sloughed off to reveal new green wood where the tree filled in where her back would’ve rested. As she watched, moss crept over sections of old bark, and the roots tightened their coils and knots, bedding down into their new position, as if the towering tree had always been that way, as if the throne had never been there.

     

                A ripple of confusion ran through the crowd, and Lena turned, weak fingers of moonlight filtering down through the high canopy as her eyes ran over those present. She swallowed thickly and pulled a small roll of parchment from her belt, unfurling it to stare at the glyphs she’d agonised over with Kara for days. Clearing her throat, she drew in a deep breath, and her eyes snapped to her wife’s face, drawing strength from the sight of her before she started to talk.

     

                “Let all present bear witness to my statement; I, Lena, Queen of the Unseelie, do hereby declare my irrevocable decision to renounce the throne for myself, my kin and for all fae, and my desire that the execution of this abolition of the Unseelie monarchy take place immediately. In renouncing my crown, I take a seat on the new Unseelie Council as a representative of the Earthfolk, and do so swear to solemnly and sincerely affirm that I will be faithful and bear true allegiance to the land, sea and sky, and all its creatures, without any acts of subterfuge or corruption, and that I take this responsibility freely, until such time comes that I resign from my seat, or another is deemed more suitable to take my place.”

     

                Finishing reading off the scroll, a sense of responsibility weighing on her shoulders as she finished speaking the oath she’s modelled after the Seelie Court oath, recounted by Kara, Lena looked up again, glancing at her wife first and then the faces of others. All, save for her Council and friends, looked surprised, silently staring back at her, and Lena slowly took a seat on one of the unremarkable roots of the old tree. It was not a seat, no markings save the knots and whorls in the bark, but it was as fine a seat as any to sit and debate with the newly formed Council, to sit and hear the grievances of their people.

     

                “Sister,” Lena called out to Alex, then, beckoning her forward. “Speak your oath and join me.”

     

                Approaching, Alex took the roll of parchment and read the section with the Councilmember oath, swapping Earthfolk for Firefolk, but otherwise recounting it word-for-word. Afterwards, she handed Lena back the scroll and took a seat to her right as a flurry of whispers swept through the crowd. Lena repeated this with each Councilmember called forward, and there was a sense of unease as she called Kelly next, but then silence as her chosen Unseelie started to get called. Perhaps it was the respect for the likes of their General, or maybe even the selection of ordinary folk like Jack and Jess, but the sense of unease dissipated as twelve Councilmembers took their oaths and perched along a forking root of the wide tree, taking their seat as the new Unseelie Council came into being.

     

                Kara approached them, slowly and with a small smile playing on her lips, and she looked to each Councilmember as they sat arrayed in a half-moon on the tree roots, before she gripped the pommel of her sword and politely inclined her head.

     

                “I come as a representative of the Seelie Council to extend friendship towards the Unseelie Council.”

     

                “Then let us be friends,” Lena coyly replied, her eyes bright with amusement. “We shall meet with your Council and see how best we can serve the forest in this new era of peace.”

     

                “We look forward to it.”

     

                With another polite nod to them all, Kara backed away, and then Lena climbed to her feet, walking towards her before her wife could back up more than a few steps. Pausing, Kara raised an eyebrow as she smiled slightly and then reached for her wife. Lena stepped into Kara’s fierce embrace and pressed her face into her shoulder, smiling as her eyes creased at the corners. “It is done.”

     

                “Come with me,” Kara whispered, drawing back and clasping Lena’s hands in her own, backing away as she towed her wife with her.

     

                Smiling, Lena let herself be led away from the tree, from the Council and through the audience, who parted to let them by. There were those deferential nods again, but Lena barely acknowledged them with her eyes glued to Kara’s face. It was almost midnight, and she walked away from the old site of the throne without a title and without the sole responsibility of the Unseelie Court resting on her shoulders.

     

     

                As exhausted as they all were, they were up before the dawn, the forest foggy and frigid, and Lena gripped her reins in cold hands as she stifled a yawn. The Council rode in single file through an overgrown stretch of the forest, brambles hemming them in on either side as low-hanging branches of conifers brushed their cheeks, the smell of pine heady in the damp morning.

     

                It was becoming a familiar ride to Lena, certain landmarks identifiable after so many passes through that stretch of the Court. She knew that over the next few months, they’d be making the journey more frequently while liaising with both Councils, trying to establish new trade routes and free travel across the river. They’d need to rebuild bridges and tend to the forest, get things on the right path, but she was hoping to have some time with Kara at Argo before. A little reprieve from their responsibilities before they had to deal with the bureaucracy of being Councilmembers.

     

                It was past lunchtime when they reached the bridge again, the sight of canopies and tents pitched on the opposite bank as their horses lightly stepped around the trees on their side. Swinging down from her saddle, Lena followed on Kara’s heels as her wife strode along the low bridge with a bright smile on her face, as she hailed the rest of her Councilmembers.

     

                Cat reached them first, the others flanking her, and she arched an eyebrow. “Well?”

     

                Spreading her hands, Lena’s mouth hitched into a crooked smile. “I am merely Lady Lena now. As promised.”

     

                “An Unseelie who keeps their word,” Selena hummed, giving Lena a once-over. “How novel.”

     

                With a quiet huff and a roll of her eyes, Lena just smiled tightly in response. Kara’s glance at the woman was a little sterner, and she clasped her hands behind her back, lingering almost at the end of the bridge as she raised her eyebrows suggestively.

     

                “So, shall we all meet to discuss this new development further?” she suggested.

     

                “If your lot doesn’t need time to recover from your journey,” Morgan snidely replied.

     

                “Their constitution is no different to ours, Morgan,” Kara sighed. “If we could please set aside all bad blood, I believe it would be a more effective discussion.”

     

                He gave Kara a sneer but otherwise remained silent. The rest of the Council waited patiently for a few moments as no one spoke or moved until Cat cleared her throat. “Well?”

     

                In short order, they were all on the Seelie side of the river, separated into the two Councils, with Lena and Kara the mediators. Of course, the new Unseelie Council had a large Seelie presence in it, which afforded them some trust, but it was still rough going as they all bickered over what the next steps would be. They didn’t break until dusk, the few attendants who’d accompanied Lena setting up tents and canopies on the Unseelie side during that time, and they retreated back to their camp to discuss matters over food as the night wore on.

     

                They remained there for three days, regularly conferring with the Seelie Council and then retreating back to their side to stand in a circle and debate the conversation further. It seemed endless, figuring out who was responsible for what, what their focus should be, and how to establish trust. By the end of the third day, the most productive decision made had been Lena delegating residences to her Council members. Rama Khan already had his own as an Unseelie General, and Lena gifted Rhea’s old home to Hector, given his grave injury from her, and deliberated over others circled on maps, weighing the locations and the Councilmembers left. Alex already had her own halls in the Seelie Court, so she gifted a joint home to her and Kelly for their time spent in the Unseelie Court. For herself, she would keep the hall at the centre of the Unseelie Court, close enough to the river to make frequent trips back and forth Argo, and with enough room for everyone else to stay when they attended Council meetings.

     

                “We have exhausted all topics of conversation for now,” Kara exasperatedly said as both Councils stood in two distinct crescents, a gap between them to ensure there was no mistaking them being unified. “We should break now, and see to the tasks we have deemed of importance.”

     

                “And when should we reconvene?” Jack asked. “I have an interest in spending some time at home; I have been away for some months now.”

     

                “I am interested in the same,” Cat agreed. “We have our tasks, and your Council is new, so we should afford you some time to get your affairs in order before we consider it worthwhile for us to assist with more important matters. I would like to enjoy my time until my assistance is required.”

     

                “Midwinter, then,” Rama Khan suggested, stoic as he stood with his hands clasped behind his back.

     

                Lena still wasn’t sure what to make of him, a General through and through, and one of the oldest fae on both Councils. He seemed duty-bound, though, and she felt a strong sense of determination in him, the same kind within her, and wondered if it was the stubborn streak of Earthfolk. He seemed reasonable, though, and Lena leapt in to try and earn some goodwill with him.

     

                “A good idea,” she readily agreed. “It will give us some time, as you said, Cat, and will allow us all some time to enjoy the new peace. Perhaps reflect on the future and think of new things to implement or fix in the Courts.”

     

                Olivia nodded, glancing around at her fellow Councilmembers. “Are we in agreement?”

     

                Nine of them raised their hands - Morgan, Maxwell and Selena opposing - which gave them the majority. Lena glanced around the Unseelie Councilmembers. “And are we?”

     

                All twelve raised their hands on her side, and she hid a smile as she nodded. “It is settled then. We shall meet back here at Midwinter.”

     

                The three opposers turned and immediately stalked away, and Kara rolled her eyes when Lena met her eyes. Turning to her Council, Lena smiled slightly. “Thank you. We shall meet before Midwinter, at my hall if that suits.”

     

                “When?” Alex asked.

     

                “I’m not sure. I intend to take a break first. Whoever has something important to discuss first can send word to us all. We should all take a few weeks, though, to rest and enjoy the peace.”

     

                “We will be at Argo,” Kara murmured, pressing a hand against Lena’s back as she looked at her, “if anyone needs us before then.”

     

                “I will return to my home for a while,” Alex replied. “Kelly and I will travel with you awhile.”

     

                “We shall check on my wife’s affairs there, and then return to the Unseelie Court to see our new home,” Kelly said with a quick grin at Lena. “We should be somewhat familiar with the Court if we're to sit on the Council.”

     

                “A good idea,” Kara agreed. “We shall travel back with you on your way back, if you stop to fetch us.”

     

                Alex nodded and clapped her sister on the shoulder before crossing back over the bridge and making for their camp. She started to gather up her belongings, readying to leave immediately, and Lena followed suit at a slower pace, chatting with a few of the Councilmembers as they slowly walked back to their side of the river, while Kara remained behind a moment longer to say her goodbyes to the Unseelie Councilmembers. Lena was saddling her horse when Kara joined her, hands on her wife’s waist and a gentle kiss to the side of her neck announcing her presence as Lena smiled, tightening a buckle.

     

                “You’re in high spirits.”

     

                “I am,” Kara agreed. “This is the most hope I have felt in a long time. I believe we are on the right path now, thanks to you. It is a future many of us have hoped for, many of us have tried to obtain, but now, with the abolishment of the monarchy, with the creation of the Council, it seems more possible than ever.”

     

                “I think so, too. At least we’ll be able to say we tried our hardest this time, no matter what.”

     

                “Ah, you must have more hope than that,” Kara murmured as Lena turned, smiling crookedly. “It will work this time.”

     

                “If you believe so, then I believe it, too,” Lena whispered, reaching up to gently brush the back of her fingers over Kara’s cheek, giving her an adoring look. “I believe in you.”

     

                “And I you. And now, I believe I promised to take you home.”

     

                “Then you should saddle your horse immediately so we don’t waste a second more than necessary.”

     

                “Wise words from my wise wife,” Kara chuckled, leaning in to kiss Lena before stepping back, as if resisting the temptation to linger.

     

                Her blue eyes were bright with amusement, and there was a sense of relief about her as well, a lightness that made Lena’s heart soar, reassured that things were all working out for the better. The pall of war, of risking their lives on a daily basis, whether it was due to battle, subterfuge or the forest itself, had weighed heavily on them all, but that weight had been lifted upon their reunion and subsequent attempts to undo a lot of harm.
