Lena had only been in the forest for a touch longer than a year, and not even a full one at that, with the way time had messed with her return, a season gone in the blink of an eye, but even she knew that this was a first in the Courts in millennia at least. There had been peace before, and now there would be peace again.

     

                Everyone parted ways then, some travelling in pairs, a few departing alone, and Eliza accompanied her daughters and their wives as they headed back into the Seelie Court. Before they made it very far, there was a panicked shout and a few splashes, before Lena caught sight of the wolf slipping into the Seelie Court behind her, shaking water from his pelt and slinking into the shadows of the trees to the north of the path she was taking. She smiled slightly, turning her attention back ahead, and her horse plodded along behind Kara’s as they continued onwards, reassured by the knowledge that the wolf was safe and still lurking nearby. Lena wouldn’t treat him as a pet, wouldn’t try to domesticate the wolf, but it was good to know that it trusted her, and would most likely stay in the vicinity and could be called if she ever needed a little protection.

     

                It was a few hours on horseback, making good time with the forest on their side, instead of trying to inhibit them, before they parted ways with the rest of Kara’s family. Just the two of them now, it was another hour before they reached the edge of the lake. The trees started to thin as they neared the edge, and they dismounted, removing saddles and bags from the horses and turning them loose into the forest, before carrying their belongings to the lakeshore. Standing on the muddy bank, they stared out at the expanse of blue sky overhead, the sun drenching everything in the warmth of its rays after days of dismal grey, and the surface of the lake stretched for miles in every direction, winking like a mirror as it reflected the sun. Turning her face towards the sunlight, Lena closed her eyes for a moment, humming with contentment as she listened to the wind sigh through the trees and breathed in the damp smell of water mingling with the forest. It was like the perfect balance between herself and Kara, and she didn’t feel frightened, standing on the shore of so much water.

     

                Opening her eyes again, she looked at the tower rising from the surface of the lake, pale and almost seeming to glow in the light of the sun, and then she turned to look at Kara, who was gazing at her home with a wistful fondness in her expression. Reaching out, Lena took her hand and gently squeezed it. “Welcome home.”

     

                Staring at her for a moment, Kara’s face split with a wide smile as she beamed at her wife. She led the way, stepping onto the first submerged stone and then pausing, glancing back at Lena with a faint furrowing of her handsome features, holding all of her supplies but deliberating over whether to dump it all on the shore and carry her wife all the way upstairs, or telling Lena she’d come back for her in a moment. With a small laugh, Lena stepped into the cold water of the lake, letting the shallows lap over her bare feet as she stepped onto slick stone. 

     

                “It doesn’t frighten me to drown anymore,” Lena admitted. “Not that I’m any fonder of water, though.”

     

                Kara laughed and hefted her bags into a more comfortable position before she took Lena’s hand. “My brave wife.”

     

                With a quiet scoff, Lena rolled her eyes. “I’m not sure about that. Everyone’s afraid of something.”

     

                “Oh? And what do you fear now?”

     

                She let Kara lead her across the wide stepping stones, one by one, as they walked further into the lake, towards the tower. Hesitating a moment, Lena wrinkled her nose and let out a sheepish laugh. “It’s obvious, isn’t it? I’m afraid of losing you.”

     

                “Ah,” Kara hummed, “of course. I should have expected that. How could I have expected anything else when your heart mirrors my own completely?”

     

                “Is that what you fear?”

     

                “Of course. Although we have both survived the impossible, so I would hope we have no need of such fears anymore. It is still hard to let go of it, when I have clung to that fear since we met.”

     

                “That long?”

     

                “At first, it was out of obligation, to protect the woman I’d been wed to. Now, I would give anything to keep you alive. Even my own life in your defence. In fact, when I believed myself to be dying, I was not thinking much of my life ending, but of how relieved I was that it was not you, how sorry I was for leaving you, and how fortunate I was to have lived a sliver of my life at the same time as you. I felt very lucky to have been wed to you for as short a time as we were. Now, I am even luckier to know that it was not the end.”

     

                “We have all the time in the world,” Lena murmured, gazing at her.

     

                Kara grinned, tugging her onwards a little faster. “We shall make good use of it, I think.”

     

                They were almost to the base of the tower now, the water deeper, up to their shins as they lightly leapt from stone to stone, until Kara paused. Lena gave her a questioning look and took in the tilted angle of Kara’s head, the furrow of confusion, and looked to see what had caught her attention. Blinking, Lena realised she’d forgotten about the tree, her grief forcing its pale branches to bloom after centuries of being bare.

     

                “Oh. Right. That was my doing,” she said with an apprehensive laugh.

     

                Kara looked at her, “you did it?”

     

                Drinking her wife in, her ocean-dark eyes, the uneven tilt of her lips as she smiled, impressed and surprised, Lena nodded. “Losing you … unlocked something inside of me. My emotions were so heightened, constantly, that everything just kept … blooming. Everywhere I went, things grew or bloomed, and I guess the tree was never really dead, so … well, when I came back here, it was because I wanted to feel close to you … at my end, um … but it didn’t really work well, and the tree just … bloomed instead.”

     

                “It’s beautiful,” Kara said with wonder, continuing the last few steps onto the submerged ground floor of the tower.

     

                Setting the saddle and her bags on the lower steps of the spiral staircase, Kara quickly crossed over to the tree and placed her palms flat against the trunk, smoothing them over the polished bark. She let out a bewildered laugh as she looked up at the flowering branches and glanced over her shoulder to smile brightly at Lena.

     

                “A marvel. You never cease to surprise me.”

     

                “Hopefully not for some time yet,” Lena drawled, giving her wife a wry smile.

     

                She waded over to the stairs and stepped over Kara’s bags, not scared of the water anymore but eager to get out of it, and started to pad upstairs, wet footprints in her wake as she carried her bags up to her room. When they’d lived there together before, they hadn’t shared a bed yet, and she had spent as much of her time as possible on her floor, sulking and keeping her wife at arm’s length. Now, she couldn’t imagine being more than a dozen feet away from Kara at any given point, and had every intention of making this her home, as much as it was Kara’s.

     

                Placing her belongings at the foot of the bed, Lena started to shed her armour, an empty stand in the corner waiting to hold it all for her. Shedding everything piece by piece, she dressed the stand and pulled her sword from its sheath, following a trail of sunshine to one of the open arches ringing the room. Standing in its warmth, she read the words that Kara had gotten engraved in the steel, and was brooding over it when Kara appeared, soaking wet as water ran off her in rivulets, a puddle starting to form at her feet when she came to a stop near Lena. She scattered kisses across the shoulders of Lena’s shirt, basking in the sun, smelling of her idp in the lake, and was quiet for a moment, before intruding on Lena’s thoughts.

     

                “What is it?”

     

                “My sword. It says Princess. That’s not true anymore.”

     

                “I shall have that rectified for you, Lady Lena.”

     

                Humming, Lena turned and gave her a shrewd look. “Hopefully, things will stop changing so much. I’d like a bit of peace and quiet for a change.”

     

                Kara grinned and reached out to take the sword from her grasp, taking a step to lean it against one of the pillars of the arches, and then took Lena’s face in her hands and kissed her firmly. Lena grabbed fistfuls of her wet shirt and pressed back against her, a thrill shooting through her at the knowledge that they were finally alone, in their own home, and she smiled into the kiss, feeling the scrape of Kara’s teeth on her lips, the pang of her hunger, a match for Lena’s. Hands smoothing over Kara’s waist and up her back, Lena tangled her hands in her wife’s hair and propelled her away from the arches. She wouldn’t truly be able to relax with the long drop down to the lake, and she had every intention of enjoying the moment for as long as possible.

     

                Pressing Lena down onto the bed, Kara kissed her softly as she braced herself above her, her mouth trailing to her jaw, her neck, kissing her pulse and feeling Lena’s quick heartbeat in the hollow of her throat. Lena felt Kara’s smile against her throat as she started to pull her wet clothes off her, sitting up to let Lena drag her shirt over her head, before she kissed her again. Burying her face in Kara’s hair as her wife kissed her neck, Lena breathed in the smell of rain as she wrapped her arms tightly around her. Attempting to even the odds, Kara pulled Lena’s shirt free from her leggings, and Lena let out a huff of breathless laughter as Kara rucked the shirt up and kissed her way across her ribs and down her stomach, before she unlaced her leggings and peeled them off. Basking in the feeling of Kara’s mouth all over her, Lena closed her eyes and smiled faintly, her fingers in her hair and her heart hammering in her chest as she was struck by the thought that everything in that moment was utterly perfect.

    Chapter 59

                They had weeks to themselves at Argo, and Lena fell in love with her wife all over again. It was all so different now, no need to repress her emotions, no need to close herself off from people, and they both knew what it meant to be honest too late, to waste time, so they didn’t waste any. The weather cooled off considerably as they dwelled there, but Lena was otherwise too preoccupied to care all that much that she woke on bitter mornings with cold extremities. It gave her more reason to linger in bed with Kara, pressing her cold nose and hands against her wife’s unfailingly warm skin, burrowing in closer as Kara grumbled at the iciness of her wife’s fingers, and then helped warm her up a bit beneath the blankets.

     

                It was like they were learning how to be married all over again, having done everything in the wrong order before, and Lena basked in the delight of finding what her wife liked and disliked, how Kara lived in her own home, how she often quietly sang to herself while repairing fishing nets or maintaining her little boats and canoes. There was an unhurried sense of peace about her wife that Lena hadn’t seen before, too preoccupied with war for Kara to let her guard down on Lena’s safety, but that stress and sense of duty and responsibility had lessened, and with it came a woman who laughed more, who was so warm and affectionate, so uninhibited in her love for her wife and her joy at not being saddled with the doomed prophecy that it was as if Lena was watching Kara truly become herself. She loved to see it, and she felt the same, no longer worried about revealing too much of her feelings, no longer feeling inadequate in her abilities or out of place amongst the forest. It was a part of Lena now, as much as she was a part of it, and she knew it had its claws in her so deep that she would not leave again, not even for a brief trip to the human realm.

     

                Instead, Lena found ways to fill her days without the looming threat of being attacked or killed. It entailed days spent reading and embroidering, playing stones with Kara beside a brazier, helping her wife cook their meals, and taking long baths until the hot water grew cool. Nearly every day, she hopped across the stepping stones to practice her archery against a marked tree, or convinced her wife to come with her and spar a while, which usually led to a scuffle in the dirt and clothes shed. She went foraging for herbs and wrote long-winded letters to her Councilmembers, and occasionally saw Alex and Kelly, making short trips with Kara on a few instances to meet them halfway and spend some time in the saddle, drinking wine and cider around campfires as they dwelled in ruins and reminisced on things of the past. It felt nice, nostalgic for things that had happened not yet a year past, and Lena enjoyed those nights in the forest, the smell of earth and trees soothing.

     

                A more surprising pastime came several weeks into their stay, after a lot of thought, when one night over dinner Lena asked Kara, in a rather serious manner, if she’d teach her how to swim. She wasn’t sure if she was more surprised to want to learn or whether Kara was about her asking, but of course, her wife was thrilled at the opportunity to spend time in the water with her wife. It was a bad time of year for it, but Lena didn’t want to wait for the spring, knowing how many times she’d found herself thrown into water, even if it wasn’t always very deep, and how lucky she was to have survived it, wading and splashing and somehow managing to keep her head above water. That wouldn’t do; she wanted to know how to stop herself from drowning. Perhaps she should’ve ensured she could swim as a child, after losing her mom, because then she might not have grown up to be so afraid, but it was that very fear that had always stopped her. Now, she was determined to overcome it in full, to be able to rely on herself in case she ever needed to.

     

                It wasn’t easy, especially not when the lake was so cold, but the very next morning, after asking Kara, Lena found herself naked with her arms wrapped around herself, shin-deep on the bottom floor of the tower, as Kara tried to coax her into the lake, already treading water a few feet away from her. It took no small amount of courage for Lena to grit her teeth and jump in, knowing that if she inched in bit by bit, it would be worse, and she was very fond of getting things over and done with quickly. She jumped in and surfaced with a wild-eyed look of panic, settled by her wife’s strong hands gripping her arms, gently coaching her through deep breaths and getting her to grip the edge of the tower floor underwater and learn how to kick her feet properly before proceeding any further. Lena hated it, shivering as her teeth chattered, feeling like she was going to sink at any moment, slick stone under her fingertips, and then no stone when she was coaxed away from it, taught how to tread water as she floundered and bobbed in the waves she made with her frantic splashing to stay afloat, but she did manage it.

     

                She’d had several lessons with Kara by now, no longer as scared, although she wouldn’t classify herself as able to swim, but able to keep herself afloat at the very least. They’d woken with the late sunrise and eaten their breakfast, warmed through with some tea and porridge, before Kara had dragged her down to the lake again, clothes shed, and the icy plunge into the lake more familiar than Lena would’ve liked now. Still, she had improved; it was undeniable. It was laughable as well, watching her clumsily swim, but Kara was encouraging and very vocal in her praise, even if she did find it amusing as well. Lena couldn’t fault her; she knew she looked ridiculous, paddling through the lake like a drowned rat as her muscles ached and her body grew numb from the cold, but she was nothing if not stubborn, so she listened to her wife’s encouragement and kept swimming.

     

                “Just a little further!” Kara called, moving further away, always moving the finish line, as if to show Lena just how capable she was.

     

                “You keep moving!”

     

                “You do not look close to giving up yet, so I shall not give up either.”

     

                Lena groaned and rolled her eyes at her response, and Kara let out a bark of laughter as she watched Lena, her hair plastered to her head as she kept herself afloat, treading water as she slowly paddled towards her, splashing as she practically clawed at the water, her legs furiously kicking far below the surface. Lena didn’t cover much distance, but her head did stay above the still surface of the lake, even if she did make such a fuss that she kept splashing water into her face and mouth, making her squint and splutter.

     

                “You remind me of my father’s hounds,” Kara teased her, “they similarly paddled through the lake when hunting fowl.”

     

                “Even a doggy paddle … is an achievement … for me,” Lena breathlessly defended herself. “If I … fall off a cliff again … at least I’ll be able to swim this time.”

     

                Cutting through the water in a few quick strokes, with all the speed and form of an Olympic swimmer, Kara was in front of Lena, reaching out to cup her face in her hands and give her a gentle kiss. Lena pushed back against her lips, frantically trying to tread water as she dipped a little lower in the water, up to her chin now, as her legs continued to kick against the water, and Kara smiled as she pulled away slightly, just far enough to put a couple of inches between them.

     

                Lena let out a yelp of panic, her eyes cutting to Kara with alarm, but she didn’t sink any lower in the water, and Kara’s hands were hovering around her, the water pressure below making it so that she wouldn’t be able to sink any deeper than she already was. Kara would never let anything bad happen to Lena in the water again.

     

                “You can do it,” Kara encouraged her, giving her a serious nod.

     

                “It’s … freezing,” Lena spat between clenched teeth as a tremor ran through her.

     

                Paddling away, putting more distance between them, Kara laughed. “You will be dry and before a fire in no time. Swim another fifty feet, and I will warm you up myself.”

     

                Lena rolled her eyes and was wracked by a violent shiver as she watched Kara back up a little more, never further than two strokes away from her wife, just in case. Her fingers were pruned and felt stiff in the frigid water of the lake, the end of autumn bleeding into winter, and her foolish insistence that she learn to swim was the cause of her inability to feel much of her toes right then, but Kara had been eager to teach her, and Lena was always eager to impress her wife. This wasn’t their first swimming lesson, but it was the first time Lena would consider herself able to swim without needing to be supported. At least she knew how to keep herself afloat on her back in dire circumstances and could manage a rather poor doggy paddle on her own, which was more than she’d been able to manage before, relying on being able to touch the bottom of whatever river or pool of water she’d been in to ensure she didn’t drown. 

     

                The confidence of being able to keep herself alive in the event of deep water had taken the edge off her fear of drowning as well, and while Lena didn’t believe she’d ever be considered a strong swimmer, she was sure that, with regular lessons with Kara and her watchful supervision, she’d at least become good at it. Hopefully, she’d manage a stroke less embarrassing than doggy paddle soon; Lena didn’t think her pride could handle the teasing from Alex or Andrea if they caught her doing it. Not being able to swim at all would be preferable to their amusement at the situation. Kara insisted that she didn’t look ridiculous, and that she was learning quickly, which Lena knew were lies, even if her wife had managed to talk enough around it to make her statements true, but she loved her for believing in her, and she managed to paddle halfway towards her, drawing in painful breaths as the ice of the water stole the air from her lungs, without struggling to keep her head above the surface of the water.

     

                Once she’d crossed the fifty feet Kara had set her, Lena was coaxed back the other way with a groan, a hundred feet back to the tower awaiting her. She supposed that had been Kara’s intention, trying to build her stamina and help develop the muscles and form to make her a strong swimmer, and a few kisses along the way worked to sweeten her annoyance and encourage her to keep going. When her fingertips finally grazed the pale stone of the submerged lower level of the tower, Lena hauled herself fully onto it, feeling algae slick beneath her hands and knees, and climbed to her feet as frigid water streamed off her skin. 

     

                Kara had brought towels for her, leaving them on the steps, above the water level of the lake, and she drew as much water from Lena’s hair and skin as she could and then wrapped her in two towels, kissing her tenderly as her wife shivered. Kissing her brow as well, Kara pulled back and smiled, her pruned, pallid palm pressing against Lena’s cheek as she beamed at her with pride, blue eyes bright with delight.

     

                “You did well.”

     

                “Well, I couldn’t get any worse, could I?” Lena grumbled through trembling lips, giving Kara a droll look.

     

                With a soft chuckle, Kara lifted her off her feet and carried her over to the steps, safely depositing Lena down above the water level and propelling her upstairs. “You seem to think it an embarrassment to be bad at something, when it is only natural. Your impatience has not improved much since your arrival here, I think. You must consider where your skill with archery, swordsmanship, or even horseriding was upon your arrival, and how much you have achieved. Even your reading and writing, your fluency in Fae - these are all things you have worked hard at for months, almost a year. Think of where your swimming will be with the same amount of time and dedication.”

     

                “I think I’d rather dedicate my time to the things I’ve already gotten semi-decent at,” Lena groused as she was steered into their room.

     

                “Come now, you are simply too proud to be bad at anything. You and I both know you will not suffer anything less than being a good swimmer. I admit to being surprised you were interested in it, given your past, and I understand your intention-”

     

                “To save your life, in case you’re riddled with arrows again in the middle of a river,” Lena interrupted, turning to poke Kara in the chest and stomach, arching an eyebrow pointedly.

     

                “Yes, in case such circumstances arise again,” Kara easily agreed, “but I am confident you will excel at it, as you have everything else.”

     

                Scoffing, Lena shed her towels as she reached her trunk, rummaging through her piles of clothes as she pulled out warm wool leggings and thick shirts, with brocaded jackets and velvet robes, sifting through it all as she found appropriate garments to fend off the chill. It was almost cold enough for them to pack up for the winter and head back to the Unseelie Court; a pigeon had arrived with a letter from Alex only that morning as they were eating breakfast, stating her intention to depart from her home a few days hence. Lena had to confess she’d miss their time there at Argo, the peace and solitude that had been afforded them, the likes of which they hadn’t had since she’d first arrived there. Things had been different this time around - she was married to a woman she loved, and she wasn’t afraid of living in a tower surrounded by the sprawling lake and the tonnes of water it contained. Lena was free to come and go into the forest without fear now and could feel the earth, instead of feeling so isolated from land. 

     

                Still, she was looking forward to returning to the Unseelie Court, being within the forest and getting back to business. Their little holiday, of a sort, had been nice, but they’d had matters to attend to, with long letters sent back and forth with her Councilmembers and the Seelie Court, mostly by way of Kara, and they’d achieved what they’d been able to on their own. Trade routes had already been opened up, and Lena and Rama Khan had arranged for Unseelie Earthfolk to help construct new bridges across the river where the water ran too deep and the banks were too far apart to easily cross. There had been a few spats along the border, but nothing that hadn’t been resolved without dissolving into open warfare again.

     

                Dressing, Lena wrapped her arms tightly around herself as she rubbed some warmth back into herself, watching as Kara dressed at a more leisurely pace, still somewhat damp, and seemingly unbothered by the cold or wet. “I’ll swim again tomorrow,” Lena conceded, her voice softening as she gazed at her wife. “We should make the most of the lake while we can. Even if it feels like needles in my skin to get into it. I don’t know how you were swimming in the sea last winter; it makes me shiver just thinking about it.”

     

                She did shiver then, both of them quietly laughing. Kara donned her shirt and grinned at Lena, raking a hand through her damp hair as she padded over to her wife and took her hand in hers. It was surprisingly cool - not freezing, which should’ve been expected, but not as warm as she usually was, either - and she ducked her head to kiss Lena’s knuckles. “Fret not, you will be spared that act. I am not cruel enough to subject you to the wintry sea, although I disagree with the sentiment of you, my family and our friends on it being an unpleasant experience. I find it … invigorating. You would most likely find it unpleasant, though.”

     

                Lena laughed, “that’s putting it kindly, I think.”

     

                “You are always most kind,” Kara murmured, leaning in to kiss her. “Now, I will show you some kindness and bring you some tea while you warm beside the brazier.”

     

                Letting go of Lena’s hand and turning away from her, Kara crossed over to the unlit brazier set near an armchair. It was where Lena spent most of her time these days, as the weather turned further, curled up with tea and a blanket over her lap as she read books, scrolls or letters and jotted down ideas and plans as she stayed warm and dry. Kara was usually off fishing or swimming, occasionally riding to one of the nearby dwellings or checking on tributaries leading off from the lake, ensuring that water levels were maintained, that the fragile ecosystems that were fed by her great lake were not interrupted. Sometimes Lena accompanied her, but more often than not, she stayed by the fire, or was left to her own wanderings through the forest, foraging for herbs to replenish the medicinal supplies in their home, or tithing her remaining power to the forest to help sustain life through the colder months. A few times, she saw the wolf cub, although it only approached her on one occasion, letting her pat its muzzle for a moment before it nudged her shoulder and then trotted off again to hunt some prey to fatten up for the coming season. She wondered what would happen to him when they went back to the Unseelie Court, whether he’d follow as usual, or find some den for the winter. She hoped he’d survive, find enough prey to sustain him, although she wondered how so big a creature, still growing, could stay full on the offerings of the forest. 

     

                Arranging driftwood in the brazier, Kara struggled with the flint for a few moments, until the kindling caught and a small finger of flame grew as she blew on it. Fanning it bigger, she glanced over at her wife and smiled fondly, blue eyes tender as they lingered on Lena, who settled into the armchair and pulled the blanket draped over the back onto her lap, huddling for warmth. Feeding the fire until she was satisfied with it, Kara dropped a kiss onto Lena’s brow, cupping the back of her head as her fingertips gently dug in for a second, as if trying to hold her as closely as she could with the act.

     

                “I shall bring you some tea,” Kara murmured.

     

                “Thank you,” Lena whispered, gazing up at her with a mix of adoration and gratitude.

     

                The warmth of the fire started to wash over her as her wife left to fetch the tea, and Lena held her cold hands out towards the brazier, feeling the sting of the heat. She felt content as she sat there, enjoying the peace of the morning as she listened to the sound of the wind through the trees, the cry and splash of water birds on the lake or in the reeds bordering it, the snap of the fire as the driftwood caught and charred. It was such a peaceful life that Lena felt as if she didn’t have a single care in the world to contend with, although she had several Council matters to deal with, and the upcoming reunion with them, but it all felt so easy now. She’d achieved what she’d set out to do, and things had been smooth sailing since then. It felt wrong for it all to be so easy after so much difficulty to get to that point, but it only made her more appreciative of the peace that held now.

     

                Rereading a letter that she’d half-drafted, Lena slowly warmed up beside the brazier, and not long after, Kara returned with a laden tray. She had a mass of water coalesce into one of her humanoid figures to move a low table to Lena’s side and set the tray down for her, sinking to her knees to pour a cup for Lena and stir in some honey, before she poured a cup for herself and sat at her wife’s feet, cradling it in cool palms while she laid her head in Lena’s lap for a while. She’d brought some barley cake and dried fruit and nuts as well, and Lena reached for the tray to serve them both a slice of the cake, picking at it in between mouthfuls of tea as she thought deeply about how to finish off her letter. It was one of a personal matter, one for J’onn, who was still up north, managing Kara’s lands along the coastline. 

     

                She’d been thinking about it for over a week now, unsure whether what she was asking was possible, but once she set her mind to something, Lena was determined to get her way. Perhaps in that sense, she was always destined to be a Queen, or in some sort of position of power, but she was used to fighting for things, and didn’t mind the obstacles that came along with it, even if it wasn’t quite so easy as it had been when she’d worn the crown and been able to snap her fingers and have people do her bidding - even if they did so reluctantly. She drained her tea and reached to set the empty cup down on the tray, delaying refilling it for a moment as she got lost in her ruminating, and Kara lifted her head off her knee to start eating her own cake, swallowing a bite and glancing up at Lena, sensing her preoccupation.

     

                “What are you thinking about so carefully?”

     

                “Just … mulling over an idea,” Lena off-handedly replied, giving her wife a flash of a smile.

     

                “Oh? And what idea is that?”

     

                Reluctant to tell her for a moment, Lena opened and closed her mouth and then let out a small exhale, smiling ruefully. “I think I will miss it here dearly when we depart.”

     

                “It shan’t be for long,” Kara reassured her. “Just for the winter, and then we shall return in the spring, to warmer weather more suited for a tower with no walls.”

     

                “I know,” Lena murmured, reaching out to rake her hands through Kara’s silken hair. “It’s only, I was thinking about last winter. At Krypton.”

     

                Smiling unevenly, Kara let out a huff of laughter. “You were miserable.”

     

                “For reasons I couldn’t explain at the time. I was not fond of the sea, of course, but it wasn’t the sole reason for my misery. I happen to have a lot of fond memories of Krypton, in hindsight. And I’ve been thinking … well, I’m sorry for what I did to your home.”

     

                “You are sorry for sacrificing stone in exchange for my life?” Kara queried, arching an eyebrow.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena clicked her tongue. “Don’t downplay it; it was your family’s ancestral home.”

     

                “One of them. I’m quite content with my tower and my lake. Even more so because it is surrounded by forest, and thus, you are content here.”

     

                “Yes, well, I had the thought that Krypton should be rebuilt,” Lena quickly replied, getting the words out in one breath as she watched surprise flash across her wife’s face. “So we can visit again, so you can go back home from time to time. I know we’ll spend most of our time here, so we can travel to the Unseelie Court for my Council meetings and be close enough for emergencies. But … it would be nice to visit Krypton sometimes as well. Not just in the winter. It would be nice for you. I can’t undo what I did, but … maybe I can help carve it into the cliffs again, make it look as it was before.”

     

                “That is a grand feat to achieve,” Kara slowly said, doubt passing over her features.

     

                “Not for my wife,” Lena whispered, leaning in to kiss her forehead. “You said you’ve met mountains less stubborn than me; I believe that’s true, because I would move the mountain for you out of sheer stubbornness alone. And in saying that, I would raise Krypton from the sea for you, no matter how grand a feat.”

     

                She had her unfinished letter in her right hand and sighed as she picked it up and then let it fall back onto the side table littered with quills, scraps of paper and ink. “It is only that I need some help to achieve it. I think J’onn will be most helpful, though, until I can get there next year to do the work myself.”

     

                “You have this all planned out,” Kara said with wonder, her head slightly cocked to the side as she stared up at Lena, a faint smile on her lips.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You will do this no matter how much I assure you that Krypton’s loss is not something for you to atone for. Why?”

                

                “From the very first day I arrived back in this realm, you have given me everything. From small things, such as remembering all that I have told you, to something bigger, like love and a family. I would like to do something for you.”

     

                “You have given me everything just by being here. You braved the river to save my life. I need nothing else from you but your love and company.”

     

                Smiling, Lena softened. “But I would like to do this for you. I would like to right the wrong that happened there because of my family.”

     

                Silent for a moment, Kara’s face was serious and thoughtful, before she nodded, meeting Lena’s eyes. “As you wish, but I have one request.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You do not recreate it. It will be our home that we build together.”

     

                “We shall design it together then,” Lena agreed with a pleased smile. “It will give us something to do through the winter months. When I am not otherwise occupied by Council duties.”

     

                “Or by your wife, I should hope.”

     

                “You may always occupy my time,” Lena murmured, leaning in to kiss her. “But we should also start packing; we will be leaving soon.”

     

     

                It was slow-going, packing up their belongings. They’d left things scattered across multiple homes, and knew they wouldn’t be gone for an entire season this time, and it would be a day’s trip there and back if they’d left anything important behind at Argo, so they were determined to pack light. With only what they could fit in small chests and saddlebags that could be attached to panniers on horseback, they spent a lot of time deliberating over their lists, packing and unpacking, then repacking again as they took things out or swapped them for things of greater importance. Lena’s belongings mostly consisted of clothing, which wasn’t of great importance, with the amount of clothes left behind in the Unseelie Court, but she had a few treasured pieces that were comfortable and suited to winter weather, and she had to make room for her gifts from Kara. Her copy of The Secret Garden was the first thing packed, already read twice since they’d reached Argo, with Kara convincing her to read chapters aloud to her, even though she’d read it herself already.

     

                They had to pack up Argo as well, the gauzy curtains pulled across archways, Kara’s harp packed away in a wooden case, rugs rolled up and certain pieces of furniture draped with cloths to protect them from harsher weather. Most of it was already weathered from decades of rain and damp, which only added to the charm of the place, but Kara was particular about her home, and Lena was more involved this time, instead of holing herself up in her room and only leaving when preparations had been completed for her. This time, she helped take the provisions of food that remained in the kitchen to nearby dwellings, small families or smaller communities thanking them for the extra food to see the winter through, and she made a personal effort to ensure they all had enough medicinal supplies as well, doling out portions of herbs she’d dried throughout the remainder of autumn, salves and tinctures she’d made. These people were kind to her now, used to her occasional visits with her wife, and Lena was pleased to see how they’d come to trust her with time. There was more hope for the future.

     

                They were finished packing when Alex and Kelly arrived almost a fortnight later, their bags and chests left on the shore of the lake as they enjoyed a last cup of tea for the day, dressed in their armour, more so out of the need to save space in their bags. It felt strange to Lena to be wearing it again, after so many weeks without needing to, and she wondered if she’d ever have need of it again. She hoped not, but knew that even without war, things would be unstable for quite some time, perhaps even decades, so they still had to take precautions. Kara had worn armour on and off for well over a decade, through sparring and drills, to skirmishes, and to war, so she wore it as a second skin, without any discomfort for not having donned it in a short while, but it was an amusing sight to watch her raise a dainty teacup with a mail-backed gloved hand, metal clinking as the scaled armour rattled with her movements.

     

                “You are quiet this morning,” Kara noted as she finished draining her cup.

     

                “Mm,” Lena hummed, her attention honing in on her wife as she gave her a small smile. “I’m going to miss it here.”

     

                “I shall as well.”

     

                “Isn’t it funny, it used to annoy me to be left alone with you, with no one else for company, but now it’s all I want. I’m too selfish to share you with everyone else.”

     

                “I am yours, my heart, down to the last drop of blood in my body,” Kara sweetly replied.

     

                “Oh, I know,” Lena laughed. “I’m not insecure to think you will replace me in your heart, only that I want you all to myself, always.”

     

                Joining in with her laughter, Kara set her cup down and reached out to briefly cup Lena’s cheek in her gloved hand. “Well, I can offer you a few more moments before my sister gets here.”

     

                “It will do,” Lena said with feigned weariness, a spark of amusement in her eye as she glanced sideways at Kara and then tipped her head back as she drained her tea.

     

                They lingered there until there was an audible shout from the shore of the lake, and Kara pushed herself to her feet, moving over to a south-facing archway and parting the gauzy curtains. “It is them.”

     

                “Do we have everything?” Lena asked as she set her cup down and climbed to her feet, before picking up the tray and making for the stairs.

     

                “Everything important,” Kara decisively nodded, following her down the spiralling stairs.

     

                Lena paused in the kitchen to hastily rinse their cups and the empty teapot before she continued down to the lowest level, stepping into frigid water and wading across the foyer, bypassing the tree, which was still flowering, despite the approaching winter, and pausing at the edge of the tower. She could see Kara nearing the shore, hopping across the last stone onto the soft, muddy bank, and embracing her sister, lifting her off her feet momentarily, before she hugged Kelly as well. Lena lingered on solid ground, despite being shin-deep in lake water, and smiled to herself as she shielded her eyes against the glare of the pale sky, watching Kara gesture behind her, towards the tower. Alex raised a hand in greeting, which Lena returned as she took a step forward, while the trio on the far shore started to walk across the stepping stones to meet her halfway.

     

                Kara let her sister go ahead, so Alex reached Lena first, giving her a brief but tight hug, looking pleased as she pulled back, appraising Lena’s face. “You look well, sister.”

     

                Patting Alex’s arm, Lena smiled and nodded. “I am. Much has changed - for the better - and I think I’ve finally adjusted. To the water, most of all.”

     

                Alex laughed, and Lena rolled her eyes, before stepping forward to hug Kelly, who reached the stepping stone only just behind her wife. “It’s good to see you,” Lena softly greeted her, pulling back and smiling brightly. “I hope you’ve both spent your free time well.”

     

                “Well enough,” Kelly replied, “although I am glad to be doing something of purpose now. I find myself restless when too idle.”

     

                “Mm, me too. I’ve been trying to make good use of my time.”

                

                “Practising with a sword, I hope,” Alex said, raising her eyebrows.

     

                “Of course. Kara is gentler than you, though - I might need to rope in your help again, or I might not actually be improving as much as I think I am.”

     

                “A wise idea.”

     

                “She has been focusing more on swimming of late,” Kara proudly proclaimed, ignoring the jibe about her going too soft on Lena.

     

                Face crumpling, Alex gave her sister a disbelieving look. “Swimming? In the lake? But Lena hates water.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena arched an eyebrow. “That’s kind of the point.”

     

                “You can swim now?” Alex echoed with surprise. 

     

                At Lena’s slightly smug nod, Alex nodded thoughtfully and then shoved her into the lake. With a startled cry, Lena went under in her armour with a big splash and surfaced with more splashing as she spat water. Coughing and spluttering as she scowled, Lena paddled and kicked to keep herself afloat as she gave Alex a venomous look.

     

                “What was that for?”

     

                “For trying to drown yourself last time I was here with you.”

     

                With a huff as she rolled her eyes, Lena swam for the stepping stone as Kara clapped a hand on her sister’s shoulder and softly sighed, giving her a grateful look. “Thank you for taking such good care of her in my absence,” Kara earnestly thanked her, before shoving Alex into the lake as her sister let out a cry of outrage before hitting the surface of the water, right beside Lena.

     

                As she surfaced, expression severe and thunderous as she tread water with more grace than Lena, Alex gestured cluelessly. “And what was that for?”

     

                “That,” Kara said with amusement, “was for pushing my wife in.”

     

                “Traitor! I should boil your lake dry,” Alex spluttered, already swimming to the stepping stones, eager to be out of the water. Lena might’ve been frightened of water, but Alex hated it more; the cold and wet was the antithesis of her element, and Lena muffled a laugh as she watched her sister-in-law hurriedly pull herself up onto the stepping stones, already shivering. “And my own wife does not raise a finger to help me!”

     

                Kelly laughed and held her hands up defensively as Alex gave her a wounded look and then took a step towards her, holding her arms open as water poured off her, while Kelly backed away. “Oh, no, no, this is not my quarrel, and I very much would like to stay dry. You are all fools if you think I will be going for a dip before we continue our travels; it will take an age to get warm again in this weather.”

     

                “I can warm you up quick enough,” Alex coyly replied, taking her wife’s hand and pressing a kiss to her knuckles.

     

                Lena looked at Kara and wrinkled her nose, still in the water, even if she gripped the edge of the sunken stepping stone to keep herself floating in place. With a quiet laugh, Kara stooped to grasp her wrists in her wiry grasp, and hauled Lena up and onto the stepping stone, and then wrapped her in her arms, heedless of the water. Lips brushing Lena’s ear, Kara’s voice was a low murmur that made Lena’s skin ripple with goosebumps - it definitely wasn’t from the biting wind and her soaked clothes.

     

                “I can warm you up as well.”

     

                With a quiet snort, Lena swatted Kara’s arm and rolled her eyes as she extracted herself from her wife’s embrace. “Please do; if I have to ride in wet clothes and armour, I’ll be miserable company.”

     

                “Your company is never miserable,” Kara murmured as she drew all of the moisture from Lena’s clothes, ribbons of water flung back into the water, while the rivulets running down her breastplate coalesced into balls of water, before she was completely dry again.

     

                Kara repeated the act for her sister, laughing as Alex bumped her shoulder and then slung an arm around Kara’s shoulders. They made their way back to the shore, a sense of pleasure filling Lena the moment her bare feet touched wet earth, toes wiggling in the damp grass as she inhaled deeply, her lungs filled with the smell of the forest. 

     

                “We shall linger a moment to eat before we continue, so you might rest a bit longer,” Kara insisted as she started picking up her pile of belongings, her sister helping, as Lena and Kelly grabbed the remainder.

     

                “We have another companion joining us, too,” Alex informed them as she strode off through the trees, where they’d left their horses. At the bewildered look on Kara’s face and the wariness of Lena’s, she laughed and raised her voice. “Sam!”

     

                Lena was mildly surprised; they hadn’t seen Sam since they’d parted ways in the Unseelie Court. It made sense that she’d be in the Seelie Court, though, and Lena knew that Kara and her friends had always been sympathetic towards the Hunter’s plight, considered her something of a friend, even, and how that would’ve been more likely since Lillian’s death. She wouldn’t pretend her feelings towards her weren’t complicated, though, even though Lena had been more forgiving than she’d ever imagined she could be, even feeling something akin to friendship with the other woman, herself. Still, she felt a flicker of uncertainty in her stomach as they continued through the trees and caught sight of Sam with the horses as they rounded a wide trunk.

     

                Kara cupped Sam’s shoulders as she greeted her warmly, if a little reserved for Lena’s sake, and Lena hesitated a moment before holding a hand out. She shouldn’t have been surprised when Sam gripped her forearm instead of shaking her hand, but Lena hesitated a moment before returning the greeting, murmuring a quiet hello, before she turned to survey the horses. Only three of them, until Kara whistled, and half a dozen more appeared after a few minutes. They were part of the wild herd that grazed around the lake, although they were only wild in the sense that they weren’t kept, free to roam where they pleased, but gentle and willing to be ridden when called. Lena busied herself with her saddlebags, ensuring the small chests were properly secured and the weight was evenly distributed, before she leapt onto the horse’s back, no saddle or bridle brought with her to make the ride easier or more comfortable. She didn’t require it these days, and the riding would be unhurried, so there wouldn’t be much risk of danger to have her galloping with urgency as she tried to cling to its mane.

     

                Once everyone was mounted, they took off at a gentle trot, Lena’s fingers knotted in her mare’s mane, and they rode in single file for the first few miles, winding around trees as the cool wind blew through the forest. Birds called out, but the forest was silent, other than the wind, the grey day and encroaching winter already adding a certain hush to the place, and Lena was left to her thoughts for a while. Once the tightly packed ferns thinned out, and the space between trunks widened, Kara rode beside her sister, the two of them talking quickly, catching up on things they hadn’t included in their letters, while Kelly rode at the front, her bow strung across her lap with a notched arrow, just as a precaution as her eyes flitted about, scouting the way. That left Lena and Sam at the rear, and she wasn’t sure if she reined her horse in or whether Sam quickened her stallion’s pace a touch, but they were soon riding side-by-side.

     

                Glancing over, Lena cleared her throat. “You’ve spent your time off well, I hope?”

     

                “Yes, very well Your-” Sam cut off, her brow faintly creasing before she gave Lena a wry smile. “Yes, Lady Lena. And yourself?”

     

                Rolling her eyes, one side of Lena’s mouth hitched into an uneven smile. “Yes. I’ve been learning to swim.”

     

                “Oh,” Sam softly exclaimed. “That is … surprising.”

     

                “To me as well. I thought it best, just in case I find myself in similar situations again.” Lena’s eyes darted sideways to Sam, watching her shift uncomfortably in her saddle. She didn’t mean to make her old guard uncomfortable, or try to make her feel guilty; there was just this old thing hanging over them, which neither could forget about, but Sam had protected Lena for months, and her lover had saved Kara’s life, and they’d both stayed with her in the months where Lena had been parted from Kara, so she was grateful to this woman who’d been part of her mother’s death. It was never quite so black and white as it had seemed upon her arrival at the Courts, and she was glad that her perspective had shifted, that she could let go of some of that old grief to move forward.

     

                “Andrea is not with you?” Lena ventured after an awkward pause.

     

                “She has returned to the Unseelie Court to prepare our home for our stay,” Sam slowly explained. “I have been with her for some years now, but … she had never met my daughter before. My time has been well spent on learning how to be a mother in full; we shall bring her to the Unseelie Court soon, so that I may raise her myself.”

     

                Lena felt oddly fond of the other woman then, that she was trying to recover what she’d been denied by Lillian, so bound in service that she couldn’t disobey, no matter how badly she’d wanted to. She didn’t think her suggestion that Sam return to her daughter had been the reason for this, but rather that Sam had always wanted it, and Lena had given her the opportunity for that freedom. Lena had seen her that day Kara had taken her and a bundle of cherries to the dwelling not far from Alex’s home, where Ruby was being raised without her mother - the blatant want had been obviously written on Sam’s face at that time.

     

                “I’m happy for you,” Lena honestly replied.

     

                A flicker of surprise crossed Sam’s face in earnest then, and she faintly smiled and dipped her chin in acknowledgement. They made idle conversation for a while, the topic turning to the Council and the work they’d been doing while parted. She’d exchanged numerous letters with the woman, and with the rest of the Council, since returning to Argo, so she was clued in on what Sam had been focusing on, but it was nice to talk about these matters with someone other than Kara for a change, someone who actually sat on the same Council as Lena, who bore the same responsibility. Kara’s responsibilities were just as great, and some of the things that took up her time were the same matters that took up Lena’s, trying to enact the decisions both Councils had made together, but others were solely for the Seelie Court, and they’d had an established Council for centuries, with more experience in their combined Councilmembers to make their business run smoother and be implemented more easily. It was nice to have someone who bore the same burden of getting the Council off the ground.

     

                The ride was peaceful, stopping off once when they reached the river, indulging in the luxury of time instead of haste as they shared a skin of wine, getting the blood flowing in their chilled hands and feet as they walked along the riverbank. They were on horseback again after that, riding the rest of the way to Lena’s home without any trouble, Kara whistling to the birds and laughing at her sister’s stories, while Lena watched her, her most enjoyable pastime. They made it to the Unseelie Court late afternoon, when dusk had already fallen, and the forest was blue and cold. Turning the horses loose, they carried their belongings into the underground tunnels, and Lena stepped into her old room with a sense of homecoming, depositing her bags and turning to kiss Kara.

     

                “It is good to be here, is it not?” Kara asked with a smile, seeing the pleasure in Lena’s eyes, in the ease of her shoulders.

     

                “It is. It’s … familiar,” Lena tried to explain, because while it wasn’t the place that she’d gone to when she’d wanted to be close to Kara, but it was the place she would’ve gone to be close to herself, this home under the earth, surrounded by trees and plants and dirt. “You know, I sometimes wonder if I remember more of the Court than my mind lets on. I know it felt familiar, coming back to the forest, that not everything was taken from me once I’d been weaned off the place, but … I don’t know, sometimes I think I remember it more through feelings than by sight.”

     

                “That makes sense. Your mind would have forgotten long before your body did.”

     

                “I remember my mom, though, and I know those memories must’ve been from here. She died as soon as we made it back to the human realm; where else could they be from?”

     

                “What do you remember?” Kara asked, her palms cradling the sides of Lena’s neck as she gave her a searching look, listening to her intently, knowing it wasn’t often that Lena reminisced about her mom.

     

                Silent for a moment, a crease forming between her brows, Lena hummed thoughtfully. “I don’t know. I guess there’s one memory, a very specific one, where I can picture her clearly. I know it’s a memory, not just something my mind made up. She’s sitting under a tree in the shade, and the shadows are very sharp around her, so I know it was summer at the time. She had red hair, you know - I’m not sure if I ever told you - and she was wearing white. It was an apple tree, I think. They were red apples; it must’ve been late summer.”

     

                Kara listened to her scattered explanation of the memory, while Lena got a distant look in her eyes, envisioning the scene in her mind. When she fell silent, she blinked and met her wife’s gaze, a weak smile crossing her lips, before she leaned in and kissed her quickly.

     

                “Anyway …”

     

                “Thank you for telling me,” Kara softly said, snagging Lena’s hand and giving it a quick squeeze.

     

                Nodding, an odd lump in her throat, Lena paced away as she started on the fastening of her cloak. “We should dress for dinner. We’ve not eaten a proper meal since dawn; you must be starving.”

     

                “I am in no hurry if you wish to linger a while longer,” Kara assured her.

     

                “I think I’d like to eat and then bathe, before having an early night.”

     

                Lena was tired, and her mind turning towards her mom had turned her brooding, and she fumbled with the buckles of her armour as she kept her back to Kara, but her wife came up behind her and gently nudged her hands away to help her, her voice quiet as she replied. “As you wish.” 

     

                Mouth thinning with annoyance for herself, Lena let Kara undo her gorget and pauldrons, carefully setting them aside, before freeing her of her breastplate. Lena felt lighter with each piece shed, and turned to kiss Kara when her chainmail came off. Kara softened beneath her mouth, her fingers lightly pressing against Lena’s scalp as she threaded them through her hair, before kissing the tip of her nose. 

     

                Quick to shed her own armour, although neither of them was foolish enough to go around unarmed, Kara held a hand out to her wife. “Come, let us eat.”

     

                Without changing into something finer, Lena let herself be escorted to the dining hall, finding Alex and Kelly already there with Sam. They weren’t the only attendees, and Lena clasped Andrea’s arm and warmly greeted Hector and Rama Khan before taking her seat. Their Council wasn’t set to reunite for almost a week hence, but she was glad that they were already starting to gather in her home, rooms set aside for each of them, with the expectation that the others would arrive soon, too. She was in better spirits as the night wore on, her momentary brooding overridden by the company as she drank warm cider and stew and let her wife dote on her as she felt relief in her chest. Truthfully, she’d worried a little about coming back; that word hadn’t reached her, and she’d find things in disarray, but it was all much the same as it had been when she’d left.

     

                They lingered in the dining hall longer than she’d anticipated, and she spoke at length with Hector and Rama Khan, making plans to meet with them in the morning and discuss a few matters, and promising Alex that she hadn’t forgotten about their sparring lessons either. Expecting to be busier than the last few weeks had been, Lena was the first to excuse herself, with Kara accompanying her. As she’d already stated, she wanted a bath first, and they washed in their favourite pool, Lena basking in the luxury of so much steaming water without having to wait to heat buckets of it for a bath, and as soon as they were back in their suite, she changed into a thick nightgown and crawled into bed. Kara had a brazier lit and joined her, sliding in beside her beneath the blankets as her arms came around her waist, and she kissed Lena’s shoulder.

     

                “I love you,” Kara murmured.

     

                “I love you, too.”

     

                “I’m glad to be here with you.”

     

                “Truly?”

     

                “Of course. For the first time, I am in the Court of my enemies and feel no dread, no threat to our safety. It is a nice feeling.”

     

                Lena hummed, “I think so, too. I didn’t know what to expect, but … well, it feels very normal. It’s been left in good hands in our absence; I’m confident in my choices.”

     

                “Yes, you picked well,” Kara whispered, nuzzling the back of Lena’s neck. “You are wise beyond your years. I know it, your Council knows it, and in time, the rest of your Court and mine will know it, too.”

     

                “You’re awfully confident,” Lena softly chuckled.

     

                “In you? Always.”

     

                With a scoff, Lena closed her eyes and burrowed into the blankets. “Go to sleep.”

     

                “And you, my heart. Sleep well.”

     

                Surprisingly, Lena did. The room was warm, and the smell of earth was comforting, with the solid presence of her wife at her side. She might’ve slept a lot longer if she hadn’t been roused an hour after dawn by loud banging on the door to their quarters, Alex’s muffled voice taking a second to make itself coherent as sleep lingered before clarity set in. Without giving her time to break her fast first, Alex had Lena in the mosaic room where Lena had first held a sword, giving as good as she got as they sparred until Lena’s clothes were stuck to her sweating skin and she was bruised and scraped all over. Alex thrashed her, naturally, with two decades of experience on her, but Lena’s skill improved by the day, and her sister had praise for her when Lena caught her by surprise, or made the mosaics ripple underfoot as the ground tripped Alex up.

     

                Sore and tired, Lena limped to a late breakfast with Alex, earning a slap on the back for her good effort, and found Kara finishing off the dregs of her tea, sitting with Rama Khan. The room was otherwise empty, everyone long-since finished breaking their fast, and Lena drained a cup of water and tea back to back, before even attempting to eat the fried tomatoes and boiled eggs she had set on her plate. She was warm enough from her workout, but she had a bowl of porridge too, garnishing it with honey and walnuts as she ate until she was full, and had another cup of tea to wash it down.

     

                By that point, she could practically feel Kara’s impatience, and gave her several questioning glances and asked numerous times, but was brushed off each time. When Lena asked Rama Khan if now was a good time to talk, she was surprised by his hesitation, his eyes flitting to Kara, before he agreed, and Lena was even more so surprised when her wife told her to leave her sword, that she’d take it back to their quarters for her. Bewildered by her behaviour, Lena just unbuckled her sword belt and departed with a quick kiss on Kara’s lips. Following Rama Khan to the suite he’d claimed for himself, Lena found herself seated across from him with a desk between them, and spent two hours discussing political matters and orders of business he intended to raise at their next official Council meeting.

     

                It was a long conversation, and they were both courteous, even if they disagreed on matters, and after they wrapped it up, she went to find Hector, her meeting with him shorter but no less informative on his opinions and intentions. He was less politically savvy than the General, but had a more informed point of view on the normal Unseelie folk, which Lena valued greatly. She’d been everything from an orphan, homeless, business owner, Princess and Queen, and had varying perspectives as a result of all of them, and she knew that in order to know what needed to be fixed, and how to maintain order, they needed all of those perspectives in a Council.

     

                Feeling pleased with her productive morning, Lena went to bathe and returned back to her suite with damp hair and a faint smile on her lips as she shut the door behind herself. Kara was sitting on the chaise and looked up at her arrival, an eagerness to her expression as she set aside a map she’d been studying and climbed to her feet.

     

                “Good, you are back. Your business has been concluded for the day?”

     

                Apprehensive, Lena raked her damp hair back. “I suppose so. As far as I’m aware.”

     

                “Dress warmly. I have somewhere to take you.”

     

                Laughing, confused but happy to play along with Kara’s almost frantic insistence, Lena walked into the bedroom and fished out warm clothes, changing quickly and fastening her cloak around her shoulders. She reappeared back in the open living area, and Kara held her scabbard out towards her. Lena thanked her, buckling the belt around her waist and adjusting it until the sword hung comfortably at her side, the dagger on her other hip.

     

                “And where are we going?” Lena asked as Kara eagerly took her hand and started towing her out of the room.

     

                “You will see. It is important.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena laughed, increasing her pace to keep up with her wife, whose long strides left Lena almost jogging to keep up.

     

                Above ground, Kara led her to the stand of willow trees woven into stables and picked two suitable horses for them, and Lena’s brow furrowed. She hadn’t expected them to be going far, not far enough to need horses, and she wondered what Kara had in mind. Perhaps she’d gotten the idea to take Lena to one of the places they’d snuck out to under Lillian’s nose, escaping the control of Lena’s mother as they stole a few minutes to themselves in the forest. They hadn’t liked each other then, their relationship a tentative truce, but those places would’ve been within walking distance - they’d never been allowed to stray far from the seat of the Unseelie Court.

     

                Lena asked her wife where they were going several times as Kara led them southeast through the forest, and each time Kara insisted it wasn’t much further. As the miles went by, Lena lost all familiarity with the forest, until they were pushing through dark patches of briars and bushes, the shadows thick and the light low as it struggled to pierce the canopy overhead. Towering trees shaded shorter trees, growing in thick and close in between the wide spaces between trunks, and Lena could feel the age of them as she sent calming waves of power into the ground, into the trunks, the trees almost seeming to sigh, to reach for her as she rode past.

     

                They rode for several hours before coming to a stop at the ruins of a building. It was built over uneven ground and roots, old stone grown over with moss, the black streaks of a fire marring thick beams that had collapsed inwards and were now being slowly overtaken by lichen and ivy. The haphazard arrangement of rooms over the tiered ledges of uneven ground nagged at Lena’s mind, and she cocked her head to the side as she stared at the eerie ruins hidden amongst the trees. It would’ve been a fair-sized building before it had been destroyed - not so grand as her home now, but bigger than the smaller dwellings of ordinary folk. And it wasn’t a watchtower or some sort of waypoint.

     

                She could feel Kara watching her and turned her attention to her wife’s face. Lena almost asked her where they were, but bit her tongue. Kara knew even less of the Unseelie Court than Lena did, but she was looking at her with anticipation. Turning her gaze back to the building, Lena studied the ruins for a moment before dismounting and walking towards where the door would’ve been. She paused in her tracks then, her face crumpling with confusion. The wall there had collapsed, and up a level, the whole face of it brought down to be reclaimed by the forest, but Lena knew that was where the door had been. It struck her with a shock of certainty, and she faltered, unsure how she knew that. Walking into the ruins, she crept over broken crockery and twisted metal, the ashes of furniture long since blown away by the wind or worked into the mud on rainy days, but she had the sense of having been there before, but couldn’t picture it.

     

                After a few moments, she didn’t want to be in there anymore and hastily walked back out, and then paused. Turning, her face furrowed with doubt, Lena followed the collapsed wall around to the right side of the house and heard her wife’s footsteps follow after her. Climbing the sloped ground, stepping over a snaking root and then scrambling up a ledge, Lena stood atop a small rise at the back end of the house, the ground sloping away from it. Pausing a moment, she continued downwards, the ground easing down to a small stream behind the old house, trickling past, and she hopped over it, catching a sweet smell in the air. Her stomach turned, and she froze, turning to give Kara an accusing look, uncertainty inside her, but her pulse quickened anyway. Kara didn’t speak, just stared at her and waited, and Lena swallowed thickly and turned back around, slowly walking forward until she was standing in an apple orchard with a sickening sense of deja vu rushing through her.

     

                “I’ve been here before,” she murmured, in a daze as she looked around.

     

                The tall apple trees were knobby, and the branches drooped towards the ground in the way she remembered, branches bearing red apples and the ground littered with the rotting remains as they fell in the winter. Animals had gotten to them, cores left behind, worms burrowing into softened flesh and flies buzzing around remains, but it was the same. In summer, the ground would’ve been green grass, the air thick with bees, and the shadows deep and harsh. Face wrenched with confusion and disbelief, and no small amount of grief, Lena rounded on her wife.

     

                “How did you find it?”

     

                “I asked Rama Khan,” Kara softly explained. “You told me yesterday you had a memory of your mother that must’ve been from here. I don’t know why I didn’t think of it before, but you would’ve had a home here when you were little. Before your mother took you and ran. Your father would have put you both somewhere near where he could visit; that would be where that memory was from. Rama Khan confirmed it and gave me directions. I thought you might like to see your home again. Forgive me if I assumed too much.”

     

                Shaking her head quickly, Lena sniffed and drew in a hitching breath, her back to Kara as she studied the clearing. “No. Thank you, I-” Her shoulders caved as she exhaled, and Lena’s voice steadied as she swallowed and continued. “It makes it feel more real to me, now. I’ve forgotten so much, but … it’s nice to know that I remember that correctly. We were happy here. She was sitting there.”

     

                Lena pointed to the place, and she slowly walked towards it, sinking to her knees as she reached out to bury her hands in the fallen leaves and mealy apples. “Right here,” she whispered, her voice wavering slightly as her eyes stung.

     

                Kara’s hands firmly came down on Lena’s shoulders in a comforting presence, keeping her grounded in the moment as grief bubbled up. The air was heavy with the smell of damp earth and apples, but also a hint of mint and sweetbriar, and wet moss and leaves. It felt like an echo of a memory, and she had already promised to come back in the summer to have that snapshot of the memory of her mom again. Lena couldn’t remember much else of their time there, so much stolen when the strange magic of the forest had been leached out of her upon her escape, but she clung to that memory and felt that old grief smoothed over just a touch more.

     

                Moving from her knees to a seated position, Lena leaned back against the trunk, sitting in the crook of the roots, and wearily sighed. Kara sat beside her and wrapped her arm around her wife’s shoulders, kissing her temple, and Lena turned her head, pressing her lips to Kara’s.

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                Nodding, Kara didn’t speak. They could’ve stayed that way for hours, and she wouldn’t have minded, stuck in the peace of the moment as Lena thought about the mother she’d lost so young, and how that had shaped the rest of her life. It was already mid-afternoon by then, and in the dense section of the forest, it felt like dusk was being ushered in, the light waning, and the first sight of bats flitting through the branches overhead, crickets droning, filled the silence. 

     

                “I don’t know what to say,” Lena said after an age.

     

                “You needn’t say anything,” Kara comforted her, taking her hand and pressing a kiss to the back of it. “When we are together, it is as though we are like water in a river; my thoughts flow through yours, yours through mine. In that way, I already know your mind as you know mine. So, you needn’t explain yourself. I know all there is to be said already.”

     

                Lena let out a small laugh and wiped her eyes, shoulders slumping as she gave Kara an aching look, a thin smile on her lips as she gazed at her. “You’re beyond all the words I’ve ever known. Indescribable.”

     

                “I have words to describe you,” Kara replied, a sheepish look on her face as she reached for the pommel of Lena’s sword and drew it in a swift motion. “I stole your sword earlier and had Alex rework what was written on the blade, considering you are no longer a Princess, and not even a Queen.”

     

                “Oh? And what am I now?”

     

                Setting the sword across their laps, Kara’s fingers ran over the glyphs, smoothing over the section that had been smelted smooth by Alex’s fire and etched with a new glyph. Lena reached out to trace it with her fingertip as they both read the words, and Kara pressed a kiss to Lena’s temple before whispering it to her.

     

                “You are simply Lena of the Unseelie.”

    Chapter 60

    Chapter Notes

    thank you to everyone who stayed with me for the Very long journey of this fic, i really appreciate it and i hope you've enjoyed reading it as much as i've enjoyed writing it 🫶🏻

                Winter arrived, and was spent holed up at Lena’s home in the Unseelie Court for the most part. It was cold and damp, but the forest felt oddly alive for how silent and bare everything was. The Unseelie Council gathered there, Lena housing them all, and the servants that had never left, and whom Lena was too polite to evict, kept the household running as they ate meals together and deliberated over laws and legislation, treaties and agreements at all hours of the day. Spending much of her time by the fire, Lena felt a comfort there that she never would’ve thought possible, no longer fearing for her life at every moment, no longer bearing sole responsibility for so many people. She got to know her fellow Councilmembers better, and they made some real headway and changes, while sorting out the mess of things her mother had left behind, so much wealth and resources hoarded, against the natural order of their Courts. 

     

                In harsher months, those from the smaller dwellings surrounding the seat of the Unseelie Court converged upon the place, and Lena made sure they were all fed and housed within the numerous homes amongst the trees. With the war over and her army disbanded, to while away their time as they pleased, there were many beds freed up, and there was a sense of satisfaction in helping those who came to her home, seeking a sack of oats and dried meats, offering up bolts of thick cloth or pouches of salt and herbs. There was a sense of surprise in it, too, and Lena knew that Lillian wouldn’t have cared that much for anyone who wasn’t serving or advising her. It felt good, made her feel purposeful, and the other Councilmembers emptied out their own stores in their homes, sending supplies out to the people in their lands, ensuring everyone made it through the winter.

     

                On Midwinter, thirteen of them made the trip to the bridge to meet with the Seelie Council, and they remained for a week. Camps were set up on both sides of the river, and the rest of the Seelie Council tentatively set foot on the Unseelie side on the fourth day, which Lena took as a big success. She had to wonder if this was the first time most of them had set foot on enemy territory, or whether they’d been warriors in their youths and had spilt their fair share of blood on the earth underfoot. Regardless, they’d decided to leave that in the past, and the way forward was looking more optimistic than she’d even hoped for. No one had drawn a weapon on someone else yet, and even their disagreements between Councils were no more hostile than the ones within their own Councils. Lena secretly thought that the Seelie Council, for all their years of experience and self-adulation for how peaceful they were, in contrast to their bloodthirsty neighbours across the river, were more prone to bickering and derision amongst themselves. She couldn’t blame them, though - the likes of Morgan and Maxwell would be enough for her to snap back on their opinions, too, if it came to it. A few nights, after particularly tense days, she’d even asked Kara how she managed to put up with them, and how they still held seats on the Council. They were shrewd-minded, though, and had aptitudes for trade and numbers, which was an asset in ensuring the Seelie Court had enough resources to ensure everyone was fed and healthy. Still, Lena never could warm to them, and they made it obvious they didn’t like her either. That was just the way of politics.

     

                Some things both Councils voted to proceed with, others were vetoed, and overall it was a mostly positive experience, or at least promising legwork had been done, with the foundation for more ahead. They decided to reconvene again mid-spring to go over their progress and decide on the next orders of business for both Courts to work on, with the agreement that they would exchange letters and pay visits if deemed necessary in the meantime, before both Councils packed up their camps and went their separate ways again. In the Unseelie Court, Lena and Kara saw out most of the remainder of the winter, leaving just before the seasons started to turn again.

     

                They went back to Argo as spring was ushered in, the tower not too cold to handle the contrary weather, and the forest bloomed around them as the foggy mornings dwindled and the frost snaps turned into spring showers.
