Lena enjoyed those early days of spring, walking through the dewy forest as everything turned a vivid shade of green, sapping her extra strength as the plants budded and flowered, daffodils in vibrant yellow pushing up through dark soil, strawberries and blueberries studding bushes, while clover carpeted everything and lavender shot up, attracting bees as they flitted from flower to flower. She picked colourful handfuls of tulips for her wife, and replenished stores of dandelions and stinging nettles, peppermint and goldenseal, as well as parsley and thyme for their kitchen. She enjoyed coming home to the tower with dirty hands and a basketful of things she’d foraged for, mushrooms and snap peas accompanying Kara’s freshly caught fish or quail on their dining table.

     

                They frequently travelled between their homes in both Courts until the Council meeting during mid-spring, before they journeyed to Alex’s halls in the foothills of the mountain afterwards. There, they lingered a week before continuing onwards, through the mountain passes, so vastly different to how they’d looked that winter they’d been forced to flee through there, and spent three nights in Eliza’s hall, before crossing the remaining distance to Kara’s lands on the northern shore of the Seelie Court. Of course, Krypton no longer stood, but they camped out in the old quarry, where Kara reminded Lena of where their relationship had taken a turn for the better, and they waited for J’onn to answer the call of Kara’s letter. There, they lingered through the early days of summer as stonemasons and woodworkers congregated in a makeshift camp under J’onn’s rule, starting preliminary works on Lena’s meticulously planned designs for the soon-to-be newly constructed Krypton.

     

                Kara gave her opinion on things, too, but mostly left the plans up to her wife, too preoccupied with swimming in the sea or taking out a little skiff with a small sail and trawling for fish. She grew tanned in the cloudless sunny days, clambering over rockpools for crabs and mussels, or splaying on the sliver of sandy shore at the base of the cliffs, while Lena holed up in the tent they’d moved to aboveground, ink staining her fingers as she sketched out rough ideas for the masonry and layout of the rooms. She brought modern convenience to some of the plans, while keeping the fantastical elements of the architecture, still so in awe of and in love with the intricate designs of fae craftsmanship. So much of her designs kept the whorls of waves, fish and seabirds, wanting to keep it firmly rooted in the element of her wife, but Kara made a few changes, insisting on lily of the valley motifs in what would be their bedroom, which she also tried to move from open air to the sea below to deeply set in the cliffside. Lena had relented on the lily of the valley but stubbornly objected to moving their bedroom, knowing Kara had always loved being a step away from the sea - and truthfully, Lena had a certain love of the sound of crashing waves now, an appreciation for how close it had made her feel to Kara when she’d thought she’d lost her and spent several nights sleeping on the sandy shore of the Unseelie Court. She wasn’t so spooked by the sound of waves lulling her to sleep anymore.

     

                As the work progressed, they moved out of the quarry to camp amongst the workers, and Lena spent a good portion of her day splinting broken fingers, washing out grazes and stitching up deep cuts from the injuries sustained. On top of that was the occasional congestion, headaches and infections, and she meted out her care with a delightful sense of purpose, endearing herself to more of the Seelie, especially on nights spent around the communal fire, drinking cider and proving a surprising source of entertainment to the Seelie as they found her witty and quick with her wry retorts. It was a peaceful time, but not spent idly, and Lena enjoyed the warmth of early summer as they dwelled there, each day filled with seemingly endless hours of sunlight, sparkling over the sea as it made its trajectory from east to west, and she was busy, her attention split between the reconstruction of Krypton, healing and all it entailed, with the gathering of herbs and plants and the proper storing or preparation of them, and spending time with her wife, of course.

     

                Time passed, though, and summer wore on with no great change in things. That was one thing about the fae that somewhat irked Lena; they lived so long that everything took an age to be completed, because there was never any rush. The stonemasons would work as they pleased, for as little or as long as that was, and each piece was a work of art, which she respected and admired, but it meant it would take a long while to reconstruct Krypton again. But Kara assured her that it would be for the better, that it would be rebuilt even more wonderful and fantastical than it had been the first time, especially with the designs Lena had laboured over, as if trying to impart her remorse into the very parchment. 

     

                She was glancing over at them again, a few weeks before Midsummer, standing on the grassy stretch along the cliff edge as the wind tousled her hair and the sun near-blinded her as it reflected off the undulating waves rushing in. Kara found her there and quietly intruded on her wife’s solitude, standing at her side, somewhat damp as she returned from her swim. Lena could smell the salt on her without turning at the sound of her footsteps, and she leaned into Kara’s touch as her wife pressed a hand against her waist and kissed the side of her neck. Glancing at a nearby stonemason chiselling away at a piece of limestone, Lena glanced at her designs and concluded the woman was working on a piece that would make up the pillar of the dock.

     

                “It will look good once it’s completed, don’t you think?” Lena optimistically voiced, her head cocked to the side as she studied the gigantic blocks of limestone. 

     

                Some had already been finished and were laid nearby, waiting to be placed once the Earthfolk had finished excavating the new halls below them. Most of the structure would be carved right into the foundations below, but many pillars would be handmade for extra structural support, before the rest of the rooms were hand-carved into the wondrous designs of the Waterfolk. She rolled the plans up in her hands and looked at Kara with hope in her eyes.

     

                “It will be better than it once was,” Kara insisted, a smile on her lips as she smoothed a hand down Lena’s dark hair, the wind tossing it about her face as they stood so close to the cliff edge.

     

                “You’re biting your tongue,” Lena observed, rolling the plans tighter and capping the ends of the scroll as she spoke. “What is it?”

     

                “We should leave tomorrow, or else we’ll risk being late,” Kara nervously insisted, her hand pressed against her wife’s back as she leaned in and kissed her temple. 

     

                Looking up, Lena raised her eyebrows a fraction. “So soon?”

     

                “I would like to spend some time with my mother when we pass through the mountains.”

     

                “Oh, then of course, we’ll leave with the dawn.”

     

                Kara’s face softened with a smile, and she cupped Lena’s chin in her palm. “We shall return afterwards to continue your work.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively, Lena wryly smiled. “I wouldn’t say my work. J’onn knows the place better than I do and has arranged it all. I’m sure he’ll have it all in hand.”

     

                “He listens to your advice.”

     

                “I don’t think I could advise him on anything he doesn’t already know about Krypton and your lands here. He does take my recommendations on board, though, which is kind of him.”

     

                With a small laugh, Kara’s cheeks dimpled, “still, he would not be helping rebuild my home without you convincing me to do it.”

     

                “Ah, well, it’s the least I could do.”

     

                Clicking her tongue and softly sighing with exasperation, Kara took the scroll from Lena and gave her a withering look. “You are not indebted to me for bringing down my hall. I am indebted to you for saving my life.”

     

                “You’ve saved mine more times than I can count,” Lena scoffed as she took Kara’s hand and started leading her towards their tent. “I’m indebted to you for that.”

     

                “Ah, but you brought this CPR to the Courts, which resulted in my resuscitation, and my being alive today, so I am indebted to you for that.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Lena bumped her shoulder into Kara. “Should I remind you how stubborn I am? You won’t win this argument.”

     

                “Indeed, I don’t believe I will, but I enjoy the bickering, regardless. It reminds me of when we first met.”

     

                “I bet you never thought you’d look back on those days with fondness,” Lena laughed.

     

                “I look back on every moment with you with fondness. Even when I could have throttled you or left you for dead at the time.”

     

                They both laughed, and Lena grabbed onto Kara’s arm and briefly rested her head on her shoulder as she mockingly crooned, “you’re so romantic.”

     

                Sighing, Kara fought a smile and towed Lena towards the tent entrance, holding aside the flap and letting her inside first. The plans were safely set on a table, and Lena flopped onto the bed, staring up at the canvas as she listened to the quiet sound of chisels on stone. The masons brought in weren’t solely comprised of Earthfolk, which surprised her, because she imagined Earthfolk of great experience would be able to mould the stone into the engravings she’d designed on her plans, but they all insisted on working it with their hands, regardless of which element they had an affinity for. It was purely for the love of the craft, for the satisfaction of working the stone with their tools and feeling fulfilled from the use of their time, and she couldn’t argue with that.

     

                Pushing herself up onto her elbows, Lena studied her wife, taking in the stern expression on Kara’s face as she gathered up letters and pages into a neat pile, tapping them against the desk to line them up, eyes glancing around at their belongings. They’d only been there for the start of summer, yet they’d accumulated a mess of belongings, as per usual, and they’d need to sort through it before retiring that night if they were to set off at dawn, as Lena had promised. She could practically see the thought turning over in Kara’s mind, and her expression softened with tenderness.

     

                “You seem anxious,” Lena observed.

     

                Blinking, Kara glanced over at her and smiled, a quick twitch of the corners of her mouth. “I’m not anxious.”

     

                “Are you sure? It’s not like you haven’t done it before.”

     

                Exasperatedly sighing, Kara shook her head, fighting a smile. “Yes, my heart, I’m sure. Excited would be more apt.”

     

                “Excited?”

     

                “Of course. Aren’t you looking forward to it?”

     

                With a quick laugh, Lena gave her a wry smile. “Definitely. It will be an altogether different experience this time.”

     

                “A good one, I hope,” Kara murmured, crossing over to the bed and stooping to plant a kiss on Lena’s brow.

     

                “Of course.”

     

                “Why? Are you nervous?”

     

                Laughing, Lena tugged at the front of Kara’s shirt, holding her in place before her wife could straighten up. Wrinkling her nose, Lena hummed a moment before shaking her head, eyes bright with amusement. “No. It can’t be worse than last time, can it?”

     

                Giving her a dark look, as if scolding her for even speaking the jinx aloud, Kara pried Lena’s fingers free from her shirt, kissing the tips of them, before she straightened up. “I would not think so, but I would not tempt fate by saying it.”

     

                “Ah, well, maybe we’ll be held up and miss it altogether.”

     

                “That would be poor form.”

     

                “Then we should pack now, and hope your mother keeps us on track. You’re incorrigible when we’re alone.”

     

                “Me?” Kara spluttered. “You would have me walk around unclothed at all times if you had it your way, I’m sure.”

     

                “I am but a mere woman,” Lena feigned a sigh and grinned.

     

                After a moment, she leapt up and made for the small chest holding the limited wardrobe she’d travelled with. “Come, let us pack.”

     

                The weather had been warm on the coast, trees sparse and the sunlight harsh, so they’d spent most of their time in shirts and leggings, with no need for extra layers, but once they were back in the forest, the deep shade would be somewhat cooler, so Lena made a quick bundle of suitable clothes and emptied a knapsack before stuffing her clothes in. She took a small store of medicinal herbs, clean bandages and certain teas and packed them as well, right alongside her treasured copy of The Secret Garden. Kara took care of their food supplies, leaving to fetch what they’d need, and Lena readied her armour while she waited for her wife to return. It was too hot for full plate armour, so she set aside her breastplate and tassets, deeming her coat of mail suitable enough, with the extra protection of the gorget and pauldrons more than was necessary. She could never be too careful, though, and wouldn’t ride unarmoured through the forest so soon after a war. It had barely been a year, a mere blink of an eye to many fae, and she didn’t want to grow complacent. Kara wouldn’t allow that to happen, anyway - she was far too cautious, especially when it came to her wife’s life.

     

                They made swift work of their packing, and Kara left their remaining belongings in J’onn’s care, informing him that they’d be back before the end of summer, to see through the first half of winter there as well. Lena left her to finalise plans and delegate responsibilities to her Steward while they were absent and made her way to the communal fire as sunset was ushered in, the horizon painted shades of pink and lavender over the expanse of flat land, and she enjoyed a bowl of stew and a few cups of cider as she basked in the peace of her life. She enjoyed the periods of being still, settled down somewhere for weeks at a time, but there was something thrilling about travelling as well. They hadn’t settled anywhere permanently since her arrival in the Courts, and Lena was glad that they still hadn’t settled yet. The thought of not exploring the vast corners of the Courts seemed boring, and she was happy to split their time between their numerous homes and those of their family and friends as well.

     

                The thought of the start of a new journey in the morning had her retiring early, leaving Kara, who had joined her at the fire as the first stars appeared in the sky, to finish her dinner. In bed, Lena slept soundly to the rush of waves breaking on the shore below the cliffs, and barely stirred when her wife slipped into bed beside her, curving around her and snuggling into her back. They were up early, dressed and ready to go, with horses that grazed nearby in a herd, saddled and waiting for them. Saying their goodbyes to those remaining, they mounted up and departed before the sun had barely peeked over the horizon, setting off south-easterly towards the stretch of wetlands and marsh between them and the foothills of the mountains.

     

                It was uneventful, each day a pleasant ride through the ever-changing landscape, picking their way through bogs and shallow pools of stagnant water, stunted trees and midges everywhere they looked. Kara caught small silver fish in the wetlands and shot a few ducks as well, Lena preparing them for their dinners, even if she couldn’t stomach hunting them herself, and then they were into the thin forest in the shade of the mountain range, climbing up and up, snaring rabbits for dinner while Lena foraged for mushrooms and strawberries. They made good time and reached Eliza’s home in three days of riding, spending a week deep inside the mountain, in the stone halls that had been the turning point of their relationship all those months ago.

     

                When they left, Eliza accompanied them, their rations restored with fresh bread and foods that grew in the forest that they’d sorely missed. Lena felt refreshed after a few nights on a soft mattress, clean clothes and a proper bath with real soap doing much to reinvigorate her, and they rode leagues to the river dividing both Courts, Alex and Kelly catching up with them along the way. The five of them made for a lively party, their laughter ringing through the trees as they rode through the forest at a leisurely pace, catching each other up on their doings, making plans for the next season. They weren’t late reaching the border, getting there the morning before Midsummer to find most of both Councils already assembled on either side of the river. They greeted the Seelie upon their arrival, before crossing over the bridge to greet the Unseelie, Lena feeling genuine delight at the sight of so many friends and familiar faces.

     

                Another week was spent on the banks, familiar now after a few seasons of it, and while it wasn’t exactly the height of excitement, it was productive and eventful, and the trust between both Courts continued to grow. The Seelie Court even agreed to let a small group of Earthfolk settle on their side of the river to help bolster the small number of Earthfolk on their side and repair some of the damage done by the endless wars. It was another achievement to feel proud of, and Lena quietly toasted her wife around the fire that night, cheeks a little rosy from too much wine, her worries no longer written in the line of her shoulders or etched on her face.

     

                They went to Argo after the Council meeting had concluded for the season, new orders under their belts and renewed motivation to continue their work. Kara’s family came with them, insisting on staying, knowing their intentions, and the tower was filled with noise for the week they all resided there. One morning, a little over a week after the Council meeting had ended, summer inching onwards towards its end, Lena woke early, when dawn was still hours away, with excitement in her belly. She scrubbed herself clean in the tub of cold water and then dressed in her finest clothes, braiding her hair as best as she could, dark locks twisted and plaited, before Lena stared at her reflection in a mirror of polished silver, pleased with the outcome.

     

                Kara was likewise resplendent in a silken dress in a shade of blue that matched her eyes, the fabric rippling like water, her golden hair neatly arranged with pearls and silver threaded through. She donned a cerulean robe, ornately embroidered, and Lena fetched herself one in a nice shade of moss, the velvet soft and light enough for the warmth of the summer morning. They departed the tower together while it was still pitch black, hand-in-hand across the stepping stones, and Kara whistled to the forest for any nearby horses, to no avail, before Lena whistled and waited patiently until the ground trembled with the slow, plodding footsteps of her wolf.

     

                He let them both scramble up onto his back, and she patted the side of his neck, speaking fondly to the wolf and pushing her intentions towards it. The forest sighed around them, and the wolf set off at a slow trot as Kara laughed, elated at the experience as she wrapped her arms tightly around Lena’s waist, craning her neck to look down at the forest floor, a dizzying drop below them. By the time the wolf reached the river, dawn was creeping in, the sky in the gaps between the canopy still a dusky blue but lightening slightly, the shadows shortening and the slight chill to the air dissipating. He padded straight into the river, and Kara dove off his back as Lena let out a squawk of surprise, twisting to look down, watching her wife cut through the current and make for the bank of the Seelie Court.

     

                Patting the wolf’s neck, Lena tried to get it to stop and put her down, but it was at least another mile before it heeded her words - or just decided on its own that it had borne her far enough - and she hurried back the way they’d come. Heart pounding, adrenaline coursing through her, Lena reached the riverbank and stopped at the edge of the bridge, the sun rising ever so slightly, leaves skittering across the cobblestones of the low bridge as the river ran below it, so close that it used to be unnerving, but now just made her skin prickle with goosebumps. Or that might’ve had something to do with the woman on the opposite bank, waiting for her, just as she’d been waiting for her two years ago to the day. 

     

                She looked as beautiful as she had then, and Lena’s mouth curved into a smile as Kara beamed at her and walked towards the middle of the bridge. Following suit, Lena stepped onto the damp cobblestones, moss slick under her feet, and met her halfway, her stomach swooping with anticipation. Kara cocked her head to the side and studied her wife for a moment, her eyes dark in the gloom but so achingly adoring that it made Lena’s heart hurt.

     

                “And here we are at last,” Kara murmured as she reached out and took Lena’s hand in her own.

     

                “Happy anniversary,” Lena softly said, a smile in her voice.

     

                Eyes brightening, Kara smiled proudly. “And you, my heart.” She gave Lena’s fingers a squeeze. “Do you remember that day?”

     

                “I thought it was a dream.”

     

                “I did, too. I had not thought my wife would be so beautiful.”

     

                “You were so serious.”

     

                With a quiet scoff, Kara wryly smiled, her cheek dimpling. “I was bound by my duty. That is why I wanted to come here today, so I might be bound by my love.”

     

                “I would just like to know what I was bound by,” Lena joked.

     

                “Ah, well, if you will allow me,” Kara murmured, letting go of her hands for a second and unsheathing her dagger from her waist.

     

                She quickly cut her palm, red blood welling up as she cradled it, and offered the dagger hilt to Lena, who cut her own with a little more trepidation, cupping her hand as the wound bled, while she offered the dagger back to Kara. Sheathing it, Kara reached for Lena’s hand and gripped her wrist, her bloody hand pressed against Lena’s. Remembering this, Lena’s fingers circled Kara’s wrist in response, their palms slick and warm as they touched. Reaching for her power, Kara twined a ribbon of water around their joined hands, and a moment later, Lena summoned roots from the riverbed to wrap around them as well.

     

                Lena didn’t remember the words from last time, spoken for her by Lillian as a proxy, but she listened as Kara spoke them then, her voice a soft burr, so tender and sweet. “You are mine, and I am yours, and let me never be whole again, from this day until my last.”

     

                Blinking in mild surprise, Lena licked her lips, her voice faintly rasping as she echoed her. “You are mine, and I am yours, and let me never be whole again, from this day until my last.”

     

                Eyes creasing at the corners, Kara pulled her in closer and gently kissed her, their hands still clasped, although the wounds were already scabbing over now. Eyelashes fluttering as her eyes closed, Lena sank into the kiss and smiled, a warmth spreading through her chest as she bound herself to her wife all over again. It was different this time; it was voluntary, and she felt as if she could feel the weight of the binding snake around her heart, tying them together for eternity.

     

                Pulling back slightly, Lena brushed her nose against Kara’s and let out a husky laugh. “My wife.”

     

                “My wife,” Kara whispered. “I have called you that for two years now, yet it feels truer today than on all the rest of them.”

     

                “Yes. It’s almost as if I can feel it. The words.”

     

                Humming in agreement, Kara smiled. “The truth of our language is a fickle thing. You can know when you have bound yourself, when something has rung true, just as much as you can know when someone tries to speak falsely by how they cannot get the words out.”

     

                “I think that’s how I knew my prophecy had been fulfilled.”

     

                “Aye, I knew it from that, too,” Kara agreed. “And how fortunate it was, so that I might love you now and forever without that uncertainty looming over us.”

     

                “Isn’t it … wild to think about how so much has changed in just two years?” Lena laughed. “Two years ago, I was married off to a stranger to make peace in the midst of a war. And now, there’s no war, and I’m not a Princess by any means, and you’re not a stranger - you’re the love of my life. Who would have ever thought that would happen? I certainly didn’t.”

     

                “None of this would have happened without you, Lena,” Kara whispered, a look of wonder in her eyes as she adjusted her grip to properly hold her wife’s hand. “Isn’t that such a beautiful thing?”

     

                With a lump in her throat, Lena smiled, squeezing Kara’s fingers. “And what about my wife? I wouldn’t have gotten very far without her.”

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter, her expression softening, Kara nodded. “Then it is good she has promised to never stray too far from your side.”

     

                “And isn’t that such a beautiful thing?”
